His body sets as he goes. The shell goes on bearing whatever is on it, and from outside he is a stone tortoise with the world on its back. His students count their own progress by the doors, and “she has opened the Seventh Room” is the highest praise the school gives.
Applications

Outlasting a duelist of souls, a worker of minds, a soul-drinker or a curse
Sitting out a siege inside the shell
A seclusion of years

Associations

Thaloré for the depth and Fixatio for the doors, on the Spirit road
EMPTY YARD opened downward

Limitations

Going deep is nearly free. It runs at the cost of the empty house, which he could pay for eleven days
The deeper he goes, the less of him is in the yard. His senses dim, his speech falls to single words, and from the deep Rooms he cannot act in the world at all unless AT HOME is standing
No light from the yard reaches the deep Rooms, so he never knows how long he was down until he sees the sky. He came out of eleven years of seclusion believing one winter had passed
A door bound in error stays bound, and Fixatio will not let him open it from the wrong side
The tell is the head drawing into the collar, the amber eye half closing, the breath slowing to a few in a minute, and the lattice dimming pane by pane like a house putting out its lamps
It is countered by waiting, which is a fool’s choice against a tortoise, or by harming what he loves in the yard while he is below

COME IN (들어오시오 · Deureoosio, “come in”)
COME IN is basically habitable anatomy of the soul: the power to take one who reaches him and asks into a Room of his house, where nothing can reach them. It came with the Class name Housekeeper.
Capabilities
He never says come with me. He says come in, and the guest makes the crossing, with the asking as the rite’s one offering. It is done by touch, a hand on the shell or his hand over theirs. Under Thaloré the guest’s soul takes the shape of what holds it and is let down into the house, and the body stays where it stood, slack and breathing slowly like a tortoise in winter. Since 702 the Room it comes to has a warm floor. Pyraeon’s banked heat runs under every Room the way a hill house is fired from beneath, and people who have sat there since remember the warmth before anything else.
Nothing follows a guest in. A curse, a Pressure, a possessing thing, a wound of the soul and the pull of a dying body all stop at the wall. A dying guest may wait there while a mender works on the flesh, or wait for a goodbye. The dead stay dead: if the body fails, the guest cannot go back out, and he carries them across the Veil himself, as a Ferryman does. On the third night of the Nine Days a stock boy crossed the yard, laid a hand on the shell and knocked, and was taken in with the blows still falling. It is the school’s favorite story.
Applications

Sheltering the hunted, the possessed or the cursed until the danger has passed
Holding a dying soul while a mender works on the body
Letting a grieving soul sit somewhere warm for a while

Associations

Thaloré, and Pyraeon since 702, on the Spirit road, at Ferryman

Limitations

The asker must reach him. Outside ALL WHO KNOCKED he takes no one in at a distance, and no one can ask for the senseless or the infant
A guest costs almost nothing to keep, a hundredth part of the empty house, so a full house of ninety-eight costs twice what an empty one does. A dying guest costs ten times a living one. The ninety-ninth Room is his own
The bodies stay in the yard and can be killed there. An enemy who knows him strikes the empty bodies
Thaloré binds what it holds. Every guest he has carried is tied to him for life, and he feels each one’s worst grief as his own. A guest walking to their Room sees what the house is built of, so he has no privacy from anyone he has carried, and every guest who leaves knows the way back in
After the guests have gone the floors stay warm and go on eating his reserve for hours, down where he does not notice it
The tell is two words, a body going slack under his hand, a smell of peat smoke, and one more pane lit in the lattice. Anyone watching can count his guests
It is countered by killing the bodies, by keeping askers from his hand, and by a guest who opens a door

THE GREAT BEAM (대들보 · Daedeulbo, “the great beam”)
THE GREAT BEAM is basically weight redirection: the power to hold a load for days by handing it down through himself into the ground, and pushing nothing back. It is the move, and the name, his fourth Class gave him.
Capabilities
The great beam of a house carries the roof to the posts, and the posts carry it to the earth, and the beam does this for three hundred years without once pushing upward. The same word means the one a family stands on. Petralon’s idea is the foundation, the thing other things rest on, and its operation is coagulation: the bearer is fixed in place, set to bear and never to rise. Thaloré takes the weight into the soul at its true measure and Petralon passes it down. He fights nothing. The load only goes through him on its way to the ground.
That is why it can last. At the Bearer’s Bend a river stood behind him eleven fathoms high for a day and a night, green as glass, while a whole district climbed past beneath it on its own feet. From one breath to the next he was never doing more than a Journeyman does. When he let the river go it went around him, and it bends there still, and the gorge wall keeps a smooth hollow six fathoms across where the weight went into the stone.
Applications

Holding a flood-door, a river, a failing gallery or a falling roof for days
Being the place where an army’s weight, a Domain’s weight or a mountain’s goes down

Associations

Petralon, with Thaloré carrying the weight in the soul, through the Body road
The Gate, the Bearer’s Bend and the Kneeling Hill
Gwibong, stone under load on a height, is the best ground he has

Limitations

It is the held house at its purest. A river costs him little more than an empty house does, and today he could hold one for the better part of nine days from full. At the Bend, a far smaller man, he lasted the day and the night and was empty at dawn
It needs ground beneath him to take the load. On a deck, on silt, on loose sand or above a drop the weight has nowhere to go
It answers pressing and never pulling. Lift him from his ground and the whole load comes loose at once
Each great hold sets him lower for good, as BEARING does
The tell is dust sagging down, a slow deep settling in the stone under him, and nothing else moving
It is countered by Cymorath, which slips the load, by Abython, by bad ground, and by lifting him

ALL WHO KNOCKED (두드린 이 모두 · Dudeurin i modu, “all who knocked”)
ALL WHO KNOCKED is basically mass inner world internalization: the power to take in at once everyone inside his yard who has asked. It is the move of his last Class, the Master of the House.
Capabilities
A house holds many. Here Orrenthal’s conjunction is turned from blows to people, all held in common under one roof, and Thaloré lets them down together. Every soul within thirty paces of him that has asked goes into a Room in the same breath, and the lattice lights from crown to tail, every pane at once. It is COME IN said once for a whole courtyard, and it is the only time he takes in anyone his hand has not touched.
Applications

Emptying a yard of the hunted in one breath
Taking a company’s souls out of the path of a working that kills souls

Associations

Thaloré and Orrenthal, on the Spirit road
COME IN, of which it is the full size

Limitations

Only within thirty paces, and only those who asked. The house is full at ninety-eight
Each guest costs what a guest of COME IN costs
The tell is the whole lattice lit together and a yard full of bodies going slack in one moment. It tells any watcher exactly where the souls have gone
It is countered as COME IN is, and more cheaply, since the bodies lie all in one place

SETTING DOWN (내려놓소 · Naeryeonoso, “I set it down”)
SETTING DOWN is basically absorption release: the power to put everything he has borne into one blow, at one place, once.
Capabilities
The beam lets go. Everything he has sent into the ground through the days of a bearing comes back up through him into a single stroke, laid on by contact or sent through the earth he stands on. Petralon’s foundation is worked the other way, by separation, the whole borne load parted from its bearer and sent to one place, and since 702 Pyraeon keeps the heat of it, so that a blow at the dusk of a long bearing lands exactly as heavy as the whole bearing was. He does not strike first, and he adds nothing of his own. The blow weighs what was put on him.
On the ninth day at the training yard north of Verath he struck once, on the stone alone, years before the ember woke in him. The hill sank six fathoms with the yard and the school upon it, and it sits level now, and the Accord’s own survey calls it the Kneeling Hill.
Applications

Ending a siege of blows with one blow
Putting a held river, a wall or a field down somewhere other than the valley beneath it

Associations

Petralon, and Pyraeon since 702, through the Body road
THE GREAT BEAM and BEARING, its only sources

Limitations

It gives back only what was laid on him. A fighter who never strikes him gives it nothing, and a short fight gives it little
It takes about a third of everything he has, on top of the bearing
It passes through the house on its way out, and the crooked plate cracks again each time
Thaloré gave the load its true weight, his griefs along with it. When the load goes, one grief he carried goes into the ground with it, and he can never feel that one at its weight again: a dead friend he can name and can no longer mourn
Afterward the ember smolders under him for hours, eating reserve and flesh, and for a day the shell takes nothing well. That day is the window
The tell is the lattice going from dim to blazing down the whole shell in an instant, thin smoke at every seam, and bright cracks along the plates. Whoever reads it has one breath
It is countered by giving it nothing, by breaking off before the load is full, by lifting him from his ground, and by Catharsis, which makes him set it down early and without aim

MAY I COME IN (들어가도 되겠소 · Deureogado doegesso, “may I come in?”)
MAY I COME IN is basically inner world manipulation turned around: the power to ask to be carried into another’s house. The doctrine of his own school names it the last movement of the inner way. He has never made it.
Capabilities
The master knocks. That is all the doctrine says, and nobody alive knows what follows. Every other movement of the way has him inside and the world at the door; in this one he stands in somebody else’s yard with his hand raised, and the art is in another’s keeping. He has not asked anyone for anything since the pens.
Applications

None that anyone has seen

Associations

Thaloré, on the Spirit road
Every other movement of the way, turned to face the other direction

Limitations

He has never done it
It needs another soul to answer, and that soul may refuse

Releases
AT HOME (집에 있소 · Jibe isso, “I am at home”) · First Release
AT HOME is basically inner world externalization: the power to be at home in the yard and in every Room at once, so that the master acts in the world without leaving the house. It is his First Release, found at Flourishing.
Capabilities
The Spirit road’s first door asks for the self said aloud and true, and he opens it with two quiet words. The lattice lights over the whole shell, and GOING IN stops costing him the yard: he sits in the ninety-ninth Room and stands on his feet in the same breath, the slow body in the world with all the depth of the house behind its hands.
A Spirit soul’s First lengthens its reach on other souls, and his own reach on a soul has always been the length of his arm. So it runs through his palms and his shell and nowhere else. A soul he lays a hand on is shown the door: its Pressure, its coat and every working it was holding are put back inside it for the space of a breath, and the struck man finds his art shut up in him like a guest who has been walked politely to the gate. It moves no stone and breaks no bone. The blow that follows is another matter, and it is usually someone else’s.
Applications

Fighting from the deep Rooms with his body in the yard
Showing a soul the door by touch

Associations

Thaloré, on the Spirit road, with the texture of the Body road he walks
EMPTY YARD and GOING IN, held together

Limitations

It empties him in about half an hour from full, and each palm laid on a soul is a committed exchange besides, a hundredth to a thirtieth of all he has. Run long it hollows him: colors go flat near him, then a word slips, then a name
Contact only. He must put his hand on the soul he means, and he is slow
The self is said aloud and true, so while it stands the yard is not empty and he cannot lie. His face can be read. No lie will leave his mouth, and a plain question gets the truth or a silence anyone can read
The door holds for one breath and no longer
The tell is the two words, then the lattice lit from crown to tail
It is countered by staying out of his hands, by striking the body, which is no tougher for it, and by asking him questions

I WILL BEAR IT (지겠소 · Jigesso, “I will carry it”) · Second Release
I WILL BEAR IT is basically damage transferal: the power to have whatever is laid on a guest borne by the whole house. It is his Second Release, found at Refraction, the deepest a Spirit soul has, and it opens and powers his Domain.
Capabilities
The second door on the Spirit road asks for a meaning borne for someone else. It is the future of jida, and it is a promise. Orrenthal’s conjunction joins the guest’s load to the house in common, Thaloré gives it its weight, and Fixatio fixes it where it lands. Within thirty paces of him, whatever is laid on anyone who has asked him is taken to have been laid on the house: a curse, a wound of the soul, a Pressure, a grief, the meaning of a debt.
A Spirit soul’s Second rules meanings and leaves the room looking as it did. But he walks the Body road as well, and that gives the claim a hold on matter, so a blade swung at a guest is taken as struck on the shell, and BEARING receives it. The guest does not flinch. The old tortoise three paces off rocks on his feet and comes back.
Applications

Taking a company’s wounds onto the shell
Lifting the weight of a curse from the one who asked, and keeping it
Opening the Domain

Associations

Orrenthal, Thaloré and Fixatio, on the Spirit road
The Bearer’s Bend, where the river was a load and the district walked

Limitations

With the Domain it empties him in about thirteen minutes from full, and in nine if AT HOME is standing too
Only for those who asked, and only within thirty paces
What he bears for another stays bound to him. The guest walks out free of it, and he keeps the scar, the curse’s term written against his own name, and the grief. Two centuries of other people’s worst hours sit in his plates
The tell is that nothing in the room changes. The blow at the guest lands on him
It is countered by striking the unasking, who stand outside it, by striking from past thirty paces, and by harm already done, a poison swallowed or a wound already given

Domain
THE ASKING GATE (청문 請門 · Cheongmun, “the gate of asking”)
THE ASKING GATE is basically sanctuary domain: the power to make the house and yard around him obey one law, no one is carried who has not asked. The first character of its name means to ask and also to invite, and the name holds both.
Capabilities
A house is opened from inside, and within his gate no soul is taken to be anyone’s load. Thaloré lays the meaning on the ground and Fixatio sets its terms as hard as written law; the operation is coagulation, each soul fixed in its own vessel past melting. It is a field of the Spirit, which rules what things are taken to mean, with a claim on matter from the Body road beneath it, and it is small: thirty paces, a house and its yard.
Inside it nothing carries off, drags, compels, reads, drains, possesses or takes a person who has not asked. A collar bound by a working goes slack on the neck. A compelling voice speaks into empty yards. A chain will not haul a body, and a hand that tries to drag a man finds that the man will not leave the place where he is standing. Every guest in it stands under I WILL BEAR IT. Called in a fight it is as dear as the Release that powers it. Laid as a house is held, with nothing pushed, it costs what the house costs, and his own hall at Gwibong has stood inside it for a century and a half.
At Principality the world entered that law in its own book, and it stands now whether he does or not. A law of the Spirit works on what people take to be so, and it puts no chain on anyone’s arms. On the day he crossed a kingdom fell quiet for one held breath, and afterward everyone in it found they agreed about something they had never once discussed. In the hill country round Gwibong nobody lifts a fallen man without asking him first. A child in its mother’s arms has asked by holding on. The senseless lie where they fell until someone wakes them, and that country’s physicians are the best wakers in the world. No drover there can bring himself to drive stock that has not asked. The Accord’s clerks file him as the Standing Exception and do not write down why.
Applications

Making a hall where no one can be taken: a sanctuary for the hunted, a yard no slaver can work in
Breaking working-bound collars, compulsions and claims on a soul inside it
Holding a company of askers under I WILL BEAR IT

Associations

Opened and powered by I WILL BEAR IT. It is NAEDO’s meaning laid on the ground
The hall at Gwibong and its yard stand inside it
The law registered in his name at Principality covers a kingdom. His own field has never grown past the yard

Limitations

The law binds everyone inside it, himself first, and Fixatio keeps it from being changed. He can end the field and cannot alter its terms. Nobody can carry the unasking inside it, so the sleeping, the senseless and the infant cannot be moved by anyone. Set a fire round a sleeping child within his gate and his own law holds her in it: he must end the field, or she must wake and ask
No one can carry him off inside it unless he asks, and he has never asked. If he falls senseless there, he lies where he fell
A guest within can open it, and a hostile asker is a guest
It forbids no killing. A blade kills a man who has not asked, since killing is no carrying
Everything past thirty paces is outside it, the bowman on the wall included
He cannot put the registered law down. The dead of that country who lay where they fell are his
It yields to a field two Stages above his
The tell is almost nothing: a chain going slack in the hands of the man hauling on it, and the air thickening toward blue

Realm
THE NINETY-NINE ROOMS (아흔아홉 칸 · Aheunahop kan, “ninety-nine bays”)
THE NINETY-NINE ROOMS is basically inner world internalization at its last size: the power to take other people’s Domains in as Rooms of his house, still running, their owners inside them, and to have their law read as a guest’s law. It is his Realm, reached through the Second Release grown whole.
Capabilities
Ninety-nine is the largest house a subject may keep. A Realm of the Spirit rules what the fields within it are taken to mean, and its operation is conjunction, two meanings joined in one vessel and each kept whole. His is the house that receives any field as a guest. A Domain that stands inside his thirty paces keeps its law entire, and that law is read in the sense of the house: it holds over its own master and over whoever asked to be inside it, and over no one else. A rival’s field becomes a Room, and the rival is the one who must stay in it.
He found the door on the Kneeling Hill. For nine days he held the Domain of Corvane Hask, the owners’ champion and a Stage his better, inside his own, and he understood its law wholly, exactly as its master meant it, because he had lived fifty years under that law in the pens. His own law stood around it and did not change by a word. Held as the house is held, the Realm costs what the house costs, and he can keep it up from morning to night.
Applications

Shutting an enemy’s Domain inside its own walls, so that it rules no one who did not walk in
Holding allied fields together as rooms of one house
Standing every field in a fight under one roof, if the fight comes into his yard

Associations

The Second Release grown whole, and the Domain’s law at its last size
Thaloré, on the Spirit road

Limitations

It holds only fields that stand inside his thirty paces. A field kept off at range is never his guest
For a day and a night after he lets it go his power sits badly on him, spilling and ill governed
A reading needs something to read. Silence, the unrecorded and a field with no name give it nothing to hold, and a field built on a meaning he has never truly understood is not held at all. He has never understood the carrying of an unasking person as anything but sale, so a field whose law is rescue by force is the one field he cannot hold whole
It counts against the cap on his own boosts, as the Domain beneath it does
Null-Light’s Mugan, the Unseeing, is its direct contrary, and so is any soul that will not be read
It yields to a field two Stages above his, and to hold a field is not to outrank it
If it breaks, it breaks with everything inside it, the held fields included

characters/ability-accounts/haldan-stain.title: Haldan Stainmore — Abilities in full
characters/ability-accounts/haldan-stain.content:
Card: Haldan Stainmore
ACCOUNT RENDERED
ACCOUNT RENDERED is basically debt enforcement: the power to take what is owed him, on the spot, in the coin it was lent, until the account is square. It is his signature, the one idea his Trait, his named moves and the One he is reaching for each express. In Nalūn an account rendered is the statement a creditor presents for payment, and his is presented aloud.
Capabilities
He was a courier’s son and a road agent before he was a factor, and for six winters on the eastern corridor he read a pack for its weight and a convoy for its lateness to the day. Then he went into the counting room, and for twenty years he has closed accounts to the grain. A soul becomes what it does longest. His has become the closing of an account.
Oblation, the Offering, is the Wellspring under the salt, and its idea is the bargain that gives back exactly what was given up. The salt cities read it as contract: two parties each giving something up before a witness. Every other soul that works it stands on the giving side. Haldan stands on the other, where the same law says that what was lent comes back, never a grain over and never a grain under. Its operation is separation. The owed thing is parted from the one who holds it and goes where the books say it belongs.
He wears the claim on his Attraction Layer the way another Fate soul wears presence, and he spends his own Essence to present it. He reaches for no Thread. An instrument sealed under the Chain Light is already a working, and a debtor in breach is a man Nalūn has already stopped working for, so the instrument does the leaning and Haldan only reads it out. That is why a sealed claim leaves no knot behind it, and why a soul standing on the lowest rung of Fate can do this at all.
Nothing in it strikes. The owed coin leaves the debtor by its own likeliest road, a purse string tied in haste, a ring a size large, a buckle with a worn tongue, and after that it will not stay in a hand it is owed out of. Picked up, it slips. Pocketed, the seam goes. It lies where it fell until Haldan or his clerk takes it up. In a fight the art takes the fight’s tools and leaves the man standing: the sword bought on his note, the armor, the horse, a hired man’s pay. Against a higher Stage the instrument still binds, since a seal holds a great soul as it holds a small one, but the reading is his own, so the coin leaves only where the grip on it has give, one thing to a reading, the loosest first.
His refusal is written into it as a law it cannot break. “I take what was lent. I do not take the borrower.” The art has no hold on a debtor’s body or breath, on his kin or his name, and a debt lent in any such coin is one it cannot collect.
Applications

Taking back what is owed the house, on the spot, from anyone in breach of a Stainmore instrument
Following lent coin into what it bought, and taking that
Holding a pledged thing where it stands, a sword in its scabbard, a gate, a cart, until the account squares
Binding an opponent to terms offered and accepted in the room, so that breaking them is a breach he can collect
Disarming and unhorsing a man before a fight begins, by buying his debts beforehand
Getting back anything taken from him by force, since everything he carries is entered and sealed in the house books, and a taker is a breacher
Closing a small man’s whole account in one reading, and a lord’s across days

Techniques

TO THE GRAIN - the Trait: every open account in earshot, felt as weight
ACCOUNT RENDERED: TERMS OFFERED - terms stated aloud and accepted, sealed by word in the room
ACCOUNT RENDERED: DISTRAINT - the owed coin parted from its holder on the spot
ACCOUNT RENDERED: THE TRACE - the claim followed out of spent coin into what it bought
ACCOUNT RENDERED: HELD AGAINST THE ACCOUNT - a pledged thing set where it stands until the account squares
ACCOUNT RENDERED: QUITTANCE - a man’s whole account closed, in one held breath where it fits and across days where it does not, the source of his epithet
A LIEN - the One, offered and not yet his: a claim staked on his life

Associations

Oblation, the Offering, the Wellspring under the salt, whose law of equivalence is Dazkar’s
Fixatio, the Knot, Atla’zon’s, his one held lens, for the Hold alone
The Fate Path does the work, as a Claim in Distraint, the Trace and the Quittance, and as a Bind in Terms Offered and the Hold
The Factor House of Stainmore and its sealed articles, and the house books, in which everything he carries is entered and stamped
The oldest instrument, and its token on the cord at his throat
His Class, Surety, the one who stands for another’s debt, gives him the touch-assay: taking any coin, bar or token in his own hand, he knows whether it is short weight or false. What never passes through his hand it cannot judge
He reads every account in full Concord Common, in the Ironlink drafting register, clause by clause, and closes on one word: “Due.” for a claim, “Held.” for the Hold, “Quit.” for a Quittance
He never says “Called,” the Nalūn word for a First Release. The room says it of him anyway, and the room is wrong, since he has no Release
His Pressure has a creditor’s weight: the unwoken feel their knees go and remember, all at once, whatever they owe anyone
His aura is Oblation’s warmest teal with an amber edge, laid flat along the lattice of his robe and then across his hands, and it does not flicker

Limitations

It works only where a real account stands, and at its full force only where the account is sealed under Parun
An unsealed or disputed debt has no working behind it, so collecting one is a true pull from the lowest rung of Fate: about three quarters of his reserve and a nosebleed for a lean that often fails, with a knot due within days. He almost never tries
It never touches the debtor: body, breath, blood, labor, kin, name, the clothes he stands in, the day’s food and the tools of his trade are outside every account
The debtor must hear the account read or read it in his hand, and nothing lands before the last word
The sum must be exact. Named under, he takes only what he named. Named over by a grain, the grain is paid out of him into the debtor’s hand
It nets. Any account he or his house owes the debtor is set off first, and if the house owes more, nothing moves and the lean runs the other way
Nobody who stands under the mountain settlement’s claim can be collected from while the eastern delivery stands undone, and that claim can be bought in shares
He stands at Touched, Fate I, with no grip, and about two parts in three of what he spends reaches the claim
He speaks a working into the world, and his soul pours slowly: a purse takes him some eleven seconds of reading and a twentieth of his reserve, and nothing he owns can be hurried
At rest on ordinary ground he refills in about ten minutes, faster at Deepvein and on any toll bridge or bargain-stone, slower above the snowline and on water
He walks one Path. He cannot coat or reinforce, and against a fighter he loses a straight exchange
Anyone watching hears it coming, because he reads the account aloud, unhurried, clause by clause
The lamp flames gutter toward the debtor as if something were being taken from beside them, there is a smell of lamp oil and burnt offering and a pull at the sleeves, and the air between the two men hangs in a drawn thread
A debtor who wears a seal-token feels it go cold against his skin a breath before the coin moves
Paying him ends it, since a payment tendered discharges the account
It is countered by never letting him finish the reading: noise, distance, stopped ears, a blow, a hand over his mouth, or a lie he must stop to answer
It is countered by being someone he owes, or by carrying a share of the mountain settlement’s claim
It is countered by giving him bread and salt at a threshold and seeing him eat it, which makes the giver his guest, and a guest’s goods are beyond his claim until they part company and the next sunrise is up
It is countered by holding the thing with nothing to give, sewn in, riveted or worn tight, because the art leans and never forces
A prior or senior claim on the same goods takes them first, and so does an instrument sealed under Council authority over his
A tokenless man with no instrument to his name gives it nothing to stand on
A Fate soul of higher Mastery can contest the claim outright
It is weakest on ground where nothing has ever been given up, which Oblation hates
Benediction, the gift with no count, is its contrary and the one idea it cannot weigh. A gift he has not paid for stands on his books as an account he cannot read, and while it stands he cannot collect from the giver
It fails in Oblation’s own manner. Past some thirty-eight clauses in a day the reading outruns the breath: a breath that is not there in the middle of a clause, the count lost on the clause after, and a wrong figure collected out of him. The Measurewrights call it cavitation and say his lungs read like a pump running dry

Traits
TO THE GRAIN · Primary Trait
TO THE GRAIN is basically debt sensing: the power to feel every open account within earshot, who owes it, to whom, in what coin, and how far overdue. It is his Primary Trait, always on, and ACCOUNT RENDERED starts from it.
Capabilities
It formed on the corridor, where he read packs, mules and men for what each owed the road, and it finished in the counting room. An open account sits on a person’s Attraction Layer as a weight, and he feels that weight in his own hands, the way a salt-taster knows a short bar on the tongue. A sealed account comes exact, to the grain. An unsealed one is a heaviness with no figure in it. A breach is a sour, slack weight, like a cord that has lost its knot. The salt has an old belief that a breaker shows on his face. To Haldan it is simply true.
He cannot put it down. He reads every friend, every lover and every child as a set of balances, and he reads himself the same way.
Applications

Knowing to the grain what a man owes before he gives his name
Knowing who in a room is in breach, and of whose instrument
Reading which of a debtor’s possessions were bought on whose credit, the first step of every Trace
Catching a lie about a debt, since the weight does not change when the mouth does

Associations

Oblation reads it, on the Attraction Layer
Lived, never taught, the road’s habit become the soul’s
“What’s your oldest?” is the greeting he never needs to ask

Limitations

It reaches earshot, a hall at most, and a man outside it is outside the Trait
It is exact only on sealed instruments. An unsealed debt reads as weight with no figure, and a debt the debtor honestly does not know he owes reads very faint
It reads balances and nothing else. It cannot tell him what a man intends
A gift given without count is a blank where a weight should be, and it unsettles him past bearing
It reads nothing on a tokenless man with no instrument to his name
It costs nothing at rest. Reading a crowded hall hard takes about a five-hundredth of his reserve a minute, less than he recovers sitting still
His eyes go to a man’s purse and belt before his face, and his hands turn palm up a little, as if weighing
It is countered by owing nothing, or by standing outside earshot

Techniques
ACCOUNT RENDERED: TERMS OFFERED · Bind
TERMS OFFERED is basically contract creation: the power to seal a bargain by word in the room, so that breaking it makes the other party his debtor in a coin the terms name.
Capabilities
A contract is two parties giving something up before a witness, and where no scribe stands by, Oblation is the witness. Haldan states the terms aloud with each side’s stake named. “Draw before the bell and the blade is mine. Hold until the bell and I pay you forty marks.” A word seals it, or a nod, a hand, a token touched to his. Each stake is set apart from its owner and held against the terms, and he closes with “Dazkar weigh the difference,” and the lamps in the room steady.
A bargain sealed by word binds lightly: for a day or its stated term, and only on what both parties said. It has no Parun behind it and it does not travel. Once it is broken, though, the breaker owes the named coin under a witnessed bargain, and DISTRAINT can collect it. The salt is full of men who accept terms by reflex, because that is how they were raised.
Applications

Setting the terms of a duel, a parley or a surrender so that breaking them disarms the breaker
Binding a hired man not to strike while terms stand
Turning a bribe, refused or accepted, into a claim

Associations

Oblation, as witness
The Fate Path, as a Bind
The salt’s own custom of closing by word before the scribe comes

Limitations

Nothing binds without a real acceptance. Silence binds nothing, and veterans in Nalūn know never to answer a factor in a fight
Both sides must give something real. Terms in which he risks nothing are no bargain, and Oblation does not witness them
He is bound as hard as they are. If he breaks his own terms he owes the stake, and it is collected out of him
It cannot name the other party’s body, labor, kin or freedom as a stake. “Your life on it” is a phrase Oblation hears and does not seal
Terms sealed by word lapse at their term or at the next sunrise, whichever comes first
Sealing costs about a fortieth of his reserve and five or six seconds of speech, and keeping the terms costs nothing. From full he could seal forty bargains, and he recovers one in the time it takes to pour tea
It leaves no knot
He states the terms in full and waits for the answer, and that waiting is the tell
It is countered by saying nothing at all

ACCOUNT RENDERED: DISTRAINT · Claim
DISTRAINT is basically repossession: the power to part the owed coin from its holder on the spot, so that it falls from him and will not stay in his hand.
Capabilities
He reads the account: creditor, debtor, sum, coin, date, term. Then one word. “Due.” The coin of the debt leaves the debtor by its own likeliest road and lies where it falls. Silver lent comes back as silver, grain as grain, and a horse lent comes back as that horse. If the debtor stoops for it, it slips his fingers. If he carries it off, the seam gives.
The same reading guards Haldan’s own person. Everything he carries is entered and stamped in the house books under the house’s sealed articles, so a man who takes a thing of his by force is in breach of a sealed instrument from that moment, and the thing comes back to him the way any owed coin does.
Applications

A purse, a ring, a pay-chest, a sword, a horse from under its rider
Getting back a weapon struck from his hand or a purse cut from his belt, in the same exchange
Stripping a hired man of the pay drawn on a Stainmore bill before he earns it

Associations

Oblation, by separation
The Fate Path, as a Claim
TO THE GRAIN, which gives him the figure before he opens his mouth

Limitations

A plain reading is six clauses at the least, and one sealed account to a reading
It takes only the coin of the debt. Silver owed does not take a sword unless the sword was bought with that silver, and that is THE TRACE
A thing held with nothing to give stays where it is
Against a higher Stage it takes one thing per reading, the loosest first
The debtor’s person and his privileged goods are outside it
A purse or a ring costs about a twentieth of his reserve and some eleven seconds of reading, so twenty from full
A sword, a piece of armor or a horse costs a tenth and some twenty-two seconds, so ten from full
A cartload costs a fifth and three quarters of a minute, so five from full
A sealed account leaves no knot
The reading gives it away, and then the debtor’s token going cold, the pull at the sleeves and the lamp flames guttering toward him
It is countered by paying, by stopping the reading, or by a grip with no give in it

ACCOUNT RENDERED: THE TRACE · Claim
THE TRACE is basically value tracking: the power to follow lent coin out of a man’s hands into whatever it bought, and take that instead.
Capabilities
Equivalence follows the value and cares nothing for the shape. What the silver became is still the silver. TO THE GRAIN tells him which things in a man’s kit were bought on Stainmore credit, and THE TRACE reads the line of exchange aloud, a clause for each trade: lent at Halcrest, paid to the armorer at Rimward on the second of May, in exchange for this hauberk. The separation is carried across each exchange in turn, the drawn thread of air runs from the debtor’s purse to the thing, and at “Due.” the bought thing parts from him as coin would.
In a fight it is the move men fear. A man armed and horsed on Stainmore credit is carrying arms and riding a horse that were never his.
Applications

Taking the sword bought with the house’s silver, the armor, the horse, the roof bought on a note
Reading aloud to a room exactly what a man’s finery cost and whose money paid for it

Associations

Oblation, by separation carried across each trade
The Fate Path, as a Claim
TO THE GRAIN finds the line, and DISTRAINT takes the thing at the end of it

Limitations

The line dies at a buyer in good faith who gave value and did not know: a soldier paid his wages in that silver, a merchant who sold honestly and was paid
It dies at anything eaten, drunk or spent and gone, and at a debt discharged
From a mixed purse he takes only his proportion, to the grain
Past three trades the line is too thin to read
Coin changed by a working instead of a trade, melted and remade by an alchemist or transmuted, is no longer the same coin, and the line loses it. Transmutatio, change with no loss, is its contrary
It costs what DISTRAINT costs for the thing taken, and about a tenth of his reserve more for each trade the coin passed through. A sword three trades off is two fifths of his reserve and a minute and a half of reading, twice from full
A long trace is a long tell
It is countered by anything that breaks the line, or by stopping a reading that takes this long

ACCOUNT RENDERED: HELD AGAINST THE ACCOUNT · Bind
HELD AGAINST THE ACCOUNT is basically lien enforcement: the power to set a pledged thing where it stands, so that it cannot be moved, opened, drawn or used until the account is square.
Capabilities
This one move runs on his second lens. Fixatio, the Knot, holds the idea of commitment: what is bound stays bound, because the way back has stopped existing. Its operation is coagulation, and salt is the matter that fixes, the virtue of the very stone his city is cut from. He lays it on security for a debt. The account is read, he says “Held.”, and the pledged thing sets where it is. A sword pledged or bought on his note stays in its scabbard. A cart does not roll. A gate pledged against a city’s loan stays barred, and a seal stays unbroken.
It holds against everyone, the debtor and Haldan alike, and when the account squares it lets go without being told. A lord who borrowed against his castle has mortgaged its gate to whoever holds the note.
Applications

Keeping a debtor’s weapon sheathed through a fight
Barring a pledged gate or door in a siege or a flight
Stopping goods from leaving a hall or a quay

Associations

Fixatio, the Knot, Atla’zon’s, at home on every Path and so worked by a Fate soul at no loss
The Fate Path, as a Bind
Laid only on what Oblation’s books already name as pledged or owed

Limitations

It takes only on a thing pledged as security for a sealed debt, or owed under one
It holds the thing and never the person. A man can drop a held sword and pick up another
A Hold placed on the wrong thing stays placed. He cannot lift it early, and Oblation books the wrong Hold as a debt he owes. This is Fixatio’s own failure, the way back gone
Fixatio thins on open water, at high altitude and on a moving deck. On a boat, in a ford or high on a pass the Hold slips and will not set, and the eastern road runs through passes
A hand-sized thing costs about a tenth of his reserve and some twenty-two seconds to set. A gate or a cart costs a fifth and three quarters of a minute
Keeping it costs about a fiftieth of his reserve a minute. That is a fifth of what he recovers at rest, so a still man can keep a Hold for days. A man who is also working drains, and with no rest at all one Hold would empty him in under an hour
A sealed pledge leaves no knot
A smell of sweet resin gives it away, the thing going sticky and then rigid to the touch, and a bead of amber light hardening at the join, the scabbard’s mouth or the gate’s bar
It is countered by squaring the account, by fighting him on water or on a pass, or by making him work until he cannot keep it

ACCOUNT RENDERED: QUITTANCE · Claim, the signature
QUITTANCE is basically total debt collection: the power to close a man’s whole account, every note, every trace and every pledge, and leave him quit.
Capabilities
The old word under quittance is quiet. A man who is quit is at rest, and nothing rests that was not paid. Before Haldan meets a man he means to break, he buys that man’s paper: every Stainmore note, and every note he can get from the other houses at discount. Then he reads it in one held breath, every clause in order, and closes on “Quit.” Everything the man holds in the coins of the debts read, traced or pledged, leaves him in the same moment. Purse, rings, sword, armor, horse, banner. A small man’s paper fits in one breath. A lord’s is read across days, one breath a day, and the account stands open between.
A quittance is a discharge. When the last of the account is read the man owes Stainmore nothing, ever again, and the account is closed for good. If what he held fell short of what he owed, the shortfall is discharged with the rest and the house bears it, and Haldan pays the house the difference out of his own pocket and tells no one.
That is where the epithet comes from. When Stainmore has finished with a man, the man is quit, and the name makes it sound like a mercy.
Applications

Unarming, unhorsing and unseating a man in one reading, before a fight, a duel or a council
Breaking a lord whose venture ran on Stainmore credit, at the source, as a campaign of daily readings and never as one stroke

Associations

Oblation, by separation, all at once
The Fate Path, as a Claim
DISTRAINT, THE TRACE and the Hold, each of which it gathers into one reading

Limitations

It takes only what is owed, only in its coins and only what can be traced, and the debtor’s person is untouched
One reading closes only what one held breath carries. He can hold one for about a minute and a half, and in that time his soul pours about two fifths of his reserve
A small man’s whole account is about a quarter of his reserve and a little under a minute of reading, and it fits
A lord’s whole account does not fit. He closes it across days, one Quittance a day, each reading closing what one breath carries, and the account stands open between them. The discharge comes only when the last of it is read, and until then the lord knows what is coming and has days to pay, sell on or run
Never more than once in a day
It cannot take what has passed to the innocent, soldiers’ wages or goods sold honestly, so it strips the master and never his men
After it he has no further claim on that man in any coin, for life. A quittance spent early is a weapon gone
It is the longest reading anyone hears him make. The whole room goes still as each item is named, and every lamp gutters at once
The held breath is the opening. Interrupt the reading or make him draw breath and it fails, with the reserve and the breath already paid
Self-deceit hollows it. Turned on an account he tells himself coin can close, when it was never lent in coin, it comes back empty and costs him the breath anyway
It fails as the whole art fails, at full size: held too long, the breath he does not have goes missing in the middle of the reading, and the figure he misreads after it is collected out of him

Releases
A LIEN · the One
Offered, not yet his. A LIEN is basically claim imposition: the power to lay his claim on the ground around him, so that everything owed inside it answers to his note. Fate has one Release, the One, and in Nalūn it takes the salt’s word for a Second, a lien, because it counts as one; the Domain it would open is called a foreclosure.
Capabilities
He stands at Glory, and the One opens a Stage above him. Refraction comes first, by its own Catalyst, and only on that Stage can the One be met, under contest, by a claim staked on his life and kept. He must name aloud a claim over something outside himself, with his life the forfeit, against someone who can take both, and hold it unyielded until the contest ends.
Oblation’s price has to be truly the giver’s own, and a claim yielded at the last hour to save his life was never staked, so the One fails.
Opened, it would make the ground do his reading for him. Inside the lien every account owed is presented at once, with no clause spoken, and every breacher within it finds the coin of his debt leaving him. Nothing pledged or owed leaves that ground unpaid. Dust lies flat from his feet to the lien’s edge, flames stand straight, every lamp gutters toward whoever owes, and people step back to give it room before anyone tells them to. Where the contest ends with the claim still standing, the stillness stays on the ground for a day, and animals will not cross it.
Applications

Presenting every account on a stretch of ground at once, without a reading
Keeping pledged and owed goods from leaving that ground
Opening and powering a Domain, as a Second Release does

Associations

Oblation, on the Fate Path, the claim grown from a voice to a place
He would call it in the drafting register, the claim read as an instrument

Limitations

It is not his. He must first cross to Refraction, and then meet the One there, in person
It is staked on his life. A claim yielded is a claim never staked, and he knows it
It governs only what is owed. A man who owes nothing walks through it untouched
It is a claim on ground, weakest on raw wild ground where nothing was ever given up and strongest on toll roads, bridges and old bargain-stones
Called aloud it rises in full. Held silent it is weaker, and the choice is his
It is countered by a Fate soul of higher Mastery, who can contest the claim outright, by a debtor with no standing, by ground where nothing was ever given up, and by anything that makes him yield the claim before the contest ends

characters/ability-accounts/hayato-amagi.title: Hayato Amagiri — Abilities in full
characters/ability-accounts/hayato-amagi.content:
Card: Hayato Amagiri
THE INDIGO ROADS
THE INDIGO ROADS (藍の道 · Ai no Michi) is basically path manipulation: the power to own every road he has ever walked, and to decide where it goes. It is his signature art, and his Traits and techniques are this one idea. The eye is the Moto blood’s and the mist is the Amagiri blood’s; in him both were turned to the road, so the north will one day use the one name for all of it.
Capabilities
Every piece is the same act at a different size: know the way, and own it. Like any practitioner he pulls Aether (mana, in the common word) out of the ground he stands on, refines it in the Soul Crystal into Essence (spiritual energy), and drives it out through the layer the working belongs to. His ground is the kind both his Wellsprings favor: a well-traveled road, wet air, moving water, cold. Phreatis, the Waters of Memory, is the keeping lens. Its idea is memory as deep water, and its operation is dissolution: what is lived is taken down and held, and what flows remembers the shape of what it flowed through, the way water that fell as rain reaches a well decades later still carrying the hills it came down. So every road his feet have been on, and every road an Amagiri before him walked and wrote down, lies in him the way a riverbed lies under the river, whole, with its fords and its bends and how long a mule takes on each.
Transference, the Give-and-Take, is the carrying lens. Its idea is that two things bound and in tune can give and take with nothing carried between them, and its operation is distillation, what one holds rising out of it and coming down in the other. Scholars compare it to two bells of one pitch: strike the first and the second rings across the room, and nothing visible has crossed. A road he has walked is exactly such a pair, its two ends joined by his having gone from one to the other, and held in tune by the memory Phreatis keeps of everything between. So on that road the distance between the ends answers to him. He can be at any point of it without the riding, he can say that nothing shall pass a line across it. Both lenses descend from the Titan Sylorin, the river that joins two souls with no body making the trip, which is why the two sit so easily in one man.
The two bloods do the rest. The Amagiri inheritance is mist: on a road, in air that will hold water, the house thins the light round itself until a column reads as weather. Mist is real water, tiny drops hung in air that has cooled to the point where it can hold no more, which the Measurewrights call the dew point. Warm that air and it can carry more water unseen, and the drops go back to vapor, which is all that is happening when the sun burns fog off a valley. The Moto inheritance is the Shingan, the heart-eye, which shows where a thing is carrying its weight. About nine parts in ten of what he spends reach the work, which is his yield. The lost tenth is paid in his Core, and what shows of it comes off him as cold and wet, a fine chill haze, the very mist his blood hides in, so that the harder he works the more weather there is round him.
Applications

Knowing the way through any ground he has walked, and how long it takes
Going down a walked road faster than he could ride it, with whoever he carries
Hiding everyone on a road as weather
Shutting a road along one line

Techniques

THE ROAD UNDER THE ROAD - the Trait that knows the way
RAIN MIST - the Amagiri blood’s cover, on the road
NOW I KNOW WHICH WAY - the road once chosen, not turned off
AMAGIRI-ASHI - the Step, which goes down the road
THE ROAD’S OPEN - the Step held open for others
MICHI-KIRI - the Cut, which shuts the road
SHINGAN - the Moto eye, which says whether the road will hold a horse today

Associations

Phreatis, the Waters of Memory, the keeping lens
Transference, the Give-and-Take, a Wellspring of Fate, the carrying lens
The Titan Sylorin, from whom both descend
The Spirit Path for the read, the keeping and the mist; his Walked Fate Path for the road that answers and every claim on ground; a Studied Body Path for the one stroke of the sword-arm
The Amagiri blood, which gives the mist, and the Moto blood, which gives the eye
The plain sword, his bonded weapon, and the gilt fox mask

Limitations

His power is only as wide as his feet have made it
Every piece that rides on mist dies in heat, in a hard dry wind and in strong sun, and is strongest at night, in the cold, beside water
When the mist goes he is left standing in the open wherever it ran out, a slight man in a rain-cape with no armor worth the name
The charge is small and always the same hand: his finger draws the road first, on a table, in the wet ring of a cup, in dust, in the air, and when the finger stops he has chosen
Before he works the gold flecks in his haze turn like moths finding a lamp, the air beads on cold iron, there is a smell of cellar stone and a mineral taste on the tongue, and the sound that was rain on a cape widens until it is rain on a whole forest, though no rain is falling
As his reserve falls, at half his breath comes short and the gray haze thins, at a quarter his fingers stop moving entirely, and at a tenth the mist round him lifts all at once and the gold flecks in it go out
It is beaten by fighting him on ground he has never walked, by bringing heat or a hard dry wind, by going round the ends of the line, or by sending what crosses without traveling
Phreatis fails by its flaw: deep water does not ask what is sinking into it, so it keeps whatever enters, the bad water with the good, and nothing can be taken back out; the Measurewrights call it contamination of the aquifer, and so he cannot forget a road, a count or a morning in the Hall of Verdicts
A road that has changed since he walked it comes back to him as it was and betrays him
Transference fails by its flaw: the exchange gives toward whoever has less and never asks who is giving, and run backward it carries off the one who opened it, which the Measurewrights call reverse coupling
The mist fails as mist does, burned off the ground by heat, torn by wind, thinned by daylight

Traits
He carries two Trait risks. Rigidity: once committed, he will ride a road after it has stopped going anywhere. His Shear Break condition is carrying something down his roads that he swore they would not carry.
THE ROAD UNDER THE ROAD · Primary Trait
THE ROAD UNDER THE ROAD is basically path detection: the power to read any ground for the way through it, and to keep every yard of it for good. It is the Trait that knows the way.
Capabilities
His soul reads ground for passage before it reads anything else: where a column can go, where a mule can carry two sacks in snow and where it must go single file, which herders’ shoulder the smugglers never had a reason to find, which deer track comes down onto the north hill of a house that did not know it had a back door. Everything he has walked stays. Phreatis keeps it the way a riverbed keeps the river, Retention keeps it whole, and Forecast turns it into time, two days, a day and a half, and he is always right.
The keeping is not his alone. Every road every Amagiri walked and wrote down since the house began lies in him through the blood’s memory, and it comes up whole when he reaches for it, the way a riverbed shows when the river runs low. At Dissonance it is more than a map. On a road he has walked, Transference treats the road as his: he can be anywhere along it faster than he could ride it, and so can whatever he carries.
Applications

Saying where a column can go and how long it will take
Knowing the paces between any two points of a walked road without measuring them
Being anywhere along a walked road faster than he could ride it
Reading through water as well as the eye: in air thick with steam he feels the shape and weight of a fighter moving through it, the way a fish feels a stone in the current

Associations

Phreatis, with Transference
The Spirit Path for the read and the keeping, with his Walked Fate Path’s share for the road that answers
The Amagiri blood’s memory of the house’s roads
His Retention and Forecast

Limitations

It reads only ground he has ridden or walked, never a map, however much he trusts it
In the Wellspring’s own terms, Transference pools on well-traveled roads and thins to nothing on unmapped ground
It reads ground and not men: he can bring twenty riders to any door in the north and has no idea what will be waiting behind it
It costs nothing to read, and he cannot stop doing it
The finger gives it away: it draws roads on tables, in wet rings, in the air
Country he has never walked beats it, and so does a road changed since he last walked it

RAIN MIST (雨霧 · Amagiri) · Inherited Trait
RAIN MIST is basically mist camouflage: the power to make himself and everyone riding with him look like weather. The Amagiri name means rain-mist, and their blood earns it.
Capabilities
On a road at night, in wet or cold air, the Amagiri thin the light round themselves and the people riding with them: a party with him goes gray at the edges and hard to fix in the eye from a wall or a hold, and a sentry looking straight at the track sees weather. It is the oldest thing the line does. The blood gives the mist and a lean toward the wet ground it stands in, and never a Path.
Applications

Hiding a party on a road at night from a wall or a hold

Associations

The Amagiri blood’s inheritance, with no Wellspring
The Spirit Path, the mist laid over what he is and over those riding with him

Limitations

It hides from eyes and readings and only from them, and best on the move, in the dark or the wet
In a hall, in daylight, standing still, it thins to almost nothing
It fails as fog fails: air that is warmed can hold more water unseen, the drops go back to vapor, and the cover is gone from the ground upward with nothing left to gather
It will not hold within ten yards of a fighter who walks in furnace heat; there it boils away round him in white rags and leaves him standing in the open like a man caught on a hillside when the mist lifts
It costs about two percent of his reserve an hour on the move, less than he recovers
To anyone who knows to look, it shows as a patch of road where the mist is thicker than the weather explains
Daylight, dogs that smell what they cannot see, a lantern on a pole, and heat beat it
When he calls KIRISAME the mist comes off him and goes out over the ground

NOW I KNOW WHICH WAY · Secondary Trait
NOW I KNOW WHICH WAY is basically indomitable will: the power to stay on a road once he has chosen it. It formed in Kiyome Byakuya’s white house the night he admitted he had spent a year mapping the roads out and had only been getting ready to run.
Capabilities
Once he has chosen his road he does not turn off it: fear still reaches him, and his hands still shake, but his feet do not stop. It pulls nothing down and moves nothing outside him. It is the processed half of the Verdict of Six, a fracture made into a feature, his own share of Fate spent the way a kept word is, and it binds only the man who chose.
Applications

Riding at the front of six hundred horse with his sword out, though he holds it badly

Associations

His Walked Fate Path, with no lens
The Verdict of Six, the fracture it was made from

Limitations

Its limit is the choosing: until he has picked his road he is the most hesitant man in any room, glancing at the door
It costs nothing to choose and everything to keep
His restless fingers going still show that he has chosen
Put two roads in front of him at once

Techniques
AMAGIRI-ASHI (雨霧足 · the Rain-Mist Step) · Bloodline Art, Amagiri
AMAGIRI-ASHI is basically mist-form travel: the power to go to cold fog and run a road he has walked the way fog runs down a river valley. It is the Step, the art going down the road.
Capabilities
On a road he has walked, at night or in wet air, he goes to mist. The edges first, the haze round him thickening and the man inside it going gray, and then all of him, body and coat and sword and whatever he holds, gone into a fine cold fog that moves along the road the way fog moves along a river valley at dusk, low and quick and following every bend, and comes back together at the far end as a slight young man in an indigo rain-cape, apologizing.
The mist is the blood’s cover and the road does the carrying: Transference hands him from one point of a walked road to the next, bend by bend, and what an onlooker sees is fog moving faster than fog should. His body is never flown through the air as vapor.
Applications

Crossing the north in a night
Taking passengers: he has carried two Grandmasters with him at once, the three of them gone to cold gray fog along every bend the house had written down
Setting a passenger down at a dead run at the far end

Associations

The Amagiri blood for the mist, Transference for the carrying, Phreatis for the road known
The Spirit Path, with his Walked Fate Path’s share for the road that carries
THE ROAD’S OPEN, which is the Step held instead of taken

Limitations

Its limits are the mist’s: it needs a road he knows, and it needs air that will hold water
It will not hold in heat, in a hard dry wind or in strong sunlight, which burn it off the ground and leave him standing where the mist ran out
It costs about a fifth of a percent of his reserve a league, which is why he can cross the north in a night and does not, since a quartermaster who arrives before his message raises questions
Before the Step he is a little grayer at the edges than the weather explains, the haze thickening from the hem of the cape upward
Heat, wind, daylight and strange ground beat it

THE ROAD’S OPEN · Technique
THE ROAD’S OPEN is basically passage holding: the power to hold the way along a road open like a door, for others to go through. It is the Rain-Mist Step, held instead of taken, and it is his own phrase, said to a king over his shoulder; nobody taught it to him.
Capabilities
He stands at a bend of a walked road with his left hand out behind him, palm open, the way a man holds a door, and the fog of the road stays standing at his back with the way through it kept, for as long as the mist will stand. Anyone he names can step into it and be carried, without waiting on him to go to mist first.
Applications

Carrying the people he names down a road without going with them
Keeping a way back open

Associations

The Amagiri blood, Transference and Phreatis, as the Step
The Spirit Path, with his Walked Fate Path’s share
AMAGIRI-ASHI, whose price it pays

Limitations

Its limits are the mist’s and the road’s: it stands only at the edge of where fog will hold, and only on a road he still has
He pays the Step’s price for the stretch he is holding, again every minute it stands
He pays with his feet too, because the open end is wherever he is and he cannot leave it
The hand gives it away: his left hand held out behind him, palm open, and fog standing at one bend of a road
Burn the mist off that bend, or move him off it

MICHI-KIRI (道切り · the Road-Cut) · Signature Technique
MICHI-KIRI is basically passage negation: the power to close a road along the line of one cut, so that whatever is traveling across it arrives and goes no further. It is the Amagiri draw, which his grandfather taught him in a barn with the doors shut.
Capabilities
The name is the old country word for the rope and straw hung across a village road to turn back whatever comes down it at night; the Amagiri kept the custom and lost the rope. He draws the plain sword, the one time he ever draws it, and cuts once across the air in one long flat line, from the left hip, with the whole arm level, at the height of a man’s chest, making almost no sound. The draw is a real cut, a slight man’s whole arm, and it would open a throat if a throat were there. The working goes out along the path the edge travels and for as far past the point as his Radius will carry it, and Transference closes the road along that line.
Whatever is traveling across it, a blade, an arrow, a man running, a charge of horse, a river’s flow, a working’s current, stops traveling. It rides one blow, and the blow strikes nothing. A rider does not hit a wall, because there is no wall, and nothing pushes back on him: his way forward simply ends at the line, the way a river’s ends at a weir, and everything he was carrying in the way of speed stands there with him, pooled.
Sheathing the sword opens the road like a gate, and whatever was pressed against it stumbles forward into the place where it had been, a step late and off balance.
Applications

Stopping a charge: cut across a wing of horse at three hundred yards, it has stopped four hundred riders against nothing in the snow
Stopping a blade, an arrow, a running man, a river’s flow or a working’s current
Holding a thing at the line until he chooses to let the road open

Associations

Transference, which closes the road
His Walked Fate Path: a claim along one line, carried on a Studied Body’s single stroke
The plain sword, his bonded weapon, which carries it in its edge
His Radius, which sets how far past the point it reaches
His grandfather, who taught it and told him never to use it where anyone could count

Limitations

It closes only what travels: heat, light and sound are no travelers with two ends to their journey, only the world’s old habit of passing from one bit of air to the next, so the exchange has nothing to refuse
A furnace stopped a hand’s width from a shield still blisters the man behind it, and a furnace on the far side of his line cooks the people behind it as if the line were not there
A man standing still on the line is not moved off it
The line is as long as one cut of a slight man’s arm and the reach of his Radius, never a wall round a city
It costs about five percent of his reserve to draw, and it holds a minute from the draw
The line lives in his sword-hand: its near end is where he stands, and if he steps off that end the end moves with him, so a cut that is holding something he cannot afford to let through pins him as surely as it pins the thing
The sword out is the tell
Go round its ends, or bring something that crosses without traveling
A fighter stopped by it can walk along the closed road with his fist against it, feeling for the end the way a man feels along a fence for the gate, toward the slight man standing at it

SHINGAN (心眼 · the heart-eye) · Bloodline Faculty, Moto
SHINGAN, turned on the ground, is basically load perception: the power to see where a slope, a ford or a wall will bear a horse and where it will give. It is the common Moto sight, which shows where a thing is carrying its weight.
Capabilities
In Hayato it turned to the ground early and stayed there, and he reads a slope, a bank, a frozen ford or the mended seam in a wall for where it will bear a horse and where it will give, before he reads the faces in front of it. In him it is the surveyor’s half of the art: the Trait says where a road goes, and the eye says whether it will hold a horse today.
Applications

Telling him that a deer track will take a horse
Reading a frozen ford, a bank or a mended wall before he trusts it

Associations

The Moto blood, with no lens; the blood gives the eye and never a Path
It spends his own share and pulls nothing down
THE ROAD UNDER THE ROAD, whose other half it is

Limitations

It resolves load in ground and stone; it reads men poorly, and the Torvald he read at the Verdict of Six he read with the other five
Held open it lasts nearly three hours from a full reserve, paid as a squint that never quite leaves the corners of his eyes
It shows as his eyes going to a wall’s mended seam before the people in front of it
Soft ground with nothing in it carrying weight gives it nothing: bog, deep snow, open water

characters/ability-accounts/hisae-thornw.title: Hisae Thornwall — Abilities in full
characters/ability-accounts/hisae-thornw.content:
Card: Hisae Thornwall
SMILE AND PAY
SMILE AND PAY is basically deception mastery: the power to let them count you bought, and keep the door. It is her signature art. She smiled and paid for forty years, and the whole time she was keeping a back door open.
Capabilities
It is one idea, and it took her forty years to say it out loud. A Byakuya girl was sent north to seal a peace, into a house that sat under Tenrai taxes and Tenrai factors and Tenrai silver, and on her wedding night an old forester told her that Thornwall kept a road open through the wood for a king who had not come. She thought him a sentimental old fool. Then she spent forty years being the thing that kept his road safe.
The smile is the keeping, the door is what was kept, and the pike is what comes through the door when the crow arrives. None of the three is a Wellspring’s work. She has harmonized no lens for them. They are a habit of the soul, a secret of her husband’s house and a drill of its foresters, and each takes its limit and its failure from itself.
Applications

Being counted bought by the people she means to turn on
Keeping a road open for a king who had not come
Sending the pikes through it when the crow arrives

Techniques

SMILE AND PAY - the keeping, a small dry smile with everything behind it
THE BACK DOOR - what was kept, the way in nobody uses
THE THORNWALL PIKE - what comes through the door

Associations

No Wellspring and no lens: a habit of the soul, a secret of the house and a house drill
The Spirit Path carries the smile, as one meaning written over herself
The Fate Path carries the door and the Command; the door and the pikes are no working
THE RED BEFORE THE WHITE, which is no part of the art and the reason for all of it

Limitations

A waiting does nothing until the crow comes
It cost her forty years behind shut doors, and her own name with them
The door, once used, belongs to everybody

Traits
SMILE AND PAY · Primary Trait
SMILE AND PAY is basically emotion concealment: the power to hold everything behind a small dry smile, so that no reading of her face or her aura gives up what she means. Her soul learned it sitting in Thornhaven under Tenrai taxes, Tenrai factors and Tenrai silver for forty years, smiling and paying, while the Tenrai counted Thornwall bought.
Capabilities
A face gives a person away in a particular manner. What somebody truly feels arrives on the face first, for well under half a second, before the face they mean to show can be laid over it, and a sharp eye across a table lives on those flickers. An aura leaks the same way: it brightens and leans toward what its owner wants. In her the flicker is not there to catch, because the dry smile is already in place before the feeling comes, and a face that is already doing one thing has no slack left to do another.
She walks the Spirit Path a third and more of her practice, and that Path works on what a thing means; she uses it on one thing only, herself. Her Core (the innermost layer of the soul, where identity sits) holds a single plain meaning over everything else, a provincial lady who likes gold thread and pays what she is asked, and that is the page any reader gets, whether he reads with his eyes or with his Gnosis (the stat of perception and understanding).
While she keeps the smile her Feint reads a step high on the hidden scale. Her aura, the near-white with its red line, stays banked so low under it that a factor across the table saw a woman and no practitioner at all.
Applications

Sitting across a table from Tenrai factors and giving nothing away
Passing as a provincial lady with a weakness for gold thread
Hiding a practitioner’s aura from a reader

Associations

The Spirit Path, as one meaning written over herself by her Core
Her own table at Thornhaven, across from Tenrai factors
The red-and-gold bodice and the icicles at her ears

Limitations

It is a waiting, and a waiting does nothing on its own; it needs a crow to come to Thornhaven
When the crow came and said that the red line lived, she had the Tenrai factor put in her cellar the next morning and called out the pikes, and the smile had done all it would ever do
It costs nothing she would mention, because nothing is made or thrown and no reserve leaves her
What it truly cost was forty years, and her own name
Its tell tells a watcher nothing: the corners of the dark red mouth lifting a very little, the heavy lids coming half down, the small hands folding, the icicles at her ears hanging dead still
The Tenrai found nothing that beat it, because they read her face for forty years and never once read her house
The smile hides what she means and cannot hide what she does
A man who counted the pike-shafts in the Thornhaven lofts, or asked the foresters why they cut the same empty rides every winter and every spring, or simply walked the Thornwood east until it ended, would have had all of it without looking at her at all
A reader whose Perception outranks her Ward by a full step on the hidden scale, with her raised Feint counted against him, sees a banked aura for what it is

THE BACK DOOR · Secondary Trait
THE BACK DOOR is basically weakness detection: the power to look at ground for the way nobody uses. It formed the night she married into the house, when her husband’s grandfather told her why the Thornwall foresters kept the corridors cut.
Capabilities
A stronghold is safe for exactly as long as the things its safety depends on stay true, and its keepers stop looking at those things long before they stop being true. That is the oldest lesson in siege work, that a pass is turned by the goat track its defenders forgot.
She is a Fate Path soul, and Fate is the Path of what has to be so before anything can happen; her Forecast, the best thing in her, goes to that and nothing else. She pulls no thread and moves nothing, which is why it is free. She only looks at a map, a wall or a bargain and finds the one condition everybody has agreed to stop checking.
She already knows where one is: the long cuts through the Thornwood, walled in by trees so old you cannot see the sky, and the stair behind the frozen fall. Thornwall cut them two hundred years ago, when the Kōkan still sat the red chair and Thornwall was their forester, and they run from Thornhaven to the foot of the Seat’s eastern face, where the rock is lowest. The Seat’s main gate had been the only way up the rock for three hundred years, so every eye, ward and garrison on the rock faced south. In the case of the Seat she did not even have to find the door, because she had been handed it on her wedding night and kept it.
Applications

Finding the low place in a rock face, the ride through a wood, the hour every eye is on another road
Reading a map, a wall or a bargain for the condition nobody checks
Bringing pikes to the foot of the Seat’s eastern face by the Thornwood corridors and the stair

Associations

The Fate Path, through her Forecast; it is no working
Her husband’s grandfather and the foresters’ marks
House Thornwall’s corridors, kept cut two hundred years
THE THORNWALL PIKE, which goes through the door

Limitations

A back door works once; after the Seat, everybody knows, and the Thornwood rides are now on every map in the north
It costs nothing
Its tell is that she looks at a map for the way nobody uses, and her finger rests where the map is blank
A man who already knows where the corridors run beats it
One sentry at the head of the stair, or one forester who talks, and twelve hundred men are strung out in single files in a wood with a cliff at the end of it

THE RED BEFORE THE WHITE · Inherited Trait
THE RED BEFORE THE WHITE is basically oath empowerment: the power to stand unafraid near the Kōkan blood. It is the oath of the white house and no part of the art SMILE AND PAY, though it is the reason for all of it.
Capabilities
It is the Byakuya oath, said over her as a girl in the white house: purity before power, peace before the blade, and the red line before the white, until the end of the red line. An oath is the small end of Fate, and this one was laid on her Attraction Layer (the outermost layer of the soul, where bonds and vows take hold) before she was old enough to weigh it. It binds her to the red line and binds the red line to nothing. Near the Kōkan blood her Anchoring holds and nothing frightens her.
She kept it over the lamp every night for forty years in Thornhaven with the doors shut, and spoke it aloud in the Hall of Verdicts beside Kiyome, the old woman and the not-so-old one, so softly only the front of the Hall could hear. The smile, the door and the pikes were forty years of keeping this one sentence alive where nobody could hear it.
Applications

Holding her nerve and her Anchoring near the Kōkan blood

Associations

The Byakuya oath, the white house’s inheritance, with no Wellspring behind it
The Fate Path, as a binding
The Kōkan, the red line it binds her to
The oath lamp at Thornhaven, over which she kept it

Limitations

The limit is the oath’s own: it guards the king, and has nothing to say when the king is the knife
It costs nothing to keep, and it cannot be set down
Its tell is her lips moving over the words, with the doors shut
To beat it, make the king the knife

Techniques
THE THORNWALL PIKE · House Art, Thornwall · Signature
THE THORNWALL PIKE is basically pike formation command: the power to bring twelve hundred pikes on at a walk as a hedge of ash and iron that horse will not go into, or to send them thirty at a time up a stair and over a wall nobody was watching. Every Thornwall pikeman is taught the step and the hedge; only the Lady knew where to send them.
Capabilities
The pikes come on in gray felt, in step, to the slow beat of a drum, with the thorn-horn sounding behind them every hundred paces. The charge is the sound, and it is meant to be heard: a drum too slow to be anything but deliberate, the horn marking each hundred paces, and then the block itself coming out of the white, gray felt and iron caps, each banner with its dark red thorn-sprig, forty men wide and thirty deep with eighteen-foot ash shafts leveled.
The reason it works is in the horse and in the arithmetic. A horse will gallop at a man; it will not run itself onto a point it can see, and a shaft that long puts the iron of the first four or five ranks out past the front man’s chest, so that a rider coming in meets five points before he reaches one face. A horseman’s whole weapon is weight at speed, and a hedge that holds its shape gives him nothing to spend it on but the ash.
So the art is all in holding the shape, and that is drill and will together: every man at one pace so no gap opens, which the drum gives them; every man certain the man beside him will stand, which the lord gives them. Her Command keeps the step and her Forecast picks the ground. She does not shout and does not need to. A Stage V soul with her Dominion (the stat of a soul’s command over what stands around it) riding at a walk beside the block is felt down every rank as a steadiness, the same plain weight that bends the attention of lesser souls toward her, turned here to holding twelve hundred frightened men to a drumbeat.
Applications

Stopping horse with a set hedge
Holding ground and taking walls
Going up a stair thirty at a time, on her quiet order: “Not all at once. Thirty at a time.”

Associations

House Thornwall, which teaches every pikeman the step and the hedge
The Fate Path, for the Command; it is no working
Her Command, her Forecast and her Dominion
The drum and the thorn-horn, which do her shouting
THE BACK DOOR, which says where to send them

Limitations

Its limit is the hedge: it holds ground and takes walls, and it is slow
It cannot chase, and it cannot turn quickly
