VIII. Traits
Full accounts: Sonzai Moto — Abilities
Every Trait reads at his lead Mastery, Fate I.
TATARI (祟り), the Calamity · Primary Trait
TATARI is basically Calamity Manipulation: the power to make misfortune hunt down whoever wronged him. Sonzai never forgives and never forgets. Every wrong done to him goes into his memory and stays there, and the longer he holds it, the stronger it grows. Most people who pull on fate pay a debt for it afterward, as bad luck that comes back on them. Sonzai holds onto that debt so hard that it lands on the person he hates instead. Straps snap on them, roofs fall on them, horses throw them, wells go sour in their halls, and nothing anyone does can explain why. It breaks the oldest rule of his house: the Moto read what a thing is meant to do and enforce it, and their Ruin only brings down what was already failing, while Sonzai’s grudge makes a thing ready to fall, and then it falls. It only works on a real wrong, and only on one target at a time. If he ever lets go, or his target dies before he is finished, every bit of that held calamity comes home to him at once.
ONNEN (怨念), the Deep Grudge · Secondary Trait
ONNEN is basically Revenge Empowerment: the power to keep going for as long as the person who wronged him is still alive. It was born the night Mizuyi was taken, when Cozbi Mahuo said “let the games begin” and Sonzai decided he would never let it go. While his target lives, Sonzai cannot be stopped. He ignores pain, does not tire, and gets back up from wounds that should have dropped him, because his soul will not let his body quit before the debt is paid. It works hand in hand with TATARI: the calamity hunts his enemy, and Sonzai keeps walking toward them through anything in the way. The price comes at the end. Once the target is dead or out of reach, the Trait lets go all at once, and every wound he ignored and every night he did not sleep arrives together. Without someone to hold on to, he may not get back up.
IX. Domain
None.
X. Techniques
TATARIGAMI (祟り神), the Calamity God · Signature Art
TATARIGAMI is basically Misfortune Embodiment: the power to become calamity itself for whoever wronged him. In the old stories a tatarigami is an angry spirit that brings disaster on those who offended it, and Sonzai’s grudge becomes exactly that. When he calls it, the grudge rises over his target as a red omen, and the world begins to turn against them. Beams crack over their head, the ground goes bad under their feet, their horse balks, their sword slips, and their luck runs out all at once and keeps running out. None of it looks like magic. It looks like the worst day of someone’s life, over and over, until they break. It runs on TATARI and ONNEN together: his grudge makes things ready to fall, the calamity hunts the target, and Sonzai keeps walking toward them through all of it.

KYŌCHŌ (凶兆), Ill Omen · He marks the target. They begin to see signs everywhere, a red bird on the sill, a crack in their cup, their name misspoken, and everything that happens to them from then on goes wrong.
FALLING SKY · Everything above the target comes down at once: beams, banners, stone, the roof itself.
SOURED GROUND · The earth under them turns against them. Footing gives, wells go bad, and the floor of their own hall will not hold them.
HYAKUSAI (百災), the Hundred Misfortunes · The finisher. Every bad thing that could happen to them happens at the same moment.

The tell: the white rose on his golden armor reddens petal by petal as the grudge grows. When it is fully red, the Calamity God is ready.
The price: his knots are the heaviest in the house, the calamity does not care who is standing next to the target, and the more he uses it, the narrower his world grows around the one person he hates.
Combo with Sodoku (unnamed; they argue about it): Sodoku ties a target’s thread to one spot with MUSUBIME, and Sonzai brings TATARIGAMI down on the knot. The calamity cannot miss, because the meeting was already written.
XI. Spirit Axes

Sodoku (brother) The one who catches him, and the one bond his obsession cannot eat. Sodoku is all that stands between him and the bottom.
Mizuyi (sister) Taken out of the hall in front of him. He went for the dark with his bare hands and got four strides.

Eyes: Pale green, sidelong and heavy-lidded, and in anger wide and wet and furious.
Face: Fine-boned and sharp, his father’s face at the Foot when the cold goes out of it.

After: On the night Mizuyi was taken the drawer broke. What was left was his father’s face at the Foot, and a grudge he means never to put down.
Voice: Blunt, fast, in plain words when he is angry, driving straight on over a break in his voice.

When the dark took Mizuyi, went for the door with his bare hands and was caught by his brother on the fifth stride.
Swore at the table to go down the Kessen road and burn Cozbi Mahuo’s capital to the ground.
Pushed his brother off and walked out of the great hall, telling Rashani Zettari the Moto did not need the Zettari’s help. Lorn Stark followed him.
ONNEN, the Deep Grudge, woke the night Mizuyi was taken.

VIII. Traits
Full accounts: Tenma Moto — Abilities
Every Trait reads at his Fate I, the early grip’s rung.
KEGARE (穢れ), the Defilement · Primary Trait
KEGARE is basically Ontopathogenesis: the power to infect what a thing is, so that whatever he carries spreads from one thing to the next like a sickness. In the old belief, kegare is the impurity that clings to anyone who touches death and passes on to whoever touches them. Tenma’s soul works the same way. Everything in the world is tied to everything else by fine threads of fate, and Tenma can send whatever he holds along those threads. It can be something physical, like a wound, rot, frost, fire or poison, or health and strength. It can be something magical, like a working, a curse or a blessing. It can be a state, like fear, sleep, courage or an oath’s hold. One touch is enough to start it, and from there it travels through touch, through bonds and through shared ground, one soul catching it from the next. At its extreme it stops being something a person has and becomes what they are: a man becomes stone, a curse becomes who someone is, and a Domain turns to rot from the inside. The price is that he is always the first one infected. Everything he spreads passes through him first, so he carries a little of every sickness he has ever started. It can only travel where there is a connection, so a soul cut off from everything cannot catch it, and the Work of Purity can wash it out.
KAESHI (返し), the Return · Secondary Trait
KAESHI is basically Damage Reflection: the power to send whatever is done to him back to whoever did it. In Japanese, kaeshi is the return, the answering stroke that comes back along the same line. Tenma’s soul is woven into everything around him, and KEGARE lets anything that touches him travel along those threads. KAESHI turns that around: when someone hurts him, the hurt follows its own thread home. Cut him and the cut opens on the swordsman, in the same place. Poison him and the poisoner sickens. Curse him and the curse goes back to whoever laid it. Strike him with a working and the working lands on the one who threw it. It only wakes while he is under attack, and it is strongest when the attack is meant to kill: the more someone wants to hurt him, the harder it comes back. The price is that he feels all of it first, in full. KAESHI does not spare him the wound; it only makes sure he is not the only one who bleeds. A blow strong enough to kill him outright can still kill him, and then it kills the one who struck it as well.
IX. Domain
None.
X. Techniques
NAGASHI-BINA (流し雛), the Floating Dolls · Signature Art
NAGASHI-BINA is basically Sympathetic Magic: the power to tie a person to a paper doll, so that whatever happens to the doll happens to them. In Japan, nagashi-bina are paper dolls that families set afloat down a river to carry their impurity away. Tenma makes his own. He folds them small and white from plain paper, and the moment he ties one to a person, a thread runs between them that only he can see. Both his Traits travel along that thread. Through KEGARE, anything he puts into a doll spreads into the person tied to it: a wound, a sickness, a curse, sleep, fear. Through KAESHI, a doll can take what was meant for someone he loves and send it back along the thread to whoever did it. On the field he looks like a child playing with paper. People laugh until the first doll tears.

KATASHIRO (形代), the Effigy · He folds a doll and ties it to a person, by a touch, a hair, a drop of blood or their name spoken over it. From then on, what happens to the doll happens to them.
NAGASHI (流し), the Floating Away · He pulls a wound or a curse out of someone into a doll and sets it loose, sending it to whoever he chooses.
MIGAWARI (身代わり), the Stand-In · A doll tied to someone he loves takes a killing blow for them. The doll tears, and through KAESHI the blow goes home to whoever struck it.
WARA NINGYŌ (藁人形), the Straw Doll · The finisher. It comes from the old curse ritual of nailing a straw doll to a shrine tree in the darkest hour of the night. He nails one, and the person tied to it feels every nail.

The price: every doll is tied to him as well as to its target. Everything a doll carries passes through his hands first, and if a doll is burned before he is done with it, whatever it held comes back to him.
With his brothers: Sodoku ties the threads and Tenma spreads along them.
XI. Spirit Axes
Sodoku (brother) · The Author ties the threads; the Carrier sends things down them.
Kimizu (brother) · Two years younger. Kimizu reads everything and Tenma carries it; Tenma is the one who stands in front of him.
Mizuyi (sister) · Taken by Cozbi Mahuo on the night of her betrothal.
XII. Resistances

Filtration 152: poison, sickness and corrupted Essence move through him without taking hold, which is why he can carry what he spreads.
Fortification 83, Continuity 98: a curse finds it hard to stay in him, and KAESHI sends it home.
Body: Vitality 436, Dexterity 293. He is a twelve-year-old in a hood, and a strong enough blow can still kill him outright.

XIII. Physical Description
Hair: Black and unruly, a thick mop falling over the brow and into the eyes, gathered loosely at the nape.
Eyes: Red, deep and steady under the black fringe; the eye people remember.
Face: Pale, almost bloodless, with a small closed mouth and a look that holds on a person too long.
Dress: A hood and wrap of dark red cloth close about the neck.
Marks: A thin gold ring at the ear.
XIV. Psychology
Voice: soft and spare, polite to everyone, and he says sorry before he does something, never after.
Underneath: the quiet one of the four, who watches too long and says little. He carries the family’s hurts on purpose, and he has learned to be careful about where he sets them down.
How he moves: small and still, hands in his sleeves, with a fold of paper always between his fingers.
XV. Equipment
He carries no weapon and does not fight with his hands; the dolls do the fighting.

XVI. Temperance Record

Stage I, Murmuring: woke young, as Kōkan children do.
Stage II, Welling: crossed in the yard at the Seat.
Stage III, Ascension: KEGARE woke with it, when a fever went through the nursery and stopped at him.
Stage IV, Flourishing: crossed at eleven.
Stage V, Splintering: crossed at twelve.
Next gate: Stage VI, Glory; it holds at Level 115, which his 135 already passes, so only the Catalyst is wanting; past Level 200 without it he would come into Residual Strain.

XVII. Fracture Log

Named Tenma, heaven’s pause.

TraitKindSourcePath and FormGatesWhat it doesLimitTellCostCounterNumbersTHE MAKING OF A GENERALPrimary———One long look at a man tells him what that man can carry and how far, and then he says, “Ah. So there he is.” (Primary Trait)It reads what a man can carry, not what he will choose. Those two summers are the proof: he read what Gimbzo could carry, and he was right, and it told him nothing about what the man would do with it.The long look, the pale eyes going over a man the way they go over a ford, the black iron ring turning in the beard-braid under his thumb, and then the line.Nothing, because nothing is made or thrown: it is a read, and it runs on his eyes and his years.A man who shows him nothing: stand still, keep your hands quiet, carry nothing in front of him, and never take the road he offers.No reserve.WE GIVESecondary———While he is giving something away, his brother, his riders, his house, his neck, fear cannot reach him and his hands do not shake. (Secondary Trait)It is all one way; nobody promises the Starks anything back, not the Sky, not the lines, not the people they give it for. It also works only on what is his. He cannot give away another man’s life and feel nothing, and the boys younger than sixteen he lets lie their way into the vanguard are a weight the Trait does not lift.A sentence and never a gesture: by the time he says “That’s just the way this life is, lad,” the giving is done and his hands are already quiet.Everything, and he does not count it.Something he would not give, and nobody has found it. The nearest anyone came was Wystan Greymane, who talked him into keeping one thing back, the boy’s own name, and Ulf sat on it like a man selling a horse with a cracked hoof under a blanket.No reserve.STARK RIMEInherited———The Stark cold at full strength: the warmth walks out of everything near him and down through his heels, the snow goes hard as a floor, and his great sword runs white to the point. (Inherited Trait)It moves heat and cannot make it. On ground already frozen to the bottom there is little left for it to take, against a real fire it is a bucket against a furnace, and pushed past what his body can pass along, the cold stops in him on the way down: white fingers first, then a slow, stupid hand on the cross, which a man two fingers short cannot afford.His breath stops steaming and the wolf-fur goes white.—Heat, and calm: a brazier at your back, a warm blade, and nothing said about his brother.No reserve at rest; reach, yards round him. · Sound: a frozen lake groaning under weight

Full accounts: Wystan Greymane — Abilities
Every Trait reads at his lead Mastery, Body I.

























































TraitKindSourcePath and FormGatesWhat it doesLimitTellCostCounterNumbersKEEPERS OF THE WALLPrimary———While somebody stands behind him, nothing that reaches him moves him back a step; he looks west first, and then at you. (Primary Trait)It faces one way; it is a wall, and a wall guards what is behind it and nothing else. With nobody behind him the step is gone and he is a strong old man with a good shield, and a blow from the flank or the rear meets no wall at all.His eyes go west, or to whatever he has been set to face, before they come to the man in front of him, because he is checking the post before he checks the threat.Nothing, since nothing is made or thrown.Come at what he isn’t guarding: go round, split him from the people he is covering, or put a second threat on the far side of them and make him choose.No reserve; Anchoring and Fortitude one step high while he holds a line with someone behind it.STILL, THEN FASTSecondary———He stops moving altogether, so that there is nothing in him to read, and the first thing he does out of the stillness is quicker than he has any right to be. (Secondary Trait)It is one move; after the first, he is only an old man of sixty-one with a sword, and winding it again takes real stillness, a few breaths of it, which nobody close enough to hit him will give him.He stops moving altogether.Nothing.Never be the first to move. A patient man wastes it, a longer weapon can make him come forward out of it, and a false start he believes spends it as surely as a true one.No reserve; the first move out of stillness one step quicker, once.LATER, ULFSecondary———One word, “Later,” and the thing he is keeping is as far out of reach as if the ridge stood in front of it. (Secondary Trait)A silence cannot defend itself except by staying silent. He cannot explain, argue or lie his way round a question, because he does not lie; he can only decline it, and a declined question tells a sharp listener that there is something there.”Later.”What keeping costs: he carried the boy’s name south with him and never got to say it.Ask him in front of the one he is keeping it from; he will walk to the window instead, and the walk is an answer of a kind.No reserve.

characters/volume-i-—-character-cards/xh.title: Xhem Valorin
characters/volume-i-—-character-cards/xh.content:
The Young Inkbinder · He Who Hears Magic Before It Speaks
I. Identity
Full Name: Xhem Valorin
Titles: The Young Inkbinder · the Vaeloris Prodigy · the Boy Without a Crystal
Age: 16
Race / Lineage: Human · House Valorin, the Scripted Soul Lattice bloodline
Faction: Vaeloris Village, Inner World, after the Sundering. Vaeloris Alchemical Scriptorium · wand-forges · Grimoire Conservatory. Sponsored by the House Valorin elders.
Family: Son of the late Rheana Valorin, who died of a soul sickness · nephew of Malex Valorin and of Dhaerin Valorin, headmaster of the Scriptorium and leader of Vaeloris · cousin Saella of the crimson branch
Status: Active
Catalyst Event: At nine he opened a sealed family grimoire that had rejected every child before him, collapsed for three days whispering unfinished formulae, and woke to say they were not curses, they were questions.
II. Soul Architecture
Stat line: Stage IX Invocation · Master (Fire) · Level 275 · Refined · Inkbinder · Fate leading, II · Spirit second, Walked, IV · Lenses: home + 2
Level: 275; it holds Invocation (215) and would hold Realization (230), and no Residual Strain builds in him short of 300
Temperance Stage: IX · Invocation · Master · stat ceiling 625
Soul: No Soul Crystal. A Scripted Soul Lattice with the same three faces, grown to the depth a Crystal would call Fire.
Path: Fate, leading (permissions, recognition, bonds); Spirit, second (comprehension and memory; gates a Stage late); Body only as far as his hands and tools.
Mastery: Fate II, Drawn, the lead, with no grip by blood or blessing to lift it past II · Spirit IV, Shepherd, Walked a rung behind · Body not walked, and nothing reads there; his hands work through his foci
Class: Inkbinder (evolves as his lead Mastery rises)
Reserve: about 8.8 million EU at full (log₁₀ EU = 3.4202 + 0.012812 × 275); a Fate-led bar reads as Essence. The Cistern of Unspoken Lines puts him on par with Crystal-bearers of his Stage.
Inner Grimoire: his since Stage VIII; the lattice is its own focus.
Releases: not known.
The climb: Stage III at fifteen to Stage IX at sixteen, every crossing lived on the Fate road.
III. Wellspring Harmonizations
Triune Core: Anamnesis (Medium; magical memory) · Fixatio (Medium; holds formulae and seals) · Ascensio (Distillation: separating a working into its parts).
Network: Transference (Fate; moves a working’s standing: Lent Script, Translation) · Judicium (names the weakest clause) · Luminalis (diagnostic light) · Coagulatio (gives ink a body) · Absolution (vents corruption).
Forms: Scriptia · Alchemia · Harmonia.
IV–V. Stats
Pool: Levels 1 to 100, 1,200 + Levels 101 to 200, 1,500 + Levels 201 to 275, 1,350 + Thresholds I–IX 4,500 = 8,550 points on Sub-Stats.



























































PrimaryTotalMeanSignature Sub-StatsGnosis1,900238Analysis 450 · Fluency 420 · Retention 330 · Perception 300 · Cognition 200Resilience1,600200Ward 480 · Integrity 360 · Continuity 250 · Fortification 200 · Persistence 150Tempering1,200150Clarity 360 · Yield 300 · Maturity 220 · Coherence 180Dominion1,050150Sovereignty 400 · Sense 250 · Radius 200 · Gravity 120 (divided by seven; Throne outside)Harmonics1,000125Axis 300 · Attunement 260 · Synergy 220 · Stability 160Dexterity800100Finesse 330 · Economy 220 · Reflex 120 · Celerity 80Vitality56070Regeneration 160 · Threshold 120 · Constitution 100 · Fortitude 80Ardency44055Penetration 180 · Compression 120 · Flux 80
Skills: Spell analysis Master · Vaeloric script Master · Alchemy Expert · Wandwork Expert · Grimoire-binding Expert · Footwork Apprentice.
VI. Physical Force
Thin: Vitality and Ardency at means of 70 and 55. Scribed Flesh has begun writing his bone and sinew, and he still will never trade blows with a warrior. His force is in Ward 480, Analysis 450, Fluency 420 and Sovereignty 400.
VII. Aether Flow
Essence routed through the lattice as living language: intent into formula, formula into structure, structure into effect, through grimoires, wands, staffs, inks, catalysts and circles. Banked lines in the Cistern pay out first.
VIII. Traits
Lineage (Valorin Family page): Scripted Soul Lattice · Primordial Scriptia · Harmonic Translation Engine · Living Spell Memory · Arcane Vessel Sovereignty · the Cistern of Unspoken Lines · Scribed Flesh · the Inner Grimoire · Errata · the Distributed Soul.
His own (each feeds his arts; every Trait reads at his lead Mastery, Fate II):

The Grammar Heard Feeds Errata, Nullgrammar, the Translator’s Hand. Hears a working’s grammar as it forms, its sequence, pressure, intent and weakest clause, in a third of a breath to one breath. Overloaded by chaos, the nameless and the truly alien.
Grimoire Symbiosis Feeds Stored Workings and the Silent Page. Vellum-Wake as an organ: pages hold longer and fire cleaner, and it opens to the page he needs. Countered by book-burning, page-sealing wax, anti-script wards, theft.
The Translator’s Hand Feeds Translation and Lent Script. After one or two looks, rebuilds a simple-to-middling foreign working at four to six tenths of its strength; every working Nullgrammar strikes out leaves its shape in Vellum-Wake as a study page. Bloodline locks, Domains, miracles and chaos resist.
Wand-Hand Precision Feeds Wand-Script Bolt and the Struck Line. A mark within a finger’s width at forty meters. Countered by hand injuries, tremors, fear, disarming.
Mystic Lock Feeds the Seal. What he seals stays sealed while his written name holds it; only his hand or a greater authority reopens. Holds the structured, not a battering ram.
Margin Notes Feeds Errata and Lent Script. Writes small annotations into a working mid-cast, his or a consenting ally’s: lengthen, quiet, quicken, narrow. Each note costs; it never changes what a working fundamentally is.

IX. Domain
The Unwritten Library. Inside it every working must be written down to exist, and he can read everything written. About thirty meters, young. Every working legible to him at once; Nullgrammar at half cost; exceptions to his Silent Pages free. Smell of ink, paper, candle smoke and rainwater; footsteps like turning pages; lies hang as smudged text. Holds about a minute before Lattice Shear. Chaos stays illegible; a Domain of greater authority overwrites it.
X. Techniques
Featured creation: Nullgrammar (anti-magic). Every clean working is held up by recognition: the Continuum recognizes the caster’s intent, read off the Attraction Layer. Nullgrammar is Fate work: through the Grammar Heard he reads a working’s authorization, through Errata he writes one clause into it on the Fate plane, backed by his Sovereignty: this was not permitted. The Continuum withdraws recognition; the working comes apart into loose Aether, a shimmer and a smell of wet ink. The caster’s spend stays spent.

The Struck Line · by wand bolt; strikes out one working (a bolt mid-flight, a ward, an enchantment, a curse) to about forty meters; cost rises with the working’s Grade against his own Stage.
The Silent Page · a torn page of Vellum-Wake unfolding into a field of about ten meters; nothing new is cast inside unless it passes his clause; holds one to three minutes; exceptions written by name, his own spells included.
The Seal · written onto the thing itself; seals a ward, door, cursed book or Essence channel shut for hours to days (Mystic Lock).
The Unwritten Word · spoken, the whole lattice behind it; strikes one clause of a Domain’s law out of a pocket two or three meters across for a few breaths; risks Lattice Shear.
Cannot: unpermit what was never permitted (Obsession-held workings); touch chaos or the nameless; stop momentum (a charge keeps its weight, a stone still falls); take hold against sacred blessings, Archon-scale workings, or Domains far above him; choose its targets inside the Silent Page.

Other arts: Errata: Correction (blunt, redirect, delay or invert a structured working) · Vaeloric Formula: Unbind (loosen a binding’s anchor clause up to his Stage) · Living Ink Barrier (a ten-meter script wall holding to around A-grade strikes) · Wand-Script Bolt (forty meters; can carry the Struck Line) · Translation · Lent Script (with consent) · Stored Workings (about a dozen prepared pages) · Ink Familiars (minutes now) · Silver Page Solvent (purges curse residue, poison-magic, corrupted ink).
XI. Spirit Axes
The Spirit of Written Memory and the Spirit of Alchemical Refinement; a faint, unborn Axis to the future idea of Magehood as a universal discipline. Vellum-Wake, his first true grimoire. His mother Rheana, dead of a soul sickness; he wears her medallion. His uncles Malex and Dhaerin, who see her face in his.
XII. Resistances
Crystal-targeting arts, possession and Crystal corruption: very high (no Crystal; Distributed Soul). Structured magic: very high (Errata, Nullgrammar, Ward 480). Memory attacks: his greatest danger. Speed and closeness, raw force, chaos and the nameless, Obsession-held workings: weak.
XIII. Physical Description
Five foot eleven, slim and long-limbed, long-fingered, narrow through the shoulders, and denser than he looks. A sharp jaw, high cheekbones, and a mouth that rarely bothers to smile. Warm Kushian brown skin, the same line as his uncles; faint gold and violet alchemical stains on his hands; luminous script along his fingers, wrists, forearms, throat and temples that changes with every new understanding. White Valorin hair in loose, heavy curls to his shoulders, usually falling across his brow and never quite combed. Royal violet eyes so pale they read almost blue in daylight, under heavy lids that make him look permanently unimpressed; when he casts, rings of red-violet Vaeloric script rotate around each pupil and the iris goes liquid like ink shot with light. Ink-burn lines on the right wrist. Out in the village, a deep burgundy mantle thrown over one shoulder and a gold high-collared tunic beneath; on a fine gold chain, his mother’s medallion, a gold roundel worked with a lion’s face. In the laboratory, violet scholar’s robes with ink-stained sleeves. Always the satchel belt of vials, chalk, pages and spell tags. Smells of black ink, lavender root, heated copper, old paper and rainwater in glass.
XIV. Psychology
Curious, obsessive, soft-spoken, brilliant; fights like a student solving a dangerous equation before it kills him. Wound: praised for brilliance before he knew whether he deserved it. Flaw: obsession that looks like curiosity. Desire: that no child is ever locked out of magic by birth. When afraid he gets more technical. He lives with the irony that his greatest work is a lock; he keeps Nullgrammar’s full formula in no book but his own lattice. “Magic does not hate us. It only refuses to answer questions asked poorly.”
XV. Equipment
Vellum-Wake · bonded grimoire of white bark paper, black hide and silver thread; holds his Silent Pages, stored workings and Nullgrammar’s study pages. The First Wand of Vaeloris · blackwood, moonbone sliver core, a strand of his hair in the handle; returns when called. The Seven-Vial Belt · solvent, ink, silver-root, binding chalk, bitter flame salt, memory oil, blank charm tags. Rheana’s medallion · a gold roundel worked with a lion’s face on a fine gold chain; his mother’s, worn since she died. A staff, half-written; maker and name not known.
XVI. Temperance Record
I · woken by the sealed grimoire at nine. III · crossed on stabilizing his first original wand formula. IV–IX · lived on the Fate road, from fifteen to sixteen.
XVII. Fracture Log

The Sealed Grimoire (age 9).
The Moonbone Wand Trial (age 13).
The Failed Living Ink Barrier (age 14): comprehension is not capacity.
The year of six Stages (15 to 16); writes Nullgrammar.
Finds the Unwritten Library.
Costs he carries: Formula Headache, Over-Translation, Arcane Drift, Lattice Shear, Memory Burden.

characters/volume-i-—-character-cards/yu.content:
He had written every one of them from the first line as carefully as the true three. And before that last writing he had done the thing that made the grin go wide. He had written each page three times over and scraped it back three times: a soldier, scraped; a clerk, scraped; a doorman, scraped. Under every stone man in the yard now, faint as old ink, lay three earlier hands that had never held a sword or a tablet anywhere in the world. The same three lay under the true ones, since he had written those apart a moment ago on a page that carried that very ghost. Read that. Read it to the grain. Then tell me which of them remember and which of them were taught to. Of all the stone men standing in the court, three had a vein and a nail. Hiromi knew which three. He took some care not to look at them. On the step of the covered walk Senna had stood up. The kunai hung still on her finger, and her lips were no longer moving. The kitchen girls would count nineteen stone men afterward and the guardsman would swear to thirty, and neither count was any use to anybody, which had been the whole idea. One of them was not stone all the way through. He had kept a single light back for the Black Gate, and that one he did not wake. He called down to it, as a man calls down a well, and waited. The dead of his line answer the claim before they answer the boy. She came half of the way. Where a false Sagwan ought to have stood there were the recorder’s long sleeves and the flat-crowned hat, granite to the breast, and above the breast the stone ran thin as eggshell, and under it was a woman’s face he had never seen painted and knew anyway, as he knew the bend of the valley road where her mound stood. Deep indigo showed at her throat where the stone had not closed, the color she had died in. A smell of cold cellar came off her. Her eyes were not blue. They went to the black coat, and then they came to Hiromi and rested on him a little longer, measuring whether the boy was worth getting up for. She did not lie down again. Thank you, grandmother. Be angry with me afterward. And there was the matter of a hope. The Zettari had told the recorder to write that down: that it was no lie, only a hope, and that there was a difference. Hiromi had been turning it over ever since, the way the tongue goes back to a chipped tooth. At the court’s edge two of the old boulders, which had sat heavier since the gold came up, got to their feet. They shook the rime off as dogs shake off water. Under it they were stone in the flank and green bronze in the scales, thick through the neck, with a single horn set low on the brow and the Scale’s blue lit behind the eyes: haetae, the beasts that stand at every gate of his mother’s dead palaces, that know the false from the true and put the horn into the false. They had no interest in the gray sword. They lowered their heads toward the black coat from the left and from the right, and they would make up their own minds what a hope was. His fist had stood loose at his side since the pillars came up. He shut it. The lid came down again, harder, on a yard that was now full. Three Jinbyeoks let go of their swords and spread their arms, and the granite ran off their wrists and went over the frost low and fast from three sides, putting out shoots as it came. The stone men walked. They went outward past the Crown Prince on either side as a river goes past a post, none of them sparing him a look, and he stood in the middle of them on his own feet with his dead hands shut on the notched blade and the knot in his chest hauling him toward a heel he could not see. They walked in step, and the court shook with it, and the woman in the recorder’s sleeves walked among them and left no mark in the rime. The two beasts came in with their horns down. The two cracks of gold closed from either hand like the blades of a pair of shears. All of it was going to the one place: a boy in a black coat twenty paces down the yard, beside a gray sword standing in the frost. The first runner was a stride from his boots. The nearer edge of the gold was a hand from his sleeve. Hiromi put his own left hand back in his pocket. “There,” he said. “Now I’ve asked.”

Dawn Guard · Heir of Kushara

Full Name: Zuberi Zettari
Alias: Dawn Guard (his father’s name for him)

Race / Lineage: Human · Zettari and Yukari; of all his brothers he took up the Zettari traits the most
Faction / Rank: House Zettari, Kushara. Fourth child of Sovereign Dougou Zettari and Naevra Yukari. Heir of Kushara.
Status: Alive
Family: Father Dougou; mother Naevra; brothers Ma’Kovu (15), Rashani (14) and Rengai (12); sister Ayaka (8). Uncle Naiser Yukari.
Current Location: The Sovereign House, Kushara Crownlands
Catalyst Event: His three elder brothers each declined the heirship. Zuberi embraced it, at ten.

Stage, Level, Path and Crystal not known.

Not known.
IV–V. Stats
Not known.
VI. Physical Force
Not known.
VII. Aether Flow
Not known.
VIII. Traits
The Everlasting Eyes · He has the eye of the Zettari line, the same line of sight his father carries. What he can read with it so far is not known.
Zettari Blood · The most Zettari of the children. Which other traits of the line have woken in him is not known.
His Father’s Eye for Faults · He can already name what gave his elder brothers away in a bout.

None.

Not known. He balances his reading with training.

Dougou (father) · Sees the most potential in him and made him heir. Zuberi thinks his father is the coolest man alive.

Naevra (mother), Rashani, Ayaka (siblings).

Not known.

Height: Five foot seven. Eyes: Jet black; the Everlasting Eyes. Hair: Short and black.

Studious and calm. Spends most of his time reading law, war and history, and took up the weight of the heirship willingly. The rest is not known.

His books.

Not known.

Named heir of Kushara at ten, after his brothers declined.
Sails north with his family on the first ship to cross the seas of the Division.

cosmology--and--metaphysics/ages-and-rec.title: Ages and Reckoning
cosmology--and--metaphysics/ages-and-rec.content:
How the world counts its years and its ages, and how its making advanced from the First Eon to the Withering. The moon crossed the sun over the Ironlink brackets in Year 690, an almanac was an hour wrong, two fighters kept going in the dark, and a bad song named the age: the Dark Ages, which is where these shelves stand.


The Concordance of Ages The Fixing of the Count, in Four Ages and One Continuous Reckoning, with the Grand World, the three arcs of the Dark Ages, the split and the turn of the century carried below the seal
Errata to the Received Registers The Conversion of Superseded Dates, with a Ruling on the Epochs
The Four Ceilings A History of Making, from the First Eon to the Withering
The Sky, the Hour and the Year The Accord asks what hour it is. The Sohai asks whose hour it is. Only one of those questions has ever had an answer everybody accepted.

cosmology--and--metaphysics/ages-and-rec.content:
The Conversion of Superseded Dates, with a Ruling on the Epochs
Over the gate of Hollingarth, in the northern quarter, the Thorsby family had cut THIRTY THOUSAND YEARS AND NEVER ONCE ASKED in letters of gilded oak as tall as a boy, and in the summer the Concordance was sealed Lord Piers Thorsby rode to the Guild’s survey camp with sixty lances in blue and butter-yellow to have the sum corrected in his favor. He let his Pressure (the weight a higher Stage lays on a room just by standing in it) roll across the camp table until the inkwells crawled. Measurewright Ingrith Sallow, who came up to about his sword belt, moved her inkwell back, handed him a shovel and walked him to the ash section, where she showed him one summer’s worth of the wall, four gray-and-rust bands where the old method had counted four years. Lord Piers hit the section with a two-handed maul to show what he thought of it.
Several of his ancestors’ centuries came down on his boots. He stood in them for a while, and then, to the great credit of the house, he began to laugh, and he was still laughing when the stonecutter’s bill arrived. Dividing by forty gave seven hundred and fifty years; the Guild’s audit of the charters gave six hundred; the stonecutter, who charged by the letter, gave a refund. Within the year the minstrels had him as Lord Six Hundred and the tenants of the north pasture had stopped paying rent on grounds of antiquity, and the instrument below is the Guild’s answer to everyone else who was about to ride out with a maul.

Issued by the Guild of Measurewrights under the Hexagonal Oath, as a companion instrument to the Concordance of Ages. Year 715 In Concordance, Withering Era, the twenty-fifth year of the Dark Ages.
This document leaves the Concordance as sealed and states how a reader holding an older register is to convert what is in front of them.

I. Why an Errata Rather Than a Recension
The Concordance withdrew the received chronology. It did not, and could not, withdraw the several hundred documents written against it.
The Archives requested a full recension, meaning that every affected register be reissued in corrected form. The Guild declined, for two reasons, only one of which is administrative convenience.

The first reason is that a recension destroys the evidence. A charter written in the old count is a record of what its signatories believed, and a bloodline claim written against a date that no longer exists is still a claim, still binding on its parties, and still the only surviving proof that the claim was made. Reissuing it silently corrected would leave the Accord holding a shelf of documents that all agree with each other and none of which anyone has read.

The second reason is that the conversion is mechanical. Where a superseded register gives a date in the old count, the correction is a substitution and calls for no judgment, and a reader who has this instrument in hand can perform it without consulting the Guild. Six substitutions cover the whole corpus.
II. The Ruling on Epochs
Before the substitutions, a distinction the Guild has been asked for since the Concordance was sealed.

The Concordance governs the Ages. It does not govern the Epochs, and no reader should attempt to convert one into the other.

The Ages are historical. They are counted, attested, and dated by physical evidence, and the whole of them runs from Year minus fourteen hundred to the present. The Epochs are cosmological. They concern the Division of Omnara, the three currents, the Plane of Fate, the Soul Plane, the Physical Plane, the Titans, and the Archons. Their durations are given in the surviving records as figures in the tens and hundreds of thousands, and the Guild has examined those figures and found that not one of them derives from a count.
No calendar existed. No observer stood outside the Epoch to mark its passage. The numbers are theological quantities in the shape of durations, and the Guild considers them accurate as statements about magnitude and meaningless as statements about years.
The ruling demotes nothing. A bloodline that traces itself to the Second Epoch is making a claim about origin and not about arithmetic, and the claim is unaffected by the Concordance. The Yukari registers stating that Senri Yukari perceived Ashura’s approach across a hundred and twenty thousand years remain as written. The Zettari registers claiming two hundred thousand years of continuous lineage remain as written, and the Guild notes that the Zettari’s own archive describes that figure as held out of conviction, which is the correct description and does the Guild’s work for it.

















FindingStatementThe ruleAn Epoch figure is not to be placed on the Age count, subtracted from it, or reconciled with it. A document that gives both is giving a myth and a measurement and expects the reader to know which is which.The consequenceNo bloodline codex, no Archonic register, no Path or Wellspring origin account requires amendment under the Concordance. The Guild has examined the principal registers of the Yukari, the Zettari, and the Moto and finds that not one of them cites an Age. They were never in conflict with the count, having been all along in a different conversation. The Alftian codices do cite one. They are stamped in the early years of the Dark Ages, and they stand on the count as sealed.
The same rule covers what the days of the Physical Epochs left lying about, when Bara, Ashura and Aegor walked in human form, and what the Great Spirit War left after them: dead and dangerous battlefields, relics people will kill for, old beings who remember. All of it is real, and much of it can be walked to and bled on. None of it can be given a year on this count, and the Guild has declined several generous offers to try.
III. The Six Substitutions
Where a superseded register uses the term at left, the reader substitutes the term at right. Where a date is attached, the reader converts it by the note given.








































Superseded termCorrected termNote on conversionThe Age of DeliberationThe Reconstruction Age, earlyDates given as “thirty thousand” are withdrawn. The era runs −450 to −225 in the corrected countThe Dragon EmpireThe late Reconstruction kingdomsDates given as “twelve thousand” are withdrawn. The period runs −225 to −60. No single polity is attested; the received name describes a trading and military regionThe Pyrrhean EpidemicThe Antediluvian collapseWithdrawn as a distinct era. The events attributed to it belong to the closing century of the Antediluvian Calendar, circa −550 to −450The Imperial CalendarThe count In Concordance (IC)The count itself is unchanged. Year Zero is Year Zero. Only the name is correctedThe Withering AgeThe Withering EraWhere a register places the Withering before the Voyager Era, the register is inverted and the reading is to be reversed. The Withering opens Year 645The Renaissance Era, The Fractured EraNo corrected termNeither appears in any sealed chronology. A register citing them is citing Divisional correspondence and should be read as opinion
Beside the last row, in a later hand: the correspondence was early with both, by a generation in the one case and most of a century in the other. Nobody has sealed either name yet. See the Concordance, Section VI.
Below the table, in the same hand, a seventh that the Guild did not sign: where any document stamps a year from 690 IC onward as “the such-and-such year of the Imperial Age”, read “of the Dark Ages” and leave the number alone, so that Year 700 is the tenth year of the Dark Ages and Year 715 the twenty-fifth. The name Imperial Age belongs to what comes after the turn of the century, Year 800, the Renaissance of banks and universities, and to nothing earlier.
Under that, in a third hand, three names the Guild never got round to: where a register says “the Creation Age”, read the First Eon. Where it says “the Era of Myths”, read the days before the Great Spirit War, which Section II keeps off this count. “The Second Accord” stands in no sealed chronology, and a register citing it is giving its author’s own reckoning.
On the Withdrawn Figures
Every number in the old count above about two thousand derives from a single stratigraphic method that read seasonal ash layers as annual ones, at a site where the ash falls four times a year. The error compounds by a factor near forty across the depth of the section.

A reader encountering an old figure may convert it by dividing by forty and treating the result as an order of magnitude rather than a date. The Guild offers this reluctantly and only because it knows the alternative is that readers will invent a worse rule.

IV. Registers Requiring No Action
The Guild has surveyed the principal holdings and records the following as conforming already, so that no clerk spends a season correcting what is not wrong.
Documents stamped in the Voyager Era at low years of the count · The Concord Codex at Year 000 IC, the Heart Vault inner seal at Year 013 IC, the Hall of the Vanguard engraving at Year 014 IC, and the High Concordant’s Lattice writ at Year 027 IC are all correct as sealed. The Voyager Era is the opening era of the count and runs to Year 070. The apparent paradox in the first edition of the Four Ceilings arose from placing it five centuries late and has been withdrawn.

Bloodline and Path registers See Section II. None cite an Age.
Wellspring registers The sixty Wellsprings are described by law and behavior rather than by date. Where a Wellspring register gives an era of discovery, it is giving the era in which somebody wrote it down, which is a fact about scribes.
Technique and glyph registers Unaffected. A glyph combination has no date.
The Guild Accord instruments The Codex articles, the Divisions, the Tiered Path, and the Gate network all date to the Voyager Era and are correct as written.

V. What the Correction Costs
The Guild has been asked, twice in writing, to state plainly whether anybody is harmed by this instrument. It is, and the Guild would rather say so here than be asked again.

Every claim resting on antiquity is worth less this morning than it was worth before the Concordance was sealed. A house that held title by right of thirty thousand years now holds it by right of six hundred. The title stands as strong in law as it ever did. It has weakened in the only currency such claims actually trade in, which is the sense that a thing has always been so, and there are several holdings in the northern quarter where that sense was the whole of the security.

Four Archives careers rest on the withdrawn stratigraphy. The Guild names none of them and states that the method was standard when it was applied, that its authors were diligent, and that they were wrong about a rate of ash and about nothing else.
The Guild has no remedy to offer for either. It observes only that the count was wrong for as long as it went unexamined, that it was wrong the entire time those claims were being made, and that a claim which required the error to hold was never resting on the years.


Attested and sealed. Guild of Measurewrights, under the Hexagonal Oath, in the Archives Eternal beneath the Council Spire. Year 715 In Concordance, Withering Era, the twenty-fifth year of the Dark Ages.

cosmology--and--metaphysics/ages-and-rec.title: The Concordance of Ages
cosmology--and--metaphysics/ages-and-rec.content:
The Fixing of the Count, in Four Ages and One Continuous Reckoning
At the midsummer brackets of Year 690, at Ironlink in the western quarter, forty thousand people in yellow awnings and sect colors had paid to watch Sister Perpetua Lunt of the Greenmantles fight Ragnall Oxblood of the Saltmarket Reds, and the Guild of Measurewrights had sold most of them an almanac promising that the moon would cross the sun at the fourth bell. It came at the third. Shiro slid over the noon with Lunt’s knee on Oxblood’s breastbone, the sky went the blue-black of a mussel shell, the sausage-sellers’ fires jumped up orange all round the bowl, and for four minutes the only thing anyone could see on the sand was two aura coats (the constant skin of colored light any trained fighter wears), hers the color of a bruised plum and his a screaming marigold, going at each other in the dark.
The two coats met with a ring that every soul in the bowl felt in the back teeth, and forty thousand throats answered it. Lunt broke his jaw in the blackest part of the eclipse, Oxblood broke her wrist and three of her fingers with what remained of his interest in the matter, and eleven people died on the south stair trying to get out from under a sky nobody had told them to expect at that hour. The bookies paid on neither fighter, on the grounds that nobody could swear to the finish. A hedge-minstrel named Tam Lackpenny was singing about it by nightfall, the dark age came at noon and the odds were four to one, and his song got the bell, the winner and the number of dragons wrong and traveled faster than the news. Measurewright Ottoline Wray, whose sums the almanac carried in every hand-copied edition, spent the remaining thirty years of her life arguing that the moon had been early.
So the age got its name from a fight, a blunder and a bad song, and the Guild, which dates an age from its first witnessed year, found that it had supplied its own rule with forty thousand witnesses. I am told the Division tried for a decade to call those years something else.
I keep the open shelf’s copy of the instrument below, and my copy has been wet twice and on fire once. Everything down to the seal is the Guild’s, sealed in Year 715, and its now is that morning: the Dark Ages twenty-five years old, the Withering seventy, and one unbroken land under everybody’s boots. I have left its now alone, because the rest of these shelves stand in that same year and a reader ought to stand there with them. What the Guild could not know when it pressed the wax sits under the seal in Section VI, in my hand, and I write it in the last winter before the turn of the century. Measurewrights will tell you the hand is careless. They are welcome to come and copy it themselves.

Prepared by the Guild of Measurewrights under the Hexagonal Oath, at the standing request of the Research and Archives Division, and sealed in the Archives Eternal beneath the Council Spire of the Concord Citadel. Year 715 In Concordance, Withering Era, the twenty-fifth year of the Dark Ages.
This instrument supersedes every register preceding it. The Guild has been asked for a count that a surveyor, a magistrate, and a bloodline claimant can all use without translation, and has produced one.

I. The Rule of the Count
One count runs in both directions from a single hinge, and no other count is recognized anywhere under Accord writ.
The hinge is the sealing of the Concord Codex in the Concord Lattice. The Accord names that Year Zero and the Guild accepts it, less for its significance than for its witnesses. Four archives attest the same season independently, and a calendar wants a witnessed date more than an important one.
Years after the hinge are notated plainly and carry the mark IC, read In Concordance. Years before it carry the negative and are read as distance backward, so that −450 stands four hundred and fifty years before the Codex was sealed. The whole of reckoned history runs from −1,400 to the present, which is two thousand one hundred and fifteen years, and the Guild states plainly that this is a shorter history than the Archives has been in the habit of claiming.

The longer figures in circulation, the thirty thousand and the twelve thousand and the twenty-five thousand, receive no reduced form. They are withdrawn. They originate in a single stratigraphic method the Guild has tested and found to count seasonal ash layers as annual ones, at a Wellspring site where the ash falls four times a year. The error compounds by a factor near forty across the whole depth of the section, and every figure derived from that method carries it.
The Guild has been asked whether this was known before now and has answered that it was suspected, and that the suspicion was inconvenient.

The consequence is a nearer world, in which a bloodline can be traced, a grudge can be inherited by someone who remembers its cause, and a long-lived person can have stood in more than one age and be asked what it was like. The Guild regards that as the count doing its job.
II. The Four Ages
The Corrected Count1The First Eon-1400 to -900EmplacementOre bodiesthe Crevice opensTitanstone and Crevice Shale2The Antediluvian Calendar-900 to -450Presence without transmissionCities built on Wellspring sitesthe Coilcollapse by exhaustion3The Reconstruction Age-450 to 000Notation inventedParunic syntax formalizedLiving RunesRunebronze4In Concordance000 to openVoyager Erathe Long Reckoningthe Withering Era5The Dark Ages690 IC to openInside the Withering Erathe Black Noonsects, brackets and bounties
The First Eon
Span · −1,400 to −900. Five hundred years.
Character · The emplacement. Ore bodies, the northern shield, the flood-basalt province, the ophiolite belt, the Crevice.
Close · No catastrophe. The Eon ends where the first kept record begins, and the boundary is a fact about writing rather than about the world.
Everything the four quarters have ever dug out of the ground was put there in this age, and nothing has been added since. Skill compounds. Ore does not. That one asymmetry has governed every economy that followed and will govern the next, and it is the reason the Old World is the first civilization able to see the bottom of the thing it stands on.

















First Eon materialStandingTitanstoneThe shattered remains of slumbering [[Cosmology & Metaphysics/Faith and the Powers Above/The Fourteen Titans/The Fourteen Titans#World SpiritsCrevice ShaleFractures nearby Realm law. Forbidden to move, hold, or trade under Article III of the Concord Codex, a law about a rock, and the only such law the Accord has ever written.
The Guild takes no position on the theology of the age and observes only that both materials behave as though something decided their properties. That is a statement about behavior and carries no claim about intent.
The Antediluvian Calendar
Span · −900 to −450. Four hundred and fifty years.
Character · Presence without transmission. Enormous individual capability, no conduit, no storage, no notation.
Close · Collapse by exhaustion, repeated across unconnected cities that had no means of warning one another.
The Antediluvians could do extraordinary things with Essence and could not move it one pace. That is the whole of their technology and the whole of their fate. A practitioner pulls Aether out of the ground and air around them, refines it in the Soul Crystal into Essence, and drives it out through the Shell, and where they stand decides how fast they fill. Aether comes in kinds that work on the Crystal differently, and those kinds are the Wellsprings, sixty of them and fixed, each a source of power and each also an alchemical principle and a spiritual transformation. A Wellspring has sites where its Aether pools, and common speech calls such a site a Core. A person standing inside a Core’s field can work with it, and a person outside that field cannot, so a civilization that wants a great many people working must put a great many people on top of the source.
They built on Wellspring sites, directly on top of them, with the foundation courses sunk into the pooled ground itself. Every excavated site shares the same plan, a dense settlement wrapped concentrically around a source with the most valuable structures innermost, which reads to a modern surveyor exactly like a diagram of field strength and was almost certainly arrived at by trial.

A body is the only Essence conduit that walks. Lacking any means of sending Essence anywhere, the Antediluvians moved practitioners instead, taken from wherever they were found and held at the works that needed them until they were used up. Surviving tablets record throughput, loss, and replacement rate in the same columns as grain.
The Accord treats this as a moral fact. It was a technical one as well, and the two readings do not compete.

The Coil
The most important instrument in the modern economy was built to sort people.
Hauling a practitioner across three hundred leagues is expensive, and hauling one who turns out to be useless is a loss the ledger notices. So somebody wound a conductor into a ring and discovered that it answers measurably to the Essence character of whatever is set inside it, and for the first time in history a question that had been a matter of somebody’s judgment produced a number instead.
Every holding coil in every Accord assay house is a refinement of that ring. The trade in Holding-grade material, which is the trade the modern world runs on, descends without a break from an instrument built to decide which people were worth the journey. The Guild has included this in the plain register rather than the appendices, over the Research Division’s written objection.

A distinction the trade literature blurs and the Guild does not. The principle is Antediluvian and among the oldest instruments in the record. The coil is younger. A ring that answers to what is set inside it tells one reader something; a coil that gives the same number in two kingdoms is a different device entirely, and that device is a Voyager Era product of shared units, sealed reference standards and annual calibration.
Fourteen hundred years separate the two, and everything the Accord’s legitimacy rests on lives in the gap.

The Collapse
When a Core began to fail, an Antediluvian city could not answer by leaving. It could only answer by pulling harder on the source that was already failing, and pulling harder meant bringing in more bodies. The archaeological record of four and a half centuries is that loop running to completion, in a dozen places, none of which knew the others existed.

What the Guild records and does not interpret. A site pulled from without reciprocity goes past thinning. The pooled Aether stops recognizing visitors and begins taking from them, which the modern register calls a site running under Obsession Force and treats as a hazard classification rather than a history.
Every excavated Antediluvian settlement sits on a source that was pulled to exhaustion by a population that had no other option. The Guild has surveyed nine of them. It has recorded the density readings and declined to publish a finding on what the sites are now doing, on the grounds that the finding would be a theological claim and the Guild does not make those.
The exclusion perimeters around all nine were set by the Enforcement Division and have never been reduced.

The Guild asks that this paragraph be read alongside Section III.
The Reconstruction Age
Span · −450 to 000. Four hundred and fifty years.
Character · Notation. The invention of writing Essence down, and everything that follows from it.
Close · The sealing of the Concord Codex, which is Year Zero.
The Age produced no machine and contains the largest single break in the history of making. Parunic syntax was formalized out of whatever the Antediluvians had been doing by feel, glyphs were assigned stable meanings, and the combinations were cataloged. Kessian Yorul cut the first Living Runes into bone, inscriptions that feed on the bearer’s own circulation. Mnirah Valein codified the Twelve Stages of Spirit Infusion and, in doing so, established that capability could be graded, taught, and required before permission was granted, which is the ancestor of every guild license now in force.

Before notation, an effect required a practitioner standing in the room. After notation, an effect could be laid into a substrate and left there, and it would keep working when nobody was watching.
Every array, every ward-stone, every mine-lift and draught-fan, every lamp a warden has set burning and walked away from descends from that sentence. The years In Concordance did not invent the array. They inherited the idea and eventually had the money to build one at scale.

Making in this age is bloomery iron, charcoal, and the first material in history designed to hold an inscription rather than merely tolerate one. Runebronze is melt-forged with minor glyphs, durable under basic enchantment, and still carried by minor guild knight orders. Somebody worked out that the glyph could go in during the melt instead of after the cooling, and the entire subsequent tradition of Holding-grade manufacture is a footnote to that discovery.
The Age’s doctrine, that Wellsprings must be respected rather than exploited, is read by the Archives as wisdom learned from the Antediluvian collapse. The Guild records a less flattering reading and does not endorse it: a civilization with no conduit and no pump cannot exploit a Wellspring at scale even when it wishes to, and a virtue that costs nothing to hold is difficult to tell apart from an incapacity that has been given a name. The doctrine was tested when the capacity arrived. It did not survive the test.
In Concordance
Span · 000 to open. Seven hundred and fifteen years and running.
Character · One continuous count, unbroken, never reset. The first age to know its own date the whole way through.
Close · None. The count has not closed and the Guild declines to say when it will.
The significance of the years In Concordance is that they can be audited. Every age before them must be assembled from ash layers, foundation courses, and the arguments of dead clerks. These years have receipts. The Accord’s power rests less on its enforcement divisions than on the fact that it can state what happened and prove the date, and every rival authority in the four quarters has had to argue against a ledger rather than against a story.
The count divides into three eras, and the third of them is the present era. The Guild stresses that these are eras of one count, none of them an age in itself, since the count does not break, the grammar does not break, and the institution sealed at Year Zero is the institution sitting in the Council Spire this morning.
The Voyager Era · 000 to 070 IC
The sealing of the Codex and the opening of the routes, and the two are the same event viewed from different divisions.
The first decades built nothing. They established shared units, sanctioned notation, and the first assay houses, which is to say they established that two people in different kingdoms could specify the same thing and mean it. Every history of the era skips this and every history of the era is wrong to. The Concord Codex, the Lattice, the Divisions, the Tiered Path, and the first nine Concord Gates all date to this seventy-year window, and the documents bearing the stamp of Year 013 and Year 027 In Concordance are correct as written and require no correction.
The enabling technology of the expansion was the chart and not the ship. What the routes brought back broke the money. Eastern placer gold is won by hand from black-sand river bars with no permission required from anybody, which meant bullion arrived in the western quarter in quantities no mint controlled and no crown could meter. Prices roughly doubled within a generation. The western guilds spent thirty years blaming hoarding, foreign merchants, bad harvests, and moral decline, and then a Babylan theorist observed that when the quantity of money rises faster than the quantity of goods the money is worth less, which is not a moral fact and cannot be legislated against.
Wage earners lost. Wages are customary and adjust slowly, prices are not and do not. The Voyager Era is commemorated with a public holiday in four kingdoms and the holiday commemorates the charts.
The Long Reckoning · 070 to 645 IC
Five hundred and seventy-five years, the body of the count, and the era in which the ceilings fell. They fell in an order nobody planned, and each solution created the problem the next answered.

Everything above the fourth tier of making comes out of that window, Aethersteel first among itHaulageRock is heavy and ropes have a limitNever fell. Was merely lied to, by Weight Ablation glyphwork that misreports the load to the rope rather than lightening it. The industry is built around that lie rather than through it
What the era built was a dependency. A pumped shaft must be pumped forever, since the array does not stop when the ore stops and the water returns at the rate it always wanted to the moment the array does. An array wants feeding, and the feeding is done by array-keepers, practitioners on a shift who pull from the ground under the pit head, refine it and drive it into the contacts, and who are paid by the hour and may decline to come in. A modern western pit is a permanent argument with the water table conducted at a fixed hourly cost, and the west lost the ability to walk away from that argument some time around Year 140 without noticing it had happened.

By the close of the era the western quarter had arranged its industry and a substantial part of its food supply so that a sustained Essence shortage becomes a mass drowning within ninety hours and a famine within a season. It did this incrementally, profitably, and with no individual decision anywhere in the chain that looks wrong on its own terms.

The Withering Era · 645 IC to open
This era is the bill, seventy years of it so far.
The ambient Wellspring density of the western quarter (Aetheric Density, in the scholar’s term: how much Aether the ground and air hold for anyone to pull) began to fall measurably around Year 645 and has fallen every year since. The Research Division describes the phenomenon as contested. Every pump-master between Ironlink and the Greaves districts describes it as Tuesday. Every bracket fighter in the same country calls it the thin, and will tell you loudly and at length how much longer it takes to fill back up between bouts than it did for his teacher, and how an eastern fighter on his rich home ground is practically cheating.
Nothing about the Withering resembles the collapse that closed the Antediluvian Calendar, which is why it took a generation to name. There is no plague, no war of sufficient scale, no visible catastrophe anyone can point at. The great houses buy Essence supply the way an army buys grain (Core-keepers’ contracts, array crews on retainer, sealed Holding vessels on mule-back), a bad year in supply closes shafts still full of ore, and the price of certainty has risen in each of seventy consecutive years without a single year in which anybody could say what had specifically gone wrong.
A civilization that feeds itself through an Essence dependency has arranged for a Wellspring failure to become a famine. The Codex made that doctrine at its sealing and the western quarter has spent seven centuries quietly outrunning it.
The Dark Ages · 690 IC to open
The Dark Ages are an age inside an era, twenty-five years old at this sealing.
The Dark Ages is the street’s name for the years since the Black Noon of 690 IC, when the moon crossed the sun over the Ironlink brackets, and the Guild has entered it here because every quarter reads it without translation. The present year, 715 IC, is its twenty-fifth. It rises inside the Withering Era and runs alongside it, so that every date written this morning belongs to both at once. The four ages above divide reckoned time between them. The Dark Ages name what the world has come to live in, and they overlap the era they rose in.
The name flatters nobody and describes very little. The Archives holds that dark refers to the state of the records, the wars having eaten a good many of them. The Sohai holds that it refers to the state of the reading. Tam Lackpenny’s heirs hold that it refers to the eclipse, and collect on the song. No visitor to a market day would guess any of it. These are the loudest years the Guild has on file: painted shields and sect banners on every bridge, crowds three deep at any bracket worth the entry, gold-leafed temples older than the count with a food-stall against every wall, lamps in amber and rose behind salt-glass, and more people who can do something impossible than at any point since the count began.
Practitioners are common and everyone can read the ranks: outer disciple, inner disciple, core disciple, elder in the sects, the Guild’s own titles in the halls, Stage brackets at every fair. A school runs like a town’s great love and greatest liability, with its colors, its songs, its grudges, and a house style a child can spot at fifty paces. Small powers are everywhere and they are trades, done by living hands for money: the hedge-worker who takes off a wart for a copper and will put it back for two, the ward-cutter, the Guild craftsman bragging about his mark over a contraption that has twice burned down his own shop. Any of them may overcharge, strike or tell you to find someone else. Fame moves on foot. Heralds cry the news at the crossroads, minstrels carry it further and wrong, lords post bounties on hand-copied bills nailed to doors, and bookies quote odds on all of it. What is built and carried is what a smith and a guild hall can make, and the road, the ship, the rider and the beacon are as fast as anything gets. The cheapest way to end a high-Stage fighter in a closed room remains a crossbow bolt from a man the fighter has not looked at, and every great house in the four quarters keeps a few such men.
Nothing before 690 IC belongs to the Dark Ages. The Guild dates an age from its first witnessed year and has done so here, and it records that the age is young.
III. The Repeating Figure
The Guild has been instructed to keep its findings to matters of date and has requested one exception, which the Research Division granted on condition that it be marked as commentary. It is marked.

The Antediluvian answer to a failing Wellspring site was to pull harder on the site that was failing, and to bring in more bodies to do the pulling. The current western answer is to contract for supply from further away, at a higher price, on a longer term.
These are the same answer with a longer haul, and the second is being given by an institution that possesses a complete written record of what the first one cost.

The Guild does not predict. It observes that in the compressed count, the distance between the height of the Antediluvian Calendar and the present day is fourteen hundred years, that this is a distance a Wellspring remembers, and that several persons now living were born before the first pump-master noticed the fall.
IV. The Concordance in Full

The instrument records four ages, three eras within the fourth, and the Dark Ages rising inside the last of them: one count, from −1,400 to the present, with no interregnum, no reset, and no gap in which a claim may be hidden.
V. What Remains Open
The Guild closes the count and records three matters it cannot close, on the standing principle that a discrepancy papered over is a discrepancy that will be found later by somebody with less patience.
The Antediluvian founding · They kept a calendar and counted forward in it from a founding the Guild cannot locate, so their internal dates cannot be converted and appear here in the count by stratigraphy alone. Somewhere under the ash there is a Year One that would fix four and a half centuries to the season.
The First Eon’s opening · The figure of −1,400 marks the oldest datable emplacement and not the beginning of the world. What lies before it is undated and the Guild declines to guess at its depth.
The Withering’s mechanism · The Guild can state the rate to three places and has done so annually for seventy years. It cannot state the cause, and will not manufacture one to satisfy a Division that has asked four times for better news.


Attested and sealed. Guild of Measurewrights, under the Hexagonal Oath, in the Archives Eternal beneath the Council Spire. Year 715 In Concordance, Withering Era, the twenty-fifth year of the Dark Ages. Every register preceding this instrument is withdrawn.

VI. Below the Seal: The Count Carried to the Turn
Added in a later hand and a different ink. The Guild has not attested it and has twice asked for it to be scraped off.
The Guild wrote open in three cells of that table and it was right to. I can fill them, more or less, from the last winter before the turn, and I will do it as a table first, since the sealers would want that, and argue afterward.
Not one year number moves. Year Zero is Year Zero, the Long Reckoning still runs 070 to 645, the Withering still opens at 645, the Black Noon is still 690 and the sealing above is still 715. Every date on every shelf that conforms to this instrument stays where it stands. What the count gained after the seal is what it could not have known, and it has kept running straight through all of it, which is the one boast of the Guild’s I will repeat without a smile.













































StretchYearsWhat it isThe Grand Worldthe whole count, from −1,400 to the split, about 740 ICThe one body of land the whole of this instrument is written on. Its four quarters are quarters of a single continent with isles off its shores, and a carter could take salt from the northern basins to the warm southern marches and never pay a ferryman. Nobody living in it needed the name. It was given afterward, the way you name a house once it has burnedThe Dark Ages690 IC to the turn, 800 ICOne hundred and ten years, inside the Withering Era. Arc is the minstrels’ word, a cycle of songs long enough to fill one winter, and I use it because the singers cut the age into three of them before any scholar got round to it. The joints between the second and the third are theirs, and the singers do not agree, so I have left that boundary without a year.
The split has no sealed date. I give about 740 because that is the middle of the argument. One Division clerk has 738 from a run of tax receipts, a Marrowkin hold has an entry number that converts to 741 if you accept the conversion, and every water clock that might have settled it stopped that day. Before it a person could walk the length of the world in one pair of boots, and after it that person wanted a boat. The count survived because a count is a very light thing to carry.
Muken Moto belongs to the generation born before the split, and he lives through it. The ballads have the rest of him wrong in at least four keys, and most of the people those ballads are about are still alive at this end of the century to complain.
The Moto read it coming, and I am obliged to record the complication. The Long Reading has the house reading the split long before it arrived, a reading that gave pressure and vector and no hour, and it has the white shelf at the land’s western edge going under a first blow while the rest of the body held. I place that breaking, with the Refusal and the Stay that answered it, at about 310 IC, on the Holy Sea of Alabaster’s own four centuries of testimony counted back from the sealing above. The Moto registers call that first blow the split because to them the whole thing was one event with a long middle. Two Measurewrights I have read file it as an unrelated coastal collapse. I hold it was the same hand’s first attempt, and I expect to be argued with.
The old works sit off this table altogether. The dead battlefields, the relics people kill for and the old beings who remember come down from the Great Spirit War and the days of the Physical Epochs, when Bara, Ashura and Aegor walked in human form, and the Guild’s own rule keeps Epoch figures off the count. See the Errata, Section II. A surveyor who tells you what year such a field was fought has sold you something.
The ink is nearly out and the bank on the corner has started keeping a light on after dark, which I am told is the future. Read the instrument above as it was written, and let the morning of Year 715 be the morning.
