factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Long Reading — Moto Ancient History
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
The Moto at Alabaster · The Refusal · The Stay · The Recension

An ancient history of the house, from Bara to the birth of Muken.


The Battle of Sorrel Water was fought in one afternoon, on a table, and it is the only battle in the registers whose losers complained about the food. Two kings had brought forty thousand spears between them to the foot of the white cliffs, in every color a dyer could sell, with their drummers and their cooks and their mistresses and a sutler’s tent the size of a barn, and both of them, being careful men, climbed the stair to Alabaster first to have the thing read. Hisame Tenrai Moto sat them down on a bench of white stone, looked at the pair of them for about as long as it takes to peel an egg, and told them in a pleasant voice who would break on which flank, which of their sons would die and of what, how many wagons the dead would fill, and that the winner would be bankrupt by the second harvest. Neither king asked whether she was sure, because in the whole of the record nobody ever had. They went back down the stair and the armies, having been told, sat on the grass; by dark forty thousand men were drunk together under the torches and a hill of unused arrows was being sold back to the fletchers at a loss. The king who was going to lose gave up the river meadows by treaty in the morning and wept with relief. His heir was carried up the stair at three weeks old to be read, and came back down with a small neat scar under the ribs, and that is the part the minstrels leave out.
I have spent nine years in these registers, and I like these people, and you should not.
I · The Seat Before the Water
The world is one body of land, and its western reach ends in a shelf of white stone, and the Moto held it. They held it as the place other kingdoms sent their questions to, which is a far larger thing than being one kingdom among several.
Bara authored the Works before chronology, and Mizuki gave that authorship a family capable of passing it down, and what the family did with it for the whole of the First Eon and long after was read. That is the era’s name in every surviving register: the Long Reading. The name covers something stranger than a conquest or an empire in the ordinary sense: a civilization whose entire product was the accurate determination of what a thing was, what it owed, and what it would become.

A contract sealed at the white shelf held anywhere, because the sealing was witnessed by the ground itself. A birth read there produced a determination no other authority would contradict. A war stopped there because both parties had already been told, correctly, how it ended.
Trade routes ran to Alabaster with no thought of its goods, because the alternative was doing business without knowing what your counterparty was.
The house held no standing army worth the name and did not need one. There is no recorded instance of the Long Reading conquering a neighbor. There was never a reason. A polity that requires the Moto’s determination to function has already been annexed and simply has not been told.

Read and Assign
This is the part the modern house does not teach and the modern Church cannot file.
Territory bored the Long Reading. It administered people, individually, at scale, from birth. A child was read at delivery. The reading established the convergence the child carried, the lineage debts standing against it, and the lawful function it was fitted to perform. The determination was then placed into the body.
The instrument · Covenant Scar. A dormant law-mark set into living flesh, holding inheritance triggers, military vows, marital obligation and punitive backlash. It remains in the house’s shared arts to this day and is taught without comment.

At Alabaster it was applied to populations. A scarred obligation leaves the body free and restrains the standing, and nobody has ever taken one for a chain.
A scarred laborer who leaves their assigned function never sees a hunter. They get caught by the law refusing to recognize them anywhere else, because the Moto’s whole art is recognition, and they had simply declined to extend it.
The house would have been offended to hear this called slavery, and the offense would have been sincere. Slavery is arbitrary. This was correct. Every determination was accurate, every assessment honest, and the accuracy is precisely what made it impossible to argue with.
A man told he is unfree by a tyrant has a grievance. A man told he is unfree by an instrument that has never once been wrong has a diagnosis.
Knowledge corrupts into devouring certainty. It is in the family’s own training register, listed beside the other six, and it was written by people who had watched it happen and declined to name the century.

II · The Reading of the Split
About 310 IC something struck the white shelf at the land’s western edge while the rest of the body of the world held. The Moto registers call that first blow the split, because to them the whole business is one event with a long middle, and this page keeps their word. Every other history in the four quarters that troubles to record it records a catastrophe that arrived, and two Measurewrights have filed it as an unrelated coastal collapse. The Moto record is the only one that records a catastrophe that approached, because the Moto were the only people in the world equipped to watch it coming. Whose hand it was is argued; the later hand in the Concordance holds it was Malakar’s first attempt and expects to be argued with.
Tengan governs probability pressure, convergence, causality bias and near-future vectors. The Tenrai and the Amagiri both carry it. Two lines with the same eye read the same approaching event and produced a joint determination: the split was coming, and the ground beneath the white shelf would not survive it in its current arrangement.

What the determination did not say, because the eye does not give it, was how long. Convergence reading gives pressure and vector. It does not give the hour.
Every subsequent decision in the house’s history proceeds from that single gap in the instrument.

III · The Refusal

Both readings were correct. That is the whole of the problem.


















PositionThe argumentThe Kōkan TotalityA thing which can be gathered can be held. Braid Purity into Balance into Totality, apply the frame to the landmass rather than to a person, and the ground does not have to survive the split on its own merits. The working required two things: every line submitting its Work to a single sovereign judgment, which is the Kōkan function and which the other six had spent millennia not doing; and the population remaining, because a rite of that scale is made of oath and witness, and oath and witness are made of people standing on the ground swearing onto it. > We can hold it. We cannot hold it if you leave, and we cannot hold it if you take themThe Six Meigan, Reigan, TenganThe reading gave pressure without duration, and a working built to hold something for an unknown period is not a hold, it is a wager with a population as the stake. The lawful Work was Süld Hataraki. Passage. Preserve continuity rather than territory, because a house is its blood and its registers and not its stone. Beneath the argument, unsaid then and stated plainly in every later account: the Kōkan could not distinguish integration from subsumption, because from inside Totality there is no difference, and a line asking six others to submit their Works to a single judgment during an emergency was doing the thing its own corruption vector describes. > You are not holding the land. You are gathering the house, and you have found a catastrophe convenient

Each side was accusing the other of the honest version of its own corruption. Neither was wrong. That is why it could not be adjudicated then and cannot be adjudicated now.

What it is called · The house calls it the Refusal, and the word carries two verdicts depending on who is holding it. The six mean they refused an unlawful working. The Kōkan mean they were refused. Both usages appear in the surviving registers, sometimes in the same document, and no compiler has ever standardized it.
IV · The Stay
The six lines went north with what they could carry: their registers, their retainers, and the population they could move. The Kōkan stayed with everyone who would not leave, and performed the working, and named it nothing.

The Stay is the name the six gave it, and it was meant as an argument. A stay is temporary by definition. A stay is what a court grants when it has not yet decided to spare you.
It worked.
It worked incompletely and for a time. The ground held. The first blow came against a frame built to contain it and the frame took the load and did not immediately fail, and the white shelf remained in its correct shape while the low country on either flank of it went under the sea.

The evacuation the Kōkan had opposed was conducted across the window the Kōkan had bought. Every Moto alive in the current era descends from someone who crossed water on time purchased by a working their own line had declared unlawful.

Nobody disputes the reading. It is arithmetic, and it is in the registers of all six northern lines, and none of them have ever taught it.

Then the frame failed, on a schedule nobody had been able to read, with the Kōkan still standing on it.
Why nobody came back
Because the record already said there was nothing to come back to, and the record was written by the survivors.
The account that hardened into canon within two generations: the Kōkan refused the reading, held doomed ground out of the arrogance their Work is known to produce, and destroyed themselves and everyone who trusted them. Every element of that account is defensible. They did refuse the reading. The ground was doomed. They did destroy themselves.

The account omits only the window, which is the one part that would have obligated somebody to sail.
The line that saved the house is remembered inside the house as the line that failed it, and Kōkan entered the family’s internal register as the standing example of tyrannical subsumption, which is where it remains.

V · What the Stay Left
The Testimony Wellspring
The Stay was an oath-and-witness rite conducted at continental scale into limestone. Every soul who remained swore onto the ground, and the ground took it, and the working broke without the swearing stopping.
It has not stopped since.

The Wellspring the Holy Sea of Alabaster measures its entire theology against (the instrument by which a name enters the archive and a person becomes counted) is the residue of a Moto working that failed.
The Church discovered no Wellspring. It built a doctrine on a scar, and has been reading the scar accurately for four centuries without once being in a position to ask what made it.
The Thaloré reading holds that testimony weight is density times depth, independent of the vessel. This is why the kingdom’s anti-discrimination doctrine is a property of the Wellspring rather than an ethical position it could revoke. It is also why the Wellspring does not distinguish between the testimony of a cleric and the testimony of a man being sold, and files both.

The Veil-Saints
When the frame failed there were tens of thousands dying mid-oath on ground that was still holding, and the passage of those souls did not go correctly. It did not go correctly for a long time afterward either, because a Veil threshold that has had a continental working collapse across it does not reseal cleanly.
Passage work became the coast’s necessary trade generations before it became its holiest office. The Veil-Saints perform Sacraments over the dying to harmonize soul transition so the dead cross without fragmentation, distortion or predation, which is Süld Hataraki, the Work of Spirit, in every particular.

The office exists because the coast needed it. It needed it because of what the Kōkan did there. The Work the six lines said was the lawful one is the Work the ground has been demanding ever since.

The Ruin
The seat stands in the hinterland above the coast, inland and up, where the shelf climbs onto exposed shield rock and the frost does not break for most of the year. Broken structures. A well. A gatepost. The residual saturation is dense enough that a Somnalis-primary practitioner cannot touch a wall there without reading what happened against it.

A woman of the house with exactly such a Crystal has lived alone in a cabin on it for the last stretch of her life, undocumented, uncounted, inside the kingdom whose entire theology is the counting of people.

VI · The Long Diminishment
The Kōkan were broken, which takes longer than dying out.
What remained on the coast after the Stay was a surviving population with no fleet, no external authority, a ruined seat above them and a Wellspring beneath them that would not stop running. They held the hinterland. They intermarried outward because there was nobody else. The Kamigan appeared less often in each generation, then rarely, then as an event.
Whoever came after built on top of them, as people do. The port grew. The Sounding Walk was laid. Four centuries of feet wore the polish off the flags. Sancta Lux eventually seated a chapter hold on the coast, the archive began, and the archive became the most complete register of births, deaths and contracts in the Inner World.

The Kōkan remnant were not in it. Their gafa was held as family property, in a First Epoch phonology no clerk in the kingdom could read, recorded in a glyph the Continuum has never been able to classify.
They had been keeping their own registers since before the Church existed and saw no reason to hand them to a body they regarded, correctly, as a tenant.

VII · The Recension
How the uncounted became available.

Nobody in the Holy Sea decided to enslave the Kōkan. This is the part that has to be understood exactly or the kingdom becomes a cartoon.
Somebody decided the register was inaccurate.

A recension is a critical revision of a text. The Church conducted one, sincerely, for good reasons, to correct accumulated drift in the archive and bring the register into conformity with what the Wellspring would actually witness. The reform was competent. The clerics read their method and their error rates aloud in open chapter and posted fair copies on the church doors. It improved the instrument measurably and everyone involved was proud of it.
What it produced downstream was a hard line between the documented and the undocumented, where before there had been a soft one. The Manumission Doctrine extends legal protection through theology to populations the surrounding world considers disposable, and it extends that protection to the counted, because a doctrine administered through an archive can only reach what the archive holds.

The hinterland families could not produce a name the register would accept. They had one. It was four hundred thousand years old. It was written in a mark the instrument could not classify.
An unclassifiable mark returns no reading. A person who returns no reading has not been witnessed. A person who has not been witnessed has not been counted.
Nalūn’s factor houses needed cutting-class labor. Bonded contracts require a party with standing to be a party, and require nothing at all of a party without it. The parchment was clean. Every instrument involved functioned exactly as designed.
The house that read people at birth and scarred their lawful function into them had its last line read out of a register and assigned one. Nobody arranged the symmetry. Nobody was in a position to notice it. Both instruments were honest, and being honest is what made them work.

VIII · Muken
Two to four generations on from the Recension, the Kōkan were a hinterland population with a family memory nobody outside could verify and no standing anywhere.
What follows is the account the salt towns of Nalūn give, and the taverns that learned it from them; the ballads carry it in at least four keys. I set it down because it is the account the house has to live with. The man’s own file reads differently at several points, and where the file and the salt towns disagree, the file governs.
Muken’s mother was taken by a lesser noble family of Nalūn. He was the result. His sister Yukazuri shares the mother and did not inherit the blood in any form the house would recognize: mortal, unbloodlined, Moto by blood only and even that she stopped answering to.
They were fed by what he could earn with his hands. Mercenary work, taken young, taken because it was there. He carried an inheritance nobody had told him about, in a body that had been produced by a crime, in a kingdom whose entire cultural apparatus is the accounting of obligation, and he learned the grammar of debt before he learned he was descended from the people who invented it.

















SourceWhat it gave himNalūnEvery commercial actor carries a seal-token representing their oldest active contract. It resonates while the contract is sound and goes inert when breached. A man raised inside that instrument as its property, who later takes a crown and makes a law where violence against sworn banners becomes measurable debt and whose signature technique is called Ruined Account Settlement, did not invent his own vocabulary. He was issued itRevari ZettariThe True Everlasting Eyes read causal lineage: the original attunement that produced a bloodline ability and the wound that shaped a doctrine. Revari looked at a sellsword nobody had reason to look at twice and read him back to his source. Whether Revari understood what he was handing a starving man is not recorded and should not be

The salt-town clerks swear that the roll has him Moto-aligned through Shingan ignition and Kharven coronation rites, and nowhere Moto by descent, and that he was never acknowledged. The eye opened in a mercenary and the rites did the rest, and every Moto who later knelt to him knew precisely what his line had been when the house was finished with it.

Why north
He went to take a seat large enough to summon them onto, and escaping them never came into it.
Kharven-Seat already stood. Its walls and its clans were old before he was born, and he took its crown and did not build it. He unified the seven lines under that crown. The unification required the subordination of lines that had governed themselves for millennia. It placed the Kōkan permanently above all of them, by law, in an institution designed to outlive him.

The house sold his mother’s people. He came back with a crown, put the house under a single judgment, and made his line senior, and he did it without a purge, which is the part nobody has ever forgiven.
A massacre could have been mourned and moved past. He out-lawed them, in the literal sense, with an institution, permanently, and permanently is the word the Tenrai could not swallow.

Azure Tenrai’s argument was that a branch immune to correction becomes tyrannical, and that removing it before the tyranny arrives is preventive governance rather than treason. He was describing, without appearing to notice, the line his own house had discarded, which had returned, and which was now beyond his reach.

They came for Muken through channels his instrument had no vector against. His one recorded flaw is that his judgment requires clear fault to function. He was made by a crime nobody was ever charged with, he built a law that works only on clean ones, and the people who want him gone come by the dirty ones.
The loop has not closed, and nobody designed it, and he is still walking around inside it.

In a later hand, in the margin: the great split proper came after him, about 740 IC, and he lived through it. See the Concordance of Ages, Section VI, whose author had the decency to expect an argument.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Moto Bloodline — Material Culture
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
The most expensive coat in the history of the north was worn for about two hours. Renji Tenrai Moto, a cadet cousin with a good leg and no sense at all, had Sigrun Hale of Thornhaven fire him a full harness-front of deep red enamel over blackened steel, with a dragon’s face at the belt and gold at the throat, and he wore it to the midwinter feast at Kharven-Seat under a white wolf pelt without a seam in it. By the second course the hall had stopped talking. By the third a clerk of the Hall of Verdicts, very polite, was standing at his elbow to ask whether he was making a claim on the throne. Renji said it was only a nice coat. He was invited to say so under oath, in a room with no windows, and he went out through the kitchens instead, and the Tenrai struck his allowance and the Kōkan took the leg. Mistress Hale sued his estate for the balance and won, the bench holding that the enamel was excellent and that whatever the enamel said was not her department.
So you will want to know what the enamel says.

The dress of the house reads the way the house reads: an outsider’s formal law laid over a native people’s practical toughness, never fully assimilating into either. Kharven is Concord-stock northern clans governed by a bloodline that arrived, enforced, and did not assimilate. A Moto in full dress carries the severity of both and the softness of neither.

The crown-line pattern is six things worn together: red enamel over dark steel, a beast-face boss, a knotwork belt, a fur mantle, a robe-over-harness silhouette, and a split between court dress and campaign dress that never collapses into one outfit with the accessories taken off. The pattern in full belongs to Kōkan. The other six Great Lines carry it in their own metal and palette, set out below.
The Six Elements
Silhouette: robe over harness · A fitted war-harness of leather and articulated steel, cut close and low-profile the way a working soldier’s kit has to be, worn underneath a robe or long over-coat that is open enough at the front and sides to show the harness beneath it. Magistrate and combatant at once, and neither is a costume over the other. A Moto strike ranks, condemns or stabilizes as readily as it hits; the robe is “judge” laid over “soldier.”
Palette: red enamel over dark steel · Enamel is glass fused onto metal by firing: it does not chip or fade the way paint does, and it is slow and costly to apply, which is why it reads as rank rather than decoration. Dark steel is steel blackened on purpose, past the ordinary quenched-dark finish of the Concord baseline: iron someone chose to make black, not iron the world has worn dark. Deep red fired over near-black steel is the crown-line’s pattern, and it repeats at human scale what the Ashen Crown already wears: garnet set into black-worked iron.
The beast-face boss · A boss is the raised medallion at the center of a shield, a belt clasp or a shoulder clasp, the one fitting that is permitted to be a picture rather than hardware. On a Moto it is worked as a beast’s face in the same near-black steel as the harness, carved shadow with at most a single garnet or red-enamel eye. Which beast marks the line before any badge is read or any name spoken; the crown-line’s is the lion or the dragon. It sits at the belt clasp in daily and court dress and moves to the shoulder or a pauldron rivet on campaign, where a belt ornament would catch on gear.
The knotwork belt · Interlacing lines with no visible beginning or end, the ornament of the native Kharven clans on belts, sword-fittings and grave-markers, and not Moto in origin at all. The one element on a Moto that is not Moto: the ruling house visibly wearing a piece of the people it governs and never assimilated into. Inherited worn leather or tooled metal, never gaudy, sitting low at the hip beneath the robe’s opening where the boss also sits. Always a specific belt tied to a specific alliance, oath or northern-born mother, earned or married in, never generic northern flavor.
The fur mantle · A sleeveless outer layer draped over the shoulders and open down the front. Heavy northern fur worn over the robe at court, reduced to a collar or a lining in the field. Climate work first, since Kharven burns fuel eight months of the year, and status work second: an unbroken pelt, even color and no patchwork mark rank by wholeness, the way the Concord baseline marks a lord’s coat. Muken’s Crown Mantle of Kharven and the wide fur collar of Sodoku’s Field Coat are the two forms already on record.
Court and Campaign

Two priority sets wearing the same lineage markers. Never one outfit with the accessories added or taken off.

At court · The full robe-over-harness silhouette as intended: the robe open enough to prove the harness’s quality, heavy with fur, dark steel and red enamel at throat, belt and shoulder. The knotwork belt is the tooled, clean piece. The boss is polished enough to be read across a hall. Every piece is a claim being made: sovereign authority inscribed rather than decorated, as the Ashen Crown itself is, and ornament that always costs the wearer something.
On campaign · The robe comes off, or survives as a weathered field version: mud-hemmed, iron-thread seams doing structural work rather than decorative work, the fur reduced to a collar for warmth. The boss leaves the belt for a shoulder rivet or pauldron, out of the way of gear. The belt, if worn at all, is the plain working version. The precedents are Artemis Amagiri Moto’s Passbreaker Mantle, an indigo over-robe with weathered campaign sigils, and Sodoku’s Field Coat: heavy, dark, wide fur collar, iron-thread seams, replaced twice. Campaign dress is survival and function wearing the markers out of necessity, not court dress with the shine turned down.
The Seven Lines
Only Kōkan holds a seat. The other six Great Lines are landless since the western seat’s fall, and their material culture is portable, worn-on-the-body wealth rather than the fixed authority Kōkan expresses through a literal crown and a literal seat. Each of the six carries the pattern in its own metal and palette: Shirogane in bright silver, Akagane in copper and red-bronze, Kurenai in black and ash with the crimson hidden, Byakuya in near-white, Tenrai in gold and banner-heraldry, Amagiri in indigo and mist-gray.





































LineDressKōkan (crown-line)Red enamel over near-black steel; gold or violet-toned metallic accents echoing the line’s own metallic hair-sheen; lion or dragon boss. The only line entitled to the full court presentation without it reading as a claim on the throne.Shirogane (Silver)Trim, buckles and boss in bright, hard silver rather than blackened steel. Harder-edged and colder than the crown-line’s palette: the dress of merciless structural punishment.Akagane (Copper)Copper and red-bronze fittings, no enamel. A warmer, rawer red than Kōkan’s fired finish: exposed metal rather than a jeweler’s work, for a line whose arts run to blood and heart.KurenaiNamed for crimson, dressed in unrelieved black and ash-gray; the crimson kept to a single hidden accent, a lining or a thread, and never shown. The contradiction is worn on purpose: a visual pun on a line whose whole function is punitive soul-law and execution.ByakuyaPale, near-white materials and a clean, almost ecclesiastical cut. Glass, veils and halos: neither heavy fur nor dark steel.TenraiGold and imperial-toned trim, and actual banner-heraldry in place of a boss. War-command dress for the line whose ambition for the throne is the kingdom’s founding wound.Amagiri (Mist)Indigo and mist-gray, lighter and less armored-looking than the other lines. Route-reading and escape, not frontal command; the Passbreaker Mantle is the precedent.


What this page does not govern · The bloodline’s birth-markers, the metallic skin-sheen at brow, clavicle, wrist and temple, the ring-lines and shard-patterns in the iris, are the body’s own and are written separately, under the shared blood markers. This page is what a Moto chooses to put on over that body.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Moto Bloodline
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
The Line of Bara · The Readers · The House That Bills

Founded by Bara Moto and Mizuki Moto. Bara stands as the mortal manifestation of the First Epoch in literal human form; Mizuki gives that primordial authority continuity, inheritance, and dynastic form.
Together they transform law-bearing myth into a human family capable of passing its power through generations.

Overview













































TypeArchaic Epoch lineage · Bara’s own line · the ruling house of the northOriginBefore measured time, by their own account; the western reach of the Inner World’s northern shield, by anybody’sFoundersBara Moto, the First Epoch in human form (the Archonic registers write him Bairos), and Mizuki MotoSeatKharven-Seat, the one seat the law allows them; six of the seven lines are landless in law and keep castles anywayAnchorsThe Works · the Loom · the register · the Hall of Verdicts · the BowSignatureAn eye and an instrument: the Shingan and Hataraki, the Seven WorksHighest eyeThe Kamigan, the Crown Eye, which appears as an eventSay itMOH-tohMaxim”See before you act. Name before you sever.”
Bram Mabry, whom the free companies called the Ox of Thrum, had burned a tithe barn with nine people in it, and on the feast of the first pressing he was sitting in the middle of Thrum Market in a coat of boiled red leather, eating a whole roast pig at a stall that had not been paid, with forty men around him and an axe across his knees the size of a door. Ikuko Akagane Moto came through the cider stalls alone, small, in copper fittings, with a warrant. He laughed so hard he got up to enjoy it, and the axe came round in a flat arc that cleared the pig and three stools. She was inside it by then, arriving at his chest on a step that nobody watching could afterward describe, as though her being there were simply the next correct thing, and her coat flared the raw orange-red of a copper pan on a hard fire as she laid two fingers on his breastbone and said, in the voice of a woman reading out a bill, “HEART-WARRANT.”
She hit him about as hard as you would test a peach. His own account, given later, is that his heart stopped being his and recognized what it owed. The axe went down into the pig fat. Bram Mabry knelt in it and recited the nine names from the barn in order, with their ages and what they had been wearing, weeping like a child, in front of the whole market, while forty hard men looked at one another and began to walk quickly in several directions. Ikuko Akagane Moto then bled from both ears, and for three days could not have told you her own mother’s name. The Akagane consider that a fair rate.
The rest of the world has never got over this. Other lineages hit you. Here is the family that serves you with papers from the inside of your own chest.
Who They Are
Bloodline nature · An archaic divine lineage marked by inherited authority, spiritual weight, and unnatural bodily refinement.
Core inheritances · The Shingan as sacred ocular lineage and Hataraki as the family’s deeper governing power.
General reputation · Beautiful, unnerving, politically dangerous, and impossible to mistake for an ordinary noble house.
Every other old family in the world tells you what it can do to you. The Moto tell you what you are for. They hold that the world began with assignments, that everything in it has been given a job, and that their house has the sight to read the job and the inherited hands to enforce it. They find this obvious. Most of the world finds it the most frightening thing anyone has ever said at dinner, and pays them anyway.
They pay because of what the house holds that everyone needs: a determination nobody can argue with. For the whole of the Long Reading, kings climbed a white stair to be told how their wars would end, and went home and signed the treaty. A contract sealed at that stair held anywhere. The stair is gone and the appetite has not moved. A judgment from the Hall of Verdicts is the only thing Kharven exports that nobody else can make, and foreigners still pay for one and then complain about it. A house that will read a bridge, a bride or a business partner is a house with a long line at its door, whatever it did the century before.
What they want is short and it has never changed: to keep the Loom (their word for the workings of Fate, the Plane of Attraction and Obsession) theirs to see, and to be correct. Their whole vocabulary of praise is one word, correct, and their whole vocabulary of blame is another, inaccurate, and I have seen a Moto lord take the second harder than a spear. What they fear is the same thing they do for a living. They have watched what happens to a family that is never wrong, because it was them, and they keep the record of it in their own training register and teach it without comment.
I have read this house for a long time, and I would rather you heard the rest from someone who is afraid of them.
Origin of the House
Bara authored the Works before chronology, and Mizuki gave that authorship a family. Bara in human form walked in the days of the Physical Epochs. He took a wife who understood what he did not, which is that a law nobody inherits ends with its author. The house’s whole story is the long working-out of that marriage: his side supplies the function, hers supplies the children, and every Moto ever born has been asked to be worthy of the first and to survive being the second. His private record, the Hataraki no Sho, survives in his own hand and his own manners.
Bara and Mizuki → the Long Reading at the white shelf → the Refusal and the crossing → the seven lines under one crown
The Long Reading. On a shelf of white stone at the land’s western edge the family held no conquest and needed none. It read: what a thing was, what it owed, what it would become. It read populations from birth and placed the determination into the body with the Covenant Scar, a law-mark in living flesh. No chain was ever needed, because a person who left their assigned function simply stopped being recognized by anyone. The family would have been offended to hear this called slavery, and the offense would have been sincere. The whole dreadful account is The Long Reading, and I recommend you eat first.
The Refusal and the Stay. The Tengan lines read a catastrophe approaching and could not read its hour. The Kōkan proposed to hold the ground by braiding every Work under one judgment. The other six called that a gathering dressed as a rescue, and went north with their registers and their retainers. The Kōkan stayed with everyone who would not leave, and the frame held long enough for the crossing, and then it failed with them standing on it. Every Moto alive descends from someone who crossed water on time purchased by a working their own line had declared unlawful. Both readings were correct. That is the whole of the problem.
The north. The lines came ashore with their registers and no standing, and superimposed themselves on clans who had never heard of them, because a people that migrates brings farmers and a house that migrates brings law. Kharven-Seat stood on its rock already. The Kōkan sat its red chair for a long time, until the Tenrai took the rock from them three hundred years ago in a manner the law has found no way to mention. Then came the forty-year war against the Zettari, the last king ruling from a saddle, and his cellars at Halcrest.

Two accounts this office has not reconciled. One has the Kōkan broken on the coast below the white shelf, a line of unregistered families read out of the record by an honest clerk and sold into Nalūn. The other has them sitting the red chair at Kharven-Seat under a thousand years of worn stone. Both are in the registers, sometimes in the same hand. The house counts eleven hundred years since the crossing, and the Guild’s reckoning is a good deal shorter; the house, as usual, has not troubled to argue. A compiler who tells you he has settled it is selling something.

The Western Shield
The Moto originate in the western reach of the Inner World.
The Old World has no claim on it. The origin is the western part of the northern shield, past the ridgeline that now marks Kharven’s border with Undaar-Keth, on ground that no crown currently claims and no border commission patrols. The fuller account is The Moto Origin.
The seat · Standing, ruined, and depopulated. Broken structures, a well, a gatepost, frost on it most of the year. A woman of the house, Somnalis-primary and counted on nobody’s roll, has lived alone in a cabin there for the last stretch of her life and no longer touches a wall without reading what happened against it, because the density of residual memory on that ground exceeds anything else in her record.
The displacement · The first blow on the white shelf, about 310 IC, which the Moto registers call the split, reshaped the western ground and made the seat untenable. The six lines scattered toward temperate ground, and the Kōkan stayed and were broken (see The Long Reading). Generations later Muken went north and east into the boreal forest, on reasoning that was strategic before it was sentimental, and took the crown of a Kharven-Seat that already stood, over clans who had never heard of the place his blood came from. The great split proper comes after him, about 740 IC, and he survives it.
What this means for the house · Every Moto seat in the current era is superimposed on somebody else’s ground. Kharven is Concord-stock northern clans who predate the Moto arrival by centuries. The bloodline arrives, governs, enforces, and does not assimilate, because a people that migrates brings farmers and a house that migrates brings law.

The ruin · The seat is described as ruined, and the residual saturation read there is consistent with mass death rather than slow abandonment. What ruined it, and when, nobody will say. The first blow is the obvious answer and is probably incomplete, because glaciation does not leave that kind of imprint and a massacre does.
A false seat · Older gazetteers give the house the Malō of Sātūlagi. They are wrong. The Moto hold one seat and it is Kharven. The six non-Kōkan lines are landless.

The Eye and the Instrument
The eye finds the job, and the hand fires the worker. That is the whole of it, and every Moto child can say it before they can say anything else.

The Shingan determines what layer of reality the bearer can perceive most clearly. Hataraki determines what lawful function the bearer can impose once that layer is perceived.

The founder puts it with less patience. The Eye without the Work is an archivist too frightened to write in the margins. The Work without the Eye is tyranny practiced by the blind.
The Shingan
The shingan is the heart-eye, and it manifests in both eyes at once with one dominant branch. Every Moto who has it starts in the same place: they see where a thing is carrying its weight. A wall, a knee, a marriage, a company of foot, a lie held in the shoulders. Where a smith reads a bar, a Moto reads the room, and what comes back is stress lines, as fine as crazing on old glaze, gathering at the place a thing will give. Any Moto brat can see where a wall wants to fall. That is the common sight, it opens by crisis more often than by schedule, and most of a Moto’s fighting is done with nothing more.
Then the line’s branch opens on top of it, and tells the bearer what else the weight is.

What it costs. Held open past its depth it opens further and does not close: the seam widens a thread, the ring stays lit. After a hard verdict comes eye bleed, a sternum ache and twenty to thirty seconds of flat nothing, and the retainers know to bring a lord his beads before his water, and they know that the flat half-minute is the moment to tell him anything he would otherwise kill you for. Worst of all, it does not switch off at the supper table. Ask a Moto’s wife.
Who beats it. A whole thing has no seam, so freshly forged, truly soft or simply sound gives it nothing to read. Bog, deep snow and open water have no load in them. The eye shows where a man will break and never what he means, which is why one of the great Moto kings could not see that what he was ranking was his own house. A ward that returns or quiets a reading (Oblivara’s mirror, a Tenebra veil) leaves it counting nothing. A man who has gone truly quiet inside, or wants nothing, gives it little. The plain unlikely act surprises a Tengan like anyone. And the Kōkan’s own mark comes back from a fate-read like a page with no ink on it, which the other six lines find extremely funny until it happens to them.
Against the other two. The Ketsumyōgan sees the threads between things where the Shingan sees the things, and it reads where the Shingan judges. The Zettari’s Everlasting Eye reads how a thing stands, and its far end asks where that thing began. The Shingan asks what a thing owes. The Moto will tell you this makes theirs the most useful question, and the Yukari will ask who gave them the right.
The Fate Ledger
Unmei-chō. A battle-reading discipline that internally ranks threat, cost, weakness, and probable turn as though the fight were a living legal inventory. It is no gift of the blood: it is drilled, every morning, from about the age of seven, and it is the single most dangerous thing the house teaches, because it works for anyone with the eye and it makes the eye useful in a hurry. A cadet is walked through a fair and asked to enter the stalls in the order they will close. Hanae Tenrai Moto, aged nine, once entered an Accord factor’s third wagon, his second son and his solvency for him at a feast at Harlsey, unasked, in that order, and then, as she had been taught, presented an invoice.
Written out for a tutor, an exercise looks like this:
[Ledger: the yard at Harlsey, an hour before Ice-out]
  1. Left gatepost. Frost-seam. Gone by the thaw.
  2. Third company sergeant. Unpaid two quarters. Will not hold.
  3. Gray mule, near axle. A week.
  To act on 1: a rope and a boy.
  To pull on 1: do not. See above, a rope and a boy.

That last line is the whole of the education. A grown Moto runs this without moving their lips, on every room, every day, and it never stops. They rank their dinner guests. They rank their children, and the children know it. In a fight it is why they seem to be two exchanges ahead and bored, and why, when it is wrong, they are wrong with complete confidence and a very neat hand.
Hataraki: Seven Grips
Hataraki, literally translated as Work, is the governing function of the Plane of Fate. The Works have their own page and the founder’s record has the arts. This is what they are in a Moto’s hand.
Because Bara authored the Works before chronology itself, the Moto inherit an unusual intimacy with Hataraki that no later student of the discipline can study his way into.

Their techniques therefore tend to feel administrative rather than merely explosive.
A Moto strike may reveal, rank, condemn, stabilize, sever, or complete rather than simply hit harder.

Attraction Force is the law of recognition: it allows names, vows, lineages, domains, wounds, and outcomes to be acknowledged and remain lawful inside reality. Many Moto arts work by making a thing recognize what it truly is, what it owes, what it hides, or what role it now must perform.
Obsession Force is the corrupted inversion. When a Moto cannot release judgment, lineage, memory, or revelation, function curdles into fixation, captivity, recursion, and spiritual suffocation.
Why Fate is the hardest thing there is. Physical Reality and Spiritual Reality are places a person can stand and push. The thing the Guild calls the Plane of Fate as a courtesy sits above them both: everything that flows, every possibility and concept, what has to be so before anything can happen. There is nothing up there to brace a foot against, and nothing in a person to brace with, because your notions of cause, of likely and of what a blow is all came down from there. You cannot reason your way to a grip on the thing your reason is made of. Measurewrights have described threads for whole careers and never lifted one, and the founder, asked by a clever child whether a gifted descendant might dispense with the Works and take hold directly, wrote down the whole of his reply: No. So I cut handles.
That is the inheritance: somewhere to put your hand. Each Work is one distinct, inherited way of taking hold of one function, and it takes hold of nothing else.

Firing the Worker: the Two-Hand Office
A blessing, to a Moto, is a job someone has assigned to the odds, and a job can be read, and a worker can be fired. Nothing else in the world does this as a matter of routine, whoever gave the blessing, and it is why people run when a Moto starts reading their thumb.
It takes two Works or two Moto, because one grip does one job. The house calls the pair the futari-yaku, the two-hand office, and a remover who arrives alone is either bluffing or has brought someone you have not seen. In the spring of 692 Little Tolland spent its treasury on a letter north, and old Tokiwa Moto came down the Kessen road with two attendants and a bill, stood a blessed man on a bridge, read the line aloud, and said one quiet sentence to it. The brass print went out like a lamp, and he lived out the week in the best mood anyone had ever seen him.

Beneath the Work: Asami and Gisei
Every Moto carries two truths, the person the bloodline built and the person who existed before any of that. The two states are what happens when they meet.
Asami, the Shallow-Seen, is the first self surfacing so completely that the trained one stops holding its shape above it. The Ledger and the sorting go quiet with nothing suppressed. The practitioner reports no power at all, only quiet. Every art becomes native, Obsession Force finds nothing to attach to, and the aura becomes a kind of law, unaimed, that hurts whatever in the room is lying about itself. It lightens no pull: the hand stops shaking and the weight stays exactly what it was. Most Moto of sufficient depth reach it, and the correct outcome, the one the house was designed to produce, is to integrate it and live as one person. The Work is not that you saw it. The Work is that you returned.
Its inversion is the Shallow-Seen Unburied, the same stillness with the attention turned inward, discharging instead of inhabiting. Nobody can tell the two apart for the first several seconds. The Sin of Wrath, the burning man in irons who frightens children from the Foot to the Grey Teeth, is what it looks like after three hundred years.
Gisei, the Offering, spends what Asami found. A memory, a bond, a capacity or a Trait goes into the fire for good, on the Oblation mechanism, and the Plane skips the Temperance and checks the payment, so a Stage VIII can perform a Form four Stages over her head. It stands outside the gates and outside the two-step ceiling on boosts, the way a blessing does, and it does so once for each thing offered, at a ruinous price on the body and a debt the house writes down against her for good. Moto Sayo did it on the chain at the Akanoe water gate with the memory of her son’s first word. It only pays if it tears a hole. Most Moto who find Asami never touch it, and the house’s literature keeps one claim on the subject that it does not teach: that the Plane is not something a Moto reaches into at all, that it is what a Moto is made of, and that the whole architecture of the bloodline exists to keep that fact from ever becoming load-bearing.
Who beats all of this
Somebody who arrives. A Work is slow to set against a straight exchange, and a Body veteran who reaches a Moto before the result lands is hitting an ordinary body at its Stage. Somebody sound: good straps, fresh horses, inspected bridges, paid companies and no bad habits give the house very little to read and nothing to pull on. Somebody with their eyes open and their fate-sight shut. Another Fate user, leaning the other way. A soul well enough bound to refuse the result. Any Spirit fighter who can see the pull on the Core before it lands and go for the hand on the thread. And the Moto themselves, who have buried more of their own children than anyone else has managed to.
How the House Wages War
The levies who marched on Akagawa, twenty thousand spears against a Moto host of three thousand, lost to a rotten bridge pile, a thrown shoe, a turn of the wind and a rumor that was very nearly true, and by noon they were running where somebody under a plain banner had arranged for them to run. No other lineage on record fights like this, and the reason is a matter of inheritance rather than talent. Fate is the hardest thing in the system. Nobody grips it bare, and each Work of Hataraki is a distinct, inherited way of taking hold of one function, so a Moto child starts with generations of somebody else’s grip. Even so, a field moved is a life’s masterwork, and it may be done once in a war.
They read first. The Tengan, the Eye of Fate, reads probability pressure and convergence, and the founder’s whole instruction on it in the Hataraki no Sho is that the adept asks which outcome has begun demanding itself of the field. Every officer of the house is drilled from childhood in the Fate Ledger, which is why their children can rank a field the way others do sums: threat, cost, weakness and probable turn, entered as an inventory. The Meigan does the same for masonry and harness, and notes where a thing has been pretending not to break.
Then they arrange. Most of a Moto campaign is ordinary war done by people who see more of it, and needs no thread at all. Mikettei no Ame, the Rain of the Unchosen, belongs to formations, command corridors, cavalry timing and the engineering of panic, and it has been done with nothing but banners, disciplined footwork and the knowledge that frightened men flee into the route that feels least chosen by them. The Tenrai are the war-command line and the Banner of the Next Turn and the Warroom Edict are theirs. The Amagiri work the roads, and Delay Harvest and Pursuer’s Ruin are why a column chasing one arrives late and short of bread.
Sometimes they pull. Hōkai Senkoku pronounces collapse on what is already hiding its exhaustion, and in fortification warfare Kaimetsu no Hasuji waits for masonry to confess where the stress has settled. Innen Kusari makes one earlier truth arrive on time. Futatsu no Tenbin tilts a field just enough that its excess begins punishing itself, and for the rare battlefield where several laws are already colliding the Kōkan hold Teiho no Oza, which ranks them. The founder sums up the method as arranging the enemy into obedience, so that one need not always strike, and when he does strike the finishing form comes last, as the legal consequence of everything the target has already failed to survive. At Akagawa that part was done on the riverbank with ordinary spears.
It is paid for and it can be stopped. The art moves only what already has a way of happening, so a sound gate stands whoever pronounces collapse on it, and a careful enemy with inspected bridges, shod horses and paid companies gives the house very little to read. The one who does the moving pays in their own body, sometimes all of it. Each Work carries its corruption, and a commander who begins to enjoy ending things is the house’s oldest way of losing. So every serious enemy’s first job on a field with Moto on it is to find whoever is doing the reading and reach them, ahead of even the house’s champions, which is one reason that person so often stands under a plain banner.
A host in order
An army, the founder observes, is a thousand straps wearing at once, and this is why his house has so seldom needed to be the larger host. So a Moto campaign has a shape, and it has not changed since his record.

A season of reading. Nobody spends a drop. The Tengan officers rank the enemy’s march, the Meigan engineers walk the bridges under some pretext, a Reigan surgeon is sent across under a flag to treat somebody important and comes home having read everyone in the tent. Most of what you will call victory is marching to the right place on the right day, and arithmetic.
Find their Fate users first. Before their champions, before their general, before breakfast. A single old woman in the baggage train can undo a season’s work with one thing going wrong at the ford, and she is thinking the same about you.
Give each Work its office. Ruin for the bridge. Purity for your own line and your own water, which you will neglect. Spirit for the dead of the last battle, who are otherwise available to anyone. Temporality for the hour. Knowledge for their captains. Balance for the point at which they have overreached, which they will.
Spend the pull once, late, on something already going. At Akagawa the old woman under the plain banner had given eleven years to being able to do it once, and it took two days to arrange. Four of her people carried her home, and she did not walk again or know her own daughters.
Then the riverbank. Ordinary spears, which is the part every song leaves out.

The Moto and the Archons
The Archons are crowned ideas, and the Moto are the only family alive who know what the crown is sitting on. A Work is a meaning at its barest, and an Archon is that meaning risen into sovereignty, with someone home. So the house stands in an awkward spot: its founder wrote what the Fourteen are crowned on, and its descendants are mortal people with bad knees.
They stand toward the Archons exactly as they stand toward a very senior officer of an employer they share, and that attitude has got more of them killed than anything else on this page.
They bow to all fourteen, and they ask for nothing. The house’s faith is Sōhai, the Whole Bow: fourteen inclinations at the hinge of the day, under two minutes in a cold room, and fourteen labors done with the hands. Singling, the elevation of one Archon, is the principal heresy. Petition is contempt: there is no Moto “help me.” The only lawful invocation in a Moto mouth is By the Fourteen. A Moto who hears a Kharven say “Irath take it” hears heresy and will mention it.
They read by delegated sight. The Archons read the Parun lattice (the root script of law) from fourteen stations, and each station gives a hand. The Moto read the same object from above, from the Loom, on a leave the Kōkan once administered, so the Shingan and a cut glyph are looking at one thing from two very different chairs. That is why the Counted Speech has no Warrant word for what the house holds. The house takes this as proof of rank. The Archons have not said.
They are not alone up there. Most if not all of the Fourteen are Sovereign across all three planes, and on the Plane of Fate they are the most powerful things that still act, because they are the laws as well as the powers. Urion and Uurgath have no peers even among the rest, because what they are cannot be conceived, and Bara stands somewhere above them all, and has not written lately. A thread pulled down from that height may turn out to be somebody’s. Some of those thrones have someone home, and a Hollow Throne runs on and never looks up. The house keeps a short list of which is which, and that list has been wrong twice.
Yorimasa Kurenai Moto, a Fate III headsman of no particular ambition, pulled on what he took for an ordinary debt at the Saltash cloth fair, and the thread turned out to have been Urion’s. Nothing struck him, and he reached home. From then on every scale he stood near came out true to the grain, whoever had thumbed it and whatever the merchant had paid. Grocers crossed the street. Three towns barred him from their markets by name. In the last year of his life his household weighed his food in another room and carried it to him, and he remained, in the words of the Kurenai register, correct, and very thin.

Physical Appearance and Dress
Shared blood markers

Hair White appears throughout all seven lines and is never exclusive to a single branch: moon-white, pearl, frost, bone, ash, silver-white, and white touched by faint blue, gold, pink or violet undertones. The family also produces black, silver, gold, bronze, auburn, copper, red, rose-gold, pink, mauve, lilac, lavender, violet, plum, and opaline metallic tones depending on line, parental mixture, and resonance strength.
Eyes Many Moto show sigilic irregularities in the iris even before awakening: ring-lines, shard-patterns, mirrored flecks, capillary lights, or vector-like spokes.
Skin Metallic birth-sheens along the brow, clavicle, wrists, spine, temples, or hands, as though the flesh remembers an older law than ordinary blood.
Presence Even untrained Moto often feel too composed, too sharply outlined, or too heavy in bearing to be mistaken for common mortals.

Stature and voice. Nothing the blood insists on: the house runs from slight road-surveyors to men broad as a door, and its power has never lived in the shoulders. What it shares is a stillness that carries weight even at rest, the look of someone who moved before they decided to, and a way of leaving a silence for you to fill. The old register has no contractions in it, so a Moto in full form sounds as though each word has been inspected.
What they put on over that
The house dresses the way it reads, an outsider’s formal law laid over a native people’s practical toughness. The whole pattern is in Material Culture, and Mistress Hale of Thornhaven will sue your estate if you get it wrong. In short: a fitted war-harness under an open robe, magistrate and combatant at once; red enamel over blackened steel for the crown line, each other line in its own metal; a beast-face boss at the belt that marks the line before any name is spoken, moved to the shoulder on campaign; a knotwork belt in native Kharven interlace, the one thing on a Moto that is not Moto, earned or married in; and a fur mantle, ranked by wholeness of pelt, cut down to a collar in the field.

Lineage Traits
[Trait] The Too-Sharp Outline — The Blood on the Skin
The body remembers an older law than ordinary blood, and strangers notice before they know what they are noticing.

Birth-sheen, ring-lines and bearing show even in the unwoken and the unread.
Clansmen’s children are taught never to meet a Moto’s eye before they are taught the forearm grip, and a clansman addressing the Hall looks at the chest, the hands or the floor.
A trained room reads the Moto in it first, which is a problem for a family that would often prefer to be furniture.

A Moto can buy a commoner’s coat. Nobody has yet sold them a commoner’s outline.
[Trait] The Heart-Eye — What the Weight Is Doing
The common Shingan, set out above. It is the house’s only universal gift, and it is enough.

Reads load and fault in matter, bodies and formations, and in the better eyes in a working or an oath.
Sharpens under strain, and each forced opening stays a little wider.
Runs without being asked. The supper table is included.
Gives Gnosis Perception and Analysis their easy climb.

Most people look at a wall and see a wall. A Moto sees the only part of it that matters, and then has to go on being polite.
[Trait] The Handed-Down Grip — Somebody Else’s Hand on the Thread
A child’s Attraction Layer comes with generations of practice laid into it, ready to close on one function.

With a Work, Fate’s first rung reads from Ascension, before Glory; after that it is read from Level like anyone’s, and the blood gives no help climbing it.
On their own Work, a pull lands far more often than a stranger’s, at the same price.
One Work is truly theirs, and which one is usually known by the time they are twelve, to the rejoicing or embarrassment of a whole household.
The cap never lifts, and a Moto hand is not one bit lighter than yours.

A Moto child starts with somewhere to put her hand. She is still lifting the same thing you are.
[Trait] The Ledger Reflex — Everything Entered
This one is no gift of blood. It is years of morning drill worn into the nerves, so deep that the house’s physicians count it among the inheritance.

Threat, cost, weakness and probable turn are ranked before a conscious thought fires.
A Moto’s first look at a room is a list, in order, and they would be able to recite it to you a decade later.
In a fight it reads as two exchanges of advance. A stranger who does something truly unlikely gets one free blow while the list is corrected.
It marks appetite as readily as malice, and a person who enters everyone at their table as a debt stops sitting at tables.

A Moto will forgive you most things. They will never stop knowing the exact amount.
[Trait] Delegated Sight — A Chair Above the Stations
What the Moto see of Fate they see from above, on a leave nobody living has read.

Moto read a blessing’s line, an oath’s terms and a thread’s lean where no glyph or Warrant can name what they are doing.
A Moto speaker of the Counted Speech opens on a sound the record writes down and leaves the value blank.
It makes no one a better cutter. A Moto who speaks or cuts a sentence spends the soul’s own share like anyone else, and glyphs and Seals never pull.
A Fourth Seal, which ends a line instead of waiting for it, needs a grip on Fate or a Warrant that carries one. A Moto with a Work can sign it, and will mention this.

Everyone else in the trade reads the law. The Moto have been told they are reading its handwriting.
[Trait] The Covenant Scar — Law in the Flesh
Keiyaku-kon. A dormant law-mark placed into flesh to store inheritance triggers, military vows, marital obligations, or punitive backlash, taught without comment in every line.

It runs on recognition: the scarred person stops being lawfully recognized outside the terms, and no hunter need ever be sent.
The Kurenai cut one into every headsman at nineteen, to hold the vow of no wrath. One such scar has since inverted, and glows black-violet through a coat.
It binds at a Bind’s price, as a condition set on the soul’s own share, and it can be read by anyone with the eye. A removal is a job for the two-hand office.

At the white shelf this was how a civilization ran. Today it is mostly marriages. The house sees no contradiction.

Doctrine and Arts
Training and Cost
Conceptual discipline · The Moto must understand what a Work means inside existence.
Operational discipline · They must learn what that Work does when expressed through body, weapon, eye, or rite.
Judicial discipline · They must know when a function is rightful, excessive, or forbidden.

Every Work carries a corruption vector.
Ruins can become annihilation. Purity, fanatic sterilization. Spirit, soul-hoarding. Temporality, recursion. Knowledge, devouring certainty. Balance, suffocating stasis. And Totality, tyrannical subsumation.

The style that comes of this looks nothing like the showmen in the bracket towns. The founder’s hatred of decorative combat is the house’s whole aesthetic: a finishing move is the final legal consequence of everything the target has already failed to survive. A Moto bout starts with a long look, goes on to one or two very small cuts, and finishes with the other fighter discovering he has been losing for some time. The insult for a swordsman who fights any other way is poet. The children of the lines are nonetheless children, and every Stage bracket in the north has one in gold or silver bawling the name of a technique at the top of their lungs, and the elders deplore it, and pay for the ribbons.

Every line teaches five of its own. A Stage bracket crowd knows these by the first step, and a Hall assessor knows what it costs to be good at them.
