The Seven Great Lines
The lines run very much like rival clubs, and no Moto will thank you for saying so. Each has its colors and its songs, its animals and its old grudges, and a fighting style a bracket crowd can pick out at fifty paces; in any Stage bracket town you will find the silver-ribbon Shirogane boys and the mourning-black Kurenai boys singing at each other across a street, and both lines deploring it, and both lines paying for the ribbons.





















































LineShinganNatureFavored WorksByakuyaMeiganCold revelation, hidden seams, exposed falsehood, clean structural breach. The Owl, The White Fox, The Heron, The StoatKnowledge, then PurityShiroganeMeiganA harder cadet revelation branch: immediate breach, anti-fortification work, merciless structural punishment. The Lynx, The Snow Fox, The Hawk Owl, The WolfcatKnowledge sharpened by RuinsAkaganeReiganSoul-reading, curse anatomy, essence surgery, intimate violence, inner-system control. The Fox, The Red Wolf, The Viper, The Red HawkSpirit, then KnowledgeKurenaiReiganPunitive soul-law, curse pressure, internal collapse, execution through contradiction. The Crow, The Night Viper, The Jackal, The Black FoxSpirit under the shadow of RuinsTenraiTenganWar-command, elegant timing, convergence reading, battlefield inevitability. The Hawk, The Falcon, The Stag, The Swift FoxTemporality and Balance, reaching into KnowledgeAmagiriTenganRoute-reading, skirmish war, pursuit-breaking, escape law, mist-like asymmetry. The Moth, The Kite, The Hare, The Grey HoundTemporality supported by BalanceKōkanKamiganCrown authority, unified judgment, triune command, the ranking of outcomes by sovereign law. The Lion, The Dragon, The Raven King, The Crowned SerpentTotality above all, with natural access to the lower Works beneath it
They sit in the Hall of Verdicts, a long black room on the crown of the rock, each in its own chair and its own metal, with the red chair a little forward of the arc. In law only the Kōkan hold a seat. In fact every line has its castle on the Castle Stair with loud opinions about the one above it, and each has a place it calls home by some means the law has not looked at closely.
Byakuya, the white line. The white house in the Shiraki hills, the Owl over the door, and a prayer room where every child swears the oath at nine with a grandmother’s hand on her head: purity before power, peace before the blade, and the red line before the white, until the end of the red line. Their oldest office is the Kōkan’s own guard, the Samurai of Fate (Unmei no Samurai), half a step ahead of the king and to his left. A Byakuya draw is taught behind a closed door and never shown, and they tie a white knot round the sword when they enter a house to keep the peace. Their daughters marry north and keep the oath over a lamp for forty years in someone else’s castle. Their one rule: it has nothing to say when the king is the knife.
Akagane, the copper line. The Kurogane valley, the granaries, the Blood and Heart Arts that keep a heart and can stop one. The Akagane never swore to the red. They only ever obeyed it. The copper book holds every name they have buried, and every lord reads it through on taking the chair. They feed armies and sign for every sack, the best provisioning books in the north are theirs, and a provisioner who knows what the columns will do with the bread is the house’s particular kind of monster. Copper comes out of a quench softer, as the Kurenai have reason to know.
Kurenai, the black line. The executioner’s office, attached to the Hall. Kurenai means crimson and they wear it hidden, which is the line’s one joke. The verdict kills and the headsman is its hand, and a hand that strikes in wrath has broken the law it serves, so they carve the vow of no wrath into every headsman at nineteen and walk with a wax-stopped bell, without a sound, until the sentence is done. They have carried out the Hall’s verdicts for a thousand years, whatever the verdicts were. Their register struck one name and wrote the word Sin in its place. Thirteen went after him and none came home.
Tenrai, the gold line. The keep on the east of the rock with gold leaf on it, twelve hundred house-guard in gold and crimson, and the most polished manners in the north. War-command, go boards, and a line that sent its best to fill rafters for fifty years. The Tenrai took the Seat from the Kōkan three hundred years ago, and their ambition for the red chair is what the house politely calls its founding wound. The north’s joke is that they are the only family that can lose a war for forty years and bill you for it. Anyone who has lived near them wears a collar.
Amagiri, the indigo line. Roads. Every pass, ford and herders’ shoulder, written down in a line’s ledgers for centuries and more of it unwritten; waystones cut with the Moth; masks left at crossroads shrines for whatever walks the roads at night. They thin the light around a party on the move, so a sentry looking straight at the track sees weather. Nobody takes them seriously in a hall, which they have been cultivating since before the crossing. A Moto host that gets out of trouble got out on an Amagiri road. So did the people running from it.
House Within: The Kōkan Line
The red line · the line of the red chair · the crown-line of the seven

































EyeThe Kamigan, as an event; the Shingan with gold in it, otherwiseWorkTotality above all, with natural access to the lower Works. Most hold Ruin or Balance and are glad toChairThe red, plain lacquer over dark wood, with the mark worked into its back in fine black linesSeatThe rock, by law; a long gray house deep-eaved and dark-beamed on the crown, used for three centuries to store Tenrai chestsLookRed enamel over near-black steel, lion or dragon boss, gold or violet at the throatWordTheir mark: a long down-stroke, a hook, a crossing and a small closed loop, like a knot in a rope, or a little like a closed eye
One of the last Kōkan king’s captains once asked him, at a fire on campaign, when he meant to sit the chair and wear the color. He gave the fire some thought and answered, “When I’ve made it worth wearing.” He died in black, and at the Seat the servants swept round that chair for forty years, knowing exactly how wide to sweep.
Every other line reads what is there. The Kōkan rank it. The Crown Eye takes what the other three see, revelation, soul-law and fate-pressure, as subordinate offices awaiting coordination, and returns a list with the worst item first. In most of the line this shows as a hairline of gold running out through the iris, the first seam of the Kamigan, and it is why any Tenrai captain who sees it in a stranger’s eye knows at once what she is looking at: any Moto brat can see where a wall wants to fall, and the gold in it is Kōkan. The whole eye appears less often in each generation, then rarely, then as an event. The founder’s only remark on it is that those who wield it well develop an unfortunate resemblance to him.
The Kōkan's two inheritances are a judgment and a page with no ink on it.
The Gold at the Edges. The eye reads fault and load, and ranks them, and forced past its depth the gold spreads toward the rim and does not go back. Its great weakness is on record, and it is a good one: Kōkan judgment requires clear fault to function. It works on clean cases. The people who want a Kōkan gone come by the dirty ones, through channels the instrument has no vector against, and the line has been dying of that for a long time.
The Unwritten Mark. The line wrote its name in a glyph the Continuum has never been able to classify, in a First Epoch phonology no clerk can read, and held the register as family property. So a working that finds a person by the house written over them finds nothing on an unregistered Kōkan: tokens go dead in the hand, fate-rings slide off. It cuts the other way too. No seal will bind under the name until the mark is set on it by hand, and a register that cannot read you cannot protect you, as the Recension (a sincere and competent revision of the Church’s archive) demonstrated to the Kōkan remnant on the coast, with bonded contracts. Plain eyes and a blade see them as well as anyone. Some hands in the line draw the mark true and some never can, whatever they are taught, and the house has no theory.
Totality, and why they are watched. The Kōkan are the line closest to the crown-function, too often resembling, in the founder’s words, judges born without the useful softening of uncertainty. He did not consider this a flaw. Everyone else does. Totality’s corruption is the hunger to gather all distinctions into one captive frame, and from inside Totality there is no difference between integration and subsumption, which was the six lines’ whole charge against the Stay and was also, a very long time later, what the cellars at Halcrest were. Twenty years before the end of the long war the last king’s own line told him no, in the hall, to his face, and he had them killed, and their children and their cousins. Four years later he went down into the cellars with a lamp after the last of his blood, with the gold coming up in their eyes as he cornered them. The Kōkan arts went into the ground with them, and the Kurenai closed the book. The butcher of Hiroe is the kinder of the things he was called, and when he fell at Shimane in the mud, the Moto began to eat themselves the same day. Naiser Yukari, who refused his riders twice, has called him a monster and, in his way, a truly great man. The line’s own word for its worst temptation is Singling, and they say it of themselves.
Later hand: a boy came home from the ice with nobody, took the Seat in three days and broke only what was already dead, and sat the red chair his father never sat. In the Hall that spring the seven lines and six Banner Houses swore one by one: the entry reads seven lines, and one blood, under one crown, and the Hallenfeld counting-house has asked that it be noted who made it. They call him the Tokenless, and the ballads get the numbers wrong in at least four keys. Of the corridor, where the north says a king and two of his sons died in a night, this hand has no death of his to record. His son Sodoku, the Arctic Lion, came back from eleven years at the polar rift with Kamigan and frost together, a Titan’s cold worked through the eye so that five ring-lines stand in it, and his father’s beads on a cord, and he said the family record out loud at a kitchen table in a house with a scullery, which no Moto had done in living memory. I know exactly what my family is, he said. It is the most frightening thing any of them has ever said.
House Within: The Shirogane
The silver line · the rival branch · the Hard Second

































EyeThe Meigan, sharpened and impatientWorkKnowledge sharpened by Ruins, with a Purity in the family that nobody praisesChairThe silver, at the red’s right handSeatThe silver house, on its own terrace halfway up the rock, tall windows glowing blue-white under worked lamps at the Guild’s priceLookBright hard silver at collar, wrist and hairpin, frost-work on silver-gray; lynx or snow foxMaxim”It’s what I would have done.”
The Shirogane have a word for the great gate at Ōmagari, which held off a Tenrai host through two winters: ornamental. They were asked in on the third spring. A woman of the line, nobody’s idea of important, walked its length at noon with two cold lunches and a clerk. She laid one silver hairpin against the base of the fourth buttress, and said in a dry little voice, “SPLINTER ORDINANCE.” Every small crack in that wall, each of which had been waiting its turn since the wall was built, was told when its turn was. They came along one at a time, in order, from north to south, over about a quarter of an hour, with a noise the Ōmagari people still tell their children about, and the gate stayed up, ornamental, with nothing on either side of it. She had the clerk enter the hour. She had a slight nosebleed, and finished her lunch.
A thousand years ago the silver line was told it would always stand second, and believed it, and could not let it go. That is the house in a breath, and everything else about them follows. The Byakuya read what is hidden so that it may be known. A Shirogane reads what is hidden so that it may be punished, and they read it faster, since a second who hesitates does not get to be first. They are the finest siege-breakers in the world, the kind of people who get sent for. Their chains have silver in the links, which drinks at a practitioner through the skin. They have the rival’s claim, the rival’s pride and the rival’s ledger, and they are the one house in the Hall that the Tenrai have ever courted instead of bought, with the silver seal set on the left of a Tenrai letter in the place of precedence.
What they hold. The Hard Second is no Trait the coil can read, and every physician who has treated one knows it: an old wound carried from mother to daughter, with the same note under it in every generation, and a Temporality reader can follow it back along one thread the whole thousand years. The Shirogane’s coin-bright rings lie in gray eyes, and most of their daughters look at a thing a moment longer than is polite and then tell you where it will come apart. Purity’s Obsession face, which purges whatever does not fit the shape, is known across the north as the Shirogane way, and it is not meant kindly.
The fostering. For three hundred years the Shirogane and the Byakuya have sent each other a child, so that each house always has someone inside the other’s walls. It is the only arrangement of its kind in the Hall, and it has produced more treason, more tenderness and more excellent silver embroidery than any other institution in the north.
How to beat them. They need a structure to punish. Soft ground, a camp with no wall, a host that does not care whether you broke its gate, and an enemy with nothing built gives them very little. A Shirogane has been known to spend an extraordinary amount of energy on a thing whose only offense is that it stands higher. Offer them first place, and watch the whole family forget what they were doing.
Later hand: what the silver house did in the last winter of the war, and what was done about it at the first bell in the Hall square, the songs have in four keys. The silver chair has a new occupant, a small careful woman who was raised in the white house and sends someone away in the night in her own voice, over and over. The boy in the red chair chose her for it because she had every reason to hate him. The whispering has not stopped, and this office does not expect it to.
Culture
Language. The old register, full forms, no contractions, and honorifics where the old tongue is used, Japonic in its bones. Full names carry the line in the middle: Miku Tenrai Moto, Artemis Amagiri Moto. The register verb is entered. A person is read. The dead are behind, and behind is a direction, and a direction can be faced. Everyone in the house is literate, in the family’s own hand and across the fourteen hands of the Archons, and a document in the wrong hand is void rather than incorrect. The Concord hand is read as a foreign script, accurately and without love.
Greeting. None on record. From senior to junior, a hand on the head and nothing said, and the nothing is enough. A guest eats the host’s food for three days before business.
Rites

The Reading. The house’s central sacrament, stripped down from what it was at the shelf: a thing read correctly has been given its Work, and a thing that has been given its Work has been praised. A newborn’s irises are looked at by the oldest woman in the house, and she says one word, and it is written down and not repeated.
The Oath at Nine. With a grandmother’s hand on the head, at the hour of the evening bell, over a lamp in the Byakuya manner and over whatever is at hand in the others. Everything a Moto will later be held to is sworn at an age when the child is mainly thinking about supper. Keeping it counts as practice on the Fate road from that evening.
The Bow. Fourteen inclinations at the hinge of the day, standing, before the bread. All fourteen, always. Cloth moves fourteen times and no voice is heard. A household that moves cuts its fourteen scratches in the new doorpost before it unpacks, and a guest is walked through the scratched door before business, on the folk belief that a man carrying a lie cannot pass it.
The Reading at Ice-out. The winter’s dead go into the ground together when it opens, and their names are read in the order they died. To read them alphabetically would be a desecration nobody could articulate. The Queen’s Saishiki, the liturgy that made an oath structural instead of verbal, went with her, so what reads the names now is a man with a list doing his best.
The Revocation. The terminal form, full register, correct contours, before a witness: “I revoke the name Moto from you.” A man revoked is entered elar-ama, held by nobody, and the name cannot be given back by anybody. Retainers say the revoked die within the year.
The Guard Settling. When a sentence is complete, the guard settles into the scabbard mouth with one small final sound, and in Kharven that sound means the verdict is complete. A Moto lord who wants a room silent need only touch his hilt.

Who they marry. Up and north and with an eye on the register. Lines marry lines (a Kurenai headsman once took an Akagane soul-surgeon, and the Hall’s verdict on her is the worst page in either family’s books). They marry the Yuno when they can, who keep the living interval and have married into the court. Byakuya daughters marry north to seal peaces nobody remembers, and a Moto’s knotwork belt is always a specific belt tied to a specific alliance, oath or northern-born mother. Blood always mixes, as a Kōkan has observed to a furious son. The children get ring-lines anyway.
Who they feud with. The Yukari, the oldest quarrel in mortal history: the Moto see the threads as property, and the Yukari see them as reality, and a chancery fears a witness it cannot swear in. The Zettari, by forty years of war and the grudge of one king. The current settlement holds, so far, in the form of an oath that no Moto marches on Zettari land. The Holy Sea, as a tenant is feuded with by a landlord who has no way to collect. And each other, always, with enormous courtesy. The Tenrai and Kōkan feud is the kingdom’s founding wound, the Shirogane’s is a thousand years old, and the Akagane have a book.
Who they owe. Hallenfeld holds the Seat’s paper, and never once lent the Kōkan a coin. Thornwall kept the corridors open for two hundred years in case. The Banner Houses swore their oaths to a person, and those oaths do not outlast the reign, so the house is forever one bad winter from having to earn them. And every Moto alive owes the Kōkan the window across the water, which is in the registers of all six northern lines, and none of them have ever taught it.
What the commoners and servants get. A retainer family gets a ration on a true scale, inspected in public, a name in a register they cannot read, and the certainty of being entered correctly. They read little, and the house’s hand not at all. They bring a lord his beads before his water and know how wide to sweep. They get no vote and no explanation, and they have the cold comfort of a master who cannot be bribed about what they are. Northern clans have long since concluded that a Moto is weather, and arrange their lives accordingly, with the door shut when the jokes start. The house’s whole faith lives, unacknowledged, in their kitchens: there are households in the Greenhollow who perform all fourteen labors daily and could not name an Archon.
The house’s own small power is a trade. The hakari-ban, scale-watch, is a commoner’s calling on Moto ground: a keeper who has weighed the ration every day for thirty years and whose beam will not settle on a false weight, by nothing more exalted than a Common skill grown past where it should have stopped. Her balance is why you trust the bread. She charges a day’s ration a month, she can refuse, and in the Thin Weeks of 697 the scale-watch of the Castle Stair put down their beams in a body over a matter of back pay, and four cadet castles found out in nine days how much of their authority had been resting on a woman with a brass pan.
Limitations and Soul-Costs
[Curse] Devouring Certainty — The Instrument That Has Never Been Wrong
The corruption of Knowledge, listed in the house’s own training register beside the other six, written by people who watched it happen and declined to name the century.

A Moto’s reading of what is there is usually correct, so they stop noticing where the reading stops.
The eye shows load and fault, and the person supplies the meaning, and has been drilled since seven not to notice that they supplied it.
A man told he is unfree by a tyrant has a grievance. A man told he is unfree by an instrument that has never once been wrong has a diagnosis.
From inside, being right and being cruel feel exactly alike.

[Curse] The Flat — What a Verdict Takes

Eye bleed, a sternum ache, and twenty to thirty seconds of nothing at all after every hard verdict. Everyone who serves a Moto has learned the timing.
Each forced opening widens the eye a thread and it stays wider, so the flat grows longer through a life, and in the old it is sometimes hard to tell when it has ended.
The Ledger does not stop. People become entries, and the family becomes a very well-kept list of people.
The founder recorded a mother who let her firstborn’s ghost go with a palm on his brow, and approved. He did not record how she was at supper.

[Curse] The Corruption Vector — Every Work Curdles
Every Work has an Attraction face and an Obsession face, and the Work presses the soul into a useful shape, so a long life in one grip tends to become a long life in its worse face. A breaker ends what was rotten and then what was near the rot, and then does not stop. A keeper will not let the dead leave, which is what the house means by clogged. A gatherer gathers. The bearer does not notice. The ground cracks around what they aim at and not only under it, and that is the tell, and by then the people who could tell them are in the cellar.
[Curse] The Noticed Hand — Somebody Else’s Thread

A pull reaches up into the laws themselves, and any Throne with someone on it may look down. See Yorimasa, and his grocers.
Removing a blessing tells the giver who took the pen, and the larger the giver, the heavier it runs.
There is no appeal, since the house’s faith forbids asking. A Moto may never petition the thing that has noticed them.
Nothing becomes more monstrous, more quickly, than a righteous fool with correct metaphysics. A very old family has had a long time to test the sentence.

How They Stand Against the Three Paths
A Body enemy is the one who kills them. A Body fighter gets there, offers no seam worth reading if well kept, and meets an ordinary body at the end of it. No Moto wants a straight exchange with a Zettari or anyone like one. Their answer is to have read the road, the ground, the straps and the man’s knee three days ago, and to be somewhere else, or to have already cut it. High enough up a Body sovereign needs no road, and a Moto’s armor grows too heavy to lift in front of her family.
A Spirit enemy reaches the hand on the thread. A pull shows on the Core before it lands, a wounded soul loses its grip, and a soul-hit goes past the coat as if it were not there. Their counter is that Spirit survives by being right, and being wrong is what the Ledger is for. One bad read and one spoiled stroke, and the Moto has entered it. A Yukari with a Regard is their nightmare: a witness who knows them whole, and cannot be sworn in.
A Fate enemy leans the other way, reads the weights and moves the same straps, usually while bleeding and usually in the baggage train. Such people are rare, and a Moto hunts them first, ahead of any champion. Most of the world’s Fate walkers have Range, Aura Pressure and a kept word and no grip at all, and for those the house has a polite condescension and a very large body of case law. The one thing that gets a Moto’s real attention is another bloodline’s edit type, or a thread that turns out to be somebody’s.
Final Definition

The Moto are a dynasty of lawful perception and lawful function. The Shingan lets them see the stratum of reality that matters. Hataraki lets them work upon that stratum as fate’s own labor.

Their seven lines preserve different emphases of that inheritance, but all remain recognizably Moto: beautiful in an unnerving way, spiritually heavy, politically dangerous, and built around the principle that reality is to be witnessed and then judged, assigned, and made to perform.
They are the line Bara left behind him, handed seven grips on the hardest thing in the world by an ancestor who did not consider this a kindness. The grip lowers the failure and never the price. Their Path is whichever one they have lived, and it is usually the plain road of someone who reads a thing and then hits it. They read the world for a very long time, and it never once told them they were wrong, and the great question of the house is what a family owes to everyone it has been correct about. Some of them are starting to ask. The rest have entered that.
“See before you act. Name before you sever. Measure before you reconcile. Release before you cling. End only what has earned its ending. Preserve only what remains fit to endure.”
And in the founder’s hand, underneath, where only a child of the house will read it:
“The Work is not that you saw it. The Work is that you returned.”

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Say itMOH-toh
The western reach of the northern shield.

The Moto origin is the western reach of the Inner World’s northern shield, and the Old World has no claim on it.
There is no Sātūlagi. The Malō of Sātūlagi does not exist and never did. The Moto hold one seat and it is Kharven.

Hrolf Oddway, a chartered surveyor with a loud mouth and a good red cloak, bet a whole inn at Kessen a month of his wages that he could spend one night leaning on the old Moto gatepost and come back bored. He came back on the third day in the same cloak with frost in his beard, swearing oaths under his breath in a phonology nobody at the inn could place, and he swore them for the rest of his life, in his sleep and at his own wedding. His wife paid the bet. The ground he had leaned on is the subject of this page.
The Ground
Past the ridgeline that now marks Kharven’s border with Undaar-Keth, on ground no crown claims and no border commission patrols. Old cold shield, glaciated, rich in ambient Essence and with no walls, roads or keepers to use it, which is the Inner World’s profile everywhere, and is why nothing has been built there since.
The seat
Standing, ruined, depopulated. Broken structures, a well, a gatepost, frost on it most of the year.

A woman of the house, Somnalis-primary and counted on nobody’s roll, has lived alone in a cabin there for the last stretch of her life, and no longer touches a wall without reading what happened against it, because the density of residual memory on that ground exceeds anything else in her record.

The displacement
The first blow on the white shelf, about 310 IC, which the Moto registers call the split, made the seat untenable. The six lines scattered toward temperate ground, as The Long Reading tells it. Kharven-Seat already stood in the boreal north, over clans who had never heard of the place the blood came from, when Muken came up to it generations later, on reasoning that was strategic before it was sentimental, and took its crown. The great split proper is still to come after him, about 740 IC, and he lives through it.
What This Means For The House

Every Moto seat in the current era is superimposed on somebody else’s ground.
Kharven is Concord-stock northern clans whose roots predate the Moto arrival by centuries. This is why the Banner Houses carry northern names and the crown does not, and why a Stark saying the King’s name aloud is pronouncing a foreign word in his own hall.
The Moto never migrated as a nation. They migrated as a founding house and its retainers. A people that relocates brings farmers. A house that relocates brings law. This is why they superimpose everywhere they land and assimilate nowhere.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Valorin Family
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Overview
Type: Primordial Arcane Lineage · Scripted Soul Lattice Bloodline · Inner World Mage Dynasty
Origin. The Valorin emerged in the earliest generations after Malakar’s division of the worlds: his first blow on the white shelf, about 310 IC, which the Moto registers call the split, and not the breaking of the continents four centuries later. Nearly every civilization kept to the Soul Crystal model. A small body of scholars, alchemists, linguists and ritualists reached a different conclusion: the Soul Crystal was not the only architecture through which the Continuum could circulate Essence. Their answer was the Scripted Soul Lattice. Around it they founded Vaeloris, a hidden village of libraries, alchemical towers, wand-forges and staff gardens, dedicated to magical study, ethical inquiry and the preservation of knowledge.
The Seat and the village. Most of the world knows only the front of the house. The Reach knows Vaeloris, the Carver’s Seat of the Silver Cedars, where the kingdom keeps its standard for the controlled texts and develops techniques for its own use. Behind that respectable office lies the village that nobody is invited to, and a Valorin who has come up after the Seat fell, as some have in living memory, has lost an office and kept the library. The Seat fell in the late summer of 701 IC to one of the house’s own: Kujo Valorin, a child born outside it with both a Crystal and a lattice, whom Vaeloris took in and named, and who turned on everything it taught.
Spiritual lineage. The Valorin descend from the First Inkbinders of Vaeloris. They inherit no divine organ and no relic. They inherit a living manuscript written into the soul, and every generation adds to the same body of understanding. Knowledge, not raw blood, is the lineage’s strength, and knowledge compounds.
Metaphysical anchor: the Scripted Soul Lattice. The lattice is a complete alternative to the Soul Crystal, and a soul that never crystallized is still a soul. Instead of crystallizing Essence into one organ, it grows as an immense network of symbolic pathways woven through the practitioner’s existence, interfacing with the Material Plane, the Soul Plane and the Plane of Fate at once. Essence circulates through living language instead of crystalline architecture, and it remains what it is in anyone: the soul’s own substance, stamped with identity, so that a Valorin spending it is spending pages of themselves.
The lattice stores understanding first and power second. Every ability mastered, technique refined, Wellspring harmonized, language learned, failure understood and theorem proven permanently rewrites it. Growth is cumulative, never repetitive: knowledge literally becomes anatomy. Unspent understanding can also be banked as script and spent later as force (see The Cistern of Unspoken Lines), which is why a mature Valorin is far deeper than a young one looks.
Because the lattice performs every structural function of a Soul Crystal under entirely different logic, ancient scholars call the Valorin the Continuum’s Second Arcane Architecture.
I. Physical Appearance
Stature and build. Adults stand between 5’2” and 6’9”, with long limbs, upright posture and remarkable bodily economy. Their build favors precision and balance over mass, but Scribed Flesh (see Traits) makes it far denser than it looks: a slender Valorin master carries the bone and sinew strength of a much heavier fighter. Even elderly masters move with the fluid certainty of experienced calligraphers. Every gesture looks deliberate, measured, almost instructional.
Eyes. Two hereditary colors, each preserved since Vaeloris’s earliest branches:

Royal violet, the elder branch, said to favor Harmonia and Dominion.
Deep crimson, the younger branch, said to favor Alchemia and Ardency.
Gold-ink (rare). A third state, not a branch. It appears only when a Valorin becomes a Living Ink Soul: the iris turns to slow-moving liquid gold threaded with dark script, and never changes back.

At rest the eyes are calm, luminous and unusually attentive; a Valorin always seems to be observing more than they say. In operation, concentric rings of Vaeloric Script rotate around the pupil and the iris liquefies into flowing ink shot with golden script-light. Accomplished Scriptians can project those rotating inscriptions beyond the eye, so the space around them becomes an extension of their written perception.
Skin and markings. Black skin from warm dark brown to deep ebony, reflecting ancient Kush ancestry preserved within the Inner World. As the lattice matures, luminous alchemical markings surface across the fingers, wrists, forearms, throat, spine, temples and, in masters, the sternum. They are not tattoos. They are the lattice visibly rewriting itself, and they change whenever the mage integrates a significant understanding. They record intellectual growth, not combat. Under Scribed Flesh the markings deepen in battle, glowing along the lines where the body is being reinforced.
Hair. Long white hair is the defining hereditary trait. The Valorin treat hair as a secondary conductor of memory: strands are woven into grimoires, wand cores, ritual circles and staff rings to carry understanding across generations. Cutting it without purpose is an act of needless forgetting, not vanity.
Sound. Valorin magic rarely announces itself with violence. It whispers: quills on parchment, pages turning in invisible libraries, distant harmonic bells, resonating glass, flowing ink, quiet voices reading forgotten languages beneath ordinary hearing. Their greatest workings often arrive with less noise than a lesser mage needs to light a candle. When a Valorin’s magic does grow loud, it is a warning: something has gone wrong, or they have stopped holding back.
II. Axiomatic Lineage Traits
Ten traits, five old and five that close the old gaps.
[Trait] Scripted Soul Lattice — Alternate Metaphysical Architecture
A living manuscript, continuously rewritten by experience, that performs every structural function of a Soul Crystal without crystalline anatomy. Every lesson alters it, every discipline expands its pathways, every genuine understanding becomes another line in the soul.

No Soul Crystal: immune to Crystal fracture, rupture, inversion, corruption and crystallization failure.
Techniques that need direct Soul Crystal contact fail, misidentify the target or anchor against incomplete information. the Valorin can now feel such a technique reach for a Crystal that is not there, and know where it was aimed.
Magical development permanently restructures the lattice; understanding is measurable growth.
Interfaces with all Three Planes at once, translating knowledge into stable circulation.
High resistance to possession, crystal-dependent parasites and Crystal corruption. Memory-targeting phenomena remain the great danger.

Narrative texture: To advanced sight, a Valorin soul is an immeasurable manuscript of luminous script reaching past the body. Every theorem writes a page. Every corrected mistake rewrites an older sentence. Their souls are not crystals but libraries authoring themselves.
[Trait] Primordial Scriptia — Absolute Inscription Affinity
No bloodline has a deeper bond with Scriptia. Where others write spells, the Valorin write permissions, recognition, consequence, memory, pathways, identities, relationships and magical law. Their inscriptions work as living systems that adapt, communicate, evolve and preserve themselves long after the author dies.

Supreme compatibility with every known form of Scriptia.
Exceptional Continuum Retention: inscriptions endure for centuries with minimal decay.
Formula translation loss is drastically reduced by lattice-guided construction.
Large-scale infrastructure can keep developing after its creator’s death if the Plane of Fate recognizes it.
Valorin script can be written into other people’s working magic, with consent, as a stabilizer or amplifier (see Harmonic Translation Engine).

Narrative texture: Valorin Scriptia does not look carved onto reality. Reality behaves as if it has always remembered the inscription.
[Trait] Harmonic Translation Engine — Universal Arcane Comprehension
The lattice instinctively translates unfamiliar magical systems into symbolic structures that can be studied without violating their principles. Translation is not imitation; it is understanding. With observation, experiment and ethical study, a Valorin derives compatible formulae from foreign traditions while keeping their logic intact.

Extraordinary cross-disciplinary learning and Wellspring harmonization across every kind.
Outstanding Synergia compatibility with practitioners from unrelated traditions.
Rapid analysis of unknown phenomena through symbolic decomposition.
Mid-combat translation. A master who watches a technique three times can name its structure, its cost and its weakest clause.

Narrative texture: Faced with unfamiliar magic, a Valorin rarely sees chaos. They see a language whose grammar has not been translated yet.
[Trait] Living Spell Memory — Hereditary Arcane Continuity
Knowledge from earlier generations is never fully lost. It persists in dreams, ancestral grimoires, preserved hair, ritual inks, enchanted instruments and the lattice itself. Descendants inherit instinctive familiarity with structures they never studied.

Accelerated mastery of ancestral disciplines.
Family grimoires wake dormant formulae for recognized descendants.
Children dream incomplete ancestral research.
Each generation refines family techniques instead of merely reproducing them.
In crisis, a recognized descendant can call an ancestor’s mastered formula forward for one casting at that ancestor’s skill. Each use is a debt the descendant must later study down (see Memory Burden).

Narrative texture: A young Valorin may wake speaking a theorem centuries older than they are, before they have the education to understand it.
[Trait] Arcane Vessel Sovereignty — Perfect Focus Integration
The Valorin build the finest instruments in the Continuum because they treat them as organs, not tools. Wands refine thought into precision. Staffs expand stability into territory. Grimoires externalize memory. Every focus becomes a working extension of the lattice.

Exceptional compatibility with wands, staffs, grimoires, rings, catalysts and ritual instruments.
Several spell channels held through one properly built focus.
Legendary foci approach perfect yield (η) for their rightful owner.
Foci evolve alongside the lattice instead of staying static.
A focus can be recalled. A Valorin’s own wand or staff, written into their lattice, returns to their hand across any distance their Transference harmonization allows, and a broken one can be rewritten whole from its memory if even a fragment survives.

Narrative texture: When a master raises a wand, they do not seem to cast a spell. They seem to continue a sentence reality briefly forgot.
[Trait] The Cistern of Unspoken Lines — Banked Essence
The lattice conducts beautifully and by nature stores almost nothing. What it can do is store Essence as unspent script: whole formulae written in the soul and left one word short of completion. Released, each line pays out its stored Essence at once.

Reserve scales with Stage and with the number of mastered formulae, not with Crystal density.
Stages I–VII: reserve below the great Crystal lineages. Stages VIII–XI: on par. Stage XII and above: a master’s cistern can exceed a Crystal user of equal Stage, because a lifetime of written understanding is a lifetime of banked lines.
Lines can be banked only during rest, study or ritual, never mid-fight. A long battle spends the cistern faster than it refills.

[Trait] Scribed Flesh — The Body as Text
The lattice writes not only spells but the body’s own law. Bone is inscribed to bear, sinew to hold, skin to close. Markings brighten along the lines being reinforced.

Vitality High; Resilience Exceptional.
Wounds close by being re-read: a Valorin who understands an injury heals it far faster than one who does not.
Masters can harden a limb or organ into script-dense tissue for a few breaths at Essence cost.
Physical strength still trails the great warrior bloodlines at equal Stage. A Valorin who can stand toe-to-toe with a Zettari has written very well, and paid for it.

[Trait] The Inner Grimoire — The Lattice as Focus
From Stage VIII, the lattice can serve as its own focus. A master who loses every instrument does not lose their magic.

Focus loss reduces Lattice Efficiency by roughly 10–15 points instead of breaking casting rhythm.
Script projects from the markings on the hands and forearms the way it would from a wand.
Below Stage VIII, Focus Dependency applies in full.

[Trait] Errata — The Counter-Script
What can be translated can be corrected. Errata lets a Valorin read a hostile formula as it is cast and write a correction into it.

Effective against structured magic: Scriptia, glyph-work, Paru-script, formation arrays, alchemical workings and any technique with readable grammar.
A correction can blunt, redirect, delay or invert a working, depending on the gap between the two casters’ understanding.
Weak against raw force with no grammar to edit (a fist, a falling dome, pure pressure) and nearly useless against true Chaos (see Grammar of the Unmade).

[Trait] Distributed Soul — No Single Point
A Soul Crystal is one organ, and an organ can be struck. The lattice is millions of pathways with no center.

Strikes aimed at a soul’s core (heart-node techniques, Crystal-shattering arts, junction strikes) hit one region of the lattice instead of the whole.
Damage reroutes: lost pathways are bypassed while the lattice rewrites around the gap.
A Valorin can be bled dry slowly. They are very hard to break all at once.

III. System Metrics & Affinities
The Valorin favor structure over phenomenon: they master how Affinities interact across the Three Planes rather than one Affinity absolutely, and build systems of many Wellsprings working in harmony.
A line with no Epoch behind it. The blood gives what any old line’s gives and never a Path, and what they carry in place of an instrument is the lattice and everything they have written on it.
Form bias: Write · Sing · Brew · Rite (in older books Scriptia, Harmonia, Alchemia, Synergia, Conjunctia and Advanced Ritual Architecture).
The lattice on the Paths. The lattice has the same three faces a Crystal has three layers, and the three Paths and Mastery reads on it the same way. The face that meets matter is Scribed Flesh and does the Shell’s work. The manuscript itself does the Core’s. The sentences the world has agreed to recognize do the Attraction Layer’s. The Valorin lean on the Spirit Path first, since a working authored in the soul and inscribed on a thing is what they are for, and many walk the Fate Path second, with the rough seat and the long years that always cost. The Body Path they study, and few walk it: Scribed Flesh is a scholar’s answer to a fighter’s question. Lattice Efficiency (below) is the lineage’s own measure and sits beside yield; Spirit Mastery is the rung that usually leads, and a master’s Body and Fate Mastery tell you what else they have spent their life on.
What they cannot read. Understanding is everything to this lineage, and Fate is the one place it fails them. A mind’s notions are made of the thing they would be used against, and a lattice is made of notions. A Valorin can write a sentence for the Plane of Fate and can wait to see whether it is recognized, which is how the Circle of Five persist and how a kingdom comes to stand on a forgotten line. They cannot read Fate, cannot reason out why one sentence was taken and another refused, and may spend generations on a line that comes to nothing. Vaeloris teaches this to its children as the first humility, and most of them spend their lives quietly convinced that they will be the exception.
Favored kinds. The lattice spreads compatibility across nearly the whole Continuum.

Primary: the Spirit, Fate and Medium kinds, and the Wild Wellsprings of matter, mind, light, water and life. These complement Write, Sing and alchemical construction naturally.
Secondary: the Wild Wellsprings of fire, force and distance. Fully compatible, but they need more preparation to reach the same refinement.

Their strongest compatibilities are listed by name under Wellspring compatibility, below.
How their power shows. Rarely as explosions. It shows as floating Vaeloric script, living manuscripts, rotating formula circles, golden harmonic geometry, ink-like Essence streams, self-writing glyph arrays, lattice projections, living ritual architecture, wand halos and staff coronas. Even in battle they look like scholars reorganizing reality, not warriors trying to overwhelm it.
Stat modifiers


















































StatReadingWhyGnosisSupremeThe lattice integrates understanding directly into architecture; masters approach omnidisciplinary analysis of Essence circulation, harmonization, plane interaction, Attraction currents, formula construction, Crystal and Domain mechanicsHarmonicsSupremeLattice partitioning lets several harmonizations run without interference; Fate recognizes their script unusually wellTemperingExceptionalEvery Threshold Event rewrites the lattice; expression grows cleaner and harder to disruptDominionSupremeTheir Domains build working magical ecosystems (see The Living Library)ArdencyExceptional (prepared) · High (unprepared)Pre-Written Fire and the Cistern let banked lines release at full forceDexterityExceptionalScriptia demands, and the lattice rewards, near-flawless sequencing and routingResilienceExceptionalDistributed Soul and Scribed Flesh: damage reroutes instead of cascadingVitalityHighScribed Flesh writes the body’s own law
Lattice Efficiency (ηₗ)
Valorin measure refinement by the share of understanding that becomes working reality.








































TierηₗWhat it looks likeCommon Valorin60–75%Basic education, stable lattice, limited script autonomyRefined Valorin75–90%Advanced Scriptia, reliable ritual, several harmonizationsMaster Valorin90–98%Near-perfect translation, independent living inscriptions, Errata usable in combatGrandmaster Valorin98–99.8%Negligible loss; script answers almost as fast as thoughtLiving Ink Soul99.9%+The lattice writes itself; gold-ink eyes**Authored Soul **Effectively 100%Thought and expression are the same act; see Current Standing
Temperance interaction
Without a Soul Crystal, Temperance reorganizes the lattice. Each Threshold Event expands symbolic architecture instead of crystalline density.

































StagesWhat opensI–IVBasic script circulation; the Cistern begins to bank linesV–VIIIndependent lattice adaptation; Scribed Flesh hardeningVIIIScript Domains; the Inner Grimoire (the lattice becomes its own focus)IX–XISimultaneous multi-Wellspring harmonization; Errata at full strengthXII–XIVPartly autonomous inscriptions that run without concentration; the Cistern overtakes Crystal reservesRevelation · ApexNear-complete metaphysical self-authorship: thought continuously rewrites the lattice
Wellspring compatibility
No lineage harmonizes with more Wellsprings at once. Masters hold several harmonizations through lattice partitioning without ordinary interference. Strongest compatibility, all confirmed in the Codex:
Judicium · Luminalis · Chthonica · Fixatio · Coagula · Benediction · Redemption · Somnalis · Oblation · Transference · Oneirion · Anamnesis · Eidolyn · Transmutatio  · Sublimatio
Transmutatio and Sublimatio are named bench operations as well as Wellsprings, so they fit the lineage’s alchemical side directly.
IV. Signature Arts
Six lineage arts and one Domain, taught only inside Vaeloris. Each costs something the lattice must pay back.
| Art | From Stage | What it does | Cost |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Pre-Written Fire | IV | A full formula is drafted in advance and left one word unfinished. Spoken, it releases at once at full strength, with no casting time | Drafting takes study time; each banked cast occupies Cistern space until used |
| Marginalia | VI | The Valorin annotates an enemy’s technique in light only allies can read: its structure, its cost, its weakest clause | Needs three clear observations of the technique; strains Gnosis while held |
| The Unfinished Sentence | VII | A conditional casting written into a place, object or person that completes itself when its condition is met (“when the gate opens”, “if he lies”) | Each open sentence draws a thin, constant trickle of Essence until it completes or is struck out |
| Palimpsest | IX | Over hours of ritual, the Valorin scrapes a place’s old magical law away and writes a new one: wards, terrain behavior, which Wellsprings flow easily there | Slow; undone by anyone who can read and out-write it; a palimpsest over sacred or Fate-recognized ground can fail violently |
| Errata Seal | X | After Errata corrects a hostile formula, the correction is sealed in place, and the enemy cannot cast that exact technique again until the seal is broken or expires | Duration scales with the gap in understanding; a far stronger caster tears it off quickly |
| Ink Wake Ward | XI | The Valorin extends a thin layer of their own lattice over allies, giving them Distributed Soul for one engagement | The Valorin feels every wound the ward reroutes; overextending it can tear their own pathways |
Domain — The Living Library
Where most Domains impose a philosophy, the Living Library builds an ecosystem. The space unfolds into endless shelves of Vaeloric script; the floor is written, the air is written, the light reads.
Law of the Library: everything spoken or cast inside is written down.

Every technique used inside the Domain is transcribed onto the shelves as it happens. The Valorin can read it, and after one reading may cast a translated version once.
The Valorin’s own inscriptions repair themselves faster than they can be damaged while the Domain holds.
Errata and Marginalia cost nothing inside the Library.
The Domain grows with use: every technique it has ever transcribed stays in its shelves for the next opening.

Its counters, which the Valorin know as well as their own hands:

What has no grammar cannot be shelved. Pure physical force with no technique behind it passes through the Library unread.
True Chaos does not transcribe; it smears. A Chaos working inside the Library spreads illegible blots across the shelves and can corrupt what is already written there.
Burning the shelves is possible. A Pyreveil or Oblivara-scale working that destroys enough of the written space collapses the Domain early and wounds the caster’s lattice.

V. Cultural & Spiritual Lattice
Language. The ancestral tongue is High Vaeloris (High Vaylarian); its written form is Vaeloric Script. To outsiders they are a language. To the Valorin they are architecture. Every sentence has structural weight, every definition sets a boundary, every properly spoken name strengthens Attraction recognition, and every written theorem changes how future formulae understand one another.
Sacred customs

The First Page Rite. Every child receives a blank grimoire page when magical awareness wakes. The first genuine spell that appears on it of its own accord reveals the child’s deepest inclination. The page is never replaced.
The Wand Bonding. Adolescents do not choose a weapon; they form a lifelong relationship with a focus. A wand is an extension of thought, and destroying one’s own without need is symbolic self-amputation.
The Staff Pilgrimage. No one becomes a Master without leaving Vaeloris to find material worthy of a staff. No crafted substitute is accepted. The staff must survive its owner speaking their complete true name across all Three Planes.
The White Hair Oath. Locks of ancestral hair are kept in grimoires, staff rings, wand cores and memorial archives. Memory is not discarded; it is inherited.
The Ink Wake. At death, a Valorin’s final writings are read before family, students and colleagues. If the ink fades, the work is complete. If it stays visible, descendants inherit the duty to finish it, not merely preserve it.
The Circle of Five. The greatest masters may choose, through consensual Fate inscription, to remain recognized within immense Script Portraits. They are not ghosts. They are preserved scholarly minds that advise, challenge dangerous decisions, correct theory and guard the philosophy of Vaeloris. Death may end a Valorin’s life; it need not end their teaching.
The Errata Vigil. Before a Master may teach Errata, they spend a night alone in the archive correcting their own oldest mistakes, in their own hand, where every student can read them in the morning. A teacher who cannot be corrected is not trusted to correct others.
The Unwritten Line. When Vaeloris goes to war, each fighter leaves one line of their lattice in the archive, a sentence only they could have written. If they fall, it is read at their Ink Wake. If they come home, they strike it out themselves.

Signature imagery
Long white hair under library candlelight. Violet and crimson eyes lit by rotating script; very rarely, gold. Golden glyphs above black skin. Towering libraries joined by living inscriptions. Staffs crowned with silver rings. Grimoires that turn their own pages. Ink that flows upward. Whole villages breathing quietly under invisible magical architecture.
Where other civilizations build walls to defend knowledge, the Valorin teach knowledge to defend itself.
VI. Limitations — The Soul-Cost
The lineage has answers to its weaknesses, and they do not erase them. Every alternative architecture pays in its own coin, and a Valorin who forgets that is the easiest kind to kill.
[Curse] Hollow Reservoir — Crystalless Physiology
The lattice is a superb conductor and a shallow natural reservoir.

Still true: Tool-less, unprepared casting drains fast. Raw Aether pressure trails the great Crystal lineages early on. The largest workings need prepared inscriptions, catalysts or ritual architecture.
Lineage answer: The Cistern of Unspoken Lines. From Stage VIII the gap closes; from Stage XII a master’s banked reserve can exceed a Crystal user’s.
True price: The Cistern refills only through rest, study and ritual. A Valorin caught in a long fight with no time to bank lines runs dry while a Crystal user is still burning.

[Curse] Focus Dependency — Arcane Vessel Reliance
The lattice was built to extend itself through instruments, and every Valorin fights around their focus.

Still true: Below Stage VIII, a destroyed wand or staff breaks casting rhythm until the lattice reorganizes; sealed grimoires deny stored formulae; anti-enchantment ground strangles prepared infrastructure.
Lineage answer: The Inner Grimoire from Stage VIII; focus recall and rewriting under Arcane Vessel Sovereignty.
True price: Even a master loses 10–15 points of Lattice Efficiency empty-handed. Against an equal, that gap decides fights.

[Curse] Formula Saturation — Intellectual Overload
Every spell, theorem, mistake and contradiction stays in the lattice and must eventually be reconciled.

Still true: Too many simultaneous calculations slow casting; contradictory systems interfere; poorly integrated research destabilizes old formulae; fast learning without reflection weakens coherence.
Lineage answer: The Index Rite: a night of ritual sleep in which the lattice files, cross-references and resolves what was learned. Masters perform it weekly.
True price: Skip the Index Rite during a long campaign and saturation compounds. Magical ignorance is easier to survive than misunderstood knowledge.

[Curse] Memory Burden — Ancestral Continuity
The lineage never forgets, and descendants carry what the dead left unfinished.

Still true: Ancestral dreams interrupt development; powerful grimoires overwhelm the inexperienced; family expectation breeds perfectionism and self-sacrifice.
Lineage answer: None that removes it. It is the same inheritance that makes them strong.
True price: Memory-targeting magic is the lineage’s deepest wound. The Lethe-touched Wellsprings (Letheveil, Lethegraal, Oblivara) do not damage a Valorin; they erase pages. Lost understanding is lost anatomy. And every ancestor-formula called forward through Living Spell Memory is a debt the descendant must study down, or carry as unresolved script.

[Curse] Grammar of the Unmade — Chaos as Illegibility
The Valorin are built of language, and true Chaos is the end of grammar.

Chaos workings that break the agreements under things (causal discord, axiom-level instability) do not merely hurt a Valorin. They make the lattice illegible to itself: sentences lose their order, definitions forget their boundaries, formulae contradict mid-cast.
Errata cannot correct what has no grammar to correct. Living inscriptions near strong Chaos corrupt or go silent.
A Valorin facing a Chaos sovereign must win quickly or not at all. Every breath spent inside that pressure costs pages.

VII. Current Standing
Pureblood line. The original bloodline survives. It never collapsed through war or decline; it chose to stay small, preferring preservation to expansion. The pureblood houses live almost entirely within Vaeloris and its hidden scholarly branches, where magical education is a sacred obligation, not a political privilege. They are few, but nearly every pureblood receives centuries of accumulated instruction.
Scions and descendants. Modern descendants are among the Continuum’s greatest scholars, Scriptians, ritualists, alchemists and magical architects. They rarely rule by conquest. They shape civilizations through education, infrastructure, diplomacy, healing, enchantment and the keeping of dangerous knowledge. Many of the Continuum’s great magical institutions rely, unknowingly, on principles first worked out in Vaeloris.
Hybrid branches. The lattice meets Soul Crystal biology unpredictably. Hybrids develop one of three ways:

























OutcomeWhat happensStandingSuppressed CrystalThe Crystal never fully forms; the lattice dominatesCommon; reads as a lesser purebloodDual ArchitectureA working Crystal and a working lattice coexistExceptionally rare, immensely powerful, unstable without careful guidance. a stabilized Dual Architecture can run Crystal reserve and lattice precision at once, and is the most feared hybrid in the ContinuumFractured DevelopmentNeither architecture maturesErratic magic until one structure asserts dominance; Vaeloris will take such children in and help one side win
Living Ink Souls. Among the rarest manifestations. The lattice becomes partly autonomous: living inscriptions emerge by instinct, formulae keep refining themselves after completion, and written constructs become semi-living organisms that adapt while staying faithful to the creator’s intent. The eyes turn gold-ink and stay that way. Many of history’s greatest Scriptians were Living Ink Souls.
Authored Souls. Above the Living Ink Soul lies a state the Valorin speak of carefully. An Authored Soul’s lattice no longer only writes magic. It has finished writing them. Thought, intention and expression become one act; the soul is a completed manuscript that still edits itself.

Only a handful are recorded, all among the First Inkbinders or the Circle of Five.
Their inscriptions are recognized by the Plane of Fate as near-law.
No Authored Soul is known to be walking the Continuum now. Some in Vaeloris believe one of the Circle of Five is close.

Traces in modern bloodlines. Even diluted, Valorin inheritance surfaces across the Continuum: unusual scholarship, inscription compatibility, a feel for magical instruments, fast theoretical learning, ritual skill, Wellspring adaptability, strong cooperative resonance and instinct for magical language. Distant descendants often become teachers, researchers, librarians, artificers or healers without ever knowing why.
VIII. Lineage Scale & Doctrine
Scale. The Valorin are recognized as one of the greatest magical bloodlines the Continuum has produced. Their supremacy is measured in sophistication, not destruction.

No lineage surpasses them in Scriptia.
None now equals them in Harmonia, where lattice partitioning puts them first.
None equals their ability to build living magical civilizations.
With the Cistern, Scribed Flesh and the Inner Grimoire, a Valorin master is no longer only a builder behind walls. Prepared, on their own ground, they are among the most dangerous people in the Continuum to fight. Unprepared, far from home and against raw force or true Chaos, they are still mortal scholars, and they know it.

Their greatest masters build magical ecosystems that keep functioning centuries after death: preserving knowledge, defending populations and adapting without supervision. Other bloodlines forge legendary warriors. The Valorin forge legendary systems. Entire kingdoms stand because a forgotten Valorin once wrote the correct sentence into the Plane of Fate.
Doctrine. The First Inkbinders left one principle that every child entering Vaeloris is taught:
“Power forgotten dies. Power understood teaches. Therefore seek not to become the greatest mage, but the greatest teacher your magic can remember.”
So every true Valorin holds that the highest expression of magic is preservation, not domination. Understanding, not secrecy. Not becoming indispensable, but building something that no longer needs you to survive.
The lineage adds a second line, taught only to those who learn Errata:
“A sentence that cannot be corrected is not knowledge. It is a cage.”
To outsiders, the Valorin are mages. To history, they are the lineage that taught reality how to keep reading after its authors were gone.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Yukari Bloodline
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Ashura's Family · Kin of the Breath · Crows of the Threshold

The Moto were chosen by an Epoch. The Zettari were forged by one. The Yukari were born to one, and they have never once let the other two houses forget it.

When the silk factor Dorrit Vance climbed to the Cedar Enclave in the spring of 548 to collect a debt, he brought two mules, three hired swords and a writ with twelve seals on it in twelve colors of wax, and a Yukari cousin in a black coat silvered at the cuffs handed him a cup of tea before he had got his hat off. It smelled of small white flowers. It was as bitter as a lawsuit. Vance set it down untasted, and since nobody in that house speaks a word of business until the guest has tasted the tea, for nine days nobody spoke a word of business to him. They were charming about it. They fed him trout and honey cakes and asked after his mother, while a hundred crows glossy as wet ink sat along the rail and watched him eat, and his hired swords drifted down to the village dance and did not come back. On the tenth morning he drank it, made the face everyone makes, and opened his writ. The cousin glanced once at the air beside his head, where the crimson had come up round the pupil of her eye, and told him kindly that the debt was his own brother’s forgery, that the eighth seal had been cut in Thrum by a left-handed man, and that the brother had been sleeping with his wife since the autumn before last. Vance sat down on the gravel. The whole of it went into the Yukari record, with the date and the tea. He paid to have the cup, and it is on a shelf in his great-grandchildren’s house, and none of them will drink from it.
That is the family at its most polite. Now the rest.
In the autumn of 633 Bartlemy Goss, Lord of the Ley Marches, a huge merry man in a gilded harness with a laugh you could hear across a river, came up the southern road to the Cedar Enclave with seven thousand Marrick spears on a season’s contract and four hundred gray horses he had not finished paying the Yan for. He had been meaning to do it for nineteen years. The Enclave sent a cousin down to the road with a tray, and Lord Goss, in front of his whole column, took the cup off it and threw it at her head, and the column roared. He then read out his terms from the saddle, and they were very good terms, and when he had finished nobody on the Yukari side said anything at all. A woman got down from the sutler wagons at the back of his own army and came walking up the line past his bannermen. Everybody knew her. They called her Honey Nan, she was stout and fifty and had sold honey cakes in the Goss camps for eleven years, every campaign, and under the windows of the Goss hall between campaigns, and half the sergeants owed her money. She took off her apron as she came and folded it over her arm, and under it was a coat of crow black with the silver on its sleeve running all the way to the elbow, and it was about then that a bannerman of the Long Fields, a boy with nothing else to look at, noticed what his steward had been arranging for nine years that nobody should notice. It was noon. The banner threw a shadow. The horse threw a shadow. The road under Lord Goss’s stirrup was clean.
“You had a lump on your liver the size of a plum, my lord, the winter your boy was nine,” said Yukari Nagi, in the voice she used for selling cakes. “You’d have been dead by spring, and your brothers would have burned three valleys over the child. So I’ve kept you. It’s been no trouble, you’ve good cooks. Your boy’s twenty now and your brothers are dead, and you’ve come up here to my house.” She looked at him a moment longer with real regret, for she knew him better than anyone ever had. Then a crow came down on the rail of the wagon, and she turned her head to look at it.
Eleven years of liver arrived in the time it takes to turn your head. The yellow came up out of his collar and filled his face as if it were being poured in, the whites of his eyes and then his teeth. His belly rose against the gilt until the buckles went, and he leaned out of the saddle with an expression of great surprise and brought up what looked like a bucket of black tar over his horse’s neck, and more after it. While he was doing that his shadow came back, short and black, the first in eleven years, and he fell on it. The Marrick captain looked at the body, looked at the man who kept the pay chest, looked at the sun, and grounded spears. Seven thousand men walked home by supper. The Yan came for their horses. Yukari Nagi finished the tea that had been brought down for him, since it was poured, and went home, and to the end of her days she could tell you what Bartlemy Goss had dreamed on any night you cared to name, and she kept his day every year, and at the Tellings she told the whole thing against herself with the price left in. The lords of the South have walked their own courtyards at noon ever since, in front of witnesses. They call it taking the air.
The Yukari are the family of Ashura, the Breath Between Worlds, third and last of the Three Epochs. Yukari was her own name. When the Third Epoch came and the Soul Plane woke, Ashura walked the waking world for a time as a woman: she kept a house, sat at a table, laughed at it, and bore children, and the name she answered to at that table was Ashura Yukari. Every Yukari since is her kin, by blood or by the Telling, and the house is exactly as old as the Third Epoch, to the morning.

What they want and what they hold
The Yukari say they want nothing more than the spiritual balance of the world kept, and the awful thing is that they mean it. They have sworn off more land, sworn off banners and sworn their knowledge out of every war. They will not rule you. They will only know you, for good, and know what you promised, and what it was tied to, and write it down.
Three things they hold that everybody needs. The record: in a quarter where every house has a price and a grievance, the only account of who did what that nobody suspects of being for sale. By that record, of the seven houses that turned a coin on the smuggler Tam Pennyroyal’s funeral in 661, six made money and the seventh wrote down who did, and a crow rode the last twenty miles on the lid. The gate posts: the wards of half a frontier, cut by people who can hear stone. And the spirit side of the world. The war broke the Soul Plane, the dead have lost their road, and the only reason there is a road left to lose is that the father of this house went into a seam in the Epoch’s own body and held it shut. Everything still alive over there is living on time a Yukari bought. Nobody can do without any of the three, and nobody at the table has ever enjoyed saying so.
The Name
In the old Japonic of the house, yukari is the word for a tie between lives: kinship, affinity, the bond that makes two people related. The same root runs through Ketsuen, the old books’ name for the thread-bound country the house holds. Her true name in the Celestial Proto-Tongue is Ashuraya, and the Empyreal Veil keeps it. Yukari was the name she chose for the world of tables and doorways, because it said what she had come to do. The Breath is what lets one life be related to another, and she named her family after the relation itself.
That is why the name is chosen and never simply inherited. A family named for the bond lets the bond decide who belongs. Ashura took foundlings into her house and gave them the name on the same evening she gave it to her own children, and the house has done the same ever since. The tie makes kin. The blood only follows it. It is the oldest thing the Yukari say about themselves, and they say it at every Telling, before the stone.
Origin of the House
The First Household
The Ketsumyōgan is Ashura’s own sight, carried in a mortal body. The Breath knows the Soul Plane from inside, as recognition, and her children were born knowing a little of what she knew: the threads of all three planes, seen at once. Nobody taught the first Yukari to see. Their mother could, and they had her eyes.
The price came in the same cradle. A mortal Soul Crystal was never built to carry an Epoch’s sight, and the triplanar load it takes in burns the lattice that holds it. The house calls that Threadburn, and every bearer pays it. The first children paid more. They were born in the first mornings of the Third Epoch, while the Soul Plane was still waking, and their eyes saw a plane half asleep and went dark under the weight of it, and came back, and went dark again. Those blindness cycles ended as the Plane finished waking and Temperance progression became possible. Threadburn never ended. The house learned to carry it.
In those first generations the eye was raw and undivided: every thread, every plane, every connection, all at once. Over the long run of the Third Epoch it settled in the blood into its eight types, Shisen and Teishi, Danshi and Orihi and the rest, one to each eye. The undivided eye still turns up once in an age, and the house treats that child the way it treated the first ones.

They asked who had taught them to see, and she said that nobody had; they had her eyes. They asked why the seeing hurt, and she sat down with them and told them, all of it, until the lamp burned out. Then she lit it again and told the next one.
the Empyreal Veil’s echo-archive

That night at the hearth is the first Telling. Every Telling since is the same act repeated: a Yukari of age is sat down and given the whole account of what they carry, what it costs and what it means, because the mother of the house would not let one of her children pay for a sight they had not been told about. The Yukari do not worship Ashura and never have. They call her by the word a family uses, and they set a place for her at the long table on the first night of every year, and nobody sits in it.
The house also holds that she looked at a battle once, from a kitchen step, and that it stopped until she had finished what she was doing. It tells this as a story about her, and about how far every one of her descendants has fallen short of the kitchen step.
Senri Yukari
Son of Ashura · Father of the House · He Who Went Into the Seam
Senri was the last child Ashura Yukari bore, late in the long run of the Third Epoch, and her blood ran fuller in him than in any Yukari since the first mornings. He was born with the undivided eye. It took his left eye before he was grown, and the left stayed dark for the rest of his life, a still black pupil ringed in old crimson; the right saw for both, and saw deeper than any eye in the house. People who met him remembered the dark eye first and the patience second.
He was a quiet man and a plain-spoken one. He said true things in the fewest words they would go into and then said nothing at all, which the house learned to read as the rest of the sentence. When the Moto offered to take his sight into the Loom’s administration, to make it a lawful subset of their own judgment and him an officer of it, he refused them in one sentence and never discussed it again. The Moto remember the refusal. The Yukari remember the sentence.
Senri’s stone
He cut it himself. It is a single slab of the valley’s limestone taller than a man, gray with a warmth of honey where the light catches it, dressed flat on the face and left rough on the flanks so the quarry chisel’s furrows still run down them. He took it out of the hill behind the gate over one whole winter and brought it down on a sledge, six men pulling and Senri walking beside it with one palm laid on the stone as if it were a horse that might bolt. There is one line on its face, set at the height of a seated man’s eyes, so that whoever reads it properly has to sit down to do it:

Master the innards, and the outer world is yours to command.

The stone stands at the back of the long hall of the Cedar Enclave, and every Telling is given in front of it. A child who asks for the name sits on the cold floor before Senri’s stone, hears the whole account, and reads the line aloud. Children read it as a promise. Young men read it as a boast. The house says that anyone who has lived long enough reads it as a question.
His family
Senri married a daughter of House Lambert of Sallowgate, the counting house of the Holy Sea’s land marches, and the match is why the Yukari record keeps its promises in figures as well as words. Their children are Naiser, the eldest; Naevra, a year younger; and Seradris, the youngest. He raised them in the cedar valleys through the worst of the forty-year war. When Naiser lost his first match in the yard at nine and the house’s custom asked for a lock of his hair, it was Senri who knelt and cut it, very gently, and laid his hand on the boy’s head after, and said nothing.
The seam
Four winters before the war ended, the Seikai forced a seam into the Soul Plane: into the place in Ashura where the dead are kept. Senri went into it. He left from the gate on a frost-white morning in his traveling coat with the pack already on his back, because a door like that will take only one, and he held it from the inside for four years. Everything that still lives on the spirit side of the world lives on the time he bought.
When Naiser broke the Seikai working at its root on the slope above the river, the seam stopped widening. Senri did not come back. The house has not given him a posthumous name, because a posthumous name is given to the dead, and the archive enters Senri as neither. The Yukari say it plainly to anyone who asks: he went into his mother to hold her shut.
The House on the Crystal
Every soul has three layers, and every soul in this family has spent its life being told exactly how the three are doing. The soul is a Crystal: its outer Aether Shell meets the physical world, its inner Essence Core holds identity and works on spiritual reality, and its Attraction Layer is a soul’s share of Fate. Aether (mana) comes in through the skin, and the Crystal refines it into Essence (spiritual energy), which is the soul’s own stamped substance. Most of the house walk the Spirit road because the house teaches it, and a Yukari who would rather hit people may do that. The name is chosen, and the eye and the Regard both come by blood, so chosen kin may stand in the long hall with neither.
The Spirit Path is everything to do with spiritual reality: souls, spirits, the dead, the Essence in a person and the meaning in a thing. That is a far larger country than the thrown bolts a bracket crowd pays to see, and this family has been its landlord since before anybody else knew it was there. A Spirit fighter’s force holds together at range and goes past the Shell, so armor and Durability never come into it, and a Spirit fighter caught out of position has a very bad day. The same soul that can tell you what the dead man in the corner wants has about the insurance value of a wet paper lantern. Most of the family consider this a fair summary of life.
Which road, and what it costs
A soul’s Mastery is read one rung per road, from its Level under its Stage’s ceiling, and two roads matter here. Spirit is how strong your influence on spiritual reality is. Fate is how much of the odds you can move. Nobody’s Mastery reads before Glory, the sixth Stage, except where an Epoch’s grip opens a ladder early, and the Yukari’s does: their Spirit reads its first rung from Ascension, so a child can hear the dead in the room years before anyone else’s coil reads anything. Fate climbs for them as for anyone, and without a Work or a blessing it stops at the second rung. Blood has never yet lifted that ceiling, and the editors who stand above it each had a blessing to thank, or to curse. The road’s people keep their own old word for each rung, and the house uses them.

The Eye and the Look
There are three great instruments in the world, one to each Epoch’s line. Bara’s line tells the world its job, and Aegor’s line asks what carries what happens next. Ashura’s line looks at you. People outside the house confuse its two inheritances constantly, so this office will say it once, slowly. The eye sees what everything is tied to. The look keeps what it sees. The first is a matter of threads and can be turned into scissors at a terrible price. The second touches nothing at all, and that is a good deal worse.
The Ketsumyōgan: she can see the strings, and she has scissors
Eleven hundred people paid the ferry toll to watch Yukari Hisame, in crow black with a folded paper fan and a head cold, let Ōtori Genba’s finest cut finish on her neck with no consequence, and put the fan’s guard-stick through his throat in the fraction of a second his body spent waiting for an answer. She spent most of what she had on that one heartbeat and did not fight again that year. That is the eye at its loudest. The Shingan is the eye of the throne, and this is the eye of the loom: a violet-black corona at the pupil’s edge, crimson threads turning in it when it wakes, one type to the left eye and another to the right, permanent once they come. Every edit is a real pull. It has a visible charge in the iris, it can take most of a reserve for a small thing (the reserve being Essence, the same store the house’s seeing and Null-Light run on), and it often fails.
