Null-Light: they look at you, and you stay exactly what they saw
Null-Light (無光, Mukō) is recognition with no light in it: a thing known completely by a light that never touches it. Two truths of knowing make it. A thing can be known by what it does not give back, which the Measurewrights, borrowing from their optics, call the null reading. And a thing known closely and without a gap does not change, as the watched pot does not boil and Zeno’s arrow never moves, while a thing known unevenly changes faster than if it had been left alone. Put them together and you have the house’s law: to be known is to be held. It gives no fire. No Regard has ever warmed a room or moved a pebble. Its full account is its own page, and every Yukari child hears the worst of it by name.

And there is the fragment. The eye carries a splinter of Null-Light, which is why a Yukari look leaves a room as it found it, and the splinter can be pushed. It will ride a good blade for one plane and one stroke, canceling a working it matches along the line of the cut. On the Kessen road Lord Naiser Yukari is said to have thrown it over a whole stretch of road at once, a man-shaped dark at the middle, with every cedar, carriage and crow around him gone shadowless, and the only shadow left in the valley lying under him and stretching toward the thing he meant to kill. The house has declined to discuss what that cost.
The crows
They are not spies, and the crow-wards of Karasuyama will explain this to you at length while banding one. They are birds, and any Fair-day fool can learn that a crow knows a face, scolds it for years and teaches its chicks to scold it too. What the house has done, for as long as there has been a house, is feed them. Hundreds of thousands roost on the mountain above the Enclave and range the whole South, and each one of them is a small soul with a good memory that a Confessor can read whole, without touching it, from across a yard.
So a karasu-yomi, a crow-reader, sits on the Karasuyama steps of an evening with a bag of grain and takes in what the day’s birds have seen. It is a lousy way to learn anything. A crow’s account of the world is food, owls, and who threw what, and the Thread Standard, the Reach’s law of what is tied to what, will not hear it without a second witness. But it does mean that the South has been watched from above, by birds with grudges, for some thousands of years, by a house that forgets nothing. It also means that a crow-reader who has kept ten thousand crows tilts her head when you speak and dreams about carrion, and has opinions about you based on an incident with a crust. Moto lords have taken to feeding them. It has been entered.
What it costs, where it stops, who beats it
The cost is written out in the curses below, and it is the worst in the family’s power to describe. What you hold you must keep looking at. What you have known you can never give back. The eye burns the lattice and flattens the heart.
The limit. The look needs a looker with the thing in mind and a thing to know. It starts nothing, mends nothing and moves no stone. The eye moves only what already has a way of happening. A Hold stands only until something else needs looking at, and a Domain past the moment of naming is out of its reach.
Who beats it. Reach her, since the body behind that eye is an ordinary body at its Stage. Arrange a second fight, so that she has to let go of the first. Bring more souls than she can hold, which is the old Vermilion answer. Stay in Thick Veil where the deeper planes go muted. Land the second blow after the heartbeat, because the world tolerates a Causal Disconnect for no longer than that. Be what you say you are. And be sound: a whole body has nothing for a Slip to finish, as Big Aldous Harrow proved at Sealhall in yellow boots with a surgeon’s certificate on his chest, to the lasting benefit of the tooth-drawers’ guild.
What the House keeps
The Yukari keep the Immortal Cross, and they have kept it since the first morning: four arms around an empty heart, which close only for someone who understands everything each arm holds, Null-Light and the six teachings, the nature of the Seikai and the nature of the Zettari. Whoever closes it is held in true immortality. A hand with an Epoch in it does not seat a single joint, however much it understands. So the Yukari keep a test no Yukari born can pass, and they have kept it for the whole of the Third Epoch, watching for the one who can. That vigil is what the house means when it says the crow watches.
Physical Appearance and Dress

Stature 5’6” to 6’6”, lean and long-limbed rather than broad, the body arranged to take in a room rather than to fill it. Narrow shoulders, long fingers, feet that sit flat and quiet.
Eyes Dark irises from near-black to deep brown, with the faint violet-black corona of the Ketsumyōgan at the pupil’s edge even at rest. Waking, the corona brightens to luminous crimson and thread-patterns turn slowly in the iris.
Skin and thread-marks Complexions from dark earthen brown to pale cool ivory. Bearers grow thread-marks over the years: fine luminous lines under the skin of the forearms, the backs of the hands, the temples and the base of the skull, branching like roots seen from beneath the soil. At rest they are the color of old scars; under strain they glow silver going violet at the edges.
Hair Most often jet black; blonde with notable frequency; deep crimson streaks in the lines that run closest to Ashura; now and then white from birth, which the house calls the Breath’s mark. Active bearers carry Thread-Shimmer, a faint glow in the hair in low light.
The Quiet Weight A Yukari voice settles instead of projecting, and a room it speaks in grows slightly more attentive, as though the walls had leaned in a fraction of an inch. People who sit across a table from one come away with the same feeling: of having been measured, thoroughly and without hostility, by someone who will remember the measurement for life.

How they flex
Black and silver, silver threading through dark, and you can pick them out at fifty paces by how little they are doing. The field coat is crow black, cut long and plain and close in the arm so nothing swings, in good southern wool with a sheen on it like a wet feather, and the eye goes straight to the cuffs. The silver at the cuff is a count. One fine line of thread goes in for each soul the wearer holds or has held, and since a Yukari never stops knowing what she has known, nothing is ever unpicked. A young Confessor has a line or two and shows them off shamelessly. An old Shepherd’s silver has climbed to the elbow. A Ferryman’s sleeve runs silver to the shoulder, and the Long Fields sergeants who see one at a muster go quiet and start doing arithmetic. Forging it is a serious offense in the Reach, and fools do it anyway to get seated at dinner.
In the house it is Yukari gray, dark cloth with a thread of silver-violet down the seams, soft and heavy, and bare feet on the boards. The Thread Guard wear crow-black harness with no crest, since the wearer has already been told what you are. The bracket fighters of the house wear a crow-black sash and make a small polite bow, and it has become the most frightening sight on the Accord’s sporting calendar. Ward-carvers go in chalk-white aprons with the mark of their station. The founder’s mantle, high-collared, wide-sleeved and worked inside with sigils from the first household, is Legendary and worn by every head of the house, and no southern lord who has stood in front of it has failed to find something to look at on the floor.
Their weapons are a deliberate insult. A Yukari who means business has a paper fan, a kitchen knife or a very ordinary narrow blade in a scabbard with no fittings worth stealing, because the point of the exercise is to be holding something where you are about to be. Lord Naiser, a Grandmaster, goes about with a Rare longblade that assayers laugh at until they have seen it used. The house gives its steel no names until a thing is finished. What it does own in quantity is ink.
A poor cousin from the lower valleys wears homespun dyed in oak gall, black that has gone a little green, with the silver worked in one cuff by her mother and darned where it wore. She will read your entire inheritance before you have finished looking down on it.
Lineage Traits
[Trait] The Breath in the Blood — Ashura’s Continuance
Ashura is the Soul Plane in some sense careful people decline to define, and a little of her runs in this blood and lengthens everything it touches.

Spiritual decay reaches them slowly. Curses, soul-rot and the long wearing-down of a Core all arrive late.
They stay young longer than most. The fuller the blood, the longer the line, and it has been thinning since the first mornings.
Refined sensory filtering strips noise from what they take in, so they can read a room’s real signal through a crowd, a glamour or a haze.
It slows ruin and never stops it, and it does nothing whatever about being hit very fast.

They will outlive most of the people who stood near them, and every one of those people will still be in there with them.
[Trait] The Long Memory — Retention as Birthright
The Core of this house does not put things down.

Faces, debts, sums, the exact words of a promise and the hour it was made stay available for life, in bearers and in the merely Regarded alike.
It works as a lean on Gnosis Retention that needs no training, and every clerk in the South would trade a hand for it.
Whatever has been read by Mushō or the eye stays whole. A Yukari cannot be bribed into forgetting and cannot arrange it for herself.
Below a tenth of reserve, where anyone’s Core begins to fray, this works in reverse, and she may start getting your name wrong, or her own.

Other families bury their dead. These ones have them all in the same room.
[Trait] Kin of the Threshold — The Dead Answer
Spirits and the dead know the family’s smell, as a dog knows who feeds it.

The Core starts to hear years early. A valley child who says there is a man in the pantry is taken seriously and asked what he wants.
The dead reply more readily to a Yukari at every rung, and Echo Beasts, what was left of the dead with nothing to say who that was, hesitate when one looks at them.
Since the split the drifting dead come to them unasked. Valley households put out a second bowl, and there are nights when the Enclave’s gate-runners go down the road with lamps to bring in somebody’s grandfather.
This is a trade and not a safeguard. Whatever is drifting knows where you live too.

Every house in the South has a door for the living. This one has been answering the other door since the first morning.
[Trait] The Quiet Weight — Presence Without Volume
Where another house’s Pressure heats a room, a Yukari’s turns the lamps down.

A coat of Yukari aura dims the air around it, and the higher the Stage, the lower the room goes. A great one walks into a feast and every flame in the hall leans away and burns small.
A room under it goes attentive. People find they have stopped chewing, and they hear themselves explaining.
Lower Stages feel seen before they feel afraid, and the unwoken usually look away first, on a sound folk instinct.
It shows nothing, roars nothing and intimidates no one who is too stupid to mind, and the Hot Tun brawlers have made a whole art of being too stupid to mind.

The Moto make a room feel judged and the Zettari make it feel heavy. A Yukari makes it feel that somebody has opened a file.
[Trait] Thread-Marks and Shimmer — The Bill Worn on the Skin
The body keeps its own account of what the eye has cost.

Thread-marks spread by years of use, so a stranger can read roughly how long a bearer has been looking and how hard.
Under strain they light silver going violet, a tell that cannot be hidden or trained away, and good duelists watch the backs of the hands.
Thread-Shimmer in low light marks an active bearer in any dark room, which makes the family poor at sneaking and very good at being noticed in the doorway at exactly the moment they meant to be.

Everybody else’s magic spends itself and goes. This family wears the receipts.
[Trait] The Taken Name — What the Telling Does
A name asked for after the whole account has been heard is a vow, and a vow is small Fate, spent from the soul’s own share and pulling nothing down.

It lays a binding on the Attraction Layer that every Reishi in the house can see and the Enclave’s wards know, in blood kin and chosen kin alike.
That is all it gives, and it is enough to get you into the long hall, the yard and the register. It gives no eye and no Regard.
It holds. Kasane Byakuya took it in the valley at fourteen, before the stone, and the house has counted her its own ever since, whatever else she was.
It can be refused with honor. Those who refuse are not pressed, and they get their dinner.

The tie makes kin, and it is the one thing in this family anyone can walk in and ask for.

Doctrine and Arts
Karasu no Michi, the Crow’s Road
The fighting style of the Yukari yard comes down to two teachings: stand where the outcome needs you and move a thread before you draw a blade. Its whole curriculum is the patient removal of every occasion for a fair fight. Know the man first. Know his hurts, his temper, his seconds, what he owes and what he had for breakfast, and be standing with a very ordinary knife where he is about to be. A Moto reads a seam and puts a sword in it, and a Yukari has done much the same thing and only looks more bored about it.
It is a good deal louder than its reputation, because it has to be. The young ones shout their moves, because they are young, because a bracket crowd pays for it, and because the Moto next door have been bawling the names of their Works across battlefields for a thousand years and somebody ought to answer. The old ones do not raise their voices. There is no call to shout at something you have already got.

The counter to the yard is to be ugly. Fighters with no form to read, who do not know what they will do next and do not care, drag a Yukari onto ground where elegance buys nothing. And anyone who fights silent gives Iinaoshi no word to catch, at the price of a weaker working, which is why the great killers of the South have never much minded the Crow House and the showmen have never stopped complaining.
At war, and what they swore
Three things a commander will pay nearly anything for: a line of the dying held in place until the surgeons reach them, every soul on a valley’s field read and told over company by company, and the wounded of the other side slipped all at once, so that the enemy’s line, which has spent the morning hearing them, hears them stop. That last one nobody puts in the song, and everybody puts in the terms of surrender. The Yukari did all three across forty years, and on the bean field at Ōmagari a quartermaster’s clerk named Yukari Sayo sat nine days on a war drum with three hundred and twelve people’s dying in her eyes. The muster book has her down as a clerk.
The house has since sworn that its knowledge goes out to mend and never to take, and the Academy has ruled in open session that a wyrm is not a war. It says nothing about what happens to people who come up the road to start one. Lord Naiser told the Sovereign of Kushara, in the long hall, that anyone who reached into the spirit side and pulled something out to throw at another house would be annihilated, and he told him over tea.
The carvers and the Reach
Spirit work includes writing on things, and the craft the Reach is built on is a cousin of the eye: ward-cutting, in which a line on a stone carries the carver’s say on what the stone is. A Cymorath-attuned carver hears the substrate before cutting, and completes a sentence the stone was already trying to say. Most carvers are not Yukari by anything but the Academy’s letterhead, and that was the design. Niran Yukari, called the Crow of Fate, came up the coast at thirteen fixing gate posts for a meal, and every town he left an apprentice in found itself, some years later, asking to join. The arithmetic was the argument. The full account of the Reach, the Council of Threads and the Proving is the realm’s own.
Culture
Language. The old Japonic of the house for formal work, plain Common for everything else, and a family habit of finishing other people’s sentences that outsiders do not love. Names are two-element compounds on thread, crow, stone, water and grief, up to five in a life, and which one a person uses for you tells you exactly how close you stand. There is no worse manners in the valley than guessing up.
Customs

The Telling. The name is given only to those who hear the whole account of what it costs and then ask for it. Refusing is honorable and nobody presses. A person marrying in sits the same account, on the same floor, and is expected to have questions.
Five names. A childhood name; an adult name chosen at the Telling; a calling-name for intimates; the true name, spoken only in Council, at a Proving or before Senri’s stone; a posthumous name given at death.
The cut nape. A fighter who loses cuts a lock from the back of the neck the morning after and lays it on the fire, and goes about with a bare nape until it grows back. Nobody speaks of it.
The tea. No word of business is spoken in a Yukari house until the guest has tasted the tea, bitter with small white flowers. Whatever is said after, the tea was shared.
The dead. The dead are laid in rows facing east with lamps between, and their names are read over them before the light comes. The house holds that death is a return.
The empty place. On the first night of each year a place is set at the long table for the mother of the house, and nobody sits in it.
Grief. The house treats grief as a known catalyst of deeper sight and says so plainly at the Telling, as a risk to prepare for.
The walk past the door. Before their first Telling every child is walked past a clean room in the east wing with a good view of the cedars. In it Yukari Tadashi has been in the middle of a sentence for thirty-one years, with a stroke waiting on him to the hour, because his wife Hisano looked up and has not looked anywhere else. She is by every measure the kindest woman in the house. The child is asked what they would do. The house does not give an answer.
The breakfast round. Every morning at the Enclave a child goes round with a bell and a list and says good morning, by name, to the people nobody else can remember. It is a chore, they draw lots for it, and they are told why. There are people in the house whose whole claim on the world is a nine-year-old with a bell.
The Looking-Away. Nobody can hand on a Hold. So when a Holder grows old, the register names a day, and everyone she is keeping is told it, and their families, and their physicians. The surgeons come in. The house lays out a meal. She takes each one in the order the wounds stand, and she looks away, and the meal is eaten afterward, whatever is left of the party. The South’s bookmakers have long since stopped pretending not to ask for the dates.
The relit lamp. A child with the undivided eye is told everything every single night, by whoever is next on the list, until they can bear to hear it and go to sleep. The family takes it in turns, as Ashura did. Neighbors bring food, and the visiting courtesy is condolence.

Words · The crow perches. The crow watches. The crow remembers.
The teachings
The Yukari teachings are short, and every one of them is something Ashura or Senri said or did in front of witnesses.

The tie makes kin. The bond decides who belongs; the blood follows it.
Tell them everything. Nobody in this house pays for a sight they were not told about.
See without taking. A thing looked at well is left as it was. A thing looked at badly is changed, and the looker is to blame.
Master the innards. Senri’s line, the one on the stone.
Stand where the outcome needs you. Move a thread before you draw a blade.
Knowledge goes out to mend. What the house knows may leave the valley to heal and never to take.

The root of all six is Null-Light, Ashura’s own way of seeing.
Who they marry, and what the valley gets
They marry whoever asks for the Telling and survives it, which has kept the bloodline a good deal wider than the Moto’s. The Lambert match brought figures into the record. For generations the house swapped its children for a summer with the white Byakuya line, as if the war were weather, until the Hiroe burnings ended that, and there are old women on both sides who still write.
The valley folk pay the house a tithe and the house remembers who was late. They look away from a Yukari’s eyes as a matter of course, and they believe that when a child’s corona comes in a parent starts to weaken, that a true name pulls the thread, and that a child with a quiet life is to be pitied. What they get for this is that no stranger has come up their road unweighed in living memory, and that when somebody’s grandmother will not go when she should, a thin person in black comes down the hill at dusk, sits with her until she will, and asks for nothing but a bowl. “You haven’t eaten,” says whoever loves you, setting it down beside tools gone cold. A Yukari says it to the woman’s daughter. Servants of the Enclave go barefoot, get the house’s long look in time, and know more than most lords. Nobody in the valleys has ever been known to steal from the Crow House, largely because there is no point.
The House Now
The house is led by Senri’s eldest, Lord Naiser Yukari, from the Cedar Enclave on its hilltop above the Yukari valleys, east of Sum-gol. Naevra keeps the archive and the register of every birth and death in the valleys, and reads the threads of a room so easily that they come out round her face unbidden, fine as cobweb in a barn door. Seradris is the youngest of the three.
The Enclave is the oldest standing seat of the family: cedar halls stepping down the slope on limestone footings, beams gone red-brown and resin-dark, bark-shingle roofs furred silver-green with lichen, a covered walk round a court of raked white gravel, and three standing stones in shawls of moss that throw no shadow at any hour. A stream runs under the floor of the long hall and talks to itself all night. The house’s lamps burn a clear honey-gold in cedar hoods and do not flicker, and the crows that come down out of the cedars to sit on the rails are glossy as wet ink, their feathers taking a violet sheen in the sun. Below it on the drowned valley floor stand the shrines nobody has ever let go, red streamers renewed each year, and the Unlit Shrine, which goes on down past where any reflection stops. A thread-reader will not look at it for long.
The wider family
Ashura’s elder children founded lines of their own across the long Third Epoch, and their descendants are the cousins of the yard, the archive and the outlying valleys, each carrying the eye in one of its eight types or carrying none of it and taking the name anyway. Chosen kin stand beside them by the same right. A child of another house who hears the Telling and asks for the name receives it; Kasane Byakuya took it in the valley at fourteen, before Senri’s stone, and the house has counted her its own ever since.
After the war
The forty-year war ended with the Yukari standing and the Seikai gone, and it ended in the house’s own courtyard. The Zettari struck the valleys in its last four years. The Seikai forced the seam. Senri went in, and Naiser broke the working on the slope above the river, and the house came home to lay out more than four hundred of its dead in rows facing east, with lamps between.
The wound in Ashura has not closed. Memory leaks out of her into the world: the dead of that day came back into the courtyard as faint silver shapes repeating one gesture each, and the living began forgetting the faces and calling-names of the people they had just lost. Springs come slowly in the valleys now. Midwives write down how long they wait for a child’s first breath. The old die late, and some do not go when they should. In the south, springs that the Seikai drank from taste wrong to anyone with the tongue to taste them.
The house’s terms to the other powers, given in the long hall, follow from all of it: no Yukari knowledge used for war; no Yukari name carried as a banner; no one touching the spirit side without Yukari counsel and teaching; every promise made in the hall entered in the Yukari record. The Yukari say they want nothing more than the spiritual balance of the world kept. They also keep the Immortal Cross, and they have kept it since the first morning.
The Cross cannot be closed now in any case. With the seam open the Soul Plane’s recognition stutters, and the house holds that a Cross closed in these years would slip and kill its bearer quicker than if it had never been touched. So every family that has ever wanted a thing from the Yukari now has one more reason to care whether that wound heals, and the Yukari have noticed which of them have stopped asking.
The Other Houses
At the Table: the seventh house
Of the seven Southern Warlords, the Yukari are the oldest blood and the least interested in ruling it, and they are the only house whose members are all volunteers. They held of the Mahou emperors for three hundred years at a tribute of one crow a year, and entered it. On the first day of autumn in 602, when the Emperor Rokju called his roll and the South stopped answering, the Yukari sent the crow, and it sat on the balcony rail for about as long as it takes to read a name, and left. After that they simply went on sitting where they were.
The warlords’ table has sat at the Cedar Enclave since the war, because every house wanted every promise entered in a record somebody else was keeping. The southern rule is that a warlord has a price for everything and the price is never only silver, and the Yukari’s is a promise put on the record. They tell the Lamberts’ clerks where the figures are off, and the Lamberts tell them, since the record has to agree. The Yan sell a horse and keep its name, and the Yukari have a copy. Maud Corwen has not yet asked them to walk her springs from mouth to source. The Ryu ask very good questions about harbor dues. Gerrit Marrick considers them the only people in the South who have never once tried to hire him, and finds that restful, and checks his feet at noon.
The Mahuo, who were carried
The Mahuo were carried at the front of other people’s armies until there was nothing left of them but the carrying, the Yukari fought under the excuse of protecting them, and then the Yukari killed them. The house says so. It says the Moto stood back and let it happen, because a house turned into a symbol is very easy to kill and nobody weeps for a symbol, and it tells this in the long hall and at the Tellings, against itself, and tells it well. That is why it swore off banners. Lord Naiser has promised the Mahuo royal line its seat back, and Cozbi Mahuo, Head of the House, has declined to accept anything from anyone who ever carried his name. The couriers run between the two seats every week and the courtesies are perfect. Since the split the Sum-gol Post has also been laying hauntings for a fee, in olive coats, with no Yukari counsel asked or wanted, and the terms given in the long hall say what they say. Nobody at the table expects that to stay a matter of courtesy.
The Seikai, who were never kin
The Seikai were a house that reached the Soul Plane alone. They had no Epoch in their blood and no Yukari to teach them, and they got there anyway, by discipline and by nerve, which is a thing no other mortal house has ever done. No Yukari carries Seikai blood, and no Seikai ever carried Ashura’s.
Their nature was the Null. Their arts ran through Mortalis and Nihiloth, the cold of the Still Gate and the clean cancellation of a boundary, and they worked precise and still, with no wasted motion anywhere. They saw the spirit side by opening it. Every look they took was an incision, and every incision changed what they looked at. They called a Yukari’s gaze the Crow’s Audit and used the phrase the way other people use the word inquest, because they feared being seen through far more than they feared being beaten.
The Yukari tell the end of the Seikai against themselves. The house held its knowledge close and let it be known that nobody outside the family could reach the spirit side; when the Seikai reached it on their own, there was nobody to show them where the edges were, and a house that had already decided they were a threat. A Moto who reads fate came to them and told them what they could become. They reached for what cannot be arranged. They forced the seam in Ashura, drank from the southern Wellsprings to do it and put back what has fouled those springs since, and on the slope above the river Naiser Yukari broke their working and the people who held it. The house believes the Seikai were reaching for what the Immortal Cross keeps. While they lasted, the Seikai never said.
How the house stands with them now is the least comfortable thing it has to say, and it says all of it. Lord Naiser told the Sovereign of Kushara to his face that the Seikai were the Yukari’s own making, by a refusal to believe anyone else could understand, and he called that insolence. Three things follow.
The road they took is still in the house. Null-Light with the Light taken out is Mugan, the Unseeing, the Seikai’s own way of looking, and it is the sixth Regard. It is taught to no one, and it turns up about once a generation, unasked for, in somebody who has lost a great deal. The house has two rooms at the back of the Enclave for its own who tried, and they are well kept. Every Yukari knows that the worst thing the Seikai ever did can be done with the family eyes. Only one Seikai document survives in the Archive, and it lists six looks, with Mugan first and no Zenkō at all, and calls the Yukari’s seventh a kitchen story.
They are not all gone. The house reads the slope as finished and the springs as not. Something still feeds what is wrong with the southern water, and the Enclave’s terms name a Seikai remnant as one of the things it will annihilate. One name has come back to the Council’s ears more than once, of someone who outlived the house Lord Naiser broke, and the Council does not say it aloud. A remnant of a people who reached the spirit side alone is the only thing in the South that this family is known to lose sleep over, and it will not say whether that is because of what such a survivor could do or because of what such a survivor might be owed.
The left arm of the Cross is theirs. Black glass, cold at every hour. Closing it asks for an understanding of what a mortal can reach alone, and why reaching alone ended in a cut. So the house’s own immortality test requires someone to have understood the Seikai wholly and not to have followed them, and most of those who were brought to try could not seat that arm, since a mortal who has understood what can be reached alone has usually already reached for it. The second teaching says tell them everything, and the first says the tie makes kin. The register has a page ruled and headed for the day a child of that house walks up the road and asks for the Telling. There is nothing on the page, the elders have agreed to give the Telling if it comes to that, and they have not been able to agree on anything else.
The Zettari, respect across the threshold
The Zettari were forged by Aegor in the Second Epoch, Path-born, dense in the body, their Crystals built for the translation of immense physical force, their blood answering to Matla and to the Sands of Kushara. Their Origin Eye reads the point where a thing began. The Ketsumyōgan reads what a thing is tied to. The Yukari eye is relational and the Zettari eye is sovereign, and each house has always understood exactly what the other’s sees.
What the Zettari know is endurance by witness. A Zettari-forged thing is declared trustworthy once, before a witness older than the speaker, and it holds that law from then on; a Zettari body that survives a strain grows harder against that strain; the Sands keep a lineage’s memory. When a Zettari wall began to fail they could feel the stress in the stone, and a Yukari could tell them why. The two houses gave each other respect, in the Zettari sense of the word: the acknowledgment that another’s function is lawful and complements one’s own. The Zettari struck the Yukari valleys in the war’s last four years all the same, and the Sovereign of Kushara has since come to the long hall to talk terms over the tea. When a Zettari meets a Yukari, the response is typically a nod, and it is returned.
The Moto, fear worn as policy
The Moto were chosen by Bara and carry the Scribe’s mandate; their sight reads the threads as an administration to be kept. The fear between the two houses is as old as Ashura’s first children and it is jurisdictional. The Yukari eye reads the same threads the Moto govern, with an intimacy the Shingan was never built for, and the Moto have the fear of a scribe who finds that someone else can read his hand and, worse, the words he chose not to write down. They tried to fold the family into their offices more than once. Senri refused them in a sentence. The Yukari hold that it was a Moto voice that talked the Seikai into the seam.
The worst insult in the valley is ledger-eyed, and it means somebody who sees people as entries, and it means the Moto, and every Yukari who has ever used it has then gone home to a family archive with a great many people in it. Both houses know this. At weddings where the two meet, they have been known to read each other’s cards aloud.
Limitations and Soul-Costs
[Curse] The Long Look — What You Know, You Keep
The price of Null-Light, and the reason for the Telling.

What you hold, you must keep looking at. When you look away, everything held slips at once, so the longer the Hold the worse the release, and all of that lands on someone.
You cannot stop knowing what you have known. Every soul ever held stays in the Core, whole, for life, and nobody has ever found a way to give a known person back.
An old Shepherd carries every deathbed she ever sat, entire, in the same place she keeps her own name. Below a tenth of reserve she is not always certain which of them she is.
A holder of one soul learns to sleep the way a mother sleeps beside a sick child, with the one thing kept in mind, and she never has a whole night again. Nobody has managed it with a field, since a looker who truly sleeps has looked away.
A hitter gets stronger and stays more or less the person who started. Each rung here means knowing more people more completely, for good.

A Moto pays in blood and reserve and a job left undone. The reserve comes back and the rest does not.
[Curse] Going Shadowless — The Slow Vanishing
Holders grow shadowless themselves, and it comes on by inches.

People forget their faces and do not feel their regard. A shopkeeper who has served one for thirty years will greet her as a stranger, and a husband will start to set one fewer place.
By sixty, nobody outside the house could say what Yukari Sayo looked like, and the song has the color of her coat wrong.
The end of the road is someone nobody but the house remembers is there. It keeps those people on its books with great care, since nobody else will. This is the real reason for the long table, the register and the child with the bell.

The family that knows everyone ends by being known by no one. The stones in the court were the warning.
[Curse] The Threadburn — The Eye’s Own Bill
A mortal Crystal was never built to carry an Epoch’s sight.

Prolonged use stresses the lattice where the three layers meet. Phantom threads show up that do not exist, and the mind starts sorting everything it sees into causal chains whether the eye is open or not.
Emotional flattening is the part they warn you about. Continuous soul-thread data makes it steadily harder to feel a connection as opposed to seeing it. Yukari Hisame could see the thread between herself and her sister, amber to the last fiber, and could have told you its weight and its age, and she read her sister’s letter twice looking for the part of it she was supposed to feel.
Sustained paired use can empty a well-developed Crystal in minutes.
At the very top Sovereign Weave and the deep Danshi severances burn the bearer’s own fate-threads as fuel, and the Yukari who have used it have, without exception, died young.

The more clearly you see the web, the less you belong to it. The family calls this the Paradox and sets a place for it at dinner.
[Curse] Keeping — The Kindest Cruelty
Obsession Force is what recognition becomes when a bond is no longer honestly witnessed. A Regard has its own version, with no thread in it, and the house says the word as other families say the name of a drinking uncle.

A Hold begun for love can go on for no reason anyone could defend, and every day it goes on, the bill for stopping gets larger. Ask Hisano.
Since nothing arrives and nothing comes back, a soul can be kept for years by someone it would not know on the road. Ask Bartlemy Goss.
The holder is usually the kindest person in the room. The house has heard a great many answers to what it asks at the door, and it does not give one.
See without taking is the third teaching because this is what taking looks like here.

Nobody has ever been kept by someone who did not mean well. The house would like that noted, and it would like you to think about what it means.
[Curse] The Insolence — The Family That Knew Best
This one the house named itself, in front of the Sovereign of Kushara.

A family that sees everything finds it very hard to believe that anyone else has understood anything. That belief made the Seikai.
Its terms now say that nobody touches the spirit side without Yukari counsel and teaching. Other houses have pointed out what that sentence is, and the family has noticed.
It offered the Mahuo a crown, and its own record says who slaughtered them. Good intentions are entered in the same ink.

The Moto’s error, they say, is to want to control the fate of other peoples. It is a very fine line, and they are drawing it themselves.
How They Stand Against the Three Paths
A Body enemy is the oldest answer, and it is a simple one. Get there. A spear does not care what you mean, a fragile body dies out of position, and a hitter who has never been hurt and is wearing good boots gives a Slip nothing to finish. But Armor and Durability do not cover the soul, a matter-reader has nothing to read on one, and the Crow has seen the charge from sixty paces and knows about the knee.
A Spirit enemy is the one person who can feel the Long Look on the Core and go for the hand behind it, and the only one who can spoil a Yukari’s say with another say. This is the fight the house has trained hardest for, the one that ended on a slope above a river. Anyone who has come to the Soul Plane without Yukari teaching is by the house’s own terms a matter of concern, and by its own confession the reason for the last war.
A Fate enemy can move what the look depends on, and every Regard depends on something: a wind that puts the smoke in her cousin’s eyes, a messenger who arrives at the right moment. Spirit survives by being right, and one wrong read is enough. Then again, every pull is made by a soul, and it shows on the Core before it lands. The Moto can read a Yukari’s threads as she can read theirs, and each house has spent a thousand years wishing it could not.
Final Definition
The Yukari are the family of the Third Epoch, a house as old as the Soul Plane’s waking, born to Ashura and kept up since by birth and by asking. Their bodies are lean and breakable. Their Cores hear early, keep everything and are answered by the dead. Their eye sees what everything is tied to, and for those who will pay for a second road it can cut. Their instrument, Null-Light, is the far end of the Spirit road, seven Regards under one law, and it can stop a death or finish one from across a valley without touching anything at all.
They will not rule you. They have sworn off your wars and your banners, they will mend what they can, and they will tell you everything, because the mother of the house would not let one of her children pay for a sight they had not been told about. Then they will write it down. They killed the Mahuo and say so. They made the Seikai and say so. A man of theirs is standing inside an Epoch’s wound right now, holding it shut, and they have not given him a posthumous name. Somewhere in your market there is a stout woman with a good recipe for honey cakes, and you may wish to look at the ground.
The crow perches. The crow watches. The crow remembers.
Beneath it, on a slab of the valley’s limestone set at the height of a seated man’s eyes, the line that a child reads as a promise, and a young man as a boast, and anyone who has lived long enough as a question:
Master the innards, and the outer world is yours to command.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
TypeArchaic line with no Epoch behind it · hereditary house of kashira · keepers of the maOriginThe Eighty Isles, in a count that comes down from the Epochs and that no Measurewright will signFounderNone named. The keizu (the family’s recited line) begins with the gods who first walked the isles and has not yet been recited to its end by anyone livingSeatYasoshima, five island branches under hyōjō (councils of the house), with no king and no standing armyAnchorsShinma · keizu · chigiri (witnessed covenant) · kotoage · the western gate at NishimoriSignatureShinma, the keeping of the ma: the interval between any two things can be measured, witnessed and made to bear loadMaximThe ma must be carried

A hereditary house of kashira, an ie whose authority runs through keizu, through chigiri, and through the keeping of ma rather than through crown or conquest.
In most provinces the sacred stillness that belongs to the za and the moving tongue that belongs to the zetsu sit in separate blood, separate halls, separate halves of the hyōjō. The Yuno hold both in the same line.
That alone is why other houses watch them the way a village watches a fire that has learned to sit still.

Black Hob Turnstile had thirty-six ships, a monkey in a scarlet coat and the whole of the Kagura tribute, and in the summer of 478 he was the most famous pirate between the Old World’s north coast and the western shield. The Eighty Isles sent no fleet after him, because they have none. They sent Tamaki of the Kagura branch, seventy-one years old, alone in a reed boat with one cup. She climbed the side of his flagship in a brocade the color of a ripe persimmon, sat down on his deck, and declined to say a word until the cup had gone round, and his crews, howling with delight, let her. She served the sakazuki (the ordered cup, where the serving order fixes who outranks whom) in its exact order, the captain second to last, and each man who drank woke the next morning already set in his place before a house older than his language. Then she spoke, in kotoage, the bound oration of the Yuno. The sentence took about as long as lacing a boot, and by its last word thirty-six crews stood obligated by its grammar to give back what they had taken, to carry their dead to Nishimori and bury them properly, and to pay their captain every honor owed him. She folded the brocade across his shoulder and went home.
He never got it off. He spent three years giving things back, thinner each season, and he died still wearing it, and the monkey outlived him and is in the keizu (the family’s recited line), under a very respectable name. Tamaki never spoke again; the sentence had cost her the voice. She sat out her last eight years in silent watch on the western shore, and the house counts that as a bargain and tells its children the price at the same hour it tells them the story.
Foundational Identity
Their identity centers on shinma, the sacred and unbreakable relational interval running between person and person, the living and the dead, the land and the sea, the ie and the gods who first walked it.

Where other lineages inherit force that breaks, devours, commands, or foresees, the Yuno inherit the harder portion. They must keep the ma, mend it where it tears, and answer, in their own bodies, for every silence a broken ma leaves behind.

Core inheritance · Ancestral keizu recited without error back through more generations than any living Yuno has counted aloud, a discipline of kotoage sharp enough to bind a hearing crowd, and the keeper’s instinct for where a ma has thinned before it tears.
Reputation · Revered, unsettling in their composure, and politically almost impossible to move against, since even rulers who fear nothing else fear the house that both blesses the hyōjō and speaks for it.

Yuno means gentle, a temperament of calm water. Nobody who knows them calls it a peaceful name.
It is a warning wearing a soft word, because a ma, once it is old enough and wide enough, holds enough pressure to drown a village, and the Yuno are the only hands trained to touch it without flinching.

What they want and what they hold. They want the ma kept, by whoever is standing in it, for as long as there are people. What they hold that everyone needs is the thing a realm cannot make for itself: an oath that stays sworn, a truce that outlives its signers, a funeral the dead will accept. Courts mock them in public and send for them in private.
Origin of the House
The house’s own account starts at Hatsuhi with the first light on the first isle, and it will give you the figure of two hundred thousand years without being asked. On islands with nothing anyone would cross the water to steal, a people had no use for walls and every use for knowing exactly what they owed each other. The other old lines were given something by an Epoch, and the Yuno were given nothing. On their mainland shrines, Kureha-in-Mist in the west the best known, the same house in time grew a whole clergy of bell-keepers, ash-recorders, vow binders and grave chanters, and still disagrees with the island branches about whether that was a good idea.
The marriage. Muken Moto of the Kōkan Line took Ayame Yuno of the Kagura branch as his queen. Kharven believes it gained an ally, and the Yuno believe they placed an obligation. The world has noticed that the Yuno endure because the Moto stand behind them.
The House on the Crystal
The Soul Crystal is the soul, refining Aether (mana) into Essence (spiritual energy).

























LayerHow it runs in themWhat showsAether ShellThin, unhurried, seldom spent. Their aura is a stillness more than a coatRooms quiet around themEssence CoreThe working layer. It holds the keizu and reads every interval in sightThe keeper’s gazeAttraction LayerSpent on, never pulled through. A kotoage is paid for from the speaker’s own share of fateThe voice, in the end
What the Blood Gives
The Yuno have no Epoch behind them, and so no instrument: everything they do with the ma, they built. Their blood gives what any old line’s blood gives, four things and never a Path.

























SlotThe YunoThe eyeThe keeper’s gaze, which settles on the interval around a face and sees where a ma has thinned before it tears. It is a read and it moves nothingThe gripOn the Spirit road. In children marked at birth it shows before Glory as the gaze at its base; [[The Magic System/The Soul and the Climb/How Power GrowsThe stat leanResilience Oath and Continuity; Harmonics Stability; Dominion CommandLens affinitiesAnamnesis, Mortalis, Fixatio, Transference and Absolution, which go easier in this blood and lock nobody out of the rest
The Seven Tsutome are on the Spirit Path with Fate behind it, as a house’s habit and never its blood. Their Forms are Rite for the great labors, Sing for kotoage, and Bind for the cup, the brocade and the witnessed chigiri. Kotoage spends the speaker’s own share of fate and pulls nothing down, which is why it costs what it cost Tamaki.
On the rungs. A shrine attendant is Spirit I, what the road’s people call a Listener. An ordained kashira seated in a hyōjō is II or III, Answerer or Confessor. Branch elders are III and IV, Shepherd. The Kagura officiants who hold a convergence reach V, Ferryman, and it empties them. Fate climbs for the house as for anyone, and without a Work or a blessing it stops at the second rung, the Drawn, which is as far as the longest-kept vow in the house has ever carried it.
Shinma — The Keeping of the Ma
Every relation has a width, and a width can be made to hold weight.
Shinma goes well past holy magic and past etiquette raised to the level of law. It is the discipline by which the interval between all living and unliving things is measured, honored, defended, and, when torn, mended before the tear widens into catastrophe.
How it works, in plain words. A rigged mast stands on ropes pulling against each other, and scholars call the principle tensegrity: a structure whose strength lives in the tension between its parts. The Yuno hold that a marriage, a truce, a hall or a kingdom stands the same way. Everyone keeps a distance from everyone: who speaks first, who may come near, what is owed and for how long. That web of intervals is already bearing load, and most of the time no one has ever looked at it. The gaze finds a line in it, and the rite names that line aloud before witnesses, and from then on the Core of each person in it holds that line as part of what they are. Breaking it costs them from the inside. Nothing moves the odds and no fire comes of it, since this is a Spirit art and the only thing it has ever touched is what a person takes himself to be.

Their arts do not overpower a thing so much as force it back into right relation with everything it stands beside. Even their harshest workings carry the shape of ceremony: closer to a verdict than a massacre.
Because the Yuno are a house of kashira rather than conquest, their power always arrives dressed. A working that could flay a man instead arrives as procession, as judgment, as the folding of a brocade across a shoulder that will never be unfolded again.

The Seven Tsutome of Shinma





































TsutomeLaborKiyome · ConsecrationSets apart a threshold, a hall, a relic, or a body as sacred and no longer available to profane or unstable useAkashi · WitnessSeals a vow, a marriage, an accusation, an inheritance, or a confession beneath a truth the speaker cannot later unmakeYomiji · PassageGoverns the funerary crossing, the vigil, ancestor continuity, and the lawful movement of a soul from this shore toward the western gate at NishimoriWagō · ReconciliationBrings enemies, broken councils, and clashing Domains into a held space where contradiction can be carried without collapsing into warYurushi · AtonementAnswers curse pressure, inherited stain, and broken chigiri through confession, payment, and the slow work of forgivenessMuki-Naoshi · OrientationTurns a person, a hall, a relic, or a whole ie back to face its correct center when it has drifted from lawful balanceTōbō no Michi · Far WisdomThe highest and rarest labor: gathering memory, oath, passage, and reconciliation into a single sacramental act
The Saishiki
The greatest thing ever built on this discipline stood in the Ashen Hall for sixteen years. Saishiki, the Yuno rite of the woven oath, was carried out of Yasoshima by Ayame Yuno, whose title in the house was Zenma no Mamori, Keeper of the Whole Ma. The northern clans had a man’s word before witnesses and nothing more. She took those oaths, and the ceremonies and formal occasions of a kingdom, and wove them into one liturgy that bound the loyalties of the Banner Houses into a single structure, so that an oath in Kharven carried spiritual weight and could not be broken without consequence. They say she once received thirty hostile clans alone in a courtyard and had them rethreaded into three coalitions by dawn, and the wards on the royal children’s doors were the same weaving at a smaller scale. Her death removed the architecture and left the ceremony. The kingdom still performs it, and the load is no longer there, and what it was like to live under the Saishiki is the best argument for the Yuno and the best argument against any one person being able to do that.
What it costs, what limits it, who beats it
The cost is the keeper’s body. Every line a Yuno holds, she carries. A tear in a ma she has witnessed comes out of her as sleeplessness, blood from the nose, a limb gone cold, and a great kotoage takes something and does not give it back: a voice, a year, the use of a hand. Hōkō is burden, and it is written into how the art functions.
Its limits. It works only on what stands in relation. It needs witnesses and it needs time, because a sentence must be finished and a cup must go round. It binds what a person holds himself to, so it reaches the living, the dead and the places they have marked, and a plain falling rock is outside its jurisdiction. Nobody has reached Tōbō no Michi alone: it needs every branch that can be gathered under one roof.
Who beats it. Refuse the cup. Stop your ears, as sailors have done with wax since the Hob’s day, or kill the speaker before the verb, since a bound sentence takes about as long as lacing a boot and a crossbow takes less. Bring something that has no relation to anyone: a beast, a Hollow thing, a person who has truly been cut off from every tie, and a sworn runaway of the Russet Crown, on whom a kotoage finds no party to obligate. A Yuno on the other side can unsay it through Wagō. Fate can lean on what the rite depends on, a cup that spills, an old man’s cough at the wrong word. And a hard thing to say of a holy house: any plain soldier with a sharp blade, who has not been listening, is a very great danger to them.
Sacred Bearing
Skin · Yuno children are born already marked: faint lines beneath the skin at the wrist, the sternum, and the base of the spine, tracing shapes that echo the finished horimono before any horishi has touched them. The family holds that the ancestors mark the child first and the living carver only finishes what was already begun.
Gaze · A Yuno’s eyes do not settle on a face so much as on the interval around it: the exact width of ma a stranger keeps from kin, from land, from grief. Villagers say a Yuno can tell what a person owes before that person has said a word.
Presence · Even an untrained Yuno holds a stillness too exact to read as ordinary manners, the seated composure of chinza worn like a second skin. Rooms quiet around them without being asked to.
Voice · When a Yuno speaks in the register of kotoage, the sentence arrives with the weight of something already decided. The voice is rarely loud; the air in a hyōjō has been trained for centuries to receive that cadence as close to law.
Adornment · Ordained Yuno wear the kanmuri only at the gravest rites, hair bound close beneath it, skin oiled, a hossu or shaku carried not as a badge but as a second limb.
Dress · Brocade, always, and it says everything. At fifty paces a Yuno is one still figure in a very expensive color, folded and never flourished: persimmon for a Kagura elder, the pale silk and silver thread of a great ceremony, and the rest in the deep mineral dyes of the isles, every fold of it a stated rank and a stated debt. A nishiki of the old looms reads Legendary, and no one has ever seen a price, since a brocade that has been given cannot be sold. A poor cousin from a lime-burners’ branch wears one narrow band of it at the collar, repaired by three generations, and carries herself exactly as if the rest were there. There are also Yuno who carry a blade and a light of their own. Those arts are theirs, and the house does not list them.
Lineage Traits
[Trait] The Birth-Lines — Marked First by the Dead

The lines come in before birth and are finished by a horishi at ordination.
They warm when a ma is near tearing and when the wearer lies.
They are the blood’s claim on the Essence ladder, and a child without them may still be Yuno, and still be trained, and never quite believe it.

The earned ink finishes what the ancestors began, and the ancestors do not ask.
[Trait] The Keeper’s Gaze — The Width of Grief

She reads who owes whom, who has wronged whom and who has stopped speaking, across a room and at a glance.
Good ones read shrine geometry at forty meters.

Children of the house learn early that a mother always knows, and they learn why.
[Trait] The Unbroken Recital — Keizu in the Body

Layered memory of names, debts, pardons and broken oaths, recited into permanence.
The list reads back as a defense, since a soul that can say everyone it comes from is very hard to unseat.

Nobody has ever got to the end of it, and they keep the monkey in.

TierWellspringsPrimaryAnamnesis · Mortalis · Fixatio · Transference · AbsolutionSecondaryBenediction · Penance · Catharsis · Redemption · Oblation · PhreatisDifficultCataclysm · Fractura · Nihiloth, and Manganthra, whose go-between walks out of every bond the house exists to keep
Doctrine and Arts

Nasake before preference A Yuno is trained to ask what the nasake of the whole ie requires, not what flatters one voice inside it.
The ma must be carried Not every tension should be erased. Some must be housed, named, and ritually held until true wagō becomes possible.
Chigiri is architecture A sacred covenant, especially the chigiri between a brother and sister, is treated as a structural force that reorders reality once it is properly witnessed and kept.
Hōkō is burden Sacred service always costs the one who performs it. A kashira who takes on nothing has mediated nothing.


No ma stands alone. A tear in one interval echoes through the social, the spiritual, and the metaphysical alike, and the Yuno are feared precisely because they act as though that were always true.

Arts Shared by the Whole House
Ma-Jirushi, the Marking of the Ma · A woven working of spoken kotoage, Aether pressure, and gesture that renders the boundary of a sacred space visible, or half visible, around people, graves, or chambers.
Sakazuki, the Ordered Cup · Mastery of the ceremony’s exact serving order, used to fix rank, precedence, and spiritual law within a rite before a single other working is spoken.
Kotoage, the Bound Oration · Formal chiefly oratory turned technique: words shaped so precisely that a hearing crowd finds itself already obligated by the sentence’s structure.
Nishiki, the Debt of the Brocade · The brocade exchange used as a vessel that carries a sworn obligation across bloodlines and generations.
Chinza, the Vigilant Stillness · Seated, silent, watchful intercession on behalf of absent kin, patient toward an outcome it cannot yet see.
Naoshi-de, the Mending Hand · A touch-rite of healing and curse extraction, named for the old proverb of the stonefish that carries its own cure in its body. Intimate, and dangerous to whoever administers it.
Keizu, the Remembered Line · A mnemonic art through which names, debts, pardons, and broken oaths are recited into permanence, keeping the ie’s accounting honest across centuries no single memory could hold alone.
When It Comes to a Fight
The house does not fight, and it has made a long study of what to do when somebody starts. These are called in one low voice, and the name is usually the last thing you hear clearly.






























MoveMeaningWhat it doesHikae”Hold back”A half-visible line on the floor. Whoever crosses it owes a step before he may take another, and his leg knows thisOikaeshi”Returned to one’s seat”On anyone who drank her cup: the knees decide that this person has not been given leave to riseShaku-Uchi”The tablet’s stroke”A hardwood slat across the wrist, delivered with a verdict in it. The bone takes the wood and the hand takes the sentence, and it opensNishiki-Gake”The brocade laid on”The Debt of the Brocade, in the field, across a living shoulder. Bookies will not take odds on anyone who has seen it done
The Five Sacred Branches









































BranchNatureBearingFavored TsutomeHatsuhiThe oldest and most sacred line, tied to the first light and to the shaping of the isles. Public sanctification, coronation, civic vows, and the rites owed to a newly raised titleUnhurried and formally dressed even outside of rite, brocade worn folded rather than displayedKiyome, then AkashiNishimoriNight vigils, funerary rites, ancestor tending, and the silent maintenance of the western gate, where the living road ends and the road to Yomi beginsQuieter than the other branches, rarely speaks first, hands often resting near a hossu even at restYomiji, then YurushiIshizueThe shrine builders, keepers of the precinct and the raised ground. Spatial law, relic care, and the geometric discipline of ritual groundPrecise about distance and placement to the point of visible discomfort in an unmeasured roomKiyome supported by Muki-NaoshiNakadachiThe mediators, drawn most often to sit as zetsu in a hyōjō, carrying truce, confession, and the bearing of contradiction between hostile partiesQuickest to speak for the whole house, slowest to raise a handWagō, then AkashiKaguraSeated in the strait between the two great islands. The rarest branch, holding the grand seasonal rites and the most dangerous reaches of Tōbō no MichiThe only branch permitted to wear the kanmuri outside a coronation, and the only one whose members are trained from childhood to expect that permission to be resentedTōbō no Michi above all, with sanctioned reach into every lesser Tsutome beneath it
Training and Cost
Oratory discipline · Layered keizu, kotoage structures, funerary law, and the exact serving order of the sakazuki, all memorized before being trusted with public office.
Gestural discipline · The body trained as an instrument of rite: seated posture, the angle of a hossu, the timing of a breath through chinza, all held to account.
Emotional discipline · A Yuno who cannot carry grief, shame, contradiction, or fury without spiritual leakage is considered unsafe to seat in a hyōjō.

Every Tsutome carries its own corruption.
Kiyome can harden into fanatic exclusion. Akashi into punitive surveillance. Yomiji into necromantic attachment. Wagō into a suffocating false peace. Yurushi into cruelty disguised as mercy. Muki-Naoshi into authoritarian fixation.
And Tōbō no Michi into the tyrannical subsumption of every will beneath one.

Cultural Customs

Child naming A Yuno child receives two names: one spoken in the hearing of the whole ie, and one whispered over them at the cup by the eldest sōke present, recorded only in the family’s keizu.
Ordination mark Full ordination is marked by the completion of the horimono, worked by a horishi who is shown where the birth-lines already run, so the earned ink can finish what the ancestors began.
Marriage law Marriage is a witnessed chigiri between houses as much as between two people. Dissolution is possible only through a formal, recorded wagō between both ie.
Deathkeeping No Yuno is buried unwitnessed. The dead are washed, named aloud through their keizu, and given three full nights of chinza before the western road is opened for them.
Seasonal calendar A sevenfold cycle across the year, one season for each Tsutome, with the rarest convergence rites of Tōbō no Michi reserved for the years when every branch can be gathered under one roof at once.
The tide pools The Yuno keep no walls at home, and they will tell you this is the most dangerous thing about them. On the islands, beastkin, humans, half-elves and demihumans of six lineages draw from one watershed and raise children in the same tide pools, and a lime-burner or a reef-pilot has a seat at a feast and a known place in the order of the cup. A Yuno queen once told her small son what she thought a kingdom was for, and he has never managed to forget it.

Limitations and Soul-Costs
[Curse] The Price Told at Bedtime — What a Sentence Takes
A great kotoage is paid from the speaker’s own share, and it does not refill. Tamaki gave her voice. Others have given sight, a year of memory, or the use of the hand that poured.
[Curse] Answering in the Body — Every Silence Left Behind
What they witness, they carry. A keeper of many intervals has a body like an old ledger: chronic pain with no wound behind it, a cold limb when a marriage fails two islands away.
[Curse] Load-Bearing — When the Keeper Falls
An architecture held in one person goes when she goes. Kharven learned this. Nobody in the house has decided what the lesson is, and three separate branches have an opinion, and the convergence at Yasoshima goes on holding what it holds, by a very few hands.
[Curse] The Hand That Stands Behind — What the Moto Are Owed
The house that bows to no crown endures because a very large crown stands behind it. The chigiri binds in both directions, and Kagura has now given Kharven a daughter and got back a grave, a ceremony and a long silence.
How They Stand Against the Three Paths
Body. Their plain danger, because a spear does not care what you mean. A Yuno survives a Body fighter by getting him to sit down first, and if he will not, she has a shaku and a very short time. Spirit. A long, courteous and appalling contest, since Spirit is where they live, and a confessor of another school can read the same lines they do and pull at them. They win by having more witnesses. Fate. A pull moves what a rite depends on and they cannot stop it, though a working that leans on an oath finds the Yuno have already seen the thread thin, and they tend to know who is on the other end.
House Thesis

The Yuno are a dynasty of sacred relation. They pray over the world, and then they force divided things to stand in right ma with one another: force memory to answer keizu, force grief to answer Yomiji, force law to answer nasake, and force every fracture to reveal the larger weave it never stopped belonging to.
Their power can wound and dominate when the ma demands it, and it is still best understood as a gentle name worn over an enormous weight: the labor of holding too many truths in one hand at once, and refusing to let the world split clean where a deeper relation still calls to be kept.

The ma must be carried.
Yasoshima — The Eighty Isles
The islands of the Yuno.
An archipelago off the great land’s shore, in the open water of the great bight between the Old World’s northern coast and the Inner World’s western shield, belonging to neither quarter and administered by no crown. The Accord’s surveys record it, price its exports, and have never found a reason to send anyone twice.
The ground · Raised coral platform over karst, low, green and riddled with caves, with fresh water in lenses that go bad the moment anyone digs too deep. No metal, no coal, no timber worth a hull. This is the whole of the reason the islands have never been conquered. There has never been anything on them worth the crossing.
Ambient Essence · Moderate and, by every Measurewright reading taken, the most stable saturation recorded anywhere in the four quarters. Nothing drifts at Yasoshima. This is why Yuno rites hold across generations without correction, why the house has never built an array, and why the Accord’s Research Division has filed four separate requests to seat a resident Measurewright there and been declined four times without explanation.
The five branches · Hatsuhi, Nishimori, Ishizue, Nakadachi and Kagura are islands before they are branches. The Kagura seat sits in the strait between the two largest, which is why the rarest branch is also the one every other branch must sail past.
Standing · A confederation of ie governed by hyōjō, with no king, no standing army, and no charter with the Guild Accord. Kharven’s marriage to the house is the only formal tie Yasoshima holds to any mainland power, and the hyōjō ratified it as a chigiri between houses, which is not the same thing as an alliance between states and which the north has never fully understood.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Paths
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Transcendent Ascension Plane · Sovereign Metaphysical Realm · the Sands, in common speech
A place, and none of the three roads of the soul. The Zettari’s blood gives them an eye, a grip, a stat lean and lens affinities, as any archaic line’s does; what the Sands add is recognition, and the instrument, Matla, is tried here.

The supreme ascension plane of the Zettari lineage — a metaphysical reality existing above realms, dimensions, timelines, divine layers, and totality itself.
Not a kingdom, nor a conventional afterlife, but a sovereign plane where the perfected will, memory, and continuity of the bloodline converge.
Time exists only when acknowledged. Matter responds to identity. Essence is stripped bare into its purest form.

The Sands
The sands of the Paths are not ordinary substance. They are condensed lineage memory — the preserved resonance of every Zettari who has ever lived, fought, failed, risen, or died.

Every grain contains echoes of ancient sovereigns, forgotten wars, extinct kingdoms, and the accumulated pain of two hundred thousand years of survival.
Only beings acknowledged by the lineage itself may enter the Paths willingly.
Unauthorized entities attempting entry suffer immediate metaphysical collapse, as the plane rejects all identities it does not recognize as sovereign-compatible.

Rule and Residents
The Paths are ruled indirectly by Aegor Zettari, though even what appears there is never his true form — only manifested avatars capable of existing beneath the pressure of the plane.
Ancient Zettari Models, perfected sovereign archetypes forged by Aegor across countless epochs, reside there eternally as guardians, teachers, and living embodiments of the lineage’s ideals.

























FigureStandingAegor ZettariFounder of the lineage; supreme sovereign entity whose avatars govern the PathsShaka-Al Zettari, The WeaponAncient Zettari Model responsible for sovereign refinement through suffering and combatRevari ZettariCurrent inheritor of the True Everlasting Eyes and acknowledged sovereign of the fallen Kushara bloodlineThe Zettari ModelsAncient perfected manifestations embodying distinct principles of ascension, warfare, sacrifice, and continuity
What Happens There
Within the Paths, wounds may be rebuilt through lineage resonance. Essence may be refined beyond mortal limitations. Fate may be rewritten or anchored. Sovereign succession may be acknowledged. And the failures of previous generations are remembered so they are not repeated.

The Paths do not remove suffering.
They transform it into architecture.

Historical Importance
The Paths are the origin point of all sovereign Zettari ascension. Every major evolution of the lineage traces back to revelations, reforgings, or trials performed there. During extinction-level events across multiple epochs, the Paths preserved the continuity of the bloodline when kingdoms, civilizations, and worlds themselves collapsed.
The Everlasting Eyes originated from the metaphysical authority of the Paths, and many legendary Zettari techniques were first forged within its sands.
The plane also serves as the lineage archive of sovereign memory, containing preserved echoes of over two hundred thousand years of history — including the First Epoch Wars, the fall and rebirths of Kushara, the Seventh Fracture War, and countless forgotten sovereign catastrophes erased from mortal history.

The Paths are considered the ultimate proof that the Zettari were never merely rulers, but metaphysical survivors woven directly into the continuity of existence itself.

Connections

Kushara The sovereign homeland most deeply tied to the Paths through Crown Resonance and lineage authority.
The Everlasting Eyes Directly linked to the perceptual laws maintained within the Paths.
Aether and Essence systems The Paths exist above conventional Essence architecture and can reconstruct or overwrite damaged sovereign systems.
Fate architecture Sovereigns acknowledged by the Paths may have their fate anchored beyond external manipulation.
The bloodline All true Zettari maintain an unconscious metaphysical connection to the Paths regardless of distance or realm.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Zettari — Agano Sand and the Witnessed Temper
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Forge Culture · A Vow Clause Application

Where the Barrel Dwarves answer “what makes a thing trustworthy?” with time — cask it, age it, never rush it — the Zettari answer with witness and inheritance. A Zettari-forged object is not aged into reliability. It is declared reliable, once, before a witness old enough to matter, and from that moment the bloodline’s own Material Covenant Resonance holds the declaration in place.
The Dawi philosophy is brewed endurance. The Zettari philosophy is witnessed law.

The Material · Agano Sand
Agano — covenant, testament. A Swahili-derived word, in the register the Zettari already keep.
The sands of the Paths are condensed lineage memory. Agano Sand is a working measure of that sand, folded into the quench when a weapon or a piece of plate is finished.
Where Dawi pitch is aged for years in a fixed hold, Agano Sand needs no years: it already carries the memory of the whole bloodline’s history. The cost is not time. The cost is access. Only beings acknowledged by the lineage itself may enter the Paths without triggering immediate metaphysical collapse, so a smith cannot simply go and take it — it must come from, or through, someone the Paths already recognize.

The Dawi wait for the material to become trustworthy. The Zettari must be trusted before the material is handed over.

The Rite · The Witnessed Temper
A Vow Clause working, not a new kind of magic. At the quench, the smith — or the sovereign the piece is being made for — speaks a bound claim over the object before a Stone Witness: a ruin, an ancestral hall, a Path-linked relic. Per the Stone Witness Oath, it must be something older than the speaker. That claim becomes a standing law the object runs, exactly as a spoken vow becomes a standing law a Soul Crystal runs.
What it does · A Witnessed-Tempered piece inherits a scaled-down Ancestral Dominion Frame. Every significant strain the item survives, in the hands of whoever it was sworn to, makes it measurably more resistant to that same kind of stress thereafter. This is not indefinite hardening: it plateaus, the way the bloodline’s own combat maturity does.
What breaks it · If the piece changes hands outside the terms of the oath, its accrued memory does not transfer. This is not the Dawi’s Crystal-Coherence self-punishment, a cost paid by the oath-breaker’s own soul; it is closer to the Weight of the Blood, where failure feels ancestral rather than personal. The object simply stops recognizing the new holder as a party the law was made for. In the worst documented cases, Physical Plane Authority’s “hold shape” reverses for that bearer alone, and the piece becomes more failure-prone in their hands than an ordinary equivalent.

The blade does not punish the thief. It declines to know him.

The Trade Entry
Carried in the Standing Index’s B and A Grade table, in that index’s own format.



















EntryClass / Fid. / CarryWhat it doesRiskPriceAgano Sand · Grade B · provenance restrictedIII / A / 26Quenched into a forging at the Witnessed Temper, laid before a Stone Witness. The finished piece “learns” the strain it survives, for whoever it was sworn toRecognizes only the sworn holder. Sourcing requires a lineage-acknowledged Zettari’s sponsorship — an unsponsored attempt risks the same collapse the Paths themselves inflict on the unrecognized. No smith outside Kushara has explained why the sand only “listens” to a claim spoken over stone older than the speaker26.0
Not a Reskin · Set Against the Cask-Oath
