factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: House Caelward
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
TypeAvian Kin house · keepers of a Core and a court · one of the four Central WarlordsOriginThe first Kin to nest on the old bridge at Caelspire, before the Guild’s count beginsFounderUnrecorded. The house names a Warden Aelis, who is mainly a songSeatCaelspire, on the twin crags of the Violet Peaks, keeping the summit pool, the hoists and the bridgeAnchorsCurrent-Reading · the Cymorath pool · the Drop · the Molt Book · a dozen rival schoolsSignatureThe Long Read: every feather ever sold is still feeling the wind for themMaximStep Off
In the spring of 702 Count Merrow Tallis of Sedgeford, who took war seriously and could afford to, armed two thousand archers for the Harl Ford with forty thousand arrows fletched in the true gray molt of Ysmay Hask, called Long Afternoon, three times champion of the Gray Kites. He paid a king’s ransom, with a certificate for every sheaf, and he told his quartermaster to leave off the Windstair almanac as an economy, since the four silver seemed to him an impertinence. The morning of the battle was the kind of morning they paint, all bright banners and yellow flag along the water. Far overhead one small figure in gray and lilac hung on the wind and took no part, having been engaged by the other side for a modest fee. At the first volley the count’s archers loosed as one, the whole black flight went up with the sun behind it, and at the top of its arc nine hundred arrows left the rest. They peeled off like starlings. They turned over in the air with every man on that field watching, and they came back on a long lazy curve and went into the count’s own banner, his banner-bearer’s saddle, and the table where his breakfast had been laid out, in a cluster you could have covered with a door. A slip of paper came down after them, on an arrow, reading Four silver. Overdue.
The remaining thirty-nine thousand one hundred were goose feathers, dyed. They fell on the enemy and did what arrows do, and Count Tallis won the battle by a comfortable margin. He then sued his supplier for fraud on the thirty-nine thousand and the Gray Kites for assault on the nine hundred, and the court at Caelspire informed him that the first complaint had saved his life and the second could be settled by stepping off the bridge.
Every bowman in the center will tell you the moral: a true feather can be called home at bowshot, so buy fakes for the battles that matter. That has kept people from asking the next question, which I put to an elderly molt-seller at Windstair who had been drinking for some time. Why does a Kite sell her feathers so cheaply to both sides of every war? He looked at the arrow in my quiver, which was a good one, and he said that they do not sell them, exactly.
Who They Are
House Caelward has not been the strongest school on its own mountain for three hundred years, and it holds that mountain anyway. It keeps the Core’s hours, works the hoists and judges at the Drop, so a dozen clubs that despise each other must all come and shout at the Warden, at present Vessaly Caelward, called Nobody’s Landing, a tall gray-crested woman of fifty with one vane burned to the bone.
They want the stair uncut, the Core’s hours kept and the Peaks left to their own quarrels. What they hold that everyone needs is the weather. Half the battles of the center have been timed off a Windstair almanac, which is right more often than one reader on one crag has any business being.
Origin of the House
Nobody knows who built the bridge at Caelspire, and it was already old when the first Kin nested on it. For a long age the Caelwards were simply the best fighters on the mountain and the most resented. Somewhere about the year 415 the Warden of the day stopped entering the Long Step, and the schools were delighted. The Caelwards had just begun keeping a book of who bought which molt and where it went, and had worked out what twelve old readers with their arms in the Cymorath flow could feel of the world if the world was carrying enough of their feathers. They have been losing on Saturdays ever since, by policy.
The House on the Crystal
The Soul Crystal is the soul, which refines Aether (mana) drawn from the world into Essence (spiritual energy). The Kin draw it out of moving air and lay it along the vanes of the forearm, and the flight they have is earned that way.

























LayerHow it runs in themWhat showsAether ShellClean, light and extended along every vane. They call the aura coat the lift, and they argue about whether a good one should show at allA blue spiraling shimmer and curved trails where it was spentEssence CoreQuiet in most, and a Reader’s whole life. A molted vane keeps a trace of stamped Essence, and the Core goes on hearing itFar-off eyes, a tilt of the headAttraction LayerEach sold feather is the thinnest possible tie, held here. Thousands of them make a sort of permanent itchNothing a coil can read, and plenty a Warden can feel
Path lean. Body, then Spirit, as a tendency of the untrained soul. The eye. None. They read with the skin. The grip. On the Body road, the road of a soul’s influence on the physical world. A fledgling who has stepped off a sill and landed well has the skin’s knack of it years before Glory, though no coil reads anyone’s Mastery until Glory (Stage VI). The cap never lifts. On the rungs. Body I is a school senior, whose fletch in the hand obeys. At II, a captain’s feather carries it onward wherever that feather is. At III a champion knows a true feather of her school by recognition, and IV is a Warden who has given up a good many Saturdays. The Readers are often Body I and Spirit III, and could not fight a goose. Fate goes unwalked.
The Long Read
Every feather the Kin ever shed still feels the wind for them, and there are several hundred thousand of them in quivers, hats, pillows and army stores across the center.
What it is. A Kin’s vane is grown with her own Essence in it, stamped with who she is, which is why the fletch flies true. When it falls out in the molt the stamp stays on it, and so does a tie as thin as a cobweb. A single feather tells its owner next to nothing, a faint draft on one patch of skin. The Caelwards’ discovery was that the number of feathers changes what kind of thing you are looking at.
How it works. No one can forecast weather from where she stands, because a storm is the size of a country. What forecasts weather is many readings taken at once across a wide land: where the air pressure is falling, how fast, and what lies upwind. Scholars call it a synoptic chart, the view taken all together, and you would need ten thousand clerks with barometers. The house has quivers. Cymorath, the Air of Ascent, teaches a soul to read the world as a set of open ways, and twelve old Kin sit in the domed hall at the lip of its summit pool with their bare vanes laid in the flow, feeling a low front over Kingsbridge in eleven thousand fletchings. They also feel that eleven thousand fletchings have gone south by the Kessen road at an army’s pace. That sitting is the Sill, and what comes off it, once the clerks of the Molt Book have matched each draft to whoever bought that batch, is the almanac. Rain Thursday, heavy, you are in a floodplain, four silver. The house also knows where you are, because you bought the arrows.









































FormFromWhat it doesCostsReads the WindAny KinHer own skin reads the air’s whole shape, a front two days outNothing, and no way to stopThe Given FeatherStage IIIA feather shed by hand to a student or client. She feels you by it, and while she attends, Cymorath holds you up in a fall. This is the Stair Wardens’ whole contractAttention. Drop it, and you are simply a person fallingThe CallStage VI, Body I and upHer own molt within bowshot leans toward her or away. A volley’s true feathers can be bent by a spear-length, or brought home by a championA sharp bite of reserve per flight, and every shaft she turns she feelsThe SillStage VIII, at the Core, with the BookThe Long Read itself, for hoursEssence, sleep and a little more of herself each seasonThe Rain Come DueStage X or so, and a field already full of her school’s moltThe house’s one great art, about once in a generation. She finds a front with every reason to arrive in two days and brings it in now, through ten thousand small leans of air, until warm wet air lifts, cools and lets go of its water all at onceA vane burned to the bone, for good. She can only call what is already coming
Whether the rain that fell on Quartermaster-General Hasketh in 709 was forecast or called, the house has declined to say, and it billed him the same four silver either way.
Domain: the Last Step. A Domain is the territory where a high-Stage practitioner’s own law holds, opened by a Second Release from Stage VIII. Law: every stair ends here. The ground stays where it is and stops being anybody’s right, footing must be retaken each step, and those who have stepped off may stand on the air as they please. Fighters on the terraces sing the skipping rhyme to tell you it is coming.
What it costs. You feel what your feathers feel, and that includes where they end up. An arrow going into a man comes to its owner as a faint hot draft, and a champion who has sold her molt across thirty years of wars has never had a quiet night in any of them. A Reader gets the whole of it, and this is why the house’s fighters have been second-rate for three hundred years: its best are sitting down.
Its limit. Only the real molt counts, a small and costly part of what the market sells. Far-off feathers can be read and only near ones called. The Sill reads the air and has no idea what a general has in his head, and it goes blind where the air goes dead.
Who beats it. Fletch in goose, as the Marrick companies have done for a century. Carry crossbows: a bolt has leather vanes, costs about three coppers and has no opinion, and every fighter in the Peaks knows someone it brought down like a goose off a marsh. Burn or salt-boil a true feather and its tie dies. Fight on a dead calm inversion morning, when half a school is grounded. Or hold one of their feathers yourself and hire a good Spirit reader, since a tie runs both ways.
The Schools
Each school has its own peak, colors and songs, and its own molt through the Book.















































SchoolPeakColorsStyleStair WardensCaelspireViolet coatsCatch you, carry you over the gulf, discuss termsGray KitesWindstairGray and lilacLong patient glides, and an hour of insulting hymn. The best-selling fletch on the marketShrikesHighroostBlack and whiteDrop from above and hang the loser on a thorn treeLongdrop SwiftsTheir own toothSky blueHave never been seen to landOld MewsA goat and a ledgeWhatever is cleanFour very elderly women, who keep winning. They have known about the Book for two hundred years, and send notesLilac StairA well-appointed oneLilac and silverRich, bad, best songs
Physical Appearance and Dress
Light-boned and narrow, hard-eyed, with crests of feather from brow to shoulder and long stiff vanes down the outer forearm, in every color from sparrow to flame. They speak in high carrying voices, having learned to talk across gulfs, and do not lower them indoors.
At fifty paces it is the colors, the scarves and the sky behind them. Sleeves are slit from wrist to elbow so the vanes run free, and coats are cut short and laced flat. A Warden’s violet coat is Rare work in storm-silk with the white lining showing at each turn. Top gear goes light: a pinned-steel gorget, hippogrif leather, a heel-spur with a name. The Highroost champion’s is named Your Collar. A poor cousin in the lower town has one good scarf and a single true feather from a dead aunt that he will not sell.
Lineage Traits
[Trait] Current-Reading — The Air’s Whole Shape

The skin and vanes read pressure, draft and heat across a whole valley.
It gives first warning of anything that moves, including you, in the dark.

They can tell you are lying about the weather, which in the Peaks is the worst kind of lie.
[Trait] Hollow Frame — Very Little to Break

The bones are light and fast and the Reflex has no equal in the center.
The unwoken can glide on a good wind, if they are brave and have an appointment with a surgeon.
A heavy blow stays landed, and a broken wrist grounds a champion for a season.

Hard men with low ceilings have ended a good many careers in the indoor towns.
[Trait] Vanes Laid Along — The Earned Sky

True flight comes with training, as Aether pulled from moving air is laid along the vane.
A plucked vane grows back crooked and flies wrong for life.

Fighters step off the cliffs each morning in their colors, as a matter of routine, and call it going to work.
System Metrics



























































PrimaryLeanSignature Sub-StatsWhyDexterity+++++Celerity · Reflex · Evasion · SequenceThe definitive stat. They use the sky as a floorGnosis+++Forecast · Perception · VigilanceThe read of the air, and the Read of everything else for those who sitHarmonics+++Attunement · BreadthEvery feather is a very small harmonizationArdency++Alacrity · PenetrationOne heel on the join of the collar with everything she weighsTempering++Clarity · LongevityLong glides need a small flow held for hoursDominion+Sense · RadiusGood reach and little weightResilience−WardThin Shell, wide attentionVitality− −Hardly any AbsorptionThey are built to be elsewhere when it lands





















TierWellspringsPrimaryCymorath · AscensioSecondarySublimare · Sublimatio · Transference · Somnalis · LuminalisDifficultChthonica and Petralon (the ground’s own law against every way open) · Monolithion · Abython
Doctrine and Arts
Who holds the stair holds the peak. A Kin fighter stays above you, makes you pay for every step, and screams her moves down the gulf by name so the terraces can sing them by evening.








































MoveSchoolWhat it doesHighroost Stoop!ShrikesA drop from a thousand feet with everything she weighs and all the air she has packed behind her, into one heel on the join of your collarLong Afternoon!Gray KitesOne spear-length out of reach on the wind, and one cut each time you breathe in, until you sit downNobody’s Landing!Stair WardensShe gets under a falling enemy, catches him as a courtesy and carries him out over the gulf to discuss termsStep Off!Wardens, house styleA hammer of descending air on one spot, the downdraft that leaves a man’s footing lighter than his shoulders. The politest way a person is asked to leaveFine!Stair WardensA Warden’s catch with a sharp little dislocation in it, delivered with the amountThe King’s Hat!Any, in a matchAnything worn at the highest point of an enemy is suddenly in her hand, three hundred feet up
Culture
Language. Common with a great deal of school cant. Their names are light and old, and their word for anyone without feathers is groundling, applied with pity. Do not order eggs.
Rites.

The First Step. A fledgling steps off the family sill with a Warden’s feather at her wrist. If she does not land, the Warden catches her and sends the fine to her parents.
The Sill-Taking. A Warden chooses a Reader, always someone at the height of her fighting years, and she hangs up her colors in front of her school. Most of them believe she is retiring.
The Wind Burial. The dead go to the wind from the bridge, and every true feather they ever sold goes quiet at once. The Readers feel it.
The Bridge Hour. A fowler taken on any stair is walked up in the sight of the assembled schools, who for that one hour wear no colors, and invited to step off. There is nobody to catch him.

Who they marry, feud with and owe. They marry across clubs with enormous difficulty. The Scalebond hold an old fine over a bird. House Nobody has asked for the high roads: a Kite captain has carried sixty people over the range on her back, and a Shrike master charged the same sixty.
What commoners get. The hoisters’ company strikes once a decade, the lower town hangs from the crag on ropes and pins, and every child gets a school to hate with. A Stair Warden will catch them too, and the fine comes out of a common fund nobody admits to.
The sore point. The fowlers. Where the Accord’s rolls read the Kin as labor stock, licensed men with nets take them for their singing and their feathers. A plucked vane is still attached in every way that matters. A woman in a cage in a Concord market town can feel the feathers they took from her go to church on someone’s hat. The Caelwards sell their wind to the Accord each season and spit afterward, and the Warden has been heard to observe that a people who can leave are always the last to stop selling.
Limitations and Soul-Costs
[Curse] Vane-Ache — Every Arrow Ever Sold
Old champions flinch at nothing in the middle of a meal. It is a volley in a war two hundred miles away, going into someone, and there is no way to give the feathers back.
[Curse] Never Quite Here — The Price of the Sill
Readers forget their own children’s names and remember the rainfall at Pennycrown, and a Warden who sits too long has been known to give judgment on a case from the last century.
[Curse] Glass and Dead Air — One Hit, One Calm Morning
A bolt or a maul in a low room stops the song and most of the career. Still air and bled ground strip the school and the Read at once, and on an inversion morning the whole mountain is very polite.
How They Stand Against the Three Paths
Body. They beat him by never being in reach, for as long as the weather holds, and one good blow settles it if he closes. Spirit. Their fear: armor and height are no help, and a reader holding a true feather has a road straight to its owner’s Core. Fate. A storm that should not be there shows on the Sill, and they can do nothing about it, and a pull on what flight depends on (a strap, a gust at the wrong second) needs to win only once.
Final Definition
House Caelward is the people who stopped trying to win. For three hundred years they have sat on top of the only stair no army ever took, losing matches on purpose and selling their own molt to every war in the center. Anyone can buy the almanac. Your arrows send their regards.
Step off.
And in the Book’s oldest hand, on its first page: What we shed is still ours. Charge accordingly.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.filePath: Factions, Bloodlines & Institutions/Houses and Bloodlines/The Houses of the Inner World/House Corwen.md
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: House Corwen
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Overview





































TypeChartered family · Lessee of the Guild · the only southern House that holds its ground on paperOriginThe Wellheads, the steaming upland at the heart of the SouthFounderJennet Corwen, cask-steward to the Dynasty, who took out the lease in 602SeatBrightwater, at the head of the spring countryAnchorsThe lease · the brass keys · the hum of the kept poolsSignatureThe Hours: on leased ground a Corwen keeper holds the key to everyone’s magic, and sells it, and can turn it offMaximThe Water Keeps Faith
The Burning Ladder came up the Brightwater road in the spring of 689 in forty palanquins, because a sect of that standing does not walk. They were the coming power of the Midmarch, red lacquer and gold fringe and a marching band, nine core disciples and a Sect-Mistress at Stage IX, Invocation, and they had decided to have the use of the Wellheads’ training pools without the tedious part. They took the Cask Yards by mid-morning. They threw the wardens’ guard off the first terrace, roaring, because any practitioner on that ground fills faster than she has ever filled in her life. By noon the Sect-Mistress was sitting in the Warden’s own hot pool with her boots off, dictating terms.
Around that time an old keeper named Hannet Corwen walked down the Hotwell Stair in a blue coat with a boiled egg, sat on the top step by the bronze ring at the pool’s lip, and finished the egg. She looked up at the water clock. “Time, ladies and gentlemen, please,” she said, in the voice of someone closing a public house, and took out a brass key the length of her hand, and turned it a quarter. Nobody felt a thing. It took about an hour to go through the chain, keeper to keeper, along the forks in the assay posts, up one terrace and down the next and out to the sites on the barge road, and the only sign of it was that a sound everyone had stopped hearing was slowly going out of the morning. The Sect-Mistress came out of the water at about the time her first disciple tried to light a lamp. She was still Stage IX, with a full reserve, and she went up that stair like the wrath of heaven and took off Hannet Corwen’s left arm at the elbow. Then she stood there, on ground gone lean as a washboard, with the whole of a very long fight’s worth of Essence in her and no way on this earth of getting any more, in the middle of two hundred miles of Cores whose keepers were all very sorry. Hannet Corwen, who was by then being carried off, is on record as saying that the arm would be on the bill.
The Burning Ladder walked home. It took them a month, carrying the palanquins, and it paid the arrears, and that was the last anybody heard of them as a power.
A chartered family, then, and the richest per acre in the South. Every worked Wellspring site under Guild lease from the Wellheads to the southern sea sells its hours through a Corwen keeper, and the keeper can close it. That is what they hold that everyone needs. What they want is the springs clean before anyone outside the Wellheads proves they are not.
Origin of the House
There were Corwens in the spring country under the empire, keeping the casks. The Wellheads paid Sum-gol in water, and a stringy, unpleasant clan of cask-stewards saw to the sealing, and they were in nobody’s histories. Jennet Corwen is the one everyone remembers. In the summer of 602 she read the salt-tax notice and went, at her own expense, to see a Guild factor at the barge basin. The Guild Accord had been trying for a century to get hold of the South’s rich sites, and the Dynasty had been refusing for just as long. She sold him a proposition: that if there were ever to be no emperor, the springs would need a lawful holder, and that it would be cheap to have the wax ready. So when the Emperor Rokju called the Corwen from his balcony, a boy brought word that the casks had been sold elsewhere, and on the same afternoon a lease was sealed in Brightwater. It covered the entire spring country. The family has spent a century making sure nobody can find that piece of wax. The Guild says the term is in it. The Corwens smile.
Their one great defeat came from their own people. In 647 Ferris Corwen raised the cask by a third and the Dyers of Kingfisher Steps tipped out their vats and turned the river blue for nine days. The lease was redrawn around that settlement, and the color went on the banner before the river ran clear.
The House on the Crystal
A Soul Crystal is the soul itself, in three layers: the Aether Shell, where Aether (mana) comes in and force goes out; the Essence Core, where it is refined into Essence (spiritual energy); and the Attraction Layer, a soul’s own share of Fate.

























LayerPlaneThe Corwen formAether ShellPhysicalGrown huge in the intake and rather soft. Raised in the pools from birth, the Shell draws in Aether at a rate that embarrasses lowland Stages and has never had to work for itEssence CoreSoulUnremarkable. It does what the books tell it toAttraction LayerFateKeys, terms and a lease. A seal spends the soul’s own share and never pulls, and that is the whole of a keeper’s business here
Path. Pool-trained guards lean to the Body Path. Keepers, after forty years of minding terms, bonds and who may enter, drift to the shallow end of the Fate Path, the way an old midwife does, without ever knowing it and without ever holding a thread. Corwens read nothing on Fate for life.
No grip, no eye, and not much blood. The family’s gift is in the ground, and anybody who grows up in a kept pool gets most of it. A lamp-warden from the Steps with no Corwen in him at all fills nearly as fast. The stat lean comes from the water, and the authority comes from a document.

























RungTypical CorwenUnwokenBrass-boys, cask-men and the family’s many cousins, with a bad knee that is always better up hereBody I, GloryWarden’s guard in blue coats. Dangerous on their own ground, and ordinary off itBody II, Spirit IA keeper, with a key and a ring and the first understanding of what they areBody III and upThe Warden’s chair. Very few, and they do not come off the ground much
The Hours
What it is. A practitioner pulls Aether from the world around her, and where she stands decides how fast she fills. Rich ground fills you and lean ground starves you. A worked site is a pool of one of the sixty Wellsprings (the types of Aether), with a bronze ring called a ferrule seated at its lip, which limits how wide anyone can pull. Whoever holds the ring decides who gets how much and when. Everyone else in the world treats that as plumbing. The Corwens took out a lease on it, sell it by the hour and carry the key on their belts.
How it works, in plain words. A hill full of water has a head on it, as any mill-hand can tell you: the higher the source, the harder it pushes at any opening below. A Core has a head of Aether, and the ring is a sluice. A keeper’s key is cut for one ring, in brass, with a seal laid on it at the lease’s signing and renewed in that keeper’s Essence on the day she takes it up. Turn it, and the ring narrows or widens. Ground for a good way round goes fat or goes lean, for everyone on it, and with long practice it will favor the names in the hour-book. The tundish, a brass funnel beside the ring, shows from the door what color is passing. Keepers along a chain feel each other’s turns through the tuned assay forks on every wellmouth, and pass them on, and that is the hum.
It does not take anything away. A closed Core takes no one’s reserve. It stops the refill. Nothing happens to you until you need more, and you always find out late. Anyone who has ever been truly dangerous in a long fight has been dangerous because they were filling as fast as they spent, and most of them have never once thought about where that came from.
The forms. They have very plain names, as the family is proud of pointing out.



































FormWhat it isWho holds itHot and ColdThe daily turning. Widen or narrow a ring for the season’s trade, and read the color in the tundishAny keeperThe BookAn hour sold to a name. A sitter on the book fills as if she owned the place, and anyone else on the same terrace gets a trickle. Sects pay more for this than for anythingA keeper of ten yearsTimeThe whole site, shut. Up to an hour’s turning to do it decently, and then every working in the district starts going thinAny keeper with the nerve and the Warden’s wordDeadwaterA quarter-turn in a fight, by hand, with the ring in reach. The ground under one terrace goes lean in about ten breaths. It kicks like a muleAn old keeper, and rarelyThe EvictionEvery ring on the chain at once, by the Warden’s word, from the Wellheads to the sea. It has never been done. It is the only argument Maud Corwen has ever needed to mention, and she mentions it with a broad smileThe Warden
What it costs. A head of Aether does not go away when you shut the gate. Close a Core and the pressure rises behind the ring, and something has to be done about that. Tenders work in pairs at the lip at night, with a fork and a lamp, bleeding it a little each shift, unpaid, because they live there. Close too long and it rises and breeds, and the abandoned pools have the sump-toads to prove it. Deadwater kicks back through the key, up the arm and into the Shell, as scald and a bone-deep humming, and it is usually the end of a keeper’s hearing. There is also the plain cost of being the person who turned it off. Every working in the district depends on that ring, and a keeper’s whole family lives downhill of a great many angry people.
Its limit. It works on ground under lease, with a ring on it. A key opens one ring. An unlicensed Well like the Gold Mouth, or the bottom of the Long Copper, a long way past where any Corwen has ever got a key to, does not care at all. A Corwen on someone else’s ground is about what her Stage says she is, with a bad sleeping habit. And all of it, every ring, stands on a piece of wax. The Guild could evict them, in theory, if anyone could find the document, and the Guild depends on Corwen keepers for every lease this far south, so it has not looked very hard.
Who beats it. Arrive full and finish fast, like the Burning Ladder’s Mistress, who only went wrong by staying. A Body fighter with a good reserve and a short plan can walk up and kill the keeper. Bring your own: bottled Drafts, or a cask, at a price. Steal the key, since it is only brass and it will turn for anyone who has taken the seal, and that has made some very quick careers. Or hire a hedge-worker with a sack of salt, for less than the price of a spear, and have her lean out their fat ground the night before, as anyone can in this country. It is the first thing a sensible enemy tries.
Physical Appearance and Dress
Big, pink and cheerful, most of them, gleaming a little, with the padded fingertips of people who spend a lot of time wet. Hair stays damp and curls at the temples. They tend to a comfortable weight, and their joints do not trouble them until they go down to the plain for a week and everything hurts at once. They talk in big comfortable voices, slightly too loud, as people do who have grown up beside a noise. A Corwen listening to you tilts her head a little to one side, and it means she is listening to something else as well.
Kingfisher blue and brass are the colors. Keepers wear a good blue wool coat, brass-buttoned, and the key at the belt on a brass chain, polished by small boys and displayed the way a Moto lord displays a grandfather. A senior keeper’s coat is dyed on Kingfisher Steps in the violent blue that makes people stop and take their hats off, Rare and worth what a good horse is worth, and the Dyers charge the family full rate on principle, and tell you so. Blue coats and brass at fifty paces, walking downhill without hurrying. A poor cousin has a brass-washed iron key to the laundry overflow, wears it just as proudly, and will explain the terms.
Lineage Traits
[Trait] Soaked — Raised in the Fat
The body of the House, and it has no blood in it. Anyone raised here gets it.

Intake far above their Stage on rich ground, and Aether seems to find them. On the Wellheads they fill as if there were a hole in the bottom of the world.
Baths, steam and the pool’s minerals do their skin, joints and lungs great good, and Vitality Regeneration runs high at home.
On lean or ordinary ground the gift simply stops, and they fall to about what the Stage says.

Every Corwen in a foreign war has written home to say the air there is thin.
[Trait] The Hum — Hearing the Pool

A Corwen feels the ring’s state from a long way off, the way you feel your own pulse.
Keepers along a chain can pass a turning, a warning or a price down the forks, faster than a horse.
It cuts both ways: see the Curses.

Children of the house who leave home cannot sleep for the silence.
[Trait] The Tongue — An Older Way of Knowing

Long before there were forks, keepers tasted. Someone raised on the pools can tell one Wellspring from another with a sip, and with practice can tell a good deal more.
It is taught less than it was. The house reads forks now, as the Guild requires, and a fork reads what it reads.

The Archives have asked why a house would give up that tongue, and have had a very polite reply about modern standards.
System Metrics
Stat lean



























































PrimaryLeanSignature Sub-StatsWhyHarmonicsExceptionalSynergy, Attunement, StabilityWhatever the ground is doing is doing it to themTemperingHighYield, CapacityFat ground, fat CrystalVitalityHighRegeneration, FiltrationThe pools. Off the ground this drops a full stepResilienceHighOath, FortificationKeys and termsGnosisModerateRetention, AnalysisThe books and the tundishDominionModerateSovereignty, CommandTheir ground in a very narrow legal senseArdencyModerateFluxLoud and wasteful, since it has never matteredDexterityLowEconomyThey have people for that
Wellspring compatibility
A Wellspring is a lens a soul tempers itself on, and it locks nobody out of the rest. The Wellheads have a great many pools, and a Corwen grows up in several.






























TierWellspringsWhyNaturalPhreatis, SolfataraWater under the ground, and pressure let out forever and never saved upEasyDissolution, Terranova, Anima Spirare, SublimareThe unbinding stream, mending ground, the breath of the invalid, and what risesWorkableAbsolution, Verdantia, Coagula, FixatioAbsolution is a Spirit Wellspring and gives no fire, and sells very well to rich sinners on the StepsAgainst the grainCinerion, Nihiloth, PyreveilAsh, the hollow law, and a fire that dries out a good bath
On the Stages

























StagesHow a Corwen readsI to III · Murmuring to AscensionA first coat and a very good appetite. They climb early, on the ground and cheaplyIV to VI · Flourishing to GloryFirst Release as a blue steam off the skin, and a key if you are lucky. Glory comes young, and Well-Attended or Second Son comes with it often enough for jokesVII to IX · Refraction to InvocationThe bought Stages are common, since the Drafts cost little at the source. Most run Overgrown and their rungs lag badly, and a Corwen of VIII reading Body I is no rarityX and up · RealizationA keeper here on her own pool is one of the most dangerous people in the South, and a person of no great consequence ten miles from it
Doctrine and Arts
Close a door. A Corwen ends the terms on which you were having a fight. Her guard hold a terrace in blue coats with good crossbows, for as long as it takes the key to work. The fine points of the trade are all about ground: fighting uphill of an opened ring, topping up between exchanges, and being on the correct side of a book entry. Shouts are in plain Northern English and mostly learned in a tavern.








































MoveMeaningWhat it doesSlack Water!Water at a standThe call before Deadwater, and the only warning you will get. Ten breaths, and the terrace goes leanOn the House!The ring thrown wideA keeper opens fully for one breath. Everyone on the book fills, a guard’s coat flares, and the head of pressure dropping behind it makes the pool jumpCask!Portable groundA sealed cask stove in underfoot, Wellhead water on the flags. For a minute or so a small circle of ordinary ground is fat, and she will fight in itSoak!ReserveA guard goes under for three breaths and comes up full. In the Hotwell raft bracket this is a foul, and everybody does itMind the Step!A boiling-water trickTerraced ground, a sluice kicked open, and the top pool comes down on the attackers in a sheet. The Stair has seen it, with eggsRead the Terms!Shouted with a key raisedA keeper’s Command. A person on the book feels the line on their window, in the middle of whatever they are doing, and it is a poor moment for it
Culture
They speak the Wellheads’ Northern English, with a good many lease terms in it. The children learn to read from the lease.

The First Soak. A child’s first hour in the home pool, on the day it is born, in the ring’s shadow. A cousin writes down what color the tundish showed, and everyone pretends this means something.
The Silence. At eleven, a child is carried down to the lean ground below the gorge and left for a night with a keeper. Most scream. Those who come back are told what the hum is.
The Sleeves. Any Corwen who raises the Dyers’ water must do it on Kingfisher Steps, in person, with sleeves rolled up. Nobody has hit one yet. It has been close.
The Fork-Tuning. At the turn of each year the assay posts are struck in sequence from Brightwater to the barge road, and the family walks them, all of them, with a band. It is a wonderful party. The wardens read the forks, and every fork rings true.

Who they marry, fight and owe. They marry Guild factors, invalid fortunes and, very cautiously, each other. The Guild Accord is their landlord, partner and permanent threat. The ward-cutters of Kharven-Seat quench their chisels in Wellhead water at the price Maud Corwen sets, and say what they think of it. The Yan have shown her a count of sick foals, the Post buys nothing from a Corwen cask, and every month the Yukari repeat an offer to walk the springs, and every month it is declined with the same courtesy. Commoners get bath-money, the free overflow, keeper’s wages for anyone who will sit on a step all night, and a Lease Court that hears anyone at all.
Limitations and Soul-Costs
[Curse] The Hum — A Soul That Needs the Noise
Off the ground the silence is a physical thing. They do not sleep. Their food tastes of nothing and their reserve fills at what seems to them a crawl. Corwen wardens abroad have gone home in the middle of very promising careers, and the family has a small quiet hospital for those who could not.
[Curse] Pressure Behind the Ring — Every Closing Is Owed
The head rises whether you have the money for tenders or not. Close too long, or stop the night’s bleeding, and something begins to breed down there, and a ring that has been shut in anger has to be opened by someone who then stands next to it. Most of what the Bestiary knows about a keeper’s death comes from this.
[Curse] The Wax — A Kingdom on Paper
The richest ground in the South can be ended by a Guild clerk with the right document. They have no blood claim, no conquest, and no answer to the question of what they are if the lease lapses, and it is the only House in the South where the heir’s first lesson is on limitations of actions.
[Curse] The Forks Ring True — Reading the Instrument
The whole house has trusted its whole power to tuned brass for a century, and since the war the water has been wrong in ways that brass does not report. Villages downstream are sick. The family reads the forks, and the forks are fine. The Warden has never in her life been seen to drink the water, and that is all this office can tell you.
How They Stand Against the Three Paths
Body. A hitter on a good reserve with no interest in topping up is the classic answer, and the blue coats are there to slow him. Fine on their own terrace, and off it a poor match for anyone who has ever been hungry.
Spirit. The ground’s wide-open gifts work fine for a Spirit fighter too, if they are on the book, and a Spirit art goes past a guard’s fat Shell with very little trouble. A soul in a pool is nakedly easy to read. Their defense against this is mostly the law.
Fate. A Fate user might look at a lease and see what it depends on. A keeper is a poor Fate fighter herself, whatever she drifts toward, and a slipped key or a tender who misses a shift can bring on what no enemy could.
Final Definition
House Corwen does not rule anything. It rents out the ability to be dangerous, with a brass key, on terms it knows by heart, to anyone at all, and lets the whole South fight its wars on ground it has already been paid for. A big cheerful woman at Brightwater could turn off the world for two hundred miles with a word to a chain of old people on steps, and no one with a Crystal in them has ever quite forgotten it, or ever been able to find the wax. They also live downstream of whatever has gone wrong, and the lease is silent on the point.
The water keeps faith. After you, Maud.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.filePath: Factions, Bloodlines & Institutions/Houses and Bloodlines/The Houses of the Inner World/House Greymane.md
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: House Greymane
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Overview





































TypeBanner House of Kharven · Garrison Bloodline · Holders of the Western WallOrigin”Since before there was a north to hold it for,” in their own tellingFounderEntered in the house’s records by title, as the First Warden. Nobody has the nameSeatThe Ridgewall, on the Slate Ridge of StormfoldAnchorsPetralon under the floor · the Roll of Posts · the wall itself · the morning look westSignatureThe Post: give a Greymane a title and a place to stand, and the wall stands there with themMaxim”The Ridge Does Not Move.”
The spring slide at Harrowgill, in Year 658, is why nobody in the Stormfold will tell you a Greymane cannot do anything but stand there.
Harrowgill was a garrison town of fourteen hundred souls in the lee of the crest, under a long slate face that had been loading up with wet snow for a month. Nineteen hands of the Grey File had been sent up that morning to clear a drain. At first light, under a clean rose sky, the whole face let go. It came down about forty feet with the noise of a city falling over, well over two hundred thousand tons of snow and shale by the Masonwarden’s reckoning, and it met nineteen rims locked across the only bench on the slope, because a section sergeant had looked up and said lock. It stopped. Every set of boots in that file went into the rock to the ankle, and nothing behind the line moved at all.
Then nothing happened for seven hours, because a Greymane under that kind of load does not speak. The Muster Aunt worked it out from the dust. She was a stout woman of seventy who had never held a shield. She cleared Harrowgill street by street, in the order of the roster, and when the last cart was over the bridge she climbed the slope with a stool and a ledger, set the stool in front of the first man, and relieved him. You stand relieved. Who has the post? He gave the answer, she entered it, and he walked off the line on legs that would not work again and fell down the hill. The load went into the other eighteen. She moved her stool. By dusk the last hand in the file, put at the far end because he was youngest, stood alone with the whole of the Harrowgill face resting on his shield, sixteen years old, with his eyes open and blood running out of his ears, and she sat down in front of him and opened the ledger.
“You stand relieved.”
He had to ask. It is part of the form. “Who has the post?”
She looked back down the valley at a town with nobody in it. “Nobody has the post, lad. There’s no one behind you.”
He stepped back. The mountain came down and took Harrowgill to the river, every roof of it, and the Aunt and the boy were found the next morning on a shelf the slide had gone around. He was three inches shorter than the roster said. He served forty years more as the Third Sentry, his stone on the ridge says that and nothing else, and by the end he could not have told you his name.
House Greymane is the north’s defensive architecture in human form. Children are raised as components of a structure, the ones who reject the framing leave, and the ones who stay become the most reliable garrison troops in the Inner World. What they hold that everyone needs is the far side of the Galecross road, and every other house pays a levy in grain and salt to keep the Mandate of Undaar-Keth over there. The outside world takes the titles for an old family’s tic. They are a working art.
Origin of the House
The Ridgewall is carved so far into the mountain that no surveyor can say where masonry starts, and under it runs Petralon, the Foundation Stone, the Wellspring of load taken and sent down. The oldest records are rosters, and the oldest roster lists posts with a stone mark for each holder. The First Warden appears to have struck his own name first.
West of the wall lies the ground the bloodline came from, which nobody holds, and the Greymanes look at it every morning. The Archives have twice asked why, and both replies said the post was filled.
The House on the Crystal

























LayerPlaneThe Greymane formAether ShellPhysicalLoad-bearing. Plain, even and well kept, inspected every morning. It grows around the holding the way a tree grows around a fenceEssence CoreSoulVery quiet. A Greymane has almost nothing in Spirit and does not try to read what it cannot. Ward runs near nothing, and this is the door everyone forgets to hitAttraction LayerFateWhere the Posts sit. Each one is a tie to a place, a charge and the holder above, and a long-serving Greymane’s Layer looks like a garrison roster
Path. The lean is Body, with a Fate lean behind it for anchoring, oath and the gravity of a line: the usual Shieldwarden reads Body Mastered and Fate Walked at about a third. Mastery. Body comes slowly, because Level comes slowly at the post. They do not seclude, and each Stage is met where they stand. Grip. None. The Post is a vow, which spends the soul’s own share and reaches for nothing above it. Wystan died at Glory with his Fate still unread, having kept every word he ever gave.
The Post
In a breath: a Greymane given a title and a place to stand holds that place with the whole wall behind them, for exactly as long as there is someone at their back, and nobody can relieve them but the proper hand.
What it is. A Post is a vow with a strict grammar: a place (this stair, this gate, this man), a charge (who is behind you and what you are stopping) and a relief (who may stand you down). A superior says it aloud before a witness, and the one posted answers with the title and nothing else. The vow goes onto the Layer and ties to the post above it, up the roster to the Shieldwarden, who is tied to the ridge. So a load landing on the youngest hand on the most distant section has a road to go down, through stone and through the chain of the garrison.
Why they talk the way they do. Every time a Greymane is addressed by title in front of someone, the vow is said again and sets a little harder. That is why the Shieldwarden is the Shieldwarden in his own bedroom, why a Greymane child calls the dog the Hound and the latrine the Lower Gate, and why the holder’s personal name is known almost nowhere: it is the loose stone in the wall.
The forms















































FormWhoWhat it doesWhat it costsA PostAny sworn handWith someone at their back, Anchoring and Fortitude read a step high and the blow goes down. It counts toward the two-step limit on self-boostsYou stayThe Grey FileA posted sectionShields rim to rim, and a blow on any runs along the file and down every set of bootsAs long as its endsThe ReliefAny post at handoverThe incoming hand lays a palm on the post and takes up what it has learned: the wind, the loose stone, the other side’s schedule. A small Anamnesis (the Wellspring of everything keeping its past)The outgoing hand loses it. Old Greymanes sit very peacefullyThe Walking PostGodfrey’s Sworn Ward is the one clean caseA Post tied to a person. Within a long stride, a blow at the ward runs through the warden’s set body into the groundThe full hit, on a body that may not be bracedThe Long PostNobody chooses thisA hand who dies unrelieved leaves the vow standing. The stair goes on refusing people, and Mandate maps mark elevenSomebody goes up with a stool and says the form to the airThe Wall is MannedDomain, Stage VIII at leastEveryone on your side inside it takes a Post and shares the load, and nobody can retreat. Called lowEvery one of them, if it breaks
Its limit. It faces one way, holds the post and not the person, needs someone behind it and needs feet set on something one with the ground. Take away what is guarded and the art goes quiet: Amelia Greymane said out loud in a tower at the Seat that she does not know what she is with nobody behind her.
Who beats it. The failure is written into Petralon’s own law: stone fails in tension. Never push the Shieldwarden. Hook the rim and haul, lift him by the belt, or fight him on ice, a deck or a moving cart. Come from the side of the column, or land two blows at once. Break the file’s end and roll it up. Kill the officer who holds the relief and watch a section stand at a dead post until it starves, as the Mandate has done twice. Or use the name, which works for a breath, from someone who knew him before, as the load comes on: the Core answers to its own name whatever the Post allows. Godfrey Greymane has been called by his name in a king’s household since the Foot, and the old men of the Stormfold do not like to talk about it.
Physical Appearance and Dress
Stature and coloring. Long, all of them, with the wide even shoulders of a shield carried from childhood, and a stride you can recognize at a quarter-mile. Pale gray faces, hair anywhere from rye-stubble gold to dark, heavy lids, and gray eyes, though rowan-red turns up. Marks. Long still hands. The stance sinks with every fight, so an old Greymane stands lower than he did. Voice. Numbers before opinions, given as a report.
The look at fifty paces. A long gray file with the dents left in: Stormfold wool, the wolf’s head in darker thread, iron clasps, and rims proud enough to lock to the next man’s and also catch an axe-beard, which nobody in the house has ever filed down. The flex is what has been left alone. The old sun, Grade A and Very Rare, has a gold sun half worn off by sixty years of blows, it belongs to the post, and the Mandate’s ridge reports list it among the fortifications. At court a Greymane wears navy closed to the jaw, cut by a tailor who regards this as a branch of masonry. The poor cousin is hardly different: a Common file shield painted over twice, a dead relative’s plate let out by hand, and eleven small nicks inside the rim.
Lineage Traits
[Trait] The Ridge Does Not Move — The Load Goes Down

With feet set on solid ground, a load that comes in does not move the bearer. Petralon routes it down through the bones in compression, the way an arch carries a roof.
The ground takes it, cracking in a ring, and a set foot is a planted foot.

The Mandate has a technical term for fighting a Greymane on solid rock. It translates as “elsewhere.”
[Trait] The Ridgewall Stillness — Still, Then Fast

A Greymane has a way of not moving at all and then moving very fast. The first thing out of stillness comes a step quicker than the sheet. After that it is only an old man with a sword.
Its counter is never to be the first to move.

Old Stormfold men have watched Wystan use his sword a dozen times, and none can tell you which hand moved first.
[Trait] The Steady Note — Nothing Rattles Them

Those who hold Basilithe, the Stone Will, lock their rhythm so nothing drives it. Godfrey’s Flat Hand spreads that a little way, a hand laid flat beside a frightened ally, until their pulse falls in with his. The one forcing that matches them rings them apart.

Nobody’s hand has ever been laid beside a Greymane’s. Nobody in the house has remarked on this.
System Metrics



























































PrimaryLeanSignature Sub-StatsWhyVitalityHighFortitude, Absorption, ToleranceWhat the blow lands onArdencyLowDensityThey do not win by hittingGnosisModerateAnalysis, VigilanceThey read ground and schedulesDexterityLow to ModerateReflex, EconomyEvasion near nothing, on purposeHarmonicsModerateStability, AxisThe file is a harmonyResilienceExceptionalAnchoring, Fortification, OathThe whole house is this numberTemperingLowMaturity, CoherenceIt rises with ageDominionModerateGravity, Pressure, CommandDensity, without raising the voice
Wellspring compatibility.

Strongest: Petralon, the house’s for generations. Fixatio, the bond that stays bound, under Wystan’s and Amelia’s Stonefast. Basilithe, the one note.
Workable: Monolithion for the oldest, Chthonica for the mountain companies, Anamnesis for gate officers.
Against the grain: Cymorath, which reads every way as open, and Abython, which holds there is no load to bear. Aurevane has its own door on the Ridge, and a sentry on it.






























StagesHow they readI to IIIThe yard, and a first Post at twelveIV to VStonefast, called low. Dust at the heels and stone climbing the shinsVIGlory, Body I. A file of them could hold a pass by leaning on itVIISecond Release. The wall starts to answerVIII and upThe Domain the house expects to be the ridge
Doctrine and Arts
The wall first, and then very fast. The ridge sword runs on taking the Before: the one who strikes second spends the fight answering, so a Greymane who attacks does it first, from the high guard they call the Roof, and otherwise stands still. The wall does a third of the fighting, since an enemy on the crest in a storm is in the hands of the violet weather.





































MoveWhat it doesLoad PathThe first lesson. Every joint set in a column from boss to heel, and the body is the road the blow travelsThe Ridge Gives BackGodfrey’s. For two breaths the ground keeps the last catch, then heaves up with the shield behind itSTONEFAST · Setting the StoneFirst Release, called low. Slate-scale on the shoulders and ridge-stone to the kneesThe Wrath-CutStraight down off the right shoulder from the RoofThe Crooked CutHands crossed on the grip, turning edge-first onto the inside of the wristThe Hook and the HewAmelia’s, self-taught after she was told no. The beard over the rim, the pull from the heels, the edge on what it opens. The one thing every Greymane fears, learned on purposeThe Long NoteOne note on a ram’s horn. When you hear it from behind you, you are late
Culture
Language. Northern Common, flat. Family offices run all the way down: the Gatewarden, the Masonwarden, the Muster Aunt, the Cook.
Rites.

The Posting. At twelve, on the wall, with a witness.
The Look West. Every morning, from every wall. A Greymane looks that way before looking at you.
Reading the Long Posts. A Muster Aunt with a stool, trying the form on the stairs that still refuse people.
The Cutting. Each new Shieldwarden’s shield is cut new. Wystan hung the old sun on a peg at the Foot the morning he rode south.
The Sewing. The women of the long houses make the cloak in one night, and the thread runs out near the left hem.

Marriage, feud and debt. They marry for the wall. Starks share the wolf on the breast, do not speak to them and would die for them. The two garrisons on the Galecross road know each other’s relief schedules better than their own wives do, and the Ashmore clerk gets the same courtesy as a siege engine.
What the commons get. A Post. Nobody on the Ridge pays rent, because you hold your room by holding your post, and every trade has a title, and a title is a very small wall. Ragna the Cook’s pot would never go off the boil. When you stop holding the post you stop holding the room, which focuses the mind of the elderly.
Limitations and Soul-Costs
[Curse] The Name Goes — What the Wall Is Mortared With

Every address by title sets the Post and takes a little from the name. After forty years a Greymane may not answer to it, and at death the Layer leaves a Name that is often only a job.

The Third Sentry’s mother came up to the wall once, and asked for him by the name she had given him, and they could not find anyone who knew who she meant.
[Curse] With Nobody Behind — The Shape of the Absence

The art needs someone to guard, and grief in them stays put and bears load. Rigidity is the usual end, and being made to abandon a ward can break the soul outright.

They hold a silence the same way, and for the same reason, past the point of kindness.
[Curse] Creep — The Stance Sinks

Petralon accepts slow settling as the price of never cracking. They get shorter and slower to turn, and a fighter inside their turning radius has a long time to work.

The Ridgewall tailor measures them every year. He has a chart, and he will not show it to you.
How They Stand Against the Three Paths
Body. Their whole training, and the one who brings a hook has been reading. Spirit. A disaster: Fortitude does not cover the soul and Ward runs at almost nothing. Fate. A well-kept garrison offers few straps to give, so a Fate user moves the relief, the cart or the one officer, and waits.
Final Definition
House Greymane is what happens when a family decides, so long ago nobody remembers deciding, that a person is a part of a wall. They gave up their names to it and the wall answers, and a boy of sixteen can stand under a mountain. They are the most reliable people in the Inner World and very nearly the saddest, and neither is a topic they have ever found inspiring.
“You stand relieved. Who has the post?”

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.filePath: Factions, Bloodlines & Institutions/Houses and Bloodlines/The Houses of the Inner World/House Hallenfeld.md
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: House Hallenfeld
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Overview





































TypeBanner House of Kharven · Toll-Keepers and Carriers · The North’s Nervous SystemOriginThe portage road round the Hallen falls, which came first. The tolls came afterFounderMaarten the Hauler, who charged for carrying a barge past a waterfall, and then charged for the roadSeatHallenfeld, the castle over the falls and the ugly counting-house at the junction of the Painted RiversAnchorsThe chain bridges · the Rate · the books · the beacon lineSignatureThe Paid Chain: every toll ever paid to cross a Hallenfeld chain is still holding that chain upMaxim”Pay or be chained.” For internal use: “I’ll want that noted.”
Chainbridge has a contraption at its eastern pier for raising the middle span in a siege, and the guild-mark on it is the most boasted-about in the valley. On a blue October morning in Year 661, with the Hallen running green and four hundred yards of plank swaying in the sun, Aldous Rook’s Long Company came down the east road, nine hundred lances in black and yellow, to take the junction by nightfall for a Midmarch king. The bridge’s clerk that morning was Griet Hoogstraat, sixty-three, in a blue-and-ocher striped apron, and she sent a boy to raise the span. It jammed. So she picked up her stool and ledger, walked out past a toll house painted to the waterline with what happens to people who do not pay, and had two bargemen haul the old road-chain across behind her, at about the height of a horse’s knee. Rook thought it was very funny.
She stood up as the first rank came into a canter, and everyone on both banks heard her.
"Nine Hundred Horse at Three Pence the Hoof! Pay or Be Chained!"
She stepped to one side. They did not pay. The lead horses struck the chain at full gallop and stopped, as though the bridge had been a cliff. There were eighty lancers in the river before the rest pulled up. Links as thick as a man’s arm stood blue-white and humming over a pile of horses, with the air shivering around them. Two hundred and six years of carters, drovers, widows and pilgrims had each paid to come across that span, and what they gave up had gone into the book and stayed there. Griet Hoogstraat wrote something down, walked up to where Rook was picking himself out of the wreck with a broken collarbone, and showed him the page.
Eleven years of receipts had just gone out of that chain, and what was left would about stop a good-sized cart. She did not mention it. She said there were a great many hooves still on the east bank, and that the damage to the planks would be added. Rook looked at the chain, still humming, and at the old woman, and he paid, in full, for all nine hundred, and went home. She got a raise of a penny a week.
House Hallenfeld has no glamour and produces no legendary warriors. It produces quartermasters, road engineers, courier captains and the kind of administrator who treats six hours as a problem worth solving with the intensity other houses bring to swordwork. They hold the junction where three rivers and three roads meet, and with it the speed at which the north can respond to anything. They would prefer to be thanked.
Origin of the House
Nothing floats past the triple falls of the Hallen. Every barge unloads and its cargo is hauled round under the castle wall, and everything hauled pays. Maarten the Hauler charged for that before there was a castle. He kept his accounts on a stair behind the falls, and it was his great-granddaughter, going further down than was sensible, who came to a flooded landing and a toll house far older than anything on the river, its rate still painted on the wall in a script no clerk has read. She came back up, put a chain across the head of the stair and started keeping better books. The house has never explained the connection.
The House on the Crystal

























LayerPlaneThe Hallenfeld formAether ShellPhysicalNothing to speak of among the clerks. The couriers have lean, long-winded Shells that do not waste a breathEssence CoreSoulTidy. An entry by a sworn hand carries a small stamp of the hand, and most read Spirit I by accident, from the sheer quantity of writingAttraction LayerFateA wall of pigeonholes. Every toll a clerk has entered runs through it. They are almost all small and all exact
Path. The soul leans Fate for the bonds and bargains, with a Spirit lean for the writing. Couriers lean Body, and the two halves of the house do not entirely consider each other family. Mastery. Most of it reads Fate I or II and never higher, because without a Work or a blessing the road stops there, and because a vow spends the soul’s own share and a toll is one of those, many thousands of times. Grip. None, and every clerk will tell you so with pride. They have receipts.
The Paid Chain
In a breath: a toll is a small real bargain, and what you give up to cross goes into the chain at exactly its worth, so a chain with three hundred years of honest books behind it is as strong as everything anyone ever paid to pass it.
How it works. Oblation, the Wellspring of the offering, keeps one law: what you give up comes back as force, and never one grain more than you gave. It favors altars, old bargain-stones and toll bridges. When a carter pays three pence at a Hallenfeld span he gives something up, freely, for a known return, and that is a true Oblation, however small. The house’s discovery was that the force need not come back to the carter. It can be left against the thing bargained for, the crossing. So the chain holds it.
Everything else about the Painted Rivers follows. The rate has to be posted, because a bargain nobody understood banks nothing, and that is why every toll house is painted with the rate in pictures. The entry has to be made, in a sworn hand, on the day. And the book has to be true. A false entry rots the balance, and the chain parts at that link. Osbert Lambert, of the Hallenfeld cadet line, read carts against their manifests for eleven years and would not change a figure when the Tenrai beat him for it. They thought they were dealing with a stubborn man. They were dealing with a man who knew what holds up a bridge.
The forms















































FormWhoWhat it doesWhat it costsThe RateAny sworn clerk, at a postThe rate called aloud to someone who has not paid. The cart will not roll for a moment and boots grow heavyNothingThe ChainA clerk of a spanCloses the chain against what is crossing unpaid, and meets it with force at exact par from the balanceWhatever it stopped, in receiptsThe ReceiptAnyone who has paidThe other half of the bargain. A chain will not stop you, and a bargee with a good one has floated through a closed river in a siegeA copperThe HaltThe Mistress, or a tariff-masterEvery crossing closed in an hour by beacon. No grain or message moves, and an army a week away starves on the road. Mostly logistics, and all the more frighteningThe house’s whole income stops as wellSix HoursCourier captainsThe Relay. Riders sworn to one road are tied by Transference, the living exchange, so a rested rider’s legs turn up under a tired one’s. A satchel moves faster than any rider who carries itA courier’s body. Nobody under the stair expects to be good at fortyThe Toll is DueDomain, Stage VIII at leastEveryone inside pays reserve, posted and at par, before a working will fire, the clerk included. The only Domain on the north’s books with a printed tariffFalsify it once and it comes apart on you
What it costs. A chain’s balance is spent the moment it is used and comes back a copper at a time, so a clerk who stops an army has just cost the next twenty years of clerks, and will be told about it.
Its limit. Exact par, never one grain more, only at that chain and only against what is crossing. A clerk two hundred yards from a span is a soft person with spectacles. Monsters do not read posted rates, and a sump-toad in a mill-race is a matter for a miller with a hoist.
Who beats it. The first and best answer, which astonishingly few armies have thought of, is to pay. The old terms give a host passage and the house will hand it a receipt. Go around: the fords are real, and so are Hayato Amagiri’s indigo roads. Spend the chain down, as Rook very nearly did. Then there is Free Water: a town that stops paying stops feeding the chain, and the Toll-Breakers, whose class names run from Chain-Thief to Free Water itself, are beloved by bargemen and hanged by Hallenfeld for exactly this reason. The Northern Road Company has lately found another way, so that a ferryman pays the toll in the morning and the Company in the afternoon, and the chain itself seems to have begun to wonder which is the law.
The money under it
Ilse Hallenfeld, Mistress of the counting-house, does not fight. When the Seat had to fall, she told a council that its wards were kept by hand by Guild keepers, paid quarterly through her counting-house on credit the Seat had been running for eleven years. She bought the wardmasters, and at the first bell every Tenrai ward on the rock died. That was only paper. She wrote the ratification of the seven lines in her own hand and would not let a clerk touch the pen. A debt is a debt, she said. It is the largest entry the counting-house has ever made, and at least one Measurewright has wondered what, under the Oblation’s law, it now holds up.
Physical Appearance and Dress
Stature and coloring. Round-shouldered, indoors, soft in the belly, sandy and pale, often in small square spectacles. Couriers are narrow, sun-dried people who look packed for a journey. Marks. Ink on the second finger of the right hand that no amount of beating has got off. Voice. Exact and unsurprised.
The look at fifty paces. Blue and ocher stripes, loud enough for the far bank, on men with boathooks, short spears and the weight of the law. Toll houses are the true gear of the house: a fresh coat means solvent, and a peeling one means you should ask to see the books. The high end is restraint: Ilse’s dark coat lined in wolf, a ledger under her arm and ink on the gloves. The river-reeve on the lip of the falls wears a long robe and carries a sounding-staff, and no holder of that office has been seen to fall, since every morning the reeve drops a copper over the edge and enters it, so the falls have been paid. Couriers spend real money on one thing, boots, Grade D and Uncommon, resoled monthly and worn to bed. A poor cousin has a single stripe on his sleeve and a great deal of knowledge about the price of barley.
Lineage Traits
[Trait] The Sworn Hand — What the Entry Does

An entry by a sworn hand on the day carries a small stamp and cannot be altered without showing. Retention and Fluency run absurdly high, and they read Concord, which almost no one else in the north can.

They do not need to open your letter to know what it says from who sent it and how fast.
[Trait] Six Hours — The Road in the Legs

In the courier line: Celerity, Economy and Reflex at a level that embarrasses swordsmen, spent only on arriving. They are the only people in the house of any use in a fight, having spent their lives getting through other people’s with a satchel.

They have no interest in winning. It has made them very hard to stop.
[Trait] A Debt Is a Debt — No Forgiveness on File

What is entered stands. They cannot be flattered out of it, and they cannot be generous without a line for it.

A lord who has forgotten what he owes can expect a very courteous reminder at a very poor moment.
System Metrics



























































PrimaryLeanSignature Sub-StatsWhyVitalityLowToleranceClerks are softArdencyVery lowDensityNothing here hits anythingGnosisExceptionalRetention, Fluency, AnalysisTheir whole inheritanceDexterityModerate, High in couriersCelerity, EconomyPen and reinHarmonicsModerateSynergy, AxisA bond you can rideResilienceHighOath, PersistenceThreatened by professionalsTemperingModerateYield, CoherenceIt wastes nothing, by lawDominionModerateFate, RadiusA chain’s reach and a posted rate
Wellspring compatibility.

Strongest: Oblation, the whole house. Transference, for the relay. Phreatis, under their falls at the Fall Cellar, where barge-masters top up by the hour and come out remembering other people’s childhoods.
Workable: Cymorath, the open way, for couriers, and Tarturon, the reckoning, for collectors with a grudge.
Against the grain: Benediction, the gift without count, Oblation’s contrary.


























StagesHow they readI to IIIThe rate on a sack of barley before their letters, and a first postIV to VA span to keep. First Release: an aura in blue and ocher lines, like a ruled pageVIGlory. Class names: Tariff-Master, Toll-Keeper, Six Hours and, for a very few, NotedVII and upSecond Release, then The Toll Is Due. People who have felt it say the worst part is that the rate is fair
Doctrine and Arts
Reluctantly. When there is real killing to be done the house pays for it, and the company is paid on the day, in full, in the most terrifying way possible, with a receipt. Brackets are fought on the chain bridges in midsummer, one fall into the river being a loss and two a very cold swim.





























MoveWhat it doesPay or Be Chained!The Toll Law, screamed. It is a courtesy, and part of what makes the chain lawfulSix Hours!Shouted down the line by the next courier. The legs arriveNotedA clerk looks up and enters you, and from then on the beacon line knows which way you wentOn the WaterBargemen’s boathook art: the hook behind the knee, and the river does the restFull and in CoinA sum of money laid before the fight’s other party. It has ended more battles than the chain
Culture
Language. Quick river Common and Concord for the books. “Six hours” is the whole of the house’s sense of humor.
Rites.

The First Toll. A child’s first copper, paid at the junction, entered in the child’s own hand.
Calling the Rate. Every morning from the lip of the falls, up to the castle.
The Fresh Coat. Every third spring, with fights between Limners and Daubers considered part of the expense.
The Boots On. Nobody takes them off in the room under the stair. There is a row of old boots on a shelf.
Closing the Page. At a clerk’s death a colleague rules off the last page and carries the balance forward.

Marriage, feud and debt. They marry other counting-houses, and the Hallenfeld Lamberts, cadets of the Lamberts of Sallowgate, sit among them. Thornwall is the long war, and the rate on logs is negotiated each year as a continuation of it. Ashmore has the grain and they have the barges. They had a tariff-master in a Moto cell for keeping honest books, and the house wrote that down.
What the commons get. A rate, on the wall, in pictures, that applies to them exactly as to a duke, and a receipt that means something, which is rarer than you may think. Signal-post women get a hut, a basket and a wage. And there is the Toll Bun, in the shape of a fist.
Limitations and Soul-Costs
[Curse] Exact Par — Never One Grain More

What is in the book is what there is, and every clerk knows the figure. A chain spent is a generation’s work gone.

Griet Hoogstraat’s penny a week was docked, some years later, on review.
[Curse] The Honest Book — A Lie Parts the Link

They cannot falsify a figure to save a life, a child’s included, and it leaves them unable to tell a comforting story.

They were told that the Tenrai had broken Osbert Lambert. The house looked at the entries he had left, and they knew better.
[Curse] The Entry at the Bottom of the Stair — Owing

Below the Fall Cellar, down a flooded stair behind the middle of the falls, is the Drowned Toll: a toll house far older than the house, and a Well beneath it where Mourning Pike grow as long as a barge. A clerk entered its rate as owing long ago, and its chain is the only one in the realm the house has never tried to collect on.
Nobody will say which side of the bargain the house is on. Every clerk has done the sums on what a three-hundred-year debt comes to at par.

Every other chain in the north is holding something back. A careful reader will ask what this one is keeping in.
How They Stand Against the Three Paths
Body. A hitter who comes to a chain finds out the balance, and one who walks around it finds a soft person with a ledger, kills him, and pays for it in late grain. Spirit. A true Spirit fighter can read a clerk’s balance off his Core and know exactly how much bluff he has. Fate. A Weaver can move a barge or a flood. Hallenfeld regards such people as extremely late with their paperwork, and outlasts them on the principle that a pull costs what it costs and a toll comes in every day.
Final Definition
House Hallenfeld is the most boring great power in the north and it would like that noted. They took the smallest honest thing a person can do, paying what was asked and getting what was promised, and wrote it down every time for three hundred years, until it could stop nine hundred horses. When one of them looks up from the page and tells you the rate, believe her, and find your purse.
“Six hours. I’ll want that noted.”
