factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: House Keld
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Overview





































TypeBanner House of Kharven, by the south’s counting · Tundra Clans · The Carried-Name PeopleOriginBeyond the treeline, as long as there have been Keld, which they say is alwaysFounderThey will give you a name, and then they will introduce you to herSeatNone. Seasonal camps on the Aurora Reach, the greatest being the Whalebone Gather, in the shadow of the palace nobody builtAnchorsThe fires · the carried names · the lifting · the Kiilut HouseSignatureThe Carried Name: every Keld is given someone dead to carry, and when the fight comes the name stands upMaxim”We follow because you are worth following, and we stop when you stop being worth it.”
Moriyasu Tenrai, a tax captain of the gold line, came out to the Whalebone Gather in the bright week of 689 with sixty lances, a fine coat of gold-trimmed black and a duelist’s name he had earned fairly on the plateau, and had it read out at the fires that the Reach owed the Seat for eleven years. An old sled-woman told him he should talk to Thora. So they brought him Thora, under a green sky with the blue domes of the palace throwing long shadows over the racing course, and she was nineteen, low and wide and dense, with blue on her chin and a mouth full of seal fat, and when he asked how old she was to be speaking for the fires, she told him ninety.
He laughed. She finished chewing, looked for a while at how he had set his feet, and told him he had his grandfather’s left foot. It was a good foot, she said. She had thought so at the time.
There was a ring cleared on the ice by then, with bets painted on a whale’s jaw. Moriyasu drew, the blade gold in that low light and his aura coming up behind it, and Thora Sennet stood with a birch lance in a girl’s two hands and took her breath in, and four hundred people stopped talking. She did not shout. “The name stands.”
Nothing happened to her body. It stayed nineteen and short. But she settled into it the way an old woman settles into a chair she has owned for sixty years, her weight going onto a bad hip she did not have, and her aura rose the color of tallow smoke in the shape of someone a head taller. When he came in on the feint his family was known for, low to the left and then up, the one that had killed the first Thora Sennet on the Teeth seventy-one years before, she was already standing where it was not going. She said in a cracked old voice, “I’ve had a long time to think about that one, boy,” and put the lance through his throat. Blood came out of her own left side a moment later, through a coat with no hole in it, at the place a Tenrai sword had gone in before her mother’s mother was born. She sat down on the ice and asked somebody to get her some fat. The sixty lances went home. Ask Thora how old she is now, and she will tell you ninety-seven. She is twenty-six.
House Keld is the smallest house, the hardest people and the most conditionally loyal. They live in conditions that would kill anyone else inside a week, and they swear to a person and never to a letter. What they hold that everyone needs is whale-oil, ivory and a tundra nobody else can use. What they hold that nobody else wants is a whole people’s worth of the dead, in working order.
Origin of the House
The Keld say their first ancestor came out onto the ice alone and was found dead by the second, who looked at the body for a while, took her name so that somebody would still be using it, and made it through. They had a word for one of the dead left without the Waiting, a corpse nobody sat with, long before they had a word for a lord: kiilut, the worst word they own. A name with nobody to carry it is the same thing to them.
Then there is the palace, the Kiilut House, which stood on the snowfield before their oldest song. Its third dome has no agreed number of sides, and Measurewright Ansell came out of it in 694 by the wrong door with his beard at his belt. They pitch their camp every year in its shadow, will not sleep inside it, and do not joke about it.
The House on the Crystal

























LayerPlaneThe Keld formAether ShellPhysicalDense, low and economical. It runs on almost nothing, as a lamp runs on fat, and gives out very lateEssence CoreSoulThe bearer’s own, with a lodger who cannot learn anything new and has very firm opinionsAttraction LayerFateWider than it has any business being, carrying a whole other life’s worth of what was owed and promised
Path. The soul leans Body, as any soul does that has hauled its own sled since it could walk, with a smaller lean toward Fate from the name on the Layer. Ladders. Aether climbs in the fighters. Grip. The Layer, and a very small one. Taking a name at the Gather opens Thread at I, Touched, long before Glory. A Touched Keld knows the ice is about to go, and on a rare day can lean on that for most of a reserve and a nosebleed. Nobody has gone past II on blood alone. Whale-Caller is the class that runs thick at the Gather, with later forms the Long Water and the Call Comes Back, and they will not discuss the third with strangers.
The Carried Name
In a breath: when a soul dies its Layer leaves a Name behind, and the Keld pick these up and put them on their children, so a Keld fighter has one dead person’s whole life standing behind her eyes, debts and all.
What it is. At death a soul comes apart by three roads: the Core goes to Echo, the Shell to residue through the body, and the Layer to Name, a shape left on the Plane of Fate of everything that person owed, promised and was owed. Everywhere else this is a matter for theologians. The Keld call out the names of their dead at the Gather and give them to children, freely, before witnesses, and the child’s Layer takes it up. They call what she then has her sauniq, a word that also means bone. It is a vow in form, and it spends only the soul’s own share.
The dead woman is dead, and nobody in the lodge is confused about it: rebirth moves pattern and never a person. What the child has is what that life left written on the Layer, and that turns out to be a good deal: how she held a lance, where she liked to camp, who she would not forgive. It is why a Keld will tell you she is ninety and not be joking.
The forms









































FormWhoWhat it doesWhat it costsThe CallingEvery child, at the GatherThe elders call the unclaimed names into the palace’s long shadow, and the families answerWhatever the name owedThe HearingStages I to IIIThe name comes up through sleep and in the hands. A seven-year-old reaches for the lance a way nobody taught herHer first words may be somebody else’s opinionsThe LiftingAny riderIn the hour before a whiteout the horizon floats. A Keld reads wind and ground by what her name remembers, because some dead woman rode this plate two hundred years ago. Old Harald moved four hundred riders past a Tenrai column so close they heard the horses blowingA road changed since then has killed a great many KeldThe Name StandsFirst Release, Stage IV and upCalled low. The dead person’s manner rises with a second aura, tallow-colored and taller, and for its length she fights with that life’s measure, reads and habits. It counts toward the two-Grade limit like any ReleaseThe name’s death-wound opens where it opened, a little, every timeThe Long LodgeDomain, Stage VIII at leastEvery person who has ever carried that name stands up behind the bearer, and the ice is theirs. It looks unchanged to a southerner, until the dogs lie downShe has to be able to tell them which one she is, at the end
What it costs. You take the debts with the skills. A Keld whose name died owing a shift on the rim will ride south alone in that heat, present herself at the nearest fort, and leave on the day the dead person would have gone home. A name that died in a feud is still in it, and this is the plain reason the Sennet and the Haldorssons have been killing each other over the Teeth: the same people keep being in it. Muken Moto read that line through the host at the Skeldmere as a crack waiting to run, and the Sennet grays turned their lances on the Haldorsson dark horses the moment the Iron Fist was busy.
Its limit. It cannot learn. The name knows nothing past the day its owner died, and its power is the bearer’s own: a Stage II girl with a great warrior’s name has a great warrior’s habits in a Stage II body.
Who beats it. Find out how the name died. The south has been paying for this for a century, over seal fat: a death-wound is a flinch that opens under The Name Stands, on a side you can learn. Bring something the name has never met. Set its old debts against the bearer’s living ones. Keep her fighting past a tenth of reserve, where any Core frays, and the wrong one may come back up. A Yukari who can say what a thing truly is can say it to a Keld in front of everyone, and the lodger hears it.
The Kiilut House
I have asked every elder who would sit with me what the palace has to do with the names, and been fed well and told nothing. Here is what can be observed. The Calling is held nowhere else, at the edge of the palace’s shadow, late in the day as the shadow lengthens toward the crowd. The unclaimed names are called in order of how long they have gone unclaimed, and the elders are visibly in a hurry. And a Keld hedge-worker, drunk, once told Ansell’s old assistant that the third dome has as many sides as there are names nobody came for, and that this is why they keep the count down. I report this as gossip.
Physical Appearance and Dress
Stature and coloring. Low, wide and dense, with barrel chests and necks like tree-stumps, broad flat faces burned red-brown, narrow black eyes and coarse black hair braided close. Marks. Three thin blue lines down the chin mark a killing in defense of the herds, and a fourth, thicker, a chief. Walrus-ivory rings go into the braids, one for each fight won. Voice. Whichever one it is today. They rise from a floor with no hand on it.
The look at fifty paces. Nothing, in a whiteout, until the white cloth comes down. Otherwise short men on short horses in two coats, reindeer hair turned in and sealskin turned out, a wolverine hood that takes no frost, horn lamellar sewn between. Arrowheads are black glass and bone, because iron cracks in the deep cold. They flex, in a country with no coin, by who sewed it, and a coat from a famous hand is worth a team of dogs. The most famous piece on the Reach was Aksel Keld’s iron hand, black iron and walrus tusk and sinew on a stump a Tenrai sword left at thirteen, closing by a cord at the shoulder into a fist the size of a man’s skull. The poorest Keld alive has the same two coats and a small ivory tooth at the throat with a dead person’s mark on it.
Lineage Traits
[Trait] The Baseline — Conditions That Kill the Enemy First

Near-immune to cold, hunger and bad air, with a body built to spend nothing it does not have to. Heat is another matter, and the rim keeps a list.

Aksel Keld at eighteen sat his horse like a man of forty. Nobody on the ice has told me whose forty it was.
[Trait] The Worst of It — Meat-Sharing

A hunter’s kill is shared by a custom so strict that the one who killed it often gets the worst of it, and it has gone into the blood as a very high tolerance for going without.

Ashmore’s Thin Weeks has been tried on them. Their report was that it felt like Tuesday.
[Trait] Weather-Weight — Touched

The grip above, in daily use: they know when the storm, the plate or the herd will turn, a little before it is reasonable to. A true lean costs what it costs anyone.

They have one word for a soul’s weight and a storm on its way. They have a low opinion of the southern argument about it.
System Metrics



























































PrimaryLeanSignature Sub-StatsWhyVitalityExceptionalConstitution, Tolerance, FortitudeThe tundra did the selectingArdencyModeratePenetrationBlack glass goes inGnosisModerate to HighPerception, Forecast, VigilanceA herd, a mile off, in a whiteoutDexterityHighEconomy, Sequence, GrappleDisputes are settled off the horseHarmonicsLow to ModerateStability, AxisOne other person, and the deadResilienceHighContinuity, Persistence, OathTwo lives’ worth of who they areTemperingLowLongevityNobody would feed them in seclusionDominionModerateSense, RadiusThey wait until the room is cold
Wellspring compatibility.

Strongest: Phreatis, memory as deep water, what is lived sinking in and coming back. Mortalis, the black gate looked at squarely, by a people who have stopped fearing it. Anamnesis, everything keeping its past.
Workable: Thaloré, the depth of a feeling, and Abython, for sealers who go down.
Against the grain: Letheveil and Lethegraal, the Wellsprings of forgetting, which to a Keld are simply evil.


























StagesHow they readI to IIIThe Hearing. Most hedge-workers stop here, keeping a lamp lit in a whiteoutIV to VThe Name Stands. The first time surprises everyone, with a small wound in the sideVIGlory, and the Whale-Caller classVII and upSecond Release, then the Long Lodge. Below a tenth of reserve, nobody can say who is at home
Doctrine and Arts
Few as they are, they are worth three of anyone else’s. They ride in the long line, which moves across open snow like weather, and in a wedge when something needs breaking. In the lifting a Keld child is taught to sit down and wait. A rider is taught the opposite.

























MoveWhat it doesThe LiftingWhiteout war. White cloth over rider and horse, hit and fade from three sides, and they die having seen nobodyGlass Out of WhiteHorn-backed bow at close range from nowhere, black glass that shatters in the woundQatuq Take YouQatuq is the cold that takes the unready. A curse, and also a Keld with a dead fire-keeper’s name walking a host in a slow circle until the wind turnsThe Iron FistAksel’s own. A fist of solid iron and his whole weight. It broke ribs through mail at the Skeldmere, and it was full of old cracks, which is how it ended
Culture
Language. Northern Common for strangers, and for themselves the old tongue of the carried-name peoples, in which most insults are about bowls: hulluk (wet wood), numra (an empty bowl held out).
Rites.

The Skin at the Door. Sour milk in a horn cup. Refuse it and you are skin-refuser, said once, and then there is a fight.
The Waiting. Lodge lamps turned down, the dead given to the sky or the shelf, and at the next Gather to a child.
Setting It Down. When a name’s debts are finally paid, the one who carries it can say so at the fires. Nobody can remember the last time.
The Boots. A certain kind of Moto goes out on the shelf to practice Domains, and the Keld find them some weeks later, and return their boots.

Marriage, feud and debt. Marriages are arranged, in part, by whose names can stand to be in one lodge. Thornwall tried to take the whale-oil by force, and the song is long. Old Harald has been too old to sit a horse since Ulf Stark’s father was a boy, and he moved those riders in the second year of the war, and if you find that hard to reconcile you should ask how many men have been Old Harald. His grandson Aksel won eleven fights, lost the twelfth to Muken Moto on the Skeldmere and was spared, and the Keld follow that king for as long as he stays worth following.
About forty Haldorssons walked off the Seat’s square alive. That left several thousand names with nobody to carry them, and at the Gather after the war every clan on the ice stood up and took them. There are Sennet children now carrying the men their fathers killed. The Sennet elders call this an obligation, and the Haldorssons call it an occupation. It is the first new thing to happen in that feud in two hundred years.
What the commons get. There are no commons and no coin. Everyone has a name older than any lord’s, and everyone’s death will be sat with. They are the only people I have studied who do not seem afraid of being forgotten, and I think that is what makes them so hard to frighten about anything else.
Limitations and Soul-Costs
[Curse] The Wound That Comes With It — How the Name Died

Each time the name stands its death-wound opens a little, and a little more each year. The old carriers wear rags where a blade never went, and there are lodges full of people coughing up water from a sea they have never seen.

[Curse] Gone to the Name — Who Comes Back

Below a tenth of reserve a Keld’s Core has someone else to ask. Some do not come back: the girl is gone and the old woman walks around in her, asking after people. The lodge feeds her and keeps a Waiting for the girl.

It is a hard thing to sit a Waiting with the deceased pouring your tea.
[Curse] It Is the Same Feud — Nobody Gets to Stop

A carried debt does not fade, and a killing stays fresh for two hundred years because the people involved keep being born. Peace on the Reach is a matter of which children get which names.

Muken Moto broke four thousand riders with a song and an old crack, and he did not have to invent the crack.
How They Stand Against the Three Paths
Body. On the ice a Body fighter is losing to the weather when he arrives. Off it, with their backs to a stair, the Keld die as well as anyone. Spirit. The real danger: two people in one Core, one of them dead, and a Spirit fighter can get between them. Fate. A very large unpaid bill on the Layer is a thing to lean on, and they are nearly alone in the north in feeling it coming.
Final Definition
House Keld are the people who decided no one goes unsat-with. They took the bare ledger every soul leaves behind and gave it to their children, and it made them unkillably hard and unable to stop any quarrel their grandmothers began. A nineteen-year-old with a mouthful of fat will tell you she is ninety and put a lance through your throat. You should have asked her how she died.
“How old are you?” “Which of us?”

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: House Lambert
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Overview





































TypeWarlord house of the Holy Sea of Alabaster · a family of counters · reads as furniture on every registerOriginThe bench at the top of the Stair, on the white shelfFounderPerrine Lambert, tally-wife, by the house’s own listSeatSallowgate, the landward gate of the Holy SeaAnchorsThe sworn count · the Struck List · the benchSignatureThe Computus: every blow the family ever saw is counted in the blood, so a Lambert is never fast and always earlyMaximCount True
In the spring of 668 a duelist named Odo Vance, the Bright Champion of three kings in the Midmarch, rode up to the tariff-hall at Sallowgate in a coat of yellow silk and a very bad temper, because he had been asked to declare his horse. The clerk at the window was Perrin Lambert, sixty-one, a soft man with ink on his cuff, and he asked again. Vance was Stage IX, and the air around him had already gone tight enough to make the water clock shiver in its housing. Half the town came running to see the stupid thing about to happen. Vance drew and cut at him across the counter, and Perrin Lambert was standing a little to the left of where the sword went. He had not hurried. Vance cut again, and the clerk was somewhere else again, a hand’s width, on his flat feet, with his pen still in his fingers, saying in a carrying voice, “That is two, sir. Assault upon an officer of the bench is two silver the attempt.” Vance was fast enough that the people at the back could only see the shine of it. The clerk had no coat and no aura, and the assay rolls had him as a dead Crystal, thirty years filed. He went through seven more like a man finding his way across a familiar room in the dark, and at nine he stepped forward, because the shoulder had told him where the elbow would be, and rapped the Bright Champion on the wrist nerve with an oak ruler. The sword hit the flags. “Eleven silver, and the horse,” said Perrin Lambert, and it was then that the mule behind him, frightened out of its wits by all of this, kicked out and broke his hip in two places. He had not seen it coming at all. They say he lay on the cobbles and wrote it down.
Vance paid. The whole South has told that story for fifty years, and most people tell it for the ruler. The Lamberts tell it for the mule, and for the other thing they know about it: Vance was angry, across a counter, using a tenth of what he had, and every cut said where it was going. Had he stopped meaning it for one breath, or spent one working, they would have buried the clerk that afternoon.
The Holy Sea weighs what people swear, on a stone that wets under a true oath, and an honest fool leaves lovely footprints. Somebody has to count what the oath is about. For as long as the Sea has had courts there has been a Lambert at the bench beside the cleric: tariffs at the gate, grain in the store, witnesses in the dock, the days between a lord’s promise and a lord’s delivery. They are the only people in the Sea allowed a sword by right, and they hold Sallowgate and the land marches. Their levies are small, drilled, and paid on the day. Their officers tell a general his numbers before battle, in front of his captains, and do not soften them. What they hold that everyone needs is a number that is right. What they want is for the count to come out true and for the Sea’s courts to be heard north of the border, and in a world full of people who would pay for a different number, that is a much stranger ambition than it sounds.
Origin of the House
The list begins with a woman. When two kings fought the Battle of Sorrel Water on a table at the top of the Stair, a tally-wife named Perrine Lambert was hired to keep the sutlers’ account, and the house’s whole claim to antiquity is that she sat through it with her thumb moving and told the first king’s steward, before the soup, how many of his men would be alive at evening. She was off by none. The steward had her whipped, and then, the bench being what it was, had her hired. Her daughters kept the marches’ grain, and her grandsons were at the gate. The Palatines came and went, and by the time the present line of them could count there was already a Lambert standing at each one’s elbow who had counted first. Sallowgate came with the job, the land marches with Sallowgate, and the sword because a holy see needs somebody who may carry one.
Cadet branches went north on the Sea’s business and stayed: the Hallenfeld Lamberts in the north, a steward whose thumb moved at the elbow of a northern king, clerks in every chapter house, and a diocesan administrator named Charles Lambert, forty-one and heavy in the stomach, whom a Primate of the Church had read for twenty-six years without noticing a thing, until the morning he watched that man step out of the way of a very great polearm four times running, soaked to the thigh, and then put a boot through the knee behind it.
The House on the Crystal
A Soul Crystal is the soul itself, in three layers: the Aether Shell, where Aether (mana) comes in and force goes out; the Essence Core, where it becomes Essence (spiritual energy); and the Attraction Layer, a soul’s own share of Fate. From Glory an assay reads a soul’s Mastery, one rung for each road. Most Lamberts never see a rung.

























LayerPlaneThe Lambert formAether ShellPhysicalSealed in a great many, for life. In a woken Lambert, thin and clean and very lateEssence CoreSoulEvery unwoken soul holds a trickle of Essence it cannot spend. A Lambert’s goes wholly into the count, and that is why nothing else ever grows thereAttraction LayerFateNothing to report on Fate Mastery. A lifetime’s kept oath shows as a very hard Oath Sub-Stat, and sometimes as Fate I
Path. A Path is the layer a soul leans on, recognized from how it lives. An unwoken soul has a Path too, though no instrument will tell it so, and the coil, reading only output, gets silence. The house’s duelists tend to the Body Path, its benchmen to a long slow Spirit road, and a Lambert who walks either at all is unusual.
No grip, no eye. The family has neither. Their Mastery reads from Glory like anyone’s, if they wake, and on the coil they read as a very dull family. A Lambert’s window has a Level, a health bar and a great many clerical skills at an alarming rank.





















Stage or standingTypical LambertUnwokenMost of them, by rumor. Clerks and tally-wives with the Computus at full strength and nothing elseIV to VI, wokenThe rare officer. Body I from Glory, and nothing read on the other two roads, is an ordinary line. A coat at last, and a read that goes with itVII and upVery few on the list. The house does not boast of them, and they do not tend to be the ones you meet
The Computus
Computus is the Court’s Latin for a reckoning, the same word its clerics use for working out the feast days. On the Stair they call it being early. In the taverns, they say a man has got a Lambert in him when he ducks before the bottle leaves the hand.
What it is. A read with no faculty behind it. Every Lambert child starts counting at about three, and something in the blood keeps the running total for the family. Shoulders, hips, hands, breaths, and which way the weight went. It comes up as a forecast, in the body, ahead of the blow.
How it works, in plain words. No blow starts in the hand. A shoulder commits first, a heel takes weight, a breath stops, and these come in an order that a body cannot hide, because it has to obey it. If you had watched ten thousand cuts you could say, with the first flicker, which of the ten thousand this one was. A good old master does that, and calls it experience. Scholars call it a forecast from priors: you lay what you see against what you have already counted, and the likeliest continuation is simply where to stand. The Lamberts are born with several generations of priors already filed. The trickle of Essence in the sealed Core has nothing else to do, and it never stops doing this. So the answer starts before the delivery it answers, by a margin so small that a spectator calls it luck and a practitioner calls it impossible. Since it comes from no working, there is nothing to sense. It has no glow, no color and no signature, and no one has ever detected it on purpose.
The forms.






























FormCourt wordWhat it isThe ThumbPollexThe first stage, and it never leaves. The right thumb moving on the pad of the index finger, counting whatever there is. In the family this is breathingThe ColumnColumnaOne opponent, read through. The whole body starts to move early against one willThe SumSummaA field, as far as the eye can go: men, horses, remounts, days of grain. A false return feels wrong in the hand like a cased weight. A woken master reads Forecast and Analysis a full step high while he countsThe Second AskingIterumThe house’s interrogation. Asked twice, with the weight of the list behind it, a man who lies the second time knows precisely what he is doing
What it costs. Nothing, in reserve. It is the only art in the South that charges no Essence, and the bill arrives elsewhere.
It never turns off. They count stairs, wedding guests and how many breaths the priest took. They cannot be surprised at a party, cannot quite stop knowing how long the people they love have left at that rate of drinking, and in the family this is not considered interesting. It eats the soul’s first room. A great many Lamberts never wake because the Core is busy, and what would have become a Crystal’s first stirring has gone to the sum since before they could walk. The house has known this for centuries. It teaches its children to count anyway.
It also cannot be lied to, least of all by its owner. Priors are only worth what went into them. A Lambert who enters a false number has spoiled the column, and the error spreads. His read drifts out of true by a hair, then a finger, and one day a blow is not where he knew it would be. That is the real reason for the Struck List. They will tell you it is honor, and it is honor. It is also that the rest of the family’s count runs through the same bench, and nobody wants to stand next to that man at the gate.
Its limit. It reads what has a will behind it and has been done before. A falling wall, a beast in a panic and a working that runs by itself give it nothing. It knows what a body is about to do, and that has never made anyone faster. Against a blow it can see coming and cannot get out of the way of, it tells a Lambert the hour. A clerk with no coat takes a hit like a clerk, and Charles Lambert had six weeks of bending as a project after one landed. It reaches as far as the eye and the reports go, and a field unseen is a hole in the sum.
Who beats it. Do something no one has done. Feint with the whole body so the intent is false, then strike with no thought at all, which is much easier to say. Send the mule. Stand out of sight. Raise your Stage until knowing does him no good. Or, if you must deal with one at a bench, give him a true number, which beats him every time, and is the one thing he has been trying to get you to do.
Physical Appearance and Dress
They run tall in the Sallowgate line and every other size elsewhere, because they have married the bench for centuries with no thought for looks. There is some gold in the hair of the main branch. What marks them is a stillness in the face, and the thumb, and something that happens in the eyes when you walk into a room, where they check over your shoulder for how many came with you. Voices are courteous and unhurried, with a short true number in the middle of a long sentence. They do not say “about.” They stand with their open hands kept low, and on wet ground they put their weight on the outside edge of the foot. You would not look twice, and the house has spent a long time making sure of that.
White and ink-black are the house colors, a balance on the field. Benchmen wear plain white wool with an inked cuff and an iron ring cut with the balance. The Warlord’s office is the exception, and on purpose: the Bear Harness, gilded plate with a rearing Sallowgate bear in relief, Very Rare, under a scarlet cloak that makes him the easiest target on the field so his men can count him. Ask its price and he will give it to you to the copper, and the leaf by the ounce. The house sword is gray and plain, and every child at Sallowgate learns on a wooden copy of its balance. A poor cousin has a wooden tally on a string and a clerk’s coat turned twice. He will know what your boots cost.
Lineage Traits
[Trait] One Before — The Inherited Margin
The Computus in the body, and it shows on the sheet as an Inherited Trait. A woken Lambert with this and the Reflex of his Stage is a horrible thing to fence.

Against a blow with a will behind it, Reflex reads a full step high in anyone woken, and in the unwoken the blade is merely elsewhere.
Costs nothing and cannot be sensed.
Slower against whatever has no intent in it.

He is not fast. Nobody who has lost to one has ever been able to accept that.
[Trait] Furniture — The Blind Spot in Every Register

The coil, the Refinement Spectrum and every other instrument that reads output report an unwoken Lambert as nothing at all.
Pressure works on them as on any commoner, and they have had years to practice looking as if it did not.
A woken Lambert gives this up on the morning he wakes. There is a real argument in the family about whether it is worth it.

Fifty-three assessments of one man, by the Accord’s own file, and the fifty-third agreed with the first.
[Trait] Open Hands — The Polearm Drill

A taught habit that the Computus makes frightening: hands low and open to feel a shaft before the eye confirms it, hips shifting a degree or two every third of a second to keep a big enemy strung along one axis.
Learned on wet decks and in tariff-halls, and taught to no one who would be expected to carry anything.

The oldest answer to a long weapon, and it needs nothing but nerve and a lifetime’s arithmetic.
System Metrics
Stat lean



























































PrimaryLeanSignature Sub-StatsWhyDexterityExceptionalReflex, Economy, EvasionEarly beats fast, with the least motion that will doGnosisExceptionalForecast, Analysis, RetentionThe count itselfResilienceHighOath, IntegrityA sworn lifeVitalityModerateFortitudeThey take hits like the people they areDominionModerateCommandA levy paid on the day needs little shoutingArdencyLowDensityNothing thrown, if it can be helpedHarmonicsLowStabilityThe count is no help to a lensTemperingLowMaturityA climb that started late and slowly
Wellspring compatibility
A Wellspring is a type of Aether and the idea a soul tempers itself on. A woken Lambert usually takes one, late and well.






























TierWellspringsWhyNaturalJudicium, AurevaneTruth told apart, and light that does not flatter. Coin-gold auras, in the wokenEasyAnamnesis, Orrenthal, Petralon, FixatioRemembrance, a thing that keeps its word under load, a gate, and what stays boundWorkableThaloré, Mirithane, MonolithionSpirit and stone. Thaloré, a Spirit Wellspring, is the common reading of the ground under the Walk, and it gives a Lambert no fire, only the weight of what someone meantAgainst the grainSomnalis, Tenebra, CataclysmOdds, hiding and broken law, and no Lambert has been happy in any of them
On the Stages





























StagesHow a Lambert readsUnwokenThe Computus entire, and a clerk’s body. Lethal to the overconfident at a bench’s width, and in the rank a good corporalI to IIIA first coat, a good deal of surprise in the familyIV to VIFirst Release if one is found, the Answer at real speed, a Class name at Glory, generally Auditor or something unkindVII to IXSecond Release, Forecast past what many a Stage above can feint. A short list of namesX and upA woken Sum across a whole campaign. If any are alive, nobody has been told
Doctrine and Arts
The answer. Lambert fencing is a counter from first to last, and it needs to be asked. Nobody at Sallowgate is taught to attack. In the field they read the numbers aloud before the first blow, and in the Court’s Latin when they feel like being unpleasant.















































MoveTongueMeaningWhat it doesLa Réponse!Sallowgate French”The Answer!”The Sallowgate Answer, taught to every child. The blade turns in the hand before yours leaves its line, takes it on the flat, and rides down into the wrist or throatEncore une fois”One more time”The Second Asking, in a duel. He gives you exactly the opening you offered before, and you are welcome to believe itMains ouvertes”Open hands”The unarmed answer to anything long, four evasions and then the kneePied de pont”Deck foot”Weight on the outside edge before committing, for wet stone and bad planks. His footing is simply better than yoursLe reste!”The remainder!”The officer’s call. Whoever is left on your flank when the sum runs out, and he has told his crossbows who that isRAYÉ!”Struck!”The cut that ends it, shouted once and rarely. It goes through the hand you lied with
Culture
They speak Common with Sallowgate French in the mouth, and Latin at Court, where each one is entered under a name he did not ask for.

The Reading of the List. Once a year in the Sallowgate hall, the Struck List is read in full, name, figure and date. It is a real object, and anyone can ask to see it. The family stands. The list includes a man’s cousin, whom he loved, and two hundred sacks of grain.
The Father’s Count. A Lambert who is dying gives the last figure he has. Someone is expected to be there to take it. A Warlord of the house died on the Grey Plain with the count of his own dead still in his mouth, and his son got there in time.
The Family Count. One night each winter the house counts itself. The figure is entered in a book that has never left Sallowgate, and no outsider has seen it, a Palatine included. People have tried.
The Bench Marriage. At his own wedding, a Lambert asks the other family how many of them there are. It is on the Stair’s list of jokes because it is in the service.

Who they marry, fight and owe. They marry clerks, officers and, once, the Yukari: Lord Naiser is half Sallowgate, and the marriage is the house’s one great political act. The Palatine they serve and do not flatter, and they have spent centuries quarreling with the clerics on their own benches. They audit Marrick companies and match tariff books with the Ryu. Sallowgate’s commoners get the rarest thing in the South, which is pay on the day, a true weight at the market and a tariff that does not change for your cousin. Men queue for their levies. Those who cheat them find the water clock very accurate.
Limitations and Soul-Costs
[Curse] The Unwaking — The Count Takes the First Room
Most of the family will never have a coat, a Stage, or an aura, and they know why. Each generation spends itself on the sum its children will need. The woken who do come are late, thin on every road, and the house argues every time about what they cost.
[Curse] The Spoiled Column — A Lie Costs the Liar First
A false count puts the Lambert’s own read out of true. It does not matter why he lied. The Computus judges the number and never the reason, and the man who shorted two hundred sacks to feed a village through a bad winter was as wrong in the shoulder afterward as any thief. He paid the same price, and so did the cousin who struck him, who bought that village’s grain the same week and carries a fourth notch on his pommel.
[Curse] The Mule — What Has No Will
They do not see the runaway cart, the falling lintel, or the frightened horse. A surprising number of Lamberts die of accidents, and their funerals have a certain tone.
How They Stand Against the Three Paths
Body. Their favored meeting, as long as the enemy has a will and a Stage in reach. A big Stage gap breaks it by plain speed, and one blow lands on a body with nothing around it.
Spirit. Their deepest worry. A working that goes past the Shell does not move like a shoulder, and it has little to read.
Fate. They read it badly and hate it. A guard that slips has no shoulder in it. But a Fate fighter who has moved the odds has still not moved the true number, and Lamberts are unusually hard to deceive about what has actually happened. Report the strap that gave, and they will have the next strap checked.
Final Definition
House Lambert is a family of frightening clerks, who stand behind the whole South’s sworn word with a thumb moving against one finger. They hold a gate and the only true number in any room, and they have paid for it with their own waking. You may think you have never met one. You have certainly been counted by one. When a Lambert tells you how many of you there are, you should thank him, and then you should look behind you, because he has already allowed for the mule.
Count True, and keep the list.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: House Marrick
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Overview





































TypeWarlord house of the Ochre Fields · the Wall for Hire · an elected captaincy over a country of spear companiesOriginThe Long Fields, levy country of the old Empire of Sum-golFounderOld Marget Marrick is who they name; the house is older and has lost the receiptsSeatHammerfordAnchorsThe Rank · the contract · the Widows’ ChestSignatureThe Shoulder: sign one contract, stand in one file, and a blow that lands on one of you lands on all sixteenMaximShoulder to Shoulder
Everyone in the Midmarch can tell you about the Red Bell of Tarn. She was Stage X, Realization, a tall woman in lacquered plate who had taken two castles alone, and at Wick Bottom in the summer of 691 she came down onto the left corner of the Sixth Blacks out of a clear sky, with a fist wrapped in enough force to stave in a gatehouse. The man on that corner was a sergeant named Joost Hallam, Stage IV, who had a wife in Musterfield and a bad back. What the field saw was Joost Hallam staying on his feet, with his teeth showing. And behind him, in file, a hard and terrible noise went back through fifteen men from front to rear, and every one of them, the whole sixteen, at the same instant, broke his left collarbone.
None of them fell. They could not; each was jammed against the next, shoulders locked, with a drum going, and the force had gone down through thirty-two boots and into the barley stubble, which was found afterward to have sunk a foot in a line as straight as a rule. She stood there with her arm out, looking honestly surprised. Sixteen spears came level, on the drum, in fifteen right hands and one left. It would not have mattered a great deal at Stage X, except that the crossbows on the wing had been waiting all morning for a target that could not be mistaken for a friend.
The Sixth Blacks held that line until sundown, singing, with sixteen broken collarbones in the left file alone. The contract expired at sundown. At the last edge of the light the drum stopped, and a clerk called the hour, and the entire file sat down in the stubble at once and began to scream. Sixteen men. You could hear it in the next parish. Gerrit Marrick was there, on the other side as it happens, and he tells that story at every Moot, and he always ends it the same way. “You stand in it because the man on your left is standing in it, lad. Brave’s got nothing to do with it.”
The north fights in knots and wedges and long Keld lines. The south fights in a wall, and that wall was Marrick’s first. What they hold that everyone needs is the only infantry in the Inner World that will stand where it is put, to the hour, for anyone who pays, and fight a Stage X on a sergeant’s wages. What they want is a long peace with a lot of small wars in it.
Origin of the House
The Long Fields are barley and spearmen, and for three hundred years they were the foot of the Empire of Sum-gol, whose levies went where the Mahou told them. Nobody thought that made them a power. When the Emperor Rokju called the Marrick from his balcony in 602, the company in the square looked up at the sun, saw it was noon, and grounded arms, because the contract had that minute run out. The Fields keep it as a holiday. It was the first time anyone had noticed that a wall of men with a clause in it was a thing that could be owned by nobody.
The family has provided the elected Captain often enough that the name stuck to the country. Old Marget Marrick made it what it is: in 631, sitting on a barley sack on Dob Harkness’s broken cart at the ford, she auctioned the whole levy for a day and a night, accepted both bids, and split it down the middle. Both armies had Marrick companies at their center at Sorley Bridge. Nine thousand went into the ground. The Marrick dead were paid to the end of the season, to the widows, on the nail, and both kings hired again next spring. Her clause is why the cart stays broken, and every recruit touches the tailboard on the morning of her first muster.
The House on the Crystal
A Soul Crystal is the soul itself, in three layers: the Aether Shell, where Aether (mana) comes in and force goes out; the Essence Core, where it becomes Essence (spiritual energy); and the Attraction Layer, a soul’s own share of Fate. On the Fields you will meet many with all three asleep.

























LayerPlaneThe Marrick formAether ShellPhysicalMost of the rank are unwoken and sealed. A corner is an ordinary woken fighter, and what is unusual is how far the coat goesEssence CoreSoulSolid and unlettered. Marrick ghosts are very well behavedAttraction LayerFateOne line on the window, the contract, and a kept word that runs for a season. It spends the soul’s own share and pulls nothing down
Path. Body, and they would not know the word. A forty-year sergeant has leaned on the Aether Shell through his whole life, and he has very likely never been told. Any Marrick who walks Fate reads it at I or II, and without a Work or a blessing that is the top of it. Nobody on the Fields has ever moved the odds on anything. They bring more spears.
No eye, no grip, no blood. The Marrick family has none of it, and their signature would work no better for a Marrick than for a Hobgoblin rope-seller. Anyone who signs gets the Shoulder. It is what the Long Fields sell, and the reason other armies who have copied the drill have never got the wall.






























StandingStageWhat they doFileUnwoken to IIStand, push, level the spear. The great majoritySergeantIII to VA first coat and the file’s whole weight behind itCornerIV to VIISomeone who can take a blow, on the outside angle of a rank, “shining for the whole file”CaptainVII and upRare, expensive, and listed on the wall of the Hiring Hall
Body Mastery reads low and comes slowly, since Level comes slowly to a corner and most of what a corner has ever done with her Shell is hold still. A Muridic sergeant with a bad back is the backbone of southern warfare.
The Shoulder
What it is. A rank under one contract, touching at the shoulder, shares its load. Blows that land on one man spread down the file and go into the ground. It can be broken, and it hurts, and every person in that file feels every blow. That is what you are buying.
How it works, in plain words. Lock sixteen men front to back, each pressed to the next, each with a leg braced back, and now the blow has to move sixteen men and everything they are standing on. That much is plain mechanics, which scholars call spreading an impulse over a greater mass, and by the rear rank the blow is a shove.
What the Fields added is the coat. A corner’s reinforcement, the coat of aura a woken fighter wears, can extend into held gear. In a signed rank it goes further. The contract is a small vow, one anybody can make, and it is written on the same terms for every soul in the company, so each signer sees the same line on the window (the soul’s private report of its numbers). Those lines tune to one another like a set of bells cast together. With shoulders touching, the corner’s coat runs along the file, thin as paint on the back row, and the unwoken get a share of something they could never make for themselves. It lets the force through without tearing anything too fast, and it goes on down to the boots and into the ground. The window shows it plainly, the moment you step in.
[Contract: Sixth Blacks · to the Lord of Oxley]
[Term: until sundown, August 19]
[Rank: Left file, 4th of 16 · Corner: Hallam, J.]
[Sharing: load, coat, a little of the gain]

The forms. They are drilled by number, like everything on the Fields.






























FormHow manyWhat it isThe PairTwoFirst lesson. Two recruits shoulder to shoulder, and a sergeant hits one of them with a plank until both can feel itThe FileSixteenThe working unit. A corner can spread a very bad blow down a file, at the price of a broken bone apieceThe SquareA companyFiles locked side by side. The ground under a good square has a settled look when they leaveThe WallSeveral companiesThe drums set the time, and what runs through it is mainly nerve: the coat is thin that far out. A Wall will take a charge, and a good many other things it has no business taking
What it costs. Everyone pays. A blow that would have killed one person now hurts sixteen, and they all keep the injury. Whole Marrick files share the same limp. Essence in the coat comes from the corner alone, at a fast rate, and a corner who has shone for a whole file through an afternoon is gray, and shaking, and sometimes dead on her feet.
Its limit. The contract ends. That is the whole of the law and it has no appeal. At the hour named, the line goes off the window and the bells stop ringing, and it is just a lot of tired people standing close together, feeling every bone they broke at the same moment. So when a Marrick company grounds spears at noon, it is no point of pride. They have nothing left to stand in. Nobody touches a company walking off, because every commander in the South knows how many spears he would be offered afterward. Before the hour named, too, the Shoulder is not there. And it needs shoulders: a broken file is sixteen ordinary people, and most of them have never been anything else.
Who beats it. Do not hit it from the front. A wall sends force to the ground, and force from two sides at once has nowhere to go: surround a square and squeeze, and it kills from the inside, standing up. Ride around and shoot, as the Yan have done without rancor for three centuries, since an arrow in the throat is not a blow on the rank. Cut down the drummer or the corner. Go past the Shell entirely, with a working on the soul, since no one ever shared a soul’s hurt with a shoulder. Fire over the top does nicely. Or look up the term on the Hiring Hall’s wall, which is posted, and arrange your battle for the next morning.
Physical Appearance and Dress
They come from every sort of family and look like it, all of them with a thick neck, a hard callus on the left shoulder and a stoop that the sergeants have spent years failing to correct. They stand very close to each other without noticing it, and stand too close to you as well. Old companies have a shared gait, and a stranger can tell which by the way they favor the same side. Scars run in lines. Voices are hoarse, and they have a habit of talking from the corner of the mouth, for use in the last minute before contact. Gerrit Marrick is sixty, loud, scarred, very funny and missing an ear, and he looks like a building someone has tried to knock down several times without getting a clear result.
Ochre and black in squares are the colors, a patch on every coat. Each company adds its own colors inside the squares and a song with disgusting verses, and you can tell them at a mile by the drum. Their gear is the point of pride, and it is entirely practical: a long ash spear shaved true by eye, a big-rimmed shield with the company’s mark, a padded jack, a kettle helm and very good boots, Uncommon and well worn. A captain has plain black half-plate with an ochre sash and every buckle mended. At fifty paces it is just a straight line of spear-points, with shadows falling across the fields like a fence that goes on forever. A poor cousin looks exactly the same as a rich one, on purpose.
Lineage Traits
[Trait] The Corner — Shining for the Whole File
A fighter who can take a blow, at the outside angle of the rank, with her coat running down the line.

Extends reinforcement through touching bodies under one contract, thinning fast with every rank.
Lets a Stage IV hold ground that a Stage VII would like to walk through, once.
Spends the corner’s reserve at a frightening rate, and the tells show on her first.

They say “good corner” on the Fields the way other people say “good wife,” and they mean about the same thing.
[Trait] No Sight, No Fear — What a Rank Does to a Mind

In the middle of a file you can see the back in front and a shoulder each side. It turns out to be a mercy.
Pressure lands on a rank as on a crowd, but a file shares that as well, thinly: dread spread over sixteen is sixteen men feeling sick. The Stage gap still shows, and they still drop, in order.
Morale in a good file runs well past anything an ordinary person would stand for.

A rank stands because it cannot trust itself to stand anywhere else.
[Trait] A Little of the Gain — Crew on the Window

A real crew bond shows on the sheet. Marrick files share a small part of each other’s gain, and veterans of one file have very similar skills.
Spear runs as high as a soldier’s Stage lets a fighting skill go on some very ordinary people. Fifty years at one thing can give a soldier an alarming sheet with very little Stage to speak of.

A Long Fields sergeant past his marching years can name his price as a drillmaster anywhere between Kessen ford and the sea.
System Metrics
Stat lean



























































PrimaryLeanSignature Sub-StatsWhyVitalityHighFortitude, Absorption, ThresholdEveryone gets hit, and everyone keeps standingResilienceHighOath, PersistenceThe contract is the lawDominionHighCommand, GravityA drum and a sergeant’s voiceTemperingModerateOverflow, MaturityCorners burn hot, and they have made peace with itHarmonicsModerateSynergy, StabilityThe file’s bellsDexterityLowSequenceOne thrust, then another, sixteen deepGnosisLowVigilanceSomeone else reads the field. Someone else also reads the contractArdencyLowDensityOne small hole in a very long pole
Wellspring compatibility
A Wellspring is one of the sixty types of Aether and the idea a soul tempers itself on. It is a lens and locks nobody out of the rest, and very few spearmen have ever had the time.






























TierWellspringsWhyNaturalPetralon, CoagulaLoad taken and sent down, and scattered pieces gathered back into one bodyEasyMonolithion, Orrenthal, TransferenceRemaining, a thing that keeps its word under load, and strength moving down a bondWorkableChthonica, Fractura, VerdantiaThe root, the breaking point, and a good barley yearAgainst the grainMortalis, Catharsis, CymorathThe Long Barrow has taught them what Mortalis does on their own ground. Catharsis, a Spirit Wellspring, gives no fire and makes a very poor sergeant. And the wind has no use for a wall
On the Stages

























StagesHow a Marrick readsUnwoken to IIThe File. Nine in ten of them, and a person can make a good life of itIII to V · Ascension to SplinteringA coat, a place near the corner, and the first Release if one is found: on the Fields you get a bigger shoutVI to VII · Glory to RefractionA Class name at Glory, usually about a wall. A true corner, and a Second Release, if the coin comesVIII and upCaptains and company-breakers, on the wall of the Hiring Hall with a price by their names. A Domain is a drill square, and all who stand inside it keep step
Doctrine and Arts
Keep the line, finish the term. They have no flourish, on purpose. Their doctrine is to arrive, stand, thrust, and go home at the agreed hour. Against high Stages it is older than anyone’s grandmother: the rank opens, lets the great one in, closes, and every crossbow in reach looses at the one target that cannot be mistaken for a friend. A bolt costs a few coppers. They consider the exchange fair. Their shouts are in plain Long Fields, and they are all orders.








































MoveMeaningWhat it doesShoulder!Lock onThe first order of any fight. Every rank closes up, and the window shows the lineLevel!Spears downSixteen ranks of ash come down as one, on the drum, with a noise like a building falling over when they start to walkLet Him in!The holeA planned gap opens in front of a high-Stage fighter, closes behind her, and the crossbow companies start workTake It!A corner’s callShe has seen it coming, and the coat goes all down the file in one breath. Sixteen men brace, and pay what it costs in boneWhat’s He Paid?ParleyA sergeant walks out under a green branch to ask the terrible stranger what he is getting for this, and whether he would consider more. It has ended more sieges than the spear hasIt Isn’t Noon!Contract’s not startedShouted across a burning town to the people screaming at you for help. Marrick is not proud of this and will not stop
Culture
They speak Long Fields, plain English and Dutch in the names and the swearing, and a good deal of the talk is out of the side of the mouth.

The Tailboard. On the morning of her first muster, every recruit touches the broken cart at Hammerford’s ford. The Guild of Wrights have repaired it nine times, and each new axle has been sawn through at the proper angle by a man with a sworn drawing. Dob Harkness’s descendants still draw the rent.
The Signing. The contract is read aloud to the company in a field, all the way through, and each soul signs or marks it. Anybody may leave before the last mark. The line comes up on every window at the same moment, and new recruits generally yell.
The Noon Holiday. The noon of 602, kept every year. Everyone stands in the square, looks up at the sun, and when it is noon they put their drinks down. Then they pick them up.
The Widows’ Chest. A cut of every contract goes into a chest in the citadel, and a Marrick dead is paid to the end of the season, on the nail. Its keeper is the most frightening person in the country.

Who they marry, fight and owe. Everyone marries into the companies and everyone goes to all the funerals, because each family pays rent in sons and daughters, a set number to each muster, or in silver at a rate the Moot fixes. They have fought on both sides of every war, and a Marrick company will fight another to the hour and share a jug with whoever is left. The Yan brawl with them annually at Mashi, and neither has seen what a real war with the other would pay. The Holy Sea audits them, and Lambert officers are the only outsiders to get an honest head-count from a sergeant, as they would get it anyway. Commoners get a place, a pay day, a song with disgusting verses, and a country where any widow can walk up to the citadel and be paid.
Limitations and Soul-Costs
[Curse] The File Bleeds — Everyone Keeps the Wound
Being kept alive by sixteen people means owing sixteen people, in bone. There are old companies at Hotwell where the whole file walks with the one left leg. It is good for morale right up until the moment it is not, and whole villages on the Fields are crippled in the same place.
[Curse] The Term — It Isn’t Noon
They cannot be there early, and they cannot stay. A company will watch a town die at a quarter to, and a company will walk off a field with the job half done, because the strength stops with the hour. It stings every Marrick who has ever stood with her arms folded in front of someone she could have saved. There is a wyrm on the Kessen road wearing nine hundred of their spears, called Old Pincushion, and it is a joke because it has to be.
[Curse] The Paid Dead — A Contract Outlasts the Man
Nine thousand men went into one trench at Sorley Bridge, on both sides, each one paid up to the end of a season. In the generation after, a Mortalis seep pooled under them (Mortalis being the Wellspring of slow death), and the ghouls that come up out of the Long Barrow come in companies, in step. Nobody on the Fields will say quite what is keeping them in step. Their children go down each spring to fight them.
How They Stand Against the Three Paths
Body. They were made for this, as far as a good Stage gap lets them be. A Body master high enough to take a wall apart as a thing, by law, is another matter, and when one arrives they send a sergeant to ask what he is getting paid.
Spirit. Very bad. A working goes past every shoulder in the file and lands in the one soul it was meant for, and the rank cannot share that. Their answer is crossbows and a very strict rule about the first person you see standing on a wagon with her hands up.
Fate. A bad morning. A Fate fighter can move what a wall depends on, and a wall depends on rather a lot: a strap, a drum, whether the pay wagon arrived. A well-kept rank offers few straps to give.
Final Definition
House Marrick sells the one thing in the world that a Stage X cannot buy: ordinary people standing next to each other. They have made a magic out of a shoulder, a drum and a signed sheet of paper, and it works exactly as long as the paper says. They have held a line against things out of nightmare for the price of a good pair of boots, and they have walked away from burning towns at the stroke of noon, and they have never told anyone that those two are different. On the Long Fields, the barley comes in and then the spears do, and a broken cart stands by the ford with its tailboard hanging, and if anyone asks them what it is for, they say the hire stands as long as it stands.
Shoulder to shoulder, to the hour, and paid.
