factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: House Stark
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Overview





































TypeBanner House of Kharven · Northern Human Bloodline · Wardens of the Eastern MarchOriginOlder than the kingdom. Three hundred and seventy-six years by the Stone Roll, and the stones are older than the RollFounderNot recorded, and not discussed with outsidersSeatHollenmark, on the Cobalt MarchAnchorsThe Stark Rime · the boundary stones · the Stone Roll · the Dire IcebearSignatureThe Long Hearth: they steal the heat out of the world and bury it under the border, and they can never have it backMaxim”Frost holds the line.” On the March they add the second half, quietly: “And we give.”
The note said The north is reminded. It came up the eastern road to Hollenmark in the Thin Weeks (the starving end of winter), in Kagenori Tenrai’s own hand, tied to a cask of brine with Torvald Stark’s head in it. Ulf Stark read it by the fire, set it down and did not raise his voice, and that is all anyone at Hollenmark will tell you about the evening.
By the next dusk every Stark on the March had walked to the nearest boundary stone. Nobody gave an order, and the Stone Roll, which enters who stood at each stone and what was decided there, enters only that they stood. They stood in their shirts with their boots off in the deepest cold of the year, old men and widows and children of nine, and they felt what they felt. The Rime runs harder under feeling. Lamps shrank in their brackets at Stonewatch, ironwood cracked like a thrown axe, and ravens came down out of the air. The white bears walked in from Bearhold unasked and lay in rings around the stones with their backs to them, and for nine days nothing else could go near.
On the tenth morning a Vessant factor on the supply road found a ring of wet black ground thirty paces wide around the first stone, smoking in the frost. Then he saw what was coming up out of it, and took off his hat, and could not have told you why. It was grass, ankle-high and thin and very green. On the next rise there was another ring, and another past that, dark green beads laid along the whole white length of the eastern line. “When the grass comes” is how the north says spring, and it has meant moss since the clans stopped riding, because the grass is on the list of things that are gone. Old women walked out of the long houses and knelt in it and put it in their mouths. It lasted six days. Ulf Stark cut one sod with his own knife, packed it in the same cask and sent it back to the Hall of Verdicts with no note at all, and the Hall’s clerks filed it under soil.
The next winter the Winter Road killed ninety riders, on stones that had kept their grandfathers alive and had gone cold under them. Every Stark on the March knew that would happen before they took their boots off. Ask one, and they will tell you that is just the way this life is.
House Stark says where things end and begin, and it holds the eastern frontier against the holds, and it held the passes for forty years beside the Greymanes, and it imports nearly everything it eats from a house it despises. What they hold that everyone needs is an edge: the north knows where it stops because a Stark has gone and looked. What almost nobody south of Stonewatch knows is that the edge is warm.
Origin of the House
The Starks did not set the boundary stones. Waist-high, lichen-green and older than any record of the house, the stones stood on every rise of the March before there was a March, and the first line of the Stone Roll, which surveyors will show you for a price and a promise, reads in full: Came to the stone. It was already warm.
The Rime itself sits outside the register of the Sixty. The Guild’s best guess, which no Stark has confirmed, begins at the Cold Larder, a day from Bearhold, where the ground runs on Vohrin, a Titan’s own cold, in which cold is a deficit and heat is let go of as a discipline. A family that lived on that ground long enough might come out with blood that lets go of heat as a habit. A Stark Measurewright asked about it in my hearing said that he had a stone to check.
The House on the Crystal

























LayerPlaneThe Stark formAether ShellPhysicalWorks like a pump with one direction. Heat comes off everything near the bearer and leaves through the heels. The Shell is cold to anyone who reads it and clouds with rime, in a hue of dark gray where other souls show a lensEssence CoreSoulPlain and shut. It sets the rate of the Rime, since the cold follows feeling, and it reaches nobody else’s. Most Starks read Silent for lifeAttraction LayerFateFull of oaths and small with everything else. What a Stark has sworn by the sky sits there like frost in a crack
Path. The soul leans toward the Body Path, with a second lean toward Fate for the line and the oath; Body VI Mastered, Fate V Walked at about a third is the family’s usual shape. Mastery. Body comes slowly, as Level does. The great Warlords have stood at Glory (Stage VI) on the first rung, Muridic, and two of the best, Ulf and his young uncle Yusif, never put a class name on the slip at all. Grip. None. Stark blood opens no ladder early, and most read no Spirit and little Fate to the grave, keeping every vow without ever reaching above the soul’s own share.
The Long Hearth
In a breath: every Stark steals the heat out of everything near them and cannot keep it, so it goes down through their heels into the ground, and after four centuries the whole border of the March is warm underneath.
How it works. Stone is very slow at passing heat. Warmth driven a hundred yards down into solid gneiss takes about three hundred years to work back up, and above it sits the permafrost, the best lid in the world. Under each boundary stone the surveyors have found what a northern digger calls a talik, a pocket of ground that never freezes, held open inside the frozen country like a coal in a fist. Heat goes in because a Stark has stood there. It stays because nothing up top can reach it, and because the stones, which were there first, hold what they are given. The Roll-Cellar under Stonewatch, a Fixatio Well (the Wellspring of commitment, where what is bound stays bound) beneath the oldest stone on the line, is the nearest thing scholars have to an explanation.
That is why the stones are lichen-green in January. It is also why the Winter Road exists. A rider who knows the line can lie down with his spine against a stone at thirty below and wake up, and a cache buried at its foot never freezes through. An army that has marched into the March is freezing to death in the middle of the largest hearth in the north, and nobody has told it.
And none of it is for them. A Stark’s blood moves heat out and never in. A Stark can stand barefoot on four hundred years of his family’s warmth and feel nothing. Ulf Stark’s soul put it in two words the day his brother came home: we give.
The forms















































FormWhoWhat it doesWhat it costsThe WalkAny StarkWeight down through the heels, even and unhurried. The heat leaves by that road, and the walker cannot be shouldered off the lineNothing. A Stark who runs has stopped doing itThe Laying-InEvery Stark, every summerThree hot weeks walking an assigned stretch with the Rime wide open, pulling August down for January. It is the only season the Rime has much to takeThe summer. Hay on the March dries badly and the neighbors know whyGiving the StoneAny Stark, barefootThe Rime follows feeling, so a grief can be stood out on a stone and paid in. It is the house’s whole approach to mourningA little of the feeling goes with it, for good. Starks get plainer with ageThe Floor GoesBody IIThrough the ground by contact, what he takes from the air goes out along a line under a marching host. The crust rots from below as the air above drops. The Roll tells it of the Cold Hand of Stonewatch, and of nobody now livingAll of it, out of a body with nothing to spareReading the LineBody IIIThrough his heels he feels a fire lit at the next stone along, which is much of how a Stark column has already movedStanding still and barefoot on campaignHere It EndsDomain, Stage VIII at leastCalled twice in the Roll. A line is drawn, and past it heat goes where the Stark saysWhen it falls, everything it took comes up at the caster’s feet
What it costs. The bank runs down. The grass cost a third of the line’s warmth by the Roll’s own survey. Moving a stone breaks its lid, which is why the penalty is a hand, and a stone left unstood for a generation goes cold, so a house losing its sons in a forty-year war is losing its road as well.
Its limit. It moves heat and cannot make it. In deep winter there is little to take, against a great fire it is a bucket, and off the March a Stark is a cold man with no bank behind him. On the Hem of the Scourge his chief use is keeping beer cold.
Who beats it. A fire, a thaw and a scout who does not sleep. A thaw drowns the Winter Road in its own warm mud. A fire tells the Stark you are there and melts the snow that hides the stone, a fair trade if you came to find it. A captain who learns to look for green lichen can bed his men down on the Starks’ own hearth, and those stones are entered in the Roll with a remark. And a Stark kept calm is a much smaller problem than a Stark kept angry.
The bargain with the bears
A Dire Icebear stands nine feet at the shoulder in a coat built for standing still on ice, and she overheats within a mile of running, as any sealer on the shelf will tell you. So when the young of the house walk out to Bearhold in a shirt, which is called the Asking, the bear that comes up to them is checking how the heat leaves. A rider with the Rime running clean takes it off her as she goes, and she can run down a stag for as long as the rider lasts.
It also means she can feel his temper through her own spine, with nothing in the way. A rider who stops being honest about what he feels stops being worth carrying, and the withdrawal is not gentle. That is the true reading of what happened to young Sweyn in 668. No Stark wears an icebear, and the Bearhold graveyard is small.
Physical Appearance and Dress
Stature and coloring. Big, rawboned and long-armed, going to doorway width by fifty, with dark hair graying early, a coppery line among the younger sons, and pale blue or gray eyes raw at the rims. Marks. The breath stops steaming first, then frost comes in the beard, and a tavern-keeper who sees that moves the glassware. Voice. Plain and short. Everyone under forty is lad.
The look at fifty paces. Wolf-fur and black wool in knots of men on foot, a heavy even walk, and the wolf of Hollenmark on the breast, silver for the Warlord alone and brass for the sons. They dress plain and carry one thing that is not. Marchstone, Grade A and Legendary, stands point-down before its bearer the way a boundary stone stands. Lorn’s sword looks as if it cost a pig and is a Very Rare nickel steel that stays tough under his own cold, with the Hollenmark yard’s small boundary stone under the guard. The poor cousin carries a market blade he will ruin in two years, since a Stark’s rime breaks ordinary steel from the inside, as Yusif’s did, and a pelt he will tell you he killed himself. Hollenmark women braid a son two cords of caged crystal, one for the going and one for the coming back, and the north can tell a lot from which riders still wear two.
Lineage Traits
[Trait] The Stark Rime — The Heat Goes Down

Heat leaves everything near the bearer, timber silvers, snow stiffens, and all of it goes into the ground. It runs harder under feeling, and a tightened jaw on the left is the usual tell.
Near-immune to cold and weak to heat in exact proportion. Its fair counter is heat, and calm.

A Stark who is not angry is only a cold man. A great many people have died trying to work out how to arrange that.
[Trait] The Point Set Down — What the Soul Holds
The house’s own Traits come out in one shape: this far, this thing, no further. Lorn draws a line in the snow. Mark’s hand does not open on a sword whatever has hold of him. Rob stood over whoever he had claimed, and Yusif kept a silence for sixteen years until it killed him. Each has its limit in the same place as its strength, and the usual counter is to go around the end of it.
You will notice how few of them involve going anywhere.
[Trait] Cold Steel — The Blade Goes First

On the bind a Stark’s cold can run through his own blade into the other man’s steel and drop it below the point where iron stops bending and starts breaking. It ruins his own ordinary swords the same way, and bronze does not care.

Yusif Stark bought a new sword every couple of years off a market stall. He could have carried a Kingsarm.
System Metrics



























































PrimaryLeanSignature Sub-StatsWhyVitalityHighFortitude, Constitution, ToleranceHave never once been warmArdencyHighPenetrationThe cut carries the deficitGnosisLowPerception; Forecast in the oldThey watch more than they readDexterityModerate to HighReflex, Economy, FinesseDrilled, without flourishHarmonicsLowStabilityNo lens to train itResilienceHighOath, Anchoring, IntegritySworn by the skyTemperingVery lowMaturityThey drill insteadDominionModerate, rising with officePressure, Gravity, CommandThe Warlord’s Pressure arrives with the cold
Wellspring compatibility. Most Starks harmonize with nothing at all, and the Rime stands where a lens would. Those who do:

Strongest: Fixatio, the amber bond that holds what is bound, sold by the hour at the Roll-Cellar. Chthonica, the root that holds on by touching everything.
Workable: Monolithion for the old, Penance for those who keep going back to one stone, and Petralon, which makes a Stark into a Greymane with worse manners.
Against the grain: Pyraeon, Pyreveil, Exuroth and every fire of the register.






























StagesHow they readI to IIIFrost on the collar when angry. Drill and the first Laying-InIV to VFirst Release, a frost name called low: Frostfall, the White Sky. Afterward a fire, for the first time in his lifeVIGlory, Body I, the Warlords’ common ceilingVIISecond Release, and Reading the Line for the fewVIII and upHere It Ends. The Roll holds two, and neither was a Warlord
Doctrine and Arts
Stark war is winter war on roads nobody else thinks are open. The killing is done by men on foot in wolf-fur moving in knots, with the bears few and enormously loud in any chronicle. Great sword and axe in the north, boar-spear on the road, short sword and limewood shield for the young.









































MoveWhat it doesThe Winter RoadHouse art. Light columns stone to stone, arriving from where nobody was watching. Old Harald Keld is the only man who ever did it betterFrost Holds the LineThe house shout, screamed in the old tongue. Sweyn’s is the famous one, for the wrong reasonA Line in the SnowLorn’s. The point drawn through the ground, and a low white wall of cold holds behind itThe Breaking ColdLorn’s. Frost-flowers bloom on your blade, and the next blow shatters itFROSTFALL · the White SkyFirst Release. The sky covers us. A skin of clear ice over the mailThe Wall of OneRob’s. He stepped across, not aside, with the rime set in the stanceThe PinMark’s. On his knees inside the reach, the blade up behind the foreleg, and he holds it thereThe Long Clean LineYusif’s. One cut with nothing shown before it. It outlived him, in another pair of hands
Culture
Language. Plain northern Common, with an old tongue kept for shouting at bears. A debt is no debt until said aloud at a boundary.
Rites.

The Asking, the Laying-In and Giving the Stone, above.
The Hand Under the Stone. Whoever moves a stone loses the hand, and it goes under when the stone is reset. A bear at Stonewatch was once entered in the Roll as a party to the dispute.
The Dish. Every midwinter, an empty pie dish to Ashbury.

Marriage, feud and debt. A Stark daughter married a Thornwall in 592, and it is still being discussed. A Stark and a Greymane will die for each other without having a conversation. They owe Ashmore for every bushel and resent every one.
What the commons get. They pay in days on the wall and split wood. And the long houses of the March are built where a surveyor says to build them, and in the worst winter on record not one child in them froze in its bed. The barley-cake woman under the twin towers has a warm stone, and has never asked where it came from.
Limitations and Soul-Costs
[Curse] Never Warm — One Way Only

The blood moves heat out and never in. Food tastes of less. Beds are a formality. A Stark’s child, held, does not get warmer.

“A Stark has no use for a scarf,” the north says of Lorn’s, “so somebody gave it to him.”
[Curse] The Bank Runs Down — Nobody Pays It Back

Every Stark who dies young leaves a stretch of line unwalked, and the forty-year war emptied Hollenmark of sons.
Spend the Hearth in a season and the Winter Road kills your own riders the next year.

A rider’s widow at Stonewatch told me that her husband gave the stone their son, and came home, and asked what was for dinner.
How They Stand Against the Three Paths
Body. The fight they trained for. A great hitter on a hot Wellspring is the classic Stark death, and a Stark’s cold is the classic death of a man with ordinary steel. Spirit. Their worst: Silent Cores and no Ward, though a Spirit fighter still has to cross a March that wants him dead of exposure. Fate. A Stark who keeps his oath offers little to lean on, but set two oaths against each other and he freezes between them.
Final Definition
House Stark is the north’s cold neighbor and its secret stove: a family that has poured every summer and every grief it ever had into the ground under a line, for people who will mostly never know it, and who cannot warm one hand at it themselves.
“Don’t take my word for it, lad. Go and look.”

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.filePath: Factions, Bloodlines & Institutions/Houses and Bloodlines/The Houses of the Inner World/House Thornwall.md
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: House Thornwall
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Overview





































TypeBanner House of Kharven · Merchant-Warrior Foresters · Holders of the Marrowhold CorridorOriginForesters to the Kōkan, from when the Kōkan sat the red chair, and foresters to someone else before thatFounderThorold Hook, a timber-cutter whose first entry in the cargo rolls is a billSeatThornhaven, in the Scarlet WoodAnchorsThe ironwoods · the mark-hook · the Ledger of Rings · the corridorSignatureThe Long Score: they cut a working into a living tree, and the tree grows over it, and a great-grandchild collects it with interestMaxim”Six months,” told of anything about to go wrong, in a tone of mild regret. The private form is longer: “Six months. Or sixty years.”
In Year 631, at the midsummer fair at Raftwick, a Marrick captain named Aldric Voss, a large and cheerful man who had just been paid, stood in front of a Thornwall hedge at drill and laughed at the length of the spears. A forester called Sigrid Orm, who had come down to sell pitch, asked the name of the gentleman, and wrote it down. That summer she went up the Hale Ride, a straight red road through the deep stands, and at forty of the great ironwoods along it she took the small cross-headed hook from her belt, cut a palm’s width of bark away at the height of her shoulder, and carved one short line in each, with his name in it and two guild marks. People who knew her said she was never quite as much after that summer. The bark closed over within a few years, and she died in 660 with her pitch accounts in order.
On a bright cold morning in the autumn of 695, under a canopy gone the color of an open furnace, eleven hundred Marrick lances on a Tenrai contract came up the Hale Ride to seize the season’s convoy. Their captain was Aldric Voss’s grandson, a large and cheerful man who had never heard of the fair at Raftwick. A woman in a red cap stood in the road ahead of them with a ledger under one arm. She read something out of it, walked to the nearest tree, a trunk wider than a house, set the hook into a place in the bark that looked like every other place, and pulled.
"Called in!"
Sixty-four rings of red wood had grown over that line, and each had carried a little more of what Sigrid Orm put there, as a debt carries interest. It came out all at once. The great tree split from the shoulder down like a door opening and came over across the ride, two hundred feet of it, with the whole forest rising into the air as gold dust and needles, and fell into the next, which opened too. They went in order, left and right, forty of them, and when the resin settled there was a wall of fallen ironwood a mile long and as high as a keep, with a column under it, and a woman in a red cap making a note. A hundred and twelve men walked out over the next week. Young Voss was one, and she met him with the bill, itemized: forty great trees at the current rate, for the laugh, at interest.
He asked her what laugh. She told him it was all in the Ledger, and that he was welcome to come up and read it.
House Thornwall reads cargo rolls the way other houses read battle reports, and they will tell you what you will run short of six months before you know you need it. They hold the ironwood the Marrowkin import for tool handles and ward-frames, and the corridor east to Collarbone. What they hold that everyone needs is wood that will outlast your grandchildren. What nobody asks is what else is in it.
Origin of the House
The first Thornwalls found marks in the ironwood when they felled it, deep inside the trunk under centuries of rings, and being who they were they priced them. Thorold Hook’s first bill in the cargo rolls is to an unnamed party for “one old debt, opened by accident, and the damage.” The cross-headed hook on every forester’s belt is copied from one he found in a tree. They inherited a practice from people they know nothing about, and got very good at it.
The House on the Crystal

























LayerPlaneThe Thornwall formAether ShellPhysicalStrong forearms and a good back, no more than any axe-crew. Coats of aura run hot copper and fox-red, and hold a shape as well as wood holds a chiselEssence CoreSoulThe working layer. A cut reads the maker’s Essence. The Core gives a little of itself into every score and does not get it backAttraction LayerFateLong and thin, with ties running out to trees and to people not yet born
Path. The blood tends to Body for the axe and raft, with a real lean toward Spirit, through the Make form, for anyone who keeps at the carving. Mastery. Body climbs in the crews and Spirit in the foresters, where the great names sit. Grip. A small one: a child of the blood who has cut wood since before shoes reads Spirit I as early as Stage IV, for a cut in living ironwood and nothing else. The Stage’s ceiling still stands above that.
Hisae Thornwall is the exception. Born a Byakuya of the white house, she married in forty years ago, and her Fate V Mastered, Spirit IV Walked is Moto schooling kept over a lamp with the doors shut. Her husband’s grandfather took one look at what the house had got and, the night of the wedding, gave her the hook. She has held the Ledger for most of the time since. Nobody knows what she has cut.
The Long Score
In a breath: a working cut into a living tree does not fade, it grows, and it pays out to whoever holds the hook, a lifetime after the one who cut it has stopped caring.
How it works. A tree cannot heal a wound as flesh does. It walls the damage off and lays new wood over it, and you can saw into an old trunk and find a blaze cut a hundred years ago with the knife-strokes still sharp in the dark. Ironwood is the densest and slowest wood in the north, and it holds an inscription better than stone. So a line cut in a live ironwood, with some of the cutter’s stamped Essence on the edge of the hook, stays. The tree goes on drawing Aether up from the ground to live on, and with each year’s ring a little of that collects around the line. Verdantia, the green pulse, has a word for it: accumulation, one good day on top of another. Sixty years of good days is a great many.
Most of what a score does is simple. It breaks, drops, closes or holds. The cleverness is in the terms, and two guild marks make it a contract, good from here to the Center, because a lie in a cut splits the grain.
How it pays









































Grade of scoreAgeWhat it doesWhat it costs the cutterA BlazeAnyA trade trick anyone can do with a knife. A handle does not loosen, a lintel keeps a family’s nameA moment’s attentionA Short ScoreTen to thirty yearsA limb that falls when told, a ride that closes behind a convoyA day’s reserve, gone for a monthA Long ScoreFifty years and upCALLED IN. A tree that splits and comes down as a working, and can open its neighborsA share of the reserve that never refillsA Deep ScoreA century and upNobody living has opened one on purpose. The Ledger lists sixty-one, and three more it cannot placeThe dead paid itSold TimberAnyA felled tree keeps what it has and stops growing, and may go into a roof-tree or a ward-frame. The house has never said whether it has sold a score, and every gate in the north hangs on its timber
The hook. A score opens to a mark-hook of the house, set in the right place by someone who knows it, and that takes the Ledger of Rings: tree, height, year, cutter, terms and who it is for. It is the most dangerous book in the north. A score nobody has the page for is buried money.
What it costs. A forester of sixty may have a third of her reserve standing in trees she will never see open, given up for someone not yet born. The interest runs whether or not the debtor is alive, and young Voss paid for a laugh he never heard.
Its limit. It cannot be used in a hurry, and a score pays only where the tree stands. It is useless past the treeline, which is why the whale-oil warband lost as it did, and why Aksel Keld at fifteen broke another four times his size in a whiteout.
Who beats it. Fire, for a start, and the beetle as long as your thumb, which has cost the house more than any war. An Anamnesis reader (a soul that can lay a palm on a thing and read its past) can walk a road laying hands on trunks. Steal the Ledger or kill the foresters with the pages, and a century of savings goes dark. Or go around, since all of this needs you on one road on one morning.
The Long Cuts
Everyone asks about the long cuts, the narrow straight rides walled in by trees so old you cannot see the sky. Hisae’s foresters had kept them open for two hundred years when she sent twelve hundred pikes up them thirty at a time, and up the stair behind the frozen fall, and over the east wall of the Seat before the Tenrai knew there was a hole in it. A back door works once. I asked a forester whether the trees along them are in the Ledger of Rings. She told me that it was for the timber, in a forest where nobody has taken a tree off one in living memory, and she looked at me until I stopped.
Physical Appearance and Dress
Stature and coloring. Northern commons, fair to fox-brown, strong in the forearm and short of a finger or two. Marks. Resin in the creases, a knife on every belt from the age of four, and the older foresters have a thinned look, like a good coat worn a long time. Voice. A Thornwall will price the damage aloud while it is happening.
The look at fifty paces. Oiled gray felt and an iron cap, in step, a thorn-sprig in dark red thread at the collar, on twelve hundred men who look like a hedge coming on at a walk. Raftsmen wear red caps and spiked boots. Everything is carved, in knots of beasts and leaves in red, ocher and verdigris blue, and guild marks are bragged about and sued over. Money shows in fire-enamel from the Hale workshop. The real flex is the hook: small, iron, on a long black cord, and the older the iron the less anyone wants to stand downhill of you. For forty years Hisae’s passed for the keys to the linen. The poor cousin has plain felt and a borrowed hook.
Lineage Traits
[Trait] A Knife Before Shoes — The Hand Knows Wood

Every child of the house can read grain and carve a Blaze by ten, and a palm on any worked ironwood gives its age, its stand and often its cutter.

They will inspect your furniture without being asked, and they will tell you what you paid.
[Trait] Six Months — The Supply Eye

The house’s Forecast runs through trade, and they can tell a shortage from a message. A Thornwall in a foreign country with no prices is a nervous person.

They were right about the Ore Council. They were right about the Tenrai. Nobody thanks them, and they have started adding that to the invoice.
[Trait] Patient Reserve — Standing Wealth

What a forester has in trees is lost to her for good, and the blood learns to fight lean: a short reserve, spent exactly.
A veteran forester’s reserve is small for her Stage, and she has usually never once opened it all the way.

A Thornwall will not tell you what she is worth. She has not finished growing it.
System Metrics



























































PrimaryLeanSignature Sub-StatsWhyVitalityModerateConstitution, ToleranceAxe crews and cold waterArdencyModerateCompression, PenetrationA hook-pole is all leverageGnosisHighForecast, Analysis, RetentionThe rolls, and the LedgerDexterityModerateFinesse, EconomyThe carver’s handHarmonicsModerateStability, AttunementThey tune to trees, slowlyResilienceHighAnchoring, Persistence, OathThey can waitTemperingModerateMaturity, LongevityThe old foresters are very oldDominionModerateCommandA drum, a horn and a slow step
Wellspring compatibility.

Strongest: Verdantia, for the growing. Chthonica, the root that holds by touching everything. Anamnesis, for reading a beam.
Workable: Fixatio, the cure in the cut. Coagula, for mending what has split. Phreatis, for the raft-bosses, whose river remembers.
Against the grain: Monolithion, Verdantia’s contrary, and Pyreveil and its kin, for reasons any forester will give you.






























StagesHow they readI to IIIKnife, felt, a first Blaze, a first driveIV to VFirst Release in copper and red. Spirit I for the bloodVIGlory. A first Long Score, not expected to be seen openedVIISecond Release. The real foresters live on Spirit II, and III waits for TranscendenceVIII and upTHE LEDGER IS OPEN, a Domain in which each named debt comes due at once
Doctrine and Arts
The house does not fight if it can bill instead. The Thornwall hedge is long ash-and-iron spears at a walk, to a drum, with the thorn-horn every hundred paces. Woodsmen fight with axes and short bows from behind things eight feet thick, and raft-crews with hook-poles and spiked boots. Technique names are named for the job.

































MoveWhat it doesThe Thornwall PikeHouse art. Drum, horn, hedge. Horse will not go into it. Horse on open ground before it is set is the counterCalled in!The hook set and pulled, and the score opens. Bawled or muttered as the forester prefers, read off a page, by anyone with the right pageFirst of the MeltAud Rannsdottir’s. Find the one trunk holding the others and put a boot through it. It took a bridgeOn AccountA Short Score’s bough, dropped on someone at a word, with a receiptThe Back DoorHisae’s. A reading of ground for the way nobody usesSmile and PayHisae’s. No read of face or aura gives up what she means. The Tenrai looked for forty years
Culture
Language. Northern Common with a raftsman’s filth, and carved marks everyone can read.
Rites.

The Knife. A child gets one before shoes.
The Birth Tree. A forester cuts a score for each child of the house, in terms the child is never told.
Tying the Flag. One faded cloth at the Red Stair for each great tree taken, by the raft-boss who took it. Anyone who has been down to the second landing drinks free in Raftwick.
Reading the Rings. At a wedding a slice of the couple’s tree is read aloud, with what the family expects to be owed by the time the grandchildren marry. Hisae’s has not been shown.
Writing It Down. When anyone insults the house, someone asks the gentleman’s name.

Marriage, feud and debt. They marry for corridors: a Stark daughter in 592, a Byakuya peace forty years ago. Hallenfeld is the long war, over the log-jam of 688. The Keld still sing about the whale-oil. They were the Kōkan’s foresters and kept the door for them, and Muken’s price for Thornwall was the house free of the Ore Council.
What the commons get. A contract that holds, paid in a share of the drive, and it is not unusual for a raft-boss to own more than the lord she delivers to. And somewhere in the Thornwood a forester long dead will have cut a line so that a village not yet founded will have a roof. Most of what the Ledger holds is not revenge. They just tell that story more.
Limitations and Soul-Costs
[Curse] Paid in Advance — What Stands in the Wood

A share of every forester is in trees, for good, and the great cutters end up thin and faded. Grandchildren visit them to ask where things are.

Sigrid Orm’s pitch accounts were perfect. Her family says that in her last years she could not always tell you which of them she was talking to.
[Curse] Interest Runs on the Dead — The Debt That Cannot Be Forgiven

A score does not know the feud is over. Terms cut in anger will fire on a guest, an ally or the descendant you just married, and the only cancellation is cutting the tree down and taking the damage.

Every forester of the house has been told, on her first day: cut it as though the person who will open it hates you.
[Curse] Standing Wealth — A Forest Can Burn

A century of savings can be undone by a dry August. They cannot leave, and the Tenrai knew it and taxed accordingly.

They paid on the day for forty years. People assumed that was fear.
How They Stand Against the Three Paths
Body. Bring them out of the wood and they lose. Fight them in it and you have walked into a sum done before your grandfather was born. Spirit. A soul that can read what a thing means can read a score. Fate. Something that moves what a road depends on can move you off it, and a score cannot chase anyone. Hisae, however, is a Byakuya with forty years of patience and a Ledger, and I would not.
Final Definition
House Thornwall has made a magic out of the most irritating virtue there is. They cut their spite and their kindness into red wood with equal care, and they spend their own souls on people they will not meet. They are almost always correct. The bill will come. It may not come to you.
“Six months. Or sixty years. I’ll need the name of the gentleman.”

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Houses of the Inner World
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Ask a Guild clerk how many great houses the Inner World holds and you will get a number, a sigh and a request that you take it up with the herald. These are the ones the clerks can’t avoid. Each holds something the rest cannot do without, and each has one thing that belongs to it and nobody else, which is usually the first thing anyone learns about them and the last thing they understand.
A house gives its children four things at most: an eye, if it has one; a grip, which opens one ladder early and never lifts its cap; a lean in the stats; and a liking for certain Wellsprings. It never gives a Path, because the Crystal only recognizes what a person has actually done. Three lines stand on an Epoch’s own work, and each of those has both an eye and an instrument. The rest stand on what they have built, which in several cases is more than the three would like.
The Three Epoch Lines

























LineEpoch and roadTheir own thingThe MotoBara, FateShingan and Hataraki: the eye finds the job, and the hand fires the workerThe ZettariAegor, Body (the Old World)The Everlasting Eye and Matla: physical law made to answerThe YukariAshura, SpiritThe Ketsumyōgan and Null-Light: the eye sees what everything is tied to, and the look keeps what it sees
The Banners of the North













































HouseSeatTheir own thingHouse StarkHollenmarkThe Long Hearth: they steal the heat out of the world and bury it under the border, and they can never have it backHouse GreymaneThe RidgewallThe Post: a title-vow, and the wall stands behind you while someone is at your backHouse AshmoreAshburyThe Count of Mouths: they feel every mouth fed on sealed grain, and throw Pressure as hungerHouse ThornwallThornhavenThe Long Score: workings cut into living ironwood gain interest over generationsHouse KeldThe Whalebone GatherThe Carried Name: a dead person’s Name given to a child, and it stands up in a fightHouse HallenfeldHallenfeldThe Paid Chain: every toll paid still holds the chain upThe YunoMarried into the Moto courtShinma: the interval between things is made to bear load
The Warlords of the South













































HouseSeatTheir own thingHouse MahuoSum-golThe Answering: what has answered once answers the blood more cheaply, and the debt is inherited tooHouse LambertAlabasterThe Computus: a family count in the blood, never fast, always early, blind to the muleThe Yan HallQingyuanThe Stud Book: whatever is entered comes home when its full line is read aloudHouse RyuThe Copper CoastThe Holding: hold a blow or a treasury unasked, and it pays back double, half from your own reserveHouse CorwenBrightwaterThe Hours: a brass key that opens or shuts a leased Core’s intakeHouse MarrickHammerfordThe Shoulder: one contract, one file, and a blow lands on all sixteen until the hour endsThe ValorinVaelorisThe Scripted Soul Lattice: a soul that never crystallized, written instead
The Warlords of the Center






























HouseSeatTheir own thingThe Moss CourtMosk-VaalThe Keeping: Soul-Trees keep what a dead body knew, and the living wear itHouse ScalebondCoilspireBoth Hands: the left makes a body relive an old wound, and the right tells a fresh one it is still morningHouse CaelwardCaelspireThe Long Read: every feather sold still feels the windHouse NobodyBrokencollarUnserved: a sworn blank Name, so writs and curses find no party, until someone hands you paper

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.filePath: Factions, Bloodlines & Institutions/Houses and Bloodlines/The Houses of the Inner World/The Moss Court.md
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Moss Court
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
TypeVerdant Orc house · Shard-kin of the wetlands · one of the four Central WarlordsOriginThe Verdant bands who slipped into the deep wetlands during the expulsion after the Crimson Order’s RefusalFounderNone on record. The Court says the great tree began it, and the Guild’s survey declines to commentSeatMosk-Vaal, grown into the roots of the great tree in the Moonlight ForestAnchorsSoul-Trees · the Ancestor-Rot Gardens · the Spoor-Meld · Swamp Parun on one breath · the OrchardSignatureThe Keeping (Ssoth-Vaal, “the rot that stays awake”)MaximWe Will Keep It For You
The Marrick sergeant Tam Ruddock walked home from the causeway in the spring of 683, with two hundred others, when the contract ran out, and told the first tavern he reached that it was the worst thing he had ever seen. Eleven years later, being a man with a bad back and a large family, he signed on for the same causeway under King Aldric Sorrel of Low Marl, whose nineteen hundred spears in orange and black had heard the story of the pears and took it to be about pears. On the fifth morning, in bright mist, a Totemdeep lodge came up out of the black water on both sides of the road: forty orcs in bark harness, eyes burning green, none of them doing anything an orc does. They dressed their ranks. They closed up by the left with the sergeants a pace out in front, and they came on at the Aldwater slow march, the exact hitching step of the Third Column, with a drummer on the flank beating the League’s old cadence on a hollow log and all forty whistling, through teeth never shaped for it, a filthy hymn about a bishop of Kingsbridge that Ruddock had last heard eleven years before.
He had marched beside that hymn for six days. He knew the step and he knew the hitch, and he knew that Piers Vantry’s column, drilled by a man with one good eye, had always wheeled wide to the right and left its flank open for the space of four breaths. “They Wheel Right!” he bawled, in front of his king and everybody, and he took his two hundred through that gap like a cart through a hedge, and kept going. That is how the Guild comes to have an eyewitness. The rest of Low Marl stayed, and it gives a small hard quince that a Kingsbridge cook will fight you for. Every autumn until he died a basket of it reached Ruddock’s door with a note on birch bark, in a beautiful hand: You were quite right about the wheel. We have spoken to the sergeants.
The dead stay dead. I set that down first because every visitor to the Moonlight Forest comes away unsure of it. Nobody marched out of that silt in 694. Forty living orcs had drawn up through the root the drill of three thousand eight hundred men in rows, the way you might borrow a neighbor’s ladder. The Moss Court buries everything that comes to it, friend or foe, keeps what the body knew, and puts it to work.
Every army in the center buys their physic and carts its dead to Rootgate, because the Court plants them free. Ask what it wants in return and you get the sentence every envoy has been given since the board went up: Nuur ssaath. The interpreters render it with care as “Nothing wants,” and the salt councils have filed it for three centuries as a statement of no territorial claim. Press them and the Court will admit to wanting the salt kept sealed and a good crop. But I had the grammar explained to me at Ghurash Hollow by a rind-wife with her arms in a sump, and in Swamp Parun that sentence has a subject. Nothing is the bare silt under the gardens, the place where a thing goes once it has stopped being a thing. It is empty and it has an appetite. The whole of Verdant religion is that you had better feed it something specific, on purpose, with a tree on top, because it will take the unspecific on its own account. She thought this was very funny. She asked how ripe I was feeling.
Origin of the House
The Verdant Orcs are Shard-kin, whose fragments of the First Impact came down in high-resonance wetlands, and when the expulsion scattered the goblinoid peoples they went into the mire for centuries and came out with a country, a tree and a very polite board.
The Court dates itself from the first Planting: a band starving in the wet buried its dead where it camped, and found next spring that the grubs on those graves knew where the eels ran. A trained soul’s leftovers go to the lens (the Wellspring it tempered on longest) and an untrained one’s feed the ground, and on the richest Manganthra and Verdantia silt in the center, lens and ground are the same mud. Nothing leaves.
The House on the Crystal
Every soul has three layers in its Soul Crystal (the organ that is the soul, refining Aether, which is mana, into Essence, which is spiritual energy). The Shell faces the physical world, the Core faces the soul’s own reality, and the Attraction Layer faces Fate. A people’s lean is a tendency of the untrained soul. It settles nothing about what Path a person later walks.

























LayerHow it runs in themWhat showsAether ShellThin and shed like a rind. They call the aura coat ssuul, and a good one is meant to be peeled off and left behindCold silver-green along old scars, dim at the dark of the moonEssence CoreWide open and shared. Spoor-Melds run Core to Core with no language requiredThe green mist at knee heightAttraction LayerHeld by kin and tree. A debt passes to the tree at death, and the living must come and hear itThin, and rarely climbed
Path lean. Spirit, strongly, at some cost in strength and schooling, and Spirit is the road most of them climb. The grip. On the Spirit road. A child who has sat her first Meld under a kin-tree hears the tree years before Glory, the gift working at its base, though no coil reads anyone’s Mastery until Glory (Stage VI). The cap never lifts. The eye. None in the sense the old lines mean. On the rungs. Rot-wives and lodge fighters are Listeners (I), garden-keepers Answerers (II), a Mother’s circle Confessors (III), and a Mother in a good century a Shepherd (IV). Fate goes unwalked for nearly all of them.
The Keeping
Everything you bury works for you, and the Moss Court has been burying people for a very long time.
What it is. A Soul-Tree is a tree grown on a corpse in worked silt, and it holds what the Court calls the keep: the residue that comes out through a dead body’s Shell. The soul’s other parts go elsewhere. The Core goes to Echo and the Name to the Layer, so the person is gone, and the Court’s cheerful talk of grandmothers does not change that. What the tree keeps is what the body knew: the step, the guard, the hitch in a march, the way a pair of hands salts an eel, the sergeant’s bark and the old man’s grudge against a particular kind of fence. A Verdant Orc can draw that habit up through the root and wear it.
How it works. Foresters will tell you a wood is one animal. Under the leaf-mold a mat of fungus threads every root to every other, and it moves food along by a plain gradient, from a rich rotting log to the starving sapling a hundred paces off, so that the dead tree feeds the young one. That is nutrient cycling across a common mycelial network, and Verdant fungus runs it through the joints of living orcs as well. Manganthra, the go-between, lets two things that should never meet share one surface without tearing it, Verdantia gives the growth, and Rebirthine pays the bill. The keep comes along that mat, through a slip of ancestor wood under the wearer’s shoulder-bark, and the living flesh takes up a dead flesh’s habit.









































FormFromWhat it doesWhat it costsThe Sitting (Ssuth)Any VerdantSit against a kin-tree in a Meld and come away for a day with one old trade habitA long afternoon and an argumentThe Cutting (Vaal-Ssek)Stage III, AscensionA slip of ancestor wood under the shoulder-bark. It carries one body-skill at the tree’s own rank. It counts as a self-boost, under the usual cap of two stepsA share of the reserve goes down the root each time it is used, as the bill for the tendingThe Row (Ssaarekh)Stage VI, in war-Meld, on a planted bed or with its fruit eaten that morningA lodge wears a whole dead company’s drill, as Ruddock saw. They hold the formation to a hair and do it in the dead men’s own timeEveryone in the Meld shares every wound, and the drill is exactly as old as the men who died knowing itThe FruitAnyA tree’s fruit carries a trace of its keep. A bought pear gives a stranger the words to a song he never learned. A dosed one, from a rot-wife, is a Draft for an hour’s borrowed skillIdentity Contamination, in small and funny amounts, or large and otherwise. No Vantry has been on time since 683The Second Spring (Uulm-Sseth)Stage IX or so, one breath, in Swamp ParunThe rot goes through leather, rope, bowstring and then men, across a field. Whatever falls there is planted where it falls, in rank, and from next spring the ground is the Court’sThe speaker’s whole breath and whatever she was keeping it for. A Mother who misjudges drowns on dry land
Domain: the Long Garden (Mosk-Ssaath). A Domain is the territory in which a high-Stage practitioner’s own law holds, opened by a Second Release from Stage VIII. Law: nothing that falls here is lost, and nothing that falls here is yours. A dropped blade, a spent working and a spilled pint of blood all come up as reserve for the holder, and a wound taken inside begins, gently, to garden. It starves on stone, fails under noon and dies on salt.
What it costs. A keep is a loan against your own body, and the Court holds the paper. Every cutting promises the wearer back to the bed, which is the plain reason a Verdant Orc withers past two days from swamp or kin: the graft is calling in the debt. Foreign scholars name this Isolation Degeneracy, and the orcs call it homesickness.
Its limit. A tree keeps what a body knew and nothing a Core authored. No Trait, Release, secret or name ever came up a root, as the Vantry family has established at some length. A habit is also dated, and knows the world as it stood on the day it was planted.
Who beats it. Salt, which is why the Court asks for yours at the landing. A Sun-aspected Domain, which costs them about a third of everything. Bled or stony ground, and a fight kept off the wet past the second day. Above all anyone who remembers the drill better than the tree does: Tam Ruddock did it with a bad back, a loud voice and no technique at all.
Physical Appearance and Dress
They stand six foot four to seven feet, in long vine-like muscle, with eyes like solid lamps of moss-green or lunar white, skin the green of old forest, hard bark along the shoulders and luminous fungus at the joints, trimmed as a northern lord trims his beard. A cutting shows as a welt under the shoulder-bark with a different grain. An old wound pulses cold silver-green, and they show their scars the way other people show their children. Their voices are slow and sibilant, and a Mire-Mother has never needed to raise hers.
At fifty paces you see the glow first and the moths second, and you get the smell shortly afterward. A lodge fighter goes out in grown bark harness coaxed off her own family’s tree, the one thing of Soul-Tree wood that ever travels, Uncommon by the Guild’s measure and not for sale at any price. Ssaaleth’s moth-wing mantle reads Legendary, and she will tell you what became of most of the former owners. A poor cousin wears a moss blanket with one thread of moth silk in the hem, and he is as loud about that thread as a Midmarch duke about his crown.
Lineage Traits
[Trait] The Silver Scar — The Rind That Remembers

Hard bark grows over old damage and turns a blade better each decade.
Scars light with the moon and read as a plain record of what the orc has survived.
At full moon the reserve fills fast. At the dark of it everyone turns short with each other.

They ask after your scars as you might ask after someone’s mother.
[Trait] Spoor-Meld — The Shared Cloud

Group meditation releases Aetheric spores into a green mist, and inside it memory and feeling pass without language for hours.
A lie shows among kin, which makes Verdant testimony reliable and family dinners bad.
Certain phrases can tip listeners into a Meld, so wedding speeches are cleared in advance.
A war-Meld moves a lodge like one animal thinking.

A decision of the Court is what the mist feels like when it clears.
[Trait] One Long Breath — Swamp Parun

Swamp Parun, the Verdant hand of the script and speech that writes boundaries onto laws, runs on a single unbroken breath, so a working can only be as large as the speaker’s chest.
A Mother’s lungs are the only credential the office asks for.
Big workings arrive slowly, and they can be interrupted by anything that makes her cough.

The bookies at Glowwater quote odds on chest measurements.
System Metrics



























































PrimaryLeanSignature Sub-StatsWhyVitality++++Regeneration · Filtration · ConstitutionRot has been through them already and found nothing left to doHarmonics++++Empathy · Synergy · AttunementThe Meld, the moon and the matResilience+++Continuity · AnchoringA self spread across a family and a woodDominion++ (wet ground only)Sense · RadiusTo sense a stranger is to ask the mossTempering++Longevity · CapacityOne breath, held for a very long timeDexterity+Evasion · FeintSuperb under water and ordinary on a roadArdency−Depth, and little FluxSlow big workings, and arms less strong than they lookGnosis− −RetentionA long road to schooling, and the tree remembers for you





















TierWellspringsPrimaryManganthra · Verdantia · LuminalisSecondaryRebirthine · Terranova · Phreatis · Thaloré · Anima SpirareDifficultAurevane · Pyraeon · Pyreveil · Ignivale (the sun and the open flame) · Fixatio and Monolithion, which fight the bed’s own law
Doctrine and Arts
The doctrine is on the board at Rootgate. Ask them politely to go round. Let them come in anyway, let the water rise behind them, and plant what you get. The lodges fight in silence on Beast-Sign, some four hundred signals, and consider a battle cry a waste of breath, so the names below get said afterward, kindly, by people passing you the fruit.






























MoveMeaningWhat it doesMahaa-SsehMire-Mother’s YesUnder the black water at one end of a fight and up behind you at the other, with friendsSseloo VaanSee You LaterThe toast. A clean cut that leaves spores in the wound, which comes up green in a week if it is not burned outNuul SsaarA Lovely SpotSilt loosens under one man’s feet. He goes to the waist, and she has been saving that spot for himSsuul-EkThe PeelingThe aura coat stripped off whole and left standing as a green afterimage while the orc goes elsewhere, cold and without it for a few breaths
Culture
Language. Swamp Parun, with more words for kinds of rot than any other tongue has for weather, and Beast-Sign for the field.
Rites.

The Planting. The dead go into a garden with drink and a great deal of cheerful advice. A family visits, quarrels with the tree and goes home feeling better, and nobody present thinks a tree is a grandmother. They will tell you that the argument is what the visit is for.
The Dive. A new Mire-Mother is whoever speaks the largest working on one breath from the bottom at Glowwater, with the shore packed and the bookies on stilts.
The Salt Sentence. Burial in salted ground, worked so that Aether will not pool and nothing will grow. The condemned gets no tree, and Nothing gets him for nothing. Nine in the record, each named as a warning to children.

Who they marry, feud with and owe. They marry at the Blooming Mire, and the speeches go wrong. They feud politely and forever with the salt cities of Nalūn, trade clients with the Scalebond, and have planted a small, well-tended bed of House Nobody’s dead as a matter of neighborliness.
What commoners get. A tree. No Verdant dyer or eel-man has ever gone into an unmarked hole, and I have seen dukes envy it.
Limitations and Soul-Costs
[Curse] The Calling In — Isolation as Collection
Past forty-eight hours from swamp or kin they wither, stacking losses until half of what the body can bear is gone, and the more cuttings an orc wears, the sooner it starts. The Court has never held a yard of land outside the wet.
[Curse] Borrowed Hands — Too Many Grandmothers
Wear a keep long enough and it stops being borrowed. Old lodge-masters have opinions on bishops they never met and walk with a dead man’s limp, and a Mother who has drawn on too many ends up as a very good account of other people.
[Curse] The Bed Wants — Nuur Ssaath
Feeding the silt has no end. A garden left unplanted through a hard decade begins to take the unspecific: livestock, a careless child, the far root-walks. Something below the Tarnish Pools drops the leaves off Soul-Trees at the dark of the moon, and the rot-wives plant a garden on top of it every generation, deeper each time.
How They Stand Against the Three Paths
Body. A maul does not care how many grandmothers you have. Their answer is to refuse a straight fight until he is tired, wet and sunk to the thigh. Spirit. The worst of it: a reader goes past the rind into the Meld, and one poisoned Core hurts everyone in the cloud. Fate. A clever pull need only lean on what the Court depends on, a salt cart’s axle at the right ford, a cloudless week. The Court has no answer except that Fate fighters also die, and the fruit is very good.
Final Definition
The Moss Court is the people who took death at its word. They will not tell you the dead come back, whatever their manner suggests, and they will show you, with every courtesy, that nothing the dead knew has to go to waste. They have a tree for you. They have had it picked out for some time.
We will keep it for you.
And under that, from the rind-wife at Ghurash Hollow, drying her arms: Nothing wants. Bring it something nice.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.filePath: Factions, Bloodlines & Institutions/Houses and Bloodlines/The Houses of the Inner World/The Yan Hall.md
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Yan Hall
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Overview





































TypeLineage hall in the old southern style · horse-masters of the Dynasty of Sum-gol · the Thousand BloodlinesOriginThe Jade Plains, which the north’s maps call the Grey PlainFounderYan Laoma, “Old Horse Yan,” whose tablet stands alone in the first rowSeatQingyuanAnchorsThe Nine Rows of tablets · the tall gray horse · the Stud BookSignatureThe Stud Book (馬冊 · Mǎcè): anything entered in it knows its way home, and comes when its full line is read aloudMaximThe Plain Remembers the Hoof
The Duke of Tarn owed the Yan Hall for eleven hundred remounts. He had owed them for four years, through two very good letters, and in the summer of 677, at Cold Harrow in the Midmarch, he put every one of those horses into a single charge with his whole household on top of them, plate and plumes and painted lances, the grandest thing anybody on that field had ever seen, the gray backs rolling down the slope like a river going over a weir. Up on a knoll well out of bowshot sat a very small old woman in a jade sash, in a folding chair, with a boy holding a parasol over her, a ledger on her knees and a speaking-horn of lacquered ox-hide across the ledger. She was Elder Yan Meilan of the third row. She had come to see about the balance. She waited until the charge was committed, because she had a sense of occasion, and then she lifted the horn and read out one name. It was a stallion called Iron Rain who had been dead for nineteen years, and she gave his sire and his dam, and the sire and dam of each of those, in the bored clear voice of someone who has read a great many things aloud.
Eleven hundred gray horses, every one of them a grandchild of Iron Rain, turned their heads. They turned the rest of themselves a moment after. The charge wheeled in its own length, at the gallop, in perfect order, as lovely a piece of horsemanship as has ever been done, and went away to the south with the Duke’s entire household still on board, sawing at the reins and bellowing, past the enemy’s front rank, who stood up and cheered. They were still going at sunset. It is three weeks to Qingyuan at an easy pace, and they arrived in eighteen days, in good condition, most of them with a knight. The Hall stabled the knights at the ordinary rate. The Duke’s heirs paid in the autumn, for horses, feed and knights, and the other side bought four hundred grays the next spring, with cash, and read the terms very carefully.
The Yan sell to everyone. The whole Inner World rides out of their pastures, and the Yan take orders, in both senses, and never a side. The Hall sold to all of them, and every one of those horses is in the book. What they hold that everyone needs is the only animal in the world a hand higher than anything the north can raise, dappled like river stones, and the written record of who has been buying how many. What they want is for every army to need horses, and for none of them to win too quickly.
Origin of the House
The first tablet in the first row belongs to a man named Yan, who has no other name on it. The Hall’s account is that he was a bankrupt salt-carter on the old plain before there were any empires on it to pay a toll to, that a spring blizzard caught him on the open grass with a dying mare and no idea which way anything was, and that he did the sensible thing and followed her. She walked for three days with her head low. She brought him to the cold spring at what is now Yuquan, where she had been foaled, and died there. He sat down beside her and, having nothing else, wrote her name on a piece of harness in charcoal, with her sire and her dam so far as he knew them, because he thought somebody ought to. Old Horse Knows the Road is the first line of every Yan child’s first lesson, and the piece of harness is still in the Great Hall, in a jade box, and no two scholars agree on what the charcoal says.
His sons bred from her filly and their sons kept a book. The Hall paid the empire in grays for three centuries, recited its way through the last Calling of 602 so that no scholar can say if it answered, and still keeps the Emperor’s stall swept at Qingyuan, entered every year as held.
The House on the Crystal
The Hall is a clan ruled by its elders and its ancestral tablets, and a person enters it by birth, marriage, adoption or a good seat on a stolen horse. Its soul is therefore nothing like a bloodline’s. A Soul Crystal is the soul itself, in three layers: the Aether Shell, where Aether (mana) comes in and force goes out; the Essence Core, where it is refined into Essence (spiritual energy); and the Attraction Layer, a soul’s own share of Fate.

























LayerPlaneThe Yan formAether ShellPhysicalOrdinary at birth, and good by habit. The riders are clean and light, and they feel a horse through the seatEssence CoreSoulTrained on recitation. The Elders of Ledgers and Tablets read high here, and the name-reading lands through itAttraction LayerFateNothing out of the way. A book entry is a small kept vow, and it spends the soul’s own share and pulls no thread at all
Path. Riders tend to the Body Path, with the arrow as their one concession to distance. The elders of the Ledgers tend to the Spirit Path. Nobody reaches anything like Fate’s deep end on this plain, and a Yan will tell you that a true thing written down has never needed it.
No eye, no grip, in the people. The blood in the Hall’s name of the Thousand Bloodlines is horse blood. A Yan’s Mastery reads from Glory, Stage VI, like anyone’s, and with no Work or blessing behind it their Fate never climbs past the second rung. The lean is taught, in the saddle. The breed carries the rest.

























Rung and StageTypical YanUnwokenOuter cousins, herders and a great many grooms, all of whom can recite. Their read horses still turn their headsIV to VIStud archers, core disciples of a stud, first coats and first Releases on horsebackVII to IX · Body II to III, or Spirit IIThe superb few: an elder of the lower rows, and captains who collect debtsX and up · Spirit III or betterThe upper rows. The Hall-Master, ninety, still rides every morning
The Stud Book — 馬冊 · Mǎcè
What it is. A set of ledgers older than the Holy Sea’s, and a method. Sire, dam and grandsire for every animal the Yan have ever sold, with the name of the man who bought it. A gray of the Yan breed knows its own line, and answers to it from any distance a voice can carry, as you would answer if someone across a crowded market began saying your mother’s name, and your grandmother’s, and the name of the street you grew up on. A horse that hears this turns round. Given its head, it goes home.
How it works, in plain words. Every soul has its three layers, a beast’s included, with the Shell sealed until something cracks it. A Yan foal is read its line morning and evening, by the same groom, from the hour it stands, at the same tone, for three years. It drinks at Yuquan’s cold spring in those years, a small worked Core (a site where a Wellspring pools) that the Elder of Tablets keeps and will describe only as water. By the time it is sold, those words are laid down in its Core as deep as hunger. Scholars read it through the Wellspring Phreatis, memory as groundwater, which comes back to the well decades after it fell as rain. The horse does not obey anything. It remembers, all at once, from the bottom up, where it is from, and everything it has ever loved is in that direction. A Yan elder reading well is only telling it the truth in the right order. The working lands on a meaning, so it reads the reader’s Essence rung, and there is no pull in it.
Because grandchildren carry the grandsire’s name in their own line, you can read a whole get at once. That is why the third name is in the book.
The forms.






























FormTongueWho or what it reachesCalling the Horse呼馬 · Hū MǎOne horse, by its whole line, within earshot. Any core disciple can do it. It will walk through a market fence, as Rain-on-Slate did, with a professional thief still on itCalling the Get呼系 · Hū XìA dead sire’s name, and every living descendant who hears it. An elder of the upper rows, a good voice, a good horn, and a truly terrible afternoon for somebodyCalling the Debt呼債 · Hū ZhàiA buyer signs the ledger, and a signature is a small vow, a line on his own window (the soul’s private report of its numbers). Read aloud in his hearing, the line comes up in front of his eyes, with the balance, and stays until he has looked at it. It compels nothing. Lords have paid a great deal to avoid hearing it in front of guestsCalling the Cousin呼族 · Hū ZúAnyone with a tablet. Read your whole line, by your rung and your forebears, and you will feel the grass under your feet from four hundred miles off. It is a homesickness like vertigo, and it can be refused, by anyone prepared to feel like that indefinitely
The window a mounted Yan sees, in a bad moment:
[Cloud-over-Slate · Tall Gray, first class · Level 88]
[Line: Rain-on-Slate × Long Evening · Slate Water]
[Bond: Yan Hua, rider]
[Reserve 41% · Near fore: bruised]
[Heard: his line, read, northwest]

What it costs. The reader pays in reserve at about what a real working costs, and in time, which is the true price. It has to be the whole line, spoken in the right order with no name skipped, and anything out of true is noise. A horse takes a breath or two, a get takes as long as the elder takes, and a Yan in a fight rarely has that long. The title-recitation every northerner laughs at is practice, and it is also necessary: it is how a person of the Hall keeps their own line laid down, and a Yan who has not recited in a season begins to feel as lost as they are. Everything called back is a stall, a groom and a line in the book, for good.
Its limit. It reaches only what has a home in it. A gray foaled off the plain, a horse with no true line, or a man who hates the place will hear only somebody talking. It needs to be heard, and it stops at what a voice can do. It moves no horse the horse’s own legs would not move. It cannot be used on enemies, unless the enemy has been foolish enough to have bought from you, which is, admittedly, how the Hall arranged things. And since a line can only be read if it is known, a horse or man with “sire unknown” in the book cannot be read home at all. The joke of the Hall is that Lucky Bao, the best horse thief who ever lived, was the one man on the plain nobody could call in. He stayed thirty years.
Who beats it. Wax in the horses’ ears, as a sensible cavalry master does before the charge, if he can bear the look on their faces, and a deaf horse is very bad at hearing a trumpet too. Crossbred remounts, which cost a third as much and run a third as well. A crossbow in the right hedge, which has killed more than one elder of the third row. Fire in the ledger-house, which has been tried four times by people who owed money, and is why every Yan child can recite a stud’s whole column. And never buying a gray, which nobody who has seen one has managed.
Physical Appearance and Dress
Many of the Hall’s people are small, because small sits a horse better, and they are bowlegged from four years old with weather-cut eyes and a hard callus inside each knee. A rider’s right thumb is hooked and thick from the ring. Voices run clear and level and rather bored, carrying well in the open, and every Yan speaks as if reading. The Hall-Master, at ninety, has inspected the teeth of most of the lords you have heard of, and tends to look at yours.
Gray and jade are the colors, with a running horse in silver. They dress in felted coats and quilted silk, cut to the hip for the saddle, and the jade is real. A jade bridle-boss from Yuquan is the Hall’s way of saying what a horse is worth, the rider’s sash says what row she sits in, by the number of knots, and every Yan keeps the small jade horse they were given at their naming on a cord, however poor. A stud archer’s horn bow, lacquered black and sea-green, is Rare when the sinew is the Hall’s own, and she will tell you whose fault it was. At fifty paces you will see a lean person on an enormous gray moving as if the two of them were poured. An outer cousin has a felt coat, a shovel and a jade horse, and is reminded of his fortune at every meal.
Lineage Traits
[Trait] The Rung — A Place in the Rows
Everyone in the Hall has a place, stated before business. A cousin who breeds a filly of the first class goes up three rows that evening, and the tablet-carver is sent for.

Taught Dominion: an elder’s presence builds with each title recited, because each is a real weight of ancestors and a real attention from everyone who knows what it means.
The lineage halls say wēiyā, awe pressing down, and teach it as manners.
It is slow, it obeys the Stage gap like any Pressure, and it does not work on anyone rude enough to interrupt.

A Yan once introduced himself at a siege, and the siege was over when he finished. They tell that one themselves.
[Trait] Water Poured Downhill — The Seat

Riders’ coats extend through the saddle into the horse, and a good rider and gray move as one body, with the horse’s power in her balance.
Their shot needs no pause in the gallop: released between the fall of a hoof and the rise of the next, when the body is at rest.
Off the horse they are small people with sore knees.

She has not been on the ground for longer than an hour since she was four, and she walks like it.
[Trait] Read the Mouth — A Trade Skill Worth Paying For

Any Yan can tell a horse’s age, wind and soundness at a glance, and a man’s likewise. Appraisal runs absurdly high in this family.
In the ledger’s senior elders this runs to Analysis of what a purchase means: a lord who orders forty remounts in spring is expecting to lose forty in summer.

Lords pay well for that column, and pay better to have their own line of it left unread.
System Metrics
Stat lean



























































PrimaryLeanSignature Sub-StatsWhyDexterityExceptionalFinesse, Sequence, CelerityThe bow at the gallopGnosisHighRetention, Analysis, FluencyThe Book, by heartDominionHighCommand, PressureTitles, and being the eldest person in any roomHarmonicsModerateAttunement, StabilityHorses, and being in tune with themTemperingModerateLongevity, MaturityThey live a very long time, out of spiteResilienceModerateOath, AnchoringEveryone knows where they are fromArdencyLowPenetrationA narrow, tidy output, and the arrowhead does the restVitalityLowToleranceSaddle-hardened and rather light
Wellspring compatibility
A Wellspring is one of the sixty types of Aether and the idea a soul tempers itself on. It is a lens and locks nobody out of the rest.






























TierWellspringsWhyNaturalPhreatis, AnamnesisMemory as deep water, and a soul that can read what a thing has been. The tablets are built on theseEasyCymorath, Verdantia, FixatioOpen ways across open ground, grass without end, and what stays boundWorkableOrrenthal, Terranova, BenedictionA sound heart, ground that mends, a bond freely givenAgainst the grainLetheveil, Lethegraal, Oblivara, CinerionForgetting, and ash. A Letheveil child is a terrible thing to have happen to a family of this kind. Letheveil and Lethegraal are Spirit Wellsprings and give no fire, and the Hall would rather have the fire
On the Stages

























StagesHow a Yan readsI to III · Murmuring to AscensionRecitation learned, first coat, a pony and a very long listIV to VI · Flourishing to GloryFirst Release, and it looks like the horse being faster. A class at Glory, nearly always a jobVII to IX · Refraction to InvocationSecond Release, and a Domain at VIII if earned: the Plain, mostly, with the ground going to grass and the far edge of it always just furtherX and up · RealizationThe upper rows. Calling the Get with a horn across a valley
Doctrine and Arts
Never stand. The Hall’s war doctrine is as simple as anything in the South. Their horsemen are few, and they ride around a force from a distance it cannot reach and take it apart from the edges, starting with whoever is shouting. They never charge. When the Yan ride out in force it is to make sure a buyer has paid, and they take a clerk.















































MoveTongueMeaningWhat it doesHUÍMǍ JIÀN!回馬箭”Turning-Horse Arrow!”Twisted in the stirrups, shot straight behind at the full gallop. You are chasing a person whose bow is looking at youBŌ BIĀN!剝邊”Peel the Edge!”A ring of riders at bowshot, shooting the outer men, moving always to the left. It eats a company slowlyXIĀN SHÈ HǍN ZHĚ!先射喊者”First Shoot the Shouter!”Doctrine and a move both. Every arrow in the volley goes to one man, and it is whoever is giving ordersSHUǏ LIÚ!水流”Running Water!”Coat through the saddle, and horse and rider together reach a speed neither has alone for a few hundred paces, leaving an afterimage in grayGUĪ CÈ!歸冊”Back to the Book!”The Reading, shouted as an order on the field. The last thing a horse thief wants to hearJIǓ LIÈ!九列”Nine Rows!”A whole line of the Hall, recited to the end by an elder under attack, with the Pressure of each row landing in turn. It takes several minutes. Nobody has yet found the nerve to let one finish
Culture
They speak the lineage halls’ Chinese-registered tongue, and every word of address carries a rung. Bracket fights on the plain are run by stable-sects, each loyal to its stud: the Silver Bridles, the Black Girths, and the Yuquan Waders.

The Naming. A child’s first jade horse, and its first reading. The elder reads the line back as far as the first row, which can take a long while, and the child’s name comes last.
The Line at Dawn. Each groom reads each foal its line every morning, walking the stalls with a bowl of warm mash. Anyone can hear the Qingyuan paddocks from a mile off at sunrise, and it sounds like a very large and sleepy prayer.
Held. Each New Year the Hall enters what has not come home: the Emperor’s stall, the Ninth Paddock’s stock, three parties sent to read it out, and one horse. The Elder of Ledgers closes the book and they eat.
The Last Reading. When a Yan dies their tablet is cut and a descendant reads the whole line at the Great Hall, and the corpse’s own horse is led in. If the gray turns its head, they say the dead has arrived. Nobody says what they do if it does not.

Who they marry, fight and owe. They dispute the salt toll with the Ryu annually, by reciting, and hold a line of boundary stones and an annual brawl at Mashi with the Marrick, the best neighbors they could ask for. The water comes from upstream, and they have started counting sick foals and showed the count to Maud Corwen. Herding families rent their stretch by the head of stock, get a share of the foals and can have a child taken up the rows on merit, which is why a Yan grandmother can reduce a horse-coper to tears from behind a tea stall by asking who his people were.
Limitations and Soul-Costs
[Curse] Entered Is Entered — The Book Holds Both Ways
Every Yan is in the book. The Hall can call any cousin home, from anywhere, at any hour, and a cousin who refuses gets to feel like that for the rest of their life. Nobody leaves the Yan. Some people go a very long way away and get used to it.
[Curse] The Walking Home — Nothing You Sell Stays
A gray sold far off pines by about its eighth year. It will carry a beloved master through anything, and when that master is dead it will turn and walk home alone across half a continent, and the Hall will send the heirs a courteous note about the balance. Nobody who rides for the Yan can count on the horse staying once things have gone truly wrong.
[Curse] The Water Upstream — One Spring Under All of It
The whole breed drinks from a very few sources, and the springs of the South have been going bad. The Hall has noticed. If whatever is wrong with the water gets into the line at Yuquan, it gets into all of the line, and it stays in the book as true.
How They Stand Against the Three Paths
Body. A hitter has to catch them. Most never do, and they die at a distance, complaining. Those who can close the gap, by a movement art or a cliff at the Yan’s back, find a small person on the ground with a bow and very little else to say.
Spirit. More dangerous, since a working thrown at range can meet them where they live, and a Spirit fighter can read an elder’s line back at him. Memory workings terrify the Hall, and an elder who has lost a row of the Book has lost part of the Hall.
Fate. The strap gives and the horse goes down, and a whole charge can be lost to one bad hoof. But a sound horse with a clean line is a poor thing to move, and the Yan have fed, shod and inspected every animal on this plain for a thousand years. It is rare to find a strap to give.
Final Definition
The Yan Hall is a very old family that writes down the truth and reads it out at the worst possible moment. They only know where everything comes from, in order, with no names skipped, and have found that in a world this far from home nothing else is needed. Every army in the Inner World rides out of their pastures, and every horse in every one of those armies knows the way back. Lords of the north hear that and laugh, and buy another gray. It is a very good horse.
The Plain remembers the hoof. Bring a lunch.
