factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Southern Warlords
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Seven houses of the Inner World’s south, below the Center and beyond any living crown, what is left of the Empire of Sum-gol, each holding a thing the whole quarter needs and none of them holding it for anyone else.
In the fat summer of 661, when the Mahou kings still sat at Sum-gol, the salt smuggler Tam Pennyroyal died owing money in every town between the Thousand Moorings and the Long Fields, and his widow, Goody Mordaunt, gave him the finest funeral the south had ever seen, in a coffin of painted cedar that took eight men to lift, because it held four hundredweight of untaxed sea salt and no Tam. The eight she hired from a Marrick company, who were paid by the day and asked no questions. The gray horses she hired from the Yan, who wrote down her name. Forty paid mourners in vermilion streamers went howling up the salt road behind it, and at the toll below Ashbury the Ryu toll-man took off his hat, charged the full toll on one corpse, and waved them through, because there are limits. A Corwen agent sold her Wellhead water to sprinkle on the bier, by the cask. A Lambert clerk at the ford looked once at the depth of the wheel-ruts, wrote down a number, and followed the procession for two days, weeping loudly, and a crow came down out of a Yukari cedar and rode the last twenty miles on the lid. At the graveside, before three hundred people and the priest, the clerk stood up and read the count: the deceased had gained a great deal of weight since market day. The sun went down at that moment, which ended the Marrick contract, and the eight men grounded the coffin and walked home, and the lid split, and the whole south stood in the road scooping up salt in its hats and singing. They found Tam in a Ryu barge three weeks later, thoroughly pickled. Sum-gol’s post delivered every house’s bill to the widow on the same morning. She paid them all, cleared seven silver on the day, and married the clerk.
By the Yukari record, which is the only one that has all of it, six of the seven houses made money off that funeral and the seventh wrote down who did. You may now read the rest of this page as commentary.
The north counts its warlords at seven and seats six. The south counts seven too, and seats six, and the empty chair is Sum-gol’s. That is the first thing a northerner learns about the south and usually the only thing he believes: that the southern houses are softer, warmer and richer than his own, and fight with money. The second half is true. The rest is the kind of thing a man says about a country he has only ever seen from the far end of a spear.
Where the Kessen road and the salt road come out from around the Scourge of Hell, past the last of the Center, the Inner World stops being a shield of cold rock and turns green. The ground drops in long steps toward the southern sea: cedar valleys climbing into cloud on the east, the open grass of the Grey Plain in the middle, the spring country of the Wellheads steaming in the morning, iron hills and salt pans around Sum-gol, and at the bottom of it all the white shelf of the Holy Sea of Alabaster, where the cliffs are the color of milk and the water under them is so clear the fishing boats seem to hang in the air. It is loud country. Market bells, temple gongs, the hum of the kept springs under every terrace and lamp, big gray horses calling across the plain at dusk, cedar-smoke and orange blossom and hot iron. The north buys its horses here, its oil, its salt from the southern pans, half its sealed casks of Wellhead water, and every one of its grudges about southern courtesy.
None of the seven was ever bound by the Kōkan crown. The Moto held the North; the warlords hold what lies beyond the Center, and the long war of the last forty years was fought across their ground as often as across the north’s. Some sold to it. Some bled in it. One was finished by it.
How the Empire Fell
They were bound by another crown once. For three hundred years the Vermilion Dynasty of Sum-gol was the empire of the whole South, from Kessen ford to the southern sea, and every house below held its land of the Mahou emperors: the Holy Sea paid in records, the Long Fields in spearmen, the Wellheads in water, the Grey Plain in horses, the Thousand Moorings kept the fleet, and the Yukari, who were old when the Mahou were young, paid one crow a year and entered it. It ended on the first day of autumn in Year 602, when the Emperor Rokju Mahuo, who had doubled the salt tax to pay for his domes, walked out to call his yearly roll before the whole South under the vermilion banners, and the South stopped answering. A Lambert clerk read out what the throne owed the Archive. The Marrick company in the square looked at the sun, saw that its contract had run out at noon, and grounded spears. The Corwen casks had been sold elsewhere. The Yukari sent a crow. The Baengnok, the White Stag of the line, came when he called, looked at him, and walked out of the East Gate. The full account is on the Dynasty’s page.
Only two houses stayed. The Yan and the Ryu still answer to the name of Sum-gol, which costs them a recitation and a letter each autumn. Lambert, Yukari, Corwen and Marrick stand apart, and the Mahou went on as kings at Sum-gol alone for three more generations, until the war. That is why the south has powers instead of provinces, and why every house on this page keeps an old imperial grievance in the same drawer as its new ones.













































HouseRealmSeatYukariThe Silver Cedars of YukariThe Cedar EnclaveMahuoThe Vermilion Dynasty of Sum-golSum-golLambertThe Holy Sea of Alabaster, held from SallowgateSallowgate; the Sea’s capital is AlabasterThe Yan HallThe Jade Plains of Qingyuan, in the DynastyQingyuanRyuThe Copper Coast of Haeseong, in the DynastyHaeseongCorwenThe Sapphire Wells of BrightwaterBrightwaterMarrickThe Ochre Fields of HammerfordHammerford

The southern rule. A Banner House of the north serves for exactly as long as the Crown serves. A Southern Warlord serves nobody, and has a price for everything, and the price is never only silver. The Yukari’s price is a promise put on the record. The Lamberts’ is a true count. The Yan sell a horse and keep its name.

1. House Yukari
Seat: The Cedar Enclave, on a hilltop above the Yukari valleys
Realm: The Silver Cedars of Yukari, the Crow’s Reach
Territory: The Yukari valleys, east of Sum-gol: a country of cedar so tall and close that the light comes down between the trunks in thin bars of green-gold
Identity: The eye. House Yukari sees what the others are doing.
Current head: Lord Naiser Yukari
Words: The crow perches. The crow watches. The crow remembers.
Colors: Black and silver, silver threading through dark
The oldest blood in the south and the least interested in ruling it. The Yukari are an archaic bloodline before they are a house, and the house is the shape the bloodline took when the world forced it to hold ground: the valleys, the villages that pay the tithe, the long cedar hall with its covered walk and its raked white gravel and its three standing stones that throw no shadow, and wards laid along every approach that touch whoever comes up the southern road long before anyone at the gate has seen him. The Yukari name is chosen at the Telling, not inherited, which makes the house the only one of the seven whose members are all volunteers.
They came through the war harder than anyone in the north knows. The Zettari struck the Yukari valleys in the last four years, the Seikai turned, the Soul Plane broke, and Lord Naiser’s father went into the seam and held it. The house came out of it having won, and has spent every month since telling everyone who will listen that it has no wish for more land. Its terms at the Cedar Enclave were plain: no Yukari knowledge for war, no Yukari name carried as a banner, no touching the spirit world without Yukari counsel, every promise made in the hall entered in the Yukari record. And when Sum-gol is settled, the Mahuo royal line restored there, whatever is left of it, and the Yukari stepping back.
In the south they are the house everybody wants at the table and nobody wants watching them across it. A Yukari reads a room the way a cartographer reads a coastline, and the warlords who have sat in the Cedar Enclave come out of it describing the same feeling: of having been measured, comprehensively, without hostility, by someone who will remember the measurement for the rest of their lives.
The full codex: The Yukari Bloodline.
2. House Mahuo, the Mahou Line
Seat: Sum-gol, vacant
Realm: The Vermilion Dynasty of Sum-gol
Territory: Sum-gol and its country, the iron hills and the salt pans at the end of the Kessen road
Identity: The crown that was carried. House Mahuo is what happens to a name used as a banner.
Current head: Cozbi Mahuo, Head of House Mahuo and Master of the Sum-gol Post, who refuses the crown and wears olive and white, leaving the vermilion on the banners.
Words: Call, and It Answers
Colors: Vermilion and white
Once the richest seat in the south, and for three hundred years the throne of all of it. Sum-gol sits where the Kessen road ends and the south begins, on iron and on salt, and for longer than the Moto have had a crown the Mahou line ruled it, as emperors of the whole South until 602 and as kings of Sum-gol after that: summoners whose arts called things across the Veil and bound them, and whose iron and salt went north in every cart that ever used the road. The Mahuo’s salt. The Sum-gol iron. Every northern quartermaster still says the two together.
The war ate them. Their name was carried at the front of other people’s armies until there was nothing left of it but the carrying; the Moto put Mahuo banners over Moto columns, the Yukari and the Zettari each fought under the excuse of protecting them, and when the time came the house was destroyed. Every one of the three tells it differently. The Yukari say the Moto stood back and let the Yukari slaughter them, because a house turned into a symbol is very easy to kill and nobody weeps for a symbol. The Moto blame the Yukari. Kushara blames them both. All three are right about the other two.
What is left is a post. The Mahuo post at Sum-gol still keeps its crows and its couriers, and every letter between the north and the Yukari valleys goes through it; Ulf Stark’s last crows south went that way. A house that was a crown now carries the south’s letters, by crow and relay rider, and carries them so well that nobody has thought to ask who is paying the couriers, or whom they answer to, or what a summoning line does with its arts when it has no hall left to call them into. The chair at the warlords’ table is kept for Sum-gol. It is the only one with nobody sitting in it, and every other house at the table has a reason to want it filled by somebody in particular.
The full codex: House Mahuo.
3. House Lambert
Seat: Sallowgate, the landward gate of the Holy Sea of Alabaster
Realm: The Holy Sea of Alabaster, whose capital is the city of Alabaster
Territory: The Sea’s land marches, from the white shelf north to the edge of the Grey Plain, and the Sea’s courts wherever they sit
Identity: The count. House Lambert keeps the Holy Sea honest about its numbers.
Current head: Léonard Lambert, Warlord of the Lamberts, Keeper of Sallowgate
Words: Count True
Colors: White and ink-black, a balance on the field; the warlord rides in gilded harness under scarlet, with the Sallowgate bear on his breast
The Holy Sea of Alabaster is a theocracy on a white shelf above the southern sea, ruled by its Palatine from the Alabaster Court, hosting a Sancta Lux chapter hold that reports past him, and built from top to bottom to weigh one commodity: a sworn account. The Lamberts are the hands that do the weighing. For as long as the Sea has had courts there has been a Lambert at the bench beside the cleric, counting: tariffs at the gate, grain in the store, witnesses in the dock, the days between a lord’s promise and a lord’s delivery. The Sea measures testimony. The Lamberts measure everything the testimony is about.
They are the Sea’s warlord house because a holy see needs somebody who is allowed to carry a sword, and the Lamberts have held Sallowgate and the land marches for the Palatines since before the current line of Palatines could count. Their levies are small, drilled, and paid on the day, and their officers are famous across the south for a habit no other house has: they will tell a general his own numbers before battle, out loud, in front of his captains, and will not soften them. A Lambert who gives a false count is struck from the house. The house has done it. It keeps the list.
There is an older thing in the blood that the house does not discuss. A great many Lamberts are born with Crystals that never wake, and some of those grow up able to fight anyway, reading a blow before it is thrown with no faculty to read it with, so that a spectator calls it luck and a practitioner calls it impossible. Nobody outside the house has ever counted how many Lamberts there are. The house has. It has not shared the figure.
Lamberts travel. Cadet branches have gone north on the Sea’s business for generations and stayed: Osbert Lambert, tariff-master at the Hallenfeld junction, kept the ledger of Tenrai grain diverted from the starving provinces and sent a fair copy north, which is about as Lambert a thing as a man can do.
The full codex: House Lambert.
4. The Yan Hall
Seat: Qingyuan, on the Grey Plain
Realm: The Jade Plains of Qingyuan, in the Dynasty of Sum-gol
Territory: The Grey Plain, the open grass between the Wellheads and the iron hills, where the tall southern horses are bred
Identity: The horse. Every army in the Inner World rides out of the Yan pastures, and the Yan know which.
Current head: The Venerable Hall-Master of the Yan, First of the Grey Plain, Keeper of the Thousand Bloodlines, Elder Yan Shouyi
Hall maxim: The Plain Remembers the Hoof
Colors: Gray and jade, a running horse in silver
A lineage hall in the old southern style, with ancestral tablets nine rows deep and a title for every rung of the family, which the Yan recite in full at every introduction and which takes, for a senior elder, about as long as it takes to water a horse. Their wealth walks. The tall gray southern horse, a hand higher than anything the north can breed and dappled like river stones, comes from the Yan studs at Qingyuan and nowhere else, and the Yan keep the bloodlines in ledgers older than the Holy Sea’s: sire, dam and grandsire for every animal they have ever sold, and the name of the man who bought it.
That last column is the Yan’s real stock in trade. They sold to everyone in the war. Ashmore’s big southern horses were Yan horses; so were the Tenrai’s. The Hall-Master can tell you which side bought how many remounts in which season, which is to say which side was expecting to lose cavalry, and when. The Yan take orders, in both senses, and never a side.
Their own horsemen are few and superb, archers who shoot from the saddle at the full gallop, turning in the stirrups, with the gray horses running flat out under them like water poured downhill. When the Yan ride out in force, it is to make sure a buyer has paid.
The full codex: The Yan Hall.
5. House Ryu
Seat: Haeseong, the sea-fortress at the mouth of the salt road
Realm: The Copper Coast of Haeseong, in the Dynasty of Sum-gol
Territory: The Thousand Moorings, the warm southern coast east of the Holy Sea, and the salt road that runs north from it to Ashmore’s junction
Identity: The sea. What comes into the Inner World by water comes in through House Ryu.
Current head: Admiral-Lord Ryu Ha-eun
Words: The Tide Pays Twice
Colors: Sea-green and copper
Once the Mahou line’s admiralty and its southern ports. When the Mahuo were emperors and then kings, the Ryu kept their ships, their harbor dues and their salt fleet, and were the second family of Sum-gol; when the Mahuo fell, the ships, the harbor dues and the salt fleet were all still sitting at Haeseong, with nobody left to send the revenue to. The Ryu left the Mahuo’s wealth exactly where it sat, and simply stopped forwarding it. The south has never settled whether that is theft. The Ryu would like it noted that the Mahuo have never asked.
Haeseong is the brightest city in the south: white walls, green copper roofs, a harbor packed with junks and coasting galleys and the long low salt barges, lanterns strung across the water every night of the year, and a company of lamp-wardens hired down from the Wellheads at great expense so the lighthouse can burn worked light that reaches forty miles out, who walk off the tower every few years over the fee and are paid before the fishing fleet can get home. The salt road begins at its quays and runs north to the junction below Ashbury, and every sack of southern salt that ever crossed the Ashmore marches paid a Ryu toll on the way.
They will be the first house to object if anybody restores the Mahuo royal line at Sum-gol, and the last to object out loud. Admiral-Lord Ha-eun sat at the Cedar Enclave and heard Naiser Yukari promise exactly that, and smiled, and asked a very good question about harbor dues.
The full codex: House Ryu.
6. House Corwen
Seat: Brightwater, at the head of the spring country
Realm: The Sapphire Wells of Brightwater
Territory: The Wellheads, the steaming upland of southern Wellspring sites whose sealed casks go north by river barge to the ward-cutters of Kharven-Seat
Identity: The springs. House Corwen keeps the south’s power in the ground.
Current head: Maud Corwen, Warden of the Wellheads, Lessee of the Guild
Words: The Water Keeps Faith
Colors: Kingfisher blue and brass
A chartered family, the only one of the seven that holds its ground by Guild lease rather than by blood or conquest, a lease it took out the moment the empire broke, and the richest per acre. The Wellheads are a high, wet, luminous country of hot springs and cold springs side by side, terraced pools in every color from milk-jade to rust, an assay post on every wellmouth and brass-bound carts of sealed casks going off downhill toward the river, and the hum of the kept pools so constant that Corwen children who leave home cannot sleep for the silence. Every worked Wellspring site (a Core, in common speech) under Guild lease from the Wellheads to the southern sea sells its hours through a Corwen keeper, and the keeper can close it. The ward-cutters who re-cut the wards on the Seat’s rock each spring quench their chisels in water out of these casks, at a price Maud Corwen sets, and have been known to say what they think of it.
Their trouble is the water. Since the war the springs in the south have gone bad, and nobody will say why. Some taste wrong to anyone with the tongue to taste; villages downstream of them are sick, and the physicians do not know what they are treating; the forks in the Corwen assay posts ring as true as they ever did, and the Corwen wardens read the forks. The Yukari say they can walk the springs from the mouth to the source and tell you where the harm is and whose hand is on it. House Corwen has not yet asked them to.
Maud Corwen is a big, cheerful, sharp-eyed woman who knows the lease terms of every spring in the south by heart, and who has never in her life been seen to drink the water.
The full codex: House Corwen.
7. House Marrick
Seat: Hammerford, on the Long Fields
Realm: The Ochre Fields of Hammerford
Territory: The Long Fields, the levy country between the Grey Plain and the marches of the Center, and every muster ground in the south that will pay
Identity: The wall. House Marrick sells the southern rank.
Current head: Gerrit Marrick, Captain of the Long Spear
Words: Shoulder to Shoulder
Colors: Ochre and black, in squares
The north fights in knots and wedges and long Keld lines that move like weather. The south fights in a wall, a rank of men standing shoulder to shoulder because they cannot trust themselves to stand anywhere else, and charging in it with a sound like a building falling over. That rank was Marrick’s before it was anyone else’s. The Long Fields have bred spearmen for three hundred years, as the empire’s levy country first and for hire since 602; the Marrick captains drill them in the stubble after harvest, sixteen deep, long ash spears and drums, and hire the finished companies out by the season to whoever has the coin.
Half the southern hosts in the war had Marrick companies at their center, and some years both halves. The house considers this a professional courtesy. A Marrick company fights for its contract to the last day of the season and not one day past it, and has been known to finish a battle at noon on the day its contract ran out by grounding spears in the middle of the field and walking home through both armies, unharmed, because both armies would be hiring next season.
Gerrit Marrick is sixty, loud, scarred, very funny, missing an ear, and the only warlord in the south who has fought in every war of the last forty years on at least two sides. He says the north never understood the rank. “You stand in it because the man on your left is standing in it, lad. Brave’s got nothing to do with it.”
The full codex: House Marrick.
The Table at the Cedar Enclave
The seven have had no emperor since 602 and none of them wants another, unless it would be them. What they have instead is a table: a meeting called when the south’s business outgrows any one house, sat at whichever seat the calling house names, with the chair for Sum-gol kept empty at it, and its decisions binding on nobody who did not agree to them. Since the war the table has sat at the Cedar Enclave, because the Yukari asked, and because every house wanted every promise entered in a record somebody else was keeping.
What the south wants, in one line each:





































HouseWantsYukariTo be left to perform a lawful function, the Mahuo restored, and nobody’s war fought with Yukari sightMahuoWhatever is left of it, its own name back off other people’s bannersLambertThe count to come out right, and the Holy Sea’s courts heard north of the borderYanEvery army to need horses, and none of them to win too quicklyRyuSum-gol left empty, the salt road open, and the harbor dues uncontestedCorwenThe springs clean before anyone outside the Wellheads proves they are notMarrickA long peace with a lot of small wars in it
The South and the North
The Kessen road. The western of the two trade roads between the north and the south, and the one the Post rides, runs from Kessen ford down the Scourge’s west flank through the low country to Sum-gol and on past the foot of the Yukari valleys. When Kagenori Tenrai Moto put it under martial law he cut the Post’s line between the north and the Yukari at once, and every southern house lost money on the same morning. That was the first time in forty years the seven agreed on anything.
The empty red chair. The north has had nobody in the red chair for forty years, and the war that emptied it has only just stopped. The Tenrai speak for the Hall of Verdicts and collect on the road, and the seven lines watch each other across it. Each southern house has made its own reading of who sits next. None of them has yet sent a delegation, because the first house to send one tells the other six what it thinks the chair is worth. Later hand: what comes out of it within these years is the Northern Empire of Whitemere, with the Kingdom of Kharven as its capital, and the south has been arguing about the price ever since.
The Moto. The Moto are eating inward: closing the roads between their own provinces, turning back their own grain convoys at their own posts. The Yukari believe the next blood the Moto spill will be their own. Every other house at the table is working out what a Moto civil war will pay.


On the record.
From the Guild’s rolls: the Yukari valleys, the Cedar Enclave and its wards; the Mahuo post at Sum-gol and its crows; the Mahuo’s salt and the Sum-gol iron; the Kessen road; the tall gray southern horses; the southern rank; the Guild’s hold on the southern Wellsprings.
From hearsay, and the Guild would like that noted: the count of seven with Sum-gol’s chair empty; the seats, heads, words and colors of the Yan Hall, House Ryu, House Corwen and House Marrick; the table at the Cedar Enclave; the last Calling of 602, Emperor Rokju Mahuo and the Baengnok; what is wrong with the southern springs.
Open. Old Lamberts who fought without a woken Crystal are carried here as house lore only, with no names.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Ten Great Houses of Drakyssia
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Vaer’Kharath: “The Ten Wings Beneath the Throne.” Outer World imperial order.
Supreme House: House Drakhalis · Sovereign allegiance: The Dragon Sovereign of Drakyssia
Function: Continental administration, military specialization, resource stewardship, trade, breeding, roads and works, diplomacy, Aether conservation, preservation of draconic civilization
Foundational principle: No House possesses the Empire. Every House possesses something the Empire cannot afford to lose.
Bess Oakes of the southern Grass Sea kept eleven red cattle and a bad temper, and in the dry summer of 604 a Dovaryn wing-lord named Sethrax the Long came down on her pasture, three hundred meters of crimson and tarnished gold, and ate the lot in the time it took her to swear. She cut the tails off what he had left, put them in a sack, and walked nine days to the Eredan assize at Ered-Vaelor, where a small green Dragonkin clerk read her complaint through twice and sent a summons. Half the Grass Sea came out to watch him laugh at it, and he obliged them, loudly, from the top of a hill. So Eredan billed him. Zhaeryn, on Eredan’s paper, froze his gold. Rhaegyr found it could not mend his barding this season, and Ishkar discovered that the ground under his roost was approaching depletion and regretted the limit on his pulling, and Maelkar wrote a courteous letter asking after the health of his eggs. Before the first rain Sethrax the Long landed at Bess Oakes’s fence, with the whole sky full of Wyverns come to see it, and set down eleven live cattle one by one out of his forefoot, and a chest. She counted them. She told him one was lame.
Dragons will tell you that story to show how just the empire is. The mortals of the Grass Sea tell it to show how much a dragon can be made to hate a piece of parchment. A note on the word before we go in: Drakyssian chanceries say “the continent” and “continental” for their own half of the Outer World, as though everything past the Twilight March were a rumor, and I leave the word as they wrote it because they sue.
The Structure
Drakyssia’s half of the Outer World does not rest on the Dragon Sovereign alone. Beneath the imperial throne stand ten ancient draconic dynasties whose territories, bloodlines, armies, trades and institutions are the structural foundation of the empire. Each holds an Imperial Charge: a responsibility whose failure can endanger the whole of the south.
The Houses deliberately overlap, and none is meant to become self-sufficient. The House with the greatest army does not hold the treasury. The House holding the treasury does not hold foreign trade. The House holding trade does not hold the Dragon Dens. The House with the greatest mines does not hold the forges. The House holding the forges does not command the Dragon Roads.
This was formalized under Kain Drakhalis, who understood that a dragon noble controlling every necessity of war eventually becomes a rival sovereign. Drakyssia therefore runs on interdependence enforced by supremacy.
1. House Drakhalis — The Royal House
Formal title: House Drakhalis, the Blood of the Eternal Throne
Seat: The Drakhalis Throne Spire, Kra’Vorrak · Heartland: Central Drakyssian Heartlands
Charge: Sovereignty, imperial command, succession, continental strategy, preservation of the Kan inheritance
Descending from Kain Drakhalis, nephew of Dova’Kan and Avo’Kan, the House carries one of the most prestigious draconic bloodlines in the Outer World. Its authority derives not from wealth alone, numbers alone or religious legitimacy alone, but from the historical unification of all three. Across a reign of more than seven thousand years Kain broke rival claimants, subdued rebellious Houses, shattered external invasions and reorganized the Great Houses around clearly defined imperial responsibilities.
The House holds the Right of Final Command. The Dragon Sovereign traditionally emerges from Drakhalis, though ancient law permits another sufficiently legitimate descendant of the founding blood to inherit under extraordinary circumstance.
Controls: the Imperial Throne · the War-Wing Synod · declaration of continental war · recognition of Great House succession · Dragon Bond permissions at the highest level · imperial treaties · recognition of foreign sovereigns · appointment of High Dragon Generals · continental Dragon Road law · final adjudication between Houses · recognition of legitimate bloodlines · imperial succession · mobilization of the Ten.
It also keeps the Throne Reserve, a military force deliberately separate from every other House, answering only to the Sovereign.
What Drakhalis authority gives the continent is exceptionally rare among dragons: predictability. A human kingdom negotiating with House Dovaryn knows an imperial treaty outranks a Dovaryn lord. An Elven enclave threatened by an unauthorized dragon can appeal to imperial law. A merchant crossing four Houses’ territory does not renegotiate sovereignty at every border. The throne turns draconic supremacy into government.

All Wings Return to the Throne.

2. House Dovaryn — The Great Wing
Formal title: House Dovaryn, Lords of the Ten Thousand Wings
Seat: Vhar’Dova, the Sky Arsenal · Heartland: Northern Drakhal Spine and the Iron Roost corridor, facing the Twilight March
Charge: Aerial warfare, Wyvern breeding, rapid deployment, sky patrol, continental interception
Dovaryn possesses the largest Wyvern host in the Outer World, and no other House comes close. Its mountain territories hold nesting valleys, cliff hatcheries, aerial training grounds, military roosts, wind-gorges and breeding sanctuaries sustaining tens of thousands of Wyverns.
Dovaryn doctrine treats the Wyvern not as a lesser dragon but as the ideal military organism for rapid aerial war. True Dragons hold greater individual power; Wyverns hold numbers, speed, maneuverability, formation discipline and replaceability. That distinction lets Dovaryn place wings almost anywhere in the south faster than conventional armies can march.
Maintains: the largest Wyvern military population · imperial aerial patrols · border interception wings · long-distance reconnaissance · Dragon Road security · relay courier flights · anti-piracy patrols · rescue wings · rider schools · military breeding · the watch on the upper air · rapid reinforcement. Its greatest formation is the Grand Spearhost, reserved for continental war.
Dovaryn makes distance irrelevant: a rebellion thousands of miles from Kra’Vorrak can be seen within days and reinforced soon after, and no enemy can assume mountains, rivers, forests or broken roads will protect them. The same wings protect the common sky-roads, merchant caravans, isolated settlements and coastal shipping, and when flood or earthquake severs a region they are usually the first imperial force able to deliver medicine, food, messages or evacuation. They are feared as the first sign of invasion and respected as the first sign that help has arrived. They also patrol the Red Marches border, where they fly half-blind under the northern veils.

Before the Enemy Sees the Mountain, We Have Seen the Enemy.

3. House Zhaeryn — The Golden Scale
Formal title: House Zhaeryn, Keepers of the Auric Depths
Seat: Zhaer-Khazad, the Golden Mountain · Heartland: Golden Escarpment and southern Serrathan Highlands, across the March from Vel Sarith
Charge: Gold, precious metals, gemstones, imperial reserves, mining law, monetary stability
Zhaeryn controls the largest concentration of gold mines in the Outer World, extending beneath the southern Serrathan Highlands through surface mines, Wyrm-dug shafts, underground settlements, fortified vaults, ore-sledge galleries and ancient extraction chambers. Beyond gold: silver, platinum, diamonds, emeralds, cobalt, manganese, nickel and several rare magical ores.
The House became enormously wealthy. Imperial law ensured it did not become enormously independent: the richest mines are Crown Resources under Zhaeryn stewardship rather than absolute private property.
Manages: imperial gold reserves · precious-metal extraction · gemstone certification · mining licenses · coinage metals · strategic stockpiles · mine safety · deep-earth surveying · anti-smuggling · royal tribute assessment · mineral taxation · wartime reserves.
Its vaults keep the empire functioning through drought, war, failed harvest and trade disruption. Its mining towns employ enormous numbers of Humans, Elves, Dragonkin, Wyrms and smaller draconic peoples, and the House enforces extraction limits around Wellsprings, the Outer World having already learned what happens when a civilization mines metaphysical resources without restraint.

Gold may be exhausted. The land may not.

4. House Avarax — The Merchant Wing
Formal title: House Avarax, Masters of Coin and Crossing
Seat: Avar-Kesh, the City of a Thousand Contracts · Heartland: Eastern Sun Coast
Charge: Trade, markets, customs, foreign commerce, shipping, caravan law, commercial diplomacy
The market-heart of the empire. Its dragons are stereotyped as negotiators, mathematicians, multilingual scholars, shipowners, money-changers, contract-keepers and extraordinarily patient political predators. Avarax keeps commercial enclaves in nearly every major Outer World port and negotiates with human kingdoms, Elven sanctuaries, independent cities, foreign empires, and draconic Houses that refuse ordinary diplomacy.
Oversees: foreign trade · imperial customs · merchant licensing · port tariffs · continental trade standards · caravan protection agreements · maritime commerce · currency exchange · trade arbitration · merchant Dragon Roads · imperial warehouses · importation of Aether-rich resources.
The House answers one of Drakyssia’s great weaknesses: the empire cannot produce everything it needs on depleted land. Avarax imports Aether-rich reagents, healing materials, Essence-bearing plants, specialized timber, catalysts, food during shortage and foreign-made wonders and relics. It also created standardized weights, shipping protections, commercial arbitration, recognized caravan marks and cross-House merchant law, so a human trader can cross draconic territory without personally negotiating with every dragon whose mountain shadows the road. Most of the grain and medicine that crosses the March from Dreadvalis passes through Avarax contracts.

What War Cannot Reach, Trade Already Has.

5. House Maelkar — Keepers of the Dragon Dens
Formal title: House Maelkar, Wardens of Egg and Ancient Sleep
Seat: Mael’Kara, the First Den · Heartland: Volcanic valleys beneath the Black Scale Ranges
Charge: Eggs, hatcheries, nesting grounds, hibernation chambers, wounded-dragon recovery, genealogy, population preservation
Maelkar holds perhaps the most sacred holdings in Drakyssia outside the Dragon Catacombs. The Dragon Dens are enormous protected environments built for every stage of draconic life: volcanic incubators, cold caverns, vast mountain chambers, artificial lakes, systems running for miles underground. Eggs are protected here. Hatchlings are raised. Injured dragons recover. Pregnant dragons receive sanctuary. Elders enter hibernation, and ancient dragons sometimes sleep for centuries. The largest Dens are effectively underground cities.
Maintains: imperial hatcheries · egg protection · nesting registries · bloodline genealogies · hibernation chambers · elder sanctuaries · recovery caverns · hatchling nutrition · breeding-health records · abandoned egg adoption · rare subspecies conservation · population censuses. Maelkar law makes theft or deliberate destruction of a recognized dragon egg one of the gravest crimes in the empire.
Armies can be rebuilt, fortresses reconstructed, gold mined elsewhere. A bloodline permitted to go extinct cannot be purchased again. The House also manages draconic population growth against ecological carrying capacity, which on an Aether-depleted continent means protecting dragonkind partly by preventing dragonkind from destroying its own habitat.

Before There Is a Warrior, There Is an Egg.

6. House Ormyr — The Deep House
Formal title: House Ormyr, Wardens Beneath the World
Seat: Ormyr-Duun, the Buried City · Heartland: Wyrmdeep beneath the Drakhal Spine
Charge: Wyrmdeep works, tunnels, groundwater, subterranean mapping, seismic monitoring, deep Wellspring protection
Ormyr governs downward. The House keeps exceptionally close ties to Wyrm populations and counts numerous ancient Wyrm bloodlines among its nobility and client families. Its engineers built much of the underground works connecting the Heartlands: some tunnels large enough for mature dragons, others carrying water, heat, ore, cargo or military forces.
Oversees: Wyrmdeep Cities · imperial tunnel networks · seismic monitoring · volcano pressure observation · underground aquifers · heat-vents and hot galleries · deep Wellspring surveying · mine stabilization · subterranean fortification · evacuation tunnels · underground military movement · detection of unauthorized excavation.
Ormyr allows the empire to survive beneath its own volcanic homeland, detecting eruptions, earthquakes, collapse, groundwater loss, magma migration and Wellspring instability. Its engineers frequently assist mortal kingdoms with wells, aqueducts, mines, earthquake-resistant foundations and reservoirs. In the driest regions of the continent an Ormyr water engineer can be worth more than an army.

Every Throne Stands Upon Something.

7. House Rhaegyr — The Iron Flame
Formal title: House Rhaegyr, Masters of Forge and Scale
Seat: Rhaegyr’s Crucible · Heartland: Volcanic southern Drakhal Spine
Charge: Weapons, armor, metallurgy, siege equipment, Dragonfire forging, military engineering, forge-work for war
Rhaegyr makes the iron and scale of Drakyssian power. Its forge-cities surround volcanic vents, magma chambers, geothermal fields and controlled Dragonfire furnaces, and its smiths combine mortal metallurgy with draconic heat tolerance and magical material science. Its greatest workshops forge components no ordinary smithy can heat.
Forges: dragon-forged weapons · scale armor · Wyvern rider equipment · drake armor · siege weapons · fortress gates · Aether-resistant chains · military tools · Dragonfire glass · heat-tempered steel · war platforms · specialized dragon barding.
The separation is deliberate and structural: Zhaeryn owns the ore. Rhaegyr owns the furnace. Drakhalis owns the final war stockpile. No single House holds the whole military production chain. The same forge network also produces farming tools, bridge components, waterworks, mining equipment, ship fittings, earthquake braces and ordinary civilian metal goods, indirectly supporting millions of non-dragons. Dreadvalis armies wear Rhaegyr steel.

Ore Becomes Empire in the Furnace.

8. House Eredan — The Harvest Scale
Formal title: House Eredan, Keepers of Herd and Harvest
Seat: Ered-Vaelor, the Granary Citadel · Heartland: The southern half of the Great Grass Sea
Charge: Food security, livestock, agriculture, dragon prey reserves, grain storage, ecological management, famine prevention
The least glamorous necessity of empire and perhaps the most important. Dragons consume enormous quantities of biological matter, and feeding Drakyssia through uncontrolled hunting would devastate the south. Eredan therefore manages immense livestock territories, breeding plains, grain reserves, fisheries, controlled hunting preserves and agricultural tributaries.
Manages: imperial grain reserves · dragon livestock herds · emergency food stores · agricultural treaties · ranch territories · hunting quotas · fishery protection · drought planning · famine relief · soil conservation · migration corridors · ecological carrying-capacity records.
During mobilization it supplies mobile herds and preserved stores to dragon armies. Its agricultural law also protects mortal populations from predatory overhunting: imperial dragons cannot simply descend on protected livestock and eat what they please, compensation law applies even to nobles, and a farmer whose cattle are legally requisitioned by a dragon army must be paid. A dragon who eats them without authorization may discover that being three hundred meters long does not exempt one from imperial taxation. In drought years Eredan buys northern grain from the Cold Granaries, and hates that it must.

Even Fire Must Eat.

9. House Ishkar — The Wellspring Wardens
Formal title: House Ishkar, Keepers of the Last Breath
Seat: Ish’Kael, the Reservoir Citadel · Heartland: Distributed holdings surrounding major Aether Wells
Charge: Aether conservation, Wellspring stewardship, Essence reservoirs (worked Wellspring sites, Cores in common speech, dragon-kept and let recharge), Dead Zone mapping, environmental recovery, magical rationing
No House better represents the reality of the modern south. Ishkar’s whole responsibility is what remains. The House monitors surviving Aether Wells, volcanic recharge systems, exhausted Wellsprings, environmental Essence flow, atmospheric Aether, Soul-plane stability and regions approaching metaphysical collapse. Its scholars include some of Drakyssia’s finest Wellspring specialists, environmental arcanists, Wyrm geomancers and Soul Crystal scholars.
Controls: The worked Cores and their keepers · how much may be pulled at each · rest for spent ground · Essence surveys · Dead Zone mapping · Hollow Wellspring records · stored Aether reserves · magical rationing during emergency · recovery projects · draconic population-impact assessment · licensing of Core keepers · continental depletion maps.
Its authority is unusual: even Great Houses can be ordered to reduce magical consumption if Ishkar proves a territory is approaching irreversible depletion, with final enforcement belonging to the throne. It closes exhausted mines, restricts nesting near fragile Wellsprings, restores damaged river systems, rotates high-consumption populations, maintains emergency reservoirs and identifies regions where magic must temporarily cease. The House is sometimes hated because it tells powerful people no. It is respected because the alternative is eventually having nothing left to argue over. It looks north at the Frozen Wells with an envy it never says aloud.

Spend Nothing the World Cannot Regrow.

10. House Akhazar — The Outer Wing
Formal title: House Akhazar, Keepers of Roads and Foreign Crowns
Seat: Akhazar Gate, the Continental Embassy-Fortress · Heartland: The southern edge of the Twilight March, between Drakyssia and the old Five River country
Charge: Tributary administration, diplomacy, frontier law, protectorates, Dragon Roads, intelligence, relations with non-draconic peoples
Akhazar governs Drakyssia’s relationship with everyone who is not Drakyssian. Its members are diplomats, frontier commanders, interpreters, intelligence officers, treaty scholars, governors, road wardens and imperial representatives.
Where Avarax handles commerce, Akhazar handles sovereignty, and the distinction is carefully kept. Avarax can negotiate the price of grain. Akhazar negotiates whether the kingdom selling that grain owes military passage to Drakyssia.
Oversees: tributary kingdoms · protectorate agreements · human-draconic diplomacy · Elven treaties · imperial embassies · border law · Dragon Road permissions · foreign intelligence · territorial arbitration · refugee corridors · frontier forts · imperial census of subject territories.
Akhazar lets the empire rule without occupying every mortal settlement, translating imperial authority into treaties, obligations, taxes, protections, borders and enforceable law. Its treaty courts give human and Elven states a formal mechanism to challenge territorial violations by lesser dragon lords. Drakyssia is no more egalitarian for it, only administratively functional. Fear can conquer a kingdom; it cannot efficiently govern one for seven thousand years. Since the Taken Winter the House has also handled the empire’s most delicate relationship, with Morvayne’s Ledger Courts across the March.

An Empire Ends Where Its Word Cannot Travel.

The Imperial Charges




























































Great HouseImperial ChargePrincipal Continental FunctionDrakhalisSovereigntyKeeps the empire politically unifiedDovarynSkyLargest Wyvern host and swiftest reinforcementZhaerynWealthGold, gemstones, precious metals, imperial reservesAvaraxTradeConnects Drakyssia to the Outer World and wider ContinuumMaelkarContinuityEggs, hatchlings, Dens, hibernating elders, bloodlinesOrmyrDepthTunnels, aquifers, Wyrmdeep works, seismic securityRhaegyrForgeWeapons, armor, ironwork, forge-work for warEredanSustenanceFeeds dragons and mortals, prevents ecological collapseIshkarAetherProtects Wellsprings, manages continental depletionAkhazarDominionTreaties, tributaries, roads, frontiers, foreign relations
Drakyssian children learn these as the Ten Necessities: Throne. Wing. Gold. Trade. Egg. Depth. Forge. Harvest. Aether. Road.
Why the Houses Cannot Simply Rebel
Several of the Ten could individually destroy mortal kingdoms. Dovaryn could put thousands of Wyverns in the sky. Zhaeryn could purchase armies. Rhaegyr commands the war-forges. Maelkar holds the Dens, essential to the future of dragonkind. Ishkar can restrict Aether reserves whole territories depend on.
Yet the system was built so that specialization creates dependence. Dovaryn can field the Wyverns, but Eredan feeds them, Rhaegyr arms their riders, Zhaeryn finances prolonged mobilization, Ishkar determines where enough Aether exists to sustain deployment, Ormyr maintains the works beneath their roosts, Avarax supplies foreign materials, Maelkar maintains breeding populations, Akhazar keeps supply routes through tributary territory open, and Drakhalis coordinates all of it.
A House rebelling against the throne therefore risks frozen money, closed trade, restricted Aether, eggs removed from imperial protection, sealed supply roads, terminated forge contracts, stopped food shipments, and neighboring Houses authorized to occupy its territory. Kain Drakhalis built the mature system around one understanding of dragon psychology: a dragon can be powerful enough to fight everyone, and still cannot forge, feed, mine, breed and govern everything alone.
The Council of Ten Wings
Beneath the War-Wing Synod sits a more political assembly. Each Great House holds one principal seat; House Drakhalis presides. The Council handles matters touching multiple Imperial Charges: a proposed gold mine near a surviving Wellspring might involve Zhaeryn for the ore, Ishkar for the Wellspring, Ormyr for the geology, Rhaegyr for strategic value, Avarax for export, Akhazar if the mine lies beneath a tributary kingdom, and ultimately Drakhalis if the Houses cannot agree.
On an Aether-depleted continent, this restraint is plain survival.
The Houses and Their Half
Drakyssia’s claim over half of the Outer World is administered not as one continuous province but as overlapping systems of authority. Dovaryn holds much of the sky. Ormyr influences the depths. Akhazar maintains roads and political borders. Avarax connects markets and ports. Ishkar protects the remaining Aether geography. Eredan holds the food-producing landscapes. Zhaeryn manages mineral territories. Maelkar protects the future population of dragonkind. Rhaegyr turns continental resources into iron and works. Drakhalis gives all of it one sovereign direction.
The empire is less a single color painted across a map than a web laid over the continent. A human farmer in the southern Grass Sea might live beneath a Valecar king, sell livestock through an Avarax-chartered merchant, receive Eredan agricultural protection, travel an Akhazar-recognized road, watch Dovaryn Wyverns overhead, use Rhaegyr iron tools, and never meet a representative of House Drakhalis. Every one of those systems still leads back to Kra’Vorrak.
The Balance of the Ten Wings
Call the Ten anything but friends: allies, rivals, relatives, competitors, creditors, political enemies, military partners, and occasionally ancient grudges wearing ceremonial robes.
Zhaeryn and Avarax dispute mineral export prices. Dovaryn demands a greater war-chest from the gold reserves. Eredan complains that Dovaryn’s expanding Wyvern populations consume too much livestock. Maelkar opposes breeding lines that prioritize military traits over bloodline health. Ishkar restricts Rhaegyr’s geothermal Aether when forge consumption runs excessive. Ormyr accuses Zhaeryn mines of destabilizing deep strata. Akhazar objects when aggressive Houses threaten agreements with mortal kingdoms. And House Drakhalis listens to all of them.
The friction is intentional. Drakyssia does not expect dragons to stop being proud, territorial and ambitious; its political system tries to make those instincts useful. Competition produces stronger Wyverns. Rivalry produces better metallurgy. Pride produces better cities. Greed uncovers new deposits. Prestige keeps roads, hatcheries, reservoirs and armies worthy of the Names attached to them. The throne’s purpose is not to eliminate the instincts but to ensure they serve Drakyssia before they destroy it.
Among mortals: Drakhalis gives the command. Dovaryn brings the wings. Zhaeryn brings the gold. Avarax opens the market. Maelkar guards the egg. Ormyr knows what lies below. Rhaegyr lights the forge. Eredan fills the table. Ishkar saves what magic remains. Akhazar carries the word beyond the mountain.
Among dragons the phrase is shorter:

Ten Wings. One Sky. One Throne.


See also: Avo’Kan · The Archonic Codex · The Geography of the Outer World · Draconic Kind.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: Sancta Lux
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
The Hand That Casts Judgment · Standing, the Oracle, the Works, the Host

A scale is not adored. A scale is consulted. The man who kneels to a measure has already agreed to be lied to.
Opening clause, the Catechism of Equal Breath

In the wool town of Aldermere, on a market day in the last years of the Long Reckoning, the Chandlers’ Guild brought the widow Ibb Corbel before an Ember Magistrate (one of the order’s circuit judges) for selling short-weight candles. Magistrate Ysane Ambrel set up where she always did, under the striped awnings of the fish stalls, a gold lamp and an azure one burning on a trestle in broad daylight, with half the county on the benches. The chandlers’ wardens came in a body in their scarlet and beeswax-yellow, with their banner, because they had paid the fee and meant to enjoy it. The widow came in her one good dress, the color of new butter. Guildmaster Wymond Wick stated the complaint at length and sat down, and Ambrel called him straight back up, because under the rule of the order the accuser is read against the same reference as the accused, in the same session, in front of the same lamps. Most of the crowd had never seen a mirror trial. They started laughing before the chandlers understood. Her Measurewright took the reading without a flicker of interest, her Lector rendered it, and it came out that the widow’s candles ran a sixteenth light, and that the Aldermere guild’s own weights, against which every pound of wax in the vale had been bought for forty years, had been filed down one grain in the pound, by order, in the hand of three successive masters. The widow paid a fine of a few coppers. Wymond Wick and ten wardens put their right hands on the fish block at noon, in scarlet, with the banner still up. No guild in that county has brought the order a complaint from that day to this, and the Corbels are still making candles at full weight, and nobody in Aldermere will buy any others.
Keep that fish block in mind when the rest of this entry starts to sound like a chancery shelf. Everything below ends there.
What the Order Is
Sancta Lux does not worship, and says so in the first line of its own catechism, before it says anything else at all. This is the single most misunderstood fact about the order and the one its Lectors are most exhausted by. Shrine cultures across four worlds describe Sancta Lux as a church, its members as priests, and Urion as a god who hears them. The order permits the error in the street and strikes it from every filing that carries a seal.

What Sancta Lux is, in its own language, is a chartered body of measurement and consequence. It holds that the Archons and the Titans are the only orders of being above mortal accounting, and it declines to call either of them gods.
An Archon is a crowned principle. A Titan is a load-bearing law. Neither wants anything, and prayer presumes wanting.
“Urion is not a listener. He is a reference.” You do not petition a reference. You compare yourself against it and you accept the number that comes back.

Common mortal usage renders that reference as the Judger. Every Attestant is taught the word on their first day and taught to strike it on their second, and every one of them keeps using it anyway, because a thirty-year career of saying the standing reference in casual conversation defeats even Concordia formalism.





















TypeChartered arbitration body and standing enforcement order. Guild Accord member with permanent standing in both the Enforcement Division and the Arbitration DivisionReferenceUrion, Archon of Balance. Judicaris, the Order Magic of measured force and lawful arbitrationTitanic GroundDazkar, the Arbiter of Purganeth, from whose law the Archonic principle descendsCommon NamesThe Hand That Casts Judgment · The Gravel of Judger · The Scale
Founding: Two Accounts, One of Which Is True
The received account
By the order’s own reckoning, which no Guild surveyor will put on the count, Sancta Lux was founded during the Great Spirit War by Sadara Izayoi, who claimed a direct reading from the Scale and vowed to enact its correction across every realm that would receive her and several that would not. She is remembered as the First Hand.
Beneath her, the first martial wing took shape under Lucius, recorded as First Grand Paladin: a plague-cleanser who purified the survivors at Veyr Chapel at seventeen without burning them alive, and who summoned seven luminous eidolons at twenty and went blind for three days for the privilege. Lucius called on Faisal’s Numen to do it, which matters later and matters enormously. Epsilon, longest-lived Grand Archmagus in the order’s history, codified the glyphwork.
The Accord’s charter recognizes this lineage. The Grand Church’s floor is inlaid with it.

Every part of that account is documented. None of it describes the order that exists today.

The author
What people mean when they say Sancta Lux in the current era is a specific apparatus: the Ladder of Standing, the separation of reading from finding and finding from sentence, the Measurewright’s oath, the annual posting of false-positive rates, and the doctrine that no clause may be enforced beyond the scope it names.
That architecture is thirty-five years old. It was written by one man between the ages of twenty-six and thirty-five, and he is still alive, and he is not the founder in any document the order has ever filed.

Darius Ignatius Sanctus Sanctorum led four hundred Sanctified Legionaries through the outer gate of the Eclipse Bastion on a correct reading made at the wrong time. The gate held them for nine minutes. He stood at the threshold with the Scale open, understood that intervention would spend more lives than it saved, and did nothing that could be called an act.
What he came out of that gate carrying was a structural conclusion: revelation is not a method. Sadara had a revelation and it produced a war-cult with six schisms and no procedure for being wrong. Four hundred men burned inside a doctrine that had never once told anyone what to do when the reading and the moment disagreed.

So he wrote the procedure. He wrote it slowly, in the recalcitrant, unornamented Concordia register he speaks in, and the order absorbed it the way a body absorbs a splint, and then, being an institution, it did what institutions do. It backdated the law to Sadara.

Because an order that can name the decade its doctrine was written must also concede the doctrine could be rewritten, and an order that concedes that cannot execute anyone.

Darius has never corrected the record. Three Accord tribunals have put the question to him directly. All three times he answered a different question, accurately, at length, and without visible feeling. The Arbitration Division’s private position is that the founding attribution is a known falsehood maintained for institutional load-bearing reasons, that it is the single largest unweighed act inside Sancta Lux, and that the only person with standing to weigh it is its beneficiary.

“I am not here to forgive you. I am here to tell you what you did.”
Attributed to Darius, and written on the reverse of every Measurewright’s writ

The Oracle of the Judger
The Oracle is an instrument. It sees no future, has no voice, and has never once produced a sentence in any mortal language. Sancta Lux is extremely clear about this internally and does nothing whatsoever to clarify it externally, because a public that believes the order consults a voice is a public that does not ask who does the interpreting.
What it is
Every authored structure in existence emits an architectural spectrum: an oath, a working, a Domain, a lie, a killing, a marriage, a treaty. Judicium reads that spectrum. Reading it means nothing on its own. A spectrum is only information when compared against something that does not drift, and the whole problem of judgment across four worlds and sixty Wellsprings is that everything drifts. Every mortal standard bends toward the hand that holds it.

The Oracle is the thing that does not bend. On filings it is written Sel-Ur, from the root glyphs of Measure and Balance. The Measurewrights who work in front of it call it the Unmoved Measure when they are being precise and the Old Woman when they are not.
It occupies the whole of the Hall of Equal Breath: a low, warm, flame-lit room with no windows, a floor of unpolished gray stone, and two standing lamps at the far ends, one burning gold, one burning azure, held in a fixed rotational relation that has not varied by a measurable degree in nine hundred years.
Between the lamps hangs the assembly itself, which nobody has managed to call a statue or a machine, and which nobody who has stood in front of it describes the same way twice.

A Measurewright brings a reading into the Hall. The Oracle returns weight. Guilt, corruption, alignment and intent are no part of what comes back. It returns mass, and a Lector converts that mass into a finding, and an Arbiter converts the finding into a sentence, and somebody in harness carries the sentence out into the world and kills a person with it.
The order’s only honest claim

Sancta Lux asserts, and no rival body has successfully disputed, that the Oracle has never been wrong.
This is true and it is worthless. The Oracle has never been wrong because the Oracle has never made a claim.
Every atrocity in the order’s history, eleven centuries of it as the order counts, lives in the two conversions between the reading and the corpse, and every one of them was committed by somebody who had passed an examination.

The Seventh Objection
How Sancta Lux knows about Hataraki.
The Oracle returns weight in a grammar. Sancta Lux expected that grammar to be one word wide.
Balance is the order’s whole subject. Urion is the Balancer, the Scale is the instrument, Baransu no Shigoto is the labor of measure and proportion, and a body founded on a single Archonic principle reasonably expects its instrument to speak in that principle and no other.

What Sel-Ur actually returns is a reading sorted into seven categories, and Balance is only one of them. The others are Ruin, Purity, Spirit, Temporality, Knowledge, and Totality.
Those are the Works.

Hametsu no Gō, which clears what must end. The labor of Purity, which establishes what must remain. Spirit, which governs passage between states of being. Jikan no Shigoto, which arranges sequence. Knowledge, which reveals what a thing is. Balance, which reconciles.
And Zentai-sei no Hataraki, the Work of Totality, which gathers all of them into one architecture, which the Oracle invokes roughly once in nine thousand readings, and which every Measurewright who has ever seen it invoked has requested reassignment within the year.
Epsilon’s conclusion
Epsilon cataloged the pattern across three centuries of readings and reached the conclusion the order has been managing ever since. The Works predate Archonic personhood. Bara authored them inside the Plane of Fate before chronology existed, and the Archons rose later as sovereign crowned expressions of meanings the Works already held in their barest operative form.

The floor belongs to something older than Urion. He is one crowned idea standing on a labor older than his name, and Sancta Lux’s instrument reads the whole floor because the floor is what the instrument was calibrated against, and the order has been calling the floor by the name of one of its tiles for eleven hundred years.

The finding is sealed. Internally it is called the Seventh Objection, after the seventh grammatical category the Oracle returns and the order does not teach. Standing above Lector is required to know it exists. Standing at the Sealed Standard is required to read it.
Its practical consequence is that Sancta Lux is the only mortal institution in the four worlds with a continuous empirical record of Hataraki operating, and it has spent three centuries suppressing that record, because publishing it would concede that six equally primordial labors exist over which the order holds no authority at all, and that its own authority is derivative, inherited, and one tile wide.
Darius has read the Seventh Objection. He is one of three living holders of the Sealed Standard. What he has decided to do about it is the thing his own record notes he has chosen and told nobody, and which he believes will justify a fifth fracture in a Soul Crystal that will not survive one.
The Ladder of Standing
Rank inside Sancta Lux describes what a member is permitted to do to a reading, and says nothing about command, and it is the single most jealously enforced structure in the order.

The entire post-Bastion architecture rests on one principle: no one person may take a reading, interpret it, and act on it.
Darius did all three at the Eclipse Bastion. He was correct. Four hundred men burned.
The Ladder exists so that nobody is ever again permitted to be that correct alone.














































StandingMayTemperanceI · AttestantWitness. May not weigh. Trained in transcription method taken wholesale from Bellwrought Celestial practice and taught, with a straight face, that the method is their own tradition. They may stand in the Hall of Equal Breath. They may not speak in itI – IIIII · MeasurewrightTake a reading. May not interpret one. The order’s largest grade and its most fatalistic. Drilled until the separation between observation and meaning is somatic rather than intellectual, and the drill costs most of them the capacity for casual conversation. The grade borrows the Guild’s word and holds none of the Guild’s office: an order Measurewright reads and keeps silent, where a Guild Measurewright keeps the world’s tables and argues about themIII – VIII · LectorRender a reading into a finding. The first grade permitted to say what something means. Also the first grade permitted to be wrong in a way that reaches a bodyV – VIIIV · ArbiterConvert a finding into a sentence. Splits at investiture into Arbiter-Militant, seconded to Enforcement, and Arbiter-Lector, seconded to Arbitration. The two halves are institutionally required to disagree, and do, loudly, in a chamber built for the purposeVII – IXV · Archpaladin · Grand ArchmagusDeliver sentence at Domain scale. Open a Threshold case on another member. Fewer than thirty living across four worldsX and aboveVI · The Word · The WillThe two seats. Doctrinal supremacy and martial supremacy, each holding one vote and each capable of vetoing the other exactly once per convocation—VII · The Sealed StandardAmend the reference itself. Three living holders. The order does not publish their names and has never confirmed the number—
Lateral offices
Standing on the Ladder is not the same as office. Three bodies sit across the rungs rather than on them, and all three are resented by the grades they cut through.
The Inquisitors carry Judica rites etched directly into their gauntlets and may pronounce sentence in the field without an Arbiter present, a suspension of the entire post-Bastion architecture, authorized for exactly that reason.
The Ember Magistrates ride a permanent circuit through Accord territory holding flame-lit equilibrium courts in towns that will never see the Grand Church. They are the only face most people ever put to the order.
The Mask, of which there is only ever one, holds a relic forged for Censure and suppresses invocation simply by being in the room. Deployed against practitioners the order has decided should not be permitted to argue.
The Two Seats
The Word of Judger holds doctrinal authority. Epsilon held the seat longer than any figure in the order’s history and used it, for most of that tenure, to keep the Seventh Objection sealed.

The Will of Judger is martial supremacy, and it is currently held by a man who refuses to be invested in it.
Darius answers to Archpaladin, signs as Archpaladin, and is addressed as Archpaladin by everyone below the Sealed Standard, because the Will’s seat carries a vote and he has never cast one.
The order’s official position is that the investiture is pending. It has been pending for eleven years. Nobody has demanded why, which is itself a finding, and which Arbitration has weighed twice and filed both times without action.

What Sancta Lux Is Standing In For
This is the part of the entry the order would most prefer nobody assembled.
The work Sancta Lux does began as other than mortal work. Verdicts were spoken by Celestials Sung out of the Lawbell for the purpose, in a Choir structure that predates every mortal institution now claiming jurisdiction over anything.
A Celestial carries Vow-Light as a substrate of its Aether: a heavy, warm-pressure radiance under which spoken falsehood becomes physically effortful, a laboring breath, a tightening throat, a headache that scales with the size of the untruth. Vow-Light detects nothing. It makes lying cost something, reliably, in every mortal and every tongue, without examination, without a Ladder, and without the possibility of an Arbiter having a bad morning.
Then Malakar cracked the Lawbell, Grand Angel Faisal went to kneel under its weight at the edge of creation, the Host went from thousands to credible sightings in the low dozens across seven centuries by the Host’s own reckoning, and no Celestial has been confirmed Sung since.

What is left of the apparatus that used to hold the world’s oaths is a mortal order with a procedure book.
Sancta Lux is a prosthetic. The Glyph of Veridiction is a deliberate mortal imitation of Vow-Light, and it is worse in every measurable respect. It makes lying costly instead of impossible. It has a false-positive rate.
The order posts that rate annually, in full, in a fair-copied roll nobody outside Arbitration has requested in eleven years, and Darius wrote the requirement to post it into the architecture himself, over the Word’s objection, on the stated ground that an instrument which conceals its own error rate is not an instrument but a weapon with a good reputation.

The lineage is concrete. Lucius called on Faisal’s Numen to raise the seven eidolons that made the order’s name, which means Sancta Lux’s founding martial miracle was performed on borrowed Celestial architecture from a being who now kneels at the edge of creation and has not stood up since.
The order’s standing interest in reaching him, in every claim to have heard Faisal at the edge, is the largest non-public program it runs, larger than its entire Wellspring holdings enforcement arm, resourced disproportionately for reasons its own internal memoranda describe only as structural and decline to elaborate.

The Guild Accord tracks the same claims with the same disproportionate resourcing and the same refusal to elaborate.
Neither institution has told the other everything it knows, and both are aware of this, and both have decided the arrangement is currently preferable to the alternative.

Practice

Wellsprings Anamnesis, Exuroth, Fixatio, Ignivale, Judicium, Lethegraal, Mirithane, Petralon, Thaloré. The Scale’s attested nine. Judicium and Fixatio are the working core; Ignivale supplies the collapse from finding into execution; Thaloré is the one most chapters neglect and the one the Ember Magistrates say separates an arbitrator from an executioner.
Root glyphs [Ur] Balance · [Sel] Measure · [Va] Law · [Hael] Flame
Working set [Krn] Crown · [IrW] Will · [Ar] Accord · [Edt] Edict · [Flm] Judic Flame · [Ed] Edgetruth · [Exile] Exile
Arts Spirit Sealing, Spirit Rune, Spirit Summoning, Sage. The Glyphs of Absolution, Veridiction and Judgment are the order’s three examined workings, and no member advances past Measurewright without all three.
Manifesti Judica, Dictum, Decretum, Censure, Mandatum. Expunction is held under the Verdiction Codex and has been lawfully invoked four times in eleven centuries, once in living memory, in the Trial of the Echoless, against its own.


Mirror trials. The accuser is read against the same reference as the accused, in the same session, in front of the same lamps.
Mirror trials are the reason the order is hated by every guild that has ever brought it a complaint.

The order’s Measurewrights maintain open Threshold cases on any member whose Stage progression and Level accumulation diverge, which is why they have an open case on Darius that has sat unresolved for eleven years.
Holdings
The Grand Church of Sancta Lux stands in the Kingdom of Altherion, a multiracial republic with an Essence Resource Sharing Act and a Trade Equality Act specifically drafted to prevent any single body from monopolizing Wellspring access, which in common speech means the Cores, the worked Wellspring sites and the keepers who can close them.
Seating an order of universal jurisdiction inside a republic constitutionally opposed to universal jurisdiction was Darius’s decision, made in the fourth year of the rebuild, and it is the single most argued-over choice in the order’s modern history. His stated reasoning ran to one sentence: a court that cannot be evicted is not a court.
A permanent legation sits at the Concord Citadel, staffed at Arbiter grade, adjacent to the Archives Eternal and pointedly not inside them. Chapter holds operate in Eresse and in Foraye.

The Hall of Equal Breath is in none of these places.
Sel-Ur is housed at Meridian Hold, whose location does not appear in any Accord filing, whose garrison is drawn exclusively from Measurewrights who have taken a second oath, and which the order describes in public documents as a training facility.

Strengths and Limits
What it does well
Martial and doctrinal wings designed together and fighting together, rather than two traditions bolted into one charter.
Extensive Wellspring rights and tax exemption under Accord law.
Procedural discipline that survives the death of any individual member, which is the entire point of it.
An instrument that does not drift, which no rival body possesses and several have tried and failed to build.
Where it breaks
Its doctrine is legible, which means it is gameable. Cozbi Mahuo’s numbered works return no reading at all: the Oracle weighs completed acts against a standard, and a thing that has never acted and carries no closed clause presents nothing to weigh. The order has known about this seam for a decade and has no answer that does not require amending the reference.
Its recovery is ground-dependent. Away from consecrated stone the active-recovery advantage collapses toward passive, and long engagements become lethal, which every serious opponent above Stage IX now knows and plans around.
Contradictory law stalls it. Kaisic Essence enforces and leaves adjudication to others; it cannot choose between two enforceable clauses. Present an Arbiter with two valid findings pointing opposite directions and the output stops dead, with no slowing first, and at the scale these people operate at, a stopped moment is a fatal one.
And the Seventh Objection is sitting in a sealed vault at Meridian Hold with three living readers, one of whom has stopped sleeping.
Relations and Reputation
Sancta Lux holds no long-standing alliance outside Accord membership and has never sought one, on the doctrinal ground that an ally is a party you have agreed in advance not to weigh.
Its relationship with the secular Accord guilds is procedurally correct and personally poisonous. Free-magic cultures regard it as a zealot body, which is unfair, and as an unaccountable one, which is not. The elven kingdoms tolerate the Eresse hold on sufferance and audit it annually. Vaelen Mourcrix and Darius maintain a professional relationship best described as adversarial affection: Vaelen weighs, Darius executes, and neither approves of the other’s half of the work.

The Gravel of Judger, in the mouths of the people it has ruled against. The Hand That Casts Judgment, in the mouths of the faithful, who are numerous and who have almost all of the theology wrong. Among the Ember Magistrates’ circuit towns the order has a third name that appears in no filing and that its officers pretend not to have heard: the Weighing Men.
Nobody in four worlds has ever accused Sancta Lux of taking a bribe. Everyone in four worlds has an opinion about what it did instead.
