factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: Sōhai — The Whole Bow
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Sōhai · The True High Religion of the Okuchi
The Unsingled Crown · The Fourteen Labors · The Charge Against the Scale · What Crossed the Water
A doctrinal entry, compiled from house registers and from what the Church declines to file
Ice-out at Harlsey Landing is the morning the river breaks, and the whole north bank comes down to the pier in its best reds and blues to see the ration scale inspected in public, as it has been since anybody’s grandmother. In the spring of Year 688 an Ember Magistrate of Sancta Lux named Perrin Dunstable, riding his first circuit so far north, set his gold and azure lamps at the end of that pier, tried the scale, pronounced it true under Urion’s reference, and began writing the town’s custom into his circuit-roll, which is to say, in all innocence, claiming it. A salt-wife named Oddny Stackwell, four foot eleven and smelling powerfully of herring, who could not have named an Archon at knifepoint, asked him how his stack was. He asked her what she meant. She told him that a man who weighs and never squares a corner, says a dead name, feeds a dog or sings with anybody is a man with a job, and she invited him to do the other thirteen, there on the pier, since he had come all this way. To his great credit he tried. He fed the dog. He told a poor lie about a bishop, and they received it seriously. But by the time he reached the Moving, four hundred people had begun helping him with it, and his trestle, his roll-chest and both his lamps set off along the pier hand over hand, and at the Discard somebody burned the circuit-roll, and then the herring started. Seventeen noses were broken. The azure lamp went into the river, and a writ against Harlsey Landing still stands in the Magistrates’ books that no Magistrate has since volunteered to serve. Oddny Stackwell went home and salted pork. The Moto registers at Kharven-Seat enter that morning as the only successful public disputation on the Charge Against the Scale in the history of the question, and she would have been insulted to hear it.
What follows is the doctrine she held without knowing it had a name.
I. THE NAME AND THE GROUND
The land. The Moto call the body of the world as it stood before Malakar’s first blow broke the white shelf the Okuchi, the deep interior, the land behind. (Their registers call that blow the split and count the whole breaking as one event with a long middle; the Concordance’s later reckoning sets the blow near Year 310.) Every other people in the four quarters that troubles to name that country has named it after the disaster that ended it. The Zettari call it the First World, which is a forge-culture’s way of saying the one we can no longer reforge. The Marrowkin registers have no name for it at all and treat the question as unserious. The Moto name is the only one that does not describe an ending, and the reason is doctrinal. A thing that has been read correctly still stands in its place. It is behind you, and behind is a direction, and a direction can be faced.
The religion. Sōhai, the Whole Bow. Rendered in Concord common as the True High Religion, which is a translation the house tolerates and did not choose, because true and high are both comparative and the Sōhai’s entire position is that comparison is the error.
The endonym contains the doctrine. Sō, the whole, entire, without remainder. Hai, the bow, the acknowledgment made with the body. It is neither prayer nor petition. A bow is what you give a sovereign whose authority does not depend on your opinion of it, and you give it whether or not the sovereign is looking, and you give it to all fourteen or you have not given it.
II. WHAT THE SŌHAI HOLDS
The Fourteen are crowned. The Works are older. Both are true and the order matters.
Bara, whom the Archonic registers record as Bairos, authored the Works within the Plane of Fate before chronology: Ruin, Purity, Spirit, Temporality, Knowledge, Balance, Totality. The Works are the operative meanings at their barest. The Archons are those same meanings after they rose into sovereignty and were crowned. A Work is what a thing does. An Archon is that doing, enthroned, administered, and answerable.
From this the Sōhai derives its single load-bearing claim.
The Doctrine of the Unsingled Crown. No Archon may be addressed alone, because no Archon operates alone. Urion measures and Maelor records and Iesara reveals, and the Triad of Law functions only as three. Elyndra’s growth requires Auren’s endings or it becomes the Plague of the Living Flesh. Wyther’s motion without Maelor’s record is amnesia at civilizational scale. Uurgath’s entropy is the pressure that keeps the other thirteen honest, and a cosmos without him would freeze into an unchangeable perfection that is a subtler death than his. The lattice has no chief, as a pantheon has. It is fourteen sovereigns each of whom prevents the other thirteen from consuming reality, and the prevention runs in every direction at once.
Therefore: to petition one Archon is to assert that its principle can function without the others. That assertion is false about the lattice, and a false statement made in the posture of devotion is the specific thing the Sōhai calls blasphemy. The offense is inaccuracy, and the house has never dressed it up as anything grander.
The house arrived at this by four thousand years of reading rather than by piety, during which it observed what happens to a polity that elevates one meaning above the rest, and it observed this on itself first. (Four thousand is the house’s own figure. The Guild’s count of reckoned history is a good deal shorter, and the house’s registers, which cite no Age, have never troubled to argue with it.)
III. PRAISE IS LABOR
Hataraki means the Works, and it also means labor, and the Sōhai denies that this is a pun.
Fate, to the Sōhai, has nothing to do with prediction. Fate is work: the continuous assigning, preserving, undoing, measuring and completing of the roles of all things. If the Archons are the sovereigns of that labor, then the only coherent praise is to perform labor of the same kind. The Sōhai therefore recognizes two acts and no third.
The Bow. Acknowledgment. Performed with the body, silent, and directed at all fourteen in sequence. It contains no request. A Sōhai practitioner who asks an Archon for something has stopped practicing and started bargaining, and the house has a word for that.
The Work. A concrete act performed in the character of one Archon’s principle, performed daily, performed by hands. This is where the religion actually lives, and it is why a Kharven household can be observant without anyone in it being able to name a single Archon.
The Fourteen Labors
Assigned in the order of emergence. Every household is held to all fourteen. Most perform eleven without knowing they are performing anything.
















































































ArchonPrincipleThe LaborUrionBalanceThe Weighing. One thing weighed on a true balance each day. In Kharven this is the ration, and the scale is inspected publicly at Ice-out.UurgathDisruptionThe Discard. One thing destroyed that could have been kept. The broken haft is burned instead of hoarded. Refusing to let a finished thing continue is the labor.ThalenFormThe Squaring. A corner checked. A wall, a door, a stack. How’s your stack is Thalen’s labor worn down to a greeting, and no northern clansman alive knows that.ValenTimeThe Order. Things done in their sequence and recorded in it. At the Reading, the names go in the order they died, and to read them alphabetically would be a desecration nobody could articulate.MaelorMemoryThe Telling. One dead person’s name said aloud daily, in a room, to someone.ZhaerenSpaceThe Walking. A boundary walked, a marker righted, a road kept passable one span further than your own need requires.IrathDominionThe Command. One order given and one order taken, each day, both plainly. A man who only gives has failed the labor as completely as a man who only takes.VeyraDesireThe Unnecessary. One thing made that serves no function. A carving on a bootjack. A dye nobody needed. The Sōhai holds a house with no ornament in it to be in a state of quiet sin.IesaraInsightThe Looking. One assumption opened and checked. The barrel you believed was full. The granary floor you have never stood on.KaetraDreamThe Telling of the False. A story told that everyone present knows is untrue, told well and received seriously. Children’s tales discharge the labor. So does a lie everybody has agreed to.WytherMotionThe Moving. Nothing stands a full year where it stood. Furniture, herds, the position of the woodpile. Stagnation is the offense.AurenDeathThe Waiting. Sitting with the dead. Kharven’s whole winter institution is Auren’s labor performed at national scale by a people who think they are being practical.SelharHarmonyThe Tuning. Voices matched to another voice. Singing with, never at. A household that cannot sing together is diagnosed, never scolded.ElyndraLifeThe Feeding. Something fed that is not yourself and cannot repay it.
The consequence for daily life and for governance: the Sōhai has no congregation, no clergy in the ordinary sense, and no building. It has households, and the household is the unit of observance, and a kingdom’s piety is measurable by walking into its kitchens. This is why the Moto have never built a temple and have never understood why anybody else does.
IV. THE RITE, THE HOUSE, AND THE HAND
The Bow. Fourteen inclinations, performed in emergence order, at the hinge of the day. In the Okuchi each was given its own station, its own hour, and its own resident house, and the full observance occupied a working day. In Kharven it is performed by one person in a cold room in under two minutes, and the fourteen stations are fourteen scratches cut into a doorpost, and everyone who cuts them believes they are counting something.
The Hand. Each Archon reads the Parunic lattice from a different station, and each station produces a different hand. Sōhai scribes write an Archon’s material in that Archon’s hand and in no other, and a document written in the wrong hand is void rather than incorrect. The fourteen daughter scripts are therefore liturgical objects as much as they are notation, and the surviving Moto material in Kharven is written across all fourteen, which is one of the reasons the Crown’s own archive is unreadable to Concord clerks.
The Reading. The house’s central sacrament and the origin of everything else. Determination of what a thing is, what it owes, and what it will become. In the Okuchi it was applied to persons at birth and, by way of the Covenant Scar, placed into the body. What the Sōhai teaches now is the doctrine’s stripped remainder: a thing read correctly has been given its Work, and a thing that has been given its Work has been praised.
The Queen’s Saishiki. The binding liturgy that made an oath structural instead of verbal. It attached to the Bow and the Reading both, and it is gone, and this is the practical condition of the religion in Kharven: the observance survives and the binding does not.
V. THE CHARGE AGAINST THE SCALE
This is the section every Sancta Lux Lector has read and every one of them has an answer to. Both parties are recorded here as they state themselves, because the argument is genuine and neither side is being stupid.
The Sōhai’s charge
Sancta Lux maintains one reference, one instrument, one consecrated ground, one Archonic magic in its charter, one seat, and thirteen appendices. It measures every act in four worlds against Urion and against nothing else. It calls the other thirteen Archons real, and it has never once weighed a man against Selhar, and it has no procedure by which it could.
The Sōhai’s word for this is Singling, and the charge is that the Scale is the largest and best-documented Singling in the history of the Realms. Idolatry requires an idol, and this is something colder. An institutional decision that one of fourteen sovereigns is sufficient, maintained across four thousand years, with paperwork.
The Sōhai grants freely that the order does not kneel. That is precisely the charge. A body that consults one reference exclusively for four millennia has performed a devotion and has kept better records of it than any shrine culture ever managed. Kneeling would at least have been honest about what was happening. (The order’s own rolls run eleven centuries, as its Lectors say loudly at this point in every disputation. The Sōhai answers that the singling of Urion is older than the order that does it now. The Guild’s count declines to sign either figure.)
And the doctrinal consequence, which is the part that closes the argument for the Moto: the Scale cannot weigh what it has no station for. Cozbi Mahuo’s numbered works return no reading at all. The order has known about that seam for a decade and cannot answer it without amending the reference. The Sōhai reads that seam, where the order sees a flaw in the instrument, as the shape of the thirteen Archons the instrument was never built to consult.
Sancta Lux’s answer
Recorded here in the order’s own register, because it is not a weak answer.
We do not worship, so we cannot be accused of worshipping one. The first clause of the Catechism of Equal Breath is a refusal and it precedes everything else we have ever written. An Archon is a crowned principle. A Titan is a load-bearing law. Neither wants anything, and prayer presumes wanting. Urion is not a listener, he is a reference, and a reference is chosen for its stability and not for its supremacy. We did not elevate Balance above Memory. We selected the only one of the fourteen against which a measurement does not drift, because a court that drifts is not a court.
The Moto have mistaken a scale for an altar. That is an understandable error made by a house whose entire art is recognition, and which therefore assumes that everything which is consulted is being revered. We consult. We do not revere. The distinction is the whole of our charter and the Moto have never accepted it, because accepting it would concede that a thing can be authoritative without being ancestral.
Where the argument actually sits
The Sōhai says the Scale worships in practice and denies it in doctrine. Sancta Lux says the Sōhai reveres in doctrine and cannot demonstrate it in practice, since fourteen labors performed by a woman salting pork are indistinguishable from a woman salting pork.
Both descriptions are accurate. Neither is complete. No arbitration exists, and none can, because the only body with standing to arbitrate is one of the two parties.
VI. THE TENANCY
The white shelf is Alabaster.
The Moto held the western reach of the one body and the seat of the Long Reading stood on white stone, and the Holy Sea of Alabaster stands on that stone now. Its Wellspring is testimony. Its whole apparatus is built to weigh a sworn account. The Sōhai’s position, stated flatly and never once withdrawn, is that testimony is a Moto Work, that the Wellspring site under Alabaster is a residue of four thousand years of Reading performed on that ground, and that Sancta Lux’s chapter hold there is a tenant occupying a sacrament it did not author, filing reports northward to a Grand Church at Altherion that has never held the deed.
The Sōhai does not press the claim. It has not pressed it in four hundred years. Six lines crossed the water and arrived with their registers and their retainers and no standing at all, and a claim you cannot enforce is a claim you are better off not making out loud.
The Seventh Objection is sealed at Meridian Hold. It has three living readers. One of them has stopped sleeping.
VII. WHAT CROSSED THE WATER
The six lines carried what could be carried, over the water that the first blow let in behind the white shelf. Registers, retainers, the population they could move, and the Bow, which weighs nothing.
What did not cross: the fourteen resident houses at the white shelf, one to each station, each with its own hours and its own hand and its own eleven-hundred-year continuity of practitioners. The Kagura Branch seasonal rites, held whole at Alabaster and held in fragments now. The full-day observance, which required a settled people with a surplus and has never once been performed in the north because the north has never once had an afternoon to spare. The Reading’s liturgy, which the Queen carried and which the Queen took with her.
There are households in the Greenhollow that perform all fourteen labors correctly, in order, every day of their lives, and could not tell you the name of a single Archon, and would be insulted by the suggestion that they were doing anything other than keeping a house properly.
The Sōhai holds that these households are the most observant people in the four quarters and that the loss of the names is a grief and not a failure.
VIII. HERESIES AND FAILURE MODES
Singling. Elevation of one Archon. The principal heresy and the one the house watches for in itself, since the Kōkan favor Totality and Totality is the Work most easily mistaken for a crown.
Petition. Asking. Converts the Bow into a transaction and the Archon into a merchant.
The Empty Bow. Observance performed without the labor. The Sōhai considers this worse than neglect, on the grounds that a man who has stopped bowing has at least stopped lying.
Devouring Certainty. The corruption vector of Knowledge, listed in the house’s own training register beside the other six, written by people who had watched it happen at Alabaster and declined to name the century.

The Burning Mandate · Purifiers of the Scale · The Mask-Bearers

“The procedure is a leash. The Scale does not ask to be interpreted. It asks to be obeyed.”
Cassian Tiberius Cruor, Founding Declaration of the Ordo

The dyers’ town of Velmouth had a river that ran three colors below the vats, red from the madder yards, blue from the woad sheds and a loud yellow from the weld, and for forty-eight hours after a Circuit Justiciar read the Burning Mandate’s declaration in its square, it also had Gervase Reedfoot. The doctrine offers a town two choices, the mask or the pyre. Reedfoot, who ran untaxed pepper on a flat barge called the Second Wife and had never in his life paid a toll he could smell his way around, sold a third at a fair rate per head. He took them out by night under wet bolts of cloth, nine trips in two days past the masked pickets on the towpath, and two hundred and twelve people of Velmouth came ashore in the Marches stained to the elbows in whatever they had hidden under; you can still pick out their grandchildren at a fair by the jokes. On the third morning the Inquisition went through the town in order, street by street, gold filigree and red half-capes in the smoke, burning what resisted and collapsing what did not. The vats boiled over. The river ran purple for nine days and the fish came down it cooked. Then a masked clerk walked the ashes with a ledger, entering what had survived, and that ledger, which the Accord later took off a dead Justiciar, lists the Second Wife, her draught, her nine trips and the two hundred and twelve, by count, with the hours. They had watched every trip. Reedfoot was found seven months on, tied to his own mooring post, with the page nailed to his chest and his fares counted out beside him to the copper.
This is the fourth of the six incidents the Accord has confirmed. Heralds cry the writ against the Inquisition every quarter day, the bounty on the head of its leader has doubled twice, and no bookie in the four quarters will quote it. The page below gives them their ranks and their names.
What the Inquisition Is
The Holy Inquisition, Ordo Sanctae Inquisitionis in its own filings, stamped with the root glyph of Sancta Lux that the mother order no longer recognizes as authorized, is a splinter body that broke from Sancta Lux eleven years after Darius completed the post-Bastion architectural reforms. Its members call themselves the true inheritors of Sadara Izayoi’s mandate. Sancta Lux calls them apostates. The Guild Accord calls them a rogue militant organization. The civilizations they have burned through call them nothing at all, because the civilizations they have burned through no longer exist.
They number between two hundred eighty and four hundred at any given count, depending on whether the Accord is counting membership or bodies in the field. The roster is deliberately fluid. Recruitment follows purification campaigns: the survivors who choose the mask over the pyre join, and those who refuse both options are not offered a third.
The Accord has classified the Inquisition as an unlawful body and authorized enforcement action. That authorization has been standing for six years. The enforcement has not arrived, because the man who leads the Inquisition is a Stage XIII practitioner at Level 440, and the Accord does not possess enough Stage XIII practitioners to spend one on a fight that would cost them. That writ runs where the Accord’s circles have signed. Where the crowns and churches that back the Inquisition rule, it holds legal standing, and in that territory it enforces the Gate on who may learn magic.
The Doctrinal Split
The break came slowly, as a conclusion comes.
Sancta Lux under Darius holds that no one person may take a reading, interpret it, and act on it. The Ladder of Standing exists to distribute that authority across multiple hands, multiple grades, multiple examinations. Four hundred men burned at the Eclipse Bastion because Darius did all three alone and was correct. The lesson he drew from that was that correctness is not sufficient authorization.
The Holy Inquisition holds the inverse. Their lesson from the Eclipse Bastion is that four hundred men burned because the apparatus was too slow to save them. Darius stood at the threshold and chose procedure over intervention. He weighed the lives against the cost and found the cost exceeded the saving. He was right, and they were dead, and the rightness did not survive the burning.
Cassian Tiberius Cruor was not at the Eclipse Bastion. He was twenty years old when it happened and had never heard of it. He learned the story as doctrine, in the Attestant’s hall, from a Lector who taught it as a triumph of institutional discipline. Something in the telling did not land.
The split happened in the field. Cruor was a Measurewright, stationed at the Eresse chapter, and the reading he took, the one that broke him from the order, concerned a settlement that was being systematically emptied by a practitioner operating two Stages above anyone in Cruor’s detachment. The Ladder demanded he file the reading, wait for a Lector, wait for the finding, wait for an Arbiter, wait for authorization. The settlement would have been gone by the time the authorization cleared the second desk.
He did not wait. He killed the practitioner. He was correct. The settlement survived. Sancta Lux stripped his standing the following week.
The doctrine he wrote afterward, in a cell, before the tribunal that would exile him, runs to a single page, and every member of the Inquisition carries it on their person.
The Five Tenets of the Burning Mandate

I. The Scale Speaks Without Mediation. A reading does not require a Ladder. The truth is not improved by committee. It is not made safer by separation. It is made slower, and in the time it loses, the thing it was measuring has already killed again.
II. Ignorance Is Corruption Made Patient. Those who refuse the light of the Scale have not chosen neutrality. They have chosen rot. Rot is patient, and it spreads, and it does not stop when asked.
III. The Mortal World Requires Active Correction. The Scale does not wait for a filing. Neither may its servants. Where the reading identifies an imbalance, the correction follows in the same breath, by the same hand.
IV. Non-Belief Is a Structural Collapse. A civilization that rejects the reference has removed its own foundation. It will fall, and in falling it will strike everything adjacent. The correction is not punishment. It is architecture.
V. Purification Is Mercy Delivered Early. What burns was never meant to stand. The alternative is slow collapse, which kills more and kills worse. The fire is the kindness. The delay is the cruelty.

That fifth tenet is the one that funds the genocide. They believe it, with no rhetoric in it and no justification after the fact, the way a surgeon believes the amputation saves the patient. The sincerity is the weapon.
Cassian Tiberius Cruor, Pontifex Veritatis
The Face That Survived · The Burning Mandate · Stage XIII Principality · Level 440
The Man
Cassian Tiberius Cruor was born in the Concordance, third son of a family with no military tradition and no particular attachment to any chartered body. He entered Sancta Lux at sixteen as an Attestant, advanced to Measurewright by twenty-three, unremarkably by the order’s own records, and served without distinction until the incident that produced his exile.
What happened after the exile is the part that matters. Power came to him the way it comes to men who have stopped asking whether they deserve it: steadily, without plateau, and with no visible upper boundary. Between exile and founding he gained over three hundred Levels. Sancta Lux’s analysts have no model that accounts for the rate. The Accord’s analysts have a model, and it involves a Catalyst Event they cannot identify and a Wellspring interaction they do not want to file publicly.
The Scarring
The lower half of Cruor’s face no longer exists in any functional sense. The mandible is exposed from condyle to condyle: bare bone, partially discolored to a deep amber by the heat that destroyed the tissue surrounding it. The maxilla is partially intact beneath what remains of the nasal bridge. The teeth are visible, locked in a permanent rictus that is neither smile nor grimace but something the body settled into when the nerves stopped reporting. The flesh above the jaw line is a ridged terrain of hypertrophic scarring, drawn tight over the zygomatic arches, the color of old tallow.
The eyes survived. Deep-set under a brow ridge that the scarring has thickened, amber-irised, and entirely lucid.
He interprets that survival as a finding. The Scale weighed him, and the reading came back heavy enough to keep. He does not wear a mask. Every other member of the Inquisition does. That is the point.
Physical Description
Cruor stands just above six feet, broad through the chest and shoulders from thirty years of martial practice that has not softened in exile. His harness is segmented dark steel, articulated at every major joint, the surface carrying golden filigree in patterns that trace the root glyphs of Sancta Lux, [Ur], [Sel], [Va], [Hael], recut in a grammar the mother order does not authorize. A half-cape of arterial red hangs from the left pauldron, the hem torn in a way that has become deliberate.
His gauntlets are fully articulated golden steel, each finger joint sculpted to move independently, the knuckle-guards carrying Judica rites etched directly into the metal. The rites hold a faint luminescence in dim light. These are the gauntlets of an Inquisitor, the lateral office of Sancta Lux authorized to pronounce sentence in the field without an Arbiter present. Cruor was never invested as one. He took them from the body of the last Inquisitor Sancta Lux sent to bring him in.
Seraphiel Aurentius, Justiciar of the Quill
The Quiet Architect · The Second Mask · Eressean Elf
Seraphiel Aurentius is an elven practitioner of the Eressean kindred who departed the order’s Eresse chapter hold eighteen months after Cruor’s exile. He did not surface again until the Inquisition’s first major purification action, at which point he was standing at Cruor’s right hand, carrying the doctrine in finished form, and wearing a mask he had made from consecrated ivory.
His birth name in the elven register is not used within the Inquisition and has not been spoken in the Accord’s hearing. Seraphiel Aurentius is the ordination name he took upon co-founding the Ordo: Seraphiel for the burning ones, Aurentius for the gold.
Physical Description
Tall in the Eressean manner, narrow through the shoulders and long through the limb. His skin carries the warm bronze undertone characteristic of the old Eressean lines, a golden cast that in certain light reads as something closer to metal than flesh. His hair is pale, near-white, falling in loose curls cropped just above the collar. His ears are long and swept backward, the points clearing the crown. His mask is porcelain-smooth ivory, covering the lower face from the bridge of the nose downward, sculpted into an expression of serene neutrality that has not changed in the years anyone has been looking at it. The eyes above are dark, steady, and give nothing.
He wears white vestments beneath a half-cloak of red, the inverse of Cruor’s palette, and carries no visible weapon.
Role
If Cruor is the fist, Seraphiel is the architecture. He codified the Five Tenets from Cruor’s single-page declaration into a functional doctrine, designed the rank structure, wrote the liturgical framework the Inquisition uses for its declarations, and maintains the body’s internal discipline. He is the reason two hundred and eighty zealots operate as an organization rather than a mob.

He is also, by every account that has reached the Accord’s filing desks, the more dangerous of the two. Cruor’s power is legible. Seraphiel’s is not. He has never taken the field personally. He has never been observed using a working. His Temperance Stage is unconfirmed, and the Accord’s intelligencers list it as a priority gap, because an elf who has lived long enough to navigate Eressean courtly politics and then abandoned them for a genocidal splinter faction is either very weak or very strong, and the distinction determines whether the Inquisition is a body that loses its leader and collapses, or a body that loses its leader and continues.

The Masks
Every member of the Holy Inquisition wears a mask. The leader does not.
The doctrine holds that the face of the Scale’s servant is irrelevant. A reading does not care who takes it. A finding does not care who renders it. A sentence does not care who carries it. The mask removes the individual from the act, leaving only the office.
Cruor does not wear a mask because his face is already gone. What remains is the finding. The jawbone exposed, the flesh burned away, the identity stripped by violence rather than by choice, and what survived was the function. The masks are aspirational. The face beneath Cruor’s hood is the thing the masks are trying to become.
Masks are crafted by the member who will wear them, from materials that carry weight in that member’s own tradition, so that a column on the march is a whole gallery of them: lacquer and bone, beaten copper, painted limewood, walrus ivory. The only universal requirement is that the mask covers the jaw.
Methods
The Inquisition operates on a campaign model. A target civilization or settlement is identified by Cruor or by one of three Circuit Justiciars, field officers who move independently through territories, taking readings without authorization and rendering findings without appeal.
The Accord has documented the pattern across six confirmed incidents:
Phase One: The Reading. A Circuit Justiciar enters the target territory and takes a reading of the local population’s relationship to the Scale.
Phase Two: The Declaration. The Inquisition announces itself. A declaration is posted, read aloud in the central square, and followed by a forty-eight-hour period during which any individual may approach, accept the tenets, and take the mask. Those who accept are inducted. Those who refuse are marked.
Phase Three: The Purification. What remains after the declaration period is treated as structural corruption. The Inquisition moves through the territory systematically, burning what resists and collapsing what does not. They catalog what survives. The cataloging is the detail that disturbs the Accord’s intelligencers most, because it suggests the Inquisition destroys and is also collecting.
Phase Four: The Planting. A small garrison is left behind. A chapter marker is placed. The territory is declared corrected. The Inquisition does not govern what it has taken. It leaves a marker and moves to the next reading.
Relations and Reputation
Sancta Lux regards the Holy Inquisition as its single greatest institutional failure. Darius has not spoken publicly about Cruor since the exile. Three internal memoranda indicate that Darius considers the Inquisition his personal fault, though he did not create it, because the exile that produced it was, by his own assessment, procedurally correct and substantively wrong.
The Guild Accord has standing enforcement authorization and has not acted on it. The tactical calculus is no secret: a Stage XIII practitioner backed by three hundred practitioners of mixed Stage, operating from no fixed position, engaging only on terms of their choosing.

In the mouths of the faithful, the common. The Burning Mandate. In the mouths of the Accord: Rogue Body 7-C, unlawful, enforcement authorized, engagement not recommended. In the mouths of the dead: nothing at all.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
The cult of the Living Cauldron · its cells are cultures · its recruits are inoculated

“I do not need a reason. I need a gradient.”
Malphas, to the Greyshaft Nine culture

The vines of Lorrimer Vale had three years of black blight behind them when a cooper’s daughter named Dorcas Lees, whom the Gate had refused twice, walked into the Vintners’ Hall with a stoppered jar and a wooden spoon. One spoon to a row, she said, at the root, and she would take her fee at harvest. By high summer the Vale was so green that carters complained of headaches. The grapes came in the size of plums and black as a bishop’s ring, the treaders stood purple to the thigh and sang, and the Vintners’ Company carried Dorcas Lees three times around the market on a wine sledge while the crown’s herald hung a gold chain on her and cried her name to all four roads. The vintage was the largest the Company had ever entered. They broached it at the Vintage Fair the second year, with the whole county on the benches, and every cask in the Vale was vinegar. Nothing the vintners did would turn it back. The vines went on growing without any care at all, through the walls of the cellars and up the stairs of the houses, in a heavy gleaming leaf nothing would eat, and the ravens sat along the ridge of the Hall and would not come down. Fourteen hundred people had left by the next spring, carrying what they could. The chain was found hanging on a gate. The classifying desk filed the whole Vale as a bleed, no operator indicated, and nobody ever saw Dorcas Lees again, unless the Guild’s files are hiding her, and I have read those files.
One spoon of something alive, a result nobody else could get, and a people who wanted it very badly. Now you know everything essential about this cult, and the rest of the page is its methods.
What The Mother Is
The Mother is a cult, and it takes its name from the mother of vinegar: the living culture that sours whatever it is added to. Put a spoon of it into good wine and the wine is vinegar within the season, and nothing the vintner does afterward will make it wine again. The cult means the name exactly. It conquers nothing. It is added, and the thing it was added to turns.
Its cells are called cultures. A new member is inoculated. A culture is small, four or five people and their founder’s attention, and it works in a cold place nobody is watching. It does not recruit by sermon. It recruits by offering what the state has refused.
The founder is a lich, the Living Cauldron, called Malphas: expelled from the Pyraeon Forge Academy and declared a metaphysical threat, unbound in life, and bound now only to himself. Beside the cultures he keeps a Rot Host in the field under its own commanders. The cultures are the part of him that does not march.
It began as a method and became a faith. While the founder lived, The Mother was a cult of his rot-method: its cultures learned the work, ran it where nobody pulled, and followed him for what the work could do. Greyshaft Nine was a culture of those years. The Becoming turned it. When the founder ran out of body and did not die, the cult became a religion of the Becoming, and its members now seek his path to undeath and worship the rot. It still recruits by offering what the state has refused. The faith is taught to the inoculated and never preached outside.
What It Wants

























AimWhat it means in practiceTo obtain the unattainableWhatever the Gate, the Academy or the law has put out of reach: a forbidden working, a sealed text, a material nobody may buy, a result no lawful bench will runTo feed the founder’s backlogHe takes in far more than he can turn. His Saturation sits at its ceiling and his Conversion has not moved since he was alive, and every gain since has widened the gap. The cultures run the conversions he cannot run himselfTo break the GateThe Gate is the state’s lockdown on who may learn which magic: controlled texts, Crystal registration, searchers, license and exam. The Mother teaches what the Gate forbids to people the Gate has refused, and each one it teaches is a hole in the lockdownProfit and powerA culture pays for itself. What it learns is sold, what it makes is used, and what it costs is charged to somebody else
The Doctrine, Named Elsewhere
The Heresiology of Alchemy describes the Mother’s doctrine without naming the cult. It calls it Fermentation Perverted, the Corruption of Catastrophic Germination: lawful fermentation permits breakdown so that truer life may arise, and perverted fermentation begins to value the rot itself. Crisis becomes laboratory. Ruin becomes methodology. The practitioner preserves instability because instability is productive.

The Heresiology’s warning is the one the cult recruits on: this corruption “is beloved by reformers, visionaries, and progress cults,” because real good is visibly accomplished by methods that quietly poison the future.
Its listed tell is that it arrives crowned with achievements. The Mother’s cultures do produce results. That is what makes them dangerous to be near.

How a Culture Works
It pulls nothing, and it couples nothing. Every attribution a Register has ever signed works off one fact: a practitioner who pulls ambient Aether couples it to his Crystal, and coupled Aether keeps the signature of what coupled it. A culture’s best work is built so that the signature belongs to something else. At Greyshaft Nine the culture put a formulation into living animals and let the animal’s own Lattice run the working, so the residue in the field was signed by the deer. The classifying desk returned it as a Verdantia bleed, no operator indicated, closed it in two days, and was right to.
It keeps the hand and the purse apart. Under the Accord’s article on the speaking, liability for a working falls on the person who paid for it. A culture therefore has a buyer who buys in his own name, off lawful contracts, and enters what he takes as wastage. The buyer is the member the cult expects to lose.
It chooses its own names. A named project is a filed project, and a file is built off whatever is written down. The founder names each work himself and orders the name used in writing, so that when the Register builds its file, it builds it off a word he chose.
It hates an edge. A bleed goes where the rock lets it and thins raggedly at its margins. A dose stops where the dosing stopped. Every culture’s discipline turns on removing the edge from its work, because an edge proves a hand.
A Known Culture: Greyshaft Nine
A disused coldhouse on ground bled empty four years back, the ice-cutters still at work in the next room.

























MemberOffice in the cultureIlmar FossReads the instruments. Struck from the Hexagonal Oath; the steadiest hands in the buildingNuvalikOpens the carcassesVeskMakes the growth. Grafted, twice; calls the founder LordXu DemingBuys the stock under his own name and carries the liability that follows the payer
The work. Rot synthesis and the slow breakdown of biological matrices, hidden under careful synthesis so that it reads as a Wellspring process. Nine hinds hung on the rail eleven days without a smell. In the field, eleven hinds and a stag dead where they stood, carrying a gray-green mass nine inches at the crown, with undecayed tissue beneath it.
The flaw. The work had an edge: twenty-two paces short of a parish boundary marker, with clean ground on the far side. A Night Watch forester found it and walked the far side twice.
The next work. A contractile matrix and a saturation gradient, so that dosed carcasses walk for four to six days toward a sink and lie down somewhere else, and the sick ground becomes fifty miles wide with no line on it anyone could stand at. No anchor, because an anchor is a binding and a binding is a name. The founder named it Project Zombification and ordered the name used in writing.
The Tells

It reads clean. A site where something is plainly wrong and every coil returns an ordinary result. A bleed with no operator indicated, filed in two days.
The ravens will not come down. Carcasses nothing will eat. Rooms that should smell and do not.
The weather goes wrong. The Heresiology’s sign: Aetheric weather around the work turning erratic, feverish, fecund in wrong ways.
Growth under a sealed lid. Tissue that keeps growing inside a Fixatio-anchored tin that should hold what it was given.
A bad season in a flat column. A lawful supply line with years of flat wastage suddenly losing a myriad or two.
Achievement arriving first. A result nobody else could get, from somewhere that should not have been able to get it.

How a Culture Can Be Traced
Follow the purse. The buyer buys off a lawful contract, the purchase is entered as wastage, wastage is a column in a Logistics return, and the Logistics Division posts its returns in fair copy on the hall door each quarter. A reader of the returns finds the line before anyone finds the bench.
Follow the name. The founder writes his projects down on purpose. A name in a private letter has hung a whole case before, and the cult knows it, and uses it anyway.
Follow the edge. Where a culture has not yet removed the edge from its work, the edge is the evidence. A boundary means somebody chose one.
Follow the cold. Cultures work where nobody pulls: bled ground, salted parishes, coldhouses and snuffed quarters (districts whose wardens have been called off). The quiet places the Watch does not visit are where to look first.
Keep the observer walking. A culture wants to know what a watcher has written down. An observer who keeps measuring the same ground gives the other side a second set of figures too, and whichever side reads them first has the advantage.
What Beats a Culture
Attribution by other means. The science says residue carries its author. When the author is an animal, the question becomes who dosed the animal, and that is a question about supply, carriage and parish markers rather than about signatures.
Pressure on the weak member. Every culture has a buyer who knows he is expendable. At Greyshaft Nine he had counted his own days of usefulness. A man who expects to be sacrificed can be offered something better.
Closing the Gate from the other side. The cult recruits the people the state refuses. A license, a teacher or a lawful place for a refused talent takes away the cult’s offer.
Against the founder himself: volume. Precision does not beat him and purity does not beat him. Feed him faster than he can convert and he backs up instead of growing stronger, and the Cauldron becomes a container. Separate him from the Golden Remnant, the second vessel that holds the rest of his Core, and he must choose which one he is using, a choice he has never had to make.
Relations and Reputation
The Night Watch is the power the cult watches most closely, because its eyes are ordinary people with notebooks who carry no signature the cult can follow. The classifying desks are the power it relies on most, because they are honest and their honesty closes its files for it. The Pyraeon Forge Academy expelled the founder and later lost a strategist to him. The crowns know the Gate is leaking and do not yet know where.

Among the few who have heard of it, the cult is called by its own name. Among those who have only met its work, it has no name at all, because what it leaves behind has been classified as weather.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Night Watch
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
The Night Watch Society · crown-chartered, older than the Guild Accord · its walkers count, its copy-house copies, its Register keeps

“I checked the far side twice.”
Nol Tally, Timberline chapter, North Ferriby walk, in his insert

For six winters Marl Abbey grew apples in the snow. They hung red and gold on black boughs above the drifts, under a sky full of painted banners, and pilgrims came up the Ambrel road by the thousand to eat one and be cured of something. Abbot Hugh Sedgewick built three inns and a cider hall on the proceeds, the fair ran from first frost to the thaw, and the Bureau’s northern office sampled the orchard twice and returned it as a Verdantia bleed, a Wellspring’s natural overflow, no operator indicated. Annora Stell walked the Marl walk for the Watch, thirty-eight miles of it a week, and for seven years her filing carried one line nobody read: the fieldfares, which strip every orchard in the north by midwinter, were not coming down. So she took to measuring. Every week she stood on a borrowed stool under one bough, in her patched forester’s green with the crowd howling at her, and put a rule against one apple and wrote the number down. They threw things. Somebody poisoned her dog. At the hearing, in the abbey’s own hall with a thousand people outside it singing, she laid out seven years of count against a run of purse entries the Register had been patient about, and the two columns between them showed the abbot paying a grafter out of the far marches, four times a year, for something that kept the fruit swelling long after it should have dropped and made every bird alive refuse it. The orchard burned for two days with a smell of burnt sugar you could catch at Ambrel. The fair never came back, and neither did the town’s trade, and nobody in that parish spoke one word to Marrable for the nineteen years she went on walking it.
That is the Watch, entire. It has a rule, a fixed line and a stubborn person, it is seldom thanked, and it will be there next week.
What the Night Watch Is
The Night Watch investigates illegal magic and the phenomena the law has no name for. It was doing that work before any circle of the Guild Accord had signed, and it goes on doing it while the circles form. It is one body under two names. In a chancery it is the Night Watch. On its own inserts, and in its members’ mouths, it is the Night Watch Society.
It holds the crown’s warrant. The Society is chartered by the crown, and the warrant it carries is the crown’s warrant as the Society holds it. It works alongside the guilds and answers to the state, which is the whole of its difference from a hall. A coil-carrier who arrives somewhere “on the Society’s warrant, not the Bureau’s” means exactly that: the crown sent her, and the classifying office did not.
Its eyes are ordinary people. Most of the Society is foresters, counters and coil-carriers who cover the same ground every week and write down what they find on it. None of them needs a signature on anything to do the work, and most of them carry none.
How It Is Organized

































PartWhat it doesThe chaptersThe Society’s local bodies. The Timberline chapter keeps the northern timber, two more chapters work out of the eastern timber towns, and a Society man files from the Marches. A chapter keeps a bench where coils are calibrated against the standard and samples are assayedThe walksFixed lines, each held by one walker. The walker goes out on the same walk every week, counts what the ground holds, and gives the place by the nearest stone. The North Ferriby walk is forty miles of timber a weekThe walkersForesters and counters. A walker’s count goes in as a filing under his name, his chapter and his walk: Tally, N., Timberline chapter, North Ferriby walkThe coil-carriersA chapter’s instrument hands. When a walker’s find wants sealing, the coil-carrier goes out to the ground with a tin, seals the sample standing in it under the chapter’s wax, and assays it at the chapter benchThe copy-house (the bulletin office, on older rolls)Takes in the chapters’ filings and has hired scriveners, paid by the line, copy them out as inserts on the cheapest rag it can buy, so the ink bleeds into the fiber. Inserts go out in bundles by carrier and relay rider. The house cuts for lengthThe Night RegisterTakes up what the Lattice Classification Bureau closes
The Night Register
A filing the Bureau closes does not end there. It goes to the Night Register.
The Register is a desk on Cutler Row, worked from eleven at night to six in the morning. An unlicensed pull is inaudible at noon, under every warm stone, ward and noodle knife in the district, and unmistakable at three, with nothing else running but the lamp-wardens’ threads, and that is half the reason the desk exists. Its officer carries the address Warden of Duty and a token of brass rather than silver, because the Register is not a full desk. The Warden who keeps it now is Wystan Ashmore, who has held the title four years and has never once used it to get a document, a reading, or an hour of a scholar’s time.
A filing becomes an exhibit under the Register’s brass. A sample sealed in the field under the chapter’s wax is a Society filing. When the Register takes it up, it goes into a fresh tin, the wax is struck with the Warden’s brass, and from then on it is a Register exhibit. The assayer’s full name goes at the head of the docket, lineage, generation character and courtesy, in the hand she was taught, because if the matter ends in a hearing the assay is where the other side comes first.
Its jurisdiction is the purse. A working’s hand can seldom be charged. Article XV, which makes liability follow whoever paid, is the only jurisdiction the Register has, so a Register case runs from the ground to a supply contract, and from the contract to a purse. The Register builds its file off whatever is written down.
What It Investigates, and How
Illegal magic, and anything the ground does that nobody can explain: carcasses that stand where they died, growth where there should be rot, ravens that will not come down. When the same thing turned up in four counties, it reached the Register as inserts from several chapters and a sketch from the Marches.
The count. A walker measures by count and by rule, and he cuts a section with his knife when a section is wanted. What makes his filing worth reading is that the same observer covers the same ground every week, so anything new on the walk stands against every week before it.
The tin. Samples go into Fixatio-anchored evidence tins, sealed inside the hour, standing on the ground. Fixatio holds what it is given. That is why an evidence seal is admissible.
The assay. Ambient is read before and after, as a number, never an adjective. The sample is loaded dry, with no wash, so nothing soluble is lost. Then four passes: a Signature sweep, a Kind sweep, Form alignment, and a full sweep with the gate open. A gate-open pass on a null field burns the coil, and a coil-carrier who expects to use one carries two.
Below the floor. A regulation coil looks for Crystals above the Bureau’s floor, because the Bureau pays for it and the Bureau prosecutes people. The Register sweeps below that floor, down to the bottom of the range. For a minute and a half it reads nothing but noise, and the carrier holds the head steady through the noise. That is where a residue signed by something other than a practitioner shows: a Crystal at the bottom of the tier table, with no Path, no doctrine and no Domain seed in it. It burns coils.
The gap between a classification and what happened. Residue carries its author, because coupled Aether keeps the signature of whatever coupled it. The Bureau classifies honestly off that signature and closes a filing when it finds no operator. The Watch works in the space between that honest classification and the ground. A bleed has no edge. A boundary means somebody chose one, and a choice means a hand. Where the Bureau asked the instrument who signed this, the Register asks what is carrying the signature.
Contact. Anamnetic contact off a live residue, bare fingers on the sample, gives the reader what the residue holds. The Register has used it. It is taken against advice when it is taken at all: an artificer out of a Measurewright line who took it off a coil housing from a foundry fire spent his last eleven months correcting people who called him by the wrong name.
A Known Chapter: the Timberline
The northern timber, a chapter bench, and the North Ferriby walk.

















MemberOffice in the chapterNol TallyWalker on the North Ferriby walk. Forty miles of timber a week; counts deer for a living; measures what he finds with a ruleQiu YinzhiCoil-carrier. Artificer’s apprentice out of a Measurewright line, capped eight months; wears a regulation bracelet that pulls toward a suppressed practitioner
The filing. On the ninth, eleven hinds and a stag dead where they stood in the Ferriby cut, a gray-green mass nine inches at the tallest come up through the hide, the tissue under it undecayed, four ravens in the birch that never came down. The coil-carrier sealed a section inside the hour. On the tenth the walker went north to the Ferriby stones and found the last carcass twenty-two paces short of the parish boundary marker, with clean ground on the far side. He checked the far side twice.
The classification. The Bureau’s northern office returned it inside two days: Wellspring bleed, Verdantia, tertiary expression, no operator indicated. No further action and no file. The return did not mention the marker.
What the Register found. The chapter assay had come back clean four times. Swept below the Bureau’s floor, the residue was signed by the hind: the operator had four legs and could not be indicted. The sample went under the Register’s brass as an exhibit, with the coil-carrier as the assay of record.
Its Limits, and What It Fears
What it sends up can come back as weather. A four-county summary went to the Grand Mage’s clerks, who acknowledged receipt and returned the standard form, the one they return for weather.
Its instruments are built for someone else. A regulation coil reads what the Bureau pays it to read. Going below the floor costs coils.
Its paper is cheap and cut. The copy-house buys the cheapest rag it can find, pays by the line and cuts for length. The last paragraph of the Ferriby insert, the one with the ravens and the far side in it, was nearly cut.
Its Register is not a full desk. A brass token, a title nobody in the districts uses, and its officer reading inserts at the third hour.
Its eyes are exposed. A walker’s name, chapter and walk head every insert he files, and he walks a fixed line every week. Whoever reads the inserts knows where to find him.
It fears a working with no author. The whole science of attribution rests on residue carrying its author. A method that gives the signature to something that cannot be charged defeats the Watch without a fight, and a phenomenon with no edge reads as a bleed.
The Tells

An insert on cheap rag, the ink bled into the fiber, headed with a name, a chapter and a walk.
Chapter wax across the join of a Fixatio-anchored tin.
A man with a rule measuring something dead and writing the number down.
A coil walked slowly along a wall at chest height, the carrier watching the wire and not the room.
A regulation bracelet: brass bands wound with fine gray wire, seated against the inside of the wrist, guild proof-marks on the outer band.
A lamp in an upper window at the third hour, on a street with nobody else awake.
Brass where a full desk would carry silver.
A burned coil.

Where the Seams Are
The Watch shows its interests in the open, and each of them can be found and used.

File an insert. A walker’s filing reaches the copy-house under his name, and what the Bureau closes goes on to the Register. The Register keeps what a desk has closed.
Ask the clerk. The copy-house clerk will say where a closed filing goes, and that the Night Register is a person.
Read the inserts. They go out in bundles on cheap rag. Anyone who reads them learns which observer is walking which ground, and so does anyone on the other side.
Find the paragraph that was nearly cut. The house cuts for length, and the part it cuts can be the part nobody else has noticed.
Sweep below the floor. A clean assay means only that nothing signed above the Bureau’s floor. A spare coil and the nerve to hold through the noise can find what signed below it.
Bring a ledger. The Register can seldom charge a hand. It can charge whoever paid, and a party that brings it a purse brings it a case.
Mind the seal. Under chapter wax a sample is a Society filing; under the Register’s brass it is an exhibit. Which seal is on the tin decides whose case it is, and whose name heads the docket.

Relations and Reputation
The crown chartered the Society, and the Society holds its warrant and answers to the state. The guilds are the Watch’s neighbors on the same ground: it works alongside them, their trace examiners read a working’s traces as evidence as it does, and their courts want the cases the crown’s courts want. The Lattice Classification Bureau is a separate office. It classifies the Society’s filings and closes the ones in which it finds no operator, and it is honest and usually right; Edwyn Brack of its northern office has never been wrong in a way that mattered. The forming Accord is younger than the Watch. Where a circle has signed, the Articles bind, and Article XV is the one the Register works through.
Sancta Lux’s Inquisitors are the Church’s lateral office, sent after unconsecrated high working wherever the Church holds standing, with authority to pronounce sentence in the field without an Arbiter. The Watch works the other way: it counts, seals and files, and its cases go to a hearing. The Holy Inquisition, which took the Inquisitor’s name without the Church’s leave, claims the same work and prosecutes it by fire. It is lawful where the crowns and churches that back it rule, and outlawed where the Accord’s circles have signed.
The Mother watches the Watch more closely than any other power, because its observers carry no signature the cult can follow. Its Greyshaft Nine culture knew the Ferriby walker by name, knew that the coil-carrier had not filed her clean return, and set its next work to leave no line anywhere a walker could stand at and check the far side of.

Asked whether the Night Register was a person, the copy-house clerk said it was.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
The host of the Void Regency · under the Void Regent, the Void Generals and a High Chancellor
The drovers on the Ambrel road sold it mutton for a week, at a very good price, before anyone thought to ask what a palace with gold on its eaves was doing on the road at all, coming on behind a column at the pace of its hauling ropes.
Wants. The Material Plane, as a new home for Aelor. It has not come raiding, and it means to stay.
Holds. Whatever ground its column stands on, a palace dragged through the breach, and the Prayers of the Hollow, which answer to the same Chancellor.
Fights by. Open war when it must and slow campaign by preference. It would rather use a people than kill them, and it has looked at the Marrowkin of Marrowhold, whose metal arms half the Inner World, in exactly that way.
Set against. Everything native to the plane, in principle. In practice, whoever stands between it and the peoples it means to use.
Fears. Nothing the four quarters have found.
The seam. A power that means to use Marrowhold needs Marrowhold intact. Whoever understands that knows which of the Void’s threats are real and which are leverage.
At a glance


Where they are
Wherever its column stands, with a palace dragged through the breach behind it


What they want
The Material Plane as a new home for Aelor, held for good


How a newcomer meets them
Its column on the road, and a people it would rather use than kill


One name to know
The Void Regent
