factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Articles of the Accord, and the Kinds of Polity
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
The actual articles, the courts that hear them, the penalties, and the kinds of polity the Accord has to reach across.

The Accord cannot hang you. It can make it impossible for you to sell anything, anywhere, ever again, and it prefers that.

Jankin Pennyloaf, baker of Stowmarch, was amerced for a short loaf four hundred and twelve times across forty-one years, which is the town’s record and, by my reading of the rolls, the Inner World’s. When he died in Year 694 the market court adjourned for the first time anyone could remember, and all of Stowmarch turned out in its best colors to bury him: the bier hung with bread, the shawms and drums of the Bakers’ company, the two sworn tasters at the head of the procession and already unsteady, as their office more or less requires, and a herald hired in from the next town to cry the total at every corner. At the graveside the Clerk of the Market took the last loaf from Jankin’s oven off the coffin lid, set it on the beam, found it light by a quarter-ounce, and in front of the whole town struck his loaf-stamp across with the six-point (the punch that voids a false measure) and set the fine to his means. His widow paid it out of the funeral collection. The crowd cheered so loudly that the Clerk had to read the sum again.
Nobody in that churchyard wanted any other court. They had been eating Jankin’s bread for forty years and knew to the crumb how short it ran, because any one of them could sound it at the beam at any hour without leave, and all of them had. Everything the Accord has ever been stands on that beam. The text follows.
Part One: What the Accord Is
A coalition with a law. The Guild Accord is a coalition of guilds across many nations: adventurers’ guilds, merchant guilds, craft guilds, alchemists, healers, couriers, free companies and more. A hall signs on for three things, shared rank, enforceable contracts and passage, and these Articles are how the second of them works and what the first and third rest on. They are why a mercer from one kingdom will sell to a hunter from another on sight.
Where the Accord stands. The text below is older than the coalition that now carries it. The formulary and its courts grew up over seven centuries in the Concord heartland, the Sealed Charter, and on the chartered routes; the Accord proper, the guilds and their crowns signing on together, is being made now, a hall at a time and a circle at a time. Where a circle has signed, these Articles bind as law. Where none has, they bind the members of signed halls and the parties who bring a case to the chancery’s courts, and that older jurisdiction is the one described first.
Not a sovereign. The Accord holds no territory, keeps no standing army, and cannot execute anybody. (All three clauses are maintained with a straight face at Sealhall, in a city it bought, a mile from the Legion’s drill plain, and it has never once been short of a crown willing to do the hanging.) What it has is a jurisdiction: a set of courts, along the trade routes and in the chartered markets, which merchants and locals alike bring their disputes to because those courts are faster, cheaper and more predictable than anything else available.
This is how the law merchant (the custom merchants carry from fair to fair) actually works, and the point is worth stating flatly because every minstrel gets it wrong. The law merchant is not a universal code invented by merchants. It refers to a jurisdiction and to certain procedural variances permitted in specific commercial courts. Ordinary local people use those courts too, under the same rules as the great houses.
And enforcement runs on reputation and repeated dealing, with force a distant third. The Accord’s real sanction is exclusion: an unregistered man, an unproofed cask, a struck weight, a house whose instruments will not bind. A merchant who cannot get an attestation cannot get credit, and a merchant who cannot get credit is finished, and everybody in the trade knows it without anybody having to say it.
The formulary’s four revisions, every one of them older than the first circle, are its whole legislative history until the last Title below, which the Sitting of Halls forced in when the guilds took the nine titles for themselves. What follows is the current text in summary, with the plain-tongue name beside the register name, because which one a character reaches for places him instantly.
Part Two: The Articles
Title I · Of Standards















































#RegisterPlainThe rulePenaltyIUnum pondusone weightOne weight, one measure, one reach, through all the land.Amercement; the measure struckIIDe verificationethe checkingEvery weight and measure in lawful trade bears its stamps and is presented at the appointed window.Trade suspended until presentedIIIDe percussionethe strikingA false weight is struck across its stamps with the six-point and destroyed.Destruction; second offense, license forfeitIVDe soliditatesolid or casedNo cased weight in trade. Any person may sound a weight at any hour without leave.Amercement to the offender’s means; the beamVDe mensura planalevel measureGrain sold by level measure, the board drawn once and evenly.Amercement; forfeit of the sale
Title II · Of Instruments















































#RegisterPlainThe rulePenaltyVIDe formathe wordingOnly formulary wordings bind. A clause improved is a clause void.The instrument failsVIICoram testibusbefore witnessesAttestation requires witnesses, and witnesses are compensated.The instrument failsVIIIDe die nullothe namelessNo instrument may be dated to Munahi.Void, and it has been tested twiceIXSalvo iure tertiithe third partyThe saving clause stands in every instrument the chancery issues.Cannot be contracted out ofXDe registroenteringRegistered within one turn, or voidable at the other party’s election.Voidable
Title III · Of the Trades
The register’s words are older than anyone’s memory of why. The cutting and the writing mean runes and tags, and the pouring means Drafts. These are skills anyone can level, and the Articles have never cared who can do them, only who is paid to.















































#RegisterPlainThe rulePenaltyXIDe examinethe examinationNone practices the writing or the pouring for hire unregistered.Amercement; tools forfeit; the work undone at his costXIIDe disciplinathe indentureSeven years for the cutting, indenture registered, a master limited in how many he may hold.Indenture void; the boy freed; the master finedXIIIProbatum estthe proofNothing sold as proofed that has not been tested.The heaviest fine in the formularyXIVDe vasethe vesselEvery charged vessel marked with maker and date of charge. Selling an uncharged vessel as charged is fraud, not error.Reservation, and the Bench does not often forgive itXVDe vocethe speakingNot licensed, and the Accord has never found a way to license it. Liability for a spoken working falls on the person who paid for it.Falls on the payer
Article XV is the interesting one. A working that was spoken has no author in its own grammar. The invocation register has no first person, so nothing in the sentence identifies who said it, and the Bench spent four hundred years trying to place a mouth at a scene before giving up and legislating around the problem entirely. The man who paid is liable. This is why speakers are hired through intermediaries, why nobody hires one in front of a witness, and why the whole trade sits one step outside every other in the four quarters.
Title IV · Of the Pool and the Round















































#RegisterPlainThe rulePenaltyXVIDe foraminethe boreNo ferrule (the fixed bronze ring at a Core’s lip that limits how wide a sitter can pull) other than standard at any pool.Barred from the pool; amercement; the fitting seizedXVIIDe tundisiothe tundishEvery ring fitted with its tundish (the brass funnel that shows from the door the color of what passes) and unobstructed. Covering a tundish is a separate offense from widening a bore, and carries the heavier penalty, because it is done to conceal.Barred from the pool; the heavier fineXVIIIDe sigillothe sealBreaking a Guild seal on a ring, a lamp stem or a lintel.Struck from the round; a termXIXDe crure mortuothe dead legA stretch of a round given up (a dead leg) shall have its stems capped and be reported within one turn.Amercement on the owner, whoever that now isXXDe arreragiisarrearsStriking a household from the round for arrears requires notice of one turn. A death-house, a physician’s house and a working forge may not be struck.—
Article XX is honored in the West and ignored everywhere the searcher is the same man as the collector, which is most places. The exemption exists, is well known, and is claimed far more often than it is granted.
Title V · Of Bread, Ale and the Common Sale















































#RegisterPlainThe rulePenaltyXXIDe assisa panisthe assizeThe weight of the loaf is fixed against the price of grain, and moves with it. The price of ale is fixed.Amercement, rising with repetitionXXIIDe gustatoribusthe tastersSworn tasters chosen annually, unpaid, sworn to assay the ale, and bound to report defaulters at the next sitting.Refusing the office is itself finableXXIIIDe praeemptioneforestallingBuying goods on the road before they reach the market, to sell them dearer in it.Amercement; goods forfeitXXIVDe remercationeregratingBuying in a market to resell in the same market at a higher price.Amercement; barred from the marketXXVDe coemptioneengrossingBuying up the whole of a commodity to control its price.The largest amercements the Accord has ever levied
Titles I and V between them are ninety percent of everything the Accord’s courts actually do. Grand commercial disputes are rare. Short loaves, weak ale, heaped measures and men who bought the carrots before the carts reached the gate are the daily business, and the rolls are full of the same bakers’ names year after year, which tells you exactly how much the fines deter.
Title VI · Of Persons and Carriage

































#RegisterPlainThe rulePenaltyXXVIDe pede pulverulentothe dusty footA traveler’s plea is heard and determined before the market closes.—XXVIIDe custodia viaethe roadThe keeper of a stretch keeps it passable, and may take a toll only where he does.Toll forfeit; the stretch reassignedXXVIIIDe pignorethe pledgeWhat may be taken in pledge, and what may not: tools of a man’s craft, and the last beast.Restitution
The dusty foot is the single most valuable procedural rule the Accord has, and it is why merchants use its courts rather than anyone else’s. A man passing through cannot wait three weeks for a sitting. A court that will hear him this afternoon, before he moves on, is a court he will bring his business to for thirty years. It is also why a crew of hunters three kingdoms from home will walk into a market court against a crowned head and come out laughing.
Title VII · Of Standing and the Token
The newest Title, and the one the guilds wrote. Every other Title binds a person because a court says so. This one is why a stranger will hand you the goods.















































#RegisterPlainThe rulePenaltyXXIXDe novem titulisthe nineNine titles and no others in every signed hall: Initiate, Apprentice, Journeyman, Adept, Expert, Master, Grandmaster, Archmaster, Paragon. Each hall confers them by its own lights and answers for what it confers.Hall amerced; title struckXXXDe fide artisthe trust of the tradeA member deals, makes, carries or treats up to the title and no further, without a second signature from a token that covers it.The sale voidable; amercement; the second offense, title struckXXXIDe signis et raritatestamp and rarityA maker’s title caps the Grade of what she may make, and a merchant’s caps the Rarity of what he may sell. Every finished piece bears the Accord’s stamp and its maker’s mark. A false stamp is a false weight.The piece struck across with the six-point; license forfeitXXXIIDe tabulathe boardEvery Commission posted at its true Grade, and taken only up to the Grade the title of those who sign allows. A hall that posts a Grade light answers for the dead.The bond forfeit; amercement to the hall’s means; the hall under reservationXXXIIIDe falso nummothe false tokenWhoever strikes, cuts, alters or knowingly carries a false token.Struck from every roll; reservation of all goods; delivered to the nearest crown, which often hangs him
Article XXXIII is the one every hall in the coalition agrees on. A short loaf is a matter of a quarter-ounce. A false Journeyman on a C-Grade bounty gets a crew killed, and a false token anywhere makes every honest token on that road worth a little less, and the whole coalition stands on those bits of silver. A good forger is also the one person the guilds will all chase together, in the only known instance of the Long Rope and the Red Caps riding out in the same week.
Part Three: The Courts
The market court sits in the market, in the same building as the beam and the guardhouse. It hears debt, detinue and broken contract, and it absorbs whatever else the market throws at it: stall disputes, the assize, short measure. In a large seat it sits thrice a week. In a village with a charter it sits monthly, and by the fourth generation its rolls contain almost nothing but bakers.
The Bench of Attribution sits above it and exercises four powers: entry, striking, attribution and reservation. Entry puts a thing on the record. Striking takes it off. Attribution assigns an act to a person, which is the hardest of the four and the reason Article XV exists. Reservation withholds a standing pending determination, and a man under reservation is not condemned and cannot trade, which is worse.
Sancta Lux hears what the Accord will not: oath, status, legitimacy, and whether a thing was done in bad faith rather than merely done. The two jurisdictions overlap and neither will define the boundary, because both prefer being able to claim a case than being obliged to take one.
Amercement is the standard penalty and it is not a fixed fine. It is set by the court to the offender’s means, which is why the same offense costs a laborer a week and a factor house an afternoon’s profit, and why the factor house budgets for it.
Arbitration hears what the signed halls will not settle among themselves: feuds, demarcation, who rides eighth. It has no power to make a hall come. It has the roll, and a hall that will not answer finds its letters slow. The Trials of Resonance, under the Ribs at Sealhall, bind the sworn. The Lattice holds nothing of a signed member to convict by, so short of a prisoner held down under a Sealwright’s hand, the market court will have to manage with witnesses.
Part Four: The Kinds of Polity
The Accord has to reach across states that do not resemble each other at all, and this is the normal condition rather than an exotic one. The characteristic state of the age is composite: several territories under one ruler, governed as if they were separate kingdoms under their own laws and traditions, with high political, judicial and economic heterogeneity retained. That is the Concord. That is also why the Accord exists at all, because a merchant crossing three provinces of one crown crosses three legal systems, and why a coalition of guilds that all use one form is a thing crowns need and cannot afford to like.
The seven forms
Composite monarchy. Several countries under one crown, each keeping its own law. The Concord, whose regalia sit in pledge to the chancery that lends them back for coronations. Chancery theorists hold that similarity of language and custom decides whether such a state holds together, which is precisely the argument the Accord makes for its own standards and its own tongue.
Oligarchic republic. Rule by a closed body of chartered houses, self-perpetuating, with formal offices and real elections among a tiny electorate. Marrowhold. It is rigidly oligarchical, and nobody in it pretends otherwise.
Mandate. Rule by standing decree, read aloud daily at every garrison, with no assembly and no appeal outside the decree archive. Undaar-Keth. Its strength is that everybody knows the law because everybody hears it every day. Its weakness is that the law is whatever was read this morning.
Sealed moot. An assembly whose rulings are issued in a register requiring interpreters, and whose interpreters are a hereditary profession. The Keth-Gorrum. Formally the most representative body in the four quarters and functionally readable by about two hundred people.
Rotating crown. An elective or rotating headship on a fixed cycle, designed so that no single will outlasts a season. Iampu, where the Crown passes at each solstice and equinox under the Treaty of Four Courts. Such crowns characteristically drift toward capture by the electing body, which is a live risk in Iampu and is what the Frost Council actually is.
Confederation. No monarch, binding decisions requiring consensus across every represented house. The Echo Elves’ Longhouse Accord, and behind it Altherion’s River Crown Council. Confederations are ramshackle, slow, and remarkably durable, and the Echo Elf version is slower than any other by design.
Calendrical principality. Governance by appointed window rather than by session: nothing is decided outside its ceremonial time, and urgency is treated as a defect. Eresse. No other polity in the four quarters can negotiate with it at speed and none has stopped complaining about this in four Eons.
And outside the typology entirely: Kharven. A crown, a seat, a household structure, and a body of custom that has never been written and cannot be cited. The Accord never issued an instrument that bound there, and the seat never asked for one, until the first circle was signed in its own lower hall. The Articles now bind there under that seal, laid over a custom that still has never been written.
What this means at the table
A character crossing a border changes legal systems, not just flags. The same act is an amercement in Altherion, a decree violation in Undaar-Keth, an unentered act in a hold, an untimely act in Eresse, and, until the first circle was signed, nothing at all in Kharven. A ferryman who works the line between two of them keeps two tally-sticks and two faces, and his children learn which to show on which bank before they learn to row.
The Accord’s courts and its silver are the only things that are the same everywhere, which is the entire source of its power and the entire source of the resentment toward it. It did not conquer anybody. It made itself the only layer that works in all seven places, charged for it, and now has hundreds of guilds in hundreds of colors asking every crown on the map to sign. The crowns tolerate it, because they cannot sell anything without it, and they fear it, for the same reason.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Procedure, Precedent, and the Record of Strikings

Issued jointly by the Research and Archives Division, the Guild of Measurewrights, and the Arbitration Division. Companion to The Provenance Doctrine and the Standing Index.
“The law does not govern from above. It resonates from within.”
Carved over the gate of every Guild Hall, and over the door of the Bench, where it is understood to be a joke.

What the Bench Is
Where the Accord stands. The Bench is older than the communion. It has sat for six centuries under the Codex, and its entries, strikings and reservations bind as law inside a signed circle. Outside one they bind by exclusion, which was most of their force before the first circle was signed and still is.
The Bench of Attribution has never been a Division. It is a standing joint instrument of three Divisions that could not agree to give the function to any one of them, and its entire procedure is the machinery of that disagreement operating at scale.
It rules on what a formula is, whether it may lawfully exist in commerce, what class of material a given lot actually contains, and who is permitted to hold the result.

Those four questions govern the alchemical economy, and the alchemical economy governs everything the Crown does not own outright.
The Bench is therefore the most consequential body in the four quarters and the only one with no seat on the Concord Council , an arrangement that has been proposed for correction eleven times.

The three chairs

























ChairQuestionIts positionDoctrine Research and ArchivesWhether the glyph chain constitutes lawful Parunic syntax. Whether Authorization, Boundary, Direction and Sealing are properly filled. Whether the Wellspring invoked would recognize the invoker as an authorized channelThat attribution is fundamentally a question of law, and the instrument is a convenience of the present ageInstrument The MeasurewrightsWhat the coil reads. Class, Fidelity, Carry, and the reference figures against which every subsequent lot in the world is measuredThat attribution is fundamentally a question of measurement, and doctrine is what a party appeals to when the needle has disagreed with themRuling ArbitrationThe Attribution is an adjudication. Enforceable, appealable at the appellant’s cost, backed by EnforcementThat attribution is fundamentally a question of who can be sued, and Arbitration is the only chair that has ever stated its position aloud, in session, on the record, and declined to withdraw it

A session requires all three. Two chairs cannot rule.
This has produced four documented deadlocks lasting longer than a year, one of which is ongoing, and the ongoing one concerns a formula that eleven thousand people are currently taking.

The Four Powers
Entry
A formula is written into the Standing Index. It may thereafter be lawfully rendered, sold, taught, priced, bonded, and pledged as security against a debt.
Nothing in the alchemical economy exists commercially until it is entered. An unentered formula is not illegal in most quarters. It is simply outside every instrument the economy uses to hold a transaction together, which in practice is worse than illegal, because a thing that cannot be bonded cannot be shipped and a thing that cannot be pledged cannot be financed.
Entry requires a petition, a reference lot, an assay against Nine-Nail Attestation Salt, a doctrinal read, and a Fidelity reference figure the Measurewrights are prepared to stand behind for as long as the formula remains in the Index. The last of those is the expensive part and the reason petitions from small houses fail.
Striking
A formula is removed. Every unit of stock produced under it becomes unlawful holding at the moment of publication. Holders have forty days to surrender, after which Enforcement’s interest becomes a matter of Concord Writ rather than of paperwork.
Grounds are three: doctrinal error discovered after entry, a reference figure that later assay cannot reproduce, and material harm demonstrated in the field. The third is the one the public understands and the least used.

What a Striking actually costs. Consider a Threshold formula that a poor eastern district has tempered its practitioners on for six generations, struck because the rendering house cannot produce a clean provenance chain for stock it has been buying honestly from people who did not keep records.
It costs the Bench a session and a seal. It costs the district a generation that does not advance.
No shafts are flooded, no walls come down. The district’s practitioners simply reach the quantitative floor of their Stage and sit at it, and their children inherit a place with no certified practitioners in it, and inside forty years the district buys its wards from somewhere else at somebody else’s price.
The Legion has never taken a district this cheaply. The Legion is aware of this.

Attribution of lineage
The Bench rules what Provenance Grade a lot actually contains, on assay, without regard to the seller’s warranty.
This is where the money lives. A house that has bought against a Grade V warranty and receives a Grade III ruling has been ruined in a sentence. Roughly forty such rulings issue in a year, and the Bench issues them without visible discomfort.

The Attribution names the class. It does not name the source.
Archives has proposed individual source attribution on the seal in three compilations and Arbitration has opposed it in three, on the stated grounds that individual attribution would give every Grade IV holding a standing claimant among the source’s surviving family, and that the resulting caseload would exceed the Division’s capacity inside a year.
Which is true. It is also the clearest statement anyone in the Accord has ever committed to writing about the actual size of the Grade IV trade.

Source-blindness, and what it lets through
The Attribution is blind to source by design, and the design is defensible on every ground the Bench has ever cited. It is also the reason the Grade IV shortfall is bankable.
Crystal Draw taken by unlawful extraction is indistinguishable on the coil from lawfully rendered stock, because the process was the same process performed without a warrant. It therefore passes Attribution cleanly, receives a Grade IV seal, and enters commerce bonded, pledgeable and financed. The seal is honest. It reports what the lot contains. It has never claimed to report where the lot came from and nobody has ever asked it to.

The gap in the procedure is one instrument wide. Entry requires two independent assays against Nine-Nail Attestation Salt, in separate halls, by two Measurewrights. Both are coil assays.
A coil reads Holding. An assay fork reads density. On stock taken out of an unsealed operation the two will not reconcile, and the discrepancy is the size of what was taken. The comparison is trivial, the reagents are already in the Index, and the procedure has never required the second reading.
Archives has not proposed it. The Measurewrights have not proposed it. Arbitration would have to hear what came back.

Reservation
A formula may be entered and simultaneously reserved: lawful, real, indexed, and forbidden to any practitioner below a stated rank.

Reservation is the most-used power and the one nobody writes treatises about, because it denies nothing to anyone. It merely arranges who is permitted to be capable.
Twenty-two of the forty-five entries in the current public Index carry a reservation, and the reservations cluster with perfect regularity at exactly the rank at which a practitioner becomes useful to the Accord and not before.

Session Procedure

      
      
      
      chain missing a Boundary rolePETITIONreference lot, full glyphchain in Parunic,and a named practitionerwho will stand as authorASSAYtwo Measurewrightsindependently, againstNine-Nail AttestationSalt, in separate hallsDOCTRINAL READArchives reads for thefour glyph rolesand WellspringauthorizationRULINGArbitration puts thequestionall three chairs answerAPPEALat the appellant's cost,before Arbitrationsitting alone, undertruth-bindingREFUSED OUTRIGHTnot appealable
The last petition requirement, a named practitioner who will stand as the formula’s author, is why a great many formulas in general use are not entered. Somebody has to put their name on it.
Disagreement between the two assays beyond tolerance sends the lot back and is recorded. A house whose lots repeatedly disagree acquires a reputation the Index does not record and every buyer knows.

A chain missing a Boundary role is refused outright without further consideration, and the refusal is not appealable, and this is the single rule in the entire procedure that has never been challenged in six centuries.
Everyone in the trade has seen what a working without limits does when it runs out of the material it was given and starts on the material it was not.

Unanimity is not required. Two chairs may carry a ruling where the third dissents, and the dissent is entered in full, which is the mechanism by which the Measurewrights’ objection to the Class VI grading practice has appeared in every compilation since the first and been overruled in every compilation since the first.
Fourteen appeals have succeeded. Nine hundred and something have not, and the Division stopped publishing the denominator in Year 680 on the stated grounds that it was discouraging legitimate appeals.
The Record of Strikings
One hundred and forty-one formulas struck in the last century. The following are the ones instructors are expected to know.

































YearStriking631The Ninefold Suture · A Verdantia binding compound in general use in field infirmaries for two centuries. Struck on doctrinal grounds after a reread found the Sealing role carried by a glyph that had drifted in meaning since entry. The Measurewrights recorded that the compound had never once failed in the field and that the Striking was doctrinally correct, and entered both statements in the same paragraph654The Fourth Bench session · Sealed. The formula struck is not named in the public Index. Its existence is inferable only from a gap in the numbering and from the fact that the Standing Index carries a product named for the session and does not explain the name668Whitethroat Draught · Struck on demonstrated harm after eleven deaths in the goblinoid workshops of the Expanse. The workshops had reported the failure mode themselves, in writing, four years earlier, and the report is in the Archives with a clerk’s endorsement on it and no action attached691Threshold Reversal Draught · Struck on demonstrated harm. Retained in the Index for identification so field officers can recognize the product. Nine seizures since, all eastern, and Enforcement’s own assessment is that the seizures represent a small fraction of circulation703The Withdrawn Draught · Struck, records sealed. An X-Grade entry with nothing in it, carried in the public Index as a name, a Grade, and the word withheld repeated eleven times. The shape of the row is the only public evidence that the session occurred714Four petitions concerning Stage VI · Four houses in three quarters petitioned within eighteen months to enter formulas claimed to supply the Glory Catalyst. All four were refused at doctrinal read. The Bench’s published reasoning is one sentence long and states that a Catalyst is not a property of matter. What the four houses had actually built, and what happened to the practitioners they built it on, is not in the public record. The sentence is mechanically correct and the Bench does not appear to know why it is correct. A Threshold product supplies the melt with a seed, and a seed is a law the subject survived into existence. Matter can carry a seed. It cannot supply the surviving
The standing dissent of the Measurewrights
The Guild has reviewed the assay basis of all one hundred and forty-one Strikings and finds the instrument work sound in one hundred and thirty-nine, a better record than the Guild expected and a worse thing to have to report than it appears.

The Guild further records that of the one hundred and forty-one:
Ninety-six originated east of the Ring or in goblinoid workshops.
None originated in a house holding a standing supply contract with a Concord Division.
The Bench has never in its history struck a formula upon which a Division’s own operations depend.
The Guild offers no explanation for the distribution and endorses none of the four that have been offered to it. The Guild’s position is that the instrument is honest, that the Guild will continue to say what the needle says, and that where the needle and the ruling agree it does not follow that the ruling was made because of the needle.

Crown and Bench
The Crown holds the land, the law, the levy, the tax and the right to hang. The Accord holds the assay, the rank, the credit, the writ and the arrays. Neither can abolish the other and both have costed it.

The Bench is where that arrangement is actually administered, and it is administered by not being discussed.
A crown that quarrels with the Bench does not lose a war. It loses entry on the formulas its own arsenals are built around, quietly, over two or three sittings, on grounds that are every time doctrinally impeccable.

Two crowns have tried. One withdrew the quarrel. The other is Kaetran, and the Kaetran arsenals are still supplied, and the terms on which they are supplied are not published, and the Bench’s Kaetran rulings since have been notably swift and notably favorable, and the Measurewrights have entered a note observing this and have not been asked to remove it.

The coalition’s heartland is the Sealed Charter of the Concord, on the ground at Sealhall. Above it stands the Citadel, and around it run the Gates that bind the sworn together and the small sworn force and the loud hired ones that defend them.


The Concord Citadel
The Concord Gate Network Filed under the Codex of Absolute Magical Law, Article XIII: “On Movement, Distance, and the Passage Between Realms.”
The Concord Military Filed under the Codex of Absolute Magical Law, Article XV: “On Defense, Dominion, and the Ethics of Force.”

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Concord Citadel
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Say itthe KON-kord SIT-ah-del
Filed under the Codex of Absolute Magical Law, Article XVI: “On the Heart of Law and the Architecture of Order.”

The Concord Citadel, called the City of Latticeglass, does not exist in one realm alone. It is a nexus suspended between planes, visible only to those bound to the Lattice. To the sworn, standing in the forecourt of the Hall of the Seal at Sealhall and looking up, a towering crystal spire encircled by radiant bridges of light. To spirits, a song made structure. To everyone else, weather, and a fee to have it explained.
The Codex says the city does not simply house the Accord. It says the city is the Accord.

Ask in any hiring hall from Kingsbridge to the arc, and they will tell you the Accord is the green door behind them and the woman who runs the board. They pay their fee to a place most of them will never see, and they have heard the same stories about it that you are about to, and they sing rude songs about those too. A Guildlord climbs to it perhaps once in a life, through the old Gate in the forecourt, if she has sworn, and comes home quiet for a week. The coalition’s business is done on the ground at Sealhall, under the bones of the Ribs. The Citadel is where the machinery of the Codex lives, and where the five Heads go to be told what the Vault will bear. This page is the Codex’s account of it, in the Codex’s voice, and nobody at Research and Archives has ever offered to correct it.
The Citadel’s Nature
The Citadel was not built by human hands. It grew around the Heart Vault, a massive Wellspring Core (Fountainhead on the survey, the top of the ladder) that crystallized into self-awareness after the Harmonial Age. A Core held and worked is a dungeon somebody cleared, so by the delvers’ reckoning the City of Latticeglass is the greatest dungeon anyone has ever kept, and who cleared it is not a question the Accord has a form for. Scholars still argue whether a dungeon thinks. Scholars posted here stop arguing, and ask for a transfer. The High Concordant’s soul is woven into this Vault; their breath sustains the Citadel’s glow.
Within its translucent walls, time flows by resonance, not sequence. Couriers cross days in minutes. Archives update themselves before events occur. Those who dwell too long forget what direction means.

      
      
      
      encircles allTHE COUNCIL SPIREsummit · hollow column ofrefracted lightTHE CHAMBER OF STILLFLAMEapex, behind eleven sealsTHE ARCHIVES ETERNALcrystalline corridors ·the Vault of ParunTHE CHORAL SANCTUMcore · the Choir of theFallenTHE HEART VAULTdeeper than the Archivesthe Wellspring of LawTHE CITY BELOWguild quarters, trainingsanctums,Gate plazas, the Forum ofBalanceTHE RING WALLSthe Halo Array · orbitingrather than standing
The Council Spire
A hollow column of refracted light where the Concord Council convenes. The chamber’s floor is an unbroken mirror of living Aether; its surface ripples whenever truth is spoken.
The High Concordant presides from the Throne of Resonance, surrounded by seven empty chairs, one for each Division, and one for the silence of the Black Concord.

Every decree issued here becomes law the moment it is spoken. The Lattice records the words before the speaker finishes them, binding them into metaphysical permanence.
It is said that even gods tremble when their names echo in this hall.

The Archives Eternal
A labyrinth of crystalline corridors containing the sum of all Accord knowledge. Each document is alive, runic paper that breathes, scrolls that whisper their own memories. The walls hum with a low tone known as the Librarian’s Chord, believed to be the voice of Urion, Archon of Memory.

The most sacred texts are stored within the Vault of Parun, accessible only through ritual bloodline resonance or divine authorization. Inside rests the original Concord Codex, a tome of translucent glass pages that rewrites itself according to the world’s balance.
When the Codex’s pages still, it means the world’s rhythm is dying.

The Choral Sanctum
At the Citadel’s core lies the Choir of the Fallen, a cathedral housing the souls of those who died in service. Their echoes drift through luminous air, singing endlessly in harmonic frequencies that stabilize the Lattice across realms.
Every Accord member can feel their hum in moments of silence, a comforting vibration at the edge of hearing. The song grows louder during Wellspring crises, guiding Sealwrights and field agents toward equilibrium.

“In service, the soul is not lost; it becomes the sound that keeps the world awake.”

The Heart Vault
Beneath the Sanctum, deeper than even the Archives, the High Concordant communes directly with the Lattice. This chamber holds the Wellspring of Law, the first metaphysical convergence ever stabilized by mortal and divine cooperation. It glows with a blinding white that casts no shadow.
Every Concord Seal, sworn oath, and Merit flows first through this light before reaching the rest of creation.

The Vault hums in rhythms that mirror the High Concordant’s pulse. If they die unsucceeded, the Vault stills, and the Guild Accord collapses. The signed halls would keep their silver and their grudges. Everything sworn would not survive the night.
Only three beings have ever entered the Vault and returned alive. None spoke of what they saw.

The City Below
A sprawling complex of halls, guild quarters, training sanctums, and Gate plazas. Here the sworn of every realm converge: soldiers, mages, Sealwrights, and scholars walking side by side, each guild quarter hung in its own colors and every one of them insisting it has the worst rooms. The air is perpetually filled with light rain, the condensation of Aether in its purest form, and on a clear morning the whole city glitters like a jeweler’s tray.
At its center stands the Forum of Balance, where the sworn bring disputes before minor Arbiters. Every verdict echoes upward to the Council Spire, imprinting itself in the Codex as precedent.

Justice in the Accord is circular, born below, judged above, recorded forever.

The Outer Defenses
Encircling the Citadel are the Ring Walls, colossal shields of prismatic stone that orbit rather than stand. They refract incoming attacks, magical, divine, or otherwise, turning them into auroral storms that feed the Wellspring Core. The system, called the Halo Array, was designed by the Titans Atla’zon and Maelor themselves.

Only twice in history have the Ring Walls fallen: once during the Eclipse Wars, and once during the Silent Rebellion of the Black Concord.
Each collapse left scars in the sky still visible to this day.

The Chamber of Still Flame
Hidden at the apex of the Spire, behind eleven seals, rests the High Concordant’s sanctum. Here the leader communes directly with the Wellsprings, receiving the law’s will as whisper and light. The chamber’s floor is a pool of liquid radiance upon which the Codex manifests messages through reflected glyphs.

No guards stand watch. None are needed.
The room itself devours intruders, rewriting them into the Citadel’s architecture. It is said the walls are made from the bones of those who broke their oaths while standing in its light.

The Citadel’s Living Law
The Citadel is not static. It rearranges its halls to reflect the Accord’s state. When peace reigns, the city glows golden and wide. When corruption festers, the corridors narrow and darken, the glass thickens, and whispers grow faint.

The Citadel’s architecture is both reflection and prophecy, a mirror of the world’s soul.

Sealwrights claim to navigate by tone rather than sight. If the city sings in minor key, danger is near. If it falls silent, the end of an era approaches.


“Here the world is written, erased, and written again. Here every breath is weighed against eternity. We are the keepers of order, the stewards of Wells, and the witnesses of our own decay. Let the Citadel endure, for while it stands, so too does the Law.”
Final engraving of the Heart Vault’s inner seal, Year 013 IC, Voyager Era

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Filed under the Codex of Absolute Magical Law, Article XIII: “On Movement, Distance, and the Passage Between Realms.”

The circulatory system of the Guild Accord, a web of metaphysical corridors linking the Mortal Kingdoms, Wellspring sanctums, and the Outer Realms through the living fabric of the Lattice. Each Gate is a stabilized wound in space, held open by Parun Glyph geometry and Aether compression.
Every Gate breathes, hums, and remembers. To step through one is to be rewritten elsewhere, and the walking has very little to do with it.

Almost nobody in the coalition has ever used one. Passage, the third thing a hall signs for, means the road: a road-writ at a fixed toll, a Long Relay stable every day’s ride, a bed and a meal at any signed hall at the hall’s price, and a market court that hears you before the market closes. That passage belongs to every token on the road, down to the Initiate carrying poles. A Gate is for the sworn, because the Gate recognizes oath and nothing else, and only a soul bound to the Lattice survives the fold. Merchants have offered astonishing sums to send a cargo through a Major Arch with a sworn carter walking beside it, and some of those sums have been accepted. Every year some drunk Journeyman with an unsworn soul tries the old Gate in the forecourt at Sealhall on a dare, and every year the Sealwright Prime on duty has the form ready.
Origin of the Network
The first Gates were forged during the Voyager Era, when the mortal world still lay fractured into isolated Wellspring territories. The High Concordant ordered the creation of the Great Arches, immense ritual structures capable of bending the Aether between distant points, built atop ley intersections and reinforced by the Titans’ residual laws of weight and continuity.
When the Codex was sealed, these became the first nine Concord Gates, immortalized as divine constructs anchored by the Lattice itself. Every Gate thereafter was patterned on these originals.
Structure and Function

      
      
      
      boundunboundTHE GATE SHELLthe physical arch, carvedofley-reactive stone orcrystal metalTHE VEIL COREa spinning Essence nucleusthat holds the Aether PathopenTHE LATTICE SEALan encoded sigil networklinkingthe Gate to the centralConcord CodexHARMONIC RECOGNITIONthe same pulse thatresonatesin Accord-bound SoulCrystalsSafe passageOverwhelming vertigoor spiritual burning
Transit feels like walking through wind and heartbeat. The world collapses into light, and the traveler reassembles where the Gate’s twin awaits.
Classifications





























TypeFunctionMajor ArchesRealm-to-Realm passages for armies, cargo and Wellspring material, each one a wonder of the world that cities have fought over and a crossing that costs a fortune to buy. Attended by a Logist and Sealwright teamMinor ArchesLocal crossings within quarters or nations, kept by whichever signed guild can afford a sworn crew, and fought over accordinglyHidden GatesRestricted or classified pathways maintained by Research & Archives or the Black ConcordMobile GatesExperimental Gate fragments that move with fleets or armies. Highly unstable and forbidden for civilian useDead GatesCollapsed portals from prior epochs, dormant until restored by Sealwrights or accidental resonance events
Command
Maintained by Logistics & Supply, directed by the Chief Logist, formally titled the Gate-Warden of the Lattice. Every Gate has three overseers: a Sealwright Prime who maintains Parun glyph synchronization, a Transit Keeper who monitors Essence drift and arrival stability, and a Concord Clerk who records every crossing in the Lattice Ledger, in ink as well, because the fee has to go somewhere.
Only the sworn bearing a valid Transit Sigil, struck in wax on a writ and paid for, may pass. Unauthorized use violates the Law of Passage and is punishable by Essence seizure or full Severance. The price of a crossing is the Logistics Division’s main income and the Sitting of Halls’ main complaint.
The Law of Passage
Five inviolable principles.





























PrincipleMeaningThe Gate Recognizes OathOnly souls bound to the Lattice can survive the foldThe World Demands BalanceEvery departure must equal an arrival. The Lattice prevents displacement paradoxDistance Is a CostEach jump burns Aether proportional to distance and Essence massSilence Protects TransitSpeaking or casting during travel risks dimensional fragmentationThe Lattice RemembersEvery crossing, even unauthorized, leaves a resonance trace that cannot be erased
The Transit Corridors
Between Gates exist extradimensional veins of light and hum that form the connective tissue of the planes. To most travelers, a corridor appears as endless mirrored pathways reflecting a thousand possible versions of themselves. To the trained mind, it is a silent river of law: pure, directionless Aether.

Time does not behave normally inside. A journey that takes seconds outside might last hours, days, or entire lifetimes in perception, depending on the stability of the traveler’s Essence. Veteran operatives call this the Drift, a test of Temperance and clarity of will.
Those who panic or lose mental cohesion can split, arriving in multiple incomplete forms across several realms. Enforcement calls this Echo Fragmentation, a form of metaphysical death worse than Severance.

Malfunctions and hazards
When a Gate destabilizes, the Veil Core emits a Lattice Surge, violent feedback of Aether that can shred travelers into resonance dust or open rifts to the Outer Realms. Causes include collapses at Wellspring sites, Essence overspend, or interference by divine entities. During such events, light bends inward, sound becomes inverted, and gravity abandons direction.
Some Gates, long abandoned, become corrupted, birthing Echo Lairs inhabited by entities known as Drifters or Gateborn, creatures assembled from failed travel resonance and fragmented souls.
The Great Lattice Lines
The entire network is built upon Lattice Lines, metaphysical arteries channeling Essence between Wellsprings. These intersect at major Gates, forming Nodes of Concord: immense energy nexuses visible from any high peak on a clear night as luminous rings.

Each Lattice Line hums with a different harmonic tone, recorded in the Accord’s archives as musical scales. The Pratorian March’s Gates hum in low C tones, representing Order, while the Eressean lines sing in high E, representing Dream.
When all tones align, it creates the Chord of Passage, the sound that holds the worlds together.

Gate Warfare
In times of large-scale conflict, Gates become both weapon and vulnerability, and the rivalry between Strategic and Logistics over who holds priority on them is the longest-running quarrel at the Citadel table. The Strategic Division can seal or weaponize a Gate by converting its Veil Core into a Resonance Burst, releasing compressed transit energy into the enemy’s realm. Such acts are forbidden under Concord Law, but precedent exists from the Eclipse Wars and the Outer Incursions.
Defensive techniques include Aether Sink Fields, which absorb Gate resonance, and Temporal Locks, which slow entry and create false exit points.
Legends speak of Gatewalkers, rare Paragon operatives capable of stepping between realms without any physical Gate, walking the Lattice Lines themselves.

“Every journey bends the law. Every return reaffirms it. The Lattice is not a road; it is a memory of where you chose to go.”
Engraved upon the first Gate of Eresse, Year 003 IC, Voyager Era

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.filePath: Factions, Bloodlines & Institutions/Powers and Polities/The Guild Accord/Seats and Arms/The Concord Military.md
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Concord Military
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Filed under the Codex of Absolute Magical Law, Article XV: “On Defense, Dominion, and the Ethics of Force.”

The Guild Accord was not founded for conquest, but preservation. Yet preservation demands teeth.
The Accord commands an army bound by resonance, with nationality left at the gate. Every soldier’s oath is a spell. Every battle a ritual of equilibrium. Their existence is both covenant and consequence.

The Articles say the Accord keeps no standing army, and the Legion drills on the plain below Sealhall every morning in blue and white, and both statements are correct, as every clerk there will be delighted to explain. A coalition of guilds does not want a great army. Merchants pay for it and hunters resent it, and no Guildlord at the Sitting of Halls wishes to see a large sworn force standing behind the clerks. So the Accord’s force of arms is three things of very different sizes: the Legion, sworn, small, and far grander on paper than on the plain; Enforcement, small, sworn and frightening; and the free companies, hired, numerous, loud, and answerable only to their instruments.
The Free Companies
Most of the fighting done under Accord wax is done by people who are getting paid for it. A free company is a guild like any other: a captain, a painted rank list, a share of the plunder written down in advance, a song, and a recruiter in a good coat. It signs under seal, and it fights like people whose wages depend on the instrument holding. The fighting guilds’ table of titles reads straight across, so a Master’s token leads a Master’s contract, and the captain’s silver says how large a contract she may sign.
The Scarlet Tally fight in painted plate and keep a running count of their dead on the side of the pay wagon, in gold leaf. The Nine-Fingered Company will take any contract and hold any bridge, and every recruit gives the company a finger on signing, or says he did. The Marrick companies of the Long Fields do not fight off contract for anyone, not by a minute. Half the rest hire out of Halcrest in the Amber Cities, whose factor houses keep contract specialists who can lay a clause across a doorway. When the Turn against the Scourge of Hell falls on the Center, the Charter pays its share by buying them in bulk.
Companies are signed, and very few are sworn. Here lies the most interesting point of law in the whole of Accord warfare. Nothing on this page that the Lattice enforces, the Law of Witness and the Law of Reversal above all, reaches a soldier who has given it nothing. A free company answers for its conduct as a contract answers: its bond is forfeit, its token struck, its letters refused. So a crown that wants an Accord-backed army without Accord scruples hires a company, and the Accord is delighted to take the fee and regrets what happens, in writing.
The Doctrine of Measured Force

“Power without restraint is corruption. Restraint without power is surrender.”

The sworn Concord military acts as a metaphysical deterrent, and no conqueror’s hand. Its forces intervene only under specific conditions: when a Wellspring site or leyline is threatened by external corruption, when a member nation violates the Codex or weaponizes Essence, when the Council issues a Realm Defense Mandate, or when the High Concordant invokes the Law of Necessary Equilibrium. It also garrisons Sealhall and the Major Arches, and it crosses the Scourge’s red-capped posts only on a Writ.

Every engagement is reviewed by Arbitration post-conflict. Each death is weighed as both moral and metaphysical consequence.
Even victory must resonate cleanly, or the Lattice rejects it.

The Enforcement Division
The Concord’s iron soul, and the one part of the machinery every hall has met. It keeps the tokens honest, hunts Codex violators and enacts the Codex’s will through direct action: arrest, containment, suppression, and when necessary, erasure.

























OrderFunctionThe Vanguard OrdersElite strike teams responding to Wellspring breaches, Domain violations, and rogue Ascendant entities. Each member bears the Sealwright Mark, allowing them to fight on metaphysical planesThe Sealwright TeamsParun Glyph specialists deploying rapid containment circles, barrier fields, and dimensional anchors. They can immobilize gods, by their own account, or stitch open rifts shut with Essence chainworkThe Null WardensSilent enforcers assigned to track and capture Codex violators and token forgers. They speak no word, their throats sealed by ritual vow, and sense corruption through harmonic dissonance rather than sightThe Tribunal MarshalsSenior Executioners of the Codex, appointed only after decades of service. They wield Concord Brands capable of stripping souls from corrupted vessels and reabsorbing them into the Lattice
Each order answers to a High Warden, who serves as both judge and general. Their presence in a realm is considered a state of martial law, and the sight of one on the road will empty a market.
The Strategic Division
Commonly called the Concord Legion, for the only thing it fields. It is the sworn force of the shared things: Sealhall, the Citadel, the Major Arches and any realm under a Defense Mandate. Blue and white, on a Writ, with the bread paid for.
Seven Legions stand on the roll, some forty thousand on paper. Two stand at strength on any given morning. The rest are cadres of sworn officers and a colored banner, filled out when a Mandate is voted and the Sitting of Halls has been talked into paying for it, with the Fifth still carried as a name and a hole in the accounts. This is the arrangement the guilds prefer. Legionaries are bound by a resonance cut into the bone, and they are the best-drilled soldiers in the four quarters and the most heavily audited.

























OrderFunctionThe War-Priests of UrionSpiritual tacticians who estimate an opposing force through resonance, reading movement and remaining strength from the Lattice hum. Their estimates are said aloud, hedged, and wrong often enough to keep them humbleThe Domain EngineersMagical architects who construct battlefield Domains, semi-real territories of controlled law, allowing Concord forces to fight on their own metaphysical termsThe Aether KnightsArmored guardians empowered by harmonic Wellsprings. Their weapons are forged through the memories of the deadThe Lattice PilotsSpecialized mages capable of guiding Concord fleets and Gate crossings through dimensional instability
At the apex stands the High Marshal of the Accord, who sits on the Council beside the High Warden and Prime Arbiter, forming the Triumvirate of Balance.
The Codex Protocols
Combat laws enforced on every battlefield the Legion takes, and on no free company that has not signed them in.





























LawProvisionThe Law of LimitationWeapons of mass metaphysical effect may only be deployed under a Master’s clearance or higherThe Law of WitnessEvery battle must be recorded by a Concord Scribe or Seer. Unrecorded wars are considered illegalThe Law of SilenceOuter Realm entities captured alive must not be named. Names grant continuityThe Law of ReturnAny Accord soldier who dies defending a Wellspring site becomes part of its flow. Their essence cannot be reclaimedThe Law of ReversalIf the Concord becomes aggressor, the Lattice strips their resonance, disabling the entire army
Violation can cause entire divisions to lose their Essence harmonics, rendering weapons inert until repentance or dissolution.
The Spirit Armory
All sworn Concord weaponry and armor is crafted within the Spirit Armory of Praevissar, known as the Thousand-Forged Hall. Blacksmiths and spiritual engineers use Soul Crystallization, shaping weapon-forms through voluntary memory sacrifice. The smiths are guild smiths, with guild titles that cap the Grade they may make like anyone’s, and they will tell you at length that nothing a free company’s money can buy comes close.

Every weapon remembers its wielder. Every shield hums with ancestral resonance.
The Lawbrand · the standard Concord blade. Seals Essence instead of spilling blood.
Resonant Harness · armor that hums with the wielder’s Temperance stage, its protective strength scaling with spiritual refinement.
Parun Rods · multi-glyph devices carried by Sealwrights, used to deploy or disrupt magical law.
Oathflame Gauntlets · wielded by High Wardens. Ignite when corruption is near, the light burns truth into the flesh of the guilty.

Weapons are never inherited. They choose successors by harmonic familiarity.
The Divine Warfare Clause
The Accord acknowledges that not all wars are mortal. When Titans, Archons, or divine manifestations threaten the planes, the Divine Warfare Clause is invoked: the High Concordant gains temporary full dominion over all Wellsprings and their armies. Ascended entities are called from the Lattice Choir to serve as divine generals, and mortal commanders defer to Aetheric Protocol, where physical tactics are replaced by harmonic resonance duels, wars fought through the rewriting of reality itself.

Such wars are measured in continuities lost, more than in casualties. A realm may survive, yet wake changed, its rivers, names, and skies rewritten by divine consequence.
Only the High Concordant may end such a war by decree, invoking the Absolute Seal, which resets the battlefield to pre-conflict conditions at the cost of countless lives’ memories.

The Enforcement Ethics
All Enforcement and Strategic personnel are bound by three sacred Oaths, carved into their bones at initiation.

The Oath of Blindness · “We see corruption, not race, creed, or kin.”
The Oath of Burden · “Our lives are weights upon the scale.”
The Oath of Still Flame · “We burn only when law demands.”
These oaths glow when the bearer lies or hesitates in their duty. Should an agent willingly break their oath, their Essence immediately collapses into the Lattice, rendering them soulless, a living husk called a White Shell.

The Oath of Blindness has been cut into the bones of the officers who enforce the Beastkin Classification Provision at Verath, and they will show you the scar. Readers may do with that what they like.
Wars of Wells
The most sacred responsibility of the Concord Legions. These are wars of Essence, fought for no one’s land. Each side attempts to alter the balance of Wellspring resonance across realms using mass Aetheric rituals and Divine Conduits.
Concord strategy focuses on harmonic interference, breaking the enemy’s rhythm sooner than their armies. To capture a Wellspring site is to hold the lens a whole country sees through; to lose one is to weaken the world’s stability.

During the last War of Wells, the Concord sealed six corrupted Wellspring sites at the cost of one hundred thousand lives and a third of the Lattice’s total light.
No victory since has felt holy.

Heroes and Legends
The Codex forbids pride in duty, and so the Guild Accord rarely speaks the names of its champions. Every tap-room on the continent makes up the difference.
Ser Varnath Rhogar, the Scorn of the Outer World, held a Gate open with his body long enough for a million souls to flee.
Aerym Snowveil, Veilkeeper of Iampu, froze an entire ocean to trap an invading god.
Karo Venrik, the Foolish Magus, turned his own Essence into harmonic resonance to stabilize a collapsing Wellspring site.
Opalis Maethryn, the Radiant Arbiter, judged ten nations in silence and restored the law through mercy.
Their names are engraved in the Wall of Resonance, deep beneath the Concord Citadel, where only the High Concordant may walk. They are also on a good many tavern signs.

“To hold the law is to become its weapon. To wield the law is to become its wound. We are the first flame and the final breath, the sound between creation and collapse.”
Engraved upon the Hall of the Vanguard, Year 014 IC, Voyager Era

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.filePath: Factions, Bloodlines & Institutions/Powers and Polities/The Guild Accord/Structure and Rank/Merit and Severance.md
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: Merit and Severance
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Filed under the Codex of Absolute Magical Law, Article X, “On Worth and Wages of Service,” and Article XI, “On Betrayal, Dissolution, and the Price of Unbinding.”

“Where coin fades, Merit endures.”
The Codex. Chalked beside it in most hiring halls: “Where’s my coin?”

Everybody in the coalition is paid. The trouble is that it has two payrolls. A signed member, a mercer or a hunter or a free company’s drummer, is paid in coin, shares and letters of credit, and if she cheats she is struck from the roll and nobody will deal with her. A sworn member, who has given a fragment of the soul to the Concord Lattice, is paid as well in something the old Codex calls Resonance Merit, and she can be struck from something a good deal older than a roll. This page holds both, because both hang on the same hall wall.
What the Signed Are Paid
Shares, bounties and fees. A crew takes shares in a venture, a craftsman takes the price of the work, a courier takes carriage, a free company takes its contract, all of it entered in ink and enforceable in any signed market court.
Rights that come with the title. A token opens what its numeral covers: the board up to its bounty Grade, the stall up to its Rarity, the forge up to its Grade, the Long Relay’s stables, the hall’s bed at the hall’s price. A rising hunter also gets entries on the roll, and those matter more than she thinks. A hall chooses who gets a patron’s Draft and who gets a hard crew by reading its roll, and the poor rise largely by being worth somebody’s bet.
The window and the roll are different documents. Level moves by hard and real work, danger overcome above all, and it shows on your own window where nobody else can check it. The roll holds what your hall will swear to. They need not agree. A crew’s luggage who landed the killing bolt will have the Level and none of the entry, and the argument has broken up better crews than any monster has.
Temperance Merits
For the sworn, each successful Commission also grants Merit Points, commonly called Echo Marks, held in the Lattice and imprinted upon the Soul Crystal as faint glyph-lines visible only under Concord light. In the Dark Ages they are entries first of all, in ink, by the Bench’s power of entry on the roll, and the glyph-lines follow. The more difficult the mission, the stronger the resonance engraved into the soul.













































TitleRecognition, for the swornInitiateMinor resonance. Proof of first steps upon the Tiered PathApprenticeSmall merit increases; early recognition by guild instructors and mentorsJourneymanTrue harmonic trace. Proof of independent capabilityAdeptThe first to earn the formal title of Concord AgentExpertSealwright designation available. Trusted with enforcement authorityMasterElevated to Warden of Duty. Authorized to lead large-scale operationsGrandmasterNamed Envoy of the Lattice. Recognized across realmsArchmasterBearer of the Concord Flame. Living arbiter between mortal and divine lawParagonNamed Chosen of the Codex. Name permanently inscribed in the Lattice Ledger as recipient of Zenith Decree
Essence Compensation
Beyond Merit, sworn operatives are compensated through what the Codex calls Aether Credits: draughts (the keepers’ unit of time at a Core’s pool) and letters of credit against a factor house, each encoded with one’s personal signature and exchangeable for equipment, reagents, or relic access at any hall.
Low-Tier · Drafts, spirit shards, training sigils. Mid-Tier · relic vouchers, rare materials, research licenses. High-Tier · divine artifacts, personal Wellspring rights, a top tempering Draft out of the Accord’s own stores, or political elevation within the Accord.

Because each sworn credit is soul-bound, theft or falsification invokes Essence Reversal, a punishment that drains the thief’s resonance until the debt is repaid in spirit or death. Forging a signed member’s letter merely gets you hanged.

Advancement rights
Relic Rights · permission to wield or bond with Concord-sanctioned artifacts. Wellspring Visitation · access to active Wellspring sites for study or attunement. Gate Access · travel through the Concord Gate Network. Ritual Command · authorization to lead Essence Sealing, Purification, and Binding rites. Political Authority · eligibility to serve as Envoy, Tribunal Judge, or Council Advisor.
All rights are granted through Arbitration following a Temperance evaluation and the signing of the Oath of Merit.
Merit conversion and legacy
Merit can be spent, traded, or transmuted into Concord Favor, a political currency used by guilds and nations. A single high-Tier Merit may equate to months of negotiation leverage or a lifetime of recognition. But:


“Merit spent is memory lost.”

Excessive conversion weakens the soul’s resonance, and many veterans retire before their Essence begins to fade from overuse.
Those who die in service become part of the Lattice Choir, fragments of harmonic memory that continue to echo through the Guild network. Their names are sung each solstice within the halls of the High Concordant.

“The Concord does not pay in coin. It pays in remembrance.”


The hiring halls sing their dead too, at a different volume, in the tap-room, and the song usually gets the details wrong.
What a Hall Can Do to You
Struck. A hall or a court strikes your title. The news goes down the road faster than you can, and by the next market nobody will hold your coat.
Excluded. A hall struck from the roll loses every token it ever issued. Its weights no longer pass, its letters no longer clear, the rider stops coming. This is the Accord’s real weapon, and it has emptied whole towns with no one raising a hand.
Reserved. The Bench of Attribution withholds a standing pending determination. A person under reservation is not condemned and cannot trade, which is worse.
Hanged, by someone else. The Accord cannot execute anybody, and it is rarely short of a crown that will. A forged token goes this way more often than not.
The Nine Laws of Severance
The Codex holds that it is law, etched into the fabric of the Lattice itself, and for those who have sworn to it this is a plain description of what happens. A signed member who has given the Lattice nothing has nothing for it to take, and faces only the hall and the court above. For the sworn, when a member violates that truth, the Lattice responds. It restores balance, and vengeance does not enter into it.























































LawTriggerConsequenceI · Fracture of OathBreaking a direct promise under the Concord sealThe Soul Crystal fractures along its outer ring; Lattice connection dims. Minor fractures cause Essence sickness or amnesia. Severe fractures cause Lattice Silence, the inability to channel or perceive Essence at allII · Seal of RejectionWillful defiance of a Concord order, or falsifying a mission reportBranded with a Reject Sigil, visible to all who bear Accord sight. Prevents use of any sanctioned Wellspring site, relic, or Gate. The branded are known as Forsworn. Many wander until they wither, for the world itself rejects their resonanceIII · Brand of CorruptionTampering with or corrupting a Wellspring site without sanctionEssence inverted; emotion becomes toxicity. Enforcement is authorized to enact Essence Severance, removing the corrupted portion of the soul by force. Survivors rarely remain whole. If corruption spreads to the site itself, the accused’s life is forfeitIV · Parunic SilenceSpeaking forbidden glyphs, teaching the Divine Language without sanction, unsanctioned Aether draftsSilencing, removal of one’s voice in body and spirit. Their speech becomes inaudible to all beings who still bear Essence, rendering them ghosts within realityV · The Concord TrialGuilt uncertainA Trial of Resonance in the Neutral Chambers under the Ribs at Sealhall, where lies cannot survive. The soul’s harmony is measured: if it hums true, absolved; if discordant, the Lattice itself convicts them. The Codex holds that this trial supersedes all mortal courts and that its verdict is final. The crown courts dispute both wherever they reach the accused firstVI · Excision of MemoryCrimes regrettable but redeemable: relic theft, negligence, desertionCleansing through Forgetting. A Sealwright removes the crime and its motive from the soul. The offender begins anew, but at the cost of self. Some accept this willingly, calling it the Second BirthVII · Shadow AbsorptionProving useful but irredeemably dangerousConscription into the Black Concord. Names, faces and records erased; memories rewritten for covert service. Only the High Concordant knows their true identity. They are called Shades of the Lattice, and they are both prisoner and weaponVIII · Total SeveranceBetraying the Accord’s foundation: attempted divine ascension, mass destruction of Wellspring sites, inter-realm rebellionThe soul is exiled from the Lattice entirely, erased from existence, with more than mere death in it. No resurrection, no record, no echo. To the Concord, they never were. Even memory recoils from their nameIX · Balance RestoredJudgment concludedRemaining Essence is absorbed by the Lattice and redistributed among the Wellspring sites. Even in death, every punishment feeds the order that governs reality. The Concord does not destroy to avenge; it destroys to balance
A sworn person feels the breach before anyone else knows of it: a Lattice oath is a vow, and the window shows its terms, and a broken vow lands at once. The Measurewrights who have studied the Second Birth report that the window keeps a blank line where the excised crime was, and that some people spend the rest of their lives looking at it.
Notes of redemption
Though the Accord is absolute, mercy is not forgotten. A soul may regain connection to the Lattice through service, confession, or the sacrifice of one’s life to defend a Wellspring site. This process, called Resonant Penance, is perilous, many attempt it, few return. Those who do are marked with a faint silver sigil over the heart, denoting a Soul Rewoven.
Enforcement and oversight
Punishments are administered jointly by Arbitration and Enforcement under the Prime Arbiter. High-level Severances require Concord Council sanction or direct approval from the High Concordant. All judgments are witnessed by three officials, a Seer, a Sealwright, and a Scribe, whose Essences intertwine to confirm the act in the Lattice Ledger.

“The Accord forgives only those who restore balance. For law is not vengeance; it is remembrance made divine.”
