factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: Structure and Rank
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Who is in the coalition and how it runs, what its nine titles promise, how it pays and strikes, the Division it will not name, and what its soldiers are taught about the people who outweigh them.


The Guild Accord in the Dark Ages — Divisions, Companies, Academies and Offices The Accord did not conquer anybody. It chartered them, and then it was the only thing that worked in all of their courts at once.
The Tiered Path The nine titles, the same in every guild, and the fighting guilds’ table
Merit and Severance Filed under the Codex of Absolute Magical Law, Article X, “On Worth and Wages of Service,” and Article XI, “On Betrayal, Dissolution, and the Price of Unbinding.”
The Black Concord Filed under Restricted Article XII, “On Necessary Concealment.” Access Level: Parun Lock Authority, Eyes of the High Concordant only.
The Practitioner Problem Standing Doctrine on Individuals Who Outweigh Regiments

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.filePath: Factions, Bloodlines & Institutions/Powers and Polities/The Guild Accord/Structure and Rank/The Black Concord.md
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Black Concord
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Filed under Restricted Article XII, “On Necessary Concealment.” Access Level: Parun Lock Authority, Eyes of the High Concordant only.

There exists a Division that the public Codex does not name. A record that does not echo in the Lattice. A shadow that moves where the law cannot tread.
The Black Concord is not evil, nor good. It is the void between truths, where the Lattice stores the acts that must never resonate.

Purpose
An archivist’s note, pinned in. Every hiring hall has a joke about the Black Concord, usually involving the obsidian wax, and nobody in Waxgate will tell you who makes it. The merchants’ Guildlords hold that a coalition which pays for this deserves to see the accounts. They have asked. The reply was a blank sheet, properly sealed. The document below comes to us from the old machinery that predates the coalition, and it does not mention the coalition at all.
The Black Concord exists to safeguard the Concord Codex from internal collapse and metaphysical exposure. When truths too great to exist threaten the order (divine uprisings, Titan awakenings, collapsed Wellspring sites, or human ascensions gone wrong), the Black Concord acts before the world can learn.
Unlike other Divisions, it answers only to the High Concordant. Its operations are invisible to the Concord Council, and its members’ names are expunged from both mortal and divine record.

“In silence, the law endures.”

Structure
Hierarchy is simple and absolute. Each rank is an echo of absence.





























RankFunctionThe OverseerThe unseen hand. Speaks directly with the High Concordant. Their existence may be theoreticalThe WraithsElite agents drawn from the Severed, Reborn, or Paragon operatives. Each holds a false identity in public lifeThe ShadesField operatives with erased lineage and rewritten memories. Infiltrators, assassins, containment specialistsThe Scribes of AshArchivists who record erased history on fading vellum, then burn the pages to seal events from timeThe Null PriestsRitualists responsible for metaphysical redactions. They silence Wellspring sites or kill gods through temporal sealing
Every mission, name, and record is burned after execution. Only the Overseer retains fragmented knowledge, stored in a sealed chamber called the Echo Vault, a temporal construct that forgets itself every cycle.
Silence Grades





























GradeOperationOne · Whisper MandatesMinor covert surveillance or extraction of dangerous relicsTwo · Quieting OrdersAssassination of destabilizing figures or sealing of forbidden domainsThree · Veil MandatesRewriting of public records, memories, and events. Alteration of historical timelinesFour · Null OperationsComplete deletion of a location, cult, or entity from metaphysical existenceFive · Codex RevisionsRewriting of the Concord Codex itself. Only by direct command of the High Concordant

The Black Concord does not kill in the traditional sense. It removes resonance, severing the subject’s connection to history, leaving no echo, memory, or shadow behind.
This process is known as Aether Nullification. To the Lattice, it is as if they never lived.

Recruitment
No one joins the Black Concord by choice. They are taken, chosen from the ranks of the condemned, the Forsworn, or the dead, and only from among the sworn, since the Lattice can do nothing to a soul that never gave it a fragment. Through the Rite of Absence, their Soul Crystal is hollowed and re-tuned to the Null Frequency. Their memories are rewritten to serve the Accord’s unseen necessities.
To outsiders, these agents appear as ordinary operatives, scholars, or travelers. But the Black Concord can recognize one another by their Resonance Silence, the faint emptiness that follows in their wake, a lack of Essence hum in the world around them.
Tools and Relics

The Null Sigil A black Parun glyph that devours light, carried beneath the tongue of every operative.
The Silence Veil An Aetheric shroud that erases sound, scent, and emotion within its radius.
The Mirror of Amnesia An artifact that transfers memory from victim to user, then self-destructs.
The Oathknife A blade forged from the heart of a dead Wellspring site. Its cut severs both body and record.
The Codex Fragment The Overseer’s most sacred relic, a lost page said to contain the Lattice’s erasure command.

Sanction and Oversight
Though answerable to no one but the High Concordant, the Black Concord is monitored indirectly by the Prime Arbiter and Grand Curator through Parun Counterseals hidden in the Codex of Law.

If the Overseer ever defies the High Concordant’s will, those seals activate the Reverse Lattice Protocol, erasing the Black Concord entirely, including all its records and members.
It has been triggered only once. The result was the Night of Unremembering, when half the Accord’s archives vanished and three Divisions forgot an entire century of their own history.

Known Operations · Declassified Fragments

Operation Ecliptica Erasure of the Divinity known as Sire Ophen, who attempted to overwrite the Harmonial Law.
Operation Pale Gate Sealing of the Rift at the Southern Wellspring site during the Withering.
Operation Emberveil Assassination of ten Archmagisters who attempted to create a synthetic Titan.
Operation White Silence Deletion of an entire city from the Mortal Plane after its citizens achieved collective Ascension without sanction.


These fragments remain partially remembered only because the Black Concord allowed them to be remembered, a warning to those who believe the law cannot bleed.

The Obsidian Seal on a board means an X- or EX-Grade bounty and a posting nobody will read aloud. A crew that takes one is paid extremely well and tends to change its name afterward. Hall gossip holds that the same hand is behind the Crystal Draw that has never balanced on the Bench’s returns, on either side of the crime, depending on who is drinking. Nobody has evidence, and the people who went looking for it are not on the Wall any more.
The Doctrine of Necessary Concealment
The Black Concord operates under one sacred paradox.


Truth unspoken preserves the world.

For every hero the Lattice celebrates, a hundred silent shadows die to make the story believable. When the Accord proclaims peace, it is the Black Concord who kills the memory of war. When the Accord restores balance, it is the Black Concord who buries what must never be known.
Their existence is both crime and salvation, the sin that keeps the law pure.
“If this record is read, you were meant to. If it is remembered, then silence has failed. May the shadows remain loyal where light cannot.”
Excerpt from the High Concordant’s personal Lattice writ, Year 027 IC, Voyager Era

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.title: The Guild Accord in the Dark Ages — Divisions, Companies, Academies and Offices
factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
The Accord did not conquer anybody. It chartered them, and then it was the only thing that worked in all of their courts at once.

At the Midsummer Riding of Aldersey in Year 688 the Worshipful Company of Chandlers, in mustard, and the Worshipful Company of Saddlers, in oxblood, reached the narrow end of Fish Street at the same moment, each with its Master on a white horse, its Beadle on foot in front with the silver mace, and a settled belief that it rode eighth. The order of the Twelve Great companies had been fixed by a ruling nobody living had seen made. The Chandlers’ Clerk, who was eighty-one, unrolled the company’s copy and read it aloud in the street. The Saddlers’ Clerk unrolled the Saddlers’ copy and read that aloud over him, and the two copies said the same words, which is the whole trouble, because the words will bear either reading. The Beadle of the Chandlers then hit the Beadle of the Saddlers across the ear with four pounds of silver.
It took the whole of the afternoon to stop. Apprentices came over the barricades of both companies’ feast-wagons, the Scalded Cats’ outer disciples joined in on the Chandlers’ side for the sake of an old grudge with somebody else entirely, and when a torch went into the Chandlers’ second wagon nine hundredweight of good wax went running down the Fish Street gutter on fire, in a long gold stream with burning hats in it, and the fishwives hauled their stock up the steps cursing both liveries. Two people died, one of them a Warden who had only come out to complain. The mayor fined both companies, the market court fined them both again for the fish, and the Bench of Attribution, asked to rule on the ruling, regretted that a precedence was not a formula. Every year since, both companies have ridden eighth. They ride on alternate sides of the street, at the same pace, not looking at each other, and the town turns out in numbers to watch it not happen.
Everything the Guild Accord is shows in that street: a charter, a Clerk who outlasted forty Masters, a Beadle who carries the mace at the feast and throws you out of the hall, a wax seal, an old ruling, two guilds who would die before sharing a place in the line and who both carry the same silver, and a crowd that knows every rank in the procession by its color. What follows is the coalition as it stands in the Dark Ages, in wax and ink, down to who eats by what.
I. A Coalition with an Old Engine
The Accord looks like two different institutions depending on which door you came in by, and both are correct.
The coalition is the guilds. Adventurers’ guilds, merchant guilds, craft guilds, alchemists, healers, couriers, free companies and every other trade with a hall, across many nations, each with its own colors and grudges. They have signed on for three things: shared rank, enforceable contracts and passage. This binds by consent and by interest. Most of it is new, and most of the people in it think of the Accord as the thing their hall pays a fee to.
The engine is what they signed on to. It has two parts, both seven centuries old. The Chancery is the jurisdiction: the formulary, the articles, the market courts, the standards, the proof-marks, the Bench. The Concordat is the covenant: the Codex, the Lattice, the fragment of Soul Crystal offered on swearing, the Trials of Resonance. This binds the sworn spiritually rather than legally, which is why a sworn practitioner cannot resign.
They are one body because they flow from one power: the charter. The Accord’s actual instrument is the ability to grant a standing and to take it away. A guild holds its charter on the roll. An academy holds its charter on the roll. A member holds a title because a hall on the roll conferred it. Remove the charter and the hall is a building full of people with no legal ability to sell what they know. The halls know this, and they know as well that without their fees the engine stops by the next quarter day, and that mutual understanding is the whole of the constitution.
What it is on the ground
Nobody should picture an office. The Accord in any given town is a stone hall with a bounty board on one wall and a beam (the public scales) in the yard, a sworn clerk who may also be the only literate person for a day’s ride, a seal press in a locked chest, a Measurewright with an assay fork who comes through on circuit and is argued with, and a Hall-Warden who can fight. In a bigger town it is six or seven halls in six or seven colors, all of them hating the one with the best site on the square, sharing one beam and one court. Every instrument any of them issues is written by hand, witnessed by people who are paid to remember, and closed with colored wax. If the clerk dies the town waits until somebody sends another. A Division, seen from the Citadel, is a great lord’s household: a Head with a seal, a sworn following of scriveners, riders and assessors who eat at its table, and chests of rolls that travel when it travels. Its reach is exactly as long as a rider can go.
A register note, applied
The original document renders the machinery in an older and grander manner: Lattice-stones throwing Commissions onto the air, sigils hung in space, Aether credits, echo marks. The Dark Ages render all of it in wax, vellum and ink, and the mechanism is unchanged.





























Old renderingDark Ages renderingLattice-stones casting CommissionsThe board. Vellum, wax, a clerk, and a hall with a wall for itSigil colorsSeal colors. Green, blue, gold and obsidian wax, struck on the postingAether creditsDraughts and the bill. The keepers’ unit of time at a Core’s pool, and a letter of credit against a factor houseScry-glyph verificationThe beacon line, the field report, and a countersigning witnessEcho marksEntries. The Bench’s power of entry, on the roll, in ink
Nothing metaphysical is lost. The Lattice still holds every sworn oath, and nobody in the four quarters has ever seen a guild’s number floating in the air. The only figures that float are on your own window (the soul reporting its numbers to its owner, unseen by anyone else), and the window has no opinion about your title.
II. Where the Accord Actually Reaches
Where the Accord stands. Halls sign on one at a time, and whole countries sign in circles, and the Articles and the Commission framework bind as law only inside a signed circle. The first was signed at Kharven-Seat. Everywhere else what reaches is the coalition’s halls and the older machinery behind them: the Codex, its courts and its standards, carried by charter and taken by consent.
The Accord is unequally strong, and the pattern follows hard facts of trade and ground far more than it follows politics.
Strongest: the New World’s arc. Chartered from nothing within living memory. There is no older law to displace because there was no older law, so its chartered halls are the jurisdiction there, with no second one beside them, running the Accord’s text by charter ahead of any circle. Every settlement holds a charter, every charter names the Accord’s standards, and a company that loses its charter loses the ground it stands on. The elven old-ground beside the arc is another matter: four Eons of Eressean law the Accord did not displace. The Divisions keep more sworn clerks across the arc than in the whole of the Old World.
Strongest: the island nations. Trade-dependent, small, and unable to survive exclusion for a season. An island that will not take Accord weights cannot sell its cargo in any port that does, and the arithmetic makes the argument without anyone having to make it. Island seats are famously punctilious about standards and famously resentful about it.
Strong: the Inner World. The heartland is the Sealed Charter of the Concord, in the Center, where the wax comes from, with Sealhall’s white hall and the chancery schools and the kept roads at their densest. The Accord runs alongside crown law here rather than replacing it, and the two have grown into each other so completely that most people cannot tell you which of them issued the rule they are obeying.
Weak: the Old World. Ancient polities with law older than the Accord and no interest in being harmonized. The holds keep two columns. The Keth-Gorrum’s rulings are unreadable to Accord clerks by design. Undaar-Keth adopted the standards instantly and the jurisdiction never.
And the seam is the relay. The Accord’s practical reach ends roughly where its riders and its beacon line end, and an institution that cannot get word to its own searchers inside a season is not administering anything. Every district the Withering thins is a district the Accord quietly stops governing. The ground goes lean, the wardens and ward-cutters leave for better rounds, the hall loses its fees, and the rider stops coming. The Lease-holders are moving into exactly those districts, and the correlation has been noticed by nobody senior.
III. The Divisions, Politically
A coalition needs somebody to keep the shared things running, and the shared things are older than the coalition and came with their own staff. Five Divisions, one unacknowledged sixth, and every one of them regards the rest as competitors. Most hall members could not name them all. Each holds a different instrument and each is trying to make its instrument the one that decides.















































DivisionInstrumentEats byStanding rivalStrategicThe Legion, and the Gates as a military assetLevy on chartered realmsLogistics, over who controls Gate priority; the free companies, over who gets paidEnforcementThe Sealwrights, token fraud, and the High Warden’s presence, which is martial law wherever it standsForfeitures and amercements, which is a scandal nobody will nameArbitration, permanentlyArbitrationTreaty, mediation, feuds between halls, and the Trials of ResonanceFees from the parties, which is the same scandal from the other directionEnforcement, permanentlyResearch and ArchivesThe Archives Eternal, the Codex, and the power to say what a thing isEndowment, chairs, and the academiesNobody openly. Everybody quietlyLogistics and SupplyGate coordination, Essence transport, the letters of creditTolls and carriageEveryone, because it holds the purse; the Long Relay, which carries its letters and will not take its ordersThe Black ConcordWhatever the High Concordant requiresNot accounted for anywhereNot applicable
The two blocs. Strategic and Enforcement vote together on nearly everything and are called the hard hand by people who are not being careful. Arbitration and Research vote together and are called the long table. Logistics is the swing, holds the purse and the Gates, and has been the swing for two hundred years, which is why the Logistics head is the most courted person in the Citadel and the least likely ever to be nominated for anything.
The Sitting of Halls. The guilds’ answer to all this is younger and a good deal louder. Each territory’s halls send up a Guildlord, and the Guildlords meet at Sealhall after the Veyra’s Day fair, in every color at once, under the great bones of the Ribs. The Sitting has no vote the Council is obliged to count. It can decline to collect the hall-fee, and it did so once, for a single quarter, in the matter of the Chancery’s seal charges, and the charges came down before midsummer. Merchants’ Guildlords lead it by wealth, the adventurers’ by volume, and the White Aprons’ by being the only people present whom everyone will need eventually.
Enforcement’s funding is the structural problem nobody will touch. It eats by forfeiture. A Division that takes its revenue from the property of people it convicts has an interest in convictions, and every clerk in the Citadel knows this, and Arbitration raises it once a decade and is voted down by the hard hand.
Who pays for it. In a river town under the hard hand, Warden Cato Pelham of Enforcement seizes a miller’s stones for a false weight, because the stones are forfeit and his Sealwrights’ winter bread comes out of forfeitures. Examiner Mathilde Brask of Arbitration, who sits on the same bench, wants the fine set to the man’s means and the stones returned, because a miller without stones cannot pay any fee to anybody. Both are honest, both swear by the same Codex, and the baker at the end of the lane, who cannot get her flour ground while they argue, has walked it nine miles to the next mill and raised her price, and has been named at the next assize for it.
IV. The High Concordant
Chosen, without any election. The Council nominates. The Heart Vault accepts or does not, and there is no procedure for determining whether it has accepted other than whether the nominee survives the weaving. This is unfalsifiable and is therefore the perfect political instrument, because a failed nomination proves the candidate was unworthy and can never prove the Council chose badly. The Sitting of Halls has asked for a say in this and has been told, with great courtesy, to take it up with the Vault.
Held for life, because the office is a condition rather than a post. The Concordant’s soul is woven into the Vault at the Citadel’s core and their breath sustains the Lattice. There is no retirement and no removal, and this is the whole shape of the office.
Powers. Appointment and dismissal of Divisional Heads. Command of the Black Concord. The casting judgment in a divided Council. The charter, and the revocation of a charter, which is the power everything else rests on.
And one enormous constraint. The Concordant cannot leave the Citadel for long. The most powerful person in the four quarters cannot travel, has not seen most of what they govern, and receives everything through five Divisional Heads, each of whom decides what is worth carrying up.
So the real politics of the office lies in curation. A Head who wants a thing done does not argue for it. They arrange for the Concordant to hear about the problem it solves, three times, from three directions, over a season. Every senior person in the Citadel understands this, and none of them would call it corruption.
The succession is the whole game and it is played before the death. If the Concordant dies unsucceeded the Vault stills and the Lattice with it, and the signed halls would wake to find their tokens still good and every sworn officer on the continent in convulsions. Everyone knows this, which means the Council will accept almost any nominee rather than risk a gap. Therefore the contest is entirely over who is standing closest when the moment comes, and therefore the Concordant’s health is the most closely held and most intensively rumored fact in the Inner World, and therefore the beacon line out of the Citadel is read by more people than any other line in the world.
V. The Guilds
How a company is built
Every chartered company in the four quarters runs the same skeleton, whatever it calls the parts.
Governance. A Master, elected annually, styled Prime Warden or Upper Bailiff in some companies and addressed by that title without exception at any formal occasion. Beneath the Master, Wardens, from whose number the next Master is normally chosen. Together with a body of Assistants, including past Masters as permanent members, they form the Court of Assistants, which governs and which is self-appointing, and that last word is the entire politics of the guild system.
Officers. The Clerk is the chief officer, keeps the records, calls the meetings, and in practice runs the company, since Masters last a year and Clerks last thirty. The Beadle assists the Clerk, leads processions, and acts as a constable, which means the man who carries the mace at a feast is the same man who throws you out of the hall.
Membership, in three classes.





















ClassHow reachedApprenticeIndentured to a master for seven yearsFreemanBy servitude (completing an apprenticeship), by patrimony (a parent was of the company), or by redemption (purchase)LiverymanFull membership, by vote of the Court, normally once the freeman is established in business on his own account
The freedom brings the right to work for whom you choose or to set up on your own, and in chartered seats it brings a vote. Redemption is the class question. A freeman by purchase is a freeman, is treated as one, and is never quite forgotten to have bought it, and every company has a word for such a man that it does not use in front of him.
Freedom and title are different things, and both show. Freedom and livery are your standing inside your own company. The nine titles, Initiate to Paragon, are your standing with every stranger on the road, and they travel as silver. An established Liveryman of the Chandlers may carry an Adept’s token, and a brilliant journey-hand who cannot afford the livery may carry a Master’s and still eat at the bottom of the table. See The Tiered Path.
Precedence. The order of the companies was settled once, by a body that has long since stopped existing, and has been argued about ever since. The Twelve Great take precedence at every civic occasion. The Chandlers and the Saddlers have been in dispute over the eighth and ninth places for four hundred years, and the dispute is genuinely unresolvable because the original ruling is ambiguous and both readings are defensible.
The apprentice’s morning. An apprentice of nine or ten goes to his indenture with his name on a sheet his mother cannot read, sleeps under the bench, and may by Article XII be freed if the master holds more boys than the formulary allows. Most never hear of Article XII. The ones who do tend to be the ones who become Clerks.
The kinds of guild
Craft guilds. Regulate a craft: standards of work, terms of apprenticeship, who may take hire. Smiths, Engravers, Drafters, Assayers, Fitters and Gaugers. Drafts, runes, tags and chants are skills anyone can level with use, and a guild’s title is how far the guild will vouch that you have gone. A smith’s title caps the Grade she may make. Scale, bone and hide off a monster make the top gear, and the smiths have never forgiven the hunters for knowing it.
Merchant guilds. Regulate a trade rather than a craft, and their members make nothing. The Mercers, the Salters, the great houses of Altherion, the factor houses of the Amber Cities. These outrank craft guilds in wealth and are outranked by them in precedence, and neither side has ever stopped minding. A merchant’s title caps the Rarity he may sell, and the second signature on a piece above his silver is a fee a great many people live on.
Alchemists. The Drafters’ Company is a craft guild and the Alchemists’ Society is something stranger. It restricts senior membership to actual practitioners, unlike the companies, most of which long ago stopped requiring that the Master of the company practice the trade the company is named for: a man may be a freeman of it by purchase and may not sit on its Court unless he can work. Between them they render the monster cores the hunters bring in, into the Essence Drafts used for tempering. Drafts can supply a Catalyst, Stages can be bought, and the great houses hoard the top Drafts, so an alchemist’s guild is the nearest thing the world has to a mint for power, and everybody treats it accordingly.
Healers. The Company of Leeches and Bonesetters, the White Aprons, run a price board by the door. Pre-modern medicine first and in plain words, then a slow recovery that leaves scars and limits, and a Verdantia hand (Verdantia being the Wellspring of living growth) only for those who can pay. A wound is a status line on your window that stays until treated, and healing is priced, so the rich walk off what cripples the poor. The guild’s title says what she may be paid to treat. It also keeps a free bench in every hall of any size, one morning a week, by a clause its founders wrote in and its Court has been trying to read differently for two centuries. Every hiring hall keeps a White Aprons’ account, and running one up is the fastest way to find out who your friends are.
Couriers. The Long Relay: yellow coats, a stable every day’s ride, and the only guild whose Grandmasters are mainly famous for being late once. A high-Grade rider travels faster than any commander in the old histories could think, and spends reserve doing it, and is the first thing an enemy kills. Their title says what they may be handed sealed. The beacon wardens, who keep the lamp line, regard the Relay as a nostalgic hobby, and the Relay regards a lamp as something that cannot carry a parcel.
Free companies. Mercenaries who sign under seal and fight on the strength of the instrument. Each has its colors, its painted rank list and its share of the plunder written down in advance. The Accord’s articles of war bind them only as contracts, a point of enormous interest to crowns. See The Concord Military.
The Adventurers
An adventurer is somebody who ventures capital. That is the original and correct meaning, and it is what the Company of Adventurers was chartered to do: subscribe money to a risky undertaking, in shares, against a return.
The Commission trade grew out of it, and the word walked down the street and moved into the hiring halls. A Commission is a venture, and a crew that takes one holds shares in it.

A subscriber puts up the outfitting: stores, carriage, Drafts, the Guild fees, and the bond posted against damage.
The venture is divided into shares, and the crew takes shares rather than wages. A captain takes more. A first venture takes less. A specialist bargained for in advance takes a fixed share off the top before division, which everyone else resents.
Losses fall on the subscribers, and deaths fall on the crew, and this asymmetry is the whole moral character of the trade.
A bottomry exists: a loan against the venture that is repaid only if the venture returns. It costs a great deal and it is what a crew without a patron uses.
Underwriting exists, at a price, and the Company keeps the tables, and the tables are the most honest document about mortality in the four quarters because they are written by people with money on the answer.

The five Commission Classes are unchanged. Reconnaissance, Containment, Retrieval, Arbitration, Extermination. What changes is that a crew discussing a posting is discussing terms, and the argument in the hall is about shares and the bond and who got the kill, with glory saved for the tavern, where it is plentiful.
The hiring hall. Today most people who say adventurer mean a hunter with a green sash and a loud name, and the hall is where they live: the board on one wall, the Wall of crews on another, the long table, the song, the Beadle, the White Aprons’ account book. Halls run like clubs and are followed like them. Sedgeby’s river-green and the Long Rope’s yellow have fans in towns neither has ever worked. A hall sponsors the promising poor, buys a patron’s Draft for a girl who cleared a floor at fifteen, and takes its share for seven years, and this guild patronage is one of the three ways the poor ever rise, beside dungeon luck and blessings.
The feuds
Signing ended no quarrel. It moved them indoors and put a fee on them.

The eighth place. The Chandlers and the Saddlers, above.
Cutters, pourers and singers. The three old trades of runes, Drafts and chants once kept separate ranks and separate examinations, each holding itself the true art and the others its servants. The ranks are long gone and anyone may level all three. The grudge has outlived them by centuries, with its own songs, its own jokes about the others’ hands, and a brawl at the Engravers’ feast that has reliably broken out in every year anyone has checked.
Halls and the Well-Hunters. Every signed hall despises the Well-Hunters’ Company for hunting under the halls’ price with one license among a dozen men, and hires its men when short.
The wound Draft. White Aprons against Drafters: who may be paid for a Draft that closes a wound.
The Tail. The Long Rope has the old right to the first bell at Sealhall’s dungeon, the Red Caps say they were promised it in Year 640, and Enforcement holds the gate and is enjoying itself.
Merchants and makers. Wealth against precedence, at every feast there has ever been.

Arbitration will hear any of these for a fee. Most go to the Stage brackets at the next fair instead, where yielding is allowed and killing is forbidden and still happens, and the bookies in green hats can give you a price.
VI. The Academies
Academies teach and examine. Societies recognize. They are separate institutions and they compete.
Ranks within an academy





























RankWhat it isScholarUnder instruction. Not yet permitted to work unsupervisedLicentiateHolds the license: permission to practice for hire. This is the qualification that matters commercially and the one most holders stop atMasterPermitted to take apprentices. A teaching qualification, with no claim to superior practice, and the distinction is constantly misunderstood outside academia, all the more since it shares a word with the sixth title on a tokenDoctorPermitted to teach the masters, examine, and dispute. Confers the right to be wrong in public at lengthChairAn endowed and appointed post, named for whoever endowed it. Held for life or until a better one is offered
The chairs are the money. An endowed chair is a fund, and the holder is paid from it, and the endower’s family frequently retains a say in appointments in perpetuity. A dozen chairs in the Inner World are in the gift of a crown rather than an academy, and those are the ones that get people ennobled.
The societies
A society does not teach. It elects, from a large pool, a small fixed number each year, and the election is by the existing members. Membership is styled Fellow, carries a postnominal, and cannot be bought at any price, which is precisely why it is worth more than anything that can.
The Society’s whole power is that it is the only body in the four quarters that confers standing without money changing hands. It has no charter to grant, no license to issue and no court to convene. It simply says, once a year, who is worth listening to, and the four quarters have agreed to care.
The Accord and the Societies have never worked out their relationship and both prefer it that way. Research and Archives funds them, and has never dared try to appoint to them.
The sects
Academies have charters and examinations. Most of the people who can actually fight learned it at a sect, a school with a wall, a ground, a color and a grudge, under a discipleship ladder any child can recite: outer disciple, inner disciple, core disciple, elder. Sects run on those ranks while the guilds keep their titles, and a good many practitioners carry both, a core disciple of one thing and a Journeyman on the Guild’s roll. Sects teach what money cannot buy, Releases, Domains, techniques, skills and the rites for their Wellspring, and they know exactly what that is worth. The Accord would like them all to register. Some do, for the right to post fighters at Guild-sanctioned brackets, and the Stage brackets at every fair are the nearest thing the four quarters have to a shared religion. Yielding is allowed and killing is forbidden and still happens. The rivalries, songs and laundries are set out on The Powers of the Dark Ages.
VII. The Great Offices
These are appointments, and nobody is measured for them. Nobody is judged to be the greatest anything. An office exists, somebody is appointed to it, and the honorific accretes afterward until people forget the office was ever a job.
The pattern is exact and worth knowing: an office is created to do something, the holder is styled by an increasingly grand informal title, the title becomes the standard usage, and eventually the office is detached from the work altogether and becomes largely honorary, awarded for distinction. Three of the four Accord offices have completed that journey. One has not, and resents the others.
In the Accord’s gift
The Grand Mage. Originally the office that visited and examined the academies, on circuit, once every three years, with power to suspend a charter. The honorific accreted over two centuries. The office is now largely honorary, detached from any particular academy, and conferred for distinction, and the visitation is performed by deputies. Guildmasters who still receive the visitation consider this an outrage, since they are examined by a man acting in the name of somebody who has never seen their hall.
The Grand Alembic. Pre-eminent in the pouring. Began as the office that certified the Draft formulary, which meant deciding what could lawfully be made. Now honorary, and the formulary is certified by a standing committee of the Alchemists’ Society, which the Accord funds and does not appoint to, and which is therefore the most independent body in the four quarters and knows it.
The Grand Engraver. Pre-eminent in the cutting. Keeper of the angle-set and of the Master Glyph Index. Honorary in name and working in fact, because somebody has to say whether a newly attested form is a form, and no committee has ever been willing to take that on.
The Grand Gauger. Pre-eminent in the measure of the pool. Created within the last century, still does its job, still sets the standard ferrule (the fixed bronze ring at a Core’s lip that limits how wide a sitter can pull), still hears appeals on the keepers’ books. The other three regard it as a jumped-up search office with a grand name. It regards them as three honorifics attached to nobody’s actual work, and it is right, and saying so has cost two holders their seat at the Citadel table.
There is no Accord office for the singing. Chants have never been an Accord examination, and the orders appoint their own Precentor of the Choirs, whom the Accord does not recognize and cannot appoint, and who outranks every one of the four inside any hall where a chant is holding something up.
In the crowns’ gift
Every crown appoints its own: Mage Royal, Alchemist Royal, Engraver Royal, and in the Inner World a Gauger Royal in three kingdoms so far. These are salaried, resident, and expected to work.
Two honor systems, and they overlap badly. The Grand Mage is the Accord’s. The Mage Royal is a crown’s. Neither outranks the other and no protocol has ever settled which enters a room first, so the compromise everywhere is that they enter together and are announced together, and the two men involved have usually loathed each other for years.

factions,-bloodlines--and--institutions/.content:
Standing Doctrine on Individuals Who Outweigh Regiments

Issued by the Strategic Division for the instruction of field commanders at Legion rank and above, and sold, at a price that keeps the Division’s bindery in vellum, to any free company captain whose token covers the contract. Sections on Voidic and the Law of Reversal are withheld from copies issued outside the Concord Citadel and appear here by direction of the High Marshal.
First of the War Cycle.
An archivist’s note: the Legion is small and the free companies are not, so most of the officers who have read this page draw their pay from a contract and paint their rank on a wagon. It is the most copied military text in the four quarters and almost none of the copies are legal.

The Question

A Stage XII practitioner walks onto a field held by four thousand men. Every officer present understands that they cannot kill this person.
The question this document exists to answer is why the four thousand are there at all.

Every field commander asks it in their first year and most are given an answer that is a slogan. The Division’s position is that the slogan has cost more lives than any enemy.
The honest answer requires admitting the premise. A practitioner at Emanation or above cannot be beaten by an army in any sense a soldier would recognize. There is no formation that kills them, no volume of ordinary steel that reaches them while they have reserve and warning, and no number of ordinary men whose deaths add up to their defeat. Commanders who have been taught otherwise have marched into the proof.
The distinction

A practitioner converts Essence into effect. An army converts time into ground.
These are different currencies and they do not exchange. The practitioner’s currency is enormous, finite, and spends itself whether or not anything worthwhile is bought with it. The army’s currency is inexhaustible in principle and worthless in a hurry.

A Stage XII practitioner can unmake a regiment in an afternoon. They cannot occupy a province. They cannot hold a bridge for three weeks, garrison six towns at once, escort a grain convoy, invest a fortress, or be awake in two valleys on the same night. They must eat, they must sleep, they must be supplied, and the moment they stop spending Essence the ground reverts to whoever is standing on it.

Ground is held by bodies. It has never been held by anything else. The four thousand are there because the war is about ground and the practitioner is not.

What a Practitioner Is, Militarily

































FindingConsequenceThey are siege engines, not infantryA weapon with a rate of loosing, a store of stones, a crew requirement, and a time to shift. Every doctrinal error in the Division’s history has come from officers who treated them as very good soldiers rather than as very expensive trebuchetsThey have a store and it emptiesEssence is finite per practitioner per day, replenishment is slower than expenditure under load, and the practitioner knows exactly how much they have left at every moment, because their window reports it to them, to the percent, and to nobody else. That knowledge governs their behavior more completely than any order doesThey cannot be two placesThe constraint the entire doctrine is built on, and the one commanders forget first, because a practitioner arriving somewhere is spectacular and a practitioner failing to arrive somewhere else is invisibleThey degradeSustained output past the second hour produces measurable coarsening in the Aether Shell. Techniques surgical at dawn are approximate by midday and blunt by dusk. A tired practitioner loses precision long before strength, a different and often worse problem for everybody nearbyThey are irreplaceableA Legion can absorb the loss of a company and continue. It cannot absorb the loss of its Aether Knights. This asymmetry is the enemy’s principal opportunity, and every experienced commander conducts their campaign around protecting an asset more valuable than the objectiveThe token is not the fighterStages can be bought. A coil and a Master’s silver will tell you a young lord stands at Stage IX, and neither will tell you that he has never once found a Release, which must be mastered by fighting. Find out before you plan around him, on either side. The bought Stage has the reserve and the numbers, and until his Level catches up it sits Overgrown, spilling power he cannot steer, and a veteran two Stages under him has been known to cost him out by mid-morning for the pleasure of it. A wealthy house will pay well to keep this question open
The Spend

“Cost him out and hand him to the infantry.”
The whole of Division doctrine, as taught in the ranks, in seven words the War-Priests have never managed to improve on.

The War-Priests of Urion read the Lattice hum to estimate an opposing practitioner’s remaining capacity. Their instrument is imprecise, their estimates are conservative by policy, and their function on a Division staff is not prophecy. It is bookkeeping.
A practitioner enters an engagement with a budget. Make them spend it on things that do not matter.
The four spends

On the worthless Screening troops, feints, decoys, empty positions defended with conviction. A technique discharged into a company of levy is a technique not available three hours later against the Aether Knights. This is what levies are for, and the Division does not say so out loud in the presence of levies.
On the ground Prepared positions, entrenchment, stakes, flooded approaches, obstacles that must be removed rather than crossed. Ground cannot be intimidated and does not rout. A practitioner faced with a properly prepared frontage must either spend Essence to unmake it or spend time to go around it, and the Division is content with either.
On suppression Sealwright interference, Parun Rod disruption, Voidic proximity. Suppression rarely stops anything. It raises the price of everything, and the price is the objective.
On the sustain A seated Domain drains continuously whether or not it is doing anything. A practitioner who has been persuaded to seat a Domain early is a practitioner paying rent, and the cheapest way to persuade them is to threaten something they must not lose.

Costed out

A practitioner who has exhausted their budget is a person. Skilled, dangerous, physically formidable, and a person, whose coat is gone, and whom a three-copper crossbow bolt loosed across a room can kill as well as it kills anyone. The same is true of any practitioner asleep, drugged or surprised, at any Stage. Every doctrine in this document exists to produce it.
The transition is not visible from outside, and this is the source of most of the Legion’s casualties. A costed-out practitioner behaves exactly like a full one until the moment they do not, and the men sent to test the proposition are the men who find out.
The Division’s standing guidance is that the test is made with expendable formations, and that the guidance is not to be read aloud.

Why Mass Still Matters
The five functions of ordinary soldiers on a field that contains a practitioner. None of them is killing the practitioner.

Frontage A line of men occupies a width. A practitioner occupies a point and a radius. Beyond that radius the war continues. Mass is the instrument by which an army makes a battlefield larger than one person can attend to.
Flank and rear The practitioner’s own supply, baggage, and line of retreat are held by ordinary men, and can be taken by ordinary men. An army that ignores this in favor of contesting the center has agreed to fight the enemy’s battle.
Depth Reserves absorb a breakthrough. A single catastrophic technique that would end a shallow formation merely wounds a deep one, and the difference between those two outcomes is measured in ranks.
Holding Ground taken must be occupied or it is not taken. This is the function no practitioner performs and none has ever performed, and it is the reason the levy exists.


Attrition economics. Ordinary soldiers are replaceable at a known cost. Practitioners are not replaceable at any cost.
An exchange that trades three hundred levy for one Aether Knight is a catastrophe for the side that lost the Knight and a routine market day for the side that lost the levy, and both commanders know the arithmetic before the engagement begins.

What a Domain Does to a Line
The Division spent sixty years teaching officers that a Domain kills the men inside it. The finding that replaced that teaching is the most important single correction in the Division’s history, and it cost the Fifth Legion to obtain.

A seated Domain does not kill a formation. It breaks it, which is not the same thing and produces the deaths by a different route.

Inside a Domain the world runs on the practitioner’s terms. Their equipment behaves fractionally wrong. Sound arrives from the wrong direction or does not arrive. Distances read false. The man beside them looks unfamiliar for a moment they cannot account for. Orders do not propagate, because orders travel on drums and voice and sightlines and a Domain interferes with all three by construction.
None of that is lethal. All of it is corrosive to the one thing that holds a line together, which is a man’s certainty that the men beside him are still there and that somebody knows what is happening.
So the line breaks. And the killing occurs in the rout, as it always has, because a man who turns his back has discarded his shield, his formation and his facing in a single motion, and a Domain that has broken a formation does not need to do anything further. The pursuit is conducted by ordinary cavalry at no cost to the practitioner at all.
The doctrinal consequences

























FindingWhat followsA Domain is a rout engineAssess it by how fast it breaks cohesion, not by how many it kills. Two Domains of identical scale can differ by an hour in the time they take to unmake a formation, and that hour is the whole engagementVeterans cost more than recruitsA formation with genuine internal cohesion resists a Domain considerably longer, for reasons that have nothing to do with Temperance. Men who know each other keep standing after the drums have stopped meaning anything. The Division’s investment in unit stability is defended in the budget as a morale expense and is in fact a metaphysical countermeasureCommand must be redundant before contactOrders that will not survive a Domain must be issued before the Domain is seated. Formations trained to continue on last instruction hold. Formations trained to await orders dissolve, and dissolve fastest at the moment they are most neededThe Domain Engineers earn their pay hereA counter-Domain does not need to defeat the enemy’s. It needs to give the men inside it one true thing. A patch of ground where the sound is right and the distances read correctly is worth more to a wavering line than a company of reinforcements, which is why Engineers are instructed to seat toward the formation rather than toward the enemy
The Five Counters
In ascending order of cost and descending order of availability.
Ground · The cheapest and the most reliable. Every campaign in the record that a smaller force won against a superior practitioner was won on ground chosen months in advance by somebody who never fought on it. Ground does not rout, cannot be intimidated, does not tire, and is not impressed. A practitioner who has spent four hours unmaking a fortified line has spent four hours unmaking dirt.
Distance · The two-front tax. A practitioner who must cover two objectives covers neither properly, and a commander who can threaten three has effectively reduced the enemy’s principal asset by two thirds without engaging it.
Attention · Screening forces, feints, and the deliberate manufacture of urgencies. The War-Priests hold that attention is depleted faster than Essence and recovers slower, and that a practitioner who has been made to choose six times before noon is functionally costed out by mid afternoon regardless of what remains in the store.
Suppression · Expensive, slow to deploy, fragile in the field, and almost never decisive on its own. A Sealwright team that has doubled the cost of an opposing practitioner’s technique has done more for the engagement than any three companies on the field, and will receive credit for none of it, and knows this going in.

The Bind. Domain against Domain: two practitioners contesting the same ground on incompatible terms, producing a standing interference in which neither can operate freely and both pay continuously to remain.
The Bind is a stalemate by design and the Division treats it as a victory condition rather than a failure. It converts the enemy’s irreplaceable asset into a stationary object paying rent, and everything else on the field proceeds as an ordinary battle between ordinary men, which is a battle the Legion knows how to win.
The cost is that the Bind consumes one of the Legion’s own irreplaceable assets to do it. Aether Knights assigned to Bind duty are frequently ruined by the assignment, and the Division’s own reviews record that the men who volunteer for it a second time are rarely the men who did it well the first.

The Fate Commander
Every finding above treats the enemy’s practitioner as a siege engine with a store of stones. Most of them are. The Division has one standing exception, and it is rare enough that many officers finish a career without meeting it.

Each side’s first job on any field is to pin or kill the other’s high-Stage champions. Fate users are pinned first, ahead of even those.

The ordinary Fate Path officer is simply a practitioner with long Range, heavy Aura Pressure and a sworn company that fights better for him, and he is costed out like anyone. The commander this section concerns is another matter, and is a life’s masterwork at high Stage or a bloodline’s art. Such a person does not spend Essence on the field so much as on what the field depends on: weather, supply, panic, the hour a column arrives, the company that breaks first and which way it runs. Every one of those already has a way of happening, and an army is thousands of straps wearing at once. It may be done once in a war and it may cost the person doing it. Nothing about it looks like a working until the after-action review, when the survivors sit down and count how many small things went wrong.

























FindingWhat followsThe champion is the loud oneA Stage XII on a ridge can be seen from two valleys away, and a Fate commander may be an old woman under a plain banner. Look for them by effect: keep a written log of what goes wrong, day by day, and read it for a pattern luck would not produce. By the time anyone can see what was decided, it has already happened and it looks like luckSoundness is a countermeasureIt moves only what already has a way of happening. A bridge somebody has inspected, a horse freshly shod, a company paid on time and two roads to the same ford give it very little to hold. The Division’s inspection regime is defended in the budget as good housekeeping and is in fact the cheapest metaphysical defense in the arsenalIt is contestedAnother Fate user can read the weights and lean the other way, at about equal cost to both. Dominion’s Fate Sub-Stat pushes, and a high enough Resilience Persistence and Continuity in the soul it is aimed at pushes back. Nothing in this finding helps a levy, which has no such soul to spareReach them before the result arrivesOutside their Domain, in a straight exchange, they are an ordinary body, and one that has been paying heavily. Light horse, a night raid or a bolt will do. A commander who has spent six days hunting one and failed has still made them spend those six days hiding
True Fate Arts are rare, mostly by bloodline, and considered incredibly overpowered, and the Division’s advice on meeting a Moto host in the field runs to one line, which is to confirm first that you have to.
Voidic

Withheld from Legion-rank copies. The Division’s position is that the fewer commanders who understand what a Voidic practitioner is for, the fewer will request one.

Voidic is the Legion’s old word for a Body Mastery held Inverted, and it is lateral rather than sequential. It is no rung, sits above none, and does not represent an advancement: a practitioner can hold any rung of the Body road that way. The Shell’s polarity is reversed, and a Voidic practitioner devours where others emit.

The military consequence is direct. A Voidic practitioner is a poor attacker and the finest suppression instrument in the world, and the two facts are the same fact.

They are not fielded as combatants. A Voidic practitioner committed to ordinary engagement is a waste of the rarest asset the Accord possesses. They are pointed, like a siege engine, at one target.
They are slow to move and cannot defend themselves. Every consideration governing a great trebuchet governs them, including a dedicated guard detachment whose only function is to keep ordinary soldiers away from an asset that cannot deal with ordinary soldiers.
Their presence is the effect. Proximity alone raises the cost of every technique executed nearby, including the Legion’s own. Voidic assets are sited with the same care as a burning brand in a pitch store, and the Division’s siting regulations run to eleven pages of which nine concern friendly forces.
They are structurally distrusted. A practitioner whose architecture consumes Essence is one the Lattice reads differently, and Voidic operatives are subject to standing review procedures applied to no other class. Whether this is a security measure or a prejudice with a procedure attached is a question the Division has declined to examine four times.

Because Voidic practitioners are the counter, and because the counter is rare, the strategic balance of the four quarters rests on how many exist and who holds them.
The Threat Codex maintains a separate register for this. The register is short. The Division has never published its length, and the fact that it has never published its length is itself the most informative thing on the subject that anybody outside the Citadel has been able to obtain.

Speed, and What It Buys
A woken courier at a full run travels faster than any commander in the old histories was able to think. This ought to have ended the fog of war. It did not, and understanding why is the whole of Concord command doctrine.
An army possessing woken couriers of rank enjoys something no force in the old histories ever had: command within the hour across a front too wide to see. What that buys is tempo, concentration against fractions, and arrival before the enemy has finished deciding. The Long Relay’s best riders are guild members and hire out to whoever has signed, under terms that exclude being shot at and are honored about as well as you would expect. For two centuries the strategic weight of any force that could hire them has rested on this and on nothing else.
Why it does not settle the matter
Speed is Essence. A courier who has run at full draw arrives depleted and requires hours before they can run again. Same-hour command is a consumable, and it is consumed fastest on the days it matters most.
Couriers are the first thing killed. Courier interdiction is the cheapest strategic operation available, and the Legion’s own courier losses in a hard campaign routinely exceed its losses in any other specialization.
Same-hour command degrades to the old slow kind precisely when it is tested. The same army on the fourteenth day of a contested campaign has runners on foot and a commander guessing. The Division’s most repeated finding across four hundred years of after-action review is that formations trained on same-hour command collapse faster under courier loss than formations that never had it.

The Law of Witness supplies a floor. Every engagement must be recorded by a Concord Scribe or Seer, and the record enters the Lattice. This is a legal requirement and functions incidentally as a communications system of last resort, since a Scribe’s record reaches the Citadel whether or not any courier survives.
Commanders have learned to write for it. The Division has never formally acknowledged that its own legal apparatus is load-bearing for its command apparatus, and would prefer the question not be asked in front of Arbitration.

Capture
A dead practitioner is a message. A living one is an asset, a hostage, a bargaining position, and eventually a witness.
A costed-out practitioner can be taken. This is the single most valuable outcome available to a field commander and the one their men are least inclined to deliver, because the men who reach a costed-out practitioner are usually the survivors of what they did before they were costed out.
The Division’s standing instruction is that capture is preferred, that the instruction is to be repeated at every level of command, and that it will be disobeyed. Commanders are advised to assign the taking to formations that were not engaged.

The Lawbrand exists for this. It seals Essence rather than spilling blood, and the Spirit Armory’s continued production of a weapon that is worse than a sword at everything except taking practitioners alive is the clearest statement of Accord priorities in the entire arsenal.

Politically · A Crown that has lost its champion has lost a category of threat it cannot rebuild inside a generation. Terms available after such a capture are terms unavailable after a battlefield death, because a corpse cannot be returned and a prisoner can.
Metaphysically · A living Soul Crystal can be read. Trials of Resonance conducted on a captured practitioner have produced intelligence that no interrogation could, and Arbitration’s position on the admissibility of such readings has been revised in the Accord’s favor on three occasions.
Materially · This entry has been redacted from all copies issued below the Citadel.
An archivist’s note, in the margin: every free company sergeant in the four quarters can fill in the redaction, and so can you. A Crystal cut from a dead practitioner makes the strongest Draft of all, and it is the worst crime in every realm and the most profitable. A field commander holding a captured Stage XII has been handed the price of a small kingdom, in a form that spoils if the prisoner is exchanged. The Division has not seen fit to say what its instruction is on this. It has repeated the instruction on capture four times.
The Law of Reversal

Withheld from Legion-rank copies. Every Crown in the four quarters knows its contents and the Division is aware that they know.
If the Concord becomes the aggressor, the Lattice strips the resonance of its forces and the army ceases to function. Not degrades. Ceases. Weapons go inert, harmonics fail, and the finest military instrument ever assembled becomes forty thousand people standing in a field holding objects.
No vote can repeal this, because it belongs to the structure of the covenant that gives the Legion its power, and it means the sworn force of the Guild Accord is constitutionally incapable of a war of conquest.

Note the word sworn. A free company has given the Lattice nothing and the Lattice can take nothing from it, so a signed company fights on under Accord wax however the question falls. Every crown knows this. So does every Guildlord who has wondered whether a coalition of merchants could have a war of conquest after all, by contract, one company at a time, and the Division would like it known that it has not raised the subject.
What every enemy does about it
The Accord’s opponents do not seek to defeat the Legion. They seek to establish that the Legion is the aggressor, a cheaper campaign conducted largely in Arbitration and requiring no soldiers at all.
Border provocations designed to produce a disproportionate response. Civilian presence arranged where the Legion must strike. Wellspring claims filed in advance of hostilities to convert a defensive intervention into a contested seizure.

The entire body of Accord military law reads, to an experienced Crown, as a list of instructions for disabling the Accord’s army by paperwork.

The Division’s counter is procedural and slow and consists almost entirely of the Law of Witness, which is why the Law of Witness is enforced with a severity that appears disproportionate to anyone who has not read this section.

Every operation the Legion conducts must be defensible in Arbitration before it is conducted, which means the Legion fights with an inherent delay its opponents do not have, on ground its opponents have usually chosen, under rules of engagement its opponents have frequently written.
This is the true asymmetry of Accord warfare and it runs the opposite direction from the one the public assumes. The Accord’s army is not restrained by its principles in the manner of a strong power exercising forbearance. It is disabled by them in a specific, mechanical, exploitable fashion, and every Crown with a competent legal division knows exactly how.

Counterplay at Scale
Three fields that convert an individual technique into a mass-combat instrument with a defeat condition. A technique that cannot be given all three does not belong on a battlefield.





















FieldWhat it governsFrontageHow much line the technique affects, in men or in paces. A frontage of twelve men is a personal weapon used in a battle. A frontage of three hundred is an instrument of war. The distinction is not power. It is width, and most spectacular techniques are narrowSustainHow long the effect can be held before Essence cost forces cessation, and what the practitioner cannot do while holding it. A Domain with an eight-hour Sustain and a practitioner who can do nothing else during those eight hours has told you exactly how the enemy should spend their dayRe-formHow long an affected formation needs to recover cohesion, and whether it recovers at all. This is the field that decides battles. A technique that breaks a line for ten minutes has bought a local advantage. A technique that breaks a line permanently has ended the war on that flank

The counterplay to any scaled technique is therefore always one of three things.
Exceed its Frontage, so the war continues where it is not. Outlast its Sustain, so the practitioner pays and gains nothing. Or shorten its Re-form, which is what drill, veterancy, redundant command and a counter-Domain seated toward your own men are all purchased to do.

Unresolved Entries
The costed-out threshold · No instrument reliably distinguishes a depleted practitioner from a full one at distance. The target’s own window knows and tells no one. A reader whose Gnosis Perception outranks the target’s Resilience Ward by a full step can read it directly, which is why such readers are bought at any price and why the target’s first act on a field is to find out who they are. Everyone else has an estimate said aloud, and an old hand can hide or fake what is being estimated. The War-Priests’ estimates carry an acknowledged error margin and men die inside it. Four proposals for a field instrument have been funded and none has left the Archives.
Whether the Bind can be conducted by a lesser practitioner · Present doctrine requires an asset of comparable Stage. Whether two or three lower-Stage practitioners can jointly Bind one greater has been modeled favorably and never tested, because the test consumes the practitioners either way.
Domain Re-form in veteran formations · The Division holds figures for recruit formations and none for veterans, because veteran formations are not made available for the trials. The gap is known, has been known for ninety years, and is annotated in the Division’s own returns as pending.
Voidic register length · Not published. Not published deliberately.

Whether the Law of Reversal has ever been invoked. The Division’s position is that it has not.
The Archives hold one sealed session from the Eclipse Wars whose subject is not recorded and whose duration was eleven days.
