geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Crimson Isles of Vorruk-Khal
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say it*Vorruk-Khal* VORR-ook KHAHL · in most mouths, the Hobgoblin Expanse, HOB-gob-lin ek-SPANS
Vorruk-Khal · The Held Ground

Vorruk is ground that tried to move and was stopped, which no farmer means by ground. Khal is held as a wound holds together after stitching, and a hand holds a cup some other way.

The Keth-Gorrum was halfway through the annual roll on kelp-bed boundaries, in the spring of 612 IC, when Gorr-Keth, nine leagues up the crescent, blew the side out of its cone. The moot sits under open sky and has refused an awning for as long as it has been asked, so the whole assembly had an excellent view. The sky over Khal-Serrat went the orange of a smith’s apron and then a deep bruised violet, the red banners along the cliff-top stood straight out in the hot wind, and stones the size of loaves began coming down on the moot floor, trailing smoke. A Tinker Voice moved to adjourn. The Speaker, a Hobgoblin named Sahl-Venn in Crimson Order scarlet, ruled that a motion to adjourn requires a roll call, that a roll call once begun must be completed, and that the kelp roll had been begun first.
So one hundred and twelve Voices stood under a rain of hot rock and answered to their names. Coats of aura went up along the benches, sulfur-yellow and basalt-blue. The Bugbear Voices planted themselves where they sat and the stones broke on them. A Fleshshaper advisor, who does not vote, walked the aisle setting bones and telling people what she thought of them in language the record calls direct. The kelp roll finished, the motion to adjourn failed by six because the ash had by then stopped falling, and four Voices who had died in their seats were marked present, since they had answered. The reef families, who had watched the mountain burn pink and gold over the water from their boats, were told about the session a week later and asked whether the kelp line had moved. It had not. It is in the Rock.
Forty-three volcanic islands make up the Crimson Isles, black rock and red banners, with a war-moot held under the open sky at the foot of a cliff and no king anyone has ever been able to find, and they would like you to wait your turn to speak.
Overview
A volcanic archipelago of forty-three islands strung across the water south of the one great land, past the sea below the Holy Sea of Alabaster and the Copper Coast, where the old charts run on toward the Outer World’s western shelf. The Concord charts name it Vorruk-Khal, which is Old Vaross, though the phrase carries a weight the translation does not. Its people are the Hobgoblins of the Crimson Order and the Bugbears who came with them, with Tinker Goblin workshops and Fleshshaper quarters besides, and every town flies the same red banner with nothing on it, since a device would imply somebody whose device it was.
The islands are young. They belong to the same volcanic arc that built the New World’s eastern seaboard, a chain of andesite peaks pushed up by the same subducting plate at a different angle. The tallest, Gorr-Keth, reaches four thousand feet above the waterline and glows orange at night when the wind shifts. The smallest are little more than basalt shelves a few hundred paces across, colonized by lichen and by Tinker Goblin signal-fire and mirror posts that have been there long enough that nobody remembers who built the first one. Black beaches, yellow sulfur crusts around the vents, green terraces up every caldera wall, a sea that goes from ink to jade over the shelves: it is the only black country in the world that anyone has ever called gaudy.
Fourteen of the forty-three are inhabited year-round. The rest serve as seasonal fisheries, volcanic-glass quarries, sulfur fields, or navigational markers. Three are forbidden entirely, with nobody enforcing the prohibition, because the ground shakes there in frequencies that make Stone-Blood vibrate at the wrong harmonic, and the Bugbear population discovered this the hard way four centuries ago and has not needed to rediscover it.

The Crimson Isles are the largest self-governing goblinoid realm in the four quarters. They have no king, no warlord and no hereditary seat of any kind.
What they have is a war-moot, and the war-moot is older than most of the kingdoms that regard it as a curiosity.

They are also, with the Iron Mandate of Undaar-Keth that they disapprove of, the standing enemy of the North, for reasons that begin with a toll: see The Unpaid Toll, below.
The Scattering · Grr-Vashuum
In the long age before the Scattering, the goblinoid peoples held territory in the western quarter’s mountain passes, where the rock was closest to the asteroid’s original composition and the Stone-Blood ran strongest.
They were ruled, loosely, by Ironblood Orc warchief coalitions. The word ruled does too much work. What the Ironblood provided was a chain of command running on kinetic hierarchy: the strongest warband held the best passes, the passes controlled the trade, and the trade funded the war-parties that held the passes. It was circular. It functioned, the way a wheel functions on a slope, which is to say it kept moving and the movement was its own justification.
The Crimson Order existed within this structure, but uncomfortably. Hobgoblin discipline and Ironblood volatility occupied the same valleys the way two predators share a forest when neither can afford to leave. The Hobgoblins administered the granaries, kept the glyph-wards, and trained the mixed formations that held the passes against Marrowkin incursion from the north and Elven pressure from the east. They were, by every measure except the one the Ironblood cared about, the architecture of the goblinoid presence in the Old World.
The measure the Ironblood cared about was violence, and they were better at it, and they said so with the regularity of a church bell.
The three stages of collapse

      
      
      
      
      
      Dokk-Vraal's deepraid into thenorthern shieldmilitarily successful,politically catastrophicTHREE MARROWKINTALLY-HOUSES UNITEa century of tunnel-accessargument set asideERESSEANEXPEDITIONARY FORCEdispatched over no injury,because the Marrowkinalliancedisturbed the KinshipDoctrine's equilibriummodelFRONTIERFOLKVALLEY-LORDSstop paying goblinoidtolls, start fortifyingNorthern passes lostin nine daysEastern approaches lost insixThe Ironblood demandthe Hobgoblinscommittheir administrativereserves to acounterattackTHE REFUSALForty years ofgrinding expulsion

The refusal is the moment the Ironblood call the Betrayal of the Mountain, and that the Crimson Order calls the First Rational Act.

What followed was a grinding expulsion over approximately forty years. Ironblood warbands broke into raiding parties and scattered to every quarter that would tolerate them. Verdant Orc bands slipped into the deep wetlands of the southern interior and were not seen again for centuries, and their heirs now hold the Moss Court in the Moonlight Forest of Mosk-Vaal. Some of the Crimson Order would not leave at all, and dug in on the western shield, and became the Mandate. The rest of the Order, with whatever Tinker Goblins and Fleshshaper enclaves would follow, withdrew southwest along the coast until they ran out of coast and found the volcanic chain rising out of the water.
The Hobgoblin name for this is Grr-Vashuum, built from grr- (a force event, kinetic, percussive) and vashuum (a thing that opens where it should not). It is the word for a fault line that splits a load-bearing wall.

The Ironblood use it too, but they pronounce the second syllable shorter, as if the breaking was quick and clean. The Hobgoblins hold the vowel. The breaking was not quick.

The Seventh Lineage · The Bugbear Peoples
Mantle-Born · Gorr-Veshaal





















TypeMajor Race, Asteroidal Depth-Kin / Endurance-ForgedOriginSecond Epoch. Born from the mantle layer of the First Impact, the intermediate mass between the core that compressed and the shell that shatteredMetaphysical AnchorEssence (Gravitational / Passive), inertial mass, with neither the kinetic force of the shell nor the structured lattice of the coreSpiritual LineageThe Weight-That-Stayed. Where the core compressed and the shell exploded, the mantle did neither. It absorbed
They are the largest of the goblinoid peoples, standing between seven feet and eight feet four, and they carry their height differently. An Ironblood Orc’s body is built for output. A Bugbear’s body is built for absorption. The shoulders are wider than a Hobgoblin’s and sloped rather than squared, distributing load across a frame that was never designed to throw a punch first. The chest is deep, not broad. The waist does not taper. The legs are short relative to the torso, thick, rooted, set wide in a stance that looks casual until someone tries to move it.
Their skin runs darker than any other goblinoid lineage: deep charcoal gray to near-black, matte, absorbing light in a way that is difficult for other races to look at directly. Their Stone-Blood runs thickest but slowest, and the asteroidal mineral deposits in their tissue are arranged in layered striations rather than the Ironblood’s jagged scars or the Hobgoblin’s geometric etchings. Under the skin the layers are visible as faint banded patterns, gray on darker gray, that shift when they move. A Bugbear in motion looks as if the mountain itself is rearranging its strata.

Their hair is sensory. Bugbear hair follicles contain a density of Aetheric nerve endings that allow them to read ambient Essence pressure changes through the scalp. They feel weather, Wellspring fluctuation, and hostile intent before any other sense registers it.

Axiomatic traits





















TraitFunctionGravitational AnchorPassive weight multiplication. A Bugbear who plants and chooses not to move becomes functionally immovable by any force below Grade A kinetic output. Stone-Blood increases effective mass by a factor of six to eight, involuntarily, under threat. Knockback, displacement, and forced-movement glyphs lose 60% to 80% of their effectiveness against a set BugbearInertial DampeningThe mantle’s inheritance. Impact force is reduced by transmission rather than deflection, dispersed across the entire layered tissue structure. Where an Ironblood converts received force into stored kinetic energy, a Bugbear simply takes less damage, permanently, passively, without activation cost. 25% baseline, scaling to 40% under sustained bombardment as the tissue compresses and hardensPresence GravityAt Stage VI and above, a passive Aetheric gravity field within roughly fifteen paces. The pull is metaphysical, with no physical force in it. Ambient Essence flows toward the Bugbear rather than dispersing, and practitioners inside find their own expenditure increased by roughly +8% AU cost on all active techniques. The Bugbear does not benefit from the gathered Essence. It simply pools and dissipates slowly. A high-Stage Bugbear warps the tactical economy of an engagement merely by standing in it

Key limitation · Inertial Lock. A Bugbear who has activated Gravitational Anchor cannot transition to full combat speed for 2.4 seconds after release, during which their reaction time drops to human-baseline. This is the window. Every opponent who has fought a Bugbear and survived learned to read the release.
Speed Deficit. Travel speed caps at roughly 60% of an Ironblood Orc of the same Stage. They are slower than the thing they are most often compared to, which has been enough to get them killed in open-field engagements where mobility determined survival.

Cultural lattice
Language · Low Goblintongue for working. Gorr-Vaross among themselves, a Bugbear dialect of Old Vaross distinguished by extended vowels held at sub-bass registers that physically vibrate the listener’s ribcage at conversational distance. Formal Bugbear speech is felt before it is understood.


The Laying of Weight: responsibilities as part of the body
When a Bugbear assumes a new responsibility, a seat in the Keth-Gorrum, a wardship, a marriage, a sworn contract, they carry a stone from the shore to the peak of the nearest island summit without stopping. The stone must be heavy enough that the climb takes effort.
The act is structural. Bugbear Stone-Blood responds to sustained gravitational load by deepening its layered compressions, and a Bugbear who has carried many stones has a measurably denser Aetheric signature than one who has not.
Their responsibilities are, in a literal metaphysical sense, part of their body.


The Long Silence: grief felt in the follicles
When a Bugbear of consequence dies, every Bugbear within earshot of the announcement stops speaking for one full day. Nobody vows it and no rite requires it. It happens to them.
The sub-bass frequencies of Gorr-Vaross carry a harmonic signature unique to each speaker, and when a known signature ceases, the absence is physically perceived by every Bugbear whose hair has ever registered it.
The silence is grief felt in the follicles, and it takes a day for the sensory absence to stop triggering a searching reflex.


Signature imagery · Layered basalt columns, deep shadow, carried stones, and the Closed Fist resting on a flat surface, the gesture that means I am staying.
Relations · Permanently allied with the Crimson Order by the moot’s integration. Respectful contempt for the Ironblood Orcs, whom they regard as an argument for rule that has been losing since before the Scattering and has not yet noticed. Cautious trade with the Marrowkin, who share their experience of building a home on ground nobody else would have. They describe Elves as “people who have never carried a stone in their lives and it shows.”
Geography of the Isles
The forty-three islands are arranged in a rough crescent running southwest to northeast, following the volcanic arc’s surface expression. The crescent opens north toward the white shelf and the Thousand Moorings, approximately two hundred leagues off. The southern horn trails toward the Outer World’s western shelf, where the water shallows over ancient craton, the fishing is good, and the Crevice’s influence is not yet measurable.

























TierCount and elevationFunctionThe High IslandsSeven, peaks above 2,000 ftThe oldest Hobgoblin settlements, built into caldera walls and leeward slopes where the volcanic soil is deep enough to farm. Terraced agriculture produces taro, breadfruit, volcanic-ash grain (a Tinker Goblin cultivar of three centuries ago that they have been failing to improve ever since), and thurr-kep, a root that grows nowhere else and tastes, according to every non-goblinoid who has tried it, exactly like charcoal mixed with honeyThe Shelf IslandsTwenty-two, 300 to 2,000 ftThe working backbone. Forges, shipyards, obsidian quarries, sulfur works, and the moot-isle of Khal-Serrat. Densest population: mixed Hobgoblin-Bugbear communities with Tinker Goblin workshop enclaves and a persistent Fleshshaper quarter on Krev-Mol, where the ambient Essence is irregular enough that their self-modification practices find raw material more easilyThe Low ReefsFourteen barely above the waterline, plus uncounted tidal shelvesFisheries, kelp farms, signal relays, and the vent-forges the Marrowkin taught the Hobgoblins to build, which run on the heat the sea floor gives up. Permanent residents are predominantly Bugbear fishing families who regard the moot with the tolerant disinterest of people who have never needed its help and expect never to
The towns
Khal-Serrat, the moot-isle. The old tallies give the island as Vesh-Undaal, a Bugbear form, and every chart since the Gold Flood gives it by the town. Serrat is an old word for the place where a weapon is set down, so the name is a setting-down of the stitched kind. It is a huge terraced fortress-city of rust-red and black volcanic rock, stacked up from a black-stone harbor, with every wall ending in curved spikes, tall red banners hung down its faces and firelit gold in its deep doorways, on ash-pale ground under an amber sky. Strangers come up the ash road on foot, two or three to a party in their cloaks, and look smaller at every step. At its heart, at the foot of the great cliff and under open sky, lies the moot floor. On moot days every room is let twice, the rope-walk closes and the families of the Shelf delegations sit on the sea wall and bet on how long the morning’s roll will run.
Krev-Mol. The fish market opens before dawn under strings of blue-glass floats, and the Fleshshaper quarter sits behind it, with its coats left open to show the work. Mokk-Vesh, on the next island along, is the great shipyard, where the volcanic-glass-hulled ships of a design found nowhere else are laid down with Tinkers swarming over the frames and the shipwrights shouting at them to stop helping.
Gorr-Keth. The caldera towns on the mountain are the oldest in the Isles, terraced and green, with a founder’s pride and the best view of the thing that might kill them. Under them are the deep slag-yards, and the page owes you an honest word on those.
Under Gorr-Keth
The great forges of the High Islands run on goblin bellows-gangs, in turns that never end, down in yards the moot’s delegations do not tour. Children go onto a bellows-handle at six. A yard goblin of twelve can tell from the note of a roof-timber how long it has left, a skill everyone on a gang has and nobody talks about, since when a forge-roof comes down the entry on the board is one line. The Tinkers hold four guild-seats at the moot and are loud about the vote they do not have. The yard goblins hold none, because the residency count runs by hearth and a bunk is no hearth, and every goblin in the deep yards knows the iron-red banner of the Mandate from its contract-foremen long before they could tell you who speaks for them at Khal-Serrat. The Isles that opened their palm have this under them. It has been raised at the moot eleven times and is cut into the Rock under the heading Deferred.
Rent, food and the street
The Shelf towns are as loud as the Rock is formal. Obsidian cutters and sulfur men wear their guild colors to the Breakwater brackets on Krev-Mol, where Bugbear anchor-schools bet on who can be moved and nobody ever wins much, and the petty trades run on every dock: a net-mender whose knots do not slip, a Tinker who sharpens anything at all and sometimes on purpose, a Fleshshaper who will take out your bad tooth and asks whether you would like a better one. Rooms on the Shelf are rented by the season and paid by weight, in sulfur or glass, since the Isles price in barter by old habit. Supper is taro, breadfruit and Shelf fish, and strangers are offered thurr-kep so that everyone can watch them try it.
Wealth
Sulfur and obsidian, first and always: brimstone for the bleachers, vintners, physicians and siege-fire of half the world, and volcanic glass for edges, lenses and the hulls no one else can build. Then fish and kelp, Tinker work with a shouted guild mark, and glyph-inscription under seawater pressure, which only they do. All of it is priced in weight-barter rather than coin, and has been since before anyone can remember a reason. The Isles buy grain and timber, because ash grain is what it is and a volcano grows few masts.
The Keth-Gorrum · The War-Moot
The moot meets on Khal-Serrat, under open sky, below a shelf-tier island’s entire western face: a sheer basalt cliff carved with the records of more than seventeen centuries, and the last seven hundred and sixty-five of them unbroken. It is called the Rock.

The records are load-bearing. Every motion passed, every treaty ratified, every war declared and every war refused is inscribed into the cliff-face in High Concord script, and the inscriptions are Engraved in the Crimson Order sense: they carry Aetheric weight.
A law written into the Rock cannot be mislaid the way a hide is mislaid. It is a fact about the stone, and the stone remembers.

The day-to-day registers are kept in Old Vaross tally-cuts, a room full of timber boards behind the harbor. Every entry in it can be destroyed with an axe. This has happened, and the Isles’ law has a hole in it where the year 411 used to be. The crest of Sir Hamon Manningtree of the Concord is nailed to one of those boards, a peacock in scarlet, from the Salt Ford parley, where he took a hobgoblin kaan’s slowing voice for surrender and told his trumpeters to sound the victory.
The name combines the Open Palm gesture (Keth-ur) universal to goblinoid culture with the Old Vaross root gorr-, meaning assembly, or mass, or the-weight-of-many-standing-together. The name is a statement of method: rule by open argument among those who carry weight, with hereditary right and combat supremacy both ruled out of order, and the accumulated mass of argument, evidence and responsibility in their place.
Why a war-moot. The first of them was called on the edge of a fight, and the form has never forgotten it. Every Voice comes armed, in harness, as to a muster, and stacks spear and blade in the racks at the foot of the Rock before taking a seat, palms open, which in every goblinoid tradition means I have already laid down the more important weapon. Foreign envoys read the gesture as peace, and have been badly surprised. The moot’s first business in any year is the roll of wars standing and wars refused, and it can decide in a morning to send the fleet.
The look of it. Black rock under a blue morning, Order scarlet down the Hobgoblin benches, the Bugbears a long dark mass that seems to take the light off everyone near it, red banners cracking overhead, guild colors and gulls. Rain is a motion, which has failed, and so is the awning.
Composition
One hundred and twelve Voices, apportioned by island and adjusted every twelve years by a count of hearths, walked house to house by two Voices who dislike each other. The present apportionment gives the seven high islands thirty-eight seats, the shelf islands fifty-six, and the low reefs eighteen. A Voice stands for six years.
There is no king and no lord. No separate court sits apart from the moot. What there is, is a Speaker of the Rock, chosen from among the seated Voices for a single twelve-year term, who controls the order of debate and nothing else, and who recites the standing law from the Rock’s foot every spring so that nobody can claim not to have heard it.
Hobgoblins under Stage VII keep the Vow of Silence, the Order’s rite against emotional corruption of their Traits, so a young Voice argues in Silent Sign-Glyphs and a sign-caller speaks for him. Rulings in the sealed register, full of old roots nobody can decompose, require an interpreter, and the interpreters are a profession, and the profession is hereditary, and it would be delighted to explain this to you at length.
Bugbear Voices hold thirty-one seats, a proportion that has increased steadily over three centuries. They vote as a bloc on sea-law and fishery rights and as individuals on everything else, a pattern the Hobgoblin Voices find alternately reassuring and infuriating depending on the issue.
Tinker Goblin guild-seats number four, allocated by trade guild rather than island: the Forge Guild, the Signal Guild, the Quarry Guild, and the Alchemical Compact. These carry voice but not vote on matters of war, a restriction the Tinker Voices have protested formally in every session for ninety years and informally by building increasingly alarming signal-relay devices on the cliff-top above the floor.
Fleshshaper representation is consultative. Two appointed advisors attend on matters of health, Aetheric contamination, and living works. They do not vote. They do not want to vote. They have made this clear in language the records describe as “direct.”
In war. The moot names a War-Kaan (kaan, an officer) for one sailing season, who may not stand again the next, and who can be recalled by a roll he must answer. Nobody has ever become king this way, though several have stood on the foredeck and thought about it.
The Orc Exclusion
No Ironblood Orc has ever held a seat. The charter does not say so and does not need to. The charter requires twelve continuous years of residency before standing for the moot, and no Ironblood Orc has ever lived in the Isles for twelve continuous years.

Several have tried. The longest residency on record is Vorrak the Patient, who lasted eleven years, two months, and six days before breaking a shelf-island dock in half during an argument about fish pricing and departing by the next available vessel.

The Hobgoblin position is exclusionary in practice only, and the practice is the point. The Crimson Order’s founding argument is that rule requires the discipline to sit still, to listen to an argument one disagrees with, and to respond with words rather than with the nearest heavy object. Individual Orcs of remarkable self-control exist and are welcomed as residents, traders, and workers. They are not welcomed as Voices, because the moot cannot survive a single session in which a Voice overturns a table, and the Ironblood have not yet produced a generation in which no tables were overturned.
How the Isles Fight
Almost never first. The Isles’ first weapon is geography: in 350 IC the moot answered an Ironblood landing by cutting off fresh water and waiting, and it cut the result into the Rock under the heading Resolved by Geography. Past that, there is the fleet, its glass-sheathed hulls riding low and strange in the water, and the Order’s formations, some four thousand spears in ochre and gold kept on the Shelf in rotation, every soul of them a stone in a Resonance Lattice. The Phalanx of the Soul, a formation whose souls lock like the stones of an arch, is nearly impenetrable to chaotic Aether, and The Red Wall Takes One Step is the move every crowd has heard of: a whole formation advances a single pace, in silence, and the room changes hands. At the shore the Bugbears plant. A reef-family line that has decided to stay is the most expensive beach in the world, and Inertial Lock (those 2.4 seconds after a Bugbear lets go) is the only clause in the contract.
Stone-Blood runs slow in deep cold, and a formation there falls back from sign to a horn count. The Isles rarely see deep cold, which is the heart of their trouble on the Greymane wall.
Fighters on the docks call the aura coat (the visible coat of a fighter’s own color) ak-gresh, the survived skin, the Order has been arguing with the Ironblood for several Eons over who wears it correctly, and the Bugbears do not see why it needs a name.
The Unpaid Toll · The Isles and the North
The hobgoblin states are the North’s enemy across the Greymane wall, both of them, and the Isles’ part of it is a bill. In the Scattering the frontierfolk valley-lords stopped paying goblinoid tolls and started fortifying, and the passes they fortified are, so far as anyone can establish, the ground the Ridgewall now stands on in the Slate Ridge of Stormfold. The Keth-Gorrum has never closed the account. Every spring, after the standing law, the Speaker reads the Toll Entry: the sum in weight owed by the heirs of the valley-lords, carried forward from before the Concord was thought of, with the passes themselves entered as surety. Nobody expects payment. It takes most of the morning.
The practice has teeth. The Isles sell brimstone and glass to anyone in the four quarters who brings weight, and on the Kharven side of the wall to nobody. Loads for the Mandate are landed on the coast of Vorrak’s Reach, at the weight, with mutual contempt. Twice the moot has voted a Loan of Spears to the wall, by narrow margins, each time over objections cut in long form, and the four hundred Order soldiers lent in 688 IC stood on the southern approach through a Greymane winter and learned about the three-quarters of a beat. House Greymane, whose words are The Ridge Does Not Move, answers the Toll Entry each year by sending the Speaker a single piece of slate, which Khal-Serrat now has a good many of and uses as roofing on the fish market.
Later hand, from the last winter before the turn: when Kharven was built out into the Northern Empire of Whitemere, the moot took three days over whether the debt passed to the new crown, and found by a margin of nine that it did.
Monsters on the Roads
The roads here are water, and the moot’s rolls file what lives on them under fisheries. Sea Serpents hunt the kelp lines and are entered as fishing disputes. Ash-crabs, shore-walking things with hot shells, come out after an eruption and eat what the ash killed, and reef children sell the shells. Of plain beasts the Isles have sea birds in their millions, which will have the eye of a quarry hand who gets between them and an egg, and turtles and reef fish, which are supper. The Isles’ Essence runs on what Hobgoblin scholars call the arc’s own magmatic source, and the Low Reefs have vent-forges the Marrowkin taught them to build.
Dungeons
The register calls a dungeon a standing item, and two stand. The Moot Vent runs down from Khal-Serrat, a Pyreveil ground (Pyreveil being a Wild Wellspring of banked heat) that smells of banked coals, where nobody sweats, and where the heat you did not feel comes due later as thermal debt, the overreach peculiar to that Wellspring. Young hobgoblins of the Crimson Order walk down it to earn a voice at the moot. The charter asks only twelve years’ residency, the benches ask whether you have been down the Vent, and no candidate has yet won a hearing by explaining the difference. It counts as worked, after a fashion, with hours sold by weight, and the keepers are whoever is left.
The other is Skaal-Mol, one of the three forbidden islands where the ground shakes at a frequency that makes Stone-Blood vibrate at the wrong harmonic, and nobody enforces the prohibition because nobody needs to. Tinker crews and foreign delvers land there anyway for the glass, down a lava tube that goes on past any rope, and a Bugbear can tell you from the hair on her scalp that they will not be back. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
The Scourge and the Turn
Nothing out of the Scourge of Hell, at the center of the one great land, has ever been recorded swimming, so the Isles are the only people on these shelves who can discuss the Turn from a position of pure interest. The Turn is the old rota by which North, South and Center each keep the Scourge’s monsters off everybody else for nine years, and each time the wheel moves the Keth-Gorrum reads it into the Rock under the heading Others’ Business, on a roll that takes a morning.
It is also a very good customer. Brimstone goes into the siege-fire on the Line, the chain of forts around the Scourge’s edge, and glass into its edges and lenses. On the South’s Turn the ships load for Rimward and the Salt Quay at Haeseong and the salt road carries it up the east flank. On the Center’s, the present one until 721, the Charter offers instruments, the Isles price in weight, and so the Center pays in Nalūn salt and complains in two directions. On the North’s Turn the Isles still sell nothing on the Kharven side of the wall, so a Northern host on the Line burns Isles brimstone bought at third hand out of the South, and its Count carries the markup as a grievance. The moot has been informed of this and considers it the Toll Entry’s most satisfactory result to date.
Some of the Isles’ people go in person. Among the hobgoblins on the western ridges above the Black Roots, stripping carcasses and hiring out as guides, are Isles outcasts and contract hands, usually people who lost a vote badly or could not stand to hear another roll. They are long-service folk with a century or more in them, and they still move to adjourn when a crew starts to panic.
Neighbors and Grudges

The Iron Mandate of Undaar-Keth The other answer. The Isles consider the Mandate a tyranny, and the Mandate considers the Isles naive, and four centuries of observers who are at once envoys and spies have kept the two from war. They trade in brimstone, glass and goblin contracts. A young Voice who wants to end a debate may ask his opponent whether he would like the matter settled by a decree.
The Ironblood See The Orc Question, below, and bring a meal. Ironblood warchiefs still land from time to time, and go home thirsty.
The Sealed Charter of the Concord The Isles sent an observer to the founding and did not sign. They trade with the Accord. They do not belong to it. Concord clerks and Isles interpreters each regard the other as a dying art.
The Marrowkin of Marrowhold Partners in the vent-forge since about 500 IC. Both deny learning anything from the other in public and acknowledge it freely in private. The Isles’ scholars would like very much to know what the Marrowkin’s tally of what was taken is for, and the Marrowkin have said that they will be informed.
The South’s harbors Alabaster’s harbor at Rimward and the Ryu sea-captains of the Copper Coast of Haeseong buy brimstone and glass by the shipload and argue about the kelp line on the Outer World shelf, every year, in writing, at length.
The Antediluvians Gone, and the moot voted on it.

What they joke about
Every Isles joke is about procedure. “May your motion carry” is a curse. “I second it” means you first. The reef families ask how many Voices it takes to bail a boat, and the answer is that the roll has been called and will be completed shortly. The dead four of 612 are still toasted, as the only Voices never to change their minds. They say of the Mandate that a decree is a motion nobody was allowed to second, of the Ironblood that an orc reads a table as an opening argument, of Elves that they should try carrying something, and of the northern lords that the bill is still open, which the Isles consider funnier than you do. Thurr-kep is its own joke, and you are it.
Timeline

































































































DateEventSecond Epoch cosmological, pre-reckonedTHE FIRST IMPACT. The asteroid strikes the mortal world. Core becomes Hobgoblin, shell becomes Orc, mantle becomes Bugbear. The six goblinoid lineages emerge over the centuries that follow as impact fragments interact with local Wellspring conditions. Stone-Blood encodes all lineages to a single origin frequencyc. −1,380Goblinoid Old World settlement. Ironblood coalitions rule by kinetic hierarchy; Hobgoblin granaries and wards support the military structure; Bugbear clans anchor the interior valleysc. −1,340 to −1,300THE SCATTERING. Forty-year compression and expulsion from the Old Worldc. −1,290LANDFALL ON GORR-KETH. First permanent settlement in the caldera. Bugbear clans claim the shelf tier. The name Vorruk-Khal enters the recordc. −1,250THE FIRST ASSEMBLY. A dispute over fresh water between three Hobgoblin settlement-commanders and a Bugbear fishing kin escalates to the edge of violence, weapons out. A Bugbear elder named Thaal-Gorr proposes the dispute be settled by open argument in a public place rather than by rank or force. The precedent holdsc. −1,200 to −1,100THE QUIET CENTURY. Consolidation. Terraced agriculture. First obsidian quarries. Gorr-Vaross develops as a distinct dialect. The Crimson Order’s Vow of Silence adapts to island conditions with a sea variant permitting speech during navigation emergencies, a pragmatic exception the mainland fortress-monasteries have never formally acknowledgedc. −1,050FORMAL CHARTER. Kethaal the Inscriber carves the charter into the cliff-face of the moot-isle with her own hands over eleven days. Establishes residency requirements, apportionment by hearth, term limits, and the prohibition on hereditary seats. It does not mention Orcs. It does not need toc. −900An established realm of roughly twelve thousand across nine islands. The Hobgoblin merchant fleet, built from volcanic-glass-hulled vessels of a design found nowhere else, makes its first recorded crossing to the Old World coastc. −700FIRST BUGBEAR SPEAKER. Gor-Thuum of the Shelf Islands. His term is remembered as the most procedurally uneventful in the moot’s history, which is the highest compliment the Hobgoblin Voices know how to payc. −500THE ANTEDILUVIAN CONTACT. Trade is attempted and fails. The Antediluvians regard goblinoids as raw material. The Isles withdraw entirely from eastern waters and keep a defensive perimeter. The first recorded instance of the Keth-Gorrum voting unanimouslyc. −450The Antediluvian civilization collapses. The Isles are unaffected. The moot debates whether to send aid and decides, after eleven days, not to. The margin is four votes. The debate is inscribed in the Rock in fullc. −200POPULATION PEAK. Roughly forty-five thousand across fourteen islands. The Bugbear population exceeds the Hobgoblin population for the first time and the apportionment adjusts accordingly. No civil unrest accompanies the shift. The Hobgoblin Voices note that the system worked as designed and say this with the specific tone of people who designed the systemc. −100TREATY OF THE WESTERN SHELF. Negotiated by a Bugbear trade delegation and notable for being written in Low Goblintongue rather than High Concord, a choice the Hobgoblin elders for outside dealings approved through gritted teethc. −50THE LAST LAPSE. A sickness on the Shelf leaves the moot short of a quorum for a full year, the only time in its history. It reseats the next spring and starts its count of unbroken years over, in the belief that an honest count is worth more than a long one. The Hobgoblins will tell you the first thousand years were practiceYear 000The Isles send an observer to the founding of the Concord and do not sign the Codex. Stated reason: the Codex concentrates enforcement in a manner incompatible with the moot’s sovereignty. Unstated reason: the Concord is built on the Old World’s institutional logic, and the Old World is the place that threw them out. They trade with the Accord. They do not belong to itc. 100 to 150 ICTHE GOLD FLOOD. Eastern placer gold destabilizes western currencies. The Isles’ sulfur and obsidian, priced in weight-barter rather than coin, are suddenly among the most stable goods in the four quarters. The moot raises shipments by twelve parts in the hundred and holds prices constantc. 350 ICIRONBLOOD INCURSION. The warchief Grakh-Tuul attempts to seize the low reefs. The response comes from the benches rather than the barracks: the Keth-Gorrum votes to cut off freshwater resupply and wait. Unable to find potable water on the tidal shelves, the warband withdraws after sixteen days. No Hobgoblin or Bugbear soldier draws a weapon. Nobody has ever admitted to it, and four families are surec. 500 ICMARROWKIN CONTACT. Factors of Marrowhold establish formal trade. The Marrowkin teach vent-forging, the art of running a forge on heat the ground gives up, which they know from furnaces of their own; the Hobgoblins teach glyph-inscription under seawater pressure. Both sides deny learning anything from the other in public and acknowledge it freely in private, which is the foundation of every durable trade partnership in the four quartersc. 612 ICTHE ASH SESSION. Gorr-Keth erupts during the kelp roll. The roll is completed. Four Voices die in their seats and are marked present688 ICTHE SECOND LOAN. Four hundred Order spears lent to the Mandate for the Greymane wall by a margin of three. They come home the following year in smaller number, with stories about the coldc. 650 to 715 IC presentRoughly sixty thousand across fourteen permanent islands. The moot is in its seven hundred and sixty-fifth year of unbroken sitting. The current Speaker is Vaal-Gorrum, a Bugbear, the ninth non-Hobgoblin to hold the position. The Withering has not measurably affected the Isles’ Wellspring access, which Hobgoblin scholars attribute to the arc’s independent magmatic Essence source, and everyone else attributes to nobody wanting the islands badly enough to deplete them
Historical Figures
Dokk-Vraal, the Breaker · Ironblood warchief whose northern shield raid triggered the coalition that expelled the goblinoid peoples. Not a member of the moot. Remembered in the Keth-Gorrum’s records as the author of the exile, cited in every debate about Ironblood participation as evidence that force without counsel produces exactly one outcome.
Thaal-Gorr, the First Voice · Bugbear elder who proposed public argument as an alternative to violence during the freshwater dispute. Did not hold formal office. Did not seek it. The tradition that grew from his proposal now rules sixty thousand people, and the only thing recorded about his personal life is that he was a fisherman who hated mornings.
Kethaal, the Inscriber · First Speaker of the Rock. Carved the charter in eleven days. Served one twelve-year term and refused a second, on the stated ground that a Speaker who serves twice has begun to believe the Rock needs them specifically, and it does not.
Gor-Thuum, the Shelf-Speaker · First Bugbear Speaker. His term was so procedurally smooth that the historians describe it as “unremarkable,” which is the word the Keth-Gorrum reserves for rule that required no crisis, no emergency session, and no personal heroism. He took this as the compliment it was.
Grakh-Tuul, the Thirsty · Ironblood warchief who withdrew after sixteen days without water. The epithet was given by the Hobgoblin record-keepers and has survived because it is funnier than anything the Ironblood call him.
Vaal-Gorrum, the Current Speaker · Bugbear, ninth non-Hobgoblin Speaker, serving in Year 715 IC. Known for a style of deliberation other Voices describe as “waiting until everyone else has finished being wrong.” Has held the Speaker’s gavel for four years without using it to call order, because the gavel is a Bugbear-forged basalt weight that would crack the Speaker’s stone, and everyone on the floor knows it, and that knowledge has been sufficient.
Gorrum Ashentusk · Za’tarch Elder, not of the Isles. The most prominent living advocate of cross-lineage goblinoid unity. Za’tarch is a village of two hundred. The Isles are a people of sixty thousand. He is doing with philosophy what the Keth-Gorrum did with law, and both sides are watching the other to see whose proof holds longer.
The Orc Question
Every Hobgoblin child in the Isles learns the Scattering before they learn to read. Every Ironblood child in the four quarters learns the Betrayal of the Mountain before they learn to hold a weapon.

They are learning one event and two lessons.
The Ironblood position, unchanged in two thousand years: the goblinoid peoples were strong enough to hold the Old World if they had fought together, and the Hobgoblin refusal to commit their reserves was the act that lost the homeland. Force was the answer. More force was the better answer. The Hobgoblins chose cowardice disguised as wisdom, and everything that followed is their fault.
The Hobgoblin position, equally simple and equally unchanged: the peoples were driven out because Ironblood leadership made enemies of every other race on the continent at once, refused every diplomatic alternative, and then demanded that everyone else die for the mistake. The homeland was lost the day Dokk-Vraal crossed into the northern shield without counsel. Everything that followed was consequence.

The Bugbear position is the one nobody asks for and both sides find uncomfortable: both are correct. The Ironblood were right that more force might have held the passes for another generation. The Hobgoblins were right that holding them for another generation would have delayed the expulsion and prevented nothing, because the fundamental problem was political.
And the Bugbears, who were in the interior valleys growing grain while the passes changed hands, were the ones who carried the heaviest load during the withdrawal and received credit from neither side for doing it.

The Bugbear position is therefore the specific irritation of someone who did the carrying while two other people argued about direction.
They chose the Hobgoblin road because the Hobgoblin road went somewhere. The Ironblood road went in circles, and the circles were getting smaller, and the Bugbears could see the bottom.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say ityah-soh-SHEE-mah
The Sea-Space. Islands of the Yuno.

Vā is the relational space the house exists to keep. Moana is the deep ocean. An aiga (a family holding land and titles together) that names its own islands after the relation they hold rather than after a founder is behaving exactly as the house thesis says it should.

The fourth application reached Yasoshima in a two-masted Accord cog painted Division blue, carrying Magister Odile Trevanion, forty crates of brass and glass, and a letter with nine seals. The fono of the Manono strait (a fono is the council of a place’s titled heads) received her on a beach hung with red and ocher barkcloth, roasted three pigs in a pit for her, seated her on the fine mats, and began the speeches of welcome, which by custom run in order of title, and the titles ran for forty-one days. She ate breadfruit in coconut cream and learned to drink kava without flinching. On the fifth day, to pass the time, she unpacked one assay fork. It rang one note and held it, morning and evening, for five weeks, and she wrote in her journal that in thirty years she had never seen a fork behave so and would give a finger to know why.
On the forty-first day an old woman of no stated rank gave her a fine mat, a basket of dried fish, and her own letter back with the seals unbroken and the compliments of the house. Nobody had said no. The cog went out on the evening tide loaded with gifts and struck the reef a league off the strait, in water so clear that the crew could watch the crates settle among the blue coral, and the island pilots pulled every soul out of the sea, fed them all again, and did not dive for the brass. The fork is still down there. The Division has her journal, and has filed it with the other three under Pending.
Yasoshima is eighty low green islands with nothing on them worth stealing, where Essence does not drift and a house has made hospitality into a wall. Land here is held under a title and paid for in fish, mats and labor at the fono’s feasts, water rights in the lens are older than anyone’s grandmother and fought over harder than any crown, and the lime-burners, reef-pilots and mat-weavers of the strait will all stop work and shout at you if you walk across a marked threshold in your shoes.
Formation
A drowned fragment of the same collisional belt that became the Old World, which never rose high enough to join the mainland and spent the intervening age being capped in limestone.
What stands above the waterline is raised coral platform over karst. Low, green, riddled with caves, holding fresh water in lenses that sit a few feet above the salt and go bad the moment anyone digs too deep.
Bearing Stock

Effectively none. No metal, no coal, no timber worth a hull. Lime, shell, coral rag, pandanus, and fish.
This is the whole of the reason the islands have never been conquered. There has never been anything on them worth the crossing, and a house that cannot be invaded profitably has been free to spend two hundred thousand years perfecting ceremony instead of fortification. (That figure comes down from the Epochs, which the Guild’s count keeps off its books, and a Measurewright will not sign it. Neither will a Yuno, who sees no reason he should have to.)

Ambient Essence
Moderate, and by every Measurewright reading ever taken, the most stable saturation recorded anywhere in the four quarters. Nothing drifts at Yasoshima.
This is why Yuno rites hold across generations without correction, why the house has never built an array, and why the Accord’s Research Division has filed four separate requests to establish a station there and been declined four times without explanation.
What the Research Division Was Not Told

What the Accord was never told. Nobody outside the Kagura officiant line knows what follows, and no Accord clerk has ever been told.

Yasoshima’s Essence is not stable because the islands got lucky. It is stable because House Yuno has spent two hundred thousand years making it a drain. Every fracture, every fanning-out of chaotic Essence that the rest of the four quarters absorbs and calls weather — the ordinary drift that keeps Measurewrights employed everywhere else in the world — the Kagura branch has been quietly gathering to itself and metabolising, one convergence rite at a time, through the deepest reach of Tōbō no Michi. Yasoshima does not merely tolerate Essence better than anywhere else. It is where a portion of the world’s disorder goes to stop being disorder.
The islands are the correct vessel for this precisely because of what the Bearing Stock entry treats as their poverty: no ore, no reactive mineral wealth, nothing conductive or catalytic to distort what is poured into them. A bowl with nothing in it holds cleanest.
This is not passive. Every rare convergence — the sevenfold calendar’s once-in-years alignment when all five branches can be gathered under one roof — is a working, and Tōbō no Michi does not come free. Hōkō is burden: sacred service always costs the one who performs it, and Tōbō no Michi’s own listed corruption is the tyrannical subsumption of every will beneath one. What that means in practice is that the officiants who hold the convergence — always Kagura, always the branch trained from childhood in the most dangerous reaches of the labor — spend a measurable sliver of their own selfhood into the pattern each time, the same Ritual Self-Dilution Ayame’s own card names as the cost of her lesser, single-city version of this discipline at Kharven. The stillness the Accord measures at Yasoshima is not a gift of geography. It is a standing sacrifice, currently being paid, by living people, on a schedule the house has never missed.
Four applications have asked, in good faith, to put instruments on the one place in the world where nothing drifts. What they do not know is that nothing drifts is not a baseline to be studied — it is a container under active load, and every one of the house’s rules about consecrated ground exists to keep exactly this kind of instrumented attention off it. A station, an array, a Measurewright taking continuous readings, is by the house’s own theology precisely the profane or unstable use that Kiyome exists to bar — not because the readings would offend anyone’s dignity, but because an outside apparatus measuring the sink changes what the sink is holding.
Why the house refuses
Three separate strands of the house’s own logic converge on silence, not a single we cannot tell them instinct.

Theological. Yuno power always arrives dressed, never as raw process. A Research Division station is the opposite of dressed: instrumentation stripped of rite. Letting it observe the convergence is not a privacy violation to them — it is a category error that risks desanctifying the sink mid-use.
The nature of partial truth. The ma must be carried; not every tension should be erased. A Yuno does not consider a partial disclosure safer than silence — an account offered under outside interrogation is itself an unwitnessed, badly formed act. Better total refusal, four times, than an explanation that is nine parts true and permanently loose in the world.
What the Accord would do with it. A confirmed, replicable Essence-stabilisation mechanism is worth every crossing there is. House Yuno is not protecting a mystery. It is protecting the only leverage that has ever kept it unconquered: the world’s total certainty that there is nothing here worth taking.

If it is ever forced into the open
Two things happen, and neither is contained. First, the mechanism itself. Because the convergence rites are tuned exactly to the load they have always carried, sudden outside interference — a station’s array, a captured officiant made to demonstrate the working under duress, a forced early convergence — does not fail safely. It backs up. The volatility the sink has been holding does not vanish when the working stops; it discharges locally and violently at Yasoshima itself, and for the first time in recorded history a Measurewright reading somewhere on the mainland spikes — the first confirmed drift ever traced back to the islands, proof the connection was real all along.
Second, the political fallout outlives the physical one. The instant any faction understands Yasoshima is not merely stable but is absorbing everyone else’s instability, the island stops being unconquerable and becomes the single most contested piece of ground in the four quarters — fought over not for what it produces but for what happens to the rest of the world if it is damaged or seized. And whoever is made to speak the mechanism aloud does not walk away clean: everything already established about this world’s oath-magic — a broken sanctuary recoiling on a Soul Crystal — tracks with treating the house’s silence as a sealed vow, not a policy.
Governance
A confederation of aiga governed by fono, with no king, no standing army, and no charter with the Guild Accord.

The five branches are islands before they are branches, and the Manono seat sits in the strait between the two largest, which is why the rarest branch is also the one every other branch must sail past.
Kharven’s marriage to the house is the only formal tie Yasoshima holds to any mainland power. The fono ratified it as a feagaiga between houses (a sacred covenant of obligation), a very different thing from an alliance between states, and the north has never fully understood the difference.
Kharven believes it gained an ally. The Yuno believe they placed an obligation.
Both are correct and neither has said so out loud.

The Queen

The Queen of Kharven is Ayame Yuno.


























NameStandingPersonal name AyameGiven at birth by the Yuno family. Japonic register.Aiga YunoKagura BranchMatai title Zenma no MamoriKeeper of the Whole Vā, and a literal description of the White ConcordSaimei Okurareta NishikiThe fine mat that was given away. Kharven’s records call her Queen, and the Yuno house calls her the same.

Yuno means gentle. It is a warning wearing a soft word. A woman named Peace who receives thirty hostile clans alone in a courtyard and has them rethreaded into three coalitions by dawn is that thesis walking around.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Bearing and the Holding
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
A Survey of the Four Quarters, Their Substrate, and What May Be Made Of Them

Fourth revision. Compiled for the Logistics and Supply Division of the Guild Accord under attestation of the Guild of Measurewrights, Hexagonal Oath. Dates conform to the Concordance of Ages, sealed Year 715 In Concordance, the twenty-fifth year of the Dark Ages. Kingdom names struck throughout. Copied by hand and circulated to Division heads, Accord assay houses, and the chartered mining companies of all four quarters. Not for open sale.

Prefatory Note
This ledger exists because two men can dig the same hole and get different answers, and because the Accord has now lost four deep workings and one city block to the assumption that stone is stone.
The block was Vat Row in Aldermarsh, and the two men were Simkin Kettleby and Osbern Tapley, who dug one trial pit together in the pale limestone behind the Dyers’ new hall and fell out over it before they had climbed back up the ladder. Kettleby read thirty feet of sound rock and said so to the Dyers, who were paying him. Tapley read the same thirty feet and the hollow note under them, and said so to the Fullers, who hated the Dyers, and the Fullers nailed his reading to the hall door on the morning of the Feast of Vats. Nobody takes advice from a rival’s door. Four hundred dyers came down the Row that noon in woad blue and madder red with the great vats carried shoulder high and the whole town leaning out of its windows to throw flowers, and at the corner by the tripe stalls the street folded in along its own length and went down into a cave that no survey had ever entered. Sixty-one people went with it, and nine hundred gallons of dye. The spring at Thornholt, three leagues off, ran blue for ten months and red for four more, and the Fullers charged a copper to see it. Kettleby’s heirs and Tapley’s still cross the street to avoid each other. Both readings, I am sorry to report, were accurate.
It is arranged by quarter rather than by kingdom. Borders move. Bedrock does not.

The fourth revision has struck the kingdom names from the deposit entries, and the reason is worth stating rather than burying. A ledger that names a seam for the crown that holds it must be reissued whenever the crown changes, and this one has now been reissued three times without a single seam moving an inch. Where a name was doing real work it has been replaced by the ground it referred to. Where a name was doing no work it is gone.

Every figure in this ledger was taken at the face, not from a chartered claim. Where a claim and a reading disagree, the reading stands.
Terms, for the new clerk
The four quarters are four quarters of one continent with isles off its shores, and a loaded mule could visit all of them without once getting its feet wet, though the Division does not recommend the mule. Inner, Old, New and Outer are chart-clerks’ names from the Voyager Era, and they record the order in which the Guild’s charts got there. They say nothing true about the ground, and the elves of the “New” World have been laughing at the word for seven centuries.
Bearing is what a material does under load: compression, tension, shear, thermal cycling, abrasion. Holding is what working it will keep, and for how long. Every entry gives both, a Tier from T0 to T9 (the Accord’s ladder of what a material can stand and who can work it), and where it applies a Resonance (the Wellsprings it answers to) and a Domain (the branch of natural law that Resonance works through).
Aether is what lies in the ground and air, and how much of it lies there is Aetheric Density: rich ground and thin in a scholar’s mouth, fat and lean in the street. It comes in sixty types that affect the Soul Crystal differently, and those types are the Wellsprings: sources of power that also represent alchemical principles and spiritual transformations. A practitioner pulls Aether out of the world, and what happens next depends on the road. A Body worker packs it raw in the Shell (the soul’s outer skin) as the Charge and drives it out from there. A Spirit worker refines it in the Crystal into Essence and spends it through the Core. A Fate worker pulls Thread and pays from the soul’s own share. All three must fill from the ground first, so Aetheric Density feeds every reserve. A place where one type of Aether pools is a Wellspring site, and a worked site with keepers on it is called a Core in common speech.
Density is one of three readings the Guild takes off a piece of ground, and the only one this ledger prices, because it is the only one that feeds an array. Echo Depth is how thickly souls, memory and meaning lie on a place: graveyards, temples and old homes run deep, and Spirit workings come cheap there. Thread Weight is how much has been decided on it: battlefields, coronation halls and crossroads run heavy, and Fate pulls come cheap there. Neither can be pulled, pumped or put in a contact. Both move rents, sieges and the choice of dueling ground, a place can run high in more than one, and the clerk who needs them will find the instruments and the famous sites in The Three Grounds.
An array is a standing runed working cut for one duty, and it does nothing by itself. It is fed by array-keepers, practitioners on a shift who pull from the ground under the pit head and drive what they pull into the contacts, packed raw in the Shell or refined in the Core according to the keeper’s own road. They are paid by the hour, and they may decline to come in. Everyone reading this ledger should keep that last clause in mind.
What Magic Actually Did to Industry
The common account is that Essence made industry possible. That is wrong in an instructive way. Essence removed four specific obstacles that had held mining and metalworking at a fixed ceiling for eleven centuries, and everything since has been the consequence of their removal.



































ObstacleWhat it heldWhat removed itWaterNo working anywhere ran more than sixty fathoms below the adit line for longer than a dry summer. The deep ore was simply understood to belong to nobodyPhreatis-fed lift arrays, filed by the Measurewrights under Fluid DynamicsAirDepth kills by the atmosphere long before it kills by the roof. Firedamp burns, blackdamp smothers, and the old answer was a man in a wet hood with a candle on a poleCymorath draught arrays, turning every deep working into a lungHaulageRope has a limit and rock is heavyWeight Ablation glyphwork, which lifts nothing and lies to the rope about the weightHeatCharcoal and a good bellows will not take you past the point where iron becomes liquid, and everything interesting lives past that pointIgnivale and Pyraeon forge-arrays, filed by the Measurewrights under ThermodynamicsAssayThe bearing press is old. The holding coil is notThe coil (the brass assay instrument), which is why the trade in Essence-active material stopped being a matter of a seller’s word. A coil reading can be falsified, and the Accord hangs people for it. What cannot be falsified is a coil reading set against an assay fork, because the two instruments answer different questions and a forged lot will not satisfy both. The comparison is trivial, both reagents are indexed, and no procedure anywhere requires it

The single most important fact in the ledger. A pumped shaft is as deep as its array can be fed, and no deeper. Which means a mine does not die when the ore runs out. It dies when the ground under its pit head thins and the keepers can no longer pull enough to feed the array, and the ore is still down there when the water comes up. The Old World is a graveyard of drowned workings that were still profitable on the day they were abandoned.

Weight Ablation halves the effective load on a winding rope for as long as the glyph holds. When the lie fails it fails all at once. Every winding house in the Old World has a bell for that and every man underground knows what the bell means. Spatial translation of ore was tried, costed, and abandoned; moving rock by Transference remains more expensive per ton than moving it up a rope, and will remain so.
The heat ceiling’s fall moved the constraint from the fire to the vessel, which is why refractory stock, wolfram and chromite and nothing else, is quietly one of the most strategic commodities in the four quarters and is priced accordingly.

What follows from all this is the shape of the world as it now stands. There is no steam engine in any mine, forge or mill in the four quarters and there never will be, because every problem a stationary engine was going to solve had already been solved by other means before anyone thought to build one.
There is instead a continent-wide dependency on hired wardens and the hours they buy at a Core for the most basic functions of a pit, pumping and ventilation, which means that a Wellspring site going thin or a Core’s keepers closing their gate does more than inconvenience a mining district. It drowns it, and then it suffocates whoever went down to see why the pumps had stopped.

The fifth obstacle, which fell last
The four above were removed and are therefore invisible. The fifth held longest, and its removal is the reason the ledger has had to be revised.
Traction. An array is a fixed work. It stands where it was cut, its keepers stand on the ground beside it, and nothing that moves can bring its keepers’ ground along. Weight Ablation lies to a rope about a load and supplies no motive power whatsoever. Spatial translation of ore was tried, costed and abandoned. So the problem of moving a great weight a long distance overland stayed exactly where it had been for eleven centuries: horses, and the road, and the weather.

Which is why the kept road is a street that does not stop. Ward-cutters keep its bridges and road-wardens its waystones, and a waystation’s stones are cut in tuned pairs: the warden fills one in the station, and its twin under a carrier’s cart-bed takes the heat across a hand’s breadth of air by Transference (the Wellspring that passes energy between tuned things without contact). Nothing burns and nothing boils, a kept wagon rolls through the frost and mud that stop a plain one, and there is no steam engine anywhere in the four quarters, on a road or off it. The horses remain horses, and the Division has received complaints from them.
It is an Accord work in every respect that matters: laid out under a company’s charter, paid for at every waystation, and stopped on any morning its road-wardens choose to sit down on the steps. It beats the one obstacle Essence took longest to reach, and it does so by carrying the fee to every town on the road.
The Logistics Division’s position is that the kept road is a haulage convenience. The Division has not yet costed what happens to a district when a kept road reaches it and the whole town goes on the fee in a single season.

The tenders who work the arrays pay for this in the ordinary way. Long array duty produces the tremor the trade calls the tender’s shake, a fine persistent palsy of the hands that arrives at about eight years of service and does not leave. Array houses hire young and they hire in numbers.
Comparative Summary



































QuarterIn one breathPrincipal exportsStanding conditionNorth · Inner WorldCold iron country with fire to spare and nothing else cheapIron, nickel, copper, salt, beryl, timberCheap array heat, expensive everything elseWest · Old WorldThe richest holes on earth, and a whole people paid by the hour to keep the water out of themWolfram, tin, lead, coal, lime, reworked slagTotal array dependency for survival, not productionEast · New WorldGround still being made, gold in the rivers, and every town ready to pick up its hall and runGold, silver, sulfur, cement, Onceglass, Cloudmetal, all of these the arc’s; the elven old-ground beside it lies outside this ledgerAlmost no array dependency outside the eastern arcSouth · Outer WorldThe poorest quarter in the world, sitting on what the other three cannot do without, with dragons on half of it and Vampires on the restPhosphate, nitre, chromite, fulgurite, serpentineExtraction by hand at scale, value added elsewhere
A survey has no column for what a place looks like, and I will trespass here once. The clerk who has read only this ledger will arrive expecting a country of holes. He will find pale western towns with sect banners on every bridge and three schools’ colors brawling at the bracket gate, lamps in amber and rose along the wharves, eastern markets selling river gold by the pinch under awnings dyed with the same sulfur that is killing the men who gather it, and coppersmiths in every quarter shouting the names of their own kettles. Rent, in every one of them, follows the ground. The ledger will tell him why. It will not prepare him for the noise.
Hazard Register, Abbreviated











































































HazardWhereCharacterArray failure, pumpingWestern deep workingsFlooding within seventy to one hundred and ten hours depending on shaft. The most likely mass-casualty event in the four quarters and the one the Accord is least prepared forArray failure, ventilationAll deep workingsFiredamp in coal, blackdamp in metal. Kills faster than water and is more easily concealed afterwardKeepers’ stoppageAll array housesAn array-keeper is a person with a wage and a grievance. A walkout starts the same clock as an array failure, and both sides of the dispute can countWeight Ablation glyph failureAll winding housesTotal and instantaneous restoration of true load. The bell is rung by hand because no contraption built to give the warning has ever been fast enoughSulfide roast fumethe RingChronic. Vegetation loss to six leagues and risingVitriol drainageWestern old workingsChronic, cumulative, irreversible at current practiceRock dust, silicateWestern slate beltsGrinder’s cough. Twenty year onsetRock dust, fibrous serpentineSouthern coastal quarriesTwenty year onset, invariably fatal, no treatment recordedLaharEastern volcanic plainsSudden, total, and faster than a horseFumarole gas poolingEastern sulfur fieldsSilent, collects in hollows, kills rescue parties secondWellspring driftEastern quarter generallyEconomic rather than physical. Bankrupts rather than killsTender’s shakeAll array houses, all quartersOnset at approximately eight years of service. Permanent. No compensation scheme exists in any quarterCrevice proximitySouthern Crevice marginUndescribed. Four-league exclusion, revised outward five times in the last sixty years
Unresolved Entries
The Measurewrights record the following as open and decline to guess.
The provenance of Ghoststeel. Attributed to the northern shield on ruin-siting evidence alone. No crucible reproduction has succeeded, and until one does the material’s formation is unexplained.
The provenance of Seerstone Resin. Attributed provisionally to eastern cloud forest canopy species. Unconfirmed by Archives.
Whether the Ring’s interdimensional passages are caused by the impact structure or merely coincident with it. The Measurewrights hold that the correlation is too exact to be accident and too unexamined to be asserted.
The Names That No Longer Attach to Ground
A separate class of open entry, and the one the Logistics Division finds most irritating.
Certain materials in continuous trade arrive under provenance names that no current survey can attach to anywhere. The material is real. It is assayed, priced, shipped, and used. The place it is said to come from cannot be found by anyone the Accord has sent to look.





















MaterialThe problemVellun CopperTrade-route evidence places the source hills in the western quarter. Four surveys have failed to confirm it. The copper continues to arriveGlassroot Fibers and Steelsilk CordTwo separate Accord records place the source in two separate quarters. Both cannot be right and neither has been withdrawnWillowblood Sap and Moonblight OreNeither source appears on any current survey, and the older registers that name them give no coordinates, only a name and a road that no longer runs anywhere
The Measurewrights offer three explanations and endorse none. That the names are commercial fictions protecting a real source, which is ordinary and would explain the shipping and not the age of the records. That the places existed and have been depopulated to the point of leaving no charter behind, which the northern quarter has seen twice within living memory. Or that the names are older than the Concordance’s count can reach and refer to ground that has since been renamed by people who did not know what they were renaming.

The Guild notes that the third explanation is the one the corrected chronology makes least available. Fourteen hundred years is not long enough for a country to be forgotten by everybody while its exports continue.
Something is still loading those ships.



The Inner World — The Northern Shield
The Old World — The Western Wearing
The New World — The Eastern Rise
The Outer World — The Southern Pan
Yasoshima — The Eighty Isles
The Crimson Isles of Vorruk-Khal
Kushara — The Land That Remembers Weight
