geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Amber Cities of Nalūn
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itnah-LOON
The free salt cities of the Center, wedged between the North and the South

Take the tunnels and you hold rock. The value is in the seals, and the seals answer to the Wellsprings, and the Wellsprings do not recognize occupation.
Every serious military assessment of the chain-cities in the last two centuries, arriving at the same paragraph

Bartlemy Quince of Ironlink Hold owed a wheel of Bridgemarch blue, and no cheese has ever cost anybody more. As a young man he had sealed a friendly instrument with a rival, one wheel a year on midsummer morning for as long as both their houses stood, as a joke, in the salt, with the glyphs done properly because he was showing off. Twenty-eight years later, at the height of his career, he forgot. It was his daughter’s wedding in the Great Chain Hall, three thousand guests under the amber walls, wine from four kingdoms, lamp-dancers in gold leaf swinging from the chain overhead, when the rival’s widow stood up on her bench and held out an empty cheese-board, and the iron disc on Quince’s chest, the oldest active contract he owned, went dead in front of everyone.
The wedding instrument failed to seal under the scribe’s hand three times running. By evening no calibrator in the Hold could read his credit. By the end of the month four more of his contracts had stopped answering and his carriers were leaving his loads at the roadside. He spent the next nine years walking cheese up and down the Iron-to-Salt Corridor in a borrowed coat, paying every back wheel by hand, and the widow ate each one in front of him. His daughter married anyway, in a Cutwall tavern, on a handshake, and she will tell you it was the better party.
Nalūn is seven free cities cut into the bed of a dead sea, where a promise is a working, every army that marches through pays for its bread, and nobody has ever worn a crown. How anyone dares live there takes the rest of this entry.
A Country With No King In It
Nalūn is the name of a country. Its cities are free, each under its own council, and the fourteen factor houses that sit across all of them meet as the Council of Links. The old style, the Kingdom of Nalūn, lives in exactly one place, the salutation of its diplomatic instruments, because the Concord Codex’s recognition framework requires a sovereign signatory and the Council refused to invent a new category. That is the name you will find on the first circle of the Guild Accord, signed in the lower hall at Kharven-Seat. Ask a Bridgemarch chain-hand who his king is and he will ask what you are selling.
The Center is where the North and the South meet when they want to hurt each other. Nobody marches through the Scourge of Hell, so all their traffic goes round it by two roads, and the eastern one, the salt road, climbs straight through the basin. The chain-cities have been marched through in every generation anyone has written down. They pay both sides, they owe neither, and they have outlasted most of the people who ever came to take them.
Seven cities, a surface port, six provinces. Roughly forty-five thousand souls underground, with a further eight thousand in surface settlements and corridor way-stations that depend on the chain-cities for their living.
The Land and the Look
Come in at dusk, up the salt road, and the first thing you see of Nalūn is Ironlink Hold above ground: a walled rise of honey-colored stone under a deep blue sky, a great domed council hall at the top of it, tall slender call-towers around the dome like reeds around a pool, and one lamp-lit street climbing through the steep dark roofs. Halfway up that street stands a triumphal arch with no top, thick in green creeper. The upper city is the part of Nalūn that gets painted, and it is the smallest part. Below it the cities go down into the bed of the sea, and there the walls themselves glow honey and amber wherever a flame stands near them.
The whole country is a sealed evaporite trough (a basin where a sea dried out and left its salt) ninety leagues by forty, on the north side of the Scourge of Hell: bounded on the north and west by the basement rock of the northern shield, on the east by the boreal forest where the eastern timber begins, and on the south by a broken rim that looks out over the dry country the cutters call the Thresh. The floor sits three hundred feet below the surrounding shield, drier, warmer and far steadier than the glaciated plateau above.
The beds are bedded halite of exceptional purity, two hundred fathoms thick, the preserved floor of an ancient sea that dried out in an era nobody alive can date with confidence. Each band of salt holds a season of that sea’s chemistry, and nobody has counted them to the end. The upper beds have been cut for centuries. The lower beds, where the Aether pools thicker with every fathom, remain partially explored and are reached only through the oldest tunnels, which the cutting houses maintain with an obsessiveness outsiders find comic until they witness the first collapse. Where a cup’s flame catches a seam of clean halite the wall throws it back in pink and violet and a faint drowned green, and the gallery children lie on their backs and count the colors.
Climate · Underground it is cold at the top, dry and stable, and the deepest chambers hold a low constant warmth that visitors describe as the temperature of a body at rest. Above ground: short summers, five months of snow, and a wind off the shield carrying the smell of wet granite and boreal resin. North of the rim lie the chain-lakes, and Long Scratch, the greatest of them, is the road every salt smuggler dreams about in a hard winter.
Marrowhold · Outside the country and inseparable from it. The ore and the worked metal of Marrowhold, which older maps call the Ring and whose rim mountains are the ribs of something the Marrowkin carve up and sell, come down the Corridor and pass through Nalūn’s supply contracts on their way anywhere else. What it was that died in there is an argument for another shelf.
The Seven Cities

Together they form a single organism: a creature made of salt and contract and the accumulated weight of seven centuries of people who discovered that the most durable thing in the world is a promise made inside a mountain.






































CityCharacterIronlink Hold the seat of the CouncilLargest and oldest, where three salt horizons cross a fault that carried the Aether up from the deep. Above ground the honey-stone rise and the dome called the Hall of Links. Below, five levels, lift-cages, and the Great Chain Hall holding three thousand under lanterns that cast warm light across walls of translucent amber salt. The most significant Parun-bound contracts in the four quarters are sealed here. The air smells of mineral warmth, lamp oil, dried ink, and the sharpness of active resonance that visitors feel as low pressure behind the eyes. The oldest walls glow faintly during a sealing, and that glow is called the Chain LightHalcrest the gate cityUppermost, where the beds thin against the northern rim. Customs house, weigh-house, lazar-house and the hiring ground of half the free companies in the north. Goods are weighed and classified here before they go down. See belowCutwall the extraction districtA city only loosely: a shifting complex of work chambers and temporary barracks that moves slowly through the basin as the cutting houses exhaust one face and open another. Permanent structures: the stamping houses, the assurance chambers where array-grade Chainsalt is tested, the offices of the six recognized cutting houses. The rest is scaffolding, sled-track and dust. The air tastes of powdered halite and lamp soot, and career workers develop a dry cough the trade calls salt-throat, which never quite goes and which the older cutters wear like a rankVaultmere the counting cityWhere the salt is exceptionally dense and dry, ideal for the long keeping of Parun-bound instruments. Sealed chambers hold the physical record of every significant agreement in the country’s history, kept dry by the salt itself. Roughly three thousand: archivists, contract scribes, and the calibrators who verify authenticity. A dead merchant’s token is carried here and shelved beside the instrument it stood for. Visiting factors describe it as the place where you can feel the country’s memory pressing against your skin, and they tend to lower their voices and then resent having done itBridgemarch the junctionThe central void, where the tunnel network converges and the largest chain-bridges span two hundred feet across open caverns. Built upward rather than outward, houses hanging from the ceiling and climbing the walls in tiers. The sound of chain is constant, a low rhythmic clanking that becomes, for residents, a form of silence, and on a still night it carries all the way to Halcrest. More egalitarian, more physical, more inclined to solve problems with engineering than with contracts, a disposition the factor houses regard with the wariness of people who understand that the person who maintains the bridge decides whether the bridge stays up. The blue cheese is theirsDeepvein the Wellspring floorLowest of the seven, where the beds are thickest and the Oblation pools richest. Contracts sealed here hold tighter, last longer and enforce with a specificity instruments sealed elsewhere do not match, and the difference is measurable. Roughly two thousand: the most senior contract specialists in the country, the Measurewright station, and the handful of scholars studying how Contraxis and Fixatio work on each other. Warm and glowing. The Chain Light is constant here, a faint amber radiance that does not flicker and needs no fuel, and the oldest residents claim they feel the Wellspring the way other people feel weatherRimward the eastern frontierNewest and most vulnerable, founded about 140 years ago to service corridor trade. Not the Holy Sea of Alabaster’s harbor of the same name, and letters go astray about once a month. Thinner salt, weaker resonance, and contracts sealed here carry a slight but measurable reduction in enforcement strength. The factor houses call this a scandal. The Rimward merchants call it a selling point, because a contract that holds slightly less hard allows slightly more give, and give is what frontier dealing needs
Halcrest
Halcrest is where most people meet Nalūn, and it is the city the songs get wrong. The upper town climbs the basin wall in pale terraces roofed with salt slab, furred white by the frost through its five months of snow, and the bridge-chains strung from terrace to terrace carry worked lamps along their length like beads on a cord. Up in the factor quarter the lamps burn behind panes of clear salt-glass, rose and amber and a clean cold white, and snow falling past them goes pink and gold for the space of a breath. Brass assay posts stand along the shaft-heads, capped in snow, slate-backed and under Guild seal. The salt here is the pale Halcrest kind, its bedding planes showing like the grain of a board, and a lamp cut from it gives a light the color of weak honey.
A worked lamp costs what a sergeant’s pay cannot cover, so the town runs on oil above the kitchen. The salt-tea houses rent their upper rooms by the week, and those rooms smell of lamp oil, wet wool and the butter-and-brine fug of the tea boiling below. Merchants wait here for clearance, couriers for dispatches, and free companies for anybody fool enough to pay them: the Lanternless, the Grey Lamps and Fennick’s all keep a table at one tea-house or another, and a captain’s word on who is a liar will travel the length of the terrace before he has finished his cup. Pay for a season’s escort is quoted in stamped bars, and a factor’s man will look at your belt for a token before he looks at your face.
Under the town lie the Cuttings, gallery below gallery, three hundred feet and more of steady warmth. The lift-cages go past the galleries with their worked lamps lit and their gates shut, carrying factor men to the stamping floor and up again, where the presses strike the house seal into every bar. The cutting families burn fish-oil in tin cups. They cut for the houses that hold the galleries, Orrel among them, and they are entered by name or number in the drainage book, because the drainage book is the one roll in the salt that everybody keeps honest.
The Six Provinces
Each governed by a Provincial Chainwarden, appointed by the Council and bound by Parun-sealed terms specifying their authority, their obligations and the conditions of recall.

































Province · Chief cityCharacterThe Ironward Ironlink HoldPolitical and financial core. Provincial and Council business are in practice the same thing, and the Ironward’s Chainwarden is traditionally the most junior Council member, given the post as a formality because the Council governs the province directlyThe Upper Basin HalcrestThe province of arrival and departure, the one outsiders see first and often the only one they see. Its Chainwarden holds the outer perimeter, the defenses of the surface port on the lake road, and the Chain Gate garrison. The most militarily significant province of a country that has no military, a distinction the Chainwarden carries with the cheerful competence of someone defending a thing that refuses to believe it needs defendingThe Cuttings CutwallExtraction, from the galleries under Halcrest out to the moving face. The six cutting houses operate under their own internal governance, which the Council regulates and does not administer, and they defend that distinction with an obstinacy that is itself a provincial trait. The most physically dangerous district in the country. The safety record is good by any standard except the standard of people who have never been undergroundThe Vaultlands VaultmereArchival. Deliberate, precise and suspicious of haste in any form. Home to the largest concentration of trained scribes in the Center, each of whom completed a seven-year apprenticeship before being permitted to draft an instrument that would be sealed. A factor without a scribe is a man with opinions. A scribe without a factor is a scribe with a full calendarThe Span BridgemarchTransit. Defined by engineering more than commerce. Has produced more Chief Engineers than Council members, a figure its residents cite with pride and the Council cites with concern. The factor houses decide where things go, but the Span decides whether they get there, and the difference matters more than anyone in Ironlink Hold is comfortable admittingThe Eastern Reach RimwardFrontier. Bears the full weight of the corridor closures: supply disruptions, stranded convoys, and mountain settlements that have received nothing for months. Deepvein sits inside its borders as a special zone under direct Council authority, administered by a Council-appointed Steward, producing exactly the friction one would expect between a frontier province and a carve-out in its middle
The Wellsprings and the Oath

Nalūn sits on a great site of Oblation, the Wellspring of what is given up, one of the sixty types of Aether that affect the Soul Crystal each in its own way, a Fate Wellspring, and a contract is two parties giving something up in front of a witness. Worked this way, on this much ground, it is able to seal an agreement into metaphysical law. This is the single fact upon which the entire country is built. A site where such Aether pools is a Core in common speech, and Nalūn’s has its keepers in the factor houses, who have never once closed it, because they know exactly what they would be closing.

Oblation · Contract and agreement, as the salt towns read it. It produces few practitioners in the conventional sense and a great ambient field in which spoken and written agreements, properly sealed, acquire metaphysical weight. A Parun-bound contract (one written in Parun, the glyph script that sets boundaries on law) executed under Contraxis resonance is a working, with no court behind it and none required, and breaking it has consequences that arrive without anyone needing to be convinced, summoned or bribed.

The consequences are structural. The breaker’s Essence (the refined power a practitioner holds and spends) becomes unreliable, their instruments fail to seal, their credit becomes physically unreadable to anyone attuned to the field.
The punishment for breaking a Nalūn contract is that Nalūn stops working for you, and in a world where Nalūn’s instruments are the backbone of long-distance credit, that is a punishment worse than any court could impose.

Fixatio · Concentrated in the salt itself, making Chainsalt an Essence dielectric of exceptional quality, which in plain words means a stuff that will not carry Essence, will not keep it and will not wear down under the strain of holding it back. The interaction gives the chain-cities their character: agreements made inside the salt are bound by the one Wellspring and shielded from tampering by the other.
Parun-bound instruments · A document inscribed with specific glyph sequences, sealed in a linked token, executed inside the resonance field. Each party holds a token, a small iron or bronze disc stamped with the chain-mark, which hums faintly in the metal while the contract is sound and goes silent and cold when it is breached.
The seal-token · Every significant commercial actor carries one, representing their oldest active contract, and “What’s your oldest?” comes before the name. A merchant without a token is a merchant without a history, and a merchant without a history is a merchant without credit. A Nalūn seal binds to a house name. A tokenless man in the chain-cities cannot sign for a sack of meal.
Who Rules
The Council of Links · The senior partners of the fourteen recognized factor houses, sworn in by Parun-bound contracts specifying obligations, term, authority and the consequences of exceeding any of the three.

Four Council members in the recorded history of the Links have been removed by the mechanism of their own oath: their tokens going inert mid-session when the Wellspring determined they had breached the terms under which they held their seat. The chairs were refilled. The four are named in the record only by what they broke.

The High Chainlord · The one who signs for the country, with a chair and a seal and no crown, chosen by the Trial of Ten Deals: ten days, ten increasingly complex commercial problems, judged by retired factors, active Measurewrights (the Guild’s sworn assayers of Aether) and one representative of the Accord’s Arbitration Division, with odds posted on every terrace from the first morning. The candidate who resolves the most without breaching any existing contract, creating any new liability, or insulting any party whose goodwill the country requires takes the office. Held for life, or until the holder’s oath-token goes inert, whichever arrives first.
The factor houses · Fourteen recognized, each a partnership bound by Parun-sealed articles. The articles are public documents and anyone may read them. Orrel and Vessant are the two a stranger most often hears named: Orrel for its cuttings under Halcrest, and Vessant for the oldest supply contract into the eastern timber, iron stock and lamp oil out, furs and resin back, every mile of it through Stark country.
The city councils · Each of the seven runs its own streets, its own watch and its own quarrel with the Hold. Bridgemarch’s sits on a platform slung over the drop, and a member who talks too long is said to find the chain being let out.
Wealth and Trade
Salt · Cast into standard bars of fixed weight and fineness, stamped by the cutting house, circulating as money across the northern quarter and well into the west. At once a food, a preservative, an array-maker’s isolation stock (arrays being standing runed workings) and a currency. A salt bar passes for a silver mark at the Accord rate, more in a bad winter, and it can be eaten, which no other money can.
Credit · Parun-bound enforceability solved the problem that defeated every other economy of the age: long-distance trust. A bill drawn on Ironlink Hold is accepted at the furnaces of Marrowhold, in the Old World’s western ports and in trade posts across the frontier, and those places need feel no respect for Nalūn, because the instrument enforces itself. A bill issued by a factor house can be carried by an unarmed man across three jurisdictions and presented for payment. Metal does not need to travel if claims on metal can.
Supply contracts · A commitment to deliver at a rate, for a term, from a named source. The most traded document in the four quarters, and the factor houses broker the majority of them because their instruments are the only ones the counterparties trust to hold. A river carrier who signs for a load feels the seal take hold of him, faintly, behind the breastbone.
The Iron-to-Salt Corridor · The principal overland route from the furnaces of Marrowhold to the chain-cities and on to the coast. Serviced by independent merchants under Nalūn-sealed contracts, most prominently the Greis Trading House, which operates eleven way-stations along the route.
Interest · Where enforcement is physical rather than moral, lending stops being a sin and becomes a schedule. The Holy Sea of Alabaster maintains that this is a distinction without a difference, and has maintained it for four hundred years while keeping its money at Ironlink Hold.
Rent, Bread and the Street
Underground has never meant hushed. Bridgemarch at change of shift is a roaring market hung over a two-hundred-foot drop, with bread-and-salt sellers working the chain-bridges on ropes, lamp-wardens’ boys running amber and rose lanterns along the tiers, and the cutting-house bracket crews in their house colors fighting on a salt floor while half the district bets sealed slips on them. Every tunnel has its petty trade: a woman at Halcrest who can find a short-weight bar with her tongue and charges by the lick, a drain-walker who hears standing water through a wall and has twice struck over late fees, a Vaultmere copyist whose ink stays wet until the signature is honest and who is booked for three years.
Rent goes to the tunnel’s holder with a drain-share on top, and a household behind on the drain-share is out faster than a household behind on the rent, for the reason Salt Law gives below. Property is measured in salt, so a family’s standing is the volume its ancestors cut.
Supper is salt fish and hard bread, salted meat when the surface has sent it, and grain and medicine that were weighed at Halcrest before anybody ate them. A host at his threshold shaves a curl off a stamped bar onto a heel of bread and hands it over, and a guest who eats it has eaten the host’s money. Salt tea (black tea boiled with salt and butter) is sold by the bowl on every terrace in Halcrest, and in the private chambers of the factor houses it is where the real positions get stated.
The classes · Three, defined by relationship to the instruments. The factor class, partners and senior employees of the fourteen houses. The cutting class, miners, processors, engineers. The agent class, everyone operating under a sealed instrument without being a partner: independent merchants, bonded couriers, ward searchers, scribes, calibrators. Beneath all three lies what the rolls decline to call a class: the tokenless, the people who came down into the galleries with no paper and no house, whom the factor houses take in the way they take in everything that arrives without a claim on it. A party without standing is not a party. They cut, they are entered in the drainage book under a number, and no instrument in the country can be broken against them, a fact the Measurewrights have noted and the Council has not been asked to discuss.
The dead · The salt keeps them. The cutting class lays its dead in a worked-out face, and the salt takes them and does not let them go soft. A merchant’s funeral is also a reading of his open contracts, because they do not die with him.
Words for the shared arts · The aura coat is the surety here, Pressure is the call, and sensing is reading a man’s seal. A Guild roll uses the proper words and everyone in the salt thinks those are the affected ones. A practitioner’s First Release is “called,” like a note, and a release held too long is standing water, which is the rudest thing you can say about anyone’s technique.
Language · Concord Common spoken with a precision that reflects the culture’s relationship to binding language. Contracts are drafted in a register so exact it has become a technical dialect. A loose word in Ironlink is a small liability.
Religion · The Holy Sea maintains a chapel in Ironlink Hold, staffed by a single cleric whose primary function appears to be changing money. Devotional life centers on the Wellspring, and the rites around sealing a great contract carry a ceremonial gravity that does the work of worship. Nobody drinks in a sealing room, and scribes blot with salt, because a spilled cup is held to void the deal.

The chain-cities do not pray. They negotiate, and the negotiation is the prayer.

Law
The Honor Challenge · Insulting a merchant’s honor is a binding challenge, because a merchant’s honor is a load-bearing financial instrument. Resolution: retraction, arbitration, or a formal counter-negotiation in which the accused must demonstrate, through prescribed transactions under full Wellspring scrutiny, that their conduct meets the standard the accuser claimed it did not. The loser pays all costs. These draw bigger crowds than most executions and the Bridgemarch bookies run a book on the third transaction.
Salt Law · Property is measured in salt: the volume a family’s ancestors cut, the tunnels that cutting produced, and the right to maintain them against collapse.

The Drainage Obligation is the single most important provision. Every tunnel owner must maintain their drainage to a standard sufficient to prevent intrusion into adjacent tunnels, because salt fails in standing water.
It is enforced by the Wellspring. A tunnel owner who neglects their drains finds their contracts going unreliable before the water arrives.

How It Fights
The Chain Guard is roughly eight hundred professionals responsible for tunnel security, the surface perimeter and the physical safety of the factor houses, in harness and amber surcoats, with crossbows on every terrace. Competent, well-equipped and entirely insufficient to resist a determined assault.

This does not matter. Taking Nalūn by force accomplishes nothing.
An invading army would find itself responsible for maintaining drainage works that require three centuries of institutional knowledge, and would fail at it within a season.
The real defense is economic. Every crown, lending house and war-chest in the four quarters depends on these instruments. A war against Nalūn is a war against one’s own account-books.

The proof stands in the upper city at Ironlink Hold. Marshal Han Do-yun, when Sum-gol was still the empire of the whole South, took the rise in eleven days with thirty thousand men and sat down in the Hall of Links, and he ordered a triumphal arch to be raised on the street below it, in honey stone, with his campaigns cut into it in letters a yard high. He paid the masons in bills on Ironlink Hold, because that was what his war-chest held. His quartermaster stopped the drains on the third level to billet a regiment. Six weeks later the water reached the first contract, the marshal’s bills went dead one after another in the pockets of his own masons, and they put down their tools at the top of the piers, with the keystone in its cradle, and went to dinner. He was out of the country by autumn. The arch stands as they left it, under its creeper, and the Council has it entered as a forfeit against an unpaid account, on which interest continues to run.
So the cities have a custom for armies. A marshal coming through is met at Halcrest or Rimward by a scribe with a march contract: a named road, a term, a schedule of what bread and fodder cost, and a token for his own belt. Sign it and the bakers open. Loot, and the war-chest paper that pays your army stops being money by the end of the week. North and South have both signed it, frequently in the same month, and the cities pay each side a quiet fee against the quartering, which each side enters as tribute and the factor houses enter as insurance.
Where it comes to blows the fighting is hired. Free companies sign under seal out of Halcrest and fight like men whose wages depend on the instrument holding, and the factor houses keep contract specialists at Deepvein who can lay a clause across a doorway that a man will feel behind the eyes before he crosses it. Those are the people the bracket crews are afraid of.
What They Joke About
The arch, always. “Paid in full,” said of anything left half built. Rimward seals, a promise with give in it, and “a man with opinions” for a factor with no scribe. Every child in Bridgemarch can do the cheese-board, holding out both empty hands with a widow’s face. They say Nalūn has been conquered eleven times and billed for it twelve. They tell northerners that the chain is what holds the South off them, and they tell southerners the same, and in the Cuttings they say a factor has two kinds of friend: the ones under contract and the ones in the salt.
Monsters on the Roads
Water is the great enemy, and what comes with it: Sump-toads (Grade A on the Bestiary’s scale, which runs from E to EX and prices every bounty in the world) in any neglected gallery, the kind of creature a drainage book exists to prevent. Lamp-drinkers (Grade S, found only as the darkest place on a dark shape) have ended whole shifts in the older tunnels, and the lamp-wardens charge accordingly. Blind white fish in the old flooded cuts and the bats of the upper galleries are the only wild animals most of the forty-five thousand will ever meet, and a blind fish at a wedding is a boast.
Above ground the beasts are the plain northern kind, and hungry. Goats on the salt-bush bring wolves, the wolves work the ice of Long Scratch in a hard winter and have learned the hour a smuggler’s sled goes out, and the ice-road taverns will sell you a pelt with the hole in the right place, for those who wish to have been brave. In bad years, stilts and greywalkers come up off the Thresh to the southern rim, a stilt being a herd animal on legs as long as a ship’s mast, thousands together, and a greywalker the upright, long-armed thing that follows them in files at dusk. In dry years haze-kites the color of an old copper pot ride the outward wind as far as the rim road and take mules.
Deepvein is the worked Core, the great Oblation site (the Wellspring of what is given up, and here of contract), and its keepers in the factor houses have never closed it. The dungeon is the Lower Beds, below the deepest maintained gallery, reached only through the oldest tunnels and only partially explored, where the Aether pools thicker with every fathom and a whole cutting house, Merrow’s, went down in 590 and has gone on sending up its drainage fee on time, in bars, by a lift nobody is working. The top of it is a country, the bottom is partly explored, and it is the only dungeon a nation’s law depends on. What the cutting houses have walled off down there they will not say for any fee. The Accord holds a bargain with a speaking spawn (the rare deep creature that talks) void at law, and no Measurewright has been able to say whether the Contraxis at that depth has read the Accord. The Bridgemarch bookies run a long book on the day Merrow’s payment fails to come up, and they have been paying out to the patient since 590. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
Beside the Scourge
The southern rim of the basin is the north side of the worst neighbor in the world. The Scourge of Hell begins past it, across the dry country called the Thresh, then the Hem (its outermost belt, fifteen leagues of black-barked thornwood and pale dust), then the Black Roots, and in high summer the wind comes up hot and dry off all of it, smelling of iron and pollen, and sets the salt-slab roofs ticking. Two trades here answer to the word cutter: the cutting class, who cut salt, and the free-company hunters on Thresh contracts (monster bounties, paid by anyone with a monster problem), who cut up whatever the bounty names. Each takes the confusion as an insult.
Halcrest, on the far side of the basin from the Thresh, is where every crew signs on, with cutters’ taverns and a map trade, and everybody on its terraces will sell you a copy of a copy of the good map. Two of those taverns face each other across one lamp-chain, the Ordinary Sword and the Other One, under the same picture on the sign: a lone figure on a ridge under a purple sky, looking up at a colossal bronze-hilted sword driven into the mountains, with a field of violet stars where its blade should be. On perhaps nine days a year you can see the real one from the Hem, a dark upright line on the sky, and the crews come back up the south road and argue about it over salt tea.
Nalūn’s one contribution everybody admires is the Salt Line: a strip of salted ground, worked by hedge-workers with Chainsalt so that Aether will not pool on it, some sixty miles along the Scourge’s north rim and a hundred paces deep, renewed each spring. Whatever crosses it comes off its Well (ground thick with one kind of Aether) and comes weaker. It costs a fortune and it holds about as well as a fence. The work is let under seal, and the cutters of Halcrest will tell you which stretches were salted honestly and which were let under a Rimward seal, with give in it.
Then there is the Turn: North, then South, then Center, nine years each, with whoever holds it keeping the Line of forts around the Hem, paying the door bounties and bleeding, while the other two watch their borders and count what it costs. The Center holds it now, from 712 to 721, and on the Center’s Turn Nalūn pays in salt and complains in writing. A Vaultmere scribe drafts its Count, the bill each party presents when a Turn ends, in a hand so exact that the Accord’s auditors at Sealhall have twice tried to hire her. On the North’s Turn or the South’s, the host bound for the Line comes up the salt road like any other army, right of passage in hand, and is met by a scribe with a march contract, and it signs, because a right of passage has never yet made a baker open. The difference carried forward between the three Counts is now larger than all the coin in the world, and claims on it trade at Ironlink Hold for a sliver of a copper on the mark. They have never once failed to find a buyer.
Every other town on the rim builds on stone footings with no cellars, for fear of what comes up through the ground. Nalūn is all cellar. No black root has ever been found in the salt, the drainage book keeps a column for it, and on the day a Bridgemarch engineer writes something in that column I should like to be elsewhere.
Neighbors and Grudges

The North The Banner Houses buy on credit and resent the rate. Stark country carries the Vessant contract, Marrowhold’s metal comes down through Thornwall’s corridor, and the Painted Rivers of Hallenfeld fight the Corridor for every load that could go by water.
The Guild Accord The Accord handles disputes between parties who did not seal under Nalūn authority. Nalūn handles disputes between parties who did. The arrangement has never been codified, because codifying it would require acknowledging that Nalūn’s Wellsprings constitute a rival jurisdiction, and the cities’ name on the first circle has only made the silence more expensive. The Sealed Charter next door regards Ironlink Hold as an unlicensed court with a very good roof.
The Holy Sea of Alabaster The theological reconciliation required to condemn the interest and keep the deposit is an achievement of ecclesiastical reasoning that the chain-cities regard with genuine admiration and no small amount of professional respect.
The Hundred Crowns of the Midmarch Owe Nalūn more than any other people in the Center, jointly and severally, and a good third of their wars are about who inherits the debt.
The Moonlight Forest of Mosk-Vaal The Moss Court’s law makes a spilled cask of salt a capital matter, and every salt carter on the Kessen road is a walking insult to it. The Court takes the coin and forgives nothing, and the city councils keep a clerk whose only work is apologizing.
The Marrowkin The best customers and the worst, since no instrument has yet settled who owns what is being sold.
The Zettari Commercial rather than political. Corridor merchants operate under Nalūn instruments in Zettari territory, creating a jurisdictional complexity both parties manage by pretending it does not exist.

The Corridors Now
The Withering, the slow thinning of the world’s Aether, has not touched Nalūn’s Wellspring in any measurable way. The cities function. The instruments seal. The credit flows.
What has changed is the world around the country. The war that ended in the mud at Shimane collapsed the authority that kept order between Nalūn and the frontier. The eastern corridors are partially closed. The factor houses sit behind their Parun-sealed doors. The mountain settlements have received no salt, no iron stock and no medicine for months.

The High Chainlord’s position is that the restoration of outside order is no business of Nalūn’s. The Eastern Reach’s Chainwarden disagrees, loudly and on record, and calls the policy of waiting an absence of policy.
The factor houses’ position, expressed less officially and over salt tea in private chambers, is that a world in which the corridors stay closed is a world in which their supply books lose value, and a factor house whose supply book has lost its value has lost the only thing it cannot replace.
The tension between these positions brought a woman named Alkia of the Thornridge settlements to speak with a merchant named Torven Greis about roads, and wards, and what a man with wagons owes to the people who depend on them.
A man who owns the ore is rich until the road closes. A man who owns the road is rich until the road falls apart. A man who owns the wards on the road is rich until he dies, and if he dies, the road falls apart, and then nobody is rich. That is the whole of the business.
Torven Greis

Later hand, from the last winter before the turn, running past the year these shelves stand in: the Northern Empire of Whitemere, when it came down from the north with a name and a capital, was met at Halcrest by a scribe with a march contract. The rate had gone up.


The Guild Accord
The Powers of the Dark Ages

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Aurora Reach of the Keld
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itKELD
House Keld · The Polar Reach · Beyond the Treeline
Cuthbert Ansell, Measurewright of the Third Hand, came north in Year 694 with four mules, a set of brass assay forks and a theory, and he arrived at the Whalebone Gather in the bright week after the sun comes back, when the whole Reach is out on the ice for the sled-races with their faces painted and walrus ivory clicking in their braids. The palace stood over the camp the way it always does, white and ice-blue, its spiral towers and blue-glass domes throwing long shadows on the cracked snow. Ansell announced to the fires that it was a perfectly ordinary Spirit War relic and that he intended to spend the night in it and measure it, and an old sled-woman asked him what he would bet. He put up the mules. She put up a reindeer team, and by evening the whole Gather had put up something, the odds were painted on a whale’s jaw, and four hundred people watched a small man in a good coat walk across the covered bridge under the green aurora with a lantern, singing to keep his spirits up.
In the morning he came out by the far tower, on the wrong side of the snowfield, in excellent spirits. His beard had grown to his belt. He had, he said, had a most interesting evening, and he asked if the race had started. He spent the next eleven years writing nine hundred pages on the dimensions of the third dome, and the Guild has three copies, and no two of them agree on how many sides it has. The sled-woman took his mules and gave him back the assay forks, on the grounds that they had stopped being his. And the Keld, who had told him all of this would happen, went on doing what they have done every year for as long as there have been Keld, which is to pitch their camp in the shadow of the most beautiful building in the world and refuse to sleep inside it.
The Aurora Reach belongs to the hardest people in the north, living beyond the last tree under a sky on fire, around a palace nobody living built, and they will follow you exactly as long as you are worth it.

Two hands on this page. It stands in Year 715. Lines marked Later hand come from the annotator of the Concordance of Ages, writing in the last winter before the turn. Later hand: the Reach is counted as a land of House Keld inside the Northern Empire of Whitemere. It is the empire that does the counting.

The Land and What It Looks Like
Past the treeline there is nothing to govern. North of the Thornwood and the Stark bears the last spruce gives out, and then it is tundra and permafrost to the polar shelf, which is a geological fact more than a border. It is also, against all reasonable expectation, one of the most beautiful places alive. Rose mountains stand far off along the horizon. The snow is white and blue and pale gold according to the hour, cracked into enormous plates where the frost has heaved it. The aurora comes out most clear nights in green and violet and hangs from one side of the world to the other, and a pale moon sits up there in it looking cold. In summer the moss goes green and scarlet and there are more birds than you would believe, and the herds come through in rivers.
The palace stands on a cracked snowfield toward the western end of the Reach: a white and ice-blue thing of spiral towers and blue-glass domes, with a long covered bridge running out to a far tower that stands alone. Snow-bent firs grow around it, curling over like breaking waves, the only trees for a hundred miles and alive for no reason any forester can give. No one living built it. It is old work, the Guild says, out of the days of the Great Spirit War or earlier, though the Guild says that about most things it cannot get into. The Keld have called it the Kiilut House for as long as they have talked, kiilut being one of the dead left without the Waiting, a corpse nobody sat with, and the worst word they own. They camp beneath it, trade beneath it and race around it. They will not go in, and they will not cut the firs.
Around it, and for a thousand miles, are hide camps and sleds. A Keld camp is long lodges of reindeer hide over whalebone, nine fat-lamps to a war-lodge, sled-dogs staked out in rows, drying racks of windmeat, and smoke going straight up. There is no wood on the tundra, so the Keld burn fat, seal and reindeer and the yellow tallow of the great horned musk-beasts that come down off the high ice in the Thin Weeks. It burns low and smoky and very hot, the deep yellow of butter, with a smell like a butcher’s yard on a summer afternoon.
The major places
The Keld have no city, and consider this an advantage in several ways.

The Whalebone Gather. The one great seasonal camp, in the shadow of the palace: ten thousand people for two bright weeks, jaws of whales set up in rows as gateposts, and sled-races, marriages, feuds settled, children named, a market in ivory and beryl and furs, and the only time in the year a southern factor can buy anything without being looked at as if he had brought his own weather. Then the camp goes, and there is a large stain in the snow and a palace.
The Teeth. The high summer pastures, fought over by the Sennet clan and the Haldorssons since their grandfathers’ grandfathers.
The shelf. Where the land stops. Sealers go out on it. A certain kind of Moto practitioner goes out on it as well, because the emptiness is the only space large enough to practice Domain-scale techniques (a Domain being a working that makes a whole piece of the world obey its user) without killing bystanders. The Keld find them, some weeks later, and return their boots.

Roads. There are none. You come by sled, north from the Thornwood or along Threeways’ northern road and past the Stark bears, in the hard months only, since the thaw turns the whole country to bog.
House and Rule
House Keld is the smallest house, the hardest people and the most conditionally loyal. They live beyond the treeline in conditions that would kill members of any other house inside a week and that the Keld consider baseline. They are low and wide and dense, built by the tundra, with barrel chests and short powerful legs, and they count their years differently from the south, or decline to.
They have no seat and no lord in the way the others mean it. The clans lead their own fires, and over the fires there is whoever every fire will follow. In Year 715 that is Old Harald, too old now to sit a horse; the talk on the ice is about his grandson, who is about seventeen and has never lost a fight he chose. The Keld are counted among the Seven Warlords, by the old count, by anyone who has met them.
Names are carried. A Keld child is given the name of someone dead and is held to carry that person, and the dead person is held to be in some sense still about; the Keld release, when a fighter’s whole power rises, is called the name stands. Ask a Keld how old she is and she may tell you ninety, and she is not joking, and she is nineteen.
The Keld swear to a man. Never to a letter, and never to a house. The oath goes to whoever comes out onto the tundra in person, sits at their fires, eats their food and stays worth following. We follow because you are worth following, and we stop when you stop being worth it. Nobody has ever got a better term out of them, and quite a lot of silver has tried.
Wealth and Trade
Whale-oil, seal-fat, walrus ivory, whalebone, reindeer hides, white-fox and bear furs, musk-beast tallow, salt fish, windmeat, and from the pegmatite dikes on the northern margin the odd crystal of Clearbeam beryl, sometimes longer than a man, which they drag south on a sled and sell for less than the Guild would have paid if the Guild had got there first. They buy iron, salt and grain, in that order, and have a settled opinion that everything else is a way to get you killed. The whale-oil trade has drawn envious southern warbands past the treeline more than once. Those warbands are the subject of a popular song cycle on the ice.
There is no coin on the Reach. Exchange is meat-sharing, labor-debt and salt, and a hunter’s kill is shared out by custom so strict that the one who killed it often gets the worst of it.
Rent, Food and the Street
Rent is a meaningless word here and you will get a blank look. A lodge belongs to the woman who sewed it. Food is seal, reindeer, fish, whale when there is whale, blood-soup, frozen fat cut in curls, windmeat, stonecurd and the sour fermented milk in horn cups, served at the door. Refuse it, and you will be called skin-refuser, which is said once and then there is a fight. Keld sit on the bare packed snow of the lodge floor, cross-legged, and rise from it all at once with no hand on the floor, and a southerner who needs a stool will get one and will never be asked anywhere again.
Street life is camp life, and it is louder than you would expect: dogs, drums, racing bets, the long throat-songs that go on all night in the dark months. Faces are painted for joy and for war in blues and reds from the shelf-clays. Practitioners are a plain matter of who can keep a lamp lit in a whiteout or sniff out a herd, and Keld hedge-workers will talk the rot out of a stored seal for a share of the seal. Their word for a soul’s weight is the same as for a coming storm, and they have a low opinion of the southern argument about it.
What they joke about. How tall southerners are. Horses a hand too high for anything. What a Measurewright says when his forks stop working. The Kiilut House, never: you can joke about your mother on the Reach, and about the dead, and you can tell any story you like about what is in that palace, but a joke is a thing you say to something that is listening. The curse is Qatuq take you, Qatuq being the cold that takes the unready; the insult is numra, an empty bowl held out.
Law and How It Fights
Law. The elders of the fires. A dispute goes to them and they talk until the lamp runs down. A killing costs a killing or a great many reindeer. A person who breaks trust is left behind at the next move, which on the Reach is an unusual kind of sentence, in that nobody has to carry it out. The dead are given to the sky or the shelf, and the Waiting is kept in the lodge with the lamps turned down.
The fighting. Keld warriors, few as they are, are worth three of anyone else’s. A fighter raised on the Polar Reach has already survived conditions that would kill the enemy before the fighting started, and the fighting itself is an afterthought beside the surviving. The Keld ride small shaggy tundra horses and fight in the long line, which moves across open snow like weather, and in a wedge when something needs to be broken, with birch lances with leaf-shaped heads and short horn-backed bows firing black-glass arrowheads out of the white. Their great trick is the whiteout. They can move through snow-blind fast and quiet by reading the wind and the feel of the ground, and southerners die without having seen who killed them. Tenrai tax columns were sent onto the ice for years, until the Tenrai learned better than to do that.
Monsters on the Roads
The beasts are the whole economy and they know it. Reindeer come through in rivers, the great horned musk-beasts come down off the high ice in the Thin Weeks, white fox work the edges of every camp, and on the shelf there are seal, walrus and whale, any of which will turn over a boat. Everything the Keld eat, burn and wear has at some point tried to kill them, and they consider this good manners.
The monsters. Monsters move, and they live across the whole of the Inner World, even out here. Droval, the Frost-Howlers or Rimegaunts, are the Reach’s own terror, spirit-touched hunters of the snowfields that lie along a ridge until the ridge is suddenly not there. Wild bears come next, and packs of what the Mandate’s northern wall calls an interesting category.
The Kiilut House
The dungeon (what a Wellspring Core makes around itself, or what grows up around one) is the palace, which the Keld call the Kiilut House, a kiilut being one of the dead left without the Waiting: white and ice-blue, spiral towers and blue-glass domes, a covered bridge to a far tower, old work no one living built. It may hold Living Armor (Grade A on the Bestiary’s scale, which runs from E to EX) and worse. No one has cleared it, since no one can agree how many sides its third dome has. Measurewright Ansell spent one night inside in 694 and came out by the far tower with his beard at his belt. The Keld camp beneath it, trade beneath it, race around it, and will not sleep inside. The register enters its kind as unknown. Crews who cross the covered bridge to the far tower are not on any roll afterward, and Ansell is the only name that has ever come back that way, which the Keld put down to the palace not having finished with him. In a Keld mouth a dungeon is a house nobody sat with, which they regard as bad manners on a very large scale, and you do not go in. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
The Scourge and the Turn
The Scourge of Hell lies most of a continent to the south, and the Seat’s clerks count the Keld in the North’s share of it anyway. The Turn is the old rotation by which North, South and Center each spend nine years keeping its monsters off everybody else, and on the North’s Turn a summons reaches the fires by letter, and the Keld, who swear to a person and never to a letter, feed it to the lamp. What the Line (the chain of forts and beacon towers round the Scourge’s outer belt) gets from the Reach is fat. Those beacon towers burn whale-oil and musk tallow on anybody’s Turn, because it burns hot and low in a hard wind, so oil sold at the Whalebone Gather to a southern factor turns up on the rim a year later at a price the sled-woman who sold it would find very funny.
Now and then the Line also gets a fighter. A Keld who carries the name of someone who died on the rim is held to have a shift unfinished, and she will ride south on her own on a small shaggy horse, in hide, in that heat, and present herself at the nearest fort, and whoever holds the Turn had better feed her. They are worth three of anyone else’s, and they leave on the day the dead person would have gone home. The Center holds the Turn until 721 and the Keld have no view on the matter. The Count, the running bill the three parties present to one another, has never yet managed to charge them anything, since there is no coin on the Reach.
Neighbors and Grudges

The Scarlet Wood. Whale-oil and a warband. The song is long.
The hill clans off the Shiogane. They come down in bad years to raid the reindeer. It is regarded as a form of correspondence.
Kharven-Seat. Tenrai silver and promises come out here regularly with Tenrai seed grain, which will not grow, and the Keld keep the silver. No love anywhere on the ice for the Kōkan either, after forty years of war.
The Cobalt March. The wild white bears of the Reach and the ridden ones of the March are the same animal, and the two houses agree on one thing, which is that nobody can tell the bears anything. A Keld elder tasted the crust of that famous pie and remarked it would have made a decent meal for one.
Each other. The Sennet and the Haldorssons, over the Teeth, without intermission.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Cobalt March of Hollenmark
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itHOLL-en-mark
House Stark · The Eastern March · Where Things End
Young Sweyn Stark was nineteen in the spring of Year 668, freshly made a rider and in love with the sound of himself, when he led forty Starks on white icebears up to the old boundary stones to explain to a survey party from Marrowhold whose moss they were standing on. It was a fine morning, the sky hard blue, the snow pink with low sun, every bear’s fur dusted in frost and every rider’s breath going up like a banner. The holds’ rib-sounders had brought a table and were eating lunch. Sweyn rode out ahead of the line on a sow called Mistress Knife, nine feet at the shoulder and the most celebrated bear in the March, stood up in the stirrups, let his hide go blue-white so the whole hillside could admire it, drew his grandfather’s great sword and screamed FROST HOLDS THE LINE in a voice they heard at Stonewatch.
Mistress Knife stopped. She turned her head and regarded him for about as long as it takes to read a short letter. Then she reached round, took him by the thigh, lifted him out of the saddle, shook him twice, put him down in the snow with the leg broken in three places, ate his saddlebags, and walked home. The other thirty-nine bears, on reflection, sat down. The rib-sounders laughed until one of them had to be thumped on the back, sent a bonesetter over with the rest of the lunch, and the border held quiet for thirty years on the strength of that afternoon. Sweyn lived to be seventy and limped all of it, and he told the story himself at every midwinter, because in Hollenmark a rider who is put off his bear has been told the truth by someone with no reason to lie.
The Cobalt March is a blue fortress at the edge of everything, held by people who ride animals that can fire them, and who have been deciding where the world stops for almost four centuries.

Two hands on this page. It stands in Year 715. Lines marked Later hand come from the annotator of the Concordance of Ages, writing in the last winter before the turn. Later hand: the March is a land of House Stark inside the Northern Empire of Whitemere. It is no kingdom, and no Stark will ever say the word “subject” about it in your hearing.

The Land and What It Looks Like
Hollenmark is a cold blue stone city under a snow mountain, and in a clear dusk the whole of it is the color of a good enamel. Its heart is a pair of heavy round twin towers joined high up by an arched bridge, with snow forever blowing through the streets under them. Blue ice grows on every battlement and nobody chips it off, since it does more for the wall than the wall does for it. Beasts are carved all over the dark walls, bears and wolves and things the masons had heard about, and high up on the right a pale citadel looks down on the town, catching the last of the light long after the streets have gone dark. The wolf of Hollenmark is on the banners, the gate and the coin-weights.
Outside the walls is the March proper, the Ironwood March on older maps: boreal forest giving way to shield upland, ironwood and black spruce under deep snow, standing water frozen blue, and at every rise a boundary stone, waist-high and lichen-green and older than the house’s records, with a Stark rider on a white icebear somewhere within sight of it. The light is extraordinary. Autumn sends the broadleaf stands up in scarlet and gold against the blue ice, for about three weeks, and then it is over and everyone goes back to work.
The major places

Hollenmark. The seat. The twin towers, the bridge, the pale citadel, the hall where the Lord of Hollenmark seals the house’s business, and a street of sword-cutlers who will tell you what is wrong with your grip before they take your money.
Stonewatch. A hard little garrison town on the eastern line with a view of the old boundary stones, the Roll-house where the Stark surveyors keep the record, and the training yard of the Thrawn Yard, who wear undyed wool and one red thumb and have a song with a single line.
Bearhold. A high stockade and a great deal of open ground in the northern March, where the white bears come in the autumn of their own will to look over the young of the house. A Stark who wants to ride walks out there unarmed, in a shirt, and stands still. This is called the Asking. There is a small graveyard.

Roads. The eastern road runs in from Threeways, timber goes out down the eastern rivers, and the Vessant supply line comes in from the Amber Cities under a tithe, with a bronze disc to show at the gates. East, past the stones, is Marrowhold. West is the plateau and the Seat, and north along the head of the March lies the Thornwood.
House and Rule
House Stark defines where things end and begin, and has done so with a straight face for three hundred and seventy-six years by its own measure. The Roll, or Stone Roll, records the position of every boundary stone on the March, who last stood at it and what was decided there, and a Stark quarrel is settled by going and looking.
The lord in Year 715 is Ulf Stark, Lord of Hollenmark, Master of the eastern March and Warlord of the house by the right of his father and his father’s father: fifty-seven, broad as a doorway, wearing the head and pelt of a great brown wolf and calling everyone under forty lad. By most counts he is the worst of the north’s Seven Warlords to have against you, and he has spent most of his life proving the count correct.
The house carries the Stark Rime, an ice-aspected inheritance that predates the Moto and operates outside the standard Wellspring framework: a cold radiating from body and blood, intensifying under emotional pressure, silvering timber and stiffening snow in a radius around the bearer. An angry Stark’s breath stops steaming and his beard goes white, and an experienced tavern-keeper will start moving the glassware at that point. The inheritance is northern, older than the kingdom and older than the Starks’ own records, and they do not discuss its origins with outsiders, because the origins are Stark business and the Starks keep their business behind their borders. The fair answer to it is heat, and keeping him calm.
The Dire Icebear is an enormous polar ursid whose white fur carries a permanent frost dusting and whose temperament is exactly what the name implies. Nobody has ever domesticated one; the arrangement is a partnership. A Stark rides one because the bear has decided to permit it, and the permission is withdrawn the moment the rider stops being worth carrying. The withdrawal is not gentle, as Sweyn could tell you.
Later hand: a cousin of the house, Zaehaerys Stark, carries the title of Warden of the Eastern March a generation on, and copies of this shelf that name him lord in 715 are reading the wrong winter.
Wealth and Trade
Timber, furs and road. The March sells ironwood and spruce down the eastern rivers, white-bear furs from animals that died of something else (ask no further), and above all safe passage. A Nalūn factor house, the Vessant, has run a supply line into the eastern timber for thirty-one years, every mile of it through Stark country, and for thirty-one years it has paid Hollenmark a tithe for the road and the contract has run sound. Hollenmark is the only town in the north whose smiths reckon in Nalūn seal-tokens as readily as in copper, and the bronze disc with the wolf on one face and the chain-mark on the other is a thing a merchant shows at a gate and a soldier never expects to be handed.
The house imports most of what it eats, by Ashmore’s allocation, and has resented every bushel of it since before the pie.
Rent, Food and the Street
A tenant in Hollenmark pays in days on the wall and split wood, and a house with a son in the riders pays nothing and is reminded of it. Lodging is a long bed over the bakehouse if you know someone. The town eats windmeat, bone broth, smoked fish from the blue lakes and whatever Ashmore sent, with a cup of the skin (fermented milk in a sealskin) at the door. There is a market under the twin towers where snow blows through the stalls year-round and a woman sells hot barley cakes off a warmed stone, and she has a hedge-worker’s trick that keeps them hot exactly until you have paid.
Street life runs on the road and on the bears. A bear in the street has right of way over the Warlord. Children play the Asking in the lanes, one of them standing very still in a shirt while the others growl. The hide, in Stark country, is expected to have frost on it, and a practitioner with a warm-colored aura gets stared at. Heralds come through from the Seat and from the holds and are made to stand at the same fire.
What they joke about. Everything south of them. Greymanes, who have the same wolf on their breast and no sense of humor about it. Ashmore’s arithmetic: every midwinter, for a hundred and twenty years, Hollenmark has sent an empty pie dish to Ashbury. Being put off your bear, which is a joke only the person it happened to may start. A Stark’s idea of a warm welcome is telling you exactly where you are standing.
Law and How It Fights
Law. The March keeps its own laws, and they are about stones. Move a boundary stone and you lose the hand, in theory; nobody has been stupid enough in living memory, not counting the bear that scratched its back on one at Stonewatch and was entered in the Roll as a party to the dispute. Disputes go to the nearest stone, with witnesses, and then to the Lord. A debt is not a debt until it has been said aloud at a boundary.
The fighting. Great sword and axe in the north, boar-spear on the road, short sword and round limewood shield for the young. The heavy walk is the signature, weight down through the heels, even and unhurried, and it frightens people who have seen where it ends. Stark war is winter war on roads nobody else thinks are open: a Stark column has already moved before you knew it was coming, and the fair answer is a fire, a thaw and a scout who does not sleep. House riders on icebears are few and enormously loud on the page of any chronicle, and most of the killing is done by men on foot in wolf-fur, moving in knots. First Releases in the family are named for frost and called in the old northern tongue, and the first person to tell a Stark they are shouting is generally the bear.
Monsters on the Roads
The beasts. Wild bears are the first danger and the most respected. An icebear with no rider on it has made its own decision about you, and the Dire Icebear that carries a Stark is the same animal on a better day. Elk and boar keep the ironwood, the great brown wolves follow the elk, and the hunting hall at Hollenmark will post a bounty on a wolf and none on a bear, on the grounds that the Roll would have to enter the bear as a party.
The monsters. Monsters move, and they live across the whole of the Inner World, and the March gets the ones that come down off high ground or out of the east. Goliaths (Grade A on the Bestiary’s scale, which runs from E to EX; giantkin who want to be left alone) hold the snow mountain above the city and throw rocks at surveyors. The surveyors go up anyway, and each rock is entered by location. On the eastern line, Stark riders and Marrowkin survey parties both hunt the odd Greater Wolf pack and whatever comes off the Ring’s fume-belt with too many opinions.
Two dungeons
The March talks about two dungeons (a dungeon being what a Wellspring Core makes around itself, or what grows up around one). The first is the Roll-Cellar under Stonewatch, a Fixatio Well (the Wellspring of anchoring) that opened beneath the oldest stone on the line. Starks cleared it three generations ago, going down with surveying chains and entering each dead thing in the Roll by location. It is a worked Core now, with Stark keepers, and practitioners pay by the hour to sit in amber light that makes a stance very hard to shift.
The second is the Cold Larder, a day from Bearhold, a Vohrin ground (Vohrin being a Titan’s cold, outside the Sixty, worked like heat run backward): blue galleries under the boreal and a cold that drinks your lamp. Renderers hold it on a Stark lease, and the winter trade cures down there what cannot be warmed. Its masks have to be run to the hall in a sack of snow, since a hall pays only while the color holds. A Stark with the Rime up is charged double at the door, because the renderers have seen what happens to their stock when the cold in the room acquires an opinion. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
The Scourge and the Turn
The Scourge of Hell is about as far from anything blue as the continent allows, and the March goes there anyway when the wheel says so. The Turn is the old rotation by which North, South and Center each spend nine years keeping the Scourge’s monsters off everybody else. A Northern Turn takes the March’s spears in long columns, by the eastern road to Threeways, the southern road to Ashbury and the Kessen ford, already gone before you knew they had left. The riders go with them, and it is the one campaign a Stark dreads. An icebear on the Hem, the Scourge’s outer belt, in that hot dry wind sheds its frost, goes off its food and sits down in any water it can find, and the rider goes slowly mad beside it. More Starks have been put off their bears south of the Kessen ford than anywhere on the March, and the bears then walk home, which takes a season and frightens a great deal of barley. A Stark with the Rime up, on the other hand, is the only cold drink for a hundred miles, and the rim taverns will stand him free beer all night to keep him sitting beside the cask, angry.
Hollenmark blue was on the field at Lastpenny in 676, at the handover the whole Center still spits about, drawn up beside the Stormfold slate and watching a wyrm eat the town because the host had been stood down an hour before. The March does not dispute it. “It isn’t noon” is a joke in Hollenmark that only a man who stood there may start, and there are fewer of them every winter. The last Northern Turn ended in 703 and the Center has it now, until 721, so the March’s share for the moment is a clerk’s copy of the Count (the running bill the three parties present to one another), some remarks on what Ashmore charges for bread on the way down, and a list of which boys will be old enough.
Neighbors and Grudges

The Ember Holds of Marrowhold. The eastern frontier, and the reason the stones exist, since the March runs out to the foot of the rib mountains and stops. Stark believes in the line. The people on the other side believe in the entry. Both are correct often enough to keep the peace.
The Golden Hollow. The pie. The allocation. See above, and see the Starks’ faces.
The Slate Ridge. The other wall of the north and the only house the Starks treat as an equal, by not talking to it. A Stark and a Greymane will die for each other without having a conversation.
The Scarlet Wood. A Stark daughter married a Thornwall in 592 and it is still being discussed.
Kharven-Seat. The Tenrai toll-post on the Kessen road, Tenrai factors on the March, and the forty-year war that has just emptied Hollenmark of sons. Every lord in the Stark camps is past fifty-five and every spear under them is carried by a boy, and that is about as much as the Hall of Verdicts should want to know about the mood here.

Later hand: the house’s standing toward the Crown is the kingdom’s oldest alliance and its most honest. The Starks serve because the Crown serves, and will continue for exactly as long as that holds. The distinction between this position and disloyalty is the distinction between a partner and a subject, and the Starks have never been subjects. See The Banner Houses of Kharven.
