geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Copper Coast of Haeseong
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itHEH-sung
The Thousand Moorings · The Salt Road’s Mouth · In the Dynasty of Sum-gol
The lamp-wardens walked off the great tower at Haeseong at dusk on the fourth night of the mackerel run in 671, in their sea-green coats, in good order, over a matter of eleven coppers a night. It was the sixth such strike in living memory and they timed it, as always, for when it would hurt. The lamp they tended burned worked light that reached forty miles out, and every boat of the fishing fleet was out past the Sawbacks with a southerly rising and no other mark on that whole black coast to steer for. On the quay the wardens’ captain, Gim Dol-soe, stood with his arms folded, explaining the terms to an under-steward who was explaining them to Admiral-Lord Ryu Seok-ju, who was at dinner.
Nobody explained anything to old Deok-sun the net-widow. She took the paper lantern off her own door, lit it, walked to the end of the mole and hung it on a boathook. The woman next to her did the same. Inside the hour every house along the Moorings was stripping its lamps and every child was running with an armful, and they strung them on fishing line from mast to mast and roof to roof clear across the harbor, red and gold and copper-green, thousands of them, and rowed more out on sampans, until the whole bay stood lit up and shaking on the water like a city on fire that was enjoying itself. The fleet saw it from nineteen miles out and came in on the backs of the waves with the men screaming with laughter. Only three boats were lost. The Admiral-Lord paid the wardens the eleven coppers, because the tower is the tower, and fined the town for the use of the fishing line, because the line was harbor property. Deok-sun paid the fine in mackerel. The lanterns have gone up across the water every night of the year from that day to this, and they say that a Haeseong child, set down anywhere in the world, cannot sleep in the dark.
The Copper Coast is the brightest city in the South, the Dynasty’s old admiralty, sitting on the Dynasty’s money, answering to the Dynasty’s name, and asking very politely whether anyone would like to come and collect.
The Land and the Look
Warm, wet and shining, from the white cliffs of Alabaster eastward. The coast is called the Thousand Moorings, a run of inlets, sandbars and pine-topped islets, and the water goes from sea-green to copper at evening with the whole shore smelling of salt, tar, charcoal and frying fish. Old copper workings in the hills behind it stain the creeks green and the roofs are sheathed in the same metal, bright as a kettle when new and going sea-green along the oldest eaves, so that a Moorings town at sunset looks as though someone had tipped a purse out on a hillside.
Haeseong itself climbs from a long stone quay at the mouth of the salt road in hundreds of copper-red and gold roofs, tile and upturned eaves stacked up the hill, over a harbor of deep blue water packed with fishing boats, junks, coasting galleys and the long low salt barges, with those lanterns on every line and huge white clouds standing behind it all. Two citadels look down on it. The dark stone fortress on the sheer green crag is the Ryu’s, and the white-and-gold palace on the next rise is the old Dynasty’s governor’s seat, swept and aired and kept for Sum-gol by the people who have stopped sending Sum-gol its money. Behind the city the salt road runs north, a raised causeway at first, between paddies and salt-ponds, then a long straight highway through the low country, past the Rose Coils at the ford of Bothhands, across the Sealed Charter and up the east flank of the Scourge of Hell to the salt basin, and so to the junction below Ashbury. There are camellias on the walls and it rains hard for ten minutes every afternoon, and everyone stands in doorways making remarks about it.
The House
House Ryu was the Mahou line’s admiralty. When the Mahuo were emperors, and later when they were kings, the Ryu kept their ships, their harbor dues and their salt fleet, and were the second family of Sum-gol. They did not leave at the last Calling: they sent a superb letter. They have answered to the name ever since, and they are by every form of law still its loyal officers.
When the Mahuo fell, the ships, the harbor dues and the salt fleet were all still sitting at Haeseong, with nobody left to send the revenue to. The Ryu left the Mahuo’s wealth exactly where it sat, and simply stopped forwarding it. The South has never settled whether that is theft. The Ryu would like it noted that the Mahuo have never asked. The counting-rooms keep the whole sum in a separate set of books under the heading held for the Throne, correct to the copper and growing, and they will show you the heading.
The present head is Admiral-Lord Ryu Ha-eun. She is fifty-three, stout, sunburned and merry, wears sea-green silk with copper at the throat, and has been at sea since she was eleven, and the fleet would follow her onto the Sawbacks. She sat at the Cedar Enclave and heard Naiser Yukari promise to restore the Mahuo royal line at Sum-gol, and smiled, and asked a very good question about harbor dues. House Ryu will be the first to object if anybody restores that line and the last to object out loud. Its words are The Tide Pays Twice. Its colors are sea-green and copper.
Cities and Towns
Haeseong, seventy thousand souls and the largest living city in the South, has its fortress on the crag, the governor’s palace on the next rise with nobody in it, the Admiral’s Hall above the harbor with its copper dragon-ridge, and the Long Mole running out to the great lighthouse. At the mole’s root is the Salt Quay, where the barges load in a white haze that gets into your teeth, and where the salt road begins, every sack of southern salt that ever crossed the Ashmore marches having paid a Ryu toll on its way. A company of lamp-wardens hired down from the Wellheads at great expense keeps the tower lit. They still walk off every few years over the fee, and are still paid before the fishing fleet can get home.
Geumpo, “gold harbor,” lies a day east along the coast, a smaller, prettier, more dishonest place, where the foreign and island ships unload away from the toll-clerks’ eyes. It got the name for the river-gold once washed down there or for the color of its mud at sunset, depending on who is selling you the house. Lacquer, pearls, dried sea-cucumber and a great many things without papers pass through its warehouses. Its Guild of Pilots has been in a state of cold war with Haeseong’s for two hundred years, and it fields the better bracket team.
Along the rest of the Thousand Moorings lie some hundreds of salt-ponds, fishing villages and customs posts, each with a shrine to the drowned and a Ryu toll-man who takes his hat off to funerals and charges for them anyway.
Wealth and Trade
Everything that comes into the Inner World by water comes in through House Ryu, by their own account, and the account is close to the truth. Harbor dues, salt tolls, the salt fleet, wreck-right on the whole coast. Copper, hammered and sheathed; green copper sheet goes up the salt road for half the roofs in the South. Fish in every form. Sea-silk, pearl, and the deep southern dyes come in from the isles and go out to wherever a lord wants to look richer than his neighbor.
The salt itself comes in part from the Dynasty’s pans at Yeomjeon, carried by Ryu barge along the coast and sold north by the Ryu at a Ryu price, which is how one sack can make its way through three lawsuits before it reaches a pot. The money that should have gone to Sum-gol has mostly become ships. Ask to see them. They are magnificent.
Rent, Food and the Street
Rent is high on the rock, ruinous on the Salt Quay and a matter of family on the water, where several thousand people live on sampans and pay mooring-fee by the lunar month to a harbor-mother who knows who is sleeping with whom. Grilled mackerel, rice, cold noodles in broth, salted shrimp with everything, sea-urchin at a stall if you have just been paid, and a clear rice liquor that visitors take for water exactly once.
The evening is the point of Haeseong. When the lanterns go up the entire city comes out on the mole, the sampans turn into floating kitchens, and the sound of the place rises to where you can hear it at the Sawbacks. Fortune-sellers will tell you the tide of your marriage. Hedge-workers sell net-charms, knot-charms, a wind in a bag that has never yet produced a wind and always produces a story about the last customer. Bracket schools wear their harbor’s color and row out to fight on barges lashed together in the middle of the bay, with the betting done by boat: the Haeseong Green Tide, the Geumpo Gilders, and a fisher school from the outer Moorings called the Bad Weather, who have no style anyone can name and are very hard to knock off a barge. On the quays the aura coat is gabot and Pressure is nureum, as at Sum-gol, and you sense a stranger by nunchi, which here also means knowing when to change the subject.
Law and How It Fights
The Tide Court sits on the Long Mole in the shade of the tower, and it hears wreck, salvage, toll and mutiny in an afternoon, with an admiral’s officer on the bench and a harbor-mother beside him to say who is lying. Goods from a wreck belong by old right to the Ryu, unless a living creature from the ship came ashore, so an unusual number of ship’s cats have been very carefully thrown overboard in time. Everything on the road pays. A man may bribe a toll-man, and it is considered polite, but it does not reduce the toll.
At sea they are the best in the South and know it: coasting galleys with marine crossbows along the rail, fire-pots, and big war-junks that carry a company of boarders in copper-scaled harness. A Ryu line takes the windward, lets the current do the work and shoots the rowers first. House practitioners stand on the fighting platforms and do what they can with wind and water, and the lighthouse wardens, on the rare day the fee is paid in advance, can throw that worked beam across an enemy’s eyes at a mile. Ashore they hold the salt road with little walled toll-forts every thirty miles, and rent spears from Hammerford for anything larger. They have never in their history fought a land battle they could avoid by raising a price.
What They Joke About
Money, loudly, and the Mahuo, quietly. “Held for the Throne” is what a Haeseong man says about his wife’s jewels, his brother’s loan, or whatever he has just put under his coat. A sailor who is late with what he owes says he is waiting for the Mahuo to ask. They say a Yan will make you wait through his grandfather’s name to sell you a horse and that a Lambert will count your fingers after shaking your hand, and that the Yukari already know what you had for breakfast and disapprove. Of Geumpo they say that its children are born with a false bottom. Of Haeseong, Geumpo says only that it pays its pilots on the wrong tide.
Monsters on the Roads
Sea Serpents (Grade S) follow the mackerel, and every Ryu fleet has lost hulls off the Sawbacks. Sirens (Grade B) work the outer islets, and everyone on the water has a story and a net-charm. Kraken (Grade EX) are named in old wreck-right and nobody has lately had the nerve to file a claim. Beasts are the daily nuisance and have their own column at the Tide Court: sharks under the sampans in the mackerel weeks, otters robbing the creek traps, wild boar in the paddies, and cormorants that have learned to work for a rival family.
The dungeons. The respectable one is the Green Galleries, the old copper workings in the hills behind Geumpo, which broke into a Basilithe Well (the Wellspring of pure pitch and clean crystal, ochre-gold). Tolling Crabs (Grade A) hold the Upper Workings, and a careful delver strikes a tuning bar and rings a crab’s own note back at it until the carapace falls apart. Geumpo’s pilots hold a lease on the Mouth. The Ryu dispute it annually. The other is the Gold Mouth, a sea cave east of Geumpo, an Oblation ground (a warm Wellspring of Fate, whose law runs on what is given up to it), unlicensed and very busy: a tide cave that pulls. Smugglers use it, and House Ryu claims wreck-right on anything that washes out, crews included. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
The Scourge and the Turn. The Scourge of Hell is a long way up the road from the Salt Quay and nobody on the Long Mole has ever smelled it, but this is where the eastern corridor starts, and every carter who dies on that flank had a Ryu toll-stamp on his sacks. The Turn, the old wheel by which North, South and Center each spend nine years keeping the Scourge’s monsters off the other two, is the one thing that goes up the salt road free. Whoever holds it may march through anyone’s land by right of passage, and House Ryu regards nine years of spears passing its toll-forts unbilled as a natural disaster. The toll-men stand at the gates regardless, hats off, writing down what each company would have owed. When the wheel comes round to the South and the old Dynasty’s realms are made to pay, the Ryu answer as they answered the Calling, with a superb letter, salt barges at a fixed price and the carters’ losses entered to the copper, and the whole unbilled sum goes into the South’s Count with the Admiral-Lord’s compliments.
In every other season the traffic comes back down the road in the other direction. Wyrm cores and bagged masks off the Hem pass the Salt Quay on their way to any crucible that will pay, a good deal of ghoststeel leaves through Geumpo with no papers at all, and a cutter with a season’s bounty and one ear short is a familiar sight on the mole, under the lanterns, eating sea-urchin.
Neighbors and Grudges
Sum-gol. Their sworn liege, in olive now and refusing the crown, and the accounts grow in their column every month. The letter the Ryu send to each Calling is much admired, and is copied out in a fair hand all along the coast.
The Holy Sea. Rimward is the only harbor on the southern sea that can hurt them, and the Lamberts’ tariff books are the only ones in the South that match theirs. Rivals by water and colleagues by temperament.
The Golden Hollow of Ashbury. The salt road ends at Ashmore’s junction, with grain coming back the other way. The north eats what Ashmore sells, seasoned with what the Ryu sell, and neither has ever been able to stop the other.
The Jade Plains. Fellow servants of the empty chair. They dispute the salt toll annually, and the Hall’s elder recites at it.
The Silver Cedars. Lord Naiser’s promise to restore Sum-gol is the one sentence in the South that could cost the Ryu everything, and it is in the Yukari record, with the date, and Ryu Ha-eun’s very good question next to it.
Further reading · The Southern Warlords

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Ember Holds of Marrowhold
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itMARE-oh-hold. In its own tongue *Luuthruk*, LOO-throok, the bone-hold.
The Ring · The Ore Council · The Lender’s House · The Seat of the Scale · Eastern Shield
King Hobart of Pennycrown, whose realm was four villages, a ford and a very high opinion of itself, decided in the spring of 651 IC that a true king ought to sit on a god. He sold his ford-tolls eleven years ahead, rode to the Cutting Fair at Collarbone in a borrowed scarlet cloak, and outbid an abbot of the Holy Sea and two northern factors for one slab of old ivory off the Twelfth Rib, nine feet tall, warm as a new loaf, with a gold grain in it that moved when the light did. Forty Marrowkin hauled it south on ox-sleds with kettledrums and pans of copper-green fire, and half the Midmarch walked out to watch it go by. In Pennycrown’s square a hold-clerk named Vappu Tarrekk Ollan, four feet tall, with furnace-colored eyes behind a slit visor of carved horn, read the sale aloud in meter, all of it, for three hours, down to the last line: returnable on the Lender’s demand, carriage at the holder’s charge. Hobart signed with a flourish and bellowed that the Lender was welcome to come and try. The crowd adored him.
The throne leaned. By the first winter a marble set on its seat rolled north. By the fifth year the court had wedged it with lead, by the ninth it was held down with ship’s chain, and visiting kings were learning to pour their wine at an angle. On midsummer night of 662, with the hall full of guests and Hobart on it in his crown, the chain let go and the throne went north, through the dais, through the kitchen wall, through the queen’s pigeon-house, and across four hundred paces of bean field with the king clinging to the armrests and roaring for his guard, until it met the town wall and stopped there. It broke his pelvis and his reign. He sued at Breastbone. The tribunal sat for two years and found that the throne had done nothing the sale had not said it might, and the Carriers’ Guild sent a courteous note offering to take it the rest of the way at the usual rate per league. A sworn Measurewright inspected the furrow and blamed bad footings and a spring under the beans, and that remains the Guild’s opinion. Pennycrown built a new stretch of wall around the thing rather than touch it. It is still leaning.
Marrowhold is a nation of smiths and clerks who live inside the ribcage of something that fell out of the Great Spirit War, cut it up, sell it to everybody, and write down every ounce, because someday the body will want it back.
Overview
A Marrowkin kingdom built into and through the bones of the Ring, the ninety-league crater holding the northern quarter’s richest sulfide ore, at the eastern end of the northern shield, past the Ironwood March and the Scarlet Wood, extending outward to take in the territories and trade routes that depend on what comes out of it. Older rolls and most of the songs call the people Dawi and the country the Guild Seat of Stannvaard, the Metal-Warden, a Concord filing name built from stannum, tin or worked ore. The Guild’s clerks have kept using it, the Marrowkin have stopped answering to it, and no state of that name is on any roll now.
Among its holdings is Altherion, the multiracial republic whose River Crown Council governs the largest surface settlement on the rim, and whose constitutional architecture provides the political stage on which Sancta Lux has chosen to seat the Grand Church. This makes Marrowhold the most politically complex sovereign entity in the Inner World: a forge, a republic and a court of universal jurisdiction, stacked one inside another, with the friction managed by a people who treat every problem as an engineering challenge and refuse to be impressed by anyone else’s theology, having a much larger one under their feet.
Roughly eighty thousand souls: about 35,000 Marrowkin, about 20,000 human, the remainder elven, beastkin, goblinoid and other, concentrated primarily in Altherion.

A man who owns the ore is rich until the road closes. A man who owns the forge is rich until the fuel runs out. A man who owns the court inside the republic inside the forge-kingdom is rich until the mountain disagrees, and the mountain has not disagreed with us yet.
Guildmaster Thordren, Ore Council address, Year 698 IC

What died
Nobody can tell you, and you will meet plenty who try. What fell into the Ring stays disputed. Every school has a candidate and every candidate has a priesthood prepared to explain, at length and with witnesses, that their god is alive and well, thank you. The Guild’s rolls of Archons and Titans show no empty chair that all the rolls agree on. One school holds that the thing was never on any roll, and another that it never had a mind and the word god is a sales term. The Marrowkin enter no opinion. They call it the Body when they are selling and Lainur, the Lender, when they are frightened, and a stranger who presses the question will be asked what he proposes to buy.
Why the Church is here
Darius Ignatius Sanctus Sanctorum, who wrote the order’s modern apparatus between the ages of twenty-six and thirty-five, understood that a court seated inside a republic seated inside a guild-state produces a jurisdictional complexity so dense that no single power can evict the court without dismantling the republic, and no power can dismantle the republic without disrupting the guild-state, and no power can disrupt the guild-state without collapsing the metal trade that every army and every forge in the four quarters depends on.

A court that cannot be evicted is not a court. Darius made sure his court was a court.

The Land and What It Looks Like
Come at it from the north road at sunset and the first thing you take for mountains are mountains, and the second thing you notice is that they lean. The rim of the Ring is a wall of sheer peaks all curving inward over the basin at the same angle, each one a single bone the color of old ivory wherever the red has not climbed it, and the red has climbed most of them. Everything that can grow in the Ring is ember red. Moss, bracken, thicket, forty-foot ferns on the bone terraces, all of it the same range of rust and coal and hot copper, running up the ribs in great burning shawls and pouring down into the basin, so that the place looks at every hour of the day like a forest in the last week of autumn, with the leaves refusing to fall. The holds call this growth emberwort, and it lives on what seeps out of the bone. Far off across the basin a silver river goes through it like a dropped chain.
Shocked quartz and an inverted rock sequence at the rim confirm the Ring as an impact scar rather than a volcanic caldera, so something came down here from a very great height and very fast, whatever else it was. The sheet of melted rock beneath the basin floor is where the ore concentrated as it cooled, producing sulfide deposits in concentrations that make every other mine in the four quarters look like a surface scraping. The ore seams follow the faults, which puts the richest deposits along the crater walls rather than the basin floor, and that is why the cities are built into the walls. The metal is in the cliffs and the Marrowkin followed it. A Guild surveyor who walked the rim in 702 counted twenty-nine standing ribs. The holds say twelve to a side, because that is what a person has, and they told him to enter a number that scans.
Through the seams and under the floor runs what the holds call hehkuveri, the glow-blood: a slow heavy melt, dull orange, thick as cold tar, that has not finished cooling since the fall. A Measurewright will tell you it is impact melt saturated with Aether. A Marrowkin will tell you it is blood. Neither has moved the other in a very long time, and the furnaces work either way. Climate inside the Ring is warmer than the surrounding shield, from that heat and from the thermal mass of the walls, and the snow that lies a yard deep on Altherion’s roofs turns to steaming rain halfway down the inner slope. The air carries the taste of sulfur, hot metal, and the dry-mineral smell of stone that has been heated and cooled thousands of times, with something under it like a tooth that has just been drilled.
The Cities
Breastbone, the capital
The picture on every guild seal is the upper city, and it is as good as they say. Breastbone is a walled citadel of slender pale spires and tiered towers rising against the sheer face of the ribs, every one carved out of the Body’s own bone and left standing where the fall snapped it upright, each tower narrowing by stacked terraces to a needle. Thin bridges with no visible means of support run from spire to spire. Inside the white wall a great ribbed dome houses the Ore Council, and below the wall lie the round terraced halls, each a wheel of pale stone with an ember garden blazing in its hub, and below those the low town, a spill of pale roofs furred with red moss. Everything that was not carved is red, because the emberwort has climbed every surface the glow-blood can reach as it cools in the bone, and the whole ember-colored country is, by the holds’ own account, feeding on the thing they are cutting up. A traveler who has crossed the gray shield for a month generally stops at the last turn of the road, and the road’s beggars work that turn for a reason.
All of that is the part you are shown. Under it, going down through the crater wall along the ore seams, are the seven working levels the old rolls call Thane-Gorr, joined by shaft-lifts, chain-bridges and tunnels, the lowest reaching the base of the impact melt sheet. Thane-Gorr’s forges burn continuously, set over the glow-blood in furnaces that hold temperatures no fuel achieves and hold them steady for days. The glow is visible from the rim at night, a dull orange pulse against the walls that travelers steer by and that poets have been comparing to a heartbeat for centuries because the comparison is accurate and nobody has found a better one. The holds enter it as furnace-light and decline to discuss the timing.
A small Tinker Goblin quarter keeps the hoists and chain-lifts running, and has been petitioning for a guild seat for over two centuries with increasing volume and decreasing patience. In 669 IC they concluded that the Ore Council had not been reading it, and cast it in bronze. Every letter stood as tall as a goblin. The whole text, fifty-three words and four tons, was strung on one chain down the great shaft with pans of copper-green fire burning on every landing, so that seven levels of Marrowkin coming off shift could watch their neighbors’ grievance descend past them in order, slowly, to horns and kettledrums, while Mag Cotterpin, master of the works, rode the top letter in her good leather cap and bellowed the name of her invention, THE SELF-ANSWERING PETITION. The brake she had designed held until about the word respectfully. Four tons of bronze then went down that shaft faster than any appeal has ever moved in the Ring, through the roof of the Assay Guild’s counting room and the floor beneath it. Cotterpin rode it as far as the fourth level, and it cost her both legs below the knee and a Guild balance worth more than her street. Nobody else died, because a Marrowkin hears a chain going wrong through the soles of the feet before it goes. The arbitration tribunal sat for two years, found that a petition delivered through the ceiling counts as received, denied it on the merits, and billed the Tinker quarter for the ceiling, which the quarter is still paying off, one letter at a time.
Collarbone
The northern hold and the front door. Collarbone runs along one enormous horizontal bone at the head of the rim road, a mile and more of galleries with windows cut through to the open air on both sides, so that its long market gets the wind from the shield in one ear and the heat of the Ring in the other. This is where the Thornhaven corridor comes in and where the outside world is permitted to buy. The Cutting Fair, held for nine days after each year’s schedule is read, fills the bone end to end with relic-hunters, sect quartermasters, abbots, smugglers, armorers from four quarters, and the bookies who will give you odds on what the top lot fetches and whether its buyer gets it home. Every piece sold is read aloud by a clerk before the money moves, so the whole place sounds like a very large liturgy being interrupted by a very large fight.
The Twelfth Rib
Ykt-kaht Kylki on the hold’s rolls, written as two words because the numeral will not harmonize. The longest bone anyone has cut into, hollow for most of its run, lying on the eastern wall. The Twelfth is the oldest cutting face still working and the source of the best ivory, and it holds Kegshard Hold, seat of the Cask Line, with its grand hall, its Oath-Breakers’ wall, its red and copper banners and the Deepvault beneath. The galleries run so long that a bowl of soup carried from the kitchens to the far shift arrives cold, and the far shift has a song about it.
The other holds of the Upper Ring
Kolmthruk, the Third Hold, cut into the Third Rib on the west, is a town of furnace-tenders who consider Breastbone soft. Barkstone on the northern wall takes its name from the scaled, weathered outer layer of its rib, and gives the tongue its standard dialect and its most insufferable metricians. All four cities of the Upper Ring are workings first and settlements second, with civic life organized around the guild shifts that decide when people work, eat and sleep.
Altherion, the republic on the rim
Altherion sits on the northern rim where the three principal roads meet, outside the bone and very pleased about it. It was not planned. Merchants needed a place to sleep, the place needed a market, the market needed law, and by the time anyone decided to write a charter the city was already there. What makes it different is that the charter it eventually received was drafted by every race that lived there, at the same table, and the table, round, without a head, one chair per delegation and no chair larger than another, is still in the River Crown Council’s chamber and is still used. Marrowkin built the shafts, and everyone else built Altherion, timber-framed over stone with rooflines pitched against snow, in the visual chaos of seven racial building traditions practiced in the same streets across three centuries. The Accord’s northern chancery and its Arbitration Division sit up on the high ground called the Seat, where it always seems to be raining.
The Seven Districts













































DistrictCharacterPop.Breastbone and Thane-Gorr the capitalSeat of the Ore Council, the citadel above and the seven forge levels below~12,000The Upper Ring Collarbone, the Twelfth Rib, Kolmthruk, BarkstoneFour smaller cities in the bone of the eastern, western and northern walls~15,000Altherion the republic on the rimGoverns itself under its own charter. The Ore Council has never attempted to override its constitutional provisions, partly because they do not conflict with authority over extraction, and partly because Altherion’s population includes the labor force that moves the product after it leaves the forge, and the Ore Council is not foolish enough to antagonize them. It is not the capital, and it is the kingdom’s face, a multiracial republic that happens to sit on top of a forge-state that happens to host the most powerful judicial body in four worlds~22,000The Rimlands surrounding territoryRoads, way-stations, timber and the agriculture feeding the crater population. Governed by a warden appointed jointly by both Councils, a jurisdictional compromise that satisfies neither body and functions because neither body has proposed a better arrangement~12,000The Corridor Holdings trade route territoryAdministered by the Carriers’ Guild: road upkeep, way-station keeping, escort coordination, above all on the Iron-to-Salt Corridor, which runs south by the Greis way-stations to the Amber Cities and the coast beyond. A transient population with the character of people who live on roads rather than in cities~6,000The Deep Reach below the basin floorUnder a Council-appointed Steward rather than a guild warden, because the territory’s Wellspring sensitivity and its proximity to the Deepkin-occupied zones require governance more cautious than standard guild administration can provide. The Deepkin maintain a significant presence and an advisory role the upper holds consider necessary and slightly unnerving, because the Deepkin know things about what lies beneath the Ring that nobody else knows and have declined to share in full~3,000The Ember Magistrates’ Circuit not geographicThe permanent traveling court riding between communities too small or distant to bring cases to the Grand Church. Operates under Sancta Lux authority and crosses Marrowhold’s borders into neighboring realms, a jurisdictional overlap the Ore Council manages by pretending it does not exist and Sancta Lux manages by filing paperwork the Ore Council has never read~40,000 served
Three Histories That Became One
The Ore · By the Tally the Marrowkin have been inside the Body since the first entry, and the Guild’s Errata would cut the Tally’s count down hard. What is on firmer ground is the climb. A High Line prospecting expedition came up out of the deep halls, assessed the crater, and sent word back down that the richest mineral deposit in the northern quarter was sitting in the open on the surface, unguarded, unmined, and waiting for someone with a forge hot enough to work it. The halls sent smiths. The smiths brought families. The families became guilds. The guilds became a kingdom, by the accumulated weight of people who never meant to found one and stayed because the work was there, and who discovered over generations that a community organized around a forge has already solved most of the problems governments are designed to solve.
The Republic · The holds offered to govern the incoming population under guild law. The newcomers declined, on the reasonable ground that guild law was designed for guilds and that most of them were not guild members. The compromise was the founding charter: a multiracial republic, the Essence Resource Sharing Act preventing any body from monopolizing Wellspring access, and the Trade Equality Act preventing any race or guild from monopolizing extraction or trade. The charter was, in essence, a promise that Altherion’s governance would measure every community the same way, which is why Sancta Lux eventually chose it as a home. The Echo Elves maintain that Altherion’s confederated structure owes more to Echo Elf political philosophy than the republic’s official histories credit. Altherion’s official historians maintain the resemblance is coincidental. The Echo Elves repeat their claim verbatim, once, every time it is made, which is their way of recording that it has been said without conceding that it is true.
The Court · The Grand Church is a consecrated stone compound within Altherion’s walls, built on rock that Sancta Lux’s Measurewrights consecrated themselves, using methods they declined to share with the republic’s architects and that the republic’s architects declined to ask about. It includes the Sanctified Hall where Arbiter-grade readings are taken, the training facilities, the offices coordinating four-quarter operations, and the chambers in which the Arbiter-Militant and Arbiter-Lector wings are institutionally required to disagree, and do, loudly, in a room built for the purpose. The Hall of Equal Breath, where the Oracle is housed, is elsewhere. Sel-Ur is at Meridian Hold, whose location does not appear in any Accord filing.
The Wellsprings

























WellspringFunctionPetralon Stone / ReinforcementThe Ring’s primary territorial Wellspring, the Aether of stone pooling in the crater walls and the bone alike. Tunnels carved through fault-stressed rock that should collapse and do not, because the stone has been reinforced by centuries of sustained exposure until the rock is stronger than the load above it. Petralon-attuned Marrowkin fighters are the hardest opponents in the Inner World to move, because their connection to the ground is literal. Breaking it requires either lifting them off the ground or destroying the ground beneath themJudicium Judgment / PriorityThe Sancta Lux installation’s primary Wellspring. The Measurewrights calibrated the compound’s stone to Judicium and Fixatio simultaneously, producing a substrate that responds to the Scale’s readings with the same fidelity that Nalūn’s salt responds to Oblation. A reading in the Sanctified Hall carries more weight than a field reading. The Hall amplifies nothing: the substrate holds the reading steady while the Lectors work, the way a good bench holds a workpiece steady while the craftsman cutsFixatio Anchoring / StabilityPresent in both the geology and the installation. The same substrate stability that holds an inscription in a tunnel wall also holds a finding in a consecrated hall, and the fact that both rest on the same Wellspring is either a coincidence or a theological statement, depending on whether you ask a Marrowkin or a LectorIgnivale Flame / CollapseThe collapse from finding into execution. The fire that falls, the moment a measured finding becomes a physical consequence. The forges of the holds do not use Ignivale. The distinction between forge-heat and judgment-fire is one the kingdom maintains with the deliberateness of people who understand that a fire that melts metal and a fire that executes people should never be confused, because confusing them produces a civilization that cannot tell the difference between manufacture and murder
Who Rules: Three Institutions
The Ore Council · Twelve guild masters (Smelter, Forge, Tunnel, Assay, Carriers, Inscription, Stone, Fuel, Merchant, Archive, Healer, Ward), chaired by a Council Chair elected for a ten-year term whose authority is administrative. The present Chair is Mirja Hiilekk Solisan, called Sixty Tuns, a former Tunnel master with arms like bridge-timbers, who once stopped a Council session to correct the scansion of a death threat. The Council governs everything that touches the ore and everything cut from the Body. The extraction schedule is the kingdom’s true sovereign instrument, and everything else is administration. It sets how much comes off which rib, how fast the world’s metal moves, and who waits. Its reading each year opens the Cutting Fair.
The River Crown Council · Representatives elected by every racial community, sitting in a circular chamber whose design reflects the founding principle: no delegation is larger than another, no seat is elevated above any other, and the speaking floor belongs to whoever holds it. The Trade Equality Act’s provisions occasionally conflict with the extraction schedule’s requirements, and the conflicts are resolved through negotiations that take longer than the Marrowkin consider reasonable and shorter than the humans consider sufficient.
The Grand Church · Does not vote on the Ore Council and does not sit on the River Crown. It maintains its own compound, staff, training, consecrated substrate and chain of command, and its relationship with the kingdom it sits inside is defined by one principle: the Church measures. It measures the Ore Council’s trade practices, Altherion’s civic governance and the kingdom’s military operations with the same instrument and the same standard it applies to every other realm in the four quarters. The government can request a measurement and cannot decline one. It cannot evict the body that performs them either, because that would require the cooperation of every kingdom that depends on the metal, and those are the same kingdoms that depend on the court.

The three coexist because the cost of separating them exceeds the cost of managing their contradictions. The Ore Council controls the economy. The River Crown controls the politics. The Grand Church controls the measurement both are judged by. The resulting governance has neither elegance nor efficiency. It is stable the way a three-legged stool is stable: remove any leg and the structure falls, and with all three in place it holds more weight than its construction would suggest.

Wealth and What It Trades
Marrowhold’s economy is the northern shield’s economy. Every Inner World realm’s economy connects to the Ring’s output, and the Ore Council sits at the center of that web with the patience of a people who know the web cannot function without them. Smelting happens at the Ring because that is where the sulfide is, and the smelters run on forge-arrays (standing runed workings) that pull directly from the ambient saturation, so a Ring furnace costs a fraction of what a western one does. In the west you pay a Core keeper for your hours, and here it is simply in the air.
Two kinds of goods come out of the Ring, and the difference matters.
Metal is the bulk of it and the part that moves armies: above all the alloys made with Blackcap Sulfide, the massive nickel and copper ore of the melt sheet, which keeps its temper inside a forge-array’s working field where ordinary steel goes soft and stupid. Every crucible tong, array clamp and furnace door hinge worth owning is Blackcap alloy. Every bar carries the assay stamp, and the stamp counts for more than the bar.
The Body is the part that made them famous, sold by the piece, by hand, each piece cut by a named person and entered under that name:








































PieceWhat it isWhat it is bought forOld ivoryRib bone, warm to the touch, gold-grained under moving lightSword hilts, ward-frames, reliquaries, thrones of petty kings. A rune cut in it does not driftSinewCord drawn from the great pale sheets that line the older galleriesCrossbow strings and bow-cord. A bolt costs a few coppers, and a Marrowhold string under it is why a sect elder should watch the windowsMarrow-tallowFat rendered from the core of the bone, dull gold, slow-burningLamps that burn orange and last a season, and a base for Drafts. It smokes, and every Marrowkin thinks an honest lamp shouldBloodslagBlack-red glass skimmed off a glow-blood furnaceAlchemists, ward-cutters, anyone wanting heat that stays where it is putEmber dyeBoiled emberwortThe hot red that no northern dyer can match and every northern tailor lies aboutRelicsA joint-cap, a splinter that hums, a hand-sized thing nobody can nameSects and kings, and people have killed for less. No tooth has ever been sold, and two hundred are on offer in the Midmarch at any time
The Return Clause closes every sale of the Body: returnable on the Lender’s demand, carriage at the holder’s charge. Nobody reads it, and it is read aloud anyway. That means every old-ivory hilt in the four quarters is out on loan, every buyer’s name is in the Tally beside it, and the clerks at Breastbone can tell you where most of the Twelfth Rib currently is. Sold pieces are reputed to lean, a hair, toward the Ring, and sailors hang splinters on threads to prove it. Guild assayers have measured the lean on some pieces and found nothing on others, and a Measurewright will explain it by the cut of the grain until you leave. The holds have one comment, which is that they keep the record for when it is asked for.
The Accord relationship is the deepest of any Inner World state. Enforcement maintains a permanent legation at Altherion. Research sources experimental metalwork from the Inscription Guild. Strategic’s weapons procurement runs through the Forge Guild. The Skyglass Archive sources its substrate materials from the Deep Reach. Marrowhold is the Accord’s armory, and the Ore Council decides how quickly the armory restocks.
Altherion runs on trade, services, and the revenue of hosting the Grand Church: pilgrim traffic, arbitration fees, legation rent and diplomatic delegations, making it the most commercially active surface settlement on the northern shield despite producing nothing itself. The merchants have a saying: Altherion makes nothing and sells everything, accurate in the way all self-deprecating merchant humor is accurate, describing a real condition and pretending to be embarrassed by it.
The dead mines of Anguz
Out past the northern roads lie the workings of Anguz, which were once a real power, with the guilds setting the price of Aethersteel and Bloodsilver on the coil and gold running second to both. The mines collapsed and took the power with them. Nobody holds Anguz now except whoever is down there this week, and what comes out is Dustquartz, from shattered veins, sold by the sack for cheap decorative charms and treated with less caution than it warrants, since in bulk its shards resonate to discordant Aether under compression. Marrowkin use the place as a proverb. A mine that owes nobody, they say, ends up owing everyone.
Rent, Food and the Street
Rent in the holds is reckoned by warmth. A gallery near a furnace shoulder costs about twice what the same room costs on the cold side of the bone, the rent goes in the Tally like everything else, and people will tell you their rent before they tell you their trade, with the same pride. Rooms in Altherion are let by the quarter, and rent on the river side has been a live question before the River Crown for three hundred years.
Food is bought in, and it shows. The Rimlands feed the crater and never quite enough, so bread is dear, grain prices make every other kingdom wince, and the stores that matter are salted, dried, cellared and packed in bulk. Underground the meal is the crib, a pastry case of meat and root carried down in a tin and eaten at the shift’s break, with a mark pressed into the corner of the crust so that a man gets his own back up. Sour barley beer in the lower levels, which every visitor calls an acquired taste and every Marrowkin calls beer. Cheap and everywhere are redcaps, the fat emberwort fungus off the bone terraces, fried in tallow, tasting strongly of iron. Marrow itself is never sold to be eaten. A child gets one smear of it on bread at the First Entry, and it goes in the Tally as that child’s opening debt.
Come in a market week and bring ear-stoppers. The low town under Breastbone’s wall is pale houses, red moss on every roof, copper-green fire in pans at the corners, and shift horns going over the top of everything. A rib-sounder will press her jaw to your party wall and tell you, for a copper, whether your neighbor is really out. Hoist-goblins in too many pockets are arguing with a Tunnel journeyman over the last chain-lift. On the rim it is louder: seven peoples’ building traditions lean over the same Altherion streets in seven colors of paint, a Bugbear porter and an elf factor are arguing the price of one mule in two languages, cookshops sell cribs to pilgrims who have walked a season to see the Church, and the fighting clubs of the rim wards march to the River Stairs brackets behind their own drums and their own insulting songs. Down in the bone the shift clubs do the same, with the First Shift Reds and the Third Shift Coals holding a grudge so old it has its own column. Lamp-wardens, ward-cutters and a thousand petty trades work these streets on their own account, and they strike when they please. One old ratcatcher will clear your cellar for a copper and leave you the receipt carved on the rat.
The Weighing Festival · Sancta Lux’s festival, held in Altherion’s streets. The senior Measurewright performs a public reading of the Grand Church’s operational integrity, and the annual reading of the false-positive rate is treated with the ceremonial gravity other kingdoms reserve for coronations. Altherion attends in numbers that surprise the order every year, because it is the one time most people see the Scale’s instrument in operation, and most attendees describe the experience as the most intellectually honest thing they have ever witnessed and also the most frightening.
The Assay · More than a test: the Marrowkin way of saying that a thing that has been measured and found correct carries a truth no salesmanship can replicate and no counterfeiting can fake. The measurement is the thing, and the thing without the measurement is just rock.
Language · The Tally-Tongue in the holds. Concord Common in Altherion. Lattice Tongue for High Line sacred and technical inscription, where the grammar of the utterance mirrors the grammar of the universe, and outside listeners describe the experience as hearing a proof being recited rather than a sentence being spoken. See The Tally-Tongue of the Marrowkin.
Law
Three parallel systems whose jurisdictions are defined by function rather than geography.
Guild Law · Practical, specific, enforced by arbitration tribunals whose appeals process is slow, thorough, and famously humorless.

The Drainage Obligation, borrowed from Nalūn’s model: structural integrity sufficient to prevent collapse into adjacent workings.
The Tender’s Obligation: lifetime support for array-tenders who develop the tender’s shake, the fine persistent palsy that arrives at about eight years of forge-array service and does not leave. You will see it in a cup that will not sit still. The guild that shook a tender keeps him for life and pays for his funeral, and a hold that defaults on this has never been found, because the clerks would have to enter it.
The Assay Standard: counterfeiting a stamp is a capital offense. The last person who attempted it was found, tried and sentenced within three days, which is the fastest judicial process in the kingdom’s history.
The Cutting Right: nothing comes off the Body without an entry naming who cut it and how much. An unentered cut is theft from the Lender, tried like murder, and the bone-runners who carry such pieces out over the rim at night are the most romantic criminals in the north and have an average career of about eighteen months.
The Reckoning: a life is settled by nothing but a life, a theft by nothing but its own return. Toll-right is honored by every branch of the people.

Republican Law · Applies to every person within Altherion’s territory regardless of guild affiliation, racial origin or institutional membership.
Sancta Lux Jurisdiction · Operating on the principle that the Scale measures everywhere and that the measurement does not require the measured party’s consent. The Ember Magistrates hold flame-lit equilibrium courts in towns that will never see the Grand Church, and their jurisdiction is one of the few legal authorities neither Council can override.
The three intersect constantly. The complexity is managed by a class of professional arbitrators trained in all three, known informally as the Three-Tongued, who make their living translating between legal traditions and who are, by universal agreement, the most exhausted professionals in the Inner World.
How It Fights
The Forge Guard · Roughly four thousand, built from the same material as the Ring’s walls: dense, patient, and extremely difficult to move. They fight in harness of Blackcap alloy under red-enameled rib-ivory shields, with hammers and short heavy spears, a line of squat figures with hot eyes behind slit visors who plant their feet and let you arrive. Every tunnel in the Ring is defensible and every road narrows where a formation benefits them. Crossbowmen on sinew strings hold the galleries above. A Forge Guardsman’s signature move is called Worked Ground: he sets both feet, the floor for three paces round him answers to Petralon, and the man who charges him finds he has charged the mountain.
A Marrowkin with his aura coat up is on shift. He calls Pressure the load, and he calls sensing a man sounding him, the way a rock face is sounded for a bad seam. A human from Altherion who tries the same words will be corrected, in detail, for as long as he stands there.
Sancta Lux maintains its own capability within the compound: the Arbiter-Militant wing, the Inquisitors with their gauntlet-etched Judica rites, and the Mask, of which there is only ever one, whose mere presence in a room suppresses invocation. It answers to the Will of Judger, currently held by Darius, who refuses to be invested in it and has been pending investiture for eleven years.
The strategic defense is economic. A war against Marrowhold is a war against your own account-books, your own armory, and the judicial body that every other kingdom’s legal system references when its own authority is insufficient. Nobody has been willing to pay all three costs at once. An invader also has the small additional problem of a Tally that will record his name, what he took, and who is to be asked for it back.
What They Joke About
Marrowkin are flat about everything except the current seam, which they will boast about at the top of their lungs in a meter you can feel through the floor. Their humor is mostly accounting.

The oldest joke in the holds holds that the god died of being invoiced.
A Marrowkin who has cut very little is teased by cut-name for life. Thimble is a real name on a real clerk, and she has outlived three people who laughed.
Altherion is “the lid.” Humans are “the weather.” The Church is “the people who check our sums,” said very quietly, in the shaft, with a look at the ceiling.
They tell a whole cycle about King Hobart’s throne, and they tell it to buyers, at the signing, with a straight face.
Everyone else says that you cannot insult a Marrowkin because he will only write it down, and that you cannot lie to one because he will read it back, and that if you want to know how a Marrowkin feels about you, check whether the entry scans. Kharven soldiers will tell you the Marrowkin sold the god its own coffin and are still waiting on the balance. Nalūn says the Marrowkin have a heart and it is on the schedule.

Monsters on the Roads
Everything red is slightly wrong to eat if you are not used to it, including the deer. The Ring’s ordinary beasts are those deer, red-stained goats on the bone terraces, and pale bats that roost in the galleries and come out at dusk against the furnace glow like smoke going the wrong way. Out in the Rimlands the timber holds the usual northern company of wolves and bears, and they are no respecters of a Carriers’ Guild escort. Bone-runners on the rim at night are the most romantic criminals in the north, and rib-lice, pale cat-sized things living on the older galleries, are the least, and every shift keeps a terrier and a low opinion of both.
Basilisks (Grade A on the hunting halls’ scale, which runs from E to EX) hunt the fume-belt, the six leagues downwind of the smelters where the smoke has killed everything else and nothing will trouble them. Along the boundary stones west of the rim, Marrowkin survey parties and Stark riders both hunt the odd Greater Wolf pack and whatever comes off the fume-belt with too many opinions, and each side enters the kill on its own side of the stone. Monsters move, here as on every road in the Inner World, and a bill for one goes up on the door at Collarbone beside the Fair’s lot list, in meter, with the reward in the last line where you have to hear the rest to get to it.
Dungeons
Petralon (the Aether of stone) pools in the walls, a good part of the Ring is worked Core, and the holds will sit you beside one for an hour at a price. Marrowkin do not use the word dungeon. They say a cavity, which is a butcher’s question: what was in it, and who has already had the good cuts. Three get talked about, under whatever name, and the full account of what such a place is sits on the Dungeons shelf.
The Deep Reach below the basin floor is a Steward’s territory, with the Deepkin in an advisory role that the upper holds find unnerving, and nobody who knows what lies at the bottom has shared it in full.
The Cold Marrow, under the Twelfth Rib, is a gallery through the god’s bone that the Marrowkin stopped working one winter, in a great hurry, leaving their tools. The Ore Council closed it. In a country that will read you the entry for a splinter, nobody will say what kind of ground it is, the halls at Altherion have stopped asking to post it, and no Marrowkin goes down there. The far shift’s song about the cold soup has one more verse, on why the soup goes cold, and they stop before they reach it.
Anguz, out past the northern roads, is dead mines, once a real power, now held by whoever is down there this week: a Wild ground of stone and ore, Dustquartz by the sack, collapses, shards that resonate to the wrong Aether under pressure. Marrowkin use it as a proverb, that a mine that owes nobody ends up owing everyone.
The Scourge and the Turn
The Scourge of Hell lies well to the south, with the whole salt basin between, so no Marrowkin has ever had a stilt walk through his barley, and the Ring has done extremely well out of the place. The Turn is the old rota by which North, South and Center each keep the Scourge’s monsters off everybody else for nine years, and the Ore Council’s position is that Marrowhold is nobody’s holding and so no party to it. On the North’s Turn, Kharven and the Banner Houses march in Ring metal and enter it in their Count as a northern neighbor’s contribution. The Ore Council enters the same metal as a sale, and the Accord’s auditors at Sealhall have looked at both columns and taken their fee. The South’s Turn and the Center’s buy from the same schedule at the same price, and the present Turn, the Center’s until 721, pays by Charter instrument, which the Assay Guild accepts and reads very slowly.
So the Forge Guard has never stood on the Line, the chain of forts around the Scourge’s edge, and most of the spearheads that do carry an assay stamp. Heavy loads go down the Iron-to-Salt Corridor to the basin and then by the salt road along the Scourge’s east flank, where a dry year’s haze-kites (Grade B, membrane and hunger, riding the outward wind) take the Carriers’ mules on the last stretch, and the Guild bills for the mule. What comes back up that road is the other half of the trade. Wyrm cores, the glassy hardened hearts of very large creatures, sell to any crucible at Breastbone that can pay, and the relic hunters bring ghoststeel out of the Shambles to the Cutting Fair, where the Inscription Guild buys it to find out, again, why it cannot be made. A young Marrowkin who has cut a wyrm core out on the Thresh may not take it as a cut-name, because the Tally has only the one Body, and several have asked. Shown the sword itself, on one of the nine clear days, the holds’ surveyors look at the Ring’s ribs, look at the blade, and suggest it is a butcher’s pin marking a cut.
More in the Gazetteer.
Neighbors and Grudges
The Amber Cities of Nalūn · The defining trade partnership of the Inner World, now that the cities have no crown to argue with. Nalūn’s credit finances extraction. The Ring’s metal backs Nalūn’s credit, and supply contracts are sealed at Ironlink Hold, never here. It is structural the way a bridge and its piers are structural: remove either and the span falls, and nobody describes a bridge as being friends with its foundation.
The Kingdom of Kharven · Imports metalwork and supplies military protection for the northern corridors, and is the most critical economic relationship the holds have and the most complicated political one. The Ore Council has long treated Kharven as a useful armed frontier, and when it wants to say so it cuts grain and keeps sending inscription substrate. Moto Fractura-attuned practitioners provide fortification assessments the holds’ engineers find useful and irritating in equal measure, because they can see stress in stone the holds’ own instruments do not detect, and being shown a flaw in your own masonry by a human warrior with a blood-inherited eye is the kind of experience Marrowkin process by building a better instrument rather than by expressing gratitude. Kharven-Seat’s crown ironwork, set with garnet, came from a Ring smith whose descendants still hold the commission.
Added in a later hand: when the banners of the north came together as the Northern Empire of Whitemere, the Ore Council entered the new name at the head of the same column and kept the same grain prices. Marrowhold is nobody’s holding. The empire is its largest buyer, and both of them know what that makes it.
The Scarlet Wood of Thornhaven · House Thornwall’s corridor runs to Collarbone. Grain and worked metal go west along it, ironwood comes east for tool handles and ward-frames, and the Thornwalls know the difference between a shortage and a message, having tracked the Ore Council’s supply decisions for generations. Their reading is that the holds are comfortable with an armed buffer and uncomfortable with an independent one. They have been saying so, correctly and unheeded, for a long time.
The Guild Accord · An essential supplier, an intractable negotiating partner, and the host of the most powerful judicial body the Accord has to answer to. All four divisions submit to the same Sancta Lux jurisdiction every other visitor submits to, producing the friction of a supra-national body being measured by one of its own chartered members inside a territory it nominally oversees. There is also the matter of the great curved bones around the arena at Sealhall. The Accord bought those somewhere and has never produced the receipt. Hold-clerks have gone to look, more than once, with a measuring cord and their mouths shut, and the Tally says only that the bones are not in it.
The Holy Sea of Alabaster · The Holy Sea measures testimony, Sancta Lux measures everything else, and both hold that a measurement that does not drift is worth more than a judgment that does. Warm, distant, mediated through the chapter hold that reports back to Altherion. Abbots keep turning up at the Cutting Fair and keep describing it as a pastoral visit.
The Silver Cedars of Yukari · Commercial, functional, defined by mutual utility, a relation the Crow’s Reach had with the holds and the Yukari land carried on. Its wards protect corridors both sides depend on.
The Iron Mandate of Undaar-Keth · A cold peace at a distance, and an unspoken embarrassment. Philologists have laid out the cognates between the Tally-Tongue and Old Vaross, down to the low numerals and the word for hand. Both peoples have read the table, and neither has commented.
The Hundred Crowns of the Midmarch · Very good customers. Roughly one in five of its kings owns something that leans.
What This Shelf Does Not Have





























GapStandingNamed personsThe twelve guild masters, the River Crown’s leadership and the Grand Church’s staff below Darius are mostly missing from this shelf, because nobody will tell it. The Chair has a name and would like that notedThe Deepkin’s roleWhat they know about what lies beneath the Ring, and what they have declined to share. Nobody going down into the Deep Reach should rely on this pageThe Tender’s ShakeDeserves a physician’s entry of its own. Hard material that the kingdom’s economy runs on and that nobody outside the guild system thinks aboutEcho Elf influenceWhether they hold a formal seat on the River Crown Council, or only an inherited philosophical influenceDarius’s investitureThe Will of Judger seat has been pending eleven years. Nobody has had his reason from his own mouth, and the people who claim to have it disagree
See also The Marrowkin.

The Body does not care about your court. The Body does not care about your republic. The Body does not care about your twelve guilds or your fourteen factor houses or your thirty-five-year-old procedure manual written by a man who refuses to hold the office he designed. There is ore in it and there is an account against it, and that is why we are still here, and that is the whole of the explanation.
Attributed to a tunnel-master, name unrecorded, preserved in the Archive Guild’s collection of statements too honest to file

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Golden Hollow of Ashbury
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itASH-bree
House Ashmore · The Greenhollow · The Grain

Perkin Oatley lit a little light,
to see the mice were gone;
the roof went up to say good night
and came down Barleyford at dawn.
Children’s skipping rhyme, the Greenhollow

The Great Tithe Barn at Sheafton is two hundred and forty feet long, with a roof of oak trusses a bishop would be proud of, and in the harvest of Year 678 it held every sack the upper Hollow had just been made to give. It also held mice, and the Ashmore steward hired a hedge-worker named Perkin Oatley to charm them out at four copper the day. Perkin was a cheerful, untidy man who could genuinely talk to mice and was, by all accounts, doing well. Toward evening, with the threshers shaking out the last sacks and the air inside gone thick and sweet and golden with barley dust, he lit a tallow dip to see into the far bays.
Fine flour in still air will burn faster than the eye can follow, and every miller knows it. Perkin Oatley was a hedge-worker. The flash ran the length of the barn, the great roof lifted off all together like a lid off a boiling pot, and the blast could be felt nine miles off. The sky over the upper Hollow filled with green roof-tiles, and for half an hour afterward it rained hot roasted barley on three villages, gently, in the sunset, with the whole country running out with aprons and baskets, shouting, children dancing in it, the smell like the best breakfast of your life. Eleven threshers died and Perkin was never found in any form that could be sat with, and the Hollow gave them a very handsome funeral. Then, the following week, the Ashmore clerks came round with tally-sticks and billed every household in three villages for what had fallen on their land, by the bushel, at the harvest rate. They paid. Everyone in the north always pays Ashmore in the end.
The Golden Hollow is the one warm valley in a cold country, whose owners know to the sack what you will need in January, and who have never once had to raise their voices about it.

Two hands on this page. It stands in Year 715. Lines marked Later hand come from the annotator of the Concordance of Ages, writing in the last winter before the turn. Later hand: the Hollow is a land of House Ashmore inside the Northern Empire of Whitemere, and the empire eats out of it.

The Land and What It Looks Like
The Greenhollow is the southern lowland of the north: forested river valleys, deep soil and enough season for grain, livestock and timber, and the only territory in the old kingdom where agriculture is the primary occupation rather than a supplement to hunting and trade. Coming down into it off the plateau in late summer is one of the great experiences of a northern life. The road drops through the last of the spruce, the wind stops trying to kill you, and there below is a long green valley gone gold, barley and rye to the tree-line in both directions, red cattle in the water-meadows, the rivers bright between the alders. And standing over the wheat in every parish, like cathedrals to a religion of bread, are the tithe barns: oak and honey-colored stone, buttressed, under great sweeping tiered roofs of verdigris teal with carved finials, hundreds of feet long, with doors a loaded wagon can turn around in. The faithful are expected to fill them.
The Hollow is green from thaw to first frost and it is still cold by anyone else’s measure, with a four-month growing season to work in. Visitors from the south find it charming and slightly small. Visitors from the north find themselves crying at a hedge.
The major places

Ashbury. The seat, on the water-meadows where the Kessen, the Marrow and the salt road from the south all meet. A storybook town of half-timbered halls under those same sweeping teal roofs (the biggest of them are tithe barns, and visitors keep taking them for churches), with golden trees in every yard, a clear stream under a stone bridge where the carts cross and small boats tie up, blue mountains behind it, and russet pennants on the gates. It has the Corn Hall where the allocation is read out at Stack-Count, and below the town at the crossroads the junction stone, a black upright older than the house, on which Ashmore oaths are sworn hand-flat, and which the Hollow believes holds them. A famous old woman at Ashbury licks a horseshoe and tells you whether the horse will see spring, and she has made a very good living.
Sheafton. The barn town of the upper Hollow, with the Great Tithe Barn (rebuilt, with larger vents, and a regulation about tallow) and a Harvest Fair that draws bracket fighters from across the north, largely for the food.
Barleyford. A malting and brewing town on a shallow crossing, smelling of sweet smoke in all seasons. It owns one green tile from the old roof, set in the church wall, and will show it to you. The best small beer north of the Center comes from here, and nearly all of it goes up the road to the Seat on Ashmore’s terms.

Roads. North by the Marrow road to the Seat, through the last of the spruce, and upriver by the southern road to Threeways and the Painted Rivers. South of the valley the North stops and the marching country begins. From the junction below Ashbury the salt road goes to Halcrest in the Amber Cities, four days by relay rider, and on down the Scourge of Hell’s east flank, and the Kessen road takes its ford for the Midmarch, five days to Kingsbridge, and on down the west flank.
House and Rule
House Ashmore is the least martial house in a martial kingdom and the most quietly dangerous. Their power is grain. Their leverage is the specific kind that comes from controlling what everyone else needs to survive the winter, and they have never lost a negotiation with anyone who was hungry, which in the north means they have never lost a negotiation. They hold every sack between the Greenhollow and the treeline, and they govern through a steward’s competence, soft voice and clean hands: an Ashmore knows exactly how many bushels each Banner House needs to survive December and is willing to adjust the allocation on political grounds. The Ashmores do not threaten. Threats are for houses whose leverage requires explanation, and Ashmore leverage explains itself every time the temperature drops.
The lord in Year 715 is Edric Ashmore, Lord of the Ashmore Marches and one of the Seven Warlords: forty, looks younger, a man who weighs before he speaks and who will look at an offer for exactly as long as it takes a cup of wine to go cold. For twenty years the Tenrai have held Ashmore’s roads, so Ashmore takes Tenrai silver because Ashmore has no choice, and the Tenrai count him bought. In the taverns of Hollenmark they say a man who owns the grain in a famine does not need to fight anybody, and he will sell to whoever stands at the gate with silver when the snow comes and call it neutrality. Edric has heard this and thinks it is a fair summary.
Wealth and Trade
Barley, rye, oats, malt, salted beef, hides, tallow, cheese, and every bit of the leverage those provide. The house runs its income in kind, through the allocation: each autumn the Corn Hall reads out how much grain goes to each house, town and garrison in the north, and the reading has ended more friendships than adultery. The salt road brings Nalūn salt bars up from the Center, and Ashbury is where salt, grain and river-barges change hands. Tolls on the three-way meeting bring in more than a duke’s rents. The Ashmores buy big southern horses from the Yan of the Jade Plains, at Yan prices, and have a low opinion of the Yan as a result.
Every farmer in the Hollow owes a tenth to the barn, a day a week in plowing and harvest to the manor, and whatever he can talk his way out of to the reeve. Ashmore clerks count on notched tally-sticks split down the middle, one half for the barn and one for the farmer, so neither can cheat without the other’s stick. Among the people who are never short of food, this is considered the height of civilization.
Rent, Food and the Street
Land here is held in strips, by old custom, and the rent is a share of the crop. In Ashbury town rent is in coin and in a sack on Sack Day, the first market after harvest. This is the only part of the north where people eat fresh bread every day, where a laborer has an onion in his pocket, and where a plowman’s wife can get fat, and no one from the rest of the north ever fails to mention it. Pease pottage, barley cakes with butter, dark rye, smoked eel from the water-meadows, plum brandy in a good year. Harvest Home runs a week, with dancing in the empty barns, sheaf-tossing, cloth-of-gold scarecrows carried on poles, and the local Stage brackets held on stubble fields under the moon, a dozen fighting schools in russet and yellow calling each other’s mothers cows. It is considered bad luck to win on the first night.
Hedge-workers do steady business: talking the frost off a rye field, the mice out of a bay (under supervision), the blight from a pear. In the Hollow they charge per acre and they can and do refuse a lord who has shorted them, and in 684 the whole upper valley’s hedge-workers walked out over a late payment and there were no pears for two years. People here call the aura coat the hide, as everyone in Kharven does, and add that a thick one is a sign of a good dinner. A great many households in the Greenhollow perform all fourteen Sōhai labors correctly, in order, every day of their lives, and would be insulted to hear they were doing anything other than keeping a house properly.
What they joke about. Thin people. The rest of the north, gently, from a position of having eaten. Perkin Oatley, always. Edric’s wine, which is said to be the coldest in the kingdom. “Which sack?” is the punchline to about half the jokes in the valley, for reasons a stranger will never get, and the answer is always the one you already gave them.
Law and How It Fights
Law. The manor court and the reeve for ordinary business, with the Corn Hall above them. A dispute over a bushel goes to the stick. A big promise goes on the junction stone, and it holds one oath at a time; two oaths on the same stone are known to grind, and lawyers have made fortunes finding out which one was first. Hollow people will not lie with a hand on stone, whatever else they do.
The fighting. The peasantry here fight with billhooks and a strong sense of grievance, and Ashmore’s own fighters come in one form, the Ashmore Line: russet pennants and a long ragged charge of those big southern horses with lances couched, lords’ sons in the saddle, very pretty, very expensive, and able to come down on a flank like a landslide of money. The fair answer is spears, set, on ground the horses cannot take at speed. Everything else the Hollow needs killed is arranged by contract, usually by not sending someone their grain.
Monsters on the Roads
The beasts. Mice, in the quantities that have shaped the region’s history, as above. Eels and herons work the ditches and red cattle the water-meadows. Everything that eats a mouse lives well here, and everything that eats a red cow will walk a long way to do it.
The monsters. Monsters move, and they live across the whole of the Inner World. The Hollow is the softest ground in the North, so everything hungry eventually comes to it. Reaching Briars (Grade B on the Bestiary’s scale, which runs from E to EX; Well-spawn hedges with a green knot over the root-crown) creep out of the woods and are burned by the parish. Greater Wolves come down in the Thin Weeks, and in a dry year a wyvern from the Ridge will take a red cow in front of the whole village. South of the valley the barns have arrow-slits, for what walks up from the Thresh as well as for armies.
The Malt Deeps
The dungeon (what a Wellspring Core makes around itself, or what grows up around one) is the Malt Deeps under Barleyford, old malting caves that went down too far and turned out to be a Verdantia Well (the Wellspring of growth). Hired Thornwall axes cleared them in the 540s at a cost Ashmore still disputes. It is a worked Core now, kept by brewers on an Ashmore license, its hours sold to bracket schools, and the air down there will sprout a dropped crust while you watch. The galleries glow a clear chlorophyll green and smell of cut grass over the sweet smoke, the old mash-tuns creak as their staves go on growing, and a brewer’s apprentice spends her first year cutting the walls back with a hooked knife. The parish hedges that have to be burned are, by general belief, cousins of what lives down there, and the brewers deny this in writing. Barleyford also denies that any of it has to do with the small beer. Thornwall sends its bill for the clearing every spring, and Ashmore sends a very polite receipt. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
The Scourge and the Turn
No land of the Banner Houses lies closer to the Scourge of Hell than the Hollow, with only the marching country and the salt basin between its last barn and the Thresh, the cutters’ name for the dry country on the rim. In the herds’ season, the late summer of a dry year, the wind on the southern parishes comes round with iron and pollen in it, right in among the smell of the harvest, and every reeve south of Ashbury goes up to look at the arrow-slits. Haze-kites (Grade B, membrane and hunger, the color of an old copper pot) have ridden that wind clean over the Salt Line and taken mules off the salt road in sight of a barn. The rim towns answer this sort of thing with bells on stakes and a great deal of paint. The Hollow answers it with a tally.
The Turn is the old rotation by which North, South and Center each spend nine years keeping the Scourge’s monsters off everybody else, and the Ashmores have never lost one in their history, which is the plainest true thing anyone has said about them. Whoever holds the Turn may buy victuals at a fixed price, and every host that goes down either road buys at the junction below Ashbury at exactly that price, by the sack, and at this point the Hollow’s favorite punchline applies. On the North’s own Turn, Ashmore enters its grain in the Count (the running bill the three parties present to one another) as supplied at the fixed price and then allocates it to the other houses as usual, which has not improved feeling about the pie. The Ashmore Line itself has ridden down to the Hem on a Northern Turn, the Hem being the Scourge’s outer belt, and it was very pretty, and it came home short a great many expensive horses. The Center has the Turn until 721, so for now the hosts at the junction are only the hungry ones going by, and a clerk with a copy of the Count has a desk in the Corn Hall.
Neighbors and Grudges

The Cobalt March. An empty pie dish arrives from Hollenmark every midwinter, and has done since 592. Ashmore sends a very polite receipt.
The Painted Rivers. The barges are theirs and the grain is Ashmore’s, and each house considers the other a useful servant.
The Scarlet Wood. Loose trunks by the thousand came down past Ashbury in 688 and warmed the grain-lords’ stoves for a decade. Ashmore did not send a thank-you, and did keep the wood.
Kharven-Seat. Tenrai factors in the Corn Hall, Tenrai silver in the strongbox, and an understanding on all sides about what happens if the Seat ever gets hungry in earnest.
The Amber Cities of Nalūn. Four days down the salt road by relay rider, at Halcrest. They pay in bars and their bars are always good. The south of the Hollow is where the North stops and the marching country begins, so the barns on that side are built with arrow-slits.
