geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Holy Sea of Alabaster
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itAL-uh-bas-ter
The White Shelf · The Bench of the South · The Country That Counts
The sale of Tobit Gurnard stopped at the second bid. It was the Feast of Saint Ebb in the spring of 683, the Rimward quay was hung end to end with blue and saffron pennons, sardines were frying on every bollard, and the wreck-merchant Gaspard Vauquelin had just sworn before the harbor bench that a storm put his galley, the Good Intent, and forty men on the watchtower rock, and that his sea-lenders therefore owed him eleven hundred silver. He was raising a little of it in the meantime by selling off the one oarsman who had crawled ashore. Tobit Gurnard, standing on the block with a rope on his neck and a gap where his front teeth had been, told the whole quay in a voice trained on a rowing bench that there had been no storm, that he had watched Vauquelin’s man douse the tower lamp and hang a false one on the point, and that he would like to say so on the Walk.
The Archdeacon of Rimward, who was Vauquelin’s brother, offered to swear the contrary. So the whole town went up the Stair behind them, fishwives and notaries and Serpentkin clerks and a Hobgoblin rope-seller with her stock still round her shoulders, and by noon the bookies had the Archdeacon at three to one. On the Sounding Walk, the long white pavement above the bay, both men took off their shoes. The Archdeacon swore in beautiful Latin and stepped back, and his soles left the limestone as dry as they found it. The oarsman swore in dockside Common with two words the clerk declined to enter, and under his bare feet the stone went dark and wet in the exact shape of his toes, as though he had that moment climbed out of a bath, and the prints stayed there till sundown with half of Alabaster filing past to look. Vauquelin hanged on the point where he had hung the lamp.
Then the auctioneer, who had been waiting patiently with his book, pointed out that Tobit Gurnard had no line in any register of the Holy Sea. His testimony had been witnessed and filed. His person had never been counted. The Manumission Doctrine protects the counted, and the sale would now resume. The roar they heard across the bay is on record. The sardine women passed their aprons, the quay and the Stair and a good part of the bench emptied their purses into them, and a Lambert clerk who happened to be going by counted thirty-seven silver aloud and corrected a bystander by two coppers. They bought him, walked him up to the Archive with a drum in front and had him written in, Gurnard, Tobit, oarsman, counted, before the lamps were lit. He spent his next twenty years as the most expensive professional witness in the south. They sell plaster casts of those footprints on the Walk today, and there are enough of them to pave it twice.
The Holy Sea is a white city that weighs what people swear on a stone that has never stopped listening, rules everyone through the registers it keeps, and keeps a family of counters at its gate to check the words against the sacks.
Foreigners expect the name to mean water. It has that too, and it will charge you for the view.
The Land and the Look
Come in by the bay if you can afford the harbor dues. Alabaster stacks up out of blue water in tier after tier of pale wall, its roofs red and rust, its towers spired, the whole palace-city climbing toward clouds that pile up gray-blue and rose over a ring of misty mountains. An arched stone bridge leaps the inlet at its foot, and out in the water a lone watchtower stands on its rock with the gulls going round it. The roofs are red because the clay is local. Everything the Court itself owns is white and ink-black, the colors of the house that counts for it, and a white wall with a black balance painted on the door means that someone inside has a right to ask your name.
Below the city runs the white shelf: cliffs the color of milk, dropping into water so clear the fishing boats seem to hang in the air with their shadows lying on the sand beneath them. On either flank the bay is drowned country. Something struck this shelf about 310 IC, the low land on both sides went under the sea and the shelf held, and on a still morning the sponge divers can show you the tops of walls. Whose hand it was is argued; two Measurewrights file it as an unrelated coastal collapse, and the Long Reading calls it something else.
Behind the shelf the ground climbs through lemon terraces, goat hill and thin chalky barley into the land marches, which run north to the edge of the Grey Plain. Higher still, inland and up, the shelf meets old hard rock and the frost hardly breaks. Up there stand broken walls, a well and a gatepost, the old Kōkan seat, where the residue lies so dense that a practitioner with the wrong kind of Soul Crystal cannot lay a hand on a wall without reading what happened against it. Pilgrims are advised not to. Pilgrims go anyway. The north’s surveyors put the ground the Moto came from somewhere else entirely, west past the Slate Ridge, and that is one of the honest quarrels on the Gazetteer’s table, since nobody able to read both places has been let near both.
All of this stands at the very bottom of the South, where the land finishes its long green steps down to the sea, with the Copper Coast warm along the shore to the east and the Jade Plains and the Long Fields between the land marches and the Center. The country is poor in grain and rich in everything that can be written down.
The Stone That Listens
The Holy Sea stands on the ground where the Moto once held the Long Reading, the seat where for four thousand years a contract sealed held anywhere because the ground itself witnessed it. Two kings once brought forty thousand spears to the foot of these cliffs and fought the Battle of Sorrel Water on a bench at the top of the Stair, which is the kind of thing that happened here. The Moto are gone from it. The bench is still there, and clerks eat their lunch on it.
What remains is the thing the Church built on. The Court calls the Aether under the shelf Attestis, a word found in its own Latin and on no Guild list of the Sixty, and every Measurewright who has sounded it gives a different account of which Wellspring it really is (a Wellspring being one of the sixty fixed types of Aether, the raw power practitioners pull from the world around them). The most respected reading is Thaloré, the Wellspring of Depth, under which emotional truth acquires a physical weight: testimony weighs density times depth, and the vessel it came from does not enter the sum. The Sōhai, the old Moto faith, hold that the whole of it is the residue of a Moto working that broke and never stopped running, that the Church discovered no Wellspring and built a doctrine on a scar, and that Sancta Lux is a tenant in someone else’s house. The Church has heard this. It has filed it.
How the Walk works. A witness stands barefoot on the limestone of the Sounding Walk and swears aloud. The oath goes into the stone. A sworn account the swearer holds true, deep down and with their whole weight, draws water up through the rock and leaves two dark footprints that last till sundown; a clerk sets an assay fork (a tuned brass fork that rings to the Aether it touches) on the flag and reads how deep the oath went. A false oath leaves the stone dry. In the street, a liar is dry-footed, and a woman who wants to insult her sister’s husband asks after the state of his socks.
What it cannot do. The Walk weighs what you hold true, and what you hold true may be a mistake, and that is the whole reason the Lamberts have a job. An honest fool leaves lovely footprints. The Sea measures testimony; the Lamberts measure everything the testimony is about. And a person whose name is in a mark the instrument cannot classify returns no reading at all, which the bench may not lawfully treat as true, false or anything else. See the Recension, below, and do not bring it up at dinner.
Who Rules
The Palatine holds the Sea from the Alabaster Court, at the top of the Stair. The present one, Aurélien Cassard, is a small, courteous, nearly blind old man who has his registers read aloud to him while he eats and is said to catch more errors that way. Below him sit the Court’s benches, each pairing a cleric with a Lambert: the cleric weighs the oath, the Lambert counts the facts, and the two of them have been quarreling over the same table for centuries. The Church of the Holy Sea keeps the saints and the Archive. Court Latin is its working tongue, and every lord who comes before it gets a Latin name he did not ask for.
The Veil-Saints do the work no one else wants. A continental working collapsed across this ground, the souls of tens of thousands died mid-oath on it, and the passage of the dead here has not gone right since. So the coast’s holiest office is a trade: Veil-Saints perform their Sacraments over the dying so that the soul crosses without fragmenting, and you can hire one by the night and you will want to book ahead in plague years.
The chapter hold of Sancta Lux stands inside the walls, reports past the Palatine to the Grand Church at Altherion, and politely declines to explain what it reports. A petition sent to the Sea is therefore read twice, once by a Court with reason to listen and once by an order with reason not to.
House Lambert are the hands that do the weighing and the only people in the Sea allowed a sword by right. They have held Sallowgate and the land marches for the Palatines since before the current line of Palatines could count. Their words are Count True, their colors white and ink-black with a balance on the field. A Lambert who gives a false count is struck from the house, the house keeps the list, and the list is a real object you can ask to see. The present Warlord of the Lamberts and Keeper of Sallowgate is Léonard Lambert, thirty-four, called Sword of the Bench, entered at Court as Leonardus Lambertus, Custos Portae Salicis. He is a tall man with wild gold curls and a clear green eye, in gilded harness under a scarlet cloak with the Sallowgate bear on his breast, and he came to the seat at twenty-nine when his father died on the Grey Plain with the count of his own dead still in his mouth. His father and grandfather fought with Crystals that never woke (a Soul Crystal being the organ of a practitioner’s power), reading blows before they were thrown with no faculty to read them with, and were feared for it; many Lamberts are born that way, nobody outside the house knows how many, and the house knows. He has told three generals their numbers to their faces, and two of them listened. “I do not doubt your courage, my lord. I am only telling you how many of you there are.”
Cities and Towns
Alabaster is the capital, sixty thousand souls by the only census in the south anyone believes, and most of them are on a stair. The Stair of Testimony climbs from the bay to the Court in eleven hundred steps, with a shop on every landing, and the Bridge of Notaries, the great arched span, carries a double row of booths where you can have anything sworn, sealed or copied in nine languages while the tide goes under you. The Sounding Walk was laid after the shelf held, and four centuries of bare feet have worn the polish off its flags. The Archive, cut back into the shelf behind the Court, is the most complete register of births, deaths and contracts in the Inner World; its works are records, with no machinery anywhere, and the records outlast everything. Out on its rock stands the Lone Clerk, the watchtower, where a harbor scribe has counted every hull entering the bay for six hundred years and where, since the Good Intent, two men hold the lamp and watch each other.
Rimward is the harbor, down at the bay’s western arm, all sail lofts, slave-blocks, sponge boats and galley sheds, a loud salt town that thinks the upper city is a pack of hypocrites and supplies it with fish. It is no relation of the Rimward among the free cities of Nalūn, and each will tell you the other stole the name. Half the tavern arguments in both concern whether the Sea’s theology or the Yukari’s arithmetic is the better reason for treating a Beastkin like a person, and these arguments end in the usual way.
Sallowgate is the landward gate, a fat walled town where the salt road’s western branch comes in, with sallow willows thick along its ditch and a stone bear rearing over the arch that every passing soldier touches for luck. Here the tariffs are taken, the land-march levies drill, and every child of the house, woken or not, learns the Sallowgate Answer, the counter-cut that turns in the hand before your blade has left its line. The tariff-hall has the South’s most accurate water clock, and the town’s favorite spectator sport is watching a merchant discover what he actually declared.
Wealth and Trade
The Sea sells certainty, by the page. Trade routes ran to Alabaster long before the Church, because the alternative was doing business without knowing what your counterparty was, and they run there still: registers of birth and title, sworn copies, sealed contracts, adjudications between foreigners who trust nobody else. Deposit-and-lending runs through the Archive’s strongrooms too, which the free cities of Nalūn consider a sin and the Sea considers a service. The Sea has in turn maintained for four hundred years that Nalūn’s distinction between lending and interest is a distinction without a difference, and it has maintained this while keeping its own money at Ironlink Hold, in the care of a chapel with one cleric in it whose primary function appears to be minding the money.
Alabaster also inherits jurisdiction over southern phosphate law, because the Marrowchalk barges (bone-rock that doubles a wheat yield and also raises the dead) all come through its lawyers. The Court has twice tried to establish that the two uses can be legally told apart at the point of sale, and has twice failed. Otherwise: lemons, salt fish, sponges, white cheese, good parchment and pilgrims. Grain comes in by sea and costs too much, and the north has been told so in writing.
Rent, Food and the Street
Rent rises with the Stair. A landing near the Court costs a Guild journeyman’s wage for a room the width of his arms, and the Laundry Steps at the bottom, wet and singing all day with washerwomen slapping linen on the stone, house six families to a floor at well under the city list. Bread is the price everyone watches. People eat sardines off a skewer, goat cheese with lemon salt, chickpea cakes, barley soup with fish heads, and on feast days a sweet white almond paste molded into the shape of a balance, which children eat from the pan that holds the lies.
The crowd is the most mixed in the Inner World, because the ground will not distinguish one race’s oath from another’s. Serpentkin scribes, Catkin sailors, Tinker Goblins and Eressean pilgrims jostle a Hobgoblin rope-seller on the same landing. Petty arts are everywhere and paid by the job: foot-washers on the Walk who scrub your soles for a copper so that the print reads clean, hedge-workers selling dry-foot charms that have never once worked, professional witnesses in good shoes, lamp-wardens who keep the worked lights on the Stair and walk off it at festival time for double pay. Two bracket schools run the city’s fights like a pair of rival parishes, the Whites of the Upper Stair and the Inks of the Laundry Steps, and on bracket days a clerk’s son in a white sash will cheerfully break a washerwoman’s son’s nose and then enter it in the proper form. Dockers call the aura coat the shine and Pressure the weight, and clerks say Reinforcement and enter the same broken nose under another heading.
Law and How It Fights
The bench. Everything is decided by the sworn account and the true count, in public, with fair copies posted on the church doors. A tribunal of examiners also keeps a graded catalog of the corruptions a soul can fall into, down to the Corruption of Non-Commitment, which is innocence through distance, the man who says “it is complicated” while the preventable catastrophe rolls past him, and which the rest of the south finds hilarious until it is read out with their name on it.
The Manumission Doctrine extends legal protection through theology to populations the surrounding world considers disposable. It is the proudest thing in the Sea, and the anti-discrimination law behind it is a property of the ground rather than an ethical position anyone could revoke. It also reaches only what the Archive holds. The ground does not distinguish the testimony of a cleric from the testimony of a man being sold, and files both.
The Recension is the part that must be understood exactly. Some two to four generations before the present, the Church reformed its register, sincerely and competently, to correct accumulated drift and bring it into line with what the stone would witness. The clerics read their error rates aloud in open chapter. It improved the instrument and everyone involved was proud of it. It also drew a hard line where a soft one had stood, and the hinterland families of the old Kōkan remnant, whose names ran four hundred thousand years back in a mark no instrument could classify, fell outside it. An unclassifiable mark returns no reading, a person who returns no reading has not been witnessed, and a person who has not been witnessed has not been counted. Nobody in the Holy Sea decided to enslave anyone. Somebody decided the register was inaccurate.
War. The Sea’s levies are small, drilled, and paid on the day, a rare enough thing in the south that good men queue for it. Lambert officers tell a general his own numbers before battle, out loud, in front of his captains, and do not soften them. Crossbow companies from the march towns hold the walls and the Stair, at a few coppers a bolt, and a Stair full of crossbows has discouraged more than one high-Stage visitor who could have flattened the gate. The Court fights its larger wars with paper: an excommunication from the registers, a refusal to witness, a line struck from a title. When it needs a wall of spears it hires one from Hammerford, and audits it.
What They Joke About
The Sea’s people are funny the way bookkeepers at a wake are funny. They tell the one about the Palatine who died and was turned back at the gate of the next world for a discrepancy. They say that a Rimward man will swear to anything and a Stair man will charge you for it. They ask what a Lambert says at his own wedding (“how many of you are there?”). Of the Yan they say that a horse there has better papers than a duke, and of the Yukari that a crow will sell you your own secrets and enter the sale. Of northerners they say only that they write very short petitions.
Monsters on the Roads
The parish has a form for most of it. Zombies (Grade D) get up in fields dressed too heavily with Marrowchalk, and the form has a box for what the thing was called when it was a farmer. Sirens (Grade B) work the rocks off the point, and two men hold the Lone Clerk’s lamp and watch each other. Sea Serpents (Grade S) are a bad year’s news. Beasts do the ordinary daily harm: gray wolves come down off the frost line into the land marches when the snow lies late, rock sharks follow the sponge boats along the drowned walls, and the gulls of the Stair will have a sardine out of your fingers, and a finger if you are slow.
The dungeon. The ground under the shelf is the great working site, which the Court calls Attestis, a word on no Guild list, and which Measurewrights read most respectably as Thaloré, the Wellspring of Depth. It is why a true oath wets the stone. The dungeon is the Drowned Parishes, the sunken low land on both sides of the bay since the blow of about 310 IC. The church bells are still in their towers, and in the autumn gales they swing, and Rimward’s sponge boats stay home. Mourning Pike (Grade A, Well-spawn bred on Thaloré ground, teal over the skull) hold the naves, the souls of tens of thousands died mid-oath on that ground, and the Veil-Saints will tell you why they charge what they do. Nobody has cleared a single parish, though the Archive still holds the deeds, and about once a generation some heir buys a sworn copy, hires a crew on the Rimward quay and goes down to collect the rent. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
The Scourge and the Turn. The Scourge of Hell lies far up at the other end of the South, past the Long Fields and the whole climb of the land, and nobody on the Stair has ever smelled its wind. The Sea pays for it anyway. Under the Turn, the old wheel by which North, South and Center each spend nine years keeping the Scourge’s monsters off the other two, the South’s share falls on the old Dynasty’s realms, this white shelf and the hired spears of Hammerford. The Sea fights its share with a pen: a Southern Turn runs by the season on subscription lists opened at Alabaster and posted on the church doors, every parish and guild with its sum beside its name, so that a stingy one can read about itself in a fair hand. Lambert officers go north with the companies to audit the spears and tell the captain-general his numbers each morning, and the Veil-Saints book out for a Turn as they do for a plague year. The South last kept the Line from 703 to 712, and the Archive is still adding it up.
Every Turn ends in a Count, audited at Sealhall and accepted by nobody. The Archive holds the South’s copies, and the most complete register in the Inner World has looked for four centuries for the original of the arrangement without finding it, which it takes as a personal insult. Three clerks of three regions have now carried their three Counts up to the Sounding Walk and sworn to them barefoot. The three figures cannot all be right, and all three men left lovely wet feet, which the Court has asked people to stop bringing up.
Neighbors and Grudges
Sum-gol. The Sea paid the old empire in records and never in soldiers, and it was a Lambert clerk who read the bill at the last Calling. It keeps the Dynasty’s old rolls, and has had a very polite letter about them from the Post.
The Silver Cedars of Yukari. Close by marriage: Senri Yukari took a daughter of House Lambert to wife, and Lord Naiser is half Sallowgate. The Sea arrives at equality through theology and the Yukari lands arrive at it through empiricism. The disagreement is genuine, respectful and permanent, because neither side can refute the other’s reasoning without abandoning its own.
The Kingdom of Kharven. Distant, and doctrinally entangled in a way no trade ledger records, since its crown descends from the people who once held this stone, which makes every exchange an inheritance question wearing a diplomatic coat. Léonard Lambert has a standing grievance with the Palatine that nobody north of the Moto border will read a petition from the Sea, and his cousins at Hallenfeld write that nobody is sitting in the red chair to read one. Later hand: within a generation of this page the north is the Northern Empire of Whitemere, and the Archive’s first response was to rule a new column.
The free cities of Nalūn. Money-keepers to the Sea and its favorite theological scandal, and the feeling is mutual; the chain-cities regard the reconciliation of the two positions as an achievement of ecclesiastical reasoning, with real professional respect.
The Iron Mandate of Undaar-Keth. The Manumission Doctrine and the Mandate’s Ironblood Clause are two different answers to one problem, how to protect a population everyone else considers disposable. The clerics find the Mandate morally inadequate, the commanders find the Sea militarily irrelevant, and each is correct and incomplete.
Sancta Lux. The Sea measures testimony, the order measures everything else, and both hold that a measurement that does not drift is worth more than a judgment that does. Warm and distant, and neither party has left the other alone in a room since the chapter hold was seated.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Hundred Crowns of the Midmarch
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
The Center’s patchwork of petty kings, and the bridge that all the armies have to cross

There have never been a hundred. The Guild survey found eighty-three in 710 and a hundred and seventeen in 712, and in the second count the surveyor was crowned at Pennycrown on his way home.
Note in a Measurewright’s circuit book

King Gerent Tuppence the Third held the whole of his kingdom in nineteen arches of pale stone, from the pier at the south wharf to the pier at the north, and on the morning of the feast of Veyra in the year 662 he had his chair carried out to the crown of the eleventh arch, with the crown on his head and the cash-box on his knees, because two armies had sent word that they intended to cross him. From the south came six thousand Marrick spears in ochre and black. From the north came the host of the Banner Houses, red and gold and painted to the eyebrows, each bound for the far bank. Neither side had a quarrel with Kingsbridge, and each side’s marshal arrived at his own end of the bridge, looked at the toll-board, and asked what a man would have to pay to keep the other one off it.
Gerent sold both of them the bridge. He sold the Marrick marshal the south nine arches and the northern marshal the north nine, with a sealed bill for each and the eleventh reserved to the Crown, and by noon the two armies had met head on in a roadway twelve paces wide, with the king’s chair lifted out onto a mason’s cradle over the water so as not to obstruct the proceedings. Every longship and barge on the Aldwater came to watch. The whole city climbed out along the wharves in its feast-day colors, the bookies went up and down the moored boats on planks, and a Marrick captain named Sella Drax, coated in a yellow you could read by, held the ninth arch alone for the time it took a bell to ring twice, with the dead going over the parapet on both sides of her. His Majesty’s bailiffs fished them out and billed for it, under an old by-law, as refuse in the navigable channel. Two thousand men died on that bridge for the right to be on the other end of it. The eldest of Gerent’s sons, who had gone out with the Standing Army to keep the eleventh arch clear, died there too, on his father’s side of the line, with his crown-prince’s circlet driven through his eyebrow, and the king did not get up from his chair until the fighting was over. Both armies were gone by harvest. He had taken in more that day than his ancestors had in a hundred years, and he rebuilt the eleventh arch with it, and his son’s name is on every stone.
That is the Midmarch. A hundred-odd kings, each sure he is the rightful one, sitting across every road between the North and the South and charging the passing wars by the head. The bill is usually paid in sons. Its people are not much troubled by it and will tell you they have the best songs in the world.
The Land and the Look
The Midmarch is the crowded country along both roads around the Scourge of Hell, thickest on the Kessen road down the west flank and thinner on the salt road up the east, river plain and low green hill, with more castles per mile than anywhere else in the world and nearly all of them small. You can stand on one keep’s roof and count nine others, and every one of them flies something loud: scarlet bulls, blue-and-yellow checks, a gold goose on purple, three fish and a ladder. Herald-painters are a respected class and are paid before the masons. Between the keeps run hedgerows, water meadows and barley, and every lane has a chain across it with someone sitting beside the chain.
North of it are the salt basin and the Banner Houses’ southern marches. South the two roads run on to Sum-gol and the Long Fields. Nobody lives in the middle and nobody goes there. The Aldwater runs down the middle of the crowded western half, broad and brown and full of traffic, and most of the country’s quarrels are about who owns which reach of the river.
There is no capital and nobody wants one. There are three places everyone has heard of.
Kingsbridge
Kingsbridge is the most painted sight in the Center, and its great stormy sky appears to be a local product. The bridge carries the Kessen road long across the Aldwater on huge arches, wide enough for a marching column, and behind it the pale stone quarters stack up the height one on top of another to a vast green-roofed minster, whose copper the rain has turned the color of an old coin. Longships and barges crowd the wharves three deep, and the wharves roar with cranes, fishwives and the men who get paid to shout about both.
A king’s whole kingdom is that bridge. The city on the height and the wharves on the bank belong in law to their own town council and to a bishop, and the Tuppence crown ends at the last stone of each pier, as generations of bailiffs have discovered while chasing people. So the House of Tuppence collects, and it does not govern anything but traffic. Every morning the entire Standing Army, about two hundred men in red with red banners, marches the kingdom from end to end, with a drum, and is home for dinner. The minster is the Scale Minster, a Sancta Lux house, and its bishop hears crown claims from all over the Midmarch and has the busiest court in the country, since Sancta Lux hears legitimacy and the Midmarch produces it by the barrowload. The present king is Gerent’s grandson, also a Tuppence, who is pleasant to everyone and has the tolls in writing.
Tollgarth
Tollgarth is a castle-town shut across the one good pass in the Harl Hills, held for three generations by Tinker Goblin kings, and currently by Queen Tizz Copperwick the Fourth, three foot five in her boots, with one arm of her own and one of her own design. Most Tinker Goblins do not live past forty, the Essence running too hot for the frame, so a Tollgarth reign is short, and the coronation feast is usually paid for by the same bill as the last funeral. Every gate is a contraption. The Self-Minding Portcullis has killed four kings and one horse, the toll is collected by a machine that makes change only when it feels like it, and the whole town smells of burned vitriol and soldering copper. Merchants pay gladly, because the alternative road adds a week, and because watching a wagon go through is free. Her subjects are goblins, humans and a large contingent of people with burn scars who came for the wages.
Pennycrown
Pennycrown is where you go to become a king. It is a town of goldsmiths, heralds and notaries, on the old fair-ground where, as the story goes, the heir to a lost crown bought a replacement for a penny and could not be shown to have done anything wrong. The law of the Midmarch, such as it is, says a crown is lawful if three neighboring crowns attend the coronation, or two and a Measurewright. Shops on Crown Row sell them at every price, from solid gold to a stamped copper ring for one penny, which by long custom is what a landless younger son wears until he has done something about it. The Coat-Turning is held here every tenth summer. It is a three-week fair at which the kings of the Midmarch, in full heraldry, announce whose side they are on for the next decade, and bookies from four quarters take odds on the order. The sides are mostly North and South. It settles nothing, and everyone comes.
Who Rules
Everybody and nobody. A Midmarch crown may hold a county, a valley, a mill, a stretch of towpath or, in one case, a well. Human kings are the most common and the loudest, usually descended from a northern sergeant or a southern marshal’s bastard who stayed. Tinker Goblin kings hold the workshops, the Harl passes and a surprising number of bridges, and their people have a saying that their reigns are shorter and their monarchs more thoroughly felt. The Chimeric-Born hold the Stitch Hills, a kingdom-in-many-pieces founded by people the Accord has no coherent policy on and therefore no way of evicting. King Ambrose Fivefold, who rules there now, has the Binding Scars that hold his body together gilded for court, and three neighbors have tried to get his coronation annulled on the grounds that he was assembled. He has so far won every case and every field. A few Beastkin hold crowns too, by the same right of nobody being able to stop them, and the Charter’s clerks enter them as nemo, rex.
Kings owe one another fealty in chains that cross themselves. A man may be overlord of his overlord in a different county. Sancta Lux’s Ember Magistrates ride circuit hearing who is whose. The Guild Accord reaches in patches: the stretches from the Brine crossing down to the marches of Sum-gol signed the first circle at Kharven-Seat, along with several kings who have since been deposed by others who say they never agreed. Past that line the Articles are a custom a merchant may take or leave, though the market court and the dusty foot are so handy that most towns keep them anyway.
Wealth and Trade
Tolls first and always. Then what travels the Aldwater: wool, barley, Marrowhold’s iron, Nalūn’s salt, and wine going north. Then war itself, the largest local industry, which pays the Midmarch at both ends: victuals sold to the host coming up, plunder bought from it going home, and free companies hired out on the Thresh contracts to anyone with a monster problem. The great herds of the Scourge, the stilts and greywalkers and the things in the dry beds nobody has named, come up into Midmarch barley some years, and a bounty posted on a Midmarch door is cried for ten leagues.
Heraldry is the next trade. Painters, embroiderers, banner-makers, trumpeters, heralds and genealogists do better here than anywhere in the world, and a good pedigree is written to order. The minstrels of the Midmarch sell their songs up and down both roads, get the details wrong, and have done more for some kings than their armies have.
Nearly every crown owes the factor houses of Nalūn, and a third of the country’s wars come from fighting over who inherits the debt.
Rent, Bread and the Street
Rent goes to whoever’s man turned up, and in a contested valley he may turn up twice. A Midmarch peasant keeps a chest of old tax receipts from dead kings against the day one of them is found to have been lawful. Coin is anybody’s, and the money-changer at every crossroads will tell you what a Tollgarth mark or a Pennycrown penny is worth this week, which is how much metal it has in it, and he has a small hammer for finding out.
They eat better than the Charter does, since food is the thing armies pay for: barley bread and river eels, smoked ham from the hill kingdoms, big onions, apple beer. Market days run one town after another so nobody can miss one. Every town has a bracket ground, a sect in a loud shirt and a fierce opinion. The Sixth Arch Boys of Kingsbridge, in red and white, and the Harl Hill Scorchers of Tollgarth, in black and copper, have fought each other at every midsummer for ninety years over a bet about a goose, and when you meet a fighter from the Midmarch they will tell you whose, before they tell you their name.
The street’s word for the aura coat is colors (“he’s showing his colors,” or, of a fighter nearly out of reserve, the Essence a fighter holds to spend, “his colors have run”). Pressure is the crown, and a strong fighter who walks into an inn is said to have put it on. Sensing is the herald, as in “my herald tells me you’re lying about your Stage.” Ordinary petty arts are everywhere and cheap: the woman who can make a chain across a lane too heavy for anyone but her to lift, the boy who knows by the smell which king’s men are coming and sells it, the toll-sitter who cannot be lied to about what is in a cart until his fee has been paid. All of them can be bought, and all of them have been known to change sides by supper.
Greet someone with “Who’s king today?” The answer is a joke unless it is not.
Law and How It Fights
Every crown has its own law, and a farmer who crosses a ditch may cross a jurisdiction. Justice is mostly by toll, fine and the king’s bad mood, and a traveler carries his plea to the nearest market court if he has any sense. A king can hang you in his kingdom, and if his kingdom is small you may be able to see the safe side from the gallows.
War between crowns is a sport with casualties. Levies turn out behind the banners for forty days and go home for harvest. Harness is mixed and much repainted. Spears do most of the work, crossbows do the killing, and a well-placed bolt has ended more Midmarch reigns than any Domain (the ground in which a high-Stage practitioner’s own law holds), at about three copper apiece. Goblin kings bring contraptions that misfire in funny and terrible ways, and everyone stands well back from their own side. Kings who are also practitioners fight each other in person, with their titles shouted out in full first, and a small dispute may be settled in a tourney ring by champions with the whole county looking on. Yielding is allowed. Killing is forbidden, and it still happens.
When a real army comes through, the kings fall over themselves to join it. Then they sell its road to the other side.
What They Joke About
That there are a hundred of them. That any of them is rightful. The Standing Army of Kingsbridge being home for dinner. “Long live whoever” is the loyal toast in about half the county, and in the other half they mean it. A man who has been promised something is said to have a Pennycrown deed. There are several hundred songs about a king whose kingdom is a mill, who went to war with the king downstream by stopping the water, and in all of them he wins in a different way. Northerners, they say, have one king and can’t tell you why, and Southerners used to have one and can’t get over it. They are terrified of the Moss Court and won’t joke about that, since the last Midmarch host to go in as far as Rootgate is now mostly a very good stand of alder.
Monsters on the Roads
The great herds south of the salt, the stilts and greywalkers and the things in the dry beds, come up into Midmarch barley some years, and a bounty on a Midmarch door is cried for ten leagues. A stilt stands on legs as long as a ship’s mast, a greywalker comes after it in a file at dusk, and between them they have ruined more kings than the Coat-Turning. Barley and monsters are the country’s two great local harvests. The beasts are those of any fat, fought-over plain: Greater Wolves follow armies, boar root up the dead, and every king’s geese have been eaten by every other king’s foxes. Manticores (Grade A on the Bestiary’s scale, which runs from E to EX and prices every bounty) have been crowned in at least one valley, by a herald who needed the fee, and its tax receipts still trade.
The dungeon is Nether Marl, the only kingdom in the world that is wholly a dungeon: a labyrinth under a hill with a Minotaur (Grade A) at the Lower Workings, whose title King Hamo the Undefeated bought at Pennycrown along with a stamped copper crown. He has never gone below the Mouth. He sells licenses at the door, charges a toll going in and a much larger one coming out, and has legally been at war with whatever is down there for twenty-six years.
Nether Marl is only the loudest. The Orchard Under Goosegrass at Hollowhay, a Verdantia ground (the Wellspring of growth) whose nine galleries of apple trees stand in leaf and fruit in every month of the year, was won by thirty crossbows and a Sealwright and then lost to its own keepers, a family called Ambrey, over three seasons’ back pay. They let the great gallery for weddings, and it is booked until 719. A crew found a Mouth (a dungeon’s first band and its way down) under a tannery in Pennycrown, and the tanner discovered that he owned a dungeon. By the custom of the Center a clearing venture takes a third of the hours at the pool for nine years, the clearers’ third, and by the law of the dead leg the fine on a lapsed gallery lands on its owner, “whoever that now is,” which is why several kings of this country have turned out to own a catastrophe by marriage. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
Beside the Scourge
Everybody in the Midmarch lives with their back to it. The Scourge of Hell fills the center of the continent, nobody marches through it, every army in history has used the same two roads around it, and the kings of the Midmarch are sitting on both. On the Kessen side the Hem (the Scourge’s outermost belt, fifteen leagues of black-barked thornwood and pale dust) lies east of the last hedges, and on the eastern patches along the salt road it lies to the west. In the late summer of a dry year the wind off it comes hot and smelling of iron, the herds come out on that wind, and that is the week the barley goes. A petty king posts a bounty on his doors, hires a free company, and now and then loses a castle.
Lastpenny, on the Kessen road, is the edge town the whole country claims. At a quarter before noon on Midsummer Day of 676 the biggest earth wyrm anyone living had seen came up through its cheese stalls, in front of eleven thousand northern and southern spears who were waiting for noon to decide whose job it was, while a goblin king the size of a child beat on the northern marshal’s stirrup with a ladle. The town has been rebuilt in stone and has kept the awning. The wyrm still comes up along that stretch every eleven years or so, wearing nine hundred spears, and everyone calls it Old Pincushion. At the Noon Fair each Midsummer the whole town stands in the square and turns its back on any soldiers present, and in the Midmarch a northerner or southerner who declines to help you has said it isn’t noon, and you are entitled to spit. The Turnstone, a black pillar on the western rim off the same road, is where a commander handing over the Turn is supposed to hand his successor a broken spear. He generally sends it by courier.
The Turn itself runs North, then South, then Center, nine years each. Whoever holds it keeps the Line of forts and beacon towers around the Hem, pays the door bounties, answers for every carter lost on the corridors, and may march through anyone’s land to do it. So the host passing through on someone else’s Turn eats Midmarch barley going up, the castles with the wall knocked in are Midmarch castles, and half the invasions in this country’s history began as a Turn that lost its way, which has been shown on maps. The Center holds it now, from 712 to 721. Every king sends nine men and a very loud banner, free companies on Thresh contracts (monster bounties, paid by anyone with a monster problem) do most of the dying, and the betting in Kingsbridge is on who will be standing to hand it over.
Then there are the sword-pullers. Near the middle of the Scourge a colossal bronze-hilted sword stands point-down in the mountains, its blade a window on a violet field of stars, and you can make it out from the Hem on perhaps nine clear days in the year. Every few years a young Midmarch king with a good jaw sets out with a following, bookies alongside and a minstrel on retainer, to walk in and draw it. Half the taverns in the rim towns are called the Ordinary Sword and the other half the Other One, after the picture on the sign, a lone figure on a ridge with a plain blade, looking up. The record belongs to a Tinker Goblin named Nixie Sprocket, who got into the Shambles (the fourth belt in, all dead battlefields) with a mule-drawn engine of her own design and sent back a letter describing the bronze as warm. The bookies have never paid out. Pennycrown does a steady trade in crowns for the walk, and it does not give refunds.
Neighbors and Grudges

The North and the South The customers. The Marrick spears remember the bridge, and so do the Banner Houses, and all of them still use it. The Painted Rivers of Hallenfeld dispute every toll on the upper Aldwater, and the Dynasty of Sum-gol has maps showing the whole country as provinces that have been temporarily mislaid.
The Sealed Charter of the Concord Sells them law at a markup and keeps the worst of the armies off its own roads by leaving them on Midmarch ones. Every king in the country resents this, and most of them send their sons to Sealhall to study it.
The Amber Cities of Nalūn Hold the paper. The kings who pay least cheerfully are the ones with the most tokens, and a Nalūn scribe with a march contract is the most frightening thing a Midmarch army ever meets.
The Central Warlords The Russet Crown takes in the Midmarch’s runaways and sells it russet cloth and information. The Rose Coils remember every pedigree anyone has ever forged and will tell you, for a fee, which one of them is yours. The Avian sects of the Violet Peaks scout for whoever pays, and they find the hedgerows very funny from up there.

Later hand, from the last winter before the turn, running past the year these shelves stand in: when the Northern Empire of Whitemere reached the Aldwater it was sold the south nine arches. The clerk who wrote this note does not record what it did about that.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Inner World — A Gazetteer
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Every realm of the one continent, from the Polar Reach to the Holy Sea: its weather, its ground, its monsters, its people, its towns and its roads

A traveler wants four things from a page: what will fall on me, what will bite me, who will cheat me, and where I can get dinner. This page answers in that order, and it has been wrong about all four in living memory.
Note on the flyleaf of the Guild’s circuit copy, in an archivist’s hand

In the bright week of Year 691, at the Whalebone Gather, a clerk of the Holy Sea made an offer to the fires. The old Palatine, the one before this one, had read that polar ice tastes of nothing at all and wished to be certain, so he would pay two hundred silver for one block of it on his table at Alabaster at midsummer. Everyone laughed except Ikka Sennet, a sled-woman nineteen years old and, by the name she carried, ninety. She cut a block off the shelf the size of a lodge door, wrapped it in reindeer hide and whale fat, whistled up thirty dogs and two cousins, and went south past the last tree with the green aurora on her back. At Thornhaven the raftsmen packed it in red sawdust and priced the melt aloud at every bend. On the Hallen a reeve chained it across the bow and billed it as grain, since the wall had no rate for ice. Ashbury gave it barley straw and a receipt. The weigh-house at Halcrest weighed it twice, a day apart, with the whole terrace betting on the second figure. In the Midmarch the tolls came every mile until she reached Pennycrown, where two kings and a bribed Measurewright attended while she crowned the thing for a penny, and King Block the First crossed the rest of the country as a reigning monarch, untaxed, with a hired trumpeter walking ahead of him.
At Rootgate an orc seven feet tall hung a basket of pears on the sled and asked her to go round. She went round, eleven days along the flank of the Scourge of Hell, and the dry wind out of the haze took a third of His Majesty in one afternoon. On the eighth evening a wyrm with scales the size of shields came up through the black roots to look at the only cold thing in a hundred miles, and it took one cousin and nine dogs, and Ikka drove on with her jaw set and the blood freezing on the block. The olive riders of Sum-gol kept her company past the iron hills, and the Yan lent two tall grays and an elder who recited his titles at the ice all the way across the grass. On midsummer morning she climbed the eleven hundred steps of the Stair of Testimony in her hides, with half of Alabaster roaring on the landings and the sardine smoke going up, holding what was left in her two bare hands. It was the size of a goose egg. The Palatine, nearly fainting with delight, put it in his mouth and pronounced that it tasted of nothing. A Lambert clerk noted that the contract said one block and named no size, paid in full, and fined her for water on the Stair. The Keld sing it still, with the fine as the last verse.
That block went through every weather this continent owns. So will you, and you may as well know what is coming.
The Shape of the Land
The Inner World is one continent, long from north to south and pinched in the middle by the Scourge of Hell, and this page covers all of it and nothing beyond. A reader standing anywhere on it in Year 715, the twenty-fifth of the Dark Ages, with the forty-year war only just stopped, should be able to find his feet from what follows.
The North is a shield of old cold rock, planed flat by ice and dimpled with chain-lakes. At the very top lie the tundra and permafrost of the Polar Reach, past the last tree. Below that Kharven holds the high plateau at the center. West, the Slate Ridge closes the border, with Undaar-Keth beyond it in black basalt and boreal forest. East, the Ironwood March and the Scarlet Wood run out to the Ring, where the rib mountains of Marrowhold stand. South, the land drops into the Greenhollow, and the Painted Rivers carry everything between.
The Center is the Scourge of Hell and whatever can live on its edges. Nobody marches through the middle, so all traffic between North and South goes around by two corridors, the Kessen road on the west flank and the salt road on the east, and those corridors are where the armies go and where the Center’s people live. The Amber Cities of Nalūn lie on the north side, in a dead sea’s salt basin, with Halcrest at the gate where the beds thin against the northern rim. The Hundred Crowns crowd along both roads, with Kingsbridge on the Kessen road. The Sealed Charter sits at the east road’s crossing. The Moonlight Forest lies on the west flank around its great lake, the Violet Peaks climb on the northwest, the Rose Coils lie on the old ruins of the southeast edge, and the Russet Crown holds the east around an inland sea.
The South turns green and drops in long steps to the water. The Long Fields come first, just below the Center. The iron hills and salt pans of Sum-gol lie west at the Kessen road’s end, the Yukari valleys climb into cloud on the east, the Jade Plains open in the middle, and the spring country of the Wellheads steams in the uplands between them. At the bottom stands the white shelf of the Holy Sea, with the Copper Coast warm to its east, where the salt road starts.
Offshore, the Crimson Isles lie south, past the sea.
What the sky does, north to south
The weather on this continent runs in three broad belts, and a Measurewright can explain every one of them with a globe and an orange.

The cold shield. Dry, bitter air off the polar ice sits on the North for half the year. The ground under the Reach stays frozen all the way down, summer scarcely thaws the top hand of it, and water cannot drain, so the summer moss stands in bog. Thirty below is an ordinary night on the plateau. Storms come in off the western shield and break on the Slate Ridge, which is why the Ridge gets the lightning and Kharven gets the clear hard cold behind it. The aurora goes over most clear nights.
The continental interior. The Center is a long way from any sea, so it swings hard: hot, bright summers with towering thunderheads, cold winters with snow in the north of it and iron frost everywhere. The Scourge makes the swing worse. Its bare ground heats fast and sheds a dry wind in every direction, its haze hangs copper and rose on the horizon, and rain that comes near it tends to fall on the mountains and forests around its rim, so the Moonlight Forest drowns while a day’s ride inside the rim nothing has seen a cloud burst in a decade.
The warm south. Below the Center the land falls toward a warm sea, and the sea sets the terms: mild wet winters and long summers, lemons and rice and camellias, with fog on the white shelf, a hard ten-minute rain every afternoon on the Copper Coast, and big autumn gales that come off the water and take roofs. High ground stays cold. Cloud sits on the Yukari valleys all year, and above the shelf the frost hardly breaks.

The two roads and the rivers
The Kessen road comes up out of the low country to the Foot, at the door of the north. Going south from the Greenhollow, it takes the Kessen ford and runs through the Midmarch, over the great bridge at Kingsbridge, down the Scourge’s west flank past the Moonlight Forest, and ends at Sum-gol, and the warded track carries on across the South as its last stretch in all but name, to the foot of the Yukari valleys. The salt road starts at the Salt Quay in Haeseong, runs north as a raised causeway through the paddies and then as a long straight highway through the low country, skirts the Rose Coils at the ford of Bothhands, runs up the Scourge’s east flank across the Sealed Charter, climbs through the salt basin and finishes at the junction below Ashbury, where it meets the Kessen and the Marrow.
The rivers of the North gather on that same junction. The Marrow comes down past Kharven-Seat, the Hallen, the Ruddle and the Sleeve meet at Hallenfeld, and below Ashbury their water comes out as the broad brown Aldwater, the river of the Midmarch, which feeds the Moonlight Forest’s mire through a hundred channels before the rest of it runs on west, off this map.

Monsters, beasts and Cores
Three things want to eat you, and the hunting halls keep them apart. Beasts are animals with an ecology, some of them very large, and they are everywhere: wolves and bears and worse, on every road on the continent. Monsters are the things beyond that, and they move, following prey, Aether and the marching of armies, so a wyvern bred on the Slate Ridge may turn up over Ashbury’s barley in a dry year. A Well-spawn is a creature born inside a Well and masked in its color. The Bestiary grades all of them, from E up to EX, and a lord’s bounty and a hunter’s funeral are both priced off that one letter.
A Core is what common speech calls a site where one of the sixty Wellsprings (the sixty types of Aether) pools. Most lie in dungeons, and some are said to lie out in the open in vast territories nobody has walked. A dungeon is what a Core makes around itself or what grows up around one: caves, drowned stairs, old workings, a ruin the ground has begun to rearrange. The Measurewrights argue about which comes first and have been wrong in writing on both sides. Delvers read a dungeon from the top: the Mouth, the Upper Workings, the Lower Workings, the Deeps and the Heart, each band richer and worse. A worked Core with keepers is a dungeon somebody cleared and now holds, and those keepers can close it. Every realm below has at least one dungeon that people talk about in taverns, and the taverns have usually got the depth wrong.
Monsters live across the whole continent. The Scourge of Hell is where they are extreme.
The North
Later hand, from the last winter before the turn: these lands become the Northern Empire of Whitemere, with Kharven its capital and the Banner Houses holding lands inside it. On the morning this shelf stands, there is no such empire. Kharven is the one true kingdom, the six Banner Houses are lands and never kingdoms, and Marrowhold and Undaar-Keth answer to nobody on this list. On the North’s nine years of the Turn (see the Scourge, below), Kharven and the Banner Houses take their long columns down the Kessen road; the North last held it from 694 to 703.
The Kingdom of Kharven
House Moto · full page: The Kingdom of Kharven
Climate. The cold is the constitution. Winter runs six months at the Seat, the growing season four, and heating eight, and thirty below is a working temperature. Snow comes dry and squeaking, the wind off the plateau finds any gap in a coat, and the first frost that will not lift opens Stack-Count. The hungry end of winter is the Thin Weeks, a date on the calendar. Spring arrives all at once with Ice-out, the morning the river breaks, followed by mud, then a short bright summer of long pale evenings and biting flies. The sky is enormous, storm stacked on storm with orange sunset at the edge, and aurora goes over most clear nights, a slow green river with violet at its hem. In the hour after sunset the snow turns blue.
Habitat. A high granite plateau scarred by ice, with boreal forest of spruce, pine and birch on thin acid soil, moss in the shade, standing water everywhere, and permafrost in patches where the ground lies open. Rye and root crops grow in the sheltered valleys and barely. The Marrow runs under the Seat. The Skeldmere, the great frozen lake, hums in the deep cold over the water beneath it. North of the Seat lies the white, a mere that goes opaque by the second week of frost and never freezes through, because something keeps the water moving down there. In these woods live elk, wolverine, brown bear, lynx and shaggy little horses, and in the rivers char and pike.
Monsters and Cores. Greater Wolves (Grade C) work the Castle Stair in packs and will flank a column in a whiteout. In a bad Thin Weeks a Wendigo (Grade S) may come down off the shelf road, and the clans say it was somebody once, and they will tell you whom. Droval, the Frost-Howlers, stray south of the treeline in the hardest winters. The dungeon everyone talks about is the Hum, a drowned stair going down from the Skeldmere’s north shore under an ice-cutter’s hut, a Well of Abyntheus (a Wellspring of deep naval blue, whose slow throb is felt in the teeth before it is heard). Its spawn wear masks of deep naval blue. It has never been cleared. The Scarlet Scarves and the Wolf Grays each claim to have reached the Lower Workings, and each has the funerals to prove it. The Owing House, the debtors’ prison on the south side of the Seat, stands on a thin Tarturon seep (the Fire of Reckoning, a Wellspring of Fate, hot amber-red to anyone who can see it). No fork will tell you. A debt contracted on those stairs has never once been forgiven, and the turnkeys will not play cards.
Peoples and culture. Two traditions that coexist without merging: the Moto, Japonic in name, seven Great Lines each in its own metal, and the northern clans, Nordic in their pragmatism, who were here first and were steppe-riders once, before the ground froze through. “When the grass comes” still names the spring. Clan names run Norse and northern English (Sigga Tolleifsdottir), Moto names run given name, Line, Moto. They eat bone broth, windmeat (dried hard in the cold air), stonecurd (a dried cheese like a pebble) and the skin (fermented milk in a sealskin, and refusing it can get you killed), with the first bowl going to the one who cannot fill it. They wear wool and hide, and paint their doors ox-blood and ocher to find them in a whiteout. The greeting is a forearm grip and “How’s your stack?” The dead lie first in the unheated death-house, and street and family sit through the Waiting; then the Seat buries and the clans give to the sky. Sōhai (the Moto’s own faith) lives in household labors done correctly, among people who would be astonished to hear they were religious. They value competence, a full woodpile and showing up, and despise wet wood (a liar) and an empty saddle. Never meet a Moto’s eye. The north fights in knots and wedges with great swords, axes and boar-spears, and a bracket fighter (brackets being the public fights, sorted by Stage, the sixteen rungs of a practitioner’s climb) on every lane. The hide is the aura coat, the visible coat of a fighter’s own color. The low sky is Pressure, the weight a stronger soul puts on a room, and smelling a man’s stack is sensing. Festivals: the Midwinter Brackets on the river ice, Stack-Count, Ice-out, and the nameless day in the dead of winter, when no oath holds. They joke about southern coats, anyone with a third pair of boots, and the Tenrai, “the only family that can lose a war for forty years and bill you for it.”
Cities and towns.

Kharven-Seat. A towering dark castle of many spires and verdigris roofs on four hundred feet of rock, with a thousand orange lights in the lower town at its foot, and about the only place in the north where you can buy something you do not need.
The Foot. The door of the north, square gray stone, two towers and a toll-post, where whoever holds it holds the Kessen road.
Harlsey Landing. A river town that turns out in its best at Ice-out to watch the ration scale inspected in public.
The Castle Stair. A long frozen valley with a cadet castle at every bend, each with loud opinions about the one above it, and the hooded stone torch-bearers on the last mile.

Getting there. Up the Kessen road from the Greenhollow to the Foot, then the valley of the Castle Stair. The shore road runs south to the Seat from the Skeldmere. West is the Slate Ridge, and past it the Mandate’s country and the ground the bloodline came from, which nobody holds. East lie the Ironwood March and the Thornwood. South are the Painted Rivers and the Hollow, and past them the two roads around the Scourge. North there is the Reach, and nothing to approach from.
The Cobalt March of Hollenmark
House Stark · full page: The Cobalt March of Hollenmark
Climate. Colder and snowier than the Seat, because the March catches what wet air gets past the plateau. Snow blows through Hollenmark’s streets all year in some fashion, and blue ice grows on the battlements and stays there. Winter is long, still and glittering, with a hard blue sky and pink snow at dawn. Autumn lasts about three weeks and it is glorious, the broadleaf stands going up scarlet and gold against the ice, and then everyone goes back to work. Summer is short, cool and full of mosquitoes.
Habitat. Boreal forest giving way to shield upland: ironwood and black spruce under deep snow, peat and bare gneiss, lichen on everything, and standing water frozen blue. A boundary stone stands on every rise, waist-high and lichen-green. There is timber and fur here and not much else that grows, so the March eats by Ashmore’s allocation. Elk, boar, great brown wolves, and the Dire Icebear, enormous, frost-dusted and never domesticated, who carries a Stark for as long as the Stark is worth carrying.
Monsters and Cores. Wild bears are the first danger and the most respected. Goliaths (Grade A, giantkin who want to be left alone) hold the snow mountain above the city and throw rocks at surveyors. On the eastern line, Stark riders and Marrowkin survey parties both hunt the odd Greater Wolf pack and whatever comes off the Ring’s fume-belt with too many opinions. The dungeon is the Roll-Cellar under Stonewatch, a Fixatio Well (the Wellspring of anchoring) that opened beneath the oldest stone on the line. Starks cleared it three generations ago, going down with surveying chains and entering each dead thing in the Roll by location. It is a worked Core now, with Stark keepers, and practitioners pay by the hour to sit in amber light that makes a stance very hard to shift. The other is the Cold Larder, a day from Bearhold, blue Vohrin galleries (Vohrin being the Wellspring of heat run backward) held by renderers on a Stark lease, where the winter trade cures what cannot be warmed and masks have to be run to the hall in a sack of snow.
Peoples and culture. Northern folk of the old clan stock, Norse and northern English in name (Ulf, Sweyn), in wolf-fur and wool, with the wolf on banners, gate and coin-weights. Food is windmeat, bone broth, smoked fish from the blue lakes and whatever Ashmore sent, with hot barley cakes in the market under the twin towers. They value the line, and a debt said aloud at a boundary, and being told the truth, even by a bear. They despise anyone who moves a stone. The dead go through the Waiting as elsewhere in the north. The Asking is their great rite: a Stark who wants to ride stands unarmed in a shirt at Bearhold while the bears look him over. Children play it in the lanes. A hide is expected to have frost on it, and the house’s own inheritance, the Stark Rime, silvers timber around an angry Stark, and the tavern-keeper starts moving the glassware. They fight with great sword and axe, the heavy walk through the heels, winter war on roads nobody else thinks are open, in knots of men on foot with a few enormously loud bear-riders. Every midwinter for a hundred and twenty years they have sent an empty pie dish to Ashbury. They joke about everything south of them, and being put off your bear is a joke only the person it happened to may start.
Cities and towns.

Hollenmark. A cold blue stone city under a snow mountain, twin towers joined by a high bridge, a pale citadel, and sword-cutlers who criticize your grip before they take your money.
Stonewatch. A hard garrison town with the Roll-house, the old boundary stones in view, and the Thrawn Yard’s training ground and its one-line song.
Bearhold. A high stockade and open ground where the white bears come in autumn to look over the young of the house, with a small graveyard.

Getting there. The eastern road from Threeways. Timber goes down the eastern rivers. The Vessant supply line from the Amber Cities runs through here under a tithe, and a bronze disc with wolf and chain-mark gets you past most gates. East is Marrowhold, past the stones.
The Slate Ridge of Stormfold
House Greymane · full page: The Slate Ridge of Stormfold
Climate. The Ridge makes its own weather, and the locals say it does so out of spite. Thunderheads come in off the western shield and catch on the iron-banded rock most afternoons from thaw to first snow, so violet lightning walks the crest over wet slate that shines like a plum, the rain goes sideways, and a band of clean bright sky opens behind it. The storms pass as fast as they come, every gully runs silver and the heather smells of hot iron. Winter is a wall of driven snow, and in spring the keeper at Galecross ropes himself to his door. The children can tell a storm’s arrival by the taste of the air.
Habitat. One long fold of slate and greystone, wind-hammered, with thin peat, heather, bilberry and dwarf birch below the crest and bare rock above. Stillband iron lies bedded in it. Gray-faced sheep too stubborn to fall off graze the shelves, with ravens and mountain goats, and snow hare in the gullies. Nothing else grows that anyone would call a crop, so grain comes up by levy.
Monsters and Cores. The Ridge has a plague of storm-things. Raiju (Grade A, lightning in the shape of a beast) run the crest in bad afternoons, and a coat of aura up there is regarded as asking for it. Wyverns (Grade S) nest on the western faces and take sheep and sentries. Harpies (Grade B) work the Galecross road. The dungeon is the Ninth Gallery: a Masonwarden’s crew cutting a new gallery through the living slate broke into an older one that nobody had cut, full of blue-white light and Glarewings, Well-spawn with arc-blue lightning trees across their brows. It is a Well of Aurevane (hard-edged electric light). The Greymanes walled it, put a door in the wall, and set a post on the door, and a sentry has stood it for three hundred years, because no one has told him to stop. It has never been cleared. Every Greymane who has been sent inside was sent by title and has been replaced by the next one of that title.
Peoples and culture. Gaunt, long, gray people raised as components of a defensive structure, Norse and northern English by descent and addressed by function: the Shieldwarden, the Gatewarden, the Masonwarden, the Muster Aunt, the Cook. They eat at the mess: mutton, barley, bone broth, rind-water in the Thin Weeks, and hard cheese you could shoe a horse with. They wear gray, with a wolf’s head in darker thread. They value the post and despise leaving it, and you hold your room by holding your place on the wall. The Waiting is kept in shifts in a cold death-house on the crest. Their one festival is an accident, the singing at the Dry Sock in Galecross on nights too bad for the wall, generally the song about the Cook, thirty verses. They fight in the Grey File, shields locked rim to rim, and the ridge sword strikes first from the high guard they call the Roof. Releases (a fighter’s whole power rising into a higher form) are called in earth-words, Stonefast and Setting the Stone. A Greymane child will address the family dog as the Hound and the latrine as the Lower Gate. Everyone else tells the one about the Greymane who sat guard over a pie all night.
Cities and towns.

The Ridgewall. A fortress carved into a sheer mountain face, one arched door at the end of a snowfield and leagues of curtain wall on the crest, with a lightning-mast on every tower and a garrison town in the lee whose whole economy is boots.
Galecross. The great pass town, a knot of slate roofs where the wind comes from four sides, with a famous mess, a smoked-mutton trade and a tavern called the Dry Sock.

Getting there. From the Seat by the ridge road, west, on foot in winter. Galecross is where the road comes up from the Mandate’s country, and the two garrisons know each other’s relief schedules better than their own wives do. Past the wall lies the ground the bloodline came from, which the Greymanes look at every morning and which is nobody’s business. Grain comes by Ashmore clerk each autumn, received with the courtesy due to a siege engine.
The Golden Hollow of Ashbury
House Ashmore · full page: The Golden Hollow of Ashbury
Climate. The one warm valley in a cold country, and cold by anyone else’s measure. Sheltered from the plateau wind and open to the south, it is green from thaw to first frost with a four-month growing season to work in. Winters bring deep soft snow and fog on the water-meadows, summers bring warm rain, thunder at harvest and evenings the color of honey. Late summer is when northerners come down the road and find themselves crying at a hedge.
Habitat. Forested river valleys and deep dark soil, the only ground in the old kingdom where farming comes first: barley and rye to the tree-line, oats, pears, plums, onions, red cattle in the water-meadows, alders along bright rivers, golden birch and beech on the slopes. Eels and herons in the ditches, and mice in quantities that have shaped the region’s history. Tithe barns stand over the wheat in every parish like cathedrals to a religion of bread.
Monsters and Cores. The Hollow is the softest ground in the North, so everything hungry eventually comes to it. Reaching Briars (Grade B, Well-spawn hedges with a green knot over the root-crown) creep out of the woods and are burned by the parish. Greater Wolves come down in the Thin Weeks, and in a dry year a wyvern from the Ridge will take a red cow in front of the whole village. South of the valley the barns have arrow-slits, for what walks up from the Thresh as well as for armies. The dungeon is the Malt Deeps under Barleyford, old malting caves that went down too far and turned out to be a Verdantia Well (the Wellspring of growth). Hired Thornwall axes cleared them in the 540s at a cost Ashmore still disputes. It is a worked Core now, kept by brewers on an Ashmore license, its hours sold to bracket schools, and the air down there will sprout a dropped crust while you watch. Lazar Green, the old plague field above Barleyford, is Contrition ground (the Broken Flame, a Spirit Wellspring, dull red with a sting). No beast minds it and nothing on it grows strangely, and a man who sits on its wall for an hour gets up having decided to write to his brother. The parish pays a warden to keep the wagons moving.
Peoples and culture. Northern commons, English and Norse in name (Edric, Perkin, Wat), plump by northern standards and reminded of it. They eat fresh bread every day, pease pottage, barley cakes with butter, dark rye, smoked eel and plum brandy in a good year. They wear russet and yellow wool and carry a clean onion in the pocket. Many households perform all fourteen Sōhai labors correctly, in order, and would be insulted to hear they were doing anything other than keeping a house. They value the tally-stick and a promise on the junction stone, and despise waste and being asked “which sack?” Harvest Home runs a week: dancing in empty barns, sheaf-tossing, cloth-of-gold scarecrows on poles, and Stage brackets on the stubble under the moon, where it is bad luck to win on the first night. Peasants fight with billhooks and grievance, and the Ashmore Line comes on as a long ragged charge of lords’ sons on big southern horses, very pretty. Everything else is arranged by not sending someone their grain. They joke about thin people, the rest of the north, and Perkin Oatley, always.
Cities and towns.

Ashbury. The seat, a fat town of honey stone and gold thatch with tiered verdigris roofs on its great halls, the Corn Hall where the allocation is read, and the black junction stone below it, which holds one oath at a time.
Sheafton. The barn town of the upper Hollow, with the rebuilt Great Tithe Barn, a regulation about tallow, and a Harvest Fair that draws fighters for the food.
Barleyford. A malting town on a shallow crossing, smelling of sweet smoke, with one famous roof slate in the church wall and the best small beer north of the Center.

Getting there. The junction below Ashbury is where the Kessen, the Marrow and the salt road meet, and nearly everything on this continent passes it sooner or later. North by the Marrow road to the Seat, through the last of the spruce. South the North stops and the marching country begins: the salt road to Halcrest, the Kessen ford and the road to the Midmarch.
The Scarlet Wood of Thornhaven
House Thornwall · full page: The Scarlet Wood of Thornhaven
Climate. Cold, snowy and sheltered, with less wind than the plateau because the trees take it. Snow lies bright as linen for six months, and under the canopy it hardly thaws until the rivers are already running. Thaw to midsummer is the great season, loud with raft-horns and ice going out, and mist hangs in the stands most mornings. Summer is green, damp and gold-barred. Autumn fills the air with scarlet leaves that blow across everything.
Habitat. Hills of giant ironwood, red-barked, the color of a fox at the crown and old dried blood at the root, wider than a house and two hundred feet to the first branch. The dense stands are too dark for anything but moss and bear. Bright towns sit in the clearings along the rivers, with barley in small fields and birch for sap. Furs, pitch, tar, resin and charcoal come out of it, and the rivers run thick with log rafts. Bear, marten, boar and red deer, and beetles that a hedge-worker must talk out of a stand.
Monsters and Cores. Sasquatch (Grade C) move through the deep stands masking their scent, and most foresters leave them food. Dryads (Grade C) guard the oldest groves and have started two wars with the axe crews. Reaching Briars take the edges of the stump fields. Hedge-workers refuse to work on the far side of a long cut (a narrow straight ride through the deep stands) after dark and give no reason, and I set that down without comment. Crews call the Long Cuts a lying-down, a dungeon with no roof, and have offered to walk one end to end, and the foresters have been very civil about refusing. The dungeon anyone will admit to is the Red Stair: a ruined carved archway older than the house, at the head of worn steps, with long strings of faded cloth flags running off between the trees. The loggers’ tally flags are tied there, one for each great tree taken. The steps go down among the roots into a Well nobody has reached the bottom of, and a raft-boss who has been down to the second landing drinks free in Raftwick.
Peoples and culture. Northern commons, Norse and English in name (Aud Rannsdottir), with a lady from the Shiraki hills at their head. They carve everything, in knots of beasts and leaves painted red and ocher and verdigris blue, and a child gets a knife before shoes. Food is smoked river fish, venison and bear in dark gravy, birch-sap beer in spring and flat barley bread bought dear; every raft has a pot that has not been washed since the raft was built. Raftsmen wear red caps and sing dirty songs in rounds, charcoal burners are the Black Hands, house soldiers wear gray felt and iron caps. They value a contract cut in wood with two guild-marks, and despise people who think a forest is scenery. Raftsmen’s brackets are fought on moving logs in spiked boots. They fight with the Thornwall hedge, long ash-and-iron spears at a walk to a slow drum, and woodsmen with axes and short bows behind things eight feet thick. Technique names are named for the job. A Thornwall will price the damage aloud while it is happening, and “six months” is their punchline.
Cities and towns.

Thornhaven. Carved red halls where the Thornwood meets the water, the Raftmen’s Hall with a famous boot on a shelf, the cargo-roll house, and the best fire-enamel in the north.
Raftwick. The great raft-town at the head of the river-drives, half of it afloat, which shifts its streets every spring and has no reliable map.

Getting there. By raft in the thaw, down to the Hallenfeld junction and beyond, with a toll fought over every spring. House Thornwall holds the corridor, the road and river-chain east to Collarbone in Marrowhold, timber one way and worked metal the other. North past the last spruce is the Aurora Reach. Starks next door, in the habit of checking the stones.
The Aurora Reach of the Keld
House Keld · full page: The Aurora Reach of the Keld
Climate. Polar. Past the treeline the winter is a months-long dark at the top of the Reach, dry and windless until it is not, and then a whiteout comes across the plates and a person cannot see his own hand. Cold takes the unready, and the Keld have a name for it, Qatuq. The sun comes back to one bright week of sled-races, and summer is a brief endless day, moss going green and scarlet, more birds than you would believe, the top hand of soil thawing into bog over ice that never melts. The aurora hangs from one side of the world to the other in green and violet, with a pale moon in it looking cold.
Habitat. Tundra and permafrost to the polar shelf. The snow is white, blue and pale gold by the hour, cracked into enormous plates by frost heave, and rose mountains stand along the horizon. No trees except the snow-bent firs around the palace, curling like breaking waves, alive for no reason any forester can give. Moss, lichen and dwarf willow. Reindeer in rivers, the great horned musk-beasts that come down off the high ice in the Thin Weeks, white fox, wild white bears, seal, walrus and whale on the shelf. Clearbeam beryl comes from the pegmatite dikes on the margin, some crystals longer than a man.
Monsters and Cores. Droval, the Frost-Howlers or Rimegaunts, are the Reach’s own terror, spirit-touched hunters of the snowfields that lie along a ridge until the ridge is suddenly not there. Wild bears come next, and packs of what the Mandate’s northern wall calls an interesting category. The dungeon is the palace, which the Keld call the Kiilut House, a kiilut being one of the dead left without the Waiting: white and ice-blue, spiral towers and blue-glass domes, a covered bridge to a far tower, old work no one living built. It may hold Living Armor (Grade A) and worse. No one has cleared it, since no one can agree how many sides its third dome has. Measurewright Ansell spent one night inside in 694 and came out by the far tower with his beard at his belt. Crews who cross the covered bridge are not on any roll afterward, and his is the only name ever to come back across it. The Keld call a dungeon a house nobody sat with. They camp beneath this one, trade beneath it, race around it, and will not sleep inside.
Peoples and culture.
