Vaeloris. A warm stone-built basin, the proving-house for new ward-work.
Reedgate. A station on the Long Water in the Lake Districts, famous for a pike.
The Thornback Ridge. A forward post at the end of the perimeter, on the northern frontier.

Getting there. The warded track from Sum-gol, the Kessen road’s last stretch in all but name, with a way-station every twenty to twenty-five leagues, three weeks by wagon, to the foot of the valleys. The Corridor runs north beside the salt road toward the Nalūn basin. Wards touch whoever comes up the southern road long before the gate has seen him.
The Holy Sea of Alabaster
House Lambert and the Court · full page: The Holy Sea of Alabaster
Climate. Warm-temperate coast. Long dry bright summers with a sea breeze every noon, mild wet winters, autumn gales that come off the water, and huge clouds piling gray-blue and rose over a ring of misty mountains. Fog sits on the shelf at dawn. Inland and up, it gets colder fast, and at the top of the land marches the frost hardly breaks.
Habitat. White cliffs the color of milk dropping into water so clear the fishing boats seem to hang in the air, and drowned country on either flank of the bay where on a still morning sponge divers can show you the tops of walls. Behind the shelf, lemon terraces, goat hill, olives and thin chalky barley climb into the land marches and north to the edge of the Grey Plain. Sardines, sponges, gulls, sallow willows in the ditches. It is poor in grain and rich in everything that can be written down. Marrowchalk barges (bone-rock that doubles a wheat yield and also raises the dead) come through its lawyers.
Monsters and Cores. Zombies (Grade D) get up in fields dressed too heavily with Marrowchalk, and the parish has a form for it. Sirens (Grade B) work the rocks off the point, and two men hold the Lone Clerk’s lamp and watch each other. Sea Serpents (Grade S) are a bad year’s news. The ground under the shelf is the great working site, which the Court calls Attestis, a word on no Guild list, and which Measurewrights read most respectably as Thaloré, the Wellspring of Depth. It is why a true oath wets the stone. The dungeon is the Drowned Parishes, the sunken low land on both sides of the bay since the blow of about 310 IC. The church bells are still in their towers. Mourning Pike (Grade A) hold the naves, the souls of tens of thousands died mid-oath on that ground, and the Veil-Saints will tell you why they charge what they do. Nobody has cleared a single parish, though the Archive still holds the deeds. Penitents’ Square, at the foot of the Stair of Testimony, is Penanceflare ground (the Light of Contrition, a Spirit Wellspring, whose hue runs the whole spectrum with the heat of what is said). Nothing burns there. A speaker who tells the whole of it feels it come up through the chest, and the crowd knows from the way she stands, and the Veil-Saints have a posted rate for hearing it first.
Peoples and culture. The most mixed crowd on the continent, because the ground will not distinguish one race’s oath from another’s: Serpentkin scribes, Catkin sailors, Tinker Goblins and Eressean pilgrims on one landing. Court Latin is the working tongue and French-sounding names are the fashion (Aurélien Cassard, Léonard Lambert), and every lord who comes before the Court gets a Latin name he did not ask for. They eat sardines off a skewer, goat cheese with lemon salt, chickpea cakes, barley soup with fish heads, and almond paste molded into a balance on feast days, eaten from the pan that holds the lies. White and ink-black are the Court’s colors, and a black balance on a white door means someone inside can ask your name. Faith is the Church of the Holy Sea, its saints and its Archive. Veil-Saints perform Sacraments over the dying so that the soul crosses whole, and you can hire one by the night. They value the sworn account and the true count and despise a dry foot; to be dry-footed is to be a liar. The Manumission Doctrine protects the counted, and only the counted. Festivals: the Feast of Saint Ebb with pennons and frying sardines, and bracket days between the Whites of the Upper Stair and the Inks of the Laundry Steps. Small drilled levies paid on the day, crossbow companies on the Stair, Hammerford spears hired and audited, and paper for the larger wars: excommunication from the registers. Dockers say the shine and the weight. They tell the one about the Palatine turned back at the gate of the next world for a discrepancy.
Cities and towns.

Alabaster. Sixty thousand on eleven hundred steps, pale walls and red roofs stacked from a blue bay, the Sounding Walk, the Bridge of Notaries, the Archive cut into the shelf, and the Lone Clerk on its rock.
Rimward. The harbor on the bay’s western arm, sail lofts, slave-blocks and sponge boats, a loud salt town that thinks the upper city is a pack of hypocrites and supplies it with fish.
Sallowgate. The fat walled landward gate where the salt road’s western branch comes in, a stone bear over the arch, the South’s most accurate water clock, and Lamberts learning the Sallowgate Answer.

Getting there. By the bay, if you can afford the dues. By the salt road’s western branch to Sallowgate. The Copper Coast lies east along the shore, and Rimward is the only harbor on the southern sea that can hurt it. Inland and up, broken walls, a well and a gatepost mark the old Kōkan seat, where pilgrims are advised not to go, and go anyway (see Where the Maps Quarrel).
The Copper Coast of Haeseong
House Ryu, in the Dynasty · full page: The Copper Coast of Haeseong
Climate. The warmest and wettest on the mainland, subtropical and shining. It rains hard for ten minutes every afternoon and everyone stands in doorways making remarks about it. Summers are sticky and salt-hazed, with autumn typhoons that come up off the warm sea and wreck the outer Moorings, and winters so soft that camellias bloom on the walls. The water goes from sea-green to copper at evening.
Habitat. The Thousand Moorings, a run of inlets, sandbars and pine-topped islets east of the white cliffs, with paddies and salt-ponds behind and old copper workings in the hills staining the creeks green. Rice, sea-silk, mackerel, shrimp, sea-urchin, pearl-beds. Cormorants, herons, otters in the creeks, and a shore that smells of salt, tar, charcoal and frying fish.
Monsters and Cores. Sea Serpents (Grade S) follow the mackerel, and every Ryu fleet has lost hulls off the Sawbacks. Sirens work the outer islets, and everyone on the water has a story and a net-charm. Kraken (Grade EX) are named in old wreck-right and nobody has lately had the nerve to file a claim. The dungeon is the Green Galleries, the old copper workings in the hills behind Geumpo, which broke into a Basilithe Well (the Wellspring of pure pitch and clean crystal, ochre-gold). Tolling Crabs (Grade A) hold the Upper Workings, and a careful delver strikes a tuning bar and rings a crab’s own note back at it until the carapace falls apart. Geumpo’s pilots hold a lease on the Mouth. The Ryu dispute it annually. The Gold Mouth, a sea cave east of Geumpo on Oblation ground (a warm Wellspring of Fate whose law runs on what is given up to it), is unlicensed and very busy: a tide cave that pulls, used by smugglers, with House Ryu claiming wreck-right on anything that washes out, crews included.
Peoples and culture. Korean in register (Ryu Ha-eun, Gim Dol-soe, Deok-sun), harbor people in sea-green and copper silk or tar-stained cotton, thousands of them living on sampans and paying mooring-fee by the lunar month to a harbor-mother who knows who is sleeping with whom. They eat grilled mackerel, rice, cold noodles in broth, salted shrimp with everything, sea-urchin if just paid, and a clear rice liquor visitors take for water exactly once. Each village keeps a shrine to the drowned, with a toll-man who takes his hat off to funerals and charges for them anyway. They value a good letter and despise being shown the wrong set of books. Every evening the lanterns go up on fishing line from mast to mast and roof to roof across the harbor, red, gold and copper-green, as they have since 671, and the city comes out on the mole to eat. Haeseong children set down anywhere in the world cannot sleep in the dark. They fight at sea, with windward, currents and marine crossbows, shooting the rowers first, and they have never fought a land battle they could avoid by raising a price. Bracket schools row out to fight on lashed barges: the Haeseong Green Tide, the Geumpo Gilders and the Bad Weather. Gabot, nureum and nunchi, as at Sum-gol, and nunchi also means knowing when to change the subject. “Held for the Throne” is what a Haeseong man says about whatever he has just put under his coat.
Cities and towns.

Haeseong. Seventy thousand, the largest living city in the South, hundreds of roofs in copper new and old climbing from a stone quay, a dark fortress on a green crag, the white-and-gold palace of the old Dynasty’s governor on the next rise, and the Long Mole with its great lighthouse.
Geumpo. “Gold harbor,” a day east, a smaller, prettier, more dishonest place where things without papers unload, with the better bracket team.
The Moorings. Some hundreds of salt-ponds, fishing villages and customs posts, each with a toll-man.

Getting there. The salt road begins at the Salt Quay and runs north, past Bothhands, across the Sealed Charter, up the Scourge’s east flank and through the salt basin to Ashmore’s junction, with walled toll-forts every thirty miles. By water from anywhere, since everything that comes into the Inner World by sea comes through House Ryu by their own account. Foreign and island ships unload at Geumpo. Ryu barges carry the Dynasty’s salt in from Yeomjeon along the coast.
Offshore
The Crimson Isles of Vorruk-Khal
Hobgoblins of the Crimson Order, no king · full page: The Crimson Isles of Vorruk-Khal
Climate. Warm, maritime and volcanic. Steady trade winds and tropical rain on the windward slopes, a dry lee, and fine warm seas going from ink to jade over the shelves. Ash falls some years, the sky over Gorr-Keth goes smith’s-apron orange and bruised violet when the mountain has a mind, and nobody has ever approved an awning. Deep cold is rare enough that the Isles’ soldiers learned about it from a Greymane winter.
Habitat. Forty-three islands in a rough crescent. Seven High Islands with peaks above 2,000 feet and deep volcanic soil, terraced with taro, breadfruit, volcanic-ash grain and thurr-kep, a root tasting of charcoal mixed with honey. Twenty-two Shelf Islands of forge, quarry and sulfur crust. Fourteen Low Reefs of kelp and fish. Black beaches, yellow vents, green terraces up every caldera wall, sea birds in millions, turtles, reef fish.
Monsters and Cores. Sea Serpents hunt the kelp lines and are entered as fishing disputes. Ash-crabs, shore-walking things with hot shells, come out after an eruption and eat what the ash killed. The Isles’ Essence runs on what Hobgoblin scholars call the arc’s own magmatic source, and the Low Reefs have vent-forges the Marrowkin taught them to build. The dungeon is Skaal-Mol, one of the three forbidden islands where the ground shakes at a frequency that makes Stone-Blood vibrate at the wrong harmonic, and nobody enforces the prohibition because nobody needs to. Tinker crews and foreign delvers land there anyway for the glass, down a lava tube that goes on past any rope, and a Bugbear can tell you from the hair on her scalp that they will not be back. The Moot Vent at Khal-Serrat is the worked one, a Pyreveil site (banked-coal heat) that young hobgoblins of the Order walk down to earn a voice at the moot, its keepers being whoever is left.
Peoples and culture. Hobgoblins of the Crimson Order in scarlet, geometric etchings on the skin, under Vow of Silence below Stage VII, arguing in Silent Sign-Glyphs with a sign-caller speaking for them; Bugbears, seven to eight feet, charcoal-dark, reef families who regard the moot with tolerant disinterest; Tinker Goblins with four guild-seats and no vote on war; Fleshshapers with their coats left open to show the work. Goblin bellows-gangs in the deep yards under Gorr-Keth hold no seat and no hearth. Old Vaross is law and Gorr-Vaross runs at sub-bass. Names are hard Vaross compounds (Vaal-Gorrum, Sahl-Venn). They eat taro, breadfruit and Shelf fish, and strangers are offered thurr-kep so that everyone can watch. A Bugbear taking on a responsibility carries a stone to the nearest summit, and when a known Bugbear dies every Bugbear in earshot stops speaking for a day without meaning to. They value the roll and the Rock and despise a king. Every spring the Speaker recites the standing law and reads the Toll Entry, the old bill against the North. They fight almost never first, with geography and fresh water, then glass-sheathed hulls, the Phalanx of the Soul, The Red Wall Takes One Step, and Bugbears planted on a beach. Ak-gresh is the aura coat. All their jokes are about procedure, and “May your motion carry” is a curse.
Cities and towns.

Khal-Serrat. The moot-isle, a great terraced city of rust-red and black rock, every wall ending in spikes, red banners with nothing on them, and the Rock’s sheer carved cliff above a moot floor under open sky.
Krev-Mol. A dawn fish market under strings of blue-glass floats, and the Fleshshaper quarter, and the Breakwater brackets.
Mokk-Vesh. The great shipyard, volcanic-glass hulls and Tinkers being told to stop helping.
Gorr-Keth. The oldest caldera towns on a mountain that glows at night, with the slag-yards underneath.

Getting there. By ship only, south past the sea, and the shipmasters of Rimward and Haeseong make the crossing for brimstone and glass, paid in weight rather than coin. On the Kharven side of the Greymane wall they sell to nobody, and Mandate loads land on the Vorrak’s Reach coast. Rooms on the Shelf are rented by the season and on moot days every room is let twice.
Where the Maps Quarrel
This page draws the land as the current survey draws it, and on nearly every border the surveyors have stopped arguing. Two questions stay open, because nobody able to settle them has been let near enough to do it.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itthe IN-er WURLD
One long continent, pinched in the middle by the Scourge of Hell: the North on its old cold rock, the Center on the two roads around the wound, and the South going down green to the sea

Go north until the ground stops wanting you and south until the sea does. If anyone offers you the short way through the middle, count your fingers before you shake on it.
Painted on a map-seller’s board at Halcrest

A smuggler called Long Inga Rawe took forty sledges of Nalūn salt out across the ice of Long Scratch, the greatest of the chain-lakes, in the hard winter of 661 IC, to dodge the weighing at Halcrest. She went by night with the northern lights running green and rose overhead, every driver singing to keep the dogs steady, and she had paid a hedge-worker two hams to charm the ice. The charm held for eleven miles. The twelfth mile had no interest in hams. A seam opened from shore to shore, wide enough to swallow a chapel, and twenty-six sledges, nine hundred bars and fifteen men went down into the black water with their lanterns still lit, so that for some while the whole lake glowed from underneath.
Rawe walked ashore with frostbite and a sled-dog under each arm. All that salt melted where it lay, the perch of Long Scratch came up pickled for three winters, and the lakeside villages held the finest fish feast in their history and then took her to law for fouling their water. She paid them off in installments, in salt, legally weighed at Halcrest, until she died.
The Inner World in a breath: the oldest ground there is at one end, soaked in Essence, worth a fortune and trying to kill you on the way to market; a warm green country falling to the sea at the other; and between them a Center that lives on two roads around a wasteland nobody crosses, and gets marched over by both. Bring a sledge and a lawyer. The shelf still files all of it under the Northern Shield, after the rock its first surveyors stood on. That rock accounts for the top third of the map, and the Guild has been meaning to change the label since before the ink dried.
The Lie of the Land
The Inner World is one continent, long from north to south and pinched in the middle by the Scourge of Hell. Read it from the top down.
The top is the Polar Reach, tundra and permafrost past the treeline, which the heralds call the Aurora Reach.
The North is a shield of old cold rock. Kharven holds the high plateau at its center. West, the Ridgewall of the Slate Ridge closes the border, and beyond it lies Undaar-Keth in black basalt and boreal forest. East, the Ironwood March and the Scarlet Wood run out to the Ring, where Marrowhold’s rib mountains stand. South, the land drops into the Greenhollow, and the Painted Rivers carry everything between.
The Center is the Scourge of Hell, which fills the middle of the continent, and whatever can live on its edges. Nobody marches through it, so all traffic between North and South goes around it by two corridors, the Kessen road on the west flank and the salt road on the east. Those two corridors are where the armies go and where the Center’s people live. The Amber Cities of Nalūn lie on the Scourge’s north side, in the dead sea’s salt basin, with Halcrest at the gate where the beds thin against the northern rim. The Hundred Crowns crowd along both roads, with Kingsbridge on the Kessen road. The Sealed Charter sits at the east road’s crossing. The Moonlight Forest lies on the west flank around its great lake, the Violet Peaks climb on the northwest, the Rose Coils on the old ruins of the southeast edge, and the Russet Crown on the east around the inland sea.
The South turns green and drops in long steps to the sea. The Long Fields of the Ochre Fields come first, just below the Center. The iron hills and salt pans of Sum-gol lie west, at the Kessen road’s end, the Yukari valleys climb into cloud on the east, the Jade Plains open in the middle, and the spring country of the Wellheads steams in the uplands between them. At the bottom stands the white shelf of the Holy Sea of Alabaster, with the Copper Coast warm to its east, where the salt road starts.
Offshore, the Crimson Isles lie south, past the sea.
What will eat you. Monsters move, and they live across the whole of this map, with beasts more widespread still, so every realm below has its own bad road and its own song about it. The Scourge of Hell is the one area known for extremely dangerous monsters, and the North, the South and the Center each take a nine-year Turn at keeping them off the other two, which all three resent in writing. Wellspring Cores (sites where one of the sixty kinds of Aether pools) mostly lie in dungeons and are also said to lie in vast territories, and every realm has at least one dungeon people talk about, cleared or not.
For the weather, the roads, the towns and who will cheat you, see the Gazetteer.
The Map of the Inner World
Older copies of this ledger listed six polities on this ground and treated them as settled. A reader holding one should use it to start a fire. Every realm on the continent is listed below by its region, from the top of the map to the bottom.

Two hands on this map. The rocks and the realms stand as this shelf stands them, in Year 715, the twenty-fifth of the Dark Ages, with one exception that a later hand, the one that annotates the Concordance of Ages, has inked over the plate. It is marked below.

The North
The Northern Empire of Whitemere
Later hand: on the morning this shelf was sealed there is no such empire, and the boy who will build it is about sixteen. Muken Moto builds it in the years the minstrels call Arc One, out of the one true kingdom in the North, and I have drawn it in because a reader ought to know what the ground is about to be called. Whitemere is a Moto name, from the white mere under the ridge at Kharven-Seat. The Kharven have never once used it among themselves. They call the empire the Stack, after the woodpile, because everything that arrives from the Seat arrives as an addition to a count somebody has to keep. Kharven is its capital. The six Banner Houses hold lands inside it, each under its own name in the heralds’ style, and every one of them is a land and no kingdom, a point on which they are sensitive.

The Aurora Reach of the Keld · House Keld · no city; the Whalebone Gather. The very top of the map: tundra under a burning sky past the last tree, hide camps and sleds, and a palace nobody living built, which the Keld camp beneath and will not sleep in
The Kingdom of Kharven · House Moto · Kharven-Seat, the Foot. The high plateau at the center of the North, and the one true kingdom: a towering dark castle of many spires and verdigris roofs on a frozen river, seven lines of the oldest blood in the world and one empty red chair. The cold is the constitution
The Slate Ridge of Stormfold · House Greymane · the Ridgewall, Galecross. The western border: a fortress carved straight into a sheer mountain face, violet lightning over slate, and a family who will address you by your function
The Cobalt March of Hollenmark · House Stark · Hollenmark, Stonewatch, Bearhold. The Ironwood March, east toward the Ring: a cold blue city under a snow mountain, boundary stones, and riders on white icebears who can be fired by the icebear
The Scarlet Wood of Thornhaven · House Thornwall · Thornhaven, Raftwick. East of the Seat and on along the head of the March: red-barked giant ironwoods, log rafts, carved and painted halls, and the corridor to Marrowhold
The Painted Rivers of Hallenfeld · House Hallenfeld · Hallenfeld, Threeways, Chainbridge. The valleys between the plateau and the Greenhollow: a pale castle above a triple waterfall that stops every barge, and below it a junction packed with chain bridges and painted toll houses, where the north’s letters get read
The Golden Hollow of Ashbury · House Ashmore · Ashbury, Sheafton, Barleyford. The Greenhollow, where the land drops and the Kessen and the salt road meet: the one warm green valley, gold grain, tithe barns the size of cathedrals, and everyone’s dinner

Beneath the crown. Kharven runs on the six Banner Houses, each holding territory, troops, and the conditional loyalty that is the north’s only currency. They carry northern names because their roots predate the Moto arrival by centuries. The Moto have never replaced the people already holding the ground, which is why the realm fragments the way it does: the houses were never absorbed, only bound, and a binding survives exactly as long as the binder. See The Banner Houses of Kharven.
Beyond the crown
Two realms on the North’s ground answer to nobody on the list above.

The Ember Holds of Marrowhold · the Marrowkin · Breastbone, Collarbone, Twelfth Rib. The Ring, at the east end of the North. They live inside a dead god, forge with what they cut out of it, and sell pieces of it. What died stays disputed
The Iron Mandate of Undaar-Keth · hobgoblins · Undaar-Gorr, Vreth-Kaan, Gorr-Shal, Keth-Vorruk, Tinker’s Gorge. West beyond the Ridge, in black basalt and boreal forest. A decree-state: a military organism with a civilian population attached, rather than the reverse

The Center
Wedged between North and South, and marched through every generation by somebody on the way to somewhere else. Much of it is not human, and the Accord’s Beastkin law and its neighbors’ very existence are its standing fight. Its middle is a wound nobody crosses, so all of it lives along two roads: the Kessen road on the west flank and the salt road on the east.


The Scourge of Hell · no ruler · The middle of the continent. A vast wasteland filled with monsters long ago, with a colossal sword standing in the mountains at its heart. No road crosses it, and the South, the North and the Center each get a resented turn at dealing with what comes out


The Amber Cities of Nalūn · city councils, no crown · Ironlink Hold, Halcrest, Bridgemarch, Vaultmere, Cutwall, Deepvein, Rimward. The Scourge’s north side, in the dead sea’s salt basin. Free salt cities going down into the seabed, who pay both sides and owe neither. Their wealth is what the tunnels are made of


The Sealed Charter of the Concord · the Guild Accord · Sealhall, Waxgate, Verath. The east road’s crossing. A white walled city whose court of judgment sits inside the bones of a dead beast, under green, blue and gold wax seals


The Hundred Crowns of the Midmarch · petty kings, changing sides every decade · Kingsbridge, Tollgarth, Pennycrown. Along both roads, thickest on the Kessen. Little castles with loud heraldry, and a king whose whole kingdom is one bridge


The Central Warlords are less known than either side, and a northerner may not be able to name all four.

The Violet Peaks of Caelspire · Avian Kin, House Caelward · Caelspire, Windstair, Highroost. The northwest. A mountain country of rival sects on rival peaks, and no army has ever taken the high stairs
The Moonlight Forest of Mosk-Vaal · Verdant Orcs, the Moss Court · Mosk-Vaal, Rootgate, Glowwater. The west flank, around its great lake. They bury armies that march through and grow things on them
The Russet Crown of the Unpapered · Catkin, Wolfkin and Bearkin runaways, House Nobody · Brokencollar, Shadowed Ridge, Nightveil Hollow. The east, around the inland sea. A kingdom of runaways seated in the Accord’s own old holding fortress, whose rolls file them under “nobody”, so they took the name
The Rose Coils of Coilspire · Serpentkin, House Scalebond · Coilspire Den, Stoneglass Hollow. The old ruins of the southeast edge. They remember everything anyone has tried to forget, and they treat and poison both armies

The South
Sum-gol was once the empire and dynasty of the whole South, and it broke up. The Yan and the Ryu stayed with the Dynasty; Lambert, Yukari, Corwen and Marrick stand apart. The houses are set out on the Southern Warlords.

The Ochre Fields of Hammerford · House Marrick · Hammerford, Spearmoot, Musterfield. The Long Fields, just below the Center. A great walled city of rose-brown stone, and muster country beyond it, spears in the thousands
The Vermilion Dynasty of Sum-gol · House Mahuo · Sum-gol, Cheolsan, Yeomjeon. The west, at the Kessen road’s end. Gold domes, vermilion banners, iron hills and shining salt pans, and the memory of owning the whole South
The Sapphire Wells of Brightwater · House Corwen · Brightwater, Hotwell, Kingfisher Steps. The uplands of the Wellheads, between the iron hills and the Plains. A white town on rock stacks over a drowned sapphire gorge, and steaming terraced springs in impossible colors behind it
The Jade Plains of Qingyuan · the Yan Hall, in the Dynasty · Qingyuan, Yuquan, Mashi. The middle of the South. A wide green valley floor under vast curved mountains, grass to the horizon beyond it, and tall horses sold to everyone
The Silver Cedars of Yukari · House Yukari · the Cedar Enclave, Karasuyama, Sugidani. The east, climbing into cloud. Green-gold light through huge cedars, crows, and a drowned shrine country on the valley floor. Its outer land is still called the Crow’s Reach
The Holy Sea of Alabaster · House Lambert · Alabaster, Sallowgate, Rimward its harbor. The white shelf, at the very bottom. A pale-walled palace-city stacked up from a blue bay
The Copper Coast of Haeseong · House Ryu, in the Dynasty · Haeseong, Geumpo. East of the shelf, where the salt road starts. Hundreds of copper-red and gold roofs climbing from a stone quay, two citadels above them, and lantern-hung boats

Offshore

The Crimson Isles of Vorruk-Khal · hobgoblins of the Crimson Order, no king · Khal-Serrat, the moot-isle. South, past the sea: volcanic islands, a terraced fortress-city of rust-red and black rock with spikes on every wall, red banners, and a war-moot under open sky

What Ties It Together

The economic spine. Nalūn’s credit finances the Marrowkin’s cutting and Marrowhold’s metal backs Nalūn’s credit; the cedars’ wards watch the eastern corridors both depend on; and Kharven and Undaar-Keth hold the two ends of a cold peace across the Greymane ridgeline.
Sever any one of those relationships and the frontier’s carrying trade collapses, and all of them know it.

What the old shelves called it
A reader will meet these names on older pages, and they still turn up in the mouths of old men.

Nalūn is no longer a kingdom. Its cities are free, and the name now means the salt country.
Ketsuen has folded into the Silver Cedars of Yukari, and “the Crow’s Reach” survives as a name for that land.
Stannvaard is gone. The Ring is Marrowhold now, and its rim mountains are the ribs.
Anguz is dead mines, a place and no longer a power, out past the northern roads. Dustquartz still comes up from it by the sack, and the guilds that once priced Aethersteel and Bloodsilver on the coil went down with the workings.
The Dawi of the northern holds are replaced on this shelf by the Marrowkin.
Thornwall’s corridor now runs to Marrowhold.
Malō of Sātūlagi has no quarter on this shield or any other, having been struck from the rolls; the Moto hold one seat and it is Kharven.

The Ledger of the Shield

The oldest exposed rock in the Material World, and it looks it. Superb bearing stock, high ambient Essence, and not one road you would call finished.

This is the Guild’s old materials ledger, and it covers the rock under the North. The Center and the South keep their ground on their own pages.
Formation
Beneath the soil, where there is soil, lies a continuous basement of gneiss and granite that was already ancient when the western mountains were first raised. It has been planed flat by successive ice, scoured down to bare rock across enormous stretches, and left dimpled with chain-lakes lying in the scratch-marks the ice left behind.
Two features break the monotony and both of them matter.

The Ring. A circular structure some ninety leagues across whose rim mountains are the only relief on the eastern shield, out where the North runs out. The Measurewrights hold, on the evidence of shocked quartz and an inverted rock sequence at the rim, that this is an impact scar and not a volcanic caldera, and that the sheet of melted rock beneath the basin floor is where the northern quarter’s richest sulfide ore was concentrated as it cooled.
The Marrowkin, who live there, do not dispute the quartz. They add that the rim mountains are the color of old ivory and curve in a line a butcher would recognize, that they are ribs, and that what struck the ground that day was already dead when it landed. The Guild keeps three accounts of what the body was, none of them agreeing with the Marrowkin or with each other. The Yukari record, kept by people whose carvers once minded wards all over the shield, adds that the passages (the thin places in the Veil) of that country occur only within the ring, and invites the reader to draw the obvious conclusion about what a strike of that magnitude does to the local thinness of the Veil.
This ledger records the correlation and declines to assert the cause.

The northern shield Basin on the southeastern margin, a sealed evaporite trough where an ancient sea dried out under salt beds two hundred fathoms thick. This is where the North gives out and the Center begins, and the Amber Cities of Nalūn are cut into that salt. Its wealth is what the tunnels are made of.
The Ground Itself
Bare rock the color of old pewter, moss as green as a bottle, and standing water that throws back the whole sky in the interior. Boreal forest across the southern third, dense, resinous, broad-leafed, going up in scarlet and gold every autumn and growing back hard over the stump fields the frontier left. The roads are new and mostly bad.
Settlements arrive as clusters of raw timber with sap still weeping from the wall boards, ringed by fifty yards of cut stumps, with crude three-layer ward work on the gate posts that any journeyman Engraver can maintain and no journeyman Engraver is proud of. They have a bracket ring before they have a chapel, two rival sects recruiting at opposite ends of the same tavern, and a herald who comes through once a month and is believed about half the time.
Ambient Wellspring saturation across the shield runs high and steady, which visitors feel as a low pressure behind the eyes within a day of arriving. A scholar calls this rich ground and the street calls it fat, and a practitioner standing on it pulls Aether straight out of the rock and refills faster than almost anywhere else in the world. It is the reason the northern quarter can afford to run its arrays (banks of glyphs cut by hand into stone and metal to hold a working steady) at all on a frontier tax base.
Bearing Stock
Shieldgneiss · T2 · Stone · Basement outcrop across the whole quarter
Banded, coarse, brutally hard, and effectively without Holding. Inert to nine Wellsprings in ten. This is the reason a Measurewright array laid on the northern shield stays exactly where it was put for a century, and why the Accord sites its most sensitive grid-work here rather than anywhere more convenient. Bearing exceptional, Holding negligible. Resonance: Petralon, weakly. Domain Material Science.
Greystone · T2 · Stone · Quarrylands of the western marches
The standard fortification stone of half the realms on this map. Minimally resistive to magic, entirely adequate against everything else. Bearing good, Holding poor.
Stillband Ore · T2 · Metal ore · Bedded across the western shield
Banded iron, magnetite alternating with gray chert in finger-width layers. Smelts to sound structural iron. The chert bands scatter Essence badly, so anything made from unrefined Stillband takes an inscription and then loses it over a season. Cheap, abundant, and the backbone of every bridge and gate in the quarter. Bearing good, Holding poor.
Sunkwood · T3 · Wood · Recovered from the beds of the chain-lakes
Oak and black spruce drowned when the ice dammed the northern drainage, buried in anoxic mud, and lifted out after two thousand years black to the heart and dense enough to sink. Takes an edge tool badly and a polish beautifully. Essence-quiet, which makes it the preferred bench and bracket stock in workshops where a stray resonance would spoil the piece being made. Bearing very good, Holding negligible.
Holding Stock

Chainsalt · T2 · Mineral · the northern shield Basin, bedded halite
The most important dull material in the four quarters. Bedded rocksalt of exceptional purity acts as an Essence dielectric: it will not conduct, will not retain, and will not degrade under sustained potential. Every gasket, every isolation collar, and every separator plate in a serious glyph array is cut from northern shield salt, because nothing else in the ledger refuses Essence so completely and so cheaply.
It also happens to preserve food. The northern oath-bound trade houses have never needed to lie about the value of what they sell.
Bearing poor, Holding deliberately nil. Resonance: Fixatio. Domain Material Science. Fails in standing water, which is why the chain-cities are obsessive about their drainage in a way outsiders find comic until the first collapse.

Blackcap Sulfide · T3 · Metal ore · Melt sheet beneath the Ring
Massive nickel and copper sulfide with a platinoid fraction, concentrated where the impact melt cooled and settled. Alloyed into iron it produces a metal that keeps its temper inside a forge-array’s working field, where ordinary steel goes soft and stupid. Every crucible tong, array clamp, and furnace door hinge worth owning is Blackcap alloy. Bearing very good, Holding moderate. Resonance: Manganthra. Domain Material Science. Roasting it releases a sulfur fume that has killed the vegetation for six leagues downwind of the Ring smelters and shows no sign of stopping.
Clearbeam Beryl · T4 · Crystal · Pegmatite dikes on the northern margin
Optically flawless beryl in crystals occasionally longer than a man. Ground into lenses it passes Essence-light without the scatter that quartz introduces, which makes it the only acceptable stock for holding coils, assay glasses, and long-range Aetheric instruments. The Skyglass Archive is glazed with it. Bearing brittle, Holding high and clean. Resonance: Luminalis, Mirithane. Domain Electromagnetism.
Ghoststeel · T3 · Metal · Recovered from Spirit War ruins across the shield
Salvaged, never mined, off the dead battlefields of the Great Spirit War, where it lies among things better left alone, and people have killed each other for a good piece of it. Partial phasing quality, reflects spiritlight, and nobody has yet reproduced it in a crucible. The Measurewrights record it here on the argument that the ruins it comes from are all sited on the shield and the shield is therefore its provenance. This is contested and should be read as provisional.
The Works
Northern work is extractive, young and short of coin. The ore is superb and the way to move it is a muddy cart track through second-growth forest.
Smelting happens at the Ring because that is where the sulfide is, and the Ring smelters run on forge-arrays that pull directly from the ambient saturation, which is the one genuine advantage the quarter has over anywhere else. A Ring furnace costs a fraction of what the same furnace costs in the west, because in the west you must pay a Core keeper for your hours and here it is simply in the air.
Everything else about northern working is worse. The shafts are shallow, the shield being so hard that sinking is slow and fire-setting is the only practical method: you build a bonfire against the rock face, quench it with cold water, and pick out what cracks. Haulage roads freeze and thaw and destroy themselves annually. Skilled Engravers are scarce enough that ward maintenance on frontier settlements is done by traveling men paid in meals, which is precisely as reliable as it sounds.
The salt basin is the exception and operates on a wholly different logic. Salt cutting requires no smelting, no array heat, and almost no capital. It requires only the tunnels, which the cutting itself produces, and the oaths, which the northern oath-houses enforce with a thoroughness that has become the quarter’s chief cultural export.
What It Costs

Frontier ward failure is the ordinary northern death. A moisture barrier thins past coherence in a well-stone, nobody reads it because nobody in the settlement can read it, and the water goes bad before anyone connects the two.
Ring smelter fume is the second. The ice is the third, which is not magical at all and which kills more men annually than the first two combined.

Trade Posture
Exports raw sulfide matte, structural iron, timber, salt, and beryl blanks. Imports finished cloth, worked tools, and Engravers. Chronically indebted to Old World money-lenders against ore it has not yet dug.
The Accord’s Logistics Division regards the northern quarter as the single greatest untapped bearing-stock reserve in the Material World and has said so, in writing, in language that has made the oath-houses extremely careful about who they let sign anything.

Art: Gooey Cube LLC.
The Iron Mandate of Undaar-Keth — The Closed Fist
Say itoon-DAHR-KETH
The Closed Fist · The Decree-State · Western Shield
One stroke of a chisel is the most faithfully obeyed mistake the northern shield has ever made. In the midwinter of 634 IC an apprentice to the Stone-Carver Hesh-Kaal, cutting the season’s muster on the Decree Stone before the whole plaza, let his hand slip on a single vowel, and the order that every reserve company of the capital district shall report to the wall came out in Old Vaross as shall report to the wolf. The Stone at any moment holds exactly and only the law that applies, so by the next morning’s Reading it was the law. Nine hundred soldiers of the Undaar-Gorr reserve in red-lacquered harness, banners up and drums going, their breath smoking in a pink dawn, marched across three frozen rivers into the forest and reported.
A pack of nine gray wolves, unused to this, took the forward rank of the Third Company and one sergeant’s throat before the line could be dressed. After that the companies stood at attention in the snow while their commanders cut boards of inquiry as to which wolf. A superseding decree needs the Ironfold’s assessment and a public re-carving, and it took nine days, in which the reserve drew rations, posted sentries around the pack it now surrounded, and entered a she-wolf on the Third Company’s roll as officer commanding. Forty men lost fingers or feet to the cold. Hesh-Kaal laid down his chisel; the apprentice was assessed, found to have the best hand of his year, and made to carve the correction himself. The she-wolf drew a soldier’s ration until she died, because nobody could find the decree that stopped it, and every child in the Ashenmoor can give you her name and rank, which were Shaarn and kaan (an officer).
Picture a fortress that grew a country, where the law is whatever is cut in one black stone this morning and nobody has ever told it no. The Mandate would like it noted that it has never lost a border war.
Overview
A hobgoblin decree-state run by a military order, the Ironfold, occupying the western reaches of the northern shield beyond the Slate Ridge, and the oldest enemy the North has. Its banner is iron-red cloth with a black basalt fist on it, closed, knuckles forward. Every goblin who ever worked a bench knows that banner before they know their own mother’s face. The goblins at those benches call the Mandate the Empire in the North when no hobgoblin is in earshot, and the Imperium when one is and they want him to smile, and the Ironfold, which has no sense of humor on the subject, has never decreed against either.

It is the answer that the other answer refused to give.

When the Scattering broke the goblinoid peoples out of the Old World, the Crimson Order sailed south and built a war-moot on volcanic rock. They opened their palm. They asked what rule looked like when force was set down at the door, and have spent their centuries refining the answer. The Crimson Isles of Vorruk-Khal are that answer.
Undaar-Keth is the other answer. It was given by the hobgoblins who did not sail, who stayed on the land, dug into the western shield’s boreal forest and granite ridgelines, and held ground against human settlers, Ironblood raiding, Marrowkin indifference, and the specific hostility of a frontier that did not want them and that they refused to leave.

The founding doctrine is one sentence carved into the basalt of the Decree Stone:
“The hand opens when the border is safe, and the border is not safe.”
The sentence has been there for six hundred years. The border has not been safe for any of them.

The Ironfold Council does not debate policy. It receives the watch-reports, assesses threats, issues decrees, and enforces them. The efficiency of this system is its strength. The rigidity is its weakness. The Mandate has never lost a border war. It has also never produced a body of law that a farmer would describe as humane, and the Isles’ moot-historians consider this a related phenomenon.
The name · Old Vaross, and argued over. The Mandate’s own heralds take Undaar from undaal, platform, elevation, the throne that sits above, and Keth as the open palm, the universal goblinoid gesture of peaceful intent (keth-ur), carried here as clan-signifier and bitter irony, the open palm offered by a state that rules through closed fist. The grammarians read undaar as the standing thing, that which does not fall, and keth as a seal, which makes the whole name a seal of the standing kind, since in Vaross the second element of a compound governs. Nobody on Decree Street minds which.

The Mandate is named for the peace it intends and has never been permitted to practice.

Roughly fifty-five thousand souls on the Grain Roll, predominantly hobgoblin, with significant Bugbear, Ironblood Orc and Tinker Goblin populations, and a good many more off the Roll, of which more below.

The Isles ask. We answer. The difference is that we do not wait for the question to finish.
Ironfold Commander Vreth-Kaan, address to the border garrisons, Year 702 IC

Geography and the Western Shield
Black basalt and boreal forest. River valleys, low granite ridgelines separating drainage basins, and the specific quality of terrain that military surveyors call defensible and everyone else calls miserable. The forest is resinous and dark green, the canopy thick enough to block sky in midsummer, the undergrowth dense enough to swallow a formation within fifty paces of the treeline, and in the short autumn the whole of it goes up in rust and copper like a banner nobody ordered. Black pines run down to the roads, and on the far side of nearly every road stands a watchtower of basalt blocks on a ridge of gray granite, squat and square and ugly as a fist, with the iron-red cloth snapping on top. Against all this the crimson ranks march in lines you can see from the next valley, which is the idea.
The ridgelines run north to south, creating natural defensive corridors the Mandate has fortified with a thoroughness that visiting envoys describe as excessive and that the Mandate’s own commanders describe as adequate.
Winters are longer, colder and more brutal than at Marrowhold or the Kharven uplands. The population has adapted the way all northern populations adapt: by developing a tolerance for cold that outsiders find alarming and an attitude toward comfort that outsiders find depressing. The tolerance has a hard floor, and the floor is in the blood: see The Ironwall, below.
The Ashenmoor interior is the picture the Mandate does not hang in its offices: steep-roofed timber towns on stilts along braided rivers under a snow mountain, smoke going straight up, long bridges railed with tusks bigger than a cart, goblinoids round a campfire arguing about the fish, and some mornings a giant Bugbear wading the shallows with a net over her shoulder. Far overhead, more often than the watch-reports care for, there is a dragon.
The capital
Undaar-Gorr stands at the confluence of three rivers on a basalt plateau chosen for its defensive geometry and its stone.

Basalt is the goblinoid’s native substrate. The Crimson Order’s asteroidal inheritance (the mineral of the First Impact, carried in the blood) responds to dense igneous rock as nothing else: the ground that feels correct, the stone that holds weight the way weight was meant to be held.

Dark, heavy, angular, with walls thick enough to absorb siege-engine impact and streets laid out in a grid that moves soldiers, grain and spears from any quarter to any gate at a dead run. Under the plateau are the dry Undaar deeps, cut vaults kept bone dry on purpose, where a fluid-worker (a Phreatis adept, who cannot act without a medium) finds nothing to work with and is shown the way out.

The grid is doctrine.
A city whose streets are laid for the rapid march is a city that has decided, at the level of its foundation stones, that defense is the architecture of rule itself.

The Decree Stone
A basalt monolith as tall as a keep, in the central plaza, carved in Old Vaross with six centuries of active law. High on its face runs the one founding sentence in cuts longer than a man, legible from the far bank of all three rivers. Below that, at the height a scaffold can comfortably reach, is the working face, twelve feet by eight, where the law actually lives.

It is a legal instrument, and anyone who calls it a monument gets corrected.

Every decree currently in force is carved into the working face, and every superseded decree is chiseled off and the surface re-carved, so that the Stone at any moment contains exactly and only the law that applies. The boards in the decree archive keep what the Stone has let go.
Both acts are performed in public by the Ironfold’s designated Stone-Carver, and both carry the ceremonial weight other realms reserve for coronations: the law arrives in stone because the stone is the law’s body, and the law departs when the stone releases it. Crowds bring their children and their lunch. A clean carving of a long clause gets applause, and the old men in the front row, who have opinions about crossbars, are worse than any tournament crowd.
Origin · The Ones Who Stayed
Not every hobgoblin followed the fleet. The territories held populations who could not leave, would not leave, or chose not to leave because the land was the only home they had and abandoning it felt, to them, like a second defeat dressed in the language of a strategic withdrawal.
The Ashenmoor Period · Reckoned at two centuries after the Scattering by the Mandate’s chroniclers and at nearer twelve by anyone with a calendar, and named for the character of the land they held: ashen, marginal, and wanted by nobody else. They survived because the territory was poor enough that no major power considered it worth conquering, and because the Stone-Blood inheritance works just as effectively in a forest as it does in a fortress.

They could not build a moot because they were too scattered and too threatened. They could not build a kingdom because they had no capital and no surplus. What they could build was a network of garrisoned settlements joined by defensible corridors, and what they built was exactly that.

Vreth-Undaar consolidated three garrison settlements onto the basalt plateau, carved the first decree, and declared the enclosed territory sovereign ground ruled by decree rather than by council, because a council requires the luxury of time and time was the thing the western shield had never provided.

Three founding principles the Ironfold has never amended.
The border defines the state. The decree defines the law. Every mouth that eats the state’s grain fights for the state’s border.
These produced a realm that is, by design, an armed order with a farming population attached, rather than a farming population with an army attached.
In Undaar-Keth the army is the state, and agriculture, trade, schooling and craft exist inside the military’s perimeter because the military’s perimeter is the only reason any of them survive.

The Ironblood
Some came as refugees from inter-clan wars. Some came as raiders who discovered that raiding the Mandate’s border was the military equivalent of headbutting a wall, and who, after sufficient headbutting, accepted the wall’s offer of a place on the Roll in exchange for standing on the other side of it.
The Ironblood Clause was enacted under Commander Gorath-Keth, who argued with the pragmatism of a commander who had spent eight years fighting orcs on the northern perimeter that the Ironblood were going to be inside the borders one way or another, and that a people on the Roll have a stake in the border’s survival while a people off it have a stake in its collapse.

It passed five to two, and the two dissenters were reassigned to the northern perimeter for the following season, which the Ironfold’s records describe as a coincidence and which the dissenters described as a very specific kind of hobgoblin humor.

The Seven Districts
An ashfold, which is the Mandate’s word for a district, is drawn along defensive lines rather than geographic or cultural ones. A ridgeline that makes a good defensive position makes a good district border, regardless of whether the farming village on one side has more in common with the village on the other than with the garrison that governs it. A garrison settlement is a kaadre, numbered and never named, and the street Vaross of Kaadre-Six is what foreigners are taught to imitate when they want to be understood and laughed at. A commander takes the district’s name with the post and gives it back with the post, which is why there has been a Vreth-Kaan on the northern wall for as long as there has been a wall, and why the name in the epigraph above belongs to a chair.













































DistrictCharacterPop.Undaar-Gorr the capital districtThe plateau, the Decree Stone, the Ironfold’s headquarters. The Stone-Carver maintains the Stone here with the specific care of someone whose chisel-work is, in a literal and legally binding sense, the act of creating law. Holds the largest number of people who are not currently soldiers~12,000Vreth-Kaan the northern wallColdest, harshest, most heavily fought. Faces the unclaimed frontier, the polar waste’s edge, and the specific category of creature that breeds on rich tundra ground and considers hobgoblin settlements an interesting food source. Its soldiers are selected for cold-tolerance, endurance, and the mental resilience required to spend a winter on a wall that overlooks nothing except the precise direction from which the next attack will come. The Fortress-Monastery of Haldrek stands at its back, where the order’s young take the Vow of Silence and the Engraving, and Echohold of Stoneblood Vale lies a day south, where they go to be taught to speak again~7,000Gorr-Shal the eastern marchThe stretch that runs along the foot of the Greymane wall, and so the district that holds both the Mandate’s war and its money: the one trade road comes down off the pass at Galecross under safe-conduct, carrying what the Ring sells west. Its customs post is the realm’s busiest gate, a post the Marrowkin factors describe as efficient and the Mandate’s own merchants describe as humiliating, because every transaction is processed through a military checkpoint and every merchant is treated as a threat until cleared. The war camps are a morning’s march up the road from the wool scales, and the sutlers work both~9,000Keth-Vorruk the southern lineHolds the barrier that has stopped human settlers for three centuries, younger sons with a charter and a cart coming up out of the Hundred Crowns of the Midmarch, each sure the forest is empty. Its Commander is traditionally the most diplomatically skilled member of the Ironfold, because the border requires managing a relationship that is at once hostile and commercial, characterized by the mutual understanding that the settlers will keep pushing, the wall will keep holding, and the space between the pushing and the holding is where the actual relationship lives~8,000Ashenmoor the interiorThe farming heartland and the Bugbear heartland, territory the Bugbears settled while their hobgoblin neighbors were building walls, farmed with the patient persistence of a people whose ancestral inheritance is the memory of a layer that took the full force of impact and survived by being too massive to move. A small Ironblood community chose farming over garrison duty and is treated by the Bugbear majority with the cautious warmth reserved for relatives who have recently stopped throwing furniture~10,000Tinker’s Gorge the workshop districtThe canyon settlement holding the Tinker Goblin workshops and the category of experimental shed the Ironfold inspects quarterly and that the inspectors describe as technically within regulations and probably not going to explode. Standing policy on Tinker invention: approve everything that does not explode, record everything that does, and never tell them to stop, because the day the Tinkers stop inventing is the day the Mandate loses its only source of surprise from the workbench.
