Za’tarch, Gorrum Ashentusk’s proving-ground for cross-lineage goblinoid unity, sits in the Ashenmoor’s southeastern corner: see The Goblinoid Peoples.
The Ironfold regards it with official indifference and unofficial attention, too small to threaten anything and too philosophically interesting to ignore. Watch-reports are cut with the annotation “monitor, do not engage”, which is the Mandate’s way of saying it does not yet know whether the settlement is a threat or a future, and that it intends to find out by watching rather than by asking.

The Gorge, top and bottom
Tinker’s Gorge is a crack in the western shield a mile long and three hundred feet deep, and it is the brightest place in the Mandate. No daylight reaches the floor, so the goblins who live there hang their own: lamps on chains from every ledge and gallery, strings of brass and green glass by the hundred, kept burning by lamp-wardens on a garrison stipend, and the light runs down the walls in lime and amber and pink and copper-gold and pools where the workshops are. The shops are cut into the rock in tiers, joined by ladders, rope-bridges and little iron cage-lifts on counterweights. Every door is painted a different color, the goblins having nothing else that is theirs to paint.
The top of the Gorge is the Mandate’s pride, with its sheds, its guild marks shouted across the galleries, and its monthly Forge-Circle. The bottom is the Mandate’s money. At the head of the road stands a tower of black basalt with the fist on its banner and a bell in it, and when the bell rings four thousand goblins put down one set of tools and four thousand more pick them up, and the benches do not stand empty. On the floor tiers they file valve-seats and bellows-fittings and the small brass hearts of half the contraptions in three realms, true to a hair, by eye and by feel, to a daily quota set by a hobgoblin foreman on a raised platform with a ledger. The rank-cut on his shoulder plate, four cuts and a crossbar, can be read at forty paces. The pay is bunk space and soup.
Readers who can add will have noticed that eight thousand goblins do not fit in a district of three thousand. The bench goblins are hired by contract out of the Gorge’s own families and the slag-yards of the Isles, and a contract hand does not eat the state’s grain in the Roll’s sense, so the Roll does not count them. The Iron Code says no one on the Roll is exempt from anything regardless of species. The decrees, on the rare occasions they mention bench goblins, use a compound that comes into Common as the lesser. The Archive offers this without comment and suggests you not offer one in Undaar-Gorr.
The Wellsprings
The western shield’s profile is sparse. The ground runs thin, lean in the street’s word, thinner than at Marrowhold, the Kharven uplands or the Nalūn salt basin, and concentrated seeps are largely absent. A fighter pulling Aether (the raw magic of the world) here fills slowly, so Mandate practitioners learn thrift early, and their aura coats run close and quiet until the moment they do not. They call the coat ak-gresh, the survived skin, and hold that the Ironblood wear it too loud.

This has shaped the Mandate’s magical culture. Where other realms build rule around Wellspring-backed instruments (Nalūn’s contracts, the Holy Sea’s testimony, the Thread Standard of the Silver Cedars), the Mandate rules through its order alone.
The decrees carry no Wellspring enforcement. They carry the Ironfold’s enforcement, which arrives in the form of soldiers rather than metaphysics.

Petralon · Diffuse rather than concentrated, providing the ambient reinforcement that makes the fortifications hold. A formation of hobgoblin soldiers standing on Petralon-bearing stone locks into the substrate in a way that makes the formation functionally immovable without destroying the ground beneath it.
Stone-Blood Resonance · A racial Aetheric signature that all goblinoid peoples carry, rather than a Wellspring, producing measurable effects when populations concentrate. The Mandate’s practitioners describe it as the weight of the stone remembering what it was before it was people. The practical consequence is a passive defensive field that makes a settlement harder to disrupt through Aetheric means, which is one reason the fortifications have held for centuries against opponents with superior magical capability.

The Decree Stone’s Question. The single most politically sensitive Wellspring question in the goblinoid world.
The Isles’ Rock at Khal-Serrat is openly Engraved: the inscriptions carry Aetheric weight, and a law written into the Rock is a fact about the stone.
If the Decree Stone carries the same property, the Mandate’s decrees are metaphysically enforced, which would mean the Ironfold rules through Wellspring-backed authority whether or not it acknowledges doing so. If it does not, the decrees are enforced purely by soldiers, which is the Mandate’s official position and which the Isles’ scholars consider unlikely, given that the Stone is carved from the same asteroidal-resonance basalt and inscribed in the same script. The nine days the reserve spent guarding a wolf are cited by both sides.
The question is unresolved. Neither side has tested it. Both sides suspect the answer and neither side wants to be the one who confirms it.

Governance · The Ironfold
There is no house here, no crown and no heir. The Ironfold is a sworn military order that happens to own a country, its officers bound by the Crimson Order’s Engraving (an oath carved into the Soul Crystal itself, so that breaking it does immediate harm to the breaker). At its head sit seven operational commanders, one per district, holding both military and civil authority. The Ironfold does not vote in the Isles’ sense. It reaches agreement through assessment: commanders present their counts and reports, the Mandate-Holder sets them side by side, and the decree that results is the decree the counts support.

Dissent is recorded but not deliberated. A commander who disagrees may cut a formal objection, which the Stone-Carver annotates beneath the decree’s text on the Stone in a smaller hand, so that the law carries its own criticism visibly and permanently.
This is the Mandate’s only concession to loyal opposition, and it is one the Isles’ moot-speakers regard as both insufficient and deeply honest.

The Mandate-Holder · Selected from the Ironfold by the Assessment, judged on published, specific and merciless criteria: border integrity, how much grain reaches the line, how quiet the villages are, how fast the line answers an alarm, and the ratio of decrees issued to decrees enforced. The bench goblins call the holder the Imperator, for the same reason they call the place the Imperium. The holder in 715 IC is Drekka Vreshen, a hobgoblin of the Gorr-Shal command, known on every wall as Drekka Never-Late, an epithet her soldiers mean as praise and the Greymane scouts mean as a dare.

A commander who issues many decrees and enforces few is not considered decisive. They are considered noisy, and noise is the Ironfold’s cardinal sin.

Three Mandate-Holders have been reassessed out of office. All three accepted the verdict. The Mandate’s own chroniclers describe this as the order’s maturity. The Isles’ historians describe it as the consequence of knowing what happens to people who refuse, a characterization the Mandate does not dignify with a response.
The Stone-Carver · The official whose chisel creates law. The quality of the carving, the precision of the script, the depth of the grooves, the clarity of the letterforms, is treated as a measure of the law’s own quality.

A poorly carved decree is a poorly made law, and a decree carved sloppily into stone is a decree that has already confessed it was not worth the effort of doing properly.

Law and the Iron Code
The Iron Code · Amended only by unanimous vote of the Ironfold. Mandatory service between sixteen and forty-five, a levy assessed on what each field and shop can yield, collective responsibility for border upkeep, and the principle that no one on the Roll is exempt regardless of rank, species or guild.

It reads as the standing orders of a garrison: clear, imperative, without ornamentation, concerned exclusively with function.

The Decree · The Code is the bones; the decrees are what you are actually told to do this morning. Decrees are composed in Thruum Vaross, the reading register, with clauses ordered by what must be done first, and they refuse in a form with nobody in it: Skaal vashk, there shall be no breaching. The Concord’s clerks enter the Mandate as the type-case of the polity they call a Mandate: rule by standing decree, read aloud daily at every garrison, with no assembly and no appeal outside the decree archive. Its strength is that everybody knows the law because everybody hears it every day. Its weakness is that the law is whatever was read this morning, as the she-wolf’s descendants could tell you. A ferryman on the southern line keeps two tally-sticks, one for each bank’s law, and his children learn which to show before they learn to row.
The Ironblood Clause · Produces the specific friction of shared standing between peoples whose traditions are fundamentally incompatible and whose ways of war are terrifyingly complementary.

A hobgoblin formation provides the Resonance Lattice (soldiers’ souls set together like the stones of an arch), the structured defensive anchor. Ironblood soldiers provide the assault, the raw impact force the formation channels rather than generates.
Together they produce the most effective ordinary way of war on the northern shield, and the effectiveness is why the Clause survives: the military argument for integration is so strong that the cultural arguments against it have been losing for four centuries.

The Petition Process · The only road for anyone below an officer to be heard. Slow, cut on boards, carried up through three commands, and surprisingly effective: the commanders discovered over centuries that a people who are heard, slowly, are a people who do not revolt, and putting down a revolt is expensive.

It produces stability, which the Mandate considers a prerequisite for justice and which the Mandate’s critics consider a substitute for it.

Economy
Military and farming, in that order. Boreal timber, furs, limited minerals, seasonal grain and roots in the Ashenmoor valleys, brass and fittings from the Gorge, and the austere productivity a people living inside a permanent perimeter develop because they cannot afford waste.
Soldiers are the unofficial export: frontier settlements and caravans occasionally hire Ironwall units for escort, a practice the Ironfold officially discourages and unofficially permits, because the fee feeds the war-chest and the road teaches the soldiers. A caravan with six hobgoblins walking its flanks in iron-red pays a little more at the start and a good deal less at the end.

The Mandate does not use Nalūn’s credit paper. It has tried to make its own, through decree rather than Wellspring, and every attempt has produced documents that are enforceable within the borders and metaphysically inert outside them.
The result is a realm whose internal money is the split ration-tally and whose external money is barter, weight-for-weight exchange, and the grudging acceptance that the salt bars of the Amber Cities are the only universally trusted medium on the northern shield and that refusing to use them is a principle the Mandate cannot afford.

From the Crimson Isles the Mandate buys brimstone and volcanic glass, at the weight, with a great deal of mutual contempt. From the Marrowkin it buys as little as it can, and the Ironfold’s decree forbidding any officer to own a piece of god-bone (the ivory stuff Marrowhold cuts out of whatever it lives inside) is among the best enforced on the Stone.
Rent, food and the street
Black stone does not make it a dull town. Every door on the Undaar-Gorr grid is lacquered in its company’s color, oxblood and yellow and a shouting blue, so that a runner can find a billet at a dead sprint, and the regimental messes on Decree Street turn out smoked elk and barley by the barrow, with Nalūn salt on every table. Out in the Ashenmoor it is roots, pickled things and rye under a Bugbear roof, low and wide, with a bench that will hold anybody; in the Gorge it is the soup. Housing is by billet, and a family that wants a better one files a petition, which is slow, and then pays a sergeant, which is faster.
Small practitioners are everywhere and every one of them is on a roll: wall-wardens who keep the watch-fires burning a true color, ration-cooks whose pots never scorch, and the Ironwall’s famous farrier who can shoe a warhorse while it is kicking him and bills the horse’s company for the bruises. Each company has its song, its color and its grudge against the company next door, and on feast days they run the Wall Games on the plaza, carrying sandbags up a scaffold in full harness before a crowd that knows every sergeant by name. Betting on the Wall Games is unlawful by no decree whatever, because the Ironfold has done the sum on the ratio and knows it could not enforce one.
Defense · The Ironwall
Roughly eight thousand, the largest standing army on the northern shield and the readiest, in the specific sense that a force defending the same borders for six centuries has honed every procedure for exactly one purpose: holding the line.

Ironwall doctrine produces companies that function, baggage trains that arrive, and fortifications that hold, and has no place for individual heroes. It does post a monthly list of officers commended, which every soldier in the Ironwall reads as a ranking and bets on accordingly.

The tactical approach is the phalanx of spears, remade for a world with magic. The Resonance Lattice absorbs chaotic Aether and channels kinetic energy; integrated Ironblood companies break the attacker’s formation once the Lattice has absorbed the first impact. The move the crowds and the enemy both wait for is The Red Wall Takes One Step: a whole formation advances a single pace, in silence, and the field changes hands. Ironblood on the Mandate’s wall add Vorruk-Da, Shard Comes Home, standing still for the first blows on purpose and handing the stored force back through one fist, and the companies that drill the two together call the combination the Door and the Knock and argue over which of them is the door. Crossbows hold the cleared lanes, because a bolt costs almost nothing and does not care about your Stage if you do not see the loose.

Devastating against ordinary forces. Less effective against Domain-scale practitioners (those who can make a stretch of ground obey their own law), because a Lattice that functions by absorbing chaos is vulnerable to an opponent who applies order, and a Domain is the most organized expression of magical authority that exists.
The cold is the other way in. Stone-Blood runs slow in deep cold, and at thirty below every Stone-Blood fighter moves about three-quarters of a beat late. The strength is all there and arrives behind the count, and a formation drilled to keep time loses its time before it loses its strength. In such weather the Silent Sign-Glyphs fail and the Ironwall falls back to a horn count, which can be heard by the people it is fighting. The Ironfold knows this as it knows the sum of its own grain.

The fortification line is the most extensive military work on the shield with no Wellspring behind it: redoubts at regular intervals, cleared shooting-lanes, Tinker-kept warded perimeters, and a chain of beacon towers and Tinker mirror-posts that carries a border alert from the northern wall to the Mandate-Holder’s table in approximately forty minutes, fast enough that the response is usually in motion before the attacking force has finished crossing the perimeter.

The strategic weakness is every military state’s: it can hold its borders and cannot grow beyond them without turning from a defensive posture to an offensive one, and the turn requires a surplus of grain and of will the Mandate has never possessed at the same time.
The borders do not expand. The borders do not contract. The Mandate exists inside its walls, and the walls are its argument that existence is sufficient.

Culture
Martial, direct, and functional in the way a well-kept fortification is functional: everything serves a purpose, and the one exception to the absence of ornamentation is color, which the Ironfold permits on the ground that a banner is a signal. The rest of the plainness is itself a statement about what the culture values.
Composition · Of the Roll, about 55% hobgoblin, 25% Bugbear, 12% Ironblood Orc, 5% Tinker Goblin, 3% other, predominantly human frontier families who crossed the southern line going the wrong direction and were offered a place on the Roll rather than expulsion, on the pragmatic ground that a family who voluntarily enters a military state has already selected for the characteristics the military state values.

The peoples’ roles are functional rather than harmonious: the hobgoblins command, the Bugbears feed, the Ironblood fight, and the Tinkers build. The roles are not prescribed in the Code, but six centuries of cultural gravity have produced a division of labor that newcomers absorb within a generation and that the Mandate’s own people regard as natural in the way breathing is natural, meaning they do not notice it until someone from outside points it out. Orcs get the walls and the northern perimeter, to be spent against whatever comes off the tundra hungry. Goblins get the benches.

Language · Old Vaross for administration and law. Gorr-Vaross, the Bugbear dialect, in the Ashenmoor: long coordinated chains joined by and, resisting subordination, idiom drawn from water, rot, growth and things that sink. The Ironblood speak Old Vaross with heavier consonants, shorter vowels, and the sub-bass frequencies that physically vibrate the iron content of nearby listeners, which the hobgoblin population has learned to filter and visitors have not. A Vaross speaker in a rage gets quieter and slower, and emphasis is carried by how long a vowel is held. A commander who starts holding his vowels has told you everything you need to know about your next few minutes.
Architecture · The Bugbear instinct is horizontal while the hobgoblin instinct is vertical, and the contrast between the capital’s angular height and the Ashenmoor’s spread-out sprawl is the most visible expression of the realm’s inner character.
The Decree Reading · A daily ceremony, roughly fifteen minutes, at every garrison, market square and settlement hall. A thruum, in Vaross, is a decree read aloud. Attendance is not mandatory. Non-attendance is noted, and in a culture where being noted is functionally equivalent to being assessed, the distinction between mandatory and expected has collapsed into a category the Mandate calls observed and everyone else calls mandatory with extra steps. Every child can recite the Third Ashfold Decree by seven, for its last lines: A thousand years. A thousand years. And we bore it.
The Forge-Circle · The monthly Tinker exhibition, held at the top of the Gorge and attended by commanders, engineers, and whatever farmers are brave enough to attend an event where the exhibits occasionally achieve unplanned combustion. The makers shout their names and guild marks. The Mandate’s closest equivalent to a festival, and its atmosphere, watching a Tinker demonstrate a device whose stability the proposal boards described as provisional, produces the only occasion in the calendar when hobgoblin commanders are observed to smile.

Za’tarch’s cultural influence. A position official doctrine does not accommodate and that the younger generation finds increasingly interesting: that goblinoid peoples can live together through soul-work rather than decree.
The Mandate’s younger soldiers visit during leave rotations and return with questions the Ironfold has not prepared answers for.
Whether Za’tarch represents the Mandate’s future or merely a village of two hundred with ideas above its station is the question the Ironfold has been avoiding for a decade, and the avoidance is itself an answer the Ironfold prefers not to examine.

What they joke about
The she-wolf, first and always: “Report to the wolf” is what a Mandate soldier says when an order makes no sense, and he says it with his face perfectly straight, because it might be lawful. An officer who is out of her depth is Kaan Shaarn. A kaanith is a jumped-up officer, and the diminutive is the only insult the Ironfold will overlook on a feast day.
Of the Isles they say a decree is a motion that got on with it, and that an Islander asked the time will call a roll. Of the Greymanes they say the house has one idea and that it is correct. Of the Kharven they say a lord’s oath is good until the thaw. Of the Marrowkin they say that you will be sold your own teeth and given a receipt. The bench goblins say a number of things about all of the above, quickly, in the Goblin dialect, with the syllabic r dropped so that the foreman has to ask.
Monsters on the Roads
The woods are full of the honest kind of danger: elk that will not move for a column, bear in every drainage, wolverine in the ration stores, salmon thick enough in the braided rivers that the Ashenmoor bears fish beside the Bugbears and neither side files a complaint. Gray wolf packs are a matter of record, and one served as an officer.
The northern wall faces the creatures that breed on rich tundra ground and consider a garrison an interesting food source, and Droval (the Frost-Howlers of the polar snowfields, which lie along a ridge until the ridge is suddenly gone) head the watch-reports in any bad winter. Monsters move, and the Mandate’s are entered by the post that first saw them. Wyverns (Grade S on the hunting halls’ scale, which runs from E to EX) nest on the western faces of the Slate Ridge and take sentries from both garrisons with perfect impartiality, the one subject on which Gorr-Shal and Galecross have exchanged notes in a civil tone. A dragon has been seen far overhead above the Ashenmoor, and it is entered in watch-reports as a dragon.
The dungeon
Concentrated seeps are largely absent here, so a dungeon is a rare event, and the one everyone mentions is Vorrak’s Standing Grove on the western frontier, where the third Stone-Carver spent her retirement cutting practice decrees into living trees. A thin Chthonica seep (a Wellspring of dark iron-oxide, all grip and ground) lay under the wood. The things in that grove now obey clauses, and a patrol that knows the wording can walk through. A company stands around it, and the foresters who say the forest has been ignoring her law make one exception, in a lower voice. The Ironfold has it annotated “monitor, do not engage.” More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
The Scourge and the Turn
The Scourge of Hell lies south and east of Keth-Vorruk, past the Midmarch and the foot of the Violet Peaks, and the Mandate holds no ground on its rim. The Turn is the old rota by which the North, the South and the Center each keep the Scourge’s monsters off everybody else for nine years. The Ironfold’s whole recorded view of it is two words on a board in the decree archive, not party, and it follows the thing more closely than some of the parties do. On the North’s Turn, Kharven and its Banner Houses march down the Kessen road with Stormfold slate in the column, the Greymane wall stands thin by however many spears went south, and every commander at Gorr-Shal knows the count by the first thaw. The Center holds the Turn until 721 and the North’s comes next, and that sum has been done on every wall in the Mandate.
The other end of it arrives on the southern line. In a dry late summer the Scourge’s herds push outward and what follows them comes too, so the Midmarch empties northward on its carts, and Keth-Vorruk sees more younger sons with charters in a bad herd season than in any other, some of them followed up the road by Hellhounds (Grade A) off the near rim. The Ironfold shoots both on the same principle. Caravans bound for the Kessen road hire Ironwall units for the flanks, and the fee goes in the war-chest.
Then there are the ridge-men, who are the Mandate’s quietest export. On the western ridges above the Black Roots, the long-service hands of the Scourge trade are hobgoblins, stripping carcasses and hiring out as guides, and a good many came from here. Service under the Iron Code ends at forty-five, and a hobgoblin may see two centuries if the world allows it, which leaves a discharged sergeant about a hundred and fifty years to fill and no decree to fill them. They keep their old company’s color on a rag somewhere about the harness, and they will tell a Midmarch boy the worst of it in the same voice they used for the morning Reading.
Relations
The Slate Ridge of Stormfold and the Greymane wall · The Mandate’s whole eastern sky. The Ridgewall, a fortress grown out of a ridge of slate under violet lightning, stands on the line between the shield’s two great militaries, and House Greymane has held it for longer than the North has had a name. Both sides have been looking at each other across the same passes for centuries; in the present year it is a cold peace, which on that ridge means raiding parties, burned watch-posts, stolen horses and a great deal of formal notice served by arrow. Hobgoblins hold that those passes are goblinoid ground, lost in the Scattering and never paid for. Greymane children are raised as components of the wall they stand on, and the Ironfold, which raises its own the same way, has never quite been able to bring itself to despise them.
Kharven and the Northern Empire of Whitemere · The cold peace across the Greymane wall, and the one border the Mandate has pressed and not taken. Both states believe borders must be held, threats must be answered, and rule is serious work done by serious people, which is precisely why neither can leave the other alone: Moto sovereign judgment and Ironfold decree-authority arrive at similar conclusions through different mechanisms, and the conclusion they have both arrived at is that the other is the threat worth the winter. Later hand, from the last winter before the turn: when Kharven was built out into the Empire of Whitemere, with the Banner Houses holding lands inside it, the new empire inherited the wall, the cold and the enemy, all three, and the Mandate’s reading of the news took fifteen minutes and changed nothing on the Stone.
The Crimson Isles of Vorruk-Khal · The most politically charged relationship in the goblinoid world. Two states, one people’s two answers to the question of rule. The Isles opened their palm. The Mandate closed its fist. Both respond to the same founding wound, and both believe the other’s response was wrong. The Isles consider the Mandate a tyranny. The Mandate considers the Isles naive. Both are correct. They agree on exactly one thing, and it stands on a ridge: no human lord has a good title to those passes, and every load of Isles brimstone landed on the Vorrak’s Reach coast is a vote on the subject.

Dealings are conducted through observers who are at once envoys and spies, and both states are aware of this and consider it the healthiest possible arrangement, because an observer who is also a spy cuts comprehensive reports, and comprehensive reports are what both states require to maintain the mutual assessment that has prevented a war between them for four centuries.

Marrowhold · The whole of Kharven lies between them, and a joint trade moot still meets annually in the customs post at Gorr-Shal, discusses the same three issues, reaches the same compromise, and adjourns until next year. It has performed this exact ritual for two centuries. Both sides consider it a model of efficient rule. Both sides are correct. The Marrowkin enter each year’s compromise in their tally of what has been taken, and the Ironfold has asked what that means, and has been told it will be informed.
The Center · South of Keth-Vorruk lies the Hundred Crowns of the Midmarch, whose petty kings change sides every decade and send their spare sons north with charters. The Ironfold deals with whichever of them has most recently stopped being a nuisance. The Concord’s Sealed Charter does not run past the southern line, and its clerks’ opinion of the Iron Code has been received and entered. Salt comes up from the Amber Cities of Nalūn under Ironwall escort, the one arrangement nobody has ever tried to change. Nalūn’s factors are the only foreigners a commander will stand up for.
The Silver Cedars of Yukari · The land the old maps call the Crow’s Reach lies far to the south, and what passes between them is defined by mutual incomprehension: the Mandate cannot understand a realm that rules through perception rather than decree, and Yukari cannot understand a realm that rules through decree rather than perception. Each keeps an observer at the other’s seat, and each observer’s reports are read with the deep suspicion that they might be accurate.
The Holy Sea of Alabaster · The Manumission Doctrine and the Ironblood Clause are two radically different approaches to the same problem: how to extend legal protection to a people the surrounding world considers disposable. The Holy Sea does it through theology. The Mandate does it through military pragmatism. The clerics find the Mandate’s approach morally inadequate, and have lately asked about the Gorge. The commanders find the Holy Sea’s approach militarily irrelevant. Both assessments are accurate. Both are incomplete.

That is our history. That is the whole of the explanation, and if the explanation is insufficient, the mountain is still here, and you are welcome to try.
Stone-Carver Vorrak, unofficial remarks, preserved in the Archive despite her objections

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Jade Plains of Qingyuan
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Art: Jonas De Ro, Wizards of the Coast.
The Jade Plains of Qingyuan
Say itching-YWEN
The Grey Plain, on northern maps · The Thousand Bloodlines · In the Dynasty of Sum-gol
Lucky Bao stole the greatest horse in the South on the night of the Lantern Fair in 694, and he did it beautifully. Rain-on-Slate was a seven-year-old stallion of the tall gray Yan breed, a hand higher than anything the north can raise and dappled like river stones, with a stud fee that would buy a village, and Bao walked him out of the Qingyuan paddocks with his hooves wrapped in silk while nine rows of the Yan family were up at the tablets toasting their ancestors. He rode north for eleven days and sold nothing, because he was a professional and meant to do it properly. In the great horse market below Ashbury, with half the Ashmore gentry bidding and a real northern lord holding up a purse the size of a cheese, Bao was counting his fortune when a child of about nine came through the crowd on a fat pony. She wore a jade sash and carried a ledger as big as she was. She looked the horse over, opened the book, and read out his name, his sire, his dam and his grandsire in a clear, bored voice.
Rain-on-Slate turned his head. Then he turned the rest of himself, went through the market fence with Bao still in the saddle, and set off for home. They say there has never been a ride like it. He ran flat out for six days, down the salt road with the copper haze of the Scourge of Hell standing on his right hand, past a string of Ryu toll-forts without paying, through two weddings and somebody’s war, with the whole country laying money on it from the hedges and Lucky Bao hanging on with both arms because by now he could not get off. The Elder of Stables was waiting at the paddock gate when the gray came in at a walk, not even blown. Bao slid down, fell over, and held out his wrists. The Elder looked at his seat and his legs and the state of the saddle, took out a brush, and made an entry: One thief, sound, excellent hands, sire unknown. Bao rode for the Yan for thirty years, and they buried him with his name in the book, which he considered the best thing anybody ever stole.
Qingyuan is a green valley and an ocean of silver-green grass, a family that has bred every good horse in the Inner World and written down who bought it, and the quiet certainty that a horse, a debt or a man will come home when the right person reads out his name.
The Yan sell a horse and keep its name. You may read everything below as a footnote to that.
The Land and the Look
It is grass from here to the sky. Silver-green, waist high by midsummer, running in long swells from the steam of the Wellheads in the west, with the rust-colored iron hills beyond them, across to the foot of the cedar country in the east, it goes pale whenever the wind turns the blades over, and that is why northerners who have only ever ridden across it in a cold wind wrote the Grey Plain on their maps. The Yan call it the Jade Plains, because in the low sun after rain it turns the exact color of the stone in the spring at Yuquan, and they will correct your map for you if you leave it unattended.
Toward its middle the plain narrows into the valley everyone paints: a wide green floor of wildflowers, still pools and low stone walls under an enormous blue sky, with long waterfalls coming down off vast curved mountains on either hand, and on a rise in the midst of it Qingyuan, a pale many-towered hall under slate roofs.
Out of the grass rise the stud-halls, each a walled compound with lacquered roofs of black and sea-green turned up at the corners, and on the rise behind every one, jade and silver banners as tall as ships’ masts. Big gray horses call across the plain at dusk, and sound carries a long way. There are no trees to speak of, a great many larks, and more sky than most visitors can stand for the first week.
This is the middle of the South. Boundary stones mark the Long Fields on the north, the Sallowgate marches climb away on the south toward the white shelf, the old imperial road comes in from Sum-gol, and salt and grain come across from the salt road, paying at every toll. Buyers come from four quarters, and horses sold from here have a habit of walking back.
The war came through here more than once, and the dead of the Grey Plain include a Warlord of the Lamberts. Grass grows back. The Yan have a column for that as well.
The House
The Yan Hall is a lineage hall in the old southern style (a clan ruled by its elders and its ancestral tablets, rather than by a lord). Its tablets stand nine rows deep, with a title for every rung of the family, which the Yan recite in full at every introduction and which takes, for a senior elder, about as long as it takes to water a horse. The present head is the Venerable Hall-Master of the Yan, First of the Grey Plain, Keeper of the Thousand Bloodlines, Elder Yan Shouyi. He is ninety, he rides every morning, and he has personally inspected the teeth of most of the lords you have heard of. The hall maxim is The Plain Remembers the Hoof. Its colors are gray and jade, with a running horse in silver.
Below the Hall-Master sit the Elders of Stables, Ledgers, Remounts and Tablets, the core disciples of each stud, and the outer cousins, who do the shoveling and are reminded of their fortune at every meal. A Yan is born to a rung, and the only way off it is a horse. A cousin of the lowest row who breeds a filly of the first class goes up three rows that evening, and the tablet-carver is sent for.
The Hall answers to the name of Sum-gol, and has done without interruption since before the empire broke. Every autumn an elder goes to the Calling and recites his titles from the square. The Hall keeps the Emperor’s stall swept at Qingyuan and enters it each year as held. As for what the Dynasty has received from the Grey Plain since 602, the Hall will be delighted to show you the ledger, and you will need to bring a lunch.
Cities and Towns
Qingyuan is the seat and the only thing on the plain you could call a city: forty thousand people inside a square of tamped-earth walls faced in pale stone on the rise, with the Great Hall of Tablets at its center, many-towered and slate-roofed, its nine rows lit by a thousand oil lamps, and the home paddocks stretching out through its north gate. The streets are laid wide enough for sixty horses abreast and smell like it. Saddlers, farriers, tack-lacquerers and ledger-binders each hold their own guild street. The Lantern Fair at midsummer fills the walls with paper light and buyers from four quarters.
Yuquan, “jade spring,” sits where a cold spring comes out of the eastern rise over beds of milky green stone. River jade comes down it after every flood and the whole town wades in after it with sieves, while the carvers who buy their finds cut bridle-bosses, ledger-weights and the small jade horses every Yan child gets at its naming. The water is the sweetest on the plain, and since the war the town has been watching very closely whether it stays that way, given what has happened to the springs upstream.
Mashi, “horse market,” is a town that exists for nine weeks a year and is a wide empty field for the rest of it. Then the tents go up in rows a mile long and everyone comes: northern quartermasters, Marrick paymasters, Lambert clerks to check the Marrick paymasters, Moto stable-lords in red, horse-copers with a dozen ways of making an old mare look young, hedge-workers who will gentle a colt or lame a rival’s for the same fee, and bookies on every rail, because there are races at noon and at sunset and on any provocation in between.
Wealth and Trade
Their wealth walks. The tall gray southern horse comes from the Yan studs at Qingyuan and nowhere else, and the Yan keep the bloodlines in ledgers older than the Holy Sea’s: sire, dam and grandsire for every animal they have ever sold, and the name of the man who bought it.
That last column is the Hall’s real stock in trade. They sold to everyone in the war. Ashmore’s big southern horses were Yan horses, and so were the Tenrai’s. The Hall-Master can tell you which side bought how many remounts in which season, which is to say which side was expecting to lose cavalry, and when. The Yan take orders, in both senses, and never a side. Lords pay well for that column, and pay better to have their own line of it left unread.
Beyond horses: river jade, felt, hides, mare’s milk spirits, lacquer, and the leather of a hundred thousand saddles. Grain and salt come in by the cart, the salt at a Ryu toll that the Hall disputes annually, by reciting.
Rent, Food and the Street
The grass belongs to the Hall. A herding family rents its stretch by the head of stock, in foals and days’ labor, and pays it at the fall gather with a great deal of drinking; a Qingyuan townsman rents a room over a stable at about the ordinary city list and gets the warmth free. They eat hand-pulled noodles, mutton roasted on the bone with cumin and salt, steamed buns the size of a fist, and tea with butter and salt from a bowl that hangs at the saddle. Everyone drinks the sour mare’s milk spirit at the fall gather, and everyone regrets it.
A Qingyuan market is all elbows and titles. Two men who meet in the street state their rung before they state their business, the lower one bows the correct number of degrees, and a Yan grandmother can reduce a horse-coper to tears from behind a tea stall by asking who his people were. Stable-sects run the bracket fights, each with its own colors and its own songs and a stud to be loyal to: the Silver Bridles of the home paddocks, the Black Girths of the eastern halls, and the Yuquan Waders, who are not taken seriously until they break your jaw. The hall’s scholars say hùtǐ for the aura coat, wēiyā for Pressure and shénshí for sensing, and they will explain to you that the Guild’s words are translations, poorly done. On the plain, a boy with a good coat is simply said to be shining like a wet gray.
Law and How It Fights
Hall law runs the plain. The Elder of Ledgers hears disputes in the Great Hall in front of the tablets of the plaintiff’s own ancestors, which keeps testimony short. Killing a man is a matter for his family and a blood-price. Stealing a horse is a matter for the Hall, and since the horse will come home regardless, the penalty turns on how well you rode it. No one on the plain has ever been able to explain to a Lambert why the ledger is not perjury when it says what it says about the buyers; the Yan hold that a true record of who bought what cannot be a lie, whoever it embarrasses.
Their own horsemen are few and superb, archers who shoot from the saddle at the full gallop, turning in the stirrups, with the gray horses running flat out under them like water poured downhill. They never stand and they do not charge. They ride around a force at a distance from which it cannot reach them and take it apart from the edges, starting with whoever is shouting. When the Yan ride out in force, it is to make sure a buyer has paid. A wall of good spears gives them nothing to charge and they have no interest in trying, which is the entire history of relations between the Yan and the Marrick, and both sides consider it a professional friendship. A crossbow in the right hedge has killed more than one elder of the third row. That goes in the ledger too.
What They Joke About
Titles first. A Yan will tell you about the elder who introduced himself at a siege and the siege was over when he finished. Of the Marrick they say they have spent three hundred years walking everywhere to prove it could be done. Of northerners they say a northern lord will pay anything for a tall horse and then fall off it in a very brave manner. Of the Ryu they say that the tide pays twice and the Yan three times, and the Hall still does not know who the third payment went to. There is one joke they tell against themselves. A Yan dies, comes to the gate of the next world and is asked his name, and the gatekeeper gives up and lets him in around the third row.
Monsters on the Roads
Neiman Lions (Grade B) hunt the plain with a stunning roar that has cost the Hall a great many foals, and every stud has a bounty standing. Hippogrifs come down from the rim mountains and are shot on sight or sold. The rest of the country’s teeth belong to beasts: steppe eagles take lambs, foxes take everything smaller, wild asses break the hay-fences, and marmot holes have lamed more good horses than the lions have killed, a figure the Elder of Ledgers will show you.
The dungeon. The cold spring at Yuquan is a small worked Core, kept by the Elder of Tablets. The dungeon is the Ninth Paddock: in the Hall’s old ledgers there was a stud east of Qingyuan whose compound sank into the plain in a single night, walls, roofs and tablets, into a hole no one had known was a Well. On a still dusk, tall horses can be heard calling from the ground. The Hall enters the stock every year as held, has sent three parties to read out their names, and got back one of the horses. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
The Scourge and the Turn. The plains lie too far south to see the Scourge of Hell, and it is on every page of the ledger anyway. The stilts (Grade B, herd animals on legs as long as a ship’s mast) that walk through the Marrick barley in a bad year do not all stop for the boundary stones, and whose contract covers a stilt past the stones is one of the things the annual brawl at Mashi is for. Greywalkers (Grade A) come behind them at dusk, and those the stud archers shoot on sight. When the Turn comes to the South, the old wheel’s nine years of keeping the Scourge off everybody else, it falls first on the old Dynasty’s realms. The Hall answers with remounts by the season, the Elder of Remounts going north with a ledger and a bill for every animal, and a few score horse archers who ride the southern Hem shooting greywalkers off the flanks of the herds from a distance nothing there has yet closed on a gray. In the other two regions’ Turns it sells to them instead, and reads each order as advance notice of how much cavalry that side expects to lose.
Bounty crews from every realm buy grays for the Hem at any price. In late summer one will come walking in at the north gate of Qingyuan with an empty saddle, thin and unhurried, having crossed half a continent alone, and the Elder of Ledgers makes a line in the book and sends the buyer’s heirs a courteous note about the balance. A good many families in the Midmarch have heard their news that way.
Neighbors and Grudges
Sum-gol. Sworn. The Hall answers at every Calling and keeps the stall, and has written down how many relay horses the Post bought this year, and how many it did not.
The Sapphire Wells. Upstream. Bad water means sick foals, the Hall has started counting them, and Maud Corwen has been shown the count.
The Copper Coast. Fellow vassals of the same empty chair, and they have been quarreling about the price of salt since before it was empty.
The Ochre Fields. Their border is a line of boundary stones, a shared love of being paid, and an annual brawl. The Yan want every army to need horses, and none of them to win too quickly. The Marrick want a long peace with a lot of small wars in it. They could not be better neighbors.
The north. Their best customer and their least attentive one. Every lord in the north who has ever bought a gray has a line in a book on the Grey Plain, and that book is what the Hall offers the next buyer.
Further reading · The Southern Warlords

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Kingdom of Kharven — The Ashen Crown
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Art: GLIULIAN.
The Kingdom of Kharven — The Ashen Crown
Say itKAR-ven
The Ashen Crown · The One True Kingdom of the North · The Moto Seat
At the Midwinter Brackets of Year 703 the whole lower town of Kharven-Seat came down onto the frozen Marrow in its scarves, four thousand people between the bonfires, with the rock standing up behind them strung with amber lamps and the green aurora hanging over the spires. The final was Scarlet Scarves against Wolf Grays, the two fighting schools of the Seat, whose grudge is older than either school’s account of it. The Scarlet champion was Big Sigga Tolleifsdottir, a cooper’s daughter with a coat of aura the color of a split beet and forearms the width of a good ham. The hedge-workers who charm the bracket ice had asked for an extra copper the yard that year and been laughed at, and at noon they had put down their tools and gone to watch from the bank with their arms folded. Nobody on the ice had been told. Sigga took a Wolf Gray’s staff across the ear in the third exchange, roared, jumped as high as a cart, bawled the one art she ever named, THE WHOLE WINTER, and came down on both heels.
The Marrow opened from bank to bank. Bonfires, bookies, sausage-sellers, a bishop’s nephew and the entire front third of the crowd went into black water in their best red and gray, and the river steamed where the fires hit it. Thirty-one people drowned, and the lower town sat with every one of them through the Waiting, all night, Scarlet beside Gray, on the cold floor of the death-house. In the morning the bookies paid out, because the wager had been on who was left standing, and the only person standing on anything was Sigga, on a slab of ice the size of a door, a quarter-mile downriver, still holding her opponent by his scarf. The Hall of Verdicts, up on the crown of the rock, sent down a clerk to determine who was at fault. He looked at the river for some time, and nobody has ever told him it was the hedge-workers.
One dark rock, one empty red chair, the oldest blood in the world arguing under one roof, and a winter that audits all of them: that is Kharven in a breath.

Two hands on this page. The ground, the trades, the law and the people below stand as this shelf stands them, in Year 715, the twenty-fifth of the Dark Ages. The crown’s own story runs past that seal. Passages in the later hand that also annotates the Concordance of Ages, carried back from the last winter before the turn, are marked Later hand where they begin. A reader standing in 715 should take them the way a farmer takes weather coming over the ridge. Later hand: this is the one true kingdom of the north, and it becomes the capital of the Northern Empire of Whitemere, which Muken Moto builds out of it.

Overview
The northernmost sovereign ground in the Inner World, and the only true kingdom in the North. “Kharven” is the old name of the high country itself, and the Seat and the Foot stood on it before anyone now alive had an opinion about them. The six Banner Houses hold their lands around it, each on its own page, and they are houses and lands, never kingdoms, however they carry themselves at table.
Kharven is defined by two inheritances in permanent tension: the divine authority of the Moto bloodline, whose Hataraki-bearing eyes make them the most spiritually dangerous ruling house in the Inner World, and the practical, unsentimental toughness of the northern clans who were there first and who have accepted Moto rule, on and off, because the alternative was the fragmented clan warfare that had been killing them for generations.

The climate is the kingdom’s primary institution. It kills the weak, preserves the strong, punishes pretension, and rewards only the virtues that survival in sustained cold requires: endurance, preparation, cooperation under duress, and the willingness to do ugly necessary work without complaint.
The cold is the constitution.
This arrangement makes Kharven the most internally coherent kingdom in the Inner World when the Crown is competent, and the most rapidly fragmentary when it is not.

The Land and What It Looks Like
You come to it up a long frozen valley with a castle at every bend, each one a little higher and a little more sure of itself, and on the last mile of the approach the road runs between the Hooded Men: stone figures twice the height of a rider, cowled, faces worn off, each holding up a torch that a lamp-warden is paid to keep lit and which goes out when the lamp-wardens are not paid. Nobody knows who carved them, and the Measurewrights have stopped asking because the answers came back in the wrong hand. Then the valley opens and the sky is enormous, storm stacked on storm with an orange sunset breaking at the far edge of it, and Kharven-Seat is standing on its rock in the snow.
Kharven-Seat is a towering dark castle of many spires with verdigris-green roofs, and every traveler who has ever seen it has stopped his horse, so that a lone rider sitting still on the last mile with his head tipped back is the commonest sight on that road, and the lamp-warden’s boy will charge him a copper for the view. The rock under it rises sheer out of the Marrow on the river’s west side, four hundred feet of cliff veined with frost that glitters rose and pale gold in the first light, and the whole face of it is strung with lamps in brass cages, up the cliff stair and along the terraces and the long curtain walls. Halfway up, the silver house of the Shirogane sits on its terrace with its tall windows glowing blue-white. On the crown, the long black roof of the Hall of Verdicts steams faintly where the snow melts off the warmed stone. The Tenrai keep stands to the east with gold leaf on it, and gold and crimson banners hang from every wall that will take a nail. Beside the Hall, older and lower than anything else up there, is a long gray house of the old Kōkan building, deep-eaved and dark-beamed, with floors of black stone worn smooth by a thousand years of feet, and for three centuries the people who live on the rock have used it to store chests. A lift-cage of black iron and brass hangs on cables from the cliff-top to the river ford, lit inside like a lantern, the masterwork of a Guild craftsman long dead and a source of steady terror; it has dropped twice in living memory, both times with nobody important in it, which the lower town regards as the true miracle.
At the foot of the rock is the lower town, a thousand orange oil-lights crowded along the river with their chimneys smoking straight up. Here the Seat speaks its second architectural language, the longhouse tradition of the northern clans, timber-framed and steep-roofed to shed snow load and hold heat through a six-month winter, doors painted ox-blood and ocher so a man can find his own in a whiteout. The squared, heavy-walled Moto stonework above it is built to channel wind rather than resist it.

Visiting architects describe it as beautiful and threatening in roughly equal measure. The population describes it as home.

North of the Seat, under the shoulder of the ridge, lies a mere the Kharven have called the white for longer than anyone has written anything down. It ices at the first hard frost and goes opaque by the second week and stays that way until the grass comes, and underneath it never freezes through, because something keeps the water moving down there. Three Measurewrights have explained what. Later hand: the Moto took the name of their empire from it.
The highland plateau is the kingdom’s core: granite uplift scarred by glacial activity, boreal forest, defensible, central, and cold enough to discourage anyone who does not genuinely want to be there. Its great frozen lake, the Skeldmere, hums in the deep cold over the water beneath it, and the shore road runs south from it to the Seat. Past the ridgeline to the west lie the Mandate’s black basalt and boreal forest and the ground the bloodline came from, which nobody holds and on which the Crown has never once filed a claim. The Holy Sea’s copies of the map keep that ground on its own high marches instead, and the Gazetteer enters both. Aurora goes over all of it most clear nights, a slow green river with violet at its hem, and in the hour after sunset the snow turns blue.
The major places

Kharven-Seat. The capital, the rock, the Hall, the river, the lower town. About the only place in the north where a person can buy a thing they do not strictly need.
Kharven’s Foot, called the Foot. The door of the north. It stands at the top of the long ridge where the Kessen road comes up out of the low country and goes on through the mountains. The old clans built the first of it, a ring of dry stone round a well, back when the land was still grass and the riders still rode; somebody built over that, and somebody over them, and eleven years ago, with the long war going badly, the Tenrai rebuilt the lot in square gray stone with a gatehouse, two towers, a curtain wall eight men high and a toll-post, and hung a gold-on-black banner you can see in clear weather from three days down the road. Whoever holds the Foot holds the road, and the ordinary people of the north have a number of remarks about the toll.
Harlsey Landing. A river town whose whole north bank turns out at Ice-out, the morning the river breaks, in its best reds and blues, to see the ration scale inspected in public, as it has been since anybody’s grandmother.
The Castle Stair. The long valley of the approach, with cadet castles of the landless Moto lines at every bend, each with loud opinions about the one above it.

Roads. You come up the Kessen road from the Greenhollow to the Foot, then through the valley of the Castle Stair. The Marrow road runs north from Ashbury to the Seat through the last of the spruce, the shore road runs south to the Seat from the Skeldmere, and the ridge road goes west to the Slate Ridge, on foot in winter. West, past the Ridge, are the Mandate’s country and the empty ground. East lie the Ironwood March and the Thornwood, running out to the rib mountains of Marrowhold. South are the Painted Rivers and the Hollow, and past them the two roads that go around the Scourge of Hell, the Kessen down its west flank and the salt road up its east. North is the Aurora Reach.
Who Rules
The Moto. Seven Great Lines sit in the Hall of Verdicts, each in its own chair and each in its own metal: Kōkan in red, Shirogane in silver, Tenrai in gold, Akagane in copper, Byakuya in near-white, Kurenai in black and ash, Amagiri in indigo. In law, only Kōkan holds the seat, and the other six are landless. In fact the Tenrai took the rock from the Kōkan three hundred years ago and have held it since, which the law has found no way to mention. The red chair has stood empty for forty years, since the long war began and the last king rode out to rule from the saddle. In Year 715 the war has only just stopped, the chair is still empty, and the man who does most of the talking from the gold one is Kagenori Tenrai Moto, who has wanted the red one for twenty years and whom nobody can accuse of having said so.
The Hall of Verdicts is the kingdom’s high court and its only real council: a dome, seven chairs, a black stone dais and a Kurenai executioner’s office attached. Under the old law it can summon every Warlord of the north to answer for the conduct of his house, and it does, and they sometimes come. The north has said “the Seven Warlords” for longer than the Guild can trace, names six houses when asked, and gets vague and looks at the fire when pressed on the seventh. This shelf has noted it and moved on.
The kingdom was built simple by design, because complexity in governance is a luxury cold climates cannot afford and because the clans would not have accepted a system they could not understand. The Crown’s authority is meant to rest on two sources that reinforce each other. Competence, the King holds the throne because the King can do the job. Blood, the Shingan (the Moto’s sight, which reads a thing’s stress lines the way a smith reads a bar), the Hataraki inheritance and the Kōkan Line’s native relationship with the Plane of Fate produce a sovereign whose authority is felt before it is argued.

A competent king without the bloodline would be respected but not feared. A bloodline heir without competence would be feared but not followed.

The Ashen Crown
Ironwork set with garnet, forged by a smith of the deep holds whose name the Moto archives record and whose descendants still hold the commission. Older copies call the smith Dawi; the people of those holds are the Marrowkin now, and the page has followed them.

The crown is inscribed, and the inscriptions do real work. They carry the sovereign’s recognition into the metal, the metal carries it into the land, and the land’s response is what the Crown’s authority actually rests on.
A pretender who placed the Ashen Crown on their head would feel the rejection the way a smith feels a bad weld: as wrongness at the structural level, visible to anyone with sufficient Attunement to read it.
The Crown selects for the bloodline. The bloodline selects for competence. The system is recursive.

The crown is kept in the Hall. The Tenrai have not tried it on, and they have been careful to be seen not trying.
The Banner Oaths
Personal, sworn by each house’s lord to the reigning sovereign. Military service at call, tax in kind and coin, maintenance of roads and signal posts, submission to the Crown’s justice in disputes between houses. In exchange: territorial integrity, military support, external trade, and no interference in internal governance.

The oaths do not outlast the reign. When a king dies or leaves the chair, each house chooses whether to re-swear.
This is the mechanism by which the kingdom expresses the conditional nature of its loyalty: the Crown earns the oaths, the oaths are not inherited, and a successor who cannot earn them does not hold the kingdom.

With no one in the chair there is no one to swear to, so in Year 715 the houses are held by the old summons law, Tenrai silver and the Tenrai toll-post on the road, and all three of those are resented in a different voice. See The Banner Houses of Kharven.
Wealth and What It Trades
A cold-climate economy is an economy of scarcity managed through discipline.
Exports: ironwood timber and furs and hides through the banner lands, preserved game, military service, and the one thing only the Seat has, a judgment from the Hall of Verdicts, which foreigners pay for and then complain about. Imports: grain beyond the Greenhollow’s yield, the Marrowkin’s metalwork, the inscription stock ward-craft requires, and sealed casks of Wellspring water from the Wellheads, carried round the Scourge of Hell by road and north from Ashbury by river barge for the Seat’s ward-cutters.

The balance is perpetually tight. A kingdom with a four-month growing season and an eight-month heating season does not generate surplus. It generates sufficiency, maintained through household discipline, communal storage, and the absolute unwillingness to waste anything.
The corridor to Marrowhold is the kingdom’s most critical external dependency. When it functions, the economy functions. When the holds restrict it, the kingdom feels it within weeks, because a northern economy has no reserves deep enough to absorb a sustained interruption, and because the Marrowkin understand this and calibrate their restrictions accordingly.

Past the last warden’s round almost nothing here is paid in coin. It is grain, salt, cloth, fuel, a day’s labor owed and settled at year’s end. A Nalūn salt bar passes as money from the river to the treeline. Where coin does change hands it is copper, and the Seat has had three copper famines in living memory, during which a dead man’s boots bought a month’s firewood.
Rent, Food and the Street
Kharven-Seat in the deep of winter is the brightest thing for a hundred leagues: bonfires in every yard, seal-fat lamps the color of butter in the longhouse windows, and on the frozen river the ice brackets, with the Scarlet Scarves and the Wolf Grays turning out to settle a year’s grudges in front of anyone with a coin for the bookies. Rent in the lower town is paid in split wood as often as in silver, and a landlord who takes your coin and lets you run out of wood has broken something no court needs to look at.
The greeting is a forearm grip, which is diagnostic, since a man can feel how thin you have got through a sleeve. Then “How’s your stack?”, which means your woodpile and means everything else as well. Stack-Count comes with the first frost that will not lift, when every house squares its pile against the wall and the headman walks the lanes with witnesses. The hunger at the end of winter is the Thin Weeks, and it is a date on the calendar, in the sense that a hanging is.
Supper is bone broth and windmeat (meat dried hard in the cold air) and stonecurd (a dried cheese like a pebble). After it comes the skin, fermented milk in a sealskin, which you drink, because refusing the skin is an insult and a man has been killed over it at a family funeral. The first bowl goes to the one who cannot fill it themselves. The heated stone beside your bed is a night-stone, and it is handed down.
Practitioners are thick on the ground, since a cold country pays well for anyone who can keep a roof warm: hedge-workers who talk the frost off a rye field, lamp-wardens who charge double in the dark months and know you will pay it, ward-cutters on the Seat’s walls who are the best paid and most frequently sued people in the north. Kharven fighters call the aura coat the hide, Pressure (the weight a stronger soul puts on a room) the low sky and sensing smelling a man’s stack, and they will argue with a Guild roll over which words are more accurate, at length, over the skin. The heralds cry the bracket results on the river stair, the minstrels have them wrong by the following week, and a bounty posted in the Hall square is copied by hand and is on doors in Ashbury inside a fortnight.
The dead. The Seat buries in the ground and the clans beyond it give their dead to the sky. Either way the dead lie first in the death-house, which is never heated, and the family and the street sit with them through the Waiting. The Sōhai (the Moto’s own faith) lives in the household labors of the kingdom, mostly among people who would be astonished to hear they were religious: the ration weighed in public, the woodpile squared, fourteen scratches on the doorpost. See Sōhai, the Whole Bow.
Culture
Two traditions that have learned to coexist without fully merging. The Moto tradition, Japonic in its naming, and its own thing in its spiritual architecture and its relationship to authority and inherited duty. The northern tradition, Nordic in its pragmatism, its honor codes, its relationship to land and earned respect. Neither fully, but something specific to Kharven: a hybrid carrying the severity of both and the softness of neither.

Honor in Kharven is a climate.
The cold does not care about your intentions. It cares about your actions. Did you store enough firewood? Did you repair the roof before the snow? Did you share food with the family whose harvest failed? Did you show up when the Crown called?
A man who speaks beautifully and lets his neighbor starve is not honorable. A man who says nothing and splits his woodpile with the household down the road is.
The system produces a population that finds southern courtesy slightly absurd, because courtesy is what you practice when survival is not the primary concern, and survival is always the primary concern in Kharven.

The northern clans respect competence and fear the Moto’s blood. Children are taught never to meet a Moto’s eye before they are taught the forearm grip, and a clansman speaking to the Hall looks at the chest, the hands or the floor. The fear is not irrational, a lord who can see the stress lines in your soul, and whose judgment carries the weight of the Plane of Fate’s administrative function, is not a lord you displease casually.
What they joke about. Southern courtesy, southern coats, anyone who owns a third pair of boots. The Tenrai (“the only family that can lose a war for forty years and bill you for it”). The lift-cage. Wet wood, which is what you call a liar, and an empty saddle, which is what you call a man who was not there when the ride went out. Moto jokes are made with the door shut, by people looking at the floor. A full stack speaks louder than a full mouth is the proverb, and every man who has ever said it was talking.
Law and How It Fights
The law is short. A man’s word given before witnesses binds him, disputes between neighbors go to the headman and then to the fist, disputes between houses go to the Hall, and what the Hall decides goes on the rock in a clerk’s hand nobody in the lower town can read. Almost no one among the clans can read at all: a man signs with his mark, the woodpile is counted and never written, and the readers are the Moto and the Hallenfeld quartermasters. On the nameless day, which falls in the dead of winter and belongs to no one, scores are settled, because a killing on a day when no oath holds carries no blood-debt. The old clans hold that the death-house takes what it takes, and the Waiting begins the first named morning after.
The fighting. The Seat’s own troops are Tenrai house-guard, about twelve hundred in gold and crimson, with banner levies behind them when anyone can make them come, and practitioners of seven lines in the Hall who would very much rather not be asked. The north fights in knots and wedges. In the Seat’s yards you will see great swords and axes in the cold, boar-spears on the road, and a bracket fighter for every lane, each of them screaming the name of a technique their mother disapproves of. Sects come with colors and songs: the Thrawn Yard of the Kharven Marches, in undyed wool and one red thumb, whose whole style is to stand still, take it and hit back once; and the Kagerō-ryū (the Heat-Shimmer School) of Moto country, who regard the Thrawn Yard as a weather event.
The primary defense is the territory itself. An army marching from the south must cross three hundred miles of forest and highland in conditions that degrade equipment, consume supplies and kill soldiers through exposure before the fighting begins. From the west, the Greymane ridgeline. From the north there is nothing to approach from.
Monsters on the Roads
Monsters move, following prey, Aether and the marching of armies, and they live across the whole of the Inner World, so the hunting hall in the lower town keeps its board three bills deep like any hall on the rim.
The beasts do most of the killing and collect none of the songs. Elk, lynx and brown bear keep the boreal woods, and a bear woken early in the Thin Weeks has taken the door off a longhouse to get at the windmeat. The wolverine is the one the clans respect, because it will carry off a drying rack with a man sitting under it and come back later for the man. Char and pike run thick in the rivers, and the shaggy little horses will bite anything that is not currently feeding them.
The monsters. Greater Wolves (Grade C on the Bestiary’s scale, which runs from E to EX and prices every bounty in the world) work the Castle Stair in packs and will flank a column in a whiteout. In a bad Thin Weeks a Wendigo (Grade S) may come down off the shelf road, and the clans say it was somebody once, and they will tell you whom. Droval, the Frost-Howlers, stray south of the treeline in the hardest winters.
The Hum
The dungeon (what a Wellspring Core makes around itself, or what grows up around one) everyone talks about is the Hum, a drowned stair going down from the Skeldmere’s north shore under an ice-cutter’s hut, a Well of Abyntheus (a Wellspring of deep naval blue, whose slow throb is felt in the teeth before it is heard). Its spawn wear masks of deep naval blue. It has never been cleared. The Scarlet Scarves and the Wolf Grays each claim to have reached the Lower Workings, and each has the funerals to prove it. The hut is still let, to a family of ice-cutters who charge a copper to stand in it and put your teeth against the doorpost. The assay fork rings true on the top step, the air smells of cold iron, and every crew reports the same two things from the first gallery: a slow pressure that comes and goes like a tide with no water in it, and a sudden sharp knowledge of what someone a long way off is doing. At the Midwinter Brackets the bookies run a depth book on the Hum alongside the ice, and the old boys of both schools will fight you in the street over the last gallery either has mapped, which on the evidence of the two maps is the same gallery from opposite ends. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
The Scourge and the Turn
The Scourge of Hell lies far to the south, past the Hollow and the salt basin, and nobody has ever seen the sword from the Seat’s roofs. It arrives anyway. The Turn is the old rotation by which North, South and Center each spend nine years keeping the Scourge’s monsters off everybody else, and on the North’s Turn the North means Kharven and its Banner Houses. The Hall of Verdicts calls the houses under the old summons law, Tenrai silver pays the bounties on the rim doors, and the columns go out through the Foot and down the Kessen road in good order, past Ashmore’s grain, to keep the Line, the chain of forts and beacon towers round the Scourge’s outer belt. The last Northern Turn ran from 694 to 703, with the long war going on at the same time, and the South will tell you the two were hard to tell apart, since a Northern Turn has a way of losing the road and arriving at someone’s castle. At the handover the commander is supposed to give his successor a broken spear at the Turnstone, a black pillar on the western rim off the Kessen road. The Seat sent its spear by courier and asked for a receipt.
In Year 715 the Center holds the Turn, until 721, so Kharven’s whole part is to watch the southern road, send a clerk to write everything down and add it to the Count, the running bill the three parties present to one another. The wheel comes back to the North in 721, and the lower town already speaks of it the way it speaks of the Thin Weeks, as a date. As for the sword, the Moto have a word for it that they do not use in front of guests, and I have been a guest.
The Neighbors





































PowerStandingThe Banner landsSix houses around the Seat, each with its own grievance and its own page: the Cobalt March, the Slate Ridge, the Golden Hollow, the Scarlet Wood, the Aurora Reach, the Painted Rivers. Tenrai factors sit in most of their towns, and Tenrai taxes come out of most of their barnsThe Ember Holds of MarrowholdThe most critical economic relationship and the most complicated political one. The Marrowkin treat Kharven as a useful buffer, an armed frontier absorbing threats from the polar regions and Undaar-Keth without requiring their own troops. The Ore Council’s standing posture, inscription stock on schedule while grain is cut, is the holds saying: we want you armed and we want you hungry, because an armed and hungry frontier serves our interests better than an armed and independent oneThe Silver Cedars of YukariFar down the salt road, with the whole Center in between. Kharven believes governance requires sovereign judgment, a crown that decides. The Yukari believe it requires distributed competence, a council that measures. The Moto and the Yukari have been watching each other across this disagreement for longer than the Guild’s count runs, and the peace is quiet because both sides know what testing it would costThe Iron Mandate of Undaar-KethThe cold peace across the Greymane ridgeline. What answers the Mandate is Kharven’s cold, well ahead of Kharven’s courage: Stone-Blood runs slow at thirty below, and the lateness is the only currency the Shield has ever hadThe Holy Sea of AlabasterDistant, poor in grain, and doctrinally entangled with Kharven in a way no trade ledger records. Its territory stands on the white shelf that was the seat of the Long Reading, which makes the Moto’s relationship with it an inheritance question wearing a diplomatic coat. Its Wellspring is testimonial and its whole apparatus is built to weigh a sworn account, the one commodity a starving kingdom can still produce in quantity. A Sancta Lux chapter hold operates inside its territory. The practical consequence: a petition sent south is read twice, once by a realm that has reason to listen and once by an order that has reason not toThe Guild AccordTreats Kharven as a peripheral power whose military capability exceeds its political influence. The first circle of the Accord signed in Kharven-Seat’s lower hall, which the Seat brings up at dinner. Enforcement holds jurisdiction in theory and limited access in practice, cooperation being calibrated to produce exactly enough compliance to avoid a formal dispute and not one measure more. The Accord has no instrument that binds here, so anything done in Kharven is lawful until someone strong enough says otherwiseThe Center and the SouthThe long war of forty years went through the Center as wars do, down the two roads round the Scourge of Hell, and the Southern Warlords sold to it and bled in it. None of the seven was ever bound by the Kōkan crown. See the Southern Warlords
The King the Songs Are About
Later hand, to the end of this section.
I will set this down short, because everyone who reads it will have heard the song, and the ballads have him wrong in at least four keys.
In Year 715, the morning that shelf is sealed, Muken Moto is about sixteen and nobody at the Seat could pick him out of a line. Within a few winters he has taken Kharven-Seat and the crown it was already keeping for someone, and he has done the thing the old kings of a hall and a day’s ride could not, which is to make that crown mean the whole north. Then he goes on past it and builds an empire, and the Moto name it Whitemere, and the Kharven have never once called it that among themselves. They call it the Stack, after the woodpile, because everything that arrives from the Seat arrives as an addition to a count that somebody has to keep. Kharven stays what it was, the one true kingdom and the capital. The banner lands stay lands.
The minstrels have the rest, and they may keep it. This hand has no death of his to record.
