geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Moonlight Forest of Mosk-Vaal
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
The Moss Court of the Verdant Orcs, one of the four Central Warlords, on the wet west flank of the Inner World’s center

GO ROUND.
Painted on a board at Rootgate in four tongues, with a basket of pears hung under it. The basket is refilled daily, and the board has been repainted more often than any royal portrait in the Midmarch.

Every autumn the fruit-sellers on the bridge at Kingsbridge cry a fat red pear called a Vantry, and every buyer over forty knows why it tastes the way it does. In the wet spring of 683 Captain-General Piers Vantry brought the Third Column of the Aldwater League, a coalition of Midmarch kings that lasted three years, to the edge of the Moonlight Forest, four thousand men in blue and yellow with a hired Marrick company at the center, because the Kessen road round the forest was eleven days longer and he was late for a battle. At Rootgate an envoy seven feet tall, in a cloak of white moth-wings, with eyes like two green lamps, handed him a basket of pears and said in excellent Common that the forest would much prefer he went round. Vantry ate a pear on horseback in front of his staff, remarked that it wanted salt, threw the core in the water, and ordered the column onto the causeway with every drum going. By all accounts it was a glorious sight for six days, blue and yellow banners under a tree the size of a mountain, the lake lit teal from below, and the men singing. At noon on the sixth day the Marrick contract ran out. Two hundred spearmen grounded their ash spears, faced about and walked home between a great many green eyes that watched them go and did nothing, and they told the first tavern they reached that this was the worst thing they had ever seen. On the seventh night the moon came up full, the black water on both sides of the causeway rose by the width of a hand with no rain falling, and the Third Column’s rear rank discovered that the people behind them had come up out of it. It took until morning. The water ran red as far as Glowwater, and the moths came down on it in such numbers that the fishers say the lake looked snowed on.
The Court buried the column where it had stood, in its ranks, in the good black silt below the causeway, and planted a pear whip on every man. The orchard is there still: three thousand eight hundred trees in company order, sergeants a pace out in front, the drummers in a neat line on the flank, and on a little rise the largest tree of all, which fruits a week ahead of the others and has the sweetest crop. Dame Emmot Vantry sued for it. She brought her claim before the Fair Court at Harrowgate, arguing that the fruit of her husband was his estate, and the Moss Court replied on a sheet of birch bark that it had no objection whatever. The Fair Court awarded her the pears. A basket has gone to the Vantry family every autumn since, with an itemized bill for the tending, and the family, I am told, has never once been ahead on the transaction.

The premise, in one breath. A nation of wetland orcs for whom death is a phase, living in a shining city grown into the roots of a glowing tree, who ask every army politely to go round and then bury and farm the ones that do not.

I catalog this page with some care, as an archivist of the Guild who has been asked to go round and did.
The Land
Come down the Kessen road from Kingsbridge and the first thing to change is the color of the night. The Moonlight Forest lies on the west flank of the Scourge of Hell, in the lowest, wettest ground of the center, where the Aldwater goes to pieces in a hundred channels and the rain that will not fall on the Scourge comes down instead, nine days across by the causeway when the causeway is dry, and it glows. At its middle stands a colossal tree whose whole height shines an ice-blue, reflected whole in a still teal lake, and in the roots of that tree the city of Mosk-Vaal is grown in shining green and gold. Around the shore rise tall stalks that carry their own light, thick as temple columns. Tree-houses sit in the crowns under masses of magenta blossom, and small soft lights drift between them with no one carrying them. On any clear night a single small ship can be seen crossing the lake on its own reflection, and the people aboard are generally selling something.
Out past the lake the forest turns to mire: moss-green glow on every trunk, white moths in drifts, and water like black glass, which is lovely until you have stepped in it. These are the most beautiful places a goblinoid has ever lived in. The orcs will tell you so while something unpleasant happens to your boots.
The light follows the moon, which earned the forest its name. The ground here is rich in Luminalis, the Hidden Light, the moon’s own kind among the sixty Wellsprings (the sixty types of Aether, the raw power of the world, each of which works on a Soul Crystal in its own way), with Manganthra, the Wellspring of rot, and Verdantia, the Wellspring of growth, lying thick beneath it. At the full moon you can read a contract by the moss. At the dark of the moon the forest sinks to a dull ember and the whole population turns cautious and short with each other. In the street’s words the forest is fat ground, which fills a practitioner quickly, and a fighter who has fed on it often comes up short when he leaves.
The Measurewrights cannot agree on what the great tree is. The Court says it is the eldest of the Soul-Trees, and that it knows whose. The Guild survey of 640 calls it a tree that happens to be growing on the richest worked site in the center, a Core in common speech, and notes that the surveyor was asked to go round before he finished. Two later readings dispute both. I have touched the bark. I can report that it is warm and that I felt I was being remembered.
The House and Who Rules
The Verdant Orcs are Shard-kin, a people descended from fragments that struck the world in the First Impact, and theirs landed in high-resonance wetlands. Where the Ironblood carry the violence of that impact, the Verdant carry its aftermath: stone turning to soil, decay feeding growth. When the Crimson Order made its Refusal and some forty years of grinding expulsion scattered the goblinoid peoples to every quarter, the Verdant bands slipped into the deep wetlands of the interior and were not seen for centuries. When they were next seen they had a country.
They stand six foot four to seven feet, with long vine-like muscle built for moving silently under water. Their eyes are solid lamps of moss-green or pale lunar white. Their skin is the green of old forest, with hard bark along the shoulders and luminous fungus at the joints and collarbone, which they tend and trim as a northern lord tends his beard. An old wound on a Verdant Orc pulses cold silver-green, and they show their scars the way other people show their children.
The Moss Court is the house, and it is grown and never built. Its hall is a chamber of living bark in the great tree’s roots, widening by about a hand each century, with bark-shapers on retainer to argue with it. The Court has no fixed roll of lords. It sits in a Spoor-Meld, the group meditation in which participants release Aetheric spores into a shared cloud of mind, visible as green mist at knee height, and inside that cloud the tribe shares memory and feeling directly, with no language required. A decision of the Court is what the mist feels like when it clears. Outside envoys are seated upwind and told the result.
The one fixed office is the Mire-Mother, the voice that speaks for the Court to anyone who does not have spores. The office goes by lungs. Swamp Parun, the Verdant hand of Parunic (the script and speech that writes boundaries onto laws), runs on a single unbroken breath, so a Verdant working can only be as large as the speaker’s chest. When a Mother dies, or as the Court prefers to say, moves on, the candidates go under the black water at Glowwater on the first full moon, with the whole shore packed, the bookies on stilts and three days of fried eel, and each speaks the largest working she can on one breath. The present Mother, Ssaaleth the Long Breath, took the office by speaking a full Third Seal (a working of the third and heaviest order of Parunic speech) from the bottom of the lake, and the moths rose off the water for a mile in every direction when it took. She is enormous, cheerful and very old, wears a mantle of moth-wing she has personally eaten most of the former owners of, and has never been known to raise her voice. The Court’s words are We Will Keep It For You. Its colors are moss-green and moth-white.
Cities and Towns
Mosk-Vaal is the seat, in the roots of the tree, and the name means roughly “the moss that stays awake.” Its streets are water and root. You go by punt or along the high root-walks, past fungus-lit doorways and market rafts, and the glow changes hue block by block, as each quarter’s gardeners feud over whose moss is finer. Foreigners may enter by leave of the Court, and they are asked to leave their salt at the landing.
Rootgate stands at the northern head of the causeway, and it is the one town where outsiders sleep without an invitation. It has the board and the pears, along with innkeepers, money-changers, guides of varied honesty and a fee-house for the causeway. It will also sell you a burial plot before you go on down the rim, at a discount for paying in advance, and it is the only place on the Scourge’s edge where the prices fall as your chances do. Half the people on the street are orcs, and the other half are carriers and factors from the Amber Cities pretending not to be nervous.
Glowwater is the lake port, a town of dyers and moss-gatherers whose forearms are stained luminous for life, and of little ships with lamp-stalks at the bow. The succession dive takes place off its main stair.
Ghurash Hollow is the oldest Verdant settlement on the Guild’s roll and holds the greatest of the Ancestor-Rot Gardens. The Verdant dead are laid there in sacred groves, and their decomposition feeds the growth of Soul-Trees, each tree carrying the compressed Aetheric signature of the person it grew from. People come to visit their grandmothers and quarrel with them. Walking through it is walking through accumulated lives.
The Blooming Mire is the marriage town, a square league of flowering fen that stinks gloriously in season. Certain phrases of Swamp Parun, spoken on saturated ground, can tip Verdant listeners into a Spoor-Meld they were not attempting, so the wedding speeches here are cleared in advance, and they go wrong every year anyway.
Totemdeep is half under water, a town of carved trunks standing in the flood, each one a school’s standard. It is where the Verdant fighting lodges train, and its children learn Beast-Sign before they learn to swim, a very short gap.
The Orchard is no town at all, yet it appears on every map, and it has a gatekeeper.
Wealth and Trade
Mosk-Vaal sells what comes up. Its fruit goes north and south by barge and carrier, and the Vantry pear is only the most famous of the cuts; the orchard of the Second Battle of Rootgate gives a small hard quince that a Kingsbridge cook will fight you for. Moss-dye that keeps its glow for a season is the next great line, and it dresses half the festival banners of the center. Moth silk is white and light as breath, and every thread of it is someone’s patient life’s work. Physic is the third, and it is the one the armies come for: a green rot-wife can pack a wound with a mold that eats the poison from it and leaves the flesh, and the molds cost dear and spoil if taken far from the wet. Tarnish-reagents, cut from the Manganthra pools, go to every alchemist from Sealhall to the Wellheads. Living lamp-stalks, cut green, burn a whole season on a little water, and the lamp-wardens of the Amber Cities have twice gone on strike against them.
The Court also takes two fees. The causeway fee is paid by anyone who insists on crossing, and it is cheap for a carrier and ruinous for a regiment. The reclaiming fee is paid by families who would like a body back, and it rises each year the tree has been growing, for the Court considers by then that the tree has rights.
Soul-Tree wood is never sold. A foreigner found with a piece of it is not asked where he got it.
Rent, Food and the Street
No one in Mosk-Vaal rents a room, because no one in Mosk-Vaal built one. A household asks a grower for a chamber, waits about nine years while it comes in, and owes that grower’s line a share of its work for as long as the room lives. Young couples sleep in a cousin’s root. A foreigner at Rootgate pays ordinary inn prices in plain coin, and the blanket is moss, and in the morning it is a little bigger.
The Verdant cook is the finest and most dangerous in the center. Swamp Parun has more words for different kinds of rot than any other tongue has for weather, and a menu reads like a calendar: black-water rice left to turn for three moons, eel smoked over punk-wood, mushroom beer the color of old brass, a cheese that has to be held down, and moon-pears poached in something you would rather not have explained. Dark-moon food is plain and sulky, and full-moon food is an event. Street stalls sell fried moth-grubs in paper-thin bark cones, and on feast nights the entire lake is ringed with cook-fires, each one a slightly wrong color.
The street is small powers from end to end. For a couple of coppers a hedge-worker will ripen your fruit overnight or put a rot in your neighbor’s fence that can be traced to no one, and a rind-wife will take the fungus off a sore joint and tell you your future from it. All of them can refuse you, and they often do, because the moon is wrong. Funerals here are merry and long, with drinking at the graveside and a great deal of cheerful advice for the deceased. Mention that you are grieving and someone will ask what you plan to plant.
Law
Death is a phase, so death is no punishment, and a foreigner who has been told this usually takes it for a comfort until the matter is explained further. The great Verdant crime is against the cycle: hoarding a body, keeping a corpse from the ground, poisoning a garden. The great Verdant penalty is the Salt Sentence, by which a convicted orc is buried in salted ground, worked by hedge-workers so that Aether will not pool on it and nothing will grow. The condemned gets no tree, and the family gets nobody to quarrel with for the rest of time. It has been carried out nine times in the record, and every one of the nine is named as a warning to children.
Salt itself is under law. A sealed cask may pass under Court license; a spilled one is a capital matter for the carter, and the carter’s employer will get a very polite letter.
A debt does not die with the debtor. It passes to the tree, and a creditor may stand in the garden and demand payment from the tree’s living kin, who must come and hear it. In a Spoor-Meld among kin a lie shows, which makes Verdant testimony very reliable and Verdant family dinners very bad. An outsider has no spores to speak with, and so has no standing unless a native speaks for him, for a fee.
Toward everyone else the whole of the law is on the board at Rootgate.
How It Fights
The Moss Court has never in its history taken a foot of ground outside the wet, and the reason is written into the people’s bodies. A Verdant Orc more than forty-eight hours from swamp or kin begins to wither, losing strength by stacking measures until half of what the body can bear is gone, which is what scholars call Isolation Degeneracy and what the orcs call homesickness. In Radiant, Fire or Sun-aspected Domains (a Domain being the territory in which a practitioner high on the sixteen Stages of the climb makes his own law hold) they lose about a third of everything. They cannot go conquering, and no general has ever managed to explain this to the survivors.
At home they are a nightmare with excellent manners. Their fighting lodges go out in grown bark harness over the bark they were born with, moss-green eyes burning under the brow. The move the crowds wait for is Mire-Mother’s Yes: go under the black water at one end of a fight and come up behind you at the other, with friends. Beast-Sign, the Verdant gesture-language of some four hundred signals, runs a whole company in dead silence, and Crimson Order operatives who have studied its basics call it the most information-dense speech they know. A war-Meld lays green mist along the ground, and every orc in it feels every other, so an ambush moves like one animal thinking. Their big workings arrive slowly, on one enormous breath, and when one lands on an army the rot goes through leather, rope, bowstrings and then men, and the whole field begins to bloom.
They have their own quarrel with the shared arts. The aura coat, the visible coat of a fighter’s own color, is ak-gresh, the survived skin, in Low Goblintongue, and the Verdant call it ssuul, the rind, and insist that a good one should be peeled off and left behind. Pressure (the weight of a higher Stage felt in the room) they call the damp. To sense a stranger is to ask the moss.
The counters are known, and I set them down for fairness. Bring a Sun-aspected Domain and the strength to hold it in a forest that hates it. Take the fight onto salted or bled ground, which means carrying a great deal of salt across nine days of people who object to it. Keep your enemy from kin past the second day, if you can catch one. Or fight at the dark of the moon, when they are at their weakest and most irritable, and bear in mind that everything you kill goes straight back in the ground and is on their side by summer.
What They Joke About
They joke about everything, at length. The Verdant consider themselves the only funny people in the center, and on the matter of Ironblood they may be right: “Ironblood rings are a very heavy way to remember your own name.” They ask a guest how ripe he is feeling, and they tell the Hundred Crowns that they have a lovely spot picked out. The standard Verdant toast translates as “See you later,” and it is a threat only if you are not family.
The others joke back. Nobody in the Midmarch will take a pear from a stranger, and “going round” is street talk in six towns for a sensible surrender. The Scalebond note that the Verdant have been making the same joke for eleven hundred years. Everyone agrees that the smell of a moth-wing cloak is one you get used to, and everyone agrees that this is the frightening part.
Monsters on the Roads
Very little here will bother you if you have been polite. Mourning Pike (Grade A on the Bestiary’s scale, which runs from E to EX, bred on Thaloré ground with teal over the skull) and Sump-toads hold the deep channels, Reaching Briars are regarded as a kind of pet, and swamp-grown Hydra (Grade X) stories are told to children and also to generals. The orchards are not, strictly, monsters. The wild things are mostly food: eels, frogs and the enormous soft moths whose grubs turn up fried at every stall. Nothing on four legs crosses the mire without someone’s leave, and the deer of the outer gardens have a thoughtful look.
The great tree stands on the richest worked site in the Center, and the Court keeps it. The Guild’s list of famous dungeons enters it as never cleared, with the note that it has joined the government. The dungeon people talk about is the Tarnish Pools below Ghurash Hollow, Manganthra sumps where rot-wives cut their reagents from the upper levels and from which, at the dark of the moon, something older sends up a smell that makes the Soul-Trees drop their leaves. The Mire-Mother’s divers have cleared it four times, in the sense of planting a garden on top. The Verdant word for any such place is a garden gone to seed, on the reasoning that something ought to be growing on all those adventurers, and something is. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
Beside the Scourge
The rain that will not fall on the Scourge of Hell comes down here, and that one fact draws the forest’s eastern edge as if with a ruler: moss and black water on one side, and a day’s ride the other way a country that has not seen a cloudburst in a decade. The Kessen road runs down that seam. Every sensible carter takes its long loop round the forest, eleven days between the eastern eaves and the Hem (the Scourge’s outermost belt, fifteen leagues of black-barked thornwood and pale dust), with the dry wind on his left shoulder going south and green lamps among the trees on his right. The forest calls this stretch the salt road, because that is what comes along it, and letters meant for the real salt road on the Scourge’s far flank have gone astray on that account. Wyrms (Grade SS) with scales the size of shields run under the black roots along here, and Hellhounds and Bicorns (Grade A) work the near rim. The Rootgate board has no opinion on any of them.
The Court’s answer to all of it is the one it gives everybody. It lets things come in, and it plants them. A stilt, one of the great herd animals on legs as long as a ship’s mast, goes down to the barrel when it wades past the third channel and stays there, and the greywalkers following it in their dust-colored files find the footing going soft and the water coming up behind them. The Scourge bed of the great garden runs a very long way down the eastern eaves on what has been fed to it, in trees I could not name and the rot-wives would not, and its fruit is kept for family. As for the colossal bronze-hilted sword at the Scourge’s center, with a field of violet stars where its blade should be, the Court holds that it is a stake, holding up something that has not finished growing, and that it can wait.
The Turn runs North, then South, then Center, nine years each, with the holder keeping a Line of forts around the Hem and the other two counting what it costs. A host bound for the Line on the North’s Turn or the South’s reads the board, goes round, and gets a pear. The Center holds the Turn now, from 712 to 721, and the Court’s share is set by its people’s bodies: an orc two days from swamp or kin begins to wither, so it mans no fort past the wet. It takes the dead. Every cart of bodies that reaches Rootgate from the Line is planted free, whoever sent it, and in the Center’s Count (the bill each party presents when a Turn ends) the Moss Court’s contribution appears as three lines on birch bark, with a cutting attached, which the auditors at Sealhall have to water.
Neighbors and Grudges
The Amber Cities of Nalūn are the great grudge, and the great customer. The Kessen road runs along the forest’s edge, and every salt carter on it is a walking insult. The Court buys their coin and their silver and has never forgiven them a single spilled cask, and the councils of the salt cities keep a clerk whose only work is apologizing.
The Hundred Crowns of the Midmarch march through. One petty king in every generation decides that the causeway is the short way, and most of the fine fruit trees of the outer gardens have a coat of arms on a little plaque.
The Rose Coils of Coilspire treat the same armies and keep a precise record of how many the Court has planted. Relations are polite, and the Scalebond are the only foreigners ever invited to read a garden.
The Sealed Charter of the Concord has no good law for a people who are neither Beastkin nor quite on its rolls. It sends a surveyor once a generation, and formal notices rather more often. The surveyors are asked to go round, and the notices come back with things growing on them.
The Ironblood and the Crimson Order regard the Verdant as cousins who have gone strange. The feeling is warm and mutual.
The North and the South know the forest as the place on the map where armies go missing, and the Moss Court is content with that.

In a later hand, in the margin: When the Northern Empire of Whitemere began to come south in the years of its building, its quartermasters read this page and paid the causeway fee in advance, in full, for a column that then went round. The Court sent back a basket. I am told it was the first time anyone in the Stack had been seen to look at a pear with respect.



The Goblinoid Peoples
The Central Warlords

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Ochre Fields of Hammerford
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itHAM-er-ford · MARE-ick
The Long Fields · The Wall for Hire · Shoulder to Shoulder
Go to Hammerford by the south road and the first thing you will see, before the gatehouse, is a broken cart. It sits by the ford at the little bridge, tipped on one snapped axle, with its tailboard hanging, in a neat cobbled square of its own, and the most dangerous infantry in the Inner World take their hats off when they go past. It has been there since the hiring fair of 631. The carter was a barley-man named Dob Harkness, who broke his axle that morning in the worst possible place, with the only ford for ten miles blocked behind him and, on either bank, the paymasters of two kings who had come to buy the same eight thousand spears. Neither would go around, and each sent men to shift the cart, and both sets of men got into a fight on the bridge. The Captain of the day, Old Marget Marrick, climbed up onto the load in her ochre and black, sat down on a barley sack, called for a jug, and offered the whole levy to the higher bidder on the spot.
It took a day and a night. Every soul in the Long Fields came down to watch, with drums and sausages, and the bookies set up on the bridge. The kings’ men shouted their offers across the barley with their voices going, and Dob Harkness, who had grasped his position by about noon, began charging them rent for the use of his cart. The price went past anything a spear had ever been worth. At dawn Old Marget accepted both, split the levy down the middle, had the contracts signed on the tailboard, four copies, and added a clause in her own hand: this hire stands as long as the cart stands at the ford. Both armies had Marrick companies at their center at Sorley Bridge that autumn. Nine thousand went into the ground on the two sides. The Marrick dead were paid to the end of the season, to the widows, on the nail, and the two kings each hired again next spring.
So the cart stays. It has been repaired from end to end nine times by the Guild of Wrights, with every new axle sawn through and the break reset at the proper angle by a man with a sworn drawing. Nobody now living could tell you whether the clause still binds anyone. Every Marrick recruit touches the tailboard on the morning of her first muster, and Dob Harkness’s descendants still draw the rent.
The Long Fields are a land that grows barley and spearmen, sells the second by the season to anyone who pays, and has fought on both sides of every war for three hundred years without once taking it personally.
The Land and the Look
Hammerford is a great walled city of rose-brown stone, its long curtain wall and gatehouse facing the cobbled south road, its houses climbing a hill to a tall pale citadel, with that broken cart by the ford and its small bridge below the wall, and green country and blue mountains all around. On a clear evening the wall goes the color of a good loaf. Marrick does not care for decoration, but it does care for a wall, and the masons have been patching this one for three centuries and sign their work.
Beyond the walls the Long Fields run out flat and enormous between the Grey Plain and the marches of the Center, with the rim of the Scourge of Hell a long ride north of the last company’s stakes. The cobbled south road comes up to the gatehouse, the Kessen road passes on the west on its way to Sum-gol, and the northern roads run up into the Midmarch. It is muster country. After harvest the stubble is laid out in ochre and black squares, a patchwork a day’s ride across, each square a company’s drill ground, marked with limed stakes and tarred rope. The tent cities go up in rows, cook-smoke over them, drums going from before sunrise, and the spears: long ash spears in the thousands, standing in racks along every road with their shadows falling across the fields like a fence that goes on forever. In summer it is all barley, the color of a lion. Spearmen are one of the two crops, and they come in after the other.
The House
House Marrick sells the southern rank. The north fights in knots and wedges and long Keld lines that move like weather. The south fights in a wall, a rank of men standing shoulder to shoulder because they cannot trust themselves to stand anywhere else, and charging in it with a noise like a building falling over. That rank was Marrick’s before it was anyone else’s. The Long Fields have bred spearmen for three hundred years, first as the levy country of the Empire of Sum-gol, whose foot they were. On the day of the last Calling in 602 the company in the square looked up, saw it was noon and that their contract had expired, and grounded arms. Marrick considers this the greatest day in its history and has a holiday for it.
Its head is Gerrit Marrick, Captain of the Long Spear. He is sixty, loud, scarred, very funny, missing an ear, and the only warlord in the south who has fought in every war of the last forty years on at least two sides. He has been asked to wear a crown a number of times, generally by people who wished to have someone to blame, and he says there is no room for one under a helmet. The land is a kingdom by every test but the coronation; the Captain is chosen by the assembled company-captains, for life or until he loses their pay. “You stand in it because the man on your left is standing in it, lad. Brave’s got nothing to do with it.”
The words are Shoulder to Shoulder. The colors are ochre and black, in squares.
Cities and Towns
Hammerford holds fifty thousand in a hard winter, and half that in the campaigning season. The citadel is plain, tall and pale, and it holds the Captain’s Hall and the strongroom with every contract the house has ever signed. On the hill below are armorers, drum-makers and spear-shavers, who take an ash pole and bring it to true by eye in a long curl of white wood. The Hiring Hall sits on the Ford Square, and on the wall by its door anyone can read what any company costs this season. Rose-brown houses, red tile, and a tavern at every corner named for a battle in which its landlord was on the winning side, or the other one.
Spearmoot, which every Marrick and most maps call Pikemoot, stands at the center of the Fields and is mostly a very large meadow with a ring of old stones and a town of inns around it. The Scourge contracts are signed here. The company-captains meet here at midsummer in the Moot to vote for the Captain, settle precedence, fix the season’s rates, and break each other’s noses in the traditional order. The Moot Law, kept by rote and shouted once a year from the stones, is the closest thing the Fields have to a constitution. A stranger may buy a place on the ring at Moot for about the price of a good meal, and it is worth it.
Musterfield is the great drill-ground town to the north, a square league of beaten earth with a permanent street of sutlers, where recruits learn the rank in the stubble after harvest, sixteen deep. It is a raw, loud, cheerful place with very few old men in it. The Midmarch is a few days’ march away, and people in Musterfield tend to know which of its kings owes them money.
Wealth and Trade
Companies by the season: that is the crop, the export and the religion. Half the southern hosts in the war had Marrick companies at their center, and some years both halves. The house considers this a professional courtesy. Barley goes out by the cart, with beer, ash poles, drums and very good boots. There is also a brisk trade in veterans, because a Long Fields sergeant past his marching years can name his price as a drillmaster anywhere between Kessen ford and the sea. A cut of every contract goes to the Widows’ Chest in the citadel, and the most frightening person in the country is its keeper.
Rent, Food and the Street
Most land is held by company, and a family pays its rent in sons and daughters, a set number to each muster, or else in silver at a rate the Moot fixes and everyone complains about. Those who send a child pay nothing for that year, and the same system means that everyone on the Fields knows someone in every company and goes to all the funerals. In town a room costs about the ordinary city list, and a pitch in the tent lines costs a few coppers a week. People eat barley bread, onions, sour beer, blood sausage, hard yellow cheese, and a stew called the sergeant, because it is thick and it has been around for a long time and nobody knows what is in it.
The companies run the place like rival parishes at a ball game. Each has its colors within the squares, a drum-pattern you can tell at a mile, a song with disgusting verses and a long grudge. The Late Arrivals, the Stubble Boys, Mother Hallam’s Own, the Sixth Blacks, who are the fourth company of that name and do not wish to discuss it. Men fight in the street over a drummer’s honor and share a jug afterward. Hedge-workers cure blisters at a copper the foot and charm a shield-strap for two, and the blister-wives who follow the tent lines are the only people in the country a sergeant will salute. Anyone with an aura coat has a place on the corner of a rank, where one fighter who can take a blow makes the line behind him braver: they say the shine and the weight on the Fields, and a good corner is said to be “shining for the whole file.” Bookies take odds on the musters, the Moot and the weather. Minstrels get everything wrong, and the companies pay them to.
Law and How It Fights
The contract is the law. A Marrick company fights for its contract to the last day of the season and not one day past it. It has been known to finish a battle at noon on the day its contract ran out by grounding spears in the middle of the field and walking home through both armies, unharmed, because both armies would be hiring next season. Nobody touches a company walking off. That custom has held for three centuries, and a commander who broke it would find no spear for hire anywhere in the South, ever, including his own. Breaking a rank while under contract is death by the file, carried out by the file. The rest is settled by the sergeants, then the captains, then the Moot, and the fines go to the Widows’ Chest.
The rank is sixteen deep, long ash spears and drums. It works because no one in it can see anything but the back of the person in front and the shoulder at each side, which is exactly why it holds when any sensible person would run. A cavalry charge stops at it. The Yan know this and never try, and go around, and shoot, so the Marrick carry crossbow companies on their wings and big shields in the second rank. A high-Stage fighter can of course cut a hole in sixteen ranks, and the drill for that is older than anyone’s grandmother: the rank opens, lets him in, closes, and every crossbow within reach looses at the one target that cannot be mistaken for a friend. A bolt costs a few coppers. They consider the exchange fair. The other drill, equally old, is to send a sergeant over to ask what he is being paid and whether he would consider more.
What They Joke About
Everything, and the dead most of all. A Marrick joke is told in the rank, out of the side of the mouth, in the last minute before contact. They say a Marrick was once offered a place in the world to come and asked what it paid. They say a Lambert will tell you there are four thousand and eleven of you and a Marrick will tell you it’s plenty. Of the Yan: they’ve been running away for three hundred years and calling it a tactic. Of the Moto: you can tell a Moto lord’s about to lose because he’s stopped looking at you. Gerrit Marrick lost his ear to a Tenrai officer at a battle in which the two were on the same side, and tells that story at every Moot with a new ending.
Monsters on the Roads
Stilts (Grade B) come down off the Scourge rim in bad years and walk through the barley, thousands together on legs as long as a ship’s mast, and the companies take the contract at a rate fixed by the Moot. Greywalkers (Grade A) come after them in files at dusk, dust-colored until they rouse. Neiman Lions (Grade B) cross from the plains after horses. Beasts are the everyday trade: hares and bustards in the barley, foxes in the tent lines, kites following the drums for scraps, and great flocks of crows that make a nuisance of themselves at any muster.
The dungeon. It is the Long Barrow at Sorley Bridge: nine thousand dead went into one trench there in the autumn of 631, on both sides, and in the generation after it the trench turned, a Mortalis seep (the Wellspring of slow death, venous black-red) pooling under so many men paid to the end of the season. Ghouls (Grade B) and Skeletal Folk (Grade B) come up out of it in companies, in step. Every spring the Moot lets a clearing contract, recruits do their first real fighting there, and it has been cleared sixty times and never stayed cleared. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
Beside the Scourge. The Fields are the south side of the Scourge of Hell, and they live with it the way a farm lives with a river that floods. In August the dusty wind from the Center goes hot and starts to smell of iron and pollen, and the farmers north of Musterfield look at the sky and cut their barley green. That is the herds’ season, when thirst pushes them outward and what follows them comes too. Every stretch of northern stakes has a drum on a pole for it, with its own pattern, and a company a day’s march away that has already asked what the farmer is offering. Cutters, the free-company hunters who work the rim on Thresh contracts, come mostly from here and the Midmarch, and half the funerals everybody goes to have nothing in the coffin but boots.
The Turn. The great harvest is the Turn, the old wheel by which North, South and Center each spend nine years keeping the Scourge off the other two. A Southern Turn runs by the season, on contract, with subscription lists at Alabaster paying the bill and Marrick companies standing the Line. It is well run and it stops at sundown on the last day, which the North holds against them, accurately. The South last kept the Line from 703 to 712, and the Center holds it now, which is better still, since the Center pays by instrument and hires nearly all of its rank.
The Fields’ own story of it is Lastpenny, on the Kessen road, Midsummer Day of 676. Five thousand of the companies stood in the square in ochre and black with their arms folded while the biggest earth wyrm anyone living had seen ate the Corn Hall and the better half of Butter Row, because their contract began at noon, and the instant the clerk called it the drums came in. They drove the thing back down by lamplight and left nine hundred spears standing in its hide. It still comes up about every eleven years along that stretch, wearing them. Everyone calls it Old Pincushion, a sergeant can tell you by the marks whose pay each spear was, and there is a standing bet at Spearmoot on which company gets the next one in. In the Center a Marrick who declines to help you has said it isn’t noon, and you are entitled to spit. On the Fields it is what they say when the jug goes round before the contract starts.
Neighbors and Grudges
The Jade Plains. A line of boundary stones, a shared love of being paid and an annual brawl at Mashi. They have never once fought a real battle against each other on their own account, as neither sees what it would pay.
The Holy Sea. A good steady customer who audits. Lambert officers are the only outsiders to whom a Marrick sergeant will give an honest head-count, since they will get it anyway.
Sum-gol. Old employer, and the holiday still stings there. The Post pays on time when it can.
The Sapphire Wells and the Copper Coast. Both rent the rank by the season. Both have tried to buy a company outright, and been told a company is only for sale by the year, and that the year ends.
The Moto. Up the Kessen road past the whole of the Center, and the most lucrative customer on the map. The Fields want a long peace with a lot of small wars in it, and every house at the warlords’ table is working out what a Moto civil war will pay; Gerrit Marrick has been heard to say he has already sent in his rates. Later hand: the north becomes the Northern Empire of Whitemere in these same years, and the rank has been quoted to it too.
Further reading · The Southern Warlords

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Painted Rivers of Hallenfeld
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Art: JJPeabody.
The Painted Rivers of Hallenfeld
Say itHALL-en-feld
House Hallenfeld · The Junction · Movement
Every toll house on the Hallenfeld rivers is painted, and for a hundred and fifty years two guilds have fought over who gets to do it. The Limners of Threeways use gold leaf and paint saints. The Daubers of Chainbridge use whatever is cheapest and paint the reeve, unflatteringly, with his wife. In the spring of Year 699 the Limners, having lost the Long Toll contract, climbed the Chainbridge toll house by night and gave the reeve’s portrait a donkey’s hindquarters, and the Daubers replied by repainting the Threeways guild-hall door with a depiction of the Limners’ master that a passing bishop had to be helped away from. It came to brushes in the street, then to boathooks, and on the morning of the eighth day a Dauber barge carrying the guild’s entire year’s stock, ninety barrels of ultramarine, ocher and madder rose, was rammed amidships at the junction itself by a Limner lighter, with the crews going at it on the decks in full view of three towns.
It went down in the exact middle of the meeting of the rivers. For a week the Hallen ran blue, the Ruddle ocher and the Sleeve rose, three bright ribbons winding side by side for eleven miles below the junction, and all the swans of the lower valley turned the color of whichever river they had picked. Every washerwoman for a day’s walk took it to law. Five men had drowned and two were knifed. A Hallenfeld clerk, Wat Pennyquill, came down to the bridge with his book, looked at it for a while, entered ninety barrels of pigment at the river toll rate, and billed both guilds for carriage. The heralds tell you the realm gets its name from the toll houses. The people on the rivers know better, and if you look at a Hallenfeld sheep’s left side in a wet year you can still see why.
The Painted Rivers are three rivers, three roads, and a house of clerks who can stop the whole north with a chain and a sharp remark, and who would prefer to be thanked.

Two hands on this page. It stands in Year 715. Lines marked Later hand come from the annotator of the Concordance of Ages, writing in the last winter before the turn. Later hand: the Rivers are a land of House Hallenfeld inside the Northern Empire of Whitemere, and the empire’s roads, rivers and letters all run through them.

The Land and What It Looks Like
The river valleys south and east of Kharven-Seat, running down from the plateau and the March to the Greenhollow, low and green-gold and busy, and in thaw or harvest more crowded than any place in the north has a right to be. The realm is a junction: three rivers (the Hallen, the Ruddle and the Sleeve) coming together at the meeting of the three principal roads of the north, and the whole of it packed with barges stem to stern, poled and sailed and hauled, loaded with grain and salt, ironwood, furs, ore and every kind of person. Above the water run the great chain bridges, plank roadways hung from iron links as thick as a man’s arm between stone piers, swaying under carts. And everywhere on the banks are the toll houses: tall narrow buildings with jettied upper stories, painted from the eaves to the waterline in stripes and saints and beasts and scenes of what happens to people who do not pay, blue and ocher and rose and a very great deal of red. The realm looks like a fairground that has been running a tax office for three hundred years.
Above the junction the Hallen comes down off the high country over red rock in a triple waterfall, three white drops one below the next with firs on both sides and misty blue mountains behind, and on the green rise over it stands Hallenfeld castle, pale and towered. On the lip of the falls, most mornings, stands a robed figure with a long staff, the house’s river-reeve, sounding the water and calling the day’s rate up to the castle. The same office keeps the stair behind the falls, and no holder of it has ever been seen to fall. Nothing floats past those falls but loose timber. Every barge unloads at the top or the bottom, and its cargo is hauled round by the portage road under the castle wall, and everything hauled pays. The portage came first and the tolls came after. It is where the house’s power comes from, and all that paint is just what the money turned into downstream.
Beyond the rivers it is farmland and alder and willow, with mills every half mile, long straight causeways, and on every high point a signal post, a tall timber frame with a basket for the beacon and a hut for the woman who lights it.
The major places

Hallenfeld. The seat: the pale castle over the falls, the portage road, and below them the junction itself. A loud, damp, wealthy town of counting-houses and warehouses on stilts, the greatest toll in the north, a Fish Market rebuilt with some bitterness since 688, and the Hallenfeld counting-house, a plain ugly building that every courier, quartermaster and road-toll between the Seat and the southern marches answers to. Under its stair is the room where the house’s couriers wait, with their boots on.
Threeways. Where the roads actually meet, a day’s ride from the water, a town of inns, smiths, wheelwrights and the Limners’ guild-hall: the eastern road goes off toward the March and on through the Scarlet Wood to the corridor for Marrowhold, the northern road climbs past the Seat toward the Aurora Reach, and the southern road goes down to Ashbury and the two great roads round the Scourge of Hell, and the water goes the same way, by barge to Ashbury and the upper Aldwater. People say you can buy anything at Threeways, and sell it back an hour later at a profit.
Chainbridge. The biggest chain bridge in the realm, four hundred yards from pier to pier over the Hallen in flood, and the town that grew up at each end of it and does not speak to itself. It is the Daubers’ town. A contraption at the eastern pier raises the middle span in a siege; a guild-master built it, it has jammed twice, and the guild-mark on it is the most boasted-about in the valley.

House and Rule
House Hallenfeld is the kingdom’s nervous system. They hold the junction, and whoever holds that junction controls the speed at which the north can respond to anything. They have no glamour and produce no legendary warriors or political masterminds. They produce quartermasters, road engineers, courier captains, and the category of administrator who understands that a message delivered six hours faster can save a thousand lives and treats the six hours as a problem worth solving with the intensity other houses bring to swordwork. They count among the Seven Warlords only in the sense that a heron counts among the great beasts of the river; try taking a fish from one.
The house in Year 715 is run from the counting-house by Ilse Hallenfeld, its Mistress: a fine cold hand, a ledger, and a settled refusal ever to leave the junction. The house’s river corridor is run under her by a tariff-master, who is expected to keep honest books and is sometimes made to suffer for it. “Clerks and couriers,” Ulf Stark says. “They’ll carry anybody’s letters.” They will, and they read Concord, which almost no one else in the north can, and they do not need to open your letter to know what it says from who sent it and how fast.
Wealth and Trade
Tolls, carriage and paper. A barge pays at the first toll house it passes and every one after that, a rate painted on the wall in pictures for those who cannot read and a second, better rate available from the clerk upstairs. Hallenfeld holds carrying contracts on every road north of the Center: grain for Ashmore, timber for Thornwall, salt bars up from Nalūn, sealed Wellspring casks from the Wellheads, which come round the Scourge by road and go north from Ashbury by river barge for the Seat’s ward-cutters. It runs the beacon line (a chain of those signal posts, each lit from the last, that can bring a yes or no from the March to the Seat in a night) and the relay riders, who change horses every twenty miles and will tell you what they think of your road.
The counting-house also holds paper. A Hallenfeld note of hand, written by a sworn notary and witnessed, is good from here to the Sealed Charter, and half the debts of the north are held in that ugly building, each in its own pigeonhole. Lords who have forgotten what they owe can expect a very courteous reminder at a very poor moment.
Rent, Food and the Street
Everything on the rivers is rented by the quarter and by the foot of frontage, with the rate going up the nearer you are to the water. Bargefolk rent nothing and pay everything. Eel pie, river perch fried in barley meal, black pudding, pickled cabbage, small beer from Barleyford and a hot spiced ale sold from a boat that comes alongside your boat. The whole realm eats standing up. Food-sellers pole around between the barges calling out, and the most famous item in the valley is the Toll Bun, sold at every toll house, in the shape of a fist.
Street life is water and argument. A Hallenfeld child knows the rate on a sack of barley before it knows its letters. Sign-painters are everywhere with a brush behind the ear and a grudge, and a house without a fresh coat is presumed to be in debt. Sects here run as bargemen’s clubs and bridge companies, in loud stripes, with brackets fought on the chain bridges in midsummer, one fall into the river being a loss and two being a very cold swim. Lamp-wardens work the bridge lanterns by the night and strike by the season, and when they do the night traffic stops and the toll goes up and everyone pretends to be surprised. Heralds cry the news from the Hallenfeld bridge first, and the minstrels who pass through rewrite it into a song by the second bridge.
What they joke about. Delivery. “Six hours” is the whole of the house’s sense of humor, and it can be told as a joke by anyone at any time. Thornwall raftsmen. Stark bears, on the subject of paying a toll. Anyone who thinks they can get to the Seat by some other way. The rest of the north jokes about Hallenfeld as well, and those jokes all have clerks in them, and in all of them the clerk gets paid.
Law and How It Fights
Law. The Toll Law: pay or be chained. A barge that has not paid has a chain put across its bow, in plain sight, and a boatman who cuts one loses his boat. The reeve sits on a bench on the bridge itself on market days, in view of the river, and hears whatever comes along. Written contracts are enforced here as nowhere else in the north, because here someone can read them. A sworn notary is a respectable trade and has been known to be knifed.
The fighting. Reluctantly. House men wear blue-and-ocher stripes and carry boathooks, short spears and the weight of the law. The house’s real weapons are the chain (every span and river-crossing in the realm can be closed in an hour), the halt (no grain moves, no message moves, and an army a week away starves on the road), and the courier captains, the only people in the house who are any use in a fight, because they have spent their lives getting through other people’s fights with a satchel. Where there is real killing to be done, the house pays for it, and the company in question is paid on the day, in full, in the most terrifying way possible, with a receipt.
Monsters on the Roads
The beasts are the river’s, and they pay nothing. Eels and perch fill the water, otters raid the fish-weirs, herons stand on every toll house roof with the expression of a clerk, and the swans have been in a bad temper since 699.
The monsters. Monsters move, and they live across the whole of the Inner World, and here they use the same rivers as everyone else. Things come up the water. Sump-toads (Grade A on the Bestiary’s scale, which runs from E to EX; Well-spawn with blued-steel rings on the brow riding level with the surface) turn up in mill-races after floods, and a miller keeps a horse-hoist and a bait lantern for them the way other towns keep a fire bucket. Greater Wolves take the causeways in winter when the river is walkable.
The Fall Cellar and the Drowned Toll
The realm has one dungeon (what a Wellspring Core makes around itself, or what grows up around one), with two names, because its top is a business and its bottom is a debt. The top is the Fall Cellar, a dripping stair behind the three waterfalls below the castle, on Phreatis ground (the Wellspring of water that remembers). It is worked, famous for it, and kept by the robed reeve on the lip. Dew beads on your sleeve as you go in, the air smells of cellar stone, and barge-masters top up there by the hour and come out remembering other people’s childhoods.
The bottom is the Drowned Toll, a flooded stair going on down from behind the middle of the triple falls, leading to a toll house far older than the house, with its rate still painted on the wall in a script no clerk can read, and a Well under it where Mourning Pike (Grade A, bred on Thaloré ground, teal over the skull) grow as long as a barge. It has never been cleared. A Hallenfeld clerk has entered the rate as owing. A chain hangs across the head of that stair, the only one in the realm that the house has never tried to collect on. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
The Scourge and the Turn
The Scourge of Hell is four or five days past Ashbury for the fastest rider the house owns, and every Northern Turn on record has gone through this junction on the way. The Turn is the old rotation by which North, South and Center each spend nine years keeping its monsters off everybody else. On the North’s Turn the columns come down the roads to Threeways, the grain comes down the water, and the house carries all of it under contract, unloads it at the portage, hauls it round under the castle wall and charges it at the rate, since the old terms give a host the right of passage and are silent on the subject of its bread. For the nine years the beacon line is carried on past Ashbury as far as Halcrest, so that a herd sighted on the north rim reaches the Seat in a few nights, and that is “six hours” at its most expensive.
The North’s Count, the running bill the three parties present to one another, is written here. The Count for 694 to 703 fills a wall of pigeonholes in the ugly building, and one of the three hands on its cover sheet is Wat Pennyquill’s. The Center holds the Turn until 721, so the North’s part for now is to watch and write it down, and the clerk it sends down the Kessen road to Lastpenny for the purpose is a Hallenfeld clerk with a satchel, whom the whole town spits at on principle. He enters that too.
Neighbors and Grudges

The Scarlet Wood. The log-jam of 688 took the bridge, the fish market and the reeve’s counting-house. Each year the rate on logs is negotiated as a continuation of that war.
The Northern Road Company. A chartered carrier out of the south with its eye on the northern roads and tolls, and its men standing guard at any bridge a house can be paid to give it. A ferryman on the junction pays the house’s toll in the morning and the Company’s guards in the afternoon, and nobody has been able to tell him which one is the law. Hallenfeld means to outlast it.
The Golden Hollow. Mutual necessity. Ashmore has the grain and Hallenfeld has the barges, and a wise person does not come between them or try to work out who is using whom.
Kharven-Seat. A customer, and a customer who has a Hallenfeld officer in its cells for keeping honest books. The house has written that down.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Rose Coils of Coilspire
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Art: Tom Kidd.
The Rose Coils of Coilspire
House Scalebond of the Serpentkin, one of the four Central Warlords, physicians and poisoners to both armies

“When did you say that was?”
The most feared question in the center. In Coilspeech it is a point of grammar.

The war of the Rose Teeth lasted nine days in the autumn of 697 and killed three hundred men, none of them with a weapon. Two armies, one under Marshal Corbel Aumery in northern pay and one under the southern captain Merrin Penhale, had camped on either side of Stoneglass Hollow for the harvest, and on the first morning Aumery’s quartermaster climbed the great stair at Coilspire Den with a heavy bag and bought a cask of Widow’s Rose, the finest well-poison in the center, at the posted price, from a gold-scaled apothecary in a very good coat. That afternoon Penhale’s quartermaster bought the antidote, from the same apothecary, at the posted price. The next morning Aumery’s man bought the thing that spoils the antidote. By the fourth day the two quartermasters were climbing the stair together, in step, with porters, and the whole plaza under the great statue had turned out in its colors to watch, with bookies working the steps and rose-sellers doing the trade of their lives. Neither side thought to ask whether the apothecary had any preference. On the ninth day she came out onto the top step and observed, once, clearly, in Common, that these same two families had done this same thing two hundred and twelve years ago, and that the casks now in both camps had been compounded on each other so many times that they contained, in effect, rosewater, a strong purge and a dye. She then went in to lunch.
Both armies had already been dosed. Thirty thousand men sat down where they stood, in full harness, in the sight of each other, for three days, and the battle was conducted entirely in insults. The dye was fast. Every soldier on that field had rose-pink teeth until midwinter, and in the taverns of two quarters men are still pointed out for it. Three hundred died of the purge, and they were treated before the end in the same long ward at Bothhands, on the same terms, in beds that ran in no particular order.

A country of gold-scaled scholars who remember everything anyone has tried to forget, who treat and poison both armies at a posted price, and who keep their conqueror’s giant statue in the main square because it reminds them who lost in the end.

Every archivist in the Guild has been sent to Coilspire at some point to be made to feel ignorant. I went at twenty-six. It worked.
The Land
The name comes from the ground. On the southeast edge of the Scourge of Hell, where the salt road comes down toward the Long Fields, the hills run in long, curved ridges of rose-colored stone, turning back on themselves like a sleeping snake, with hot springs on one flank and cold seeps on the other and narrow green valleys wound between. Old ruins and old battlefields lie in those valleys like pressed flowers. The Serpentkin chose this country for that reason: they settle at historically significant sites, Wellspring ruins and event-dense lines of the earth, anywhere the Coiling Memory (their name for the principle that the echo of a thing persists in the world’s Aether longer than the thing itself) can be reached. It is rich ground of a peculiar kind. A visitor with any training feels the afterimages before he has found an inn.
Coilspire Den is the seat, and you approach it up the finest stair in the world. It opens on a grand ornate plaza of carved gray stone, sweeping steps on every side, glass-globed lamps burning on posts cast as rearing serpents, and pink cathedral spires standing up beyond it against the sky. The crowds on those steps are gold-scaled scholars in good coats, reading, arguing, and being consulted by anxious people from elsewhere. And in the middle of it all stands the statue, colossal and nearly black: a giant wrestling a dragon, a serpent and a beast, all at once, and winning.
The giant is Gorvaine, called the Unanswered, who took this city with an army and raised the statue to tell the world what he had done to it. The serpent is them. His people kept no record of him and his name appears in no history outside this country. The Serpentkin have never moved a stone of it. They keep it spotless. They hold the Reading of Gorvaine on its steps each year, with his full titles and the exact manner of his death, and then children climb on him. Ask any scholar there why they left it standing, and she will ask you who else knows his name.
The House and Who Rules
The Serpentkin, who go by Scalebond on every Accord roll, were formed in the Dissolution Period of the Second Eon, near the Scorchline Wellsprings, when memory-essence from collapsing realms etched itself into scaled bodies shaped for it. Their function was the condition of their creation. Their spiritual lineage runs to Zseraxil the Coil, ancient guardian of the Anamnesis site called Ancestral Echoes.
A Serpentkin Soul Crystal (the organ that refines the world’s Aether into the Essence a person spends) lays down memory in structural layers, and an old one, read with enough skill, looks like sedimentary rock. What they touch, they remember, and what they remember, they can use. On waking they gain Chronos-Vision, the sight of past Aetheric events still standing in physical space, and the great elders stop consulting their own memory and begin consulting the world’s. Anamnesis is their native Wellspring, with its faded violet and its smell of old paper and attic dust, and Mirithane, the Wellspring of the mirror, stands close behind. The cost is written into the same stone. A Crystal so full resists all restructuring, and so most of their great ones stall at Stage VIII of the sixteen Stages of the climb, where going further would mean Transcendence, unwilling to pay for it with anything they have kept. I have met four of them, and each regarded the matter as settled by the evidence.
The young take the Coil-Rite, meditating in an Anamnesis zone until the Crystal receives its first deep layer, which holds the shape of the whole lineage and no one person’s recollection. I am told that it is like learning you have always known a very long song.
House Scalebond rules by the Standing Record, a body of the hundred eldest Crystals in the Rose Coils who are consulted on all matters and who decide very little. Its working head is the Remembrancer, chosen by the Record to go and speak to people. The present Remembrancer is Zsovrath Oda-riss, whose soul-name means “born into plenty, the coil that remembers,” a narrow, unhurried person in a coat of old gold brocade, who is said to have corrected a Palatine’s grandmother’s birthday during a peace negotiation, in passing, and to have ended the negotiation by doing so. The house words are It Has Been Tried. The colors are rose and gold.
Cities and Towns
Coilspire Den, described above, is the capital, the house of the Record and the seat of every notary in the center worth the seal. Under the plaza the living archives run for miles, and they consist mostly of people: rooms of scaled elders, warm or cold by preference, who may be asked things, by appointment.
Stoneglass Hollow is the second city and the older one, a bowl in the hills whose walls were fused to rippling rose-black glass by some working no one will discuss for less than a very large fee. A Memory Domain has accumulated there across so many centuries that the town’s practitioners live inside it (a Domain being the territory in which a high-Stage practitioner’s own law holds, and this one the residue of many such lives). Past events show in the glass if you stand in the right place at the right hour, and the Hollow’s guides know the hours. Tourists pay to see the battle of their choice. Armies have camped outside it for nine hundred years, because the water is good and no general believes the stories.
Bothhands is a hospital town at the ford below the Den, where the salt road crosses and every army crosses with it, with one long ward for each direction of the march. It has the only street in the center where men from opposite sides of a war routinely share a cookshop, because the physicians enforce it, and no one here has yet been willing to anger the person who is about to set his leg.
The Pale Fang Archipelago is claimed by the house, and disputed, and it lies a long way off. The Record will tell you who disputed it first.
Wealth and Trade
Coilspire sells three things, each at a posted price cut into the stair.
Physic first. Serpentkin surgeons are the coldest-handed and the most experienced in the world, and a great many of them can tell you how the last person with your wound died. Every commander of means in the Inner World has a Scalebond surgeon on retainer, and every one of them knows that the other side has one as well.
Poison second, compounded by the same people in the next room, and the antidote is always for sale. They consider this an ethical position. A household that buys both is said to have “kept its accounts.”
Memory third, and the rest is small change next to it. A notary’s testimony from living Crystal is sought by every court that will admit it. A Stage VII practitioner standing on a contested field can query it: what happened here, in what sequence, by whom. Heirs pay for that. So do widows, who come in great numbers for memory-weaving, in which a practitioner shares a Crystal layer through sustained touch and matched breathing, and the recipient receives the feeling of a lost time with none of its content. It is the center’s great grief-trade, and I have seen hard captains weep on those steps and go home lighter. And then there are the people who come to pay for silence on what they have done. The house has never once sold a secret to a third party, and it has never once agreed to forget one. Its discretion and its menace are the same service.
Rose stone goes out by barge in small amounts. Rose-dye, after 697, has an ironic following.
Rent, Food and the Street
The Serpentkin are comfortable at either thermal extreme and at their weakest in between, so every Scalebond house has a hot room and a cold room and a short, unwelcoming corridor at the temperature everyone else likes. Rents are set by thermal comfort, and a good steam-room near the plaza costs what a house would elsewhere. The hard part of a Coilspire lodging is the bill: every stair-side lodging-house will take the usual few coppers for a bed in the room of twelve, and the cheapest of them, in Lamp Stair, will also take a true story you have told nobody, at the same value. Half the spies in the center started their careers on Lamp Stair, and they all know the other half did too.
A Serpentkin eats one great meal a fortnight and lies still after it, so the street food is entirely for the benefit of everyone else: hot peppered snails, iced rosewater, flat bread with river-fish and pickled plums, and a pale pink wine that comes from the terraces and is better than it needs to be. Food-sellers on the great stair know their customers’ grandfathers’ orders. Children sell rhymes giving the kings of the Midmarch in order, and the rhyme takes four hours and has never once been accurate for more than a season.
The petty crafts run to memory too. A stair-wife will find your lost ring by walking you backward through your afternoon, and a hedge-worker will take a stain out of a garment by persuading it of an earlier time. The lamp-wardens who tend the serpent posts are a hereditary company, and they have been on strike exactly once, in 512, and the Record is still discussing it.
Law
In Coilspeech, a statement that does not say where it sits in time is incomplete, as a sentence without a subject is incomplete in Common. Every assertion carries the speaker’s judgment of when it is true, in relation to what came before. So a Coilspire court does not begin with what happened. It begins with when you knew, and a good many foreign liars have talked themselves into a corner at that point, just by trying to say the sentence correctly.
Law here is precedent and nothing else, and all of it is living. A contract needs no paper among the Serpentkin; a notary witnessed it, and the notary will outlast you. Foreigners get a sealed copy as a courtesy. The worst crime is tampering, which covers altered records, a falsified boundary stone or a bought witness, and the second-worst is asking someone to forget. Poisoners cannot be prosecuted for selling. They can be prosecuted for mislabeling.
The Accord’s law hangs over all of it. Under the Beastkin Classification Provision a Scalebond is contestable stock unless she carries the scholar-class exemption, and the exemption has to be renewed, in person, in a good coat, at Sealhall. The Accord’s historical division treats Serpentkin records as anecdotal, because their source is living memory and not inscribed record. Then, at the end of a long winter, its clerks come quietly up the great stair and ask for the answer. The Serpentkin find this classification clarifying. If you ever hear a Scalebond use that word about you, I would make arrangements.
How It Fights
Very few armies have thought to find out. House Scalebond keeps a small, exact guard in rose and gold, and otherwise regards a siege as a kind of case. Any host that takes the Coils finds its wells have been considered in advance, its surgeons want to discuss their fees, and its best officers have started receiving small, accurate notes about their families. Gorvaine is the only conqueror who ever got as far as raising a monument, and the notes were how they finished him.
A Scalebond fighter is a slow horror. The move the crowds wait for is As Previously: a coiled strike with the exact force that settled this same fight two hundred years ago, against someone who fought like you. They read your body against everyone who ever stood where you are standing, with Chronos-Vision showing them the last man’s footwork in the air beside you, and they talk throughout. Their glyph-chains in Ma, Zo and En (Memory, Echo and Lattice, units of Parunic) feed on the Crystal’s own layers and never fade, so a chamber they have prepared stays prepared for a century. At Stage VII and past, a fighter’s Domain can be queried in the middle of a duel, and it will tell him every feint you tried on the way in.
They call the aura coat (the visible coat of a fighter’s own color) the entry, as in an entry in a record, and they keep it thin and pale gold. Pressure, the weight of a higher Stage felt in the room, is the objection. To sense another fighter is to look him up.
Now the fair counter, which every student of the Coils learns first. Negation breaks them. Uur and No, the glyphs of Disruption and Negation, produce a gap in the Crystal’s filing logic where a backlash ought to be, and a Scalebond hit by a clean negation will stand very still and be, for a moment, truly at a loss. Moderate temperatures dull them; fight on a mild spring day in a shaded field. And the only other reliable answer is to do something that has never been done before, in the whole recorded history of the art, which is harder than it sounds.
What They Joke About
They joke dryly and with dates. A Scalebond’s idea of a great joke is to wait for the right occasion, and they have been known to wait a hundred and forty years. “A Bearkin is the only person who is older than my grudge” is as near as they come to affection. Humans they regard with no contempt at all, as a civilization that consistently fails to consult the available record before repeating a documented mistake, and they will tell you which one. A favorite story among them concerns a young human who said “that will never happen,” and it has no other content.
Everyone else has one joke, in many forms. Ask a Scalebond the time and he gives you the year. “A Scalebond has been wrong before, and can give you the date” goes around every market in the center. North of the salt country they say a man with pink teeth has been to school. In the Midmarch, “keeping your accounts” means sleeping with a knife, and in the Moonlight Forest they consider the Scalebond a people who have never once allowed anything to be finished, and they say so kindly, while passing the fruit.
Monsters on the Roads
Nine centuries of armies have left this country well supplied with Ghouls and Skeletal Folk (both Grade B on the Bestiary’s scale, which runs from E to EX) on the old fields, and the Hollow’s guides know which ones you can tour. Basilisks (Grade A) and Lamia (Grade A) keep to the far valleys, where they are entered by name, with dates. The ordinary animals are basking lizards on every warm flank, river-fish in the valleys and peppered snails, which are dinner. Serpents of the plain kind are left strictly alone, and the house will not discuss them.
The dungeon is the Lower Reading beneath Stoneglass Hollow, an Anamnesis Well (the Wellspring of memory, faded violet, smelling of old paper) under the fused rose-black glass. It breeds Roll-callers (Grade S), Well-spawn of the Deeps who speak in the voices of people the Well has killed, and has never been seen above them. The house has not cleared it and regards it as a source. Scholars go down on a rope to hear a dead witness and pay the posted price per question. Stoneglass Hollow itself is the odd case on the Guild’s list, a dungeon with a town inside it and guides who know the hours, and nobody has tried to clear it, since no one can say what there is to kill. The Serpentkin call such a place a long memory with a bad temper. They have the names of everyone it ever ate, and their rates are reasonable. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
Beside the Scourge
Every ridge in the Coils has a fine view of the Scourge of Hell, and the northwestern slopes get its dry wind along with the view. The haze stands along that side of the sky all year, and the vines beneath it give the sharper wine. A survey taken from Stoneglass Hollow reckons the colossal sword at the Scourge’s center, bronze-hilted, driven point-down into the mountains, with a field of violet stars where its blade should be, at about three leagues above the peaks. A rival survey from the Windstair makes it four, and the two authors did not speak afterward. The Record holds both, with dates. The Scalebond say they remember what the sword was, and they will tell you for a sum nobody has ever been able to raise. It is posted on the stair, and children recite it.
This corner of the rim takes the Scourge’s survivors. Crews and soldiers off the southeast Hem (the outermost belt, fifteen leagues of black-barked thornwood and pale dust) come down to Bothhands by the salt road, and in every edge town on the rim a Scalebond surgeon has a door by the hunting hall, between the renderers and the core-buyers, and knows how the last man with your wound died. Whoever comes out alive is treated at the posted price, and the house keeps a record of everything anyone says in fever. Half of what crews rave about is lies. The other half is the best map of the Black Roots and the Haze that no surveyor ever drew, the only one with the dead marked by name, and you may guess how much it costs. In the late summer of a dry year the great herds push outward and what follows them comes too, and the far valleys fill with greywalkers, long-armed and dust-colored, who have no idea whose old battlefield they are standing on, and are corrected.
The Turn runs North, then South, then Center, nine years each, with the holder keeping a Line of forts around the Hem and the other two counting what it costs, and the Coils treat all three as they treat both armies. A Northern or Southern commander on his Turn has his Scalebond surgeon on retainer, like any commander of means. The Center holds the Turn now, from 712 to 721, and the house pays its share in surgeons, each one entered in the Center’s Count (the bill each party presents when a Turn ends) at the posted price. The Record will recite every Count ever presented, by all three parties, with the arithmetic corrected. No party has asked twice.
Neighbors and Grudges
The Sealed Charter of the Concord is the standing fight, polite and without end. The Record holds the true date of every Accord promise and it reads them out at inconvenient moments.
The Holy Sea of Alabaster weighs sworn accounts, and the Lamberts count everything, and each regards the other as a very good amateur. The Sea admits Scalebond testimony on alternate centuries, and this is one of the off ones.
The Moonlight Forest of Mosk-Vaal plants what the Coils have failed to save. They get on well, in the manner of two tradesmen who keep sending each other clients.
The Russet Crown of the Unpapered gets a quiet fair hearing here. Zsalla Underscale, the Scalebond advocate of the Harrowgate gate, was of this house, and the Record has kept the name of every soul in those pens, including the nineteen who were caught. The Crown would like the list. The Record will sell it to anyone at the posted price, and that includes the Crown, the Accord and the men who hunted them, which is why nobody at Brokencollar will share a drink with a Scalebond.
The Violet Peaks of Caelspire owe the Record a very old fine over a bird that fell on the plaza. It accrues.
The Marrowkin of the Ember Holds keep a tally of everything cut from their dead god, and the Scalebond keep a parallel count of how the tally has been altered, in a mutual respect grounded in preservation, material on the one hand and Aetheric on the other.
The Hundred Crowns of the Midmarch consult the Record on matters of succession and then ignore the answer. It is the most reliable income the house has.

In a later hand, in the margin: The Northern Empire of Whitemere sent a Scalebond surgeon its bill of thanks while it was still being built, and the surgeon sent it back corrected. The great stair has cut no new posted price for an empire. The last one was Gorvaine’s, and they are holding it open.
