geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Russet Crown of the Unpapered
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
House Nobody, the runaway kingdom of Catkin, Wolfkin and Bearkin, one of the four Central Warlords, which the Guild Accord does not recognize

Holder of the lands aforesaid: nobody. Owed by: nobody. To be served upon: nobody.
The Assessor’s return for the Russet Forest, sealed at Sealhall, 668 IC. It is the most expensive clerical error in the history of the Accord, and the Accord has never admitted that it was one.

A Provision Assessor named Pell Wickham rode up to the landward gate of Brokencollar in the autumn of 668, with a clerk, a roll-book and forty coated bravos of the Red Bar school in their red and white, to enumerate the unlicensed beastkin of the Russet Forest for the purposes of the Labor Provision, which classes any Beastkin without sealed papers as available for sale. He set his table up in the old sorting yard, at the foot of the great heap of cut iron collars, which even then stood higher than a mill. He called the first person forward, an enormous Bearkin in a fir-green apron with a chair she had brought herself, and asked for her name and her owner. “Nobody,” she said. The clerk asked her to repeat it, and wrote it down. The Catkin behind her was named nobody and belonged to nobody. So were the four Wolfkin after that, in chorus, and by noon the whole town had come down off the terraces in its painted fur and its brightest cloth, four thousand one hundred people in a line that went twice around the heap, with cider going along it and fiddlers working, each stepping up in turn to give the same answer to the same tired man. Wickham’s bravos looked at the line and then up at the ring-walls, where a great many pairs of eyes were looking back, and they asked him quietly whether it might be a good idea to finish the job.
He finished it. He was a conscientious man. He carried the roll back to Sealhall and entered it, and sealed it, because an Assessor swears to record what is declared. It took the Accord’s lawyers about a year to understand what he had done. By the Provision’s own wording, a writ for the recovery of property must name the holder, and the holder of the whole country, in a good clear hand under a green seal, was nobody. Nothing could be claimed from them. No one could be sued. A raid on the forest was now an assault upon no one’s land by no one’s warrant, and the licensed returners who hunted runaways for the bounty could not get paid for it. The Accord has spent the better part of fifty years trying to file a correction, and a correction must be served upon the party concerned.
The town held a feast that lasted a month. They hammered the first collar ever cut there into a band and put it on the head of the oldest runaway they could find, and it had gone a fine deep red by the first rain, and they have refused to clean it since.

A kingdom of runaway Beastkin in a forest of permanent autumn, whom the Accord will not recognize and whose own rolls file them under “nobody,” so they took the name and put the rust on as a crown.

I keep this page at the request of no one, and the Guild’s Beastkin desk has twice asked me to stop.
The Land
The Russet Crown holds the east of the Center, around a bright inland sea, with the salt road and the Concord’s uneasy flank on its west and the Scourge of Hell beyond them. Inland from the water lies the Russet Forest, in hill country, and it has been autumn there for as long as anyone can say. Oak and beech and great old chestnut stand in every shade from rust to bright gold, the fallen leaves lie knee-deep on the slopes, and the air has smoke and apples in it in every month of the year. New leaves bud, turn and fall at once, on the same branch, without any winter ever arriving. The Measurewrights have sent three surveys to explain this. One blames a Verdantia site gone out of its season, one blames the Bearkin who have been Weight-Bound here since before the count, and one blames the surveyor before it. The Bearkin were asked and said that it was fine.
The forest towns stand on stilts over the leaf-drift and the floods that come down off the hills, walkways and ladders and rope bridges strung between platforms, everything carved and painted because nobody here was ever allowed to own a painted thing before. People go about in bright cloth with their fur dyed in bold bars, stripes and handprints, in colors that would earn a flogging in a licensed pen. You can tell how long someone has been free from how loud they are.
The House and Who Rules
There is no blood in this house, and that is the entire idea of it. House Nobody is anyone who has arrived and spoken. Its people come in three kinds, with old law and older habits between them.
Catkin (Feline, in the Accord’s terms) make up the largest number, and they are among the most frequently enslaved people in the world, because human buyers find their faces pretty. They descend from the Clawbound Accord, formed during the Watcher’s Eclipse, and their Soul Crystals (the organ that refines the world’s Aether into the Essence a person spends) store feeling as a reservoir and turn it to speed. In the Spirit War their ancestors were the Concord’s preferred assassins, and they hold no parades for that. Their discipline is the Emotional Covenant: before any important act a Catkin stands still and counts up what she is carrying, and decides whether it is ready. Wolfkin (Lupine) are the most hunted, under the “wild beastkin clearance” provision, and their tether-bonds and the slow death of Isolation Decay make it easy to run one down alone, so they do not go alone. They run on the Pack-Soul, in which enough of them close together think as one, bound palm to cut palm under a full moon by the Kinbinding, and they keep their history in the ground by the Howls of Mourning, sung into the local lines of the earth. Their packs guarded collapsing Wellspring sites during the Verdant Siege, under the Moonwake Accord, and received formal recognition for it and no membership, and they understood the difference. Bearkin (Ursine) were here first, and they are generally free-status where documented, which puts them in little danger and makes their staying a very pointed thing. A Weight-Bound Bearkin has tethered her soul to one mountain or glade and feels what it feels, and a Stillness Trial is two of them standing under pressure to see who breaks stance first, which can take up most of a festival. When the first runaways came through in the last days of the Third Eon the Bearkin of the Glade of the Slumbering Root looked at them, looked at the hunters coming up behind, and declined to move. They have been declining since. Catkin and Wolfkin share the oldest beastkin alliance there is, and the Wolfkin and the Bearkin have an old saying between them: Lupine move; Bearkin stay.
The Russet Crown itself is that hammered band of collar-iron, rusted the red of the forest, and whoever wears it is the Queen or King of Nobody for as long as the town allows. The Crown holds three powers: to speak to outsiders, to call the muster, and to be blamed. The one requirement is a scar at the neck. The present Queen is Sefa Tuen-zhiv, whose soul-name means “born in flight, charged with quickness,” and who was sold twice as a grown woman, first as “skilled labor” and then at a rather better price to a man who wanted a rival’s accounts stolen, and who describes that second owner’s death in detail to visiting envoys while they are eating. She is a small, gorgeous, furious Catkin in a coat of nineteen colors, and has held the Crown for eleven years. She can vanish in the middle of a sentence and finish it behind you. The house words are the one word of the Name-Keeping, Ashe: I remain. Its colors are russet and gold, in any combination the wearer can afford.
Cities and Towns
Brokencollar is the seat, and you can see it from a day out on the water: a great walled city of russet roofs terraced up a rocky headland over the sea, ring on ring of high walls, a domed hall, needle spires on the summit and a sheer stone platform jutting out from the cliff, all of it peach-colored in the low sun. The Accord built it, as the holding fortress of the labor trade, and every one of those rings faces inward, because they were made to keep people in. The platform is where the barges loaded. The runaways took it, on a night Sealhall has never entered, and they live in it now, with their washing on the inner walls and doors knocked through wherever anyone wanted one. When the rings filled they spilled out of the landward gate, and at the fortress’s foot a stilt-town of nine thousand stands around the old sorting yard and around the Heap. The Heap is what it sounds like: every collar, shackle and neck-ring ever cut off a runaway in that place, thrown down in one spot since the Third Eon, grown now to a rust-red hill with a stair up it and small shrines and flowers tucked into it by people visiting their own. At its foot stands the Underhill Forge, kept by the descendants of Orsa Underhill, the Bearkin smith who lifted a pen gate off its pins at Harrowgate. They will cut any collar free of charge, on any day, and the only price is that you hold the tongs for the next one.
Shadowed Ridge is the Catkin town, and its map is carried in the heads of those who live there. It is very hard to find from the outside and instantly obvious once you are in it, since it is built around the shadow-map its residents share and has no visible landmarks whatever. The Clawbound Trial is held on the Ridge, where a young fighter must shadow-walk through ground her elder has anchored, following a map written in darkness, and come out bound to the elder for life, with the burden running both ways.
Nightveil Hollow is the second Catkin town and the Crown’s great den of thieves, forgers and retired assassins. Its people go to the Dusk Quarter of Altherion and back by roads nobody else knows. Most of the good false papers in the center start here. Fine penmanship is the most respected art in the Hollow, and the master forgers walk around with bodyguards.
Greyfang Crossing is the Wolfkin town at the river ford on the Concord road, set where it is for reasons of lunar sight-line that no outsider can follow, and it holds the border. The Shrine of Nine Howls stands in the hills above it. A pack goes there to sing their dead into the ground, and it can be heard in Brokencollar on a still night.
The Glade of the Slumbering Root is the Bearkin heart, among the oldest continuously occupied places in the world, its stone halls unchanged since the Age of Glacial Memory. Its people keep a three-day silence every year for the Siege of the Seventh Fold, where the Bearkin held the final line for three days while a Domain (the territory in which a high-Stage practitioner’s own law holds) collapsed around them, so that other peoples could escape, and none survived intact. They call the silence recognition, and they will not have it called grief.
Wealth and Trade
The Crown is poor and proud of it, and it has more money than it admits. Chestnut flour, smoked trout, strong honey and russet cloth go out by the sack and the bale, with a good deal of information folded in the cloth, along with apple spirit that the Accord’s excisemen have been unable to tax because they cannot identify the owner. Bearkin workings are the great export; glyph-chains in Ir, Tar and Ky (Endurance, Weight and Structure, units of Parunic) last for decades without renewal, the only inscribed beastkin work that outlasts its maker, and a Glade-cut lintel on your door is the best ward money can buy. Catkin scouts, spies and knife-hands hire out by the season, to both armies, with a clause that no one on the job will wear a collar or guard anyone who does. Those fees are large.
Then there is the Long Way, which is both the Crown’s reason for being and its worst drain. The Long Way is a chain of safe barns, friendly ferrymen and bought clerks running from Verath to Harrowgate and beyond, down which runaways come. A pen-breaker’s work is expensive. It costs far more to buy one person out of a licensed pen with good papers than to buy a good horse, and the old price at Verath Township is seventeen gold marks a head. The Crown spends every bit of what the fighters and forgers earn on that, and it has never yet paid for anyone who could not be stolen instead. Forged free-holder papers go out by the hundred, and they are good enough that the Accord now charges a fee to check its own seals.
Do not ask at any stall for furs. They will think you are joking, and you do not want them to find out otherwise.
Rent, Food and the Street
A runaway owes nothing for a year and a day. After that a household owes one day in seven to the common work of the town, on the stilts, the roads or the watch, and that is the whole of the rent. Coin from outside is good everywhere, and locally people pay each other in collar-bits, small sawn pieces of cut neck-iron stamped with a thumbprint, each good for a day’s work and no use at all beyond the first ford. They are considered unlucky to hoard.
The eating is loud and generous. Bearkin bring their own chairs to it. Chestnut bread and smoked trout and blackberries stewed with venison come out on long tables on the platforms, and cider is passed around in anything that holds it, by people who remember a pen ration and take a second helping out of principle. Above the leaf-drift the walkways are full all night, because a Catkin’s day runs from dusk. Pickpockets practice on each other and return the takings. You will hear three languages on any bridge: Purrspeech, with a second conversation running under the first that is usually about you, Moontongue with its growl even in a greeting, and Urganic Growlscript, in which ordering breakfast takes a while. Small powers are for sale at every ladder-foot: a Wolfkin who can tell you how your brother is, without being told his name, by the weight of him; a hedge-worker who takes the smell of you off a road, for a price, and will refuse you if the hounds are too close and she has her own children to think about.
The other thing you will see on the street is the bad day. A woman in her thirties stops walking in the middle of a bridge and stands shaking at a sound. A man cannot sit with his back to a door. Nobody in Brokencollar remarks on it. Somebody comes and stands next to them, and in a while they go on.
Law
The whole constitution is one rite. A person who arrives stands at the foot of the Heap and speaks her soul-name, the name of her birth and her charge, aloud, and whatever else she has lost: Fen Tuen-zhiv, Baru, “the last thing, Tuen-zhiv, spoken aloud.” Whoever is nearest answers Ashe: I have heard, you remain. That person is now her witness, her ndoto, for life, responsible for her first year and answerable for her. That is the whole of citizenship. Nothing is written down.
The refusal of writing is the deep law of the country, and it is meant. Paper is how they got you. No birth, debt, marriage or land in the Crown has ever been recorded, and to keep a list of names here is the one crime for which the town will hang you without a hearing, because a list can be stolen, and the people on it can be found. A dispute goes to the witnesses of the parties. Bearkin elders hear what the witnesses cannot settle, slowly, at a pace that encourages settling. Theft from a Crown neighbor is fined and theft from an outsider is admired.
The Accord’s law applies, in the Accord’s view, to every inch of this. Any Catkin or Wolfkin here without sealed papers is contested stock, and a hunter who catches one beyond the forest eaves may lawfully bring her to a licensed pen. Inside the eaves the law of 668 holds, and a returner cannot be paid by any owner. Sealhall keeps a standing Enforcement line for its own collectors to go in anyway, on forfeiture, and their iron comes out cut and goes on the Heap. So the border is a matter of feet, and there are people on both sides of it who know exactly where it runs.
They do lose people, and I record it, as the Crown will not. A bad decade sells off two or three hundred at the fairs. A raid by men who do not care about the fee is simply a raid, and there have been children taken from the outer platforms, and a whole Wolfkin hamlet at Lower Sedge run down in a single Lunar Inversion, when the moon had them half out of their minds. There is a Howl for it. Every year the Crown’s knife-hands go out to find the names of those responsible, and the Accord’s rolls show a higher than usual mortality among licensed returners in the weeks that follow.
How It Fights
House Nobody has no army, and it keeps three thousand people at the ready who would tell you the same. What comes at you is a tactic that the Hobgoblin staffs have studied with envy.
The Catkin go first, and you will not see them. Before You Decided is the reservoir going off through one precise step, and the knife was already in you when you thought about parrying. Then the Wolfkin: the Nine-Howl Run puts a whole pack in one gait, and the distance you were relying on stops existing, since inside a Lupine Pack-Hunt Domain the space between predator and prey obeys the pack. Then you turn around to retreat to the ford, and there in the middle of the ford is a very large Bearkin, in an apron, who was not there this morning and has no plans to leave. Inside her Earthen Domain things weigh more and fast techniques cost more, and The Mountain Has Thought About It waits on the far side of a lifetime of patience. The muster is called by Howl, and from the time of calling, the first knives are moving before the sound has crossed the valley.
The words for the aura coat (the visible coat of a fighter’s own color) start fights here: Catkin call it the lie, since the skill is in not showing one; Wolfkin say the pelt and ask whose; Bearkin call it the weather and do not understand why you are worrying about yours. Pressure, the weight of a higher Stage felt in the room, is called the old man by all three, in memory of whoever held the whip. To sense someone coming is to smell the iron on them.
The counters are known to every licensed returner. Light hurts them: a Catkin’s lattice is built for the space between light sources, and in a Radiant Domain she loses nearly a third of everything, which is why the good raiders march at noon with priests. Structure backlashes on Lupine, for Ko and Al, Order and Edge, land in the Pack-Soul like a wall appearing in a field. Run a Wolfkin alone past a few days and Isolation Decay will finish what you started. Wait for a Lunar Inversion and Bloodmoon Corruption will turn the pack’s great strength into a screaming thing with no plan in it. As for Bearkin, go around them; everyone does, and they will still be there when you come back.
What They Joke About
They joke about their name, mostly, and they have heard yours already. “Who’s your king?” is the oldest joke in the center and every child in Brokencollar has a better answer to it than you do. A toast goes “To the health of nobody,” and a curse goes “May you be somebody.” When a thing goes badly, they say the Assessor will hear of this. A Catkin will tell you that a Lupine cannot go to the privy alone, and a Lupine will tell you that a Catkin will swear she was never there, and for once you should believe her. Everybody tells jokes about the Bearkin, slowly, in the hope one will reach them in time for the next feast.
Outside the forest, an Accord clerk who has made a very stupid mistake is said to have “enumerated.” Market thieves all over the center give their name to the watch as Nobody, and it does not work, and the watch writes it down anyway, out of a sort of tired love.
Monsters on the Roads
Sasquatch (Grade C on the Bestiary’s scale, which runs from E to EX) in the high glades, Tanuki (Grade D) who pick the same pockets the Catkin do, and in the leaf-drift the long low things locals call drift-eels, that hunt by the shiver in the leaves and are the reason nobody walks at ground level after dusk. Returners, licensed hunters of runaways, are entered in the same list by local habit. The beasts are deer, trout, boar and the fat acorn-hogs that fight back, and a Brokencollar child’s first real fight is generally against a hog.
The dungeon is the Seventh Fold, up in the hills beyond the Glade, where a Domain collapsed around a Bearkin line in an old siege and left a pocket that will not settle. The ground weighs more the further you go in and the fast get slow. Its Mouth is three days from anywhere. The Glade’s people keep it, in the sense of standing near it. Crews have another name for the whole forest, the Autumn Country, which the Guild’s list enters as a lying-down, a dungeon with no roof, with an edge you can walk across without noticing and a center nobody has mapped, and as Verdantia (the Wellspring of growth) by one survey of three. It is inhabited and closed to surveyors. The Unpapered do not care what it is, and have reasons to dislike people arriving with forms. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
Beside the Scourge
Below the Charter’s edge the salt road runs with the forest eaves on its east and the Hem of the Scourge of Hell on its west, the Hem being the Scourge’s outermost belt, fifteen leagues of black-barked thornwood and pale dust. The breeze off the inland sea keeps the worst of the heat out of the chestnut woods. Nobody here has signed anything about the Scourge, and the things that come out have never asked to see a roll, so the Crown fights them anyway. In the late summer of a dry year the Howl goes up, the Catkin go out along the eaves ahead of whatever is coming, the Wolfkin run it down, and in the morning there is a very large Bearkin in the ford.
Catkin out of the Russet Crown run some of the best-regarded bounty crews on the eastern side, working out of Goodmorrow on the salt road, and they are paid in actual money, which goes down the Long Way. A good many of their people learned the trade at the back of someone else’s line. A licensed labor-stock porter hired out of Verath is equipment on a clearing’s instrument, written nemo along with the rope, and a porter who comes over the wall has generally seen more of a dungeon than the captain who hired him. That is why Brokencollar has so many people who can read a fork, the brass assay instrument that rings truer as the ground thickens. The Crown’s crews sign under the same clause as every Crown hire: no one on the job wears a collar or guards anyone who does.
The Turn runs North, then South, then Center, nine years each, with the holder keeping a Line of forts around the Hem and the other two counting what it costs. The Center holds it now, from 712 to 721, and “the Center” means everybody who lives along the rim, which is a story in itself here. The Unpapered are on no roll. The Center’s Count, the bill audited at Sealhall when a Turn ends, must carry this stretch of the rim as held by nobody and owed nothing, because the Crown fights regardless and bills nobody, and I am told it is the most aggravating line in the document. On the North’s Turn or the South’s a host may march through anyone’s land by right of passage. Every marshal who has come up the salt road has been advised by his lawyers that the forest is nobody’s, and by his scouts to stay on the road.
Asked about the colossal sword at the Scourge’s center, with a field of violet stars where its blade should be, an elder of the Glade thought about it for most of a festival and said that it was a long way off.
Neighbors and Grudges
The Sealed Charter of the Concord is the whole of the matter. The Accord does not recognize the Crown and has a standing committee on how to do so without having recognized it. Sealhall’s lawyers, every generation, produce a new form of the correction, and every generation someone goes through the wall of their counting-house.
The Rose Coils of Coilspire gave them Zsalla Underscale, and the Crown honors her name at Brokencollar. They also hold a complete list of everyone who has ever passed through a Harrowgate pen, for sale, at the posted price. The Crown has been trying to buy it, and burn it, for a century, and has also tried to steal it, and this is why no Scalebond is served a drink at the Heap.
The Violet Peaks of Caelspire sell the Accord its wind and shelter the fowlers’ victims, depending on which school you ask. Some of the Long Way goes over those high roads, and the Crown keeps a list of its friends up there in the only place it keeps any list, which is in the head of one old Catkin.
The Moonlight Forest of Mosk-Vaal accepts Crown dead when asked, on the Moss Court’s terms, as a matter of neighborliness, and has planted a small and very well-tended garden of them. Not a single returner has ever crossed the causeway in pursuit.
The Hundred Crowns of the Midmarch sometimes offer the Queen a marriage alliance and are always surprised by the reply.
The Iron Mandate of Undaar-Keth has Hobgoblin staff officers who hire Catkin scouts, and who call the pairing the most uncomfortable military alliance that consistently wins engagements.
The Ember Holds of Marrowhold have an honor-bound kinship with the Bearkin of the Glade, forge-culture and endurance-culture having enough in common that the two need no contract, and a good deal of the iron that the Crown does not get from the Heap comes down that road.
The Amber Cities of Nalūn buy forged papers, Crown knives and honey, and pretend not to. The North, for its part, has a Banner House or two that hold their own Beastkin under older words, and a few northern lords quietly send coin to the Long Way for reasons that are their own.

In a later hand, in the margin: The Northern Empire of Whitemere, in the years it was building, sent the Crown a letter. It was addressed to Nobody, and they thought that was quite good. The Accord’s correction was still pending in my time, and I am told that the file now fills a room.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Sapphire Wells of Brightwater
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itBRITE-wah-ter · the WELL-heads
The Wellheads · The Leasehold Kingdom · The Spring Country
The Warden’s cask-men caught Annis Blewitt drawing water out of the Hotwell overflow for her dye-vats in the spring of Year 647, and took her to Brightwater for it. Nobody could have called it stealing, in the ordinary way, since it was running into the ditch at the time. But the lease said water from a kept pool was sold by the cask, and the Warden then, a long stringy man named Ferris Corwen, had just raised the cask by a third. Annis Blewitt was the mistress of the Dyers’ Guild of Kingfisher Steps. That overflow did something to woad that no other water in the world would do, and it made a blue so violent that people had been known to stop and take their hats off to a bolt of it. She paid the fine on the steps of the Warden’s Hall in clipped silver, told him he could keep his ditch, and walked home.
On the third morning, every dyer on the Steps tipped out her vats into the top pool at once. It went down the terraces in a sheet. It went through the bathhouses and the laundries and the cheese-cellars of Brightwater, it went into the river and the barge basin, and it dyed every cask-man’s breeches where he stood. It dyed the Warden’s white mare, four hundred sheep, a bishop on retreat, the whole of a Guild assay party that had been wading in to find out what was happening, and the river itself, a clean roaring kingfisher blue, all the way down to the barge-towns for nine days, with people running along the banks in their thousands with buckets and bedsheets and a hired band of pipes and drums. Six dyers were held under to the shoulders in the last vat by Corwen’s men and came up with arms that never faded. Then the Guild’s own factor at the barge basin, a man of practical mind, sent up to ask what the Warden wanted per bolt.
The settlement took two years and the whole Wellhead lease was redrawn around it. To this day the Dyers pay a third less for their water than anyone else, and any Corwen who raises it must do so on the Steps, in person, with his sleeves rolled up. Ferris Corwen, who was no fool, put the color on his banner before the river ran clear. You will still meet old families on the Steps with one blue-armed ancestor in the portrait, and “blue to the elbow” is what the spring country says of anyone who has been in a fight with the management and lived.
The Wellheads are a high steaming upland of pools in impossible colors, the richest ground per acre in the South, held on a Guild lease by a cheerful family who keep the keys to everyone’s power, and whose water, since the war, has been going wrong.
The Land and the Look
Up through mist, on a wet road, and you hear the place before you see it. The Wellheads steam in the uplands at the heart of the South, with the iron hills of Sum-gol off to the west and the Jade Plains opening to the east. They are a high, wet, luminous country of hot springs and cold springs side by side, terraced down the hills in step after step of pale stone, every pool a different color from milk-jade to rust, from a green that hurts to a sapphire so deep and clear you can watch a dropped copper fall for a long time. Steam stands over all of it in the morning and goes gold when the sun comes through. Brass is everywhere, brass-bound carts, brass wellmouth rings, brass stair-rails kept polished by small boys, an assay post on every wellmouth with its tuned fork humming. Kingfishers are real here and shameless. They dive through the steam and come up blue as the banners, and the house has them on its spoons.
Under it all is the hum of the kept pools, so constant that Corwen children who leave home cannot sleep for the silence. A scholar calls this rich ground, and the street calls it fat. Any practitioner standing here pulls Aether from the air and the water far faster than down on the plain, and within a day feels twice the size she is and is liable to pick a fight about it. Below them the springs have drowned an old gorge to the brim, with the minerals in the water giving it that color, and past the gorge the land falls away to the river, the cask road and the western edge of the Grey Plain.
The House
House Corwen is a chartered family, the only one of the seven southern houses that holds its ground by Guild lease rather than by blood or conquest, and the richest per acre. It left the Empire of Sum-gol in the most Corwen way possible, sending word to the last Calling that the casks had been sold elsewhere, and then took out a lease from the Guild Accord on the entire spring country the moment there was no emperor to object. It is a kingdom of its own by any reckoning a southerner would use, with its own law, levies and table at the warlords’ council, and it could in theory be evicted by anyone holding the right piece of wax. The house has spent a century making sure nobody can find that piece of wax.
Its head is Maud Corwen, Warden of the Wellheads, Lessee of the Guild, a big, cheerful, sharp-eyed woman who knows the lease terms of every spring in the south by heart, and who has never in her life been seen to drink the water. She takes no crown, says the lease does not provide for one, and has a very fine brass one in a box. The words are The Water Keeps Faith. The colors are kingfisher blue and brass.
Every worked Wellspring site (a Core, in common speech) under Guild lease from the Wellheads to the southern sea sells its hours through a Corwen keeper, and the keeper can close it. That is the true crown. The keepers, in blue coats with brass keys at the belt, can seal a site in under an hour if paid and willing, and a keeper in a bad mood has ended more arguments in the South than Marrick ever did.
Cities and Towns
Brightwater stands at the foot of the spring country, twenty-five thousand people in a white town with red-tile roofs, stacked on sheer rock stacks and arches over the brilliant sapphire water of the gorge. Stone and rope bridges run between the crags, sailboats work the water, boats are drawn up under a great arch, and horses stand about on a sunny terrace looking pleased with the view. In it are the Warden’s Hall with its brass doors, the Cask Yards where coopers hammer from dawn with a noise you can hear on the Plain, the Lease Court, and the barge road going down to the river. Every morning the sealed casks go off downhill toward the north, and everyone comes out to count them, on principle.
Hotwell is the bath town, cheap and bawdy, built around a boiling pool in a bowl of the hills. Sick men, old soldiers, Marrick companies between contracts and anyone who has been told by a physician that it might help come to sit up to their necks in water the color of tea and tell lies. There are eggs boiled in the street gutters, there is a fighting ring on a raft, and there is no record of anyone in Hotwell ever having been sober at a funeral, including the corpse.
Kingfisher Steps is the terrace town, thirty-one tiers of pools and workshops down the side of a steep green valley. Here are the dyers, the glassmen and the brass-founders, every wall hung with drying cloth in blue, and the richest invalids in the Inner World being carried up and down in chairs by men with calves like bedposts. Dye-water runs down the street gutters in stripes. Anyone who has argued with the Warden gets a free drink on the top landing.
Wealth and Trade
Power in the ground, by the hour and by the cask. Sealed casks of Wellhead water go down by barge and north by brass-bound cart, round the Scourge of Hell by one corridor or the other, to the ward-cutters of Kharven-Seat and half the alchemists of the world; the ward-cutters who re-cut the wards on the Seat’s rock each spring quench their chisels in water out of these casks, at a price Maud Corwen sets, and have been known to say what they think of it. Every practitioner wanting hours at a rich site pays a keeper. Every sect that wants a training pool for its core disciples pays a keeper more. Add bath-money, blue cloth, brass work, physicians’ fees, and a thriving trade in small sealed vials sold by persons with no connection to the house to pilgrims who will not know the difference.
Rent, Food and the Street
Rent is steep in season and steep out of it, with a room in Brightwater running above the city list and a lower price in winter for anyone who can stand the damp. Everything is cooked in the springs because the fuel is free. People eat eggs boiled in a net, trout steamed over the vent, watercress, sulfur-tasting black bread baked in hot sand, pickled plums, and on feast days a whole sheep lowered into a pool in a basket and hauled out with a good deal of shouting. The poor bathe for nothing in the overflow, and the rich pay a hundred times that to be alone.
Hedge-workers work every ditch here, reading pools for a copper and charming a bad knee for two. Brass-boys polish all day and fight all evening. Lamp-wardens from this country are hired all over the South, because a person raised on this ground takes to the craft young, and they carry the habit of the strike wherever they go; the wardens of the tower at Haeseong are Wellhead men. The Blue Bracket on the Hotwell raft fields the Steps Dyers, the Brightwater Coopers and the Hotwell Dregs, and it is said that the Dregs have never won anything and have the best songs in the South.
And the water. Since the war the springs in the south have gone bad, and nobody will say why. Some taste wrong to anyone with the tongue to taste. Villages downstream of them are sick, and the physicians do not know what they are treating. The forks in the Corwen assay posts ring as true as they ever did, and the Corwen wardens read the forks. Street life goes on around this the way it does around a family member nobody mentions. The Yukari say they can walk the springs from the mouth to the source and tell you where the harm is and whose hand is on it. House Corwen has not yet asked them to.
Law and How It Fights
Lease law is the law, and a wellmouth is its church. The Lease Court, in brass and blue, hears water rights, hours, contamination, and who touched whose fork. A false assay is the worst crime in the country, and a Corwen warden will tell you this with great sincerity while looking you directly in the eye. Assay-searchers walk the pools by rota. Water may never be taken from a kept pool without payment, a rule from which only the Dyers’ Guild has an exception, and they will show you the arm.
The house does not fight, in the sense of owning an army. It keeps a small warden’s guard in blue coats, good crossbowmen and pool-trained practitioners who are dangerous on their own ground and ordinary off it, and it hires everything else from Hammerford. What it actually does when threatened is close a door. A besieging force finds that its own practitioners have no hours at any Core within two hundred miles, that its enemy’s stand open, and that the keeper is very sorry. To fight in the Wellheads at all is to fight on ground the other side has paid for: come here with a sect behind you and you may find that a hedge-worker was out the night before with a sack of salt, and that the lovely fat ground under your feet has gone lean as a washboard, with Aether that will not pool. Anyone can hire that done. It is cheaper than spears.
What They Joke About
The lease. Every Wellhead joke ends with someone checking the wording. They tell the one about the man who drowned in a kept pool and whose widow was billed for the water he drank. They say a Lambert clerk bathes with his hat on so as not to miss anything, and that a Marrick company will fight for you all day and then sit in your bath till the contract runs out. And there is one joke that everyone in the spring country knows and nobody tells the Warden’s people to their face, which is just to raise a cup of the water and hold it out and say, After you, Maud.
Monsters on the Roads
Every kept pool is a worked Core, and most were cleared dungeons once, which is what the coin in a keeper’s purse is really paying for. A keeper can seal a site in under an hour. Sump-toads (Grade A, Well-spawn with blued-steel rings on the brow riding level with the surface) breed in the abandoned pools, Glarewings are rare and much bet on, and Hotwell’s boiling bowl has a resident Sea Serpent’s smaller cousin that nobody admits to. Beasts come for the free lunch: hill wolves after the fat sheep, boar in the watercress, otters in the trout runs, and kingfishers that have taken rings off bathers in broad daylight.
The dungeons. The one the keepers show you is the Hotwell Stair, boiling springs under Brightwater’s lease going down beneath the bath town, worked for so long that invalids boil eggs in it. It is the proof that a dungeon can be tamed, as the Corwen keepers will tell you with a brass key in their hand. The one they do not is the Long Copper, a sapphire pool at the gorge’s head so deep and clear you can watch a dropped copper fall for a long time, and then keep watching. A Phreatis Well (the Wellspring of water under the ground, copper-green) lies under it. Divers from the Steps have gone down on a rope for two centuries, and a Corwen keeper holds a key to the top landing and no idea of the bottom. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
The Scourge and the Turn. The dry wind of the Scourge of Hell gives out a long way north of the steam, and the Wellheads meet the wasteland through the books. A Southern Turn, the South’s nine years in the wheel of the Turn, runs on hours. Every practitioner a host takes north has to fill somewhere, this is the fattest ground on the way, and keepers charge what they like. Captain-generals write very long letters about it. Right of passage covers roads and victuals at a fixed price and, the Lease Court has found, does not cover hours, and the Warden replies each time that the lease makes no provision for patriotism. The bill then goes into the South’s Count, the other two regions read it, and it is the one item all three have agreed to resent.
What comes home comes to Hotwell. Marrick companies off the Line and bounty crews off the Hem sit up to their necks in water the color of tea, coughing up rim dust and lying about the Black Roots, and a one-eared cutter on the raft will fight anybody in the Blue Bracket for his supper. The small sealed vials sold to pilgrims have lately begun to promise protection from wyrms, by persons with no connection to the house.
Neighbors and Grudges
The Jade Plains. Downstream. The Yan have started counting sick foals and have shown the Warden the count.
The Silver Cedars. They have offered to walk the springs. Every month the offer is declined with the same courtesy and every month it stands in the record.
The Guild Accord. Their landlord, partner and permanent threat. The Guild’s assay is the house’s legitimacy, and the Guild depends on Corwen keepers for every lease this far south, which is a marriage both would like to see written down more clearly.
Sum-gol. The Post buys nothing from a Corwen cask. The Corwen have noticed. Cozbi Mahuo likes to put the Corwen first in the list of houses that do a job the world cannot do without, and the Warden has not decided how she feels about that.
The Kingdom of Kharven. The north’s ward-cutters depend on these casks every spring and resent every copper, and the Warden sets the price each year with a broad smile. Later hand: a Northern Empire pays the same price as a kingdom. She checked.
Further reading · The Southern Warlords

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Scarlet Wood of Thornhaven
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itTHORN-hay-ven
House Thornwall · The Thornwood · Timber and Trade
In the thaw of 688 IC the raft-boss Aud Rannsdottir of Thornhaven brought eleven thousand trunks down the Hallen in a single drive, her red-capped raftsmen dancing on the logs with their hook-poles, the river running green and brown and as loud as a market, and at the three-road junction the drive met the Hallenfeld bridge, the bridge’s toll-men and a late plate of river ice all at once. The trunks stood up on end. By noon a dam of red timber forty feet high had the whole spring flood stacked behind it, the upper town stood knee-deep, and the Hallenfeld reeve was shouting across the water that she could pay the toll on every log before he would send one man to help. Aud Rannsdottir, who had a coat of aura the color of hot copper and a low opinion of reeves, walked out on the jam in front of both towns, found the one trunk holding all the others by kicking them in turn, bawled the only technique she ever troubled to name, FIRST OF THE MELT, and put her boot through it.
The jam went all at once. It took the bridge, the fish market, the reeve’s counting-house and seventeen people who had come down to watch, and Thornwall and Hallenfeld fought over the bill with boar-spears in the road for the rest of that spring, while the loose trunks drifted south past Ashbury and warmed the grain-lords’ stoves for a decade. Then winter came. Both towns were short of bread and roofs, and in January the men who had been killing each other in May were splitting wood at one pile, because the alternative was to be found in the spring by whoever was left. Thornhaven still has her boot, on a shelf in the Raftmen’s Hall, and it can be viewed for a copper.
The Scarlet Wood is a red forest of trees as tall as a keep, floated downriver by the shipload by merchant-warriors who can tell you what you will run short of six months before you know you need it.

Two hands on this page. It stands in Year 715. Lines marked Later hand come from the annotator of the Concordance of Ages, writing in the last winter before the turn. Later hand: the Wood is a land of House Thornwall inside the Northern Empire of Whitemere, holding the empire’s road to the Marrowkin.

The Land and What It Looks Like
The Thornwood runs across the hills east of Kharven-Seat and north along the head of the Ironwood March, and nobody forgets it. These are giant ironwoods, red-barked, the color of a fox at the crown and of old dried blood at the root, their trunks wider than a house and going up two hundred feet before the first branch, standing in snow as bright as linen. In the low sun the whole forest turns the color of an open furnace. Under the canopy the light comes down in long gold bars and the air smells of resin and woodsmoke, and every sound comes close until the raft-horns start and drown the lot. The dense stands are too cold for anything but moss and bear, and the Wood’s bright little towns sit in the clearings along the rivers.
Those towns are the second thing you notice. Everyone here builds in the wood, because it is there and because it will outlast your grandchildren, and they carve it, with every gable, doorpost and beam-end a knot of beasts and leaves painted red and ocher and verdigris blue, so that a Thornwall hall looks like a chest somebody has spent forty winters decorating. The rivers are thick from thaw to midsummer with log rafts, hundreds of feet long, with a cook-shack and a family and a goat on each one.
Where the old road goes in, mist lies under the trees and scarlet leaves blow across everything, and at the head of a flight of worn steps stands a ruined archway of carved stone, older than the house and older than anyone’s account of the house, an old clan gate with nothing left of the clan. Long strings of faded cloth flags run off from it between the trunks as far as you can see. They are the loggers’ tally, one flag for each great tree taken, and every raft-boss has tied some of them. People call the place the Red Stair.
The forest also has the long cuts, narrow straight rides through the deep stands, walled in by trees so old and so close you cannot see the sky. Foresters of the house have kept them open for longer than the house will discuss, and when you ask why, they tell you it is for the timber.
The major places

Thornhaven. The seat, in the northern March where the Thornwood comes down to the water. A town of carved red halls, the Raftmen’s Hall, the cargo-roll house, and on the hill the Thornwall hall itself with its black roof-tree. It is also the best place in the north for fire-enamel: the workshop of the Hale family has fired harness-fronts for lords who should have asked the price first.
Raftwick. The great raft-town at the head of the river-drives, half of it afloat. It shifts its streets every spring and has no reliable map, and you tie up where you can. Raftsmen’s brackets are fought on moving logs in spiked boots, and spectators bet from the bank.

Roads. By raft in the thaw, down to the Hallenfeld junction and beyond, with a toll fought over every spring. East runs the corridor, road and river-chain, to Collarbone in Marrowhold. North past the last spruce is the Aurora Reach, two weeks by sled from the Whalebone Gather in the hard months. South along the March are the Starks, in the habit of checking the stones.
House and Rule
House Thornwall is merchant-warrior, comfortable with commerce in a way most northern houses find slightly undignified and the Thornwalls consider essential. Their wealth comes from the ironwood stands the Marrowkin import for tool handles and ward-frames, and their function as the house on the Marrowhold corridor gives them an outsized voice in the north’s trade. They read cargo rolls the way other houses read battle reports, and consider the ability to predict a supply shortage six months out a more valuable military skill than the ability to hold a shield wall, on the grounds that the shield wall is useless if the men behind it are starving. They are almost always correct about trade, which is why the other houses find them slightly irritating.
The ruler in Year 715 is Hisae Thornwall, the Lady, about sixty and looking thirty-five. She married north forty years ago from the Shiraki hills to seal a peace nobody now remembers, and the rest of the north calls her the old woman while being careful where she can hear. She has sat in Thornhaven all that time under Tenrai taxes and Tenrai factors and Tenrai silver with a small dry smile, paying on the day. Her husband is not named on the record, and no one has ever got far by asking about him. The Tenrai count Thornwall bought. People who trade with her count their fingers after.
Wealth and Trade
Ironwood, first and always. Dense, hard, slow to rot, wanted for tool handles and ward-frames and ships’ keels, and floated down to anyone with money. The corridor next: the road and river-chain east to Collarbone in Marrowhold, up which Thornwall sends timber and down which come the worked metal and the inscription stock ward-craft needs. Thornwall carriers move both and are paid for both. Then furs, pitch, tar, charcoal, resin, carved goods, and a small but well-loved line in tall painted drinking horns.
Thornwall reads a trading partner’s behavior like a physician reading a pulse. When the Ore Council of Marrowhold cuts the grain it resells up the corridor and keeps sending inscription stock, the Thornwalls notice first, because they have tracked the holds’ trade for generations and know the difference between a shortage and a message. Their standing reading: that kind of cut is political rather than logistical, because the holds are comfortable with an armed frontier buffer and uncomfortable with an independent one. They also tried once to take the whale-oil trade off the Keld by force, with a warband past the treeline, and the Keld still sing about it, and so does the wood, more quietly.
Rent, Food and the Street
Foresters and raftsmen hold their posts by a house contract and are paid in a share of the drive, and it is not unusual for a raft-boss to own more than the lord she is delivering to. A room over the rope-walk in Thornhaven runs in copper, in split wood (everyone has wood, so it is priced badly), or a fortnight on the drive. Food is smoked river fish, venison and bear in a dark gravy, birch-sap beer in spring, flat barley bread bought dear from Ashmore. Every raft has a pot on it that has not been washed since the raft was built, and they will tell you this is why it tastes of something.
Thornwall’s street life is carving. People whittle at table and in court, and a child gets a knife before shoes. Guild-marks are cut into every worked beam, and carvers brag about theirs and sue each other. Raftsmen wear red caps and sing dirty songs in rounds, and have a low-grade bracket scene between the red caps of Raftwick and the charcoal burners, the Black Hands, who are fairly sure the raftsmen are all thieves. Hedge-workers talk bark-beetle out of a stand and frost-crack out of a trunk, and they refuse to work at all on the far side of a long cut after dark, and give no reason for it.
What they joke about. Prices. A Thornwall will price the damage aloud while it is happening, and did so at his own wedding. Hallenfeld reeves. People who think a forest is scenery. “Six months” is the standing Thornwall punchline: told of anything that is about to go wrong, in a tone of mild regret.
Law and How It Fights
Law. A contract cut in wood with two guild-marks on it is good from here to the Center. The Raftmen’s Hall settles everything on the water, the cargo-roll house everything off it, and the Lady whatever is left, and the Lady is rarely troubled.
The fighting. House soldiers wear Thornwall gray felt and iron caps. The signature is the Thornwall hedge: long ash-and-iron spears, coming on at a walk, in step, to the slow beat of a drum, with the thorn-horn sounding behind them every hundred paces, then setting a hedge that horse will not go into. A Marrick captain would laugh at the length of those spears and has done, and the Thornwalls wrote his name down. It holds ground and takes walls, it is slow, and the fair answer is horse on open ground before the hedge is set. Woodsmen fight in the stands with axes and short bows, from behind things eight feet thick. Raft-crews fight with hook-poles and spiked boots, and they will drop a trunk on you. Technique names in the Wood tend to be named for the job, and nobody south of Ashbury should believe FIRST OF THE MELT was a joke.
Monsters on the Roads
The beasts are the Wood’s real landlords. Bear keeps the dense stands, where it is too dark for anything but moss and him. Marten, boar and red deer take the rest, and a boar in the stump fields has put more axe-men in bed than the Keld ever did. The beetle that a hedge-worker must talk out of a stand is about as long as your thumb, and over the years it has cost the house more than any war.
The monsters. Monsters move, and they live across the whole of the Inner World, and in a forest this old some of them have stopped bothering to. Sasquatch (Grade C on the Bestiary’s scale, which runs from E to EX) move through the deep stands masking their scent, and most foresters leave them food. Dryads (Grade C) guard the oldest groves and have started two wars with the axe crews. Reaching Briars take the edges of the stump fields. Hedge-workers refuse to work on the far side of a long cut (a narrow straight ride through the deep stands) after dark and give no reason, and I set that down without comment.
The Red Stair and the Long Cuts
The dungeon (what a Wellspring Core makes around itself, or what grows up around one) is the Red Stair: a ruined carved archway older than the house, at the head of worn steps, with long strings of faded cloth flags running off between the trees. The loggers’ tally flags are tied there, one for each great tree taken. The steps go down among the roots into a Well nobody has reached the bottom of, and a raft-boss who has been down to the second landing drinks free in Raftwick.
The other thing crews talk about is the Long Cuts themselves. The Bestiary’s shelf files them as said to be a lying-down, the crews’ word for a dungeon laid flat with no roof: an edge you can cross without noticing, ground that thickens as you go on, and stock that changes with the ground. Nobody in the Wood admits they are anything. Crews have offered to walk one end to end, and the foresters have been very civil about refusing. It is for the timber, they will tell you, in a forest where nobody has taken a tree off one in living memory. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
The Scourge and the Turn
The Scourge of Hell is a very long haul from the Wood, and the Wood has been selling to it for as long as the house has kept rolls. The Turn is the old rotation by which North, South and Center each spend nine years keeping its monsters off everybody else, and the party whose Turn it is keeps the Line, a chain of forts and beacon towers round the Hem, the Scourge’s outer belt. Those forts want roof-trees and stakes that will not rot in country that is dry overhead and damp under the surface, and ironwood does not, so whoever holds the Turn ends up buying Thornwall trunks, floated down to Ashbury and carted on from there, at a rate the cargo-roll house quoted six months before they knew they needed it. The house has sold to all three parties in one year and regards this as the whole point of a rotation.
On a Northern Turn it also owes spears, and the Thornwall hedge has gone down the Kessen road at its walk behind its slow drum. A hedge is a fine thing against horse and an indifferent one against whatever comes up through the ground beneath it, as the surviving sergeants reported, with the cost per yard. On the last such Turn, which ended in 703, a Thornwall forester went in as far as the Black Roots on a bet, to see what tree those roots came from. He cut a slice with a hand-saw, smelled it, priced it at nothing and walked home, and that is the Wood’s entire published opinion on the subject. The Center has the Turn until 721. The wheel then comes back to the North, and the cargo-roll house has already begun buying ash.
Neighbors and Grudges

The Painted Rivers. The log-jam of 688, still in the ledgers on both sides. Thornwall calls it the toll-men’s fault, Hallenfeld calls it murder, and every spring they renegotiate the rate on logs through the junction in a spirit of mutual loathing.
The Ember Holds of Marrowhold. Their largest customer and their largest worry. The Marrowkin treat the house as a door they would like to keep ajar, and they can close it from their side.
The Aurora Reach. The whale-oil, the warband, the song.
The Cobalt March. Next door, and in the habit of checking the stones. A Thornwall groom priced the damage at the Stark wedding of 592 aloud while the bear was still eating. The Starks remember, and the bride laughed.
Kharven-Seat. Their old employer, from when the Kōkan still sat the red chair and Thornwall was its forester. The Tenrai tax them now. Thornwall pays and writes it down.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Scourge of Hell
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Art: lyraina.com.
The Scourge of Hell
Say itthe SKURJ of HELL · also Hell's Scourge
The vast wasteland at the center of the Inner World: no ruler, no road through it, one colossal sword, and the worst monsters on the map

Item, for the keeping of the Line, nine years: see attached. Item, for the dead: see attached. Item, owed to us by the other two: see attached.
Cover sheet of the Count, the same in every copy, in three different hands

At a quarter hour before noon on Midsummer Day of 676, in the market square of Lastpenny on the Kessen road, the biggest earth wyrm anyone living had seen came up through the cheese stalls. It came straight out of the ground in a fountain of paving and yellow rounds, a long bronze hill with scales the size of shields and a crest of stone spines, and it took the herald who was reading the speech. Around that square, under every banner they owned, stood eleven thousand soldiers in perfect order. Six thousand Banner spears of the North were drawn up on one side in Hollenmark blue and Stormfold slate. Five thousand of the Marrick companies stood on the other in ochre and black, with their drums. They had come for the handing-over of the Turn, the old arrangement by which the realms of the North, the South and the Center each take nine years keeping the Scourge of Hell off everybody else, and the Turn passed at noon, by the Accord’s water clock, which stood on a trestle in the middle of the square under a green awning with a clerk beside it.
The northern marshal had formally stood his host down an hour before, with a very fine speech. Past that moment a Northern man who fought did so at his own cost, with no bounty and no pension for his widow. The southern captain-general’s contract began at noon and not one drop earlier, and the Marrick companies do not fight off contract for anyone. So the two commanders looked at the water clock, and then at each other, and folded their arms. Eleven thousand spears stood and watched while the wyrm ate the Corn Hall, the reeve, and the better half of Butter Row. The whole town screamed at them in the Midmarch tongue, and a goblin king the size of a child beat on the marshal’s stirrup with a ladle. Nine minutes in, someone tipped the water clock. The Center says it was a cheese-wife called Gytha Rowe, who had lost her stall and both her sons. The North says it was the wyrm’s tail, the South says the clock was fast, and the clerk, who was sworn to read the instrument as it stood, looked into the bowl and called noon in a voice like a nail.
The Marrick drums came in before he finished the word. It took them until the lamps were lit to drive the thing back down, with four hundred dead and nine hundred spears left standing in its hide, and the South presented the North with the bill for all of it, as the North’s last act of negligence. The wyrm still comes up every eleven years or so along that stretch of the road, still wearing the spears. Everyone calls it Old Pincushion, and the companies can tell you by the marks whose pay each one was. In the Center, to this day, a northerner or a southerner who declines to help you has said it isn’t noon, and you are entitled to spit.
Here is the place in a breath: a wasteland as big as a kingdom at the center of the continent, filled with monsters so long ago that the oldest rolls already call it full, under a purple sky, with a sword in it. Nobody rules it and nobody marches through it, which is why the Center is shaped the way it is, why every army in history has used the same two roads, and why three great regions of the world hate one another with such careful bookkeeping.
Where It Lies and How Far It Runs
The Inner World is one long continent pinched in the middle, and this is the pinch. The Guild gives the Scourge as some hundred and eighty leagues from north to south and a hundred and forty across, a league being about three miles and the figures being, by the admission of the man who drew them, a matter of walking round the outside and multiplying. No survey has crossed it. No road crosses it. All traffic between North and South goes around by two corridors, the Kessen road down the west flank and the salt road up the east, and every realm of the Center lives along those roads with its back to the thing.























































SideWho holds itWhat they do about the ScourgeNorthThe Amber Cities of Nalūn, in the salt basinKeep the Salt Line (below), and pay for everything in bars. Their cutters call the dry country south of them the ThreshNorthwestThe Violet Peaks of CaelspireAvian scouts read the wind off the Haze from the high stairs and sell what they see, and every herd sighting on the western side comes from them, at their priceWestThe Moonlight Forest of Mosk-VaalThe Moss Court lets things come in, and plants them. Its garden has a very long Scourge bedWest and east, on the roadsThe Hundred Crowns of the MidmarchPetty kings who post bounties on doors, hire free companies, and lose a castle now and then. Barley and monsters are the two great local harvestsEast, at the crossingThe Sealed Charter of the ConcordKeeps the law up to the marker posts. Past Verath, where the guild’s jurisdiction ends at two iron posts with red-painted caps, lies the Verath Expanse, the Charter’s own name for its stretch of the HemEastThe Russet Crown of the UnpaperedRefuses to sign anything, and fights it anyway, since the things that come out have never asked to see a rollSoutheastThe Rose Coils of CoilspireTreats everyone who comes out alive, and keeps a record of everything anyone says in feverSouthThe Ochre Fields of Hammerford, and the Long FieldsMuster ground. Marrick companies sign their Scourge contracts at Spearmoot, and the land turns green and starts its long drop to the seaSouthwestThe Vermilion Dynasty of Sum-gol, at the Kessen road’s endIron hills and salt pans, and a long memory of an empire that once claimed the Scourge on paper
What It Looks Like
The first thing to say is that the name led me to expect something drab, and the name is a liar. It is the most violently colored country I have ever been frightened in. The stone is iron red and rust and in places a wet-looking purple. The haze goes copper at noon and rose at evening, and past the middle of it the sky itself turns the color of a bruised plum and stays there, day and night, with stars in it at midday if you are far enough in to be wrong about the time. Thorn-vines flower in vermilion after the spring rains. Lightning walks around the dry beds in green and violet with no storm behind it. A painter would be delighted, briefly.
The Sword
Then there is the thing everybody came to see. Near the center of the Scourge, driven point-down into a range of mountains, stands a sword.
It stands about four leagues above the peaks by the best reckoning, or about three, those being the two surveys, taken from the Windstair and from Stoneglass Hollow, whose authors did not speak afterward. You can make it out from the Hem on perhaps nine clear days in the year, when the wind off the interior drops, a dark upright line on the sky. It has a bronze hilt with a guard as wide as a city, and in however many ages it has stood there the bronze has not gone green. The blade has no metal in it that anyone can see. Look at it and you are looking through a tall sword-shaped window at a starfield, deep violet and crowded, and as you walk along a ridge the stars shift against the blade’s edges, near ones faster than far ones, the way the view through a real window shifts. Every star-clerk who has seen it agrees on two things: that the sky in there is no sky over this world, and that it should not be possible to agree about that from so far away.
Every edge town has the picture on a tavern sign, painted by every hand from masters to drunks: a lone figure on a ridge, under a purple sky, holding an ordinary sword and looking up. Half those taverns are called the Ordinary Sword. The other half are called the Other One.
The Land by Depth
The Scourge gets worse as you go in, and it does so in belts, which is the first thing that made the Guild suspect it of being a dungeon laid flat. The wind comes outward from the middle in every season, hot and dry, which is why the whole rim country smells of iron and pollen and why nobody has ever had the wind at their back going in.















































BeltWidth, roughlyClimateHabitatGround (scholars’ rung)The Hem15 leaguesLong hot summers under a dry wind, clear hard winters, a short violent green after spring rainForest and desert forced into one country: black-barked thornwood, dry hissing grass, iron-colored stone jutting up at angles, soil dark in patches and then pale dust. Damp under the surface, alwaysRill thickening to FreshetThe Black Roots20 leaguesDry wind above, and warm and wet an arm’s length down. Sinkholes steam on cold morningsA mat of black roots with no tree anyone has found at the end of them, wrist-thick at the outer edge and thick as a cottage further in. Lime and violet fungus, thorn-groves, hollow ground. The ground stops feeling like ground and begins feeling like a lidFreshet to MillraceThe Haze25 leaguesHaze that has never been recorded clearing, a fine dust of iron and pollen. The sun is a copper coin. Dry lightning, and very rare rain that does not reach the groundDead river courses, salt flats in pink and white, seas of stiff red grass. Herd country, and the dry beds run water some years, sometimes uphillMillrace to RiptideThe Shambles20 leaguesWeather in patches with no relation to each other: frost on one ridge, a furnace on the next. The sky begins to go purpleMountains, and the dead battlefields of the Great Spirit War on every slope: fused glass, ghoststeel lying about in drifts, things the size of churches with their armor still on. Time runs wrongRiptide to WhirlpoolThe Socket10 leagues, if anyone knowsNobody has returned with an opinion on the weather that a physician would acceptThe broken mountains around the blade. A violet sky with stars at noonNot placed
The rungs are the sites ladder (the register’s scale of how strong you must be to stand on dense ground and stay yourself), and those past the Hem are estimates by people in a hurry. The Northern Shield as a whole reads Rill. Each rung up asks more, and a Millrace is survivable for an afternoon and not for a season, which every crew in the Haze is aware of and has decided to think about later.
Ground as a lid. People who have walked the Black Roots all say the same thing, and it is the thing to listen to. The roots hold up a thin crust over warm hollow dark, and the big things travel below it. A small party can feel it through the boot soles, a shudder running along under the mat. Edge towns have a petty trade in it: the lid-listeners, hired for a few coppers a night, usually old women with one small gift, who lie with an ear on a stake in the ground and tell a crew how many legs are coming.
Why the Monsters Are Worse Here
Monsters move, and you will meet them on every road in the Inner World, and beasts are more widespread still. Every realm in the world has its own bad road and its own song about it. But this is the one area known for extremely dangerous monsters, and a Realm Hazard (Grade SS on the Commission’s bounty scale, which names the Accord title it would have to send) gets a name and a ballad anywhere else on the map, and here it gets eaten. The Guild’s accounts for this:
Age. It was full before the rolls begin, and no one has ever thinned it. Everywhere else a thing that grows dangerous gets a bounty on the doors, and a crew comes, eventually. Here it has had thousands of years of being left alone.
Stacked Wells. A Well (ground where one kind of Aether lies thick enough to rewrite what lives in it) elsewhere has its own country around it and its own stock. Here they lie on top of each other like dropped cards. A crew in the Haze may break masks in five colors before lunch.
They eat each other. Nothing native to the ground above an ordinary Well will touch a Well-spawn. In the Scourge, wyrms and worse have learned to, and masks have been cut out of stomachs here, and nowhere else on file. What survives a hundred thousand generations of that is very good at what it does.
The Scourge-born. Its great herds breed true and wear no masks, which the register’s own rules say should not happen, since an animal warped by dense ground is supposed to come out short-lived and sterile. These have been at it so long that they stopped being warped and became a kind of animal. The entries sit under Natural Beasts, under protest. Beasts plus time plus Essence, as one old cutter put it, ecosystems with teeth. And unlike a shallow spawn they hold ground. Above a certain size a thing has a range, and it will not chase you out of it, since you are simply its until you leave or die.
The wound. The reading I favor, and no one can prove: the sword went into something, and all of this is what has been leaking out around it since.
