A wyrm steadies the Aether around it, so crews in the Haze are always a little glad to find one, for about as long as it takes to see itGrade SSThe crownedThe Shambles and whatever comes out of itSurveyors mark the ones they call great with a little crown on the map. Individuals, each one its own kind of disaster, with names and bookiesGrade SS and up
A wyrm core. This is the fourth meaning of the word, and I apologize for it. Inside a big creature’s chest the Essence Core (the seat of its nature) hardens over centuries into a fist of glassy stuff in the wyrm’s own color, and a good one sells for a small fortune anywhere there is a crucible. Every body on the Scourge gets cut open for it before it is cold. Do not confuse this with the Core at a worked site, and be careful which one you promise a factor.
The herds’ season. In late summer, in a dry year, the wind and the thirst push the herds outward, and what follows the herds comes with them. That is when the barley goes, and that is the season the whole arrangement below exists to meet.
Dungeons and Cores
Dungeons, the Bestiary explains at length, are what a Wellspring site makes around itself, and the Scourge has more of them than it has surveyors. Cores (a Core being a site where one of the sixty kinds of Aether pools) mostly lie in dungeons and are also said to lie in vast territories, and the first thing anyone says about a vast territory is this one. There is a respectable school which holds that the whole Scourge is a single Core with no roof, so large it has weather. It has not been able to explain the other Wells, and has not stopped trying.
The ones crews talk about:

The Lamplit Stair, in the Verath Expanse. An Aurevane stair going down from a thornwood gully, its walls a hard blue-white. It has been cleared twice and lost twice, and it is where half the Green Sigils in the Charter get their first bad night.
Nine Wells Gulch, in the Black Roots. Nine separate Mouths inside a morning’s walk, no two of the same Wellspring, and a mask market on the lip in good years with its own cook-tents and bookies. Crews have won it nine times by count. Nobody has held it through a second winter.
The Upside Abbey, in the Haze. A whole abbey hanging from the underside of a rock arch, an Ascensio ground (a Wellspring of lift and weight), with its floors over your head and its bells hanging up. Relic hunters adore it. You go in by rope, and nobody agrees on which direction you fall when you stop.
The Dry Harbor, in the Haze. A Thaloré ground (the Wellspring of crushing depth) in a dead river mouth. No water has been there in the memory of anyone, and yet men are found on bone-dry stone crushed flat as if from a great depth, with their ears burst and, in a few cases, a Mourning Pike’s mask nearby in deep teal.
The Long Muster, in the Shambles. A dead camp of the Great Spirit War on a slope, tents long since gone and the lines still straight, which takes the roll every dusk in a language no one has placed. It has more ghoststeel lying about than the rest of the shield together. Nobody who has answered to their name there has been of further use.
The Wound, at the foot of the sword. Said to be a Core. Said by people who have not been there, mostly, to people who are buying them a drink. Bookies will take any bet on it, at any odds, on the sound principle that nobody will ever come back to collect.

The Turn
The arrangement has no good name. The chancery calls it the Rota, the wheel. Everyone else calls it the Turn. North, then South, then Center, nine years each, then round again, so that a full wheel takes twenty-seven years and most adults have seen enough of it to hold firm views. Nobody can produce the original. The copy at Sealhall refers to an older copy, and that one refers to “the ancient custom.”
The three parties. The North, the South and the Center each mean whoever can be made to pay. On the North’s Turn that means Kharven and its Banner Houses. The South’s means the old Dynasty’s realms, the white shelf of Alabaster and the hired spears of Hammerford. The Center’s means everybody who lives along the rim, which is a story in itself.
What it costs. The party whose Turn it is keeps the Line, a chain of forts and beacon towers around the Hem. It pays the bounties posted on doors for anything that comes out, fields a host every herd season, and answers for every carter lost on the corridors. It may march through anyone’s land to do so, by right of passage, and buy victuals at a fixed price. The other two owe it nothing but a fixed subsidy that has been paid in full on no known occasion.
The Count. The other two watch their borders, send a clerk, and write it all down. Every Turn ends with each party presenting a Count of what the last nine years cost it and what it is therefore owed. The Accord’s Arbitration division audits them at Sealhall, for a fee, and has never yet produced a figure that any party accepted. The accumulated difference is now larger than all the coin in the world. It is carried forward.
The resentments.
The North says the South hires its killing done, and walks off the field on the last day of the contract in the middle of whatever it was doing. This is accurate. A Northern Turn runs like a campaign, in long disciplined columns down the Kessen road, with icebear riders from the March going slowly mad from the heat. And it says the Ashmores of the Golden Hollow, who sell grain at the junction where the two roads meet, have never lost a Turn in their history, which is also accurate.
The South says the North only ever comes down to look at the Center’s castles, and that half the invasions in the Center’s history began as a Turn that lost its way. This has been shown on maps. A Southern Turn runs by the season, on contract, with subscription lists at Alabaster and keepers at the Wellheads charging what they like for the hours. It is well run and it stops at sundown on the last day.
The Center says the other two take turns. The Center lives here. The host passing through on someone else’s Turn eats its barley going up, and its castles are the ones with the wall knocked in. When its own Turn comes round, the Charter pays by instrument, the Midmarch kings each send nine men and a very loud banner, Nalūn pays in salt and complains in writing, the Scalebond send surgeons at their posted price, the Violet Peaks pay in sightings and seniors, the Moss Court plants what it is sent, and the Unpapered, who are on no roll, fight regardless and bill nobody. Free companies on Thresh contracts do most of the dying. The Center holds the Turn at present, from 712 to 721, and the betting in Kingsbridge is on who will be standing to hand it over.
The Salt Line. Nalūn’s one contribution everybody admires. A strip of salted ground, worked by hedge-workers with Chainsalt so that Aether will not pool on it, some sixty miles along the north rim and a hundred paces deep, renewed each spring. Whatever comes across it comes off its Well and comes weaker. It costs a fortune and it holds about as well as a fence, and on the far side of it the cutters of Halcrest will tell you which stretches were salted honestly.
Who Goes In
Bounty crews. There is more bounty on the doors of the rim towns than anywhere else in the world, and a wyrm core on top of it. Crews come from every school in every realm, in every color they can afford, because a tally from the Scourge is worth three from anywhere else, and a song comes with it. Catkin out of the Russet Crown run some of the best-regarded outfits on the eastern side, and they are paid in actual money. The hobgoblins on the western ridges are the long-service men of the trade: outcasts and contract hands from the Mandate and the Isles, working the ridges above the Black Roots, stripping carcasses and hiring out as guides. A hobgoblin may see two centuries if the world allows it, so a ridge-man who says he has been doing this for a hundred and thirty years may well mean it.
Relic hunters. The Shambles are the richest dead battlefield known. Ghoststeel, the phasing metal nobody has ever reproduced in a crucible, lies there in quantities that would ruin the market if anybody could get it out, and so do old gear with names and legendary arts carved or bottled by the dead. People have killed one another over a good piece on the road home, three days short of the rim, within sight of the tavern.
Sects. Most of the fighting schools of the Center send their seniors to walk the Hem, and the proud ones send them to the Black Roots, with the school song and a banner. Coming back with a mask is how a Journeyman gets a name. The schools of the Violet Peaks keep an annual tally of kills per student and post it on the bridge, and a school that loses a season’s seniors will recruit twice as hard for the glory of it.
Sword-pullers. There is one every few years. A young Midmarch king with a good jaw, a sect heir, a farm boy with a dream, who sets out with a following, bookies alongside and a minstrel on retainer, to walk to the middle and draw it. The Hundred Crowns have a particular weakness for this. The record is held by a Tinker Goblin named Nixie Sprocket, who got into the Shambles with a mule-drawn engine of her own design and sent back a letter describing the bronze as warm, and whether that means she reached it or wished to, the bookies have never paid out.
Surveyors. Measurewrights go in with forks to settle things, and porters go in with them.
What Scholars Argue About the Sword
Most agree it is an old work of the Great Spirit War, from the days of the Physical Epochs when Bara, Ashura and Aegor walked in human form. Everything else is open, and a good Guild dinner can be ruined by asking.

Who drove it in. Every list of the great combatants of that war has its partisans, every partisan has a passage, and the passages were written long afterward by people who already held the opinion. I have seen a knife drawn over this at a funeral.
What it was driven into. A foe, say the romantic schools, and the mountains are what grew over the body. A rift, say the sober ones: a place like the Crevice in the Southern Pan, torn open in the war and stopped with the only plug to hand. If so, nobody should pull it, and every few years somebody sets out to.
Whether it is a sword. A small and very pleased school of Measurewrights holds that the thing is a standing tear in the Veil, and that “hilt” and “blade” are what a human eye does with a shape it cannot read. The bronze is an awkward fact for this school, and it has a whole volume on why bronze is an illusion.
What the stars are. One star-clerk at Sealhall has spent his career recording the field in the blade from borrowed reports, and he holds that it has moved twice in three centuries. Others hold that this proves the reports are bad.
What the neighbors think. The Marrowkin look at the Ring’s ribs, look at the sword, and suggest it is a butcher’s pin marking a cut. The Moss Court says it is a stake holding up something that has not finished growing. The Scalebond remember what it was, they say, and they will tell you for a sum nobody has ever been able to raise. The Moto have a word for it that they do not use in front of guests.

The Edge Towns
Everybody expects an edge town to be a sad little place of ash and widows. It has the widows. It is also the loudest, brightest, most expensive and most cheerful town you will ever try to get a night’s sleep in, because every person in it either just came back alive or is about to find out.

Lastpenny. On the Kessen road, in the Midmarch. Rebuilt in stone, and they have kept the awning. The Noon Fair every Midsummer sells a hard yellow cheese with a bite out of it, and at noon the whole town stands in the square and turns its back on any soldiers present.
Goodmorrow. On the salt road, under the Charter’s edge. A town of painted stilts over a sinkhole country, every bridge a different color so you can tell them apart through the haze. It has the best mask-clerks on the east side and the worst beer.
Halcrest. Nalūn’s gate, where the salt thins against the northern rim, the far side of the basin from the Thresh and the place every crew signs on, with cutters’ taverns and a map trade. Everybody here will sell you a copy of a copy of the good map.
Rootgate. The Moss Court’s gate on the western flank, where the orcs will sell you a burial plot before you go, at a discount for paying in advance, and it is the only place on the rim where the prices fall as your chances do.

The houses all sit on stone footings with no cellars, which is the first thing you notice and the last thing they will joke about, and above the street run plank walks from roof to roof. Every wall is painted vermilion, yellow and blue, because it has to be seen through the haze, and every eave hangs with ground-bells on iron stakes that go a good way down, so that a shudder under the lid sets the whole street ringing. In the taverns the crews’ tallies are painted over the door, and the board at the hall goes three bills deep. Outside the hall are the renderers, the core-buyers, the Scalebond surgeon who knows how the last man with your wound died, and the bookies on barrels with the depth odds chalked up for every crew that went out this week. Hedge-workers salt your doorstep for a copper and your bed for two.
Black-root tea is the local drink, bitter as a lawsuit, and every kind of meat in the stew is a matter of faith. A careful man pays for his own wake before he goes in, and the wake-houses keep the money in a marked jar. If he comes back he drinks it, with everyone he knows, and that is the great daily festival of an edge town: somebody at the door, burned and laughing and one ear short, shouting for his jar. The Widows’ Bench outside the hall is an actual bench, and the women on it are among the best-informed investors on the rim, holding more shares in more crews than any factor. They will tell you to your face what you are worth.
At dusk the lamp-wardens go round and the whole town lights up in every color its keepers have, and out past the last wall the wind comes in off the Hem smelling of iron and flowers. On one of the nine clear days everybody stops what they are doing and goes up on the roof walks to look at it, the dark line standing up out of the end of the world, and then the bookies call the odds again and they all go back in.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
The heartland of the Guild Accord, in the Center, where the wax comes from

The Accord holds no territory. I have read that sentence many times, in a room it owns, on a street it owns, in a city it bought.
Marginal note in the open shelf’s copy of the Articles, in an archivist’s hand, unsigned

On the second morning of the Veyra’s Day fair in the year 677 a Catkin named Whitlow Sixtoes, who carried wax for a chandler at Waxgate and had been sold at Verath for seventeen gold marks when she was nine, stood in line at a market-court window in Sealhall with six copper in her fist. She reached the front at about the hour the clerk reached his seventieth petition. He was a man named Corbin Ashlar with forty years on that window, and she told him she wished to bring an action of detinue, the plea for the return of goods wrongfully held, against the chandler, for one Catkin. He took the coin, wrote out the form, entered her in the party line, and struck it in green wax without looking up. She had read the formulary aloud to herself on the wax wagon for eleven years, and she took the instrument from his hand with both of hers and walked outside and held it up.
A party is a person. Nothing in seven centuries of chancery text has ever let a chattel plead, and only formulary wordings bind, and the wording was perfect. By noon the wax-carriers of every quarter in the city had downed their baskets and were carrying her through Long Spine Street on their shoulders, under the blue and orange banners, with Catkin on every roof and the bookies giving nine to one. For three days she was the only Beastkin in the Charter with standing nobody could dispute, and on the third they heard her in the Ribs, under the great curved bones, with more people on those benches than the Measurewrights will swear can fit. A Scalebond advocate spoke for her for free, from memory, for six hours. Enforcement wanted the clerk’s head. It fell to an Examiner of Arbitration, Dame Isolde Averell, to find the way out, and she found it in the accounts. She rose and ruled that the fee had been accepted in error. She walked down to the beam in the middle of the floor, in front of all of them, counted out six copper and the interest due on them, to the fourth part of a copper, and put them in Whitlow’s hand, and the instrument was void from the moment of the refund, before witnesses, because a person whose fee has been returned has never been a party to anything.
Nobody in the Ribs made any noise at all for about as long as it takes to breathe twice. Then Whitlow Sixtoes threw the coins at the bench, and the riot lasted until Irath’s Day. The Legion took the carriers’ quarter back street by street, and forty-one people died. Corbin Ashlar refused to say he had made an error and was struck from the roll at seventy-one. Whitlow went over the wall of the Ribs that night, up the bones, in a way no Measurewright has since been able to reproduce, and Brokencollar says she reached it. Brokencollar says many things. Every window in the Charter now carries a standing instruction that a petitioner without free-holder papers be written in the party line as nemo, nobody, so that it can never happen again. In the market towns a bad bargain with a smile on it is called a Sealhall refund.
The Sealed Charter is the country the Guild Accord swears it does not have: a bright white land of wax, weights and windows, where the law is faster than anywhere in the world and everybody who can pay for it adores it. The rest of this entry is how that works, and who it was written against.
The Land and the Look
The Charter lies in the Center, on the good low country on the east flank of the Scourge of Hell, where the salt road crosses the roads to the Russet forest and the Bearkin hills, with the salt basin to the north of it. It is green and blue and yellow in summer, all hay meadow and bee-country, with lavender and clover grown by the mile for the hives, and white towns on brown rivers, each with a beam in the yard and the bronze reach (the Accord’s standard length) set into the market wall at hand height. Every town flies its wax colors over the hall door. A kept street burns its lamps in the color of whoever keeps them, amber, rose or kingfisher green, so the country at dusk looks like a jeweler’s tray.
Sealhall dominates it, and you will see Sealhall from a day away. It is a vast walled city around a single vast white hall, with obelisk towers standing along its roofline and blue and orange banners the size of mainsails running down them. Two great statues stand on the wall above the south gate, each ninety feet of pale stone in a long robe, with their spears crossed over the road, and over the crossing hangs a horned skull bigger than a barn. Inside the walls, at the center of everything, there is a round arena ringed by the colossal curved bones of a dead beast, and the beast’s spine trails away from it across the city and out through the wall into the barley.
The Three Places You Will Be Sent
Sealhall
Sealhall is a city of perhaps sixty thousand who all claim to be there on business. The Hall of the Seal is where a Regional Envoy’s business comes to be finished: the high windows of the chancery, the rolls of the formulary, the great water clock that keeps the Guild hour, which older rolls place at Stannvaard and which every clerk in the Charter will now tell you has always been here. The obelisks carry the head of the beacon line, and the beacon line coming down out of the Concord Citadel is read by more people than any other line in the world, so that a change in the lamps on the third obelisk will move the price of bread by evening.
The Citadel itself is elsewhere. The City of Latticeglass stands between planes, visible only to those bound to the Lattice (the living web of Essence signatures that records every oath), and Sealhall is the place on the ground from which the bound look up at it. A sworn agent crossing the Hall’s forecourt can see a crystal spire and bridges of light standing in the sky over the skull. Everybody else sees weather, and pays a fee to have it explained. One of the older Concord Gates stands in the forecourt under a Sealwright Prime’s guard, and the Gate recognizes oath: only a soul bound to the Lattice survives the fold, and every year someone tries it on a dare.
The Ribs is what everyone calls the arena. The Accord bought those bones from a bankrupt town council in the fourth century of the count, on a bill of sale that reads, in full, one carcass, condition as seen, and it has been the best-attested purchase of an unidentified object in the history of commerce. It raised its court of judgment inside them. The tiers go up between the ribs, the great bones curve over all of it the color of old cream, and in the middle of the floor stands the First Beam (a beam being the public scales), on which any person may sound a weight at any hour without leave. The Neutral Chambers run under the tiers, and that is where the Trials of Resonance are heard, where lies are held not to survive and the Lattice convicts or clears. The Chambers’ armory is in the third rib. The door of the Bench of Attribution opens off the Chambers, with the Guild motto carved over it, where it is understood to be a joke.
What the beast was stays open. Research and Archives holds to three accounts and the Measurewrights to a fourth, and the assayers who have worked on the bone have returned figures nobody can place. The Marrowkin send an assessor every ten years, who taps it, looks thoughtful, and offers a price. It has never been established that anyone was offering to sell.
The two statues are the Witnesses, named for the Article that makes an instrument good only coram testibus, before witnesses. The town calls them Cory and Tess, and brides leave them ribbons.
Waxgate
Everything in the Charter is closed with colored wax, and that wax comes through Waxgate, a loud yellow river town of hives, rendering sheds and pigment yards that smell of honey and scorching and paint the river four colors in a day. Green comes from verdigris scraped off copper in the sheds, blue from ground smalt, gold from leaf worked in by the small hammer, and the whole town has stained thumbs. The Worshipful Company of Waxmakers holds the charter, and the wax-carriers who walk it out on their backs in baskets are the poorest people in the place, Catkin and Bearkin for the most part, papered or otherwise. Nobody in Waxgate will tell you who makes the obsidian wax. The carriers say there is a shed. Waxgate’s gate-toll is a dab of hot wax on the back of your hand, in the color of your business, and strangers walk around town for a week with it on.
Verath
Verath is a township at the crossing of two trade corridors on the Charter’s far western edge, the last clean street before the Scourge, and it exists for the reason the page opened on. Beastkin law belongs to this country. The Verath Township Labor Authority runs the largest licensed pens in the Center, under a provision that bears its name, with enforcement men in gambesons carrying its seal, a crossed hammer and chain in copper thread. It is a clean town. The pens are inspected, the brass on the assay post is polished, and the going price at Verath the last time anyone published it was seventeen gold marks a head, less than a horse. “Those aren’t people, boy. Those are labor stock. Licensed and documented.” That sentence, from a Verath enforcement man called Darvo, has been repeated in more songs than he would have enjoyed.
The Law That Lives Here
The rest of the four quarters takes the Articles as a custom or a circle. Here they are the weather. The market court sits in the market, three times a week in a big town and monthly in a village, and Titles I and V between them are ninety percent of what any court in the Charter ever does. Short loaves, weak ale, heaped measures, men who bought the carrots before the carts reached the gate. The dusty foot gets a traveler heard before the market closes, which is the reason merchants will walk three days out of their way to be sued here. Amercement, the Accord’s standard fine, is set to the offender’s means, and the factor house budgets for it. For the full text, see The Articles of the Accord.
The Beastkin Classification Provision
It was written in the Third Eon, in a good clear hand, on purpose, and it divides the living peoples it groups together into free-status, bonded-status and labor-stock on criteria the Accord’s own practitioners consider inconsistently applied. A Beastkin who cannot show free-holder status through guild membership, a sealed indenture of service or bloodline recognition is available for labor contracts: purchased, held in licensed pens, sold at Accord-adjacent fairs. Read the licensed and documented qualifier closely, because it protects nobody. It is the mechanism by which the transaction is made legal. Demihumans default to free-status pending investigation of their lineage; Beastkin default to labor stock pending documentation. Bearkin are generally free where documented, Catkin and Lupine are contested, Serpentkin may claim a scholar-class exemption, and the Chimeric-Born have no coherent policy at all, which is a worse thing to live under than it sounds. See The Beastkin and Demihuman Peoples.
This is the Center’s standing fight. Half the Charter’s neighbors are peoples its statute has opinions about. It will not recognize the Russet Crown, whose subjects are by its own rolls nobody and who took the name. It trades with the Serpentkin through the exemption and the Avian Kin by the territory, and it sends the Moss Court formal notices that come back with things growing on them.
Who actually rules
On paper, the Crown in Charter. The Concord is the oldest composite monarchy of the age: several countries under one crown, each keeping its own law. In the ruin of the Great Concord Splintering its crowns pledged their regalia to the chancery against their debts, and the instrument that did it, the Sealed Charter itself, is the document the country is named for. The present holder keeps the land, the law, the levy, the tax and the right to hang, as crowns do, and is permitted to borrow the crown for coronations, on signature. The Accord holds nothing but a pledge, and so it may say with a straight face that it holds no territory. It holds the assay, the rank, the credit, the writ and the arrays, and every Mage Royal or Gauger Royal in the Charter enters a room together with a Guild officer who loathes him. Other crowns are further from the chancery’s chest, and some, Kaetran among them, have fought the Bench and come away on terms nobody has published.
In fact, the Guild Accord. Sealhall’s Regional Envoy (the Accord’s senior officer in a realm) outranks anyone within a week’s ride who is not a Divisional officer, and the Divisions fight each other for the rest. Strategic and Enforcement vote together and are called the hard hand. Arbitration and Research are called the long table. Logistics holds the purse and the Gates and swings. Enforcement eats by forfeiture, which is why a miller here can have his stones seized on a Tuesday and his fine reduced by a different officer of the same Codex on the Wednesday. The High Concordant cannot leave the Citadel and has not seen any of this. See The Guild Accord in the Dark Ages.
Wealth
The Charter makes very little and charges for everything. Its fortune is fees: attestation, registration, the entry in ink, the proof-mark, the license, the seal. Under that sit wax and honey, parchment and iron-gall ink, standard weights cast at the Founders’ Yard in Sealhall, and scriveners by the regiment. The great hiring halls run their boards from here, and the Company of Adventurers keeps its underwriting tables here, the most honest document about mortality in the four quarters. The alchemical economy runs through the Bench’s Standing Index, and a formula not entered cannot be bonded, shipped, pledged or financed. The Legion has never taken a district as cheaply as the Bench has.
Beastkin labor, sold at Verath and the fairs, carries the wax, cuts the hay, works the rendering sheds and is entered in the accounts under stock.
Rent, Bread and the Street
Rooms are by the month in tenement, with the warden’s fee on top, and a house on a kept street pays its bill to a chartered company in a sealed household grade; the lead seal on the lamp stem by your door says who did the work, what was paid and until when. “Still on the round?” is how neighbors say good morning. The poor boil their pots at the waist-high parish stone in the road, warm, iron-bound and quarreled over, and the water tastes of it.
Food is honest and exact and there is not quite enough of it. The assize loaf has its weight fixed against the price of grain, white for those with money and dark for the rest; pulse porridge; ale at the fixed price, passed by two sworn tasters, who are chosen each year, unpaid, may not refuse, and are visibly unsteady by the sitting. Meat is a feast-day matter. Honey is everywhere, on everything, the one cheap sweet thing the country has, and the Charter’s children have bad teeth and very good manners.
Everybody here can read. A window clerk may be the most powerful person you meet in a year, and he knows it, and his ink is on his cuff. Titles come before names at any door, without exception. Across the street from any hall sits a sect in its colors, whose elders consider the establishment a tax on talent and whose core disciples carry Guild tokens anyway. The Scalded Cats hold the river towns in orange and soot, open hands, and sing Who’s Got the Lid flat on purpose, and the Stage brackets at every fair are the nearest thing the country has to a shared religion, bookies in green hats and all. In Aldersey the Chandlers and the Saddlers still both ride eighth. In Stowmarch they still bury bakers with the loaf.
The Charter’s words for the shared arts are the Guild roll’s, reinforcement, Pressure and sensing, and its people use them proudly and correctly, and the bracket crowds around them say shine, weight and nose to annoy them.
How It Fights
Its first weapon is the charter, and the real sanction is exclusion. A town that crosses Sealhall finds that its weights no longer pass, its letters no longer clear and the rider has stopped coming. The Accord cannot hang you. It can make it impossible for you to sell anything, anywhere, ever again, and it prefers that.
The Articles say the Accord keeps no standing army, and the Concord Legion drills on the plain below Sealhall’s walls every morning, in blue and white, bound by resonance where other men are bound by pay, every soldier’s oath a working cut into the bone. Its doctrine is measured force, and every engagement is reviewed by Arbitration afterward. Enforcement brings the worse news: Vanguard strike teams; Sealwrights (the Accord’s specialists in binding glyphs) laying containment circles that can pin down things no one should have to pin down; the Null Wardens, their throats sealed by vow, who track a violator through the dissonance he makes and have never been heard to say they are sorry. A High Warden’s presence in a realm is martial law, and the sight of one on the Waxgate road will empty a market.
And the spear-points are crossed over the road for a reason. Armies do cross the Charter, in every generation, because nobody marches through the Scourge, the salt road is one of the two ways round it, and the salt road runs under those spears. They cross on a Writ, by the named road, with their bread paid for at the assize, and the ones that did not bother with a Writ are why Sealhall has walls. Most marshals save the fee and the argument by taking the Kessen road on the far flank, across the Midmarch, which is one of the things the Midmarch holds against the Charter.
What They Joke About
Paperwork, with love. “Before witnesses,” said of anything done in the dark. “Nullum et irritum,” of a husband. Both companies ride eighth. Nobody dreams in Latin, and a clerk who talks in his sleep is reported to his Warden. Cory and Tess are said to have been married since the Second Eon and to have stood with their spears crossed the entire time. The beast, they say, was the last creature to dispute a bill in Sealhall. The Beastkin who carry the baskets have jokes of their own in Purrspeech, with a second conversation running underneath the first, and it is usually about you. They ask each other who is coming to dinner, and the answer is nobody.
Monsters on the Roads
Everything here has a form. Cockatrices (Grade A on the Bestiary’s scale, which runs from E to EX) get into henyards along the river towns and a warden has to be sent for. Harpies raid the wax wagons. Stilts, the great herd animals of the Scourge on legs as long as a ship’s mast, have been sighted from the western hay-country in bad years, and the Concord Legion drills for them on the plain. The ordinary beasts are kept in good order. Wolves on the sheep-walks carry a fixed bounty under the assize, paid by the pair of ears at any hall door, and a bear in the clover must be reported within the week by whoever owned the hive, with the hive’s number.
The hiring halls run their boards from here, and the Company of Adventurers keeps its underwriting tables, the most honest document about mortality on the continent. The dungeon is the Tail: the spine of the dead beast of Sealhall runs out through the city wall and away into the barley, each great bone bigger than a chapel, and a stair goes down at the fourteenth vertebra into a Well the survey has never identified. Enforcement holds the gate on it, the Company rates it, and past the Lower Workings the tables simply print a dash. Farmers on either side plow round the vertebrae and let the shade to drovers.
The chancery rolls call such a place a domnio, an asset with a defective title, and the Articles never use the word dungeon at all, saying a pool, which the courts have had to stretch one lawsuit at a time. The greatest of them is the Heart Vault in the Concord Citadel, a true Wellspring Core (Fountainhead on the survey, the top of the ladder) held by the Accord, and who cleared it is not a question the Accord has a form for. The darkest line in the whole ledger is the porter clause. A licensed labor-stock porter, bought or hired by the season at Verath, is equipment on a clearing’s instrument: he cannot hold a share, cannot be named in the saving clause, and goes on the roll as nemo along with the rope. He carries the poles at the back of the line. He is generally the first to say that something down there is wrong, and nobody is obliged to listen. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
Beside the Scourge
The west of the Charter lives with the Scourge of Hell the way a good house lives with a bad neighbor, by fixing the boundary exactly. Its dry wind reaches the western hay-country a few weeks a year and dries the hay on the stalk. Past Verath the guild’s jurisdiction ends at two iron posts with red-painted caps, and beyond them lies the Verath Expanse, the Charter’s own name for its stretch of the Hem (the Scourge’s outermost belt, fifteen leagues of black-barked thornwood and pale dust). On this side of the posts you get an assize loaf, two sworn tasters and a court that will hear you before the market closes. On that side nothing holds. Crews going out touch the red caps for luck, and the paint is renewed every spring at public expense, on a form.
The dungeon every young hunter in the Charter has a story about lies out there. The Lamplit Stair is an Aurevane stair (Aurevane being the Wellspring of hard white-blue light) going down from a thornwood gully, its walls a hard blue-white, cleared twice and lost twice, and it is where half the Green Sigils in the country, Green being the first license color a hunter can carry, get their first bad night. Goodmorrow, on the salt road under the Charter’s edge, is the great edge town of that side, painted stilts over a sinkhole country, every bridge a different color so you can tell them apart through the haze. It has the best mask-clerks on the east side, Charter-taught every one (a mask being the colored plate a Well-spawn wears, and the thing a hall pays on), and the worst beer.
The Turn comes to Sealhall in the end, whoever holds it. North, then South, then Center, nine years each, the holder keeping the Line of forts around the Hem and paying the bounties while the other two count. The copy of the arrangement at Sealhall refers to an older copy, and that one refers to “the ancient custom.” Every Turn ends with each party presenting a Count of what it cost and what is owed, and the Arbitration division audits them, for a fee, and has never produced a figure any party accepted. It was an Accord water clock, on a trestle under a green awning, that eleven thousand soldiers stood and watched in 676 while a wyrm ate Lastpenny, and Sealhall maintains that the instrument performed correctly.
The Center holds the Turn now, from 712 to 721, and the Charter’s share raises the prettiest point of law on the map. The Accord holds no territory, so by its own argument it owes nothing. The Crown in Charter owes, and the Crown’s regalia are in pledge to the Accord. So the Charter pays by instrument, a bill drawn on one pocket and accepted by the other, which buys free companies and keeps the eastern forts in bolts, and the Legion in blue and white crosses the posts only on a Writ. On the North’s Turn and the South’s a host may march through anyone’s land by right of passage, which would seem to dispose of the Writ and the fee together, and Enforcement has spent some centuries on the question of when an army under those crossed spears has stopped being on its Turn. As for the colossal sword at the Scourge’s center, with a field of violet stars where its blade should be, one star-clerk at Sealhall has spent his career recording those stars from borrowed reports, and he holds that they have moved twice in three centuries. His office is funded by a fee on something.
Neighbors and Grudges

The Amber Cities of Nalūn A rival court with a very good roof. The arrangement between Sealhall and Ironlink Hold has never been written down, because writing it down would admit it exists.
The Russet Crown of the Unpapered The runaways’ kingdom, unrecognized by every roll in Sealhall and the subject of a standing Enforcement line item. The Charter’s collectors go in. Their iron collars come out, cut, and go on a heap.
The Hundred Crowns of the Midmarch The Charter sells them law at a markup, and the worst of the armies go across their ground so as to stay off the Charter’s.
The Rose Coils of Coilspire The Serpentkin take the exemption, argue every case, and remember the clerk’s grandfather. No Scalebond advocate has ever needed to look anything up. Two chairs at the Bench have wanted their archives entered for a hundred years, and Research treats what they hold as anecdotal, since the source is living memory.
Sancta Lux and the Holy Sea Sancta Lux hears oath, status and legitimacy, the Accord hears everything else, and neither will define the boundary. Both prefer being able to claim a case to being obliged to take one.
The North The first circle was signed at Kharven-Seat, over a custom that has never been written. Sealhall regards that as its greatest triumph, and Kharven regards it as a thing that was signed.

Later hand, from the last winter before the turn, running past the year these shelves stand in: the Northern Empire of Whitemere found the crossed spears still over the road, and sent up its own clerks, in their own wax.


The Guild Accord
The Bench of Attribution

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Silver Cedars of Yukari
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say ityoo-KAH-ree · keh-TSOO-en
The Crow’s Reach · Ketsuen, in the old books · Domus Vinculi, in Accord filings
Three summers ago a wedding barge came down the Long Water with the bride’s whole family aboard, a hundred and twenty otter-folk of the Lake Districts in scarlet and reed-gold, with drums, a roast pike the length of a door, and the bride’s four brothers up in the bow singing louder than anyone. At the Reedgate station the perimeter read them and called a threat. The Thread Guard turned out sixty in crow-black harness to meet a party of drunk fishermen at the landing, and Maren Ottertail, in a crown of marsh-marigolds, broke the sergeant’s arm with a boat pole for laying a hand on the pike. Nobody died. The pike was a total loss. Within the week the Corridor was laughing at the Guard and at the Academy that trained it, and the bookies at Senri’s Gate were giving odds on which carver would be disgraced for cutting a station that could not tell a bride from a bandit.
Then the case came up under the Thread Standard, and a reader went through what was connected to what, and found that the ward had been right. The four brothers had come to kill the groom over a debt of nets, and each of them had a filleting knife under the scarlet. The court traced the debt to a bad sale made by the groom’s father twelve years before, ordered the groom to make it good, set the brothers to mending the Reedgate landing every spring under the sergeant’s eye, and gave the sergeant a seat at the table on every anniversary. All of them still come. The sergeant says the pike has improved.
This is the oldest blood in the South on a cedar hill, all around it a frontier that asked to be governed because its gateposts were failing, and every promise anyone makes written down by people who can see what it is tied to.
The old maps call the outer country Ketsuen, “Binding Bond,” and give it a border and a flag. It never was much of a state. What it has always been is the Yukari valleys and the settlements that hired the Yukari to mind their wards, and the South calls the whole of it the Silver Cedars for the trees and the Crow’s Reach for the people who watch from them.
The Land and the Look
On the east of the South, past the Wellheads and the whole width of the Jade Plains, the ground climbs into cloud, and the cedars begin. They stand so tall and close that the light comes down between the trunks in thin bars of green-gold, on moss, on black water, and on the silver lichen that furs every north face, and a person walking under them lowers their voice for no reason they could give you. Crows go over all day, high up and talking. The house colors are black and silver, silver threading through dark, and they are the colors of the place at any hour after noon.
The Heartstone valleys sit in limestone six hundred feet above the country around them, walled on three sides by ridges whose faults have been exhaling Essence into the soil for centuries, so that the ground presses on your temples within a day of arriving and does not stop. Scholars call this rich ground, and so does everyone else after the first headache. The valley’s entrance is a pair of standing stones under a carved lintel, bearing one unbroken line of thread-notation in a language older than Parunic; the stones stood before the house came, and nobody will say who set them. The limestone goes gold at evening. Above the valley on its hill stands the Enclave, with raked white gravel in its court.
Below the Enclave the valley floor drowned long ago, and nobody has ever let it go. Mossy dark pagodas and towering carved temple spires stand up out of still water that gives the whole of them back, lily pads crowd their steps, huge pale waterfalls come down behind them, and long red cloth streamers run from spire to spire across the sky, renewed each year by people who row out to do it. The shrines are still kept. A robed figure in red can generally be seen on the shore, and the valley will tell you that is a keeper and will not tell you which one.
Beyond the valleys, north and east, the Reach proper runs out through long lakes, birch and cold upland toward the salt road and the old ruins of the Rose Coils: raw timber settlements with sap still weeping from the wall boards, ward-posts cut last season, new roads and mostly bad ones. A market town out there is loud in the way of any place where everyone arrived recently and has an opinion, with carvers’ apprentices in chalk-white aprons racing each other to a failed gatepost for the fee, Lake District fishers selling dried fish off the tailboard, and a hedge-worker on the corner who will tell you the Academy’s standards are a racket while charging you half of what the Academy’s graduate would.
The House
The Yukari are an archaic bloodline before they are a house, the family of Ashura, the Breath Between Worlds, and the house is the shape the bloodline took when the world forced it to hold ground. The name is chosen at the Telling, when a child of age sits on the cold floor before Senri’s stone and hears the whole account of what the blood carries and what it costs, and is never simply inherited. That makes this the only house in the South whose members are all volunteers. Their words are The crow perches. The crow watches. The crow remembers. The bloodline’s own page has the rest, and you should take the tea.
Lord Naiser Yukari, the Bearer of Weight, is head of the house, a man of near thirty, Senri’s eldest and half Lambert by his mother, known across the South as the lord who won the war and asks for nothing. His father went into the seam when the Soul Plane broke, and held it. The house came through the last four years of the war harder than anyone in the north knows and laid out more than four hundred of its dead in rows facing east. It has spent every month since telling everyone who will listen that it has no wish for more land. Its terms at the Cedar Enclave were plain: no Yukari knowledge for war, no Yukari name carried as a banner, no touching the spirit world without Yukari counsel, every promise made in the hall entered in the Yukari record. His sister Naevra keeps the archive and the register of every birth and death in the valleys. Seradris is the youngest.
The Reach and how it came. The Reach accreted, and there was no conquest in it. Frontier settlements joined because the alternative was worse, and the thing that made the alternative worse was what Yukari carvers could do that nobody else could: maintain the ward-craft that kept the frontier from collapsing in the night. The story everyone tells starts with Niran Yukari, called the Crow of Fate, who came up the long coast to the valley gate at thirteen with salt in his pack and a ward-carver’s tools at his hip, able to hear a failing bridge by listening to its footing. He fixed wards as he traveled, a cracked gate post or a thinned well-stone, in twenty minutes for the price of a meal and a dry place to sleep, and each time he left a trained apprentice behind. If the valley maintained your wards, the valley set your ward-standards, and if it set your standards it was already minding your gates and wells. The eighth settlement petitioned on birch bark, carried by a merchant who had observed that towns under Yukari maintenance had not lost a building to structural Essence failure in three years, while towns outside it had lost an average of four per season. The arithmetic was the argument.
The Council of Threads runs the Reach, under the house and at arm’s length from it: seven Thread-Wardens, one per province, and the Crow’s Seat, a post Niran designed for himself with no executive power at all, carrying only the right to speak last, to call an emergency session, and to place before the Council any crisis his Thread-Sight shows him. Roughly eighty thousand souls live under it. The charter says the Seat passes to whoever holds the most comprehensive Thread-perception and otherwise stays empty. A blind Crow is worse than no Crow at all. The house stays out of Council business as loudly as it can, and everybody knows who owns the stones.
The Proving is how anyone gets anywhere. It is a public review of demonstrated performance, with no examination in it. Candidates present what they did, what came of it, what they learned from the failures. The panel sits in public, the deliberations are recorded and the criteria are posted in advance. Incumbents re-Prove every six years and about one seat in three changes hands. A Proving draws crowds that would shame a tournament, since it is the one contest in the South where a sitting lord can lose in front of his own tenants with his own numbers, and the Corridor’s bookies post odds on every seat.
Cities, Towns and Provinces
The Cedar Enclave is the seat, on its hilltop above the valleys: cedar halls stepping down the slope on limestone footings, beams gone red-brown and resin-dark, bark-shingle roofs furred silver-green with lichen, a covered walk around a court of raked white gravel, three standing stones in shawls of moss that throw no shadow at any hour, and wards along every approach that touch whoever comes up the southern road long before anyone at the gate has seen him. A stream runs under the floor of the long hall. Senri’s stone stands at the back of it. Since the war the warlords’ table has sat here, because everyone wanted every promise entered in a record somebody else was keeping.
Karasuyama, “crow mountain,” is the bare limestone peak above the Enclave and the rookery town on its shoulder. Hundreds of thousands of crows roost there, and the crow-wards who feed and band them will tell you, without being asked, which ones have been reading your mail. Every autumn the sky over it goes black for an hour at dusk, and people walk in from three valleys to see it.
Sugidani, “cedar valley,” is the house’s market town and the only place in the valleys with a decent inn: sawpits and shingle-makers, the great cedar rafts going down the river, ink-grinders, and paper made from bark, which every clerk in the South prefers and complains about the cost of. Its tea tastes of small white flowers and is as bitter as a lawsuit.
Senri’s Gate is the town that has grown up around the standing stones, at the mouth of the valley, and the capital of the Reach. It holds the Council, the Ward-Carver’s Academy and the Archive of Provings. Old books use its name for the whole Enclave, and are wrong in a way that has annoyed three generations of the family. The warded track runs out from here to Sum-gol, one hundred and forty leagues, three weeks by wagon and nine days by mounted courier, with a way-station every twenty to twenty-five leagues, each with a Yukari-standard perimeter and a resident carver. The Kessen road proper ends at Sum-gol, and this track is its last stretch in all but name, carrying on across the South to the foot of these valleys.













































ProvinceCharacterPop.The Heartstone Senri’s GateAdministrative, educational and spiritual center, and a great carvers’ school. Every carver, Thread-reader and governance candidate in the land trained here or under someone who did. Its Warden is traditionally the Academy’s most senior active instructor~14,000The Thornback March northern frontierWhere the perimeter meets the wilderness. The wildlife has been marinating in high-density Aether for centuries and has opinions about territorial boundaries. The old rest-point on the Thornback Ridge still stands as a forward post~6,000The Corridor trade routeThe long narrow province following the road toward the Nalūn basin. Settlement clusters have grown at station-points where travelers stop, resupply, and occasionally decide to stay. Its Warden manages independent merchants who consider themselves citizens of commerce, a legal fiction tolerated because the alternative is taxing them into using a different road~12,000The Lake Districts western settlementsThe breadbasket: lake-margin grain, forest timber and game, freshwater fisheries. Otter-folk and other beastkin fishers, and a small and influential Marrowkin community whose people came to sell bone and stayed because the fishing was better than expected~18,000The Uplands eastern heightsSparsely settled, with seasonal grazing and the high-altitude herbs alchemists value. Its importance is the highest-concentration natural seeps in the land. Its Warden is traditionally a practitioner with advanced Ketsumyōgan, the Yukari fate-eye, because reading threads at that density takes it~4,000Vaeloris the Carver’s SeatA warm geothermal basin fed by an old vent, built in quarried stone where the rest of the land builds in cedar. The proving-house for new work, where techniques are developed and standardized before they go out on the road, in the structural grammar of the master Dhaerin, who taught there~10,000The Frontier Marches contested borderThe most unstable province, full of people who chose the frontier to avoid being governed by anyone and tolerate the Council only because the wards work. Its Warden is typically the Council’s most diplomatic member~16,000
The Mahuo province that the older surveys list here is gone from this table: Sum-gol is sovereign southern ground, as it always maintained, and the Dynasty’s page has its people.
The Wellsprings and the Ward
The land has no single dominant territorial Wellspring. What it has is more diffuse and in practice more versatile, a composite ward-network running on several types of Aether at once.





















WellspringFunctionCymorath Vibration / ResonanceUnderlies the entire ward-net. Lets a practitioner hear the substrate’s internal frequency before carving, find the paths of least resistance, and design inscriptions that work with the material’s architecture. A Cymorath-attuned carver completes a sentence the stone was already trying to sayFixatio Anchoring / StabilityThe network’s holding power. A properly sealed ward holds its function for years if the substrate remains intactMonolithion Thread / CausalityFeeds the Ketsumyōgan. The Thread Standard depends on it, the Council is named for it, and the valley sits on a fault system that concentrates it. The Yukari settled there because the valley was the place where Thread-Sight worked best
The valley’s limestone walls carry a Boundary function that predates any inscription system. Whether this is a local Wellspring phenomenon, a geological artifact, or evidence of a tradition too old to identify is undetermined, and three Measurewrights have stopped speaking to one another over it. The wards function. The Reach maintains them. The explanation will arrive when it arrives.
Wealth and Trade
Ward-craft is the defining product. A Yukari-standard ward carries a mark that frontier settlements recognize, Accord searchers accept, and rival ward-cutters have been unable to copy, because the glyph formulae are posted on the Academy door and the quality lies in the attuning of the substrate, which requires Cymorath perception most practitioners do not have.
Practitioners are the second. The Academy trains anyone who can pass the entrance Proving, and a land whose graduates keep the wards on half the frontier’s settlements is a land everyone depends on and nobody wants to antagonize. Cedar, shingle and bark paper come out of the valleys, and herbs from the Uplands. The land does not feed itself and buys its grain and preserved goods through the free cities of Nalūn.
The house itself trades in what it sees and never sells it outright. Its wealth is its archive. What the Yukari know may leave the valley to mend and never to take, and they are the first to admit that this makes them very expensive friends.
Rent, Food and the Street
Land is held by stewardship rather than ownership. Neglect forfeits a holding through the Proving of Absence: unmaintained ward-craft degrades, a Cymorath-attuned searcher can hear it, and the finding triggers a review of whether the holder is still competent to hold. Nobody in the Reach pays rent, exactly: they pay dues to their station, which keep the carver in dumplings. Under the valley’s cedars the tenants pay the house a tithe, and the house remembers who was late.
Broth with root vegetables and dried lake fish tastes, the Heartstone says, like the country. Dumplings at a family table, lake fish, forest game, bitter tea. The sentence that does most of the work in a Yukari household is “You haven’t eaten,” said by whoever loves you, as a bowl is set down beside tools that have gone cold.
“Who keeps your posts?” is the greeting on the road; it says which carver maintains your settlement’s wards and which station answers for you. Every building sits on a ward-carved foundation, tied to the ward-line around it, so that every house is also a knot in the net. Ward-carved foundations do not glow and do not advertise their presence, and the only way to know one is to listen to it. The Proving Festival runs every six years at the summer solstice. The Ward-Lighting falls at the autumn equinox, when the Academy’s graduating carvers cut their first permanent station in a public ceremony the whole district treats as the great day of the year, with chalk thrown in the street. At midwinter the Thread-Reading is given from the flat stone above the gate, and people walk for days to hear what the web shows.
Law and How It Fights
The Thread Standard. Other courts ask what happened and who is guilty. These courts ask what was connected, what was damaged, and what needs to be restored for the connections to hold. It takes in the threads that bound the parties before, the threads the act damaged, and what happens to the community if the damage is left unrepaired. Outsiders find the outcomes either profoundly just or deeply confusing, depending on whether they understand that a fine paid to the wrong party can leave the real damage unrepaired. It is slower than conventional adjudication and more accurate. No other land has copied it, because no other land has a population of Thread-readers.
Citizenship is earned through service. Any person of any race contributing demonstrated capability for three continuous years may petition through the Proving, and race, bloodline, wealth and origin are not factors. The population divides into the Proven and the Unproven, and the Unproven are protected by law and may work and earn. More than half the Reach is human of mixed frontier stock, about one in six Yukari by blood or by name, about one in seven beastkin, and the rest Marrowkin, Mahuo and a small growing goblinoid population in the Marches. The Telling goes to every new citizen on completing the Proving. Not gentle, not abbreviated, not optional.
The Thread Guard is roughly three thousand strong, in crow-black harness, organized around the ward-network, and holds no fortified positions. The perimeter detects entry and makes no attempt to prevent it. It classifies an entrant’s intent through vibration in the substrate and alerts the nearest post. A bandit crossing is read as hostile before she clears the treeline, an army before it finishes forming up, and a wedding party according to its brothers. The land is never surprised, and a prepared answer is cheaper than an improvised one. Its strategic weakness is concentration: the perimeter is only as strong as its worst station, and an attacker who understands the inscription architecture could open a gap. Yukari fighting is quiet and unnerving, with long fingers, flat feet and eyes that close for a deep read, and the house’s own teaching says to move a thread before you draw a blade. The house has sworn no Yukari knowledge for war. It says nothing about what happens to people who come up the road to start one.
What They Joke About
Being looked at. A valley child learns early to look away from a Yukari’s eyes, on the belief that the Crow’s Audit sees what you have done wrong, and the valley makes all the jokes you would expect about it. “Ledger-eyed” is the worst thing you can call someone who sees people as entries, and that means the Moto. “Blind crow” is someone holding a post his sight cannot carry. “Loud” covers any unnecessary motion, and Yukari visit Haeseong in order to feel it. “Absent” is a neglectful holder. Out in the Reach, the commonest joke runs: how many carvers does it take to fix a gate? One to fix it, one to listen, and a panel to review them both.
Monsters on the Roads
The wildlife of the Thornback March has been marinating in high-density Aether for centuries and has opinions about territorial boundaries. Tanuki (Grade D) cheat travelers on the valley roads. Psy-Apes (Grade B) troop in the upland cedars and everyone in earshot suddenly knows what they ate. Beasts are plentiful and well informed: crows in their hundreds of thousands, otters who know the fishers by name, bears on the upland herb slopes, and in the Long Water pike the length of a door. A perimeter reads an entrant’s intent through the rock, which tells you when something is coming and not what to do about it. The Uplands hold the land’s highest natural seeps.
The dungeon. Everyone’s name for it is the Drowned Shrines, the low valley floor below the Enclave, Thaloré by the look of it, kept and never cleared. The Yukari row out to tend the pagodas and renew the streamers, they decline all commissions, and the water is a good deal deeper than the valley. The worst of it is the Unlit Shrine, a pagoda whose lower stories go on down under the water past where any reflection stops. A Yukari thread-reader will not look at it for long. The house has not told anyone what is in it, and what the Yukari know may leave the valley to mend and never to take. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
The Scourge and the Turn. The Corridor’s merchants go north beside the salt road along the east flank of the Scourge of Hell, and that is as close as the Reach comes to it by choice. The South’s share of the Turn, nine years in every twenty-seven keeping the Scourge’s monsters off the other two regions, falls first on the old Dynasty’s realms, and the Yukari stood apart from the Dynasty long before it fell. Every captain-general since 602 has come up the road to ask anyway. The house has sworn no Yukari knowledge for war, and the Academy ruled in open session that a wyrm is not a war, so Academy carvers go north by the season at the posted rate to cut perimeter stations on the southern arc of the Line, and answer afterward at a Proving for any that failed. A station on the Hem reads a herd and reads what follows the herd. Carvers who have stood one report that what comes up through the stone from under the Black Roots is nothing they can enter as an intent, and that the edge towns’ ground-bells, on an iron stake at a copper’s worth of hedge-work, gave the same warning first. The Academy has reviewed this finding, in public, with odds.
Neighbors and Grudges
Sum-gol. The Yukari tell the story of how the Mahuo were killed against themselves, and tell it well. Lord Naiser has promised the Mahuo royal line its seat back and the Head of House Mahuo has declined the gift. The Post carries every letter between the north and these valleys, and the courtesies are perfect.
The Holy Sea. The Sea arrives at equality through theology and the Reach through empiricism, the disagreement is genuine, respectful and permanent, and it constitutes approximately forty percent of the content of tavern arguments in both Rimwards. Kin as well, through Lord Naiser’s mother, which is why the Yukari record keeps its promises in figures as well as words.
The Moto. Fear worn as policy. Their sight reads the same threads the Yukari read, and they have been watching each other across a table for two hundred thousand years. The Moto believe governance requires sovereign judgment, a crown that decides, and the Yukari that it requires distributed competence and a council that measures. Both have been wrong in public. The whole Center lies between them, and the peace is quiet because both know what testing it would cost.
The free cities of Nalūn. The Reach’s wards protect the corridor and the chain-cities finance it. Neither cares about the other’s philosophy. They care about whether the wards hold and whether the bills clear.
The Ember Holds of Marrowhold. The Marrowkin keep a tally of what they have cut from what they live in, the Yukari keep a record of everything else, and each suspects the other’s book of being the one that gets read out at the end.
The Iron Mandate of Undaar-Keth. The Mandate governs through decree and the Reach through measurement. No direct trade, no military cooperation, and a mutual understanding that the distance will not be tested, because neither is foolish enough to fight a war it cannot model.
The Zettari struck the valleys in the war’s last four years, and the Sovereign of Kushara has since come to the long hall to talk terms over the tea. Their page is their own.
Further reading · The Yukari Bloodline · The Southern Warlords · The Ketsumyōgan
