geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Slate Ridge of Stormfold
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itSTORM-fold
House Greymane · The Western Wall · The Ridge Does Not Move
The garrison cook at Galecross in Year 671 was Ragna Ottarsdottir, and her whole gift as a practitioner was that a pot under her hand would never go off the boil, for which the Greymanes paid her a soldier’s wage and a second blanket. In the first week of that spring, a column of three hundred and eleven hobgoblins of the Mandate came up the Galecross road in crimson lacquer and iron, in step, under a thunderhead the color of a bruised plum, with the violet lightning walking along the ridge above them the way it does there most afternoons. The pass garrison was sixty and most of those were eating. Ragna looked at the sky, looked at the column and looked at her kitchen, and had the eight great iron cauldrons of the Galecross mess dragged up onto the crest by mule, with every chain in the fort run from them down the rocks to the road, and the last of the chain she laid across the road herself, in an apron, with the head of the column in plain sight. Then she stood on the rocks and shouted, in the voice that had called sixty men to dinner for thirty years, COME AND GET IT.
A storm looks for the easy way down, and iron is a far easier way than air. The first stroke took the crest cauldrons and came down the chain in a violet rope you could see from the Ridgewall, and the second and third came right behind it, and it went along that column from the front, from iron to iron, so that for about as long as you could hold your breath a hundred men in crimson stood lit from the inside, every buckle a star. The rest ran. The Mandate entered it as an unforeseen loss, Ragna lost her left arm at the shoulder and all the hearing she had, and the Galecross mess went without a hot meal for a month. The Greymanes do not do parades. They gave her a title, as they do for everything, and for the eighteen years she had left she was addressed by the entire ridge as the Cook, and no one in Stormfold has used her name since, which is the highest honor they know.
The Slate Ridge is a fortress cut out of a mountain, under its own private lightning, held by a family who have turned being a wall into a religion and do not know they have done it.

Two hands on this page. It stands in Year 715. Lines marked Later hand come from the annotator of the Concordance of Ages, writing in the last winter before the turn. Later hand: the Ridge is a land of House Greymane inside the Northern Empire of Whitemere, and its western edge is the empire’s.

The Land and What It Looks Like
The Stormfold is the western highlands of the north, exposed and wind-hammered, one long fold of slate and greystone running between Kharven and Undaar-Keth. The ridge makes its own weather, and the local belief is that it does so out of spite. The rock is banded with Stillband iron, and the thunderheads that come in off the western shield catch on it most afternoons from thaw to first snow, so that violet lightning walks along the crest over dark wet slate, which shines like a plum, with the rain going sideways and a band of bright clean sky behind it. The storms pass as fast as they come, and then every gully runs silver and the heather smells of hot iron.
The Ridgewall is a fortress carved straight into a sheer mountain face, so thoroughly that no surveyor has been able to say where the mountain stops and the masonry starts. You come to it across a white snowfield in the usual blizzard, toward one arched door, with great ice-sheathed pillars standing up on either side of it, a single tall tower cut from the rock above, and gold light in its tall windows, the only warm thing for ten miles. Galleries run back through the living slate, and from the fortress’s shoulders the curtain wall goes on for leagues along the crest in the same stone, with watchtowers rising out of the outcrops like the outcrops’ own idea. Gray banners with a wolf’s head worked in darker thread hang wet on every tower, and the old shields of the house, steel-faced and green-rimmed with a gold sun rising on them, are worn half blank by centuries of blows. The whole thing has an iron lightning-mast on every tower, and the storm hits those instead of the sentries as a rule.
West of the wall lie two things. Down the Galecross road is the Mandate’s country, black basalt and boreal forest under crimson ranks. Past the ridge lies the ground the bloodline came from, which is not Greymane business and not anyone else’s. Nobody holds it, and the Greymanes look at it every morning from the wall. The Holy Sea’s copies of the map put that ground somewhere else entirely, and the Gazetteer enters the quarrel.
The major places

The Ridgewall. The seat, the long wall, the galleries, and a garrison town in the lee of the crest whose whole economy is boots.
Galecross. The great pass town, a knot of slate roofs at the crossing where the wind comes through from four sides and the road comes up from the Mandate’s country. It has a famous mess, a smoked-mutton trade, and a toll-house whose keeper has to rope himself to his door in spring. Its children can tell a storm’s arrival time by the taste of the air.

Roads. East to the Seat by the ridge road, on foot in winter. West and down from Galecross into the Mandate’s country. Grain comes up by levy each autumn, in the care of an Ashmore clerk.
House and Rule
House Greymane is the shield, military to the point of institutional. Children are raised to see themselves as components of a defensive structure rather than individuals with personal ambitions; the ones who reject the framing leave, and the ones who stay become the most reliable garrison troops in the Inner World. Their words are The Ridge Does Not Move, which describe the house, and which the house has never once found inspiring. They have held the ridge, by their own telling, since before there was a north to hold it for.
The lord is the Shieldwarden, always, regardless of given name, because the function matters more than the person. Lord of the Ridgewall and one of the Seven Warlords of the north, addressed by title in his own bedroom, gaunt and long and gray like all of them: the Greymane stride is a thing you can recognize at a quarter-mile, and so is the Ridgewall stillness, by which a Greymane does not move at all and then moves very fast. The personal name of the current holder is known within the family and to the kind of person who reads cards. Family offices run the same way down the ladder. There is a Gatewarden, a Masonwarden, a Muster Aunt, and the Cook.
Wealth and Trade
Very little. The Ridge sells greystone (the standard fortification stone of half the realms in the north, bearing good and holding poor), Stillband ore off the western shield, wool from gray-faced sheep too stubborn to fall off, smoked mutton, and soldiers. Its real income is a levy that every other house in the north grumbles about and pays, in grain and salt, because everyone south of the crest would like the Mandate to remain on the far side of it. Mountain companies from the Ridge hire out for a season or two; they are expensive, humorless and worth it. The long war has cost the house more sons than it has ever admitted on paper. It imports grain, and the Ashmore clerk who arrives each autumn with the allocation is treated with the same exact courtesy as a siege engine.
Rent, Food and the Street
Nobody pays rent on the Ridge. Everyone holds their room by a post on the wall, and when you stop holding the post you stop holding the room, which focuses the mind of the elderly. Food is the mess: mutton, barley, bone broth, rind-water (the honest northern name for thin broth) in the Thin Weeks, and hard cheese you could shoe a horse with. Galecross has the only real tavern on the ridge, the Dry Sock, and its one boast is the name. There is singing there on the nights the storm is too bad for the wall, generally the song about the Cook, which runs to thirty verses, and it is the only time you will hear a Greymane raise his voice for a reason other than an enemy.
Local aura-talk runs the same as everywhere in Kharven (the hide, the low sky, smelling a man’s stack), with the addition that a coat of aura on the crest in a storm is regarded as asking for it. Hedge-workers here do a brisk trade in charming sentries’ boots dry, and lamp-wardens have refused the upper towers altogether. A signal post on the ridge is kept by a garrison hand and costs nothing, and it is the only free service in the country.
What they joke about. Hardly anything, in front of you. Among themselves, the joke is titles: a Greymane child will address the family dog as the Hound and the latrine as the Lower Gate. The other Banner Houses tell the jokes about them, and the best known is the one about the Greymane who sat guard over a pie all night because no one had told him to stop. Greymanes consider that a fair description of a good soldier and do not see why it gets a laugh.
Law and How It Fights
Law. Garrison law, from the Shieldwarden down: post, relief, watch, and what happens if you leave one. A dispute goes to the senior hand on the section, and from him to the wall. Greymanes have their own version of a death-house on the crest, cold and wind-scoured, and the Waiting is kept in shifts.
The fighting. Shield and sword, the wall first and then very fast. The Greymane school is the ridge sword, and it is built around a single principle known as taking the Before: the man who strikes second spends the whole fight answering, so a Greymane strikes first, from the high guard they call the Roof, hilt by the ear and point standing up behind the head. Its two great cuts are the Wrath-Cut, straight down off the right shoulder, and the Crooked Cut, hands crossed on the grip, turning edge-first onto the inside of the wrist. They march in the Grey File, shields locked rim to rim. Greymane Releases are called in earth-words (Stonefast, Setting the Stone), dust settling around the heels as the body takes on the ridge’s refusal to go anywhere, and the fair answer is to pull him, lift him or fight him on ice. A horn on the belt calls the next section, one long note, and the sound of it coming from behind you is a thing Mandate veterans will mention quietly, after some drinks.
The wall itself does a third of the fighting. Mountain companies watch the western approaches and survive conditions that would kill most soldiers before the fighting started, and an enemy on the crest in a storm is in the hands of the violet weather with everyone else.
Monsters on the Roads
The beasts are the ones too stubborn to leave: gray-faced sheep on the shelves, mountain goats above them, snow hare in the gullies, and ravens who know the mess schedule and have taken a sentry’s dinner off the wall in front of his whole section.
The monsters. Monsters move, and they live across the whole of the Inner World, and a good many of them start out here. The Ridge has a plague of storm-things. Raiju (Grade A on the Bestiary’s scale, which runs from E to EX; lightning in the shape of a beast) run the crest in bad afternoons, and a coat of aura up there is regarded as asking for it. Wyverns (Grade S) nest on the western faces and take sheep and sentries. Harpies (Grade B) work the Galecross road. In a dry year a Ridge wyvern will turn up over Ashbury’s barley and take a red cow in front of a village, and the Ashmore clerk has twice presented the Shieldwarden with the bill, which came back with a note that the animal had left its post. The western nests are also the one subject on which the Galecross garrison and the Mandate’s exchange messages.
The Ninth Gallery
The dungeon (what a Wellspring Core makes around itself, or what grows up around one) on the Ridge is the Ninth Gallery: a Masonwarden’s crew cutting a new gallery through the living slate broke into an older one that nobody had cut, full of blue-white light and Glarewings, Well-spawn with arc-blue lightning trees across their brows. It is a Well of Aurevane (hard-edged electric light). The Greymanes walled it, put a door in the wall, and set a post on the door, and a sentry has stood it for three hundred years, because no one has told him to stop. It has never been cleared. Every Greymane who has been sent inside was sent by title and has been replaced by the next one of that title. You can stand at that door and hear it, one clean high tone like a wet finger on a glass rim. The sentry keeps smoked glass on his belt and wears as little iron as a Greymane can bear to, which is a great deal to ask on a ridge made of it. The Accord has twice offered to post the place as a commission, and the Shieldwarden replied both times that the post was filled. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
The Scourge and the Turn
The Ridge regards the Scourge of Hell as somebody else’s wall, badly kept. The Turn is the old rotation by which North, South and Center each spend nine years keeping its monsters off everybody else, and on the North’s Turn the Greymanes send their mountain companies down the Kessen road to hold the forts of the Line, around the Hem, the Scourge’s outer belt. They have stood those forts in a heat they could not have imagined, on ground that shudders under the boots, and they ask only what the relief schedule is. Stormfold slate stood at Lastpenny in 676 with the Hollenmark blue, while a wyrm ate the town, and the Greymanes are the only northerners who have never apologized for it, because they were ordered to stand and they stood. The companies also hire out on other people’s Turns, the Center’s at this moment included, until 721, when the wheel comes back to the North.
A Ridge section on the Hem may well hire as its guide one of the hobgoblin ridge-men, Mandate outcasts who work the high ground above the Black Roots and may see two centuries. So a Greymane sergeant can find himself following a man who stood the far side of Galecross a hundred years ago and can recite the relief schedule of the sergeant’s grandfather. By all accounts they get on very well, and neither mentions it at home.
Neighbors and Grudges

The Iron Mandate of Undaar-Keth. The reason for everything. Both sides believe borders must be held, threats answered, and governance is serious work conducted by serious people, which is why neither can leave the other alone. The two garrisons know each other’s relief schedules better than their own wives do, and the Stone-Blood (the hobgoblins’ own inheritance) runs slow at thirty below, a fact the Greymanes rely on and think about constantly.
The Cobalt March. The other wall of the north. The Starks and Greymanes share a wolf on the breast, stood together through the long war, and are not on speaking terms in any way a stranger would notice.
The Golden Hollow. Grain. See the Ashmore clerk, above.
Kharven-Seat. The Hall of Verdicts holds that it can summon the Shieldwarden to answer for his house. The Hall did exactly that, within living memory, over a brother and some salt, and the Ridge has not forgotten the weight of either.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Vermilion Dynasty of Sum-gol
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itSOOM-gol, from *sum*, breath, and *gol*, a hollow
The Crown That Was Carried · Breath Hollow · The Empire Deposed by Attendance
On the first day of autumn in Year 602 the Emperor Rokju Mahuo walked out onto the Balcony of Answers to call his roll, as an emperor of Sum-gol had done every autumn for three hundred years. The square below him was packed to the fountains. The palace behind him was hung from its gold domes to its pale twisting towers with banners of vermilion and white, and down both sides of the square stood the tall red standards with the pale antlered stag of the line, row on row, each with a sweating boy to hold it straight. The custom was simple and the whole South came to see it. The house words are Call, and It Answers. The Emperor called each great name of the South in turn, and the house stepped forward, answered, and had its tribute carts driven past. He had doubled the salt tax that spring, to pay for the domes.
He called the Holy Sea, and a Lambert clerk stepped forward with a roll under his arm and read out what the throne owed the Archive for three centuries of registers, to the copper, which took until the fried dough sellers had sold out twice. He called the Marrick, and the spear company in the square looked up at the sun, saw that it was noon, and grounded arms, because their contract had that minute run out. He called the Corwen, and a boy brought word that the Wellhead casks had been sold elsewhere. He called the Yukari, and one crow came down and sat on the balcony rail for about as long as it takes to read a name, and left. He called the Yan, and an elder of the Grey Plain began reciting his own titles in a carrying voice, and was still going when the sun moved, so that to this day no scholar can say whether the Yan answered. He called the Ryu, who sent a superb letter.
Then Rokju Mahuo did the thing his line was for. He raised his hands and called across the Veil, and the Baengnok came, the White Stag on all those banners, the great bound power of the dynasty, stepping out of the air above the square with its antlers full of cold light and a hush going out from it across a hundred thousand people. It looked at the Emperor. Its compact, as the Mahou scholars later explained at length, ran for as long as the realm answered. It walked down out of the sky, through the crowd, which parted, out by the East Gate and up into the iron hills, and has not been summoned since. There was a long pause, and somewhere near the fountains a fish-wife started to laugh. By nightfall the standards were firewood, every girl in Sum-gol had a vermilion sash, and the only emperor in history to be deposed by attendance had gone inside to think about it. The Empire of the South ended that afternoon with very few casualties. They came later.
Sum-gol is the name of an empire with no empire left, the richest ruin in the South, two great houses that still answer to it and keep its money, and a young postmaster who holds what is left and will not put on the crown.
The Empire and How It Broke
For three hundred years the vermilion ran from Kessen ford to the southern sea. Every southern power held its land of Sum-gol: the Holy Sea paid in records, the Long Fields in spearmen, the Wellheads in water, the Grey Plain in horses, and the Thousand Moorings kept the imperial fleet. The Yukari, who were old when the Mahou were young, paid a tribute of one crow a year and entered it. The Mahou line were summoners, whose arts called things across the Veil and bound them, and whose iron and salt went north in every cart that ever used the road, for longer than the Moto have had a crown.
After 602 the lands went their own ways, and nobody invaded anyone, which is what makes it so embarrassing. The Lamberts kept Sallowgate for the Palatine. The Corwen took a Guild lease and a charter of their own. The Marrick found that a spear company hires out better when it has no emperor to serve, and the Yukari simply went on sitting where they were. Only two stayed. The Yan Hall of the Jade Plains and House Ryu of the Copper Coast, the Dynasty’s horse-masters and its admiralty, go on answering to its name today. What that means in practice is the subject of the rest of this page and a good many lawsuits.
The Mahou went on as kings of Sum-gol for another three generations, still rich, still loud, still hanging the banners. Then came the long war of the last forty years, and it ate them. Their name was carried at the front of other people’s armies until there was nothing left of it but the carrying. The Moto put Mahuo banners over Moto columns, the Yukari and the Zettari each fought under the excuse of protecting them, and when the time came the house was destroyed. Every one of the three tells it differently. The Yukari say the Moto stood back and let the Yukari slaughter them, because a house turned into a symbol is very easy to kill and nobody weeps for a symbol. The Moto blame the Yukari. Kushara blames them both. All three are right about the other two.
The Land and the Look
The pictures you have seen are of the old glory, and the minstrels have not updated them: gold domes and pale twisting towers, a huge palace hung top to bottom with vermilion and white, tall red standards with the pale antlered device, a dark crowd massed in the square. All of that stood, and most of it stands yet. The domes have been stripped on their north faces by people who could reach them, so that they flash gold and bare in turns when the sun comes round. The towers have been hit by things. Crows sit on every cornice. A city built for ten times its present people still has its colors, and at evening, when the salt pans go red to the horizon and the banners that remain lift in the wind off them, it is one of the most beautiful sights on the one great body of land, and it charges less for lodging than any other.
Around it lie the iron hills, rust-red and bare-backed, and the salt pans, shining flat out to the south in rows of white and rose. Up the river behind the city the rice terraces climb in green shelves to Breath Hollow, the old valley the name comes from. Sum-gol sits at the southwest corner of the Scourge of Hell’s rim country, where the Kessen road comes off the wasteland’s west flank and ends and the South begins, and everything that moves between north and south has to pass through its gate or go a long way round by the salt road on the east. From the top of the iron hills to the north you can see the haze on the horizon, copper at noon and rose at evening.
Who Holds It
Cozbi Mahuo, Head of House Mahuo and Master of the Sum-gol Post, is twenty-five. On the Sum-gol road they call him the Post-Master who never loses a letter. In the rest of the South he is the man the Zettari–Mahou Accord condemns by name, and among those who deal with the dead he is the Keeper. He is the greatest summoner the South has seen in generations, a patient and lavish host who laughs loud and at the right moment, wears an olive greatcoat under a mantle of white fur, and speaks of his dead in the present tense.
He has refused the crown. Lord Naiser Yukari promised at the Cedar Enclave to see the Mahuo royal line restored at Sum-gol and to step his own house back, and Cozbi takes nothing from a house that ever carried his name: no gift, no crown, no protection, no counsel. He has also refused the color. The Mahuo colors are vermilion and white, and he kept the white. Vermilion is what other houses’ armies carried into the field over Mahuo banners, so the Post wears olive, and asked at dinner when he will wear the red again he says, with every sign of enjoying the question, on the day Sum-gol is his by his own hand.
So the throne stands empty, in a hall kept swept by a woman the Post pays. The chair at the warlords’ table is kept for Sum-gol, it is the only one with nobody sitting in it, and every other house at the table has a reason to want it filled by somebody in particular. The Dynasty still has its name, its salt and its iron, its two loyal houses, its heralds, and every autumn its Calling: an old herald stands on the Balcony of Answers and reads the roll to a large cheerful crowd that has come for the food. An elder of the Yan recites his titles. A letter arrives from the Ryu. The Post-Master attends in olive and does not answer, since the roll is the crown’s and he has no crown.
Cities and Towns
Sum-gol is the seat and the name of the whole country. By the last Yukari count the city and its country hold about fifteen thousand souls among streets laid out for a hundred and fifty, so that whole quarters stand open to the sky and a family can rent a prince’s stable for the price of keeping it standing. The Palace of Answers fills the north side of the square, with the Balcony above it. The Post-House stands in what was the imperial mews, its roofs white with crow droppings and its yard full of olive coats and blowing horses, and it never closes. The teaching house in Breath Hollow keeps a school in the city as well, where children of the line and any others who can pay learn the soul-breath arts.
Cheolsan, “iron mountain,” is the hill town of the mines, built in red stone up the side of the ore it stands on, full of smiths and fire-setters and a vile black beer. Its smiths brag about their marks the way Moto lords brag about their grandfathers. The same hills give cinnabar, the red ore that made the vermilion, and the dye works still run in the lower town, staining the river for a mile, and sell to everyone in the South except the Post.
Yeomjeon, “salt field,” is a low white town on stilts at the edge of the pans, where the rakers go barefoot with their feet wrapped in linen and the wind tastes of what you would be paying for anywhere else. The Mahuo’s salt. The Sum-gol iron. Every northern quartermaster still says the two together.
Breath Hollow is the valley itself, emptied as the house went out of it by attrition, and what remains is sixty roofs and a teaching house. Ask anyone there about the Seven Debts, the cohort of cousins whose grandfather gave them all the generation-syllable for debt. It is still the best lawsuit the valley ever had.
Wealth and Trade
Salt and iron first, as ever, though the salt sells through other people’s toll-gates now. House Ryu sits on the sea end of the old revenue and has stopped forwarding it, and the South has never settled whether that is theft. Cinnabar and dye. Rice from the terraces. Mahuo soul-breath knowledge, sold as healing, spiritual diagnosis and lineage-reading, which no amount of ward-craft can replicate.
And the Sum-gol Post, by crow and relay rider. Every letter between the north and the Yukari valleys goes through it, along the whole length of the Kessen road, in sealed bags on olive-coated riders who change horses at the old imperial stations. A house that was a crown now carries the South’s letters, and carries them so well that nobody has thought to ask who is paying the couriers, or whom they answer to. Beside the letters the house runs its other trade, in the same coats. Cozbi Mahuo means the world to know the Mahuo as the Order of the Spiritual Reality, the Keepers of Death, a function nobody can do without, held the way the Corwen hold the springs and the Lamberts the count. Since the Soul Plane broke, hauntings have spread across the South and the dead drift. The Post will lay a haunting, exorcise a house, clear Well-creatures where the dead have soured a site, or escort a soul home, each job priced, recorded and done in olive and white. “The Corwen keep the water. The Lamberts keep the count. We keep the dead. Nobody else would take them.”
Rent, Food and the Street
Rent is the wonder of the South. A journeyman can live in a duke’s kitchen, and a hedge-worker who keeps the rats out of a dead minister’s library pays nothing at all. Food is cheap and salted: rice and barley with salted radish and fermented bean, blood soup at the Post-House gate, grilled river eel, and pans of sour greens put up against the winter. The valley counts breath before it counts coin, and a nursemaid teaches a child to count the ox’s breathing before she teaches it the copper. At the Stubble-Burn, when the terraces are fired after harvest, the whole hollow smokes for three days and everyone comes down to the city to eat and argue.
The street is loud because there is so much room to be loud in. Scavenger crews in painted hoods fight over the gold on the domes. Children race crows. Scribes who cannot read Common sit outside the Post-House and write your letter anyway. Everyone but the Post-Master wears vermilion, a sash or a rag or a dyed hat, partly from pride and partly because it is cheap here. The city’s bracket crowd says gabot for the aura coat, nureum for Pressure and nunchi for sensing, and it will tell you at length that the Yukari do not understand any of the three.
Law and How It Fights
The old imperial code still runs in the courts because nobody has written a new one, and a dead emperor’s seal will still pass in Yeomjeon if it is the right color. Mahuo burial law stands alone in the four quarters in not requiring the family to keep the body. Post law is the only law everyone respects. A sealed bag is holy, a rider’s horse may be taken for no debt, and the last man who robbed a courier on the Kessen road returned the letters himself, by hand, at night, and would not say why.
Sum-gol has no field army now and has not had one since the war. Its ancient art is summoning: a Mahou summoner shapes a vessel, lends it an identity and holds it by recognition, so a single trained summoner can bring a small host to any field, and the great ones of the old line brought whole bestiaries to the square. The house style among the riders is the hwando, a short curved saber worn across the shoulders on the road, and a ring of salt poured quickly around anyone who needs one. As for the Post-Master, he fights the way he gives a dinner, and his summons are his guests. Nobody who has been to one has asked for a second invitation. The Guild Accord’s assessors gave up trying to list his forms in their third year.
What They Joke About
Attendance. Every Sum-gol joke comes round to the Calling. A boy who skips school “answered like a Marrick,” a husband who comes home late “sent a very good letter.” They say the Emperor’s stag is still walking and will be back when someone pays it. They say the Yan elder finished his titles last spring and has started again from a new angle. Of the Lamberts they say that one came to read a dying man’s will and stayed to read the man. Of the Moto they say nothing polite, and they spit before they say it.
Monsters on the Roads
Since the Soul Plane broke, hauntings have spread across the South and the dead drift, and the Post will lay a haunting, exorcise a house or clear Well-creatures where the dead have soured a site, each job priced and recorded. Ghouls (Grade B) work the empty quarters, where a city laid out for ten times its people offers them any number of quiet kitchens. Brine-walkers, pale long-legged things that follow the rakers at dusk, are the salt pans’ own contribution. Beasts are the smaller bill: wild goats and hill wolves on the iron hills, herons on the pans, and crows on every cornice that will have the eyes out of anything left lying. The Baengnok, the White Stag, bound power of the old line, walked out by the East Gate in 602 and has not been summoned since, and hill people leave it alone.
The dungeons. The one everybody tells is the Answering Vaults, under the Palace square, where the great summoners of the old line kept whole bestiaries in bound vessels against the next Calling. Nobody living has the roll. Scavengers in painted hoods go down for the gold and bring up reports of a host still standing in rows, waiting to be called. The one nobody tells in front of a smith is the Ninth Adit at Cheolsan (an adit being a level tunnel driven into a hillside), a Chthonica Well (a Wellspring of dark iron-oxide, all grip and ground), worked for its iron, with the Eighth sealed. The Dynasty’s iron mountain goes down further than the miners were ever told, Post riders carry the adit’s accounts under seal, and the smiths of Cheolsan have stopped asking what the Ninth is being fed. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
Beside the Scourge. The empire claimed the Scourge on paper, the whole of it to the foot of the sword, and the Palace still has the deed. Yeomjeon’s forgers will sell you a barony in the Black Roots (the belt of root-mat just inside the rim) under a dead emperor’s seal, and it will pass. The wasteland is less impressed. In late summer of a dry year the wind goes round to the north and comes over the iron hills hot, smelling of iron and pollen, the rakers look up from the pans, and whatever the herds have pushed out of the rim comes down the last of the Kessen road: dire wolves off the Hem, and haze-kites (Grade B, membrane and hunger the color of an old copper pot) after the mules at Cheolsan. Every relay station on the flank keeps a ground-bell on an iron stake and a horse saddled. Olive riders work that road in every year of the wheel. A sealed bag is holy, the things that come up through the roots have not read Post law, and on the Post’s books a rider taken by the ground is a letter delayed, and the next rider leaves on time.
The Turn. The South’s share of the Turn, nine years in every twenty-seven keeping the Scourge off the other two regions, falls first on the old Dynasty’s realms, and Sum-gol has no field army to send. It answers in iron, salt and road. When the South’s western column goes north it forms up in the square under the empty Balcony, eats the city out of eel and leaves with Cheolsan bolts in its pouches, and the stakes under the ground-bells of every edge town from Lastpenny on were as likely as not forged here. The Post holds the job of laying the South’s drifting dead along the Hem, each line priced and entered in the South’s Count. In the other eighteen years it sells the same bolts and carries the same letters for whoever’s Turn it is, and at the Calling the old herald still reads the Scourge out among the Dynasty’s holdings, to general applause.
Neighbors and Grudges
The Silver Cedars of Yukari. The house that offered the crown back. The couriers run between the two seats every week, on a warded track, and the courtesies are perfect.
The Copper Coast and the Jade Plains. Sworn to the name. The Ryu have left the Mahuo’s wealth exactly where it sat and would like it noted that the Mahuo have never asked. The Yan hold an empty stall for the Emperor’s horse at Qingyuan and enter it every year as held.
The Holy Sea. Keeps the empire’s old rolls and has never been paid. The Post carries its letters promptly, and reads their addresses with interest.
The Sapphire Wells and the Ochre Fields. Both left at the Calling and both have done well from it. Sum-gol still buys Marrick spears when it can pay, and does not drink from anything that comes out of a Corwen cask.
The north. Every northern lord’s letters go through the olive coats. The Moto put the Mahuo banner over their columns in the war, and no Moto rider has ever been refused at the Post-House, and no Moto rider has ever been comfortable there.
Further reading · The Southern Warlords · The Mahuo Family

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Violet Peaks of Caelspire
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
House Caelward of the Avian Kin, one of the four Central Warlords, over a mountain country of rival schools

One step for the farmer,
Two for the king,
Four thousand for the army,
And the last one’s the thing.
A skipping rhyme from Windstair. Children there skip at the cliff’s edge, as a matter of honor.

In the high summer of 704 King Odo Gambrel of Upper Marl, the eleventh of that name in a kingdom about nine miles wide, crowned at Pennycrown in a crown of good middling price, marched nine hundred men up the Windstair to demand arrears of tribute that he had found mentioned in an old letter. He picked his moment well, or thought so: it was the week of the Long Step, the great match between the schools of the Violet Peaks, when every fighter on the mountain is known to be busy. It took his men eight days to climb. They arrived at the top in their best red, gasping, with their king carried in a chair and his herald too winded to herald, and they found the entire peak population on the terraces with their backs turned, roaring, because the Gray Kites of Windstair and the Highroost Shrikes were at that moment throwing each other off a cliff. The herald eventually got his breath and began the demand. A Shrike in black and white came up out of the gulf at that moment, three hundred feet of bad temper riding a column of air, and took the crown off Odo’s head on her way past, because the rules of that year’s match said the side holding the highest object at sundown won, and it had occurred to her that the king was standing on a table.
The Kites took it back by nightfall. No one on the mountain ever spoke to King Odo at all. He stood about for two days, was charged by a basket-man for the air his men had been breathing, and went home bareheaded down four thousand steps, with the hoisters laughing and his army selling its boots. The match has been fought for his crown ever since. It is called the King’s Hat, it has a dent in it from the Finals of 711, and when the Gambrel family wrote to ask for it back, the schools invited them to come and win it, and sent the list of fixtures.

Twin crags above the clouds, where feathered fighters from a dozen rival schools step off cliffs and read the wind for a living, who have never lost the high stairs to any army and who will not stop their match to discuss it.

I do not care for heights, and I wrote the following from an inn at the bottom, with reports.
The Land
Look up from the farmland on the northwest of the Center on a clear morning, with the haze of the Scourge of Hell at your back, and there is a line of lilac cloud where no cloud should be, and above it, floating on nothing, the Violet Peaks. The chief of them, Caelspire, is two crags rising side by side out of that cloud and joined near the summit by a long arched bridge hung with so much green that from below it looks like a line of living forest crossing the sky. On the crags stand pale domed halls and steep violet roofs, stacked wherever rock will hold them. At the very top is one huge old tree, and beside the tree a pool that spills straight off the edge of the world as a waterfall so long that much of it blows away before it lands, with a rainbow standing in the spray from morning until the sun drops. Flights of white birds go round it all day. The whole country of the farms lies spread far below like a map on a table, patched and tidy, and the people of the Peaks speak of it as a map.
Beyond Caelspire the range runs on in a broken line of violet-shadowed summits, and each peak is its own school. Windstair is the great way up, four thousand cut steps on the north face. Highroost is the far peak, narrow as a tooth and in constant high wind. There are a dozen others, some inhabited by four old masters and a goat. Feathered banners stream from every roofline, and on any fine morning you will see fighters in their school’s colors simply stepping off the cliffs.
The pool at Caelspire’s summit is a worked Wellspring site, a Core in common speech, and its Aether is Cymorath, the Air of Ascent, one of the sixty Wellsprings (the sixty types of Aether, the raw power of the world), a blue spiraling thing that smells of ozone and dry air and leaves curved trails where it is spent. Its keepers can close it, and the keepers are the Caelwards. Rich ground fills a practitioner quickly, which is why a dozen schools have climbed up here and stayed, and why they have been fighting ever since about who gets the mornings. No one knows who built the bridge. It stands on no pier that anyone has found, and it was already old when the first Avian Kin nested on it. The Measurewrights say the Great Spirit War, and the Kin say the bridge has never mentioned it.
The House and Who Rules
The Avian Kin stand on the Accord’s roll under the name Current-Reading, the habit of their blood, with Dexterity (the Guild’s measure of reaction and of moving at the right distance) as their definitive gift and a legal standing marked “variable by territory.” In person they are light-boned and narrow, hard-eyed, with crests of feather from the brow to the shoulders and long stiff vanes down the outer forearm, in every color from sparrow to flame. The unwoken among them can glide a little, on a good wind, if they are brave and have an appointment with a surgeon. The ones who truly fly have earned it, pulling Aether out of the moving air, refining it in the Soul Crystal (the organ that turns Aether into the Essence a person spends) and laying it along those vanes. Current-Reading is the gift underneath: an Avian Kin feels the air’s whole shape on the skin, reads a front two days out, and can tell where you are in a dark room from the way the draft goes round you.
House Caelward holds Caelspire, the bridge, the tree and the pool. It has not been the strongest school on the mountain for three hundred years, and it keeps the Core’s hours, runs the hoists and sits in judgment at the Drop, so every other school must come and shout at it. The head of the house is the Warden of the High Stair, at present Vessaly Caelward, called Nobody’s Landing, a tall gray-crested woman of fifty with one vane burned to the bone, who won the Long Step three years running in her youth by never once appearing to hurry. She presides over a mountain of feuding clubs with a dreadful courtesy. She has thrown exactly one ambassador off the bridge, and he was caught. The house words are Step Off. The colors are violet and white.
Schools, Cities and Towns
Schools here run like football clubs. Each has its peak, its colors, its songs, its old defeats, and a style you can spot at fifty paces, and a child in Windstair is born owing loyalty to one and despising the rest. Their followers travel, drink and riot.
Caelspire is the seat, with the Warden’s domed hall, the markets on the bridge and the Caelward school, the Stair Wardens, whose violet coats mean they will catch you if you fall and fine you afterward. Its lower town, hung from the crag on ropes and iron pins, is the most crowded and most cheerful slum in the Inner World.
Windstair is the working town of the Peaks, strung along the top third of the great stair, full of hoist-lodges, feather-sellers and inns that have had the same argument for a century. Its school, the Gray Kites, in gray and lilac, fights on long patient glides and wears you down from a distance, and their crowd sings an insulting hymn that lasts an hour.
Highroost is the home of the Shrikes, in black and white, a butcher’s style that drops from above and hangs the loser up by the coat on the nearest thorn tree. It is a brutally cold town, and it is proud of that. People there eat standing up because of the wind.
The smaller clubs each have their devotees: the Longdrop Swifts, who have never been seen to land; the Old Mews, who are four very elderly women and who keep winning; the Lilac Stair, who are rich and bad and have the best songs.
Wealth and Trade
The Peaks grow almost nothing and they are rich anyway. Their first trade is the wind itself: a Windstair almanac, hand-copied, tells a shipmaster on a far coast or a general on a far field what the weather will be doing on Tuesday, and readers of the air are hired by captains and commanders on every side. Half of the great battles in the center were timed by someone in a gray coat.
Their second trade is the molt. Feathers shed by the Kin are the best fletching anyone has found, because a Kite’s feather holds a trace of its owner’s read of the air, and arrows fletched with it fly straighter than they have any right to. Molt-sellers go through the school dormitories every season with sacks. The feather of a champion is sold with a name, and fakes are everywhere. To pluck one is a killing matter, and that is the root of the worst thing on this page, below.
The third is the schools. Young fighters from every realm climb the stair with their parents’ money to be taught, and some of them, being wingless, have to be taught what falling is. The fourth is the passes: the high ways over the range are the only roads between the salt country and the west that have never been cut by war, and the Caelwards take a toll. The fifth is the match. In the week of the Long Step every bed on the mountain costs what its keeper says it costs, and the bookies take more than the schools.
Rent, Food and the Street
Height costs money, and the direction it costs in depends on who you are. A loaf is cheapest at the foot and it rises a little every thousand steps, because everything up here comes up in baskets, on ropes worked by the hoisters’ company. They are paid by the load and go on strike about once a decade, at which point the whole mountain lives on goat and spite until someone pays. For a person of the Kin, rent runs the other way: a room on the outer edge, with a clean drop from the sill, is worth more than a palace on the inside of the rock. A family of means leaves its front door opening onto nothing. A lowlander is put in the cheap inner rooms and told he should feel lucky.
The food is goat cheese and lilac honey, barley cakes from the small terraces, dried fish that has climbed four thousand steps and resents it, and thin sharp wine that gets stronger as you go up, or seems to. Do not order eggs. It is very funny the first time, and no one on the mountain will ever explain why they have stopped speaking to you.
Everyone on the street has a petty air-trick and a price: the laundress who dries your shirt on a private breeze, the boy who will drop a note down to the third terrace for a copper, the hedge-worker who keeps the smell of the Highroost tanners from drifting across the bridge, until someone stops paying her. Fans are bet on, scarves are sung about, and two strangers in the wrong colors in a narrow alley have an understood procedure.
Law
The law of the Peaks is the law of the stair: who holds the stair holds the peak, and the stair may not be cut in time of match. Disputes between persons go before the Warden, and any that cannot be settled go to the Drop. Both parties step off the Caelspire bridge, and whoever lands last has won the case. It sounds like a joke, and it is also an exact measure of skill and nerve. A lowlander may appoint a champion, at ruinous rates. It has happened, in 633, that both parties won the case very thoroughly and left their estate to the lawyers.
Falling is lawful. Pushing a person off a height is murder, unless it can be shown that the person might reasonably have flown.
The one law that has no comedy in it concerns fowlers. In the territories where the Accord’s rolls read the Kin as labor stock, there are licensed men with nets who take them for their singing and their feathers, and a bird-maker in a Concord market town will show you a cage with a person in it, with the long vanes clipped so she can never leave, and quote you a price. A plucked vane does not grow back straight. A fowler taken on any stair of the Violet Peaks is walked up to the bridge, in the sight of the assembled schools, who for that one hour wear no colors, and invited to step off. There is nobody to catch him, and they all watch him the whole way down.
How It Fights
No army has ever taken the high stairs, and they have been at it since before the Guild’s count begins. The problem is mostly arithmetic: four thousand steps, cut one man wide at the worst points, under cliffs, in a high wind, with fighters who can stand in the air beside you and take your head off and go home for lunch. Rocks are also available. A siege fails for lack of anything to besiege, for the hoists can be pulled up at any time and the Kin can go out over your head to the farms. Mostly, an army that reaches the top is too tired to be anything but embarrassed.
In the single fight, they use the sky as a floor. The Highroost Stoop drops a Shrike from a thousand feet with everything she weighs and all the air she has packed behind her into one heel on the join of your collar. The Kites’ Long Afternoon stays one spear-length out of your reach, on the wind, and cuts you once each time you breathe in, until you sit down. The Stair Wardens’ Nobody’s Landing gets under a falling enemy, catches him as a courtesy, and carries him out over the gulf to discuss terms. Fights end in a crowd’s roar, with the winner calling the move by name so the terraces can sing it, and any good fighter on these peaks has an epithet before his crest is grown.
They call the aura coat (the visible coat of a fighter’s own color) the lift, and argue endlessly about whether a good lift should show at all. Pressure, the weight of a higher Stage felt in the room, is the downdraft, for what it does to your shoulders. To sense another practitioner is to feel the draft go round him.
The counters are real. Still air grounds half a school, and on a dead calm inversion morning, with the fog lying flat, the Peaks are as near to helpless as they ever come, which is why those mornings are the only ones on which the schools do not train and everyone is very polite. Bled ground starves them. A light-boned fighter who gets hit once by anything heavy stays hit, so hard men with low ceilings have ended a good many careers in the indoor towns. And a crossbow bolt costs about three coppers, its threat Grade met by the fighter’s Speed (the Guild’s measure of how fast a body can answer) like any other missile’s: a Kite who does not see the loose comes down like a goose off a marsh, and every fighter in the Peaks knows the name of someone it happened to.
What They Joke About
They joke about everyone who has to walk. A groundling is anyone with no feathers, and the word is applied with pity. “Eight days up and one breath down” is the Windstair summary of all foreign policy. They say a Bearkin is the only thing on the map that might be a mountain, and they say a Scalebond remembers the fall and a Kite remembers the view. Most of all they joke about each other: the Lilac Stair have been told at every match for ninety years to try landing on purpose, and the Shrikes’ away songs are not to be set down here.
The groundlings joke back. In the Midmarch, a person with a very high opinion of himself “has a sill.” Every bowman in the center claims his fletching came off a champion. And anyone within a week’s march of the range knows that the fastest way to get a Violet Peaks scout to tell you what she has seen is to ask her who she thinks will win on Saturday, and then to stand well back.
Monsters on the Roads
Griffons (Grade A on the Bestiary’s scale, which runs from E to EX) nest on the east faces and will leave a fight to keep the nest. Hippogrifs (Grade B) are caught and sold, Harpies are a nuisance on the Windstair, and a Wyvern taking a fighter out of the air is a thing that happens during fixtures. Bear keep to the northern faces, goats go anywhere they please, and the white birds that circle Caelspire are under the Warden’s protection and know it.
The dungeon is the Chimney inside Highroost: a shaft up through the hollow tooth of the peak, an Ascensio Well (the Wellspring of rising and hoist, steel gray) where the Mouth is at the bottom and the Heart at the top, so delvers climb and everything else falls on them. The Shrikes claim to have cleared it in 588. The Old Mews, four very elderly women, send them a note every year correcting the date and the word. The Summit Pool at Caelspire is the other place the Guild’s list names, a Cymorath site worked by House Caelward for longer than the house can document, and every other school on the mountain has to come and shout at the Caelwards to buy its hours. More on the Dungeons shelf and in the Gazetteer.
Beside the Scourge
The Peaks stand off the northwest corner of the Scourge of Hell, high enough to look down on the whole problem, and they have found that this can be sold. Its wind comes outward from the middle in every season, hot and dry, and a Current-Reader on the high stairs can feel the Haze (the third belt in, where the great herds walk the dry beds) shifting before any hedge-worker on the rim knows a thing. Every herd sighting on the western side comes from an Avian scout, at her price, and the Windstair almanac carries a dry-year column that the kings of the Midmarch pay for and then ignore. The herds do not climb. Haze-kites do, membrane and hunger the color of an old copper pot, riding that same wind to the foot of the stair in dry years and taking mules from the hoisters. The Gray Kites regard the name as a slander and kill them on sight.
The schools go in. Most of the fighting schools of the Center send their seniors to walk the Hem (the outermost belt, fifteen leagues of black-barked thornwood and pale dust), and the proud ones send them on to the Black Roots, with the song and the banner. The schools of the Violet Peaks keep an annual tally of kills per student and post it on the bridge, the Long Step’s bookies study it closely, and a school that loses a season’s seniors will recruit twice as hard for the glory of it. The Lilac Stair’s tally is excellent, and no one has ever seen the kills.
Windstair also has the view. On perhaps nine clear days in the year a dark upright line stands on the sky far to the southeast, the colossal sword at the Scourge’s center, bronze-hilted, driven point-down into the mountains, with a field of violet stars where its blade should be. A survey taken from the Windstair reckons it about four leagues above the peaks. One from Stoneglass Hollow says about three, and the authors did not speak afterward. On those days the whole town goes out on its sills in every color to look, and the odds on the next fixture are chalked up on the way back in.
The Turn runs North, then South, then Center, nine years each, with the holder keeping a Line of forts around the Hem and the other two counting what it costs. The Center holds it now, from 712 to 721, and the Peaks pay in sightings, at a discount the Warden describes as generous, and in seniors, who would have gone anyway. On the North’s Turn or the South’s a host comes down the Kessen road below the range in long columns the terraces find very funny, and its marshal sends up for the almanac. The same sighting has been sold to the holder of a Turn and to both of the clerks sent to count what it cost him.
Neighbors and Grudges
The Hundred Crowns of the Midmarch are the map below, and their kings send demands. The King’s Hat has been defended against three of them by name.
The Sealed Charter of the Concord licenses the fowlers, buys the almanacs and has been refused a Warden’s audience for two centuries. The Caelwards take its coin for the wind every season and spit afterward, and this is the sore point at home. A faction of the clubs wants the trade cut, and the Warden has been heard to observe that a people who can leave are always the last to stop selling.
The Russet Crown of the Unpapered has asked for high roads for its runaways. Some of the schools run them, for love, and some sell the crossings. There is a Kite captain who has carried sixty people over the range on her back, one at a time, and there is a Shrike master who charged them.
The Rose Coils of Coilspire hold an old fine over a bird that fell on their plaza, and they will tell you which bird.
The Moonlight Forest of Mosk-Vaal buys the almanac for the moon’s sake. It is the only customer that has never once tried to get a discount.
The North and the South know the Peaks mainly as arrow-fletching and a good place to send a difficult son. The real war, as far as any Kite is concerned, is against Highroost.

In a later hand, in the margin: When the banners of the Northern Empire of Whitemere came as far as the foot of the Windstair, in the years it was building, their herald read a very fine proclamation. It was the week of the Long Step.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The New World — The Eastern Rise
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itthe NOO WURLD
The Eastern Rise

The eastern quarter is still being made. An oceanic plate is going down beneath it along the whole seaboard, and young ground is rich ground.

The Scarlet Bellows has moved its school forty leagues in a hundred and twenty-seven years, and it has done so at a run. In the autumn of Year 588 the Pyraeon pool at Pennock’s Bar, the Core (a worked Wellspring site with keepers on it) that had fed the school for two generations, thinned to nothing in a single night after the caldera above it settled, and by the next evening a shepherd nine leagues up the ash plain was reporting warm stones and a color in the air like the inside of a peach. Mother Hawise Tregar had the hall down by dawn. Six hundred disciples in scarlet and yellow set off across the plain with the roof beams on their shoulders and the demountable array in numbered crates and every drum in the school going, and behind them came the dumpling sellers, the bookmakers, two minstrels and most of the town. Unhappily the Blue Sluice school had a shorter road and its own shepherd. The two met on the warm stones on the fifth day and fought for six more, coats blazing vermilion and kingfisher across a flat of white ash, in front of a crowd that had brought its children. It cost twenty-two dead and Mother Tregar’s left hand. An Arbiter of the Accord came up on a mule, opened a hearing on the question of who owns a Wellspring site that has walked, and was on his second witness when the pool moved again in the night. Both schools got up and ran. The clerk followed with the docket.
They are still at it. Pennock’s Bar is now a town on skids, called Walking Pennock on every chart and redrawn each decade, where rent runs by the season and the hearing is in its fifth Arbiter. Ask anyone there what the New World is and they will tell you it is the place where you keep your hall in crates.
In one breath: a country so young it will not hold still, with gold lying in the rivers for anyone who cares to stoop, and every town in it ready to pick up its roof and run after its luck.
The name misleads. There has never been a sea between this quarter and the rest of the land. A carter can walk here from the western kingdoms if he has the months and the ash leaves him a road. It is New because the Voyager Era’s charts reached it last, and because the ground under it is younger than some of the families on it.
Two Grounds
The eastern quarter holds two countries on one rim of the land, as different as a cathedral and a gold camp, and this ledger surveys one of them.
The elven old-ground. Eresse’s ancient country, under four Eons of elven law: the Grand Principality of Eresse; Iampu and its Seasonal Courts; Rovann; the Sylvaar Dream Groves; the Echo Elves’ Longhouse Accord; Velthaeir, the Floating Archive-City; the Sunroot Court at Vaelmarr. Its Wellspring sites have been pulled from since the first Eon. Two of its materials are entered below, Ironwood and Glacium, with the old-ground as their region. Nothing else of it is surveyed here.
The arc. The young volcanic ground the Guild Accord chartered from nothing, beginning when the Voyager Era’s routes first brought its gold home and still adding charters within living memory: the andesite chain, the caldera belt, the ash plain between them, the coral platforms of the northern coast; Caedor and its four Cloudmetal arrays, Foraye, the Tsohanto Reach. Everything from Formation to Trade Posture below is the arc’s ledger and no other’s. Where the text says the eastern quarter, read the arc.
Eresse and every elven branch sit here and not in the Old World quarter, which keeps Varūn. The Accord’s doctrine that the New World was chartered from nothing, with no older law to displace, is true of the charter and of the charter alone.
Formation
The consequence of that subducting plate is a volcanic arc running the length of the quarter: a chain of andesite stratovolcanoes, an inland belt of calderas, and between them a plain of ash and lahar deposit measured in fathoms rather than feet.
The hot fluid systems above a live magma body deposit gold and silver in shallow veins that are still there because nothing has had time to erode them away. Where an intrusion has pushed into limestone, the contact zone has cooked into skarn and thrown out silver, lead, and zinc in bodies workable from surface. The rivers cutting through all of this have concentrated gold into placer bars that a man can work with a pan and no capital whatsoever, which is why the eastern quarter has the population it has.
The wet flanks weather differently. Under high rainfall and heat the ash breaks down into a deep red laterite crust, leaching out everything soluble and leaving behind a residue extraordinarily rich in aluminous and nickeliferous minerals. That crust is worthless to anyone who cannot reduce it, and reducing it takes more Judicium capacity than the Old World has ever been willing to divert from its pumps. (Judicium is the Wellspring of the lightning’s line, an array is a standing runed working fed by keepers on a shift, and reduction is the old smelter’s word for tearing a metal out of its rock.)
The Ground Itself
Ash plains that carry a crop in three seasons and bury a village in one night. Cloud forest on the volcanic flanks, dripping, layered, loud with birds the color of a dyer’s apron, and full of things nobody has classified. Obsidian flows glassy enough to cut a boot through. Sulfur fields around the fumaroles where the ground is warm and yellow and nothing grows. Red crust on every wet slope, rivers running gray with suspended pumice and turning gold at the bars, crater lakes of a green no painter has been paid enough to match, and off the northern coast, coral platforms building on drowned volcanic cones. Western visitors call it a beautiful way to die, and then they stay.

The Wellspring sites here move. This is the fact eastern practice is organized around and that western surveyors consistently refuse to believe until they have lost a season to it.
Ground this young does not hold a pool of Aether (the raw stuff in ground and air that a practitioner pulls and refines) in a fixed position across generations. A working sited on a strong local source can find that source thinned or shifted after an eruption, a caldera settling, or nothing anyone can identify. Fat ground this year is lean ground next, and the whole trade of the place is knowing which.
Eastern arrays are built to be moved. Western arrays are built to be permanent. Neither quarter thinks the other is sane.

Who Lives On It
A list of minerals will not tell you that this is the loudest quarter on the map. Every practitioner with a grudge and every younger son with a pan comes east sooner or later. Sects follow the pools and craft guilds follow the sects, so that a bar-town of nine hundred can hold four schools with four sets of colors, each one sure of the local Core, and an Essence-work stall on every corner. Rent runs by the season, because nobody signs for a year on ground like that, and is paid in dust by the pinch, which every landlord’s thumb has trained to be larger. Food is ash-plain yams and beans, river fish split and smoked in red pepper, eggs boiled in a basket lowered into the vent by a child who has been told to hold her breath, and western flour at a price that makes bread a boast.
The politics of the place come straight out of the river. Gold won by hand needs nobody’s permission, so a bar governs itself by bar-moot, an open meeting of whoever is standing in the water, which sets claim-lines, hangs thieves and sells its vote to the Accord’s factor on alternate Thursdays. The Accord holds the charters and the debts, and the moots hold the rivers. Neither has yet found a way to collect from the other without a fight.
Caedor is a walled city wrapped around four white-blue fires, and everything in it, rent and songs and wars, comes down to keeping them fed. Rooms within sight of the arrays cost more than a house on the plain, because that is where the guild-sworn live, and the militia drills on the ramparts every evening under a light that turns everyone’s teeth lavender. It eats other people’s grain, and it has fought for its own roads more often than anyone has troubled to count.
Foraye is griffon country over a black glass valley, where the High Aerie Riders keep bonds seven centuries old and every militia child carries a pocketful of single-use glass. It is the nearest thing the arc has to an old town. Sancta Lux keeps a chapter there, and the rents on the high terraces are set by how far the griffon droppings fall.
The Tsohanto Reach is the long barrow-country at the arc’s edge, with its own people and its own dead, who hold a settled opinion of the word nothing in the Accord’s charter. Prospectors go in by the river for the black-sand bars. The ones who come back recommend asking first.
The bar-towns are everything else: Walking Pennock and a hundred like it, standing on Alchemelt floors and timber frames, each one sure it has found the real fat ground at last. Half of them will be elsewhere within your lifetime.
Bearing Stock
Bearing is what a material does under load, Holding is what working it will keep. T0 to T9 is the Accord’s Tier ladder, and a Domain names the branch of natural law it works through.
Alchemelt Brick · T2 · Synthetic stone · Artisan guilds of the arc
Volcanic ash ground with burned lime and water, which sets hard, sets fast, and sets underwater. This last property is why the eastern quarter is building deep-water harbors at a rate the west finds indecent while western harbors silt shut. It resists ambient magic and crumbles under sustained structural stress, so it is used for floors, foundations, moles, and cisterns rather than for anything that must span. Bearing moderate, Holding deliberately low. Domain Material Science.
Pumice Float · T1 · Stone · Caldera ignimbrite sheets, universal
Abrasive, filtration medium, and lightweight fill. Floats. Rafts of it come down the rivers after an eruption thick enough to walk on for a week, which has killed a number of people who tried.
Redcrust Laterite · T2 · Mineral · Weathered flanks, wet eastern seaboard
The red caprock. Useless as stone, useless as soil, and the feedstock for Cloudmetal. Bearing poor, Holding nil.
Roughgold · T2 · Metal · Placer bars, black-sand rivers
Won by hand, by anyone, with no permission from anyone, which has produced the eastern quarter’s characteristic political condition. Carries Benediction and Sublimatio well, which makes it the standard substrate for ecclesiastical and oath work. Bearing soft, Holding high.
Ironwood · T3 · Wood · Deep forest of Eresse, the elven old-ground
Hardened to the equivalent of tempered steel, prized by the elves for ceremonial bows and shamanic staves, and cut under restrictions that make it functionally unavailable to the trade.
Holding Stock

Onceglass · T3 · Crystallized stone · Obsidian flows quenched within an active Wellspring field, Foraye and the caldera belt
The eastern quarter’s signature and the material western guilds most resent. Obsidian that cooled fast inside a live field of Aether takes a full inscription with unusual clarity, holds it perfectly, and shatters completely on discharge. One casting, and then you have gravel.
It cannot be repaired, cannot be recharged, and cannot be traced back to its Engraver, which is a separate problem the Enforcement Division has raised four times. What it can be is cut in quantity, cheaply, by moderately skilled hands at a bench, and sold to people who could never afford a permanent working. An eastern militia carries Onceglass charges the way a western militia carries arrows.
Bearing brittle by design, Holding high and terminal. Resonance: Fractura, Tenebra. Domain Abstract and Entropic Systems.

Cloudmetal · T4 · Metal · Reduced from Redcrust laterite, the eastern arc works
A structural metal at a third the weight of iron, silver-pale, corrosion-proof, and impossible to produce without a sustained Judicium reduction array of a scale that exists in four places in the world, all of them along the eastern arc.
Caedor did not discover the metal. Everyone knew it was in the laterite. The eastern arc was simply the only polity willing to commit that much array capacity to something other than pumping water, because the eastern arc has no old flooded mines to pump. This is the clearest case in the ledger of a capability following from geological accident rather than genius, and the arc guild would prefer it were not written down in those terms. Bearing good for its weight, Holding low. Domain Electromagnetism.
Skarnrose Ore · T3 · Metal ore · Intrusive contacts with limestone, inland caldera belt
Silver, lead, zinc, and garnet in banded contact bodies, worked open from surface because the deposits outcrop. Silver here is a byproduct of a zinc operation, which is an inversion that western silver houses have found financially unpleasant.
Yellowbreath Sulfur · T1 · Mineral · Fumarole fields throughout the arc
Sublimate sulfur, collected by hand off the vent rims by men who work in wet cloth and do not work long. Feedstock for every acid in the eastern alchemical trade and a primary Pyraeon reagent. Domain Thermodynamics.
Ember Flint · T2 · Stone · Foraye
Sparks a mild magical flame when struck. Field-mage survival stock, and the single most widely distributed Essence-active object in the eastern quarter by simple count.
Seerstone Resin · T4 · Liquid essence · Canopy trees, eastern cloud forest, provisional attribution
Stores visions and is dangerously volatile. Provenance recorded on the strength of the resin’s physical character and the tree species involved. This attribution has not been confirmed by the Archives Division and is flagged accordingly.
Glacium · T5 · Frost-infused mineral · Iampu, the elven old-ground, grown in the ice-caves under Winter Court license
Grown rather than quarried, slowly, in caverns held below freezing for the purpose, by a process the Winter Court does not document and does not permit anyone to inspect. Frost-bound weaponry and the frost-infused stock that supplements Iampu’s gold in the mercenary trade. Bearing brittle, Holding high and narrow. Resonance: Vohrin. Domain Thermodynamics.
The Works
Shallow, fast, run on borrowed coin, and enormously productive. The eastern quarter works almost nothing at depth, because it does not need to. Its ore outcrops. Its gold is in the rivers. Its cement makes itself out of the ash that falls on the works. It has, in consequence, almost none of the array dependency that defines the west.
The characteristic eastern operation is small, mobile, and expects to be somewhere else in five years. Buildings are Alchemelt over timber frame. Arrays are demountable, and their keepers walk beside the crates. Nobody sinks a shaft that assumes the ground will still be there.
The exception is the eastern arc, which has built the only permanent great works in the quarter and has organized its entire polity around defending the four reduction arrays that make Cloudmetal possible.
What It Costs

Ash fall, which buries. Lahar, which is a river of wet ash moving at the speed of a horse and which does not leave bodies to bury. Caldera collapse, which is rare and total. Fumarole gas, which kills silently in the hollows where it pools.
And the Wellspring drift, the wandering of a site’s pool, which is rarely lethal and has bankrupted more eastern ventures than every eruption in recorded history combined.

Trade Posture
Exports Cloudmetal, silver, gold, Onceglass, sulfur, and cement. Imports iron, tools, wolfram, credit, and expertise. The arc owes the west heavily and resents it. This is the arc’s posture. The elven old-ground owes nobody and says so at length.
The Accord’s Arbitration Division spends a disproportionate share of its calendar on the arc’s colonial rights, Wellspring access, and the question of whether an unregistered Onceglass charge is a weapon or a commodity.
