geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: Kushara — The Land That Remembers Weight
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itkoo-SHAH-rah
The Land That Remembers Weight

🌐 An ancient Aether-dense supercontinent of desert, rainforest, savanna and rift, ruled from Kushara by eight houses, containing no elves or dwarves at all. It is no part of the western quarter of the four-quarter ledger: a different landmass, which spent a long time carrying the wrong name.

Continental orientation
Classification: Ancient Aether-Dense Supercontinent · Epithet: The Land That Remembers Weight
Primary sovereign power: the territories unified beneath Dawn Guard
The broad shape of a broken shield. Ancient even by the standards of the Continuum: its mountains have been eroded, raised and broken several times over, its rivers run through the ruins of civilisations whose names did not survive, and Wellspring pressure has worked the geology deeply enough that stone, metal, river and forest sometimes carry recognisable spiritual memory.

North — the largest deserts, salt basins, sandstone kingdoms, buried cities and volcanic glass fields. Immense aquifers and mineral seams beneath the dunes, left by ancient inland seas.
West — warm, humid, heavily forested. Rainforest descending toward dark estuaries, mangrove deltas, cliff-lined coasts and tropical islands.
Center — savanna, wooded grassland, broad rivers, seasonal wetland, and the sovereign heartlands surrounding Kushara. The continent’s largest migrations and many of its oldest continuously inhabited cities.
East — a massive rift system, volcanic mountains, deep lakes, elevated grassland and isolated highland kingdoms. Geologically unstable, extraordinarily rich in metals, gemstones and geothermal Aether.
South — rolling mineral plateaus, temperate forest, red grassland, warm gulf coasts and the storm-beaten cape. Some of the greatest ports on the continent.

The Twelve Great Regions






































































RegionWhat it isWhat comes out of itThe Zafaran Expanse northNot one sand sea but dune oceans, gravel plains, salt depressions, sandstone mountains, dry valleys and green basins. Dunes migrate on seasonal wind and underground Wellspring current, swallowing roads, tombs and whole settlements and returning them generations later. Features: the Singing Dunes · the White Salt Mirror · the Buried Stair · the Red TeethSunstone, copper, gold, red salt, desert glass, fire opal, ember iron, solar quartz, pale gypsum, Wellspring amberThe Blackglass Basin west of ZafaranVolcanic desert fused to black glass by ancient eruption and magical warfare. Obsidian flats, basalt ridges, gray ash dunes, collapsed chambers. The surface can look solid over hollow lava voids. Features: the Mirror Wastes · the Furnace Trenches · Mount Qarash · the Field of Melted KingsObsidian, basalt, black diamond, volcanic sulfur, ember iron, nightglass, ash crystal, deep cobaltThe Kharu Belt transitionalDry grassland, thorn forest, seasonal rivers, mesas and scattered groves between the northern deserts and the central savanna. Rain is unpredictable; empty channels become violent rivers without warning. Features: the Thousand Wells · the Thorn Crown · the Walking Rivers · the Copper MesasCopper, tin, malachite, salt, iron, ochre pigment, fossil resin, thunderstoneThe M’Bala Great Savannas centerGolden grassland, wooded plain, seasonal wetland and broad river. Not wilderness: old roads, pastoral communities, fortified cities, agricultural valleys, royal estates, ancestral shrines and protected migration corridors. Features: the Crowned Grass Sea · the Twelve Migration Roads · the Stone Herds · the Thunder BasinsIron, gold, manganese, quartz, blue agate, red clay, fossil ivory, starstone fragmentsThe Kusharan Crownlands eastern centerElevated ground where high savanna, river valley and ancient stone plateau meet. Reddish-brown earth, rocky hills, clear rivers, great shade trees, golden building stone. Roads from desert, forest, mountain and coast converge here.Kusharan gold, blue sapphire, red granite, iron, silver, river pearl, deep quartz, Material Covenant stoneThe Nyoka Rainsea equatorial westRainforest vast enough to make its own storms. Layered: sunlit branch, hanging garden, dark middle forest, flooded rootland, fungal cavern, underground river. Some settlements never touch the ground. Features: the Roof of Leaves · the Drowned Roots · the Emerald Abyss · the Thunderfall · the Sleepless GroveGreen diamond, cobalt, gold, spirit amber, medicinal resin, bloodwood, Memory bark, luminous fungi, deep-earth saltsThe Great Akar Rift eastCliffs, fault valleys, volcanoes, geothermal fields, deep lakes and plateaus where the crust is separating. Among the most Aetherically active ground on the Material Plane; Wellspring currents rise near the surface and produce strange weather, mineral growth, mutation and local gravity distortion. Features: Lake Nureth · the Red Escarpment · the Breathing Fields · the Hanging Lakes · the Broken SpineDiamond, sapphire, ruby, obsidian, geothermal crystal, silver, rare-earth metals, Riftstone, gravity ore, black saltThe Orunthal Highlands northeastTable mountains, cool valleys, alpine grassland, cloud forest and terraced agriculture. Near the deserts but high enough for rain and snow, feeding rivers that run both to Zafaran and to the central plains. Features: the Crown of Clouds · the Stair Fields · the Sky Monasteries · the Echo ValleysPlatinum, silver, highland iron, pale sapphire, sky quartz, white marble, cloudstoneThe Nahal River System central arteryNot one river but a living network of channels, flood basins, seasonal branches and deltas, rising in the Orunthal, the Rift, the Crownlands and the western forest. Its annual expansion enriches soil across several kingdoms. At its widest the far bank cannot be seen. Features: the Sundi Inland Sea · the Golden Floodplain · the Reed Labyrinth · the Nine-Mouth DeltaRiver gold, clay, salt, pearl, freshwater crystal, black silt, blue pigment stone, medicinal reedsThe Zamara Gulf southwest coastTropical beaches, limestone coves, mangrove wetland, coral shelf and broad natural harbor. Cities of coral limestone, painted plaster, dark hardwood, blue tile and copper roofing; narrow streets near the old ports opening into music squares and harbor markets. Features: the Painted Harbors · the Mangrove Thrones · the Sapphire Shelf · the Bellwind CoastSea salt, coral limestone, pearl, blue copper, shellstone, tropical hardwood, ambergris, Tide crystalThe Auric Plateau southeast interiorRolling grassland, red canyon, wooded ridge, rocky upland and deep cave network. The earth runs red, gold, violet or black according to what lies beneath it. Mining cities throughout, many under strict spiritual law because careless extraction damages buried Wellspring routes. Features: the Golden Veins · the Deep Choir · the Red Crown Hills · the Iron ForestGold, platinum, diamond, chromium, manganese, iron, silver, cobalt, violet crystal, Harmonic ore, star-metal fragmentsThe Cape of Storm Drums southernmost pointSea cliffs, temperate grassland, dark forest, mountain passes and violent water. Two ocean currents meet offshore and make storm, fog and unpredictable sea; water striking hollow caves sounds like distant drumming. Features: the Drum Cliffs · the Twin Current Sea · the Silverwood · the Last LanternSilver, tin, black pearl, cold iron, storm crystal, granite, saltwood, deep-sea coral
The City of Kushara
The city rises across natural plateaus over the River Kesh, districts joined by broad avenues, terraced gardens, bridges, stairways and fortified gates. The oldest districts are carved partly into the plateau itself; newer neighborhoods run out into wooded hills and river plain.
The Golden Steps, the processional stair down from the sovereign district to the old river markets, with a grass slope beside it that children race on. The River Gardens, shallow waterways and flowering arches and small painted boats, candlelit at festival and carrying messages downstream. The Grand Court, the largest Zettari training ground in the city, adults in the central court and children in the enclosures around it. The High Gardens, terraces on the upper walls holding ancient trees, fountains and elevated pools. The Ancestral Halls, stone sanctuaries preserving family cords, weapons, Zettari patterns, witness tablets, royal oaths and the records of the dead. The Bridge of Evening Voices, where musicians gather at sunset without arrangement and sometimes play until morning. The Market of Twelve Roads, where goods from every region of the continent arrive.
Mountain systems

The Broken Spine volcanic chain following the Akar Rift. Obsidian, diamond, geothermal crystal, deep Wellspring pressure.
The Orunthal Crown high northeastern mountains feeding many of the continent’s largest rivers.
The Golden Back eroded chain west of Kushara. Gold, iron and ancestral ruins in its lower valleys.
The Southern Teeth sharp mountains dividing the Auric Plateau from the Cape.
The Cloudwall western system that traps ocean air and feeds the Nyoka Rainsea.

Government
Ruled from Kushara by House Zettari, the Sovereign House, with the Seven Pillars — N’Kharu, Vokari, Malani, Obaru, N’Yari, Jomari, Zembari — each preserving one structure the continent cannot do without: armies, gold, food, medicine, strategic minerals, maritime trade, desert water. House Zettari is not a pillar; it is what keeps seven pillars from becoming seven crowns.
Full house-by-house detail — seats, continental duties, greatest assets — is documented at The Eight Great Houses of Kushara. Kept there rather than re-tabled here, so the continent has one table of the Eight Houses, not two.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Old World — The Western Wearing
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itthe OHLD WURLD
The Western Wearing

The root of a mountain belt that no longer exists. The most geologically generous ground in the four quarters, and the most thoroughly emptied.

Every year on the feast of the first thaw, the people of the Aerne valley bury their river. They have done it since the water below the old adits turned the color of a tangerine and everything in it died, which was before anyone’s great-grandmother. The Mourners’ Guild turns out in marigold and white, seven painted barges come down with drums and pipes, and a lead-lined coffin the size of a hay cart is filled at the bank with a hundred gallons of the river itself and rowed to the sea reach with the whole valley weeping on the towpath and thoroughly drunk by noon. On the wharf at the end of the procession sit the Chancery’s buyers at their folding tables, because that orange water, refined, is the mordant that fixes ink to vellum, and the Accord has bought every codex it has ever written out of the Aerne’s drainage. In the spring of Year 652 Gunnora Hextall, Mistress of the Mourners, stopped the coffin in front of those tables and asked what they had paid for the deceased. They told her. She had it tipped over the ledgers. Vitriol at that strength does not burn the skin, so the junior clerk who leaned in to save his page felt nothing at all until he could no longer see it; fourteen people died in the riot on the wharf, and four years of the Aerne’s accounts dissolved on the planks. The buyers came back the next spring at double the rate. So did the coffin, which is now weighed before it is rowed, and the Mourners take a tenth.
That is the Old World, and I recommend the funeral. Here everything has been dug, sold, poisoned, mourned and reworked at a profit, in the best-kept country in the world.
In one breath: the deepest mines on earth, the oldest money, and a whole people paid by the hour to keep the water out, who have known for seventy years that the ground is thinning under them and have not stopped arguing or singing.
Formation
Two continental masses collided, in an age nobody can date, threw up a range on the scale of anything now standing, and then spent an unimaginable stretch of time being worn back down to the stumps. What is left at the surface is the deep interior of that range brought up into daylight: slate belts and mica schist folded like cloth, with granite bodies intruded up into them from below. The old masses have been one land since long before there was anyone to walk across the join.
Those granite bodies are the point. As each one cooled it sweated out a hot mineralizing fluid into the cracks in its own roof, and that fluid deposited tin and tungsten in sheeted veins around the granite cupolas. Further out, cooler, the same fluids left lead and silver in the limestone. Along the seaward foreland, in the basins that formed while the range was still rising, plant matter accumulated and became coal. Along the coastal plain, buried salt has risen through the overburden in domes, dragging up sulfur and oil-shale with it.
It has been worked continuously for longer than any current kingdom has existed.
The Ground Itself
Worked country, and handsome with it. Terraced hillsides, coppiced woodland cut on rotation for eleven hundred years, hedgerows on field boundaries older than the treaties that name them, pale towns on green hills with a slate roof and a sect banner on every rise. Spoil heaps stand at the head of every valley, grassed over on the outside and still poisonous within, and the sheep on them are the fattest in the quarter and are not eaten by anyone who knows. In the tin districts the ground subsides without warning over workings nobody recorded, and in the coal foreland it subsides on a schedule everyone has learned to plan around.
The rivers run orange below the old adits and have done for generations. Nothing lives in them above the tidal reach. The harbors silt, because eleven centuries of mining spoil has to go somewhere and it goes downstream.

Aetheric Density (how much Aether, the raw stuff of magic, the ground and air hold for anyone to pull) is low to moderate and locally depleted around the old districts, which is the western quarter’s defining problem and the reason its arrays are so expensive to run. An array is a standing runed working, and it stops when the keepers who feed it can no longer fill themselves from the ground they stand on. Since Year 645 the figure has fallen every year. The Research Division calls this contested. The bracket fighters of the west call it the thin, and will tell you at length how much longer it takes them to fill back up between bouts than it took their teachers. Its Echo Depth (the weight of memory a place holds, which cheapens a Spirit worker’s hold on souls) has not fallen with it: the old districts are thick with their dead, which is why the west keeps its Spirit schools long after its Body schools have gone east looking for better ground. See The Three Grounds.

Who Lives On It
The west is the crowded quarter, the one with the guild halls, the law and the bad manners. Its cities are built of that pale limestone with the color put on afterward: painted shields over every door, Greenmantle green and Saltmarket red fighting it out on the bridges, lamps in rose and amber on the wharves, each one burning the aura of whoever keeps it. Ironlink is the great example, a pit town that became a fairground without closing a single pit, whose midsummer brackets draw forty thousand under yellow awnings and whose keepers’ hall sits opposite the bookmakers for convenience. The Greaves districts live on tin, and every family there can tell you to the fathom how deep the lode has gone since their grandfather’s day and exactly who is to blame.
Rent is a map of the ground. Fat ground is where the wardens work cheap and the lamps stay lit, so a room on it costs what a house costs on lean, and a good many western fortunes consist entirely of owning a street that has not thinned yet. People move downhill as the ground fails. The landlords move first.
Food comes from somewhere else. The quarter imports it, because its rivers are dead and its best land has been under spoil for centuries. A western table is pease and barley, salt fish off the coast road, mutton from the clean hills, a great deal of pickling, and a pie on every corner whose contents are between the baker and the magistrate. A bad harvest in the east reaches a western loaf before the news does, since the news moves by beacon at a price and a factor moves by instinct.
The politics are water. The great houses own the shafts and the pump-masters run them, the array-keepers man them by the hour and can walk off at the change of shift, and everyone can count to ninety. Companies, crowns and sects sign and break charters over Core-keepers’ contracts the way other countries fight over a river crossing. No king in the quarter has ever won an argument with his own keepers’ hall, though several have tried, and their successors have a good view of the result from the palace, which is on higher ground.
Varūn keeps to its mountains, and its dwarves sell you veinwood at a fair price and psionite at no price at all. It has outlasted every western kingdom it has traded with, and it mentions this.
Bearing Stock
Bearing is what a material does under load, Holding is what working it will keep. T0 to T9 is the Accord’s Tier ladder, and a Resonance and Domain name the Wellsprings a material answers to, and the branch of natural law they work through.
Forge-Iron · T2 · Metal · Altherion, Inner World, northern rim
The standard armament and structural iron of the western kingdoms. Durable against blades, poor Essence retention, made in quantity and to a specification that has not meaningfully changed in three hundred years. Bearing good, Holding poor.

Slagbloom · T2 · Metal · Recovered from ancient spoil, western foreland and tin districts
The signature material of the quarter and a fair summary of its condition. Old smelting was inefficient enough that the slag heaps of dead kingdoms still assay well for iron, and today’s forge-arrays are hot enough to get it out.
Slagbloom is cheap, sulfurous, brittle in the cold, and carries a persistent oddity: inscriptions laid on it read doubled, because the metal was worked and marked once already and something of the earlier marking survives the second melt. Engravers charge extra to work it. Superstitious foremen will not have it in a mine cage.
Bearing moderate and inconsistent, Holding erratic. Resonance: Anamnesis, unwelcome. Domain Material Science.

Palegrit Limestone · T2 · Stone · Platform carbonate across the central west
Ashlar for building, lime for mortar, and flux for every iron furnace in the quarter. Three uses, one quarry, and the reason the western kingdoms build in pale stone while the north builds in gray. Karst country: the same rock dissolves, which gives the west its cave systems, its sinkholes, and its habit of losing rivers underground for leagues at a time. Bearing good, Holding poor.
Veinwood Plank · T2 · Wood · Mountain trees of Varūn
Semi-hardened grain, briefly enchantable, standard stock for ritual shields.
Kirkyard Lead · T2 · Metal · Galena in the limestone belt, worked with the silver
Roofing, coffin lining, pipe and sling bullets. Its real importance is single: lead sheet attenuates Essence more effectively per unit thickness than anything else in common supply, so every assay house and every array isolation room in the west is lead-lined. The men who smelt it do not last. Bearing soft, Holding nil, shielding excellent.
Holding Stock

Blacktooth Wolfram · T3 · Metal ore · Sheeted veins in the granite cupolas, western tin districts
Wolframite, black, absurdly heavy, and possessed of the highest melting point of any workable metal in the ledger. This is the vessel problem’s answer. Forge-arrays can reach temperatures that will slump any ordinary crucible, and wolfram will not slump. Every nozzle, every hearth crown, every array-furnace lining above T4 work is wolfram or is lined with something wolfram holds.
It has no glamour, no legend, and no substitute, and the Accord tracks every ton of it. Bearing extreme under heat, Holding low. Resonance: Ignivale, Exuroth. Domain Thermodynamics.

Greaves Tin · T2 · Metal · Cassiterite, lode and stream-work, western tin districts
Bronze, solder, and the tinning of array contacts. Contact corrosion in a working glyph array is a slow, invisible, cumulative failure, and a tinned contact does not corrode. Unglamorous, essential, and running out. The stream works were exhausted six generations ago and the lodes are now worked at depths that only exist because of the pumps. Bearing moderate, Holding moderate. Resonance: Coagulatio. Domain Material Science.
Attercrop Vitriol · T2 · Liquid reagent · Drainage of abandoned workings, universal in the west
Green vitriol, drawn off where pyrite in old spoil weathers into acid water. It is the poison in the orange rivers and it is also, refined, the mordant that fixes ritual ink to any organic substrate. The same fluid that killed the Aerne valley writes the Accord’s own codices. Western alchemists have stopped remarking on this, and the Aerne has not. Resonance: Dissolution. Domain Material Science. Blinds on contact with the eye and does so without warning, since it does not burn on the skin at working dilution.
Psionite · T4 · Mineral · Varūn deep workings
Mental fortification stock, worked only by psionically attuned Varūn dwarves under the Psionic Mastery Code. Effectively unavailable outside the kingdom.
Vellun Copper · T1 · Metal · Source hills unlocated
Malleable, a good spiritual conductor, and melts far too easily to be useful past apprentice work. The trade name is retained because the shipments are continuous and the assay is consistent. The hills it is named for do not appear on any survey the Accord has commissioned.
The Works
Deep, mature, money-heavy, and running on borrowed ground. Western shafts are the deepest in the world and every one of them is a standing bill: the pumps must run whether the mine is producing or not, and the pumps run on Essence that the ground under the pit head no longer gives up in sufficient quantity. The great western houses buy Essence supply the way an army buys grain (Core-keepers’ contracts, array crews on retainer, sealed Holding vessels coming in by mule), and a bad year in supply closes shafts that are still full of ore.
The compensating advantage is that everything else exists. Roads, canals, winding houses, assay offices, guild schools, burial clubs and sea-loans, and eleven centuries of accumulated practice about how to keep men alive underground. A western pit does more work per man than any pit in the other three quarters and it does it in a hole that should have drowned a hundred years ago.
Reworking is the coming trade. Slag heaps, old tailings, flooded levels pumped out and picked over. There is a whole class of western operator who has never sunk an original shaft and never intends to.
What It Costs
Firedamp in the coal foreland, which the draught arrays manage until they do not. Subsidence in the tin districts. Vitriol drainage everywhere. Silicosis in the slate belts, which the trade calls the grinder’s cough and which is simply what happens to men who breathe rock dust for twenty years.

Above all, the array dependency. The western quarter has arranged its whole livelihood so that a sustained Essence shortage, or a long enough walkout by the keepers, becomes within about ninety hours, a mass drowning.

Trade Posture
Exports finished goods, worked metal, wolfram, tin, expertise, and credit. Imports raw ore from all three other quarters, phosphate from the south, and food. Holds the debt of the north and much of the east.

The western position rests less on what the west has in the ground than on being the only quarter that can turn anyone else’s ground into finished work, and the western houses are entirely aware that this is a service and that a service can be taken elsewhere.



Older books also call Kushara the Old World. It is a different landmass entirely, and the two were long confused for carrying one name.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: Bluvest — The City Beneath Dawn
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itBLOO-vest
The Blood Throne · The City Beneath Dawn · Capital of the Dreadvalis Empire
In the autumn of Year 711 the lamp-wardens of Bluvest went on strike, and the greatest night-city in the world discovered that it could not see in the dark. The Vampires could, of course. Their eyes drink the moon through a mile of stone. But the upper districts belong to the living, to the channel-keepers who open the sluices, the bakers and coopers, the Tithe physicians and the porters on the Lantern Stair, and every one of them works by moon-lamp, and every moon-lamp in the city is filled, trimmed and charmed to its soft blue burn by a guild of four hundred mortals who had asked for a copper more a lamp and been told by a Night Governor’s clerk that the dark was free. The guild-mistress, a tall cheerful widow named Hessa Brannock with frost-white braids and a laugh like a dropped tray, put out the lamp on her own doorstep first, in front of the clerk, and then went home and had her supper by touch.
For three nights the deeps did not notice. On the fourth the ration came late, because the keepers on the blood channels could not read their gauges, and the Common Vampire families of the middle city stood in line at the ration-wells in their best red coats for eleven hours, hungry, insulted and perfectly able to see one another’s faces. On the sixth a lord of one of the Seven Blood Estates came up the Stair in a fury, in sable and garnets, to explain the situation to the upper districts personally, and walked straight off the end of the Third Landing into the water channel, which had been moved in Year 704 and which nobody had thought to tell him about, since he had not come up in nine years. On the ninth the Ledger did something it had never done for anything that was not blood. It entered the lamp-wardens’ wage as a protected contribution, payable in grain and tithe-exemption for every warden’s household, and made a crime of stinting it. The lamps went back on at dusk, all of them at once, from the Western Gate to the Third Landing, and the upper districts came out into the streets and cheered as if it were the Long Night.
The Throne, they say, sent Hessa a single red-metal ring for her braid. She wears it to market. Dreadvalis rules by being the one who never runs out, and for nine nights it ran out of the one thing it had never thought to count.
In one breath: a capital sunk a mile into black stone under the oldest veil in the world, where the rent goes up the deeper you live, noon never comes, and a sea of blood is kept in the cellar against the day the north runs short.

Two hands on this page. It stands in Year 715, the twenty-fifth of the Dark Ages. Lines marked Later hand come from the annotator of the Concordance of Ages, writing in the last winter before the turn. Later hand: the lamp-right of 711 is still in the Ledger at the turn of the century, and the wardens still strike over it about once a reign.

Overview





































What it isCapital of the [[Geography & the Four Quarters/The Geography of the Outer World#IV. The Dreadvalis Empire — The Veiled NorthWhereBeneath the northern edge of the Moonlight Forest, under the oldest of the Great VeilsBuiltWithin a single lifetime, by the first High Vampires, after the Taken WinterWho lives thereThe Census of Morvayne says something over a hundred and sixty thousand souls, counting the living and the dead in separate columns and then arguing about which column the Turned belong inRuled byThe Blood Throne and the Royal Vein, with the Seven Blood Estates around itThe groundRich: Aetheric Density near Old World levels in the forest above, and the Great Veil lets it pool. Echo Depth runs high in the deeps, where the Ash Wake masks of every sunburned Vampire since the founding hang in the ancestral vaultsIts nameBlu-vest in Dreadvalic: the city whose night was built, never given
Bluvest is the answer to a single problem, written out in stone. A Vampire burns in true sunlight in seconds, and a race that must go underground before every dawn will either build a world underground or be hunted to ash on the surface by anyone with a clear sky and a grudge. The first High Vampires built it. They sank the city down through black stone, reflective mineral, enchanted metal and blood-wards, under a veil that turns noon into deep blue twilight, and they arranged it the only way the curse allows: the deeper you live, the further you are from the sun, and the more you are worth.

The city is a ladder, and everyone in it can tell you which rung they stand on. Turned Vampires and the living at the top, where a breach in the veil would reach first. Common Vampire families in the middle. The High Vampires, the royal halls and the Red Sea at the bottom, where no natural light has ever fallen.

The City and What It Looks Like
You come to Bluvest through the Moonlight Forest, and for the last day of the road the forest is the brightest thing you have ever seen in the dark. The silver-barked conifers and pale hardwoods hold light like new snow, so that under the veil every trunk glows faintly blue-white, and the canopy overhead (the Silver Ocean, the foresters call it) rolls like surf under a moon that shows through the veil at noon. Then the trees open on a broad hollow of black stone, and in it stands the Western Gate: two leaves of black iron forty feet high, worked with red-metal vines, under a lintel cut with the inscription every child of the empire can recite. The Sun was made our enemy. Hunger was placed inside us. Neither fact determines what we choose when the doors close and night begins. Beyond the gate the ground simply stops, and the city goes down.
The Lantern Stair is the great spiral of the upper city, a shaft a quarter mile across with the districts built into its walls in rings, terrace under terrace, every balcony hung with moon-lamps in brass cages, so that from the gate it looks like a well full of blue fireflies. Bridges cross it. Lifts run on chains. Mortal porters run the stairs with baskets on their heads, and every hundred feet of descent the Stair passes another Landing, a broad market terrace with its own bells, shrines and quarrels.
Under the streets run the Three Channels, which Arkhaven Bluvest laid out before anyone had built a house to put over them. Water runs in pale limestone. The alchemical nutrients that keep the living districts healthy run in channels of green glass. Blood runs in red-lacquered pipe with brass gauges every forty yards, and keepers in grey aprons walk them day and night reading the dials. Nobody mixes the three. A Bluvest proverb holds that a city is three rivers and a promise to keep them apart.
Light comes down the Mirror Shafts: tall bright tubes lined with polished mineral that carry the glow of the Moonlight Groves from the forest floor into the middle city, so that the Common Vampire districts live under a soft silver daylight of their own, borrowed from trees. The light is Luminalis glow and never sunlight, which is the whole of the trick, and every shaft has a Tenebra shutter at the top that can drop in a heartbeat. Children in the middle city grow up believing the sky is silver and the forest is the sun.
The major places

The Western Gate. The only surface gate open to foreigners, with the inscription over it and a Tithe Hall beside it, where the mortals of the forest villages give their portion to a physician and go home with a stamped tin and a bag of twilight barley.
The Lantern Stair and its Landings. The upper city: Turned barracks, mortal workshops, the lamp-wardens’ guildhall, the bakers’ row on the Second Landing and the breach-crews’ bell towers. Cheapest rent in the city and nearest to the sky.
The Middle City. The Common Vampire districts under the Mirror Shafts: broad galleried streets, warm-houses, fighting yards, the ration-wells where the Red Sea’s allowance is drawn, and the loudest night markets in the north.
The Deeps. The High Vampire estates, the ancestral vaults, the High Courts and the royal halls, cut into the black stone below the last Mirror Shaft and lit by nothing but red-metal lamps and the wearer’s own aura.
The Red Sea. The great alchemical reservoir at the city’s heart: donated, taxed, purchased, inherited and enslaved blood, kept cold in a vaulted basin so wide a lamp on the far shore looks like a star. Lord Sevran Molovar, Keeper of Seventeen Veins, drew its sluices, and every Tithe Hall in the north runs on his designs.
The Arkhaven Door. A small black door on the Fourth Landing with a brass sunburst on it, behind which is the experimental solar chamber where Arkhaven Bluvest, the city’s architect, died after misclassifying one wavelength as harmless. The door has not been opened since. Every apprentice ward-glazier in the city touches it on the first day of their training, and the sunburst is worn bright.
The Veilspire of Bluvest. The anchor tower of the oldest Great Veil, rising from the forest above the city like a black needle, worked through Vantabriel and Tenebra, with Therosan masons living in its foot and charging the empire for every flaw they find.

Roads. The Veil Roads run out from the Western Gate under the veils, strung with the Hollow Lanterns, little undercities of waystations, granaries and Tithe Halls a day’s walk apart. East through the forest to the Seven Blood Estates and the Elyran Green Crowns. North across the Moonlight Snow Plains to the black walls of Morvayne. South, by Veyran’s grain roads and the long way down to the Red Marches, toward the sun.
Who Rules
The Blood Throne. Bluvest calls whoever sits it simply the Throne, in the way a farmer says the weather. It belongs to the Royal Vein, the line descended from the blood authority of Vaelora Dreadvalis, First Blood Empress, and the Vein does more than govern. Its blood is woven into the city’s oldest wards, reservoirs and oaths, so that the gates answer it, the Red Sea recognizes it and the Ledger’s law takes its standing from it. Succession runs in the blood, in the soul and in the stone at once: a lawful heir inherits a crown and a place inside the systems that keep the city alive. A pretender without the blood can sit the chair, and the doors will not open for them.
The Seven Blood Estates ring the city in the deep Moonlight Forest, each a Great Clan’s blood-system with its own wards, reservoirs and founder’s blood. A mortal of the upper districts is taught to say their names only in Old Bluven, and only at a bow. The Estates sit in the deeps when the Throne calls them, keep town houses on the lowest galleries, and each holds a key to one sluice of the Red Sea, which is the city’s oldest constitutional arrangement and its most frequently threatened.
The offices. Night Governors run the districts and the provinces beyond the gate. The Warden of the Sluices keeps the Red Sea’s ledger of what goes in and what comes out, an office the Molovar line has held since the first basin was cut. The High Courts of Bluvest try what the Crimson Ledger Courts of Morvayne send up to them: clan feuds, blood crimes of the nobility, treason against the Vein. Morvayne holds the machinery of the empire. Bluvest holds the throne, the blood and the last word, and each city thinks the other is a branch office.
The silence. Malakar walks the Material World again, and every Vampire in Bluvest can feel their maker in their blood like a second pulse. The Throne has said nothing in public. In the deeps the oldest High Vampires, the ones who remember the Taken Winter, are asking whether the thing that made them has come back for them, and the Malakarian loyalists have stopped asking and started leaving, south, in ones and twos, with the city gates logging their going in a book nobody is allowed to read.
Wealth and What It Trades
Bluvest makes very little and holds a great deal. It is a capital, which is to say a place where the empire’s surplus comes to be counted, and the surplus of Dreadvalis is everything its rulers cannot eat: grain, metal, medicine, timber and time.

Blood. The Red Sea is the city’s treasury and its granary at once. In famine every recognized citizen draws a ration, the size set by rank. In plenty the Warden of the Sluices sells the surplus forward to the Estates as vein-notes, promises of blood in a lean year, and vein-notes trade in the deeps the way gold does in the south.
Ward-glass and moon-lamps. The light-proof glazing that seals every window in the empire is cut on the Fourth Landing, and so are the moon-lamps of every Hollow Lantern from the Archipelago to the Red Marches. Both carry the city’s mark.
The red alchemists. In the catacombs below the High Courts the red alchemists keep forges that run on blood instead of coal, and make the empire’s finest worked gear in their own long, cold way. Their masterworks have names and reputations.
What comes in. Twilight barley from Veyran and the Cold Granaries for the living districts; moonlight timber, spirit amber and preservation resins from the Elyran Green Crowns, by treaty; frozen fish and whale oil from the Archipelago; and Rhaegyr steel from the far side of the Twilight March, by way of Calverne’s road, because Dreadvalis armies wear dragon-forged plate and nobody in Bluvest finds that funny.

Rent, Food and the Street
Rent runs upside down. On the Lantern Stair a room costs almost nothing and a household owes breach duty besides, nights on the shutter crews that would seal a tear in the veil above. In the middle city rent is reckoned in ration-share, so many cups a month to the landlord’s clan. In the deeps nobody rents; a gallery there is inherited, married into, or taken by a court. A mortal family that saves for three generations can buy one floor further down, and does, and holds a party on the new landing to which the old neighbors come in order to complain about the stairs.
The living eat twilight barley bread, pale and faintly sweet; moon elk and smoked pale stag; frozen Archipelago fish fried in elk fat; frostroot mash; and moonpetal tea, which every Tithe physician prescribes after a draw and every child hates. The bakers’ row on the Second Landing sells hot barley rolls stamped with the Western Gate inscription, and a widow there has a hedge-worker’s trick that keeps them warm exactly as long as you are polite to her.
The dead drink by law. The ration comes from the ration-wells, drawn by rank. Above the ration a Common Vampire with money goes to a warm-house, where donor houses sell blood across the counter by its legal kind: sevrathi, freely given, is the luxury, poured warm in small glass cups and paid for in silver, and the donor’s name is chalked on a board behind the bar so the drinker knows whom to thank. Draal, blood with no recognized owner, is cheap, comes cold and comes without questions. The difference between the two is the first thing a reformist wants to talk about and the last thing a traditionalist will.
The street runs on bells and pulses. The bells are the Veiling of Dawn, rung before every sunrise though no sun will reach the city: gates close, the Mirror Shaft shutters drop to half, and the whole of Bluvest pauses for the length of one breath it does not need to take. The pulses are Bloodcant, the Vampires’ language of heartbeat and touch, so that a crowd in the middle city is always quietly talking under its talking, and a Turned porter feels a passing High Vampire’s displeasure as pressure in his bite scar before he hears a word. Children play Noon, in which one child shouts the word and the rest dive under anything they can find, and the last one standing is ash.
Shared arts. The aura coat is the shroud in Bluvest, worn close and dark, and a Common Vampire who lets theirs flare red in the street is showing off for someone. Pressure is the cold, for what a stronger soul does to the air of a gallery. Sensing is hearing the vein: Vampires read heartbeats, wounds and fear the way other people read faces, and a Bluvest card-player who can hear the vein will not sit at a table with one who can.
What they joke about. The south, where people live in the sky with no lid on it and cry at the brightness. Morvayne’s clerks, who are said to have filed the Taken Winter in triplicate. Dragons, who eat the ground. The Turned, mostly by the Turned. Lords who have not come up the Stair in nine years.
Culture
Old Bluven is the city’s ceremonial tongue: long, quiet and full of pauses, many of its sentences meant to be spoken with the heart stilled. Blood marriages, trials, royal declarations and investitures are held in it. Dreadvalic is the street, and its grammar shifts with whom you are addressing, prey, protected mortal, kin, maker, fledgling, clan sovereign, elder or royal blood, so that a sentence in Bluvest carries a social map inside its verbs.
The calendar has three holy nights. Kethra, the First Thirst, when a fledgling’s first sanctioned feeding is witnessed by its clan, and the proof of civilization is the moment the fledgling lets go. The Moon Hunt, at full moon, when the clans that keep the custom hunt the forest together. And the Long Night, every few winters, when the far north goes weeks without real daylight even outside the veils, and the entire city goes up through the Western Gate at once and lives on the forest floor: banners on the trees, red lanterns strung through the Moonlight Groves, fighting schools in the hollows, the Throne’s household walking among the crowds, Vampire children seeing snow under an open sky for the first time and the mortal ones laughing at them.
The dead. The sun leaves little but ash. A Vampire who burns is mixed with black resin and sealed inside a named memorial mask in the Ash Wake, and the masks hang in the ancestral vaults of the deeps in rows that run back to the founding. Their weight is why the deeps run high in Echo Depth, and why a Spirit-led duelist will pay a great deal to be challenged down there.
Executions at the High Courts are dressed for like weddings, in red and white, with music, and seats near the block sell at a premium, because the city believes a death should be witnessed as fully as a marriage, and both are entries in the Ledger.
Doctrine. The Imperial Doctrine of Blood is cut into the lintel of the High Courts: blood is sustenance, memory, inheritance, evidence, consent, debt and power, the record of a life carried in liquid form. The radical reading, that whoever drinks a life takes responsibility for what it held, is preached openly on the Third Landing and quietly denied in the deeps.
Law and How It Fights
Law. The Crimson Ledger governs every clan in the city: blood consumed, mortals protected, debts, unlawful killings, births, turnings and inherited obligations. Its courts sit at Morvayne; the High Courts of Bluvest hear what Morvayne sends up and what the nobility does to itself. The crimes that matter most in Bluvest are blood crimes: feeding on a protected mortal, a child or a diplomat; stealing another clan’s donor; illegal turning; wasting valuable blood; and drinking another Vampire. Red Guest-Law protects any mortal under declared hospitality, and a household that breaks it loses standing in Fate as well as in society, which starts blood feuds that run for decades. Since 711 the Ledger also protects the lamp-wardens’ wage, and is a little embarrassed about it.
The two faces. The tributary kingdoms are shown the Tithe Hall by the Western Gate, with its clean tins, physicians and exemptions. They are not shown the donor houses of the deeps, some of them hereditary prisons under polite names, or the livestock pens the traditionalist Estates keep on their own land, which the Ledger tolerates and the Throne does not discuss. Bluvest lives with both faces at once, and every reformist in the city has a theory about which one is the real one.
How it fights. Bluvest is a vertical fortress, and the only attack that really frightens it comes from above. An army at the Western Gate is a nuisance; a tear in the Great Veil over the Stair at noon is a massacre. So the city drills for breaches the way a port drills for fire. Every upper household serves on the breach crews, every Landing has a bell tower and a shutter-gang, and at the first gleam of real sunlight in a shaft the crews drop Tenebra shutters, roll ward-glass screens across the galleries and drive the Turned and the living down past the Mirror Shafts in an order every child has practiced since they could walk. The fair answer to Bluvest is the sky: tear the veil, bring daylight down a shaft, and the city’s strength becomes a trap. The fair answer to that is the shutter, and the Veilspire, and the Therosan masons who are paid very well to keep it standing.
The garrisons. Turned soldiers hold the upper districts and the gate, Common Vampire companies the middle city, and the deeps defend themselves, since a High Vampire in their own gallery, on their own ground, with their clan’s founder-blood in the walls, is about as dangerous a thing as the north contains. Moonlight and shadow strengthen every Vampire, and a fight in Bluvest is always a fight under both.
The Wild Around the Gate
The Dreadvalis do not hunt for food, so the forest around Bluvest is crowded with game that only mortals and predators pursue. Moon elk cross the Veil Roads in herds whose antlers glow under the veil, and the gate guard will stop a caravan for an hour rather than argue with one. Veil owls, great pale hunters of the permanent twilight, nest in the Veilspire and are a city emblem. Pale stags shed the Groves’ glow from their coats and leave the forest floor sparkling where they bed down.
The danger is the Night Gaunts, light-swallowing hunters of the darkest veil-country, and the veil over Bluvest is the darkest in the empire. A gaunt can drink a moon-lamp out from across a clearing and take whoever was holding it, and they are dangerous even to Vampires. The Night Governor of the forest posts a standing bounty, paid at the Western Gate in silver or ration-share at the hunter’s choice, and the gaunt-hunters of the Hollow Lanterns are a famous, loud and short-lived profession.
The ferals. Every Vampire can fall into the Feral State, and a starving one goes down through the five stages, Drying, Crimson Fever, Blood Frenzy, Soul Consumption and Feral Hollowing, until hunger is all that governs. The old construction shafts under the Stair, sealed when the Mirror Shafts were cut, are where Bluvest’s ferals go to ground, and the Hollow Watch, a company of Turned volunteers with silver and stakes, goes down after them. Early ferals can be brought back with blood and time. A Blood Hollow is put down, and its mask is made like any other.
Neighbors and Grudges

Morvayne. The city of law, under the Moonlight Snow Plains behind its black walls. Morvayne thinks Bluvest is a beautiful cellar with a chair in it. Bluvest thinks Morvayne is a filing cabinet with a wall around it. Both are right, and the empire runs on the arrangement.
The Seven Blood Estates. Close enough to be family, which is the problem. Each holds a sluice key, and each has threatened at least once to stop turning it.
The Ashen Courts. The oldest High Vampire nobility, on the gray stone of the Northern Tablelands, who keep their distance from the Throne and their opinions to themselves. Bluvest invites them to every Long Night, and they send masks.
The Elyran Green Crowns. The Elven canopy cities of the Moonlight Forest, who pay no blood and tend the Groves whose glow lights the Mirror Shafts. The city depends on them for its daylight, and the Elves are courteous enough to mention it only once a year.
The Kingdom of Veyran. Grain, horses and the tithe, paid on a schedule of harvests. Veyran’s ambassador in Bluvest lives on the Second Landing by choice, says it is for the bread, and is a very good spy.
The Red Marches and the south. The frontier is a long way down the Veil Roads, and Bluvest thinks about it the way a sleeper thinks about a window left open. See The Twilight March.

Read beside this: The Vampiric Peoples for the people and their law, The Geography of the Outer World for the land, and the Atlas of the Two Skies for where it all lies.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Outer World — An Atlas of the Two Skies
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itthe OW-ter WURLD
The Land Beneath Two Skies, laid out band by band · Vampire North, Dragon South, the March between
In one breath: a continent that runs long from north to south and warms the whole way down, split evenly between a young empire of night in the cold north and an old empire of fire in the hot south, with a frontier band of mortal kingdoms across its middle where the veils give out and the sun comes back.

How to use this sheet. It stands in Year 715. The bands and the named corners (Northeast, Southwest, Southeast) are fixed by The Geography of the Outer World, which governs. Where this atlas puts a place west, center or east inside its band, it is this sheet’s reading, and the governing page wins if the two ever disagree.

The Sheet
Read it top to bottom as north to south. Every band south of the line gets hotter, brighter and poorer in Aether; every band north of it gets colder, darker and richer.









































BandWestCenterEastFar North · ice and the Frozen WellsThe Frostfang Cordillera’s western glaciersGrimhold Deeps in the heart of the Frostfang, over the Frozen WellsThe Last Archipelago, offshore, under a light titheNorth · the Veiled ProvincesThe Moonlight Forest: Bluvest beneath its northern edge, the Seven Blood Estates in its depths, the Elyran Green Crowns in its canopyThe Moonlight Snow Plains and Morvayne behind its black walls; the Northern Tablelands and the Ashen Courts on their gray stoneThe northern Serrathan Highlands: iron and silver uplands around Vel SarithThe Twilight March · where the veils endThe Red Marches along the whole northern edge; the Great Grass Sea, Veyran in its north and House Eredan’s ranges in its south, with Dovaryn’s roosts watching from the SpineThe old Five River country: Therosan, Calverne and Saren north of the Dusk Line, Valecar and Ordas south of it, Sallow Ford on the Horse Rivers and Akhazar Gate on the southern edgeThe Golden Escarpment of the southern Serrathan, House Zhaeryn’s gold facing Vel Sarith’s silverSouth · the Burning SouthThe Southwest: the Drakhal Spine, the Drakyssian Heartlands around Kra’Vorrak, the Wyrmdeep, the Black Scale Ranges and the Aurelian Dust CoastThe South-Central interior: the Veloran Rainsea, the Thousand-River Basin, the Varakh DrylandsThe Southeast: the Eastern Sun Coast and its port cities under House AvaraxFar South · the sacred fireThe Ash WastesZyraxia, the ancient flame-realm where the last Salamanders sleepThe Ash Wastes
1Far North: ice, Grimhold Deeps and the Frozen Wells2North: the Veiled Provinces, Bluvest and Morvayne3The Twilight March: the Dusk Line, Grass Sea and Five Rivers4South: Kra'Vorrak, the Rainsea and the Sun Coast5Far South: the Ash Wastes and Zyraxia
Who Holds What
The two empires hold the continent in even halves, each half directly or through its tributaries.

The north is Dreadvalis. Everything from the Frostfang down to the Red Marches lies under the Blood Throne in Bluvest, held directly in the Veiled Provinces and through Grimhold Deeps, Vel Sarith and the tithe kingdoms beyond. A northern border follows the veil: a village is Dreadvalis land if a veil hangs over it or a Tithe Hall stands in it.
The south is Drakyssia. Everything from Akhazar Gate down to Zyraxia lies under the Dragon Sovereign at Kra’Vorrak, held through the Ten Great Houses and their tributaries. A southern border is layered: a mortal king on the ground, a Wyrm below, a House on the mountains, a Wyvern wing above, the Sovereign over all.
The March is both. Across the middle runs the Twilight March, where both systems run at once and the Dusk Line moves south in winter and north in summer.

The Gradient on One Line





























NorthThe MarchSouthSkyDeep blue twilight at noon under the Great VeilsVeil in winter, open sun in summerOpen sun, volcanic stormsAetherHealthy, near Old World norms in the Moonlight ForestUneven, good in wet years and poor in droughtExhausted outside the Aether Wells and the volcanoesWhat is worth owningThe land itselfThe crossingsThe volcanoes and the last Wellsprings
About the Painted Atlas
The painted World Atlas on the Four Quarters page shows the Outer World in its older arrangement, from before the even split was written: Drakyssia, the Drakhal Spine and Kra’Vorrak spread down the west side of the pan, the Frostfang Cordillera and the Last Archipelago drawn at its southern tip, and no Dreadvalis, Bluvest or Twilight March at all. This sheet is the corrected layout until the painting is redone. The other three quarters on the painted sheet are unaffected.
For a repaint. One brief, kept with the sheet so whoever paints it next has it:

Keep the Outer World as the southern pan of the whole sheet, in the house atlas style.
Inside it, put the cold at the top and the heat at the bottom: the Frostfang and the Archipelago at its northern edge nearest the Central Expanse, the Ash Wastes and Zyraxia at its southern tip.
Shade the northern half under a blue-violet veil, with the Moonlight Forest silver-white; leave the southern half in open gold and ash-red, with the volcanic Spine down its west side.
Draw the Twilight March as a broad green band across the middle, with the Dusk Line as a dotted line that does not quite meet either coast.
Label, at minimum: Bluvest, Morvayne, Grimhold Deeps, Vel Sarith, the Great Grass Sea, the Five Rivers, Akhazar Gate, the Golden Escarpment, Kra’Vorrak, the Veloran Rainsea, the Eastern Sun Coast and Zyraxia.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Twilight March — Where the Veils End
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itTWY-lite MARCH
The Frontier of Two Skies · The Grass Sea, the Five Rivers and the Golden Escarpment · Where Blood-Law Meets Tribute
In the spring of Year 709 the reeve of Corran’s Hollow, a hamlet of thirty-one households on the Horse Rivers, walked into the Twin Assize at Sallow Ford carrying two pieces of paper and a wheelbarrow of turnips. The first paper was the northern Edge Roll, sealed in red wax by Morvayne’s Tithe Ministry, and it said that Corran’s Hollow had lain under the veil for the whole of the year past and owed a full blood tithe. The second was the southern Edge Roll, sealed in gold by the clerks of Akhazar Gate, and it said that Corran’s Hollow had lain under open sun for the whole of the year past and owed a full tribute in grain and cattle. The turnips were what Corran’s Hollow had left after paying both.
The reeve was a short, freckled, extremely polite woman named Ottilie Marsh, and she set the two rolls side by side on the Assize table, in the arc-blue light of the Judicium reader who sits at every Assize, and asked the court which of them was lying. The reader looked for a long time. Then she said, in front of both delegations, that neither roll was lying: both clerks had copied the same survey, taken in the Long Night winter of 706 by a Therosan mason who had been drunk, and who had marked Corran’s Hollow on both sides of the Dusk Line at once out of a sense of fairness. The northern delegation laughed. The southern delegation did not, being dragons, but one of them was seen to look at the ceiling for a while.
The Assize ruled that week that the weeks dark and the weeks of sun on the two rolls must add up to one year and no more, and that where they do not, the town pays the lesser of the two bills until the clerks agree. It has been called the Marsh Rule ever since, and every reeve on the March can recite it. Ottilie went home with her turnips, a refund in grain from the south, a refund in blood-days from the north, and the first copy of a ruling that both empires have been trying to read narrowly ever since. On the March the law is the one thing both skies have to share, so a hamlet with a wheelbarrow can make both of them blink.
In one breath: the frontier band across the middle of the Outer World, where the veils run out and the sun comes back, so that whether a town owes blood north or tribute south depends on how many weeks of the year the dark lay over it, and both empires keep their own count.

Two hands on this page. It stands in Year 715, the twenty-fifth of the Dark Ages. Lines marked Later hand come from the annotator of the Concordance of Ages, writing in the last winter before the turn. Later hand: the Marsh Rule outlives the March it was written for, and both successor courts after the split cite it as their own.

Overview





































What it isThe frontier band between the [[Geography & the Four Quarters/The Geography of the Outer World#IV. The Dreadvalis Empire — The Veiled NorthWhereAcross the middle of the Outer World: the Red Marches, the Great Grass Sea, the old Five River country and the Golden Escarpment of the southern SerrathanWho lives thereMost of the continent’s free mortals, by the Census of Morvayne and the Akhazar registers alike, and the two disagree by about a sixthSworn northThe Kingdom of Veyran, the Kingdom of Therosan, the Kingdom of Calverne, the Free March of Saren, under the Red Marches of DreadvalisSworn southThe Kingdom of Valecar and the Principality of Ordas, under House Akhazar’s Gate, House Eredan’s ranges and House Zhaeryn’s mountainsThe groundUneven Aether: good in wet years, poor in drought. Thread Weight runs high at every ford, crossroads and old battlefield, and the March has more of all three than anywhere in the Outer WorldThe weatherFour true seasons, the only ones on the continent: a warm growing season, cold rains, a dry windy autumn, frost months
The March exists because neither empire can live in the other’s sky. A Vampire burns in the southern sun, and no veil can be raised over the volcanic belt. A fire-dragon slows in the northern cold, and under the veils even House Dovaryn’s Wyverns fly half-blind. So between them lies a broad band of grassland, river country and escarpment where neither empire is comfortable, and there the mortal kingdoms that survived the Taken Winter make their living by being worth more alive than conquered.

The March is the only place in the Outer World where both laws apply at once. In the north a border follows the veil. In the south a border is layered, mortal king below, House above, Sovereign over all. On the March both systems run on the same farm, and the farmer keeps two sets of books.

The Dusk Line
The veils fail at the March. They thin along the empire’s southern edge, and somewhere in the Grass Sea the last of them gives out altogether, and that edge is never still. In winter, when the sun is low and the nights are long, the Therosan veil-keepers can push it south. In summer the sun burns it back north. A farm on the Horse Rivers can spend the frost months under deep blue twilight at noon and the harvest months under open sky, and the line where the dark stops is called the Dusk Line.
Along it stand the dusk stones: waist-high posts of black Therosan basalt, each with a red band painted on its north face and a gold band on its south, set a mile apart from the Red Marches to the Golden Escarpment. Every week of the year a Ministry surveyor and an Akhazar clerk walk the stones together and note on which side of each the dark lay at noon. Neither trusts the other to walk alone, and both are usually right.
Weeks dark. Every town on the March is assessed by how many weeks of the year the veil lay over it. The northern tithe is owed in proportion to the weeks dark, the southern tribute in proportion to the weeks of sun, and a town wholly under the veil owes only blood, a town wholly in the sun owes only tribute, and a town in between owes both in their shares. The two counts are kept on the Edge Rolls, one in red wax at Morvayne’s Tithe Ministry and one in gold at Akhazar Gate, and the two rolls have never once agreed. Since 709 the Marsh Rule holds that the weeks on both rolls must add up to one year, and where they do not, the town pays the lesser bill until the clerks settle.
The arrangement makes the line itself valuable. Land a mile north of the winter mark owes almost nothing but blood; land a mile south of the summer mark owes almost nothing but grain. Land between the two marks owes a little of both and is raided by both, so it sells cheapest on the continent, and the March is full of people who bought it anyway.
The Land and What It Looks Like
From the Red Marches the land opens south into the Great Grass Sea, the Endless Green, a temperate grassland on deep black soil running further than a Wyvern can fly in a day. In winter its northern reaches lie under the last thin veil, a dim silver dusk over pale stubble and frost-white grass, and you can watch the twilight end on the horizon like the edge of a lake. In summer the whole sea stands green and gold under open sky, horse herds moving through it like weather.
East of the Grass Sea lies the old Five River country, the most crowded land in the Outer World: river towns, bridges, mills, walled market-cities and toll-houses on every crossing, five broad rivers running south out of the cold and every one of them crossed by the Dusk Line twice a year. Further east the land climbs onto the Golden Escarpment, the southern face of the Serrathan Highlands, a weathered wall of yellow stone and waterfalls where House Zhaeryn mines gold within sight of Vel Sarith’s northern silver.
The major places

The Red Marches. The empire’s southern frontier province, a belt of Hollow Lanterns, Turned garrisons and Vein-Marshals’ forts along the winter mark, built low and half underground, with ward-glass shutters that close the moment the summer sun comes over the line.
Sallow Ford. The neutral crossing on the Horse Rivers where the Twin Assize sits each autumn. It stands on a Judicium site, dry and windy in the season the Assize meets, and its Thread Weight is the heaviest on the March: a treaty sworn there in the arc-blue light holds, and a lie told there comes away from its maker in front of everyone.
Ered-Vaelor, the Granary Citadel. House Eredan’s seat in the southern Grass Sea, a dragon-fortress built around barns the size of cathedrals, where a drought in the south is answered in grain bought north.
Akhazar Gate. The Continental Embassy-Fortress on the southern edge of the March, between Drakyssia and the Five River country, where every road permit, tribute schedule and southern Edge Roll is sealed in gold.
The Saren towns. The fortified towns of the Free March of Saren, founded by refugees from dragon conquest who chose the tithe, with walls built thick against fire and Tithe Halls in every square.
Zhaer-Khazad and the Golden Escarpment. House Zhaeryn’s Golden Mountain at the March’s eastern end, where the Escarpment’s gold is weighed, certified and sent south, and where Ordas’s silver gets its stamp.

Roads. The March Roads are the busiest on the continent, grain and medicine going south, gold and steel going north, with a toll-house on every bridge and an Akhazar permit required on the southern side. Calverne holds the road from the northern mines to the coast and charges everyone for it. Dovaryn’s Wyverns fly the line overhead, and a caravan that sees a wing turn toward it stops and shows its papers to the sky.
Who Rules
Nobody, and everybody. The March has no throne of its own. Each kingdom on it rules its own ground, each empire rules the kingdoms sworn to it, and between them the treaties drawn after the first raids, between Western Dragon diplomats, the envoys of House Akhazar and Morvayne’s Ledger Courts, are recognized by Fate and taken seriously by both.
North of the line. Veyran holds the northern Grass Sea, a horse-and-grain monarchy that feeds the Cold Granaries. Therosan’s engineers and masons built most of the Veilspires and still keep the frontier veils, which makes them the people who decide where the Dusk Line sits in winter, and they know it. Calverne holds the mine road. Saren holds its walls. Over all of them the Vein-Marshals of the Red Marches keep the frontier for the Blood Throne, with Turned garrisons who can stand a gray winter noon and not much else.
South of the line. Valecar sells cavalry, grain and mercenaries; its herds feed Eredan’s ranches, and its companies fight in Drakyssian wars for pay. Ordas is small and rich, and its silver pays for a professional army that Zhaeryn certifies by the coin. Over them stands House Akhazar, Keepers of Roads and Foreign Crowns, who govern everyone in the south who is not Drakyssian, and who since the Taken Winter have also handled the empire’s most delicate relationship, with Morvayne’s Ledger Courts across the March.
The Twin Assize. Once a year, in the dry windy autumn, both empires send a delegation to Sallow Ford and sit at one table under a Judicium reader. They hear the year’s border disputes, raid claims, Edge Roll quarrels and treaty breaches, and their rulings bind both sides. It is the only court on the continent where a dragon and a Vampire lord sit on the same bench, and the only one where a reeve with a wheelbarrow can win.
Wealth and What It Trades
The March is rich because everything that crosses the continent crosses it.

What crosses. Grain, preserved food, medicine, physicians, surgical steel, the common metals, Frozen-Well crystals, moonlight timber, spirit amber and resins go south. Gold, dragon minerals, House Rhaegyr’s weapons and scale plate, volcanic glass, war beasts, hides and livestock come north. Almost all of it moves under House Avarax contracts and Akhazar permits on the south side and through Morvayne’s Tithe Ministries on the north. A Drakyssian war raises the price of grain in Bluvest; a hard northern winter raises the price of steel in Kra’Vorrak; and the March takes a toll both ways.
What it makes. Grain, livestock, leather, wool, salt and iron from the Grass Sea; cavalry horses, engineering, ward-work and mercenary contracts from the Five Rivers; gold and silver from the Escarpment.
The crossings. On the March the land matters less than the bridges, fords and passes. A good ford is worth more than a county, and every one of them has been fought over at least once.

Rent, Food and the Street
Rent comes in two coins. A room in a Five River town is quoted in silver by the week and in blood-days by the season, and a landlord who wants a tenant from the other side of the line will take either. Farmland is priced by weeks dark: the more weeks of the year a field lies under the veil, the more of its rent is owed in blood, and the less a southern buyer will pay for it. The cheapest land on the continent lies between the winter and summer marks, owing both bills and raided from both directions, and it is farmed by people who say they like the view.
The table. Grass Sea beef and black barley bread; river eel smoked over willow; Valecar horse-milk cheese, sharp enough to start an argument; frostroot and onion stew in the cold rains; hot spiced cider through the frost months. A March tavern keeps two price boards, red and gold, and a meal eaten exactly on the Dusk Line is said to be free, which is why so many taverns claim to stand on it.
The street. Every market town on the March has a tithe cart and a tribute wagon, often parked at opposite ends of the same square, and children are raised knowing which one their family’s name is written on this season. A Turned soldier and a Dragonkin drover can drink at the same bar, sit at opposite ends of it and pretend not to notice each other, and the barkeep charges both a little extra for the pretending. Children play Line, in which one child is the Dusk Line and walks slowly across the yard, and everyone on the dark side must speak only in a whisper, and everyone on the bright side must shout.
Shared arts. Bluvest calls the aura coat the shroud and wears it close. On the March it is the half-cloak, worn loose and plain so that nobody at a crossing can tell which sky taught it. Pressure is the lean, for the weight a stronger soul puts on a conversation at a crossing. Sensing is reading the weather, because on the March you learn early to feel which way the next raid is coming.
What they joke about. Morvayne’s clerks and Akhazar’s clerks, who are said to have married each other’s sisters in order to argue at home. Therosan masons and their surveys. Wyverns who land in the wrong field. Bluvest, where people pay rent to live in a hole.
Culture
The March speaks Dreadvalic in the north, Drakyssian in the south and the common mortal tongues of the Five Rivers everywhere, and most traders speak all three badly. Its peoples keep their old kingdoms’ customs, and over them the March has grown customs of its own.
The Turning of the Stones. Twice a year, at the first frost and the first green, every town on the March walks out to its nearest dusk stone and watches the line go past. In autumn the northern families sing and the southern families bank their fires; in spring the other way about. The day the line crosses a town is a holiday in both calendars.
Hybrids. The rare Vampire-Dragon hybrids have only ever been born in the borderlands where the two empires meet, and the March is where people tell stories about them, mostly untrue. Saren towns treat the subject as unlucky. Valecar companies treat it as a recruiting opportunity.
The Long Night. When the far north goes weeks without real daylight, the Dusk Line runs further south than in any other winter, and whole Grass Sea counties spend a month under the dark. Dovaryn doubles its patrols for as long as it lasts, and the March holds its breath until the sun comes back.
Law and How It Fights
Law. Three laws run on the March at once: the Crimson Ledger north of the line, Akhazar’s frontier law south of it, and the Fate-recognized treaties over both. A crime committed on the Dusk Line is tried at the Twin Assize, and it is a well-known March trick to commit one there on purpose and wait for autumn. Red Guest-Law holds in the north; Drakyssian hospitality holds in the south; a traveler on the line is safest with both.
How it fights. Raids are common, and the raiding calendar follows the line. In winter, when the veil comes south, the Vein-Marshals’ Turned can ride further into the Grass Sea, and the north raids. In summer, when the sun burns the line back, Dovaryn’s wings and Valecar’s cavalry can reach further north, and the south raids. A March town learns to read the season like a farmer reads the sky. Neither empire wants a real war on the March: conquest there is expensive, the kingdoms on it are more useful whole, and no single Drakyssian House can march north alone. So the raids stay raids, and every autumn the Twin Assize sits and the damages are counted.
The fair answer. To the north’s winter raid, the sun: every Red Marches fort has to be back under the veil before the line moves, and a garrison caught on the wrong side in the first warm week burns. To the south’s summer raid, the cold and the dark: a Wyvern wing that follows a raid too far north flies half-blind under the veils, and the Turned are waiting.
Monsters on the Roads
The Grass Sea’s herds draw hunters of every kind. Wild horse-herds run the Endless Green, and the drovers who follow them for Eredan or Veyran fight off the big grassland predators every season. Along the line itself the danger is hunger: ferals drifting south out of the Red Marches in the gray weeks, starved past the Crimson Fever and looking for a farm the Ledger does not protect, and young drakes flown off from Dovaryn’s roosts who have learned that cattle near the line are seldom guarded by anything they fear. Both empires post bounties, and a March bounty-hunter is paid in whichever coin the corpse came from.
Neighbors and Grudges

The Dreadvalis Empire. The north sees the March as its pantry, its toll-road and its front door, and keeps the door locked from the inside. See Bluvest.
Drakyssia. The south sees the March as a granary it rents and a border it watches. The Council of Ten Wings has never agreed that the north is worth the cost of taking.
Each other. Veyran and Valecar share the Grass Sea, the Horse Rivers and a centuries-old argument about where one ends and the other begins, settled every autumn at Sallow Ford and reopened every spring.
Malakar. Since the Vampires’ maker returned, the Council of Ten Wings has ordered Dovaryn to double its patrols along the Red Marches and Akhazar to learn what the Ledger Courts are not saying. Malakarian loyalists leaving the undercities have to cross the March to go anywhere at all, and the Saren towns have begun asking travelers questions at the gate.

Read beside this: The Geography of the Outer World for the continent, The Ten Great Houses of Drakyssia for Eredan, Akhazar, Dovaryn and Zhaeryn, and the Atlas of the Two Skies for where the March lies.
