geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.title: The Outer World — The Southern Pan
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-be.content:
Say itthe OW-ter WURLD
The Southern Pan

Old, low, dry, and structurally strange: the only quarter whose geology cannot be described without reference to something that is not geology.

The best wheat ever grown in the western kingdoms came up at Yarrowby in the summer of Year 667, chest high and the color of old ivory, on forty tons of ground chalk that the factor Reynold Attwater had sold the parish off a barge from the southern shelf. That barge had carried a lot prepared for a Dorrosfenn temple on its previous run, and nobody had swept it. The parish held its harvest supper at the field’s edge with ribbons on the wagons and a fiddler up on a barrel, and at moonrise the churchyard wall went over and three centuries of Yarrowby’s dead walked in among the tables, took the scythes down off the wagons, and started on the top field in a straight line. They were superb. They had, after all, been the parish’s reapers. Some of the guests cheered, and old Marjory Lusk carried a cup of cider out to a man she had buried in Year 629 and stood holding it while he went past her. They had three hundred acres in by dawn and showed no sign of stopping at the boundary, and sixteen living people who stood in the row to reason with them were reaped with the wheat. The Holy Sea of Alabaster took the factor to law for selling a necromantic reagent as fertilizer. Attwater set two lumps of chalk on the Arbiter’s table, one from the barge and one from a sack the Sea’s own almoner had bought for the abbey garden, and invited the court to tell them apart. It could not, and neither could anyone after. The Yarrowby flour went to market that autumn under a different name, and I am told it made excellent bread.
Almost everything the rest of the world knows about the south arrives that way, on somebody else’s barge and in need of explanation.
In one breath: the poorest quarter in the world, red plain and white pan and black basalt under a blazing sky, sitting on the handful of things the other three cannot make anything without, and half of it belongs to dragons who issue no survey permits, with a young Vampire empire under veiled skies on the other half.
Formation
The bulk of it is a worn craton (a slab of the oldest and most stubborn crust) comparable in age to the northern shield but never glaciated, so instead of scoured rock it carries a duricrust: a hard iron-cemented caprock that formed by chemical weathering over an inconceivable stretch of time and now armors the interior in a stony gibber plain, rust red to the horizon, that turns a wagon wheel and breaks a horse’s leg.
Across the western third lies a flood-basalt province, a stack of lava sheets erupted in a single geological convulsion and now weathered into stepped terraces league upon league. Along the eastern coast runs an ophiolite belt, a slice of ancient ocean floor shoved up onto the land, which is why the coastal ranges are serpentine and chromite and support almost no vegetation. In the interior basins lie the pans, dried inland seas floored with nitrate, borate, and gypsum. Along the old shelf margins in the south lie the bone-beds.

And through all of it runs the Crevice, which is not a fault in any sense the Measurewrights are willing to certify, and along which the rock stops obeying the ordinary rules at a distance the Accord has fixed at four leagues and revises upward roughly once a decade.

The Ground Itself
Gibber plain, silcrete, salt pan, and basalt step. Marsh in the Dorrosfenn basins where the drainage fails and the water sits, thick with lilies and things that eat lilies. Serpentine barrens on the eastern coast, green-gray, sterile, and dusty in a way that is worse than it looks. The Veil-tide shores in the far south where the bones wash up. After one of the pans’ rare storms the lightning stands on the white crust in columns as far as the eye goes, and every child in the confederations can tell you what it is worth by the armload.
There is very little water and what there is, is mostly undrinkable. There is very little wood. Almost everything the southern quarter builds, it builds out of stone or out of something that used to be alive.
Aetheric Density (how much Aether, the raw stuff of magic, the ground and air hold for a practitioner to pull) is low across the interior and violently irregular near the Crevice, which is the reason the southern quarter has no array work worth the name and the reason it never developed any. An array is a standing runed working fed by keepers on a shift, and keepers on lean ground starve. The other two measures of ground run the other way. The south’s old battlefields lie heavy in Thread Weight, where great things were decided and a Fate pull comes cheap, and Dorrosfenn’s kept dead give its marsh towns an Echo Depth few places anywhere can match. See The Three Grounds.
Who Lives On It
The ledger’s three polities are loud in the way of people who have never once been left alone by anyone with a boat.
Dorrosfenn is the marsh theocracy that will rent you your own dead. Its temple-towns stand on Trapstone piles over black water, hung with green lamps and bone wind-chimes and crowded with sect processions, and a tenant there pays one rent to the temple on the house and a second on the grandfather, who is kept on and does useful work. Food is eel, reed-bread and marsh duck, salted with nitre from the pans and tasting faintly of it. The priests rule, the priests argue, and the priests are the one buyer on earth who want Marrowchalk raw.
The Braqthian confederations hold the terraces and the pan margins, tribal, proud, and arranged around standing stones that nobody in the west has ever troubled to read. They pay no rent, since a clan’s ground is its stones and whoever can lift them. They live on goat, dried fruit and pan-salt meat, and they gather lightning glass after storms and sell it to Accord factors at one-fortieth of what it fetches at the other end of the road, a piece of arithmetic every Braqthian child can do and the factors wish they could not.
Epprenea quarries the bone-beds under its Spire, in open benches white enough to blind a man, and its town is loud with barge-masters, chalk-dust and Alabaster’s lawyers. It feeds half the western wheat fields and buys its bread back from them at a price it has had four riots about.
Below all three there are the pan-scrapers’ camps and the quarry towns, where a petty folk-worker who can sweeten a cistern is the most important person for forty leagues and knows it, and may decline to come out for less than a goat.
Bearing Stock
Bearing is what a material does under load, Holding is what working it will keep. T0 to T9 is the Accord’s Tier ladder, and a Resonance and Domain name the Wellsprings a material answers to, and the branch of natural law they work through.
Trapstone · T2 · Stone · Flood-basalt terraces, western interior
Columnar basalt, split naturally into six-sided posts that require almost no dressing. The universal building stone of the quarter, quarried by prying rather than cutting. Resonates readily with Coagula and Fixatio, which the Braqthian tribal confederations exploit in their standing-stone work and which the west has never bothered to study. Bearing good, Holding moderate. Domain Material Science.
Greenskin Serpentine · T2 · Stone · Ophiolite belt, eastern coastal ranges
Soft, green, easily carved, and pleasant to work. In certain pods it is fibrous, and the fibers separate into a dust so fine it does not settle. Men who quarry the fibrous pods develop a scarring of the lung that appears twenty years after they leave the trade and kills them regardless of what they did in the interval. The Accord’s Enforcement Division has posted no writ on this, and the coastal quarries have raised no objection to the absence.
Mireclay · T0 · Clay · Marsh basins of Dorrosfenn
Brittle, dissolves wherever Aether runs strong, used for short-lived summoning totems in rural spirit rites and for very little else.
Coilhide Leather · T2 · Beastkin hide · Ironcoils, native to Braqth
Training armor and gloves. Common enough in the southern quarter to be unremarkable and expensive enough in the west to be a minor trade.
Coalthread Cloth · T1 · Fabric · Southern weave, distribution uncontrolled
A black-laced weave that dulls aura flicker and burns readily. The Accord notes without further comment that its principal known users are smugglers.
Holding Stock

Marrowchalk · T2 · Mineral · Phosphorite bone-beds, southern shelf margins, Dorrosfenn and Epprenea
The most consequential material in the southern quarter and the one that explains its politics. A bedded rock composed of the accumulated skeletal remains of an ancient shallow sea, phosphate-rich, chalky, and quarried in open benches by the thousand tons.
Ground and spread on western fields it doubles a wheat yield. Ground and prepared otherwise it is the primary reagent of every necromantic practice in the quarter. The same bench, the same rock, the same barge.
The Holy Sea of Alabaster has twice attempted to establish that the two uses can be legally distinguished at the point of sale and has twice failed, because they cannot be distinguished at the point of extraction either.
Bearing negligible, Holding high and specific. Resonance: Mortalis, Rebirthine. Domain Biochemistry.

Palebed Nitre · T1 · Mineral · Nitrate caliche, interior pans
Crusted nitrate salts left in basins that have not seen rain in living memory. Oxidizer for alchemical charge work, preservative for meat, preservative for corpses, and fertilizer where Marrowchalk cannot be got. Harvested by scraping. The pans have been worked for eight hundred years and are not measurably diminished. Resonance: Exuroth. Domain Thermodynamics.

Ashfast Chrome · T3 · Metal ore · Chromite pods in the serpentine belt, eastern coast
The southern quarter’s one strategic export. Chromite ground to sand and rammed into a furnace hearth will not react with slag, will not fuse, and will not fail at temperatures that destroy every other lining material in supply.
Between Ashfast hearth sand and Blacktooth wolfram nozzles, the entire high-temperature capability of the four quarters rests on two ores that occur in two places. The Logistics Division has said so in every annual return for nineteen years.
Bearing extreme under heat, Holding nil. Resonance: Fixatio. Domain Thermodynamics.

Stormfulgur · T4 · Natural glass · Fulgurite fields, nitre pans of the interior
Where lightning strikes the pans it fuses a branching tube of glass down through the crust, sometimes to the depth of a man’s height. These tubes are naturally hollow, naturally continuous, and naturally aligned along the path a discharge took, which makes them the cheapest ready-formed Essence conduit in the world. The Braqthian confederations gather them after storms the way coastal people gather driftwood, and sell them by the armload to Accord factors who resell them at forty times the price for the long runs of an array. Fragile, irregular, and impossible to manufacture. Resonance: Mirithane, Aurevane. Domain Electromagnetism.
Driftbone · T1 · Organic · Veil-tide shores
Hollow bone bleached by the tides, carrying whispers when hollowed, ritually carved by dream shamans. What the tides are bleaching, and where it comes from, is not recorded, and the shamans decline to speculate in front of Accord surveyors.
Gloomhide · T5 · Leather · Beasts born in forgotten spirit zones, southern interior
Repels light-based castings and weak divine strikes. Spiritually inert and physically hyper-resilient, which makes it the one material in the ledger that is simultaneously an ideal armor backing and completely useless as a substrate.
Grimbarite · T6 · Stone · Buried beneath the Crevice fault system
Repels both Fate and Name manipulation. Heavy, silent in all forms, absorbs prayer. Extraction requires working within the Crevice margin, and the mortality figures for Grimbarite crews are not published.

Crevice Shale · T9 · Rock · The Crevice itself
Glows black. Fractures nearby Realm law. Required in the crafting of unmaking weapons and forbidden to move, hold, or trade under Article III of the Concord Codex.
Recorded here because a ledger that omits it is a ledger somebody will trust.

The Works
There are no southern works in the sense the other three quarters use the word. There is extraction, which is quarrying and scraping and gathering, performed by hand at enormous scale with almost no gear beyond a pick and a sledge, and there is shipping, which is what the extracted material is immediately subjected to.

The west calls this backwardness, and it is the correct answer to the conditions. Array work requires reliable ground to pull from and the southern interior does not have it. What the quarter has instead is materials that require no processing at all before they are worth carrying: nitre you scrape, phosphate you dig, chromite you crush, fulgurite you pick up off the ground.
The southern quarter has arranged itself around the fact that its wealth needs nothing done to it.

The consequence is that almost all of the value added to southern material is added in western furnaces, and almost all of the profit stays there. Dorrosfenn’s necromantic theocracy is the only southern polity that has built a trade at home on a material from home, and it has done so by being the only buyer that wants Marrowchalk in the form it comes out of the ground.
What It Costs
Thirst, which is the ordinary death. Serpentine dust, which is a slower one. The pans, which reflect enough light to blind a man in a season and which have no shade for forty leagues in any direction.
And the Crevice, which does not kill in any way the Measurewrights have found language for, and which is why the four-league line exists and why it keeps moving outward.
Trade Posture
Exports phosphate, nitre, chromite, fulgurite, hides, and labor. Imports well-diggers, cistern-masons, timber, iron, and grain. Holds almost no credit and almost no debt, because western moneylenders and factors will not write paper against ground they cannot survey.

The southern quarter is the poorest of the four by every measure the Accord records, and it sits on two of the six materials without which the other three quarters cannot make anything above T4.
Nobody involved considers this arrangement stable.

The Quarter Above the Ledger
Clemence Rooke, Measurewright, petitioned the Dragon Sovereign’s court for a survey permit six times between Year 631 and Year 640. The sixth answer came by Wyvern, which landed in her camp on the Dust Coast, ate the mules with every courtesy, and left under a rock a sealed refusal correct in every point of treaty form. She filed it, walked home, and wrote up what she had been able to see, which is the whole of the page above. What follows came from people who had wings to ask, or who did not ask.

Two accounts of this quarter, and they disagree, though not in the way the Old World’s do. The note at the foot of this page says why.
Everything above is the Measurewrights’ survey: an unglaciated craton, duricrust and gibber, flood basalt, ophiolite coast, nitre pans, bone-beds, the Crevice. Almost no water, almost no wood, no array work, and the polities are the Braqthian confederations, Dorrosfenn and Epprenea.
Everything below is drawn from The Geography of the Outer World, which has the whole of it: a long land split between an Aether-starved dragon south, spined by a colossal volcanic cordillera and carrying a vast rainforest, and a cold, veiled Vampire north whose ground still holds its Aether.
The two agree on the southern metaphysics and disagree on the water. That is a different failure from the Old World’s, and it points somewhere useful.

Orientation
Classification: Divided Supercontinent, Aether-Preserved Vampire North and Aether-Depleted Dragon South · Epithet: The Land Beneath Two Skies
Sovereign powers: the Draconic Empire of Drakyssia in the south and the Dreadvalis Empire in the north · Territorial share: even, each holding half of recognized territory directly or through tributaries
Other peoples: human kingdoms, elven enclaves, free cities and frontier peoples, split between the two empires.

The south possesses plenty. It is poor because too many ancient things have already eaten.


Far North: the Frostfang Cordillera with its glaciers and Frozen Wells, and the Last Archipelago. Dreadvalis holds the mountains from Grimhold Deeps; the island peoples owe a light tithe.
North: the Moonlight Forest, the Moonlight Snow Plains and the Northern Tablelands, the Veiled Provinces of Dreadvalis, where noon under the Great Veils is deep blue twilight.
Northeast: the northern Serrathan Highlands, old, worn, and rich in iron and silver around the undercity of Vel Sarith.
The Twilight March: the frontier band where the veils end and the sun returns. The Red Marches, the Great Grass Sea, the old Five River country and the Golden Escarpment, split between northern tributaries above and Drakyssian Houses and tributaries below.
South-Central: rainforest, river basin, wetland and transitional dryland. The richest biological diversity and some of the weakest ambient Aether. Forests physically alive and metaphysically exhausted: plants grow, animals breed, rivers run, and magical abundance does not return at the rate it is consumed. The further inland, the less ordinary borders mean; dragon territory is often marked by flight range instead.
Southwest: the Drakhal Spine, a colossal volcanic chain of snow peaks over fire, with high desert, deep valleys, a narrow coastal strip, and the largest surviving concentration of geothermal Aether in the south. Drakyssia’s heart lies in its central volcanic highlands.
Southeast: the Eastern Sun Coast and its port cities, under House Avarax and treaty protection.
Far South: the Ash Wastes and the ancient flame-realm of Zyraxia, Drakyssian sacred territory, where the last Salamanders sleep.

The Aether Gradient

The defining geographical fact here is how much Aether the ground still holds, and that falls steadily from north to south.
The north kept its reserve for plain reasons. No dragon ever lived there, because for seven thousand years it was too cold for fire-born bodies. A Vampire takes its Essence through blood and draws nothing from soil, forest or river. The Vohrin-touched cold slows depletion along with everything else, the Great Veils let Aether settle and pool, and the Dreadvalis tax careless magic, license every Wellspring and plan like people who do not age.
The southern ground is alive and spent. Wild Aether that would circulate through soil, plant, weather, seam, river and animal has been pulled down across enormous territories, many of which carry a fraction of the Aetheric Density considered normal elsewhere. Natural Wellspring sites remain, but deep, unstable, dormant, tightly localized, or claimed by dragons whose territories formed around them generations ago.
This is the principal reason dragons dominate the south. A dragon needs energetically viable territory, and calderas, deep faults, ancient Wellspring sites, geothermal basins, Soul-rich forest, storm corridors and subterranean seams therefore carry political value equal to farmland, ports or gold. The strongest draconic states hold land only as the way of holding what remains beneath it.

Five processes emptied the southern reserve, and no account of them is disinterested.
Draconic consumption. Large dragons passively pull more ambient Aether than entire mortal settlements. A region carrying hundreds of mature dragons is under a constant metaphysical drain. Drakyssia learned to manage this through territorial rotation, volcanic recharge zones, controlled access to Wellspring sites, migration law and subterranean reservoirs. Less disciplined draconic territories simply drained themselves.
Ancient warfare. Dragon wars rarely leave ordinary battlefields. Breath alters geology; elemental conflict at scale destroys forests, evaporates lakes, fractures Wellsprings, destabilizes Soul-plane recognition, vitrifies valleys. Many of today’s Dead Zones are old battle zones.
Wellspring extraction. Ancient civilizations found methods of pulling directly from Wellspring sites and treated the pools as limitless. They were not. Several collapsed after emptying local pools faster than the pools recovered, and the south is still scattered with enormous abandoned works around sites that no longer answer: relics of the Great Spirit War and the days of the Physical Epochs (when Bara, Ashura and Aegor walked in human form), dangerous to enter and still killed over.
Heat and storm. In the southern heat, Aether that might have pooled is burned off by volcanic storms and heatwaves almost as fast as it rises.
The great drain. The land appears to have lost part of its ability to circulate ambient Aether at all. Some Measurewrights hold that repeated extraction damaged the metaphysical equivalent of groundwater flow; others that the draconic population simply prevents recovery. Drakyssian scholars reject the accusation that dragons alone caused it and point at pre-imperial human, elven, demonic and vanished ruins demonstrating Essence use on a ruinous scale. The safest conclusion is that everyone inherited a wounded south and nearly everyone made it worse.
The Great Regions, North to South































































































RegionWhat it isWhat comes out of itThe Last Archipelago far northern coastLand fractured into islands, channels, fjords, mountains, glaciers, peatland and black-water sea. Cold, remote, storm-heavy, extraordinarily hard to govern. Small human and mixed-blood settlements survive on fishing, whaling, sealing, ship repair and navigation, and owe Dreadvalis a light tithe and the use of their harbors. Features: the Broken Horns · the Sea of Knives · the Black Lantern · the Grave of WingsFish, whale oil, seal, salvage, pilotageThe Frostfang Cordillera far northBlue ice, ice field, fjord and narrow valley. Ancient ice has locked away pockets of Essence older than the depletion itself. These Frozen Wells are intensely valuable, and the fortress-city of Grimhold Deeps guards them. Features: the Blue Teeth · the Steam Fjords · the Frozen WellsSilver, copper, cold iron, blue crystal, glacial quartz, black granite, froststoneThe Northern Tablelands above the forestHigh frozen plateaus of gray stone, home to the Ashen Courts, where the oldest High Vampire nobility keep their distance from the throne, and to the anchors of the VeilspiresSalts, stone, Frozen-Well crystalThe Moonlight Snow Plains veiled northOpen snowfields past every horizon, lit under the veils only by the moon and the snow. In winter the snow lies a man’s height deep; in the short summer it thins over hardy grass and the herds move through. Features: the Pale Sea · the Starfields · the Black Walls of Morvayne · the Lantern RoadGame, Frozen-Well crystal, and the stores of the Cold GranariesThe Moonlight Forest veiled northThe largest healthy forest left on the continent, silver-barked conifers and pale hardwoods that hold light like snow, so that under the veils the whole forest glows faintly blue-white. Ambient Aether here is close to Old World levels. Bluvest lies sunk beneath its northern edge, and the Seven Blood Estates ring the capital in its depths. Features: the Silver Ocean · the Moonlight Groves · the Still RiversMoonlight timber, spirit amber, preservation resins, moonpetal, frostrootThe Elyran Green Crowns within the Moonlight ForestNot one kingdom but a network of elven sanctuaries, canopy cities, river groves, plateaus, Spirit-tree settlements and hidden valleys. Their discipline of Essence is a way of life: excess ambient casting is forbidden, wasteful display is culturally offensive, and the young are taught to circulate and recover Essence before they are taught to discharge it, which makes them one of the few mortal civilizations Dreadvalis respects. By treaty they pay no blood; they tend the Moonlight Groves instead. Seats: Elyr-Vael · the Saelith Plateau · the Quiet RootsSpirit amber, medicinal plants, memory wood, rare fungi, living fibers, green gemstones, river pearls, preservation resinsThe Serrathan Highlands northeast and the MarchWeathered plateau, steep escarpment, rolling mountain country, waterfall, grassland and mineral upland, much older than the Spine, shorter and more eroded, and extraordinarily rich where the geology is exposed. The line runs through it: the northern uplands around Vel Sarith mine iron and silver for Dreadvalis, and the Golden Escarpment in the south is House Zhaeryn’s. Features: the Golden Escarpment · the Table Kingdoms · the Thousand Falls · the Red CavernsIron, gold, manganese, diamond, quartz, emerald, tin, bauxite, nickel, cobalt, black crystal, Aether-resistant stoneThe Great Grass Sea the Twilight MarchTemperate grassland on deep fertile soil, and it feeds both halves of the continent. Its northern half grows grain for the Cold Granaries under the Kingdom of Veyran, a horse-and-grain monarchy; its southern half raises the herds of House Eredan, so that dragons who hold volcanic energy and Wellspring sites still depend on mortal farmers and drovers. Features: the Endless Green · the Blacksoil Belt · the Horse Rivers · the South GranariesGrain, livestock, leather, wool, clay, salt, iron, river stone, hardwoodThe Old Five River Country the Twilight MarchA small fraction of the continent carrying a disproportionate share of its mortal population, its kingdoms broken apart along the north-south line after the Taken Winter. Sworn north: Therosan, engineers and masons who raised many of the Veilspires; Calverne, a merchant monarchy holding the road from the northern mines to the coast; the Free March of Saren, fortified towns founded by refugees from dragon conquest who chose the tithe. Sworn south: Valecar, cavalry, grain and mercenaries; Ordas, small and wealthy, silver financing a professional army. None could survive open war with either empire. They survive by being worth more aliveGrain, iron, silver, cavalry horses, engineering and ward-work, mercenary contractThe Veloran Rainsea south-central interiorA vast hot rainforest. Rivers wide enough to resemble inland seas, canopy past several hundred feet, whole ecological regions that never receive direct sun. Physically magnificent, metaphysically dying slowly, with vast biological mass and very little magical vitality. Spirit-sensitive travelers describe the body of something enormous and the exhaustion of something ancient. Its surviving Aether Wells are almost all held by dragons and guarded by House Ishkar. Features: the Green Ocean · the Great Verdant River · the Blackwater Labyrinth · the Sunken Towers · the Breathing ForestGold, iron, bauxite, green diamond, spirit amber, medicinal resin, bloodwood, rare hardwood, deep clay, mana-poor crystal, river pearl, blackwater saltsThe Thousand-River Basin south-centralFloodplain, swamp, grassland, braided river, seasonal lake and floating island. Periodically receives diluted magical sediment carried down from the Spine, so local Aether fluctuates violently, nearly mundane some months, temporarily saturated in mountain flood years. The wildlife is correspondingly adaptive. Mostly draconic tributary ground, with several human fishing confederacies living under negotiated tribute. Features: the Mirror Marsh · the Floating Grasslands · the Seven Serpent Rivers · the Flooding ForestRiver gold, clay, iron sand, freshwater pearl, medicinal reeds, black peat, amber, blue-green stoneThe Varakh Drylands south-central interiorThorn scrub, dry woodland, red earth, salt pan, seasonal river and very hot lowland basin. It does receive rain; the problem is inconsistency, several abundant years followed by severe drought, and heatwaves that kill. Weak Aether and difficult agriculture make it not worth a major dragon’s permanent occupation. Features: the Red Thorn Sea · the White Pans · the Broken Rivers · the Bone HillsIron, salt, tin, copper, fossil resin, red quartz, manganese, pale silver, bone phosphateThe Drakhal Spine southwestern backboneColossal young volcanic chain. Snow peaks over fire, stratovolcanoes, black-rock plateaus, high lakes, geothermal basins, obsidian fields, mountains tall enough to move continental weather. Its northern reaches hold the Wyvern country of House Dovaryn and its southern reaches the forge-cities of House Rhaegyr. Features: the Thousand Peaks · the Black Steps · the Sky Graves · the Red FaultGold, silver, copper, tin, obsidian, cobalt, volcanic iron, Dragonfire crystal, sulfur, red quartz, tungsten, Aetheric magma ore, black adamant fragmentsThe Drakyssian Heartlands imperial coreWhere the Spine widens into volcanic plateaus, calderas, lava plains, aerial basins and elevated nesting territory. One of the few places where deep Wellspring pressure, volcanic energy, mineral concentration, atmospheric Aether and ancient Soul-residue all remain strong enough for a permanent dragon civilization. Divided vertically as much as horizontally: mortals in the valleys, drakes on the fortification belts, Wyrms below, Wyverns in the air lanes, trueblood lines on the upper mountains, and the oldest dragons in peaks, calderas and deep chambers. No foreign settlement without the Sovereign’s permissionDragonfire ore, volcanic steel, obsidian, black diamond, gold, copper, titanium-rich black sand, Soulfire crystal, flame opal, magma glass, Wyrmstone, scale iron, adamant fragments, deep Wellspring crystalThe Aurelian Dust Coast west of the mountainsMineral desert trapped between range and ocean. Districts pass decades without rain; fog rolls in from the sea and sustains isolated ecosystems, and almost no permanent river reaches the coast. The dryness preserved the wealth: metals buried elsewhere under forest or river sediment lie exposed here. Ambient Aether is too weak for large dragons to nest permanently, so smaller draconic houses, mining enclaves and mortal city-states hold it instead. Features: the Copper Sea · the Glass Coast · the Fog Gardens · the Dead WellsCopper, lithium salts, silver, nitrate salts, gold, molybdenum, cobalt, desert glass, blue crystal, iron, sulfur, pale Aether saltThe Eastern Sun Coast southeastern seaboardThe largest concentration of mortal port cities on the continent. Warm seas, long beaches, estuaries, forested hills, natural harbors, barrier islands, mangrove and coastal plain, densely settled by comparison with the interior. Technically outside direct imperial administration in many districts, and nobody mistakes that for independence, since Drakyssian war dragons reach most major eastern ports within days. Cities: Velisar · Aureth Bay · Kethra · SolenmarSea salt, tropical hardwood, sugar-grass, pearl, fish oil, iron, coastal gold, clay, coral limestone, ship timberThe Ash Wastes and Zyraxia far southThe burned end of the continent, gray with old ashfall, the ground steaming underfoot and the heat never fully breaking, even at night. Even dragons feel the depletion here: a large one remaining too long without stored Essence, prey, or an internal elemental reserve may begin burning dangerously through its own Soul Crystal. Beyond it lies Zyraxia, the ancient flame-realm and last refuge of the Salamanders. Features: the Petrified March · the Gray Lakes · the Hollow HillsCoal, iron, oil-bearing shale, silver, uranic stone, black basalt, pale crystal, fossil resin
Kra’Vorrak
In one breath: a volcano with a city stacked up the inside of it, where your rent climbs with your altitude until the next floor is let only to things with wings.
The Imperial Sky-Capital occupies the interior of a colossal volcanic complex. The city rises rather than spreads. Its lowest districts hold mortals, smiths, servants, markets, bonded houses, foundries and armorers’ rows, loud and sulfur-yellow and smelling of hot iron and roast goat, fed on grain that comes up the mountain as tribute. Higher districts hold dragon landing terraces, War-Wing barracks, noble roosts, ritual temples, command platforms, scholar keeps and avenues built for beings hundreds of meters long. At the highest levels stand imperial structures visible from dozens of miles out.
In the caldera’s living heart burns the Ember Crown, the strongest living Wellspring left in the south: a current of Pyraeon, the ember that stays lit, that has never cooled in any record. Every Dragon Road bends toward it, and every Dragon House measures its rank by how close its roost lies.
Around it: the Dragon Catacombs, subterranean chambers where ancient dragons sleep and Bond Rituals are performed. Avo’Kara Sanctum, a ritual city for bond law, Soul Crystal rites, hatchery custom, draconic music and spiritual recognition. Dova’Ruun Fortress, the greatest military complex in the empire. The Black Scale Ranges, reserved for trueblood nesting. The Wyrmdeep Cities beneath the plateau. The Iron Roosts, Wyvern breeding and aerial-war fortresses. The Ember Vaults, treasury-forges built against controlled magma chambers. The Drakhalis Throne Spire, monument, imperial archive, mausoleum and ceremonial structure attached to the name of Kain Drakhalis.
The Great Volcanic Belt
The southwestern margin is among the most geologically violent regions in the Continuum: thousands of active, dormant and extinct volcanoes along the Spine, several large enough to carry independent ecosystems.
Mount Kra’Vorrak, the complex holding the capital. Dova’s Furnace, an active stratovolcano used historically for military trials and large-scale dragon forging. The Avo Caldera, a partly collapsed basin of ritual sanctuaries and geothermal lakes. Mount Veyrath, among the highest active peaks, with lightning standing around its summit. The Black Mother, dormant, its lava tubes holding ancient Wyrm settlements. The Hollow Flame, extinct, its magma chamber emptied into an underground cavern hundreds of miles across.
Volcanic ground is among the only places in the south where natural Aether replenishment stays comparatively strong, so nearly every major volcano is claimed, sometimes by an empire, sometimes by a noble House, and sometimes by one dragon powerful enough that nobody has successfully informed it the land belongs to anyone else.
Metaphysical Terrain
The continent cannot be read from ordinary geography. Depletion in the south and preservation in the north have produced classes of ground barely known on other land.
Living Land. The veiled north, above all the Moonlight Forest. The Three Planes connect normally and the land gives back Aether at a natural rate.
Frozen Wells. Aether reservoirs locked in ancient ice in Vohrin-touched country, in the Frostfang and the Starfields.
Veil Country. Land in permanent twilight under the Great Veils, where Aether pools rather than burning off and shadow-leaning workings run strong.
Exhausted Land. Most of the south. The Three Planes stay connected and magic still works, but the environment contributes almost nothing. Practitioners run on their own reserves, recovery is slow, large ritual working becomes expensive, and natural magical phenomena are uncommon.
Aether Wells. Localized pockets where Aetheric Density holds, around active volcanoes, deep fault intersections, ancient forest, underground crystal systems, glacial reservoirs, surviving Wellspring sites, old nesting grounds, and places deep in Echo Depth or heavy in Thread Weight, where Soul or Fate is thick enough to draw the Aether after it. Almost every major Well has an owner. In the south, most owners have wings.
Draconic Saturation Zones. Ground held by a powerful bloodline for centuries develops its own metaphysical climate from scale fragment, breath residue, Soul Crystal emission, shed blood, death sites and continual elemental expression. A fire territory may carry warm stone centuries after its owner dies. An ice lineage may permanently lower groundwater temperature. A storm lineage raises atmospheric charge. A Wyrm dynasty leaves stone unusually responsive to seismic speech.
Hollow Wellsprings. Sites gone empty, which is a different and milder thing than a Dead Zone: old works with nothing left in them. A skilled practitioner can still read what kind of law once ran through them, and they occasionally answer weakly during major celestial events or continental Essence surges.
Dead Zones. Far worse. Material, Soul and Fate relationships are fractured past any draining. Magic may fail. Names may lose local recognition. Spiritual projections may not return correctly. Structures behave inconsistently. Drakyssia marks the known ones on imperial flight charts and even dragons avoid several.
Dragon Roads and Veil Roads. Thousands of years of repeated migration have made certain southern sky corridors recognized by Fate: reduced atmospheric resistance, stabler thermals, clearer spatial orientation, occasionally shortened effective distance. Most converge on Kra’Vorrak. In the north, permanently veiled corridors link the undercities through the Hollow Lanterns, and a Vampire can travel the length of the empire on them without ever seeing the sun.
How Dragons Hold Ground
Drakyssia’s half of the continent, under direct, tributary, inherited or uncontested draconic control, is not a province governed by imperial officials. A dragon may legally possess a mountain range, a valley, a watershed, a hunting territory, a cloud layer, a volcano, or several hundred miles of airspace without maintaining any settlement at all.

































FormWhat it meansImperial TerritoryGoverned directly by DrakyssiaNoble Scale TerritoryHeld by recognized Dragon Houses owing allegiance to the SovereignTributary TerritoryMortal kingdoms governing themselves while acknowledging supremacy through tax, military obligation, resource access or treatyRoost TerritoryClaimed primarily as nesting and hunting groundWild SovereigntyHeld by independent dragons powerful enough that no state has displaced themUnclaimed Depletion ZonesToo Aether-poor, inaccessible or dangerous for anyone to govern meaningfully. Far smaller than outsiders assume
A dragon does not need to build a castle to own a mountain. Sometimes the territorial marker is simply the fact that everyone who entered without permission stopped returning.
In the north, sovereignty runs by veil and by tithe instead. A village is Dreadvalis land if a veil hangs over it or a Tithe Hall stands in it, whether or not an imperial officer ever visits. A settlement does not need a governor to know whose dark lies over it.
How Mortals Survive
Humans, elves, mixed peoples, free cities and small frontier civilizations hold what they hold under one sky or the other, five ways. Economic necessity: producing what an empire wants and prefers not to administer, grain kingdoms being the clearest case. Geographic irritation: land too wet, cold, dry, fragmented or Aether-poor to justify occupation. Treaty recognition: both empires take treaty law seriously where the original agreement was properly recognized by Fate. Patronage: a powerful House or clan has declared the place protected. Military cost: a mortal kingdom has only to make conquest less useful than cooperation, since defeating either empire was never on the table. That distinction governs most of Outer World diplomacy.
Tribute is the rent in the south, and everyone can quote it. Valecar pays in horses and mercenary companies, Ordas in silver, the Sun Coast in salt, pearl and ship timber. A family in a Valecar river town pays the town, the town pays the factor, the factor pays the House, and the House’s Wyvern, passing overhead, is the receipt. North of the line the rent is the blood tithe, drawn by physicians in the Tithe Halls and paid back in rations, medicine and protection, and the Kingdom of Veyran’s treaty is a schedule of harvests besides. Between those payments the mortal towns are as loud as any in the world, because they have had a long time to learn that nobody is coming to tax a street party: painted river-fortresses, cavalry fairs on the Horse Rivers, Therosan masons and Calverne merchants insulting each other across a market full of plantains and river fish, and on the Sun Coast a harbor lit in every color its wardens can manage, with an eye kept on the western sky.
See The Ten Great Houses of Drakyssia, Draconic Kind and The Vampiric Peoples.


Why the ledger and the land disagree. The ledger is an Accord document about ground Accord surveyors can reach. Everything it records for this quarter is dry, low, treeless and westward-facing, which is precisely the Dust Coast, the Varakh Drylands and the Ash Wastes. If half the continent is draconic and issues no survey permits, then the Measurewrights never wrote the wet half because they were never let in, and the ledger is not wrong so much as it is a partial survey wearing the confidence of a complete one.
Southern phosphate law falls under the Holy Sea of Alabaster.

geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-ge.title: The Geography of the Outer World
geography--and--the-four-quarters/the-ge.content:
Overview





































ClassificationDivided supercontinent: Aether-preserved vampire north, Aether-depleted dragon southNorthern powerThe Dreadvalis Empire: Common, High and Turned Vampires and their sworn mortalsSouthern powerThe Draconic Empire of Drakyssia: Draconic Kind, from the last Salamanders to the Bonded Mortals, under the Dragon Sovereign and the Ten Great HousesBalanceEven. Drakyssia holds 50% of recognized territory and Dreadvalis the other 50%, directly or through tributariesOther peoplesHuman kingdoms, Elven enclaves, free cities and frontier peoples, split between the two empiresAgeDrakyssia: more than seven thousand years. Dreadvalis: a few decadesEpithetThe Land Beneath Two Skies
The Outer World is a long continent split by a line nobody has drawn on a map but everyone can feel: where the veils end and the sun begins.
The north is cold country: long winters, the silver Moonlight Forest and the moonlit snow plains, glaciers, frozen tablelands and a broken coast of islands. It belongs to the Dreadvalis Empire, a vampire civilization only decades old, born when Malakar took the northern peoples in the Taken Winter and remade them. Its rulers live in great undercities and hang veils across the sky to keep the sun away. The north is the healthier half of the continent: its land still holds its Aether, its mines carry most of the continent’s ordinary minerals, and its storehouses hold most of its food and medicine, because the people who rule it eat neither.
The south is fire country: volcanoes, heatwaves, red deserts, steaming rainforest and grasslands crowded with great beasts. It belongs to Drakyssia, the oldest empire on the continent, built around a single living Wellspring burning inside the volcano Kra’Vorrak and held together by the Ten Great Houses. The south is poorer in Aether, ancient, hungry and dangerous, but it holds the continent’s gold, its dragon minerals, and the only forges hot enough to make its finest arms and armor.
Between them run the mortal and Elven kingdoms, some sworn north and some sworn south, and a frontier called the Twilight March, where cold meets heat.
Travelers sum it up in one line: the north keeps what the south has spent, and the south forges what the north cannot.
I. Continental Orientation
The continent runs long from north to south and warms the whole way down. Cold and darkness hold the north; heat and light hold the south. Where they meet, the Outer World’s politics happen.


















































BandLandHeld byFar NorthThe Frostfang Cordillera, its glaciers and Frozen Wells; the Last ArchipelagoDreadvalis from Grimhold Deeps; the Archipelago peoples under a light titheNorthThe Moonlight Forest (Bluvest, the Seven Blood Estates, the Green Crowns), the Moonlight Snow Plains (Morvayne), the Northern Tablelands (the Ashen Courts)The Dreadvalis Empire directly: the Veiled ProvincesNortheastThe northern Serrathan Highlands: old, worn, iron- and silver-rich uplands around Vel SarithDreadvalis and its mining tributariesThe Twilight MarchThe frontier band. The Red Marches (Dreadvalis’s southern frontier province), the Great Grass Sea, the old Five River country, and the Golden Escarpment of the southern SerrathanSplit: northern tributaries above, Drakyssian Houses and tributaries below. House Akhazar’s Gate watches it from the southSouth-CentralThe Veloran Rainsea, the Thousand-River Basin, the Varakh DrylandsDrakyssia, its Houses, and wild dragonsSouthwestThe Drakhal Spine, the Drakyssian Heartlands around Kra’Vorrak, the Wyrmdeep, the Black Scale Ranges, the Aurelian Dust CoastDrakyssia directly; the heart of the Ten HousesSoutheastThe Eastern Sun Coast and its port citiesHouse Avarax and the protected portsFar SouthThe Ash Wastes and the ancient flame-realm of Zyraxia, where the last Salamanders sleepDrakyssian sacred territory
Reading the map. In the north, borders follow the veils: a village is Dreadvalis land if a Dreadvalis veil hangs over it or a Tithe Hall stands in it. In the south, borders are layered: one valley can belong to a mortal king on the ground, a Wyrm below it, a Dragon House on the mountains around it, a Wyvern wing in the sky above it, and the Sovereign over all four. Along the Twilight March both systems apply at once, and a single river town may owe blood to the north and tribute to the south in the same year.
II. A Short History of the Two Skies
The flame-realms. Long before any empire, the south belonged to the primordial flameborn: the Salamanders, first creation of the Titan Omnis, living in the ancient flame-realms of Zyraxia. From them came the dragons, and from the dragons every people of Draconic Kind.
The founding of Drakyssia. Dova’Kan and Avo’Kan bound the powerful draconic territories of the volcanic south into an alliance around the Ember Crown at Kra’Vorrak. Their nephew Kain Drakhalis made that alliance an empire. Over a reign of more than seven thousand years he broke rival claimants and rebel Houses, threw back invasions, and reorganized the great dragon dynasties into the Ten Great Houses, each bound to an Imperial Charge the empire could not survive without.
The depletion. Through those millennia, the south was drained. Dragon metabolisms, dragon wars, and the Wellspring extraction of vanished civilizations emptied the land of Aether. Drakyssia learned discipline (territorial rotation, recharge zones, House Ishkar’s rationing), but it inherited a wounded south, and still lives inside one.
The mortal north. The dragons never wanted the north. It was too cold for fire-born bodies and too far from the volcanoes, so for most of Drakyssia’s history the north was mortal country: hardy human kingdoms, Elven forest sanctuaries and island peoples, bound to the empire only by light frontier treaties kept by House Akhazar. Because no dragon ever lived there, its land kept its Aether.
The Taken Winter. A few decades before the Moto–Zettari war began in the Old World, Malakar, the First Demon, came north. Over one winter he emptied the northern kingdoms of thousands of their people and remade them in the First Thirst as the first Vampires. Then he lost interest and left them, starving, leaderless and hunting each other across the snow.
The rise of Dreadvalis. Out of that chaos, within a single lifetime, Vaelora Dreadvalis and the first High Vampires built an empire. They wrote feeding law and the blood tithe, raised the Great Veils, sank Bluvest and Morvayne into the ground, and absorbed or swore to tribute every northern people the Taken Winter had left standing. Some mortal kingdoms, like the refugees of the Free March of Saren who had fled dragon conquest, chose the tithe willingly.
The two skies. Drakyssia did not ignore the new power in the north. There were years of raids and burnings along the Grass Sea before Western Dragon diplomats and the envoys of House Akhazar sat down with Morvayne’s Ledger Courts and drew the first Fate-recognized treaties across the Twilight March. Since then, the continent has been balanced: an ancient empire of fire and a young empire of night, each needing what the other has.
Now. At the close of the Moto–Zettari war, Shaka-Al Zettari banished Malakar into Hell. Now that prohibition has broken, and Malakar walks the Material World again. Every Vampire in the north can feel their maker in their blood. Malakarian loyalists are slipping away from the undercities; the Blood Throne has said nothing in public. In Kra’Vorrak, the Council of Ten Wings watches the north, and wonders which way the night will turn.
III. The Aether Gradient
The defining geographical fact of the Outer World is not its climate. It is how much Aether the ground still holds, and that falls steadily from north to south.
Why the north kept its Aether

No dragon ever lived there. For seven thousand years the north was mortal country, too cold for fire-born bodies. Nothing in it drew on the land the way a dragon does.
Vampires do not feed on the land. A dragon’s body pulls ambient Aether constantly, the way a furnace pulls air. A Vampire takes its Essence through blood. Dreadvalis rule draws on people, not on soil, forest or river.
The cold preserves. Much of the north is Vohrin-touched country: its deep cold is a Titan’s power at work, not one of the Sixty, and it slows everything, depletion included. Ice has locked away pockets of Essence older than the depletion itself, the Frozen Wells.
The veils shelter it. Under the Great Veils, Aether settles and pools instead of being burned off by heat and storm.
The Dreadvalis are misers. The empire taxes careless magic, licenses every Wellspring, and builds wards to last. Its rulers do not age, and they plan accordingly.

Why the south lost it

Draconic consumption. Large dragons passively draw more ambient Aether than whole mortal towns. A region carrying hundreds of mature dragons lives under constant drain.
Ancient warfare. Breath reshapes geology, boils lakes, vitrifies valleys and fractures Wellsprings. Many of the south’s Dead Zones are old battlefields.
Wellspring extraction. Vanished civilizations treated the southern Wellsprings as bottomless and drew on them until they stopped answering.
Heat and storm. In the southern heat, Aether that might have pooled is burned off by volcanic storms and heatwaves almost as fast as it rises.

Drakyssian scholars insist that dragons alone did not wound the south, and point to the ruins of older peoples who mined Essence on an industrial scale. The fairest reading is the old one: everyone inherited a wounded south, and nearly everyone made it worse. House Ishkar exists so that it does not get worse still.

IV. The Dreadvalis Empire — The Veiled North
The youngest great power in the Outer World and, by most measures, the most sophisticated: a vampire civilization ruled from the Blood Throne in Bluvest, built in a single lifetime by people who remembered being human. Its rulers do not eat bread or meat and have no use for herbs, so the north grows, stores and preserves food it does not need, mines metals for others, and brews medicine for bodies it does not have. All of it keeps the mortal world fed, healthy and dependent. Dreadvalis rules by being the one who never runs out.
The Veils
The sun burns a Vampire to ash, so the Dreadvalis took it out of their sky. Across the heart of the empire hang the Great Veils: vast, slow-turning screens of darkened Aether anchored on mountaintops and on towers called Veilspires, worked through light-swallowing Wellsprings such as Vantabriel and Tenebra on the theory of the alchemist Arkhaven Bluvest. Under a veil, noon is deep blue twilight and the moon shows through as if it were night. The veils thin at the empire’s edges and in the short summer; at the Twilight March they fail altogether.
Mortals under the veils live by lamplight, moon-lamps and the silver glow of the forest, and grow crops bred to ripen without direct sun. Northern children visiting the south for the first time often weep at the brightness.

The Seven Blood Estates. The noble estates of the Great Clans, ringing Bluvest in the deep Moonlight Forest; blood-systems with their own wards, reservoirs and founders’ blood.

The Land
The Moonlight Forest. The largest healthy forest left on the continent: tall silver-barked conifers and pale-leaved hardwoods that hold light like snow, so that under the veils the whole forest glows faintly blue-white. Its oldest stands, the Moonlight Groves, are worked by Luminalis, the light that hides, and give off a radiance mortals can farm and read by. Ambient Aether here is close to Old World levels; it is the only forest in the Outer World where wild magic still visibly returns each year. Features: the Silver Ocean of the canopy, the Moonlight Groves, the Still Rivers that never freeze, the Hanging Gardens of Elyr-Vael.
The Moonlight Snow Plains. North of the forest, open snowfields past every horizon, lit under the veils only by the moon and the snow. In winter the snow lies a man’s height deep; in the short summer it thins over hardy grass and the herds move through. Features: the Pale Sea at its widest, the Starfields where Frozen Wells lie shallow and the snow sparkles with Essence at night, the Black Walls of Morvayne, the Lantern Road to the Archipelago.
The Outer North. The Frostfang Cordillera, all blue ice, fjords and narrow valleys, its ancient ice holding the Frozen Wells. The Northern Tablelands, high frozen plateaus over the forest, home to the Ashen Courts and the Veilspire anchors. The northern Serrathan Highlands, old worn uplands rich in iron, silver, copper and nickel. And the Last Archipelago, a broken coast of islands and storm seas whose sea-peoples fish, hunt whales and owe the empire a light tithe and the use of their harbors.
The Peoples of the North
Common Vampires are most of the empire: its soldiers, workers, hunters and citizens, living in the middle cities and the Hollow Lanterns. High Vampires hold the Blood Estates, the Ashen Courts and the deeps of Bluvest. Turned Vampires man the upper districts and the Red Marches garrisons. Beneath them all live the northern mortals: protected citizens, tithe subjects, donor houses and labor castes. The rare Vampire-Dragon Hybrids have only ever been born in the borderlands where the two empires meet.
The Blood Tithe
Every kingdom, town and household under a Dreadvalis veil or treaty pays the blood tithe. Tithe Wardens set each household’s portion; the young, old, sick and pregnant are exempt. Blood is drawn in the Tithe Halls by physicians, never by a Vampire’s mouth, and stored cold. In return, tithe-paying lands receive rations in lean years, physicians and medicine, protection under the veils, and the empire’s guarantee against conquest. That is the face Dreadvalis shows the world. Inside the empire, in the old traditionalist estates, the law is uglier.

V. Drakyssia — The Burning South
The south is the home of the dragons and of the great wild creatures, and its center is a single burning heart.
The Ember Crown
Deep inside Mount Kra’Vorrak, the colossal volcano at the heart of the empire, burns the strongest living Wellspring left in the south: a current of Pyraeon, the ember that stays lit, power that gives up its flare and keeps its heat for a lifetime. The volcano around it has never cooled in any record. Dragons call its Wellspring Core the Ember Crown.
The Ember Crown is why Drakyssia exists where it does. In a south that has spent nearly all its Aether, it is a hearth that never goes out: it recharges the land around it, warms the deep reservoirs, and feeds the greatest permanent dragon civilization in the world. Every Dragon Road bends toward it, and every Dragon House measures its rank by how close its roost lies.
Kra’Vorrak, the Imperial Sky-Capital
Built inside and around the volcano, the capital rises instead of spreading. Its lowest districts hold mortals, smiths, markets, bonded houses and foundries. Above them come landing terraces, War-Wing barracks, noble roosts, temples, command platforms and avenues built for bodies hundreds of meters long. At the summit stand the imperial structures; at the bottom of it all, in the caldera’s living heart, the Ember Crown.
Around the capital: the Dragon Catacombs, where ancient dragons sleep and Bond Rituals are performed · Avo’Kara Sanctum, the ritual city of bond law, Crystal rites, hatchery custom and draconic music · Dova’Ruun Fortress, the greatest military complex in the empire · the Ember Vaults, treasury-forges over the magma · the Drakhalis Throne Spire, archive, mausoleum and monument to Kain Drakhalis.

The Ash Wastes and Zyraxia. The burned far south, gray with old ashfall, where the ground steams underfoot, and beyond it the ancient flame-realm of Zyraxia, the last refuge of the Salamanders.

VI. The Ten Great Houses of Drakyssia
Vaer’Kharath, “the Ten Wings Beneath the Throne”
Drakyssia’s half of the continent does not rest on the Dragon Sovereign alone. What Each House Gives the Continent

Drakhalis turns draconic supremacy into government. A mortal king negotiating with a Dovaryn lord knows an imperial treaty outranks him; a merchant crossing four Houses’ land does not renegotiate at every border. The House holds the Right of Final Command and its own Throne Reserve.
Dovaryn fields the largest Wyvern air force in the world, the Grand Spearhost reserved for continental war. Its wings make distance irrelevant, and they are as often the first sign of rescue after a flood or earthquake as the first sign of invasion. They also patrol the Red Marches border, where they fly half-blind under the northern veils.
Zhaeryn holds the empire’s gold, silver, platinum and gems as Crown Resources under stewardship, not private property. Its law is simple: gold may be exhausted; the land may not.
Avarax imports what depleted land cannot make, and set the continent’s weights, measures, caravan marks and merchant law. Most of the grain and medicine that crosses the March from Dreadvalis passes through Avarax contracts.
Maelkar keeps the Dragon Dens, underground cities of incubators, hatcheries, recovery caverns and hibernation chambers, and manages dragon numbers so dragonkind does not eat its own habitat. Stealing or destroying a recognized egg is among the gravest crimes in the empire.
Ormyr governs downward: Wyrm cities, freight tunnels, aquifers, seismic and volcano watch. In the Drylands an Ormyr water engineer is worth more than an army.
Rhaegyr turns Zhaeryn ore into steel. Its forge-cities make dragon-forged weapons, scale armor, rider gear, siege engines, and the farm tools, bridge parts and ship fittings that millions of mortals use daily. Dreadvalis armies wear Rhaegyr steel.
Eredan feeds the empire without letting dragons eat it into collapse: herds, ranches, hunting quotas, famine stores. A farmer whose cattle a dragon army requisitions must be paid. In drought years Eredan buys northern grain from the Cold Granaries, and hates that it must.
Ishkar keeps what remains: Aether Wells, recharge zones, Dead Zone maps, emergency reserves. It can order even a Great House to reduce consumption. It looks north at the Frozen Wells with an envy it never says aloud.
Akhazar governs everyone who is not Drakyssian: tributaries, protectorates, treaties, frontier forts, Dragon Road permissions. Since the Taken Winter it also handles the empire’s most delicate relationship, with Morvayne’s Ledger Courts across the March.

How the Houses Bind Each Other
No House is self-sufficient, by design. Dovaryn fields the Wyverns, but Eredan feeds them, Rhaegyr arms their riders, Zhaeryn pays for the campaign, Ishkar decides where there is Aether enough to deploy, Ormyr keeps up the mountains beneath their roosts, Avarax supplies foreign materials, Maelkar keeps the breeding lines, and Akhazar keeps the supply roads open through tributary land. Drakhalis coordinates them all.
A House that rebels does not only fight Drakhalis. It risks frozen gold, closed trade, rationed Aether, eggs removed from imperial protection, sealed roads, canceled forge contracts, stopped food, and neighboring Houses authorized to take its land. A dragon can be strong enough to fight everyone. That does not mean it can feed, mine, forge, breed and govern everything alone.
Beneath the War-Wing Synod sits the Council of Ten Wings, one seat per House, with Drakhalis presiding, for questions that touch several Charges at once. A new gold mine near a Wellspring might bring in Zhaeryn for the ore, Ishkar for the Wellspring, Ormyr for the strata, Rhaegyr for its strategic value, Avarax for the export, Akhazar if it lies under a tributary kingdom, and Drakhalis if they cannot agree. On a depleted continent, that restraint is not idealism. It is survival.
The Houses are not friends. Zhaeryn and Avarax fight over export prices; Dovaryn demands more of the gold reserves; Eredan complains that Dovaryn’s Wyverns eat too much livestock; Maelkar opposes breeding for war over health; Ishkar cuts Rhaegyr’s geothermal Aether when the forges burn too hot; Ormyr accuses Zhaeryn’s mines of cracking the deep strata; Akhazar objects whenever a hot-headed dragon lord endangers a treaty. The throne’s purpose is not to end those instincts, but to make them serve Drakyssia before they destroy it.
“Drakhalis gives the command. Dovaryn brings the wings. Zhaeryn brings the gold. Avarax opens the market. Maelkar guards the egg. Ormyr knows what lies below. Rhaegyr lights the forge. Eredan fills the table. Ishkar saves what magic remains. Akhazar carries the word beyond the mountain.”
Among dragons, it is shorter: Ten Wings. One Sky. One Throne.

Nearly every one has an owner; in the south House Ishkar licenses every oneThe Ember CrownMount Kra’VorrakThe strongest single Wellspring in the south: a living Pyraeon current that has never cooledDraconic Saturation ZonesOld dragon territoriesLand altered by centuries of one dragon line: stone that stays warm after a fire dragon dies, groundwater chilled by an ice lineage, air charged by a storm lineageHollow WellspringsAcross the southWellsprings once strong, now exhausted or severed; a skilled reader can still tell what law once ran through themDead ZonesOld battlefields of the southMaterial, Soul and Fate relationships fractured. Magic fails, Names lose recognition, structures misbehave. House Ishkar maps them; even dragons avoid several
The Roads of Fate
Centuries of repeated travel have made certain routes recognized by Fate, and each empire has its own.

Dragon Roads. Sky corridors in the south where dragons fly with less resistance, steadier thermals and sometimes shortened distance. Nearly all converge on Kra’Vorrak, and their law belongs to House Drakhalis, their permissions to House Akhazar, and their security to House Dovaryn.
Veil Roads. Corridors in the north kept permanently under veil, linking the undercities through the Hollow Lanterns. A Vampire can travel the length of the empire on them without ever seeing the sun.

The Three Planes Under Scarcity
In the healthy north, Material, Soul and Fate interact normally. In the depleted south, Soul-based workings need more internal reserve, Attraction bonds weaken faster unless tended, old magical infrastructure loses recognition, and Wellspring harmonization needs deeper phase-locking because the land gives so little. That makes bloodlines, relics, bonded creatures and internal reserves disproportionately important in the south, and it is one more reason dragons rule there: a dragon carries its magical environment inside it.
X. Power, Trade and the Balance
What crosses the March





























The north sends southThe south sends northGrain, preserved food and ration stores, bought by House Eredan in drought yearsGold, from House Zhaeryn’s vaultsMedicine, physicians and surgical steelDragon minerals: dragonfire ore, soulfire crystal, wyrmstone, scale iron, adamantIron, silver, copper, tin, nickel, cobalt and the other common metalsHouse Rhaegyr’s weapons, scale plate and siege enginesFrozen-Well crystals and Aether-rich reagents, for House Ishkar’s reservesVolcanic glass, obsidian and geothermal crystalMoonlight timber, spirit amber and preservation resinsWar beasts, hides and livestock from Eredan’s ranges
Almost all of it moves under House Avarax contracts and House Akhazar road permits on the southern side, and through Morvayne’s Tithe Ministries on the northern side. The exchange runs the continent: the north holds what civilizations need every day; the south holds what civilizations cannot replace. A Drakyssian war campaign raises the price of grain in Bluvest; a hard winter in the north raises the price of steel in Kra’Vorrak.
Why neither empire swallows the other

The sun and the cold. Vampires cannot fight in the southern sun, and no veil can be raised over the heat of the volcanic belt. Most great dragons are creatures of fire; the Vohrin-touched cold of the north slows them, and under the veils even Dovaryn’s Wyverns fly half-blind.
Each needs the other. Drakyssia eats northern grain in bad years and heals with northern medicine. Dreadvalis armies are armored in Rhaegyr steel and paid in Zhaeryn gold.
Treaty law. The treaties drawn across the March after the first raids are recognized by Fate, and both empires take recognized treaties seriously.
The March. The mortal kingdoms between them make conquest expensive and trade easy. Neither empire wants to govern them; both want to profit from them.
The Houses. No single House can march north on its own, and the Council of Ten Wings has never agreed that the north is worth the cost.

Two kinds of sovereignty
In the south, sovereignty is layered. One point on the map can belong to several powers at once (land, depth, water, sky), each answering to a different House, and all of them to the Sovereign. A mortal king may truly say “this valley is mine,” and a dragon may answer, “yes, and the mountain around it is mine,” and both are legally right. Drakyssia is less a color painted on the map than a web laid over it.
In the north, sovereignty runs by veil and by tithe. A village is Dreadvalis if it pays the tithe or lives under a veil, whether or not an imperial officer ever visits. A settlement does not need a governor to know whose dark lies over it.
The shadow over both
Malakar’s return has unsettled the balance. In the north, every Vampire feels their maker’s presence in their blood, the loyalists are leaving the undercities, and the Blood Throne is silent. In the south, the Council of Ten Wings has ordered House Dovaryn to double its patrols along the Red Marches and House Akhazar to learn what the Ledger Courts are not saying. Neither empire knows yet whether the thing that made the Vampires has come back for them, and whether, if it has, the March will hold.
XI. Continental Travel
Distance in the Outer World is measured twice: once in miles, and once in how much Aether the journey costs and where you can recover it.























































RouteWhereNotesVeil RoadsThe northPermanently veiled corridors between the undercities, with Hollow Lanterns as waystations. Dreadvalis license requiredThe Lantern RoadMorvayne to the ArchipelagoThe northern trade road across the Snow Plains, marked by lit cairnsThe March RoadsThe Twilight MarchThe busiest roads on the continent: grain and medicine south, gold and steel north. Toll-houses on every bridge, Akhazar permits on the southern sideDragon RoadsThe southThe fastest long-distance network on the continent, all leading to Kra’Vorrak. Drakhalis law, Akhazar permits, Dovaryn patrolsThe WyrmdeepUnder the Spine and the HeartlandsHouse Ormyr’s freight tunnels, large enough for grown dragons; the safest way to move cargo through volcanic countryThe Great Verdant RiverThe RainseaThe main freight route through the southern interiorMountain Pass RoadsThe Drakhal SpineWestern crossings; nearly all need Drakyssian permissionCoastal ShippingBoth coastsOften cheaper than inland travel, because the sea asks less of a traveler’s reserves; on the Sun Coast, under Avarax charterAether StationsSouthern roadsFortified stops, regulated by House Ishkar, selling stored Essence crystals, enchanted food, Soul-supporting medicine and licensed Wellspring access. In the south, Aether is infrastructure
Closing Geographical Phrase
“The north keeps the dark, the cold and the grain. The south keeps the fire, the gold and the steel. Between them the March keeps the peace, for as long as both are hungry. Above the north hangs the veil; above the south, ten wings and one throne. In the volcano’s heart the Ember Crown burns for a continent that has almost spent itself, and in the snow the Dreadvalis wait, patient as only the undying can be, for the rest of the world to need them.”

Read beside this. The Southern Pan, for what the Accord could survey of this quarter; The Ten Great Houses of Drakyssia, for the Houses in full; Draconic Kind and The Vampiric Peoples, for the two empires’ peoples.
