materials,-alchemy--and--trade/alchemy/m.title: Master Works
materials,-alchemy--and--trade/alchemy/m.content:
The one piece at the end of a lifetime that does what it has no right to: what they are, the famous ones in every trade, why the bench’s great prize is the hardest of all, who has died trying, and what any of it has to do with being called a Master

Pot, iron. Lid for same. Stamp: Marked. Rarity: Unique. Clerk’s note: I have struck this entry out twice and written it in again.
Assay roll of Pennycrown, the Hundred Crowns, for the year 672

The siege of Pennycrown was in its ninth week when Ser Lucan Vaye came through the Bakers’ Gate. He was the Comet of Tollgarth, Stage VIII, in plate enameled sunset orange, with a banner on his back and two hundred men shouting his name behind him, and he came in a full Release (the named, staged power-up a fighter calls aloud) with his Domain (the ground on which a high-Stage practitioner’s own law holds) rolling out ahead of him like a burning carpet and a lance of lit air four yards long running out from his right fist. He called its name so they could hear it in the next kingdom. The whole of Bakers’ Row had already run, apart from a Tinker Goblin of eighty-three called Mother Spragg. She had been making pots in that street for sixty-eight years, she had a stew on, and she had got up on a barrel in the middle of the road in her apron and a pair of smoked-glass goggles, holding up a pot lid in one small green hand.
“The Last Lid!” she screamed, because craftsmen shout the names of their works, and this was the only time anyone ever heard her raise her voice about one. “Finest Guild Work! Spragg’s of Pennycrown! Sixty-Eight Years no Complaints!”
The Comet of Tollgarth hit it at the speed of a falling star. A strike at that Grade against that lid should have gone through it as if the lid were not there, and through Mother Spragg and the barrel and the next nine houses. It stopped. All of it stopped, four yards of lit air folding up flat against a circle of pig iron stamped Marked, the lowest stamp the Guild Accord (the great coalition of guilds across many nations) has, and everything he had put into it went back the only way left to go. It took his arm out at the shoulder in a great red fan across the bakery fronts, and it put him on his back in the road with his plate burst open and his Domain going out around him like a kicked fire. Two hundred men stopped shouting. Mother Spragg climbed down off the barrel, and she looked at him for a while, and then she told him he had got blood on her step. She went back in and put the lid on the stew.
It is an ordinary lid. Anyone can see that, and the coil says so: Grade E, plain iron out of a bad pot. What goes under that lid stays exactly as it was, and nothing that means it harm gets in. She died that winter, in her sleep, at the bench, with a run of nine new lids around her that were all perfectly good lids. It has covered a family stew in Bakers’ Row for forty years, and nobody at that table has ever been poisoned, despite several sincere attempts, and the family will let you look at it for a copper. The Comet of Tollgarth lived, one-armed, to be a very thoughtful old man.
The trade has a term for such a thing, and I will now spend some time explaining why you will never make one.
What One Is
A Master Work is a piece that does what its Grade and material should not be able to, made once at the end of a lifetime, always Unique or Mythic, and named.
Each of those clauses has been fought over in the assay rooms, so here they are one by one.
What its Grade and material should not be able to. The law of Grade and Rarity holds everywhere else without exception: a material holds what it can hold, a maker cannot put in what she does not have, and a strike two Tiers over the proof passes through. A Master Work is the one standing exception. The coil (the brass assay instrument) reads it at its proper Grade, the material is the material, and it does the thing regardless. It usually does only one thing, the same one forever.
Made once. Nobody has made a second, and nobody has made one by trying harder. A maker who has done it can go on working, with sound hands and all her skill, and everything else she makes is merely excellent. Most say they felt something go out of them, and that they knew. Most die within the year. Mother Spragg lasted till the frost. The few who lived on tended to give up the trade and take up something like keeping bees.
At the end of a lifetime. Fifty years at one thing at the least, and most of them longer. A person’s skill rises with use and shows on the sheet (the window’s list of a person’s numbers, which only they can see) as one of the nine ranks, Initiate up through Paragon, and fifty years at one thing can make a Paragon of a trade with no Stage to speak of. Such a master is frightening. They usually still lose a fight, and a Master Work is what they have instead. It takes place when it takes place: no maker has yet known in advance which piece was going to be the one.
Always Unique or Mythic. Rarity is scarcity, and it comes with the definition. Mythic means a handful in the world, and Unique means one. A small number of pieces get written Mythic in place of Unique because a trade insists they are one of a family, such as the bench’s Fate Essence Drafts. A Master Work’s other rating, its Grade, can be anything down to the bottom of the letters, and it often is.
And named. By the maker if they had the breath, and otherwise by whoever the thing first astonished. The name goes on the roll with the Grade, and the clerk generally writes something like sic beside it.
Each area has its own. Every trade has a list and brags about it, and every region is sure its own list is the only real one. Bonded gear grows with its owner, and other gear does not, and a Master Work stays exactly as it was made however long anybody holds it. It has no opinions, and that sets it apart from a true relic of the Great Spirit War or the Physical Epochs, which reads as question marks to every appraiser, which cannot be copied, and which may have views about who holds it. A Master Work reads perfectly well:
[Appraisal: A]
Pot lid. Grade E. Rarity: Unique.
Stamp: Marked. Mark: Spragg, Pennycrown. Reads true.
Does: ???

The Famous Ones
Every piece below is real, by which I mean that someone will fight you about it. The makers are all long dead, and the stories have improved.





















































































































TradeThe pieceMaker and placeWhat it doesWhere it is nowPots and tinThe Last LidMother Spragg, Pennycrown, 672See aboveBakers’ Row, on a stewMasonryEnoughAldous Wray, AmblefordA doorstep of plain Greystone that nothing has yet broken. A drunk Expert of the Blue Herons broke his wrist on it at a spring fairThe assay room’s front door at Ambleford. Eleven treatises have been written about it, and people wipe their feetThe swordMajimak Mal (마지막 말), The Last WordGang Deok-su, smith of CheolsanBloom iron, Grade C, ugly as a fence post. A cut begun with it finishes. No guard, no ward and no parry has ever stopped a stroke once it started, and the stroke arrives where it was aimedNine owners on the public list, all of whom died of something else entirely, usually a person who wanted the swordArmorTwice ShyGreta Flint, a mail-knitter of the Slate RidgeA plain riveted shirt. Any blade or hand that has once marked it can never mark it again, so it only ever takes the one wound from each enemyLost at the Hallenfeld falls with its wearer. Divers go after it annuallyCrossbowsApologyIvo Marl, bowyer, the Golden HollowA cheap yew-and-sinew hunting bow. Its bolt goes where it was pointed, past wind and wards, whoever is holding it and whatever their Grade. Ivo said he was sorry, the first time he saw what it did, and the name stuckThree Stage X lords have died to it in the last century. Possession is a hanging matter in four realms and it is still somewhereDyeThe Standing RedMarget Loy, of the Cardmere dyersOne bolt of red wool that does not fade in Vantabriel light, the stolen dark of certain deep galleries where color and lamp both die. Under it, nothing else fades either. It has been cut into a bannerThe dyers’ guild hall at Cardmere, when it is not being carried into a Heart by somebody’s very expensive crew. Nine crews have died going down to get it backCordageDunn’s HitchOld Mabry Dunn, ropewalker on the salt roadA knot, in plain hemp, as far as anyone can see an ordinary hitch. It holds a footbridge at Bridgemarch that has been rotten for two centuries. Eleven masters have tied exact copies, and all of those came undoneThe bridge. The rope has been replaced around itNetsThe Patient NetA net-maker of the coast, name disputed by nine villagesHas never once come up empty. No fisher will agree to own it, because it always comes up with something, and the something has included a drowned bishop, a sealed chest that was reclaimed the same evening, and on one occasion the man’s brotherIt moves from village to village, by night, left on doorstepsMedicineKindlyGoodwife Annis Lark, a midwife of HallenfeldA bone suture needle. A wound closed with it does not fester and does not open again. The healing trade prices its work, so a rich fighter walks off what cripples a poor one for life, and she left this to the charity wardStill at the ward. It has been stolen eleven times, and has returned each time, by means no one will discuss, usually with the thief’s handBakingGrandmotherBerta Sowle, baker of AshburyA crock of sourdough leaven, unwoken work with no Stage in it at all. Bread raised on it feeds about twice what it should and has never gone moldy. War was fought over the crock in 644, briefly, between two towns with the same nameDivided by treaty. Each town has half, and each says the other half has diedPaper tagsThe SpareTam Ashlock, tag-cutter, WaxgateA ward tag, cut on a butcher’s wrapper in his last week. A tag is fueled once and burns once. This one has fired some four thousand times and it is still in dateHeld at the Lamp-Wardens’ Hall. They have tried very hard to find out what it is costing someoneChantThe Last VerseAilith Moor, hedge-singer of the Painted RiversSix lines to an old tune that close a wound of grief. It works in any mouth, woken or not, with or without a Crystal, once for each singer. People who hear it cannot quite remember it. Written down, it has never workedThe roll enters it as Unique and the assay room would like somebody to explain how they are supposed to stamp itThe ledgerThe True BookMerrin Dane, of a Kingsbridge counting-houseA plain account book. Nothing false can be entered in it: the ink will not take. Every merchant in the Center has wanted to hold it, and no one has wanted to be the person who keeps itHeld by the Accord, in a locked room, by a committee that has stopped opening itThe stoveStill WarmA ward-cutter of the Cobalt March, by reputeA parish warm stone that has held its heat for ninety years without refilling, in a village that has since forgotten that this is unusualThe middle of the road, in Bearhold’s lower town. People boil eggs on itThe benchThe Turned CoinAlchemarch Hesper Ludd, of Candle WharfA Fate Essence Draft, of which more below. For forty-one years no wager, ford or lawsuit went against the Thresh horse-coper who drank itDrunk. He died at ninety in a scarlet bed with a county in his debt, and no one has yet collected from his grandchildren
On the bragging. Craftsmen shout the names of their works and brag about their guild marks at all times, and a Master Work is the one thing every one of them will bring up in a tavern within the hour, as evidence that their trade is the serious one. A cooper of Raftwick will tell you with tears in his eyes that the barrel at Thornhaven is the finest thing ever done by human hands. It holds water. He will explain to you what is remarkable about that, and it will take him all evening.
Why They Cannot Be Ordered
Everyone has tried. Great houses keep old-maker’s pensions: a fine stipend and a warm room in the family’s own grounds for any master past seventy-five, with every material they could want, a guard on the door and a clerk to write down anything they say. It looks like charity from outside, and the makers are all perfectly aware of what it is. Some of them have got ten very good years out of it and a number of excellent chairs, and at least two have spent their last winter making something deliberately appalling and leaving it on the steward’s pillow.
Why it happens is the oldest argument in the Measurewrights’ hall. The favored account at present runs like this. A soul that has worked one way all its life hardens along that way, woken or unwoken, in what the trade calls grain. Carry, in any rendered material, is a law something survived into existence and which came along into the stock. So a Master Work would be carry with no rendering: fifty or eighty years of one person’s grain, the whole law of how they worked, gone out through the hands in one stroke into whatever was on the bench, and held there by what the thing is rather than by what it is made of. It explains the once, and it explains why they die. It does not explain the lid. The Guild’s best instrument finds no Essence in the lid at all, and four Measurewrights have had it on their tables and gone home to think. The account’s great defender, Magister Rule of Sealhall, held that a person could therefore be assayed for one in advance, and he assayed some three hundred old craftsmen and published his predictions. None of them made anything. The woman who cleaned the instrument did.
What a forger does. A fake Master Work cannot be disproved by assay, since the coil reads a real one as an ordinary thing. It can be disproved by trying it, and sellers are very good at explaining why you should not. A good forger beats a weak appraiser, and in this one corner of the market a good story beats a good appraiser. Every fair has a stall with the True Hammer of somebody on it.
How one changes hands. Rarely. A merchant’s title caps the Rarity he may sell, so a lawful sale of a Mythic piece needs an Archmaster’s token and a Unique one needs a Paragon’s, and there are not many of those. So they go the other ways: inheritance, marriage, murder. A great many famous pieces are held by people who are wondering how to keep them, and there is a list of past owners on all of them that a sensible person reads to the end.
The Fate Essence Draft
At the bench a Master Work is a Draft, and every alchemist alive dreams of pouring one kind. A Fate Essence Draft bottles a share of the Plane of Fate, the control of Attraction Force (the pull that makes a name, a bond or a vow take hold) and Obsession Force (that same pull when it will not let go), and through those two the workings of reality itself: the manipulation of probabilities to work outside what reality already knows. Real Fate Arts are rare and mostly by bloodline. For nearly everyone else alive, the only ways to touch Fate are a blessing (see Blessings and Curses) or one of these. It lends the touch. It no more makes a Fate Path practitioner than a borrowed horse makes a cavalryman, and it attaches readily to an oath. There are a handful in the world at any time, and there has never been a price. Great families have spent a county to stand near one.
[Draft: unnamed lot, sealed]
[Appraisal: S]
[Grade: B. Rarity: Mythic.]
[Does: ???]

The stock. Nothing in a monster’s stone will do it, because a stone is Core and nothing else. The Attraction Layer is the part of a soul that holds its share of fate, and the only Layer that has ever reached a bench was shaved off a dead practitioner’s Crystal by a dresser and sold in a twist of waxed paper (see barber’s curl). So the grandest bottle in the trade begins in the same back room as the Dead Man’s Cordial. The masters who will talk about it say a great Spirit Beast’s Layer would serve as well, and that they are still waiting for someone to bring one up the stair. No Alchemarch has entered the purchase in a day book.
Why it is the hardest
Every other Master Work is a person doing the thing they have always done, one more time, and something happening. This one has five separate problems, and each of them has killed somebody.
It has no Wellspring. Each of the seven stages of the Great Work takes its law from a Wellspring of its own, excepting Conjunction, the stage where two things that pull toward each other close the gap, which runs on Attraction alone. A Fate charge is a Conjunction with nothing to wed: the maker takes the charge up to the Wedding and has it marry the pull itself. So the bench has no Authorization to invoke and nothing that already knows the maker, and the discount a harmonized alchemist gets on her own Wellspring’s Drafts does not apply.
The boundary has nothing to hold. A chain with no Boundary role is refused at the Bench outright, because a transformation without limits does not stop when the intended material is consumed. Odds have no edge. There is no glyph that says here to a probability, and the masters who have got anywhere have mostly done it by binding the working to a named person or an oath, which gives it somewhere to end. An unbounded lot is the bad day described below, and on a bad day it gets into the whole street.
The maker is in the vessel. The Essence Core (the seat of a soul’s own nature) seeds whatever it is broadcasting into the material, so an alchemist’s state is a working variable in any Draft. In this one it is the whole of the Draft. A maker who wants the thing to succeed has poured wanting. Wanting is Attraction with a grip on it, and that is the road to Obsession Force. The maker has to arrive at the last pour after a lifetime’s ambition having stopped caring, and nobody has found a way of doing this on purpose, and the fact that you are trying is the entire difficulty.
It takes a walk nobody takes. The received account is that a master has to have walked Conjunction twice, once at Flourishing, Stage IV, in the first round of the Work and again at Dissonance, which is Stage XI, or else to have come as far in grain with no Crystal at all. That cuts the field to very few, and they are all very old, and each of them has been in a house’s pension for some time.
You cannot test it. Any other Draft can be assayed. A Fate lot reads at whatever its energy says, usually something modest. The coil cannot see luck, a lucky man cannot prove it, and the only trial is to drink it, which consumes the sample. Nobody at the bench has ever known whether they had succeeded. Several of the most celebrated lots may be nothing. And anyone who pours one is, by the nature of the stock, surrounded by odds that have stopped behaving, in a room where everything now either goes unusually right or unusually wrong, for years.
The ones that are known
The Turned Coin, by Alchemarch Hesper Ludd of Candle Wharf (an Alchemarch being the conferred honor of perhaps forty people in the four quarters, whose signature the Bench accepts without assay). She poured it in the last year of her life and sold it to a Thresh horse-coper named Oswin Gant for a horse. She was, by the account of her Luteboy (the apprentice who mixes the clay that seals a vessel), laughing at the time. The Coin is the only lot in the record whose effect is agreed.
Nine Mornings, by Alchemarch Ishbel Tarn of Vaultmere, was given as a dowry into a great house of the South two centuries ago and has never been unsealed. The family has prospered without a break in all that time, through three wars and more than one change of crown. Nobody knows whether possession is the effect, whether it is doing anything, or whether they are just very good at what they do, and nobody in the family will risk opening it to see. It has its own guard, its own chapel, and a steward who has gone slightly strange.
The Even Hand, by a master of the lineage halls named Wen Baozhi, after forty-one years of seclusion on a mountain. It was drunk by a magistrate in 590 who had asked to be fair. For the eleven years that remained to him, every judgment he gave came out exactly right, and he could not make any other kind. He sentenced his own son on the Thursday.
The ones who died trying








































WhoWhereWhat happenedAlchemarch Bram HurstCutwall, the Amber Cities, 602Poured it wrong and got Obsession Force. Every member of the workshop now comes back to that bench, every day, and they have since their retirements. Their children come. The city has bricked up the door three times. The workshop spends the rest of its days unable to stop returning, the Bench’s note says, and the Bench’s own inspector is in there nowSister Perpetua HaleCobblers’ Row, Alabaster, 617A Boundary failure. For nine days everything on the row went to its least likely outcome, and every die came up six, every ladder fell and every cough went to the lung. Three hundred and six people died of coincidence, and she died first, eleven ways in one afternoon, and it was noted that a roof tile had to wait its turnThe Carmine Twins, Odo and Oda ThorneWindstair, the Violet PeaksThought two makers could divide the wanting between them. One poured while the other wanted. Each now has the other’s luck, and neither has been seen for long in the same room since. It is said the first one is still alive, and the second one is whyMaster Tobias WykeA cellar in Kingsbridge, 633Believed he had done it and drank to prove it. Crossed the road, in a very good mood. A wain, a falling sign and a horse, in that order. The vial was analyzed and contained a good claretHouse Morrow, entireThe Midmarch, 601 to 604Never went near a bench. They fought the three-year War of the Stoppered Inch against the toll-kings of Tollgarth over a vial of Fate Essence Draft stolen out of a dowry. Nine thousand dead, two crowns gone and every Morrow but one in the ground. The vial, when it was finally recovered, proved to be cough syrupAt least thirty othersEverywhereThe Bench does not keep the list. The families do, and they are proud of it
Forged lots are the most profitable counterfeit in the world, since nothing can prove them false. A buyer who has bad luck afterward is told it is working in a way he does not yet understand. There has been more than one lord who took a bottle of colored water, marched on a neighbor out of sheer confidence, and won.
What the Title Has to Do With It
Almost nothing, and the assay rooms have been saying so for centuries, to no effect whatever. People hear Master Work and assume it is the piece that makes you a Master. The two words have only a spelling in common.
The title. Initiate, Apprentice, Journeyman, Adept, Expert, Master, Grandmaster, Archmaster, Paragon: the same nine in every guild, grading how far that guild trusts you in your trade (see The Tiered Path). Master is the sixth of them. You earn it by certified work and it lets you make up to a stated Grade. A title is other people’s opinion, which is why it sits on a silver token at the belt and appears nowhere on your window.
The rung. A house’s own ladder has a Master of the Circle on it, who scribes and seals and carries the liability. It is a job in one workshop, and it is a different thing again.
The Work. A Master Work is an event. It happens to the person who has the fifty years, and the token at their belt has no bearing. Aldous Wray never rose past Journeyman. He had a bad opinion of the Masons’ examiners and declined to sit. Mother Spragg held an Apprentice’s token in tin for sixty years, having failed the Journeyman’s board twice for bad temper. Goodwife Lark had no token of any kind. A good many Grandmasters and Archmasters have lived out a magnificent career of sealed, certified, perfectly correct work at the top of their guild, and gone to their pyres with no Master Work behind them, knowing exactly who down the street had got one with a pot.
The law, such as it is. A smith’s title caps the Grade she may lawfully make, and a merchant’s caps the Rarity he may lawfully sell. A Master Work is the one thing no title caps, because a Grade E lid is well inside an Initiate’s license, and whatever it does is nobody’s license at all. The assay rooms have never agreed what to stamp on one. Usually the proper stamp for its Grade goes on, with Unique beside it, and the clerk’s handwriting gets worse.
Which means. A guild can certify everything but this, so every guild has a very awkward relationship to it. They claim each one as theirs as soon as the maker is dead. Guild halls in every trade carry the name of some cantankerous old person whom they refused to promote, in gold letters, over the door.
What They Call It













































WhoThe wordThe argumentAccord assay roomsA piece outside the tableIt should not exist, and it is entered under protestNorthern craftsmenThe Last One; “her Last One”; she did her LastSaid with the hat off. Generally followed by a drinkMotoSaigo no shigoto (最後の仕事), the last workA person’s whole labor discharged at once. Their own house’s word for labor is close enough that they do not find it surprisingMahuoYujak (유작), the work left behindProperty of the Dynasty, and of the maker’s district, with a stone put upThe lineage hallsJuézuò (绝作), the work that endsThey add it to the family’s title, even if the maker was the cookThe MarrowkinA true cutTheir forges have a list, and they do not discuss it. They will say that a master’s last blade was one the body permittedThe KeldA thing that sat with its makerThe only respectable kind of object

materials,-alchemy--and--trade/alchemy/m.content:
Where the stone sits, what it fetches by the beast’s own Grade and Level, how fast it dies, what the bench makes of it, what happens if you eat it, the crime that looks exactly like it, and the people who live off all of the above

One stone, of the wyrm called Grandfather Rent. Received of: the rope.
Receipt in the Verath hall’s day book for the harvest of 677, in the hand of a clerk who resigned the same afternoon

For sixty years an SS-Grade earth wyrm called Grandfather Rent took one wagon in ten off the salt road below Verath, regular as a landlord, and the bounty on him had reached twelve hundred gold and been painted on every rim-town door when a crew called the Copper Lanterns finally killed him in the summer of 677, under a sky the color of brass, at a cost of five of their eleven. It took three days to cut him open. The stone came out of him at dusk, a fist of amber glass with a slow light turning in it, worth more than the town: twenty thousand gold by private treaty before anyone had said his name, and the name would have doubled it. The six survivors carried it up to the hunting hall behind every drum in Verath, and they were on their third keg and their second knife fight over who had got the kill, when somebody noticed they had put it down.
It was on the hall roof. It was in the right fist of the crew’s porter, a Bearkin woman the size of a cider press, who had hauled their tent poles and their wounded for six years. Under the Accord’s porter clause she was entered on the crew’s instrument along with the rope, as nemo, nobody, and so she had no share in the wyrm she had bled for and no name on any roll, and people called her Nem. She stood up there against the sunset with the amber light coming through her fingers and her mouth open, holding the stone an inch from her teeth, and she told all of Verath in a voice you could hear on the salt road that she would very much like to discuss terms.
Everybody knows what comes out of a person who goes raw on a stone that size, which is to say nobody does. Most die. The rest might be anything, standing on your roof, with sixty years of a wyrm’s tempering going off inside them at once. So the town stopped. For three days the Charter’s reeves, the hall’s master, the crew, an envoy from a Midmarch king and four factors stood in the square negotiating with a porter on a roof, while the sausage-sellers set up and the bookies gave nine to one she would swallow by Sunday. It was the hall’s advocate who found the real difficulty, around noon of the second day, and he sat down on the steps and put his head in his hands. By law she could not be a party. She could not sign, could not be bound, could not receive consideration and could not be bribed, because she was equipment, and the whole Sealed Charter of the Concord was being held hostage by a length of rope.
They settled the only way the formulary allows. The safe-conduct out of Verath, which is still framed in the Waxgate law library, is made out to “the rope, and whatever it may be carrying.” Nem came down off the roof with the stone in her shirt and walked north to Brokencollar with forty porters behind her, and she opened an inn there, and it has never once been robbed. The stone is still in a strongbox over the bar. Her granddaughter keeps the bar now, and bookies still quote odds on the box. A commoner holding a big monster core is the most frightening sight a lord will ever see, and this page is about why, and about the much larger number of people for whom it is merely Tuesday’s wages.
At a Glance
What it is. A monster’s core, which crews and renderers call the stone, is in a way its Soul Crystal: the seat of the beast’s nature, hardened over its life into glassy stuff in its own color. It is the lawful Crystal Draw (Grade IV stock, rendered from something that carried a soul) of The Standing Index, and worth more the stronger the monster.
How it looks. A lump of colored glass with a slow movement of light inside it, warm to the hand, with fine bands in it like the rings of a tree. The color is the hue of the Wellspring the beast ran on: ember orange off Pyreveil, the deepest teal off Thaloré, ochre-gold off Basilithe, chlorophyll green off Verdantia. A dead stone is gray.
What it costs. A crew, usually. See below for what it pays them.
What it becomes. An alchemist renders it into Essence Drafts, about a dozen doses at the grade it serves, drunk as a course to feed tempering and lift the drinker’s Level (the melting-down and rebuilding of the soul, layer by layer, that refines Essence and leaves the body stronger and carrying Traits). Swallowed raw it gives everything at once.
Example. Tib Hask, porter, goes back into a Green Sigil gallery for the C-Grade stone the crew’s captain left in a Greater Wolf. It goes in his shirt, walnut-sized and faintly warm. The hall’s clerk writes him a chit with the date and the beast’s name, and a rendering house by the hall pays him four and a half gold, which is more than he has held in his life. He spends one night with the stone against his skin before he sells it, and for a week afterward he does not like dogs.
Where It Sits
An animal has a soul with all three layers, as the register’s table sets out, and it lives on the first of them. Its Essence Core (the seat of its own nature) is awake, and its Aether Shell, the door through which Aether comes in and a working goes back out into the world of matter, is sealed, the same as an unwoken farmer’s. What a beast takes in from the ground and from its kills has nowhere to go. So the Essence Core lays it down, kill by kill and year by year, as hard bands around the old center, and that is the stone. Evolution or a Level threshold may crack the seal, which is when a beast starts to show an aura and put something behind its howl, and even then the crack is a small vent on a great store. Monsters gain Levels by killing, each other included, and an old one has done a great deal of tempering of its own, all of it still in there.























































Kind of beastWhere the stone sitsWhat the cutter has to knowNatural beasts and the Scourge-bornBehind the breastbone, up against the heartThe easy kind. Cut in under the last rib and reach up. A big one needs someone on the ribs with a barWell-spawn (creatures bred at a Well, born masked)Under the mask’s line, in the chestThe hall pays on the mask and the house pays on the stone, so a hunter may be paid twice. Break the mask of anything bred in the Deeps or the Heart and the body comes apart into raw Aether and goes down the Well with its stone. A deep crew that wants the core has to kill the thing the long way, mask whole, and this is how deep crews get rich or stop being deep crewsWyrms and the draconic lineLow in the neck, in a sack of its own behind the second heartDig with a crew and shore the cut. The body stays hot for days, and every wyrm on the Scourge gets opened before it is cold, by whoever is nearestSerpents, sea serpents, the long onesTwo thirds of the way down, never where the last person saidThe stone shifts when the beast feeds. Cutters walk along it with a forkHydras and the many-headedIn the trunk, and in none of the headsEvery song about a hydra is wrong on this pointSpirit BeastsA body may hold one, and many leave no body at allKilling one for its stone is legal, usually fatal, and the sort of thing a whole valley will rememberElementalsThe whole thing is built around it, and it is the one solid part when the rest stopsMind the falling lavaLiving Armor and other constructsNone of their own, as a rule. Whatever was seated in them to make them goSometimes a stone, sometimes a Crystal. See the crime, belowThe LichA Crystal, because it used to be a person, and the phylactery holds itTaking it is the crime, below, and no court has yet decided how to feel about that
Monsters on the Three Roads
A monster that has cracked its seal leans on one layer of its soul, as a person does, and the register’s Leans on line says which. How the thing lives sets the lean. The kind of Wellspring it fed on only tips it, so a stone’s color tells you its Wellspring and never, by itself, its road. The lean decides how the thing fights, and it decides what its stone is made of, because the Essence Core bands up whatever the beast lived on.

































The roadHow commonWhat they areWhat is in the stoneWhat the bench makes of itBody monstersThe common kind, nine stones in ten on any hall’s counterDrakes, wyrms, crushers, the tunneling things, anything whose whole argument is hide, weight and heat. They pack raw Aether (mana) in a cracked Shell and hit with itBanded Core like any other stone, with the beast’s packed Charge set into it. A Body monster holds raw Aether in its cracked Shell all its life, and what it held sets into the bands, unrefined, as a hard mineral weight. The bands are thick, the stone is heavy for its size and it comes out of the carcass hotSalts. The set Charge parts out as heavy Salt ash, so the Parting throws far more white ash than Essence, and the house pours it as Salt fractions, which pack a Body fighter’s Shell. A fight Salt goes down like a burn, and its crash is cramps and feverSpirit monstersRarer. A good hall sees a few in a seasonWraiths, mourners, the things that eat memory, anything that goes past your armor to get at you. They work on souls and leave the furniture aloneEssence (spiritual energy), already refined by something that was not you. Fine close bands, cool to the hand, lighter than it looksCore stock, the richest there is, and the heaviest in carry. This is the stock a Spirit fighter wants, and the lot a tally-man watches hardestFate monstersThe rarest, and the most feared. Most crews never meet one and are gladA beast that turns bad luck on its hunters. The straps give, the bowstring is damp, the caller’s voice cracks on the word, and the thing itself has hardly moved. The Hask Moor drovers call any such animal a jinx and will not say what it looks likeCore like any other, wrapped in a thin skin of grown Layer, since a Fate line’s Attraction Layer thickens where every other beast’s stays thin. The skin has no color. Coins dropped near it land on edgeThe Layer reagent. The skin is shaved off and sold as Layer, and no bench can tell it from Layer shaved off a dead practitioner, so no realm licenses it and every ounce moves on the black market. The Core under it renders as ordinary stock, with luck in the carry that nobody has found a way to wash out. The reagent refills nothing and is no fight Draft: a Fate fighter’s reserve is Essence, and what she drinks in a fight is Core stock, the same as a Spirit fighter
What the hunters say. A Body monster kills the crew in front of it. A Spirit monster kills the one at the back who was not warded. A Fate monster kills nobody, and the crew is dead by Thursday anyway, of a wheel, a well-rope and a kitchen fire. The Saffron Hoods took a jinx-hare the size of a calf on the Hask Moor in 695, clean, with no losses, and sold the skin off its stone in a cellar in Verath for eleven hundred gold. Within the month four of the seven were dead of separate accidents and the buyer’s house had burned. The hall posts no bounty on a Fate monster. It posts a warning, and the bookies will not quote it.
The breakthrough bottle follows the road. A breakthrough Draft has to supply the Catalyst the buyer’s own road demands, so the house asks which layer the client leans on before it quotes. A Body buyer’s bottle is poured on a Salt base, out of Body stones. A Spirit buyer’s is poured on Core stock, the finer the better. A Fate buyer’s needs the Layer reagent, which makes it the dearest of the three and the only one that is a hanging matter before the cork is drawn. A soul that walks two roads buys for the one it leads on.
Reading the road off a stone. Weigh it, and feel it. Heavy and warm is a Body stone, light and cool is a Spirit stone, and a stone that makes the dice on the next table behave oddly should be put down and reported, which it never is. The price table below is the same for all three by Grade, and a Fate skin sells apart from its stone, by private treaty, for more than the stone.
Cutting. A stone comes out hot from the bigger beasts. A crew’s cutter, generally whoever has the strongest stomach and worst sense of smell, uses a long hook and a leather sling for anything at A or above, because skin contact with a fresh one starts the leak (see Keeping it, below). Most stones go home in somebody’s shirt regardless, since a shirt is what people have.
What It Is Worth
The stone is read off the beast. The coil (the brass assay instrument) reads a stone and a carcass at the beast’s own Grade and Level, the way it reads any lot on a counter, and that read sets the Stage the stone serves and what it fetches. The Commission posts every beast at a Grade of its own as well, E to EX, the same letters lords post bounties by, and the whole trade uses the posted Grade as shorthand for danger and price, because for most beasts the two line up. Every table on this page is written in that shorthand. Older hall rolls give the same rows as Threat Tiers, T1 to T9, and a hunter of the old school still calls an S-Grade beast a T6.
Where they part, the coil wins, because the posted letter also counts what a beast does to a crew, a road or a coast, and none of that is in the stone. A Lamp-drinker is posted at S for what it does in the dark, and it comes off a floor of D-Grade stock with a hardest blow at Hamlet-bane, so it reads B at the very best and pays out a hen’s egg, whatever the hunters expected for a Gold Sigil. The Leviathan is posted at EX for its reach, its plate and its tie to the deep, and its hardest surge is a March-bane’s, so its stone reads S to SS and serves Stages VIII to X. A very large stone it is, and nobody will sell it to you.
The price table. Prices are raw, on the coil, at a renderer’s door, for a clean stone with a hall’s chit. Monsters level and evolve, so the coil prices the beast on the day it died rather than the row its kind usually sits in. An old wolf with a name can fetch the row above. The figures here are those of What Things Cost, and the rest of the page explains them.































































































Posted Grade, as the shorthandStage it usually servesSizeAt the doorA course poured from it, licensedRarityWhat that meansEI, MurmuringA pea3 to 5 silver10 silverCommonA laborer’s week, from something that had been at the henhouse. Children hunt these, and some of them come homeDII, WellingA hazelnut12 to 18 silver30 silverCommonAbout a laborer’s monthCIII, AscensionA walnut3 to 6 gold7½ goldUncommonA soldier’s half-year and a crew’s first good nightBIV, FlourishingA hen’s egg8 to 15 gold22½ goldRareMost of a laborer’s year. A village remembers who brought it homeAV to VII, and the coil tells you whichA plum30 to 300 goldAbout 68 to 600 goldRareThe bottom buys two horses and the top buys a clerk’s four yearsSVIII to XA woman’s fist800 to 8,000 gold1,800 to 16,200 goldVery RareMore than the crew’s home village will see in a generationSSXI and XIIA big man’s fist20,000 gold and upNot quotedLegendaryBy private treaty, with an armed escort and several new friendsXXIII and XIVReported as a child’s headNot quotedNot quotedMythicUnder the Obsidian Seal, the Accord’s black classification, and never on a counterEXXV and XVI, on paperNobody has saidNot quotedNot quotedUniqueThe Commission posts the Leviathan, the Lich and the Kraken here, and the coil reads each of them lower, the Lich at the necromancer’s own Stage. If you have one of these, you are reading the wrong page
A house pays between a third and a half of what the course will fetch poured, and a stone rendered in a hunting town sells a third under the city price, having been nearer the beast. A famous monster’s core carries a premium for the name, on top of any bounty, and the bounty is usually the smaller part. Hide, bone and scale sell separately (Hide, Horn and Bone), for about as much again while fresh, falling every day from the kill.
What the shares look like. A crew argues about all of it. Level moves by danger overcome, so killing something stronger moves it more than a hundred weak kills, and everybody wants to have landed the blow. The money follows the instrument, which by custom gives the captain two shares, the caller and the fork one and a half, each fighter one, and the porter a wage and nothing else. The hall takes its tithe at the door. The hall’s own tally of crew arguments that have ended in a killing, by Grade, is a very popular document in Verath.
How Fast It Dies
A stone begins to die when the beast does. With no heart behind it and no ground feeding it, Essence seeps out through its skin, the outer bands first, and the color drains inward. Small stones go fast and great stones hardly seem to go at all. Rendering houses read the bands with a glass and a coil, and they pay by what is left.



























































Posted GradeHolds full forHalf gone byGray and dead byEA day or twoA weekA monthDThree daysA fortnightTwo monthsCA fortnightTwo monthsA yearBTwo monthsA yearFive yearsAA yearFive yearsA generationSFive yearsThirty yearsA long lifetimeSSThirty yearsTwo centuriesNot yet observedX and EXNot observed to fade. Some are said to have grown
By that table Nem’s stone has lost a shaving off its outermost band. The bookies have not revised their odds.
Keeping it. Salt and cold about double the times above, which is why stones from the Cold Larder go to the hall in a sack of snow. Heat halves them. On ground of its own Wellspring (rich with the same kind of Aether it ran on) a stone stops fading altogether and may even take a little back, so the richest vaults in the world are built on top of worked Cores (a Core, in the street’s sense, being a site where one Wellspring’s Aether pools, and worth more than the entire vault). On ground its Wellspring hates, or the ground of one of its Contraries (each entry in the Sixty names both), it dies twice as fast. In a shirt, against a living person, it leaks into you.
A stale stone is the dangerous one. What seeps away is Essence. The beast’s nature stays behind in the bands, so a half-dead stone renders fewer doses and every dose has twice the wolf in it. Stale stock dressed with a fresh color is to the core trade what spoiled Cutwater is to the apothecary, and people who buy cheap courses from a stranger’s cart are the ones who end up living in the barn.
Gray stones have no Essence worth pouring. They still go to the ward trade by weight, where carry is all anyone is buying (carry being what a creature’s life leaves in the material rendered out of it), and a child in a rim town can get a few copper for a sackful.
Why the sizes matter, for those who ask. A Measurewright will tell you the fade runs like a pot cooling, since what a stone holds goes as its bulk and what it loses goes as its skin. Double the width and you have eight times the stock behind four times the skin. Stronger stones are also denser, and that does the rest. This account is correct as far as it goes, and it does not explain the X-Grade stone at Sealhall that has been putting on weight.
The Bench: Rendering
The full chain is in Alchemetrica, under The Core at the Bench. Here is what a client should understand before paying for it.

The read. Beast, grade, carry and age, off the bands. The Appraisal skill and the coil, and a good renderer’s nose. A careful house enters the beast’s name and the crew’s chit against the lot.
The burn and the Parting. The stone goes through the first Turnings of the bench, burned and taken and parted, and what comes off the Parting is Essence with the beast’s nature still in it.
The washings. Here is the entire art. Each washing lowers the carry and loses Essence with it, and the house decides with the client how much wolf to leave in.
The pour. By the stone’s road: a Body stone pours mostly as Salts for the Shell, a Spirit stone as Core stock, and a Fate stone as Core stock once its skin is off. Core stock refills a Spirit reserve and a Fate one alike, both being Essence, and no house pours a fight Draft for the Fate road. Bottled to the Stage it serves, with the beast’s Grade on the seal, and usually the beast’s name, because people like to know.


































The lotWashingsDoses from one stoneCarryWho buys itHeavyOneAbout sixteenMarked to heavy. A fast melt and a good deal of animalHunters, soldiers, people in a hurry, sect brawlers who want the appetiteHouseTwo or threeAbout twelve, the figure the price table assumesLight to markedEveryone with a purse. The backbone of every apothecary’s yearLightFive or moreSix to eight, at twice the price a doseNear cleanThe rich, for their children
The course
A course is twelve doses, one every few days up to the melt. Essence refines in the Soul Crystal, the body gains, Level climbs, and a neighbor who did it the slow way on a good hill gets the same lines on the window in four times the years. What the course gives is Level; the Catalyst that opens the next Stage is a dearer bottle, or a life.
[Course: Greater Wolf, grade III · dose 9 of 12]
[Melt: ████████░░ 80%]
[Tempering Clarity: rising]
[Level: 41 → 44]

Doses are priced in The Common Drafts, which also says what a course of one beast does to a fighter who runs on another Wellspring, and which layer of the soul each stock reaches. Everything a course does shows on the window, with one exception.
Identity Contamination
The window does not report it. The soul making the report is the soul it happened to, and it feels fine.
Identity Contamination is the beast’s way of being coming across with its Essence, a band at a time. A Trait is a law a soul survived into existence, and carry is a law something else survived. A melt cools around whatever seeds it finds, so tempering on core stock grows parts of a person around an animal’s convictions. Serious houses keep a tally of doses against each client’s name, and every other house keeps a story about someone who growls.






























Doses from one kind of beastWhat showsWhat the family saysUp to a dozenDreams of running, or of the dark under a gallery. A new taste in meatGrowing boyTwo or three coursesHabits. Sleeps at noon, circles a room before sitting, cannot pass a carcass without lookingTakes after his uncleFive or moreAppetite and reflex. Reads a dinner table for who is weakest. Bites, once, and apologizesWe do not take him to the Harvest SupperPast thatAn Essence Core that can no longer say which convictions are its own. They remain very sure, about thingsNobody has asked the family
Different beasts bring different weather, and buyers shop accordingly.













































StockWhat comes with itWho wants itGreater WolfThe pack. Fierce loyalty, hatred of being alone, a nose for who has gone lameSworn companies, whose captains prefer itHellhound, ManticoreHeat, spite, enjoymentDuelists, and people who are about to lose them as friendsMourning PikePatience and long still hours. Other people’s memoriesAssassins, widowsTolling CrabA love of one exact pitch, and a hard shell in every senseSealwrights, who deny itGlarewingQuick, bright, cannot abide a closed roomCouriers, tournament fliersLamp-drinkerDislike of light. A gentle wish that you would put that outNobody admits to itA wyrmHoarding, long sleep, the conviction that all of this is yoursGreat houses, who see no problem
Mixed courses do not cancel. They argue, and the drinker gets to listen.
Going Raw
A stone can be swallowed or broken raw, with no alchemist and no fee. The trade’s phrase is going raw, and it is used mostly of the dead.
Everything arrives at once: every band the beast laid down in its life, all the Essence and all of the nature, with no Parting and no washing, into a Soul Crystal that was built to hold a good deal less. The Crystal goes to the melt on the spot. If the stone is near the eater’s own Stage the odds are merely bad. If it is several Stages above, the Shell scalds, the Crystal cracks along whatever it was feeling at the time, and what comes out is built on that.





















Of a hundred, by the Verath hall’s count over two centuriesWhat happenedAbout seventyDead inside the hour. Fire in the chest, blood from every opening, a coat of the beast’s color roaring out of them and then going outAbout twentyAlive and wrong. Some are the beast, more or less, in a person’s body, and some are a person who can feel it pacing. The body may change to suitAbout tenWhole, or near enough, several Stages up on one bad afternoon
The wrong ones are the ones crews tell stories about. Hob Wendle of Rimward ate an S-Grade stone off a tunneling thing at Nine Wells in 640, and came up three Stages with the strength of a siege ram and the need to dig. He dug out through the floor of his own house that night and through two neighbors’ cellars by morning. He was still recognizably Hob, he kept apologizing, and his voice could be heard coming up through the well for most of a year.
The whole ones are why it keeps happening. Sister Wenlyn Oake, a kitchen servant at a sect in the Violet Peaks, swallowed an A-Grade stone in 655 with the elders’ dogs at the door, and walked out through them at Stage VI with a Level the swallow itself had paid for, since nothing she had ever faced was as dangerous as that stone, a Skill column with nothing in it but Soup, and a coat in a blazing kingfisher blue. It takes a bold person to hunt somebody like that, and the sect did, for eleven years. A raw climb has all the gaps of a bought one, with no Release until it is found and mastered by fighting, and the hunters come quickly.
Why lords care. A raw stone in a commoner’s fist is the one thing a lord’s whole apparatus of grain, land, debt and Draft supply has no hold on, and it costs nothing to threaten. Most realms therefore hang people for holding an unrendered stone above B without a hall’s chit, and lords have burned villages on the rumor of one. Nem’s terms have been studied by more peasants than the catechism.
The Crime
A Crystal cut from a dead practitioner makes the strongest Draft of all. It is the worst crime in every realm, and the most profitable, and it is why Grade IV has never balanced on the Index. No monster ever tempered as deliberately as a person who spent a lifetime at it. A beast lays down what happens to it, while a practitioner chooses, for decades, what to become, and that is what the buyer gets.
The Dead Man’s Cordial, as the trade says when it is sure of the room, runs several times the price of a core lot of the same grade. It tempers faster than anything alive. It also carries a person, identity-shaped and complete, and a drinker may wake with a stranger’s way of seeing, a grudge against someone they have never met, or a very good left-hand parry and a language nobody at home can place. Buyers report that it is good company.
How it passes. A practitioner’s Crystal comes out with all three of its layers grown, the Essence Core, the Aether Shell and the Attraction Layer. A beast had all three as well, but its Shell never opened wide and its Layer never thickened, so an ordinary stone is banded Core and nothing else. A Body monster’s stone is no exception to that: the Charge it packed has set into the Core’s bands as Salt, and there is no Shell on it to shave. The thin skin on a Fate monster’s stone is the one exception. So the first job is done by a dresser, who shaves away what remains of the Shell and Layer, buffs the surface, and stains in some bands. The shavings have a market of their own, and The Common Drafts says what it buys. After that it reads the same on the coil. A rendering house can still spot one on the bench if it cares to look, and the two-instrument comparison described in The Standing Index would catch it on the shelf: the coil’s Holding and the fork’s density will not reconcile. Most benches own one instrument. Then there is a chit that says wyvern, from a factor three towns away, and a house that has decided not to ask.
Where they come from. Undeclared wars, first of all, since a declared one has a quartermaster counting. Battlefields after dark, behind the licensed rendering houses, which may take the flesh, the bone and the residue of the war dead and never the Crystal (see The Crossing). Hanged men whose families cannot pay a guard. Duelists’ graves. Sect elders, sometimes, from their own students. Famous fighters above all, because a Crystal with a name on it sells for what a kingdom sells for, and every generation has its scandal in which a great family’s fortunes improved abruptly after a war.
The wake. This crime is why a practitioner’s body is never left alone. Across most of the Inner World the kin sit an armed wake, weapons across their knees and lamps lit, in the dead one’s school colors, until the Crystal has been broken by a relative’s hand or the pyre has burned down, and the wake is often the best party the family has thrown in years. A Moto house speaks to its dead and keeps them under guard while it does. Marrowkin enter the Crystal in the Tally. Kharven families have been known to sell theirs quietly and hold the wake anyway. A person who dies with no one to sit up with them is what the night-cutters look for.
The law. Every realm hangs for it, and most hang the bench and the buyer too on paper. In practice the cutter hangs. The three old warrants for rendering the human dead (see The Standing Index) reach the body and stop at the Crystal, and a surprising number of great houses have had that explained to them at length, under seal, without consequence.
Penning, its cousin, is lawful in some places and ought to worry you more. Monsters gain Levels by killing. So you can raise a line in a pit, feed it things to kill, stronger each season, and cut it at the top of its growth for a far better stone than its row would ever fetch. The Hundred Crowns have kings who do this. Most of what gets fed to the pit is goats. The Accord has struck three charters over the rest of it, and the fourth is pending. Every pen in the record has ended the same way, and the only variable is how far the town was from the pit.
Who Lives Off It











































































WhoWhat they doWhat the street calls themCrewsKill it and cut it. See DungeonsWhatever they are calling themselves this weekThe stone-walkerThe steady one who walks the core home in a shirt or a sling while the mask-runner sprints for the hallSlow MoneyThe hall clerkWrites the chit: date, ground, beast’s name, the Sigil of whoever engaged it. Everything lawful starts hereInkCore-boysChildren and old men on the Mouth, with spades, after E and D stones. Lawful, and not on anybody’s rollMarble-pickersFactorsWait at the top of the stair with a very good dinner and a purse. They buy now for what the house will pay in a month. A merchant’s title caps the Rarity he may lawfully deal, so an S stone needs a Master’s token or a second signature, and an SS needs a GrandmasterUncleRenderersRun the house by the hall. Any town with a dungeon on it has one, with a chimney of a strange colorThe KitchenAlchemists of the great housesPour the high lots under seal. A stone at S or above generally passes straight into a vaultThe family physicianTally-menKeep each client’s dose count, as a sworn clerk at the serious houses. A good one will refuse to sell to youNannyDressersStain stale stone and shave dead men’s Crystals. The best of them are also the best-paid forensic witnessesThe BarberPaste menPour colored glass with a skin of something that fools a weak coil, and sell it in bad light to people in a hurry. A good forger beats a weak appraiserBottle-boysNight-cuttersSee aboveNothing, in companyStone-reevesA lord’s officer in a hunting town, there to take the lord’s refusal first and the lord’s tithe afterThief, and it is usually said in a friendly wayQuartermastersMonster cores and bought Stages are war materiel. A war makes a stone’s price double, and a lord will strip a county’s halls before he marches, because a Draft in a champion is worth a companySir
The money, in one line. The great houses hoard the top stones, poured and unpoured, in vaults on their own ground; the middle of the trade feeds the fighters and sect disciples of every realm; and the bottom feeds a boy with a spade. The whole of the class war of the age can be read off the top three rows of the price table. I know of one inn in Brokencollar that has been reading it for forty years.
What They Call It













































WhoThe wordThe argumentCrews and renderersThe stone; going rawIt pays, or it does notThe BenchCrystal Draw, Grade IVIt is entered, it is graded, and the arithmetic will be looked intoMotoTamashii-ishi (魂石), the soul stoneA beast had a soul, and a thing that is eaten ought to be spoken to first. They do, briefly, with the knife already inMahuoHon-seok (혼석)Property of the Dynasty, wherever it was found, with a dispute about the dateThe lineage hallsYāodān (妖丹), the demon’s pillA family asset, and the great ones are named in the family register alongside the childrenThe MarrowkinA cutThey live inside a dead thing and sell pieces of it. They have no notion what the fuss is aboutFaithsThe beast’s confession, the sin in the stoneIt should be burned, and it has been noted that most of the bishops are in very good health

materials,-alchemy--and--trade/alchemy/p.content:
The common tags of the field kit, as cut by licensed hands, copied by unlicensed ones and guarded by the schools · prices in Accord marks

A wall cut by an Engraver holds for three hundred years. A tag holds for three weeks and fires once, and in a fight that is the better bargain. Twelve tags make up most of what is carried into battle.


Tamsin Cordwain warranted tags at Quenby for forty-one years under a mark the whole county could sketch from memory, and her will asked for one thing: that she go into the ground the way she had lived, loudly and at her own expense. So on the morning they buried her, forty apprentices in amber sashes lined the Cutters’ Stair with the four hundred and twelve tags laid up in her strongbox, every one of them fired on the air or on a stored charge, and as the bier came down they touched them off one by one. Flash tags went up the Stair like a string of small white suns. Smoke rolled down the steps a room’s worth at a time. A Hush tag dropped the whole hill into silence for a few held breaths, and two Blast tags took the weathercock off the chandlery, by prior arrangement with the chandler. Under all of it ran the thing every cutter knows and few ever see in bulk: an ambient or stored tag lights in its maker’s color, so that for a quarter of an hour, three days dead, Tamsin Cordwain went on signing her name up the length of the Stair in honey amber, and grown men wept into their hats.
Then the ninety-first tag lit spark blue, and so did the ninety-second.
In the second rank of mourners, in his good black, stood Fulk Pyke, Warden of the Company of the Slate, whose own color every cutter in Quenby had been looking at across a feud for thirty years. Twenty-seven tags in that box carried Tamsin Cordwain’s mark and burned Fulk Pyke’s blue. She had spent nine years tracing them through the ports, each one a forgery of her warranty that had already killed somebody or would, and in her last month she had bought twenty-seven fresh off the boats, through a nephew, and left instructions about the order in which they should be laid out. Forty apprentices turned around. The fight went down the Stair and through the churchyard with a hundred people in it and every sleeve in the trade emptying at once. Three mourners died on those steps and a fourth went home without his jaw. Pyke ran with his coat alight and the Accord hanged him at the autumn assize, and the Slate and the Cordwain apprentices still break each other’s windows on her day. The children of Quenby count out their games by it: Amber holds and amber stays, blue will hang you all your days.
That funeral is a working knowledge of tags, delivered at volume. What a tag is, who can fire it, what color it lights and why the mark on it matters are set out below, with fewer casualties.
What it is
A tag (a slap or a strip in any tavern with fighters in it) is a rune (a working written into a material so that it holds without its maker) cut fast onto paper, leather or slate, carried in a sleeve, a belt or a boot, and fired in a single beat. A wall needs a season because it has to stand for centuries. A tag needs an hour because it only has to stand until it is used, and its last line is its own burning: when the tag is spent the material is ash, and the working ends with it. Cutting is a skill and a trade like any other. Anyone with a steady hand and a teacher can level it, it shows on the cutter’s window (the soul reporting its numbers to its owner, unseen by anyone else) as a Grade, and a cutter’s guild title caps what they may lawfully sell under their mark.
Only practitioners can fire a tag. The trigger is a touch of the user’s own Essence (the stuff a working is made of) through a woken Soul Crystal (the soul itself, opened for use), with a word or a hand sign. An unwoken hand holding a tag is holding paper.
A tag is also why low-Stage fighters love them. Below Refraction (Stage VII, the seventh rung of the sixteen-step ladder of power) every working needs something outside the body to hold its shape: a voice, a hand, ink or blood. A tag is that ink, already written. The user supplies the trigger and the tag supplies the rest.
Every tag runs on one of three fuels, and the tag decides which:

























FuelWhere the power comes fromWhat it means in a fightAmbient AetherThe magic in the air around it, at the room’s Density (how much Aether, the raw stuff of magic, a place holds)Cheap and never stale. Fails in dead ground (salted ground, worked by hedge-workers so Aether will not pool on it; bled ground, pulled empty; a place beside a Core, a worked Wellspring site, whose keepers have closed it; or a place no Wellspring’s Aether reaches) and weakens anywhere thinThe user’s reserveThe Essence the person firing it can spend before running dryAs strong as the user, up to the maker’s Stage. It costs the user, and the more they feed it the longer it holdsThe maker’s stored chargeReserve the cutter poured into the tag when it was madeWorks anywhere and for anyone who can fire it. Goes stale: strongest the day it is cut, weaker each week, dead in a season
A tag can never work above its maker’s Stage. A reserve-fed tag works at whichever is lower, the maker’s Stage or the user’s.
How it looks
Fine lines cut or burned into the material, sometimes inked, always in a fixed order the eye can follow if it knows the school. Paper is cheap, quick and dies in the rain. Leather lasts months and survives a soaking. Slate is heavy, lasts a year, and shatters when it fires.
As it fires, the lines light up in an aura color: the maker’s own color for an ambient or stored tag, the user’s color for a reserve tag. A trained eye reads who is paying for the working from the color alone. Then the material chars from the edges inward, with the smell of hot paper or scorched hide, and each kind of tag has its own sound: the flash tag’s crack, the ward tag’s glassy ring, the blast tag’s rising whine in the last second before it goes.
A tag is slapped onto a surface or a body, laid in advance, or wrapped round a knife and thrown.
What it costs
Coin. Tags compete with enhanced bolts (crossbow bolts carrying a working) and are priced against them, by the maker’s Stage:








































Maker’s StagePrice, one tagNoteI · Murmuring4 to 8 copperPenny tags. One in three failsII · Welling2 to 4 silverThe field standard; about the price of one enhanced boltIII · Ascension1 to 2 goldBought singly, by people who expect to live because of itIV · Flourishing3 to 6 goldOfficers’, bounty hunters’ and sect disciples’ kitV · Splintering9 to 18 goldRarely on a counterVI and up25 gold and upNot sold. Issued, inherited, or stolen
Failure. Cheap tags fail, and they fail three ways. Most often the tag fizzles: the lines glow and nothing comes. Sometimes it fires wrong: the ward comes up a hand’s breadth to the left, the smoke comes out as sparks. Rarely, and worst, it does not stop: the closing line was cut badly, so the working runs on after the tag should be ash, a flash tag that keeps flashing, a kindling tag that burns until the building does.
The license. Licensed tags carry the cutter’s mark (a cutter’s mark is a signature and a warranty at once) and an excise stamp. Cutting without a license is a crime the Accord enforces with real violence, and the black market runs regardless.
How it is beaten

Wet it. A soaked paper tag swells and its lines blur. Leather and slate shrug it off.
Cut the line. A tag torn through its lines will not fire, or fires wrong. A blade across a stuck tag is the fastest answer to a Binding or a Seal.
Take the fight off rich ground, onto salted, bled or thin ground. Ambient tags need Aether in the air.
Read the color. A reserve tag tells you who is feeding it. Hit them, and the tag starves.
Wait it out. A stored-charge tag weakens by the week. An old tag from a dead cutter is a gamble.
Watch the hand. Slapping, laying or throwing a tag takes a beat, and the hand that goes to the sleeve is a tell.

Example
Orla Venn, a Stage III bounty hunter, walks into a warehouse after a forger. She lays a Tripwire Tag across the back door, keeps a Flash Tag in her left sleeve and a Binding Tag in her right. The forger runs, the Tripwire shrieks, and she throws the Flash Tag wrapped round a knife; it cracks white in his face. She closes and slaps the Binding Tag on his thigh, and the lines light up in her own color as she feeds it. The forger’s partner sees the color, knows who is paying, and goes for Orla instead of the tag. She has to choose between holding the leg and defending her throat, and the tag goes dark the moment she lets go.
The catalog













































































































NameWhat it doesFuelMaker’s StagePriceWho cuts themFlash TagA white burst and a crack. Shrieks loud enough to hear a street away when a body crosses it. At Stage II it blows a door off its hinges; at Stage IV it brings down a wallThe maker’s stored chargeII to V3 silver to 15 goldLicensed to armies and mines; black market in every portWard TagThrows up a flat pane of hard Aether a pace wide that stops one blow or one volley, then shattersThe user’s reserveII to IV2 silver to 6 goldLicensed cuttersSplint TagWrapped round a broken limb, it sets hard as a cast and holds the bone straight for a dayThe user’s reserveII to III2 silver to 1 goldLicensed; standard field issueHush TagKills all sound inside a small room, or around the user, for a few minutesAmbient AetherII to III3 silver to 2 goldBlack market; licensed only to the Accord’s own officersBinding TagSlapped on a body, it locks the muscles beneath it: a limb, or at higher Stages the whole frame, for as long as the user keeps feeding itThe user’s reserveIII to V1 to 18 goldSect-secret; the forms are guarded and stolenAnchor TagPasted under a boot or on the ground, it holds the user to the spot against a blow or a blast that would throw themThe user’s reserveIII to V1 to 15 goldSect-secret in the East; licensed copies in the WestTracer TagA scrap the size of a thumbnail, stuck to a person or a cart. Whoever fired it feels its direction and rough distance for a dayThe maker’s stored chargeIII to V1 to 15 goldSect-secret; bounty hunters buy it on the black marketSeal TagStuck to a practitioner’s skin, it clamps down their Trait (their inborn power) and chokes their reserve’s flow until it is torn off or its charge runs outThe maker’s stored chargeIV to VI6 to 50 goldLicensed to the Accord’s enforcers only; black-market copies, many of them bad
Who cuts them

Licensed cutters. Accord-licensed hands working under a master’s mark, selling over a counter with an excise stamp. Most tags on the kept streets (the city quarters whose lamps and wards are kept by hired crafts) come from them, and the Accord guards the monopoly hard. Stage brackets bar purchased tags outright, which has done nothing for the trade in tags sewn into a fighter’s hat.
The black market. Unlicensed cutters, failed apprentices and forgers of other men’s marks. Cheaper, unwarranted, and the source of most tags that do not stop.
The sects. The schools and great houses of the East keep their best tag forms as secrets, taught by rank, and a school’s tag-hand can be spotted at fifty paces by the way the sleeve is cut. A disciple who leaves with a Binding or an Anchor form in their hands is hunted for what they know.


In the north almost nobody cuts. What tags the north carries come from Accord quartermasters, and a northern soldier pays for them in kind.


Read next: The Working Trades, for the craft that cuts them; Stacking and Spending, for what they do to a fighter’s budget.

materials,-alchemy--and--trade/alchemy/t.title: The Common Drafts
materials,-alchemy--and--trade/alchemy/t.content:
The standard catalog of the Draft trade, as kept by quartermasters, licensed apothecaries and the excise office · prices in Accord marks

Twenty-two Drafts account for most of what is poured, sold, smuggled and drunk across the four quarters, and the Essence Drafts rendered from monster cores, set out after them, account for most of the money. This is the list every counter-clerk learns first, every smuggler forges first, and every practitioner should be able to name by the color of the seal.


By dusk Goody Nettlebed of Skerrow, seventy-one and lame in one hip, who had used her Soul Crystal all her life to feel weather in her knuckles, had a coat of teal fire spitting sparks off both arms and was carrying a herring barrel over the chapel roof for a wager. The net-menders went along the harbor wall faster than a horse will go on cobbles, blood pouring from their noses, howling with joy. The whole strand burned like a fairground in the auras of people who had never in their lives been bright, while two hundred and sixty unwoken neighbors held the lanterns and shouted advice, and when six excise riders came down the cliff road to secure the Accord’s property, they went into the harbor, and after them, in a spirit of thoroughness, their horses. A steersman named Wat Cobbold, four doses of Windglass to the good, ran off the end of the mole at full stretch, certain he was gaining on the horizon. The next tide brought him back.
All of it had come ashore that morning. The Dorcas Merry had gone onto the Skerrow Teeth in the first gale of autumn with forty cases of fight stock stowed under a cargo of onions and no excise stamp on any of it: Vein Cordial, Beastheart Serum and Windglass Snuff, poured at grade VI for somebody’s sect in the East, twenty-four vials to the case, close on three and a half thousand gold at the plain band, and by noon the cases were rolling in the surf among the onions. Skerrow was three hundred fishing people, forty or so of them woken (their Soul Crystals opened), none above Welling and most of them at Murmuring and proud of it, and nobody on that strand had ever read a numeral off a seal. They could read red wax, and they knew red wax was dear.
The excise returned at noon the following day with twelve men and a handcart, and arrested the entire woken population of Skerrow lying down. Twenty-six of the forty had torn a hamstring. Every one of them had a scalded Shell, five had cracked their Crystals, and two of the five have not held a working since. Goody Nettlebed’s hands still shake, and she will tell you for the price of a drink that she would do it again. The minstrels say it was cider. Every counter-clerk on that coast tells the true version to anyone who asks why a seal carries a number, and the catalog below is the rest of what they would say if you stayed for it.
What it is
A Draft (a working poured into a substance, so that it can be carried and drunk) is the one form of magic a stranger can sell you. Every Draft is graded by the Stage it serves (the Stage is a practitioner’s rung on the sixteen-step ladder of power). A Draft at your own grade does what the label says. A Draft below your Stage does little, because a stronger body simply outclasses it. A Draft above your Stage is dangerous (a scald, on any fight street): it pours more into the Shell (the Aether Shell, the skin of power around the Soul Crystal) than the Shell is built to carry, and the excess comes out as burns, nosebleeds, a scalded aura, or a crack in the Crystal itself.
The commonest Drafts are poured at several grades. A grade-II Windglass and a grade-VII Windglass share a name, a recipe and a crash, and almost nothing else.
How it looks
Glass or stoneware, a wax seal, an excise stamp, and sediment at the bottom that a careful buyer tilts to the light. A licensed Draft carries its grade in a Roman numeral pressed into the seal; a fight vial carries it on the cork as well, so it can be read by touch in the dark.
A fight Draft takes a beat to drink, which is why fighters call it a swallow and why Stage brackets bar it by rule and search belts at the rope. Thumb off the cork, swallow, and the half-second the body takes to answer. In a duel that beat is an opening, and every trained fighter watches for the hand going to the belt. What follows shows: a refill brightens a dimming aura back toward its full color, a speed Draft leaves the drinker’s footing light and quick, a strength Draft flushes the skin and swells the veins in the neck.
What it costs
Coin. Prices climb roughly threefold with each Stage a Draft serves, because each grade holds roughly three times the Essence (the stuff a working is made of) and the rendering loses more of it at every step:




























































Grade servedStage nameBand price for a plain fight DraftIMurmuring4 copperIIWelling12 copperIIIAscension1½ silverIVFlourishing4½ silverVSplintering13½ silverVIGloryabout 3½ goldVIIRefractionabout 10 goldVIIITranscendenceabout 30 goldIXInvocationabout 90 goldXRealizationabout 270 gold

Twenty-four copper make a silver mark and twelve silver marks a gold. A laborer earns a silver mark in a good day. A grade-X Draft costs a clerk four years of wages, and the households that keep a case of them keep it in a vault.

The crash. Every fight Draft leaves a crash once its window closes, and the crash is the real price. Two or three in one fight is ordinary. Five is how veterans describe the worst week of their lives.
The stack. A strength or speed Draft is one layer of boost, and boosts from every source stack: Drafts, Trait (a standing law carried in the soul) surges, release forms (a practitioner’s named, staged power-up), allies’ help. The stack tops out at two steps above what the body can sustain, on the hidden scale the Measurewrights keep under every figure, and every layer a fighter adds raises the chance of a Crystal fracture (a crack in the Soul Crystal, which is literally the soul).
Provenance. Every Draft came from somewhere, and its source type says where the risk lives:






























Source typeWhere it comes fromWhat it risksCreature-SourcedRendered from magical creatures, monster cores above all, and at the top of the trade, against every law there is, from peopleThe strongest, and it carries the identity of what it was made from (Identity Contamination)Material-SourcedHigh-density minerals and salts taken off a Wellspring vein (a Wellspring is one of the sixty alchemical and spiritual transformations, the governing idea that shapes how a soul uses Aether, and each is a type of Aether too; a vein is the channel that feeds a place where one type pools)Clean but weakerEnvironmentalMatter steeped in a Wellspring field until it took the setGentle and slow; close to no riskSyntheticBlended at the bench from several sourcesThe least predictable; the parts can react inside the drinker
How it is beaten

Take the beat. A fighter who stops to drink has stopped. Hit the hand, the vial or the throat.
Outlast the window. Every fight Draft runs out. Stay alive past it and fight the crash instead of the Draft.
Read the grade. A drinker who has gone above their own grade bleeds from the nose and runs hot within a minute. They will burn out without help.
Read the source. A Creature-Sourced Draft brings its creature’s appetites with it, and those appetites can be baited.
Break the supply. Drafts are bought. A fighter who has drunk their belt dry is a fighter at half strength.

Example
Hesk Tarrow, a Stage III caravan guard, holds a bridge against two raiders. Halfway through he is down to a quarter of his reserve (what he can spend before running dry), his aura thinning to a flicker. He steps back, takes the beat, and drinks a grade-III Vein Cordial; the light comes back up his arms, and the raider who saw the hand go to the belt has already closed the gap and cut his forearm. Hesk wins the bridge. That night he cannot recover a drop on his own, his forearm is still open, and a grade-III Willow Gray costs a silver and a half. He buys the four-copper grade I instead, which does almost nothing for a Stage III body, from a stall whose seal he did not check.
The catalog
Fight Drafts
