materials,-alchemy--and--trade/work,-tra.content:
Ask what it is made of. Then ask who made it. Then believe the smaller answer.
Painted over the door of the assay room at Ambleford

Dame Ragnild Thurstan wanted her granddaughter married with the family sword in the room, and the family had no sword, so she had one made out of the family hearth. The hearthstone was Greystone, quarried from the hill the Thurstans had sat on for nine generations, and she paid a smith of Master standing forty gold to cut it into a blade and to set a working in it worthy of the name, in the courtyard, on the wedding day, in front of two hundred guests in every color the valley’s dyers could sell. Master Ordway Hesketh arrived in a scarlet apron with his guild mark embroidered across the chest as large as a platter. His own Journeyman told him, in front of the cook, that the stone would hold a D-Grade working and nothing above it. Hesketh told the courtyard that stone could be persuaded, named the sword Grandmother’s Patience in a voice they heard at the mill, set both hands on the flat, and drove in an A-Grade working with his aura standing off him like a sheet of hot brass. The blade held for about as long as it takes to say so. Then it went white along the edge and came apart in every direction, through the bridal canopy, through the goose, through the left ear of the bridegroom and the right eye of the steward, and one long splinter went forty feet up into the chapel door, where the Thurstans have left it. The wedding went on, because the bride insisted. Hesketh paid back the forty gold and the steward’s pension, and the shards still sell at Ambleford fair for a copper apiece as a charm against boasting. The hilt hangs in the Thurstan hall with a card under it, in the old lady’s hand, giving the sword’s item Tier as none.
Hesketh knew every word of the law below, and so does every apprentice who has been told that story, which is why they tell it. What keeps them awake is the other half of the trade’s folklore, that stone can be persuaded, once, by somebody at the end of a lifetime, and you will find that under Master Works.
Two Ratings
Every worked piece in a lawful shop is sold on two questions, and a buyer who confuses them is about to be robbed.
Grade says how much power it has, on the same letters the Commission posts beasts and missiles by, Hollow up through EX+. The Measurewrights keep the same scale hidden under every person’s figures and never say it of a person aloud. It is a measurement. A coil reads it, and two coils in two kingdoms give the same answer.
Rarity says how scarce it is: Common, Uncommon, Rare, Very Rare, Legendary, Mythic, Unique. It is an argument, conducted by people with money on it, and the assay house that writes it down is mostly recording who won.
The two run independently. A hard-working sect forge can turn out Grade S blades by the rack and call them Rare, and the last scarf ever cut from a burned loom can be Grade E and Mythic. A piece’s Grade stays where its making left it, unless it is bonded. Its Rarity moves whenever the world does, and when a kiln falls in or a war melts a family’s plate, every surviving piece goes up a step overnight and the clerks are very busy.













































RarityWhat it meansHow you get oneCommonEvery market has it, and nobody remembers the makerAny counterUncommonA good town’s best shop stocks it, or will by springAsk, and wait a seasonRareA city has a few, and the shop knows whose they wereKnow somebodyVery RareA realm can name its holdersBuyer and seller are introduced, by someone paid to be thereLegendaryKnown by name across realms, with a public list of past ownersAn estate sale, a war, a very large auctionMythicA handful in the world: lesser relics and most Master WorksInheritance, marriage, murderUniqueOne, and there will not be anotherWhatever its holder says, while they can still say it
The Old Words Are the Stamps
Before anybody spoke of Rarity the Accord’s mark carried one word, and it still does. That word is the stamp, the older trade calls what it measures the item Tier, and every assayer alive will read you the old rule by heart:
An item carries an item Tier, Plain through Proscribed: the lower of what its material can hold and the title its maker held in the trade when it was made. A Journeyman’s blade is at most Tempered, holding a C-Grade working and no more. A master cannot put an A-Grade working into Greystone: the stone fails first.
The maker’s side of it is a guild title, read in the maker’s own trade (the old assay books call it the Tier of Standing), and the stamp is simply the Grade said in the Accord’s words. A composite item is graded by the material that carries the working, and the handle and the fittings do not enter into it. Beside its tier a material has its virtue, and the virtue decides which workings it holds well and how it fails: stone remembers, salt fixes, gold will not corrupt, quicksilver will not keep a shape, so a working that must remember sits well in stone and nothing that has to keep its shape will settle in quicksilver. A plain item with no working in it has no Tier at all; it performs as plain matter does, by the world’s old habits, multiplies nothing in the person holding it, and it can still be Rare, since there are only so many ways to come by a two-hundred-year-old yew stave.
Material tier n holds a working up to item Tier n, level with the nth title. Each Tier is the word stamped on the Accord’s mark, in Accord Latin beside the old Probatum est, and said in plain English at the table and the counter.





























































































Item TierStampSaid asGrade it holdsMaterial tierExample materialsnonenonePlainHollow–FT0 FragileMireclay, Glassroot Fibers, Dustquartz1SignatumMarkedET1 SoftVellun Copper, Willowblood Sap, Sunreed Paper2ProbatumProofedDT2 Common DurableGreystone, Shieldgneiss, Stillband Ore3TemperatumTemperedCT3 HardenedSunkwood, Blackcap Sulfide, Ghoststeel4InstrumentumInstrumentBT4 Reinforced MagicalClearbeam Beryl, Psionite, Runeglass5ConsecratumHallowedAT5 Rare / Spirit-ForgedAethersteel, Bloodsilver, Twilite Glass6InsigneStoriedS–SST6 Arcane-ResistantSoulquartz, Frostwool, Grimbarite7InventumFoundSS–SSST7 Titan-ForgedTitanstone, Drakehide Steel8NuminosumNuminousX–EXT8 Mythic / CelestialEclipsium, Sunsinew, Moonblight Ore9InterdictumProscribedEX+T9 Transcendent / ForbiddenNullglass, Ash of Names
Where a Tier spans two Grades (Storied, Found, Numinous), the upper Grade needs a Grade IV or V provenance on the Standing Index, or a maker at the top of their own title.
What a Title Lets You Make and Sell
The same nine titles run through every guild in the Accord, and they grade trust in that trade. A smith’s title caps the Grade she may make. A merchant’s title caps the Rarity he may sell. Neither title says a word about whether its holder can throw a punch, and a Grandmaster merchant may well go down to a thrown cabbage.

































































TitleA smith may make up toA merchant may sell up toAn adventurer may take commissions up toInitiateMarked, Grade ECommona beast posted at EApprenticeProofed, Grade DCommonDJourneymanTempered, Grade CUncommonCAdeptInstrument, Grade BRareBExpertHallowed, Grade ARareAMasterStoried, Grade S to SSVery RareSGrandmasterFound, Grade SS to SSSLegendarySSArchmasterNuminous, Grade X to EXMythicXParagonProscribed, Grade EX+UniqueEX
Three ceilings stand over any smith at once: what the material can hold, what her title lets her stamp, and the strength of the Essence she can put in, since an enhanced weapon performs no higher than whoever put the Essence into it (The Bolt and the Enhanced Weapon has the law). Nobody makes Expert in a smiths’ guild on a hand that cannot put more than a C-Grade working into steel, because the test piece goes on the coil in front of the examiners, and the guild’s whole value is that the coil agreed.
A merchant above his title is a merchant selling on somebody else’s. Every port has a Grandmaster who lends a token to a sale for a fifth of the price and sits in the corner eating the seller’s pears, and since a Paragon merchant is a thing most realms have never seen, a Unique piece is almost never lawfully sold. It is given, inherited, lost at cards or taken off a body, and the Accord enters whichever of those it can prove.
What the Tier Caps, by Kind



































KindIts Tier capsFigure read offWeapon (melee)the hit a working addsAttack output bandProjectile, bolt, arrowspeed, and the hitAttack Speed and Attack outputArmor, ward, shieldwhat it stops: a strike whose Penetration reads at or below its Tier’s Grade on the hidden scalethe striker’s Ardency Penetration, against the proof-markFocus, staff, instrumentthe working it can channel without failingthe channeler’s own figure, capped at the item’s GradeRelic with a standing effectthe effect’s strengththe table the effect uses
Armor’s Tier is its proof. A strike against worked armor is read on the striker’s Ardency Penetration against the proof, whatever force sits behind it: high Flux with low Penetration hits like a padded wall, and the harness holds while the man inside takes the bruise. Proofed harness stops any strike whose Penetration reads no higher than a D-Grade working’s. The mark states the Tier, the house that tested it and the test. A strike one Tier above the proof breaks it; a strike two Tiers above passes as if it were not there. Plain armor has no proof and fights by its kind.
What a Piece Does for Its Wearer
Everything above is the piece fighting at its own Grade, and that law stands: a blade hits as its working, a harness stops what its proof says, and the Rarity is the argument it always was. A worked piece does a second thing besides. Worked gear multiplies its wearer. Its line names a Primary and a figure (a helm at Gnosis ×1.15, heavy plate at Vitality ×1.3 and Dexterity ×0.85), the wearer’s own numbers under that Primary are multiplied while the piece is lit, and the Primary is read again from there. Plain gear multiplies nothing, bonded gear’s multipliers grow with the bearer, and a relic’s read as question marks.
It is paid for out of the wearer’s reserve as a draw, light, steady or heavy, and the draw is taken through the layer the piece works on: armor and weapons draw on the Shell, soul-wards and charms on the Core, oath-rings and luck-tokens on the Layer, and all of it comes out of the one reserve. Everything worn together multiplies any one Primary by ×1.5 at most. A person’s sustainable figure is read with the gear off. Gear multiplies on top of that and can move the figure the sheet shows, and the two steps a fighter may boost are counted from the bare figure, never from the dressed one. A piece above its wearer’s Stage gives half or fights them. Worn Power has the whole law, with the sums, the trouble, and the charms and rings that do the same work for the soul.
Gear and the Three Roads
A proof-mark is a statement about matter, and matter is one of the three things that can happen to you. The Three Paths gives the long account. A buyer who means to live should know what the mark on his harness does and does not say.
Against a Body fighter everything above holds as written. At the top of that road the harness itself can be read: armor made too heavy to lift and a blade rusting in the hand. That is the Material Force working on existing substance, which is why a Plain coat of no great substance is sometimes the safer thing to be wearing on that day.
Against a Spirit hand, armor does nothing, because it does not cover the soul. No Tier of plate stops a Read, a Write or a hand on the Core, and the man inside defends with Integrity and Anchoring of his own, and his Ward against a read. A ward can be cut into a piece, or a Hallowed coat consecrated, and then it reads as a working at its own Tier and against the maker’s Spirit Mastery. A soul-ward, a charm or a reliquary worn against the skin goes further and multiplies the wearer’s own Ward and Harmonics. That is real protection at a very real price, and a smith who sells you a plain Hallowed mark as proof against the dead is selling you a Hallowed mark.
Against a Fate hand, a good mark is the best defense money can buy, for a reason the assay never tested. A pull moves only what already has a way of happening. A strap inspected this morning, a buckle from an honest house and a blade with no hidden flaw offer it nothing to lean on, and a forged mark is a way of happening with a stamp on it. The rich man’s untested Legendary and the poor fighter’s mended Common are both more dangerous to their owners on this road than on any other. At high Stage a pull can assign the result outright, and then no strap saves anyone, but it costs the hand a ruinous share of reserve to do it, and most would sooner have an easier target. Oath-rings and luck-tokens multiply the bearer’s Dominion and Resilience against such a hand, and a knot-cutter will take one knot’s debt onto itself and break.
A bonded piece is seated on the Attraction Layer, because a bond is what the Layer holds, and takes the owner’s own power through the Shell, Charge from a Body fighter and Essence from a Spirit or Fate one. So it can be pulled at through the bond, and a hand who breaks it hurts the owner on both layers. A Master Work is the nearest a craftsman comes to Fate in an object: a term on the world, that this door will hold and this cut will finish, which is why it ignores its material and why nobody has made one by trying.
What an Item Costs to Make
Costs are paid out of the maker’s reserve (the Measurewrights’ conversion is 1 EU = 1 MJ):






























ItemCost to makeLastsEnhanced bolt or arrow1% of the maker’s reserve each, whatever speed or hit is worked into it, with a floor of 0.001 EUthe maker’s Duration; consumed when loosedEnhanced weapon (standing working)10% of the maker’s reserve, onceuntil the working is broken, read or unmadeProofed armor25% of the maker’s reserve, onceuntil struck by a strike two Tiers above its proofRelicthe maker’s whole reserve, once, and a spell of Starvation after (Charge Starvation for a Body maker, Essence Starvation for a Spirit or Fate one)permanent while its material holds
A practitioner can equip themselves but cannot equip an army. A Stage II maker (reserve a few thousand EU) can prepare about ninety enhanced bolts from a full reserve before Starvation sets in, or nine enchanted blades, or three suits of proofed armor, or one relic.
Hide, Bone and Scale
Monster parts make gear, and the best gear going is monster gear, because something spent a long life and a great many other animals growing that scale. A part goes to the bench as a material like any other. On the day it comes off the carcass it assays at the beast’s own Grade and Level on the coil, so an A-Grade beast’s plates hold what Aethersteel holds and a drake that reads SS is where Drakehide Steel gets its name. The trade says all this in the Grade the Commission posts a beast at, and for most beasts that is close enough, an A-Grade beast’s plates and an SS drake’s hide being the common way to put it (older hall rolls give the same rows as Threat Tiers, T1 to T9). Where the posted Grade comes from what a beast does and not what it is made of, the coil wins, and a Lamp-drinker’s hide does not hold what its Gold Sigil promised. Then it starts to fall, because a part begins losing grade from the moment the animal stops, and the whole beast trade is an argument with decomposition. Crews have run a wyvern’s wing-leather forty miles in a sack of snow on the understanding that the runner keeps a share and his feet are his own affair.
The old law sits on top of it without any exception. The maker’s title still caps the stamp, so an SS-Grade scale in a Journeyman’s hands makes a Tempered coat with an extremely handsome surface. What the material gives for nothing is its plain toughness, since a hide that turned spears on the living animal goes on turning them whether a working is in it or not.
Two things come with monster gear that a buyer does not get with steel.
It carries the beast. Scale and bone are Creature-Sourced, the same as the Drafts rendered from a core, and a little of what the animal was stays in what it became. A Tinder-fox-hide jerkin keeps its wearer up at night. A coat cut from a pack-hunter has been known to make a quiet man uneasy when he is alone. Good tanners cure most of it out, cheap ones sell it as character, and the Index lists the trouble as Identity Contamination wherever anybody has troubled to measure.
It carries the name. A famous monster has an epithet and a bounty on it before it has a buyer, and the gear made from it inherits both. Rarity runs on this, because there was only ever one Anner Moss Wyvern, and every hunter in the hundred swears he owns its left wing.
Bonded Gear
Gear stays what it is. A Hallowed blade in a Stage XII hand is a Hallowed blade, and it will fail him on the same day it would have failed its first owner, with its stamp still telling the truth about both of them. What it multiplies in him is the same share it multiplied in that first owner, and a share of a Stage XII number is a great deal more.
A bonded piece is the one kind that grows. A fighter who has carried a weapon or a coat for years and worked their art through it can seat it in the soul, and from then on it is part of them: it carries part of their art and part of their body, there is no seam between it and the hand, and it takes its part in a release. Its multipliers on the bearer grow as it does. It has no voice of its own, whatever its owner tells people in taverns. As the owner climbs, so does the piece, and the soul reports the change on its owner’s window, in the plain text block that nobody else can read:
[Bonded: Long Harriet]
Grade: C ▸ B
Holds: 62%

The maker’s title stops mattering at that point, because the Essence in it is now the owner’s. The material still matters. A bonded piece climbs until it reaches what its stuff can hold and there it stops, so a farm boy who bonds his grandfather’s Stillband hatchet at fifteen will find, at about Stage IV, that the hatchet has gone as far as hatchets go, and he has a decision to make that no minstrel has ever got right. A wise master tells a student to bond nothing cheap. The student has generally already done it.
The stamp on a bonded piece is a portrait of it as a child. Assay houses will strike a new one for a fee, and most bonded fighters do not bother, on the sound ground that a stranger who reads Proofed on the hilt is a stranger who has made a mistake.
Master Works
The whole register, piece by piece, is in Master Works.
Here the law on this page stops holding, once per lifetime, and the trade would very much like you not to count on it.
A Master Work is a piece that does what its Grade and material should not be able to, made once at the end of a lifetime, always Unique or Mythic, and named. The coil reads it at its proper Grade, the material is the material, and the thing goes on doing what it does regardless. Nobody has made one by trying harder, nobody has made a second, and most of the people who have tried to learn how from the maker found them unhelpful, or dead. Each area of the world has its own, and each trade.
The doorstep of the assay room at Ambleford is one. Aldous Wray, a mason of eighty-eight with four teeth and a bad opinion of everyone, cut it out of plain Greystone in his last winter and called it Enough, and at the spring fair of the following year a drunk Expert of the Blue Herons, invited to try, broke his own wrist on it. By the table above a strike two Tiers over the proof goes through as if the stone were not there. The Accord has tested that step with everything it could get to Ambleford. It is stamped Proofed, because Proofed is what the coil says, and Unique beside that, because the clerk could think of nothing else, and people wipe their feet on it. Measurewrights have written eleven treatises on why it cannot be doing that. One of them has been shown to be right about why, and the step has not been informed.
Every trade keeps its own list and its own bragging. The Cardmere dyers have a red that does not fade in Vantabriel light, the salt road has a knot, and the coast keeps a net that has never once come up empty and that no fisher will agree to own. Each is the last thing its maker did. In the alchemists’ halls the great one is a Fate Essence Draft: the working of probability itself bottled in a vial, extremely hard to make, a handful in the world at any time, and very coveted. For nearly everyone alive it is the only way Fate Arts will ever come within reach, and great families have gone to war over a stoppered inch of it without being entirely sure what it would do.
Relics, and the Ones That Are Not on This Page
Made relics and the lesser relics that come up off old battlefields are written the same on the roll: a Grade, a stamp and Mythic Rarity, because very few makers have ever been willing to spend themselves empty on one piece.
True relics are off the ladder. The works of the Great Spirit War and of the days of the Physical Epochs, when Bara, Ashura and Aegor walked in human form, read as question marks to any appraiser of any strength, on any instrument. They cannot be repaired or copied, and they may have opinions about who holds them, which the holder generally learns by having the matter settled for them. People kill for them anyway. The Accord stamps them with nothing and enters them under a dash, and a merchant who offers you one has found a very old sword, or has found a way to die.
Appraisal and Forgery
Three things read an item. An assay instrument does it best: the holding coil gives Grade on a good day and the assay fork gives density, and between the two a careful house can tell what a piece is and sometimes what it has been. The Appraisal skill is the one you carry, a trade skill that rises with use and shows on your own sheet as one of the nine ranks, Initiate to Paragon, like Baking or Swordsmanship. Strong Gnosis (the stat of perceiving, reading and noticing) helps both, and it is why a Harmonist can tell a working’s alignment and Duration without touching it. An appraiser’s read arrives as a window, and the window reports what the skill found:
[Appraisal: Journeyman]
Short sword. Grade C. Rarity: Uncommon.
Stamp: Tempered. Mark: Hesketh, Ambleford. Reads true.
Past owners: ???

A relic off the old fields gives the same window with nothing but question marks in it, and experienced buyers treat that as a reading.
A good forger beats a weak appraiser. Forgery is a skill too, on the same nine ranks, and the rank of the skill in use decides the contest. A Journeyman forger has cut a Tempered mark that an Apprentice appraiser’s own soul will report as true, and that appraiser will swear to it before a magistrate with a clear conscience. The usual frauds are a real blade with a false stamp, a low working dressed to run bright for a month, a past owner added to the list, and a Common piece aged into a Rare one in a bucket of cow urine. A cheap proof-mark on repaired steel is hardly even a crime. Provenance is the dearest thing to fake and the hardest to catch, because no instrument has ever measured who died holding something.
So a sane buyer above Rare hires two appraisers who dislike each other and puts the piece on a coil besides, and the coil will not read Rarity at all.
A forged title token is another order of crime. A stamp lies about a sword. A token lies about a person, and the whole coalition runs on a stranger being able to hand you the goods because the silver at your throat says so. Every hall in every realm hangs for it, including halls that are at law with each other, and a forged token is one of the few subjects on which the Accord has ever been observed to agree with itself.
Marks, Names and Past Owners
Two things ride on a good piece besides its Grade, and a buyer who ignores either one has already met the people above.
The guild mark. A stamp under the Accord’s stamp, naming the maker and the shop. Craftsmen shout their marks in the street and brag about them at table, a Marked knife from a loud shop outsells a Proofed one from a quiet shop, and the Accord’s stamp is the only part of the arrangement anybody can sue over. A guild mark tells you who to blame. It changes nothing on the ladder.
The name. Top gear has a name, a reputation and a list of past owners that the public knows, and heralds and minstrels carry all three, wrongly. A piece does not need a Hallowed stamp to get a name; it needs one famous evening. By the Storied Tier a piece has usually had several names, the most famous one winning, and a buyer pays for the list of who died holding it as readily as for the Grade. The oldest and worst of them come off the dead battlefields, and the people who sell those generally cannot say who made them or what the maker’s ceiling was, which the next owner finds out.
The name sits on the same ladder as everything else. Grandmother’s Patience has the second-best-known name in its valley and no Tier at all.
On a Card
Name · Kind, stamp (Grade X), Rarity, material Tn. One line of what it does. For example: Slyvine’s Scarf · Relic, Proofed (Grade D), Mythic, T2 or above. Can stretch, tighten, or harden to act as a rope or a weak shield.

Read next: Worn Power, for what worked gear multiplies in its wearer and what it costs to keep lit; Master Works, for the pieces outside the ladder; The Three Paths, for how each road reads your armor; Tier Grade, Bands and the Aether Shell, for the scale the letters share.

materials,-alchemy--and--trade/work,-tra.content:
A sword tells you what it can do. A coat tells you what you can do in it, and charges you by the hour for the news.
Said at the Ambleford assay counter, usually to a young man holding his father’s purse

The Vance twins rode into the Kessen brackets in the same summer with the same inheritance, and the bookies priced them as one fighter. Aubrey Vance spent his half the way the minstrels would have advised. He walked onto the sand in the Larkspur Harness (Legendary, sky-blue enamel over Grimbarite, the plate three dead champions had worn), with the Legendary helm Widow’s Lantern on his head and the Legendary gauntlets called the Tax Collectors on his hands, and for the first minute he was the most beautiful thing in the county and very nearly the strongest. The crowd could see the blue of his aura standing off the plate like noon on a lake. What the crowd could not see was his window, where three lines each read Shell draw: heavy and the bar under them was going down like a tide. He was at half before he had been hit. At a quarter his hands were shaking inside the Tax Collectors, the harness went dark piece by piece as his reserve could no longer keep it lit, and a caravan guard in mended Common mail walked in and knocked him flat with the boss of a borrowed shield.
His sister Odile sold two of her three pieces before the season opened, kept a single Very Rare brigandine she could afford to feed, and spent the rest on a trainer and on dinner. She won the Kessen bracket four years running. Asked about her brother, she said he had been wearing more than he could eat.
Both halves of that story are the law. Good gear makes a strong fighter stronger than anything else money can buy, and every piece of it has to be paid for twice, once at the counter and again out of the wearer’s own reserve for as long as it is worn.
What a Worked Piece Does
Grade and Rarity says what a piece is. A blade still cuts at its own Grade, a harness still stops what its proof says it stops, and none of that changes here. This page is about the other thing a worked piece does, which is change the person inside it.
A worked piece multiplies a Primary. Its line names one or two of the Eight Primaries (Gnosis, Vitality, Dexterity and the rest, each the sum of eight of the sixty-four single measures set out in the Eight Primaries and the Sixty-Four Sub-Stats) and a figure, and while the piece is worn and lit every one of the wearer’s eight numbers under that Primary is multiplied by it. The Primary is then added up again from its eight entries and read off the new mean. Older stamps name a single Sub-Stat (a helm at Perception ×1.15), and the soul reads such a line on the Primary the Sub-Stat sits under, here Gnosis.
Take a scout whose Gnosis stands at a mean of 160 and put a helm on her that reads Gnosis ×1.15. Her mean is now 184, a full step higher on the scale the Measurewrights keep hidden under every figure, and in any contest that calls on what she sees and reads she now wins exchanges she used to have to fight for. Nobody gives her a letter for it; the bracket says she has eyes in the back of her helm. The helm has made her better at one broad thing by a clear margin and left the rest of her shape alone, and that is how gear generally behaves.
There are four kinds of gear, and the sheet treats each differently.



































KindWhat it isWhat it does to the wearerOn the windowPlain gearIron, leather, wood and cloth with no working in itNothing. It performs as plain matter does, by the world’s old habits, and good plain steel is still good steelNo lineWorked gearRuned, Draft-tempered, or cut from monster partsMultiplies the Primaries named on its line, for a Shell drawA Worn block, with the multipliers and the drawBonded gearA piece seated in its owner’s soulMultiplies as worked gear does, and its multipliers grow as the bearer climbsA Bonded block, with the figures movingRelicsThe true works of the old wars and the walking EpochsWhatever it pleasesQuestion marks
Plain gear is most of what anybody owns, and nobody should be ashamed of it. A levy pikeman’s kettle hat multiplies nothing and has saved more lives than every Legendary on the continent together.
Worked gear is the trade. The three common ways of making it give three common flavors. Rune-cut pieces carry clean, narrow lines and are the easiest to read on a coil. Draft-tempered pieces, quenched or soaked in rendered stock, tend to carry Vitality lines and a faint smell of the alchemist’s yard. Monster gear carries what the animal was good at, so a night-hunter’s hide sharpens Gnosis and a river beast’s plate thickens Vitality, and it carries a little of the animal’s temper along with it.
Bonded gear begins as worked or even plain, and after the bond its line is the owner’s affair. The multipliers rise as the bearer rises, up to what the material can hold and no further.
Relics multiply, or do something that looks like multiplying, and no window, coil or appraiser has ever got a figure out of one. The wearer’s own sheet shows the piece’s name and a row of question marks. Holders report that the figure appears to depend on whether the relic approves of what they are doing.
Why It Favors the Strong
A multiplier is a share, and a share of a great deal is a great deal. This is the whole reason the wealthy fight better than their training deserves, and it deserves an example with the sums written out.
A field harness of worked plate reads Vitality ×1.3. Buckle it on a levy sergeant whose Vitality stands at a mean of 60 and he stands at 78, tougher by eighteen points and not a step higher on the hidden scale. Buckle the same harness on a sworn champion at a mean of 250 and she stands at 325, a full step up. One full step decides an exchange outright. The sergeant got a better coat and the champion became a different kind of problem.
So the purse and the training compound. A house that can buy its heir a Stage, a trainer and a harness has bought three things that each make the other two worth more, and a poor fighter of equal talent meets that heir a step behind on the one or two Primaries that matter. Poor fighters do win. They win by making the rich one pay the draw, by getting past the harness to something it does not cover, and by not being where the strong Primary is pointing.
The Shell Draw
A worked piece is dark until its wearer lights it, out of the wearer’s own reserve, for as long as it is worn in earnest. Armor and weapons, which are most of what anybody means by gear, are lit through the Aether Shell, and the window calls this the Shell draw and grades it in three words.

























DrawWhat it is likeTypical ofLightA trickle a fighter stops noticing. It can be worn all dayMost Uncommon and Rare pieces with one or two modest linesSteadyA real, constant spend. Every working the wearer runs holds for less time from full than the card saysVery Rare pieces, and anything with a strong lineHeavyAs costly as holding a working of your own the whole time it is litLegendary and Mythic pieces, and nearly anything that carries three lines
One heavy piece is a decision a strong reserve can afford. Two is a short fight. Three is Aubrey Vance. The tells are the same ones any spending shows, the short breath at half and the tremor at a quarter, and an opponent who sees them on a fighter who has not yet thrown a working knows where the reserve is going. When the reserve cannot feed a piece it goes dark, its line drops off the window, and the wearer is suddenly standing in plain plate with the trade-off still attached.
The draw goes by the piece. A piece is lit through the layer of the soul it works on. Armor and weapons draw on the Shell. Soul-wards, charms and reliquaries draw on the Core, and the window prints Core draw. Oath-rings, luck-tokens and knot-cutters draw on the Attraction Layer, and the window prints Layer draw. There is still only the one reserve, and all three are paid out of it, so a Body fighter with a ward at his throat is spending the same store on his plate and his locket. What changes is where the strain shows: a heavy Shell draw runs the wearer hot, a heavy Core draw leaves them a little flat and far away, and a Layer draw shows as nothing at all until the small luck around them starts to sour.
A fighter may let a piece go dark on purpose to save the draw, and light it again when it is wanted. Lighting it takes a breath and shows, since the aura runs out over the piece as it wakes. Veterans do this constantly. It is the main skill of wearing good gear, and no shop teaches it.
The Cap
All the gear a person wears, taken together, multiplies any one Primary by ×1.5 at most. A harness at Vitality ×1.3 and a tempered belt at Vitality ×1.3 do not make their wearer nearly twice as hard to break. The soul reads ×1.5, stops, and goes on charging the draw for both. Two lines on one Primary multiply together (×1.2 and ×1.1 make ×1.32), and whatever the product comes to, the window holds it to ×1.5. Nor does any amount of gear lift a figure past the ceiling its owner’s Stage allows: the line still prints, and the stat stops where the Stage stops it, which is the whole reason a rich nobody in Mythic plate is still a nobody, only a better-dressed one.
This cap is gear’s own. It stands apart from the cap on a practitioner’s own power-ups, the two steps over sustainable that Stacking and Spending sets out, and gear does not count toward that one. The sustainable figure is read bare, with every piece off and dark, and it is the bare figure the two steps are counted from. Gear multiplies on top, and it can move the figure the sheet shows, as the champion’s harness moved her Vitality a full step. Her boosts still stop two steps above the figure she owns, and the harness then multiplies whatever number that comes to, under its own ×1.5. So a fighter in a good coat may still focus, vow, call and release to her full two steps, and no coat has ever bought anyone a third. Gear adds no fracture risk either. What it adds is the draw, and the draw is why a fighter in three Legendaries has very little reserve left to stack anything with.
Gear Above Your Stage
A piece can be too much for the person wearing it. When its Grade stands above what the wearer’s Stage can carry (the Grade a maker of the wearer’s own rank could put into it, by the table in Grade and Rarity), the Shell cannot carry the whole working, and one of two things happens.
It works at half. The piece gives half its gain, so a line of ×1.3 reads ×1.15, at the full draw. Most pieces do this, and most heirs never notice, because nobody has told them what the line ought to say.
It fights them. A proud piece, a monster piece with a strong temper, or anything bonded to somebody else for a long time may refuse outright. The line reads below one. The plate drags, the helm narrows the eyes it was cut to open, and the draw climbs. Every armorer has a story about a boy who could not get his grandfather’s gauntlets off.
A bought Stage helps with this exactly as much as it helps with anything, which is to say that it opens the ceiling and the fit follows.
Trade-offs
Lines below one are honest, and nearly all heavy gear carries one. Heavy worked plate reads Vitality ×1.3 and Dexterity ×0.85, and no rune yet cut has made forty pounds of steel weigh nothing. On the champion above, with Dexterity at a mean of 240, that is 204, the same step on the hidden scale but a slower one, and against a fighter who was level with her on speed it is now a contest she loses on the first step. On the levy sergeant the same line takes him from 80 to 68.
The common bargains are well known to the trade. Plate gives Vitality and takes Dexterity. A deep hood or a closed helm cut for Gnosis often takes a little off Harmonics, since it reads threats and stops reading faces. Draft-tempered pieces that thicken Vitality tend to take a little off Tempering, so the wearer feels every hour of the march. A smith who tells you a heavy piece has no second line is either a Master Work’s maker or a liar, and the first kind are all dead.
Multipliers below one are not softened by the cap. Nothing in the law stops a fool from stacking three slow pieces and standing still.
Trouble
Forged lines. A forger who cannot fake a working can dress a low one to run bright for a month, and a line that reads Gnosis ×1.15 at the counter may be a true ×1.03 with a bright coat of paint. The buyer’s own window reports what the working is doing on the day, so it agrees with the forgery until the dressing burns off, and it burns off faster under load. The usual moment is the first hard exchange of the first real fight. An Appraisal a rank above the forger’s skill catches it, and so does a coil. The stamp does not, since the stamp is the thing that was forged.
Cursed gear. A curse on a piece is nearly always a line with terms, written by whoever made it, and the window shows the terms only as the maker chose to write them (see Blessings and Curses). Vitality ×1.4 while the bearer has not retreated is a fine line until the day the bearer needs to retreat and discovers what the rest of the sentence was. The well-known kinds are the piece that will not come off, the piece whose draw doubles at night, and the piece that is generous to its wearer and takes the difference out of whoever stands nearest.
The flex. Gear is worn to be seen, and its lines are said out loud by everybody. Owners announce their multipliers at dinner. Rivals halve them in the retelling. A smith will price a stranger’s coat across a street to within ten gold, loudly, as a courtesy to the trade. An appraiser may read the line off a piece without asking, if the skill is good enough, and at a bracket ground there is always one sitting at the rail calling the figures to the bookies. All of this brings what it has always brought: thieves, challengers, creditors, and the man who has heard exactly what your harness does and has come dressed for the Primary it leaves alone.
The Window
The wearer’s soul reports a worked piece in a short block, unseen by anyone else, when the piece is lit and whenever its state changes:
[Worn: Ashjaw Helm · Rare · Grade B]
[Gnosis ×1.15 · Vitality ×1.1]
[Shell draw: light]

A piece working at half says so, and a piece that has gone dark drops to its name alone:
[Worn: Larkspur Harness · Legendary · Grade S]
[Vitality ×1.15 (half) · Dexterity ×0.85]
[Shell draw: heavy]

A Primary that gear has moved shows its shifted figure on the sheet, with the piece named beside it, in the manner Windows and the Sheet gives for any shifted figure. A bonded piece shows its multipliers ticking up as its owner does. A relic shows this, and experienced holders have stopped asking:
[Worn: ???]
[??? ×???]
[Shell draw: ???]

Soul-Wards and Thread-Pieces
Plate covers the body. Two older trades cover the rest of a person, and neither looks like much on a rack.
Spirit gear is worn against hands that reach the soul. Soul-wards, charms and reliquaries multiply Resilience and Harmonics, and the wearer feels it most in Ward, Stability and Attunement. A soul-ward is a cut or consecrated thing worn against the skin, a disc, a cord, a stitched band inside a collar. A charm is its cheap cousin, sold at every shrine gate, and the honest ones carry a small true line. A reliquary holds something of a person who was hard to move in life (a finger bone, a braid, the ash of a letter), and it lends the wearer a little of that steadiness. Their draw is usually light, it is a Core draw and not a Shell one, and they show nothing to the eye when lit, which is half their value. No plate does this work at any Grade, and a fighter in a Legendary harness with nothing at his throat is a strongbox with the lid off as far as a Spirit hand is concerned.
Fate gear is rarer, dearer and harder to prove. Oath-rings, luck-tokens and knot-cutters multiply Dominion and Resilience, felt most in Continuity. An oath-ring is cut when a vow is sworn and strengthens the standing of the one who swore it, Command and Pressure most often, for exactly as long as the vow is kept. A luck-token steadies its bearer against being moved, displaced or made the one the accident happens to, which is Continuity’s business. Fate gear is lit through the Attraction Layer, out of the same reserve as everything else. Counterfeits outnumber true ones perhaps fifty to one, since a false luck-token is very hard to tell from a true one on a quiet day.
A knot-cutter is the strange one. Every pull on Thread leaves a knot, a debt the world collects from the puller later and in its own coin. A knot-cutter carries a small Resilience line while it is whole, and it can do one further thing, once: it takes a single knot’s debt onto itself and breaks. The bearer chooses the moment by cutting, snapping or unpicking it. The misfortune that was coming lands on the piece, and the piece is gone, generally in a manner that makes clear what it spared its owner. Fate houses buy them by the case and never admit to it. Nobody has made one that takes two.
Some Pieces on the Roll
Each entry gives the kind, the stamp with its Grade, the Rarity and the item Tier. The T on a piece is the item Tier, the rung of material and maker’s standing set out in Grade and Rarity, and has nothing to do with the Grade posted on a beast. The soul-wards and rings below draw on the Core and the Layer, as above.
The Ashjaw Helm · Helm, Instrument (Grade B), Rare, T4. Gnosis ×1.15, Vitality ×1.1, light draw. Cut by Adept Brannoch Sele of the Kessen road from the lower jaw of an Ashjaw, a gray tunnel-hunter that finds its prey by the heat of breath, with the teeth left in along the brow and the bone smoked the color of slate. Sele’s mark is a hooked tooth under the left cheek-plate. It has had three owners. The first was the crew captain Dunmore Halse, who paid for the kill, and the second was his caller, who took it off him when he did not come up. It last sold at Kessen for 240 gold to a woman who would not give a name, and the trade considers the price fair and the buyer’s silence worrying.
The Larkspur Harness · Full plate, Storied (Grade S), Legendary, T6. Vitality ×1.3, Dexterity ×0.85, heavy draw. Sky-blue enamel over Grimbarite plate with a Frostwool arming coat, made by Master Ysolde Carrow of Altherion for the champion Ser Edrik Lark, who died in it of old age, to general surprise. Two champions wore it after him and one of those did not die of old age. House Vance bought it at the Lark estate sale for 11,000 gold. It hangs in their hall now with the straps let out, because Odile Vance bought it back from her brother’s creditors and has never worn it.
Sister Maud’s Knuckle · Reliquary, Proofed (Grade D), Uncommon, T2. Resilience ×1.1, Harmonics ×1.05, light draw. A pewter locket the size of a walnut holding one finger bone of a spital sister who is said to have sat up forty years with the dying and never once been frightened by what came for them. The spital at Marchbank had the bone cut into eleven lockets by a Journeyman it will not name, and sells one when the roof needs doing, at 9 gold. Soldiers going north buy them. The bone in at least four is mutton.
The Tollkeeper’s Promise · Oath-ring, Tempered (Grade C), Rare, T3. Dominion ×1.15, Resilience ×1.1 while the oath on it is kept, light draw. A plain Ghoststeel band cut by the Adept ringwright Hale Morrow for a bridge-warden who swore that nobody would cross his bridge unpaid. It worked for thirty-one years. The warden’s son inherited the ring without inheriting the oath, wore it to a bracket, and found that it reads ×1.0 on a hand that has promised nothing. It is in a pawnshop at Ostrey at 85 gold, and the pawnbroker tells every customer the story, since he would rather not be sued.
A Kessen knot-cutter · Knot-cutter, Instrument (Grade B), Very Rare, T4. Resilience ×1.05 while whole, light draw, and the one cut. A finger’s length of red cord with nine knots tied by a cordwright who walks the Fate road, sealed in wax and usually worn sewn inside a cuff. From the two houses known to make them the price is 600 gold, by introduction, and the houses do not give receipts. The best-known use is that of the factor Peregrine Stroud, who pulled once on a grain auction, unpicked his cord that evening, and watched his own warehouse roof come down an hour later on nobody. He bought another the following morning.

Read next: Grade and Rarity, for what the stamp and the scarcity mean; Stacking and Spending, for the cap gear does not count on and the reserve it eats; What Things Cost, for what a gold mark is beside a laborer’s year.

materials,-alchemy--and--trade/work,-tra.content:
A Register of Occupations, Trades, and Technology Across the Four Quarters
Compiled for the Research and Archives Division, with the assistance of the Logistics and Supply Division

“He asked what I did. I told him I kept the array running. He asked what magic I used. I told him I used a mallet. He did not know what to do with me after that, and I have found that this is the general experience.”
Brida Voss, Senior Tender, Greyshaft Twelve, testimony to the Logistics Division

Ranulf Scarrow, called the Anvil-Eater, grandmaster of the Scarlet Rams of Harrowgate, bit a corner off an anvil every midsummer for thirty years in front of anyone who would pay to watch, and at the feast for his seventieth year he got up on the high table in his scarlet and gold, with three thousand people in the yard and the school’s drummers going, and told them that a fist of Master standing owed nothing to any pair of hands in the four quarters, and that the bakers, ditch-diggers and washerwomen of Harrowgate were welcome to kiss the part of him that sat down. The yard loved it. The bakers kept on baking. The layer-outs of Harrowgate, thirty-one old women who wash the town’s dead for a few silver and are not asked to dinner, said nothing whatever, and one of them wrote it down.
Nine years later a herring bone killed him at supper. Harrowgate gave him the funeral of the age: Ram banners the length of the Long Market, twelve-foot candles, core disciples in red weeping aloud on a catafalque built over the school’s fountain, and pie-sellers working the crowd from both ends. No layer-out came. A woman of Master standing does not stop when she stops, and neither does a man; the Crystal goes on producing Essence for a good while after the heart has quit, and the woman who knows how long, and what to do to the body until then, is the woman you sent for. On the first day the aura stood up off the bier in a scarlet column as tall as a house and the crowd took it for glory and sang. On the second day every candle in the hall burned scarlet, the funeral cakes turned to charcoal on the trestles, and the eleven core disciples who rolled up their sleeves to wash their grandmaster themselves were carried out with their forearms cooked. On the third, in the heat of a Harrowgate midsummer, the red ran down the gutters and into the dyers’ vats, the school’s own rams broke their pen and left town, and the gravediggers, asked to open the ground, explained with some pleasure what a Master laid in at the wrong depth does to a churchyard for the next four hundred years. A hundred disciples dug it themselves and dug it wrong, and had to stop when the spades began to warm.
At dusk Elder Hawise Bretton, who was said to be able to put her open hand through a town gate, walked down to Tanners’ Row, downstream and downwind and outside the wall, and went onto both knees in the fish-guts in front of Gammer Thirza Lubbock, who was shelling peas on her step. It is recorded that the Gammer finished the bowl. It is recorded that the fee was paid three times over and that the Elder was made to say a sentence out loud, in front of the street, about whose hands a Ram needed. The thirty-one came up the hill at nightfall with salt, vinegar, and a long wooden spoon nobody has ever explained, and by morning the gutters ran clear. The rival Blue Herons of Lower Harrowgate have sung “Who’ll Wash the Ram?” at every bracket since, children sing it in every lane from here to the coast, and a Ram disciple who hears it in a tavern is expected to fight or buy, and generally does both.
This register exists because of that bowl of peas, in the sense that it concerns the people who were in the room when the grand thing stopped working. It lists what they do and what they cost, and it begins, as the Gammer would have wished, from the bottom.
The Governing Question
The coil classifies people by what their Soul Crystal can do. The economy classifies them by what their hands can do.

These two systems overlap in approximately one person in twelve. This register concerns the other eleven.

(The Soul Crystal is the soul itself, which holds power and sends it out. The Accord reads what it puts out with the brass coil, the instrument that gives every practitioner a Stage, one step on a ladder of sixteen, and the word “instrument” in this register always means that coil and the people who stand behind it. A Wellspring, which this register mentions constantly, is one of the sixty governing ideas of magic, an alchemical and spiritual transformation that changes how a soul uses Aether, the world’s medium of power. A practitioner pulls Aether from the ground around them and refines it in the Crystal into Essence, the power they hold and spend, and a place where one Wellspring’s kind of Aether pools is a Core.)
Every occupation below exists because something needs doing that has not yet been done by an array (a standing working cut into stone and metal), a glyph, or a practitioner. The day any of those three replace it, the occupation vanishes, and the person who held it discovers what Value, Coin and Trade describes with perfect accuracy and no sympathy at all: that a meritocracy is an excellent arrangement for people with merit that the instrument can see.
The Three Floors
Almost every argument about dignity, wages, and what a person is worth can be resolved by asking which floor they stand on.





















FloorStandingFirst people the instrument seesTitled practitioners carrying silver tokens that are simultaneously badges, passports, lines of credit, and bullion. In the Arbitration Division’s language, attributable capability, sitting second on the creditor schedule behind only contracted Essence (bonded work and Core hours already sold). Roughly one in twelve in the west, fewer in the east, and falling in the Withering era because Welling-stage children are fewer and the instrument’s floor has not movedSecond people the instrument needsThe people who work with Essence without touching it. Someone builds the array, maintains it, supplies its substrate, calibrates its inscriptions, mines the ore, smelts the metal, weaves the cloth the Engraver wears, bakes the bread the Engraver eats, and buries the Engraver when the occupation kills him. A practitioner can do extraordinary things. A practitioner cannot do extraordinary things without a conduit somebody forged, a substrate somebody mined, a lens somebody ground, and a meal somebody cooked. Plenty of them carry a token too, a Master cooper or a Grandmaster merchant, on the strength of their work and their guild’s word, and the coil has no opinion of either. The floor the economy pretends does not exist, and the one that stops existing for a single day and the economy notices by the second hourThird people the instrument does not seeEveryone else. Farmers, herders, fishermen, porters, washerwomen, ditch-diggers, rag-pickers, nightsoil collectors, and the vast category of people who do whatever needs doing that day and are paid in whatever is available. Invisible to the Accord because they hold no title, invisible to the factor houses because they hold no contract, and invisible to the archives because nobody is paying a scribe to write down what a field hand did this morning

This register begins with the Third Floor, because they are the majority, and any account of the world’s work that begins with the practitioners is describing the exception and calling it the rule.

A careful reader will have seen one in ten elsewhere in these shelves, that being the share of people who wake a Crystal at all, and will want the difference accounted for. The market stall has it. Somebody who wakes a Crystal, learns one trick and never pays for a silver token is on nobody’s roll, and the section on the Small Powers below is about her. The other way onto the First Floor has a price: a Waking Draft, very dear, which often kills or warps a child. Most of the rich buy one for their children, and commoners sell themselves into guild debt for the chance.
What the instrument is actually missing
The floors are usually explained as a difference in capability. They are a difference in what one machine can read.
A coil reads the output of a woken Crystal. A Trait (a standing law carried in the soul) is not output. It runs in people whose Crystal is Seed and always will be, and awakening arms what was already there rather than granting anything new. So the eleven in twelve have laws of their own, and nothing in the Accord is built to detect them.
And they have sheets. The Soul Crystal is the soul and the Continuum measures it, so a window, the soul reporting its numbers to its owner in their own tongue, comes to everyone, the unwoken included, and nobody else can read it. Skills rise with use and show on the nine ranks, Initiate, Apprentice, Journeyman, Adept, Expert, Master, Grandmaster, Archmaster and Paragon, the same words as a Stage’s rank and an Accord title. A baker has a Baking skill and a little sheet. Gammer Thirza Lubbock, asked by this compiler what hers said and having decided she disliked him, reported the following and shut the door:
[Laying-Out: Master]
[Shelling: Journeyman]
[Patience with Rams: Initiate]

What a Third Floor soul undergoes instead of Temperance (the remaking a practitioner’s Crystal goes through to climb) is the Weathering: refinement under sustained strain with no melt and no recasting, the soul hardening in place along the direction it was already being used. The trade word is grain, borrowed from the joiners, and a man is said to have taken his set clean or to have set crooked.

Every occupation in this register is a grain-forming occupation, and the register has been describing the process throughout without a word for it.
The mason who reads stone by hammer-tap after a lifetime touching one material. The fisher family’s taxonomy of catch-by-Wellspring-exposure that outperforms the Bestiary. The midwife who knows the local births the way a farmer knows the local weather. The tender who can hear that a Phreatis pump sounds different on Tuesday than it did on Monday.
The window calls some of that a skill and gives it a rank, and it is one. Under the skill lies something the window has no line for: a law, hardened along the axis the work pushed it, real, measurable if anyone measured it, and useless in any other direction for the rest of that person’s life. The tender who walks into a city carries a genuine and specific capability that the urban economy cannot recognize. His own soul reports it to him every morning, and the reason nobody else knows is that the instrument was never pointed at him.
A meritocracy is an excellent arrangement for people with merit that the instrument can see. People tend to read that sentence as bitter, and it also happens to be a technical description.

The Ground Trades
Agriculture employs the majority of the four quarters, feeds the entirety of it, and appears in the Accord's classification apparatus exactly nowhere.

The omission is deliberate. A field does not have a Soul Crystal, and the Accord’s instruments do not assess dirt.

Grain and the table
The western staple is spelt wheat, ground on stone querns at home or at the lord’s mill, for his share of the flour. The nutritional distinction is texture. The social distinction is vast: mill-ground flour, sifted through a bolting cloth, is white, fine and urban; hand-ground flour is brown, gritty, and what the person eating it could afford.

A western peasant eats dark bread, pulse porridge, whatever grows in the kitchen plot, whatever was salted or smoked in autumn, and the occasional egg. Meat is a feast-day occurrence for most households and an ordinary meal for none.

The Marrowkin grow nothing underground and import everything at prices that make every other kingdom wince, which is why their cuisine is built around what can be preserved, concentrated and stored in bulk, and why the sour barley beer of the lower Ring levels is described by every non-Marrowkin visitor as an acquired taste and by every Marrowkin as beer.






























TradeThe workWhat it costsThe FarmerPlow, sow, weed, harvest, thresh, winnow, and pray that the weather, the insects and the local Wellspring density cooperate in that order. On a prosperous farm the plow may be weight-ablated (glyph-cut so the load bears lighter), which does not pull it but halves the labor of the team. The farmer who owns this has never called it magic. To him it is the harness that cost two seasons’ surplus, and he sleeps with it inside the houseThe specific musculoskeletal damage of forty years behind a plow, and the levy, which takes the young men at planting and returns them at harvest if it returns them at all. Withering-era agriculture in formerly high-density districts is a slow catastrophe: the soil remembers the yield it used to produce, and the farmer is working ground that has been taught to expect more than the local Wellspring can now deliverThe HerderA herder in a low-density valley manages animals. A herder on the Thornback March manages animals that can occasionally see through walls and object to being moved. A beast grazed on Wellspring-consistent pasture produces leather that takes an inscription. One grazed on variable pasture takes it badly, and the premium has doubled in a generationMarginal standing. Settled communities treat herders the way settled communities have always treated people who move: as necessary, unreliable, and probably stealing somethingThe FisherNet, trap and line. In the Lake Districts of the Crow’s Reach, Phreatis-aligned waters produce fish that are larger, more regular, and occasionally capable of behaviors freshwater fish should not exhibit. The fisher families’ practical taxonomy of fish-by-Wellspring-exposure bears no resemblance to the Bestiary’s classification and is considerably more useful for predicting where the catch will beCoastal fishing is the most dangerous common occupation in the four quarters. The mortality rate exceeds surface mining by a factor the Accord tracks and the fishermen do not want published, because published numbers attract regulation, and regulation attracts people who have never been on a boatThe ForesterFell, coppice, burn charcoal for every smith and bloomery in the four quarters, since the forge arrays stand in four places and everyone else has a fire. It takes an appalling quantity of wood to make a little iron, and the charcoal-burner is the man standing between the forest and the forge, reducing one to feed the otherThe charcoal-burner’s cough. And in high-density forest: a Verdantia-touched wood grows back faster than it should, which sounds like a gift until the forest decides the clearing you made last season was a wound and closes it
The Material Trades
Mining

Before the arrays, no shaft went deeper than sixty fathoms below the adit line. After the arrays, in the few great shafts rich enough to keep one, a shaft is as deep as the Essence somebody will pay to pour into its pumps. Everywhere else it is still the adit, the horse gin and the rag-and-chain.
The technology changed. The danger did not.

The Miner · The cutting has not changed in five centuries: a man with a pick, a man with a shovel, a candle, and a prayer. The array pumps the water and moves the air. The miner cuts the face. Between the array and the face is a distance measured in fathoms, and every fathom of it belongs to the miner and the rock and nothing else.

Weight Ablation glyphwork on the cage halves the load on the winding rope. When the glyph fails, it fails all at once, and every winding house has a bell for that.

Paid piece-rate by volume of ore broken, not by the hour. A miner who is sick, slow or injured earns less, and the shortfall appears as his problem on his ledger, not as the company’s problem on theirs.
The Array-Tender. A tender does not cast spells. They replace worn packing, clean conduit junctions, test inscription integrity with a coil-calibrated assay fork, and report degradation before it becomes failure.
The distinction between a tender and a practitioner is the distinction between the master who drew the conduit and the person who goes down to it in the dead of night with a lamp and a bad knee.
Most are Stage I–III: enough sensitivity to feel when the array is running wrong, not enough to do anything about it except report it.
The Tender’s Shake. Prolonged proximity produces tremor, sleep disruption, and a narrowing of affect that continues past the point where the professional can choose to stop.
The Accord has known for a century. There is no pension for it, because paying one would mean pricing the cost of every great shaft in the four quarters at a figure the owners have already reckoned and already decided against. The miners’ brotherhood keeps a box at the pit-head, and the box buys the coffin.
A tender who walks into a city is a person with no legible credential, and the specific expertise of knowing that a Phreatis pump-array sounds different on Tuesday than it did on Monday, and what the difference means, does not translate into anything the urban economy recognizes.
The pool trades
Every worked Core (a Wellspring site, a place where one kind of Aether pools, in the common word, and as a rule a dungeon somebody cleared and now holds) has its keepers, and under the keepers it has the people who do the wet part. The pool and the city’s night-pits share a good many of those people, since a man who will do one will generally do the other.
The Core-Tender · Works the lip of the site in pairs, with an assay fork and a lamp. Checks seals, clears residue from the channels, bleeds the pool when it runs too thick, and reports density drift before the site goes dry. Wet, cramped, poorly paid, and performed at the edge of a pool at densities that would be logged as an Active Concentration if a surveyor found the same reading in open country.

No baseline is taken before a man goes down, because no baseline exists for a soul whose Crystal never woke. Which means nothing anywhere establishes what twenty years at the pool does to a man, and the trade knows exactly what it does, and has a word for the late stage that appears in no company document.

The Seal-Clerk · Presses and records. Literate, indoor, resented by the men below and by the householders above in roughly equal measure.
The Fee-Walker · Walks. The only representative of the entire magical apparatus that most people in a city will ever meet, and the reason the apparatus is understood by most people as a bill.

The Snuffer · Attends when a household stops paying, strips its lamps, scratches through its wards and drops his iron cap over the lamp stem. The most despised of the four and the best paid, for the same reason the executioner is: somebody has to, everybody knows it, and nobody wants to be adjacent to the person who did.
A snuffer works down a list drawn up by a company clerk who has never seen the room. The silence arrives before the dark does, and the snuffer is still on the stair when it does.

The lamp-wardens, ward-cutters, hedge-workers and keepers who stand above these four have their own chapter, Who Pays for the Lamp, which the reader should take as read.
Smithing
The Blacksmith · The most important tradesman in any community too small for a guild hall. His forge is the warmest building in winter, which makes it the social center by default and the information exchange by accident.

The anvil is the single most expensive object most smiths own, often inherited, frequently older than the building it sits in.
Standing is high: a smith sits at the intersection of every other trade and is trusted by proximity. People bring their broken things to a person they trust, and the smith sees every broken thing in the village.

The Aethersmith · Forges Holding-grade material: metal designed to accept, retain and discharge inscriptions. The relationship to the Engraver is that of papermaker to scribe: the Aethersmith makes the surface, the Engraver makes the meaning.

Stage III minimum, because the Aethersmith must sense the Essence properties of the metal during the pour and the quench, and her title in the smiths’ guild caps the Grade she may make (Grade and Rarity). A Journeyman stamps Tempered and no higher, whatever came out of the quench.
This is done by hand and by ear. An Aethersmith listens to the metal cool, and the pitch of the cooling tells them what the coil will confirm after the fact.

Products: Aethersteel, whose crystalline structure accepts inscription at a depth cold-forged iron cannot match; Bloodsilver, alloyed under Anima Spirare conditions to bind the metal to a single bloodline; the substrate bars and blanks the inscription trades begin with; and, when a crew comes in with something on a cart, scale and bone worked up as gear. A good Aethersmith shouts the name of a finished blade across the yard and stamps a guild mark on it the size of a thumbnail, and will fight you about that mark in any tavern you care to name.
Cloth, hide, and stone
The Spinner · Spinning is the most widely distributed craft in the four quarters, and the worst paid. Every household that cannot afford bought cloth makes its own, a clothier’s mule comes up the lane with wool for the ones who need the coppers, one loom keeps half a dozen spinners busy, and spinning is the task that fills every hand not otherwise occupied, in every season, at every hour of the day.

A distaff is more common than a sword, more essential than a plow, and less discussed than either.

The Dyer · Ancient, essential, and unspeakably foul. A dye-works smells of stale urine, rotting plant matter and heated metal salts in a combination no amount of familiarity makes tolerable, which is why dyers occupy the same district as tanners: downstream, downwind, and outside the wall. The result of all that stink is the reason a city street is the color it is: madder reds, weld yellows, the blues a whole quarter goes to war over.

Aetheric Residue (the trace a working leaves in a place) alters dye chemistry. Wellspring-touched dyes produce a depth and luminance ordinary chemistry cannot replicate, and the most valued dyes in the world exist where a specific Wellspring’s Residue meets a specific mordant, guarded as trade secrets by the families that found them.

The Tanner · Months of soaking, liming, unhairing, fleshing, bating in a warm slurry of dog or bird dung whose enzymes break down proteins, then oak bark in pits of increasing strength.

Leather from stable-Wellspring pasture takes an inscription. The tanner who can produce Holding-grade leather from a consistent herd commands a price the ordinary tanner cannot touch.
Which produces the specific class inversion where the most despised trade in the settlement is also, occasionally, the wealthiest, and the settlement processes this by continuing to despise the tanner while borrowing money from him.

The Mason · A mason’s skill is reading the stone: where it wants to split, where it will carry weight, where it will fail, by eye, by hammer-tap, and by the tactile knowledge of a lifetime touching one material.

Greystone fortification uses stone selected for minimal Essence conductivity. A wall that does not conduct magic is a wall a practitioner cannot work through.
The mason needs no Temperance. The mason needs to lay a wall a Stage XII practitioner cannot crack, and the fact that this is possible is the single most reassuring fact in military architecture.

The Ward-Carver · A mason with Gnosis (the perceiving faculty that reads Essence). Second Floor by training, First Floor by output. Stage III–V, enough to verify the inscription is seating, because a ward-carver who cannot feel the glyph seating is a mason who makes expensive mistakes in expensive stone. The ward-cutter on your street corner is her poor cousin, who does lintels, and she will tell you so.

The highest standing of any artisan trade. A ward-carver who maintains a settlement’s perimeter is the person standing between the community and whatever the perimeter is keeping out, and the community knows it.

The Inscription Trades

The Reconstruction invented writing Essence down. Everything since has been the consequence.

The Engraver · Cuts Parunic syntax (the grammar of the glyphs) into prepared substrate. The scribe of the material economy, the person who turns inert matter into working goods. Stage IV minimum; Stage VII and above for recursive arrays, living runes, or anything that must interact with another soul’s architecture.

The requirement comes from the work and owes nothing to politics. An Engraver whose Gnosis cannot read the substrate at inscription depth is carving blind, and a blind carving in a material that holds Essence is an object waiting to fail.

The loupe · Ground from Clearbeam beryl, letting the Engraver see the pattern at inscription depth and verify the glyph is seating into the crystalline structure rather than sitting on the surface. The single most valuable object an Engraver owns and the one most likely to be stolen, which is why Engravers’ guild halls have better locks than the counting-houses.

First Floor by classification, and resented for it by every other artisan trade, because the Engraver does not mine the metal, does not smelt it, does not forge it into shape, and earns more than all three combined for the final step of cutting a pattern into what other hands made.

The Glyph-Scribe · Drafts the pattern the Engraver cuts. The Scribe is the draftsman, the Engraver is the builder. Seven years minimum, and the Journeyman’s examination is the most failed in any guild of the Accord, because an error produces a template an Engraver will follow into a substrate that will hold the error permanently and discharge it at the worst possible moment.
The Calibrator · Puts the finished product on a coil, measures output against specification, and signs the certificate that says it works. Or does not sign it, in which case the Engraver starts over. The calibration log is the legal record standing between the Engraver and liability if the product fails in the field.
The Small Powers
Nobody compiled this section for the Logistics Division. It was added by the Archives, because the compiler’s own laundry came back dry in the rain.
Walk any market in the Old World on a working morning and count the people doing something impossible for money. About one person in ten wakes a Crystal, very few of those climb far, and a Crystal that will never see Stage III can still do one small thing thirty times a day for forty years. These people pull a thread of Aether from the ground under their stall, refine it, and spend it on the only trick they own. On fat ground (rich ground, in a scholar’s mouth) they work till dark. On lean ground they are done by noon and charge double. They wear whatever their aura happens to be, so a fish market in full cry is a smear of little colors at wrist height, and nobody looks up.
Each of them is a tradesman first. Each of them costs money, has bad days, and can tell you to come back tomorrow, and the street treats that as it treats a baker’s temper. Each has the trick on their own window as a skill, at a rank they will tell you about over a second drink. The hall in any signed town has a rule against taking pay for a working without a token, and the fee-walkers have long since learned which stalls to walk past.



























































TradeThe small powerWhat it paysThe bad day, and the refusalThe Cold-WifeLays a palm on a basket of herring and it stays sea-cold till evening2 copper the basketDone by noon on lean ground. She has declined the Fishmongers’ steward since the day he called her “girl,” and his fish know it by the second afternoonThe Link-ChildWalks you home after dark by the light of her own open hand, in whatever color she woke1 copper the streetChildren tire, and they stop where they tire. She will also set you down at the corner of any street where someone once kicked herThe Knot-WifeTies a knot that will not slip until she says so. Sailors, hangmen and brides3 copper a knot; 1 silver for a ship’s lashingShe can die. A Measurewright (one of the Guild’s scholars of the art) once wrote out in three copied folios why a Cold-Wife’s palm could not lawfully chill a basket below the temperature of the market, on grounds of heat having to go somewhere. He was correct about the heat. It goes up her arm, which is why they all wear short sleeves in the dead of winter. Whether a small power of this kind is a learned technique or a grain that happened to wake with its owner has been argued in the Guild halls for two hundred years, and the Cold-Wives have not been consulted.
Guild craftsmen stand one rung up from the stalls and let you know about it. They shout the names of their works across the square and fight over their marks, and what they build is medieval in everything but its ambitions: glyph-cut gearing, wheels with opinions, contraptions that misfire in funny and terrible ways. Dame Mabel Madder’s Cradle of Perpetual Slumber, Warranted Against All Colic, has rocked three infants clear over the foot-rail and carries two guild marks, one of them in approval.
The Yard and the Token
A title is a job. Nobody on the street has ever been confused about this, and only the holders of titles have ever needed it explained.
Practitioners are common, and their ranks are as well known as the grades of a butcher’s cut. A carter can tell you what an inner disciple is good for and what one costs. A boy’s family has been Heron for four generations, he wears the blue rag on his arm to haul sacks, and he will explain to you which Heron core disciple ought to be dropped from the bracket and why. Any city of size has a dozen fighting schools with their colors out, and a school is an employer of the ordinary sort, with a kitchen, a landlord, a roof that leaks and wages that are usually late.
