The Crew and the Commission
Nobody’s mother wants this for them, and half the children in any Mouth town want nothing else.
The Merry Thimbles of Pennycrown came up from the Upper Workings one wet spring evening with a Tolling Crab on a sledge, all six of them alive, and fell to fighting in the tavern yard before the mask-runner had her boots off. Level moves by danger overcome, so a kill on something far above you moves it more than a hundred on something beneath you, and the soul reports the gain to whoever it judges overcame the thing. Five of the Thimbles had spent an hour taking that crab apart with hammers and a tuning bar. The sixth was Nan Hobday, their cook, who had come down to bring them soup and had hit it with the pot as it fell over, and it was Nan’s window that lit up. Their captain demanded to see it, which cannot be done. Nan described it, with feeling, for the whole yard. They were still arguing at closing, they broke two benches and a nose, and the Thimbles have gone down ever since with a written rule about the soup, and with Nan, who is a better fighter now than the captain and goes first.
Adventuring is a trade, conducted through some of the loudest halls in the Accord, and a hall is a guild like any other, with a green door, a board, a grudge against the hall across the square, and the same nine titles. Hunting halls post commissions by Grade, E to EX, the same letters monsters themselves are posted at, and a title lets you take them up to its own letter and no further (old hall rolls call these Threat Tiers, T1 to T9). Monsters live everywhere, on the roads and in the barley and under the mill, so the work is not all stairs. Most of it is smaller and meaner than the songs, an E-Grade commission at a henhouse for a few silver and a Green Sigil’s worth of hedge-pests along a toll road. The depth, the crew’s posts and how a clearing goes are at Dungeons, and this register will confine itself to the money.
An adventurer is somebody who ventures capital. A big job is raised with subscribers and shares, so a crew holds a piece of its own luck and draws no wage, which is why it will go one more gallery than is wise. Six to twelve is usual. A real crew bond, the earned kind, shows as a line on each member’s window, shares out a little of the Level gain, and shows the others’ bars in a fight, and betrayal breaks it in front of everyone concerned. Every captain will tell you the bond is worth more than the shares, and has generally just finished arguing about the shares.
What comes up the stair is the whole economy of the thing. The hall pays on the mask or the bounty. The core is what the crew came for: in a way the monster’s Soul Crystal, worth more the stronger the beast, a few silver off an E-Grade beast, most of a laborer’s year off a B, and a sum that changes a family’s history off an S (What Things Cost has the rows). Hide, bone and scale go to the armorers. Anything left behind by the last crew goes to whoever can carry it past the next crew. A commoner who comes up holding a core has walked out of a hole with the one thing the great houses cannot simply refuse to sell her, and every factor in the valley is at the top of the stair with a very good dinner. A lucky crew is the nearest thing to a revolution most of the four quarters will ever see, and the houses have noticed, and they buy early, in several senses.

The Works and the Mill

The arrays made the Old World deep. Cloth is making it crowded. A wheel on a fast river pounds the wool thick, a bell on a hall tower starts and stops the day, and the hands that do everything in between are coming in from the country faster than the town can roof them.
This is the new floor of the age, and no register can count it, because it is never all in one room.

Four years after Jonet Teasel’s wheelbarrow of coppers (the Apparatus has it, under The Hour), in the hot summer of Year 699, the masters of Cardmere quadrupled the fee for entering the Weavers’ Hall, on the stated ground that the wrong sort of people had begun saving for it. The carders of that town, the people who drag raw wool between spiked boards until it will spin, belonged to no guild, were forbidden by statute to meet in any number above ten, and had been meeting in their hundreds for a generation under cover of a burial club. They came up Tenter Hill at dusk with teasels in their hats, grease to the elbow and a banner somebody’s aunt had sewn out of the masters’ own scarlet. The dyers and shearers fell in behind them in every color the vats could throw, and by midnight the wool hall stood open, the debt rolls were burning in the square, and a comber named Dickon Burr was sitting in the Provost’s chair, in the Provost’s gold chain, over a smock you could smell from the door. Inside the week Burr’s people had made three new guilds, stopped all debts under twelve silver, and ordered the work bell rung at a decent hour.
Then they governed, and that is the part the masters lower their voices about. For three and a half years the poorest people in the richest town in the quarter ran its courts, its walls, its grain and its accounts, and ran them about as well as anyone ever has. The valley lord’s horse came against them twice, in plumes, and the carders’ muster met it at the weirs with long spears and wet ground. The gilt spurs are still nailed up in the carders’ chapel, several hundred pair, and the chaplain will show you for a copper.
What finished them came with no sword at all. The clothiers went to their country houses and stopped putting out wool. A town can be seized, and a wool clip can be sold to the next town down the river. By the fourth winter there was nothing to card, and Cardmere’s newest guild was three thousand hungry people with an excellent charter. The masters came home at the thaw and struck the three guilds from the roll. Burr, who had kept the accounts honest, got a pension and a house outside the walls on condition that he never again come through the gate. The Division has not decided whether that was mercy. The carders have.
What follows is how such a town comes to be possible, and it is how most of the hands in the four quarters that are not on a field actually earn.
The Thirty Hands · A bolt of Cardmere scarlet passes through about thirty pairs of hands between the sheep and the duke, and most of those hands never meet: sorter, beater, washer, carder, comber, spinner, warper, weaver, burler (who picks out the knots), fuller (who pounds the woven wool thick), tenterer, shearer, dyer, presser and the rest, in lofts, cellars, cottages and yards from the town wall to the hill farms. No one of the thirty can make the cloth, and each is paid only for the step they do. A thing cut into thirty steps needs no craftsman after the first, only thirty people who cannot each sell the whole, and the clothiers found that out before the guilds did.
The Clothier · This is the putting-out system, and it is the great invention of the age’s money. A clothier (a draper, in the old towns) buys the wool, carries it out to a hundred cottages to be spun, collects the yarn, carries that out to a hundred rooms to be woven, pays by the piece, and owns the cloth at every step without ever touching it. He keeps a counting-room, a mule and a list. When trade goes slack he stops coming, and a hundred rooms find out on the same morning. The loom is the weaver’s own, and so are the rent, the debt on the loom and the bad year.
The Fulling Mill and the Dye-Hall · The only roofs that gather the hands together: timber-framed, loud at the near end and warm at the far one, and raising no chimney. A fulling mill is a long shed with a wheel at one end and a shaft overhead, the shaft turning cams that lift great oak stocks and drop them on wet wool from first bell to last. A great dye-hall is the same shed with vats in it, and half of what goes on there is magic from end to end, done under trade work by thirty people who have never woken, each performing one licensed step. Visitors from the provinces expect smoke and find a hum, and cannot understand why the people inside look so tired. The grime of the age is in the conditions. The dye and cloth trades hang their work from the rafters to dry and peg it out on tenter frames (long racks that stretch wet cloth square) across the nearest hillside, so the tiredest people in the city labor under a ceiling of crimson and saffron, and the slope above Cardmere can be read from ten miles off, in stripes.
What it makes · What a household cannot make for itself and a stranger will pay for. A household still spins, bakes, brews and mends. The town sells it the rest: cloth by the bolt, each one sealed in lead at the cloth hall, and by the same arrangement of list and mule, nails by the keg, pins, needles and pewter. Boots are still a cordwainer’s, one pair at a time, at the price in What Things Cost.
The Crown’s bolts · Crossbow bolts come from a castle. A Crown keeps its quarrel forge in charcoal country, one master and a dozen hands at their own anvils, thirty thousand heads a year cut to a pattern gauge, so that a head goes onto any shaft of the same mark, at about three coppers the bolt, barreled and carted to the armory by the wagon. The master’s name is on the Crown’s rolls and the gauge is the only true one in the quarter, and he sleeps on it.
Who owns it · Chartered houses, great houses and the factor houses that fund both, with the clothiers’ own hall sitting in front of them. The raw stock comes in under charter from the eastern arc and the south, the fine reds and the alum (the salt that fixes a dye to a cloth) above all, the finished bolts go back out along the same routes at the price the charter sets, and the margin stays in the west. The age calls this trade. The places at the far end of the charter have other words for it.

The guilds at war
The register records these because every one of them is a lawsuit, and several have been a battle.
The Handloom Weaver · Once the aristocrat of the cottage. Now working longer hours for a third of the town rate, for a clothier who carried the wool out past the town’s three-league line because a cottage pays no guild, and teaching the trade to children who will never earn by it. The town weavers call him an interloper and hold a charter that says so, and every generation or so they march out in full muster to break his looms. In the Loom War of Year 671 the weavers of Cardmere went twelve miles in scarlet, with drums and a wagon of axes, to Nether Wadding, where the village women had carried forty looms up the church tower in pieces and were standing on the stair with distaffs. The expedition came home with one loom, a broken nose and a lawsuit that is still open.
The Cordwainer and the Cobbler · A cordwainer makes shoes of new leather, a cobbler mends them with old, and each company holds a charter against the other. The whole dispute comes down to how much new leather may go on an old shoe before it becomes a new one, and the searchers of both companies walk the town with rulers.
The Nailer and the Chainmaker · Whole villages at the hearth, the family’s hands making nails by the thousand. A nail-monger puts out the rod iron by the bundle at the start of a turn, takes back the nails by weight at the end of it, weighs them on his own scale and pays in whatever he has. Pins, girdles and bad ale are the usual coin, and there is a statute against that, which he can show you.
The Carter and the Carrier · Beaten wherever a river runs (a barge carries what a dozen ox-wagons carry and pays no road-warden), tolled wherever a kept road runs (one of the few great old roads whose sunk waystones, tended by hired road-wardens, ease a heavy wain across a hand’s breadth of air), and pushed out to the roads nothing else can reach, which are the roads that break axles. The Weight Ablation harness that cost two seasons’ surplus is worth half its price the day a bargeman ties up at the same wharf.
The Lamplighter · The man with a ladder and a can of oil. The good corners are lost to the wardens with their boys and poles. He keeps every alley, inn-yard and back stair that cannot pay for a warden’s color, and the Oil-Men’s Company has been at law with the wardens’ companies for eighty years over which corner is which.

The fee-bound poor are the age’s own invention. The hand who came in from the country for the cloth lives in one room on a stair, on sealed household work (a warden’s lamp and a cutter’s ward, split among six doors) at a quality below what the fee implies, pays the round-fee before bread, and is snuffed the month the clothier stops coming. He came to the city because the lamps were there. He is now the person the lamps cost most.

The City the Cloth Built
The great city of the age is timber, brick and stone, four to six stories where the walls will not let it spread, each story leaning a little farther over the street than the one beneath, and its newest quarters were mostly built inside one long lifetime.
The Street · Rows for the clerk, rents for the hand (a rent being a tall house let by the room), walled houses with a tower for the owner, and a market cross in the middle for all of them to shout at. Brick in the west, gray stone in the north, painted plaster on the fashionable squares. Stone bridges cramped and banded in Stillband iron over every river, mud and pigs underfoot and a gutter down the middle. The good streets are Essence-lit in every color their wardens happen to burn and are never quite dark, the rest go black at curfew, and the country-born do not sleep for the first month on either.
The Cloth Hall · A covered street of stalls a bowshot long under a vaulted roof, with colored glass in its clerestory and the town’s belfry on top of it, lit on market nights, warmed in winter by a warden’s stones, patrolled by beadles who keep out the poor. Every bolt in town is sealed here and every town built it before it built anything else. The age’s cathedral, and it charges no tithe until you buy something.

The Service Trades
The Innkeeper · A social institution first and a bed second: the place where news arrives before it is announced, where prices are set by conversation before they are set by the factor house, and where the innkeeper’s opinion of a guest determines whether the guest’s horse is stabled where it can be stolen.

In practitioner-heavy districts: a high-Stage practitioner sleeping in a thin-walled room leaves Residue the next guest can feel. Good innkeepers install dampening inscriptions in their best rooms, which cost more than the furniture, and charge accordingly.
The innkeeper knows everything. The innkeeper is trusted by nobody.

The Merchant · Carries a seal-token representing their oldest active contract. Torven Greis is the template: eleven way-stations on the Iron-to-Salt Corridor, metal one way and salt the other, making money on the spread and on the station fees and on knowing, better than anyone in a factor house ever will, what a week on the road actually costs.
The Carrier · Does not own the goods. Paid in weight and distance, the oldest arithmetic in commerce. Weight Ablation harness halves the effective load, which means a carrier without one is worth half as much, so every carrier who can afford the harness buys it, and every one who cannot is aware of his own obsolescence.
The Way-Station Keeper · An innkeeper stripped to essentials and stationed where nobody would live by choice but everyone needs someone to be. Quality runs from the Corridor stations, well-stocked because Greis-house money runs through them, down to a roof, a well, and the specific hospitality of a person who has been alone for three months and is willing to feed you in exchange for conversation.
The Healing Trades
The Physician · In a Guild city the physician examines, puts the patient under with the sleeping sponge (poppy, mandrake and henbane, or a hired hand from the healing trades), and scrubs in vinegar and spirits of wine before anyone cuts. Past the Guild cities the older school still does not touch the patient. It reads: urine, pulse, complexion, tongue, the character of the breath, and where Gnosis-trained, the Essence Signature. A two-tier system results, and the two tiers disagree about everything except that the patient is their problem.
The Surgeon · Cuts. Below the physician, above the barber, and angry about both. The jurisdictional dispute is always the same: the physician claims diagnostic authority, the surgeon claims procedural authority, and the patient claims the right to see whoever will actually help.

The Midwife · The most experienced practical clinician most people in the four quarters will ever be touched by. She knows the local births the way a farmer knows the local weather: from no book, and from a lifetime of being in the room when it happens.
A birth is the formation of a Crystal, and thin-Veil districts produce complications the midwife recognizes and the physician has never studied.
Her practical taxonomy of birth-by-district is the closest thing that exists to a medical account of what Wellspring density does to the formation of a new soul, and no physician has ever asked for it.

The Herbalist · Knowledge arrived at by giving people things and seeing what happens, which is exactly how every pharmacopoeia in history was built, and exactly how every college describes it in terms designed to obscure the similarity.
The Death Trades

Indispensable and untouchable. Their touch pollutes. Their presence at a feast pollutes the feast. Their money spends, and nobody asks where the coin was before the gravedigger’s hand held it, because the question pollutes the asking.

The Layer-Out · Always a woman. The person who stands between the family and the physical reality of what a body does when it stops being occupied.

A dead practitioner’s Crystal does not cease producing Essence immediately. A body that is still radiating is a body the ambient Continuum has not yet acknowledged as gone. The layer-out in a practitioner community knows how long the Residue lasts by Stage, by the Wellspring the dead one tempered on longest, by Path (a Body fighter leaves the most of it in the flesh, which is what renderers race for; a Spirit hand haunts; a Fate hand leaves vows still binding), and by whether the death was peaceful or violent, and knows it by having been in the room enough times to count. The Scarlet Rams can tell you what it costs to forget this.

The Gravedigger · Burial depth matters metaphysically. A body interred within Residue decay range of the surface bleeds Essence into the topsoil, and the accumulation over generations produces Heavy Earth: soil that reads to Gnosis as remembering being alive.

Burial grounds in old settlements are measurably different from surrounding terrain. Crops grow differently on them. Animals avoid them.
The gravedigger who works them is standing in the accumulated memory of every person he has buried, and the occupation’s reputation for strangeness is simply an accurate observation that got into the folklore.

The Executioner · Usually hereditary, always polluted, and the only person in most communities who possesses genuine expertise in how bodies fail.

A practitioner’s execution is a difficult piece of work. The Crystal’s death-response varies by Stage, by Path and lens, and by the conditions of the death, and an executioner who does not understand what happens to a Crystal at the moment of severance is an executioner who will be killed by the discharge.
The lowest standing in the four quarters. The family does not marry outside the trade. His money is spent at a specific window. His children attend no school.
And his expertise in Essence-at-death is the most practically valuable body of knowledge in the death trades, transmitted entirely within the family, wanted by the Research Division, which has asked three times and been refused three times, because publishing it would require acknowledging where it came from.

The Paper Trades

The Accord is a coalition that runs on paper. Outside its own Sealed Charter it holds little ground and raises no levy, and what binds a mining hall in one kingdom to a merchants’ hall in another is a contract each of them can enforce. A thing that has not been entered has not happened, and a thing that has been entered in three copies has happened three times.

A hall sells three things, shared title, enforceable contracts and passage, and every one of them comes out of an inkwell. A commission on the board, a venture’s share-list, a hall’s charter, a token’s entry, a pass for the Concord Gate, a letter of passage over a border, a stamp on every contract and a stamp on the stamp. Each is made out in triplicate by hand, one copy for the party, one for the hall and one for the Archive, and the Archive’s copy is the one that survives. Crowns tolerate all this and are afraid of it, for good reason, since a kingdom can hang a hall’s clerk and still find that nobody in it can get a shipment of tin across the river.








































TradeThe workWhat it costsThe ClerkCopies, files, enters and totals, on a high stool, by the Guild clock. The largest respectable trade of the age, and the one every family off the land wants for its cleverest sonShort sight, a stoop, a wage paid quarterly in arrears, and the knowledge that a bench of cheaper copyists is coming for the copying half of the workThe CopyistWorks the copy-bench: reed pen, ruled sheet, a boy to mix the ink, and three fair copies by nightfall for a hard-pressed hand. The one office bench a woman can commonly sit at, because a scrivener’s widow or daughter has always held the pen in the back room, and there are more of them every year than the men in the next room find comfortablePaid less than the clerk for more copies. Half the offices of the age call the bench “the ink,” and half of those call the women at it the sameThe Scrivener and the StationerThe scrivener keeps a bench by the church door and will write your letter, your will or your lie for a couple of coppers, and his boy can make forty dozen-word bills in an hour. The stationer, in a university town, rents out a book’s exemplar a quire at a time to whoever means to copy it. The only literate person most people will ever hireInk-galled fingers, the contents of every will in the parish, and the people who would like to know themThe Beacon ClerkReads and sends on the Guild’s beacon line (hilltop fire-towers in sight of one another beside the few great roads the Guild runs, lit by wardens in shuttered colors and shut by any fog), counts the words, charges by the count, a silver for twenty with the addresses counted and a copper for each word after, and reads every message that passes. Sworn to the Guild’s secrecy, and the best-informed person in any town that has a towerNight duty, smoke, and a reputation for knowing what the neighbors paid to sayThe Hall CallerStands on the great stair of a Guild hall in the big cities and bawls the name of whoever has a message waiting, as it comes up from the towers and the relay riders, until somebody claims it. Chosen for a clear voice, and paid a little extra by certain people to mispronounce certain namesA ruined throat by thirty, and a steward on the stair behind, countingThe Hall DeskStamps, countersigns, returns forms for the wrong color of ink, and is the face of the Accord to anyone who wants anything from a hall. The seal-clerk’s cousin, and as resentedNobody has ever thanked a hall desk, and the hall desk has long stopped expecting it
The Evening Trades
The feast calendar leaves the age some ninety days with no work bell on them, and the age keeps a trade ready to fill each one.
The Pageant and the Tavern Hall · The pageant plays to the whole town and the tavern hall plays to whoever is still standing. On a great feast every craft rolls out its own play on its own painted wagon and does it at each corner in turn, shipwrights a flood, bakers a famine broken, butchers a martyrdom with real props. The tavern hall has a host, a bar, a comic singer, a strong man and a turn that closes the night. Wagon-wrights, scene-painters, dressers, the hired warden who throws colored light from a rooftop. A comic song from a tavern hall reaches every street in the city within days and every province within the year, and nobody can say who wrote it.
Sport and Spectacle · Racing through the streets and down the meadow on feast days, ward against ward in their colors, with the bookmaker at the rope and the whole city betting by runner. Prize-fighting, half-legal, under a bridge arch or in a tavern yard. Football on a feast afternoon, parish against parish, which is the same war as the schools’ with fewer rules. And the spectacle nobody else has: the Stage bracket, with colors, songs and a bookie on every bench. The great tournaments are the world’s sport: realms send champions, schools play for colors and Cores, and a win can be worth a bought Stage. Beside the bracket stands the licensed practitioner exhibition, where a titled hand shows before a paying crowd what a Stage can do, under Accord license and on Core hours somebody has paid for.

Ordinary people regard a titled practitioner as half a saint and half a racehorse, and the exhibition sells benches on it. The license caps the working at exhibition grade and requires a warden on the floor, and every promoter knows that the crowd came for the moment the warden might be needed.









































TradeThe workWhat it costsThe Herald and the CrierCries the news at the cross and the bracket results at the gate, by the cry and by the corner. All the news most people will ever get, at a volume you can hear across a fish marketA ruined throat by fifty, and a beating from whichever side the news went againstThe MinstrelSells songs about people who did things, and gets the details wrong in the direction that sells. A fighter’s name travels at the speed of a minstrel who needs supperBeing found by the person the song was about. Several have been asked to correct a verse, and at least one did it with a broken jawThe BookieTakes odds on brackets, duels, sieges, how long a stoppage will last, and whether the grandmaster will really eat the anvil. Keeps the only figures anyone trustsBroken fingers, on a regular basis, and the debts of people who outrank himThe Bounty-ClerkKeeps the board where lords, sects and houses post what they will pay and for whom, chalks up the changes, and takes a fee for posting and a fee for striking off. Knows what everyone is worth, to the copper, and to whomHaving his own name go up, which happensThe List-KeeperMaintains one of the rankings: the Accord’s roll, a herald’s list, a realm’s, a sect’s, a bookie’s. They all disagree, and each sells copies to the people on the othersBeing visited by whoever came in ninth. Getting on a list makes you a target, and so does keeping oneThe FixerArranges for a bracket to go the way somebody has already paid for. A word to a second, a swapped vial, a sick mother. Fixing fights is a major crime and a major business, and every tournament town has one who dines with the magistrateThe rope, the river, or an honest fighter who was not told
The Tea-Stall, the Drinking-Hall and the Confraternity · The stall for talk, the guild’s drinking-hall for men of one craft with nowhere else to sit, and the confraternity for everybody else. A confraternity is a burial club with a saint, a banner, a feast and a box of dues, and any carder may join one, which is why the statutes against meeting have never once stopped a meeting. Guild halls keep a reading room with the rate sheets and the registers chained open to any member, and the confraternities keep the crier’s bills and a preacher every turn. More plans are made on confraternity benches than in council, and the Guild has noticed.
The Feast Garden and the Fair · Lit walks, hired trumpets, a hired hand throwing colored fire over the water and a rope-walker on an Ascensio line, when a great house opens its park on a feast day for the respectable; the fair for everyone: the traveling show with its menagerie, its strong woman, its shadow-play booth worked by a girl with a light in her hands, and its fortune-teller who will read your Crystal for a copper, wrongly. The park at Merrow Hythe has a bridge that drops its guests in the lake and a stone ape that spits at ladies, both by a Guild master long dead, and neither can be turned off. The fair arrives in the provinces with the only lantern show the town will see that year, and leaves with a year’s pocket money.
What the Trades Are Paid
Compiled, under protest, from What Things Cost, for readers who skipped the rest. One gold mark is twelve silver marks, and one silver mark is twenty-four copper. Past the last warden’s round most of this is paid in kind.






































































WorkPayNoteA laborer, by the day12 to 24 copperHalf a silver in a slack season, a silver in a good one. Often paid part in board or kindA soldier, by the month12 to 15 silver and his keepLess stoppages for kit, which take a third of itA clerk, by the month4 to 8 goldPaid quarterly, in arrears. The copyist gets less for more copiesA searcher, by the month10 to 18 goldAnd the gifts nobody records. Searchers inspect for the companies, with a seal press and an assay forkA minerPiece-rate, by volume of ore brokenSick, slow or injured means less, on his ledgerA carrierBy weight and distanceHalved in practice if he lacks the harnessA tender or mill-wardenPaid like each other, and Stage I to IIINo pension for the ShakeThe snufferBest paid of the pool tradesThe executioner’s reasoningLamp-wardens, ward-cutters, hedge-workersRound-fee; by the job and the glyph; in kind, usuallyThey can walk off the round, leave the last stroke uncut, or live a long way from youPetty folk artsA copper here and thereSee The Small Powers, aboveA titled practitionerBy title, 3 gold a month and upSee The Yard and the Token, aboveA crewBy share, and by what comes up the stairSee The Crew and the Commission, above. The porter gets a flat fee
Technology by Region
The Age by Place

There is no year in which the age arrived. It arrives by distance from rich ground and a Guild hall. A traveler on this continent moves through time as well as across it, and the register cannot give a date for any object without first asking where it stands.
The wardens’ rounds go out a few streets further every year, the chartered houses push further into the eastern arc every season, and every mile either of them gains is a mile of somebody’s fee.

The Accord and the Guild cities · The age at its newest, and ahead of it where money allows. An old kept road on the few great routes that have one and a beacon on the hills beside it, lamps of every color at the rich curb, a water clock in every hall and the Guild hour on every bell, Guild surcoats in the barracks, clerks and copyists in every office. The sleeping sponge and vinegar in the hospitals. A clerk here carries a pocket dial that is no use to him indoors, and thinks of working by the light as something his grandmother did.
The provinces · Decades behind, and in no hurry. The road reaches the county town in ruts; the inn is where the letters wait, and the carrier’s wagon is the news; the fulling mill stands beside a street where the country looms are still working and the town muster has not yet come to break them. Horses on every road, the militia in bright tabards, tallow in most houses and an Essence lantern on the bishop’s porch, and the spital and the barber for medicine. A provincial town keeps two times, the Guild’s and the church’s, and lives by the second.
The north · The age at its oldest, and in Kharven nothing later. No warden’s round north of the arrays, no kept road past the last waystation, no beacon past the last Guild post. Tallow and rushlight, peat and dung on the fire, letters by rider, the levy in gambeson with a crossbow if the armory had one, the light and the bell, and medicine from the barber and the old women. Almost nobody reads. The north cuts the lake ice a southern duke drinks his wine over and has never once wanted an ice-house. It sends the age its cold and shares in none of its comforts.
The east and the south under charter · Every decade of the age at once. A Cloudmetal works, one of four in the world, stands a day’s walk from villages the age has not reached, and the chartered grove, the chartered wharf and the Guild post are the age at its newest set down in the age at its oldest. The charter brings the works, and the works bring the wage, the fee and the snuffer, in that order.

A journey from an Accord capital to Kharven-Seat runs the whole age backwards. A carrier’s wain over the old stones to the edge of the fat ground, the same wain off the stones behind a tired team to the county town, an ox wagon to where the road is paved, a hired hack to where it stops being paved, the mule to the pass, and the last of it on the road the first cart made.
The traveler who makes it folds away his pocket dial at the last Guild bell, changes his coat at the last waystone and his manners at the pass, and arrives in a country where his dial is a curiosity and his title token is the only thing about him anyone understands.

What the Division Has Not Surveyed

































PolityWhat it builds, and what that saysMarrowholdExtraction technology. The Marrowkin invented nothing that does not come out of a hole. Pumping, ventilation, winding and forge arrays, and the Aethersteel process that exists because Ignivale kilns hold temperatures charcoal cannot reach. Between a miner’s pick and an Engraver’s burin lie roughly forty named occupations that the Accord classifies as Second Floor and the Marrowkin classify as the reason they eatNalūnTrust, where Marrowhold builds extraction. The Parun-bound instruments, the seal-tokens, the bills that present for payment across three jurisdictions because the bill enforces itself. Nalūn makes no things at all. Nalūn makes the agreements that allow other people to make things at a distance from each other, the physical expression of a culture that discovered the most valuable thing in the world is a promise you can verifyThe Silver CedarsPerceptual. Ward-perimeters, Boundary-layer monitoring, the Yukari contribution of perceptual governance. Technologies of watching, reading and knowing, with very little of making in them. The Reach builds walls out of awareness rather than stone, and treats maintenance as a civic sacrament and novelty as a risk to be assessed before it is adoptedKharven (redirected from the struck Sātūlagi entry)Martial. The Moto Fractura attunement gives a structural advantage in fortification assessment, demolition, and the military engineering that involves looking at a wall and knowing where it will fail. Kharven builds for war the way Marrowhold builds for extraction: with no elegance whatever and the specific brutal competence of people who have been doing one thing for a very long time and have stopped pretending it is anything other than what it isThe Holy Sea of AlabasterTestimonial. The Wellspring, the most complete archive of births, deaths and contracts in the Inner World, and the deposit-and-lending operations Nalūn considers a sin and the Holy Sea considers a service. Its works are records, with no machinery anywhere, and the records outlast everythingThe Eastern ArcWhat happens when a polity commits array capacity to something other than pumping water. Cloudmetal reduced by Judicium arrays at a scale that exists in four places in the world. Onceglass charges sold as consumable munitions. Ascensio-augmented looms the west cannot match. It demonstrates the thesis of The Four Ceilings in real time: technology owes more to geological accident and institutional willingness than to genius, and a people sitting on different rock with different priorities will build a different world

The Logistics and Supply Division commissioned this register to establish what work exists and who does it, and it has done that. It has touched entertainment only where entertainment is a trade, and it has not touched food and cuisine, ground-level justice, domestic life and courtship, or funerary custom, and the omission is consistent rather than accidental.
Every one of those is something the Third Floor does when it is not working. The Division surveys labor because labor is what the Division buys. A register compiled by a purchaser will describe what is for sale and will be silent on everything a person is when the day ends.
The Archives has proposed a companion survey on four occasions. Each proposal has been referred to the Division that would have to fund it.

materials,-alchemy--and--trade/work,-tra.content:
What a pound is, who decided, and who has never accepted it. The same political act as standardizing the tongue and the hour, performed by the same institution, resisted by the same people.

One weight, one measure, one reach, through all the land.
The Accord’s formula, repeated in four successive revisions of the formulary, each of which was necessary because the previous one had not worked

On the last morning of the Barley Fair at Saltby the grain cog Fat Margery warped off the town quay with her red sail going up, painted eyes on her bow, a band on her foredeck and five hundred loads of barley in her, and half the fair came down to wave, because her master owed money to most of them. She had been filled by the Saltby measure, heaped, and her master had signed for five hundred loads by the Accord’s measure, level. The difference between those two words is about a quarter, so she was carrying a hundred and twenty-five loads nobody had written down, and she rode so low that the boys on the quay were laying odds. A furrow out, a seam opened. Dry barley that takes on water swells with patient and enormous force, and the hold of a cog is a closed box. Fat Margery let go at every plank from the keel up, in full view of the fair, and five thousand measures of barley went out across the green harbor in one long gold slick with the band still in it, and every gull on that coast arrived to see.
Her owners sued the quay-factor for the cargo. The factor sued the master for the signature. The master, in a wet red coat, sued the town for its measure, and the town, wanting somebody smaller, sued the strike-board man who had filled her, Rolling Ned Tolland, who came before the Bench in his best hat and demonstrated his stroke on a sack of peas, slowly, three times, to the delight of the gallery, while two clerks tried and failed to describe it. The court sent out for the town’s standard measure, which was brought in on a cart with some ceremony and turned out to carry a six-pointed strike, filed halfway smooth. The suit ran thirty-four years, outlived three judges and every party but Ned, and produced one finding anyone remembers: that nobody in Saltby, then or since, could be made to say on oath how big a measure is. The barley came up that spring on the harbor mud in a long green stripe. It is called Margery’s Acre, and the question of who owns it is still before the Bench.
What follows is everything Saltby could not say on oath, set out by an archivist who has checked his own rule against the wall twice this week.
Why This Is Political
Three institutions already built cannot function without standard weights: the assay, which determines fineness by comparing masses; the proof-mark, which certifies that a thing was tested; and the Bench of Attribution, whose four powers are entry, striking, attribution and reservation, and two of those are exercised on weights.
Somebody had to make the four quarters agree what a pound is. The Marrowkin did not want to. Nobody wanted to, because a local measure is a local advantage, and the man who knows the district bushel is a heaping bushel is the man who buys in that district. The Accord is a coalition of guilds across many nations, so it could not simply decree the thing. It made the standard a term of signing on: a hall that wants the shared titles, the enforceable contracts and the passage takes the pound along with them, then goes home and keeps the old bushel in the back.
The pattern is unambiguous, here as in every history that has ever tried it: central authorities issue uniformity statutes over and over across centuries, and the fact that they keep issuing them is the evidence they are not working. The Accord’s formulary has been revised four times. Every revision says one weight and one measure through all the land. Every revision was needed.
I. The Grain
Everything is built on a seed.
The base unit of both length and weight is the grain, a single counted seed of standard barley, dried. Three laid end to end give a thumb. Seven thousand by mass give a pound. Nobody designed this system and nobody would call it elegant. You arrive at it when the only thing available in every village in the four quarters that is reliably the same size is a seed.
Which is also the flaw. Grain from different soils is not the same size, and the Accord’s grain is Western grain, and northern clerks have been saying so for six hundred years and have never once been able to prove it in a room.
II. Length













































UnitEqual toNotesgrain—one seed, end to endthumb3 grainsthe joint of a thumb, near enoughspan12 thumbsthe working unit; a mason’s rule is a span longreach3 spansfingertip to fingertip is close; the Accord’s standard reach is a bronze barrod5½ reachesawkward, universally complained about, never changedfurrow40 rodswhat a team plows before it turnswalk8 furrowsan hour’s walking on level road, which is why distance and time are the same word in most of the four quarters
The Accord wanted fourteen and did not get it. Fourteen is the doctrinally correct number and the chancery proposed it in the second revision: fourteen thumbs to the span, on the reasoning that the Bow counts fourteen and so should everything else. Every trade in the four quarters refused, in unison, for a reason that has nothing to do with theology. You cannot halve fourteen twice. A carpenter needs the half, the quarter and the eighth, and twelve gives him all three, and fourteen gives him one and then a fraction he has to think about.
The Sohai retains a fourteen-count for rite measurement only. It is the one place the Accord’s number lost to a carpenter’s, and the chancery has never referred to the episode again.
III. Weight, in Two Systems
Two parallel systems, exactly as the real world ran troy against avoirdupois, and for the same reason: what you weigh gold with should not be what you weigh coal with.
Market weight. Sixteen ounces to the pound. Bulk goods, food, fodder, ore in the raw, timber, cloth, people. The pound of seven thousand grains.

































UnitEqual todram—ounce16 dramspound16 ouncesstone14 poundshundredweight8 stoneton20 hundredweight
Assay weight. Twelve ounces to the pound, with finer subdivisions, and it is the only system the Bench recognizes. Precious metal, gemstone, Draft ingredients, monster cores, physic, and anything a proof-mark will be struck on. Nothing is ever priced in both. A merchant quoting assay weight for a commodity has said something either technical or dishonest and the room will decide which.
The assay pound is deliberately scaled so that a bead’s mass reads directly as fineness against the sample taken, and the assayer does no arithmetic at all. This is the single cleverest thing in the Accord’s metrology and was borrowed wholesale from a trade that had worked it out centuries earlier.
The stone is fourteen pounds and the Accord did not choose that either. It arrived from the wool trade, where it had been fourteen for so long that the second revision simply wrote down what was already happening. It is the only place where the doctrinal number turns up in commerce, and it got there by accident, and the Sohai has never made anything of it, which the Sohai considers a discipline.
IV. Capacity, and the Oldest Argument in the Four Quarters
The measure, for grain, with a quarter-measure below it and a load of eight above.
The entire dispute is one word: level or heaped.
A level measure is struck flat with a strike-board across the rim. A heaped measure is filled to the cone. The difference is roughly a quarter, which is a fortune across a harvest, and every statute in the Accord’s formulary insists on level, and heaping is universal, and everybody knows it is universal.
The strike-board is therefore the most political object in any market. Who holds it, how fast they draw it, and whether they roll it or drag it, decides the trade. A slow, rolling strike leaves more in the measure. There are men who are known for it and are hired for it, and there is a word for the practice in every dialect on the Common page, and it is never the same word twice.
V. The Beam
The public weighing beam stands in the same building as the toll office, the customs table, the council chamber, the courtroom and the guardhouse. It stands in with them, closer than any neighbor, because they are all the same function: the place where the polity touches a person and takes a reading.
The standards are physically fixed to the outside of that building. The bronze reach is set into the wall at hand height, worn smooth, and anybody may check a rule against it at any hour without asking, and people do.
The building hires out its own small powers, too. A true-hand is a market’s petty folk art (one small working and one small living): somebody with a woken Crystal who can heft a weight and call it to the grain, at a copper the call, with a Heft skill on her own window that she will tell you about at length. Nobody has ever beaten a good one fairly. Everybody knows what a true-hand costs to be wrong, and on a busy morning she may decide she is tired and go home, which has closed markets.
This one arrangement tells a stranger more about a town than any amount of description. A man taken up in the street is taken into the building where his grain is weighed and his rule is checked, by people he has seen weigh grain and check rules.
VI. Verification, Striking, and the Cased Weight
The stamp
Every weight and measure in lawful trade carries verification marks struck into it: the maker’s mark, the town’s mark, the system it belongs to, and the searcher’s stamp from its last check. A rim of small marks around a bronze measure is a history of every time it has been tested and passed.
The striking
A weight found false is struck: cancelled with a deep six-pointed mark cut across the verification stamps. A struck weight is unfit for trade, must be destroyed, and frequently is not, because bronze is expensive and a struck weight still weighs something.
Struck weights in circulation are one of the most reliable indicators of how far the Accord’s reach actually extends. In a Western market you will not see one. In a district the searcher has not reached in nine years you will see nothing else, and the six-pointed marks will have been filed halfway smooth, and everyone trading there knows exactly what they are looking at.
The cased weight
The classic fraud, taken whole from the real trade because it cannot be improved on.
A solid weight is bronze all through. A cased weight is a bronze shell filled with lead, which is heavier for its bulk, so a cased weight of the correct external size weighs over, and a hollowed one weighs under, and either can be made to look perfect.
And it is detectable by ear. A solid weight rings when struck. A cased one gives a dull note. Every market searcher in the four quarters carries a small hammer and taps before he does anything else, and every child raised near a market knows the two sounds, and the sound of a dull weight in a quiet market is the sound of something about to happen.
VII. The Draught
The keepers of a worked Core (in the common word a Wellspring site, a place where one kind of Aether pools, and in most cases a dungeon somebody cleared and now holds) sell time at the pool, and a practitioner pulls Aether from the ground around them, fast on rich ground and slowly on thin, which means what the keeper sells had to be measured. The Guild solved the problem the way trades always do: it measured the aperture and the time, and left the substance alone.
The standard ferrule is a bronze ring of fixed bore, glyph-cut and set into the stone at the lip of the pool, and a practitioner sitting at it can pull no wider than the ring allows. A draught is that bore, held open on ground of the site’s stated grade, for one Guild hour by the water clock. (The keepers hold to the old spelling on purpose, so that nobody will mistake it for a Draft, the bottled working, and everybody does anyway.) Nothing about the metaphysics enters into it. The keeper’s book counts apertures and hours, the bill is written in draughts, and neither the fitter nor the clerk nor the sitter has any opinion about what is actually passing through the ring.
Consequences, all of them mundane and all of them useful.
A Core on falling density bills the same for less, because the book counts time and bore rather than delivery, and the lamp-wardens who top up there pass the loss on to every street they keep, and this is the single largest source of Withering-era grievance that no minstrel has made a song about. A sitter who widens a ferrule is stealing and can be caught by a searcher with a rule. The tundish, a small brass funnel of a fitting set on the ring so that the color of what passes can be seen from the door, exists so that the widening cannot be hidden. And the Guild bills in Guild hours, which is the second reason the equal hour won: a draught measured by the light would be worth more in summer.
VIII. Who Uses What

































PeoplePositionThe Accord and the GuildTheir own standard, in every hall that has signed, in all things, and the formulary revised four times to say soConcord townsThe Accord standard in the market and the old local measure in the back of the shop, for regularsThe holdsBoth, in parallel, the same as the two-column hour ledgers. Hold weight for the Tally, Accord weight for the beacon line. A Marrowkin will not enter an Accord figure without converting it, and the conversion is itself an entryEresseAccepts the Accord’s weight and rejects its authority to set it, on the grounds that a standard nobody witnessed is a standard held contingentlyThe MandateAdopted instantly, as with the hour. A decree specifying a quantity is a better decree when everyone means the same quantityKharvenThe ration, the bowl, the stack, the fire’s length. The scale is inspected publicly at Ice-out and that inspection is a rite, not an audit
IX. Where the Weighing Is Also Worship
Urion’s Labor is the Weighing: one thing weighed on a true balance every day. It requires no priest, no building and no scale but the household’s own, and it is performed by more people in the four quarters than any organized rite.
So the same physical act carries three meanings at once and the actors are usually unaware of two of them.

The Accord weighs to establish a fact and charge for it.
Sancta Lux weighs to establish worth, and holds the establishing to be sacred.
The Sohai weighs to acknowledge Balance, expects no answer, and considers the other two to have confused a Labor with a transaction.
Kharven weighs the ration and inspects the scale in public at Ice-out, and would tell you it is doing none of the above and is simply making sure nobody starves.
A scene in which a man weighs something in front of another man is never only about the weight.

When the Vintners and the Coopers of Rushford fell out over how much a tun should hold, the Long Quay ran purple for a week, two master coopers went into the river in their own barrels with their guild colors nailed to the lids, and the tun is still the size the coopers said. Everything on these shelves is a quarrel of that kind, conducted with a tool in one hand.
The trades and their tools, the guild titles that say who may be trusted with what, the equipment of the age and how it is rated, and the standards everything is weighed by.


The Apparatus of the Age — Equipment and Material Culture A Register of Equipment, Technology, and Material Culture Across the Four Quarters
Grade and Rarity The two ratings on every worked piece, the old words that survive as the Accord’s stamps, what a smith’s and a merchant’s titles cap, monster gear, bonded gear, Master Works, and the people who forge all of it.
The Works and Days — Occupations, Trades and Technology A Register of Occupations, Trades, and Technology Across the Four Quarters, from the people the coil never reads to the crews who go down for monster cores
Weight, Measure and the Standard What a pound is, who decided, and who has never accepted it. The same political act as standardizing the tongue and the hour, performed by the same institution, resisted by the same people.



Read next: Who Pays for the Lamp, for what magic does on an ordinary street; What Things Cost, for what it all costs.

races--and--peoples/index.title: Races & Peoples
races--and--peoples/index.content:
At the Goose Fair at Tarnbridge in 612 IC, a Cask Line cooper, a Varrisak piper in moss-green and an Ironblood drover with nine iron rings in her topknot came to blows over which of them a harvest song had insulted, and by nightfall they had flattened the goose market, the pie row and a good part of the magistrate’s awning, in three languages and under a sky full of feathers. All three were right about the song. This archivist has read the depositions, and that is the whole section in small.

The pattern that runs under every people in this section: one origin, several sincere and mutually incompatible answers to what that origin demanded. Read it as a set of arguments that nobody won, and throw away any family tree that shows decline from a purer ancestor.
“She sang one note. We have spent every Eon since arguing about how it should be sung back.”

The Shape of Every Schism
Every major people in the four quarters was made once, from one source, with one instruction. And in every case the instruction turned out to admit more than one honest reading, and the readings turned out to be irreconcilable, and the irreconcilability was discovered under maximum pressure, with the roof coming down, rather than at a scholars’ disputation over a good dinner.
THREE ORIGINSHow the elder peoples were made, and how each made sense of itTHE ELVEN PEOPLESFLORWYN sings theRealmsong of Edenisthe Vey-Elarin are tuned intobeingTHE KINSHIP DOCTRINEthe land is a relative, not aresourcethe Great Spirit War asks what itactually meantFIVE THEOLOGIESTHE MARROWKINVARŪN THE DEEPWRIGHTthe universe requires endurance,not strengthONE ARCHITECTUREthree pressures, then twocollapsesEIGHT ANSWERSTHE GOBLINOID LINEAGESTHE FIRST IMPACTcore, shell and mantleSTONE-BLOODone origin frequencyfragments meet local WellspringconditionsTHE GOBLINOID LINEAGES





























PeopleThe one sourceThe instructionWhat split itThe Elven PeoplesFlorwyn’s RealmsongThe Kinship DoctrineThe Great Spirit War asked, under maximum pressure, what the Doctrine actually demanded. Five sincere and incompatible answers came backThe MarrowkinVarūn the DeepwrightEndurance, not strengthTwo doctrinal divergences in the deep halls, then two collapses that stranded five populations on ground that shared nothing with a mountain’s interiorThe Goblinoid PeoplesThe First ImpactStone-Blood, one origin frequencyCore, shell, and mantle became three different kinds of body before anyone had an opinion about it. The Scattering did the rest

The useful reading is that no branch here is the degraded version of another. Each is a complete and internally consistent answer to a question the source left genuinely open, and each is living with what its own answer cost.

On Reading These Entries
The codices in this section are partisan, and I would distrust any that claimed otherwise. Each people’s entry is written from a position close enough to that people to make their reasoning legible, which means the same event is described three different ways depending on which page you are standing on. Go in armed.
The Betrayal of the Mountain and the First Rational Act are the same refusal. The Sylvaar Rebellion Schism is a rebellion from one side of the forest and a homecoming from the other. The Sundering of the Deep Halls has a trigger that the surviving branches’ oral records and the High Line archives describe differently, and the difference has never been resolved because neither party has offered to open the question.

Where a document records both accounts, both are reproduced. Where the record contains only one, that is itself a fact about who kept the record.

Entries
The Elven Peoples carries all five surviving branches and, beneath it, The High Empire of Eresse, the single people they all were, described as it stood before it knew it was about to end.
The Marrowkin carries the origin, the fractures, and all eight branches in summary, among them the five that were put somewhere else entirely and had to decide, from first principles, what enduring even meant once the mountain was no longer underfoot.
The Goblinoid Peoples carries the First Impact, all six lineages, the languages that branched from a metaphysical event rather than a spoken root, and Za’tarch, whose people will correct you, at length and around a fire, if you call it a refuge.
The Beastkin and Demihuman Peoples carries the Labor Provision and what it actually means, the demihuman categories, and the languages, with The Five Beastkin Lineages beneath it at full architectural depth.


The Elven Peoples
The Marrowkin
The Goblinoid Peoples
The Beastkin and Demihuman Peoples
Draconic Kind — The Dragons of Drakyssia
The Vampiric Peoples
The Tongues of the Realms



Tongues. The constructed languages live here rather than under The Magic System, because a tongue belongs to a people before it belongs to a working. The Tongues of the Realms is the framework: what counts as a language against what is only a naming register, the seven conventions binding every grammar, and the family tree. Old Vaross, Eressean and Varrisak, the Tally-Tongue, Accord Latin with its two spoken registers, and Common. Accent sits under Common as a menu for placing a speaker without spelling a single vowel.
Parunic is the exception and stays where it is. It is a script for writing boundaries onto laws, and nobody was ever raised in it, so it lives under The Magic System with the Descent of Parun and the Counted Speech.
Two more are known from outside and have never been written down by anyone who would talk: Drow Shadow-Veil notation, and Mirror-Sign, a full manual language with its own grammar.



The Ashkaru



Read beside this. Every people here has a soul with the same three layers, and The Three Paths says what they are. A lineage tilts them and gives no Path. The Sixty Wellsprings is where a people’s favored Wellsprings are entered, and The Archaic Bloodlines covers what a bloodline gives.
