races--and--peoples/the-peoples/the-marr.title: The Marrowkin
races--and--peoples/the-peoples/the-marr.content:
Say itMARE-oh-kin. In their own tongue *Ytinkreis*, the hearth-line of the marrow.
Eight Answers to One Endurance · One Debt · Revised Codex

“Varūn did not make us strong. He made us the thing still standing after strength finished arguing with itself.”
Marrowkin saying, lineage of origin disputed by all eight branches equally

The worst wedding in the history of Kegshard Hold took place in 431 IC, and the guests still rate the ale. Aino, daughter of the rune-forger Kalervo Straightedge of the High Line, was marrying a Cask Line cooper’s son, the first such match in four generations, and Grand Brewmaster Ulla Sevenhoop had spent ninety years on the wedding cask: a tun the height of three Marrowkin, barley gold and amber through its glass bung, sung to every morning of those ninety years in the Old Alchemic Song so that the liquor inside had learned the tune. Master Kalervo walked in on the morning of the feast, in his good iron rings, and looked at it. He observed that the hoops ran a hair out of true. He observed this several times. And when Ulla had gone up to dress, he took out a chisel, because he loved his daughter, and cut one small correcting rune into the top hoop, so that the vessel would at last be correct.
A thing that has been patiently becoming something else for ninety years does not care to be told what it is. The rune said the cask was finished, and the ale, which had been promised another hour, disagreed. The hoops stayed perfect. The ale went out through the staves in a roaring gold column that carried off the head table, four tiers of honey-cakes and the Hold’s second-best organ of brass pipes, and the foam kept rising, singing its own wedding song in a key that loosened teeth, up the great stair, through three levels of Kegshard, while Kalervo cut more runes into the walls ahead of it, faster and faster, each one making the geometry truer and the pressure worse, and Ulla Sevenhoop stood in the flood in her bride-mother’s braids singing at it to calm down, with her beard on fire from somewhere. It stopped at the fourth landing. At the fourth landing a guest nobody had invited was standing with a mug, a gray, quiet person from a long way down, and the foam reached his boots and died, along with the torches, the singing, the glow in every rune on the wall and the feeling in Kalervo’s left hand. Two hundred people stood chin-deep in the finest ale anyone has ever tasted, in the dark, with a Deepkin in the middle of them. He finished his drink and went back down. The wedding roll lists him as a Deepkin, and the High Line and the Cask Line have been sending each other the bill ever since.
There you have Varūn’s three faces at one party: the geometry, the fermentation and the threshold. There you also have a hold of people four feet tall with fire behind their eyes, standing in a gallery cut through the bone of something the size of a province. Both accounts take longer than the ale did.
The Marrowkin are the people who live inside a dead god and sell pieces of it. They are smiths by trade, clerks by faith, and debtors by birth, and the older rolls and most of the songs call them the Dawi, the name they carried before the Body finished with them. The realm is the Ember Holds of Marrowhold; this page is the people.
What the Body Did to Them
Nobody goes on drinking what runs through that bone for as many generations as this without paying for it. Their water comes off the ribs warm and iron-tasting, their walls give off heat, their children take a smear of marrow at the First Entry, and the Ring has been altering them for longer than the Guild’s count can follow. Here is what you will notice, in the order you will notice it.
The eyes. They are large, set wide, amber through furnace orange to the red of a coal, with a bright layer at the back that throws lamplight back at you the way a cat’s does. A gallery full of Marrowkin at shift-change is a dark full of paired sparks. Open daylight hurts them. Out of doors they wear slit visors, a band of carved horn or ivory with one narrow cut across the eyes, and a clan’s visors are as recognizable as its banner. A Marrowkin who takes off his visor to look at you in the sun is paying for the privilege and would like you to know it.
The heat. Their blood runs hot and dark, the color of old rust, and in a cut it shows a dull glow in a dark room. Snow melts on them. They steam on a northern morning, a handshake feels like a loaf from the oven, and across nose and cheekbones they carry a deep forge-flush they are born with and then bake in. A long winter away from the Ring brings on a gray, shaking cold-sickness that ordinary fires do not touch, and the cure is to go home.
The bone. They stand about chest high to a human, as wide as a door, and weigh twice what they look. A Marrowkin cannot swim, sinks like an anvil, and regards rivers as a matter for other people. From about the thirtieth year the rise begins: ivory-colored ridges of new bone push up through the skin along the knuckles, the brow, the collarbones and the outer forearm, in both sexes, and go on growing for life. Their skin has a grain in it, warm ivory to dark amber, like old tusk with a lamp behind it.
The record on the bone. The Soul-Rune practice is cut into the rise. An elder’s body is a reading of their life, the entries in the Tally register, accumulating and impossible to revise, so that an old rune-forger’s forearm is effectively a bracer with a biography on it.
The beard. Both sexes grow one, starting ash-white and yellowing over decades toward the color of the ribs, untrimmed, ringed with etched iron or copper that records time served, and frequently singed. A bare-jawed adult is a scandal or a recent accident.
The sound. Their chests are built like rooms. A Marrowkin voice comes with an under-note, a second tone lower than the word, which you feel in the breastbone before you are sure you have heard it, and in formal speech, when the meter runs, a clerk’s reading can be followed through the floor from the next gallery. They speak low and flat and they do not raise their pitch to make a point, because their tongue does not work that way. They also hear through bone. A Marrowkin with a jaw-ridge laid against a rib can follow a conversation a long way off and tell you which chain is about to go. They can talk this way too, in a tapped code on the wall that every child learns before the alphabet. When one of them goes quiet and leans a cheek on your doorpost, you should stop talking.
The smell. Hot iron, tallow smoke, sulfur and yeast, from across a market.
Dress runs to soot-black leather, copper hoop-bracelets, red-dyed wool in a shade nobody else can get, and work aprons kept as carefully as other peoples keep court robes. They are a loud people about one subject: put a Marrowkin in front of a good seam or a clean pour and the flat voice goes, the fists go up and the whole shift hears about it in meter. About everything else they will tell you the figure.
The Debt
Everything in Marrowkin life is downstream of three facts: they have been cutting pieces off something enormous for longer than anyone can date, the language has no future tense, and a broken oath is audible in a name.
They do not worship the Body. They owe it. What it was stays disputed among scholars and is a matter the holds refuse to enter; they call it the Body when they are selling and Lainur, the Lender, when they are frightened. The account runs from the first cut, each person’s take is entered under their name, every sale closes with a clause making the piece returnable on the Lender’s demand, and each death pays something back: the dead are returned, walled into a cut gallery in the bone their line has worked, the only ground a Marrowkin will accept. A hold’s roll of the dead is cut beside them. It is read aloud on the Drawing-Off with the balance after it, and the balance has never once gone down.
Why they keep it, when no creditor has ever called, is the one question you will get a straight answer to. Someday it will be asked for. They would like to be able to say who took what.
The faith that is not one
Never previously named as a religion, including by the Marrowkin, who would deny it is one.
Claim. That an act either happened or did not, that the record is the world’s memory of it, and that the record is sacred because nothing else is durable. They keep the Tally, and by their own reckoning they have kept it for six thousand years, a figure the Guild’s Errata would cut down hard and which no clerk has yet dared carry to a hold. The entering is itself an act that gets entered.
Daily. The entry. Every completed lawful act, in fixed wording, scanned to Mathematical Cadence, because a statement that does not scan has not been entered whatever it says. Clergy. The clerks, and they eat by the hold. A Marrowkin would say these are administrators, and every other people in the four quarters, shown a caste of hereditary record-keepers using a fixed liturgical meter to enter acts into a book that has never been closed, would say something else.
Heresies. The unentered act, kurnur. The broken oath, which counts as a change of grade rather than a sin, audible in the name, permanent, and published on a wall. And the deepest one, the Deepkin’s Mirror-Sign, the only language of the people in which a broken oath does not announce itself. Cost. The future tense, as the grammar explains at length. Wrong about. That the record is the world’s memory. A record can be destroyed with an axe, as the Keth-Gorrum’s has been, and a faith built on permanence has no doctrine for the hole.
The word they swear by is older than the debt. Varūn the Deepwright taught that the universe requires endurance, not strength, and everything in the Fractures below is an argument about what he meant. The holds refuse to say what Varūn and the Body have to do with each other, and the refusal is entered.
Names
The full account is in The Tally-Tongue of the Marrowkin. A Marrowkin carries four names and earns two of them.






























SlotWhat it isExampleGiven nameTwo elements from a fixed inventory, conferred at the First Entry around the seventh year; a smaller child is called by birth-shift and countVappu, Mirja, Hettrun, Oskrin, UlviOath-nameSecond place, conferred at oath-taking, spoken in the strong grade while the oath stands and the weak grade once it has brokenTarrekk / Tarre, Kaltekk / KalteLineHearth-line or parent, in the genitiveOllan, Sarnan, VanhananCut-nameThe largest single thing you ever took from the Body, by weight or by part, and everyone uses itSixty Tuns, Half a Rib, Thimble
The cut-name is the only boast in the four quarters that is also a confession. It goes on the roll when you die, and your line inherits the debt beneath it and has to find a name of its own.
One Architecture, Three Original Pressures
The people were made from one thing: Varūn the Deepwright’s understanding that the universe requires endurance, not strength.

























LineageVarūn’s faceOriginThe High LineHis geometryThe Rite of Bound Geometry, Second Eon: structure as the ground of realityThe Cask LineHis fermentationThe Subterranean Crucibles, Second Eon: patience as transformation over timeDeepkinHis thresholdThe Third Eon’s Depths Collapse: the principle of endurance stripped to its minimum and found, against all expectation, to still be standing
These three held the deep halls, the oldest galleries under the basin floor, for the whole of the people’s recorded history. What happened afterward is why there are eight lineages now instead of three.
The Fractures
Each fracture is still operating. To understand current Marrowkin politics, read them as ongoing conditions, and never let a clerk hear you call them ancient history.
The Fractures1Second EonThe Rite of Bound GeometryThe High Line organizes around geometric precisionThe Cask Line around alchemical pragmatismThe disagreement has never closed2Third EonThe Depths CollapseA population stranded in Void-scarred territoryThey stayedThe Deepkin's founding wound and founding purpose at onceThe Temple Rift CrisisThe blood-feudOne withdrawal, two irreconcilable names for it3Later Third EonThe Sundering of the Deep HallsFive populations severed in five directionsVolcanic archipelago, forge-pastures, steppe, sealed valley, worst passes4OngoingThe Withering PactKeepers of the Bunker-RealmsPermanent exemption from Archon serviceStill operative
The Rite of Bound Geometry · First Divergence
It began without hostility. Varūn’s two primary aspects were understood as complementary by practitioners close to the original teaching, and as competing by those who needed to govern populations. High Line communities organized around geometric precision; Cask Line communities around alchemical pragmatism.

The disagreement about which was truer to Varūn’s nature has been running ever since and has never produced a resolution, because both positions are correct and neither side is willing to say so.

The Depths Collapse · Second Divergence
A catastrophic failure deep beneath the Innerworld’s foundations left a population stranded in Void-scarred territory with no way back to the lit halls.
They did more than survive it. They stayed, and have guarded the collapsed zones ever since, uncredited by most formal Accord record. This is the Deepkin’s founding wound and their founding purpose at once.
The Temple Rift Crisis · The Blood-Feud

The High Line record describes a strategic withdrawal from an untenable position during a Void-incursion into collapsed temple zones.
The Deepkin record, maintained in Mirror-Sign and not translated for outside eyes, describes what the Deepkin experienced on the other side of that withdrawal: being left alone with the Void while the people who shared their teacher and their bloodline left.
The Deepkin held the collapsed zones. They have been holding them since. The distinction between the High Line withdrew and the Deepkin were abandoned has never been formally adjudicated.
The blood-feud is the Deepkin’s position on who gets to name what happened.

The Sundering of the Deep Halls · Third Divergence
A separate, subsequent collapse, the exact trigger still disputed between what the surviving branches’ oral records claim and what the High Line archives admit to, severed five further populations from the tunnel-network entirely, in five different directions, stranding each in terrain that shared nothing with the interior of the Body.
None of the five could simply wait to be rescued. Each rebuilt Varūn’s teaching from the ground up, in whatever shape the new ground demanded. Out of the heat and the bone for generations, they have drifted further from the people in the Ring than the Ring’s people care to admit: cooler hands, duller eyes, and a habit of being surprised by the bill.
The Withering Pact · The Cask Line Withdrawal
When the Archons made their claim on the people’s service, the High Line’s refusal produced confrontation that ended in autonomous status. The Cask Line’s refusal produced the Withering Pact, an agreement in which they accepted the designation of Keepers of the Bunker-Realms in exchange for permanent exemption from Archon service.

The Pact is still operative. The vaults are still maintained. The contents of those vaults are the primary reason external powers treat the Cask Line with considerably more diplomatic care than their surface-level political profile would otherwise warrant. Kings who would not cross a street for a brewer have crossed whole provinces for this one.

The Eight Answers


















































BranchDoctrineEndurance means…The High LinePermanence as Truththe correct structure never needing to changeThe Cask LineTransformation as Truthpatience applied to something that is allowed to change slowly, on its own scheduleDeepkinThreshold as Truthstanding guard in the one place no one else can stand at allKuntur ReachVerticality as Truthclaiming every elevation a body can reach as one territoryTallow ClansSeason as Truthmoving between two homes so completely that neither one is ever truly leftWindward HerdsMotion as Truthnever needing a fixed place to still be wholeTower-KinDebt as Truthremembering exactly what is owed for as many generations as it takes to pay itPasswardensPassage as Truthbeing the one fixed, trustworthy point in everyone else’s movement
Every branch talks about the shared arts in the same flat words, and they are the only people who do. A Marrowkin fighter with the aura coat up (the visible coat of their own color, which on most of them is some shade of furnace) is on shift. Pressure, the weight a strong soul lays on a room, is the load. Sensing another’s Essence is sounding you, as a rock face is sounded for a bad seam, and it is as polite as it sounds. All of it goes in the Tally, and all eight branches will argue over who pays.
The Three Deep Lineages
A note on terms for readers from the surface. In the blood names what a lineage’s souls tend toward, a thing of blood and upbringing and never a lock; Untrained lean gives the tilt of the three layers before anyone has trained them, and never sets Mastered or Walked (The Three Paths); a Wellspring is one of the sixty types of Aether, each working on the Soul Crystal in its own way, and a lineage may be able to harmonize with it, or may reject it outright. Stage is a rung of the sixteen-step climb. A Domain is the territory in which a high-Stage practitioner’s own law holds.
The High Line: Rune-Forgers of the Bound Geometry
Varūn’s geometric will given biological form, and the Ribs’ own builders, who carved Breastbone’s towers. In their understanding, reality is order tolerating the illusion of chaos, and anyone who says it the other way round has simply measured badly.
A High Line inscription has nothing decorative in it. It is the actual Aetheric vibration a concept is made of, rendered so exactly that reality stops needing to be told what to do.
In the blood · Geometric permanence, and pattern revealing structure
Untrained lean · Spirit 70% / Body 20% / Fate 10%
Wellsprings · Monolithion (primary), Judicium (strong secondary), Fixatio and Basilithe (accessible). Rejects Nyxial, Tenebra and Nihiloth outright: Geometric Cohesion is constitutionally antithetical to the void

Advantages · The most corruption-resistant Crystal architecture in the Continuum; hostile intrusion shatters against its lattice the way glass shatters against stone.
Geometric Domains where lies leave measurable Aetheric residue, with no punishment involved, because inaccurate description is structurally detectable.
Limitations · Stage VII Refraction is disproportionately hard for this lineage: an architecture built to describe the world accurately struggles badly to turn that same precision on itself.
Geometric Lock overgrowth risk: an overextended Domain can produce zones of absolute spatial permanence that trap the unwary before the practitioner even notices.

The Cask Line: Alchemical Architects of Kegshard Hold
Where the High Line is Varūn’s geometry, the Cask Line is his fermentation: the understanding that some endurance is brewed, and stone does not get to be the only structure.
Kegshard Hold’s Deepvault, in the hollow of the Twelfth Rib, and the Great Cask-Oath are the same instinct in two forms: the conviction that the most dangerous and the most precious things both deserve to be aged, watched, and never rushed.
In the blood · Transformation through contradiction
Untrained lean · Body 85% / Fate 15%, the only lean toward Fate in the Continuum to emerge from watching barrels rather than the sky
Wellsprings · Basilithe (primary), Manganthra (strong secondary), Rebirthine (accessible, and uniquely so among the lineages, rot feeding what grows), Verdantia (accessible). Poorly compatible with Aurevane, Luminalis, and Judicium

Advantages · Alchemical aging: their Crystal genuinely compounds potency the longer it holds Essence rather than spends it, so veterans outperform beginners in ways Level comparisons do not capture.
The Great Cask-Oath makes their word structurally reliable, and socially reliable besides; breaking one costs the Crystal’s own Coherence automatically.
Limitations · Spirit-Blindness. Roughly 40% of the Cask Line approaching Stage VIII without deliberate Spirit Path supplementation plateau or enter an unrecognized slow spiritual compression.

Deepkin: Guardians of the Collapsed Zones
Varūn’s threshold: endurance reduced to its bare minimum and found to still hold. Stranded by the Depths Collapse in Void-scarred territory nothing else can safely enter, they stayed, and have guarded it since, continuously, largely uncredited, in a single paragraph of Third Eon Accord record that has never been updated. Their heat has gone out. A Deepkin’s eyes are the gray of cold slag, their rise has gone chalk white, and they stand in a Ring hold like a draft from a cellar.
Their names, in the Deepkin’s own record, are kept in Mirror-Sign and deliberately not transliterated for outside use.
Wellsprings · Nihiloth (primary, native), a collapsed Basilithe (accessible), corrupted and collapsed Wellspring sites generally (primary access unique to this lineage). Rejects Benediction, Oneirion and Aurevane outright: 2× damage from Divine Light or Holy-frequency glyphs

Advantages · Aura Dead-Zone: passive Aetheric suppression, +35% AoE resistance, reduced enemy technique yield (η) in radius.
Dissonance Anchor: passive Stage X zone stabilization within 15m, allowing others to work briefly in collapsed zones under their coverage.
Total immunity to Madness and Spiritual Fragmentation; Full-yield Void-aspected access no other lineage safely approaches.
Limitations · Psychological Void at Stage VIII: roughly 30% risk of permanent Catatonic Stasis on a failed Transcendence check without prior Soul-Caving preparation.
The Aura Dead-Zone plays no favorites. It suppresses the Aetheric environment for allies as thoroughly as for enemies, complicating any collaboration with Wellspring-dependent partners. See the wedding, above.

Languages of the Marrowkin
Their languages share one structural feature: they are built for endurance rather than efficiency. Each is physically adapted to what the lineage needs to survive. The grammar of the main tongue is on its own page, and the two facts every visitor should carry in are that every act in it has a doer at the front and the Tally slot at the back, and that nobody in it can say I will.
Lattice Tongue · The High Line
Less a separate language than the foundational Parunic access level at which phonemes are Aetheric vibrations that constitute the concepts they represent, with nothing symbolic left in them. The High Line does not translate from language to glyph; they produce the glyph directly through speech. Asking a High Line rune-forger to mind their language is therefore sound practical advice.
Outside practitioners who have attempted to learn it through immersion describe the experience as learning to think geometrically rather than learning a new vocabulary. Some succeed. Most find that the architecture required to produce Lattice Tongue phonemes correctly is not available to them without significant Crystal restructuring.
The Tally-Tongue, Barkstone Dialect · The Cask Line and the holds
The working language, with material-world resonance built into the phonemic structure. Old Alchemic Song is the tonal register used in brewing chants: it physically vibrates the liquids being crafted, producing a direct mechanical-acoustic effect on the alchemical substrate.
A Grand Brewmaster singing the Alchemic Song into a fermentation vessel produces measurably different results from a silence-brewed equivalent. The Song is physical, the effect is real, and the priests may keep their theories. Outside practitioners can reproduce it with sufficient practice and an adequately calibrated voice range, though they have to fake the under-note.
Low Tally, the Hollow Dialect, and Mirror-Sign · Deepkin
Their spoken language is produced by vocal cords that operate within the Aura Dead-Zone’s dampening field. Sound dies in their throats before achieving full resonance, the plain physical consequence of their Void-fold architecture, and no affectation. The Hollow Dialect carries information in the quality of the sound-absence as much as in the sound itself, and trained Deepkin listeners read the hollow quality’s variations as a secondary channel of meaning.
Mirror-Sign is the primary operational language: micro-reflections, hand gestures, and Entropic Vein micro-movements that communicate through reflected absence. It cannot be detected by standard Harmonics Attunement. It produces no Aetheric signature. It is, in the most precise sense, undetectable by anyone who has not been taught to see it.


“You are still here.”

Varūn the Deepwright’s singular principle, expressed to each of his three peoples in the specific language each of them needed to hear it in.

Moves, Costume and What Everyone Says





























LineageThe moveThe lookWhat they say about the othersThe High LineSuora Viiva, the True Line: a single rune spoken along the path of your blow, after which your blow may travel that line and no otherIron rings, squared beards, a rule at the belt in place of a dagger, and they will measure you with it”A Cask Line oath is good until the cask is empty”The Cask LineNinety-Year Pour: the reserve they have been sitting on since their grandmother’s day, let out all at once, gold and steaming, over youLeather aprons, copper hoop-bracelets, a smell of malt from across the market”The High Line has never once been drunk, and it has never once helped”DeepkinYou Are Still Here: they walk up. Your coat goes out, your fire goes out, your Trait stutters, and they are still walkingGray on gray, no metal that rings, and no one has ever asked them to danceThey sign it. You will not see what they said, and it was about you
Everyone else’s opinion of the Marrowkin is a variation on one line, and it goes round every tavern from Hallenfeld to Sum-gol: lovely steel, read the bottom of the sale.
Where the Registers Disagree
Attested, not reconciled.
The parties to the Temple Rift Crisis. The detailed record places the blood-feud between the Deepkin and the High Line, arising from a withdrawal from collapsed temple zones during a Void-incursion, and this account is reproduced above. A second register describes the Temple Rift Crisis instead as ongoing tension between the High Line and the Cask Line. Both cannot describe the same event. The Measurewrights note that only the first account names what the feud is actually about.
The count of fractures. One register lists three fracture events and omits the Depths Collapse and the Sundering. Another lists four and omits the Withering Pact. All five are reproduced above, on the reasoning that no register has withdrawn any of them.
The count of branches. An earlier framework describes seven branches, two deep lineages plus five surface, while the current codex describes eight, counting the Deepkin as a full branch rather than as an adjunct of the deep halls. This register follows the eight.
The dwarves of Varūn. The mountain kingdom of Varūn in the Old World keeps its own dwarves and sells veinwood at a fair price. The holds decline to say whether those are cousins, and the kingdom declines to say anything. Unreconciled.


“Eight ways to still be standing, and Varūn has never once told any of us which one he actually meant.”
Attributed to a joint Kegshard–Qori Anka trade summit, exact speaker disputed


Read next: The Three Paths, for what a lean means and never sets; The Sixteen Stages, for the climb; The Tongues of the Realms, for the Tally-Tongue.

races--and--peoples/the-peoples/index.content:
The elder peoples and the newer ones: their origins, their soul architecture and their ways. All of them walk the one great body of land, so sooner or later all of them are at the same inn, and the innkeeper at the Copper Goose in Tarnbridge charges a Marrowkin for the ale, a Drow for the silence and a Lupine for the door.
Where a lineage below gives an Untrained lean, the figure says how its blood tilts the three layers of a soul before anyone has trained them. It never sets Mastered or Walked, which are a person’s own practice (The Three Paths).

races--and--peoples/the-peoples/the-vamp.title: The Vampiric Peoples
races--and--peoples/the-peoples/the-vamp.content:
Overview
Races · Mechanics · Bloodlines · Languages · Cultures · Dreadvalis
Every Vampire in the world descends from one act of cruelty. A few decades before the Moto–Zettari war began, Malakar, the First Demon, came to the Outer World, took thousands of its people, and remade them. He did not kill them. He inverted the machinery that kept them alive, so that they could go on living only by taking life from others, and could never again stand in the sun.
From those captives came the Vampiric peoples, and from their hunger came the Dreadvalis Empire: a young, fast-growing, ferociously organized civilization in the cold north of the Outer World, built to keep a predatory race from eating itself to extinction.





























ClassificationWhat they areCommon VampiresThe majority: Malakar’s first captives and the children born to them. Soldiers, workers, hunters, citizensHigh VampiresThose whose curse stabilized into something self-sustaining. The nobility and rulers of DreadvalisTurned VampiresMortals transformed by deliberate blood transmission. The empire’s underclassVampire-Dragon HybridsExceedingly rare beings of Malakarian and draconic bloodMalrik FangThe one true Dhampir who will ever be born. A singular anomaly of a future age
There is no Dhampir people, no Dhampir history and no hidden Dhampir bloodline. There will only ever be Malrik.
“The Sun was made our enemy. Hunger was placed inside us. Neither fact determines what we choose when the doors close and night begins.” — Inscription beneath the western gate of Bluvest
The Origin: Malakar and the First Thirst
The First Demon
Malakar “Abaddon” Kusho is the First Demon, sovereign of Hell, and the Embodiment of Evil: a primordial thing Aegor made in the Paths, Chaos given a coherent identity. His presence does not merely break things. It persuades things to betray the principles that hold them together.
Stone forgets load. Fire stops telling fuel from air. Oaths come loose from intention. Bodies lose their agreement with their souls. Where Malakar passes, the world produces consequences without keeping the causes that should have made them.
In the years before the Moto–Zettari war, before Shaka-Al Zettari stripped him of his spatial authority and locked him in Hell, Malakar walked the Material World freely, and he went where he liked. One winter, he went to the cold north of the Outer World.
The Taken Winter
The northern peoples of the Outer World were hardy, stubborn and hopeful. They lived through long winters on the strength of their families, their villages, their faith and their plans for the spring. That was what drew him.
Over a single season the north began to empty. Whole villages were found with their doors open, fires out and tables laid. Healing houses, farms, shrines, refugee camps and noble halls lost their people in the night. Northern chroniclers call it the Taken Winter.
Malakar did not take only warriors. He took farmers, healers, artisans, children, priests, merchants, soldiers and nobles. He chose people who still had something to lose: families waiting for them, communities depending on them, futures they still believed in. A person without hope can simply be killed. A person with hope can be changed, and made to remember what was lost.
The First Thirst
Deep beneath the northern ice, Malakar forced his chaotic Essence through the captives’ bodies, Soul Crystals, Attraction Layers and Names all at once. The event is called the First Thirst.
He did not erase their humanity. He inverted the machinery by which humanity continues.

Their hearts stopped carrying the full burden of biological life.
Their bodies stopped aging.
Their Soul Crystals could no longer sustain themselves on their own Essence.
Their Attraction Layers could no longer hold their place in the world without feeding on living consequence.
Their minds stayed human enough to understand hunger, and their memories human enough to know what they had become.

These were the first Vampires.
He gave them one more gift. He made them unable to bear the sun. The sun is regularity, exposure, renewal, the oldest kept promise in the world: that morning comes. Malakar’s brother, the Grand Angel Faisal, had spent his existence keeping promises like that one. Malakar made a people who could never stand in it.
Why
Malakar did not hate the northern peoples. He did not fear them, and they had done nothing to him. He is evil by nature, not by injury, and he did it because he wanted to see what they would do.
“He did not curse us because he hated us. He cursed us because he wanted to watch us choose between our hunger and our children, and he wanted to watch for a very long time.” — Vaelora Dreadvalis, First Blood Empress
After the Thirst
For a time, the new Vampires were Malakar’s nocturnal hosts in the Outer World. They emptied villages, sabotaged defenses and spread terror across the north. Then his attention moved on to other entertainments in the Old World, and he left them behind.
His creations were starving, leaderless, and hunting each other. Out of that chaos, in the decades before and during the Moto–Zettari war, Vaelora Dreadvalis and the first High Vampires built an empire. When Shaka-Al stripped Malakar of his reach and banished him into Hell at the close of that war, Dreadvalis was already standing.
Now the prohibition has broken, and Malakar walks the Material World again. Every Vampire alive can feel their maker’s presence in their blood, and the whole Dreadvalis Empire is asking the question it has dreaded since its founding: what does he want from us now?
The Malakarian Sanguine Inversion
Vampirism is not a disease, demonic possession, necromancy or a walking corpse. It is a hereditary, transmissible curse working across all three layers of the Soul Crystal at once, formally called the Malakarian Sanguine Inversion.
A mortal life sustains itself in a closed loop:

The Vampire must import what it can no longer make, and blood is the medium of the theft. On the Material Plane, blood carries matter, minerals, heat, oxygen-bearing compounds and regenerative substrate. On the Soul Plane, it carries residual Essence, emotional impressions, memory fragments and traces of identity. On the Plane of Fate, it still carries the recognition that it belonged to something alive.
The Vampire consumes that recognition and spends it on its own cursed continuation. Blood is not food. It is borrowed life, and stolen recognition: an outside answer to a question the Vampire’s body can no longer answer for itself.
The Three Hungers
Vampire scholars divide the curse into three linked appetites. Any one may run stronger than the others, but no stable Vampire escapes all three.
The Hunger of Flesh. The body needs blood to keep its unnatural functions running: regeneration, muscle output, sensory acuity, body heat, the look of a living thing. A well-fed Vampire breathes, blinks, sweats, keeps a heartbeat and sheds tears. As starvation advances the imitation fails: the skin cools, the heart slows, breathing stops unless remembered, the eyes fix, and the muscles lock into a predatory rest. In the end the body resembles a corpse that can still hunt.
The Hunger of Soul. The Essence Core needs the Essence carried in living blood to fuel magic, keep Traits stable, hold memory together, regulate emotion, and resist the Malakarian imprint inside the curse. Without it, the Core eats its own reserves: first stored blood-memory, then memories it judges unnecessary. Names go. Faces lose their weight. Moral prohibitions vanish. Language decays. A badly starved Vampire may keep every combat skill and the ability to track prey while forgetting its own children.
The Hunger of Recognition. The deepest hunger lives in the Attraction Layer: the need for proof that the Vampire still takes part in living consequence. Fresh blood carries the recognition of the one it came from, and the Vampire steals a share of it. The old ones describe it not as eating but as becoming briefly visible to the world. This is why some Vampires grow addicted to particular people rather than particular blood: emotionally significant blood sustains more than good blood does.

The oldest Vampires understand the truth under the curse. They do not only hunger for blood. They hunger to be acknowledged by life.
The Curse of the Sun
The Sun Curse is not sensitivity to heat or light. Ordinary flame does nothing; artificial light does nothing. The curse answers to the Sun as a celestial and metaphysical authority: regularity, exposure, biological rhythm, renewal without corruption, the daily return of a world that goes on despite suffering. Everything Malakar is not.
Under true sunlight, rejection happens on all three Planes at once:

Material. Cursed tissue combusts as stolen vitality loses cohesion.
Soul. The surviving human origin and the Malakarian continuation are forced into open contradiction.
Fate. The Sun identifies the Vampire as a being continuing outside the cycle of life it was born into.

Common Vampires ignite within seconds. Skin splits, blackens and burns through to the Crystal, and long exposure leaves only ash. Malakar arranged it so they would always remember daylight, always hear mortal cities waking, always remember warmth, and always have to go underground before it came. The Sun Curse is not just a weakness. It is part of the joke.
Common Vampires
Major Race · Malakarian Bloodborn · Night-Bound





















TypeMajor Race · Cursed Post-Humans · Nocturnal PredatorsOriginThe survivors of the Taken Winter and the children born to them sinceSpiritual lineageThe First Thirst: human souls restructured by the Sanguine Inversion
Common Vampires are most of the Dreadvalis Empire: its soldiers, workers, hunters, craftsmen, merchants, clerks, farmers, servants and ordinary citizens. They outclass ordinary humans in almost every physical category, and they carry Malakar’s original curse closer to the skin than any other Vampire. Their strength rises with blood. Their identity weakens without it. Their whole existence is arranged around surviving the daily approach of the sun.
Soul Architecture
The Crystal. Usually crimson-black, dark violet or the brown of dried blood, its surface branched with vein-like channels that contract in rhythm. It works as a spiritual second heart: each contraction draws blood-borne Essence in, each release spreads stolen vitality through body, Shell and Attraction Layer.
Path. Common Vampires overwhelmingly lean on the Body Path: speed, strength, regenerating tissue, heightened senses, predatory musculature and disease resistance. A substantial minority, mostly blood-mages, lean on the Spirit Path instead, for blood magic, memory extraction and death-state persistence. The Fate Path is rare among Common Vampires; their Attraction Layer is strong but dependent, working only on recognition imported from living blood.
Mastery. Untrained Common Vampires, most of whom never reach Glory, read none. Those who do settle at Body I, Muridic as the roads say. Soldiers, hunters and trained blood-practitioners of Refraction reach II, Harmonic. Disciplined elites past Transcendence clarify into III, Resonant. IV, Luminous, and V, Radiant, take exceptional Temperance, a long life of hard Levels and the Stages that open them. A few old shadow specialists come to hold their rung Inverted, their Aether traveling through silence, absence and darkness instead of normal circulation; this is a change of kind, not a sign of greater power.
Crystal’s look. Clouded through Faceted at racial maturity, the disciplined elders’ stone fully Faceted; Fire at Transcendence for the few who reach it.
The two great fractures. The first is the Thirst Crisis: whether hunger is something the self experiences, or the self’s governing identity. Fail it, and hunger becomes part of the Crystal’s central architecture; every living thing thereafter registers as unfinished food. The second comes near the Radiant threshold (Mastery V, in the roads’ word), when accumulated victim-memory grows too dense to stay passive, and voices, reflexes, dreams and fears taken through blood begin to speak inside the Vampire’s own mind.

Traits. They gather in three families. Blood Traits: blood weapons, coagulation, blood threads, wound control, vitality theft, blood armor, lineage tracking. Ascension: Crimson Sovereignty. Authority over blood spilled in a territory, wounds opened in recognized enemies, or servants sustained by shared circulation.

Domains are predatory territories: moonless courtyards, underground cities, flooded crypts, pale forests, black-red cathedrals, hunting estates, streets beneath an unmoving eclipse. Typical laws: Blood remembers its bearer. Every wound is an entrance. Night recognizes the predator. What is consumed belongs to the consumer. Feral Domains look like slaughterhouses; disciplined ones look like hunting preserves and courts of blood taxation.
Culture

The First Thirst (kethra). A young Vampire’s first sanctioned feeding, witnessed by the clan to see whether the fledgling can stop on its own. Releasing prey is the first proof of civilization.
The Veiling of Dawn. Bells before sunrise. Gates close, reflective shutters seal, the population moves into protected districts.
The Crimson Ledger. Each clan records blood consumed, mortals protected, blood debts, unlawful killings, births, turnings and inherited obligations.
The Red Guest-Law. A mortal under declared Vampire hospitality may not be fed on without consent. Breaking it damages the household’s Fate-recognition and can start a blood feud.
The Ash Wake. The sun leaves little but ash. It is mixed with black resin and sealed inside a named memorial mask.
The Maker’s Burden. Whoever turns a mortal answers for the fledgling until it feeds with control and holds its own coherence.
The Moon Hunt. Moonlight and shadow measurably strengthen Common Vampires. Some clans hold controlled communal hunts at full moon.

Languages: Dreadvalic, Bloodcant, Old Bluven, northern mortal tongues. Realms: the Dreadvalis Empire: Bluvest, Morvayne, the Red Marches, the Ashen Courts, the Veiled Provinces.
Advantages: agelessness; superhuman strength, speed, reflex and senses; blood-fed regeneration; affinity for blood, soul and dark magic; disease and toxin resistance; moonlight and shadow empowerment; sensing blood, wounds, heartbeats and fear; memory acquisition through feeding; the ability to turn compatible mortals.
Limitations: fatal sunlight; silver rejection; the living stake through the heart-seat; sacred and holy magic; blood dependence and blood-memory contamination; feral decay through starvation; Malakar’s emotional inheritance. Decapitation, Crystal destruction, total incineration and absolute anti-regeneration remain fatal.
High Vampires
Major Race · Elder Bloodlines · Curse-Stabilized Nobility





















TypeMajor Race · Stabilized Vampire Lineage · Malakarian AristocracyOriginThose first captives whose curse settled into a coherent, partly self-sustaining form, and the bloodlines born to themSpiritual lineageThe First Captives, the Blood Thrones, and the strongest hereditary expressions of the Inversion
High Vampires are not simply stronger Common Vampires. Their curse has become internally coherent. A Common Vampire borrows nearly all its continuity from blood; a High Vampire’s Crystal holds enough of its own recognition to generate part of that continuity itself. They still need blood. They are only harder to starve, harder to destabilize, and able to treat blood as magical authority instead of the next meal.
The Thirst did not land evenly. A few of the captives (nobles with old blood, priests with disciplined souls, people of high Temperance) came out of it with a curse that held its shape. They became the first High Vampires, and in a few short decades they made themselves the nobility, the officer corps, the priesthood, the provincial governors, the occult scholars and the ruling houses of Dreadvalis.
Soul Architecture
Path. High Vampires lean on the Spirit Path (inherited blood sorcery, ancestral and consumed memory, soul domination) or, in the ruling houses, on the Fate Path (clan law, bloodline sovereignty, enthrallment, dynastic authority). Their bodies remain superhuman, but physical expression no longer leads.
Mastery. Body III, Resonant, among the noble elites, IV, Luminous, among the great rulers, and V, Radiant, only for the rare one who reaches Emanation. The rung held Inverted among shadow sovereigns and occultists whose curse has learned to conduct through absence. Anything beyond takes an exceptional individual, an artifact, a transcendent Trait or royal blood.
Crystal’s look. Fire through Flawless, with an inverted architecture: the curse has become a self-sustaining foundation. Blood becomes law, inheritance becomes anatomy, memory becomes territory. The very greatest rulers, whose identity has survived decades of feeding without being absorbed by their own line, reach something steadier still.

Overgrowth: the Living Dynasty. The bloodline matters more than its members, and descendants slowly become extensions of a founder.

Domains look like imperial courts, endless palaces, ancestral cities, sealed estates, galleries of blood portraits and throne rooms under artificial night. Typical laws: The bloodline recognizes its sovereign. Every debt is carried in blood. The court remembers every guest. No blood leaves the throne uncounted.
Culture

The Blood Throne. A ruler feeds their blood into the ancestral reservoir, and the throne tests it against the line’s accumulated recognition.
The Vein Census. Noble houses record births, turnings, inherited Traits, curse variations and blood purity.
The Scarlet Table. Diplomacy by measured blood exchange; each party adds one drop to a shared vessel.
The Long Name. A High Vampire’s titles grow with every absorbed clan, conquered estate and inherited line.
The Closed Coffin. A noble lies sealed without blood for one hundred nights to prove mastery of hunger. Some die. Some come out feral.
The Unlit Procession. High Vampires gain nothing from moonlight; their curse sustains itself. At full moon they let Common Vampires lead the processions, in recognition of the difference.

Languages: Old Bluven, High Dreadvalic, Bloodcant, ceremonial Parun. Seats: the High Courts of Bluvest, the Ashen Courts, the Seven Blood Estates, the Royal Vein, the Veiled Imperial District of Morvayne.
Historical role. High Vampires turned scattered predators into a civilization. They wrote feeding law and the blood tithe, sealed the cities, built the military hierarchy, organized the mortal populations, and founded dynastic government. They stopped the race from eating itself to extinction. They also institutionalized predation: Dreadvalis survives because High Vampires invented restraint, and countless mortals have suffered because that restraint was built for sustainable exploitation, not freedom.
Advantages: limited sunlight resistance; resistance to silver and holy magic; superior blood sorcery; high Dominion and clan authority; lower feeding needs; strong identity stability; access to ancestral blood-memory; resistance to possession and curse alteration.
Limitations: long sunlight is still fatal; the hunger remains; accumulated memory threatens individuality; dynastic obligations can become metaphysically binding; no moonlight empowerment; inherited blood can carry old curses into descendants.
Turned Vampires
Cursed Variant · Made Bloodborn · The Bitten





















TypeTransformed Mortal · Transmissible Curse Variant · Social UnderclassOriginMortals transformed by deliberate blood transmission rather than bornSpiritual lineageThe bloodline of whoever turned them
A bite alone makes no Vampire. The maker must drain the victim close to death, then introduce cursed blood into the failing circulation, so that it reaches the Crystal as the body collapses and offers it another way to go on. The victim must accept that continuation at some level. The acceptance may be conscious, coerced, instinctive, or no more than a dying body choosing anything other than death. Once accepted, the curse replaces the terminal state with blood-dependent continuation.
Soul Architecture
Path and lens. The mortal’s original Path and Wellspring lens survive underneath the curse, which is what makes Turned Vampires unpredictable. A former fire practitioner stays fire-aligned, but the flame may turn blood-fed or lightless. A healer may keep wounds as channels to move vitality through. A dream-worker may enter the dreams of anyone they have bitten. Body-leaning mortals usually stabilize physically; Spirit-leaning mortals become stronger blood and soul practitioners at the cost of more identity contamination; Fate-leaning mortals risk severe dependence on their maker.
Mastery. Unread below Glory; after stabilization, Body I at Glory and up to II at Refraction, Muridic to Harmonic in the roads’ words, and III for the disciplined who reach Transcendence. Turning often collapses part of the original Mastery, which then reads low against the Level; a skilled practitioner can climb back over time.
Crystal’s look. Clouded, often fractured, through Faceted. The turning builds a second curse-architecture around the original Crystal, and the bite scar usually stays visible because it is the first Material anchor the new continuation came through.
The common crisis: Maker Echo. The fledgling starts reproducing the maker’s speech, habits, emotional rhythms, hunger patterns or Traits.
Temperance
Turned Vampires often regress after transformation. Their great stall is the line between the mortal who died and the Vampire who went on; many stay trapped around the moment of turning. At Dissonance, the original self and the curse-made continuation can appear as two separate identities.
Typical ceiling: Stage VI for the untrained; VIII for disciplined individuals who break free of their maker. By the Measurewright’s yardstick: the average Turned hits like a Grade C beast, trained guards and independent Turned communities like a B, and one who hits like an A is rare.

Culture
Turned Vampires hold the lowest recognized rank in Dreadvalis. They serve as servants, guards, soldiers, laborers, infiltrators and expendable agents. Unlike born Vampires they keep their original skin tone, and the bite stays visible as puncture scars or dark vascular marks. Some High Vampire houses treat these marks as impurity; others prize Turned Vampires because they pass among mortals with less suspicion.
Advantages: they keep their mortal racial abilities and training; gain Vampire speed, strength, senses and regeneration; produce unusual hybrid magic; and blend into mortal societies more easily.
Limitations: every standard Vampire weakness; an unstable Crystal; maker compulsion; low status; a high frenzy rate; trauma around death and transformation; possible loss of mortal memory.
Vampire-Dragon Hybrids

Hybrids rarely survive their own making. Draconic Essence carries immense constitutive authority; it reads the curse as an invader and tries to burn, crush or overwrite it. The borderlands where the Dreadvalis north meets the dragon south are the only places they have ever been born.

Malrik Fang — The Only Dhampir
Singular Hybrid · Blood-Moon Born · Bastard of the Royal Vein





















TypeSingular Hybrid · Future Royal Anomaly · Human-Vampire SynthesisOriginA future age. Born beneath a Blood Moon, the illegitimate child of the Dreadvalis royal line and a mortal parentSpiritual lineageThe Royal Vein of Dreadvalis joined to living human continuity
There are no Dhampir peoples. There has never been a confirmed Dhampir before Malrik, and no Dhampir line will be waiting to receive him. The word will be coined after his birth, because nothing in the existing classifications will be able to hold what he is.
Malrik will not be half a Vampire. He will be a complete being made of two contradictory continuities. His mortal side will give him a living heartbeat, his own Fate-recognition, and a Crystal that takes part in the Material cycle naturally. His royal side will give him blood affinity, an aging curve far slower than a human’s, soul predation, darkness resonance, and the refined curse-architecture of the Dreadvalis royal line. The Blood Moon will let both form without either destroying the other.
He will have the strengths of Vampirism without its ordinary weaknesses. That is why his birth will be treated not as a scandal but as a theological threat to the Empire. If one child can carry Vampire power without Malakar’s punishment, then sunlight, hunger, silver and sacred rejection are not part of what a Vampire is. They are separable parts of the curse. Malrik will be living proof that the race could have been something else.
Soul Architecture
Path. Malrik will lean on the Spirit Path, carrying blood, soul, shadow, alchemy and inherited royal magic, with a natural Body lean beside it that most souls earn only at great cost: Vampire strength, speed, regeneration and senses running through a genuinely living body. His Fate layer will make its own recognition. He will never need to steal continuity just to stay present in the world.
Mastery. His architecture will support Body IV, Luminous, through V, Radiant, without the curse-stabilization High Vampires depend on. Anything past that will take real Temperance and exceptional circumstance.
Crystal’s look. Clouded early, with a strong natural road toward Fire and Flawless. His Crystal will look nothing like the inverted vascular structure of an ordinary Vampire: a living central Crystal, ringed by a royal crimson lattice. The core will make its own continuity; the lattice will treat blood as power, memory and magical substance, never as a need.
The great fracture: the Conflict of Inheritance. The royal line will try to classify him as property, defect, heir, weapon or blasphemy. The mortal world will try to classify him as monster, victim, weapon or proof of Vampire corruption. He will advance by refusing every identity anyone tries to impose.
Temperance
No Thirst Crisis. Steady progress through the early and middle Stages. His great stall will come at VIII · Transcendence: is he a bridge between mortals and Vampires, an heir to the throne, an enemy of both, or a sovereign self unrelated to any of those? At XI · Dissonance, his architecture may divide into two legitimate but incompatible inheritances, the living heir who can walk under the sun and the royal predator carrying the oldest Blood Throne authority. Unlike ordinary Vampiric Dissonance, neither side will be false. The danger will be treating them as enemies.
By the Measurewright’s yardstick: by nature he will hit like a Grade A beast at maturity, and like an S and beyond through training and major Threshold growth.
Stats



























































PrimaryLeanSignature Sub-StatsNoteTempering++++Clarity · Yield · MaturityHis defining strength: he processes living, blood, soul, darkness and alchemical currents cleanlyHarmonics++++Attunement · EmpathyHe recognizes others without turning recognition into hungerVitality++++Regeneration · ConstitutionVampire regeneration through living biology; he ages slower than humans, faster than VampiresDexterity++++Celerity · ReflexVampire speed without starvation collapseResilience++++Integrity · WardImmune to the standard Vampire weaknesses; strong resistance to curse disruptionArdency++++Flux · DepthBlood enhances output, while ordinary Essence recovery still worksGnosis+++Analysis · FluencyHuman adaptability, royal blood-memory, exceptional alchemical thinkingDominion+++SovereigntyRoyal blood gives natural authority; his bastardy denies him institutional recognition, so he must win it in conflict
Metaphysical Identity
Wellsprings. All the core Vampiric currents (Phreatis, Mortalis, Rebirthine, Anamnesis, Transference, Somnalis, Manganthra), and safe access to the ones that harm ordinary Vampires: Luminalis including its solar spectrum, Benediction, Absolution, Verdantia, Catharsis, and Penanceflare, though its judgment may still react to his royal blood. This cross-compatibility will make him an extraordinary alchemist, able to study living and cursed biology as two valid systems instead of treating one as the contamination of the other.
Glyphs. [Leth] Blood, [Ma] Recall, [Lei] Binding, [Au] Death, [Thal] Silence, [El] Life, [On] Light, [Ora] Truth, [Vael] Renewal. His fundamental architecture is [Leth] + [El] + [Ur]: blood, life, balance.

























ChainMeaning[Leth] + [On]Blood lit without burning[Leth] + [Vael]Blood purified through renewal[Au] + [El] + [Ur]Life and death held in living balance[Ora] + [Leth]Truth carried in royal blood
Traits that reconcile what ordinary Vampires cannot: blood that heals rather than steals; shadows that protect the living; fangs that draw out poison, curses or foreign Essence instead of vitality; sunlight conducted through Vampire blood; entry into mortal and Vampire Domains without being read as prey, invader or curse; blood as both living reagent and spiritual record; royal blood-command without domination. Overgrowth: the Perfect Predator. With none of the usual restraints, he may come to believe himself exempt from every limit. His great danger will not be the Red Hunger. It will be superiority.
Domain. Likely twilight rather than night: a palace split between dawn and moonlight, a red moon over a sunlit graveyard, an alchemical city with blood running through glass channels, a royal court where every shadow has a living reflection. Probable laws: Life and death share one circulation. Blood may carry power without carrying ownership. The Sun recognizes what the curse cannot condemn. No inheritance possesses the one who carries it.
Place in the World
He will have no people and no accepted place. To the royal line, a bastard carrying royal authority without lawful legitimacy. To traditional High Vampires, proof that the weaknesses used to justify their hierarchy are not fundamental. To Common Vampires, freedom, blasphemy, revolution or an unreachable privilege. To Turned Vampires, a sign that cursed continuation can be separated from subjugation. To mortals, too dangerous to see as anything but Vampire blood. He will destabilize the Empire before he chooses any side.
Advantages: every principal Vampire strength; no sunlight weakness; no silver rejection; no special vulnerability to stakes beyond ordinary injury; no automatic holy rejection; independent Essence recovery; affinity for blood, soul, darkness, life, light and alchemy; no blood dependence; royal authority; slowed aging.
Limitations: no true agelessness; the only one of his kind, with no precedent and no one who can fully teach him; a political target for his blood and a social suspect for his mortality; magnet for experimentation, assassination, religious condemnation and attempts to control his reproduction; his powers may become a battleground between royal inheritance and personal identity.
The Feral State
Feral Vampires are not a race. They are the collapse state every Vampire can fall into: the point where hunger replaces identity as the organizing principle of the Crystal. The body stays powerful and the senses sharpen. The person shrinks.
A feral may still speak, plan, imitate affection and think with real intelligence. Intelligence is not recovery. Some of the most dangerous ferals stay calculating and simply sort every relationship by feeding. A parent becomes protected food. A lover becomes owned blood. A friend becomes a resource whose moods improve the meal. A city becomes a herd. The final condition, the Blood Hollow, has no central identity left at all: a hunger-architecture wearing its accumulated memories as disguises.
The Five Stages of Starvation





























StageWhat happens1 · DryingRegeneration slows, the body cools, the senses grow irritable, the Vampire grows restless around blood2 · Crimson FeverHeartbeats become impossible to ignore. Emotional control frays. Ordinary movement reads as prey behavior3 · Blood FrenzyEmpathy collapses. Allies, family and strangers all become food. Techniques grow stronger and wilder4 · Soul ConsumptionThe Crystal eats the Vampire’s own memories. Names go, morals weaken, personal history fragments5 · Feral HollowingIdentity stops governing. The body becomes a self-directing predator
Recovery is possible in the early stages. The Blood Hollow is rarely reversible.
The Racial Curses













































CurseWhat it doesWho it sparesThe SunTrue sunlight triggers Material combustion, Soul contradiction and Fate rejection at once. Common and Turned Vampires burn fast; High Vampires resist for a while, then igniteVampire-Dragon Hybrids are generally immune. Malrik will be immuneSilver RejectionSilver conducts the curse’s opposing frequencies into each other: burning, circulation seizure, slowed regeneration, Crystal disruptionHigh Vampires resist. Hybrids and Malrik are immune to the curse-specific reactionThe Living StakeWood through the heart-seat carries a living organic pattern into deathless circulation, pins the Vampire to biological mortality and stops blood from sustaining the curse. It must reach the heart-seat or the Crystal junction; wooden wounds elsewhere are not automatically fatalMalrik, beyond ordinary injurySacred and Holy MagicBenediction, Absolution, Penanceflare, sacred relics and coherent holy Domains can force the human pattern and the curse apart: pain, paralysis, combustion, purification or deathHybrids partly; Malrik largelyBlood ContaminationBlood carries Essence, emotion, memory, disease, curses and Trait residue. Feeding on corrupted, divine, possessed, demonic or unstable beings can change the VampireNo one entirelyPredatory AttractionVampires recognize life through hunger. Without discipline, affection becomes possession, loyalty becomes enthrallment, grief becomes refusing to let the dead go, protection becomes ownershipNo one entirelyThe Maker’s PullEvery Vampire’s curse still carries Malakar’s imprint. Now that he walks the Material World again, every Vampire can feel his presence in the blood, and the Malakarian Liturgical answers him. The weak-willed feel drawn; the feral may simply goMalrik, perhaps. No one knows
The Languages of the Vampiric Peoples
Every Vampiric language carries the First Thirst. Words for blood, ownership, memory, invitation, hunger, debt and consent hold distinctions most mortal tongues lack, and Vampire grammar almost never treats blood as neutral. The form of the word changes with whether the blood is inside its rightful body, freely given, taken by force, inherited, spilled in battle, offered in ritual, taken as punishment, or owed by law.

























LanguageWhat it isDreadvalicThe common and imperial tongue, grown from the mixed northern languages of Malakar’s captives. Formal, slow and deeply contextual. Pronouns and verb endings shift with whether the listener is prey, a protected mortal, kin, maker, fledgling, clan sovereign, elder or royal blood. It has no neutral word for feeding: every equivalent specifies the legal and emotional terms on which the blood is takenOld BluvenThe ceremonial tongue of Bluvest’s nobility, built by the first High Vampires out of their own northern dialects. Long, quiet and full of controlled pauses; many sentences are meant to be spoken with the heart still. Used for blood marriages, royal declarations, trials, ancestral recitations and investituresBloodcantA ritual language of heartbeat, blood movement, subaudible Harmonics, tongue-clicks and shared resonance, passed by touch, bloodline or closeness. A single pulse can say danger, hunger, recognition, submission, location, injury or command. Turned Vampires feel it as pressure in the bite scarMalakarian LiturgicalFragments of Malakar’s own demonic tongue, surviving in the oldest rites. It acts directly on the curse: long use can sharpen bloodlust, wake dormant command-architecture, or let Malakar’s emotional imprint reproduce inside the speaker’s Crystal. Loyalists call it communion. Most Dreadvalis scholars call it self-inflicted possession, and since Malakar’s return its words have begun, very faintly, to answer back
Core Vocabulary: Dreadvalic











































































WordMeaningNotesvareshblood inside its rightful bodyBound up with personhood, privacy and protected lifedraalblood with no recognized ownerBattlefield blood, abandoned blood, blood lawfully free for usesevrathiblood freely givenCarries consent and remembered trustmalvethblood taken by dominationNot automatically illegal under traditional lawkethrathe first controlled feedingThe mark of maturity and self-commandvel-draenone who shares your hunger but not your bloodRoughly “comrade”saar valethdebt carried in bloodAn inherited obligationnoth-varenone remembered only through consumed bloodA victim whose memory lives on inside the Vampiredrevakarhunger speaking in another’s voiceA symptom of blood-memory contaminationsolvethsunlight touching cursed fleshLiterally: the world recognizing the errordraevalisdominion beneath the rejected dawnThe root of Dreadvalisblu-vestthe city whose night was built, not givenThe origin of Bluvestfang-malrikblood outside the law of inheritanceA later phrase tied to Malrik Fang’s birth
The Dreadvalis Empire





























LocationThe veiled, cold north of the Outer World: undercities beneath the Moonlight Forest, the Moonlight Snow Plains, the Frostfang and the Serrathan HighlandsCapitalBluvest, seat of the Blood ThroneSecond cityMorvayne, seat of the lawPopulationHundreds of thousands of Vampires, most of them turned in the empire’s first desperate years or born since; millions of mortal subjects and tributariesGovernanceThe Blood Throne, the Royal Vein, the Great Clans, provincial Night Governors, the Vein-Marshals, and the Crimson Ledger Courts
Dreadvalis did not begin as a kingdom. It began as a solution to starvation. The first Vampires hunted without restraint. Villages vanished, mortal populations collapsed, and Vampire packs destroyed their own food and then turned on each other. The clans formed because uncontrolled hunger could not last. The Empire formed because the clans could not stop fighting over blood.
It is young (a matter of decades, not centuries) and it grew fast and hard, under rulers who remembered being human and remembered the Taken Winter. Its whole civilization rests on one contradiction: it is an ordered society built to preserve a predatory race. Its laws prevent extinction. They also regulate exploitation.
Bluvest — The City Beneath Dawn
The largest Vampire city and seat of the Blood Throne, sunk beneath the northern edge of the Moonlight Forest under the oldest of the Great Veils. It is built down through layers of black stone, reflective mineral, enchanted metal and blood-wards, and its deepest districts have never seen natural light. Artificial rivers carry water, alchemical nutrients and blood in separate channels beneath the streets.





















LevelWho lives thereUpper districtsNearest the surface and most exposed to solar breach: Turned Vampires, mortal workers, soldiers and labor castesMiddle cityCommon Vampire familiesThe deepsHigh Vampire estates, ancestral vaults, the royal halls and the great reservoirs
At Bluvest’s center lies the Red Sea, an immense alchemical reservoir of donated, taxed, purchased, inherited and enslaved blood. In famine every recognized citizen receives a ration. How much depends on rank.
Morvayne — The City of Law
The empire’s second city lies beneath the Moonlight Snow Plains behind a ring of black walls and Veilspires. Where Bluvest holds the throne, Morvayne holds the machinery: the Crimson Ledger Courts, the Tithe Ministries that run the blood tithe across the tributary kingdoms, the physician-colleges, and the vast Cold Granaries that keep the north’s mortals fed. The Veiled Imperial District of Morvayne is where foreign envoys are received, because it is easier to impress a mortal king with a city of law than with a sea of blood.
The Royal Vein
The royal line descends from the blood authority of the first Blood Throne, Vaelora’s. It does not merely govern. Its blood is woven into the empire’s oldest wards, reservoirs, oaths and Attraction architecture, and the sovereign’s blood is what gives imperial law its recognition. Succession is biological, spiritual and territorial: a lawful heir inherits a crown and a standing inside the blood-systems that keep Bluvest alive.
Malrik Fang’s future birth will strike at exactly this. He will carry royal blood without legitimacy, yet his blood may hold more metaphysical authority than those seated above him. The Empire will have to decide whether royal blood is legitimate because the law recognizes it, or whether the law is legitimate because royal blood sustains it.
The Great Clans
The Great Clans are blood-systems, not families. Their members share inherited Traits, curse adaptations, memories, weaknesses and Fate-recognition, and a founder’s preserved blood can anchor a clan estate long after the founder dies. Destroying a Great Clan takes more than killing its living members: its ancestral blood, turned descendants, memorial vessels, Domain anchors and records must all go too.
The Crimson Ledger Courts
The Ledger Courts regulate lawful, protected and coerced feeding; blood theft; illegal turning; clan executions and unsanctioned killing; destruction of valuable blood; feeding on protected children or diplomats; consuming another Vampire; and stealing another clan’s donor. They are not humanitarian. Their purpose is political and biological sustainability.
Mortals Within Dreadvalis
Abroad, Dreadvalis shows the tributary kingdoms its best face: the blood tithe, drawn by physicians in the Tithe Halls, with the young, old, sick and pregnant exempt, paid back in grain, medicine and protection. Inside the empire, the law is older and uglier.





































CategoryWhat it meansProtected CitizensSkilled mortals granted status for service and a regulated blood contributionTithe SubjectsTributary peoples who pay the blood tithe under treatyDonor HousesFamilies contracted to give blood across generations. Some are rich; others are hereditary prisoners under polite namesLabor CastesMortals who keep the farms, mines, construction, alchemy and surface trade runningCaptivesPrisoners taken from enemy landsLivestock PopulationsMortals denied legal personhood and bred for consumption by traditionalist clans. The Ledger Courts tolerate them; the tributary kingdoms are not shown themRed GuestsForeigners protected for a time by Guest-Law
The Internal Conflict
The empire’s deepest question was never simply whether Vampires should feed on mortals. It was: what may a Vampire become, now that its maker is gone?
Reformist clans seek voluntary donors and a future past Malakar. Traditionalists treat mortals as managed resources. Malakarian loyalists call every feeding restriction a betrayal of the race’s purpose. Some seek coexistence, some empire, some a cure; others fear that a cure would not restore humanity but kill the people Vampires have become.
And now the question has changed, because the maker is not gone. Malakar has returned to the Material World. Every Vampire alive can feel him in their blood. The loyalists are already slipping away south toward him. The Blood Throne has said nothing in public. In the deeps of Bluvest, the oldest High Vampires, the ones who remember the Taken Winter, are asking the only question that matters: whether the thing that made them has come back for them, and whether they can refuse it if it has.
Malrik Fang’s eventual existence will turn all of this into open crisis, because he will show that Vampire power and Malakar’s punishment can be separated.
Famous Figures
Vaelora Dreadvalis — First Blood Empress
Founder of the Empire · High Vampire · One of the First Captives
Tall, pale and unnaturally still. Black hair in a long braid threaded with red metal rings, one for each clan she conquered or absorbed. Eyes a dark crimson with no line between iris and pupil. Her crown was forged from the melted fangs of the clan founders she defeated.
She was a northern noblewoman taken in the Taken Winter, and she came out of the First Thirst with a curse that held its shape. She did not believe Vampires could become human again. She did not believe hunger excused stupidity. Her laws were brutal because she preferred brutality to extinction: she ended the clan feuds, wrote the Crimson Ledger, created the blood tithe, and executed Vampires who destroyed mortal communities without strategic purpose. She is called both savior and tyrant, and she has never argued with either word.
“You mistake restraint for kindness. I restrain you because blood spilled today cannot feed the city tomorrow.”
Arkhaven Bluvest — Architect Beneath Dawn
High Vampire Alchemist and Geomancer
Thin, with translucent skin marked by black alchemical channels from fingertips to throat; layered protective lenses and sealed mineral powders at his belt. Arkhaven treated sunlight as a technical problem, not a divine punishment. He studied solar spectra, reflection, sacred recognition, heat transfer and the Sun Curse across all three Planes, designed Bluvest’s deepest light-sealed districts, and laid the theory behind the Great Veils. He died inside an experimental solar chamber after misclassifying one wavelength as harmless.
Lord Sevran Molovar — Keeper of Seventeen Veins
High Vampire · Architect of the Reservoirs
The architect of the imperial blood-reservoir system, the Red Sea of Bluvest, and the first regulated donor castes. Every Tithe Hall in the north runs on his designs.
Khaedros Vyrkan — The Scaled Hunger
Vampire-Dragon Hybrid
Nearly nine feet tall in humanoid form. Pale bronze skin broken by crimson-black scale along the neck, spine, forearms and ribs; backward-curving horns; blood that burns on contact with air. The first widely documented Hybrid. Khaedros despised ownership. When three Vampire clans tried to claim him through his Vampire parent’s blood, he destroyed all three and drank their ancestral reservoirs, ending their bloodline recognition for ever. Then he went south into the volcanic country of Drakyssia, and no one has found him since.
Malrik Fang — The Only Dhampir
Bastard of the Royal Vein · Future-Born
His adult appearance belongs to a future age. He will combine mortal coloring with unmistakable royal Vampire traits: no born-Vampire pallor, eyes of royal crimson under a living human brightness that shifts with blood, sunlight and exertion. His fangs will retract completely. His body will stay warm. The sun will not burn him.
Too Vampiric for mortals to trust. Too alive for Dreadvalis to classify safely. Royal by blood, illegitimate by law, heir to a power his own dynasty cannot publicly recognize without undermining its succession. He will not be the last of a lost people. He will stand alone, and that solitude will be both his greatest weakness and the root of his independence.
The Imperial Doctrine of Blood
The official doctrine of Dreadvalis:
Blood is sustenance. Blood is memory. Blood is inheritance. Blood is evidence. Blood is consent. Blood is debt. Blood is power. Blood is the record of life carried in liquid form.
The radical reading follows from it: if blood carries the record of a life, whoever consumes it takes responsibility for what that life contained. Traditionalists reject this. Reformists call it the only future in which Vampires become more than Malakar intended. Malakarian loyalists call responsibility a mortal weakness.
Malakar’s return has sharpened every side of the argument. Malrik Fang’s blood will one day add the hardest question of all: if blood can carry Vampire power without carrying Malakar’s punishment, how much of Vampirism belongs to the race, and how much still belongs to the demon who made it?
“The Sun was made our enemy. Hunger was placed inside us. Neither fact determines what we choose when the doors close and night begins.” — Inscription beneath the western gate of Bluvest

Read beside this. The Geography of the Outer World, for the land under the veils and the balance across the March.
