races--and--peoples/the-tongues-of-the-r.title: Element Inventories — Mahuo, Yukari, the Elven Branches, Beastkin
races--and--peoples/the-tongues-of-the-r.content:
Ask anyone at Sum-gol about the Seven Debts. A cadet grandfather of the Mahuo, who kept the family’s accounts in green ink and the family in fear of them, chose Chae (debt) as the generation-syllable for every child born to his line that decade, and so seven cousins went through life as Chaewon, Chaejin, Chaeyeon and the rest, in bright Breath Hollow silks, announced at every feast as what they owed. At twenty they sued him jointly, in a suit that ran nine years and outlived him, and the whole hollow turned out for the verdict with food. A name is a small inheritance with a fixed grammar, and these are the parts.
Four element inventories: Mahuo, Yukari, the Elven branches, Beastkin. Read alongside the Marrowkin and Moto inventories and the Naming Guide’s per-culture registers. Each inventory keeps the format of those two except where the culture’s own anchor does not fit it.
A glossary note. An “element” is a short syllable or root with a fixed meaning, like Latin “-ius” or the “Wolf-” in Wolfgang. A “compound” name is two elements stuck together (Wolf + gang). “Morpheme” means the same thing as “element.” A “coda” is whatever sound closes out a syllable (the “-t” in “cat”). None of this needs to be understood to use the inventories themselves.
I. Mahuo — Breath, Soul and the Ledger (Korean stratum)
Two-syllable given names built from a fixed inventory. One syllable is the generation-syllable, shared by every child of one generation within a line; the other is the personal syllable. Either syllable may occupy either position: the records show both “Ara Min” and “Mu-jin” orderings. The family name attaches per the existing pattern; the records show it both preceding (Kwon Mu-jin) and following (Cozbi Mahuo) the given name, and this inventory does not resolve which is “correct” — both are attested.





























CategoryElementsBreath & soulSum (breath: attested), Hon (soul), Ryeo (echo of a soul), Yeong (spirit), Won (origin), Sae (new, first breath)Ledger & recordJang (chapter), Kye (bond, a tallied account), Bo (safeguard), Ye (a recorded rite), Chae (debt), Rok (record)House & clan-seatGol (hollow, valley: attested), Ga (house), Ju (sovereign), Chang (prosperity), Dae (great), Ryeong (order)Precision & correctionJin (truth), Jeong (correct), Chak (exact), Ban (reflect), Kyeol (resolve), Seol (state plainly)Care & healingEun (grace), Sun (purity, gentleness), Hwa (harmony), Yeon (bond, compassion), Bit (light), Soo (water, healing flow)
Worked example. A cohort sharing the generation-syllable Jin (truth): elder daughter Jin + Won → Jinwon (“the truth of where we come from”); younger son Sae + Jin → Saejin (“a fresh truth”). Either could appear as “Jinwon Mahuo” or, in the Kwon cadet branch, “Kwon Saejin.”
II. Yukari — Thread, Fate and the Crow (Japonic stratum)
Two-element compounds. A full name carries up to five life-stage forms: childhood name, adult name (taken at the Telling), calling-name (used by intimates), true name (taboo — spoken only among family or before Senri’s stone), and posthumous name.
Only Ketsu, En, Jin, and Mu are attested in the old records; every other element is a compiler’s reconstruction to fit the register.





























CategoryElementsThread & fateKetsu (thread-bound: attested), En (bond: attested), Sen (a drawn line), Un (fate), Kizu (the mark a pulled thread leaves), Toki (the moment a thread draws taut)Crow & silenceKarasu (crow: attested), Shizu (stillness), Yami (dark), Kage (shadow), Koe (a withheld voice), Aida (the interval between threads)Divine & dreamJin (divine: attested), Mu (dream: attested), Rei (spirit), Getsu (moon), Yoru (night), Asa (the hour before dawn)Water, stone & griefSui (still water), Ishi (stone, resolve), Namida (tear, grief), Shizuku (the droplet before impact), Nagi (calm after grief), Fuchi (the deep pool grief settles into)Weight & officeKuro (black, formal-office color), Nushi (the one who holds a seat), Tsugu (the one who continues a line), Kari (a borrowed calling-name), Imi (taboo, the withheld true name), Oku (the deep name, spoken only at the Telling or at death)
Worked example. Childhood name Asagetsu (Asa + Getsu, “dawn-moon”); adult name chosen at the Telling, Kizuun (Kizu + Un, “the mark fate leaves”); calling-name Kizu; true name “Kizuun Yukari” spoken only in Council, at a Proving, or before Senri’s stone; posthumous name Okuen (Oku + En, “the bond that goes deep”).
III. The Elven Branches — Shared Roots, Branch Affixes
One shared root inventory plus five branch-specific naming rules, rather than five flat lists, because that is how the source grammar itself is organized and it avoids pretending the five branches do not share a language. The five are Eressean, Varrisak, Drow, Eladrin and the Echo Elves; the grammar is on Eressean and Varrisak — The Tongue of the Vey-Elarin.
Roots are disyllabic and open, codas restricted to a vowel, a liquid (l/r), a nasal (m/n/ny), or th. Every element carries a grammatical pitch contour (level/rising/falling).
Shared roots (attested).





























































RootMeaningelarnote, name, personveykinthaerthe kept thing, archivesylvagrowing groundmarinattested root, meaning not on recordseralwinterlythsilencedhaethe dreamvenseentortoldmato holdurto witnessiethe grant, the transfer
Shared affixes (attested).

























































AffixFunction-urenvalidated-amacontingent, unwitnessed-ieurself-witnessed, Varrisak only-itha small name, a by-name-ethan office, a rite-role-aerhigh, raised-akforeign, outside the form-incollective-engenitive, “of”-saein-window, timely-loout-of-window, hasty or erroneouszorestatement clitic, Echo Elf
New branch-specific roots (one per branch, not previously attested).



































BranchRootGlossEresseankalenthe unvarying riteVarrisaksovathe vision sought aloneDrowmorelthe ledger of what is owedEladrinfaelothe frost that holds rather than endsEcho Elvesveraththe term memorized exactly
Worked example, showing branch divergence on the same root. Eressean Kalenuren (Kalen, and the assembly stood for it); Varrisak Kalenieur (held, self-witnessed by the forest); Drow Morelsae (a debt within its term) against Morello (a debt in default); Eladrin Faelo followed by a measured four-count silence (assent, no spoken suffix needed); Echo Elf Verath. Zo Verath. (introduced, then ritually restated).
IV. Beastkin — Soul-Names and Name-Keeping
Three linked layers rather than a flat category list, because the amendment’s own anchor for the Beastkin (Akan day-naming plus the Name-Keeping tradition) is a fixed circumstance-to-name correspondence and no combinable phoneme pool. The expectation layer draws each lineage’s definitive stat (Catkin = Dexterity, Lupine = Harmonics/pack, Bearkin = Vitality, Fox-Spirit = Harmonics/memory, Serpentkin = Gnosis).
A soul-name has two parts spoken together: the circumstance-element (what the birth was like, Akan-day-name style) and the expectation-element (the attribute the child is charged to grow into). The held-name is whichever fragment survives when everything else — home, rank, kin — has been taken.





















LayerElementsCircumstance (the birth)Vel (born into stillness), Rhaka (born during storm or violence), Tuen (born in flight, escape), Miro (born under threat), Oda (born into plenty, safety), Kess (born far from kin, alone)Expectation (the attribute charged, lineage-flavored)Zhiv (quickness: Catkin), Kaal (the pack that holds: Lupine), Dorn (the weight that stays: Bearkin), Sana (kept by scent and memory: Fox-Spirit), Riss (not forgotten, the coil that remembers: Serpentkin), Vantu (raw courage, unbound to any lineage)Held-name and Name-Keeping ritual vocabularyAshe (“I remain”), Ndoto (witness, the one who receives the name), Fen (the last thing, what cannot be taken), Baru (spoken aloud), Tolo (the return, a name given back to a survivor), Chike (kept, held safe)
Worked example. A Bearkin child born into safety (Oda) charged with steady endurance (Dorn): soul-name Oda-dorn, recorded but unused daily; an ordinary use-name serves in public life. Having later lost home, rank, and kin, she performs the Name-Keeping: “Fen Oda-dorn, Baru” (“the last thing, Oda-dorn, spoken aloud”) before a witness, who answers “Ashe” (“I have heard; you remain”).

races--and--peoples/the-tongues-of-the-r.content:
Some generations back a retainer of the Akagane named his firstborn Tendoku, heaven and alone, at the spring naming, in a forge-yard hung with so much red-bronze cloth that the sparrows would not land in it. The Kōkan’s envoy, in red enamel, asked over the rice whom exactly the sky had left standing, and whether the sky had been consulted. The boy had a new name by supper, kept the old one anyway, and fought six duels across forty years over which of the two would be read at Ice-out. A Moto element weighs that much.
Moto naming is Japonic, and this is its element bank. Same shape as the Yukari inventory: thirty elements in five categories, two-element compounds, two to four syllables, vowel-forward, no clusters. Nothing here changes a name already on the record.
Attested and coined: the elements marked attested are lifted from names and terms already in use. Every other element and every gloss is coined.
Slot structure (attested)
Given name + Line name + Moto. The surname is a fixed hereditary fact of the
bloodline (§5.1: “the family name is a fixed structural fact”). The Line sits
between given name and surname for the six landless Great Lines — Artemis
Amagiri Moto*, Souma Byakuya Moto — and is omitted for Kōkan, the line
that holds the seat, and for a Moto whose Line is not the point of the sentence
(Sodoku Moto, Muken Moto, Mizuki Moto). The seven Lines are attested:
Kōkan (the crown, the seat), Shirogane (silver: the mint and the assay),
Akagane (copper: the forge), Kurenai (crimson hidden in black and ash),
Byakuya (near-white), Tenrai (gold, banner-heraldry), Amagiri (indigo,
mist-gray), from The Moto Bloodline — Material Culture.
The thirty elements

Crown & seat: Kō (crown: attested, Kōkan), Kan (the seat held: attested, Kōkan), Za (the chair itself), Ōmi (the one who is looked at), Tsukasa (office), Ren (the drilled, the tempered: attested, Kairen, gloss coined)
Metal & line: Shiro (silver, white: attested, Shirogane), Aka (copper, red: attested, Akagane), Kuro (black: attested, Kurosetsu), Gane (worked metal: attested, the -gane Lines), Byaku (white: attested, Byakuya), Beni (the crimson kept hidden: attested, Kurenai)
Sky & weather: Ten (heaven: attested, Tenrai), Rai (thunder: attested, Tenrai), Ama (rain, heaven: attested, Amagiri), Giri (mist; also the duty that binds: attested, Amagiri), Fū (wind: attested, Fūkoku), Yuki (snow: attested, Yukazuri)
Severance & exile: Doku (alone, the severed one: attested in Sodoku and Rikudoku, gloss coined), Setsu (the cut: attested, Kurosetsu), Zuri (what is dragged behind: attested, Yukazuri), Muken (the unseen, the withheld: attested as a name, gloss coined), Bara (the root, the origin: attested, Bara Moto, gloss coined), Riku (the land left: attested, Rikudoku)
Water & the Works: Mizu (water: attested, Mizuki), Ki (the tree, what stands: attested, Mizuki), Sou (the pair, the double: attested, Souma), Ma (the interval: attested, Souma), Kai (the sea, the open: attested, Kairen), Sai (the rite performed: attested, Saishiki)

How a name is built
Two elements, either order, joined plainly; a coda consonant is doubled or dropped
by ear, never clustered. The given name states what the line expects or what the
child was born into; the Line name says which metal they answer to; Moto says
whose they are. Renaming at promotion, vow or change of allegiance is a feature of
this stratum (§6): the exile’s renaming is a Moto story, not a Yukari one.
Worked examples (coined): Kōsetsu (Kō + Setsu: “the crown cut”) for a Kōkan
child born after the seat’s fall; Shirokai Shirogane Moto (silver + the open
sea: the assay-line’s factor at a port); Amayuki Amagiri Moto (rain + snow);
Tendoku (heaven + alone: the one the sky left standing). Compare the attested
Sodoku, Yukazuri, Mizuki, Byakuya, Kairen, Fūkoku, Rikudoku: every
one of them reads as two of these elements.
Notes on the bank

Tenrai is both a Line and a house that was massacred (Tenrai Moto); Ten and Rai remain elements of the bank.
Artemis and Emira are attested Moto given names outside this register: outliers, and no evidence against it.

Six peoples and how they curse · the Kharven, the Moto, the Marrowkin, the Accord, the elves and the Zettari · and the words every people shares

Every people swears in its own words first, and in the common tongue’s plain body-swears as well. What a people swears by is what it holds sacred, and what it insults with is what it fears to be. The Sky, the Fourteen (together, or each of them by name), the named Archons, the Veil, the Realmsong, Varūn and the ancestors carry the most weight, and beside them every people swears by its own Wells, its trades and its dead, as each people’s Standing Inventory sets down.

The oldest layer of this page reached the Guild on a strip of ship’s sail. When the wine cog Long Hester opened her belly on the Sowmarsh bar, thirty-eight people spent nine days on a spit of yellow sand with two casks of water and no shared opinion about anything: Kharven sealers, Marrowkin coopers, a pair of Eressean sisters, a Moto retainer in lacquered harness who corrected everyone, and a chancery clerk named Drogo Fulke. By the third day they had stopped fighting over the water and started fighting over whose insults were worse. By the sixth it was a contest with judges, and a Marrowkin cooper was winning it by saying one word three times, very quietly. Fulke took it all down on red sailcloth in fish blood, and lost the top of an ear for asking a sealer to repeat Kiilut. The boats that came for them found thirty-eight people hoarse, sunburned and on excellent terms. The strip is in the Altherion rolls, and these tables are its great-grandchildren.
How to Read the Tables
Strength, four grades:

mild: said in front of children, a grunt at a dropped tool.
firm: rude; said to a peer’s face it is a rebuke.
hard: an insult that has to be answered or swallowed.
grave: fighting words, or a curse that some people will not say aloud at all.

Kharven
The clans swear by the Sky and the fire, curse with the cold, and insult by scarcity: bad wood, empty saddles, cracked bowls, short stacks. The Sky is never named beyond the Sky.





































































































SwearLiteral meaningStrengthWho says itBy the sky that covers us.An oath taken under the whole Sky.firm (solemn)Anyone swearing a thing true; elders at a death-house; never said lightlyBy the fire.An oath on the hearth that keeps the household alive.mildEveryday emphasis in any household; “by the fire, I told him twice”Sky take it.Let the Sky have it, since the Sky takes the dead.mildThe everyday “damn it” in any mouth, riders, wives, children who think nobody is listeningWet wood.Wood that smokes and will not catch.hardSaid of a liar or a man who cannot be relied on; the whole proverb, “wet wood burns eventually, a liar never dries,” is the formal versionEmpty saddle.A saddle with nobody in it.harda man who is not there when the ride goes out; riders, veterans, the banner houses’ menCracked bowl.A bowl that cannot hold its share.hardone who takes the first bowl from the one who cannot fill it (breaks the proverb); women at the pot, eldersShort stack.A woodpile too small for the winter.firmSaid of a lazy or improvident man; neighbors, the answer to “how’s your stack?” given about someone elseFull mouth.All talk, since the full stack speaks louder.firmSaid of a boaster; young men to young men, old men to young menThin Weeks on you.May the late-winter hunger find your house.hardA curse between households in a feud; not said in a lean year, when it is too close to trueQatuq take you.Qatuq: the cold that takes the unready.hardHunters and sealers; a curse that wishes a man dead the northern way, slowly and by his own mistakeKiilut.One of the dead left without the Waiting; a corpse nobody sat with.graveThe worst thing one Kharven can call another; old women say it and men go quiet; never shoutedHulluk.The native word for wet wood.hardThe same insult as “wet wood,” in the older mouth; carried-name households, the Keld, sealersNumra.An empty bowl held out; a mouth that eats and brings nothing.firmSaid of a guest who never hunts, a relative who only arrives at meat-sharingSkin-refuser.One who refused the skin (the fermented milk offered at the door).graveAn accusation of contempt for a host; said once and then there is a fightFrozen piss.Exactly that.mildThe body-swear in its winter version; riders, soldiers on the wall
Moto
A house that holds the offense is inaccuracy, so its heaviest words are verdicts. The house speaks in the old register: full forms, no contractions, honorifics where the old tongue is used. The Moto never swear by a single Archon, since addressing one alone is Singling, the principal heresy; a Moto who hears a Kharven say “Archons take it” hears nothing wrong, and a Moto who hears “Irath take it” hears heresy. They also do not petition, so there is no Moto “help me.”





































































































SwearLiteral meaningStrengthWho says itBy the Fourteen.Before all fourteen Archons at once, as the Bow is made.firm (solemn)The only lawful invocation in a Moto mouth; senior line members, the Kōkan, retainers taking an orderIncorrect.Wrongly read.hard; from a senior, graveThe whole of blame, as “correct” is the whole of praise; lords to retainers, fathers to sons; one word, no heatEmpty Bow.Observance performed without the labor.graveSaid of a man or a house that keeps the forms and does none of the work; held worse than neglectSingler.One who elevates one Archon above the fourteen.graveA charge of heresy; the Kōkan say it of Sancta Lux, and of themselves when Totality starts to look like a crownPetitioner.One who asks an Archon for something.hardContempt for a beggar at the altar, and for any man who bargains where he should laborClogged.A house that will not let its dead leave.hardSaid of a house that keeps its dead in portraits, relics and rehearsed griefLet him go unread.May nobody read his name at Ice-out.graveA curse wishing a man’s death to go unentered and unfaced; spoken by the old, rarely, and never over a bodyWritten in the wrong hand.A document in the wrong Archon’s hand, void rather than incorrect.hardSaid of a bastard, a false claim, a forged order, or a man who holds an office he was never read intoPoet.A swordsman who fights decoratively.firmWeapons masters to students; “against harness, do not behave like a poet”A snake dressed up as a Moto.What it says.hardSaid of a false claimant to the nameBureimono.Rude person; insolent wretch: a person of discourtesy.hardA lord to an inferior who has forgotten his place; the classic feudal rebukeKisama.You: once honorific, long since contemptuous.hardA superior to an enemy or a disgraced inferior; used as a form of address, which is the insultShiremono.Fool, idiot, in the old form.firmAn elder to a reckless younger man; also, grudgingly, of a man daring past senseHikyōmono.Coward; one who acts basely.graveAmong the line and its retainers; to call a Moto this in front of a witness is to ask to be revoked or to fightHeld by nobody.Elar-ama: entered as a name nobody stands for.graveOnly as a verdict after “I revoke the name Moto from you”; as an insult outside that, it is a threat
The Marrowkin
Marrowkin have no light oath. “Kurme” is the swearing itself, so a Marrowkin who says “I swear” has sworn, and they do not say it for emphasis. Their curses fall on the cask, the angle, the entry and the grade.































































































SwearLiteral meaningStrengthWho says itKurnur.Unentered: you did it and nobody will stand behind it.hardAny Marrowkin to any Marrowkin; the three-times form (“Kurnur. Kurnur. Kurnur.”) quotes the Oath-Breakers’ wall and is graveThe name in the weak grade.Torve for Torvekk: the oath-name said as broken.graveThe worst thing one Marrowkin can do to another in one syllable; done on purpose only by enemies and the wallOllu kuolee.The brew dies.hardThe Marrowkin “damn it” for real disaster, a collapsed gallery or a lost cask; the Cask Line will not say it within sight of a Cask-Oath barrelNikkat ei on.The angles are not [true].hardThe flat damnation of a piece of work, the Tally’s “Nikkat on” turned over; clerks, rune-forgers, masters over apprenticesWrong angle.A rune cut askew, which does nothing.firmSaid of any failed work or failed man; “askew” for his work in generalVoiced.Said the way somebody not paying attention says it (b for p).firmSaid of a careless speaker, and of Concord men generallyJust rock.The thing without its measurement.firmSaid of worthless ore, a worthless plan, a man with no recordThe seam’s out.The ore seam is played out.mildResigned exclamation, “we are done here”; miners, shift crewsVarūn never said.The god never told us which answer he meant.mildA shrug-oath at a question with no answer; the old, the Reach branchesCask-cracker.One who ends a brew that holds an oath.graveSaid of an oath-breaker; the Cask Line above allPiss in the brew.Exactly that.graveAimed at the one thing Marrowkin hold sacred; said to start a fight, or by outsiders who do not know betterWill-sayer.One who says “I will,” which the tongue cannot.firmSaid of a Concord envoy, a braggart, a young Marrowkin who has spent too long in AltherionBare-chin.A beard with no rings: no time served.mildElders to the young, forge Marrowkin to outsidersKurlo. Ei kurme.Unbegun. Not undertaken.hard (as a refusal)The “no, and do not ask me for the other word” that ends a negotiation
The Accord and the Concord
Chartered, tolled and entered people swear by paperwork and the Archons’ days, and insult by weights and measures. The chancery Latin turns up in any educated mouth, and in a temper most of all. The Accord’s calendar gives the Archon days: Auren’s for the dead, Veyra’s for markets, Irath’s for musters, and Uurgath’s, which nobody chooses on purpose.





































































































SwearLiteral meaningStrengthWho says itArchons take it.Let the Fourteen have it.mildThe everyday “damn it” of the Concord, in every classBefore witnesses.Coram testibus: said in front of people who could swear to it.mildThe everyday emphatic; “I told him, before witnesses”Uurgath’s day.The day of the Devourer of Forms, when no sane court sits.firmExclamation at a disaster or a bad start; clerks, market people, soldiersUurgath te devoret.May Uurgath devour you.hardLatin curse from the educated; Division officers, advocates in a temperUrion te ponderet.May Urion weigh you.hardA curse that wishes judgment on a man; Sancta Lux-leaning speakers, MeasurewrightsNullum et irritum.Null and void.firmSaid of a man, a plan or a promise that is worth nothing; clerks and anyone who has spent time around themSalvo iure tertii.Saving the right of a third party.mildSaid drily of a promise with a hole in it, “yes, salvo iure tertii”; advocates, merchantsPondus falsum.False weight.hardA cheat; market searchers, merchants, the Assize courtsSine sigillo.Without seal.hardUnregistered, unlawful: said of a bastard, a smuggler, an unlicensed speakerShort loaf.A loaf under its assize weight, the commonest charge on any market roll.firmA small cheat; street and market speechCased.Looks solid, rings dull when struck.hardSaid of a fraud; anyone who has heard the small hammerPass his door.Let the warden walk past his lamp for arrears.hardA threat or curse on any kept street (one with a lamp-warden’s round): may he freeze in the darkMay your Echo stay in the house.May your dead self linger after the layer-out is gone.graveA curse among the poor; not said in a death-house, and not said twiceBlank.No craft at all.firmCraftsmen of the untrained; also a snob’s word for most peopleBloody bastard.What it says.firmAny Concord mouth; the educated say “sine sigillo” instead and think it cleaner
The Elves
The elves swear in the common tongue and in Vey-Elarin words dropped into it. The five branches share the tongue and differ on what the worst thing is.

















































































































SwearLiteral meaningStrengthWho says itOut of season.Done outside its appointed window.graveThe worst Eressean insult; worse than “badly done”Lo.Out of season, as one word.mild as an exclamation, hard said to a person”Lo,” at a missed moment is the elven “damn it”; Drow use it for a debt past its term-ama on a name.The name held, and nobody stood for it.hardPut on a name to its owner’s face; Eresse and Korvaeth bothMa-ama.Held, and nobody stood for it.hardSaid of a usurper, a stolen thing, a child nobody witnessed; from the proverb “Ma-ama, lyth”A bare clause.A thing said that claims nothing.firmSaid of a speaker who will not own his words; courts and councilsHeld contingently.Holding what nobody has stood for.firmA cold insult to an office-holderFlat-tongued.Speaks without the pitch contours.firmSaid of Concord speakers, who have greeted nobodyLoud.Using the singing mechanism for speech.firmMeans drunk or blasphemous depending on the room-ak.Outside the form: foreign.hardTagged onto a name; the suffix that made “Varrisak”Be a silence in the chord.May your name fall vacant.graveA curse of erasure; Eressean elders, never in a riteSung in the wrong key.A rite in the wrong key has not been performed.firmSaid of botched work or a botched apology; it did not happenUnasked.Taken without the Asking over wood, water, game or stone.hardSaid of a thief of the land, a poacher, a road-builder; any branch, Varrisak mostTranscript.One who mistakes a filing system for a memory.firmVarrisak of Eresseans, and of any clerkSeral take it.Let the winter have it.mildThe Eladrin “damn it”; the northern courtsPast nine.A silence held past the nine-count.graveEladrin; not a word at all but a silence counted past refusal into judgment; to say “past nine” of a man means he is judgedUnpaid.Worse than absent: a position, not a fact.hardDrow of Korvaeth; also “out of term” for a debt gone past its dayBy the Realmsong.On the song Florwyn sang the kin into being with.firm (solemn)Elven oath-exclamation outside a court, where “Uren” (witnessed) is the formal one
The Zettari
The Zettari swear in their own tongue. Their oaths need something older than the speaker to hear them (the Stone Witness Oath), their pride is weight and bearing, and their shame is lightness, broken cords and unmarked skin.

























































































SwearLiteral meaningStrengthWho says itJiwe limesikia.The stone has heard.firm (solemn)Closes a vow as binding; any Zettari, and a Zettari who says it has swornKwa damu ya mababu.By the blood of the ancestors.firm (solemn)The formal oath of the royal line and the Pillar housesMababu wanaona.The ancestors are watching.mildA warning to a child or a peer about to disgrace the line; also a muttered “damn it” when something goes wrong in front of eldersMzigo wa damu.The weight of the blood.mildAn exclamation of burden, “the weight of it”; the young of high blood, tiredHold shape.What the Zettari presence tells the world.mildAn oath-exclamation in the common tongue, “steady”; soldiers, forge workersRadi ikupige.May thunder strike you.hardSouthern and Cape speech, where the Storm Drums are; a curse between equalsMwepesi.Light one: a person with no weight.hardThe core Zettari insult; weightlessness is the shame of a people whose body is the first throneKamba iliyokatika.A cord that snapped.graveSaid of a vow-breaker or one who shamed the line; the Cord of Becoming brokenBila shahidi.Without a witness.hardA liar: a vow nobody older than the speaker heardMchanga mtupu.Bare sand.firmA worthless promise: Agano sand with no claim spoken over the quench; forge peopleMjinga.Fool.firmThe ordinary insult, any rankClean skin.No ink: no thresholds survived.firmSaid of the untested young or a soft outsiderKneeler.One who kneels to pressure.hardSaid of a man who gives way under Crown-Blood Pressure, or who takes orders from anyone heavier
Across the Realms
Some words belong to no one people. They come from the faiths, from the Gate, from Stage and Path, from the halls, the round and the dead, and any mouth in the four quarters may use them in its own accent. Pathless and undeclared are one fact in two mouths: an Inquisitor means a soul that walks under no Archon, a practitioner means a Crystal that never named its Path, and the Inquisition holds that the two are the same failing.
The Faiths
The Holy Inquisition
The Ordo files in Latin and speaks in its Tenets. Its insults are classifications: a word from a mask is an entry, and an entry is the first step of a correction (Tenet III: the correction follows “in the same breath, by the same hand”).



























































SwearLiteral meaningStrengthWho says itPathless.One who walks under no Archon.grave from a mask, hard from anyone elseThe Inquisition’s word for anyone who follows no Archon. It cuts twice: an instrument that reads a Crystal with no Path declared also says “no Path,” and the Inquisition holds the two are one failing, so every unwoken porter is pathless twice over. Ranked practitioners hear the second sense first and take it worseAvius. (pl. avii)Latin: pathless, off the road, straying.graveThe filing form of “pathless,” stamped on an Inquisition entry; a settlement that sees the word on a writ knows what comes nextThe patient.Rot that waits.graveInquisitors of the unrepentant, from Tenet II (“Ignorance Is Corruption Made Patient”); it carries the surgeon’s other meaning on purpose, the body on the tableKindling.What burns was never meant to stand.graveA person or a settlement marked for the fire (Tenet V). Commoners turned it round: “a mask’s kindling” is anyone who will be nextFomes.Latin: tinder, kindling.graveThe filing form of “kindling,” on the entry for a placeSecond desk.Where the authorization was still sitting when the settlement died.hardInquisitors of Sancta Lux men, and of any official who hides behind procedureLadder-man.One who files and waits.hardInquisition contempt for the Ladder of Standing and everyone on itUnmasked.Not yet chosen the mask over the pyre.hardSaid by Inquisitors of a survivor still deciding; also, inside the Ordo, of a member who is weakening
Sancta Lux
The order does not worship, and it says so in its catechism’s first line. Its insults are about measurement done wrong, and its worst word for a man is that he was never read at all.





















































SwearLiteral meaningStrengthWho says itUnweighed.Never brought to the Scale.hardOf a man, an act or a claim nobody has examined; the Arbitration Division uses it of the order’s own founding story, in privateAdorer.One who kneels to a measure.firm from a Lector, hard from a MeasurewrightOf shrine-worshippers who pray to Urion, and of the Inquisition, which the order holds has turned a reference into an idolApostate.One who left the order and kept its name.graveSancta Lux of the Inquisition, formally and alwaysUnscoped.A sentence that names no limit.hardMeasurewrights of Inquisitors, and of any officer who enforces past his warrantFalse positive.A reading that convicted the wrong man.firmAttestants and Measurewrights to each other: you were a mistake, entered and postedOff the reference.Out of true.mildEveryday in the order and around it; a crooked plan, a bent wall, a bad argumentThe Judger’s number on you.May your reading come back, and may you have to accept it.hardThe street’s curse, never the order’s; the order strikes “the Judger” from every filing and every Attestant says it anyway
The Archons in the street
Shrine cultures and the Concord street curse by the Archon whose work fits the offense. A Moto hears every one of these as Singling, the principal heresy, and a Moto in a mixed room will take note of who says them.

































































SwearLiteral meaningStrengthWho says itAuren’s quiet on you.May Death silence you.hardA curse between equals; never said in a sickroomMaelor forget you.May Memory itself let your name go.graveThe worst of the street curses: not death but being unrememberedIrath’s dog.A man who obeys any voice that commands.hardOf a toady, a turncoat soldier, a clerk who licks upwardVeyra-led.Led by what he wants, usually his prick.firmOf a fool in love or in lust; wives, sergeants, sistersKaetra’s child.One whose word is a veil.firmOf a liar or a dreamer; said fondly of a child who tells stories, unkindly of a man who sells themWyther-footed.Cannot stay put.mildOf a drifter, a deserter, a husband who wandersValen’s late.Even Time is waiting on him.mildA joke at the slow and the tardyA flat note.The one out of tune with Selhar’s accord.firmOf a troublemaker in a crew, a choir, a councilUurgath-get.A thing that should be unmade.hardOf a monster, a cruel man, a child one is very tired of
The Gate
Nearly everyone carries a Crystal, about one in ten wakes it, and very few of those climb far. The line between porter and practitioner was drawn by somebody, and both sides of it swear about it.













































































SwearLiteral meaningStrengthWho says itNought.Unwoken: a Crystal never woken.hard to a faceAcademy and hall slang for the unwoken; “noughts” for the commons at largeSleeper.A Crystal nobody attended to.firmThe politer form; a ranked man’s word for a porter, said without looking at himBirth-gate.Came through on his father’s fee.hardAbility-gate practitioners of the house-bred; a stirring child from a poor quarter says it for lifeCapped.Crystal-sealed, as a snuffer (the officer who puts out an unpaid lamp) caps a lamp.graveOf a sealed practitioner; said of an unsealed one it means powerless, and a man will fight over itOff-roll.Unregistered.hardOf an Unregistered Natural, a criminal practitioner, and by extension anyone whose papers will not bear looking atBack-room.Taught in a back room for a fee.firmOf a black-market practitioner; licensed men to unlicensedCopied.Learned off a copied Primer.firmOf a fraud, or of a man whose skill is somebody else’sKind-read.Paid a kind reader to be told he was more.firmOf a pretender to rank or powerStill in his seven years.An apprentice under indenture.mildOf anyone green; masters, hall sergeantsGone to vinegar.Joined the Mother.graveA charge, not a joke; said of someone who has disappeared from the roll, and the room goes quietInoculated.A recruit of the Mother.graveThe same charge, in the cult’s own word; Night Watch men use it flatly
Stage and Path
Practitioners talk exact numbers, so they insult in them. Commons round, and mostly do not use these.





















































SwearLiteral meaningStrengthWho says itUndeclared.Climbed without a Path.firmOf a dilettante, a man who never committed to anything; the practitioner’s form of “pathless,” without the theologyMason.Body Path: works like a forty-year mason.firmSpirit and Fate men of a Body Path brawlerMidwife.Fate Path: works like a forty-year midwife.firmBody Path men of a Fate practitioner, meaning soft; midwives would disagreeGraded hollow.Below F in the thing that matters.firm”Graded hollow in Gnosis” is “stupid” among the rankedAn F.Lowest lettered Grade.mildAny ranked speaker, of any weak showingDropped.Fell to Pressure in front of people.hardOf a man who went to his knees at a Stage gap of three or more; said of a practitioner it is a humiliation that follows himSweats at a Flourishing.Two Stages under the man he is facing.firmA sneer at someone who talks above his Stage
The Halls and the Wells









































SwearLiteral meaningStrengthWho says itPosted.Named on a hall’s board.hardOf a man the halls want; “he’s posted” ends a hiringOff-board.Takes postings without a license.hard from a licensed hunterOf the cheap unlicensed hunters every district hires anywayWell-bait.Good for drawing something out, and for nothing after.firmHunters of the uselessWell-get.Something that came out of a Well.graveOf a person, it says he is not oneCommissioned.There is an Extermination posting with your name on it.graveA threat more than an insult; hunters, Sealwrights, the halls’ own enforcers
The Round
Lamps, warm stones and warded doors come from hired people on their rounds, past the last round the commons burn oil, and the whole arrangement is a fine thing to swear about. The Accord’s “pass his door” belongs with these.

races--and--peoples/the-tongues-of-the-r.filePath: Races & Peoples/The Tongues of the Realms/Naming and Usage/The Celestial Host — Naming.md
races--and--peoples/the-tongues-of-the-r.title: The Celestial Host — Naming
races--and--peoples/the-tongues-of-the-r.content:
The bell-founders of Tollerby still tell this one to apprentices, and I record it as told. Alditha Hobday, casting the great tenor for the Salters, had a Celestial’s whole three names off a drunk pilgrim and raised them on the bell’s shoulder in letters a hand tall, for the glory and the extra fee. On the night of the pouring, with the bronze running orange and half the town up on the walls to watch, a tall figure came and stood in the foundry door with no wings and no light about it whatever, walked through the sparks, took a chisel to the mold, removed one suffix, and left. The minstrels had given it wings by the next fair. The bell has hung in Tollerby ever since, and the Measurewrights who have climbed up to look at the lettering disagree about the chisel work.
The Host’s names are built in three slots (a function-name, a rank-suffix, and a Lawbell-name) on a Hebrew-theophoric shape (element + a divine-register suffix) built from original elements, and they obey the Host’s idiom rule: measure, position and law; never light, never fire, never wings. The names Faisal, Verantha, Kaethren Vareth, Dazgrim and Urstia are read back through the register rather than replaced.
Everything not marked attested is coined.
The three slots

Function-name: what the Celestial was Sung to do. The personal identifier; it
never changes. Two elements: a function root and a measure root.
Rank-suffix: where it sits in its Choir. Changes with every promotion; a
Celestial that loses it has been stripped.
Lawbell-name: the Archonic principle it is an instrument of. Permanent; losing
it is the Severance. It is the Archon’s own name, unmodified, carried as a third

name: the fourteen are attested and need no coining: Urion, Uurgath, Thalen,
Valen, Maelor, Zhaeren, Irath, Veyra, Iesara, Kaetra, Wyther, Auren, Selhar,
Elyndra.
On the page: Function-name-Rank Lawbell — Verantha-eth Maelor, “Verantha,
senior, of Memory”. Among mortals only the function-name is heard; in the Host’s
own registers all three are written, and a register entry with the third name
struck is the document of a Severance.
Function roots (what the absence needed)
Coined on the Host’s own vocabulary: the Vow, the Verdict, the Boundary, the Seal,
the Record, the Tally, the Toll.

Ver (the verdict spoken: attested, Verantha, Vareth), Tal (the tally kept), Oth (the oath witnessed), Dahl (the boundary walked), Sarn (the seal set), Ruth (the record entered), Kaeth (the gavel, the strike: attested, Kaethren), Daz (the exile escorted: attested, Dazgrim, gloss coined), Urs (the bell’s own toll: attested, Urstia, gloss coined), Fai (the kneeling, the servitude: attested, Faisal, gloss coined)

Measure roots (how the function is measured)

-an (the count), -eth (the weight), -ren (the distance: attested, Kaethren), -ia (the standing: attested, Urstia), -sal (the position held: attested, Faisal), -grim (the order of precedence: attested, Dazgrim), -antha (the unbroken line of a ledger: attested, Verantha)
A function-name is function root + measure root: Ver-antha (the verdict as an

unbroken line), Kaeth-ren (the strike measured by distance), Tal-an (the tally
as a count), Oth-eth (the oath weighed), Sarn-ia (the seal as a standing).
Rank-suffixes, by Choir tier
The Choirs are attested (Midreach Oath-Keepers, Highspire Verdict-Bearers, Lowmere
Sealkeepers, Bellwrought Witness-Choir); the suffixes are coined.

-ith: newly Sung; carries function and nothing else
-eth: a standing officer of the Choir
-vareth: a senior officer (attested as Kaethren’s second name; read here as the rank he holds, the Last Gavel)
Grand Angel: a title and no suffix. The handful who complete the accretion into selfhood drop the rank-suffix and carry the title in front (attested: “Grand Angel Faisal, the Bound Flame”). Their by-names (“the Bound Flame”, “the Last Gavel”) are mortal coinages and break the idiom rule on purpose — mortals name what they see.

The working names, read back



































Working nameRead asNotesFaisalFai + sal: the kneeling as a position heldGrand Angel, Midreach; no suffix; Lawbell-name unrecordedVeranthaVer + antha: the verdict as an unbroken ledger line”of the Unbroken Tally” is the mortal gloss of the same name; Midreach; suffix and Lawbell-name unrecordedKaethren VarethKaeth + ren, rank -varethHighspire, the most senior surviving officer; Lawbell-name unrecordedDazgrimDaz + grim: exile ordered by precedenceLowmere by function; suffix unrecordedUrstiaUrs + ia: the toll as a standingBellwrought by function; suffix unrecorded
All five are kept as they stand. None is renamed.
Outside the register

The mortal by-names (“the Bound Flame” and its like) lie outside the register, as the Host’s idiom rule implies they should.

races--and--peoples/the-tongues-of-the-r.filePath: Races & Peoples/The Tongues of the Realms/The Grammars/Accord Latin — The Formulary and the Two Spoken Registers.md
races--and--peoples/the-tongues-of-the-r.title: Accord Latin — The Formulary and the Two Spoken Registers
races--and--peoples/the-tongues-of-the-r.content:
A formula set and a register guide. The Tongues of the Realms governs.

Nemo in lingua sua mensuratur.
No one is measured in his own tongue.
Cut above the door of the Accord’s chancery at Sealhall

Anyone on Marrow Lane in Sealhall will show you the doorstep for a copper. Noll Quillet, a hedge-speaker (one who speaks workings for hire, with no guild and no schooling), was paid to stop a chandler’s fire at the threshold, and he had the words from his aunt and the endings from nobody. Ignis. Intra limine. Consiste. came out of him with the wrong case and a clipped vowel, and the fire stopped and sat down. It stayed nine days in the doorway, knee high, the color of a kingfisher’s back, burning nothing and warming everybody, with children toasting bread on it and the chandler unable to reach his own front door. On the tenth morning it left by way of the roof, and took the roof. The chandler went to law. The chancery sat in full black silk and found for nobody, on the settled ground that an ungrammatical invocation was never an invocation, that nothing had therefore occurred, and that the roof had been lost to no cause. His heirs bring the suit again every seven years. I have read all the filings, and I have also held my hands over that doorstep, which is still warm.
The language that ruling was written in is the strangest instrument on these shelves, and I say so fondly.
I. What Accord Latin Is
It descends from nothing. It was assembled, deliberately, by committee, as a neutral instrument for contracts between parties who could not read each other and would not agree to be measured in a rival’s language. It is nobody’s mother tongue, nobody dreams in it, and no child has ever been raised speaking it.
That is the point, and it is the Accord’s actual foundation. Every polity in the four quarters has agreed to be bound in a language that gives none of them an advantage, and that agreement is more load-bearing than any treaty it has ever recorded. A gate-toll in Kharven, a proof-mark on a Marrowkin barrel, a marriage settlement in Eresse and a Mandate decree’s external copy are all written in the same fixed formulae, and none of the four peoples involved likes it.
Because it was assembled rather than grown, it does not need a grammar in this archive. Its grammar is fixed, copied out under seal, and taught the same way in every chancery school in the four quarters. What it needs, and what follows, is the formula set: the fixed wordings that do legal and Aetheric work, the registers those wordings sit in, and what happens when one of them is spoken wrong.
II. Attestation
The chancery at Sealhall holds the master formulary, revised four times in six hundred years, each revision itself recorded in the formulary it revised. What is in the formulary is valid. What is not in the formulary can be argued and usually loses.
The gate registers across every chartered crossing carry the same six wordings, hundreds of thousands of times, in every hand from a master clerk’s to a bored corporal’s. This is the best attestation of how the language is actually pronounced, because gate-clerks say the formula aloud and the misspellings record what they heard.
The choirs’ office books. The sung register is preserved by the orders rather than the Accord, and the office books are older than the chancery. This is a jurisdictional fact before it is a philological one, and it is the reason Chantcraft has never been an Accord examination category.
III. Pronunciation
One pronunciation, fixed by the chancery and taught identically everywhere, because a contract that sounds different in two rooms is two contracts.
Vowel quantity is phonemic and is taught as such. Long vowels are held to roughly twice the duration of short ones. In the chancery register this is pedantry. In the sung register it is the entire mechanism, and Section VII is where that matters.
c and g are hard in every position. v is a consonantal w in the liturgical register and a labiodental v in the chancery, and the two schools have been sniping at each other about it for four hundred years without either side ever losing a case over it.
Regional accent is tolerated and regional quantity is not. A Marrowkin clerk reading a formula with Barkstone consonants is reading it correctly. A Concord clerk who shortens a long vowel has, in the sung register, said a different word, and in the chancery register has simply revealed where he trained.
IV. The Registers, and the Doublet
The old chancery register spoke of the trades as crafts and sorted them under five words. The words name no real kinds. What they cover are skills and trades, Drafts, runes, chants and workings, taught and priced today like any other trade, and the five words are only what the old register called them, and the words stuck. Every one carries an Accord name in liturgical Latin and a plain name in the common tongue. Which column a character reaches for places them by class before they have finished the sentence.















































The old register’s wordAccord registerCommon tongueThe practitionerContemptMagicraftArs Operisthe work, workinga workerSpellcraftArs Vocisthe speaking, sayinga speaker, a castera mouthRunecraftArs Scriptithe writing, the cuttingan Engraver, a Runesmitha cutterDraftcraftArs Vasisthe pouring, vessel-worka Draftera potboyChantcraftArs Cantusthe singinga Chanter, a Chorister
An Accord examiner says Ars Scripti. The woman who paid him to cut a ward into her doorframe says the cutting. A Kharven soldier says he wants a man who can do the writing, and everyone in the room knows exactly what he means and exactly what he could not afford.
The doublet governs every craft term, not only the five. Where a Latin word and a common one both exist, the choice is characterization.
Four registers of the language itself.
Chancery. Contracts, tolls, registrations, judgments. Fixed formulae, no invention permitted, and a clause not in the formulary is a clause an advocate will attack.
Liturgical. Consecration and rite. Older, more archaic, and the register the orders guard.
Vox, the invocation register. Spoken workings. Section VI.
Cantus, the sung register. Section VII.
V. The Formula Set
These are the fixed wordings. They are not translated in use, they are not paraphrased, and a clerk who improves one has voided it.




























































FormulaSenseWhere it appearsActum et signatum sub sigillo Concordiae.Done and sealed under the seal of the Accord.The closing of any instrumentCoram testibus.Before witnesses.Any clause requiring attestationQuod dictum est, dictum stat.What has been said stands said.Binding clause; the Accord’s oldest formulaIta spondeo.Thus I pledge.The speaker’s own oath, first person, and the only place the chancery permits itProbatum est.It has been tested and it holds.Proof-marks on metal, glass, harness, casksSolutum et transitum.Paid and passed.Gate registersIn registro relatum.Entered in the register.Registration of a working, a Draft, a birth, a deathSalvo iure tertii.Saving the right of a third party.The escape clause, and the most litigated six syllables in the four quartersNullum et irritum.Null and void.AnnulmentSub pignore.Under pledge, held as security.Debt, hostage, and pawn alike, which is not an accident
A note on Salvo iure tertii. It is in every instrument the chancery issues, it costs nothing to include, and it is the reason no Accord contract has ever been fully enforceable against a party who was not at the table. Every polity knows this. Every polity insists on it. Nobody has proposed striking it, because each of them expects to be the third party one day.
VI. Ars Vocis, the Invocation Register
A spoken working is three parts, in fixed order, and the order is not stylistic.
Nomen. What is addressed, named in the vocative or accusative. Never a Wellspring, never a kind, never a Principle. The thing in the room.
Mensura. The bound. A prepositional phrase setting the limit inside which the order applies.
Iussum. The order itself, in the second person imperative or the third person jussive subjunctive.

Pondus. Per axem. Descende.
Weight. Along the axis. Come down.
Ignis. Intra limen. Consiste.
Fire. Within the threshold. Halt.

There is no first person in the invocation register. The grammar has no slot for the speaker. Ita spondeo is chancery and belongs to an oath; in Vox it does not exist and cannot be constructed. A speaker cannot put themselves into a working.
The consequence is legal rather than metaphysical, and it is enormous. A spoken working has no author in its own grammar. A ward that was cut carries the cutter’s hand. A Draft that was poured carries a maker’s mark and a registration. A working that was spoken carries nothing at all, and the Bench of Attribution has spent four hundred years devising ways to place a mouth at a scene that the language itself declines to place there.
This is the real reason the guilds hold Spellcraft in contempt and the real reason they are afraid of it. A speaker needs no substrate, no vessel, no workshop, no seven years and no guild, and when he is finished there is nothing to point at.
VII. Ars Cantus, the Sung Register
Pitched, not asserted. Quantitative, not stressed. The chant runs in metrical feet built from vowel length, and the length is the mechanism. A short vowel held long or a long vowel clipped makes a different line, whatever accent excused it, and the chant stops.
It scales with throats, and it cannot be practiced alone. Anything above trivial requires more than one voice, and the requirement is not ceremonial. The sustained vowel has to be carried continuously while the line advances, which one set of lungs cannot do, so the voices overlap and hand the vowel between them. Three is the working minimum. Serious work runs to nine and to more.

Teneat murus. Teneat. Teneat.
Let the wall hold. Let it hold. Let it hold.

The jussive is the register’s normal mood, and the repetition is structural rather than rhetorical: the line is passed between voices and each restatement is a fresh throat taking the vowel.
That single constraint makes Chantcraft institutional by necessity. Orders, choirs, liturgies, a schedule, a roster, a novice-master, and the particular catastrophe of a choir that loses three singers to fever in a week and cannot hold a wall it has held for two hundred years. No other trade can be broken by an illness.
Chantcraft is not an Accord examination category and never has been, which is why the old register’s crafts are conventionally counted as four. The orders examine their own, in their own office books, in a register older than the chancery, and the Accord has never pressed the point because it has never wanted to be told no in public.
VIII. What a Mistake Does
In the chancery register, an error is a defect of the instrument. A misquoted formula does not misfire. It fails to bind, and the failure is discovered later, in a room with an advocate in it.
In Vox, a solecism does nothing at all. The Accord’s stated position is that an ungrammatical invocation was never an invocation, so nothing happened and nothing could have. This is taught in every chancery school as settled.
Hedge-speakers dispute it. They report, consistently, across four quarters and six centuries, that badly formed workings sometimes land, and that when they land they land differently. The Accord has never investigated. The reason the Accord gives is that there is nothing to investigate. The reason offered by everyone who has ever asked a hedge-speaker is that an investigation would have to begin by admitting the question is open.
In Cantus, a false quantity breaks the chant, and breaking a chant that is holding something is the specific disaster the orders are organized around. There is no partial failure in the sung register. The line either scans or it stops.
IX. Script
The chancery hand. Upright, separated letters, no ligatures, no abbreviation except a closed list of eleven, and every one of the eleven is in the formulary. Legibility is the whole design brief, since a document must be readable by a Marrowkin clerk, an Eressean jurist and a Mandate garrison officer with equal ease.
Accord Latin is not written in any of the Fourteen Hands and this is deliberate. The Hands write boundaries onto laws. Latin writes agreements between people. The chancery has resisted every proposal to render the formulary in a Parunic hand, on the stated ground that an instrument which does Aetheric work of its own has stopped being a contract and become a working, and the parties would then be signing something none of them can read.
Seals do the authenticating, not the script. Wax over ribbon, the Accord’s own device countersunk, and a proof-mark struck rather than written.
X. Lexicon of the Accord
Ars, a craft, the old register’s word for a trade. Opus, a work. Vox, the voice, and the invocation register. Scriptum, the written thing. Vas, the vessel. Cantus, the sung line.
Concordia, the Accord itself. Sigillum, the seal. Registrum, the register. Formularium, the master formulary. Cancellaria, the chancery.
Testis, a witness. Pignus, a pledge. Ius, a right. Tertius, the third party. Iussum, an order. Mensura, a bound. Nomen, a name.
Limen, a threshold. Axis, an axis. Pondus, weight. Murus, a wall. Ignis, fire.
XI. Sample Texts
The closing of a standard instrument.

Actum et signatum sub sigillo Concordiae, coram testibus, salvo iure tertii. Quod dictum est, dictum stat.
Done and sealed under the seal of the Accord, before witnesses, saving the right of a third party. What has been said stands said.

A gate register line, written a hundred times a day and spoken as it is written.

Solutum et transitum. In registro relatum.
Paid and passed. Entered.

A proof-mark, struck rather than written.

PROB EST
It was tested and it held.

A spoken working, complete.

Aqua. Intra vas. Mane.
Water. Within the vessel. Remain.

Three words and nobody in the grammar to blame for them.
A choir's holding line, from an office book older than the chancery.

Teneat murus. Teneat porta. Teneat qui tenet.
Let the wall hold. Let the gate hold. Let the one who holds, hold.

The third clause is the one novices are made to sit with. The orders do not gloss it and have never agreed on whether it means the chorister, the wall, or something the wall is standing on.
XII. Speaking It Badly
Concord speakers have the easiest time of it and the worst habits, because the chancery register is close enough to their own legal vocabulary that they improvise, and improvisation voids instruments. A Concord clerk who paraphrases a formula has produced a document that reads perfectly and binds nothing.
Goblinoid speakers cannot produce a vowel-initial word without effort and cannot hear quantity at all, since Vaross marks weight by holding rather than by phonemic length. Mandate clerks are trained on the chancery register exclusively and are excellent at it. Mandate choristers effectively do not exist.
Marrowkin speakers are the best in the four quarters at Cantus and the reason is mechanical: quantity is phonemic in the Tally-Tongue and Mathematical Cadence trains the ear on meter from childhood. A Marrowkin chorister hears a false quantity before the syllable has finished. Marrowkin clerks in the chancery register voice nothing and are read as blunt.
Eressean speakers handle the meter easily and the invocation register with visible distaste, because Vox has no first person and no witness slot, and an Eressean is being asked to speak a sentence that names nobody and stands for nothing. Most simply decline to use it, which the Accord records as a preference and which is, in Eressean terms, closer to a refusal.
Notes on the Count
Chantcraft counts as a fifth word in the old register. Ars Cantus stands. The alternative was folding it into Spellcraft with tone as a delivery vector, and that loses the institutional reading, which is the most valuable thing in it: a trade that scales with throats cannot be practiced alone, and a trade that cannot be practiced alone must have orders, rosters and a novice-master, and can be destroyed by a fever. Nothing else in the system produces that.
The count stays four in the Accord’s own mouth, and the reason is jurisdictional rather than arithmetical. Chantcraft has never been an Accord examination category, because the orders examine their own in office books older than the chancery, and the Accord has never pressed a claim it expected to lose in public. The document called The Working Trades is therefore correctly named from the Accord’s side and undercounts from everyone else’s, which is exactly the kind of thing the Accord does.
The doublet takes the wider scope. It governs every craft term, not the five names alone.
Latin is both a written and a spoken register. Vox and Cantus are spoken registers with their own grammar and their own failure modes, and the chancery register remains document-only within its own domain.

races--and--peoples/the-tongues-of-the-r.filePath: Races & Peoples/The Tongues of the Realms/The Grammars/Common — The Tongue With No Distinctions/Accent — Placement, Prestige and the Shibboleth.md
races--and--peoples/the-tongues-of-the-r.title: Accent — Placement, Prestige and the Shibboleth
races--and--peoples/the-tongues-of-the-r.content:
A menu, not a law. Sits beside the Speaking It Badly sections in the four grammars rather than replacing them.

A man is placed by the third sentence. Everything after that is him deciding whether to fight it.

For fourteen years Alard Sefton was the most Northern man in the Cold Ford garrison. He stressed his first syllables, he said tally and cask, he drank ollet he hated, and he had told the story of his Northern grandmother so often that he cried at it. Then at the Midwinter Fair, with the whole company around a chestnut-seller’s brazier and the square red and green and drunk on spiced ale, a hot chestnut went down the back of his neck, and he announced in a clipped Western voice, with the main verb held to the very end of the sentence, that an accounting would be required. The quiet spread about three paces. His sergeant, who had shared a wall with him for a decade, asked him very kindly to say that again, and somebody else asked about the pay chest, which turned out to be the right question.
Nobody ever wrote down how he sounded, and that is the first thing to know about writing accent.
The Rule That Governs Everything Below
Accents go down in full phonetic spelling, each speaker as heavy as the ear finds them. The levers below carry a speaker either way.
Eye-dialect, rendering a speaker’s vowels phonetically on the page, is barred outright. It slows the reader, it makes the speaker look stupid, and it is never applied evenly, because nobody ever spells the duke. A page that writes ‘appen for a Northern soldier and prints the Palatine’s vowels in standard orthography has made an argument the author did not intend to make and cannot take back.
Accent here is carried by word choice, syntax, function words, silence, and what a speaker calls things. All five are invisible as spelling and audible in dialogue.
The four grammars already do this for foreign speakers, and they do it by deriving the accent from the first language: a goblinoid drops articles because Vaross has none, a Marrowkin will not state an intention without swearing because there is no verb form for it, an Eressean names his witnesses because his own tongue will not let him possess anything silently. That method stands. This page extends it to the harder case, which is Concord humans speaking Common to each other.
I. The Asymmetry
The fact that makes accent worth writing in this world at all.
Foreigners are exempt. Natives are on trial.
Common has no chancery, no guild and no order with jurisdiction over it, so there is no prestige standard a foreigner is expected to reach. A Marrowkin with forty years of blunt, article-dropping Common is understood, served and cheated in it as fluently as anyone, and nobody corrects him, because nobody has the standing to.
But a Concord man is placed instantly, by everyone, in a sentence or two, and it costs him. His own people own the standard and enforce it on each other constantly and informally, with a look. The outsider’s accent is a fact about where he is from. The insider’s accent is a verdict on what he is worth.
This inverts the usual fantasy handling, where the foreign accent is the marked one and the human cast all speak neutrally. Here the human cast is the marked group.
II. The Six Levers
One. Which stratum the abstractions come from. Nearly every abstract noun in Common is Latin. A speaker reaching for a general idea either uses the Latin word or works around it. He violated the terms against he broke his word. The workaround is not a failure; a man who habitually works around Latin abstractions is telling you he learned the idea before he learned the word for it.
Two. Where the main verb lands. High Common holds its main verb late, borrowed wholesale from chancery syntax. The vernacular core never does. A long sentence that arrives at its verb in the last clause is a schooled sentence, whoever is speaking it.
Three. Function words and fillers. The cheapest and most reliable lever. What a speaker says while thinking. What he says instead of yes. Whether he opens with a concession. Two or three fixed habits per character, used consistently, place a man more firmly than any amount of spelling.
Four. What he calls the crafts. The doublet in action. Ars Scripti is an examiner. The inscription is a guild clerk. The writing is a customer. The cutting is a man who has watched it done. A mouth is contempt for a speaker, and it is a word a certain kind of person uses in front of the wrong company exactly once.
Five. The loan strata he reaches for. At seth or on time. Cadre or the lads. Tally or the book. Eressean loans are court and calendar and mark the East and the educated. Vaross loans are garrison and mark a man who has served or lived beside those who did. Marrowkin loans are trade and drink and mark the North.
Six. How he handles a silence. An easterner who goes quiet has said something, because the lith is a real practice there. A westerner reads the same silence as having run out of words and fills it. This lever costs no dialogue at all and is the one most often left on the table.
III. Style-Shifting: The Accent Thickens When He Stops Watching
The single most useful finding to steal, and it is the oldest one in the field. Labov’s 1966 New York department-store study found that a speaker’s use of prestige forms rises with attention to his own speech, so the same man produces one accent in careful speech and another when he is not monitoring.
The use here is direct, and it tells you who a speaker is more than it tells you any linguistics.
A man’s origin surfaces when he stops attending to himself: when he is tired, angry, frightened, drunk, wounded, or talking to someone he has decided does not matter. So the accent moves with the load, and it reads like a tell. A character whose vowels have been Western for four scenes and whose function words go Northern in a crisis has been shown to be under load without a line of narration saying so.
This is also the honest way to write a character who has climbed. He still has his accent and he is holding it down, and the holding takes effort, and the effort is visible in the moments it fails.
IV. Hypercorrection: The Man Who Overshoots
Labov’s other finding, and the crueler one. Hypercorrection is strongest in the group just below the one it is imitating, because that group is most conscious of which forms are prestigious and overshoots them in careful speech.
In Common this lands on the Latin overlay, and the failure mode is exact: a speaker who has learned that Latin words are the educated ones uses more of them than an educated speaker would, in places an educated speaker would not, and stresses them chancery-fashion when he heard them at a gate.

The clerk. I have inquired as to the remittance and can attest the pledge was retained.
The jurist he is trying to sound like. I asked. It’s paid.

The man with real standing reaches for the plain word without anxiety, because he has nothing to prove. The man one rung below cannot afford to. The Latinate register is a ladder that is most visible on the people still climbing it, and everyone above them can hear exactly where they are.
This is the best available way to write an ambitious minor functionary and it never needs to be commented on in narration.
V. Covert Prestige: Keeping the Accent on Purpose
The counterweight, from Trudgill’s Norwich work. Non-standard forms carry their own prestige inside the community that uses them, valued for solidarity rather than status, and speakers maintain them deliberately.
So not every character is climbing. A Northern officer who has spent fifteen years among Western captains and kept his stress is making a claim: that he is still one of the men he came up with, and that the room can take him as he is or find another officer. Covert prestige is what makes a sergeant trusted by a company and disliked by a marshal.
The Spellcraft version is the sharpest one available. The guilds call a speaker a mouth. Speakers use the word about themselves, in each other’s company, with pride. A craft with no guild, no seven years and no master has nothing to defend but the fact that anyone can do it, and the contempt term is the flag.
The honest caveat, and it belongs on the page rather than in a footnote. Some critics hold that covert prestige romanticizes constraint, that speakers keep vernacular forms because they were never given access to the standard rather than because they value them. Both are true of different people, and the difference is exactly the sort of thing a scene can be about. The man who kept his accent and the man who never got the chance to lose it sound identical from outside, and one of them knows it and the other does not.
VI. Accommodation: Accent as an Act Performed at Somebody
Giles’s framework, and the one with the most immediate scene use, because every item in it is a thing one character does to another.
Convergence. Moving toward the other speaker. Softening the stress, borrowing his slang, matching his pace. Usually warmth.
Divergence. Moving away deliberately. Thickening what he had been holding, refusing the other man’s vocabulary. A weapon, and a quiet one.
Upward and downward. Convergence up the scale is a man asking a lord for a place. Convergence down is an officer dropping into the vernacular with his men. Divergence up is speaking faster and more finely at somebody who cannot follow. Divergence down is a nobleman reaching for the docks in front of his peers to make a point about who he is willing to be.
Over-accommodation is an insult and does not know it is one. A speaker converging too hard reads as patronizing, and this is the single most useful item on the list. The Western officer who arrives in a Northern hold and starts saying tally and cask in his own accent has not built rapport. He has performed a Northerner at Northerners, and the room has marked it, and nobody will tell him.
Converging with divergent intent. The subtlest one. A speaker can move toward the other’s forms precisely to keep him in his place. In Catalonia a norm held that Catalan was spoken between Catalans, so Castilian speakers attempting it were answered in Castilian. The surface act was accommodation; the meaning was exclusion. A Kharven table that answers a Concord officer’s careful Kharven greeting in flawless Common has just told him something. He will not work out what for three days.
VII. The Shibboleth
Accent as an instrument of identification, and history is unambiguous that it is a lethal one.
The pattern recurs across centuries. In 1282 the Sicilians reportedly asked suspected Frenchmen to say cìciri, chickpeas, and killed those who could not. In 1302 the Flemish at Bruges are said to have used schild en vriend, and every man who failed was stabbed where he stood, in his nightshirt. Kraków ran the same procedure in 1312 against German-speaking burghers with a phrase about lentils and a mill. Each time the test is a mundane word, each time it is chosen because the target’s own phonology cannot produce it, and each time the point is that the test cannot be studied for.
What makes this usable rather than decorative is that the word is always ordinary. Nobody would take it for a password or a challenge, and no spy would think to prepare it. Chickpeas. A mill. The horror is that a man dies over a food word.
The local versions are already sitting in the grammars.

The syllabic r. Concord speakers universally insert a vowel and produce gurr for grr, audible in the first word, and cannot be trained out of it under pressure. Anywhere the Mandate wants to sort goblinoid from Concord in the dark, one word does it.
Vowel length. A Vaross speaker holds vowels for emphasis and a Marrowkin treats length as phonemic, so a Concord man reading a formula aloud shortens a long vowel and has said a different word. A gate that requires the toll formula spoken rather than shown is a gate that filters.
Grade. A Marrowkin name in the weak grade is an oath-broken Marrowkin. A hold that asks a stranger to say his own name is not being polite.
The pitch contour. A Concord speaker cannot hear it and cannot produce it, so any Eressean claim spoken by one is void, which means an Eressean court can identify a forgery by having it read aloud.
And the quieter application, which is the one that will earn its keep. Eighteenth-century advertisements for runaway servants and apprentices routinely identified them by accent, with descriptions like speaks broad Yorkshire. In the Realms the same words go out hand-copied and nailed to doors. A deserter notice, a bond-runner’s description, a Bench of Attribution circular hunting a mouth who left no mark: accent is the only description available for a man who cut nothing, poured nothing, and signed nothing. Given that a spoken working has no author in its own grammar, accent is very often the entire case file.

VIII. Profiles
Two or three fixed habits each, consistently used. Not spelling.
Edward Lambert. Chancery syntax, main verb late, Latin abstractions without anxiety because he has nothing to prove. Says the inscription. Under load his sentences get shorter rather than warmer, which is the opposite of most people and is how you tell he is worried.
Renard Greymane. Vernacular core almost exclusively. Does not reach for a Latin word even where one would serve, and does not work around it either; he simply stops the sentence. Says the cutting. Answers questions with actions more often than with clauses, which reads as taciturn and is in fact a man who has been placed by his speech before and declines to hand anyone the material.
Pietro. Cant, fluently, in rooms where cant is a provocation. Uses the Latin column mockingly and correctly, which is the tell: he can do the high register and chooses not to, and the choosing is the contempt. Attest in his mouth means to lie for a friend.
Kharven commons. Not a Concord accent at all and should never be written as one. The Standing Inventory carries the idiom: the forearm grip, how’s your stack, wet wood, the fixed proverbs. A Kharven speaker’s Common is placed by which proverbs he translates and which he leaves in the original.
