races--and--peoples/the-tongues-of-the-r.title: The Tongues of the Realms
races--and--peoples/the-tongues-of-the-r.content:
Framework document. Read before any individual grammar.
At the Ford Fair on Withy Reach, in the year the salt came late, a Concord wine factor named Fulbert Pimm climbed onto a trestle table in a plum-colored coat, raised his cup to his three new partners, a Marrowkin cooper, a hobgoblin ship’s officer and an Eressean lady of the calendar, and told them through one hired interpreter that he would see them all paid by the new moon. The cooper heard an oath and began, with great ceremony, to enter it. The officer heard a man promise money without saying who would bear the cost, and his voice sank and slowed until the benches near him emptied. The lady heard a date named by somebody with no standing to open it, went silent, and started counting. The interpreter, who was paid by the day, finished his ale and left through the kitchen. By sundown the Goose Riot had the bridge, four hundred people in their fair colors were pelting each other with roast birds and then with the spits, the wine was on fire, and Pimm stood bound in three languages to a thing he had said in none of them.
These grammars are on the shelf because of afternoons like that one, and the interpreters of the Reach have charged double ever since. Start here, before any of them.
What Is Actually a Language
The Realms have more naming registers than they have languages, and the distinction has to be settled before anything gets built, because the work involved differs by an order of magnitude.
A register is a naming and idiom system used as a cipher for a culture: Japonic for the archaic bloodlines, Korean for the Mahuo, Chinese for the lineage halls, Northern for the chartered families, Far-Northern carried-names for the tundra peoples. These do not get grammars. They get naming rules, idiom inventories and dialect levers, and those live in the Naming Guide and the Racial Voice Guide.
A constructed language is one the reader sees untranslated on the page, whose morphology carries meaning the translation cannot, and where a character’s grasp of it is a plot fact. These get full grammars.
By that test there are five, and one script system. Common is the fifth and is a deliberate exception, admitted below.








































TongueStatusWhy it earns a grammarOld VarossBuiltAlready met untranslated, and its old roots survive. Its morphology carries the goblinoid worldview: no adjectives, weight-and-cost verb pairs, emphasis by vowel length.Eressean and VarrisakBuiltThe Korvaeth quarrel turns on what constitutes valid transfer of a name. The schism is a linguistic dispute before it is a legal one.The Tally-Tongue, the tongue of the holdsBuiltOath-names are a real morphological slot. Consonant gradation means a Marrowkin name changes shape by grammatical case, which is a naming problem and a clerk’s problem at once.Accord LatinBuiltReal Latin, assembled rather than descended. Needs a fixed formula set rather than a grammar, plus the two spoken registers.CommonBuiltThe exception. The reader never sees it untranslated because the reader sees everything in it. Its Latinate and vernacular doublet is alive in every line anyone speaks.The Fourteen HandsBuilt, as The Descent of Parun under The Magic SystemEach Archon reads the lattice from a different station and produces a different daughter script, and a document written in the wrong hand is void rather than incorrect.
The Seven Shared Conventions
These bind every grammar in the set. Anything a language document says that contradicts this section is an error in that document.
One. The reader never needs the language. Every untranslated line must be comprehensible from surrounding narration, a character’s paraphrase, or context. A reader who skips every foreign word loses texture and never loses plot.
Two. Untranslated text earns its place by doing something translation cannot. A word appears in the original when the translation would lose a distinction the scene depends on. Nakh against brakh survives untranslated because Common has no matched pair for taking-without-cost against bearing-cost, and the whole Mandate war argument sits on that pair.
Three. Register before vocabulary. Every language has at least three: what people say in a street, what a document says, and what the archaic legal layer says. Most of a language’s dramatic value lives in a character moving between them at the wrong moment.
Four. Grammar carries worldview, and it does it by what it makes impossible. Old Vaross has no adjectives, so a quality must be attached to somebody and an insult becomes an accusation. Eressean has no unwitnessed possessive, so my name is a construction that requires naming the witness. Build the hole first and the philosophy comes out of it.
Five. Sound follows material conditions. Marrowkin consonant gradation exists because the tongue is shouted across a working forge floor and evolved to keep root identity legible through noise. Old Vaross holds vowels because the goblinoid peoples emphasize by duration, and they emphasize by duration because volume is for signaling across water. Phonology is never chosen for flavor alone.
Six. Orthography on the page. Hyphens join compound elements. Doubled vowels mark length and length marks weight. Diacritics are forbidden across every tongue without exception. Long vowels are written doubled and nothing else.
Seven. Nobody speaks a language perfectly. Every grammar ends with a section on how the tongue is spoken badly, by whom, and what the errors reveal. A speaker’s first tongue shows through in their second.
The Family Tree
Two unrelated stocks, and one bridge. The Old World and the New are regions of the one great land, and the names are older than anybody’s reason for them.
The Old World stock. Old Vaross and the Tally-Tongue descend from a common ancestor spoken before the Scattering, and both peoples would rather be dead than say so. The evidence is in the numerals and in the body-part roots, which is where relatedness always survives. The Accord’s philologists read it into the record at Altherion four decades ago and were expelled from both the Keth-Gorrum and the Ore Council in the same season.
The New World stock. Eressean, and behind it whatever the archaic bloodlines spoke before they came into the New World. Unrelated to the Old World stock at every level.
Accord Latin is the bridge, and it is nobody’s mother tongue. It was assembled, deliberately, as a neutral instrument for contracts between parties who could not read each other, and every polity in the four quarters has agreed to be measured in a language none of them dreams in. That agreement is the Accord’s actual foundation, and it is more load-bearing than any treaty it has ever recorded.
Document Format
Every grammar follows the same eleven sections so they can be compared and so gaps are visible.

Attestation. Who recorded it, when, and whose bias is in the record.
Phonology. Consonants, vowels, length, permitted clusters, what is forbidden.
Prosody. Stress, timing, and the emphasis mechanism.
Morphology. Root shape, derivation, inflection, compounding.
Syntax. Neutral order, and what the order does under stress.
The semantic architecture. The two or three distinctions the language forces on its speakers.
Registers. Street, document, archaic.
Dialects.
Script.
Lexicon, organized semantically.
Sample texts with interlinear gloss, and a section on speaking it badly.

The Build Order
Complete. Old Vaross, Eressean and Varrisak, the Tally-Tongue, Accord Latin and the Fourteen Hands are all built.
What remains is maintenance rather than construction: the Drow Shadow-Veil notation is described from outside in three places and has no entry of its own, and Mirror-Sign is named as a full manual language with its own grammar and has never been given one. Neither is urgent. Both are real gaps.


Old Vaross — The Goblinoid Tongue
Eressean and Varrisak — The Tongue of the Vey-Elarin
The Tally-Tongue of the Marrowkin
Accord Latin — The Formulary and the Two Spoken Registers
Common — The Tongue With No Distinctions
Element Inventories — Mahuo, Yukari, the Elven Branches, Beastkin
Moto Element Inventory — Japonic Stratum
The Celestial Host — Naming
Swears, Oaths and Insults



Read next: The Descent of Parun, for the one script system here that does work on the world; The Working Trades, for why the guilds care how a working is said; Races & Peoples, for the speakers.

start-here.title: Start Here
start-here.content:
On the last morning of the Salt Succession two armies stood across a field of green barley at the ford of Orrendale, scarlet shields on one side and gold-and-black on the other, and a cook’s daughter named Perrine Dorrow walked out alone between them in a butcher’s apron over borrowed mail. Her aura was the wet arterial red that makes a stranger’s pulse jump. She filled her chest and called the name of the only art she had across the whole valley, the Hunger of All Kings, and six thousand men laughed. A knight in the gold-and-black stood up in his stirrups to laugh better. Then the third day of a fast landed in every belly of the enemy front rank at once, and the line buckled, men sat down in the barley and wept for bread, warhorses dragged their heads down to tear at the crop while their riders slid off them, and the scarlet shields walked across and took the ford almost without a blow. Perrine’s ribs stood out through the apron by then, because that art eats the woman who works it, and she ate for nine days and never again kept down a whole meal. The minstrels had the song in every tavern by harvest. The queen who had hired her held a feast in her honor, since a fighter who can starve an army is a problem at table, and the third course was poisoned, and forty people in cloth of gold watched her die with their spoons in their hands. They buried her in the old barrow above the ford, on a battlefield of the Great Spirit War where nothing has grown straight since, and nobody who has dug there will say what the barrow was built to hold down.
The newcomer’s road into the wiki. Walk the short route below and you will know enough to follow any scene. Everything else can wait until a story sends you looking.
What War of the Realms is
War of the Realms is mythic epic fantasy: Tolkien’s sense of age, Martin’s courts, Le Guin’s magic, and souls that climb. It is a medieval world that runs on old magic, with great houses at odds, lethal courts, deep and frightening powers, and a cultivation system running underneath all of it. The stories are set in the Dark Ages, the hundred and ten years from 690 IC to the turn of the century, on one great continent of four quarters, and the present year is 715 IC, the twenty-fifth of them. The name flatters nobody and misleads every visitor, because these are the loudest years on record: practitioners are common, schools run like football clubs with their colors, songs and grudges, heralds cry the news, minstrels get it wrong, and bookies take odds on all of it. Magic is done by living people and their crafts, and it runs on the alchemist’s lens rather than the natural philosopher’s: every working is a transformation the worker makes in themselves, an idea burned, dissolved or fixed in the soul, and the world gives way as far as that soul has truly changed. What burns in the crucible burns in the one who tends it. A city’s lamps burn the color of the warden who keeps them, and she can walk off the round, while the towns and the wilds still burn oil. There are no guns in any era, and a three-copper crossbow bolt can still kill a great fighter in a closed room. People who wake the power in their own souls climb sixteen Stages, and everyone says them as ranks: an Initiate, a Journeyman, an Expert, a Master. A Stage opens when the soul meets the one deed it asks, its Catalyst, and has lived enough, its Level, to hold it. Surviving what nearly breaks you meets the deed, and so does a bought Draft, which is why the rich are strong and why a lucky commoner with a monster core keeps great houses awake at night; a Stage bought ahead of the life to hold it sits loose and spilling in the soul until the life catches up. A soul comes to lean on one of three Paths: Body, which knows and works physical reality and has to close with you; Spirit, which works on souls, the dead and what a thing means, from across the field; and Fate, the hardest of them, which moves what has to be so before anything can happen, and at a ruinous price. None of them is better, and each has a way of killing the others. Each person’s soul reports their numbers to them alone, in a block of text called a window. Crews go down into dungeons, floors of living danger grown around a pool of power, to kill what guards the heart. Monsters level up, earn names and carry bounties. Guilds of every kind hand out the same nine words as titles that the fighters use as ranks, gear and beasts carry a Grade (a person never does), gear a Rarity besides, and blessings show on your sheet and sometimes lie. Each arc sets its own darkness: cruelty and loss land hard where the story turns, and then people fight back, and they win often, each win at a price you can see. Tolkien’s age lies under everything, and the land is its own thing: wildly fantastical and earthlike at once, grand and lived-in, and beautiful all the way through.
In a hurry? Magic on One Page is the whole system on one screen, the page to hand a guest at the table before anything else.
The climb in one sentence
Your soul climbs Stages, and each Stage asks one thing of you. Your life climbs Level, by everything hard and real you have done. Your hands climb skills, by use. Everything else is read from those three.

























What climbsHow it climbsWhat people sayStage, the soulIts Catalyst met, one deed per Stage, and Level enough to hold itThe rank: Initiate, Apprentice, Journeyman, Adept, Expert, Master, Grandmaster, Archmaster, ParagonLevel, the lifeAnything hard and real: danger overcome above all, but also a flood night held or fifty years at a tradeA number, and from it how well the soul works its own road, its Mastery (Body IV, Spirit III)Skills, the handsUseOne of the nine ranks: Initiate, Apprentice, Journeyman, Adept, Expert, Master, Grandmaster, Archmaster, Paragon
Letters (the Grades, F up to EX) belong to things: gear, missiles, beasts and bounties. Nobody calls a person by a letter. How Power Grows walks the whole climb in one reading.
The short route: six pages

How Magic Works. One page on the whole system in plain words: the Soul Crystal (the soul itself, which holds power and sends it out), windows, the three Paths, Wellsprings, Traits, skills, classes, Stages and their Catalysts, Stages for sale, monster cores, dungeons, guild titles, gear, Releases by Path, Drafts, Fate and what everything costs. Start here even if you skip everything else.
From Omnara to a Blow. The same system as one chain, from the first thing there was down to a fist on a toll bridge, one step at a time, with a pointer at every step to the page that goes deeper.
A Reader’s Codex. The world on one page, the history in brief, and a short glossary of the terms the stories assume you know. Keep it open in a second tab.
The Measures at a Glance. The numbers a scene throws at you (Stage and rank, Level, Mastery, reserve, skill ranks, class, title, a beast’s or bounty’s Grade, item Grade and Rarity) on one sheet, with what each one means at the table and what a window shows of it.
One Exchange, Annotated. One fight between two fighters, with every rule marked and each fighter’s windows shown, so you can see how the pieces work together.
Factions at a Glance. The crowns, guilds, houses and sects that push the stories, each in a line or two: what it is and what it wants.

The Magic System, in one reading order
The Magic System is the section’s own front page: the six rules that carry everything, the four measures, the sheet, and then the reading order. That order runs down the six shelves and the workbook below, and it is the only one that visits every page. Every other list here is a short route through it.

First Steps. The newcomer’s road: the whole system in brief, the numbers, one annotated fight, the words.
The Foundations. What a working is, the laws it conditions, and the boundaries it is written in.
The Soul and the Climb. What a soul carries, what advancement does to it, and how it reads from outside.
Power in Use. How power is put into the body, stacked, spent, carried in tags and beaten.
Practice and Institution. Who may practice, what they are called, how they are trained, and what the practice is set against.
Reference and Craft. Consulted rather than read.
Fracture of Worlds — The Living System. The workbook, for when a value is in question.

A short route before your first fight scene
When you want more than the primer and less than the whole section, these nine pages are the quickest way through. They cut across the shelves on purpose, and each one leans on the one before.

The Gate: Who May Learn Magic. Who wakes their Crystal, who never does, and why that is no longer an accident.
The Core Vocabulary. The basic words: the three planes, Aether (the medium the world is made of) and Essence (Aether a person has pulled in from the world around them and refined into their own), the Crystal, abilities and techniques, and the sheet and the climb.
How Power Grows. The climb in one reading: Stage said as rank, the Catalyst each Stage asks and the Level that holds it, Mastery read from Level, skills on the nine ranks, and the Releases each Path reaches.
The Sixteen Stages. The ladder of power, Stage (one of sixteen steps of the soul’s refinement) by Stage, told plainly: its rank, its Catalyst, what it feels like inside, what it looks like outside, what ordinary people call it, and what it costs to buy.
The Trait System: Law, Function and the Forge. Where powers come from. A Trait (a standing law in the soul, formed when lived experience hardens into something the world accepts as true) is survived into being, never taught, and works as deep as its owner’s Mastery of the lead Path, so it grows as the life does.
The Three Paths: Routing, Recognition and the Gate. The road a soul walks, Body, Spirit or Fate: what each one is, how each beats the others, what one, two or three of them cost, and what a Path (the layer of the soul it has learned to lean on) gates.
The Working Trades. The ways a working (a deliberate act of magic) is set down: spoken in the moment, cut into stone, steel or paper, poured into a bottle, or sung by many voices together, each a skill and a trade, and all but the pouring want a woken Crystal. Also why the guilds look down on fighters who speak their workings, while the crowds cheer them anyway.
The Sixty Wellsprings. The sixty Wellsprings (each an alchemical and spiritual transformation, the governing idea that changes how a soul uses Aether, a lens on magic already potent, each a transformation a person works on themselves that shows in the world, which the Measurewrights explain with one law of physics apiece as their own theory) sorted by kind, Wild, Spirit, Fate and Medium, by the plane each one calls home, each of them a way some Titan’s law shows up in the world.
Counterplay: What Beats a Practitioner. How a practitioner (a person whose Crystal is awake) is actually beaten, in four routes. Read this before your first fight scene.

Everything else, when a story sends you there:

The sheet and the climb: Windows and the Sheet, Classes and Mastery, Skills and Their Ranks, Releases and Domains by Path, Release Forms, Domains, The Ladder and the Draft, The Color of Essence.
Power in the hand: Reinforcement, Stacking and Spending, Runes and Tags.
How magic lives in the world: Who Pays for the Lamp: The Living Crafts, The Standing and the Title: Guild Titles as Trust, Training and Sects, Blessings and Curses, Vows and Oaths.
Going deeper: The Physical Account: Two Sets of Books, Mechanica: Extraction Without Recognition, On Walking Into the Current — Wellspring Encounter and Recovery, Fracture of Worlds — The Living System.
The reference shelf (look things up, do not read straight through): The Lexicon of Magic — Master Terminology, The Working Vocabulary — Trade Jargon and Its Metaphysical Extensions, Forms, The Master Glyph Index — 136 Attested Forms, The Descent of Parun — The Fourteen Hands, The Practitioner’s Field Manual — The Forge.

Where the scenes are
The stories themselves live in The Scene Archive: every scene on the live record, one page each, sorted by thread and in reading order, with the fuller New Lore reading order beside it. A good first scene for each live thread:








































ThreadWhere it is setBegin withThe Uncounted: Muken Moto and his sister YukazuriThe high north, from Halcrest to Kharven-SeatThe Uncounted, Chapter One: The Map at HalcrestThe cedar enclave: Naiser and Naevra Yukari, the Zettari talks, the Moto breakawayThe Cedar EnclaveThe Bearer of WeightAfter the Seat: Muken as king, six months after the Great War of the NorthKharven-Seat in springThe Grey WallThe Sins: Shōki, the Sin of Wrath, loose from the PitThe Pit, then the drovers’ roads north of the borderThe Wrath WakesThe fourteenth day: Faisal the Grand Angel and his brotherMidreach and the blackened plainThe Last CombustionThe Kessen road: Shōki at the ford, Muken in the cedar wood, Cozbi Mahuo and Hiromi at the Sum-gol PostKessen, the cedar wood and Sum-golThe Ford
The threads cross, and they were not written in story order. If a scene seems to start in the middle, it probably does; the Scene Archive page puts them straight.
Where to go next

The people: Volume I — Character Cards. One card per character: who they are, how they fight, how they sound.
The land: Geography & the Four Quarters, then The Bearing and the Holding for each quarter of the world.
The powers: Factions, Bloodlines & Institutions, with The Guild Accord first, the coalition of guilds whose nine titles you will see on every token and every bounty.
The peoples and their tongues: Races & Peoples and The Tongues of the Realms.
Money and daily life: What Things Cost.
Monsters and dungeons: The Bestiary and Dungeons.
Gear and materials: Grade and Rarity, for Grade, Rarity and Master Works, then Materials, Alchemy & Trade.
Named arts and schools: The Disciplines, with Named Arts and Schools and Bloodline Arts.
Gods, planes and the deep past: Cosmology & Metaphysics.
Letters, treaties and first readers: In-World Documents & the Narrative Archive.

the-bestiary/dungeons.title: Dungeons
the-bestiary/dungeons.content:
What a Core makes around itself, what comes to live in it, who goes down to clear it, and who gets the bill

Item, one hill. Item, one orchard, under same. Item, one crown, received from the hand of the late proprietor at some speed, in part settlement of wages.
Household roll of the Kingdom of Hollowhay, entry for the wedding year, in the hand of its new owner

King Bertran Ferrant ruled a hill. Hollowhay is one of the smallest realms in the Hundred Crowns, two miles of hedge and a cider press around one green lump called Goosegrass, and what made it a kingdom at all lay under the lump: nine galleries of apple trees in the living rock, in leaf and fruit together in every month of the year, lit a clear spring green by nothing anyone could point to. Bertran’s great-great-grandfather had taken the place from the things that bred in it, with thirty crossbows and a Sealwright, and ever since the Ferrants had let the great gallery for weddings. For the wedding of his own daughter Isemay to the heir of the toll-king at Tollgarth, in the summer of 708, Bertran hired every herald-painter on the Kessen road, hung the trees with scarlet and gold, and spent the last of his credit on four hundred guests. He had also not paid his keepers in three seasons.
The keepers were a family called Ambrey, who had tended the pool at the bottom of the ninth gallery since the Ferrants first won it, and on the morning of the wedding Mother Odalie Ambrey brought all of them up to the top of the stair in their clean aprons, sat them on the steps, and handed round the bread and onions. They had stopped bleeding the pool at midwinter. Nobody at the feast knew what that meant, and the toast went up at sundown the way a Midmarch toast does, with every guest who owned a woken Crystal lighting their coat at once for the pride of it, rose and amber and kingfisher blue and one enormous drunken crimson, four hundred people’s worth of Aether pulled in a single breath out of ground that had been filling for half a year. The green in the gallery went bright enough to read by. Then the apple trees began to walk, and the floor came up in loops of thorn as thick as a horse’s barrel, each with a knot of hard green plate at the crown of its roots, and the first loop took the groom’s uncle off his bench and through the top table.
Isemay Ferrant, who could read a bill, understood first. She went up nine galleries in forty yards of saffron silk with a carving knife in her hand and somebody’s blood on her to the elbows, and she asked Mother Ambrey to close the ring. Mother Ambrey finished her onion and named the arrears. Bertran, arriving on one leg with a briar on the other, had nothing on him worth a season’s pay but the thing on his head, and he threw it up the stair. She looked at it, bit it, and said it would do for the first season, and the bride tore off her dowry pearls for the other two. Then an old woman in an apron walked down through a battle with a brass key and shut the pool, and the briars lost their footing in the ground in the time it takes to say so, and four hundred drunk people in their best clothes went for the green knots with candlesticks, cake saws and the legs of benches. Thirty-one died. The marriage is still standing, and a bookie on the Tollgarth road will still give you four to one against it. The Ambreys hold the crown, which makes Hollowhay the only monarchy in the Midmarch founded on back pay, and they let the great gallery for weddings at double the old rate, because couples now ask for the bench with the stain.
The word for what lies under Goosegrass is dungeon, and this page is the Bestiary’s account of the things, since most of what the Bestiary lists either came out of one or is on its way back in.
What the Word Means
The word began as a castle word. On the old chancery rolls a domnio is a lord’s great tower, the place where his writ runs and nobody else’s does, and in the mouths of delvers it wore down to dungeon and moved underground, because the first crews to go down into these places noticed that a different lord’s writ ran there. They were closer to the truth than the scholars who corrected their spelling.

A Wellspring is one of the sixty kinds of Aether (the raw stuff of magic, lying in the ground and air), each working on the Soul Crystal in its own way. A Core, in common speech, is a site where one of them pools. A dungeon is what a Core makes around itself, or what grows up around one. The Aether rewrites the ground, things come to live on it and breed in it, and people build, dig and die there until the whole is one place with one law in it. A worked Core with keepers is a dungeon somebody cleared and now holds.

Most Wellspring Cores lie in dungeons, and the rest are said to lie in vast open territories, a matter taken up below. Three words crowd each other here, and each has killed somebody. A Well is the delver’s word for the ground itself, a Core Concentration in the survey’s terms, thick enough to rewrite what lives in it. A dungeon is the crew’s word for the whole place, galleries and beasts and all, and it covers a Well with a roof on and a worked site whose keepers have walked off. Core means any worked site in the street, the innermost and densest band of a concentration on the survey (see On Walking Into the Current), and the seat of a soul in a physician’s mouth. When a porter says he has sat beside a dozen Cores, he means the first. Find out which one your captain means before you go down.
At a Glance
What it looks like. A way down, first of all: a shaft, a stair, a cave mouth, a split in a hillside, an old cellar door with warm air coming up through the cracks. Behind it, galleries that go on longer than the hill has room for, in the color of the Well’s own Wellspring, getting brighter the deeper you go.
What it costs. Reserve to hold your own law on its ground, bolts by the pouch, a clock you cannot argue with, and a share of everyone who went down with you. A practitioner pulls Aether in fast there, and that is the bait. A Well-spawn goes toward the pull.
How it is beaten. Kill out the deep lines and then the guardian at the Heart, which is the only true clearing. Those who cannot do that seat a ring at a depth people can stand at, install keepers, and pay them forever.
Example. Ama Brockway’s crew of six takes a Green posting on a Mouth found under a Pennycrown tannery. The fork rings thin and teal at the cellar door, the cellar is perfectly dry, and the porter has started to cry and cannot say why. Thaloré, then, or something near it: a Spirit ground, all weight of feeling. She sets her caller on the top step, turns a one-hour glass, takes four people down, breaks eleven smoke-brown masks in a gallery that smells of cold brine, and is back on the step with a quarter of the sand to spare, because the man carrying the rope has gone quiet and that is the sign to leave. She reports it to the hall by nightfall, as the law requires, and the tanner discovers that he owns a dungeon.
How One Grows
The seep. It begins where a Wellspring’s Aether starts to pool, on conductive rock, along a fault, over a dead battlefield, or for reasons no surveyor has ever established. Wells breed, and a seep is a Well too young to breed anything, a warm patch where the moss runs a strange color and the dogs lie down.
The Mouth. The ground goes on thickening until it alters what stands on it and the alteration stays. On Wild ground the rock begins to move on its own time, a crack widening over a decade, a sinkhole with very regular sides. On ground where people have already dug, the Well simply takes what is there, which is how a mine, a wine cellar, a drowned abbey or a forgotten crypt becomes the top floor of something. Dungeons come both ways, grown and inherited, and most of the great ones are both at once: a thing the Core started, some people improved, and the Core then finished with their tools still on the bench.
The workings. Animals move in, or wander in, and the Aether fills their Essence Core with nowhere to go. Over generations a line stops living by its own nature and begins to breed by the Well’s, masked at birth (the full account is under Well-spawn). Now the place has an inside. Ground thickens downward in bands, and each band favors its own stock.
The Deeps and the Heart. Given centuries, the bottom of the place thins the Veil (the boundary between the planes), the deep lines gather minds out of what the Well remembers, and at the very center the law of the Wellspring stands as the only law, with a guardian grown to keep it. A dungeon that has reached that point is grown up. Anything it can still do from there it does at its leisure. The bottom of such a place is also one of the few doors through which a living body can walk into another plane, and The Veil gives that road and what it costs.
What makes it grow faster. People. Every crew that dies down there leaves its reserve in the ground and its memory in the walls, and hard pulling at the top thins the ground at the face and brings the spawn up after it. A Well worked hard breeds more, and a Well left alone breeds deeper, and between those two the entire trade of Core keeping has to find a living.
The shape of a dungeon follows the ground, and the ladder is the same one everywhere. Each band is a rung on the sites ladder, and the numbers below are the same ones the hunting halls use.





















































DepthGroundWhat the survey calls itThe spawn’s blowGrade of the bounty, and the title to take itWhat the ground asks of you if you mean to stayThe MouthFreshetActive Concentration, at its edgeHollow to ED, an Apprentice’s title (Green Sigil)JourneymanThe Upper WorkingsMillraceActive ConcentrationDC to B, a Journeyman’s or an Adept’s title (Green or Blue)AdeptThe Lower WorkingsRiptideActive Concentration, Veil beginning to thinCB to A, an Adept’s or an Expert’s title (Blue)ExpertThe DeepsWhirlpoolVeil-Thin NexusBA to S, an Expert’s or a Master’s title (Blue or Gold)MasterThe HeartFountainheadWellspring CoreA, and the guardian above themS to X, a Master’s title and up (Gold Sigil or Obsidian Seal)Grandmaster
A beast’s Grade is the Accord’s danger rating, the letter its bounty is posted under, and the title a hunter holds says which letters she may lawfully take; the Sigil is the badge of that license, in its colors. Each Grade answers to a rank and its Stages, E to B against Stages I to IV one for one, A against V to VII, S against VIII to X, and so upward, by the table in the register. The spawn’s blow is a different reading, the output of its hardest stroke on the Ledger’s own letters, and the two are seldom the same letter. Spawn carry Pressure, a Path and Mastery like anything else that has cracked its seal. What a deep line feeds on tips it toward a road, and how it hunts settles the matter, so a Wild Well can still breed a thing that goes for the soul. The guardian of an old Heart is commonly famous enough to show a Release, and nothing down there, guardian included, has ever been offered a class. Read the two columns on the ends together, because the gap between them is the first thing every hall teaches. On every floor you can kill what lives there one rank before you can safely stand there. An Apprentice party can break masks at the Mouth, on ground that asks for a Journeyman, and it has an afternoon to do it in. A Millrace is survivable for an afternoon and not for a season, and at a Whirlpool a Spirit-type onset gives you no warning at all. So every crew works by the glass, and the turn of that glass has ended more careers than the masks have.
Territories: the dungeon with no roof
Wellspring Cores are also said to lie in vast territories, and “said” is doing honest work in that sentence. Some regions of the Inner World read like a dungeon laid flat: an edge you can walk across without noticing, bands that thicken as you go on, stock that changes with the bands, and a center nobody has mapped. You walk in where you would otherwise climb down. The Scourge of Hell is the great example, and the forest of the Unpapered, in autumn for as long as anyone can say, is the argument nearest to hand. Crews call such a place a lying-down. The Guild has never confirmed a Core in one, because confirming it would require somebody to return with the reading.
What It Looks Like
Three questions, in this order: how does the ground take you, which Wellspring is it, and how far down are you.
How the ground takes you



































TypeWhat you seeWhat you feelWhich crews die in itWildThe dungeon of the songs. Stairs of floating stone, rivers going the wrong way, a gallery with a skyThe body knows first. Your pack shifts, a tool hums in your belt, metal tastes wrong. Your Crystal reads normalClever ones, who explain the rock awaySpiritAn orchard, a nice dry cellar, a chapel with good light. Nothing is wrong with itHeat in the hands, a sudden happiness, a nosebleed, a working half-forming that you are sure you decided onConfident ones, who are having the best day of their livesFateNothing whatever. A sound stair, a dull gallery, and a surveyor’s plan that keeps working until the one time it mattersNothing in the body, and nothing on the fork. Your luck goes strange, oaths bite, and you keep meeting the same two strangers on a stair with one way downLucky ones, and anyone who swore something on the way inMediumAll of it at once. The stream runs backward, your dead mother is on your mind, and the dice have stopped behavingEverything is wrong and each symptom blames the otherSensible ones, who sit down until it passes
The Spirit dungeon is the one to fear, and the worst thing about it is how few people believe that on the way in. A crew that comes up from one reports an easy job and a wonderful feeling about the next. A Fate dungeon shows up in nobody’s report at all. It shows in the hall’s ledger, as three seasons of crews whose luck was too good, and then a season when the same crews stop coming back. Nothing a Fate ground does is worth a working to it, and a sound crew with a kept harness, paid shares and two ways out gives it very little to hold.
By Wellspring
Each of the sixty has its own hue and its own ground, and the register has them all. These are the ones crews meet most, sorted by kind.

































































KindWhat the place becomesOn the registerBringWild, the hot onesSlag-glazed galleries in ember orange. A Solfatara dungeon wears yellow crust on every wall, spits steam from the seams and stinks of rotten eggs and hot minerals. A Pyreveil one smells of banked coals, and nobody sweats there, which should alarm you. A cold site runs the other way, heat pulled out of the world, blue ice and a cold that drinks your lamp. That one is no Wellspring of the Sixty at all but Titan-touched ground, the Titan Vohrin’s own power pooled in the rock, and the register files it among the Wild Wellsprings under [[The Magic System/The Foundations/The Sixty Wellsprings/Wild Wellspringsa marked note]]Tinder-foxWild, the high onesA Cymorath dungeon goes upward, wind-whistling towers and trails drawn on the air, and a Judicium one rings arc-blue, with colored fringes on every straight line and hair standing upGriffons, and whatever falls on youRope, and no iron you cannot afford to loseWild, the heavy onesNear-black Abython halls where loose things drift and a dropped wedge floats away at chest height. Petralon floors that press you down until the stair feels twice as long. Concentric rings in every poolSump-toadLoose silt, a horse-hoist, a good bait lanternWild, the stone onesOchre and amber strata, grit on the hand. Basilithe ground holds one pure pitch in the bones and draws standing waves in the dust. Terranova ground knits itself, so your chalk marks and your wedges are gone by morning and the broken door is whole againTolling CrabA tuning bar, and no faith in your mapWild, the green onesChlorophyll green and the smell of cut grass, wood creaking as it grows, the walls in leafReaching BriarAxes, fire if you dare, and a very clear idea of which way you cameWild, the dark onesThe color that should be there has been stolen. Vantabriel galleries where your lamp dims though the oil is full, and Nihiloth rooms where it goes outLamp-drinkerNoise, a crowd, a white flareSpiritNothing to see, or very little, and every crew reads the wrong thing first. Thaloré ground is the deepest teal and dry as a loft, and a grief settles on the whole party that belongs to nobody in it. Hypnather galleries are simply very restful. Oneirion ones have good beds. On Lethegraal ground the crew stops being able to say why it came down, and a Nyxial post is where a frightened sentry stops being frightened, of anythingMourning PikeSomebody outside to say what you came for, a harpoon, and a slow walk outFateViolet rooms that read as ordinary rooms, and a passage that always happens to be the way you meant to go. Ruled lines cut in the stone that never quite meet. Transference ground passes things along, and you come up with somebody else’s debt. On Oblation ground the stair asks a toll and you find you have paid it, and on Somnalis ground every plan crosses another plan at the worst landingLeveling LeechKnotted line, two people counting aloud who are allowed to disagree, and nothing you have swornMediumHard blue-white glare down polished Aurevane corridors, shadows split in two, one clean high tone like a wet finger on a glass rim. Anamnesis walls with afterimages of what once happened on them, a dry whisper like old pages, the smell of an attic. Phreatis beads dew on your sleeve and smells of cellar stone, and you begin to remember things. Mortalis is venous black-red, grave soil and a cold at the edge of everythingGlarewing, Roll-callerSmoked glass, the pay-book left upstairs, and somebody outside to tell you whose memories those are
By depth
Color tells you where you are, on the same smelting scale as a mask. At the Mouth a gallery is smoke brown with a tint under the murk. At the Upper Workings it is warm dark gray with the color suggesting itself along the seams. By the Lower Workings the true color veins through the rock and flickers when something rouses, and in the Deeps the walls are silver-gray suffused with it, bright enough to throw their hue on your face. People who have seen the Heart and can still describe things say the color bleaches to white at the edges, and they say it wistfully. Crews have an old rule for all of this: count the colors, and when the wall is brighter than the last wall, ask yourself what you are being paid.
The three grounds, with a roof on
A surveyor takes three readings off any ground, and a dungeon can run high in all of them. The Three Grounds gives the measures in full. Down a stair they behave as follows.

























MeasureWhere a dungeon has itWhat it does to a crewAetheric DensityAlways, and more with every floor. The Core is the richest ground most delvers will ever stand on, and the five bands are Density and nothing elseEvery reserve fills fast, whatever the Path, and Body fighters above all can afford to spend. It is also the bait: a Well-spawn goes toward the pullEcho DepthIn old dungeons that have killed many. Every crew that dies below leaves its memory in the walls, and a place that has eaten crews for four hundred years reads fathoms deep on the still-glass before the Mouth is out of sightSpirit workings come cheap, for the crew’s reader and for whatever is reading the crew. Echo Beasts walk sooner and stay longer, and porters with no training come up with soul wounds nobody saw dealtThread WeightIn a dungeon where something great was decided: a siege that ended in the galleries, a battle whose dead were buried on the seep, a crown lost on the stairFate pulls come cheap and their knots come small, for anyone who can pull. Everyone else finds that harness fails, oaths bite and small choices at a landing count for more than they should
The fork reads the first of these and is silent on the other two, which is how a Green crew walks into an old killing-ground believing it has a Freshet and an easy afternoon. A sound hall sends a still-glass and a hundred casts down to the Mouth before it posts a rating.
The Long Barrow at Sorley Bridge carries all three at once, Mortalis Density over nine thousand dead on a field where a battle was settled, and it is the one posting where a recruit of any Path will tell you the work came easily and the sleep afterward did not. The Seventh Fold took its Weight from the siege that made it. Stoneglass Hollow and the Drowned Parishes are deep before they are anything else. Nether Marl has been at war for twenty-six years without a decision, and the Measurewrights consider that the one thing keeping the Weight off it.
Crews hire by the reading. A Body-heavy crew wants a young, rich, shallow dungeon and gets through it like a scythe. An old deep one wants a Spirit reader and a mender on the step, and pays them more than the captain. A heavy one wants a Fate puller if the hall can find such a person, and failing that a crew with kept gear, paid shares and nothing sworn.
What Lives In It
Well-spawn are the proper inhabitants, born masked and bred along the Well’s law, and they are why a hall pays anyone to go down. They go toward the pull, shallow ones with no more plan than a moth, deep ones with a very good plan. Their own page has the masks, the ladder and the counters.
Strays. A badger that dug too far, a hound that followed a crew in. It comes out strange, short-lived and unable to breed true, and wears no mask. It enters the register under Natural Beasts, or under Aberrations if corruption made it, and it can still have your face off.
Echo Beasts. From the Deeps down, the visitors’ own grief and rage take form and walk for a while, and go when the thinning closes. Every long-serving crew has met somebody it recognized.
Spirit Beasts. Formed from Wellspring resonance, carrying a mind, and capable of making an alliance. A very old dungeon may have one sitting in it who regards the whole place as its garden and the crews as weather. Be polite.
Wyrms. A wyrm steadies the Aether around it, a living anchor on rich ground, and a big one may have dug half of what a crew takes for galleries. Mining clans have made blood-oaths with them for safe passage, and a crew that kills the wyrm in a dungeon may find the ground it was holding down goes off like a dropped pot of lamp oil. See The Draconic Lineage.
Speakers. The rare deep spawn who talk, in the voices of the people the Well has killed. They bargain and they lie in the same breath. Every one on file has wanted to go up.
The ones who stayed. The register has no entry for them and every crew knows about them. A practitioner who holds too long at a Riptide or below is retuned, and from the inside that feels like finally understanding your own gifts. They may have a whole camp down there, cooking, keeping a watch, very glad to see you, with their coats a color they never used to be. Nobody at any hall will tell you what they are owed.
Who Clears Them
Hunting halls license the hunters, post the board and pay on the mask. A hall is a stone building with a green door and a grudge against the hall across the square, and the hall’s color is worn in the street and sung against in the tavern. Chartered companies undercut them by putting one licensed captain over a party of cheap crossbows, and in the Hundred Crowns and along the Thresh you can hire an entire free company by the season. Holdout guilds keep their own boards and grades and are often older and richer than the Accord’s. Unlicensed crews take what no licensed party will touch, for whoever cannot afford a fee.
Sects go down for their own reasons, since a first descent is how a school bloods its young. Each runs its own dungeon the way a club runs its home ground: school colors on the stair, a song for the walk down, a grudge against the school that holds the next valley, and old boys in the taverns telling you how much harder it was in their day. Rich lineage halls keep a small one in the family as a training yard, and lose a child to it about once a generation, and go on keeping it.
Crowns rarely clear anything with their own soldiers and always claim to have done. A levy on a stair panics at the first smoke, and the proper use of a king is to pay.
The crew
Six to twelve is usual, because a dozen is the most one caller can talk out. A proper crew is more than fighters, and the people who get left off the song are the ones who bring the fighters home.

Hired, ranked and bet on
The hire. Postings go up on the board at a hall, pinned three deep, and on tavern doors as hand-copied bills. A big clearing is raised as a venture with subscribers and shares, an adventurer being a person who ventures capital, so that a bishop, a widow and a pair of bakers may own a third of a crew’s luck and come down to the stair to shout advice. The crew holds shares and does not draw a wage. That is why a crew in the Lower Workings will go one more gallery than is wise, and why it bribes its caller’s glass. Hiring happens at the Lamp Fairs each spring, where captains stand on barrels and lie, and a young practitioner with a good coat can be signed by lunchtime and dead by harvest.
The rank. A hunter’s license is her Accord title, worn as the Sigil, Green through Gold, and Obsidian if you are the sort of person nobody discusses. The street ranks a crew by what it brings up, in the same slang the mask-clerks use. A smoke crew works Mouths. A vein crew has been to the Lower Workings and come back with most of itself. A deep crew gets its name painted over a tavern door with the tally beside it. Anybody who says they run a bright crew is either a legend or trying to sell you something, and “bright” is usually spoken as advice to leave. Every crew has an epithet that travels ahead of it, often unflattering, and the Saffron Hoods and Scarlet Aprons have spent generations proving that hatred is cheaper than advertising.
The book. Bookies follow crews the way gulls follow boats. The depth book takes bets on how far a crew gets, the long book on how many come up, and the race book on which crew reaches a new Heart first, with a clerk at each stair who writes down the color of every mask coming out. Heralds cry a great clearing from the market cross for a fee, minstrels have it by the next fair with the color wrong and the dead doubled, and a crew that wins a famous descent will find its bar bill paid in one town and a bounty on it in the next. Betting against your own crew is held to be very bad luck, and the crews that do it have the best-kept books in the trade.
How a Clearing Goes

The look. A Reconnaissance commission, the survey’s Protocol III with a crew attached: one person in, one outside, marking the perimeter. The kind and the Wellspring are named, or the hall will not post it. A Medium dungeon goes to the top of the board and the price goes up.
The kill-out. An Extermination commission, floor by floor, from the Mouth down, on the rule that you read the mask first and lure the thing up off its ground if you can. Bait lanterns on ropes, drawn up a shaft at the gallop, have killed more big spawn than any arbalest. Salted ground helps, worked by hedge-workers so that Aether will not pool on it, and so does bled ground, pulled empty. On its own Well a spawn stands one rung higher than off it.
The Deeps. Here the work passes to Masters with crews behind them, and the speakers come out to negotiate. Break the mask of anything bred at this depth and the body comes apart into raw Aether and sinks away down the Well, leaving a gray split shard. Whether what the Well breeds next is the same creature, nobody has been able to prove.
The guardian. Something guards every Heart. It is what the Well grew to keep its own center, bred along that Well’s law, no two alike, with A-Grade spawn for a household and every crew that ever came down for its education. The rolls say the guardian and the taverns say the landlord. Kill it and that is the true clearing: the law at the center has nothing left to hold it in place, the deep lines stop breeding true, and the Core lies open for whoever can stand beside it. Almost nobody clears a Heart. The law down there rewrites anyone below Grandmaster standing who stays, and from the inside it is the truest thing that ever happened to them, while the guardian has the whole ground on its side and has seen your tricks.
The ring. What people do when they cannot. A Containment commission. A Sealwright and a keeper choose a depth where people can stand and seat a bronze ring at the lip of the pool (the ferrule, which limits how wide a sitter can pull) with a brass tundish beside it, a funnel that shows from the door the color of what passes. Everything below that is walled, warded and left alone. A “cleared” dungeon is usually one with its upper floors held and its Heart sealed off and bled from a safe distance, with the guardian still alive behind the seal, still learning.
The keepers. Somebody moves in, for good. Then it is a Core, and everyone in the next valley starts calling it that as though it had always been one.

What a Cleared One Is Worth
More than most kings, which is why so few of them are held by kings.
Hours. The living is selling time at the pool, by the hour, the season or an old obligation. Rich ground fills a practitioner fast, and half the lamp-wardens in a city top up at a Core they do not own. A modest worked site out-earns a good county in a good year, and when every working in a district depends on its hours, its keepers need never raise their voice. See Who Pays for the Lamp.
Masks. A worked dungeon still breeds, so the hall still pays. Prices are on the Well-spawn page: a copper a tail at the Mouth, 2 to 5 gold a mask from the Upper Workings, 10 to 25 from the Lower, 60 to 150 from the Deeps, by contract from the Heart. A dungeon with a town on it has a season, a trade in hammers and a Mask Night.
The harmonization. A place where a person can deliberately sit at the edge of a known Wellspring, with a keeper and a baseline, and come away harmonized with it. Sects go to war over this one.
What is down there. Dungeons keep what people left in them. Old works, relics of the Great Spirit War (the dead battlefields of the days when Bara, Ashura and Aegor walked in human form), a dead Master’s gear with its reputation still on it, an art bottled at the Well and never collected. Every map of a famous dungeon has a room marked on it that has already been looted three times, and the fourth crew always finds something.
Rent. Weddings, as above. Cider, cloth dried in a warm gallery, cheese aged at a steady cold, bath-houses, shrines. A dungeon held for a few generations ends up with a street on its roof and rents that rise with the ground, because a map of a city’s rents is very nearly a map of its ground.
What the crew gets. By custom in the Center and the South the clearing venture takes a third of the hours for nine years, called the clearers’ third, after which the ground-lord pretends he has forgotten who cleared it. The crew usually sells its third in the first week, to a factor, at a price that looks enormous until they have seen what the factor does with it.
When the Wardens Stop Being Paid
Keepers can close a site, and they do. A keeper’s whole family sits on the steps, the hours stop, and every working in the district that depends on them goes thin within the week. A closing has a useful side: with the ring shut, anything fighting on the Well’s ground loses the rung the tie gave it, and a town will pay keepers to close for exactly that reason. It is the ordinary weapon of the trade, and every keeper keeps tending while it lasts, at night, unpaid, for the plain reason that they live there.
The danger comes when the tending stops. The Core-tenders work the lip of the pool in pairs with a fork and a lamp, clearing it and bleeding it a little each shift. Too little and it rises and breeds. Too much and it goes lean and will not recharge by the season. Ward-cutters renew the seals, and a hired crew walks the upper floors every spring. All of them want paying, and when the owner dies, goes to law, or decides the place has been quiet for ninety years and the fee could be spent on bunting, this is what follows. It runs the same way in every register.

Accord Law
Where a circle has signed, the following holds, and where none has, the halls keep their own charters and it holds if you can make it. Past the iron posts of a marker line, the Accord’s jurisdiction ends and nothing holds. Full text is in The Articles of the Accord, which never uses the word dungeon. The formulary says a pool, and the courts have had to stretch that word over everything else, one lawsuit at a time.
Grading. A dungeon is graded by its deepest confirmed band and posted as a Commission of a named Class: Reconnaissance, Extermination, Containment or Retrieval. Nobody may lawfully engage above the title the posting asks. Anything at Grade X or EX goes under the Obsidian Seal, to the Black Concord, and is not posted anywhere you can read it.
Reporting. A new Mouth is reported at the nearest hall within one turn, or the holder of the ground is amerced (fined to his means). Most landholders report late, because a reported Mouth loses them the use of their cellar and gains them a searcher. A Medium-type site is reported first, ahead of all else.
The instrument. A clearing venture binds only on formulary wording (Article VI, and a clause improved is a clause void), before compensated witnesses (VII), registered within one turn (X), with the saving clause for third parties (IX), which is the clause a dead crewman’s widow will bring to court. Crews who improve the clause over beer find out what it costs.
The ring. Once a ring is seated the site is a pool under Title IV. No bore but the standard (XVI). Every ring has its tundish, and covering one is a separate and heavier offense than widening the bore, because that is done to conceal (XVII). Breaking a seal is a term in the cells (XVIII).
The dead leg. A stretch of a round given up shall be capped and reported within one turn, and the fine lands on the owner, “whoever that now is” (XIX). Courts have read this onto abandoned galleries since the middle of the count. That wording is why a lapsed dungeon changes hands so cheaply, why the buyer rarely reads to the end, and why several Midmarch kings have turned out to own a catastrophe by marriage.
The masks. The ground belongs to the ground-lord, the mask to whoever broke it, and the color to nobody, which is the whole of the law on the matter after Pennyhythe.
The check. Essence Resonance Checks are mandatory after a mission, to catch what the ground has done to a crew’s Crystals, and baselines are required before one. Crews dodge the first and forge the second. Nobody has ever been required to baseline a porter.
The porter clause. Here the law stops being funny. Under the Beastkin Classification Provision a licensed labor-stock porter, bought or hired by the season at Verath or its like, is equipment on the instrument. He cannot be a party, cannot hold a share, and cannot be named in the saving clause, and the roll writes him down as nemo, nobody, along with the rope. The deep crews of the Center go down with Catkin and Bearkin at the back of the line carrying the poles. They are the first to say this is wrong, and nobody is obliged to listen, and they are the reason Brokencollar has so many people in it who can read a fork.
Speakers. A bargain with a speaking spawn is void at law. The Accord has never said what remedy it has in mind.
