How a Measurewright Explains It
In the winter of 688 Magister Odalric Penhallow gave the Gradient Lectures at Sealhall to packed benches, and he remains the finest explainer of a dungeon the Guild has produced. His account deserves attention, since a good part of it is true.
A dungeon, said Penhallow, is sediment. Aether at a site runs from thick ground to thin at a rate set by how steep the difference is, the same law that spreads a drop of dye through still water (diffusion, governed by what a modern hand would call Fick’s law). Add a source below and a leak above and you get a steady slope, thickest at the bottom, and any lake with warm water lying on cold will show you how such a slope settles into layers with sharp edges between them. That gives you the five bands. Each band then weeds what can live in it, the way salt weeds a marsh, and over generations each grows its own stock, with clarity of mask tracking density because a harder law leaves a cleaner print. That gives you the ladder. As for the galleries, chemists have long known that a solution soaking through a gel drops its salts in regular rings with nobody arranging them, and rain makes a limestone cave without a plan. That gives you the rooms. There is no will in a dungeon, he told them, thumping a lectern shaped like a Tolling Crab, any more than there is in a bog, and a clever man could read one with a fork and run it from a counting-house.
The bands are right, the weeding is right, and every hall in the world has quietly used his tables since. Then a town called Reedmarch, holding a troubled Millrace under lease, hired him to prove the rest. His prediction followed cleanly from the slope: pull evenly and hard from the top, flatten the gradient, and the breeding must fall. They pulled, with every warden for thirty miles on double hours. By the second season the entire stock of the Lower Workings had come up the shaft after the pull, and most of Reedmarch is now a floor. A Well worked hard breeds more, and his equations had no place for an animal that walks toward its dinner.
The rest of it has troubled better minds than the crews’. A gradient does not explain why a gallery cleared and collapsed in one century grows back in the next with the same turns. A ring in a gel does not explain a stair with a step height of nine inches, in country no one has ever dug, cut for the stride of no people on any roll. It does not explain the handrail. A bog does not let the first party pass to take the porters at the back. Penhallow had answers, and they were very good. At last, to settle it, he went down into a Riptide himself, with a fork and a good staff, and he came back up nine days later in excellent spirits with his coat a shade he had never worn. He has since published four further volumes showing that the dungeon’s behavior is entirely natural, and that it is, on the evidence, rather fond of us. The Guild still funds the chair. His porter left the service that same month, and has not been heard to speak.
The current opinion in the taverns where Measurewrights drink is that a dungeon is a Domain with nobody home. A Domain is the ground in which a high-Stage practitioner’s own law holds, and a Core is a law with no practitioner attached, doing what a law does, extending itself until it is stopped. That explains the bands and the walls, and it invites the question nobody has been willing to fund: a Domain forms around a person’s idea of what the world should be, so whose idea is this one, and what does it want with stairs. I have asked three Measurewrights. I got five answers and a bill for the wine.

Read next: Monster Cores, for what comes back up; The Sixty Wellsprings, for what pools at the bottom; The Bestiary, for what lives on the way down.

the-bestiary/index.title: The Bestiary
the-bestiary/index.content:
Fifty-four attested creatures · Spirit-born, Draconic, Natural, Aberrant, Undying, Divine, Well-bred, and the Scourge-born, under protest

Every entry answers the same eleven questions, and the order of the questions is itself a doctrine. Origin before appearance. Essence Affinity before abilities. Weaknesses in the same breath as powers.
A field guide that tells you what a thing can do without telling you what feeds it has told you nothing.

The register began with a wager and a one-armed man. At the Hide Fair at Cold Ansty, late in the Long Reckoning, when the upland drovers came down in their red felts to trade fleeces and lie about wolves, a Guild copyist named Piers Wetherby climbed onto a wool-bale with a ledger under his arm and offered a silver to anybody who could show him a beast he had not already written down. By noon he had paid out for a two-headed lamb, which turned out to be a lamb and a half, and refused a goat that could count, which could not. A little after the third bell a griffon came down the sheep-lane on foot. She stood taller than the horse-lines, bronze and gold from beak to shoulder, with the great lion haunches rolling behind, and she smelled of hot feathers and high cold air, and the laughing crowd opened in front of her like a pulled curtain, because at the far end of the lane a drover’s boy had a basket, and in the basket, for sale at six coppers, sat something the color of egg yolk with strong opinions about him. She took down an awning, two stalls and a cheese-seller’s ladder without hurrying. She took off Piers Wetherby’s left arm below the elbow, because he had stepped in close to look at her feet. Then she lifted the basket in her beak, handle and all, and walked out through four hundred people and thirty hunters with boar-spears, and looked at none of them, and none of them followed.
Wetherby wrote the entry that night with the hand he had left, feverish on a heap of fleeces, and the page survives, brown at one corner where he bled on it. It gives what feeds her before it gives what she looks like. Under Weaknesses, in letters that run downhill, it says leaves the fight to keep the nest. Give back the chick. Every keeper of this register since has worked to his form, and I have the same rule and a smaller scar.
Read upward and the register changes its nature as it climbs. At the bottom sit the pests and the fen-things, every one of which has eaten somebody’s chickens. At the top sit creatures that were old when Bara, Ashura and Aegor still walked in human form, whose names sailors will not say on a falling tide, and those are written here with the same eleven questions, because a thing can be worthy of a hymn and still have a diet.
An entry describes a line, and the animal in front of you has been eating. The Hask Moor drovers will tell you about the she-wolf they called Aunt Teeth, posted in the spring of 702 as an ordinary C-Grade Greater Wolf at forty silver marks. She ate her pack by midsummer, then the party sent after her, then a wyvern’s fledgling, and by the autumn fair she stood as tall as a dray horse with her coat gone the color of a bruised plum, and the bill on every door between Hask and the sea read Grade A, three hundred gold, and she has been seen to open a gate. The bookies had her at nine to two against the Saffron Hoods. Her hide is a coat now, and two towns claim the skull.
The Entry Skeleton













































NamesThe High or Old Parunic form, plus whatever the people who actually live near it call the thing. The two are rarely complimentary of each otherTypeSpirit Beast · Draconic Lineage · Natural Beast · Aberration · Undying · Construct · Divine or Archonic Beast · Elemental · Well-spawn · Hybrid · Scourge-born, filed with the Natural Beasts under protestOriginWhich Age, which Wellspring convergence, and which Archon or Titan is credited, credit being a matter of tradition rather than record in most casesEssence AffinityThe Wellspring the creature runs on (one of the sixty alchemical and spiritual transformations, the governing idea that shapes how a soul uses Aether, a source of power to pull from, and a type of Aether as well). This is the operative field. Everything the thing can do and every way it can be beaten follows from itLeans onThe layer of the soul its power runs through, which is its Path. How the thing lives sets it: what hunts by weight, hide and heat leans on the Aether Shell and the flesh, what feeds on memory and meaning leans on the Essence Core, and what lives by turning luck leans on the Attraction Layer. The Affinity’s kind only tips the scale (a Wild Affinity toward the Shell, a Spirit one toward the Core, a Fate one toward the Layer, a Medium one toward whichever the line has grown into), and the register has plenty of Wild-fed things that live as Spirit monsters. This tells you who to bring, and the entries say so road by roadRealm AffiliationWhere it is native and where it has been recorded strayingGradeE through EX, the same letters the Commission posts its bounties by. An SS bounty may be lawfully taken only under a Grandmaster’s titleWeaknessesRecorded in the same detail as the abilities. This is what separates a bestiary from a bestiary of rumorsHistorical EncountersNamed engagements with dates where the Archives hold them, and folk accounts where they do notCultural SignificanceWhat the thing means to the people who share ground with it, which is frequently at odds with what it is
The Grades
Lords post bounties by these letters, heralds cry them from the market cross, and a hunter’s fee and her funeral are both priced off the same column.
A beast is lettered and a person never is. The Grade is the register’s whole verdict on a line: what it usually climbs to, what it takes to lawfully engage, and what the bill on the door will say. Underneath the letter a monster that has cracked its seal stands on the same climb a person does (How Power Grows gives the long account): it holds a Stage of the Sixteen, it has a Level, it lays Pressure by the Stage gap exactly as a practitioner of that rank would, it leans on a Path, and from the height of Glory the coil can read its Mastery on that road.

















































































































GradeThreatStages and rank it runs withLevelIts auraMastery on its roadAttestedE(none entered)I, Murmuring: an Initiate’sFrom 1None to speak of. Most are sealed beasts with no auraUnreadThe rat in the grain store and the fox at the hens. No hall has ever opened a Commission for one, so the register asks its questions of nothing hereDMinor / Moderate ThreatII, Welling: an Apprentice’sFrom 5Felt by the unwoken as dreadUnreadZombies · Tanuki · Tinder-fox · Leveling LeechCModerate ThreatIII, Ascension: a Journeyman’sFrom 15Weight in the room, for the unwokenUnreadGreater Wolf · Sasquatch · Dryads · Lid-crawlerBHigh ThreatIV, Flourishing: an Adept’sFrom 30, and to 100 at most before the pressure turns to strainWeight in the room. The first Grade at which a named one may show a ReleaseUnreadUnicorn · Harpy · Skeletal Folk · Neiman Lion · Psy-Apes · Ghouls · Bai Ze · Hippogrif · Siren · Pegasus · Glarewing · Reaching Briar · Haze-kite · StiltAExtreme ThreatV to VII, Splintering to Refraction: an Expert’s101 to 200The unwoken go to their knees. At the top of the band a room of Splintering hunters sweats and sickensUnread until Glory’s hold, then I, and II at Refraction from Level 150Bicorn · Griffon · Goliath · Raiju · Lamia · Living Armor · Minotaur · Cyclops · Basilisk · Cockatrice · Hellhound · Manticore · Sump-toad · Tolling Crab · Mourning Pike · GreywalkerSDomain ThreatVIII to X, Transcendence to Realization: a Master’s201 to 300As its Stage. This is the Domain band, and the oldest of them hold ground as lawII or III, and IV at Realization from Level 260Wyvern · Sea Serpent · Arachne · Wendigo · Lamp-drinkerSSRealm HazardXI and XII, Dissonance and Emanation: a Grandmaster’s301 to 400As its Stage. The weather answersIV, and V at Emanation from Level 340Wyrm · Night Gaunt · Gorgon · PhoenixXCataclysmic EntityXIII and XIV, Principality and Zenith: an Archmaster’s401 to 500As its StageVHydra · Voidwyrm · CerberusEXApocalyptic BeastXV and XVI, Revelation and Apex: a Paragon’sPast 500As its Stage, which is to say a coast at a timeΩLeviathan · Lich · KrakenC to XVariableAcross the whole rangeAcross the whole rangeAs its StageAs its StageElemental, the only entry in the register whose Grade is a range rather than a letter, running from a minor natural disturbance to a colossus that reshapes landscapeNot enteredA blank rowUnknownUnknownUnknownUnknownThe things in the dry beds of the Scourge of Hell. Nobody has come back to name them, and what they leave is half-carts and very clean bones
The Commission also counts what a creature does to a road, a crew or a coast, so a line can be posted a Grade above the band its Stage sits in, and the coil settles any quarrel. The Accord sets which title may take which Grade of bounty, letter for rank: an Initiate’s title takes an E, a Master’s an S, a Paragon’s an EX. A named beast’s Mastery is read the way a person’s is, from its Level under its Stage’s ceiling, and a Fate monster’s climbs with its Level like the others and stops at II unless a blessing has given it the grip. A famous monster can show a Release, the full form of what its evolutions were reaching for, with a name the heralds give it since it has none of its own to call. No monster takes a class. The soul offers a class to a life that has been chosen, and a beast’s has only happened to it. What stands in a monster’s window where a class would is the name of its last evolution.
The old registers counted the same nine steps as Danger Tiers, T1 to T9, and drovers still say “a T5 wolf” for an A.
The ladder beside the Grade. A Grade is the Commission’s rating: what it takes to lawfully engage a creature. The Bestiary ladder in The Tier Ladders reads the same creature by what it can break, from Hearth-pest to Sky-eater, and by what lifts it: reach, persistence and the ground that feeds it. The two often disagree, and the difference is where a hunter finds the answer.
Monsters Climb
They level and they evolve. A monster gains Levels by killing, each other included, and changes form at its own thresholds, and when it does the register enters a new name beside the old one. It climbs the same Stages and Level a person does, and only the beast is lettered. A Grade on this page is what the line usually reaches, and the bill on the door is what this one has become.
They are everywhere. Monsters move and live across the whole Inner World, and beasts more widely still. Every realm has its bad road and its song about it. The Scourge of Hell is the one area known for extremely dangerous ones.
They get famous. A famous monster earns a name, an epithet and a bounty, and lords post it, heralds cry it, minstrels get it wrong and bookies give odds. On the survey of the Scourge the great ones carry a small crown on the map, and each of those is its own entry in everything but the paperwork.
They have windows. A window is the soul reporting its numbers to its owner, unseen by anyone else, and a beast’s soul reports like any other, though what a beast makes of it no one has asked. A faculty whose Gnosis Perception outranks the creature’s Resilience Ward by a full step can read it like a person’s, and the rest of us are estimating aloud at speed. A hunter who could read Aunt Teeth in her last autumn would have seen something like this:
[Moor Tyrant, formerly Greater Wolf]
[Level 163 · Grade A]
[Strike Force: B · Celerity: A]
[Pack Hunter]
[Reserve: 41%]

The last line is the one to read, because an ordinary wolf has no reserve to report. It has a sealed Shell and a stone. By her last autumn Aunt Teeth had cracked hers, and had something to spend.
They are worth money. A monster’s core is in a way its Soul Crystal, worth more the stronger the monster, and an alchemist renders it into Essence Drafts for tempering. Its parts make gear. The rows and prices are in Hide, Horn and Bone, and the Drafts in The Common Drafts.
They walk the three roads. A monster leans on one layer of its soul, set by how it lives and only tipped by the kind of Wellspring it feeds on, and the lean sorts the whole register. Body monsters are the common kind: drakes, crushers, anything that packs raw Aether in a cracked Shell and hits with it. Spirit monsters are rarer: wraiths, and the things that eat memory, which go past armor and work on souls. Fate monsters are the rarest and the most feared, a beast that turns bad luck on its hunters, so that the straps give and the bowstring is damp before anyone has seen it move. The road decides what the stone becomes on the bench as well: every stone is mostly Core, but a Body monster’s packed Charge sets into its stone and parts out as heavy Salt ash, so a Body core renders chiefly to Salts, a Spirit core to the richest Core stock, and only a Fate core grows the thin skin that is shaved off as the Layer reagent of the black market. See Monster Cores.
Many come from below. A dungeon grows down in floors around a Core (a site where one Wellspring’s Aether pools) with something guarding the heart, and it is alive and learning, and most of what this register lists either came out of one or is on its way back in. See Dungeons.
The Scourge-born are the register’s standing embarrassment. The great herds of the Scourge of Hell breed true and wear no masks, which the register’s own rules say should not happen, since an animal warped by dense ground is supposed to come out short-lived and sterile. They have been at it so long that they stopped being warped and became a kind of animal. The Lid-crawler, the Haze-kite, the Stilt and the Greywalker are filed with the Natural Beasts, under protest, and above a certain size each holds a range and treats you as its own until you leave or die.
What Has a Soul
The physicians’ question, which hunters ask with a spear in their hands. Every soul has three layers: the Aether Shell, where Aether (mana) comes in and a working goes back out into matter; the Essence Core, the seat of what a thing is; and the Attraction Layer, its share of fate. The Three Paths gives the long account. What differs across this register is how much of each is working.





























































What it isAether ShellEssence CoreAttraction LayerWhat followsThe unwoken (a baker, a porter)Sealed. Waking cracks it, and most never wakeAwake, holding a trickle of Essence it cannot spendA small share, enough to swear onA window with a Level and a few trade skills, and no workings. Pressure falls on them by the Aura table. A Draft reaches them through the CoreA beast (born of a mother, not yet much of anything)SealedAwake. What comes in from the ground and its kills has nowhere to go, so it bands up as the stoneThin, holding a mate, a pack or a range and little elseNo aura and no reserve. What a saturated line does is passive, and leaks through the seal: a cold, a dread, a glow in a maneA monster (a beast that has climbed)Cracked, by an evolution or a Level threshold, and a small vent on a great storeBanded and old, with a stone worth cutting outThin, thickening where the line runs on a Fate WellspringAn aura, a named howl, a Reserve line on the window. This is the difference between the wolf and Aunt TeethWell-spawnSealed in the shallow lines, cracked in the deep onesFlooded with the Well’s Aether until the line lives by the Well’s law, and it carries a stoneThin, until the Deeps, where a line gathers a mind out of what the Well remembersThe mask stands where a glyph would and holds the law in place. Break it. See [[The Bestiary/The Corrupted and the Risen/Well-spawnA Spirit BeastWhatever it has grown to keep a body, often little, and sometimes no body at allWhole. It was formed from a Wellspring’s resonance and it began here, with a mind and a memoryWhole enough to bargain, bond and blessA hitter can kill what it is wearing and has then told it to leave. Its stone, where there is one, is seldom worth the valley’s opinionA Divine or Archonic beastGenuine and very clean, carrying far more than any practitioner’sGenuine, and often a single function where a person has a biographyGenuine, and bonded to a place, a route or an officeRead on the climb exactly as a person is, and lettered like any beast. These are the ones that answer a summons on their own termsA CelestialWhole, folded out of the Lawbell’s resonance with no upbringing behind itWhole, carrying what its function requires and, in the young ones, very little elseExternally anchored, tied to the Throne-network in place of a share of its ownAdministration made flesh. See [[Cosmology & Metaphysics/Faith and the Powers Above/The Celestial Host
Who to Bring
A creature’s Leans on line reads the same way a person’s Path does, by how the thing lives and not by its Affinity alone (the Affinities named in the table are the usual case), and the three roads beat one another the way The Three Paths says they do. Each entry below gives the short form. Stage, ground and preparation decide which of it holds on the day.



































It leans onBringWhyWhat goes wrongThe Shell (a Wild Affinity: matter, force, heat)A Spirit hand, or a Fate hand with time to setSpirit goes past hide and plate, since Durability does not cover a soul. Fate moves what its charge depends on (the footing, the pack’s timing, the wind), so the blow never arrives. A Body fighter meets it at its own strength and needs to be the strongerSpirit dies out of position, and a Wild thing’s whole idea is to close. Fate cannot move a sound avalanche, and some of these are soundThe Core (a Spirit Affinity: meaning, memory, mind)A Body fighter if it has a body, because a spear does not care what it means. A Fate hand, because a thing that survives by being right needs only one spoiled readIf it has no body, a blade has nothing to bite, and only a Spirit hand can reach itBody fighters walk in without a ward on their own Core. Spirit against Core is a straight contest of souls, and it has been doing this longerThe Layer (a Fate Affinity: bonds, debts, odds)A Body fighter, for force and soundness: a well-kept harness offers no strap to give. A Spirit hand, since every pull is made by a soul and shows on the Core before it landsKill the thing the bond runs through and the bond has nothing to pull withFate against Fate is a contest of weights at about equal cost to both, which is why nobody with a choice does itMedium (at home on all three)One of each, and read it firstIt may answer on any layer, and it usually answers on the one you did not bringEverything, which is why a Medium site goes to the top of the board
Set that beside the three old answers below and the register sorts itself. A Sealwright is a Spirit trade (a Writ on the thing’s law), a priest is usually a Spirit hand with a congregation behind him, and the long march is a Body answer to ground, open to anybody with boots.
What the Register Shows at Scale

Almost everything above Grade S is a Wellspring event wearing an animal. The Leviathan, the Kraken, the Hydra, the Voidwyrm and the Cerberus all owe their danger, far more than their size, to their relationship to a Wellspring site, a Crevice, or a plane boundary.
The Lich is the exception, and the Lich is the exception because it used to be a person.

The weaknesses cluster. Read across the register and the same three vulnerabilities recur: Essence-dampening, removal from the native Wellspring (getting the creature off the ground where its kind of Aether pools, or starving it there), and radiant or holy current. The practical counter to the majority of the register is therefore seldom a weapon. It is a Sealwright, a long march, or a priest.
Corruption is a lineage rather than a condition. The Bicorn, the Voidwyrm, the Wendigo and the Blackened share a grammar: something that was one thing has been converted by Abyssal, Void or Crevice contact into something that cannot go back. The register treats this as taxonomy. The Heresiology would treat the same material as a diagnosis.
And the register is honest about the thing bestiaries usually lie about. Griffons abandon a fight to protect a nest, as Piers Wetherby could have told you with the arm he had left. Unicorns evade rather than engage. The Bai Ze is physically fragile and avoids conflict entirely. Four of the register’s most feared entries would rather leave.
Entries
Read beside the entries: the Sixty for what a creature’s Affinity is and what ground it hates, The Physical Account for what a blow is, and Windows and the Sheet for what a monster’s window can tell you.
Six pages, grouped by Type. Spirit Beasts · The Draconic Lineage · Natural Beasts · Aberrations · The Undying and the Constructs · Divine, Archonic and Elemental.


Spirit Beasts
The Draconic Lineage
Natural Beasts
Aberrations
The Undying and the Constructs
Divine, Archonic and Elemental


The bound and the bred
The six pages above catalog what exists. The two below are different kinds of entry. A called thing has somebody answerable for it. A Well’s get has nobody answerable for it, and is every delver’s problem.


Summoned and Bound
Well-spawn


Where they live
Most of the register lives on ground that is trying to kill you for its own reasons.


Dungeons
Monster Cores



Read next: Dungeons, where most of this register is met; The Three Paths, for who beats what and how a creature’s lean plays; Monster Cores, for what a dead one is worth.

the-bestiary/the-called-and-the-divine/d.title: Divine, Archonic and Elemental
the-bestiary/the-called-and-the-divine/d.content:
Four entries · what is not an animal at all

Three of the four are Grade X or EX, the top of the register. The fourth has no fixed Grade because it has no fixed size.
Size is the least of what makes any of them dangerous. Each is dangerous because of its relationship to a Wellspring site, a trench, or a gate.

The herring came up the streets of Morrowhythe before the water did. That was the first morning of the Year of the Seven Tides, and the whole harbor had turned out in its market colors for the Blessing of the Nets, saffron and sea-green and the fishwives’ red kerchiefs, when the sea went out past the bar and left the fleet lying on its side, came back silver and stinking to the third step of the Fishmongers’ Hall, went out, and came back again, seven times between dawn and dusk. On the seventh the whole bay lifted. Something rose out of it crowned in coral and jagged bone, abyss-black, traced down the neck in faint blue light, and it went on rising long after everyone on the quay had agreed that it must be finished. It never looked at Morrowhythe. It looked at a patch of empty water four leagues out, and the eye that crossed the harbor on the way there dropped the Reeve and his whole watch to their knees, along with a great many people who had only come for the fish. Then it went under, and the wave it left put nine boats on rooftops and the bell tower in the bay, and for the rest of that season the cod ran where the mackerel had run, three towns went broke, one got very rich, and every pilot on the coast had to learn the water again from the beginning.
Morrowhythe entered a plea against the Titan Zar’thuun in the Reeve’s court for nine boats and a bell tower, and served it by rowing out past the bar and throwing it in the sea. I have read the file, and it is still open, and I have seldom felt so warmly toward a town. Everything on this page is the sort of thing you sue anyway. I have handled a shed Kraken beak and been singed through a good boot by an ember off a Cerberus, and I will tell you what I tell the apprentices: these four are worthy of every hymn ever sung about them, and they also eat, sleep, tire, and keep to their ground, and the eating and the ground are where you start.
Elemental

Called Wellspring Incarnates or Primordial Spirits depending on region and Essence affinity.

Elemental Behemoth, Pure Manifestation · Grade C through X · found wherever their respective kind of Aether pools thickest
Leans on · the Shell, nearly always, since one is a Wild law with a body built around it, and the kind of Aether decides the rest. Body: a big enough hit at the one solid part. Spirit: the thing has a Core at the center and no idea you can reach it. Fate: it stops when the ground stops feeding it, and a site can be made to fail.
Living manifestations of raw Wellspring power, formed when one kind of Aether concentrates with nothing to refine it, around rich Wellspring sites or wherever elemental energies surge unchecked. (The old books say Essence concentrating in an unmediated state, and a Measurewright will correct them at length.) Their existence predates many mortal races, and they act as guardians or destroyers depending on circumstance and alignment.
There is no skeleton to describe and I have stopped looking for one. The body is whatever the Aether is doing at the moment: roaring flame, crashing wave, jagged stone, swirling gust and lightning. They shimmer with Wellspring power and may manifest elemental runes glowing faintly along their bodies. The nearest thing to a metabolism is the ground under them. A small one feeds at a site the way a flame feeds at a wick, and a colossus reshapes the landscape because the landscape is what it is eating.



































TypeBorn fromCharacterPowersFireThe molten veins of Theros and volcanic Wellspring sitesFierce and destructiveFlame manipulation, explosive bursts, heat aurasWaterThe flowing currents of Etherea and aquatic Wellspring sitesFluid and adaptiveTidal surges, water manipulation, healing mistsEarthMountains, deep caves, and ancient stone Wellspring sitesStoic and relentlessTremors, rock armor, seismic shockwavesAirStorm clouds and wind-swept peaks, linked to Caelum and DraconisSwift and capriciousGusts, lightning strikes, invisibility in fog or storm

They share a core identity as forces of nature rather than thinking beings. Some develop rudimentary awareness or bond with mortals. Others act as impersonal natural phenomena and never notice that anyone was there.

Vulnerable to Essence opposition: water douses fire, earth grounds air. Dispersible by powerful ritual magic or Essence-dampening wards. And some require constant Wellspring power to hold form, so that depletion causes collapse: walk one off rich ground and it comes apart behind you like a wave going back down a beach.
The Great Eruption of Helstra was blamed on a rampaging Fire Elemental that shattered an ancient volcano’s seal. The Storm of the Thousand Winds marked a surge of Air Elementals summoned by a lost sorcerer’s folly. Some tribes seek to bind them for protection or war. Others leave sacred Wellspring sites untouched to honor their guardianship.
Leviathan

The Drowned Crown in Old Mariner’s Cant. Vor’thalass, the Maw Beneath All Waves, in Abyssal Tongue.

Divine / Archonic Beast, Abyssal Apex · Grade EX, Apocalyptic Beast · Abython, the Abyssal Pulse, secondary Nihiloth and Cymorath aspects · primarily Abythron, surfacing only in Crevice-linked oceans
Leans on · the Shell, by Abython, Wild, with Nihiloth and Cymorath. Body: nobody on record. Spirit: a very great Core a very long way down. Fate: it surfaces only through what a Crevice allows, and that is the only lever anyone has ever suggested.

Singular oceanic behemoths birthed directly by Titans of the deep. Most descend from a time before Gaia’s shaping of the Material World, when the oceans were unbroken voidwater.
The most feared is the Leviathan of Abythron, created by Zar’thuun as a guardian of the deepest void trenches, an amalgam of abyssal essence, deep-sea adaptation and ancient draconic bloodline, giving it an unnatural combination of resilience and cunning.

A colossal sea serpent stretching hundreds of meters, armored in abyss-black scales traced with faint bioluminescence. Coral-like horns and jagged bone crests crown the head, and the coral is living coral, which tells you how long it can hold still. The maw is lined with layered teeth capable of crushing iron-bound hulls, set in rows like a shark’s and replaced like a shark’s, and the Abythron shelf-fishers have sold me three of the shed ones at a price I still resent. The eyes glow deep abyssal blue and can induce fear or paralysis in weaker wills.
Solitary and immensely territorial, it is drawn to disturbances in deep Wellspring sites: anything that stirs the pooled Aether of the trenches brings it up. It moves slowly and deliberately in the deep and with blistering speed when striking.

It hunts both physically and metaphysically, dragging ships and creatures beneath the surface while severing their soul’s tether to the living realm.

Tidal Maelstrom generates whirlpools large enough to pull fleets under. Void Gaze locks eyes to inflict soul-severing dread and Essence disruption. Abyssal Breath exhales pressurized supercooled abyssal water (water chilled below its freezing point and kept liquid by the crush of the deep), which freezes the moment it strikes and shatters fortification. Domain Anchor makes it a living stabilizer of abyssal Wellspring ground, warping local sea and sky.
Vulnerable in prolonged shallow-water combat where its maneuverability is reduced. The Abyssal Breath requires recovery time, and disrupting the buildup prevents the strike. And its bioluminescent markings, if targeted, disrupt its camouflage.

The Fall of Altherion’s Eastern Fleet was attributed to a leviathan attack during the Third Concord War. No survivors, and a shattered coast.
Sailors still tell of the Year of the Seven Tides, when the Leviathan of Abythron surfaced repeatedly and altered ocean currents for an entire season.
Abyssal cults worship it as a herald of Zar’thuun’s return. Coastal nations mark it as a doomsday sign in their prophecy records.

Kraken

Tsal’gar, Terror of the Depths, in Old Parunic. The Abyssal Maw among sailors.

Divine Beast, Abyssal Colossus · Grade EX, Apocalyptic Threat · Abython and Thaloré, with powerful chaotic Essence surges · the deepest ocean trenches and the Abyssal Depths
Leans on · the Shell by Abython, Wild, and the Core by Thaloré, Spirit, which is why a town goes down grieving. Body: the arms, by a fleet, for as long as the fleet lasts. Spirit: the sorrow on the water is not yours, and knowing that is most of what a priest can do. Fate: do not be the boat it is going to meet.
A primordial sea monster born from the violent convergence of Abython and Thaloré in the deepest trenches. Legend places their creation during cataclysmic oceanic upheavals.
The body is a cephalopod’s on a scale that makes the comparison feel like an insult: dozens of powerful barbed tentacles around a massive beaked maw, eyes glowing with abyssal light, and skin shimmering with bioluminescent pattern that crawls and changes the way a cuttlefish’s does when it is deciding about you. The beak is the only hard part of the animal, and a shed one will not fit through a barn door. Its sheer size dwarfs most sea vessels.
Territorial and overwhelmingly destructive, they are solitary hunters, believed to be ancient and near-immortal.
Tentacle Crush grapples and pulverizes ships. Abyssal Roar raises waves and disorients. Ink Veil releases Essence-infused ink that obscures vision and dampens magical senses, so that a practitioner in the cloud loses the sea and his sensing together. Water Manipulation generates currents and whirlpools.
Vulnerable to Essence-purging magic and to fire-ships and the Guild’s fire-casks. Slow on land and exposed when beached. And it rarely ventures far from deep Wellspring sites, which limits encounters to those who go looking.
The Sinking of the Iron Leviathan, a Concord flagship named for her iron-sheathed ram, remains a cautionary tale of a Kraken attack. Coastal communities hold festivals to ward off its wrath, invoking ancient sea rites, with a great deal of dancing and a great many paper tentacles.
Cerberus

Gar’thak, the Threefold Maw, in Abyssal tongues. The Hellhound Guardian in frontier legend.

Divine Beast, Infernal Guardian · Grade X, Cataclysmic Threat · Tarturon and Nihiloth, infused with potent Pyreveil and Vantabriel Essence · Abyssal Depths, corrupted crevices, forbidden Outer World gates
Leans on · the Layer first, by Tarturon, Fate, and the Shell by Pyreveil, Vantabriel and Nihiloth. Body: soundness, a great many hands, and no debts. Spirit: three heads and one hand on the reckoning, showing on the Core before it lands. Fate: it holds a gate as a condition, so the contest is over the condition and never the dog.
A colossal three-headed hellhound born from corruption on Tarturon ground and ancient infernal bindings, crafted as the eternal guardian of Abyssal gates and cursed Wellspring breaches. It embodies raw destructive power and unwavering loyalty to its dark masters.
The build is a massive canine’s, with three snarling heads, each with fiery eyes and razor fangs. Thick shadowy fur is laced with flickering embers, which come off when it shakes and burn through a boot sole faster than you would believe. The claws burn with infernal heat, and flames flicker along a spiked tail. Each head keeps its own watch, and I have never met a hunter who caught all three asleep.
It is fierce, relentless and highly territorial. It hunts intruders without mercy and can track Essence signatures across realms.
Tri-Headed Strike attacks multiple foes simultaneously. Infernal Breath lets each head unleash fire, shadow flame, or poisonous smoke. Essence Tracker senses Wellspring and life Essence to pursue prey relentlessly. Hellfire Aura burns nearby enemies and disrupts Essence flow.

Vulnerable to coordinated assaults targeting each head separately. Sensitive to radiant Essence magic and holy wards.
And it is bound by infernal contracts, and breaking these can weaken or banish it outright. Which makes the Cerberus the only entry in the register with a legal counterplay.

The Siege of the Black Maw details Concord forces struggling to breach Abyssal gates guarded by a Cerberus. Tales of hunters facing the Threefold Terror circulate among frontier camps, and every one of those hunters is somebody’s cousin.

Read next: The Fourteen Archons and The Fourteen Titans, for what stands behind these; The Sixty Wellsprings, for the sites they guard.
