the-bestiary/the-called-and-the-divine/i.title: The Called and the Divine
the-bestiary/the-called-and-the-divine/i.content:
Things that come because they were asked, and things that were never asked at all.
Ask a Commission hunter the difference and she will roll up both sleeves: the left arm is from a thing somebody called, and she got damages, and the right arm is from a thing nobody called, and there was nobody to sue but the sea.


Summoned and Bound Called things, entered as creatures. What a summoner keeps on a chain and what the chain is actually made of.
Divine, Archonic and Elemental Four entries · what is not an animal at all



Read next: The Bestiary, for how the register reads; The Fourteen Archons and The Fourteen Titans, for the laws these things answer to.

the-bestiary/the-corrupted-and-the-risen.filePath: The Bestiary/The Corrupted and the Risen/Aberrations/Aberrations.md
the-bestiary/the-corrupted-and-the-risen.title: Aberrations
the-bestiary/the-corrupted-and-the-risen.content:
Ten entries · what corruption makes when it is given a shape to work with
Long Sim Tupper smuggled the egg into Harl’s Cross in a crate of speckled hens, on the morning of the Feather Fair, under a forged Guild mark, for a buyer who wanted cockatrice feathers for a purpose he did not care to describe. It hatched at noon on the poultry row, between a stall of blue ribbons and a man selling hot chestnuts. Its first look fell on the hens, a dozen of them, mid-squabble, and they went gray from the beak backward and stayed that way. Its second look found the auctioneer, Mistress Ilse Thackray, with one arm up and her mouth open on a bid, and it climbed the awning on wet green wings and looked down the whole length of the fair. Twenty-six people stopped where they stood, Long Sim among them, with his left hand in a purse whose owner has been unable to complain. The lord’s bill was on the church door by dark. By morning a crew out of Durnath who called themselves the Looking-Glass Company had bought every copper pan, tin tray and polished shield in the county, at prices the tinkers’ guild still recalls with tears of joy, and they went up the row behind a wall of kitchenware, at a walk, singing to keep step. It took until dusk, two of their men and one very large frying pan. Harl’s Cross charges a copper now to walk the stone row, and on feast days the children dare each other to put a hat on the auctioneer.
A cockatrice was a hen and a serpent before it was a calamity, and that is the whole reason it has a place on this shelf.

Every entry here was something else first. Serpent Essence and corrupted human souls. Cursed unions. Mortals who succumbed to hunger. Draconic bloodlines that fractured.
Aberration is a verdict on a lineage, and the word has never once described a species.

A note for crews before you take the bill. An Aberration carries no mask for a hall clerk to weigh, so these are paid by bounty, under a Grade and the title to take it like everything else, and each bill names the proof it wants: the horn, the stinger, the head. Read it twice. A crew once carried a gorgon’s head forty miles under a blanket and learned at the castle gate that the lord had wanted it looking at his brother.
Bicorn

Zarvak, Twin Horn, in Old Parunic. The Shadow Charger among occult circles.

Aberrant Beast, Infernal Charger · Grade A, Extreme Threat · Tarturon and Nihiloth, infused with infernal Essence · Abyssal Depths and cursed Outer World wastelands
Leans on · the Layer first, by Tarturon, Fate, and the Shell by Nihiloth, Wild. Body: force and soundness, and nothing owing. Spirit: the hand on its reckoning shows on the Core before it lands, and that Core is corrupted and cannot go back. Fate: it collects on what you already owe, so owe nothing.
Fiendish mounts and warriors born from corruption on Tarturon ground, mingled with ancient infernal bloodlines. Legend places their creation as steeds for dark warlords and demon princes.
Large muscular equines with glossy black coats and two curved sharp horns rising from the forehead. Eyes glowing crimson, hooves burning with faint embers. Shadows cling to their forms, flickering like living smoke.
Aggressive and territorial, forming small herds under dominant stallions. Their presence is accompanied by unsettling whispers and shadowy auras.
Infernal Charge shatters armor and barriers. Shadow Aura saps morale and disrupts Essence flow. Hellfire Hooves leave burning wounds that resist healing. Dark Whisper causes fear and confusion.
Vulnerable to radiant Essence and holy magic. Sensitive to coordinated ranged attacks disrupting the charge. Require proximity to Tarturon ground to maintain peak power.
The Blood Sundering of Vellsorea details a bicorn herd charging through Concord ranks and scattering them. Their horns and hides are prized in dark rituals, and some forbidden tomes name them harbingers of apocalyptic wars.
Hellhound

Khal’zor, Infernal Fang, in Abyssal tongues. The Flamehound among frontier warriors.

Aberration Beast, Infernal Tracker · Grade A, Extreme Threat · Tarturon and Nihiloth, with an intense Pyreveil overlay · Abyssal Depths and corrupted warzones
Leans on · the Layer first, by Tarturon, Fate, and the Shell by Pyreveil and Nihiloth, both Wild. Body: it tracks a debt and arrives hot, so meet it on open water if you can. Spirit: reach the Core, and it has very little left in it but the trail. Fate: the trail is a thread, and it can be moved at the usual price.
Summoned or spawned from cursed battlegrounds and Abyssal rifts, serving dark warlords, demons and necromancers as relentless hunters and guardians.
Large canine forms wreathed in flickering flames and shadow. Eyes blazing molten red, fur smoldering with internal fire. Jaws dripping acidic saliva.
Aggressive, loyal, relentless. They hunt in packs or alone and are capable of terrifying coordinated attacks.
Flame Breath ignites foes and terrain. Infernal Paws leave burning tracks that trap pursuers. Essence Tracking detects signatures across vast distance. Shadowmeld makes them nearly invisible at night.
Vulnerable to water and cold-based Essence. Their fire can be extinguished or redirected with elemental skill. And they depend on Tarturon ground to maintain peak infernal power.
The Burning Hunt of Durnath describes a pack slaughtering a Concord supply convoy. Infernal cults raise them as war beasts or gatekeepers to Abyssal realms.
Night Gaunt

Skathul, Silent Shadow, in Outer World tongues. The Black Whisper among occult circles.

Aberration, Void-Touched Hunter · Grade SS, Realm Hazard · Vantabriel and Nihiloth · the Outer World's shadow domains and Abythron borderlands
Leans on · the Shell, by Vantabriel and Nihiloth, both Wild. Body: light and a crowd first, and then a spear. Spirit: it does not hide from what reads souls as it hides from eyes. Fate: a thing that hunts by the dark depends on the dark holding.

Spawned at the intersection of Vantabriel and Nihiloth, their existence predating mortal memory. Believed to be shadowy servants of ancient Archons tasked with harvesting souls and spreading fear.
Their bodies phase between dimensions, allowing them to appear and vanish at will.

Skeletal gaunt figures with elongated limbs and membranous wings that absorb light. Skin deep shadow-black, almost translucent in moonlight, eyes burning with cold pale blue fire. Joints crack audibly as they move with unnerving silence.
Cold, predatory, relentless. They stalk in darkness before striking with lethal precision, exploiting fear and confusion. Their presence causes unsettling whispers and hallucinations, weakening mental defenses.
Phase Shift slips between shadow and reality, becoming intangible briefly. Soul Rend: strikes sever Essence threads, causing instant paralysis or death. Whispering Veil induces terror and hallucination. Silent Flight.

Vulnerable to light-based Essence and sacred wards. Physical attacks harm them during phase-shift recovery. And they are highly sensitive to sound: loud noise disrupts their stealth.

The Black Whisper Hunt chronicles a Concord operation to purge an infestation from a remote frontier town. Survivors recount eerie voices and vanished neighbors before the final battle.
Lamia

Serpentara, Mistress of Scales, in Old Parunic. Veilbinder among southern frontier tribes.

Aberration, Enigmatic Spirit-Hybrid · Grade A, Extreme Threat · Anamnesis and Nihiloth, with a minor Oneirion influence · Material World borderlands and shadowed enclaves
Leans on · the Core, by Anamnesis, Medium, with Oneirion and Nihiloth. Body: she is close and she is flesh, once you can find which one. Spirit: a contest, and she has eaten better minds. Fate: her enchantments survive by reading you correctly, and they can be spoiled.
Ancient spirit-touched beings born from the fusion of serpent Essence and corrupted human souls. Legend places their origin in forbidden rituals attempting to bind primal Wellspring serpents with mortal will, producing creatures that blur the line between flesh and otherworldly Essence.
The upper body a hauntingly beautiful human female, pale or iridescent, with faint scale patterns along arms and neck. The lower body a sinuous serpent tail in dark shimmering scale. Their movements are hypnotic and unnervingly graceful, accompanied by faint whispers.
Cunning, patient and predatory. They favor psychological manipulation: seduction, deception and trap over direct confrontation. Solitary, though they occasionally form covens to expand their influence over a region.
Illusory Veil disorients and ensnares minds. Essence Drain saps vitality through prolonged contact or hypnotic gaze. Serpent’s Coil constricts physically and metaphysically, disrupting Essence flow. Dreamweave invades dreams and builds nightmare constructs.
Vulnerable when illusions are pierced. Physically weaker than most predators. Susceptible to harmonic Wellspring purging rituals.
The Whispering Grove Massacre saw an entire caravan fall to a coven’s illusionary trap. Several accounts tell of travelers lost to their own nightmares in border forests.
Arachne

Silkraeth, Weaver of Fates, in Old Parunic. The Spider Queen’s Hand among shadow cults.

Aberration, Spirit-Hybrid Predator · Grade S, Domain Threat · Oneirion and Nihiloth · Outer World shadow forests and crevice-webbed zones
Leans on · the Core, by Oneirion, Spirit, with Nihiloth, Wild, in the web. Body: cut the anchor lines, and a body in a dropped web is a body. Spirit: her illusion is a sentence on your Core, and it can be read before it finishes. Fate: every web depends on what walks into it.
Descended from cursed unions between mortal weavers and shadow spirits of the Outer World. They embody the dual nature of artistry and predation, using supernatural webs to trap Essence, memories and flesh alike.
Upper bodies gaunt humanoids with elongated limbs, pale skin and sharp predatory eyes. The lower body a giant spider abdomen with iridescent chitin and multiple glowing eyes. Their hair resembles fine silk threads that shimmer with Essence.
Calculating patient hunters. They spin vast webs of magical and physical thread, entrapping prey to drain Essence and memory, and weave illusions that distort time and space within their lairs.
Essence Web traps both physical and metaphysical entities. Memory Snare captures fragments of consciousness, causing confusion and amnesia. Spatial Distortion alters perception of distance and time within the web domain. Venomous Bite injects neurotoxic Essence venom.
Webs can be burned or shattered with Essence flames. Physically vulnerable outside their lairs. Disoriented by harmonic Essence surges.
The Falling Webs of Zarn chronicles a coven that nearly strangled the region’s Wellspring trade routes; Concord forces broke the hive with a combined assault of fire and spirit magic. Some cults venerate them as weavers of destiny.
Gorgon

Sthenara, Stone Veil, in Old Parunic. Petrashade in Outer World dialect.

Aberration, Stoneborn Predator · Grade SS, Realm Hazard · Coagulatio and Nihiloth, with a heavy petrification overlay · shadowed caves and ruined temples of the Outer World
Leans on · the Shell, by Coagulatio and Nihiloth, both Wild. Body: do not look, and hit by sound. Spirit: the gaze sets matter, and a soul is past it, so a Spirit hand can work with a blindfold on. Fate: a gaze needs a line of sight, and a line of sight has many ways of failing.
Born from the twisted fusion of corrupted Wellspring Essence and ancient petrifying magic. Said to descend from the cursed bloodlines of fallen spirits who sought dominion over life and death, they embody the raw power to unmake living flesh into stone.
Humanoid in shape with thick stone-like skin cracked with glowing fissures. Hair a writhing mass of crystalline serpents or jagged mineral spikes. Eyes blazing with molten essence. Claws and teeth hardened like obsidian.
Lurking predators preferring ambush over brute force. Solitary and territorial, often defending Wellspring scars or crevice breaches.
Petrifying Gaze turns flesh to stone instantly or slowly depending on focus. Essence Venom Breath weakens flesh and disrupts the Aether around it. Stone Armor. Terrifying Roar causes psychological terror.

The gaze requires line of sight and focus: distractions or reflections break its effect. Vulnerable to rapid close-quarters assault before petrification sets in. Essence purifying rituals degrade their petrification powers temporarily.

The Siege of the Stone Gate recounts a gorgon’s defense of a crevice breach, turning entire companies into statues. Tales of the Crystal Cursed originate from victims who slowly petrified over years.
Basilisk

Sserak, Stone Stare, in Old Parunic. The Death Coil among frontier hunters.

Aberration, Reptilian Predator · Grade A, Extreme Threat · Coagulatio and Nihiloth, heavily overlaid with petrification Essence · shadowed forests, deep caves, crevice-riddled wastelands
Leans on · the Shell, by Coagulatio and Nihiloth, both Wild. Body: a mirror, a blindfold and a long spear. Spirit: reach past the scale without meeting the eye. Fate: it hunts by being where you will look.
Ancient reptilian creatures emerging where the Aether of a Wellspring site has been twisted by Abyssal and Corrupted forces.
Lizard-like beasts with thick scaled hides in mottled dark green, brown or stone gray. Eyes glowing sickly yellow or amber, bodies adorned with jagged spines. Their movements are slow and deliberate, lethal patience embodied.
Solitary and territorial. They ambush by stealth and patience, relying on the gaze to incapacitate before closing. Intelligent hunters that avoid unnecessary confrontation unless defending territory or hunting large prey.
Petrifying Gaze. Corrosive Venom weakens Essence flow and damages flesh over time. Camouflage in rocky or forested ground. Stone Hide: mineralized scales resistant to physical and magical attack.
The gaze requires line of sight; mirrors and reflective surfaces repel it. Vulnerable to swift attack and Essence purging. Slow movement makes flanking possible.
The Petrification of Elderwood is blamed on a basilisk that turned entire hunting parties into stone statues. Concord expeditions map basilisk lairs to avoid them and rarely attempt direct confrontation.
Cockatrice

Strathal, Venom Eye, in Old Parunic. The Deathclaw among frontier hunters.

Aberration, Reptilian Avian Predator · Grade A, Extreme Threat · Coagulatio and Nihiloth, overlaid with toxic and petrification Essence · dense swamps, ruined temples, corrupted Wellspring zones
Leans on · the Shell, by Coagulatio and Nihiloth, both Wild. Body: a gloved hand and a warden who has done this before. Spirit: very little in there to read. Fate: a henyard offers plenty of ways for a thing to get caught.
Fearsome hybrids born from the unholy fusion of corrupted reptilian and avian Essence, emerging from the darkest swamps and crevice-shadowed ruins where Wellspring Aether churns and goes bad.
A monstrous blend of rooster and serpent: feathered wings, scaled legs, sharp beak, a long serpentine tail. Eyes glowing with poisonous light; plumage from sickly green to dark mottled hues.
Aggressive and territorial, nesting in hidden lairs and defending them fiercely.
Petrifying Gaze. Venomous Claws inflict toxic wounds causing paralysis. Flight: agile flyers capable of swift aerial strikes. Territorial Screech stuns and disorients.
Gaze requires line of sight; reflective surfaces block or reflect it. Vulnerable to swift coordinated attack. Susceptible to Essence purifying rituals and fire magic.
The Swamp of Stone recounts numerous expeditions lost, with petrified remains marking their hunting grounds. Their feathers and claws are sought for crafting potent poisons and magical wards.
Manticore

Zha’keth, Spine Sting, in Old Parunic. The Sand Scourge among desert tribes.

Aberration, Venomous Beast · Grade A, Extreme Threat · Manganthra and Nihiloth, with venomous Essence overlays · arid deserts, rocky canyons, crevice-touched wastelands
Leans on · the Shell, by Manganthra and Nihiloth, both Wild. Body: the tail first. Spirit: it enjoys itself, and that shows on the Core a long way off. Fate: its volley needs the height and the canyon it picked.
Predators born from corrupted Wellspring Essence blending primal feline and scorpion traits.
Large feline body with a spiked armored tail resembling a scorpion’s stinger. Fur from tawny to deep crimson, eyes burning predatory amber. Wings resembling those of a bat or dragon enable short bursts of flight.
Territorial and aggressive, hunting alone or in small family groups. Highly intelligent for beasts and capable of calculating attacks.
Venomous Sting delivers paralyzing or necrotic venom. Winged Ambush surprises prey from above. Savage Claws. Sand Camouflage blends with desert terrain and dust storms.
Vulnerable to cold and water-based Essence. The wings are fragile and susceptible to damage. And their territorial instincts can be exploited by skilled hunters.
The Blood Sands Massacre recounts an attack on a desert caravan that left few survivors. Local tribes tell of the Scourge’s Shadow, a legendary manticore feared across vast regions.
Wendigo

Ghrosk, the Hunger Eternal, in Old Sylvaar. Frostbane among northern frontier tribes.

Aberration, Spirit-Cursed Predator · Grade S, Domain Threat · Titan-touched cold, the Titan Vohrin’s, with Nihiloth and an overlay of ancestral torment and despair Essence · frozen tundra and the Innerworld’s icy wilds
Leans on · the Shell, by a Titan’s cold and Nihiloth, with a Core torn into something that used to be a person. Body: heat, and an open fire with people around it. Spirit: Recognition, in the old sense of saying who it was, is what the clans mean when they tell you to know its name. Fate: it comes to what you did in the hungry winter, and owing nothing helps.

Cursed spirits born from mortals who succumbed to overwhelming hunger and despair, their souls twisted by corrupted cold sites and ancient famine curses.
Legend says the first Wendigo rose from a tragic winter where entire villages starved and the land itself seemed to wail in anguish.
They are embodiments of insatiable hunger and cold death. The only entry in the register whose origin is a famine.

Gaunt towering humanoid forms draped in frost and rags, glowing icy blue eyes, elongated limbs. Skin cracked and frozen, mist eternally rising from the breath. Antler-like bone growths sometimes adorn the skull; claws resemble jagged shards of ice.
Relentless, driven by endless hunger and madness. They hunt anything that moves with terrifying endurance and predatory cunning. Their presence chills the air and freezes water in their wake. Usually solitary, though they have been known to form packs during the harshest winters.
Frost Aura chills and slows, freezing surfaces it touches. Insatiable Hunger absorbs Essence from prey to heal and grow stronger. Howl of Despair saps morale and induces hallucinations of starvation. Iceclaw Strike pierces armor and freezes wounds.
Vulnerable to fire and heat. Their madness causes unpredictable, reckless behavior. And prolonged exposure to Harmonic Essence weakens their corrupted core.
The Blight of Frost Hollow tells of a Wendigo terrorizing mountain villages for decades until shamans and hunters banished it. The Winter’s Maw campaign suffered severe losses to Wendigo ambushes on supply runs.

Northern tribes conduct rites to protect against their hunger, and to honor the spirits of those lost to the curse.



Lich



Read next: The Sixty Wellsprings, for the Wellsprings these went wrong on; On Walking Into the Current, for what the same ground does to a person; The Bestiary, for the rest of the register.

the-bestiary/the-corrupted-and-the-risen.filePath: The Bestiary/The Corrupted and the Risen/Aberrations/Lich.md
the-bestiary/the-corrupted-and-the-risen.title: Lich
the-bestiary/the-corrupted-and-the-risen.content:
Three generations of the Erebus court kept the lich lord Vharzoth on the tax roll, on the clerk’s argument that a man who will not die owes like one who has not, and in the sixth year of the war he paid it in full, in old gold, by a bone courier in a green cloak who waited politely for the receipt. The coin had come out of the graves of the collectors.
Undying, Archmage Undead · Grade EX, Apocalyptic Threat · Mortalis, Nihiloth and Anamnesis, intertwined through necromantic rites · native to ruined fortresses, ancient crypts, and shadowed sanctuaries throughout the Innerworld and Outer World
Leans on · all three, since it used to be a person, and a Spirit Path one by long habit, on Mortalis, Nihiloth and Anamnesis. Body: the bones are the least of it, and getting there is still how most of them die. Spirit: the phylactery holds the Crystal, and a soul can be reached in it. Fate: it has outlasted a great many reasons to die, and each of them is a thread somebody can look for.
Liches are necromancers who bound their souls to phylacteries, transcending mortality through dark Wellspring rituals. The transformation grants them mastery over death and Essence manipulation, and binds them eternally to the arcane prison they made for themselves. Most were once mortal rulers or sorcerers, and a lich pursues forbidden knowledge and dominion over life and death long after the throne or the title has been forgotten.
Skeletal figures draped in tattered robes embroidered with necromantic glyphs, their eye sockets glowing with sickly Essence light and their hands clutching arcane staffs or relics of power. Some carry visible remnants of the person they were: patches of decayed flesh, a spectral overlay of the face they wore in life.
Cold, calculating, and utterly relentless, a lich commands armies of the undead, bends the Aether of Wellspring sites to its will, and weaves schemes that outlast the mortals who oppose it. Its intellect and magical reach make it a far more dangerous adversary than brute strength alone would suggest.


Abilities

Necromantic Mastery raises and controls vast undead legions.
Essence Drain absorbs life force to fuel spells and regeneration.
Arcane Dominion wields destructive and binding magic across multiple Essence disciplines.
Phylactery Binding keeps the lich immortal unless the phylactery itself is destroyed.



Weaknesses
The phylactery is the lich’s only true vulnerability. Sustaining its Essence flows demands extensive preparation. Holy or harmonic Essence purges weaken it.


The Fall of Erebus’ Shadow records the war against the lich lord Vharzoth, whose armies nearly overwhelmed the Innerworld’s defenses, and Concord campaigns since have focused on locating and destroying lich phylacteries to end their reigns. Liches are feared across the realms as embodiments of corruption and forbidden knowledge; some seek their power regardless, but most regard them as abominations to be purged to preserve the natural order.

the-bestiary/the-corrupted-and-the-risen.filePath: The Bestiary/The Corrupted and the Risen/The Corrupted and the Risen.md
the-bestiary/the-corrupted-and-the-risen.title: The Corrupted and the Risen
the-bestiary/the-corrupted-and-the-risen.content:
What corruption makes, what the Wells spawn, and what will not stay dead.
The bounty door of the hunting hall at Cold Ashby once carried three bills side by side, nailed up on the same wet morning: forty gold for a bicorn on the Durnath road, a copper a tail for foxes, and a sworn offer from a widow, payable in orchard land, to whoever would kill her husband a second time. This shelf covers all three.


Aberrations Ten entries · what corruption makes when it is given a shape to work with
Well-spawn Creatures bred by a Well, masked in their Well’s color, ranked by how deep it bred them
The Undying and the Constructs Five entries · what is still moving when it should not be, and what never lived at all



Read next: The Bestiary, for how the register reads; Mechanica, for how a soul is taken apart on purpose; The Crossing, for the ordinary road these went wrong on.

the-bestiary/the-corrupted-and-the-risen.filePath: The Bestiary/The Corrupted and the Risen/The Undying and the Constructs.md
the-bestiary/the-corrupted-and-the-risen.title: The Undying and the Constructs
the-bestiary/the-corrupted-and-the-risen.content:
Five entries · what is still moving when it should not be, and what never lived at all
Dob Tanner of Grey Marsh sat up at his own wake, in the second verse of the burying hymn, with marsh-marigolds on his chest and his best yellow coat buttoned wrong, and forty mourners cheered. His widow had paid a hedge-worker six coppers to keep him fresh until the cousins arrived, on ground the hedge-worker swore was sound, and for the space of one long breath the whole village believed it had bought a miracle at a very fair price. Then Dob bit the priest. The priest went home and bit his sister. By the next market day the Blight of Grey Marsh was walking the causeway in its feast-day ribbons with the Concord’s quarantine companies burning bridges behind it, and a bill on every chapel door between the marsh and the sea offered a silver for each right hand brought in. That bill founded the Second Burial, thirteen cheerful ruffians in undertakers’ black and red sashes, with a priest, a handcart and rather more lamp oil than the law allows. They sing while they work. The song has Dob in it, and his widow, who to this day wants her six coppers back.
The hedge-worker had nothing to do with the rising, as it turned out, and was hanged anyway. The trouble lay in the marsh, and it lay in what a corpse is supposed to do.

Four of the five are holes in the Crossing (the nine days after a death, in which a person comes apart into three things that go their separate ways: the Echo, the residue that goes home to its Wellspring, and the Name-record). A Skeletal Folk, a Zombie, a Ghoul and a Lich are all bodies whose three products have been prevented from parting, which is exactly the configuration the necromancy prohibition exists to describe.
Living Armor is the exception, and Living Armor is the exception because there was never a body.

Zombies

Khalrak, the Lost Flesh, in Old Parunic. Rotwalkers among frontier survivors.

Undying, Animated Corpse · Grade D, Moderate Threat · Mortalis and Nihiloth, fueled by lingering necromantic energies · battlefield graveyards and plague-ridden wastelands
Leans on · the Shell, by a Medium Mortalis and a Wild Nihiloth working what is left of the flesh. Body: the head, the knees and a good pitchfork. Spirit: nothing is home, and a priest can tell the ground so. Fate: they follow the last thing they were told, so change it.
Corpses reanimated by corrupted Wellspring energies, necromantic ritual, or abyssal taint. Unlike Skeletal Folk they retain decayed flesh and sluggish motor function, driven by primal hunger or necromantic command. Their numbers swell rapidly in plague zones and on battlefields scarred by Abyssal or Corrupted Essence.
Decaying corpses with rotting flesh, exposed bone and festering wounds. Jerky uncoordinated movement, eyes glowing faintly with corrupted Essence or pale blue light. Clothing and armor remnants hint at their past lives, and a practiced crew checks the purse before the head, since the dead pay no fees and the living do.
Mindless and relentless. They wander in hordes and attack any living creature they detect. Their slow steady approach makes them dangerous in numbers, overwhelming through sheer volume. Rare variants show signs of minimal instinct or rudimentary coordination.
Horde Tactics. Contagious Bite: some carry infectious necromantic plagues. Endurance, continuing after severe injury. Necrotic Aura slows living creatures and weakens Essence flow.
Vulnerable to fire, radiant Essence and dismemberment. Slow and uncoordinated against skilled opponents. And their necromantic bindings can be severed to disable them.
The Blight of Grey Marsh chronicles a zombie plague that devastated frontier villages. Concord quarantine forces have long worked to contain outbreaks spawned by Crevice taint.
Ghouls
Undying, Ferocious Corpse-Eaters · Grade B, High Threat · Mortalis and Nihiloth, with residual necromantic influence · cursed graveyards, abyssal borderlands, plague-ravaged zones
Leans on · the Shell, by a Medium Mortalis and a Wild Nihiloth. Body: fire, and do not let the wound go bad. Spirit: a little is home and it is hungry, and it can be read and baited. Fate: a pack depends on the next grave being there.
Corpses cursed or corrupted on Mortalis ground, spawned where necromantic energies blend with savage hunger. Unlike zombies, ghouls retain agility and ferocity, hunting living flesh with brutal efficiency.
Gaunt rotting humanoid figures with sharp claws and elongated teeth. Skin mottled and stretched tight over bone, torn and bloodied. Eyes glowing with a fierce hungry light; movements jerky but swift and calculated.
Savage relentless predators hunting both living and undead prey. They move with unnatural speed and cunning, attacking in packs with coordinated ambush tactics, and their hunger drives them to desecrate the dead.
Pack Hunt. Feral Claws tear through flesh and armor. Essence Corruption: their bites taint victims with necromantic decay. Regenerative Hunger recovers wounds rapidly when feeding on fresh flesh.
Vulnerable to radiant Essence and fire. Poor resistance to magical wards and purification. And they rely on close combat: ranged attacks disrupt their aggression.
The Ghoul Plague of Mirewood devastated frontier villages before Concord forces intervened. Several necromantic cults raise ghouls as shock troops.
Skeletal Folk

Khal’thar, Boneshade, in Old Parunic. The Bonebound among necromancers.

Undying, Animated Remnants · Grade B, High Threat · Mortalis and Anamnesis, with traces of ancestral torment Essence · Abyssal Depths, Material World graveyards, cursed Innerworld tombs
Leans on · the Core by Anamnesis and the Shell by Mortalis, both Medium. What holds the bones is what they remember. Body: a hammer, for the time it takes. Spirit: tell them what they were and that it is over. Fate: an old oath often keeps them standing, and it can be discharged by someone with the standing to do it.
Corpses reanimated through dark Essence rituals or cursed Wellspring taint, often arising from battlefields or tombs gone bad on Mortalis ground. Bound to necromantic masters or wandering as restless spirits seeking vengeance or purpose.

Unlike mindless undead, many retain fragmented memories and rudimentary intelligence.

Bare bones and skulls often encrusted with ancient runes or wrapped in tattered remnants of once-sacred garments. Some bear lingering aetheric glows or cracks where corrupted Essence leaks. Joints grinding with unnatural stiffness; eyes, where present, burning with cold pale light.
Relentless and unyielding, operating in packs or under command, driven by binding curses or lingering hatred. Their cold emotionless persistence makes them dangerous foes, attacking in coordinated waves.
Bone Shard Barrage detaches and launches fragments as weapons or barriers. Essence Lash extends limbs or creates whips of bone. Unholy Resilience. Necrotic Aura saps life force and weakens Essence.
Vulnerable to radiant or purifying Essence. Fragile physical structure: concentrated damage shatters key bones. And they are bound by necromantic rituals: destroying their masters can render them inert.
The Bonefield Campaign saw entire companies wiped out by Skeletal Folk raised from ancient war graves. Tales of the Crypt Lords describe powerful necromancers controlling vast skeletal armies beneath the Innerworld.
Lich

Zar’khan, Death’s Sovereign, in Old Parunic. The Eternal Wraith among necromantic circles.

Undying, Archmage Undead · Grade EX, Apocalyptic Threat · Mortalis, Nihiloth and Anamnesis, intertwined through powerful necromantic rites · ruined fortresses, ancient crypts, shadowed sanctums
Leans on · all three, since it used to be a person, and a Spirit Path one by long habit, on Mortalis, Nihiloth and Anamnesis. Body: the bones are the least of it, and getting there is still how most of them die. Spirit: the phylactery holds the Crystal, and a soul can be reached in it. Fate: it has outlasted a great many reasons to die, and each of them is a thread somebody can look for.

Powerful necromancers who have bound their souls to phylacteries, transcending mortality through dark Wellspring rituals.
The transformation grants immense mastery over death and Essence manipulation and binds them eternally to their arcane prisons.
Often once mortal rulers or sorcerers. The only EX entry in the register that used to be a person.

Skeletal figures draped in tattered robes embroidered with necromantic glyphs. Eye sockets glowing with sickly Essence light, hands clutching arcane staffs or relics. Some display remnants of their former selves: patches of decayed flesh, spectral overlays hinting at their past lives.
Cold, calculating, utterly relentless. They manipulate armies of the undead, bend the Aether of Wellspring sites to their will, and weave complex schemes to extend their influence. Their intellect and magical prowess make them formidable far beyond mere brute strength.
Necromantic Mastery raises and controls vast undead legions. Essence Drain absorbs life force to fuel spells and regeneration. Arcane Dominion wields destructive and binding magic across multiple Essence schools. Phylactery Binding: immortal unless the phylactery is destroyed.

The phylactery is their only true vulnerability. They require extensive preparation to maintain Essence flows, and can be weakened by holy or harmonic Essence purges.

The Fall of Erebus’ Shadow details the war against the lich lord Vharzoth, whose armies nearly overwhelmed the Innerworld’s defenses. Numerous Concord campaigns have focused on locating and destroying phylacteries to end their reigns.
Living Armor

Arkh’zan, Sentinel Shell, in Old Parunic. The Bound Sentinel among magical artificers.

Construct, Animated Armor · Grade A, Extreme Threat · Eidolyn and Fixatio, infused with Spirit Rune binding · ancient fortresses, Innerworld sanctums
Leans on · the Shell, by Eidolyn, Wild, and Fixatio, Medium, with no Core of its own unless one was seated in it. Body: Penetration above the proof, and then the joints. Spirit: find what was seated in it and speak to that, or read the binding rune and spoil it. Fate: every strap is a thing that can give, and the armor knows this no better than you do.
Suits of enchanted plate and chain forged in ancient workshops and animated through potent Wellspring Essence and Spirit Rune Arts. Created to guard Wellsprings, tombs and arcane repositories. They possess no flesh but exhibit independent will and relentless dedication to their wards.

Some are remnants of lost orders, still patrolling forgotten ruins. Others serve present-day spellbinders as guardians or shock troops, each one the costly work of a single master’s hands, and no two of them agree about the proper way to hold a door.

Heavy full-plate or ornate segmented armor with arcane glyphs etched into the plates (old work, and a hunter who finds a whole suit of it should ask who made it and when, because nobody at a forge makes such plate today). Some bear ethereal blue or green Essence glows emanating from inside; others are cracked or rusted with age. They move with a clanking gait, wielding swords, axes or polearms forged from rare materials.
Obedient and unyielding, following their last command or bound purpose with unerring precision. Indifferent to pain or exhaustion, and exhibiting tactical awareness far beyond mundane constructs.
Unyielding Guard · resistant to physical damage, immune to fatigue and pain. Arcane Strike · weapon attacks channel bound Wellspring Essence. Spirit Shield · generates protective glyph barriers. Tactical Recall · remembers combat scenarios and adapts tactics in prolonged engagements.
Vulnerable to Essence-dampening fields and anti-magic wards. Slow and cumbersome beside living combatants. And severing the binding runes or disrupting the Spirit Rune network disables them outright.
The Siege of Verdant Bastion recounts Living Armor defending ancient Wellspring shrines against Abyssal invaders. Several Concord companies specialize in dismantling Living Armor contingents through coordinated Essence disruption. Among artificers they are revered as pinnacle creations of Spirit Rune binding.

Read next: The Crossing, for what a death does when nothing interrupts it; Mechanica, for the forbidden way to build one; The Three Paths, for what each road can do about them.

the-bestiary/the-corrupted-and-the-risen.title: Well-spawn
the-bestiary/the-corrupted-and-the-risen.content:
Creatures bred by a Well, masked in their Well’s color, ranked by how deep it bred them
On Mask Night in the Well town of Pennyhythe, in the ninth year of the Dark Ages, Sluice Street was packed from wall to wall with children in paper masks painted deep teal when the two best hunting crews on the Thaloré road came up out of the ground a spear’s length apart, and one of them was carrying the only real mask in town. The Margrave of Sallowmere had nailed a bill to every door between the shaft head and the river: three hundred gold and a winter’s ale for the plate of the Mourning Pike that had eaten eight of his sluice-keepers. Jennet Ludd of the Saffron Hoods had broken that plate in the lower workings with a harpoon and a very bad word, and the shards rode in a wet sack at her hip, gray and veined with a teal so deep it seemed to crawl. Godwin Bracken of the Scarlet Aprons, whose men had bled the Pike for two days before she ever got there, held that the plate was his, and he said so with his aura coming up the red of a slapped cheek. The hall at Cold Ashby lay nine miles down the Well road. A mask pays only while it holds its color.
So they ran. Yellow hoods and red aprons went out through the Mask Night crowd with half the children of Pennyhythe pelting after them, and the sack changed hands four times in nine miles. It went through a dyer’s yard, where a porter called Tib Fennel was thrown bodily into a vat of madder and came out the color of a cardinal and still running. It went over the Sluice bridge, where Tib, with the sack in his teeth and three Aprons on his back, broke his neck on the far rail. Ludd took it off his body without stopping and has apologized to his mother every year since. She came through the doors of the hall with one ear gone and Bracken hanging off her belt, upended the sack on the clerk’s green felt, and every person in the room leaned over to look. Two veins of teal were still alight. The clerk reached for his pen, and the last of them went out while his fingers were closing on it.
The hall paid nothing, as halls do. The Margrave’s bill had said “the plate” and said nothing of color, so the two crews took him before a sworn notary and then took each other, and the suit outlived the Margrave, Bracken and the notary. The shards were split at last, and one hangs over the door of each hall, gray as dishwater. Pennyhythe runs the race every Mask Night now, with a sack of painted tiles, and the winning child is called Tib. Everything that happened that night is on this page: why the plate carries color, why it fades, why a clerk will not pay on gray, and how anyone gets near enough to break one.

A Wellspring is an alchemical and a spiritual transformation, one of sixty, the governing idea that shapes how a soul uses Aether, and each is also a kind of Aether working on the Soul Crystal in its own way. A Wellspring has sites where its Aether pools, which common speech calls Cores, and a Well (the delvers’ word for a Core Concentration, the survey’s name for such a site run deep) is ground where one of the sixty lies thick enough to rewrite whatever lives in it. A Well breeds, and what it breeds wears its Well on its face. Delvers call them the Well’s get. Hunters call them masks, because the mask is what they are paid on and the mask is where they aim. Most Wells lie inside dungeons, and the galleries, the crews and the bills are on Dungeons.

What it is
A Well-spawn is a creature born and bred inside a Well, whose body runs on the Well’s law instead of its own biology. It wears a mask of hard plate in its Well’s color, and the mask is where that law is held: break it, and the creature is finished.
How it looks
Shaped like whatever its line was bred from, a fox, a toad, a crab, a bramble, but with a plate grown over the face (or over whatever serves it for one). The plate carries the hue of the Well’s own Wellspring (one of the sixty) and a pattern drawn from that Wellspring’s kind. The deeper the spawn was bred, the clearer and brighter the mask. Its aura, where it shows one, is the same color, and every line has a sound of its own: the Tolling Crab’s one clear note, the Tinder-fox’s dry crackle.
What it costs
A Well-spawn eats Aether (the stuff all magic is pulled from, lying in the ground and air around us) and the Essence people refine out of it. It goes wherever the pull is strongest, which means wherever people are working the Well, and it costs a Well town its lamps, its timbering, its practitioners’ reserves and, often enough, its delvers. Facing one costs a hunter proofed or enhanced bolts by the pouch, and a practitioner the reserve he spends holding his own law on the Well’s ground while he fights.
How it is beaten
Break the mask. Everywhere else a spawn takes wounds as an animal of its shape would; through the mask, one clean break ends it at any size. Beyond that, every spawn is beaten by the same four things: lure it off its Well, turn its Wellspring’s own failure against it, fight it on ground its Wellspring hates, and bring a Sealwright (a ward specialist) for the night.
Example
Edda Marsh, a licensed captain with a party of five crossbowmen and a porter, takes a contract to clear the upper workings of a Basilithe Well. The porter hears a note ring in the dark, the same note twice. Edda reads the mask by lamplight before anyone looses: ochre-amber, banded like quarry rock, dull as a charcoal ember. Basilithe, upper workings: a Tolling Crab, and bolts will flatten on it. She keeps the bows quiet, strikes the tuning bar from her kit, rings the crab’s note back at it and holds it. The carapace falls into gravel all at once, and the porter is on the mask with a hammer before the dust settles, because the hall pays on a colored shard and a gray one is worth nothing.
How a Well Breeds Them
The Aether makes the body. An animal has an Essence Core (the soul’s seat, where its own nature is kept) and a sealed Shell (the vent through which a practitioner’s soul drives Essence out, and it stays sealed until something cracks it). At a Well the Aether pours into that Core and has nowhere to go, and over generations the line stops living by its own nature and starts living by the Well’s. Its young are born already made. That is a Well-spawn: a bred line, flesh and blood and bone, organized along a Wellspring’s law.
The mask is the law made solid. A practitioner’s working is bounded by its glyph, the shape that tells the Essence where to stop. A Well-spawn’s body is bounded by its mask. The plate grows over the face in the first season of life, and everything the creature can do is held inside the boundary it draws. Kill the body and the mask still reads as its Wellspring for a day or two. Break the mask and the body has no law left to keep it in shape, and goes back to being ordinary meat.
Only the Well-born are spawn. An animal that wandered onto dense ground and stayed too long comes out strange, short-lived and unable to breed true. The register enters it with the Natural Beasts, or with the Aberrations if corruption made it, and it wears no mask. The Scourge-born herds of the Scourge of Hell are the one exception on file: warped so long ago that they breed true, still with no mask, and they sit with the Natural Beasts under protest. Aether-warped beasts, Spirit Beasts, the corrupted lineages and summoned things all keep their own pages. A mask means a Well, every time.
A Well worked hard breeds more, not fewer. Hard pulling thins the ground at the face and brings the spawn up the workings after it, and a Well corrupted into Obsession Force (a site that takes from whatever enters it, compatible or not) breeds lines that hunt rather than follow.
The Mask, by Wellspring
Hue from the Wellspring, pattern from its kind, clarity from the depth.






























KindPatternHues a hunter learnsWildA print of the thing itself: crazed like slag cooling on a foundry floor off hot ground, branching like a lightning tree off charged ground, concentric rings like a stone dropped in still water off heavy ground, strata and facets with a fine grit that comes off on the hand off stone, veins and growth rings off green ground. Off the light-eaters it is an absence: the eye slides off it, and finds the face by where the darkness is deepestAbython, near-black · Anima Spirare, bright arterial red · Ascensio, steel gray with Clarity reads the depth, on the same smelting scale as a practitioner’s Essence color:





























Bred atThe mask looksThe MouthSmoke-brown, the color a tint under the murkThe Upper WorkingsWarm dark gray, the color a suggestionThe Lower WorkingsGray veined with the true color, flickering when the creature is rousedThe DeepsSilver-gray suffused with color, bright enough to throw its hue on a gallery wallThe HeartBrilliant, the color bleaching to white at the edges

A hunter reads a mask the way an assayer of power reads an aura: the hue says which Well, the clarity says how deep. A delver who meets a mask brighter than the last one has learned where he is standing.

Ranked by Depth
A Well has depth. Its ground thickens from the mouth down to the heart, and each band of it is a rung on the sites ladder (the register’s scale of how strong a person must be to stand on dense ground and stay themselves). A spawn’s power starts from the ground that bred it, and it climbs the same Stages and Level a person does. Two letters are read off it, and neither is ever read off a person. Its blow is a band of peak output, read off what a working delivers, its EU times its yield (η, how much of what is put in reaches the world), from Hollow and F at the bottom to EX+ at the top, and the Measurewrights render the bands in joules. Its Grade, E to EX, is the beast’s own letter and the one its bounty is posted under, and each letter answers to a rank of practitioner, Initiate to Paragon. Like any monster a spawn gains Levels by killing, each other included, and an old one climbs off its depth and may change form at its own thresholds. The table below reads what a depth breeds, and a mask brighter than its depth is the warning that this one has been eating.
On the Bestiary’s own ladder a creature stands on a rung (nine steps of what it can break, from Hearth-pest through Field-bane, Road-bane, Hamlet-bane and Town-bane up to Sky-eater), and each rung matches a letter of output. The Accord prices the same creature by its Grade (its danger rating, E to EX, naming the rank of practitioner it sends and the title that may lawfully take it), and the hunter wears that title as a Sigil (the license color of her badge).
A spawn’s own output sits two rungs below the ground it was bred on. On its Well it holds the tie (a creature fed by its Wellspring site stands one rung higher there than off it), so it fights one rung stronger at home than anywhere else.



























































DepthGroundSpawn’s blowRung on its WellGrade of the bountyA party ofAlone, you wantThe MouthFreshetHollow to E · Hearth-pestField-baneD, Green SigilApprentices, or a watch with plain boltsAn Apprentice; a Journeyman on its WellThe Upper WorkingsMillraceD · Field-baneRoad-baneC to B, Green or BlueJourneymenA Journeyman; an Adept on its WellThe Lower WorkingsRiptideC · Road-baneHamlet-baneB to A, Blue SigilAdeptsAn Adept; an Expert on its WellThe DeepsWhirlpoolB · Hamlet-baneTown-baneA to S, Blue or GoldExpertsAn Expert; a Master on its WellThe HeartFountainheadA · Town-baneMarch-baneS to X, Gold Sigil or Obsidian SealMastersA Master; a Grandmaster on its Well
How to read it. The bounty’s Grade sits at the letter of the spawn’s rung or one above, higher where the line persists, carries a mind, or does something to a working level that no single blow shows. A party fights a spawn at its own rung; a lone fighter wants one rung above it, which is why the ordinary spawn of the Deeps is work for a squad of Experts and a lone hunter there had better be a Master.
The unwoken feel them by rung. A spawn of the upper workings fills a commoner with dread; one from the lower workings puts a weight in the room; near a heart-bred spawn, knees bend.
Most hunters fight below the table. The Accord’s reckoning says what is safe. A porter with a spade still kills a Tinder-fox, and a crossbowman who reads the mask still kills things the table says he should run from. The counters below are how lesser people beat higher masks, and every hunting hall teaches them before it teaches anything else.
How They Behave
The shallow lines are animals. From the mouth through the lower workings, a spawn has the cunning of its shape and no more. It does not hate and it holds no territory. It goes toward the pull and stays until nothing is left to take: a lantern, a warded door, a practitioner’s reserve. Anyone with a good nose (trained sensing, the read of Aether and Essence) can predict it, and nobody can scare it off with noise alone. Its line does not migrate as a herd does, though strays follow a pull a long way, and monsters of every other kind move across the whole Inner World. It does not age by seasons, and nothing native to the ground above a Well eats it. The Scourge of Hell is the exception, where wyrms and worse have learned to, and masks have been cut out of stomachs there and nowhere else on file.
The deep lines think. Below the lower workings the Veil (the boundary between the planes) wears thin, and the Deeps are where the planes turn together: spirits show, time runs wrong, and the dead leave more behind them than bones. A spawn bred there gathers a mind out of what the Well remembers. It plans, lies in wait, lets a party pass to take the porters at the back, and brings the lesser spawn of its Well along behind it, because they follow its pull the way they follow a lamp.
Rare deep spawn speak. They talk in the voices of the people the Well has killed, and sometimes in a voice that belongs to nobody. They bargain, offering what the Well remembers in return for a fed lamp left burning below or Essence spent on the spot. They lie in the same breath. Every one on file has wanted to go up.
Some serve Malphas. A few speaking spawn have been found working for Malphas and his circle. What he offers them, the register does not know.
Deep spawn are banished. Break the mask of anything bred in the Deeps or the Heart and the body comes apart into raw Aether and sinks back down the Well, and its core goes with it. It leaves its mask behind, split and already gray. Whether what the Well breeds next is the same creature, nobody has ever been able to prove.
How They Differ
From ordinary and Aether-warped beasts. A beast has an ecology; a Well-spawn has a law, and a mask to keep it in.
From Spirit Beasts. A Spirit Beast was formed from Wellspring resonance, carries a mind and can make an alliance. A shallow spawn was bred from an animal and is still one. It cannot be bargained with, and no spawn of any depth can be bonded. A deep spawn can be bargained with, which is worse.
From Echo Beasts. An Echo Beast is the Veil’s residue, condensed for a while out of what visitors carried into a Veil-thin place and gone when the thinning closes. An Echo Beast is the concentration’s consequence. A Well-spawn is its product. It is born, it lives for years and it breeds.
From the corrupted lineage. The Bicorn and the Wendigo were converted by Abyssal or Void contact into something that cannot go back. A shallow spawn was shaped by a clean Wellspring law, and break its mask and it does go back: to meat.
Fair Counters
The mask. One break ends it. Shallow masks are thin, and a plain bolt, a spade or a boot heel goes through. From the lower workings down a mask holds a working’s strength and stops common bolts the way a worked cuirass does, and hunters carry proofed bolts (Guild-marked heads), which strike against it as one step higher, or enhanced bolts (bolts carrying a working) made by a hand of the rank the spawn’s Grade names.
The tie. Lure it off the Well, or take the fight onto salted ground (worked by hedge-workers so that Aether will not pool on it) or bled ground (pulled empty), or pay the keepers of a worked site to close it, and the rung the tie gave it is gone. A spawn chasing a lamp up a shaft is a spawn walking away from its strength.
Its Wellspring’s failure. A spawn is its Wellspring’s law in a body, and it inherits the law’s way of going wrong. Every entry’s weakness column is that failure turned into a hunter’s method.
Its Wellspring’s ground. Every entry in the Sixty says what its ground favors and hates. An Ignivale spawn in saturated cold is a small animal. A Vantabriel spawn in a loud, crowded, well-lit gallery has nowhere to stand. A Spirit spawn cares for little except how thick the Aether lies, and off the Well it is mostly a very sad fish.
The right road. A spawn leans where its Wellspring’s kind says, as the hub sets out. The register below names it.
The Sealwright. Ward-chalk holds the shallow lines off a sleeping party for a night. It does not hold a speaking one, which will sit outside the chalk and talk until somebody steps over it.
Living Beside a Well
For fighters. Clearing Wells is a trade. Mine-holders, towns and crowns contract hunting parties to keep spawn off their works; the guild hunting halls license the hunters, and the chartered companies undercut the halls by putting one licensed captain over a party of cheap crossbows. The halls pay on the mask, and only while it holds its color, so a party breaks the plate, bags the shards and runs them to the hall within the day.





























Bred atThe hall paysThe MouthA copper a tail on the Well roads; no clerk will handle a hundred fox masksThe Upper Workings2 to 5 gold a maskThe Lower Workings10 to 25 gold a maskThe Deeps60 to 150 gold a mask, half for a banished one’s gray maskThe Heart, or any speakerBy contract, from a crown or a chartered town
The core is the second purse. Under the mask a spawn carries a core, which is in a way its Soul Crystal, and a shallow one left in a carcass is what the porter goes back for. The hall pays on the mask and the rendering house pays on the core, which goes into the Essence Drafts every practitioner with a purse takes to temper. Prices are on Hide, Horn and Bone. The plate and hide make gear, and a spawn with a name makes gear with a name.
The guilds still call hunters mouths with crossbows. The Well towns call them by name, buy them drinks, and paint their mask tallies over the tavern door. A young practitioner’s first descent with a hunting party is the most common way a name is made in the Dark Ages, and the first mask a hunter breaks is kept, gray or not, for life.
Bills, crews and songs. On top of what the hall pays, any lord who has lost enough men posts a bounty on the doors, and a crew may hold the hall’s coin and the lord’s on the same shard if it gets there in time. Crews and halls wear colors and hate each other on purpose: the Saffron Hoods and the Scarlet Aprons have not shared a tavern since Pennyhythe, each has songs about the other that cannot be sung in front of a priest, and a boy in a Well town can tell you which hall a stranger drinks with from the way she carries her harpoon. A herald will cry a heart-mask from the market cross for a fee, the minstrels will have it by the next fair with the color wrong and the number of dead doubled, and bookies take odds on a crew’s tally for the season. In the crews’ own mouths a mouth-bred mask is a smoke, a lower-workings mask is a vein, and anything from the Heart is a bright, usually spoken as advice to leave. Scholars say depth and clarity, and scholars mostly stay upstairs.
For commoners. Well towns live with spawn the way river towns live with floods.

Smoked glass by the door, a hammer by the bed. Every house near a Well keeps both. The glass is for the bright ones; the hammer is for the mask.
The gray shard over the lintel. A broken mask, gone gray, is nailed above the door to keep others away. The register says it does nothing. Hunters nail them up too.
Mask Night. Once a year the children of a Well town paint paper masks in their Well’s color and run the streets with pots and whistles, shrieking. It teaches every child the color to run from, and the noise is supposed to send the shallow lines back down. Delvers do not stop it.
Count the colors. A delver who sees a brighter mask than the last turns round. Nobody calls it cowardice in a Well town.
Never answer your name from below the lamp-line. The dead do not call the roll. Something else does.
The first cup for the old man below. Deep crews leave the first cup of a shift’s tea at the shaft head, and drink the second.

The Register
Every bred line on file, its mask and its depth. Full entries for three follow; the rest keep their entries as recorded.











































































EntryWellspring, leans onBred atMaskGrade · Rung on its WellTinder-foxIgnivale, the ShellThe MouthEmber-orange crazing over the muzzleD Moderate, Green · Field-baneLeveling LeechTransference, the LayerThe MouthA violet disc over the sucker, its ruled lines never meetingD Moderate, Green · Field-baneReaching BriarVerdantia, the ShellThe MouthA green, ring-grown knot over the root-crownB High, Blue · Road-baneGlarewingAurevane, MediumThe Upper WorkingsAn arc-blue lightning tree across the browB High, Blue · Road-baneTolling CrabBasilithe, the ShellThe Upper WorkingsOchre-amber strata set into the carapace frontA Extreme, Blue · Hamlet-baneLamp-drinkerVantabriel, the ShellThe Upper WorkingsFound only as the darkest place on a dark shapeS Domain, Gold · Hamlet-baneSump-toadAbython, the ShellThe Lower WorkingsBlued-steel rings across the brow, riding level with the waterA Extreme, Blue · Hamlet-baneMourning PikeThaloré, the CoreThe Lower WorkingsDeep teal streamlines over the skullA Extreme, Blue · Hamlet-baneRoll-callerAnamnesis, MediumThe DeepsSilver-gray threaded with black-violet, finely stripedS Domain, Gold · Town-bane
The Briar, the Crab and the Lamp-drinker hold persistence as well as the tie, which is why they stand above their depth.
Tinder-fox

Vulpes ignita in the Guild register. Tinder-fox or the red nuisance on the Well roads.

Well-spawn · Grade D, Moderate Threat, Green Sigil · Ignivale · bred at the mouths of Ignivale Wells; strays up the workings
Leans on · the Shell, by Ignivale, Wild. Body: a boot on the mask. Spirit: keep your own working in hand, because Ignivale’s whole trick is that you will not. Fate: nobody has ever needed to.
On the ladder · output Hearth-pest; holds the tie; stands at Field-bane. Mask · a scrap of smoke-brown plate over the muzzle, ember-orange under the murk and crazed like cooling slag.
Bred at Ignivale Well mouths from whatever small hunter first denned there. No Archon (one of the Fourteen, the great powers tradition credits with making beasts) is credited.
Fox-sized, coat singed short and black at the tips, warm to the hand through a glove, breath shimmering in cold air. It crackles when it runs. It is dangerous by what it lowers. Ignivale drops the barrier between intent and working, and near a Tinder-fox that barrier drops in anyone with a woken Soul Crystal (the soul itself, which refines Aether into Essence): a startled practitioner fires, a frightened one fires twice, and a gallery full of both burns.


Abilities

The low barrier · practitioners within a few paces fire workings they did not choose
Warm den · a nest keeps a gallery hot enough to scorch what is stored there
Quick · a bite before anyone has finished seeing it



Weaknesses

The mask. A thin plate; a spade or a boot heel goes through
Preignition runs in it too. Startle it in the open with dogs, bells or shouting and it flares its own coat off and lies spent
Saturated cold and still, even ground leave it a small, slow animal The unawakened are its answer. A porter has no Crystal to fire




Delvers agree on the order of events: a scorch smell in a gallery with no fire in it, a practitioner who says he did not mean to, and then the timbering alight. The survivors are always the ones carrying the tent poles.

Sump-toad

Bufo profundus in the Guild register. Sump-toad, the bottom-sitter; among delvers, the old man below.

Well-spawn · Grade A, Extreme Threat, Blue Sigil · Abython · bred in the deepest sumps of the lower workings of Abython Wells
Leans on · the Shell, by Abython, Wild. Body: a harpoon at the rings. Spirit: an old toad’s mind is very simple, and it can be read from the far end of a shaft. Fate: its pulse needs water and silt to push against, and a flood has its own ideas.
On the ladder · output Road-bane; holds the tie; stands at Hamlet-bane. Mask · a broad gray plate across the brow, near-black steel veined with a clearer gleam, ringed like a stone dropped in still water. It rides level with the sump, eyes set in it, and a winding-man’s first sight of the toad is a plate floating in black water that is not floating.
Bred where the Aether is heavy enough to suffocate a practitioner who has not trained for it. No Archon is credited.
A toad the size of an ox, flat and slick, hide loose on it like a sack. Abython matches pressure instead of resisting it, and the toad lives equalized with depths that crush anything else. It waits for the pull to come down the shaft: the lamp, the practitioner in the hoist basket, and the men. Its strike is a pulse, all the pressure it has been matching let go at once, with a sound like a cellar door slammed underwater, and it staves in timbering, a hoist basket or a chest.


Abilities

The pulse · a pressure strike that brings down timbering and breaks a hoist
Equalized · no pressure, heat or cold at depth troubles it
Patience · sits for weeks at the sump



Weaknesses

The mask. Worked plate: common bolts skip off it, a proofed bolt or a harpoon at the rings does not
Rapid ascent. Brought up too fast it comes out of solution;
a horse-hoist run at the gallop with a lantern on the rope for bait has killed more of them than any arbalest
Loose silt gives the pulse nothing to push against




Winding-men keep a rule that the basket never stops halfway down when the sump has been quiet a month. The rule has no author and is never broken.

Roll-caller

Vocator sepultorum in the Guild register. Roll-caller; among deep crews, the Foreman, because it calls the roll in the voice of whoever kept the pay-book when it last heard one.

Well-spawn · Grade S, Domain Threat, Gold Sigil · Anamnesis · bred in the Deeps of Anamnesis Wells, where the Veil runs thin; has never been seen above them
Leans on · the Core, by Anamnesis, Medium. Body: a spear’s length and a Master’s blow. Spirit: it reads by touch, and a good Read can tell which of the things it says are true. Fate: it survives by being right about you, and one spoiled name breaks its whole bargain.
On the ladder · output Hamlet-bane; holds the tie; stands at Town-bane. The Commission rates it a Domain Threat for the mind and the voice, and sends Masters. Mask · a whole face of silver-gray plate threaded with a black-violet the eye cannot hold, striped fine and even like cooled lava rock. It glows faintly when warmed.
Bred in the Deeps of Anamnesis Wells, the Aether that lets a thing read the history stored in stone, metal and bone. No Archon is credited. What the line was first bred from, nobody knows.
Man-high when it stands, long in the limb and pale as a cave fish, it goes on all fours and rises to talk. It knows every death the Well holds. The gallery walls remember, and it reads them: names, voices, last hours. Touch is all it needs to read a person the same way, and a delver it has brushed against hears his own dead brother asking for him by the nickname nobody else knew.
It bargains. The last words of your dead, for a fed lamp left lit. Where the other party went, for an hour of your reserve. It lies in the same breath as it tells the truth, and it is right about the dead often enough that men go back down for it. Lesser spawn of its Well follow it as they follow a lamp. It wants to go up; every one on file has asked to be carried to the surface. Some serve Malphas and his circle.
Its strike is the Recollection: everything it has read and stored let go at once as light and heat, a white-violet flash with a sound like a hundred voices drawing breath, enough to bring a gallery down.


Abilities

The roll · speaks the names and voices of everyone the Well has killed
The reading · one touch, and it knows your history and your dead
The bargain · trades what it knows for fed lamps and spent reserve, and lies while it does
Following · the lesser spawn of its Well move with it
The Recollection · a discharge of stored light and heat that collapses a working level



Weaknesses

The mask. Worked plate at its own Grade; it wants a Master’s blow, an enhanced bolt of the same rank, or the failure below first. Broken, it banishes the creature down the Well
Thermal resetting. Heat the mask, with a Guild craftsman’s white flare, a furnace brand or a held heat working, and the stored record pours out of it as light; for a while it remembers nothing, speaks nothing and is only an animal
The Recollection empties it. Bait the discharge and the same thing follows
It must touch to read. Keep it at a spear’s length and keep your coat out of its hands
Saturated Aether, crowds and noise give Anamnesis nowhere to stand




A deep crew on an Anamnesis Well heard the roll called at shift change in a foreman’s voice twelve years dead, the names in the order of the old pay-book, and the last name on it was the youngest man in the basket. The crew came up. The young man went back down that night on his own. The Gold Sigil who went after him came back with a gray mask, split clean across, and would not say what it had told her.
On Anamnesis Wells the pay-book is kept above ground, the dead are never named below the lamp-line, and “the Foreman’s asking for you” means a grief that has started to talk back.


Read next: Dungeons, for where they gather; The Sixty Wellsprings, for the ground that breeds them; Monster Cores, for the stone.

the-bestiary/the-wild/natural-beasts/dro.title: Droval — The Frost-Howler
the-bestiary/the-wild/natural-beasts/dro.content:
Frost-Howler · White Maw · Rimegaunt · Skarn-Ursai
Jarl Eyvind Tvilling of the polar shelf went out to kill a Droval the way other young men go to a wedding. He took sixty hunters, a bounty sworn by his own father of a hundred cattle and a seat at the high table, red banners with the gold ship on them, two drummers, a skald to get the details right, and a pavilion of striped wool that took four sleds to carry. On the first night out they pitched it on the open ice beside a long white ridge, lit the fat-lamps, and sat down to roast seal and a great deal of shouting, with the aurora going green and rose overhead and the skald trying out rhymes for Tvilling. Toward the middle of the second song the ridge got up. It had been lying there with the snow piling on its back since before they crossed the skyline, thirty meters from the head of the table, and it covered that distance in one bound with no more noise than a falling coat. The cook’s boy, Ulf Ketilsson, was under a sled looking for a dropped spoon. He crawled out at dawn among the striped wool and the red snow, and he lived to be very old, telling it at fairs for his dinner. He always said that the worst of it was the song stopping before anyone had heard a thing. The skald’s rhymes for Tvilling were never finished, and they are said to have been bad.
The register enters the Droval as an animal, and the Measurewrights who keep the entry have been to the polar shelf about as often as you would expect. What follows is the best anyone has managed, mostly from the people who bonded with them and the people who ran.

Type: Natural Beast / Spirit-Touched Behemoth
Rare elder specimens and Titan-class Droval cross into Elemental Behemoth classification due to extreme Wellspring saturation.
Grade: D to EX (variable by age, lineage, environment, and specialization)
Essence Affinity: Primary: Elemental (Ice / Winter) · Secondary: Harmonic (Fear, Silence, Stillness)
Leans on: the Shell, by the Titan Vohrin’s cold, which stands outside the Sixty and is worked like a Wild Wellspring. Body: tight ground and thin ice, for the size. Spirit: the bond, since a rider’s Droval has one idea, and the dread goes on the Core and can be named for what it is. Fate: there is little to pull on such a sound animal, and a great deal to pull on a rider.

Common Names





















Frost-HowlerFrontier mortal dialects. Named for the low owl-like war cry that carries through snowfields and frozen valleysWhite MawNorthern settlement common usage. Named for the hooked beak and the rows of jagged teeth behind itRimegauntAncient hunter clans of the polar shelf. The name that experienced trackers use and that inexperienced trackers hear once before they stop being trackersSkarn-UrsaiNorthern spirit shamans who view the Droval as partly spirit-born. The name implies kinship with the ice itself rather than residency on it
Origin & Evolution
Droval evolved as apex megafauna during the First Winter Age, when the Inner World’s polar bands were locked in a supernatural deep freeze following the collapse of a nearby Solfatara site. Over long ages, constant exposure to Titan-touched cold ground, where the Titan Vohrin’s power pools in the rock, altered their bodies and instincts, infusing the species with elemental resonance beyond ordinary natural evolution. They are still mortal-born creatures, with no artificer’s hand in them and no summoner’s, but their bloodline has been permanently shaped by ancient Winter essence in the same way that geological pressure permanently shapes the crystal structure of the stone it acts on. The cold found a very large bear-shaped predator and went on refining it until the refinement was all anyone could see.
Droval are native to the Material World, specifically the polar shelf and polar regions of the Inner World where the deep ice holds Aetheric density high enough to sustain Winter-saturated biology. They inhabit frozen mountain ranges, glacier basins, white forests, arctic plains, and the specific liminal territories where the shelf’s geography intersects with the ice’s older Aetheric architecture. Wild Droval claim immense hunting ranges measured in hundreds of square kilometers. They do not migrate, and they sit out whatever comes.
Winter Eladrin later began selective bonding, ritual imprinting, and war-line breeding, refining Droval into elite mounts without ever fully taming their wild nature. Treaty is the right word for the bond between a Winter Eladrin rider and a Droval, and an Eladrin will correct you if you say domestication. The rider earns the mount’s recognition through a rite of winter kinship, and the mount extends its territorial instinct to include the rider as part of its own being. The distinction matters: a tamed animal obeys, and a bonded Droval cooperates, on its own terms, for as long as the terms are honored.
The rarest among them, known as Titan Droval, are believed to be ancient individuals that survived for centuries in direct proximity to major Vohrin-touched sites until their bodies partially transformed into living elemental matter. Size has very little to do with it. A Titan is a Droval that has crossed a threshold, permanently, and every other terrifying thing about it follows from that.
Appearance
Standard Adult
A standard adult Droval is a colossal predator built on a bear’s chassis by a colder intelligence than any bear has ever answered to. Most adults stand between ten and twelve feet at the shoulder and stretch over twenty feet in body length, carrying several tons of dense muscle beneath a pelt the polar shelf cannot distinguish from itself.
The body is built for patience and violence, in that order. Broad forelimbs are made for mauling, sprinting across ice, and breaking through glacier crust to reach prey sheltering beneath. The musculature across the shoulders and upper back is disproportionately developed, dense enough to absorb impacts that would shatter the skeleton of lesser megafauna, and layered beneath the fur in a way that makes the creature look almost sculpted at rest, a thing carved from snow. The hindquarters carry enough explosive power to launch the full mass into a pounce that covers thirty meters in a single bound, and the landing is silent, because the paws are the species’ masterpiece.
The paws are wide and heavily padded, with a toe-spread that distributes the creature’s weight across deep snow the way a snowshoe distributes a human’s. Each pad is backed by thick cartilage that absorbs impact vibration before it can reach the ice surface, and the combination of spread and absorption produces what this bestiary calls Silent Tread: a creature the size of a longhouse can cross packed shelf-ice without cracking it and deep snow without compressing it. The claws are thick, black, hooked, and set at an angle that bites into glacier surfaces the way a climbing axe bites into vertical ice: forward-curved, self-sharpening, made for grip and traction, though they will slash when slashing is needed.
The Head
The head is the species’ most distinctive feature and sets the Droval apart from every other megafaunal predator in the Inner World’s bestiary. It resembles a monstrous owl fused with a polar bear’s killing apparatus. The skull is broad and blunt, with a pronounced brow ridge that protects the eyes from glare and impact. A hooked beak, bone-hard and pale as old ivory, terminates the muzzle, and behind the beak-line sit rows of jagged teeth that do the feeding after the beak has done the killing. The beak punctures and the teeth process, two separate tools in one skull, each with its own mechanics, and the few hunters who have seen one up close and come home have all remarked on how few mistakes such a head allows.
Large forward-facing eyes sit beneath the brow ridge, adapted for low-light and storm-dark visibility, binocular for distance tracking. The irises carry a pale luminescence, blue, silver, or aurora-green, that intensifies in darkness and during emotional arousal, the glow produced by Wellspring-saturated optic tissue permanently altered by millennia of Winter resonance. It shows at a long distance, and most of those who see it have only that long to act.
Short tufted ears, stiff frost-lined whiskers, and layers of dense white or pale blue fur complete the silhouette. At rest in snow, a Droval is the snow, as a consequence of being made of much the same stuff as the place it lies, and no one has ever seen one take any trouble over it.
Titan Droval
Titan Droval differ from the standard baseline in ways that make the word “differ” inadequate. They can exceed twenty feet at the shoulder, with fur partially crystallized into translucent frost-fiber that catches light the way ice crystals do, refracting and splitting it into a faint prismatic play along the flanks and shoulders. It looks beautiful from a safe distance, and nobody has described it from any other.
Their eyes burn with the specific intensity of cold stars: a harder, deeper, more concentrated light than the standard Droval’s luminescence, which reads to the human eye as ancient. Wellspring saturation produces it, showing through the only transparent tissue the body contains, and the signature it writes in the dark says: I have been alive longer than your civilization.
The air around a Titan Droval produces drifting ice crystals at all times. They form spontaneously from ambient moisture, pulled in by the Titan’s Winter field, and they hang without falling, orbiting the creature’s body in slow, purposeless circuits. Nothing in this is a technique. The Titan has carried Winter for so long that the air around it gives way to that one idea and holds it as its own law, the way a star’s gravity bends the path of nearby matter; the Measurewrights say its Aetheric mass warps the local thermal equilibrium.
When enraged or preparing to charge, frost spreads visibly along their flanks, claws, and shoulders. Their breath rolls out in shining plumes. A faint shell of rime forms along the fur. The sound changes too: the Silent Tread stays no louder but grows heavier, the footfall of a mass that has stopped troubling to be quiet.
Temperament & Behavior
Droval are solitary, territorial ambush predators with exceptional patience and almost unnatural stillness. In the wild, a Droval may remain motionless for hours while snow piles over its back, waiting for prey to come close enough for a sudden killing rush. There is nothing passive in that patience. Every muscle is loaded, every sense engaged, and every calculation runs on behind the luminous eyes, and the prey that walks up to a motionless Droval has no idea what it is walking up to.
They are deliberate, intelligent, and brutally efficient, with no frenzy in them at all. Once a Droval commits to an attack, it does so with full lethal intent and does not disengage until the target is dead or the Droval has determined that the cost of continuing exceeds the value of the prey. That reckoning sets them apart. Ordinary predators weigh risk, and Droval weigh investment: a Droval will abandon a hunt without shame if its economics stop working, will pursue one across kilometers if they stay favorable, and makes both decisions with the same absence of emotion.
Wild Droval claim immense hunting ranges and tolerate almost no intrusion unless the trespasser is prey, a potential mate, or a bonded companion. Outside breeding season or a mother-cub bond, they do not gather in groups. When two Droval occupy overlapping territory, the resolution need not be violent.
