the-magic-system/first-steps/the-measure.title: The Measures at a Glance
the-magic-system/first-steps/the-measure.content:
Ottilie Crake had run the slate at the Harvest Brackets in Thornby Cross for nineteen years when she chalked up the Expert Bout at evens, because both fighters carried the same silver token and she had a headache. One of them was a Stage V cooper’s son in a borrowed green sash. The other had been lit for six years and had come into the double sight the previous winter (Stage VII, in the Accord’s numbering), a fact he had mentioned to nobody. When they walked out, every banner on the field leaned over toward the older man, the crowd’s noise dropped to a mutter, and the cooper’s son, sweating like a cheese, looked at his opponent, looked at his boots, and was sick on them. Nobody had thrown a punch. By sundown a Measurewright’s apprentice with a very good memory for tables owned a brewery that had been Ottilie’s, and Ottilie, a fair woman, had the whole of this page chalked on the side of her new, smaller premises, where you may read it for the price of a beer.
Learn the numbers. Some of them decide the fight, some of them decide the rent, and the two most expensive mistakes in the trade are confusing one for the other and trusting a token. Ottilie’s chalk has been added to since by people with worse handwriting, because the world now asks you to read a dungeon crew’s sheet, a sword’s stamp and a monster’s bounty as well as a bout.
Every number a practitioner, a monster or a piece of gear is read by, on one page, and what your own soul shows you of them. For the whole system in brief, see How Magic Works.
A practitioner is measured on the Soul Crystal (the soul itself, which holds power and sends it out). Their strengths are counted on sixty-four Sub-Stats (single measured abilities, such as Flux for the force a working carries or Fortitude for how well bone takes a blow), grouped under eight Primaries (Vitality, Ardency, Gnosis, Dexterity, Harmonics, Resilience, Tempering, Dominion). Their power is spent from a reserve (the one store a soul carries, counted in EU, Essence Units, which the guild reckons at a megajoule each, whatever fills it). That reserve fills as they draw Aether (mana) in from the ground and air around them. A Body fighter packs it raw in the Shell and holds it as the Charge, and a Spirit worker refines it in the Crystal into Essence (spiritual energy), which is why a fighter’s numbers and a fighter’s ground get argued over in the same breath. The measures below are the ways the Archives, the Accord and the street describe all that.
Essence is the soul’s own substance, and Charge is the world’s. The Crystal has three layers and every soul has all three: the Aether Shell meets the Physical World, the Essence Core holds identity on the Soul Plane, and the Attraction Layer holds a soul’s own share of fate on the Plane of Fate. Aether refined in the Crystal takes the stamp of whoever refined it, the Core is the center of all identity, and the Crystal is the soul, so a Spirit worker’s reserve is the person, and spending it is spending yourself: what is lost on the way is paid as a hollowing in the Core. A Body fighter’s reserve is raw Aether that was never refined, so spending it is spending the world, the lost share burns off as heat in the Shell’s furnace, and the body pays for the handling. A Fate worker holds no Thread at all: each pull is paid for out of the soul’s own share and leaves a knot, a debt the world collects later. Fighters call the three Aether Manipulation, Essence Manipulation and Thread Manipulation. Ottilie’s chalk prices all of it by the guild’s megajoule regardless.
The owner sees most of it for free. A window (the soul reporting its numbers to its owner, in the owner’s own tongue, unseen by anyone else) shows numbers, ranks, percentages, bars and Level. EU, AU/s and yield (η) never appear in one: those belong to the coil, the Measurewrights and the notes. A normal look gives the Eight Primaries as totals, with no letter on them, and a Sub-Stat appears when it is used or when it moves. Everyone else’s numbers take a stronger Gnosis Perception against a weaker Resilience Ward, or an instrument, and anything short of that is an estimate said aloud, which people can hide or fake.

Paragons pass 500 unnumbered.The owner’s window, as an exact number. Assessors, off the coil. Commoners round it or never hear it.Sets the size of the reserve (it multiplies by ten every 78 Levels) and the Stat Points a practitioner has to spend; holds a Stage open (Stage II holds at Level 5, III at 15, IV at 30, V at 101, VI at 115, VII at 130, VIII at 201, IX at 215, X at 230, XI at 301, XII at 320, XIII at 401, XIV at 420, XV at 500); and places a soul’s Mastery under its Stage’s ceiling. Level runs on whether or not the next Catalyst comes, and only past the top of a rank group (over 100 below Expert, 200 below Master, 300 below Grandmaster, 400 below Archmaster) does a waiting soul build Residual Strain.Level 160: a reserve of about 295,000 EU.RankHow everyone says a Stage, in the nine words the Accord also uses for its titles.Initiate (I), Apprentice (II), Journeyman (III), Adept (IV), Expert (V-VII), Master (VIII-X), Grandmaster (XI-XII), Archmaster (XIII-XIV), Paragon (XV-XVI).Everyone, from the bracket crowds to the crowns. “A Journeyman, Ascension, close to Flourishing” is the careful form.What a stranger expects of you before the fight, the cap on your fighting skills, and how Pressure lands on the unwoken: dread from an Initiate or Apprentice, weight in the room from a Journeyman, knees bending from an Expert. A gap of a whole Crystal look between two people changes the weather in the room. The older books grouped the Stages in five Bands (Mortal Foundation, Awakened, Sovereign, Mythic, Absolute); veterans still speak of “the wall at two hundred”.An Expert: anyone from a Splintering novice to a Refraction veteran.StageHow far the Crystal has been remade, one Threshold at a time. A Threshold is a remaking: Tempering melts the Crystal down and rebuilds each layer, refines the Essence and makes it stronger, and the body gains Traits. It opens when its Catalyst (one deed per Stage, met in the lead road’s terms) is met and Level can hold the Stage. A crisis, a seclusion, a tribulation, a Draft or a blessing can supply the Catalyst, so Stages can simply be bought, and a soul holding a Stage its Level cannot yet hold is Overgrown.Sixteen: Murmuring, Welling, Ascension, Flourishing, Splintering, Glory, Refraction, Transcendence, Invocation, Realization, Dissonance, Emanation, Principality, Zenith, Revelation, Apex.Everyone, mostly by rank. Each Release has a Catalyst of its own, however the Stage was got. Nothing in a fight: two Experts may stand two Stages apart, and a Grandmaster merchant may not be able to throw a punch. Master Venn at the forge may be an Apprentice on the road, and people mix the two up. The older books called the title a Tier of Standing and numbered it one to nine. A bought Stage raises the roof and not the rung.A Body Path fighter at Level 160 and Stage VI: Body I, his Stage’s roof, and nothing read on the other two.The Crystal’s lookHow the stone looks at its Stage, all three layers together, a jeweler’s reading and no track of its own.Seed (the unwoken), Clouded (Initiate to Adept), Faceted (the Experts), Fire (the Masters), Flawless (the Grandmasters), Starred (the Archmasters), Absolute (the Paragons). Older books called it the Soul Crystal Tier and gave the Refraction stone a look of its own, Clear, now read as Faceted.Assay houses, healers, Mancers. Everyone else reads it off the aura: one hue for the Wellspring, smoky at Clouded and clearing with every look, sitting where the Path puts it (The Color of Essence).What the Crystal can structurally do: Traits arm at Clouded; a second lens can be harmonized without tearing at Faceted, and one more at each rank after; the first true Domain stands at Fire.Faceted Crystal: steady rhythm, no Domain yet.Soul Crystal stateThe Crystal’s condition today, whatever its look.Refined (balanced, the healthy state), Overgrown (holding more pressure than it has shaped, so power spills; also the standing state of a soul holding a Stage its Level cannot yet hold, bought or met early, until Level catches up), Fractured (split by strain; it leaks).Healers, rivals, anyone with eyes.The aftermath. Overgrown spills and is easy to read, reads low on Mastery, and finds no Release while it lasts; Fractured leaks and weakens. A Second or Third Release held inside its limit leaves a Crystal Overgrown till morning and does no structural damage. Fractures earned by overreach often become permanent.Refined this morning; after the bout below, close to Fractured.PathWhich layer of the Crystal a soul has learned to lean on, read off how it has lived. Nobody picks one.Body (the Aether Shell, the Physical World; works raw Aether, held as the Charge), Spirit (the Essence Core, the Soul Plane; spends Essence, and its force lands on souls), Fate (the Attraction Layer, the Plane of Fate; pulls Thread and holds none). Each stands as Mastered (its gates are no obstacle at the person’s Stage), Walked (three parts in ten of their practice or more) or Studied (knowledge and small uses, open to anyone, opening no gates). A card gives each road a Path Stage, the highest Stage whose gates it has opened: Body VII Mastered · Fate VI Walked 35%.The owner’s window, on the top line. Assessors, off the gated Sub-Stats. The bracket crowds say hitter, thrower, talker and stayer.How far a gated Sub-Stat may rise, and the force bonus: full on one Path, three-quarters on each of two, half on each of three. Two Paths take about two and a half times as long to master and three about six, past a mortal span. It does not decide who wins: no Path is better, each has plain limits, and each can beat each.Body, Mastered: the full bonus by hand, and at his Stage he has to close.Yield (η)The share of each spend that arrives as intended effect, as a distillation has its yield; the Measurewrights’ older word is efficiency. The rest is lost on the road it left by: as heat through the Shell, the furnace burning, with sound, light and bleed, as a hollowing through the Core, as a knot on the Layer.From Glory the Mastery of the road in use sets it, on one table: Body through the Shell, Spirit through the Core, Fate for a pull. Below Glory the Stage’s own figure stands for the unread (about 0.30 at Initiate, 0.60 to 0.70 by Splintering), and above it the same table gives a field average for a stranger not yet read, rising past 1.0 at Archmaster, where the room itself adds to the working. A read rung overrides that average, and a card’s own figure governs its holder.Measurewrights and diagnostic talk. Everyone else says loud or quiet.How hard a fighter hits, how far a reserve goes and how loud they are. Delivered force is spend multiplied by η, and the rate spent at full output (AU/s) is Flux Density times η, so the yield counts twice on purpose: once for how much the layer in use can move and once for what survives the trip. At full output a higher yield empties the reserve faster; for the same delivered effect it lasts longer. A low yield runs dry first on any given blow and announces every working; a master’s work arrives almost silent.η 0.62: of every 100 EU spent, 62 strike home and 38 roar off him as heat.SkillOne thing a person does and has got better at by doing it: swordwork, haggling, brewing Drafts, cutting runes, Appraisal.One of the nine ranks: Initiate, Apprentice, Journeyman, Adept, Expert, Master, Grandmaster, Archmaster, Paragon, the same words as a Stage’s rank. Rises with use. A trade has no cap and can reach Paragon with no Stage; a combat skill never ranks above its owner’s own Stage rank, so an Expert’s sword stops at Expert. Older books wrote skills in letters (Brawling B, now Adept) and later on six craft ranks, Novice to Legend. Anyone can level a skill hands alone can do, pouring Drafts included; cutting runes, firing tags, chanting and speaking a working want a woken Crystal.The owner’s window. Teachers, by eye.How well the thing gets done, and what named techniques can be built on it. Techniques themselves show no level: one jumps when its skill gains a rank and a fight pushes it past its old limit, and takes a bigger name.Brawling, Journeyman: a good right hand, and a window line the day it moves.TraitA standing law in the soul, survived into being.No level of its own. It works at its owner’s Mastery of the lead road, and at its base below Glory, where Mastery is unread; Release and Domain are the same Trait escalating. The older books and some old windows gave Traits levels (The Forge Holds, Level 34).The owner’s window. Rivals guess.How much the Trait does and how reliably, inside its own law.The Forge Holds, worked at Body I.Beast and bounty GradeHow dangerous a job or a monster is, on the Commission scale (a Commission being a sanctioned Accord job).The letters: E, D, C, B, A, S, SS, X, EX, from a Minor Threat to a Realm Hazard, a Cataclysmic Entity and an Apocalyptic Beast. Under the letter a monster also has a Stage, a Level and a lean on one Path, read by Gnosis, with question marks for a weak reader. A famous one earns a name, an epithet and a bounty. The older Commissions counted nine Threat Tiers, T1 to T9, and the crews still say T4 for a Grade B job.The Accord’s bills, every tavern, the crews.Who may lawfully take the job (the Accord sets which title may take which Grade), and how much of your crew comes home. The Grade is also the shorthand for price, and most beasts line up with it, but a monster’s stone and parts are read from its own Stage and Level on the coil.Grade S, under a Gold Sigil, three hundred silver marks on every door in the hundred.Item GradeHow much power a piece of gear carries, on the Measurewrights’ letters, which only things wear.The Grade letters. A smith’s title caps the Grade she may make. Bonded gear grows with its owner; other gear stays what it is.Smiths, the Accord’s stamps, an Appraisal skill, an assay instrument.What it does when it hits or is hit. An enhanced weapon performs no higher than whoever put the power into it.A B-Grade hammer in a Master’s hand.Gear multiplierWhat a worked piece (runed, Draft-tempered or made of monster parts) does to its wearer: it multiplies one whole Primary, all its Sub-Stats together, and the figures are read again from there.Plain gear has none. Worked gear shows them on the window, with a Shell draw (light, steady or heavy) paid from reserve to keep it lit. A bonded piece’s multipliers grow with the bearer, and a relic reads as question marks. All gear together multiplies any one Primary by ×1.5 at most, a cap of its own beside the two-step cap on self-boosts. Above the wearer’s Stage a piece works at half its multiplier or fights them.The owner’s window. Smiths and appraisers, who price by it.How far a kit lifts the person inside it, and what it costs them to wear: heavy plate may read Vitality ×1.3 and Dexterity ×0.85. Soul-wards, charms and reliquaries multiply Resilience and Harmonics; oath-rings, luck-tokens and knot-cutters multiply Dominion and Resilience.[Worn: Ashjaw Helm · Rare · Grade B] [Gnosis ×1.15] [Shell draw: light]Item RarityHow scarce a piece of gear is, which is a separate question from how strong.Common, Uncommon, Rare, Very Rare, Legendary, Mythic, Unique. A merchant’s title caps the Rarity he may sell. The old words (Marked, Proofed, Tempered, Instrument, Hallowed, Storied, Found, Numinous, Proscribed) survive as the Accord’s stamps. A Master Work (a piece that does what its Grade and material should not be able to, made once at the end of a lifetime, named) is always Unique or Mythic.Merchants, appraisers, and thieves. A good forger beats a weak appraiser.The price, who may sell it, and who will kill you for it.Very Rare: you will be followed home.
How they connect
GRADESThe letter on a thing: an item, a missile, a beast, a bounty. Under a person, the hidden scaleHollow1–10F11–25E26–50D51–100C101–175B176–275A276–400S401–550SS551–725SSS726–950X951–1,200EX1,201–1,500EX+1,501 and upOne step upwins the exchange outrightTwo stepsis one-sidedThree stepsis an event the lower side survivesA sword, a bolt, a beast and a bountycarry a Grade aloud. No person does:the card keeps a person’s numbers,and the assayers read them on thisscale, where nobody has to hear it.
Your soul climbs Stages, and each Stage asks one thing of you; your life climbs Level, by everything hard and real you have done; your hands climb skills, by use; everything else on this chalk is read from those three. A Stage opens when its Catalyst is met and Level can hold it, and a Catalyst can come out of a crisis or out of a purse; a Stage got ahead of the Level to hold it leaves the soul Overgrown, and Level run far past the top of a rank group with no Catalyst builds Residual Strain. People say the Stage as its rank. The Stage caps every Sub-Stat and every rung of Mastery, and the numbers of whichever Sub-Stat a moment calls on, read against the other side’s on the hidden scale, decide that moment. Add a Primary’s Sub-Stats and you have the total the register prints. The Accord title is a guild’s word for how far it trusts you, earned by commissions, and it carries no weight in a fight. Power leaves through a layer, so the Mastery of that road sets the yield (before Mastery reads at Glory, the Stage’s own figure gives it), and the yield sets how much of the reserve arrives as force and how much is lost on the way: burned off as heat and noise in the Shell’s furnace, paid as hollowing through the Core, left as a knot on the Layer. Mastery is read from Level under the Stage’s roof, and a Trait works at it. Skills sit beside all this on the same nine ranks and rise by use, and they decide what a practitioner can do with the numbers his life gave him. A bought Stage shows that gap plainly: high ceilings, a low Mastery, a thin skill column, and no Release at all. Drawing Aether in fills the reserve, as fast as the ground allows. Spending runs it down, written as time from full (how long a working holds, begun on a full reserve, before the reserve falls to a tenth and the practitioner starves). The Crystal’s look says what all of this has built; its state says what today has done to it. Gear runs on its own two ratings, Grade for what it can do and Rarity for who wants it, with a worked piece’s multipliers on top, and monsters run on the same Stages and Levels as the people hunting them, with a Grade on top, which no person carries. How Power Grows walks the climb end to end.
Example: one practitioner, read on every measure
Garrick Vane, a senior disciple of a city fighting school, the Brazen Lantern, known from Lantern Street to the river as the Bellows, pays a silver mark at an assay house and stands in the coil. The clerk writes his First Name, the instrument line: Exuroth, Stage VI Glory, Expert, Level 160, Body I Muridic, η .62.






































































MeasureHis readingWhat it means for himLevel160A reserve of about 295,000 EU, nearly all of it held as Charge, since his road is the Body. Thirty Levels past the hold for Refraction, so he can take Stage VII the day its Catalyst comes, and forty Levels of grinding before a soul left waiting at the Expert’s top begins to strain.RankExpertThe same word on his silver token as on the Stage V disciple he will fight this afternoon, and the same rank. Refraction’s Catalyst, the first flicker of a Domain seed, is what he is waiting on.StageVI, Glory (“lit”)His Sub-Stats stop at 400. One Stage over a Splintering rival, his presence bends her attention; lamp flames lean toward him. Glory puts his cherry-red where any civilian can see it.Sub-StatsFlux 352, Fortitude 240, Celerity 210, Perception 120He hits a full step harder than he takes a blow, moves about as well as he takes one, and notices things two steps worse than he hits. A Measurewright would say he hits like a Grade A beast and soaks like a B.PrimaryArdency 2,080, a mean of 260The register prints the mean. His fist does not read it.ClassHammerhandThe name his soul offered him at Glory, for a life spent hitting things, and it has leaned his growth into the right arm ever since.MasteryBody I, Muridic; nothing read on Spirit or FateGlory’s roof is rung I, so his Level, which would carry him to II, waits on Refraction to raise it. His Shell leaks a third of every spend. He has never used his Core on anyone, and has never felt a thread.CrystalFaceted, RefinedSound, steady, and a long way from a Domain. His color sits on the skin like heat-haze, as a Body fighter’s does, a thin haze with the cherry-red standing in it.PathBody VI, MasteredThe full force bonus at contact, and he has to get there first. He works raw Aether through the Shell, and when he tires he runs hot.Yield (η)0.62His workings arrive hot and loud. Opponents hear him coming and can count what he has left.SkillsBrawling, Journeyman; Showmanship, Master; Footwork, ApprenticeHe can hit, he can sell a hit, and he should look at his feet more often. An Expert’s fighting skills may go to Expert, and his Brawling has room left.TraitThe Forge Holds, at Body IHis Primary Trait, well worn on one side, and working only as deep as his Mastery lets it.
That is the view from outside. Garrick, standing in the same coil, sees this, and nobody else in the room does:
[Garrick Vane · Human · Level 160 · Stage VI, Glory · Path: Body]
[Class: Hammerhand]
[Mastery: Body I]
[Vitality 760 · Ardency 2,080 · Gnosis 240 · Dexterity 480]
[Harmonics 140 · Resilience 180 · Tempering 160 · Dominion 160]
[Reserve: 100% ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓]
[Trait: The Forge Holds]
[Skills: Showmanship, Master · Brawling, Journeyman · Footwork, Apprentice]
[Blessing: none]

No EU, no yield and no Flux until he uses it. Those Primaries are totals, and Stat Points are few: a man at Level 160 has spent about 4,200 of them across all sixty-four Sub-Stats, half on Ardency, so nearly everything he has never had reason to use sits low, and only the few entries his life has leaned on reach the figures in the table above. The coil knows what his window leaves out, his window knows what the coil leaves out, and a Measurewright will explain over a long dinner why neither is the true account.
The coil’s line is accurate and, by itself, useless. What Garrick is in a fight lives in the gap between his Flux and his Fortitude, and in the roar every working makes: a fist a full step heavier than the body behind it, loud enough to be timed. One Exchange, Annotated shows what a lower-Stage fighter does with exactly that reading.

the-magic-system/fracture-of-worlds-—-th.title: Fracture of Worlds — The Living System
the-magic-system/fracture-of-worlds-—-th.content:
The System does not reward survival. It rewards contact with things larger than you.
Every scar the Soul Crystal carries is a record of how far you reached beyond what you were.
The most expensive sentence ever spoken at the Haymarket Fair in Altherion cost forty silver marks, the good name of a councilman’s son and most of a pie stall. Aldous Thwaite had hired a Measurewright (a Guild scholar who assays souls for a fee) to read his Soul Crystal from a scarlet-draped stage, with trumpets. The man set a brass assay fork against Thwaite’s breastbone, listened to it sing, and then, the fork still ringing and himself an honest fool, turned it toward the groom holding the horse. “Your groom reads higher, young sir.” Thwaite called the groom out on the spot, and the groom hit him once, apologizing, and six hundred people watched a gold-stitched coat leave through the pies. What follows is the ledger that fork was reading. Measurewrights who read it aloud to paying customers learn to stand near a door.
What the System Is
The Fracture of Worlds progression framework is the metaphysical skeleton beneath every character in War of the Realms. It is not a game overlay imposed on the world from outside. It is a natural consequence of how the Continuum observes, measures, and responds to the maturation of living souls. When a practitioner grows, the Continuum recognizes it. When they stagnate, the Continuum applies pressure. When they fracture, the Continuum waits to see what re-forms in the break.
The System tracks eight dimensions of a soul’s development, each called a Primary Stat, and beneath each of those, eight finer measurements called Sub-Stats. These numbers are not just mechanical data. They are the Continuum’s honest accounting of who you actually are, not who you claim to be.
Level is simply the count of how many times your Soul Crystal (literally the soul itself, where a practitioner’s power is held and shaped) has meaningfully densified. It is not a measure of age. It is not a measure of training hours. It is the sediment of genuine contact with consequence, counted, compressed, and expressed as a number. Level moves by any real work a life does: danger overcome above all, so killing something stronger moves it more than a hundred weak kills and crews argue over who got the kill, but also a flood night held, a plague nursed through, fifty years at a trade. The baker can stand at Level 140 and never have been in danger. Level does not open a Stage by itself. A Stage opens when its Catalyst is met and the soul’s Level can hold it; How Power Grows has the short road.
The ceiling is 500 for everyone below Stage XV. Paragons (practitioners at Stages XV and XVI) exceed it, and the Codex does not number what they reach.
The Window
Everyone carries a private copy of this ledger, the unwoken included: a baker has a Baking skill and a little sheet. The Soul Crystal is the soul and the Continuum measures it, so the soul reports its numbers to its owner in their own tongue, and nobody else can see the report. That report is the window. It comes up often and in detail, in a fight as readily as on a quiet morning, for damage, for skill gains and for reserve, and it sits in the owner’s sight as a plain block of text: [Reserve: 41%]. It shows numbers, percentages, bars and levels, and it never gives its owner a letter: Grades are for things. The EU, AU/s and yield (η) of the later Parts stay out of it and live on a Measurewright’s slate. The groom at the Haymarket had been reading his own every morning for years, and a normal look at it went something like this:
[Stage IV Flourishing · Adept (Clouded)]
[Level 64]
[Race: Human · Lineage: none of note]
[Vitality 552 · Ardency 310 · Gnosis 141 · Dexterity 604]
[Harmonics 120 · Resilience 133 · Tempering 150 · Dominion 112]
[Reserve: 100% ██████████]
[Skills: Horse-handling, Journeyman · Short Right Hand, Apprentice]
[Blessings: none]

A normal look shows the Eight Primaries with their totals. A Sub-Stat surfaces when it is used or when it moves, and the full set stays there for anyone with the patience to study it. Race and lineage show, and they shape base stats and what comes easily. Skills rise with use and show on the nine ranks, Initiate, Apprentice, Journeyman, Adept, Expert, Master, Grandmaster, Archmaster and Paragon; techniques are named things done with them, show no level, and take a bigger name when they jump. A Trait has no level: it works at its base until Glory and at the lead Path’s Mastery after. A blessing sits on its own line, and since the giver wrote that line, it can lie. To read anyone else you need an assay fork or a Gnosis Perception stronger than their Resilience Ward; everything short of that is an estimate said aloud, and people can hide it or fake it, which keeps the Measurewrights in pie.
The Twenty-Four Parts
The full system is split across child pages below, grouped by what a session actually needs to reach for.

I. Levels, Experience and Stat Points, Parts One through Three. Level and what holds a Stage, Temperance Gates, Resonant Accumulation, the point economy.
II. Grades, Gates and Thresholds, Parts Four through Ten. The hidden scale under the numbers, stat ceilings by Stage, speed by Grade, per-Sub-Stat Path gates, Threshold Catalysts, Resonant Pairs, stagnation.
III. Force of Hand, Part Eleven, the old Physical Force. Strike Force, Lifting Strength, Durability, Range, Aura Pressure.
IV. The Eight Primaries and the Sixty-Four Sub-Stats, Part Twelve.
V. Wellsprings, Attraction and Obsession, Magic Integration, Parts Thirteen through Fifteen.
VI. The Sixteen Temperance Stages, Part Sixteen.
VII. Mastery, Paths and the Lens, Aether Flow, Parts Seventeen through Nineteen.
VIII. Traits, the Crystal’s Look, Domains, Parts Twenty through Twenty-Two.
IX. The Essence Ledger, Part Twenty-Three. What an EU buys and what the guild reckons it at in joules, what a reserve costs to spend, and how fast it comes back.
X. The Tier Ladders, Part Twenty-Four.

The Short Version
Ringside, nobody says any of this. They ask what rank a fighter is and what he is good for, and the Measurewright in the judges’ box winces and writes down the real terms, which are these.
Three things climb. The soul climbs Stages, and each Stage asks one thing of it. The life climbs Level, by everything hard and real it has done. The hands climb skills, by use. Everything else on the sheet is read from those three.
Stage, said as rank. Sixteen Stages, and everyone says the rank: I Initiate, II Apprentice, III Journeyman, IV Adept, V to VII Expert, VIII to X Master, XI and XII Grandmaster, XIII and XIV Archmaster, XV and XVI Paragon. The Stage name is the precise term (“a Journeyman, Ascension, and close to Flourishing”). The Crystal shows it in its look, which is how the stone looks and not a track of its own: Clouded (I to IV), Faceted (V to VII), Fire (VIII to X), Flawless (XI and XII), Starred (XIII and XIV), Absolute (XV and XVI). The old reckoning of five Bands of a hundred Levels, Mortal Foundation through Absolute, survives only in old books.
Level cap 500. A Stage opens when its Catalyst is met and the soul’s Level can hold it: Stage II holds at Level 5, IV at 30, V at 101, VIII at 201, XI at 301, XIII at 401, XV at 500, and Level keeps rising past 500 at Paragon with no number the Codex will give. A Stage held above its Level, bought or met early, leaves the Crystal Overgrown until Level catches up. Level that runs past the top of its rank’s group with no Catalyst to the next (past 100 below Expert, 200 below Master, 300 below Grandmaster, 400 below Archmaster) builds Residual Strain, and the veteran stuck at that gate is the strange and dangerous one.
The hidden scale is a fixed threshold on the raw Sub-Stat value, universal across every stat: 1–10, 11–25, 26–50, 51–100, 101–175, 176–275, 276–400, 401–550, 551–725, 726–950, 951–1,200, 1,201–1,500, 1,501 and above. On a thing it is read aloud as a Grade, Hollow and F through EX+, and a sword, a bolt, a beast or a bounty carries its letter openly. On a person it is never named: the sheet shows the number, and a stat a full step ahead on the scale wins its exchange without a contest. A Primary is the combined total of its eight Sub-Stats; Dominion counts seven, since Throne stands outside it. A Measurewright may still say a woman hits like a Grade A beast, and she will not thank him.
Same words, two worlds. The nine ranks are also the Guild Accord’s nine titles, Initiate through Paragon, and the Accord grades trust in a trade with them: a merchant may deal up to his title, a craftsman make up to hers, an adventurer take commissions up to the Grade of bounty the Accord allows that title. Titles are earned by commissions; fighting guilds also ask the title’s own rank in Stage, and trades ask none. So “Master Venn” at the forge may be an Apprentice by Stage on the road, and a Grandmaster merchant may still be unable to throw a punch. People mix the two up, and lose money doing it.
Temperance Stage caps the value. A character cannot allocate past a ceiling their Crystal cannot structurally sustain. A transient boost passes that ceiling lawfully inside two steps on the hidden scale, read from the sustainable figure on the sheet; only a stat forced there to stay produces Crystal Fracture Events at an exponentially increasing rate. A Catalyst can be met by crisis, seclusion or tribulation, or handed over in a breakthrough Draft or a blessing, so a Stage can simply be bought. A bought Stage opens the door and no more: Level, Mastery and every Release must still be lived.
A Class is a name the soul offers for how the person has lived, first at Glory, Stage VI, with Mastery I. It is a name and never a number, and it evolves when the lead Path’s Mastery rises, each evolution giving one move that fits it. Mastery is one rung per Path, I to V and Ω, written on the card as Body IV or Spirit III. It is never tracked: the Stage sets the ceiling and Level places the soul under it, and it is unread below Glory, where the Stage’s typical figure serves. From Glory it sets the yield of workings through its Path’s layer: matter reads Body, a soul or a meaning reads Spirit, a condition reads Fate. Fate climbs with Level like the others, but without a grip, a Work of a bloodline or a blessing, it stops at II. Each road keeps its own folk words for the rungs (Muridic, Harmonic and the rest on the Body road; Listener, Answerer on the Spirit; Touched, Drawn on the Fate), and a rung held in the feared wrong way is called Inverted. The old Aether, Essence and Thread Classes, each running Ø to Ω, are the scholars’ old name for it. Classes and Mastery has the one table.
The reserve is one figure, and what fills it follows the road. Essence is Aether refined in the Crystal and stamped with identity. The Essence Core is the center of that identity and the Crystal is the soul, so Essence is the soul’s own substance, and spending it is spending yourself: it is what the Spirit Path spends, through the Core, and what it loses on the way is paid there as a hollowing and never as heat. The Charge is Aether packed raw in the Shell and never refined. It is what the Body Path spends, shaped by the lens right there and driven out through the Shell; spending it is spending the world, the body pays for the handling, and the lost share burns in the Shell’s furnace as heat. Thread is what the Fate Path pulls: never held, paid from the soul’s own share, and every pull leaves a knot the world collects later. Below a tenth of the reserve a Spirit worker’s Core frays, names first and then memory, and a Body fighter’s Shell starts drawing on the flesh. The Three Paths has the three routes and their prices.
A Wellspring is an alchemical and a spiritual transformation, the governing idea that transforms how a soul uses Aether: a lens on magic already potent, which a soul bases its tempering on. The Titans are the Wellsprings themselves, and each of the Sixty is one way a Titan’s law shows up. It is got at a Core in a dungeon, from a school, from a Draft or blessing, or by birth. Each of the Sixty has a kind naming its home, Wild (thirty-three), Spirit (fifteen), Fate (six) or Medium (six, at home on all three), and a kind is a qualifier and never a lock: any Path can use any Wellspring.
A Path is the layer of the Crystal a soul leans on, and there are three: Body (the Physical World, through the Aether Shell, spending Charge), Spirit (the Soul Plane, through the Essence Core, spending Essence) and Fate (the Plane of Fate, through the Attraction Layer, pulling Thread). The Shell is the only door into matter, so a Spirit worker’s thrown force lands on souls and on nothing else. One Path masters fastest. Two take about two and a half times as long and three about six. A card gives each road a Path Stage, the highest Stage whose gates it has opened, and Mastered means that equals the soul’s Stage. No Path is the better one. Each has plain limits and each beats each of the others, and the Stage, the ground and the preparation decide which of those holds on the day.
The Plane of Fate is the control of Attraction Force and Obsession Force and the workings of reality itself. Physical Reality under Aegor and Spiritual Reality under Ashura are the two lower realities; Fate, under Bara, sits above them and is no reality at all, being everything that flows, every possibility, idea and concept. People fight and wage wars with it, and it is the hardest thing they do. Real Fate Arts are rare and mostly by bloodline, and most people only touch it through a blessing.
Eight Primary Stats: Vitality, Ardency, Gnosis, Dexterity, Harmonics, Resilience, Tempering, Dominion. Eight Sub-Stats each, sixty-four in total.
The Crystal does not lie. It only counts what you actually are. The line a blessing’s giver wrote on it is another matter.

the-magic-system/fracture-of-worlds-—-th.content:
Jory Eel-Hand of the Slackwater fens, below Altherion, holds a record nobody has tried to take from him. Over thirteen years he killed the same kind of marsh eel, violet and thick as a thigh, with the same stroke of the same gaff, somewhere past forty thousand times, in the firm belief that a man who killed enough of anything must eventually climb. He gained two Levels (a Level is one count of the Soul Crystal growing denser), both in the first year. The children on the Eel Steps sang a counting song about whether he would ever make a third, and they had reached the rude verse on the morning a Well-spawn eel (a creature born where a Wellspring’s Aether pools) the length of a tithe barge came up through the fen with a mask of shining gold across its face. Jory put the gaff through the mask because it was the only stroke he knew, and then spent an hour in the thing’s coils being broken in ways no eel had ever broken him. He crawled out at sunset minus an ear and three fingers, nine Levels higher, weeping and laughing, and the whole of the Steps carried him to the taverns on a door. His gaff hangs in the fish guild’s hall, with a brass plate. Young fools come to touch it, and the Crystal counts that for about as much as it counted the eels.
The Guild has a word for what forty thousand eels were worth, Familiar, and you will find it in Part Ten on the next page. This page is the arithmetic of that afternoon.
Part One — The Level Structure
The Hard Cap
The system operates on a maximum of Level 500 for every practitioner below Stage XV. This number is not arbitrary. It represents the structural limit of what a mortal Soul Crystal (literally the soul itself, where a practitioner’s power is held and shaped) can contain before the distinction between practitioner and Principle collapses entirely. Characters below Stage XV who reach Level 500 do not advance in level; the pressure builds against the cap until the Catalyst to Revelation comes or the Crystal breaks under it. Paragons exceed Level 500. At Stages XV–XVI, Level keeps rising past 500 with no ceiling; the Codex does not number it, and the last of it is the Apotheosis approach, a qualitative event outside the scope of numbered progression.
What a Level Holds
Level does not lift a soul to a Stage. A Stage (one of the sixteen rungs of a soul’s refinement, said aloud as its rank) opens when two things are true: its Catalyst is met, the one deed that Stage asks, in the terms of the soul’s lead Path, and the soul’s Level can hold it. The Catalyst comes by crisis, seclusion or tribulation, or it is handed over in a breakthrough Draft or a blessing. The Level comes only by living. How Power Grows has the short road; the Catalysts for every floor are in The Sixteen Stages.













































































StageRankHolds at LevelStageRankHolds at LevelI MurmuringInitiate1IX InvocationMaster215II WellingApprentice5X RealizationMaster230III AscensionJourneyman15XI DissonanceGrandmaster301IV FlourishingAdept30XII EmanationGrandmaster320V SplinteringExpert101XIII PrincipalityArchmaster401VI GloryExpert115XIV ZenithArchmaster420VII RefractionExpert130XV RevelationParagon500, and on past it unnumberedVIII TranscendenceMaster201XVI ApexParagonthe Apotheosis approach
Overgrown. A Stage held while Level is under its hold, whether bought or met early, leaves the Crystal Overgrown: power spills, lamps lean toward the holder, Mastery reads low and no Release will answer, until Level catches up. The heir with a bought Stage and the prodigy who met a Catalyst at fifteen are the same case to the Crystal, whatever their families say.
Residual Strain. Level runs on whether a Catalyst comes or not, and grinding to the top of a rank’s group is ordinary. Past that top with no Catalyst to the next Stage (past Level 100 below Expert, 200 below Master, 300 below Grandmaster, 400 below Archmaster, 500 below Paragon), pressure builds. It shows in the room first and then in the body, and it may fracture the Crystal. The veteran stuck at the gate is the strange and dangerous one. Strain can also wake the unwoken: a commoner who has lived hard enough builds pressure until something breaks the seal, and late wakings are a known thing in every market town.
The Rank Groups
The ranks gather the sixteen Stages into the groups people talk about. Scholars once counted them as five Bands of a hundred Levels, Mortal Foundation, Awakened, Sovereign, Mythic and Absolute, and older books still do.
Initiate to Adept, Stages I through IV, mostly Levels 1 through 100. The era of first contact. The Soul Crystal is Clouded, porous, receptive and relatively unformed. Growth here is the fastest in a character’s life because the Crystal is still learning the shape of Essence. Practitioners of genuine but bounded power, dangerous to mortals, irrelevant to Archons.
Expert, Stages V through VII, mostly Levels 101 through 200. The character has survived their first genuine encounters with forces larger than themselves. The Crystal turns Faceted and begins to show its character, the specific resonance signature that will define this practitioner’s identity across every future stage. Techniques begin to cohere, Mastery is first read at Glory, and a Domain seed (the first root of a space where the practitioner’s law overrides local law) becomes possible at Refraction.
Master, Stages VIII through X, mostly Levels 201 through 300. Genuine metaphysical authority. The Crystal has taken Fire. Their Aura suppresses weaker resonances without effort. Their techniques carry the weight of doctrine rather than improvisation. The world responds to their presence before they act.
Grandmaster, Stages XI and XII, mostly Levels 301 through 400. Power is no longer measured in individual techniques. It is measured in how significantly a practitioner’s existence reshapes the metaphysical landscape of the space they occupy. The Crystal is Flawless. Domain becomes law, and Soul Crystal density generates passive environmental effects.
Archmaster, Stages XIII and XIV, mostly Levels 401 through 500. Cosmological presences, their Crystals Starred. Metaphysical output measured against Archon and Titan-scale phenomena. Individual combat becomes a secondary concern; the primary arena is the contest of Domains, Principles, and accumulated doctrine pressing against the laws of the Continuum itself. Stage XV Revelation and Stage XVI Apex, the Paragons, lie beyond canonical mortal progression.
Zenith, Stage XIV, is not a stage that ends. It is the state of a soul that has reached the upper boundary of mortal architecture and remains there, pressing against what it has not yet become, with only Revelation’s Catalyst and the Apotheosis approach beyond it.
Part Two — Experience and Resonant Accumulation
What Experience Actually Is
Experience is Resonant Accumulation, the compression residue left inside the Soul Crystal when a living being makes genuine contact with forces, choices, and consequences that exceed their current metaphysical comfort. Level moves by any real work a life does, and by danger overcome above all, so killing something stronger moves it more than a hundred weak kills, and crews argue over who got the kill, loudly and for years. A flood night held, a plague nursed through, fifty years at a trade all count, more slowly; the baker can stand at Level 140 and never have been in danger, and a lifetime’s work counts toward everything Level is read for once the soul wakes. The window settles nothing, since it reports only to its owner: [Level 12, up 9].
The Soul Crystal is not impressed by repetition. It measures growth pressure. The question it asks of every event is: did this stretch the soul’s architecture toward something it has not yet become? If yes, the Crystal records it. If no, the event passes through without deposit.
This is why experience cannot be farmed indefinitely. A threat that demanded everything from you at Level 12 demands nothing of you at Level 47 against the same opponent type with the same techniques. The Crystal has already solved that shape.
How Experience Is Earned
Combat and Genuine Threat. The System does not reward the number of enemies defeated. It rewards the degree of genuine pressure sustained, the novelty of response demanded, and the scale of force engaged relative to the practitioner’s current ceiling.
Same rank, previously used technique against the same opponent type: base XP at diminishing rates beginning at the second repetition, reaching ten percent of base value by the fifth engagement with no meaningful variation.
Same rank, novel adaptive response: one hundred percent of base XP regardless of repetition history. The Crystal rewards the new sentence, not the repeated word.
Fighting above your rank is the single most efficient form of experience generation in the system. One rank above: 1.8x. Two ranks above: 3.2x. Three ranks above: 6.0x. Four or more ranks above, survived: minimum 12.0x, scaling further with the degree to which survival required genuine soul-edge engagement.
Fighting at zero personal risk, no Essence burned, no wound sustained, no moment of genuine threat registered: thirty percent of base combat XP. The Crystal is not impressed by efficiency. It rewards contact with consequence.
Wellspring Contact Events. Direct first contact with the active Aether of a Wellspring not previously encountered produces a Resonant Surge, a significant one-time XP event. Minor Wellspring contact for an Initiate to an Adept: roughly 500 XP. First contact with the raw, untamed Aether of a primary Wellspring for a Master: upward of 40,000 XP. The very first such contact, a Wellspring’s raw Aether touched under pressure, is the Catalyst of Stage II itself. Non-repeatable with the same Wellspring. Deepening existing attunement through sustained channeling, by long breathing and pulling at a Wellspring site or in dense Aether, and by seclusion before a Threshold, moves no Level. It tempers the Crystal and builds the slow, persistent pressure toward the next Threshold that Part Eight asks for.
Gnosis Events. Deciphering an unknown Parunic (written in Parun, the language of magical law) glyph-construct independently. Reading a Wellspring’s structural composition without prior instruction. Diagnosing a Soul Crystal fracture through Aetheric Diagnostics alone. At a desk they move Level as any real work does, slowly, and build pressure toward the next Threshold besides, because conceptual growth registers as structural deepening in the Crystal as well as a life lived. Done with a life riding on the answer, they count as the danger they were.
Soul-Cost Events. Using Overchannel (forcing more output than the Crystal can safely sustain) and sustaining structural Aether Shell (the Crystal’s outer layer, which turns Essence into force) damage to protect something irreplaceable. Breaking a technique before completion at personal mechanical cost to prevent harm to another. Not counted: theatrical self-harm, deliberate damage with no real stakes, cost manufactured strategically for accumulation. The Crystal reads intent, not form.
Oath and Covenant Formation. Swearing a genuine oath, before a Witness Stone or on nothing but your own breath, builds pressure toward the next Threshold commensurate with the weight of what is risked, and Level moves only when keeping it walks the swearer through real danger. An oath that costs nothing builds nothing. A significant pulse on swearing, and again on fulfillment. A broken vow lands at once by its own terms, and catastrophic violation registers as a Temperance strain event that builds its own painful pressure. See Vows and Oaths.
Temperance Threshold Completion. The largest single XP event available. It generates a retroactive surge that partially fills the road to the next Stage’s hold. Temperance advancement is not a product of experience. It is a generator of it. The Crystal that survives a Threshold is a larger vessel than it was before. A Threshold crossed on a bought Catalyst pays no surge, since nothing was overcome: the vessel is larger and sits empty, Overgrown if Level is short of the hold, until living fills it.
XP Thresholds by Level
XP requirements are not linear. The early hundreds move swiftly because the Crystal is soft. The later hundreds require cosmological-scale pressure because the Crystal at that point is nearly stone.

Part Three — Stat Points
Allocation Per Level
Every level grants a fixed allotment of Stat Points. Points are spent on Sub-Stats only. A Primary Stat is never purchased and holds no value of its own. It is the combined total of its eight Sub-Stats, recalculated the moment any one of them moves. Vitality is what Fortitude, Absorption, Constitution and the other five add up to. Dominion is what Radius, Sovereignty, Sense and the rest add up to. The Crystal does not record a category. It records where the pressure went, and the category is the arithmetic afterward.
This is the model every sheet is built on. A sheet that records a Primary as a figure bought in its own right, a second layer of spend laid over the Sub-Stats, is wrong by this page and is re-costed to this shape: points on the Sub-Stats only, the Primary as the total of its eight.
Life spends most of these points. A level’s allotment lands where the pressure went, by what the person actually does, and a farrier’s points do not wander into Feint because he would have liked them to. A few are the owner’s to place, at each Stage, on whatever Sub-Stats they choose. Both obey the concentration cap below, which applies per Sub-Stat per level-up.



































LevelsPoints per levelConcentration cap per Sub-Stat, per level-up1–100125101–200155201–300188301–4002110401–5002412
Temperance Threshold events grant bonus Stat Points equal to the Stage number multiplied by 100, landing in Sub-Stats on the same terms: most where the life that reached the Threshold has been spending itself, and a few wherever the owner sets them. A Stage VI Threshold awards 600 points. A Stage XIII Threshold awards 1,300.
Stage I counts as a Threshold worth 100 points. Every practitioner starts with those 100 Threshold points, and the totals below count them: 1,000 from Thresholds I through IV, 9,100 through Stage XIII.
The Full Point Economy
Levels 1 to 100 contribute 1,200 points. Levels 101 to 200, 1,500. 201 to 300, 1,800. 301 to 400, 2,100. 401 to 500, 2,400. Total from leveling at Level 500: 9,000 points. Threshold bonuses through Stage XIII total 9,100 points. Full lifetime pool through Stage XIII: approximately 18,100 points, spendable across sixty-three Sub-Stats, Throne excluded.
The allotment was cut by two fifths from its original figures when the Sub-Stat count was consolidated from a hundred and twenty to sixty-four. The old pool was sized against a phantom count of twenty stats and produced an overabundance the ceiling could not absorb. The cut restores scarcity without making versatility a luxury.
A sheet costed on the old figures, twenty, twenty-five and thirty a Level across the first three hundred Levels, is re-costed to the table above: allocations trimmed to fit the current pool, the Path gates of Part Seven applied in the same pass. The Threshold grants are unchanged and stay in the pool. A Temperance Stage ratified on such a sheet stands. Only the numbers move.
Breadth is affordable. Mastery is not. A character who spreads the lifetime pool evenly carries roughly 287 in every Sub-Stat, at Stage XIII against a ceiling of 1,200. That is the versatile build, and it is a legitimate one: competent everywhere, dominant nowhere, its Primaries all reading the same modest mean. The specialist pushes a handful of Sub-Stats toward the 1,200 ceiling and pays for it with entries left near the floor. Both are viable, which is the point of the cut.
Worked examples. An Adept at Level 100 and Stage IV holds 1,200 from leveling and 1,000 from Thresholds I through IV. Spread evenly that is 35 a Sub-Stat. Concentrated into fifteen entries it is 147, against a Stage IV ceiling of 275.
An Expert at Level 200 and Stage VII holds roughly 5,500 cumulative. Spread evenly, 87 a Sub-Stat. Concentrated into twenty entries, 275, against a Stage VII allocation cap of 400, with 401 to 475 reachable only under strain. An Expert whose best entries sit a full step under his ceiling is the correct shape, not an anomaly requiring justification.
Temperance Ceilings
The ceiling binds the Sub-Stat. No Sub-Stat may exceed the ceiling imposed by the character’s current Temperance Stage, regardless of how many points are available to spend. The Stage’s allocation cap binds: a Sub-Stat may not be allocated past the top of the step on the hidden scale that the Stage allows. Where the Stage’s numeric ceiling sits above the bracket, at Stages V, VII, IX and XI, the band between them is the instability zone, reachable only under strain, never by allocation. Stage V caps allocation at 275, and 276 to 350 is its instability zone. Stage XIII caps a Sub-Stat at 1,200. The pool generates the points. The Crystal determines whether those points can be held. Points earned and refused by the ceiling are not lost; they sit as pressure until a Threshold enlarges the vessel.
Throne is the single exception. It carries no ceiling and is excluded from the Dominion total. Dominion’s mean is therefore the total divided by seven, the seven counted Sub-Stats; Throne sits outside both the total and the mean.
The mean is what an assessor reads. A Primary’s total divided by eight, or by seven for Dominion, gives the value an assessor sets against the hidden scale. A practitioner whose eight Ardency Sub-Stats total 2,400 has a mean of 300. The total is what the sheet records. The mean is what an assessor reads and what a Measurewright says aloud, as a number, never as a letter: Grades are for things, and a man who calls a woman a B to her face has bought himself a fight. A contested exchange is decided by the number of the Sub-Stat actually in use, under the Stage-gap rules; a Sub-Stat a full step ahead on the hidden scale wins its exchange without a contest.
Because the ceiling sits on the Sub-Stat rather than the mean, the original rule holds and is restored: a character’s Sub-Stats and their Primary’s mean sit in the same step of the scale. If the mean reads 200, their stats broadly read about 200. Spread shows what they are good at, and a specialist’s favorites may stand a bracket or more above the mean.
What the mean does to specialists. A Primary is dragged down by its neglected entries as hard as it is lifted by its favorites. A practitioner with three Dominion Sub-Stats at the ceiling and five near nothing reads as a modest Dominion on any assessor’s ledger while legislating local reality with the three. The institutions measure the mean. The fight is decided by the peak. That gap is not a defect in the accounting; it is the reason a register is worth lying to.
The Sheet in the Window
The owner sees all of this in numbers and words, and never a letter. A normal look at the window shows the Eight Primaries with their totals. A Sub-Stat appears when it is used or when it moves, and the full set remains there to study. Race and lineage show on the sheet and shape base stats and what comes easily, and skills sit beside them, rising with use and shown on the nine ranks, Initiate, Apprentice, Journeyman, Adept, Expert, Master, Grandmaster, Archmaster and Paragon. A trade may climb to Paragon with no Stage at all; a combat skill never ranks above its owner’s own Stage rank. Jory’s window, on the evening they carried him to the taverns, ran something like this:
[Level 12, up 9]
[Fortitude: 19, rising]
[Threshold: 14, rising]
[Skill: Gaff, Apprentice]
[Points to place: none until your next Stage]

The figures are the same ones a sheet costs out and a Measurewright reads, and Jory could not have told you what a Sub-Stat was on the best day of his life, which this one was.
Read next: Parts Four to Ten. The account in words is How Power Grows, the Aether Shell and Skills and the Hands.

the-magic-system/fracture-of-worlds-—-th.content:
Gudmund Never-Hit worked the ice fairs of Kharven for nine winters with one act. He stood on a square of swept ice in a blue cloak and a hat with a bell on it, and for a copper a bolt anyone with a crossbow could try him at twenty paces. His Reflex read 74 on a Guild roll, which is the very figure for the trick, and his Vitality read 141 all told, because nobody had ever hit him. He watched the finger, he watched the tiller kick, he leaned, the bolt went past his ear into a wall of straw bales, the wind of it set the bell on his hat ringing, and the crowd bawled for more. At the Sunmeet Fair he slipped nineteen in a row from a line of grinning sergeants, with the odds on a hit drifting out to forty to one. The twentieth came from behind him. A chandler’s widow to whom he owed nine silver marks had paid her copper, climbed into the hayloft over the mead tent and rested the stock on a beam.
The bolt went in under the hat and out through his teeth, and the bell went on ringing a good while after he had stopped moving. His coat (the aura a practitioner wears as armor) did nothing for him, since a coat is a thing a man holds and a man taken by surprise is holding nothing. The widow had put one silver mark on a hit before she climbed the ladder, which at forty to one covered the debt four times over and bought a mourning band for the hat. Every line of that afternoon is a matter of numbers, and the numbers are on this page.
Part Four — The Hidden Scale and the Grades of Things
A Grade is a letter for a thing: a blow’s output, a sword, a bolt, a beast, a bounty, a Draft. Under every person’s numbers the same thresholds run as the hidden scale, the steps that decide what scale of force, phenomenon or entity a practitioner can meaningfully engage, resist or overcome. The scale is never named of a person, aloud or in a window: a sheet carries the number, and the Measurewright who says “she stands where a Grade A beast stands” is making a comparison and knows it. A stat cannot hold a step if the Soul Crystal has not undergone the Threshold required to sustain that density. The scholars called the whole system Tier Grade, and on things they still do.
An attack Grade reads off EU delivered, the EU spent times the yield (η), the share of what is spent that reaches the world. The thresholds are the trade’s old ones, and the Measurewrights still reckon them in joules and tons of TNT at one EU to the megajoule; that column is their conversion and never the reading. The speed column is speed, measured. When two characters clash, who wins a contested exchange is answered first by the step between their numbers on the hidden scale, read under the Stage-gap rules, then by technique and tactical intelligence, then by Soul Crystal architecture.
One full step above an opponent in the relevant stat wins a direct exchange of that stat category without meaningful contest. Two steps above is overwhelming to the point of one-sided. Three steps above means the lower character is not engaging in a battle, they are surviving an event.
Where the Step Sits
The table below measures a Sub-Stat’s raw value, and the Temperance ceiling in Part Five binds the Sub-Stat. Every figure in the Path gates of Part Seven and the Resonant Pairs of Part Nine is a threshold on that Sub-Stat’s own number.
A Primary is the combined total of its eight Sub-Stats, and an assessor reads it off the mean, the total divided by eight, or by seven for Dominion, whose Throne is not counted. Eight Ardency Sub-Stats totaling 2,400 give a mean of 300. The total is what the sheet records; the mean is what an assessor reads, and a contested exchange is decided by the number of the Sub-Stat actually in use. See I. Levels, Experience and Stat Points for the point economy.
Because the ceiling sits on the Sub-Stat, a character’s Sub-Stats and their Primary’s mean sit in the same step. Spread shows what they are good at, and a specialist’s favorites may stand a step or more above the mean. The owner’s window reads in these numbers, never in the letters, which belong to things.
A Primary is dragged down by its neglected entries as hard as it is lifted by its favorites. A practitioner with three Dominion Sub-Stats at the ceiling and five near nothing reads as a modest Dominion on any assessor’s ledger while legislating local reality with the three. The institutions measure the mean. The fight is decided by the peak.
Throne is the exception. It carries no Temperance ceiling, its floor sits at 1,201, and it is excluded from the Dominion total. It is carried as its own line on the character sheet. Dominion’s mean is the total divided by seven, the seven counted Sub-Stats; Throne sits outside both the total and the mean.

In the notes below, the scale names (Wall, Building, Town) say what a blow at that Grade can bring down, and the tons of TNT beside them are the Measurewrights’ reckoning of the same thresholds, a conversion for the trade.
Hollow, 1 to 10. The unawakened baseline. No genuine contact with Essence. Output indistinguishable from ordinary mortal capacity. The System counts it all the same: a baker at Hollow keeps a Level, a Baking skill and a little sheet, with no Essence on it until waking.
F, 11 to 25. First resonance contact has occurred. The Soul Crystal has opened. Technique nascent, Essence output barely controlled, but no longer fully mortal in potential.
E, 26 to 50. Essence is deliberately shaped. Wellspring attunement fragile but genuine. Techniques constructed rather than erupted. Street to low Wall level.
D, 51 to 100. Technique coherence established. Multi-step Aetheric expressions without collapse. Wall level, 0.005 tons TNT at the ceiling.
C, 101 to 175. The step a Journeyman’s Crystal can hold. Intermediate-complexity techniques supported. Dominion at this step has the density a Domain (a space where the practitioner’s law overrides local law) will one day stand on, though the Stage grants a Domain and a number never does: a seed flickers at the Threshold into Refraction, a true Domain comes at Transcendence. Small Building to low Building, 0.005 to 0.25 tons TNT.
B, 176 to 275. Presence felt before techniques land. An unwoken crowd feels the weight in the room from a Journeyman on; between the woken, Pressure runs on the Stage gap and Dominion, as Part Eleven sets out. Building to Large Building, 0.25 to 11 tons TNT.
A, 276 to 400. The top of an Expert’s reach. A Domain held at this step, from Stage VIII on, is live and law-bearing. City Block to Multi-City Block, 11 to 1,000 tons TNT.
S, 401 to 550. A Master’s step. Full-output techniques register at natural-disaster level. Aura passively suppresses anyone standing two steps lower. Small Town to Town, 1 to 5.8 kilotons TNT.
SS, 551 to 725. Continental threat entry. Full-output events measured against major geological disruptions. A Domain at this level begins reshaping its local environment rather than merely existing within it. Town to Large Town, 5.8 to 100 kilotons TNT.
SSS, 726 to 950. Small-country scale destructive equivalence. Domain law can override localized Wellspring behavior within its territory. Full-power expression is a regional metaphysical event. Large Town to Small Country, 100 kilotons to 1 teraton TNT.
X, 951 to 1,200. Archon-adjacent (near the power of the fourteen Archons, the beings who hold conceptual law). Existence exerts passive influence on the metaphysical laws of the surrounding environment. Domain produces Archon-echo effects. Country to Moon level, 1 teraton to 29.6 exatons TNT.
EX, 1,201 to 1,500. Archon-equivalent. The distinction between a practitioner at this step and a functioning Archon is qualitative, a matter of metaphysical doctrine and the Principle they embody, not raw output. Moon to Large Planet, 29.6 exatons to 16.506 ronnatons TNT.
EX+, 1,501 and above. No formal upper ceiling beneath the Apotheosis threshold (where the line between practitioner and living Principle collapses). Titan-adjacent space. Characters here are not participants in ordinary conflict. They are metaphysical events that other characters survive or fail to survive. Brown Dwarf level and beyond, scaling toward stellar and solar-system scale.
At Zenith, Stage XIV, speed and attack output are no longer assessed by conventional metrics. The character exists in a state where the Continuum’s ordinary measuring systems require metaphysical recalibration to even register the practitioner’s presence. Zenith characters do not move faster than light. They exist within frameworks where the question of movement speed has ceased to be the relevant variable.
Part Five — Temperance Gates and Stat Ceilings
Temperance Stage functions as a hard ceiling on every Sub-Stat in the system, and a Primary’s mean therefore cannot exceed it either. A character cannot allocate their way past a ceiling their Soul Crystal cannot structurally sustain. Throne alone carries no ceiling. The Crystal must have undergone the corresponding Threshold Event before it can hold a stat at the step above. The ceiling binds what a Crystal holds to stay. A transient boost (a vow, a Release, a Draft, a strain lift) passes it lawfully inside two steps on the hidden scale, read from the sustainable figure on the sheet, and outside help adds no risk unless it is forced on someone; a blessing counts as outside help.
The allocation column binds: a Sub-Stat may not be allocated past it. At Stages V, VII, IX and XI the Sub-Stat ceiling sits above that figure, and the band between them, 276 to 350, 401 to 475, 551 to 625, 726 to 750, is the instability zone, reachable only under strain, never by allocation.
Forced advancement past Temperance gates is not impossible, but it is catastrophic. Stats pushed above their sustainable figure to stay, into the instability zone or past the ceiling itself, by alchemical augmentation, bloodline exploitation, or external metaphysical imposition generate Crystal Fracture Events at an exponentially increasing rate until the stat collapses or the Threshold is passed. This is a stat dragged past a Threshold nobody has crossed. A Draft or a blessing that supplies the Catalyst crosses the Threshold itself, and Part Eight sets out the terms.

Stage XIII is the First World Spirit threshold. Stage XIV is Full World Spirit, the furthest reach of canonical mortal coherence. Stage XV is Archon-participant territory.

The Rank column is what people say. Everyone names a fighter by rank, and the Stage name is the precise term. The same nine words are the Guild Accord’s nine titles, and the Accord is a coalition of many kinds of guild across many nations, grading trust in a trade: a merchant may deal up to his title, a craftsman make up to hers, an adventurer take commissions up to the Grade of bounty the Accord allows that title. Titles are earned by commissions. Fighting guilds, adventurers’ guilds included, also ask the title’s own rank in Stage, so a Journeyman’s title there needs Stage III, and trades ask none, so a Grandmaster merchant may not be able to throw a punch. The scholars once called the column the Tier of Standing and numbered it one to nine, and before that kept lettered Coherence Bands that shared their letters with the Grade table. Yield still runs underneath the ranks as the diagnostic axis, and two Experts with different yields are the same rank and not the same problem.
The combat skill cap is how far a fighting skill can climb at that rank, and it is the rank itself: skills read on the same nine words, Initiate through Paragon, and a fighting skill never ranks above its owner’s own Stage rank. A trade has no cap: a fifty-year baker may be a Paragon with no Stage to speak of. An unwoken soul holds no rank on a fighting roll, because the Accord does not register what it cannot examine.

Dissonance, Stage XI, carries unique behavior. Characters who pass through Dissonance rather than becoming trapped within it reach Stage XII with stats that are fractured but denser than the clean advancement path would produce. Certain Sub-Stats, particularly Overflow, Overchannel and Persistence, can only reach their true ceiling in a character who has passed through Dissonance. The fractures are not damage. They are architectural features. Emanation, Stage XII, is where those fractures become features that radiate outward.
Part Six — Speed by Step and Level
Speed divides into three components: Attack Speed, the velocity of technique execution; Reaction Speed, the capacity to perceive and respond to incoming force; and Travel Speed, movement velocity across space. All three are influenced by Dexterity’s Sub-Stats, particularly Celerity, Reflex and Sequence, but each responds differently to Temperance advancement.
These values are the natural ceiling achievable at each step through pure stat advancement, without technique amplification. Techniques built around Alacrity and Celerity can push further within overchannel risk parameters.
