Hallow. Archmaster scale. A Hallow’s act moves country and moon. What a Hallow is planted in stops being a place with a thing in it and becomes a place that is the thing.
Covenant. The rung with no ceiling. A Covenant is not held; it is entered into, and the bearer is bound to it at least as surely as it is bound to the bearer.

Counterplay
The rung says the most one act of the thing can deliver, and the binding says where the answer lives. A Free artifact’s rung goes wherever the object goes, so taking it, burying it or starving what it feeds on removes the rung whole. A Keyed artifact stands one rung lower the moment its key is contested: challenge the Writ, break the vow’s terms, deny the harmonization, and the thing works in its crudest form or not at all. A Soulbound artifact can never outrun its bearer’s Tier, and stolen it is inert, so there is nothing to gain by taking it and everything to gain by making the bearer pay; every act crosses the bearer’s Shell and is spent out of the bearer’s reserve toward the bearer’s floor. A Grown-in artifact cannot be separated from its bearer at all, and the fight is with the ground or the conditions it depends on. A store empties. An artifact placed by what it holds steps down the ladder with every discharge, and a patient opponent can count the rings.
The Summons ladder
Summons, on the spine. A called thing is a working that stands up and walks. Whatever it does once it is standing, the one figure every entry in the register carries is what it cost to call, and that figure is the ladder’s. A summon is placed by its call cost read through its yield: the EU spent to call it, times the yield of the crossing. The EU delivered finds the row, and the row is the rung; the guild multiplies by a megajoule and writes joules.
Whose yield. The crossing is the summoner’s Shell, so the summoner’s own yield is read wherever it is recorded. Where it is not, the crossing is read at the summon’s own Mastery, because Mastery governs how much of the donated Essence survives the crossing into form: rung I loses thirty to forty percent (η 0.60–0.70), II fifteen to twenty-five (η 0.75–0.85), III five to ten (η 0.90–0.95), and V delivers one hundred percent or more (η 1.00 and above). A call cost given as a share of reserve is as large as the summoner’s reserve makes it, and where the reserve is not recorded it is set by the law of reserves at the summoner’s Level.
The rung says what was paid to put the thing on the field. It does not say what the thing will do once it is there, and it does not say what it costs to keep it there. The modifiers say those.

The modifiers
None of the modifiers moves the rung. The rung is the call, and the call is paid once. The modifiers are what the call bought.
Sustain: the clock. A summon held past its arrival costs a sustain, and the sustain is read as a clock against the summoner’s reserve: reserve ÷ sustain is how long the summoner can hold it at full, and nine tenths of that is how long before Essence Starvation. A summon whose sustain empties its summoner inside a minute is placed at its call and fought at its clock.
Cost off the Ledger. Several entries record a sustain of nil and a cost paid in something other than Essence: a name taken per summoning, sensation that runs late for hours, heat carried in the summoner’s own body. A cost of this kind is recorded beside the rung and never converted into it. It does not make the summon cheaper. It makes the summoner the place where the summon can be reached.
Provenance: what holds it together. The register’s four provenances decide what survives the fight.

Not placed. No call cost is recorded for Nisuke, the soul-forged effigy in a Titan’s shape; for the Amalgamation constructs; for the seven Requiem constructs, whose price was a permanent share of their maker’s reserve in an amount the record does not give; for the reflection-constructs of the Hall of Shattered Mirrors; or for the Page-Wyrm that buds from the Ocular Codex. Each has a rung, and the rung waits on its figure.
Counterplay
The rung tells an opponent what the summoner has already spent, and that is the most useful thing a called thing ever says about itself. A Townfall called from a Grandmaster’s reserve is a twentieth of the afternoon gone; the same rung called from a Master’s reserve may be the half of it. Read the rung against what the summoner can carry, then read the provenance: a Donated summon is answered by the summoner, a Native one is not, and an Anchored one is answered by the ground it stands on. Every construct broadcasts its authorizing glyph and its summoner’s resonance to comparable Perception, so the rung is findable before the thing arrives. What to do about it is not.
The Domains ladder
Domains, on the spine. A Domain is inner law made local reality, and it is held, not thrown. What the spine reads is what the Domain holds: the EU standing in its territory at one time. Two figures fix that, and the ladder reads them together: the radius the law is held over, and the EU held across it. The EU held finds the row and the row is the rung, and the guild writes it in joules. The radius says how far it is spread, and the two multiplied back together are the size and density that Part Twenty-Two makes the measure of a Domain’s collapse.
How what is held is read. A Domain is paid for as a rate, and the Ledger turns a rate into a quantity over its own unit of time, the six-second turn. What is held is the maintenance drain across one turn, delivered through the holder’s yield: drain in EU/s × 6 × η, and the guild’s joules held are that times a megajoule. A Domain expression paid per activation rather than per second is read at its activation cost through the same yield. A Domain spent whole, detonated or collapsed on purpose, is read at what the spending cost, and stands on its own row beside the held one.
Density is the tell. The Measurewrights divide the joules held by the area of the disc the radius draws, π r², for the charge on each square meter of held ground, in J/m². It does not move the rung. It is what an opponent standing at the edge can estimate, and it is the figure a collapse is felt in.

Arm’s-reach. Law held no further than the holder can touch, at no more than a mortal’s force. The ground under the feet agrees with the holder and nothing else does. A Domain held at this rung is felt as a person’s presence and read as one.
Doorstep. A territory the size of a threshold, held at Wall-level force. It decides who crosses a doorway and how hard the crossing is. Most seeds that flicker at Refraction and collapse when attention fractures are held here or at the rung above.
Yard. A courtyard’s worth of law at Journeyman scale. What stands inside a Yard fights on the holder’s terms for as long as the holder’s attention holds.
Holdfast. A territory at the scale of a building, held at Building to Large Building force. Nearly every Domain on record whose drain is written down stands here, from Refraction to Transcendence, which is the rung’s own statement of what a live Domain costs to keep.
Precinct. A district-scale charge: City Block to Multi-City Block held standing. The rung measures the charge and leaves the Domain to the Stage that grants it, and a Precinct spent whole is a disaster at that scale.
Burgh. A town’s weight of law held at once. At this rung a Domain begins reshaping the environment it stands in rather than merely existing within it, and the Continuum must accommodate it.
Dukedom. A small country’s weight held standing. Domain law at this rung can override the local behavior of a Wellspring, which is why a Wellspring Core, the seventh rung of the sites ladder, is the first ground a Dukedom meets as an equal.
Globe. Country to Large Planet, held. The Domain produces Archon-echo effects and the ground it covers carries the holder’s doctrine after the holder has gone.
Firmament. The rung with no ceiling. Domain and holder are no longer separate figures, and the ladder keeps the rung because the spine has a top.
The modifiers
Reach. The radius is recorded beside the rung and never moves it. A wide Domain on a low rung is thin, and a narrow Domain on a high rung is dense, and the rung is the same figure in both: what the holder has standing at once.
Phase. Part Twenty-Two gives the Domain’s life by Stage, and the phase says whether what is held can be read at all.








































PhaseStageWhat the rung meansSeedVII Refractionheld by active concentration; the rung stands only while attention doesTrue DomainVIII Transcendenceheld for hours; the rung survives minor disruptionRealmIX–Xholds other Domains; pacts, artifacts and law imprint on terrainAmbientXI–XIIleaks without maintenance; no drain to read, so the rung is read at what a collapse or a spending releasesRegisteredXIIIthe Continuum registers the law; biomes carry the doctrineIndistinctXIVDomain and holder are one figure; read the holder
Ground. Maintaining a Domain inside someone else’s costs significantly more, and terrain works on the yield by what the ground holds against the idea of the Wellspring in use. Hostile ground does not lower the rung. It raises the drain the same rung costs, and shortens the clock on the holder’s reserve.
Persistence. Some Domains stand after the holder leaves them. A Domain that persists after exit holds its rung for that long without a holder to strike.
Collapse. A Domain collapses when EU drops below the maintenance floor, when concentration is shattered, or when a stronger Domain overwrites it, and the Resonance Shockwave is proportional to size and density. The rung prices the shockwave: a collapsing Domain can release up to all it holds onto everything inside, the holder included. A Domain spent on purpose releases what the spending cost, and is read on its own row.
The hierarchy is unchanged. When two Domains overlap, Temperance differential, then Dominion Sovereignty and Gravity with a read able to flip them, then Wellspring compatibility, then doctrine coherence decide, as Part Twenty-Two writes it. The rung is not a step in that order. It is what is standing on the ground when the order is applied.
Placement

































































Domainholderradiusfigure readyield (η)guild reckoning: joules helddensityrungWhite Tiger Mandalaan Expert holdernot recorded1,200 EU, per activation0.60–0.70, Expert7.2 – 8.4 × 10⁸ J, C—YardMeridian Press, the Domain compresseda Stage VIII Master25 m passive, 65 m deliberate; the press a 30° cone at 40 m28,000 EU, per activation0.812.27 × 10¹⁰ J, B11.6 MJ/m² at 25 m; 1.7 MJ/m² at 65 mHoldfastHaikyo no Jiten, the Ruined Dictionarya Stage VII Expert35 m, 8 minutes4,800 EU/s1.053.02 × 10¹⁰ J, B7.9 MJ/m²HoldfastMurder of Crowsa Stage VII Expert18 m active pressure, 40 m warning8,400 EU/s at full0.894.49 × 10¹⁰ J, B, at the rung’s ceiling44 MJ/m² at 18 m; 8.9 MJ/m² at 40 mHoldfastHaikyo no Jiten, spent: Sōkoku no Hia Stage VII Expert35 m190,000 EU, the Domain detonated1.052.0 × 10¹¹ J, A52 MJ/m²Precinct
The four held Domains stand on the third and fourth rungs, and the one spent whole stands a rung above them. A Holdfast detonated is a Precinct for one instant, and that is the whole difference between keeping a Domain and using it.
Recorded by reach, not placed. These Domains carry a radius and no drain the ladder can read: the Open Crucible, 40 m and past active maintenance; the Adamant Forge, anchored to the Forge complex; the Sounding, fifty kilometers at η 0.89; the Forge of Endurance, 3.2 km and 8 km in Overdrive; the Verdict Domain, a fifty-kilometer law field; the Ember Sanctum, thirty kilometers of pressure radius around a smaller Realm; an influence of one to two kilometers under full Emanation; a Domain-Precursor at up to three kilometers; two Domains of sixty and fifty meters; the Settled Domain of ten; the Waiting Room of about twenty; a seed extended to 120 meters through the Crook of Turned Seasons; the Garden of Still Snow at twelve, the Cinder Court at thirty-five, the Origin Court at eight; the Null, whose radius is environmental; and the Hall of Shattered Mirrors, the Quiet Hour and the Kōkan Totality Domain, which carry no figure at all. Each has a rung, and the rung waits on its drain.
Counterplay
The rung tells an opponent what will come down on the ground if the Domain breaks, and the radius tells them where to be standing when it does. Density is readable from the edge: a narrow Domain holding a Holdfast’s charge is dense enough to punish anyone who enters it and dense enough to punish its holder if it collapses; a wide one on the same rung is thin everywhere. A seed stands on attention and an Ambient Domain on nothing an opponent can reach, and the phase says which. A Domain held on hostile ground pays more for the same rung, and the difference is a clock anyone can count.
The Wellspring and vein sites ladder
Sites, on the spine. A Wellspring is an alchemical and a spiritual transformation, the governing idea that transforms how a soul uses Aether, and its own type of Aether pools: it concentrates where the substrate conducts, where no competing Aether crowds it, and where time has let it saturate the field until the ground expresses the law on its own. A site is that pool, and a vein is the channel that feeds it. Common speech calls any such site a Core. Cores are mostly found in dungeons, which grow down in floors around them with something guarding the heart, and they are said to lie in vast territories too. A worked Core is a dungeon someone cleared and now holds: it recharges and has keepers, who can close it. The survey keeps the words Wellspring Core for the seventh rung alone and has stopped correcting people at the door. A site is placed by hazard: the output a practitioner must be able to command to keep their own law inside the site at its worst ground. That figure is read in EU delivered like every other peak, the row it lands in is the rung, and the rung says how strong you must be to stand there and remain yourself.
Why hazard is read this way. A site does not strike. It retunes. Harmonization is a soul taking a Wellspring’s idea as its own, and Aether holding an idea strongly enough to press it on a Shell against its bearer’s will is Aether the bearer’s own output has failed to hold off. The survey calls it phase-locking, which is the Measurewrights’ word for it. So the ladder asks the question the survey asks, from the other side: what Grade of output holds a Crystal’s own architecture against this Aether. The density scale answers it in words, and the spine answers it in EU delivered. The two meet at one fixed point: Domain law at SSS can override the local behavior of a Wellspring, and a Wellspring Core is the ground where the Wellspring’s law is the only law operating. A Core therefore stands on SSS, the seventh rung, and the density scale is laid down the spine from there.
The nine rungs











































































NameGrade(s)output to hold one’s own law, guild reckoning in joulesdensityspine TierTrickleHollow, F, Ebelow 1.5 × 10⁴Ambient Saturation (how thickly a place is charged with Aether), low or depletedInitiateRillD1.5 × 10⁴ – 2.092 × 10⁷Ambient Saturation, high and steadyApprenticeFreshetC2.092 × 10⁷ – 1.046 × 10⁹Active Concentration, at its edgeJourneymanMillraceB1.046 × 10⁹ – 4.6024 × 10¹⁰Active ConcentrationAdeptRiptideA4.6024 × 10¹⁰ – 4.184 × 10¹²Active Concentration, where the Veil (the boundary between the physical and spirit worlds) begins to thinExpertWhirlpoolS, SS4.184 × 10¹² – 4.184 × 10¹⁴Veil-Thin NexusMasterFountainheadSSS4.184 × 10¹⁴ – 4.184 × 10²¹Wellspring CoreGrandmasterGyreX, EX4.184 × 10²¹ – 6.906 × 10³⁷past the Core: ground whose law no survey has namedArchmasterChasmEX+6.906 × 10³⁷ and abovethe Aether and its material indistinguishable, at the extremeParagon
Trickle. Ground where the Aether barely wets the field. A Sage can tune to it and an ordinary person feels vaguely uneasy or vaguely at peace. Arrays run here at a loss, and a practitioner recovers here slower than anywhere with a vein.
Rill. High, steady ambient saturation, felt within a day of arriving as a low pressure behind the eyes. It is the ground arrays pay for themselves on, and it harms nobody. Its danger is that it teaches a population to live beside a Wellspring.
Freshet. The edge of a concentration, where the field is altered persistently and the alteration stays after the flow that made it. Streets read wrong on every instrument and wrong to the people in them. Children awaken early here, and Traits appear in families that were never screened.
Millrace. A true Active Concentration. Wild ground shows altered terrain, Spirit ground produces physiological or psychological change the visitor did not choose, Medium ground produces both at once. Fate ground shows neither: luck goes strange, oaths bite, and strangers keep meeting. A practitioner who stays too long receives Wellspring Baptism (a Wellspring’s forced realignment of the soul) whether they wanted it or not, and sustained residence here or above leaves a Trait by Wellspring Convergence in anyone, Crystal or no Crystal.
Riptide. A concentration at its densest, where the Aether pulls the visitor toward the core and the comfort points the wrong way. At this rung the window between Spirit-type onset and commitment is measured in seconds, and the Veil has begun to give.
Whirlpool. A Veil-Thin Nexus. The planes turn together: spiritual entities visible, causal threads perceptible, time wrong. Bifold Perception arrives untrained, the soul drifts from the body’s position, and Echo Beasts take form out of what the visitors brought in with them. At Veil-Thin density the window of a Spirit-type onset is functionally zero.
Fountainhead. A Wellspring Core, the point its Aether wells up from. The physical and the metaphysical environment are indistinguishable and the law the Wellspring carries is the only law operating, including on the visitor. Recovery is re-anchoring by a specialist standing outside the radius, and it works, and it is not fast.
Gyre. Ground past anything the density scale was written for: a site that does not kill in any way the Measurewrights have language for, whose edge is fixed by the Accord and revised outward. At this rung the survey measures the perimeter because nothing inside it has been measured and come back.
Chasm. The rung with no ceiling. Aether and its material so far indistinguishable that the law is written about the rock rather than about the place, and the ladder keeps the rung for the one site that already stands on it.
The modifiers
Encounter type: where the danger comes from. The encounter type never moves the rung. It sets the warning time, and the warning time is what decides who walks out.






























TypeWhat reports firstWarning at the rungWildthe body and the groundgenerous: the anomalies are legible before they are dangerous, at every rungSpiritthe Crystal, and not to the conscious mindseconds at Millrace and Riptide; none at Whirlpool and aboveFatethe run of events, and only to someone keeping countnone in the moment at any rung; body and instruments read normal, and the one thing that reads this ground is a written log kept over daysMediumall of it at once, and none of it is trustworthythe worst of them; the visitor has lost the reference frame and needs an observer outside the radius
Force: whether the site recognizes or takes. A site under clean Attraction Force reads the Crystal and either permits harmonization or ignores the visitor. A site under Obsession Force takes, compatible or not, and stands one rung higher than its density, because the output that held against Aether that asks does not hold against Aether that pulls.
Stability: whether the reading drifts. A site whose saturation never drifts is read at its rung and stays there. A site violently irregular is read at its worst ground, never its average.
Pull: what working the site does. A site pulled on steadily falls as it is pulled: the old districts of a worked quarter read a rung or more below the ground beside them. Left to rest it recharges, and its keepers can close it to anyone for exactly that reason. A site worked past what it can give does not fall a rung. It gives out, and the ground that is left reads as ordinary depleted earth.
The unawakened. An unwoken soul’s Shell is sealed and cannot take a Wellspring’s idea (cannot phase-lock, in the survey’s word), and no harmonization occurs, and the rung reads the same for a porter as for a practitioner. What differs is the exit. A practitioner in a Spirit-type onset vents the load through the Shell; an unawakened soul keeps it, and no recovery protocol has been written for one returned from a Fountainhead.
Objects. A Wellspring’s Aether bound inside a vessel is an Object Wellspring, and it is read on this ladder by the material that holds it: material tier n stands on rung n. An object has no perimeter and no gradient to give warning. It is held or it is not, and its internal law meets the Shell at zero distance.
Placement

































































Sitewhat is recordedtyperungThe old districts of the Old Worldambient saturation low to moderate, locally depleted around the old districtsby its WellspringTrickleThe interior of the Southern Panambient saturation low; Aether-exhausted ground; no array tradeby its WellspringTrickleThe Northern Shieldambient saturation high and steady; the arrays run off it; felt behind the eyes within a dayby its WellspringRillYasoshimamoderate, and the most stable saturation recorded anywhere; nothing driftsby its WellspringRill, stableThe residue streets of a slow veinresidue accumulating where flow is slow; a persistent alteration to the field; Crystal awakening at abnormal ages and Trait incidence in long-settled familiesSpirit, by symptomFreshetThe deep galleries of a worked veindensities that would be recorded as an Active Concentration in open country; worked for careers by unscreened vein-menby the vein’s WellspringMillraceThe Heart Vault, the Concord Citadela Wellspring Coreby its WellspringFountainheadThe Crevice margin, inside the four-league linesaturation violently irregular; the rock stops obeying the ordinary rules; Grimbarite crews work it and their mortality is not publishednot classifiedGyreThe Crevice, Crevice Shalea T9 material and the most extreme Object Wellspring in the register; forbidden to move, hold or tradeobjectChasm
Not placed. The Oblation vein that Obrenkael’s enclosure runs on; Halloway Mire, which held Vaelmorn for fourteen years; the passages inside the Ring on the Northern Shield; the deep Wellspring pressure of the Drakyssian Heartlands and the Draconic Saturation Zones; and a bloodline’s ancestral seat. Each is recorded as a site and none carries a density the ladder can read.
Counterplay
The rung tells an opponent how strong they must be to fight on this ground and still be the one fighting. A Millrace is survivable for an afternoon and not for a season; a Whirlpool gives a Spirit-type onset no warning at all; a Fountainhead rewrites anyone below its rung who stays. The type says which sense to trust on the way in, or on Fate-type ground that none of them can be, and the perimeter is marked from outside: withdrawal is not retreat, and a fight drawn onto ground a rung above one side’s Grade is half won before it starts. Which side that is depends on who read the site first.
The Weapons and armor ladder
Weapons and armor, on the spine. Plain arms in the four quarters are Bearing-grade material with no Essence in them, and they perform as their physics; cheap runed pieces are nearly as common, and the great pieces are old and rare. The ladder reads the ones that carry a working, and it reads them the way the spine reads everything: in EU delivered, with the guild’s joules beside it. A weapon is placed by the hit it delivers: the attack output of the working in it, at the Grade of whoever put the Essence there. A piece of armor, a ward or a shield is placed by what it stops: the attack output band of the strongest strike it holds against. The EU delivered finds the row, and the row is the rung.
Whose hand. An enhanced weapon performs no higher than the figure of whoever put the Essence into it. Channeled through the weapon in the moment, that is the wielder’s own Ardency; enchanted, glyphed or worked beforehand, it is the maker’s at the time of making, and a relic keeps its maker’s ceiling in any hand. A weapon’s rung travels with its maker’s work and not with its current owner, except where the working is channeled, and then it travels with the hand.
Beside the Bearing and the Holding
The ladder does not replace the grades the trade already stamps. It reads a different quantity from the same object, and the two readings are held side by side.
The Bearing and Holding grades say what the material is. Bearing is its physical work: what it stops, carries and survives as steel, stone or hide. Holding is its Essence work: what working it can carry and for how long. Beside its Grade and Rarity, a material’s virtue decides which workings it holds well and how it fails: stone remembers, salt fixes, gold will not corrupt, quicksilver will not keep a shape. Every material has both Bearing and Holding, they run independently, and the material’s tier, T0 to T9, is where the Master Material Ledger enters it.
The item Tier says what the object may hold, and the rung says what it does. An item Tier is the lower of what its material can hold and the rank its maker stood at, counted one to nine from Initiate to Paragon, and material tier n holds a working up to item Tier n, level with the nth rank. So the material tier is the rung’s ceiling for any standing working: a weapon or armor placed above its material’s tier is a working the material cannot carry, and the material fails first. A plain item with no working in it has no Tier and no rung; its Bearing is the whole of it.
The stamp and the rung read the same Grades. The Accord’s stamp is read off the Grade it holds; the rung is read off the spine. They agree everywhere except where one stamp covers two rungs or two stamps share one:























































Stamp, said asGrade it holdsrungPlain, MarkedHollow–F; ESidearmProofedDLinepieceTemperedCWallbiterInstrumentBSiegepieceHallowedAFieldwinnerStoriedS–SSKingsarmFoundSS, or SSS with Grade IV or V provenanceKingsarm, or Landbreaker at SSSNuminousX–EXMoonsplitterProscribedEX+Unmaker
Grade and Rarity. An item carries two ratings: Grade for power, on the fighters’ letters, and Rarity for scarcity, which runs Common, Uncommon, Rare, Very Rare, Legendary, Mythic, Unique. The old words in the table above survive as the Accord’s stamps. A smith’s title caps the Grade she may make, and a merchant’s caps the Rarity he may sell. Bonded gear grows with its owner; everyone else’s stays what it is. An Appraisal skill and an assay instrument read an item, and a good forger beats a weak appraiser, which is why a shop’s best assayer tends to be its most suspicious relative.
Master Works. Each area has its own: a piece that does what its Grade and material should not be able to, made once at the end of a lifetime, always Unique or Mythic, and named. It is the one standing exception to the material ceiling below, and nobody has yet made a second by trying harder.
Bearing is never on the ladder. Plain steel stops a plain bolt by its Bearing and no rung is involved. The ladder begins where a working is added to the steel, and where a working meets the steel, the rung decides.
The nine rungs











































































NameGrade(s)guild reckoning: hit delivered or strike stopped, joulesEU delivered at the ceilingspine TierSidearmHollow, F, Ebelow 1.5 × 10⁴0.015 EUInitiateLinepieceD1.5 × 10⁴ – 2.092 × 10⁷20.9 EUApprenticeWallbiterC2.092 × 10⁷ – 1.046 × 10⁹1,046 EUJourneymanSiegepieceB1.046 × 10⁹ – 4.6024 × 10¹⁰4.602 × 10⁴ EUAdeptFieldwinnerA4.6024 × 10¹⁰ – 4.184 × 10¹²4.184 × 10⁶ EUExpertKingsarmS, SS4.184 × 10¹² – 4.184 × 10¹⁴4.184 × 10⁸ EUMasterLandbreakerSSS4.184 × 10¹⁴ – 4.184 × 10²¹4.184 × 10¹⁵ EUGrandmasterMoonsplitterX, EX4.184 × 10²¹ – 6.906 × 10³⁷6.906 × 10³¹ EUArchmasterUnmakerEX+6.906 × 10³⁷ and aboveno ceilingParagon
Sidearm. Arms at the scale of one person: a marked knife, a charm-wound cudgel, a jack that turns a blade. Any rung kills a man, and this one is where most killing is done. A steel-bowed windlass arbalest’s bolt, about 440 J by the guild’s reckoning, sits low on this rung, met by the target’s Speed Grade against the fixed threat Grade of its kind like any missile, and still the cheap thing that can kill a high-Stage fighter in a room, and a working that adds to it by the hit rather than the speed usually keeps it here.
Linepiece. The arms of the battle line: Proofed plate, an Apprentice smith’s enchanted blade. A Linepiece stops or delivers a Wall-level blow, and every piece of it costs a practitioner’s reserve, but a maker’s reserve comes back by the hour, so the workshops turn it out cheap and a whole line can be kitted to it.
Wallbiter. Arms that open a wall or hold one shut. A Tempered blade, plate that stops a Journeyman’s strike. This is the rung at which a working in the steel outweighs the steel.
Siegepiece. Arms at the scale of a building. A Siegepiece’s hit breaks a gatehouse and its proof holds against one being broken on the wearer. It is carried by one person, which is the whole of its danger.
Fieldwinner. Arms at the scale of a city block. A Fieldwinner decides a field by being on it, and the first rung at which taking the piece from its bearer is a war aim.
Kingsarm. Arms that deliver or stop a town’s destruction in one blow, Town to Large Town. Kingdoms go to war over a Kingsarm, because most were made long ago and few smiths now living could make another.
Landbreaker. Arms at the scale of a regional event. What a Landbreaker strikes is changed in the Continuum’s account, not only in the world’s.
Moonsplitter. Country to Large Planet, in one piece of worked matter. The material tiers that hold this rung are mythic and celestial, and the material is rarer than the smiths who could work it.
Unmaker. The rung with no ceiling. Arms that do not defeat what they strike so much as end it, forged from material the Accord forbids.
The modifiers
Proof: the armor’s rung is a promise. Armor at rung n stops a strike at rung n and below. A strike one rung above the proof breaks it; a strike two rungs above passes as if it were not there. Against worked armor the strike is read on the striker’s Ardency Penetration Grade, so high Flux with low Penetration spends its force on the plate and goes no further. The proof-mark names the house, the test and the bow, and a proof is a promise about a specific bow and bolt made by a workshop that may no longer exist.
Two dials: speed and the hit. A working on a projectile moves its speed, its hit, or both. Speed tops out at the enhancer’s Attack Speed and the hit at the enhancer’s Attack output band; the rung reads the hit. An enhanced bolt is dodged as a worked missile, by the target’s Speed Grade against its maker’s Grade, not at its rung.
Standing or spent. A standing working on a blade lasts until it is broken, read or unmade and costs its maker a tenth of their reserve once; proofed armor a quarter, and it lasts until struck two rungs above its proof; an enhanced bolt or arrow a hundredth, and it is consumed when loosed. The rung is what one piece does; the price says how many pieces a maker can put in the field. A lone practitioner can equip themselves; it takes a workshop of them to arm a host with cheap runed pieces, and no workshop now living makes the great ones.
Material ceiling. The material tier caps the rung for a standing working. A piece whose recorded hit or discharge reads above its material’s tier is placed at the hit, and its material is where it fails.
Off the proof. A few pieces deliver something that is not an EU figure: a strike that unthreads what it touches regardless of proofed Grade, dissolution applied past the Shell to the Crystal. Such a piece is placed at its ceiling, and no proof on the ladder answers it. Its answer is never the armor.
Placement

Not placed. Named in the record without a figure this ladder reads: the Black Aperture, whose Event-Edge ignores Strike Force entirely; Banisher; the Band of Frozen Brambles; Horizon’s Reach; Lurien’s Hearthvine; Shirokiba; the Aureate Paladin Plate and the Lux Aeterna Blade; the Gloamblade Absolver; the Ember Fang; the Stormcoat plate called Mail-White; the Crown of Tempered Roar; the Voidflame Gauntlet; the Slab; a spiked shield; a halberd; and a Guild-proofed arming sword. Each has a rung, and the rung waits on its Grade.
Counterplay
The rung tells an opponent what the piece can do and, just as plainly, what it cannot. A weapon’s rung is its maker’s ceiling or its wielder’s, and the piece says which: a channeled blade is answered by the hand, a made one by its proof, and a relic in a stranger’s grip still hits at its maker’s Grade. Armor tells its own limit on its mark: one rung above the proof breaks it, and two go through it as if it were not there. Every enhancement radiates its working’s signature, and a Harmonist reads the rung without touching the piece. The seam, the joint and the material’s failure are where the answer lives; which one is the fight’s business.
Back to Fracture of Worlds. For what the ladders mean to a living person, see Classes and the Three Ladders and The Measures at a Glance.

the-magic-system/power-in-use/counterpla.title: Counterplay: What Beats a Practitioner
the-magic-system/power-in-use/counterpla.content:
Leave the working alone. Choose which of the four things you are taking away from him, and count how long you have before he notices which one you chose.

Every washing-house north of the Reach sings about Thorvald Eikhagen of the Red Anvil school, and every one of them has the soap wrong. Eikhagen stood at Stage IX (ninth of the soul’s sixteen steps, high enough that weather takes an interest), and that spring he had walked through the whole Blackwater levy at a stroll, four hundred spears, with his aura standing a hand high off his shoulders in the deep ochre of a quarry at sunset, while the bookies at Skarrow stopped taking money against him because nobody could be found to hold the other end of the bet. Then he went to the Three Herons bathhouse to soak. Behind the towel heap sat Wenna Sprat, a laundress of sixty-one with a bad hip and two sons who had been in that levy, and across her knees lay a secondhand crossbow that had cost her eight silver, spanned with a goat’s-foot lever an hour before, because she could not trust her back to do it in a hurry. Nobody reinforces in the tub. He was humming.
The bolt went in at the hollow of the throat and stopped against the neck bone. He stood up, and that part the song has right: the water ran arterial red to the rim of the tub, the ochre came roaring up over him in the one beat a coat takes to rebuild, around a bolt already in, and he crossed four steps of wet tile with the whole house shaking and the steam going gold around him. He got as far as the towels. The song gives him a vow there. The bath-boy, who was under a bench, gives him the word “Who?” He was dead by the ninth breath. The Red Anvil posted two thousand gold on her head, and it was never collected, because every washerwoman in Skarrow went before the bailiffs that month and swore she was Wenna Sprat.
Four hundred spears, then, and eight silver. I keep this register for the Guild as a Measurewright (one of the Guild’s sworn measurers of Aether, and of anything else that holds still), and I have assayed that corpse’s records at length. My colleague at Altherion maintains that Eikhagen’s reaction speed would have slipped the bolt with room to spare. He is correct, and he has spent thirty years failing to see why it does not matter. The man did not see the loose.
The Four Routes
Everything in this register reduces to one of four. Deny the field. Break the boundary. Break the body. Break the man. They cost different amounts, they take different lengths of time, and a competent commander picks by what is available rather than by preference.
The Four Answers
The routes are a soldier’s list, and they go after the man. The confessors and the benches keep a second list of four, older than mine, and it goes after the working itself. Its contrary idea. A soul further refined in its own idea. Ground that already holds another idea. A refusal of its claim. A frost lens laid against a fire lens is the first. The second is the old master who has lived the same idea longer and truer than the boy throwing it at her, so that it comes to her as a thing she already owns. The third is a graveyard thick with Echo, a battlefield heavy with Thread Weight, or somebody else’s Domain, ground where the world has already agreed to a different law. The fourth is a soul that will not consent to what the working says about it, and it is the one the Fate section below calls being too well bound to move. The two lists sit side by side and do not quarrel. Choosing the ground by his Wellspring is the third answer in a soldier’s coat, and the routes against the body and the man take the speaker away before any of the four has to be argued.
None of the four is promised to be within reach. The register lists what answers an art, and for some arts that is a soul two Stages up, a bloodline nobody can hire, or nothing yet found, and I write it down as it is rather than as a commander would like it. When a working does give way, under any of these, it gives way along its own idea’s flaw, at the place its idea never asked to hold, and never by some general collapse. My guild’s names for those failures (thermal debt, quench cracking and the rest) are good bookkeeping and wrong about the cause, as the entries in the Sixty say plainly.
I. Deny the Field
Take away what he pulls from. The working is correct and produces nothing.
Take him off rich ground. A practitioner pulls Aether out of the environment around him before he can do anything at all, on every road. A Body fighter packs it raw in the Shell (the outer layer of the Soul Crystal, which is the soul itself) as his Charge; a Spirit worker refines it in the Crystal into Essence (the soul’s own stamped substance) and spends that through the Core; and a Fate fighter fills his reserve off the same ground, refining it into Essence exactly as the Spirit worker does, before he reaches for anything higher, since Thread is pulled per working and never stored. Nobody works a grain he has not first pulled inside, so where he stands matters: rich ground fills him faster and thin ground starves him. Wherever there is a yard to choose, this is the first move and the cheapest, and it is settled with purses as often as with swords. Fight him on salted ground, worked the night before by hedge-workers (the hired hands of the petty arts, paid by the job) so that Aether will not pool on it, on bled ground, pulled empty by a long fight or a greedy crew, or on plain thin ground, and he has what he walked in with. A worked Wellspring site, which common speech calls a Core and which is a dungeon somebody cleared and now holds, recharges and has keepers, and a keeper with the right seal can close it in under an hour, if he has been paid, if he has not been paid more by the other side, and if he has not simply refused. The practitioner is not weakened; the room is. Every serious action inside a Concord city begins with somebody deciding what ground it will happen on, and that decision is made by people who will not be present at the fighting.
Choose the ground by his plane. Ground is measured three ways, and each road cares most about one. Aetheric Density (wild ground, mines, Wells) fills every reserve, so thin ground starves all three. Echo Depth is how thick a place is with memory, graveyards, temples and old homes, and it cheapens Spirit workings: meet a Spirit worker in a barn built last spring or a rented hall nobody has ever wept in, and every stroke costs him the full price. Thread Weight is how much has been decided on a piece of ground, battlefields, coronation halls and crossroads, and it cheapens Fate pulls: meet a Fate fighter in a turnip field where nothing has ever been settled. Where a fight comes down to the ground, the measure that counts is the one for his road, so read that one and deny it. The Three Grounds has the famous ground and what was done to hold it.
Choose the ground by his Wellspring (the lens he has tempered on; each entry in the Sixty lists the ground it favors and hates). Terrain is a modifier on yield (η, the share of what he spends that reaches the world) and the modifiers are large. For the Wild kind the ground the Wellspring’s idea cannot abide tells you most of it, and I give the cases below in my guild’s terms, which are right about how much and say nothing of why. A heat lens fails in thermal equilibrium, saturated cold, and oxygen-poor air. A lens of current fails against boiled leather, fired clay, dense fog and a shielded interior. A stone lens has opinions and no tools on open water. A lens of water cannot act without a medium, so a dry vault is a prison. The counter-lightning kit has been leather and ceramic for four centuries and everyone knows it, and it stays cheaper to ignore until somebody dies of it. A lens of absence needs a gradient, and saturated ground has none left to offer. For a mind-worker a crowd is noise. Light him, and fill the room with people. A lens of distance needs a survey it can trust to say where here is, so unmapped ground, warp-scarred ground and ground two Domains (regions where the world runs on one practitioner’s terms) are arguing over all leave the transform nothing to solve against. A lens of force needs something to push back. Loose sediment, scree, mud, deep water and free fall take the third law away from him. A lens of growth is rate-limited chemistry. Rates roughly halve for every ten degrees you take out of the air, so winter, bare stone and salted earth are a sentence on it. The Spirit kind cares nothing for weather: its ground looks ordinary, and what it hates is a place where nobody is carrying anything, or where everybody is carrying the wrong thing. The Fate kind hates a clean ledger and a room of strangers with no history between them.
Saturate it. Flood the area with released power faster than it disperses and everyone present takes Fracture (damage to the Soul Crystal itself) risk, including whoever did it. A weapon of last resort and a real one, and its practical use is the threat rather than the act. The threshold is a density and not a total: ten thousand EU (Essence Units) in each cubic meter, or a hundred AU/s (Aether Units per second, a rate of output) through each square meter of the region’s edge. It grows with the surface while output does not, so below Archmaster you cannot flood a field, only a building, and you have to be inside it. A Master’s full output a kilometer wide is about a five-hundredth of threshold. The same output in a hall is five times over it. A Zenith’s full output across that same kilometer stands close to the threshold, and at the top of his band well over it, which is one reason nobody invites a Zenith to a siege twice.
Shrink his authority. The radius in which a practitioner’s own law is the operating law is his field standing above the ground’s, and the ground wins on a square root. Addressing range, anchor reach and authority radius all fall as the root of the local density. The square root is my guild’s rule of thumb, and the bench’s reason for it is older and plainer: a voice is harder to hear in a crowded room, and rich ground is a room crowded with the world’s own Aether. Fight him on concentrated ground and all three drop to an eighteenth. At a Veil-Thin Nexus, a thousandth. Inside a Wellspring Core (the site where a Wellspring’s Aether pools and its law runs strongest) a Master’s Domain is a fraction of a millimeter wide, because there the only law operating is the one the Wellspring carries. This is why a commander who cannot starve him takes the fight to the vein instead. It runs the other way too: Aether-thin ground gives him ten times the reach and almost nothing to pull, which is the whole of the bargain the lenses of absence strike. A Fate fighter feels this rule hardest, because Range and the radius of his Domain are most of what he fights with. Rich Aetheric ground crowds both, however well it fills him. What gives them back is Thread Weight: on ground where a great deal has been decided his Range and his Domain’s radius run longer than the Density alone would allow, so a Fate lord on an old battlefield holds more of the yard than the same man in a mine, and the cheapest answer to him is rich young ground, a new-sunk shaft or a fresh Well, where there is Aether in plenty and nothing has ever been settled.
Silence. The removal of magical possibility from a region, a stranger thing than any shield or counterspell. Lawful transformation cannot be authorized at all inside one. Animatria constructs fail completely because their continuity runs back to a source the Silence has severed. A soul held in one reports the sensation as loneliness rather than weakness, and that distinction is the most reliable field diagnostic for whether a quiet place is Silence or merely thin.
II. Break the Boundary
Attack the sentence and leave the speaker for later.
Interrupt the chain. Below Refraction (Stage VII) a working requires an external anchor: voice, hand, ink or blood. Take the anchor and the sentence does not complete. Break his wrist and a gestured chain is finished. Put a hand over his mouth and a spoken one is. Above Refraction the chain is internal and none of this applies, which is the practical reason Stage VII is the line every soldier is taught to fear rather than the reason the Codex (the Accord’s master register of laws) gives.
Force the Seal early. The Seal closes an operation against the warrant that opened it, and a warrant overstating standing seals anyway, with the difference deducted from the speaker at the moment of closing. A third party who can compel an early close has stopped defending and started billing him.
Knot and Lock. The only two Counter forms in the index. Laws cannot be opposed, so these two condition the conditioning. Knot entangles a path so it cannot be traced cleanly. Lock occupies a limit so no other limit can be set there. Every counter-working ever recorded is one of those two moves.
Wards. A cut working standing on a substrate, and therefore beaten the way any cut work is beaten: damage the substrate. Nobody argues with a ward. It is chiseled off, or the wall it sits on is brought down, or the third layer is scraped through by somebody who knows which layer to scrape. An inscription with a defective Sealing role has been failing continuously for two centuries, and whoever owns it owns a liability.
Countersigning. Some Seals end when countersigned in writing, and some end when the sum is spoken back correctly by another. A working that carries either of those closing conditions can be ended by an opponent who is literate enough, which is why Accord field practice avoids both and why they persist in the old inscriptions everywhere.
III. Break the Body
The Crystal is inside a person and the person is flesh: harder than common flesh, never proof. Taken asleep, drugged or by surprise, he keeps only the base his stats give the body and loses the coat of reinforcement he pushes over it, which is why ambush is the oldest answer on this list.
The bolt. Cheap, mechanically simple, and it does not care about Stage below the point where reaction speed outruns it. A crossbow costs about what a trooper’s saber costs, a child can be taught the lever in an afternoon, and it is the cheap thing that can kill a high-Stage fighter in a room. It is read like any missile: every missile carries a fixed threat Grade by its kind, sling stone, hunting arrow, war-bow shaft, crossbow bolt and ballista bolt, a worked one taking its maker’s Grade, and the fighter’s speed, read on the same scale the Measurewrights keep under every number (though only the bolt wears the letter), meets it. A practitioner whose speed stands in the bolt’s own step, as a quick Apprentice’s can, may read a crossbow bolt loosed across a room and slip it, if they see the loose. Two steps higher, where an Adept’s best stands, they can stand in a volley of bolts and arrows without significant reactive disadvantage. Everything below that line is arithmetic, and everything above it is still a body in a tub. A volley is a volley. This is the entire reason armor is still worth a lord’s rents and the entire reason ranks still stand in them. Bows, thrown things and siege engines belong on this line too, at their own threat Grades and their own prices.
Numbers, correctly used. One practitioner beats twenty men. Twenty men who have been drilled to spread, to make him choose, and to keep a lane open for the crossbows at all times will take casualties and kill him, and the doctrine that produces this is a hundred and forty years old and taught badly everywhere.
Distance. Current, by my guild’s reckoning, falls off with the square. Force has to close. A fighter working through his own body is a body, and a body has reach. Most practitioners are a threat about closing range and are written as though they were not. A Body Path fighter has to close until very high up, when his reach runs as far as there is matter to read. A Spirit Path fighter wants the reverse and survives by being right, and once you are inside his reach he is in more trouble than anyone else on the field.
Exhaustion. Below ten percent reserve a practitioner suffers Starvation (Charge Starvation in a Body fighter, Essence Starvation in a Spirit or a Fate one, whose reserves are both Essence): reduced stat expression, Shell degradation, Traits flickering. A defender who can afford to spend nothing wins a long engagement against an attacker who cannot afford to spend nothing, and sieges are decided by this more often than by any working. What starving does to him depends on his road, and so does the way to hurry it. Make a Body fighter spend. His Charge is raw Aether, and every share he spends for nothing burns in his Shell’s furnace and comes off him as heat, so make him swing at air, hold his coat through a long approach and hit things that do not matter. At a quarter he is steaming and cramping, and at a tenth the Shell cracks, the skin splitting in fine lines as it draws the Charge out of his own flesh. A Spirit worker run down goes hollow and cold and starts losing words and then names. A Fate fighter run down frays like the Spirit worker, since it is Essence he has run out of, and goes unlucky besides, which is worst for whoever is standing nearest. Stacking and Spending has the table.
Overfill him. A practitioner who absorbs banks the load in his own Crystal, and what bounds the bank is its rated Flux Density (how densely power packs into the Crystal) rather than his reserve. To half again over rating he holds it and bleeds. Past half again the lattice takes a permanent set and he is Overgrown. At two and a quarter times rating it bursts, and the Fracture is his, from power you handed him. Feeding an absorber is cheaper than out-hitting him. And the bank is short. It leaks at one minus his yield per second, three seconds for a poor Crystal and twenty for a fine one, so a defender who declines to be hit for ten seconds has taken it off him without touching him. The bleed is the tell, and it lasts exactly as long as the bank does.
Armor tiers. Padded takes bruising and not gore. Mail is immune to cuts, vulnerable to thrusts and blunt trauma, and vibrates under Essence shock in a way the wearer feels in the teeth. Brigandine hides its plates and the gaps are the openings. Proofed plate turns a bolt at range and turns most edges entirely, leaving joints, grapples and the close end of a room. Ceramic and shard are sacrificial and fail on the second hit in the same place. None of it covers the soul. A Spirit Path working goes past the Shell and past whatever is buckled over it, and the answer to that man is to get there, because a spear does not care what he means. The second answer is to ward the soul: a temple charm, a reliquary or a warded band, worn, the worked ones lifting Resilience Ward and Harmonics by a real margin for a little draw on the wearer, at five silver for a charm and two to thirty gold for a worked piece. The fair-stall kind lifts nothing. Know also what his stroke cannot do. It lands on souls only, a soul knocked out of true, a dread laid on a mind, a Core wounded, and it will not move a stone or break a jaw; a Spirit worker who wants matter moved has to do it through his own Shell, at his own Body Mastery, like anyone. What does get through leaves a soul wound, and a second stroke on the same place sets it for life, so do not let him find the pale place twice (Soul Wounds and the Menders).
IV. Break the Man
The most reliable and the least discussed.
Check whether he paid for it. Stages can be bought with Drafts and given by blessings (The Ladder and the Draft has the price list). He has the ceiling, the door and the color, thin underneath, and none of the fighting that normally comes with them, and his Release, if it is not yet found and mastered, is not there to be feared. He may also stand Overgrown, his Level short of what the Stage asks, which reads low on Mastery and spills where you can see it. A veteran two Stages below him who has been hit before is a better bet than the ranks say, and the bookies at the better bout-rings know which heirs to lay against. Learn it by making him fight past his first plan.
Read him. Start with his road: an opponent who has identified a Path knows what the other man cannot do, and The Three Paths sets out how each beats each. Taught techniques are documented and counterable by anyone who studied. Self-derived techniques must be read live, in the two or three exchanges before they kill you. Every fighter whose Crystal acts before conscious thought has a pattern, because one road walked long enough produces one, and a pattern learned is a pattern interruptible.
Make him hold Pressure (the felt weight of his power on everyone near him) in. Suppression is a skill and it is tiring. A practitioner who cannot afford to be identified is paying continuously for the privilege, and a long approach through populated ground costs him more than the fight will. It cuts both ways: people hide Pressure and people fake it, and unless your Gnosis Perception outranks his Resilience Ward by a full step, what you think you are facing is an estimate said aloud.
Read the blessing, if you can. A blessing grants power out of a person’s natural reach, sits on the sheet as its own line, and can lie, because the giver wrote the line. A man who has built his plan on what his own window says about a gift has handed a stranger the wording. The answer almost nobody has is Hataraki, the Fate Art that can take a blessing back or remove it outright, with two Works or two Moto, which is one reason its holders are spoken of the way they are.
Rigidity. A Trait’s law is not negotiable by its bearer, and the more absolute it is the less he can contradict it. Present him with the situation his own law handles worst and he will handle it that way regardless, because he has no other way available. This is the cruelest counter in the register and it requires knowing the man rather than the technique.
The vow. A vow kept buys Coherence (the match between a practitioner’s stated law and his conduct) with conduct. A vow broken lands at once, by its own terms, and repeated denial of the truth behind it makes a Shear Break (a Trait turning on the bearer who denied it), so an opponent who knows the terms of a vow holds a weapon that does not require touching him. Maneuvering a sworn man into breaking his own oath is legal everywhere, universally despised, and has ended more careers than any duel.
Coherence drift. A practitioner whose lived behavior has drifted from his stated law is degrading before anyone lays a hand on him: output falls, Thresholds refuse to authorize, and his Traits begin to argue with him. Nobody has to cause this. Somebody has to notice it and wait.
Beating a Fate Fighter
His blade had not moved. Your strap gave, your foot found the one wet stone, and the blade was already there. Now look at his nose.
The four routes were written against people who push, and a Fate Path fighter (one whose Crystal leans on the Attraction Layer, the soul’s own share of the Plane of Fate) is mostly fought the way anyone is. On most days and in most fights his weapons are long Range, heavy Aura Pressure, presence and the people sworn to him, and every route above applies to all of those. What earns him a section of his own is the rare day he pulls: he reaches for what has to be so before anything can happen and moves what the blow depends on, so that the result arrives without having been forced. The strap wears through, the back foot lands wrong, and the cut is an ordinary cut.
Do not be frightened of it in the wrong way. This is the hardest thing in the register. Nobody reasons their way into it, since reasoning is made of the thing it would be used against, and I have corresponded for twenty years with a colleague who can describe a thread to the last decimal and has never lifted one. One lean on the odds can take a large share of a man’s reserve and leave him bleeding from the nose and eyes, and it often fails. He knows that, and it decides when he tries. If he tries, you have a charge to read: the eyes gone still, the breath held on a count that is not the count of the exchange, the air around him gone slightly too tidy. Between that and the wet stone is all the warning you get: a breath for a lean on the odds, several heartbeats for a prerequisite removed, longer for a field.
There are three answers, and they are routes I, II and III wearing his name.
Bring another Fate user. This is the boundary route. A second reader of the weights can see what he is leaning on and lean the other way, and the contest then runs soul against soul, Fate Sub-Stat against Fate Sub-Stat. It is the one case in this register where answering a practitioner with a practitioner counts as a decision, and the two of them will pay for it about equally. Mind that you can find one, since the road is hard enough that most armies have none to spare.
Be too sound, or too well bound, to move. This is the field route, and it is by far the cheapest. It moves only what already has a way of happening. A strap that is wearing can give and a strap that is not wearing will not, so the answer is a good strap, good footing and no bad habits, inspected that morning by somebody who is not you. Young Moto Naoki pronounced collapse on a sound gate at Tobishima in front of nine thousand people and the gate stood, and a Fate Art is no exception to this: his aunt’s stand folded because a carpenter owed money. The soul has its own version. Dominion’s Fate Sub-Stat pushes and the target’s Resilience Persistence and Continuity (the soul’s hold on going on being true) push back, and a soul bound well enough simply refuses the result. Nobody has ever written a song about a well-kept strap, and that is a pity, as it has outlasted several people who have one.
Reach him before the result arrives. This is the body route, and it is the one every Fate fighter fears. In plain force he takes the smallest bonus in the table, and outside his Domain, at the end of a straight exchange with a Body Path veteran, he is an ordinary body, one that may have spent half of itself on the last pull. So close. Keeping your distance is a present to him, because his force degrades least across it and his presence fills the volume you are standing in, and a long wary circling is the time he needs to set. The tell is the window, and reaching the puller inside it is the counter: three crossbowmen who loose a heartbeat late have only watched. Everything under Break the Body applies, the tub included. A Spirit Path fighter has the shortest way of doing it, because every pull is made by a soul, it shows on the Core before it lands, and a wounded soul loses its grip.
A true Fate Art is the same three answers at a worse price. Real Fate Arts are rare and mostly by bloodline, and their reputation as incredibly overpowered is the opinion of the survivors. Nobody grips Fate bare, and a Work of Hataraki is an inherited way of taking hold of one function, which is why that house can do on purpose what others do by accident. It still needs something to exploit, and it still costs its holder. You will not meet this in a tavern. On a field, turn to The Practitioner Problem, which says to find him first.
And then collect. Every pull he makes, landed or failed, leaves a knot, and the world collects it later, as an ordinary accident, on him or on what is his: within days for a lean, within the arc of the business for a removed prerequisite. A Work makes his hand surer and has never lowered the price or the knot. So a Fate fighter who pulled last week is a man waiting for a strap to go, and a patient enemy makes him pull often, counts the days, and offers battle in the week the bills fall due. Ask what he wears. A knot-cutter will take one knot’s debt onto itself and break, half of those sold are fakes, and a cracked ring on his hand tells you he has already used his. The Tell and the Knot has the law of it.
What Does Not Work
Matching him. Two practitioners whose numbers stand in the same step resolve by technique, positioning and Sub-Stat (the finer stats beneath each main stat) architecture, and the exchange is a coin toss dressed as a plan. A commander who answers a practitioner with a practitioner has declined to make a decision.
Shielding. Nothing in the register stops a working by standing in front of it. Armor changes what the working does to a body. Wards condition what may be authorized in a space. Neither is a wall and both are written as one constantly.
Waiting for the cost. The reserve’s tells show inside a fight, and a fighter who can read them will spend to the last tenth anyway; the deep costs are rarely due until afterward. A plan that consists of surviving until he tires is a plan to be killed by a tired man.

The doctrine, stated once. A practitioner is beaten by taking away one of four things: the field, the sentence, the body, or the man. Pick before contact. Everything that goes wrong in the record went wrong because somebody tried to decide during.

End of the shelf. Next: Practice and Institution. For how each road beats each and how each tires, see The Three Paths. For what a monster answers to, see The Bestiary.

the-magic-system/power-in-use/index.title: Power in Use
the-magic-system/power-in-use/index.content:
At Sallow Bridge, Dunstan Pike spent his whole reserve on the first swing, in glorious orange, in front of the betting crowd, and was then beaten by a man eating a pear. These pages are how power is put into the body, stacked, spent, carried in tags and beaten, so that it need not be you.


Reinforcement The coat of one’s own aura over the body’s base, what it costs, and when it fails.
Stacking and Spending How boosts stack to the cap, how the reserve runs down, how the body tells on it and how the window reports it.
Runes and Tags Workings cut into objects ahead of time: who fuels them, who fires them, who cuts them.
The Working Trades Drafts, runes, tags, chants and the spoken arts: what each medium can do that the others cannot, what outlives its maker, and what the guilds fight about.
Counterplay: What Beats a Practitioner What beats a practitioner, and in what order the decision is made.


Next shelf: Practice and Institution. Back to The Magic System.

the-magic-system/power-in-use/reinforcem.content:
How a practitioner’s body holds its power, and how they push it further. For the whole system in brief, see How Magic Works.

“Gather it where the blow is. Then pray there was only the one.” Copybook line, set for novices in most lineage halls and ignored by all of them.

The minstrels call it The Bell and the Fork, it runs to forty verses, and about nine of them happened. At the Bell Feast in Ninefold Market, Gao Baoshan of the Nine-Ladle Hall, a cook by trade and an Expert, Stage VI (sixth on the soul’s sixteen-step ladder), by every account, bet his master’s broth recipe against a rival hall that he could take the Evening Bell of the Temple of Clear Water on his forehead, dropped from its own tower. The whole of Ninefold Market came, and the roofs sold out. He gathered everything. Every scrap of the ochre aura on his body ran up his neck and heaped on his brow, until he wore a lump of amber light the size of a goose egg and the rest of him stood bare as a plucked bird, and the riggers knocked out the pin.
The bell cracked down the lip. Baoshan stood under it with his eyes crossed and his sandals driven a thumb’s depth into the flagstones, the lanterns on the temple steps all swung one way, and the crowd lost its collective mind. Then Sister Ran of the Copper Steamer, who had money on the other side, stepped up behind him and put a coated toasting fork into his left buttock up to the handle, on the sound legal ground that the wager had specified a bell. He bled through three aprons. The Nine-Ladle Hall lost the recipe, its broth has been worse ever since, and Baoshan ate his dinners standing for a season.
Every fighting school I have visited tells this story on the first day, and they are right to. What he did to the bell is a focused coat. What she did to him is the price of one. A colleague of mine in the Measurewrights (the Guild’s sworn measurers) holds that the bell was already cracked, and he has written thirty pages on the subject, and he has never stood under anything.
What it is
A practitioner’s stats (the measured strengths of body and soul, read off the Soul Crystal, which is the soul itself, the thing that stores and sends out their power) live in the body all the time as a passive base: always on, costing nothing. Reinforcement is the active layer on top: power pulled in as Aether from the ground around them and laid over flesh, bone and whatever they hold, to push the body further for a price in reserve (the one store a soul carries). What the coat is made of follows the road. A Body Path fighter wears raw Aether, the Charge packed in the Shell and never refined; a Spirit Path worker wears Essence (Aether refined in the Crystal and stamped as her own); a Fate Path fighter wears her claim, the grip her Attraction Layer has on what happens near her, paid for in Essence like the Spirit worker’s; and all three pay for it out of the same kind of bar. What the coat guards follows the road as well. Only a Shell coat hardens a body, and it does so at its wearer’s Body Mastery, whatever road she leads on.





























LayerWhat it doesWhat it costsWhen it is lostPassive baseThe body at its sheet values: a Durability of 240 takes a blow at 240, waking or sleepingNothingSags under Starvation (the state below a tenth of reserve)Spread coatThe whole body lifted within the step of the Measurewrights’ scale its numbers already stand in, toward the top of that stepAbout ten minutes of holding from a full reserve, for an Adept (Stage IV)Asleep, drugged, surprised, or starvingFocused coatOne place (a fist, a forearm, the ribs) lifted one full step on the scale; everywhere else drops to the passive baseAbout five minutes from fullAs above, and wherever the focus is not
How it looks
A coat of their own aura. Reinforcement shows as a skin of the practitioner’s own color: the hue of the Wellspring they have tempered on longest (a Wellspring being the governing idea that transforms how a soul uses Aether) at the clarity of their Stage (their step on the soul’s sixteen-step ladder): clouded and smoky low down, clearing as they climb. A Pyreveil fighter’s coat shimmers ember-orange; a Judicium fighter’s crackles arc-blue along the forearms; a Petralon fighter’s shows as nothing but a weight the dust leans toward. It is thickest where they push. That first Wellspring sets the base color, any others add texture and sound, and a Class (the name the soul offers at thresholds) or a big Trait adds a shape, so that two Pyreveil fighters may share a color and nothing else: one coat crawling like coals, the other standing off the shoulders like a mantle.
The body under it. Veins stand up, skin tightens and takes a sheen, the stance settles lower, and the breath deepens. Heat comes off a hard-pushed Body coat in waves, and a Spirit coat pushed as hard goes cold instead.
Focus leaves gaps. Gathered into one place, the coat blazes there and goes pale everywhere else. A fist burns; the far flank fades to bare skin. Reading where it went is half the fight, and a good fighter moves the focus faster than an enemy can read it.
Everyone has a word for it, and an argument. The coat is the most famous art in the world, and each people names it to suit their opinion of it. A Moto calls it matoi, the wearing, and holds that a person of breeding does not show it in company, which is why Moto courts are so full of calm people who may or may not be about to kill you. The Mahuo call it gabot, armor, drill it like armor in ranks at dawn, and say a coat you cannot see is a coat you have not paid for. The lineage halls call it hùtǐ, guarding the body, and have been fighting for six hundred years over which hall thought of it first. A Marrowkin is on shift when it is up, and enters the minutes. A Kharven soldier calls it the hide and compares prices. In the bracket crowds of the Accord towns it is your shine, as in he’s lost his shine, get your money down. All of them mean the table above, and any of them will explain at length why the others do it wrong.
The coat by road. Anyone woken can wear one, and it is bought with reserve on every road. The table above is the Shell’s table: it is what a coat of raw Aether does for flesh and bone, and anyone may lay one, since every soul has a Shell, though a soul that leads elsewhere lays it at its own Body Mastery and no better. The other two Paths wear coats of their own that guard other things. What it is made of and how it sits follow what the road spends, and a trained eye reads the road off the coat before the first blow.

A Body coat is raw Aether. It hugs the skin like heat-haze off a summer road, close enough to move when the muscle under it moves, and it runs warm, because it is the Charge itself standing in the Shell, and the Shell is a furnace that never goes cold: what it burns comes off as heat. This is the coat the copybooks draw. It guards the hide, and the fist and ribs under it take the Body Path’s full force bonus.
A Spirit coat is Essence. It hangs a half-step off the body, like a second outline that has not quite caught up, and shadows fall a little wrong around it. It is cool to stand near. It wards the soul and not the hide: a thrown dread or a stroke at the Core has to get through it first, which is a thing no Body coat can offer, and a maul goes through it as through fog. The older copybooks say it lifts the body by the same table, and the halls have stopped teaching that line. A Spirit worker who wants her ribs hardened lays a Shell coat under it like anyone else, in raw Aether, at whatever Body Mastery her Shell has reached, which in a pure thrower is seldom much. Pushed hard, it is paid for in the Core, as a hollowing, and none of that is heat.
A Fate fighter’s coat barely shows. A faint edge of color in the right light and no more. What gives it away is the room: dust lies still near them, and a dropped coin lands face up. It is the claim worn as presence, and what it lifts is Pressure and the settling of the room, so that a blow aimed at its wearer has a little more to get past before it starts. It hardens nothing; for that a Fate fighter lays a Shell coat at her Body Mastery like the Spirit worker. It is easy to take for no coat at all, which has been the last mistake of a number of people.

Someone who walks two roads wears the coat of whichever layer they are pushing through at that moment, and a good one changes it in the middle of an exchange.
Held gear, never other people. The coat runs into what the hand is holding: a blade, a shield, a staff, the hilt of a hammer. Let go and it leaves the steel within a breath. It cannot be laid over another person, however close or however loved.
Masters can hide it. Most practitioners must choose: hold their Pressure (the weight their presence puts on a room) in, which is tiring work, or coat up and show their color. A master can reinforce with no color showing at all, and that calm is a warning in itself. Few manage it below Master standing, and the bookies shorten their odds the moment one walks in unlit. The other direction is just as old: a fighter short on reserve can flare a coat bigger than the body behind it, which is why anything but a true read (a stronger Gnosis Perception against a weaker Resilience Ward) is an estimate said aloud.
What it costs

Reserve, by the second. A card writes it as time from full: how long the coat holds, started on a full reserve, before the reserve reaches its tenth. A spread coat runs about ten minutes for an Adept, longer as their yield (η, the share of a spend that arrives) climbs; a focused coat runs about half that. The practitioner’s own window (the soul reporting its numbers to its owner, unseen by anyone else) shows the running figure as a percentage and a bar, and nobody else in the fight gets to see it.
A layer on the stack. A focused coat’s one-step lift is a power-up like any other and counts toward the cap (no more than two steps on the hidden scale over the sustainable figure on their registered card) and toward the fracture risk that comes with stacking (see Stacking and Spending). A spread coat lifts only within its step and adds no risk.
Starvation. Below a tenth of reserve the active coat fails outright and the passive base itself sags: the body reads weaker than its sheet, worse the deeper the reserve goes, and Traits (the soul’s standing laws) begin to flicker. Then the road sends its own bill: a Body fighter’s Shell starts drawing the Charge out of the flesh, and the skin splits in fine lines; a Spirit worker’s Core frays, names first; and a Fate fighter, whose reserve is Essence too, frays the same way while her own name starts to sit wrong in other mouths (Stacking and Spending has the table).
Rebuilding. A coat dropped by surprise comes back in one beat once the practitioner knows what is happening. One beat is a long time with a knife already in.

How it is beaten

Ambush. Asleep, drugged or surprised, a practitioner keeps only the passive base. Assassins, bandits and jealous rivals live by this. Guards are posted over sleeping masters for exactly this reason.
Read the focus. Strike where the coat has gone pale. A fighter who gathers everything into the guarding arm has left the ribs at base.
Outlast it. Every second costs reserve. Make them chase, make them hold the coat through a long approach, and fight them when the coat fails and the base sags.
Disarm. Knock the weapon loose and the coat leaves it. A coated blade is a different object from the same blade on the floor.
Go past it. A Body coat guards the hide and nothing behind it, so a Spirit strike goes through to the soul as if the coat were not there. A Spirit coat guards the soul and not the hide, so a spear does the same from the other side unless there is a Shell coat under it. Read which coat it is before choosing the blow.
Go after the ward. Reinforcement protects the reinforced body only. The child, the client or the wounded friend beside them stands in plain skin.
Cut the ground. On thin, salted or bled ground (Aether-poor by nature, worked against pooling, or pulled empty), or beside a Core (a Wellspring site, in common speech) whose keepers have closed it, nothing fills the reserve back up, everything costs more and the coat runs down sooner.

Holding a break shut
A practitioner with a broken bone can keep fighting on it by holding the break shut with a working, which the trade calls an Essence splint. It is a Bind: the two edges of the break are held to one shape, the way a Bind holds anything to a form, and the limb carries load as if it were whole for as long as the hold lasts.

What it costs. The splint is a focused coat laid on the break, so it runs on the focused coat’s clock: about five minutes from a full reserve at Adept standing for a small or single bone (a finger, a rib, a forearm), roughly two percent of reserve every turn. A load-bearing break (a thigh, a hip, the spine, the skull) draws twice that, about two and a half minutes from full, roughly four percent a turn. Both sit on top of whatever else the practitioner spends, and both outrun passive recovery, which gives back about one percent a turn.
How long it can be held. Tempering decides how long the soul can keep the hold at all, whatever is left in the reserve. A low Tempering lets go of the break long before the reserve runs dry.
When it ends. It ends at Starvation, when Tempering gives out, or when the Bind is broken, and the wound is worse afterward than if it had been left alone: the bone has been worked on while broken, and it heals on the slower count.
How it is beaten. Anything that breaks a Bind breaks the splint, and Silence drops it at once. The simplest answer is to outlast it: make the holder move, keep the limb loaded, and wait for the clock.

Example
Mags Tolley, a Stage V hired hunter tempered on Judicium (the Wellspring of Truth, arc-blue, which reads flaws), sleeps at a waystation with her boots on. A thief with a knife comes through the shutter. She is asleep, so she has only her passive base, but her Durability stands at 240, a long way above any knife, and the blade skids off her collarbone and opens a shallow line instead of a deep one. She wakes, and in one beat the coat comes up a smoky arc-blue over her forearms, hissing like a wet wick.
The thief has a partner at the door, Stage V like her and swinging a coated maul. Mags gathers the coat into her left forearm and takes the maul there: the arm is lifted a full step and the iron rings off it. But the blue has drained from her right side to bare skin, the partner sees it, and his second swing goes for her right ribs. She turns her hip, eats half of it at base, and feels a rib go. Her window reports it the moment after, in the tongue she grew up with:
[Hit: right ribs, one cracked]
[Reserve: 81% ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓░░]

From here she has a little under four minutes of focused coat from what is left in her, and she knows it.
Read next: Stacking and Spending. For what each road spends and pays on top of the coat, see The Three Paths.
