the-magic-system/power-in-use/runes-and-.title: Runes and Tags
the-magic-system/power-in-use/runes-and-.content:
Runes in the hand and on the field: runed gear, prepared tags, bonded weapons, and runes cut into living bodies. For the whole system in brief, see How Magic Works; for the cutting beside the other working trades, see The Working Trades.

“Check the seal, check the date, check who sold it to you, and then stand well back.” Painted over the door of the tag-sellers’ row at Skelby, since the events described below.

Nobody in Skelby calls it anything but the Long Noon. A back-alley tag seller known as Cheap Perrin sold a drover named Dob Lumley an unstamped flash tag for one silver, and Dob slapped it on the door of his brother-in-law’s privy for a laugh. It lit up white, as advertised, and then, because the seal had been cut by somebody’s nephew, it did not stop.
It burned for thirteen days and thirteen nights. There was noon over Tanner’s Row at midnight, hard and white and throwing shadows the wrong way down the street. The cocks crowed until they lost their voices, the bees came out at the second bell and worked till they dropped, the burglars of the quarter had a ruinous season, and pilgrims walked in from three valleys to pray at a privy. The lamp-wardens (the living craftsmen who keep a town’s runed lamps cut, paid by the street) demanded triple to walk the round, on the grounds that nobody could prove they had done anything. It took that long because the first Engraver refused, the second wanted the Guild’s fee in advance, and the third, Mistress Alys Thorne of the chartered cutters, finally went up to it with a chisel and a smoked glass and cut across the line. It cost her the sight of the left eye. Cheap Perrin sold the rest of his book the following week at double the price, as the man whose tags really work.
The door is in the Guild’s strongroom at Altherion and is still warm, and for a copper the porter will let you hold your hand near it. Every word below is what Dob Lumley ought to have known.
What it is
The cutting (a working written in Parun, the root script of law, into a substance so that it holds without its maker) is a skill anyone with a woken Crystal can level and a trade its guilds rank above every other, loudly, and it is what a fighter carries most. A cut sentence sets a limit on what a Wellspring is doing, at the layer of the soul the cutter’s working leaves through: a Body cutter’s ward stops the bottle, a Spirit cutter’s is taken for a wall, and a Fate cutter’s sets a term on the cutter’s own share of fate. The Glyph Index works one sentence through all three. Whichever it is, a cut reads its maker’s Spirit Mastery, and even a hand with none yet read can do small stamped work. It reaches the field in four forms, from the common to the very rare.






























FormWhat it isHow commonRuned gearA standing working cut into an everyday objectEverywhere in the cities, cheapPrepared tagsA short working cut on paper, hide, bark or thin foil, carried and set off by touchCarried by most fighting practitionersBonded weaponsA weapon carried and fought with for years until it takes part in its owner’s releaseSome fightersBody runesA working cut into the Aether Shell (the Crystal’s outer layer) of a living personRare, and feared
How it looks
Runed gear. Lamps that burn without oil, stove plates, door wards in a clerk’s house, a knife that holds its edge, a coat that sheds rain, a lock that knows its key. The cuts are fine and shallow, stamped with a cutter’s mark and an excise seal, and often repaired, worse each time. All of it was cut by a living hand and is kept up by one: lamp-wardens walk their paid rounds re-cutting worn lamps, ward-cutters charge by the doorframe, and when either of them goes on strike or decides your street owes them money, your street finds out what the dark looks like. The great pieces are another matter: a gate-array, a sword that has killed in nine wars, a ward under a fortress. They are all old, relics of the Great Spirit War and the days of the Physical Epochs that people still kill for, several can no longer be fully read, and nobody living can make another, because what was lost was the condition the old cutters worked in, and no amount of skill brings that back.
How a piece is rated. Everything cut carries two ratings: a Grade for power, on the Measurewrights’ letters, which only things wear, and a Rarity for scarcity, Common up through Mythic and Unique. Beside both sits what the stuff itself is, because a material holds a working by its virtue: stone remembers, salt fixes, gold will not corrupt, and quicksilver will not keep a shape. Which workings a piece holds well, and how it fails when it fails, follow from that, which is why a ward is cut into a wall and a promise sealed in gold. A cutter’s guild title caps the Grade she may lawfully cut, and a merchant’s caps the Rarity he may sell. The Accord’s old stamps (Marked, Proofed, Tempered and so on up) still go on the steel beside the maker’s mark. Gear stays what it was made; only a bonded weapon grows. An Appraisal skill and an assay instrument read a piece, and a good forger beats a weak appraiser every market day of the year.
Prepared tags. A strip a finger long, cut with a short sentence and its seal: a flash, a smoke, a binding, a ward on a doorway, a spark to light a torch. The user presses it to a surface or slaps it onto a body and pushes their own power into it with the thumb, whichever kind their road holds: a Spirit or a Fate hand pushes Essence (spiritual energy), and a Body fighter fires it with his own Charge, raw Aether out of the Shell, which the strip takes just as readily. It flares in the user’s color, makes its own small sound, and works. Fighters carry them in belt-books, sleeve-cuffs and hat-bands. Every tag runs on one of three fuels, and the fuel is written on the strip for anyone who can read it:

























FuelHow it worksIts weaknessAmbientDrinks the Aether (mana, the world’s medium of power) of the place it is set. Cheap and quiet to carryDies on thin, salted or bled ground (Aether-poor by nature, worked against pooling, or pulled empty), beside a Core (a Wellspring site, in common speech) whose keepers have closed it, or in Silence (a region where magic cannot be worked)The user’s reserveTakes its force from the one who sets it off. The stronger the user, the stronger the tagCosts the user, mid-fightThe maker’s chargeCarries power the maker stored in it, Essence from most cutters and Charge from a Body-led one. Works anywhere short of a Silence, at the maker’s strengthDear, and goes stale, as an enhanced bolt does
Only practitioners can use a tag. The working waits for a woken Crystal (the Soul Crystal, the soul itself, opened and taught) to close it, and a sealed Crystal cannot: the Authorization is read at the firing, off the soul behind the thumb, and a sealed one has no harmonization to show. That is why the commoner’s magic is the bottle and not the strip. Licensed cutters, Engravers under a hall’s mark, make them, and a black market sells unstamped ones beside every hall.
Bonded weapons. A practitioner who carries one weapon through years of hard fighting leaves their own power in it the way a hand leaves a shine on a hilt: Essence from a Spirit or a Fate hand, and from a Body fighter his own Charge, which is how most bonded steel in the world was bonded, since it is Body fighters who carry one weapon for thirty years. In time the weapon answers them: it takes their color when they reinforce, and when they release (let their Trait loose in its learned form), it carries part of the release. A blade may burn with its owner’s heat, a staff hold the edge of their field. The weapon grows as its owner grows, the one kind of gear that does, and its part of the release is written on the owner’s card.
Body runes. At the far end of the skill, a cutter writes into a living Aether Shell rather than stone. The lines show as pale scar-tracks, or as nothing at all until the working runs, when they light in the bearer’s color under the skin. A body rune can do what nothing else can: a ward that is part of the person, a working that never needs carrying.
What it costs













































ItemPriceNoteRuned household gearAn Essence lantern 3 to 8 silver, and the inscription fee on topThe fee is the dear partA runed knife or tool1 to 2 goldHolds its edge or its grip; re-cut every few yearsAn ambient tag1 to 3 silverApprentice-cut (by a cutter holding the second of the nine guild titles); the commonest on any beltA reserve tag3 to 6 silverJourneyman-cut and stronger, because the user paysA charged tag1 to 2 gold from a Journeyman, climbing steeply with the maker’s title and Stage (step on the soul’s sixteen-step ladder)Goes stale on the maker’s schedule; a stale book is a loss nobody refundsBlack-market tagsAbout half the stamped priceNo mark, no guarantee, and sometimes a bad sealA great pieceNot soldInherited, won, looted or given by a crown
Time and the cut. A tag takes a cutter an hour or a day; a ward on a wall, a season. A bad cut misfires every time it is used, and a bad seal makes a working that does not stop: the most dangerous thing on any black-market tag. A strip missing its seal altogether does nothing at all, and it is the seal cut wrong that lights Tanner’s Row for thirteen days. Duration comes from three places: the seal sets the term, the paper or the stone caps it, and the anchoring laid down as the sentence closes holds it. A working left unsealed has nothing holding it and nothing stopping it, so it drinks the Aether of the place until the place runs out or someone cuts across the line.
Bonding. Years of the same weapon in the hand, and the loss of part of a release if it is broken or taken.
Body runes. Months of cutting into a living person, pain the whole way, and no undoing. An error misfires on the bearer continuously, for as long as they live, and a faulty seal is a working that runs inside them until it kills them or is cut out.
How it is beaten

Damage the substrate. A tag is paper or foil: tear it, wet it, burn it, smear the ink. A ward is beaten by chiseling it, or by bringing down the wall it sits on.
Starve the ambient tag. Fight on thin, salted or bled ground, beside a closed Core, or in a Silence, and every ambient tag on the belt is a strip of paper.
Make them pay. A reserve tag costs its user reserve, Charge or Essence as the road has it. A fighter who sets off three of them has spent what he needed for his coat.
Strike the beat. Pressing a tag takes a hand and a moment. Pin the hand.
Check the date. Charged tags go stale. A raider with an old book is carrying blanks and does not know which.
Take the bonded weapon. Disarm the owner and the weapon’s part of the release goes with it.
Cut across the line. A body rune is a sentence in the skin, and a deep cut across it breaks the sentence. It is a brutal answer, and sometimes the only one.

Example
Elsie Marrow, a Stage II hired hunter, goes into a flooded mill after a Well-spawn (a creature born out of a Well) with a belt-book of six tags. Two are ambient flash tags at 2 silver each; two are reserve binding tags at 5 silver; two are charged ward tags, 1 gold apiece, cut by a Journeyman she trusts.
The mill’s ground was bled a decade ago, when a sect ran its novices there for a season, and the Aether in the wet stone is thin: her first flash tag sputters and dies on the wall. She knew it might. She slaps a reserve binding on the spawn’s foreleg, it takes a long breath of her own reserve and flares a dull, smoky orange, and the leg locks. The second binding she cannot afford; her reserve is near half and she still needs her coat. She sets the two charged wards on the doorway behind her instead, and they run at her Journeyman’s strength, not hers, which is the whole reason she paid a gold mark for each. The spawn hits the ward and stops.
Read next: The Working Trades.

the-magic-system/power-in-use/stacking-a.title: Stacking and Spending
the-magic-system/power-in-use/stacking-a.content:
How power-ups add together, and how a practitioner’s reserve shows as it runs down. For the whole system in brief, see How Magic Works.

“Two layers is a gamble veterans take. Four is a story told about the dead.” The Guild’s own rule of thumb, and Cullen Fair’s favorite thing to shout at it.

Sigrun Ox-Hand told the whole of Cullen Fair that she would lift the miller’s ox with the cart still hitched to it and the miller still in the cart, and the fair gave forty to one against. She was Stage V (fifth on the soul’s sixteen-step ladder), a drover’s daughter tempered on Pyreveil, a Wellspring of heat, and half the county had come to see her lose. She gathered her coat (her own aura, laid over the body) into her shoulders until they glowed a smoky ember-orange through her shirt. She swore aloud, with the priest as witness, that she would not set that ox down until the sun went behind the church, and she had picked her moment, since the sun was already sitting on the roof ridge and a sun takes about four minutes to get behind a roof. She drank a lifting Draft (a bottled working that pushes a stat) with her teeth and spat the cork at the bookie. Then she got under the axle and bawled HEARTH-BACK at the sky, a surge within the band for one beat’s cost, and up it all came, ox, cart, miller and the miller’s opinions, with half the county howling and the bookie sitting down in a puddle.
That was four layers. For the first minute the crowd cheered the steam coming off her. In the second the blood started, from the nose, from the corners of the eyes, and with the last red sliver of the sun still showing the orange began to go, bright lines running through it like the crazing on an old glaze, and everyone in the crowd with a day’s training had stopped cheering and started shouting at the sun. She held it to the minute, because a vow is a vow.
They heard the aura go at the far end of the horse lines. The ox, I am pleased to report, landed well. She lived, she collected six hundred gold at her bedside from a very quiet man, and for the rest of her days she could not light a pipe without her hand jumping. Asked whether it had been worth it, she bought the fair.
Everything she did is on this page, in order.
What it is
STACKINGEvery boost of one’s own counts toward a single cap: two steps over sustainableBase statsthe body’s passive floor, always onThe coatactive reinforcement, bought with reserveFocusthe coat gathered to one place: +1 step thereA vowto the top of its step; a great vow, one stepA releaseFirst to the top, Second or the One +1, Third +2 on one effectYour own Domainfrom Stage VIII: +1 step, inside the fieldA Draft or an overchannelas graded; overchannel always damagesTHE CAP · +2 STEPS OVER SUSTAINABLEHelp from outsideAn ally’s working, a standingarray, a Domain someoneelse holds, a step held upby a blessing.Stacks freely, above the cap,and adds no risk to theone receiving it, unless it isforced on them.Each layer stacked at once raises the risk of a Crystal Fracture Event. Two is a gamble veterans take.
A practitioner’s own power-ups stack on one another, up to a hard cap of two Grades (letter bands of force, F through EX+) above the sustainable Grade on their registered card, the level their Soul Crystal (the soul itself, which stores and sends out their power) can hold safely. That Grade is read bare, with every worked piece off and dark; gear multiplies on top of it under a limit of its own, and the two Grades are counted from the bare letter. A boost held for the moment may pass the Stage’s own ceiling lawfully inside that cap; only a lasting forced stat takes the fracture rate the tables give for it. A Grade held up for years by a blessing is the exception that proves the rule, because the giver carries the load until they let go, and on the day they let go it lands on you. Every layer the Crystal runs at once adds risk of a fracture, and every second of it spends reserve (the one store of power a soul carries, held as Charge by a Body fighter and as Essence by a Spirit one or a Fate one, since a Fate soul refines what it draws exactly as a Spirit soul does and pays its pulls out of that, Thread being pulled per working and never stored), which the body shows on a fixed ladder of tells.




























































LayerWhat it addsCounts on the capFocused reinforcement (the coat gathered into one part of the body)One Grade, in that place onlyYesA vow (a condition spoken aloud, which needs no witness)Up to the top of the technique’s Grade band; a great vow, staking life, a limb or Crystal mass, one full GradeYesThe Call (a technique’s name shouted as it fires)A surge within the band, for one beat’s costYesA release (the soul’s standing law, its Trait, let off its limit in a learned shape)First: top of the band. Second: one Grade, inside its field. Third: two Grades, for one effectYesYour own Domain (from Stage VIII; the Second Release opens and powers it)The Second Release’s one Grade on your workings, inside the field; a Third’s two on its one stated effectYesA lifting Draft (a bottled working that pushes a stat)As its grade saysYesAn overchannel (forcing the Crystal past its safe ceiling, unshaped)Two to five times sustainable force for a momentYes, and always damagesYour Path’s force bonus and your lens (a Wellspring reaching double at home, half again away)Force inside the letter. Both apply after the Tier is read, so neither ever moves a GradeNo, and they add no riskWorked gear (runed, Draft-tempered or monster-cut pieces, worn and lit; Worn Power has the law)Multiplies the Sub-Stats named on its line, by ×1.5 at most on any one Sub-Stat from everything worn togetherNo. Gear has that cap of its own and adds no fracture risk. It can move the letter the window shows, and the assessor still reads the sustainable Grade with the gear off. It is paid for in Shell draw, out of the same reserveHelp from outside: an ally’s working, a standing array, a Domain (a space where one soul’s law outranks the world’s) someone else holds, a Grade held up by a blessingWhatever the helper can giveNo. It stacks freely and adds no risk to the one receiving it, unless it is forced on them
The stack line. Every registered card (the record a guild or assay house keeps on a practitioner) carries one: each layer the person can run, what it adds, and where they reach the cap. An assessor reads it the way an engine-master reads the marks on a trebuchet’s arm. A Stage bought with Drafts or given by a blessing comes with a gap in that line, because a bought Stage brings no Release, so a rich heir at Stage VII may have a whole rung of the table above he cannot yet run. Assessors look for that gap first and say so loudly at dinner.
How it looks
READING THE RESERVEThe body tells on the reserve, and the ladder is the same for everyoneFullThe aura bright inits own color;breath easy.HalfBreath shortens andstays short. The auradims, as if a handcupped the lamp.A quarterA tremor in the handsand knees. The colorthins toward gray;the edges fray.A tenthThe aura flickerslike a lamp on itslast spoonful of oil.Traits stutter: late,half, or not at all.StarvationThe coat fails andthe base stats sag.The Shell degrades.Maxing out shows heat first, then blood, then a cracking aura. Waste is loud and hot; mastery is quiet.
Running low. The body tells on the reserve, and the ladder is the same for everyone:





















Reserve leftThe tellsHalfThe breath shortens and stays short between exchanges. The aura dims, as if a hand had cupped the lamp.A quarterA tremor in the hands and the knees. The color thins: the hue washes toward gray and the edges of the aura fray.A tenthThe aura flickers on and off like a lamp on its last spoonful of oil. Traits (the soul’s standing laws) stutter: a working comes out late, or half, or not at all. Below this is Starvation, where stats sag and the Crystal’s outer layer degrades.
Maxing out. A Crystal pushed to its ceiling and past it shows heat first, a fever-flush and steam off wet clothes, then blood: from the nose, the corners of the eyes, the gums. Last, the aura cracks. Bright fault-lines run through the color like crazed glass, and every trained eye in the room knows what they are.
The window. Everything on this ladder the room reads off the body, the fighter also reads off their own window, the soul reporting its numbers to its owner in their own tongue and to nobody else. It shows Grades, percentages, bars and levels. A Release or a Domain fills it with the name and what changed, and a timer bar drains:
[FIRST RELEASE: THE LONG YOKE]
[Ardency: top of band]
[Reserve: 47% ▓▓▓▓▓░░░░░]
[Holds: ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓░░░]

The body tells first and the window confirms after. Plenty of fighters have died reading the bar instead of the man in front of them.
Below the tenth. Starving is not only a matter of stats, and what goes after the stats follows the road. A Spirit worker’s Essence is the soul’s own stamped substance, so past that last rung the Core starts to fray: a name will not come, a year goes missing, a veteran stands in a burning yard trying to think whose quarrel this was. It comes back with the reserve, most of it. A Body fighter has spent the world and not himself, and keeps his names; his Shell, with no Charge left to work, starts drawing on the flesh itself, and the skin splits in fine lines where it was taken. A Fate fighter’s reserve is Essence too, so her Core frays like the Spirit worker’s, and her own road’s tells come on top of it: the luck around her curdles, then her name sits wrong in other mouths, and at the bottom every knot she owes falls due together. The table under What it costs has all three roads.
The lost share. Every working loses a share of what it spends, and how much is set by the practitioner’s yield (η, the share of spending that arrives as effect, as a distillation has its yield), which from Glory reads off the class ladder of whichever layer the working goes out through. What the lost share becomes follows the layer too. Through the Shell it burns in the Shell’s own furnace, the athanor that never goes cold, and comes out as heat, noise and light, so a novice’s Body working is loud and hot: a roar, a blast of warm air, light spilling everywhere. Through the Core none of it is heat: it is paid as a hollowing, and a careless Spirit worker goes gray and cold with a dry collar. Through the Attraction Layer it becomes the knot. A master’s is quiet on any road. The same force arrives with almost nothing around it, and the quiet is often the first thing that tells an opponent what they are facing.
What it costs

Fracture risk, per layer. One layer run inside its limit is safe. Each further layer stacked at the same time raises the chance of a Crystal Fracture Event (a crack in the Crystal, healed slowly or never). Two layers is a gamble veterans take. Four is a story told about the dead.
The cap is absolute. Nothing of the practitioner’s own lifts them past two Grades over sustainable. A Third Release already stands at the cap for its effect, so nothing else can be stacked on that effect while it holds. Gear sits outside this count: a worked piece multiplies the Sub-Stat underneath, under its own limit of ×1.5 from all gear together, and it can carry the shown letter up a band by doing so. The two Grades are still counted from the bare Grade, the one read with the gear off, so a fine helm buys a better number and never a higher ceiling for the fighter’s own layers.
Drain, written as time from full. A card states how long a working holds if started on a full reserve, before the reserve falls to a tenth: “holds six minutes from full”. Two workings at once burn both clocks together. A working started at half reserve has a little under half its time left, because the clock runs to the tenth. The exact EU, AU/s and yield behind that line stay on the card and out of the window.
Gear draws. A worked piece is lit out of the wearer’s reserve for as long as it is worn in earnest, a Shell draw the window grades light, steady or heavy. A heavy piece spends like a working held the whole fight, and a fighter in three of them reaches half before the first exchange.
Fight Drafts refill. A fight Draft (a bottle made to be drunk mid-fight) puts power back into the reserve, and it follows the road of whoever drinks it. Each costs a beat to drink and leaves a crash when it wears off. A Spirit worker’s is Core stock: the Essence arrives unstamped, and the crash (the shakes, a heavy head, and a sleep that will not be refused) is the Crystal stamping it as its own after the fact, all at once, with nobody home to help. A Body fighter’s is a Salt: raw Aether in a fraction that packs straight into the Shell. It goes down like swallowing a burn, and its crash is cramps and fever. A Fate fighter has no bottle of her own, whatever the man at the back of the market says: her reserve is Essence, so she drinks Core stock and takes the Spirit crash with it, and nothing in a bottle puts Thread in the hand. There is no rule against drinking several; there is only the price, which climbs about threefold for each Stage (step on the soul’s sixteen-step ladder) the Draft serves, and the counterfeits.
The road’s own bill. The shared tells above are the same on everyone. On top of them each road tires in its own way, because each is spending a different thing: a Body fighter spends the world and the body pays for the handling, a Spirit worker spends herself, and a Fate fighter pays for each pull in Essence and then again in luck that has to be made up later.




































Reserve leftBody (raw Aether, its loss burned as heat)Spirit (Essence, lost as hollowing)Fate (Thread, paid for in Essence, lost as knots)HalfHeat-haze thickens on the skinThe colors near them go flatSmall luck curdles nearbyA quarterSteam off the shoulders, cramps, fibers tearingA hollow cold, a slipped wordThings start going wrong around them, nowA tenthThe Shell cracks: the skin splits in fine lines, and the Charge is drawn from the fleshNames and memories slipTheir own name sits wrong in other mouthsMaxedHeat stroke, burst vessels, a Shell that may not closeA memory gone for good, and a faintThe knots all come due at once
A hitter runs hot and cracks, a thrower runs hollow, and a Fate fighter runs unlucky, so a watcher can name the road by how its walker flags. A pull on a thread carries one more price that no bar shows: landed or failed, it leaves a knot, which the world collects later on the puller or on what is hers. The Three Paths has the roads, Soul Wounds and the Menders the Spirit bill in full, and The Tell and the Knot the knot.
How it is beaten

Read the ladder. The shared tells are the same on everyone. A short breath and a dimming aura means half; when the color flickers, close. The road’s own tells say what is running out: steam means a body about to crack, a wrong name means a soul about to slip, and a bench leg giving under a bystander means it is time to move your chair.
Strip a layer. Break the focus that holds a release, make a vow-sworn fighter choose between the vow and his life, knock the weapon that carries his coat. Each layer lost is a Grade lost.
Make them stack. A fighter at the cap who is losing has one move left, another layer, and it is the one most likely to crack him.
Make the gear eat. A fighter in heavy worked plate is paying for it by the breath. Draw the fight out and the pieces go dark one at a time, each taking its multiplier with it.
Strike the drink. A fight Draft costs a beat with the neck of a bottle at the lips. Break the belt of bottles before the fight and the reserve is all they have.
Wait for the crash. A fighter who drank to finish the fight and did not finish it is about to be worse than when they started.
Listen. A loud working means a low yield, and for the same blow delivered, a loud fighter runs dry first.

Example
Hob Garrow, a Stage VI caravan guard tempered on Monolithion (the Enduring Monument, a Wellspring of stone), has a stack line that reads: coat, focused (+1); vow, no step back (to the top of the band); IRON GRIP, called (surge); cap at +2. Against a Stage VI raider on a pass road he focuses his coat into his right fist and swears his vow aloud: he will not take a step back. That is two layers, a Grade up and the top of the band above it, and the risk is real.
Two minutes in, his breath is short and his deep amber aura has dimmed: half. The raider sees it and starts circling. Hob drinks a fight Draft with his free hand, a Salt that goes down like a swallowed coal, a beat with his guard down, and takes a cut along the jaw for it. His reserve comes back up. At a quarter again his hands shake and the amber washes gray, and the bar in his window says what his hands already told him. He calls IRON GRIP as he swings, the surge cracks the raider’s shoulder, and the fight is done. An hour later the crash lands, the cramps first and the fever after, and Hob sweats it out across two sacks of meal while the wagons roll on without him.
Read next: Runes and Tags, then The Working Trades. For what worn gear multiplies and what it draws, see Worn Power. For what each layer of the stack reads, see Classes and the Three Ladders.

the-magic-system/power-in-use/the-workin.title: The Working Trades
the-magic-system/power-in-use/the-workin.content:
Drafts, Runes, Tags, Chants and the Spoken Arts · The ways a working is set down, and the quarrel over which is best

“By the hand that cut it.” Kharven oath, usually sworn just before something gets thrown.

Nobody can say who threw the first bottle at the Feast of the Five Hands, and everybody can tell you the word that started it. Master Engraver Hallvard Stenn of Marrowhold, in his gold chain and on his sixth cup, leaned down the long table at Ostermark Hall and called a Kharven pourer a potboy. She was known from the Reach to the sea as the Widow’s Ladle. She answered with a bottle of something green that stank of pears, and it glanced off his chain and burst across the plum brandy. Her second bottle died in the air a pace from his head, in a shiver of gold letters, because Stenn had cut the doorframe behind him that spring against precisely this sort of evening, and the whole room learned what a season’s chiseling looks like when it gets to do its job. Loud Peg Arkwright, a hired speaker brought in for the entertainment, climbed on a table and bawled CINDER WALK, which took out the east windows, the musicians and two of her own teeth, and she stood there grinning blood at everyone as she paid for it on the spot. Up in the gallery twenty choristers, who held the hall’s sung ward and whom nobody had thought to tell, kept the same long golden note going through all of it, in perfect pitch, as the benches went past below them.
Thirty-one broken noses, two dead, an ear, a chain, and a hall that smelled of burned brandy and pears for a year. The Accord’s examiner tried to get all of it onto one form, found no heading that would hold a bottle, a doorframe, a shout and a choir at once, and in the end wrote brawl.
A bottle poured over a season and bought with money. A doorframe cut in spring, still working. A shout, now, paid for with teeth. A note that needs twenty throats at once. Those are the trades of this page, with the tag in the belt-book as a fifth, and the brawl is the shortest honest account of them I know. Older books sorted them into ranked kinds with a grand heading over the lot, and sold the chart to schools for two centuries. No such kinds exist. There are skills that rise with use, trades that people make a living at, and guildsmen who will fight you about whose is better, and that last part is all the chart ever described.
The Governing Definition

A working is a sentence given a medium.
The grammar is fixed and identical in every trade that writes. What differs is the substance the sentence is written into, and everything else follows from that one choice.
The singing is the one that does not write. A chant does the same four jobs in tone, and it is no Parun (see below). The account all five share, of how long a working lasts and what a fault does, is in the Glyph Index.
Duration follows from it. Cost follows from it. Who can perform it follows from it. Whether it can be sold, stolen, taxed, inherited or burned follows from it.
Call them media, then, and leave schools of thought to the people who sell schools: a practitioner chooses among them the way a craftsman chooses between speaking, writing, distilling and singing.

The four roles of a sentence
Every sentence in Parun (the language of law every working is written in) does the same four jobs in the same order, and the order is the point. Authorization says by what right a limit is set. Boundary sets it. Direction states which way the law is to run across it. Sealing takes the limit back down. A glyph creates nothing. A Wellspring (the governing idea that transforms how a soul uses Aether, which is mana) was already at work, and the sentence only tells it where to stop, and it does so at whichever layer of the soul the maker’s Essence (spiritual energy) leaves through. In a spoken sentence these four roles are the Warrant, the Ground, the Vector and the Seal of the Counted Speech.
A role left wholly empty does nothing. No seal, no working, no cost, and a very embarrassed apprentice. A role filled badly is another matter, because that sentence fires, and a sentence that fires with a bad limit runs. A bad Authorization or Direction goes wrong while the operator is still in the room. A bad Boundary goes as far as the broken limit lets it, which is how the Long Loaf of Mothwick came to take the bakery.
Which is why Sealing is the role that kills people. Sealing failing produces a working that does not stop, because the law goes on obeying itself after the operator’s attention has left the room. Every burned workshop in the Accord’s incident record is a Sealing failure and roughly a third of them are recorded as something else.
Skills first, trades after
Every one of these is a skill before it is a living. It rises with use and shows on the sheet as one of the nine ranks, Initiate up to Paragon, a trade having no cap on it, and nothing stops a soldier who shouts from learning to pour, or a pourer with a woken Crystal from cutting her own bottle seals. Pouring is the one any pair of hands can level; the speaking, the cutting, tags and the singing want a woken Crystal. A trade is what happens when somebody does one skill well enough for money. A guild title (see The Standing and the Title) is how far that guild will trust them with it, and a cutter’s title caps the Grade she may lawfully cut, a pourer’s the Grade she may lawfully pour. A skill gain arrives the way all of them do, as a line only its owner can read:
[Skill: Cutting, Apprentice to Journeyman]

Techniques are named things done with a skill, and they show no level.
What each one does, side by side



























































TradeMediumHow long it holdsDoes it outlive its maker?Who can use itWhat it billsHow it failsThe speakingBreath, hand, body or a chain held in the CrystalAs long as the saying, or to the term of a spoken Seal while the speaker can carry itNo. It ends when attention lapses, or with the speakerThe wokenThe body, in the same sceneIt dissipates, and the reserve committed is goneThe cuttingStone, iron, bone, crystal, wood, a living ShellTo the term of its Seal, and never past the substrate’s retention thresholdYes, by centuriesMade by the woken; works on anyone who passesA season, a stone, and no second chanceIt misfires continuously until someone finds it and breaks itTagsPaper, hide, bark, thin foilUntil fired; a charged tag goes staleYes, until it goes stalePractitioners only: the working waits for a woken Crystal to close itIts fuel, and a hand and a momentIt dies on thin ground, or a bad seal makes one that does not stopThe pouringA substance in a vesselUntil drunk or spoiledYes. The bottle is the pointAnyone with a mouthProvenance: the ledger behind the ingredientsIt does nothing, works on the wrong person, or works exactly as a lying buyer wantedThe singingSustained tone, in resonance rather than ParunAs long as it is sung, then decays predictablyOnly by replacing the singersAbove trivial, only a groupOther people’s time, indefinitelyA choir that loses three singers to fever in a week
The register table
Each trade carries an Accord name in the old tongue and a plain name in the common one. The old names are the examiners’ filing words for a trade and name no kind of magic.








































TradeAccord registerCommon tongueThe practitionerContemptSpeechArs Vocisthe speaking, sayinga speaker, a castera mouthInscriptionArs Scriptithe writing, the cuttingan Engraver, a Runesmitha cutterDistillingArs Vasisthe pouring, vessel-worka Draftera potboySongArs Cantusthe singinga Chanter, a Choristernone on file, and nobody wants to be the first to insult forty people at once

Which column a person speaks from places them before they have finished the sentence. An Accord examiner says Ars Scripti. The woman who paid him to cut a ward into her doorframe says the cutting. A Kharven soldier says he wants a man who can do the writing, and everyone in the room knows what he means.
Nobody has a word for the whole of it that anyone would say aloud. A person asked what they do names their trade, and if they have two they name the one that pays.

The Examiners and the Workers
The discipline of building a lawful sentence and committing it to a medium is what the guilds of the Accord test, license and tax, and what their courts prohibit. Nobody practices it in the abstract, because practice always means one of the trades below.

The theoretical worker studies it and performs nothing. They know the Codex (the Accord’s master register of glyphs, Wellsprings and laws), the Sixty and their kinds, the Wellspring assignments, the case law. They can tell a Runesmith that his Boundary layer is malformed and be right. They have never in their lives put a working into anything.
The research halls are full of them, the examination boards are made of them, and the most senior chairs require no demonstrated capacity to cast whatsoever.
The practical worker performs. Their standing among the theoretical is roughly that of a farrier at a physicians’ dinner.

The examination. Four gates, in order, and the order is the argument: knowledge of grammar, then a demonstrated working, then a masterpiece submitted to the board, then the oath. A worker who fails the masterpiece may practice under supervision indefinitely and will never sign their own name to an inscription.
I · The Speaking
Ars Vocis. The vulgar one, according to everyone who can afford a workshop.
Medium · the ephemeral sentence, carried by breath, hand, or trained interior chain. Most of it is sealed on attention, the cheapest term there is. A full spoken Seal can run longer, as far as the speaker’s own Attraction Layer can carry it, and it bills them the whole way. Only spoken Parun has to add up to the sum, and the Counted Speech is the reason most speakers buy their sentences whole.
What nothing else can do · It happens now. A rune takes a week and a Draft takes a season. A spoken working takes as long as it takes to say it, and that is the entire case for it.
What it costs · The body, immediately, in the same scene. There is no substrate to absorb the strain, so the practitioner is the substrate.

Its standing: low in the guilds’ eyes, and only there.
To a guildsman, a man who can only speak is a man who could not afford to learn to cut. The soldier’s art, the hedge-worker’s art (the hedge-worker being the hired hand of the petty arts, paid by the job, who can overcharge you or refuse), the traveling fraud’s art and the art of the desperate.
It requires no substrate, no vessel, no workshop, no seven years, and no guild. That is precisely why the guilds hold it in contempt. Anyone can shout. Cutting takes seven years and a master willing to take you. The world outside the halls has never agreed. The public, the armies and the sects idolize a great speaker as they idolize any champion, the songs are all about speakers, the bookies quote their odds, and the man the examiners call a mouth is the one the crowd came to see.
The examiners license the hire of it grudgingly, at the lowest fee band, with the shortest examination, and refer to the license among themselves as the shouting ticket.

Delivery vectors · all of them the speaking
Spoken · Voice into air. The default. Loud, legible, and it tells everyone within earshot exactly which Wellspring you just invoked.
Gestured · The hand carries the chain. Quieter, slower, useless with a broken wrist or a bound arm.
Bodily · Martial integration. Corporis. A practitioner’s stats sit in the body always, a passive base nothing switches off, and bodily speaking is the active reinforcement spoken over it, pushing past the base at a price in reserve. It shows as a coat of the practitioner’s own aura, thicker where they push, with the body changing beneath it, and it can be gathered into one fist or one shin while the rest runs thin, so reading where it went is half the fight. A fist with combustion on it is a sentence with the body as the pen, and the sentence is still ephemeral, which is why the fist stops burning, and the coat drops, the moment attention lapses. Asleep, drugged or taken by surprise, a practitioner keeps the base and loses the layer, which is why ambush is the oldest answer to one. It is not a separate art, whatever the fight schools charge for it.
Internalized · The chain held silently in the Crystal (the Soul Crystal, which is the soul itself). The high form. Below Refraction (Stage VII) a working needs voice, hand, ink or blood as an outside anchor for its boundary; the registers call this the Law of Material Anchor, or Law V. At Refraction a practitioner can hold the Crystal itself as an object of study, and the four roles compress into an inner chain that needs no anchor at all. So a man who works silently in a room has told everyone present his Stage without saying a number.
Failure mode · It dissipates and takes something with it. The reserve already committed (Charge or Essence, by the speaker’s road) does not come back. Loud, immediate, embarrassing and survivable: exactly the wrong shape for the respectable trades and exactly the right shape for a battlefield. In some rooms a working spoken aloud in company is an obscenity, and nobody polite says casting.
II · The Cutting
Ars Scripti. The writing. The runes. The one the oldest guilds are built on.
Medium · the permanent sentence, cut into substrate. Stone, iron, bone, crystal, prepared wood, and at the far end of the skill the Aether Shell (the soul’s outer layer, turning inner power into outward force) or the Soul Crystal itself in a living body.
What nothing else can do · It outlives the person who made it. A ward cut into a fortress wall by an Engraver dead three centuries still suppresses hostile Essence, provided the stone has not fallen below its retention threshold. The Continuum reads what is written. The author may leave. The sentence remains legible. It was anchored once, as it closed, and the surface carries that claim from then on, by its own virtue: stone remembers what it was told to hold, which is why the great wards are in walls, and a cutter picks her material for what its virtue will keep and how it will fail. Unlike the spoken sentence it need not add up to any sum.
What it costs · Time, substrate, and irrevocability. A season of work, a stone that will never be cut again, and the knowledge that an error does not misfire once.

It misfires continuously, for as long as the carving holds, on everyone who passes it, until somebody finds it and breaks it.
There are inscriptions in the world that have been quietly wrong for two hundred years.

Its standing: highest, say the cutters, and they own the building. Masterpiece requirement, seven-year term, trade secrets that are genuinely secret, and a monopoly the cutters’ guilds enforce under the Accord’s seal with real violence. An Engraver’s mark on a wall is a signature and a warranty and a legal instrument at once.
And it is degrading
The best inscriptions in the world are all old, work of the Great Spirit War and the days of the Physical Epochs, when Bara, Ashura and Aegor walked in human form. People kill for the portable ones. The great arrays at the Concord Gates, the deep wards under Marrowhold, the standing work in the Kharven death-houses: none can be reproduced by any living Engraver, and several can no longer be fully read.

The Accord’s published position is that this is a matter of lost technique which its research halls expect to recover within a generation.
They have expected this for four generations.
Look at any standing inscription and you will find a date, an author or a repair, and the repair is worse than the original. The wall is older than the war. Cheap runed gear is journeyman stamping, common as nails, and carries no more than a maker’s mark, and the lamp-wardens and ward-cutters who keep a street’s small cuts in repair are paid by the job and go on strike like anyone else.

III · Tags
The cutting made small enough to carry and cheap enough to lose.

Medium a short sentence and its seal, cut on paper, hide, bark or thin foil and fired by touch. The full account, with prices and fuels, is under Runes and Tags.
What nothing else can do It brings a prepared working into a fight without the fighter having prepared anything that day. It takes an hour or a day to cut and a thumb to fire.
What it needs A woken Crystal to close it. Only a practitioner can fire a tag, which is why the commoner’s magic is the bottle and not the strip. Every tag runs on one of three fuels: the Aether of the place, the reserve of whoever fires it, or a charge its maker stored in it, and the fuel is written on the strip for anyone who can read.
What it costs By the fuel. An ambient tag dies on thin ground, a reserve tag bills the user mid-fight, and a charged tag goes stale on its maker’s schedule.
Failure mode A bad cut misfires every time, and a bad seal makes a working that does not stop. A strip with its seal left off altogether does nothing and is merely a waste of a silver. See the glyph roles above, and then see the privy door at Altherion.

IV · The Pouring
Ars Vasis. Vessel-work. The richest trade there is, and the one the rest of the world drinks.
Medium · the distilled sentence. A procedure, with no standing instruction left behind: Aether plus Essence plus Vessel plus Glyphica (the glyph-writing that shapes a working), resolved as a reaction, and the working ends up inside a substance.
What nothing else can do, and this is the point of the entire page:
It puts a working into the hands of somebody who cannot work.
The speaking, the cutting, tags and the singing all require a woken Soul Crystal. The pouring requires one only at the moment of manufacture, and there only behind the seal on work made to stand: under the Law of Alchemical Independence a pure alchemist, whose Crystal never woke, pours Drafts all the same.
After that the working is a thing in a bottle, and the bottle can be carried by a courier, sold by a factor, taxed at a gate, stolen off a corpse, watered down by a dishonest apothecary, and drunk by a farmer who has never harmonized with anything in his life.
The bottle is how the other ninety-odd percent of the population holds magic in their own hand. Everything else they touch, they hire: the warden’s lamp, the cutter’s doorframe, the hedge-worker’s charm against the cough. Everything a market in magic needs falls straight out of that: smuggling, counterfeiting, guild monopoly, excise, adulteration, shortage, addiction, and a black market with names in it.
What a Draft does to a soul whose Crystal never woke. A Draft acts on the Essence Core (the soul’s inner layer, holding identity, memory and Traits), and an unwoken soul has a Core like anyone else. Its Shell is sealed and cannot phase-lock, and no harmonization follows, so the farmer gets the working and none of the architecture.
He also gets no melt. Nucleation (the seeding that decides how a melted Crystal sets again) is a Crystal event, so an ordinary Draft cannot seat in him, cannot recast him, and cannot be argued with once it is in. (The one exception is the Waking Draft, made to open a sealed Crystal, very dear, and often the death or the warping of the child who drinks it.) It runs its course through the Core and leaves whatever it leaves. Repeated dosing over years advances nothing and deepens the grain, hardening the man further along the direction he was already set, which is why the second and third generation of a village on cheap Drafts are recognizable at a distance and the fourth is a problem.
The Accord has no category for this because its ledgers count practitioners. The apothecaries have known it for two centuries and price accordingly.
What a Draft does to a woken one. Everything the top of the market pays for. An Essence Draft feeds tempering, the melting-down and rebuilding of the soul layer by layer that refines Essence and leaves the body stronger and carrying Traits. A Draft can give a Wellspring. A Draft can supply the Catalyst a Stage demands, so that Stages can simply be bought, and the great houses hoard the top Drafts and marry their way into the rest. The Ladder and the Draft has what that buys and where it stops.
Fight Drafts. A bottle made to be drunk mid-fight costs a beat with the neck at the lips, refills the reserve and leaves a crash that pays for it. It follows the road of the drinker: Core stock feeds a Spirit worker’s Core with unstamped Essence and leaves the stamping crash, and a Body fighter drinks a Salt, raw Aether in a fraction that packs straight into the Shell, which hits like a burn going down and leaves cramps and fever. Each Draft is graded by the Stage it serves, the price climbs about threefold a Stage, and counterfeits are common. See Stacking and Spending.
Where the strength comes from. A monster’s core is in a way its Soul Crystal, worth more the stronger the monster, and an alchemist renders it into Essence Drafts. It is the lawful Crystal Draw of the Standing Index, with Creature-Sourced potency and the risk of Identity Contamination in every bottle. Swallowed raw it gives everything at once, and most who try it die or come out wrong. A Crystal cut from a dead practitioner makes the strongest Draft of all, the worst crime in every realm and the most profitable, and it is why the Index’s Grade IV (its top Grade of stock, no relation to Body IV) has never balanced.
What it costs · Provenance. A Draft requires ingredients, and ingredients come from somewhere, and somebody sold them to you, and there is a ledger. The bill here is social and legal, and the enforcement arm of every guild in the Accord exists to collect on it.
Its standing: middling in dignity, enormous in coin. Below the cutters in the halls and far above them in turnover. A Drafter is a tradesman. A great Drafter is a merchant house. The Accord’s revenue depends on the pouring to a degree it does not enjoy discussing.
Failure mode · It does not work, or it works on the wrong person, or it works exactly as intended for a buyer who lied about what he wanted it for. Quiet, deniable, and traceable through paperwork. Check the seal, check the excise stamp, and remember that somebody knows the difference between the label and the bottle and is saying nothing.
V · The Singing
Ars Cantus. Pitched, where the other trades assert.
Medium · the sustained condition, carried by tone. Neither ephemeral nor permanent. It holds for as long as it is sung and decays predictably afterward.
A chant is not Parun. A sound may not repeat inside a Parun word, and a chant is mostly repetition. It sets its condition in resonance, the way Gravetongue does, and it does the four jobs in tone: who sings and by what right, how far the sound carries, which way it runs, and the decay when it stops. Its words carry a sentence only when Glyphica (the writing of law) is present, as when a chorister who has the count sings over a cut ward, and then that sentence answers to the same rules as any other.
What nothing else can do · It scales with throats. Everything above trivial requires more than one voice, which makes it the only trade that cannot be practiced alone. A chant needs its voices in tune, its hours kept and somebody to replace the singer who dies, and it follows the register of whoever sings it, a soldier’s chant sounding like a soldier and a nun’s like a nun.

That single constraint makes it institutional by necessity: orders, choirs, liturgies, schedules, a roster, and the particular catastrophe of a choir that loses three singers to fever in a week.

What it costs · Other people, and their time, indefinitely. A sung ward is a standing labor obligation. Somebody is singing right now or the thing is failing.
Its standing: sacral, and outside the guilds entirely, which is why the Accord finds it difficult and why Sancta Lux and the Sohai live here.

Harmonia (magic worked by tone and sympathetic vibration) takes the singing as its medium-home.

Two Trades That Set Nothing Down
The five above put a working into a medium. These two take something off a person, and both send a bill.
Soul-menders. A Spirit strike that gets past the Shell leaves a wound no surgeon can find, and closing it is a trade with a bench, a fee and a reputation to lose. A mender is a Spirit Path practitioner, an Answerer at the least for shallow work (Spirit II, in the assessors’ numerals) and a Confessor or better for anything deep. She reads the wound, sets the soul back in true, and holds the edges of the cut together while the patient tells the thin thing over until it has somewhere to stay. The Guild-city rates run 1 to 2 silver for a reading, 2 to 6 silver for a shallow sitting, 10 to 60 gold the season for a course on a deep wound, and 100 gold and up, by private treaty, for a Shepherd (Spirit IV). A deep wound left past a season sets for life, which makes this the trade where being poor costs the most. Temples keep menders, the great houses retain them, and every fighting hall has one on a stipend it complains about. Soul Wounds and the Menders has the full table.
Knot-cutters. Every pull on a thread leaves a knot, a debt the world collects later on the puller or on what is hers, and a knot-cutter is the one piece of work that will take a knot’s debt onto itself. Knotwrights (Fate IV, which takes a bloodline’s Work or a blessing to reach) make them and nobody below can: a ring of twisted iron, a cord with a lead seal, a small hooked blade on a chain that has never been sharpened. Each takes its maker weeks in bed, each carries one knot no larger than it was made for, and each breaks when it is used. They go by private treaty, in the range of a good warhorse for one that will carry a lean and a small estate for one rated to a removed prerequisite, and half of those on the market are fakes that are very good until the week they are needed. The Tell and the Knot has the law of it.
What these are not. Ordinary Draft-making and chanting stay what this page has called them, trades and skills, however grand the customer. The name Seam Art is kept for something else: a combat art whose Form crosses two Paths, a Brew fought with for Body and Spirit or a Song for Spirit and Fate, worked at the Veil’s seams. Those are rare, unstable and feared, because nothing on one plane counters them cleanly. A pourer who fills belts is a pourer. Forms has the Seam Arts at length.
Whose Trade Is Best
A feud, and it changes with the ground. The Concord ranks cutting first. The Marrowkin rank it first and hardest, since a hold is a permanent substrate and everything they own is inscribed. Kharven ranks pouring first: nothing in a camp that moves is permanent, a Draft travels in a belt, and the standing runework in the death-houses is imported work no living Kharven hand can read, a fact the seat does not raise and the Accord does not stop mentioning. The speaking ranks higher in Kharven than anywhere else in the Concord’s reach, because a soldier is not embarrassed by an art that works now. Potboy is the word that starts fights there, as the Feast of the Five Hands can tell you.
Master Works
Every one of these trades ends in the same place, for the very few who get there. A Master Work is a piece that does what its Grade and material should not be able to, made once at the end of a lifetime, always Unique or Mythic, and named. Each area has its own: a cutter’s wall that does what no stone should, a smith’s blade, a pourer’s bottle. The most coveted thing in any cellar is a Fate Essence Draft, which bottles a share of the manipulation of the probabilities of reality itself. It is extremely hard to make, and more than one house has gone to war over a rumor of one.
Read next: Counterplay: What Beats a Practitioner.
