the-magic-system/practice-and-institutio.title: The Gate: Who May Learn Magic
the-magic-system/practice-and-institutio.content:
Nearly everyone is born with the Crystal. About one in ten is taught to use it, and the other nine can tell you exactly whose fault that is.

Every market town tells a version of the Carter’s Cross auction, and I have checked enough of them to say most are lies, so here is the one with a Guild record behind it. In a hot August a laundress named Joan Pellow had a daughter of eight, Tib, who put both hands in a full washtub and froze it solid with the shirts inside, and by the third day Joan Pellow’s drying yard held a hunting-guild scout in a wolfskin, a recruiter with an Aetherion letter, a crown screening officer with a roll under his arm, and two rival schools in full color: the Green Herons on the left with their elder and their song, the Red Ladles on the right with their elder and a louder song. A bookie chalked odds on the church wall. The bidding passed fourteen gold and a mule. When the Ladles offered a new roof the Heron elder called their grandmaster a soup thief, the Ladle elder’s coat went up the color of boiled beets, and a jaw broke in the first exchange, and then the whole yard came down, poles and wet linen and sixty people, with sheets burning green overhead like flags. Joan Pellow got up on the frozen tub with a washing bat and bawled that the girl went to whoever would let her come home at harvest. Nobody could promise it, as each of them knew, and while they were still hitting each other about it the screening officer walked around the wreck, found the child behind the rinsing trough, read her, and wrote her name down. An entered child belongs to the roll. Tib Pellow went to the crown. Her mother got three silver and the bill for the church wall, and when her younger boy stirred the following winter she walked him thirty miles by night to the Herons and never told a soul.
That yard held the whole of this page. Here is the machinery under it.
I. A Crystal in Nearly Everyone
Nearly every person alive carries a Soul Crystal from birth, the porter and the laundress as surely as the heir of a great house. The Crystal is the soul, so a few are born with one so slight that no coil has ever found it, and scholars argue about what that makes them. The rest carry a Seed Crystal: sealed and silent, present in full, and doing nothing a coil (the assay instrument that reads a Crystal) can read.
A dormant Crystal stays dormant for life unless somebody wakes it while it is young. Waking is taught, and taught early. It takes a teacher, a regimen and a place to practice before the soul sets, and a Crystal nobody attends to in childhood seals and goes on sleeping, and refines sealed by the Weathering (the slow hardening hard living gives a soul, without magic) into whatever its work made it. That is the unwoken, and it is nine people in every ten, which is most of the world.
The tenth wakes, nearly always as a child. One in ten is a great many people. A market town of four thousand keeps four hundred woken souls, nearly all of them low on the ladder, warming kettles and selling small tricks and drilling at dawn in somebody’s yard, and that is why every quarter has a school with a song, why sects and their ranks are common knowledge, and why a child of six can rank the local fighters and fight you about it.
A small number stir without being taught. A child raised on a badly worked street in a crowded quarter wakes at an odd age; a child with a strong Inherited mark (a bodily sign of a Trait carried in the blood) shows it before the first winter. These are the ones the screening seasons find, because screening reads a Crystal that has already stirred and returns nothing on one that has not.
Then there is the bottle. A Waking Draft opens a Crystal with no teacher and no seven years, and it is the rich family’s road and the desperate one’s. It is very dear, sixty to a hundred and twenty gold in a good year, and it often kills or warps the child who drinks it. Most of the rich buy one for their children anyway, generally with a physician standing by and a second child in reserve, while commoners sell themselves into guild debt for one. A blessing can wake a soul too, and the Crystal may go on answering to the knock that woke it.

So what stands between a practitioner and a porter is almost always the lesson, given in time. Once a Crystal has sealed it is woken rarely, by a crisis, a master’s forcing, a tribulation, a Waking Draft or a blessing, and always at great cost.
Every crown of the Dark Ages has understood this, and these are the generations in which they began trying to lock the lesson away.

The gates a Path (the layer of the Crystal a soul has learned to lean on, Body, Spirit or Fate) sets on a Sub-Stat (one of the finer stats) decide how far a stat may rise. This gate comes first, and decides whether the Crystal wakes at all.
II. The Lock
For most of reckoned time teaching passed through households, orders and masters, and a crown cared what its practitioners did rather than how they learned. The wars of the Dark Ages changed the arithmetic. A practitioner is a siege engine that eats at your table. A nation that can teach its own subjects and refuse everyone else’s has a standing advantage no treaty gives it, and a nation that lets anyone learn anything has handed that advantage to whoever is paying.
So every nation now keeps a schedule: which kinds of people may learn which magics, from whom, and under what oath. The schedules differ from crown to crown and they are the most jealously kept documents in any chancery. Three powers hold the keys between them.
The low lesson got out long before anyone wrote a schedule, and there are far too many yards and sects to shut. A schedule licenses them, fines them and counts them. What it actually guards, where it guards anything, is the next rung: the upper manuals, the glyph tables, the high working and the people who take pay for it.
The Accord, the coalition of guilds whose halls sit in every nation, controls the academies’ training, issues the Magister credential and funds the academies. The Guild made the system. The Guild owns the gate. Inside a signed circle the Accord’s examination is the license; outside one each crown and each hall keeps its own.
The crowns decide who among their subjects may enter an academy at all, appoint the Mage Royal and the crown chairs, and write the schedule.
Sancta Lux credentials nobody and has no need to: it declares what lies on the far side of the gate consecrated or profane, and that is often enough to close it.

The Bench’s power of reservation is the lock in its purest form. A formula entered and reserved is lawful, real and forbidden to anyone below a stated Tier. It arranges who is permitted to be capable, and denies nothing to anyone while it does.

III. The Five Gates



































GateWho passesWho holds itAbilityA Crystal that stirs unbidden and is noticed. Recruited to an academy or sought out by a guildScreening officers, academy recruiters, guild scoutsBirthThe children of houses that can pay for a teacher, a fee and seven years, or for a Waking DraftGreat houses, academies, the companies’ freedomNationThe crown’s own subjects, sworn before the first lessonCrowns and their chanceriesLicenseWhoever sits the examination and passes itAcademies, the Accord, the hallsBloodlineThe blood, and nobody elseThe archaic bloodlines and the lesser houses that copy them
Ability. Screening is seasonal and it is looking for a stirring Crystal. A child who shows one is noticed, and a noticed child is recruited. The Aetherion Academy takes its entrants by letter and recommendation; the Ward-Carver’s Academy at Senri’s Gate by an entrance Proving. Hunting guilds and sect elders go to the same screenings and bid for the same children, and a family with a stirring child in a poor quarter receives more offers in a season than in the rest of its life.
Birth. An academy charges fees, and the companies grant the freedom by patrimony, servitude or redemption. A great house reads its infants for Inherited marks inside the first month and knows by the first winter what it has. A commoner’s child reaches a teacher by indenture, seven years for the cutting, bound to a master the formulary limits in how many he may hold. Class is decided at the door of the schoolroom long before it is decided anywhere else.
Nation. A crown teaches its own. The oath comes before the first lesson, and a foreign student learns what the treaty between the two crowns allows and nothing more. Vaeloris, the Carver’s Seat of the Silver Cedars, develops and standardizes techniques for the Reach’s own use, and a technique standardized there belongs to the Reach before it belongs to anyone who learned it.
License. The academy ranks run Scholar, Licentiate, Master, Doctor and Chair on the diploma, while on the training floor the older ladder of outer disciple, inner disciple, core disciple and elder holds, settled by ranking contests, and the Licentiate is the qualification that matters: permission to practice for hire. Past it lie the Accord’s credentials. A Magister holds an academy credential and a documented training record. A Registered Natural learned by other means and submits to monitoring instead: periodic reassessment, demonstration, disclosure of every new harmonization (a soul’s tuning to a Wellspring). A school pays for its own license by the year, and in any large city about half the yards hold one and the other half hold something that looks very like one.
Bloodline. The archaic bloodlines teach their arts to the blood and to nobody else, and lesser houses imitate them. A bloodline art taught outside the line is theft in the eyes of the house and, in most schedules, of the crown as well. The deep of the Fate Path needs less guarding than a schedule supposes, since nobody can be drilled into it or reason their way in, and a Work of Hataraki, being an inherited grip on the thing, is the one lesson in the world that a stolen manual does not carry.
IV. The Second Gate: A Purse
The lesson gets you onto the ladder. What carries you up it is very largely money, and the schedules hardly pretend otherwise.
A Stage can simply be bought, as The Ladder and the Draft sets out: Drafts and blessings can supply the Catalyst (the particular experience a Stage demands), and a soul that has the Draft crosses. The great houses hoard the top Drafts, and here the lock and the purse are one object, since a formula the Bench has reserved may lawfully be drunk only by those it names. A coil reads the Stage the same however it was crossed, though it reads the seat differently. A schedule does not care, either, so long as the fee was paid and the formula was lawful.
The poor have three roads. Dungeon luck: a crew goes down, and comes up with a monster’s core worth a year’s wages, or a Wellspring got at a Core no one had found, or does not come up. Guild patronage: a hall stakes a promising hand a Draft against a signed term of service, and the term is the real product. Blessings: a higher spirit or a person of higher Temperance gives what no purse could reach, for reasons of their own, on terms that may be written badly or not at all. Every mother who walks a child to a gate has heard of someone who rose by each of the three, and every bookie can tell her the odds.
What it does not buy. Its Release must be found and mastered by fighting, and sects teach what money cannot buy: Releases, Domains, techniques, skills and the rites for their Wellspring. Nor does a purse buy a Path, because the Crystal reads a Path off what a life has been spent on, and a bought Stage arrives with its gated Sub-Stats exactly as shut as they were. So the richest heir on the river stands at the same gate as the laundress’s son, a few rungs higher and with better boots, asking the same school for the same thing, and the school can refuse him. That refusal is the most valuable thing the schools own, and they know it.
V. What Needs No Leave
The schedules watch three things: who teaches, who takes pay, and high working. They do not watch what a woken soul does at home with what it already knows.
A woman who woke as a girl and warms her own kettle breaks no law. Teaching the neighbor’s son does. Charging for it does. Taking pay for a working or a hunt without a guild license does, and is common anyway, because unlicensed hunters are cheap and there are always more postings than licensed parties. High working without a license is the gravest offense the schedules name, and each schedule defines it by Tier and by trade. The Divine Language sits inside every definition.
VI. How the Lock Is Kept
Controlled texts. Primers, grammars and glyph tables are copied by sworn scriveners under license, numbered, and issued against a registration. The Apprentice’s Primer reaches a new practitioner the day they are entered and not before. Teaching the Divine Language without sanction is a Law of Severance for anyone sworn to the Codex (the Accord’s master register of laws), and a crown offense under most schedules.
Crystal registration. A stirred Crystal is entered on the roll of the place it was found. The Bureau of Strategic Assessment manages registration and cares only whether an output has been observed and assessed. Those who refuse are entered anyway, as Unregistered Naturals, on a separate list that is never published.
Searchers and trace examiners. Nearly every working leaves traces. A ward that was cut carries the cutter’s hand; a Draft that was poured carries a maker’s mark. A trace examiner reads those traces as evidence, and a good one can name the teaching lineage behind a technique more often than not, which is how an unlicensed school is usually found: through its pupils’ mistakes. The company searcher hears the rest, and an unlicensed working on a kept street is audible to anyone listening at the wrong hour.
The Night Watch. The Night Watch Society, a crown-chartered society holding the crown’s warrant, older than the Accord’s circles, that investigates illegal magic and phenomena the law has no name for. The Night Watch works alongside the guilds and answers to the state, which is the whole of its difference from a hall.
The Inquisitors. Sancta Lux keeps a lateral office, the Inquisitor, authorized to pronounce sentence in the field without an Arbiter present, and it sends them after unconsecrated high working wherever the Church holds standing. The Holy Inquisition, the splinter that took the name, claims the same work and prosecutes it by fire. It holds legal standing where the crowns and churches that back it rule, and enforces the Gate there itself; where the Accord’s circles have signed, it is outlawed.
The guilds. Locally, the halls police their own ground. A hall that finds an unlicensed practitioner working its district posts him on its board, and an Extermination Commission against a corrupted practitioner is a lawful posting under the five classes. Inside a signed circle, Enforcement’s Sealwrights take the cases no hall will.
VII. Hire and Jurisdiction
A licensed practitioner works for pay as a hired hunter, a workshop inscriber, a company soldier, or in private practice, and the license is what separates each of those trades from a crime.
When a crime is done with a working, it is proved by the trace examiners, and then the guild courts and the crown courts fight over who hears it. The guild court claims the case because the accused holds a guild license, or because the act was a working. The crown court claims it because the body lies on crown land. Which of them wins differs by place, and in most places it is decided by whoever has the accused first.
VIII. The Magister and the Natural

The fire was always in her. The understanding of fire was always in him. Both produce fire. The institution that cannot tell the difference will be burned by both.
Attributed to the third Provost of the Bureau’s classification office, upon her resignation

The scorch is still on the market cross at Tarn Cross, and for a copper they will show it to you and tell you about the Day the Battery Burned. A Bureau party had pitched its striped pavilion there to run the standard test on a bargeman’s daughter of fifteen named Hesper Lowe, who had been lighting her father’s pipe from across the river, and half the county came to watch, with chestnuts. On the frost pan she produced nothing whatever. On the stone pan, nothing. On the fire pan she took a breath and the pavilion stopped being there, a white-gold sheet going forty feet up with three years of Bureau forms inside it, and the crowd roared and ate chestnuts roasted on the embers while the examiners ran in circles. Magister Corvin Aske of the examining party, who had lost his good robe and been ten years at the Collegium for the privilege, asked her very politely to do it again. She did it four more times in the open square, each one brighter, and each time he stood a little nearer with his hands in his sleeves, and on the fifth, as her chin came up and her left shoulder dropped, he stepped in and put one cold finger on the hollow of her throat. The flame went out like a pinched wick. She had hit harder than he could ever hit, and he had read the song by the fifth verse. They both remembered it as a victory, and the Bureau, which had nothing left to write on, entered her score on a borrowed tablecloth: 0.08.
The battery sets a soul before a row of pans and divides the mean of what it does by the best of what it does, so 0.08 means there is one thing this girl can do. The Bureau still publishes the figure, and nothing else in the world has any use for it. No window shows it, no coil reads it and no card carries it. What survived the tablecloth is the Bureau’s three words for people, which are the ones that open and close doors.

























The wordWho it meansWhat it certifiesMagisterHolds a credential from a recognized academyThat what they know came through supervised training, that their techniques are documented, and that their output can be assessed from training records. An asset the institution manufacturedRegistered NaturalLearned by any other road, and submits to monitoring: periodic reassessment, technique demonstration, disclosure of every new harmonizationThat the Bureau is aware of the capabilities and has documented them by watching. A phenomenon the institution discoveredUnregistered NaturalLearned by any other road, and refusesA separate ledger, not published. The Bureau’s position is that unregistered high-Tier output is a proliferation risk the Concord’s framework was not designed to address. Strategic Assessment’s position is more concise: an asset the Bureau cannot see is a threat the Bureau cannot assess, and a threat the Bureau cannot assess is a threat the Bureau cannot counter
On a card all of this is one word on the Source line, Taught or Lived, and whether the art can be handed on follows from it. A Magister can teach it to any student who meets the bar, because the technique was built from principles and comes apart from the person. A Natural frequently cannot: they can demonstrate, and they can refine it by repetition, and the student stands there watching a thing that is not separable from the woman doing it.
The Bureau measures the shape and argues about the cause. The cause is the seat. A Threshold is a melt, and a melt cools into order only around what survived the heat, the Traits a soul brought to the fire. A melt seeded by one dominant Trait cools narrow and deep, and every working after it runs cleanest along that one law. A melt seeded by several weaker Traits that do not contradict each other cools distributed, reaching no such depth and fracturing under no unfamiliar current either. Training regimes decide which Traits get promoted to load paths at Splintering (Stage V). A collegium that puts a cohort through eleven varied years is running a distributed seeding program without a word for what it is doing. A girl who walks out of a heat concentration at fourteen was seeded once, hard, by one current, and everything she will ever be was decided in an afternoon.
This also disposes of the word native, though the forms go on printing it, and of Natural with it. Older books sort souls by an inborn bias, and they would have told you the fire was always in Hesper Lowe. The trade has given that up. A native gift is a first hard imprint and the life lived along it, and a river is made too, only nobody signed for the work. The Bureau never asked. Ask on the water at Tarn Cross, and they will tell you that the barge she was born on burned to the waterline under her in her sixth winter, with her mother aboard. None of that went on the tablecloth.
In a fight it comes down to a pattern and a gap. A Natural on their own ground is faster, more powerful at peak and more instinctive, and a Magister against them is slower and more analytical. Every Natural has a pattern, because a Crystal that can only hear one frequency plays one song, and a song you have learned is a song you can interrupt. Every Magister has a gap, because attention spread across everything hears everything poorly, and a channel that is overwhelmed has collapsed regardless of what the others are doing. The whole engagement is whether Hesper can end it before Corvin finishes reading her.
Three kinds of people stand in the queue who do not fit the forms. The first has a very good coat and a receipt. A Stage can be bought, a Wellspring can come out of a bottle, and an advancement Draft brings a seed of its own, a single borrowed law, so a soul raised on the bottle tends to read narrow along a law it did not live, and a blessing’s line can misreport itself outright. One colleague holds that the bottle-raised are a third kind of person altogether, and another that they are ordinary Naturals with an expensive excuse. Both have been paid by the same family.
The second cannot be seen at all, since every word above assumes a woken Crystal, and a Trait does not. An unwoken soul carries its laws in ordinary material and refines by the Weathering, which hardens a man further along the direction he was already being used. A weathered fisherman off forty years of cold water would put a peak on his one law that would embarrass a credentialed Magister. Nobody will ever test him. The battery is administered to registrants, registration follows screening, and screening looks for a Crystal that has already stirred. The Bureau’s stated tolerance for unmodeled variables is low and declining. Its actual exposure is the population of the four quarters.
The third has found another way to get the output, by not running the process at all. A Mechanica operator has neither learned the grammar nor had the instrument set in them by what they survived, and sits on none of the Bureau’s forms. There is a separate designation. It exists, it is not published, and the Bureau does not discuss the criteria or the number assigned.
Three institutions hold this gate and agree on exactly one point: unregistered high-Tier Naturals are a problem. They disagree on why. The Guild considers them a credentialing failure and wants to educate them. Sancta Lux considers them a theological concern and wants to assess their spiritual condition: -turgy means divine work, as its doctors are glad to remind the Guild, and if the work is divine the Church has standing. The Bureau of Strategic Assessment considers them a strategic risk and wants them on the ledger, and it does not care whether the output was trained or self-taught, consecrated or profane. The disagreement matters because it determines what happens when one is found. When the Unregistered Natural refuses all three, the question of what happens next is answered differently by each institution, and none of the answers is comfortable.
The Bureau does not use the word goetic. It appears in the historical literature, meaning sorcery by personal will, used by the Sancta Lux theological apparatus to describe unconsecrated wonder-working. It remains in common use outside formal channels, particularly among credentialed Magisters referring to Unregistered Naturals, and guidance discouraging it has been issued on four occasions. Each guidance document was longer than the last.
The irony the Bureau notes without comment is the New World survey. The Voyager-era teams were nearly all Magisters, and Spirit-type, Fate-type and Medium-type concentrations were undercounted because literacy across every current lacks the sensitivity of someone set hard along one. A mixed team would have produced a more complete survey. The recommendation was declined, on the grounds that deploying Unregistered Naturals in an official capacity would constitute credentialing without the credential.
IX. Those Who Learn Anyway
Black-market teaching. A back room, a fee, a stolen or copied primer, and a teacher who was licensed once. The kind readers already sell a reading of what a person is with nothing forwarded to the Accord, and some of them sell the next lesson too.
The Mother. A cult, named for the mother of vinegar, the living culture that sours whatever it is added to. It recruits across the Gate: its cells are called cultures, its recruits are inoculated, and what it teaches them no schedule would allow.
Self-derived workings. A Natural who has been set hard along one law can work on it without ever having been taught, and some do. The Bureau watches for them with particular care. Self-derivation in the written arts is nearly impossible, which is why the schedules guard the texts hardest.
The guild loophole. Hunting guilds train their own. A hall indentures a boy under its own charter, wakes him on its own floor and teaches him what a hunter needs, and the state’s gate never sees him until he is registered as a finished hunter. Crowns hate this and every crown relies on it, because the halls are what stand between a district and the things that come up out of the dungeons and down off the roads.
The speaking. The shouting ticket licenses a speaker to take hire, and that is all it does. The speaking itself has never been licensed and nobody has found a way to license it, because a spoken working has no author in its own grammar. Liability falls on whoever paid. A speaker needs no substrate, no workshop and no seven years, and when he is finished there is nothing to point at.
The penalties. A small offense costs an amercement to the offender’s means. Unlicensed hire costs the tools and the fee. Unlicensed high working is punished hard: branding in the Accord cities, and Crystal sealing, in which a Sealwright shuts a woken Crystal on itself, the way a keeper closes a Core. A sealed practitioner is unwoken again in everything except memory.
X. How the Common Folk See It
Ordinary people know there is a gate and roughly where it stands. They know the screening season comes, that a stirring child is either a fortune or a danger to the household, and that the ranked practitioner walking down their street got through something they were never offered, even when they went to school with his brother. They follow the yards the way they follow a cockfight, wear the colors, and sing the songs. The awe they feel is partly for the power and partly for the door.

Some mothers hide a stirring child from the screening, because an entered child belongs to the roll. Others walk one three days to the nearest academy and wait at the gate until someone reads him.

Read next: The Standing and the Title, for the names that follow all this around.

the-magic-system/practice-and-institutio.title: The Standing and the Title: Guild Titles as Trust
the-magic-system/practice-and-institutio.content:
On the Three Names Every Practitioner Carries, What the Second One Promises, and Why the Last One Follows You Anyway
Compiled for the Research and Archives Division · companion to The Gate, The Guild Accord, and The Works and Days

“The Accord knows what I am. My guild knows what I rank. The man across the room knows what I feel like. He is the one I worry about.”
Attributed to a retired Arbiter-Militant, identity withheld at the subject’s request

Aldith and Edony Moor of Kelderbridge were cousins who had trained in one yard under one master, and at the Hallowmark Fair the coil gave them one reading to the last decimal, the same Wellspring and Stage, the same hot orange coat, which made theirs, the herald said, the fairest bout on the river. The herald, who was paid by the word, cried both profiles in full from the rail. Nobody cheered. The stands cracked walnuts and waited for it to be over. Then Aldith walked into the ring, and the front rows breathed out, and a baby that had been screaming since noon went quiet, and a boy on somebody’s shoulders yelled “The Still Water!” and the whole west stand took it up. Edony came through the east gate, and the east stand got to its feet without anyone deciding to, a fishwife began to cry and could not say why, the dogs under the benches left in a body, and the same boy, who had a future in the trade, yelled “The Storm!” An old pie seller named Goody Rudd, who had spent the morning sitting on a bench beside each of them in turn, had put her stall and her house on Aldith, and an hour later, with half the ring on fire and the east stand down on forty broken legs, she collected them and a third of the bookie’s boat. The instruments had told everyone the truth. It was the wrong truth to bet on.
The Moors had three names each, like every practitioner alive, and the crowd had only ever cared about the third. The third follows you into a tavern. The second is the one that lets a stranger hand you the goods, and since half the world has it wrong, it gets the middle of this page.
The Three Names

Every practitioner carries three names. They acquire them in order, they lose them in reverse order, and only one of them is real.

The First Name · what the instrument says. A string of measurements reading as a sentence in a language designed for ledgers. Pyreveil, Shape, Body VIII Mastered, Stage VIII Transcendence, Master, Level 218, Body III Resonant, η .91. This is what the coil (the Accord’s assay instrument) says when you stand inside it.

Impersonal, diagnostic and correct. It tells you what the soul does the way a scale tells you what a thing weighs. It cannot tell you what the weight means to the person carrying it, and it is therefore the name that matters least in every room that does not contain a coil.
Nobody introduces themselves by their instrument profile. The halls publish it. The factor houses price it. The person it describes has already stopped listening.
The bearer has a private copy. A window (the soul reporting its numbers to its owner, in their own tongue, unseen by anyone else) shows them their numbers, ranks, percentages, bars and Level, and it leaves out the yield, the η on the coil’s line. Everyone else needs a coil, or a Gnosis Perception that outranks the bearer’s Resilience Ward by a full step, and short of that, what the room has is an estimate said aloud, which people hide and fake.
It is also the one name a purse can change overnight. A Draft-bought Stage moves the ceiling, the door and the color on this line, thin underneath and Overgrown until Level catches up, since a reserve and a Mastery follow Level and Level follows a life lived, and it does nothing whatever to the third name below.

The Second Name · what your guild will trust you with. Initiate through Paragon, earned by commissions. It travels with the silver token. The nine words are the same nine everyone uses to say a fighter’s Stage, which is the whole of the confusion this page exists to clear up: a fighter’s rank is her Stage, a tradesman’s is his title, and Master Venn at the forge may be an Apprentice on the road. It opens doors, closes borders, and tells a stranger what he may safely hand you.
The Guild Accord (a coalition of many kinds of guild across many nations: adventurers, merchants, craftsmen, alchemists, healers, couriers and more) has one thing every hall in it signs on for, and this is it: the same nine titles in every guild, each one grading trust in that trade.
Dame Ottilie Marsh, Grandmaster of the Mercers’ hall at Waxgate, stands about as high as a flour barrel and was once knocked down a flight of stairs by a goose. In the spring two kings of the Hundred Crowns, at war over a bridge, handed her the crown jewels of both kingdoms on one afternoon to hold against the ransoms, in scarlet silk bags, in the middle of the battlefield, because of a bit of silver at her belt, and neither of them counted. A Stage VI captain in a coat the color of a bonfire stood over her and thought about it where his whole company could watch him think. She looked up and asked who he imagined would ever buy them from him. He went away. Her token says she may be trusted with anything short of a Mythic piece, and nowhere does it say she can throw a punch.

































































TitleA merchant may sell up toA craftsman may make up toAn adventurer may take bounties up toInitiateCommonE (stamped Marked)Grade EApprenticeCommonD (Proofed)Grade DJourneymanUncommonC (Tempered)Grade CAdeptRareB (Instrument)Grade BExpertRareA (Hallowed)Grade AMasterVery RareS to SS (Storied)Grade SGrandmasterLegendarySS to SSS (Found)Grade SSArchmasterMythicX to EX (Numinous)Grade XParagonUniqueEX+ (Proscribed)Grade EX

Rarity is scarcity and Grade is power, and an item carries both. A merchant’s title caps the first, a smith’s title caps the second, and an adventurer’s title and a monster’s bounty read off the same letters, which the Accord sets title by title. The old bills counted nine Threat Tiers instead, T1 to T9, and the older hall-lists numbered the titles as Tiers of Standing, one to nine; both are clerks’ words now. A courier’s title says what he may be handed sealed, a healer’s what she may be paid to treat, and every other hall has written its own line under the same nine words.
A hall confers a title by its own lights: a term and a masterpiece among the makers, a ledger that balanced for twenty years among the merchants. A title needs no woken Crystal, and most of the merchants’ Grandmasters have never so much as warmed a kettle.
A forged token is a great crime in every realm that has signed, and the forger is often hanged. The title is the whole reason a stranger hands you the goods, and one forged token that gets found out makes every honest token on that road worth a little less. A title lost is a scandal of the same family: the hall strikes it, the news goes down the road faster than the owner can, and by the next market nobody will hold his coat.

The fighting guilds keep one more table. Adventurers’ guilds, company soldiers and the rest who are paid to be dangerous still make you earn the title by commissions, and they ask besides that you stand at the title’s own rank in Stage, because in that trade the thing they are trusting you with is the fight: a Journeyman’s token in a fighting hall wants Stage III, an Expert’s Stage V. A trade title asks no Stage at all.

































































RankStagesFighting skills capped atOffice it can carryInitiateMurmuringInitiatenoneApprenticeWellingApprenticenoneJourneymanAscensionJourneymannoneAdeptFlourishingAdeptConcord AgentExpertSplintering, Glory, RefractionExpertSealwright, enforcement specialistsMasterTranscendence, Invocation, RealizationMasterWarden of DutyGrandmasterDissonance, EmanationGrandmasterEnvoy of the LatticeArchmasterPrincipality, ZenithArchmasterBearer of the Concord FlameParagonRevelation, ApexParagonChosen of the Codex
A hall’s certificate and a fighting rank are different things, and people have lost a great deal of money confusing them. The table above asks a Stage floor and a record of commissions and nothing else, so a fighter at Transcendence (Stage VIII) with the jobs behind her carries a Master’s token on the commission boards whoever she is and whatever her soul looks like inside. A certificate is the paper a hall signs for its own purposes: that it will stand behind this person to hold an appointment, teach in its name or sit its examination. Examinations read the seat before they read output, and the halls cap a rough seat (a soul that cooled around Traits pulling across two Paths) at Adept on certification. So a two-Path woman at Stage VIII is a Master on her token and an Adept on her certificate on the same morning, and both are true. The token says what the board will let her take. The certificate says what the hall will put its name to. Neither one says how hard she hits, and she is the reason Slagwright’s Draught sells.

So a title on a token says how good you are at your trade, and only in a fighting guild does it also say how dangerous you are. A sellsword who bows to a Grandmaster at Waxgate has made a mistake about which table he is reading, and she will sell him something for it.
A bought Stage meets a fighter’s token floor like any other. The table does not ask how you crossed, though the commissions behind the token have to be real, and an Overgrown heir spilling power across the hall is hard to miss. Crews ask, in the hall, before they go down a stair with you, because a commission does not care what you paid.
The unwoken have no row on this table. It begins at Murmuring because the halls do not register what they cannot examine, and a soul whose Crystal (the soul itself, which stores Essence and channels it outward) has not opened has no Stage to examine, however high its Level or its trade. The older fighters’ register began at the letter E, which came to the same thing. They drill in the yards, sell their small tricks and argue about rank in taverns all the same, and every one of them can recite this table.
A Paragon is the reference standard, the thing other measurements are checked against. Among fighters it is the name an institution gives a practitioner it can no longer measure, and the Codex files it as a rank because filing it as a rank is the only alternative to admitting the apparatus has run out of scale. Among merchants it is the person whose word other markets check their own weights against.
A Grandmaster who has been a Grandmaster for thirty years does not think of herself as a Grandmaster. She thinks of herself as whoever she was before the rank, plus whatever the rank cost her, and the title for that composite is a word that fits on a credential and misses everything that doesn’t.

The Third Name · what the world calls you. This is the one that matters.
No instrument assigns it and no institution confers it. It is generated by the experience of being near you, shaped above all by the behavioral signature of your Archetype, which is the thing your soul does to the room when you walk into it. Your Class, the name your soul was offered at a threshold for how you have lived, is a separate matter: it is known to you, to anyone with Gnosis Perception strong enough to read it off you, and to everyone else as far as you care to tell it. The Archetype is on everybody’s skin.

Two practitioners at identical Stage, Level, Wellspring and Form. The coil gives them the same numbers. One walks into a tavern and the fire steadies, the barman relaxes, the dog under the table puts its head down. The other walks into the same tavern and the fire spits, the barman reaches under the counter, and the dog leaves.
The numbers are the same. The souls differ. The world is reading no coil. The world is reading the weather their soul makes.
It is earned, imposed, or inherited, and it follows you until something bigger replaces it, or until you die and the name outlives you, in which case the name was the real thing all along and you were just the body it was wearing for a while.

The Weather Your Soul Makes
The Archetype names what you are like to be near, whatever it is you do. Some practitioners settle a room. Some charge it. Some empty it. The Third Name comes from the pattern. Older hall-lists call the first of these Harmonic, and the trade has been meaning to stop using that word three ways since before the Accord. No card has a line for any of them: they are the weather the room reports, and the room is the only instrument that reads them.




























































ArchetypeWhat it feels like nearbyTitles it generatesConstant the room settlesCalm, with no comfort in it, the way a well-built wall is calm. Breathing steadies and thoughts clarify, and the calm does not care whether you want itNames of stability. The Constant · The Standard · The Foundation · The Pillar · The Still WaterAberrant the room tightensPressure, the way a scar is pressure. People feel watched and slightly off-balance. Animals react before people do, and veterans know it at onceNames of damage. The Scar · The Break · The Wrong One · The Storm · The Crooked · The Remnant. Frequently unfair and never inaccurateElegiac the room remembersWeight, the way a cemetery has weight. People think of their own losses unprompted, and nothing has reached into themNames of memory. The Mourner · The Keeper of Names · The Gray · The Wake · The CandleBound the room belongs to something elseOccupancy. Something else in the room is paying attention through the practitioner. The practitioner is the houseNames of service. The Sworn · The Chain · The Vessel · The Instrument · Urion’s Scale. One bound to an Archon is addressed by the Archon’s name, and one bound to a debt is addressed by the debtAscendant the room kneelsGravity, the way a throne has gravity. People adjust their posture and lower their voices from the instinct that makes a body lean downhillNames of elevation. The Chosen · The Crown · The Anointed · The Radiance · The ThroneCatalytic the room changesProductive discomfort. Deferred decisions present themselves, and false equilibria stop holdingNames of effect. The Teacher · The Catalyst · The Wake · The Turning · The Opener. Mu-jin is The Teacher because people near him learn whether they intended to or not, and the title has nothing to say about his pedagogyConvergent the room holds two truthsAmbiguity. Warm and cold, safe and dangerous, held at once and steady enough to rule out indecisionNames of paradox. The Both · The Contradiction · The Scales · The Twin · The Fulcrum. The only titles that routinely contain a conjunctionSymphonic the room fillsFullness, the acoustics of a cathedral more than its grandeur: a space with room in it for the people insideNames of abundance. The Chorus · The Many · The Deep · The Orchestra · The CathedralEcho-Walker the room is older than it wasAge, the way an old house has age. To an Echo-Walker the dead are collaborators, on terms negotiated in real timeNames of ancestry. The Ancestor · The Return · The Archive · The Lineage. An Echo-Walker born into a family of the dead’s record-keepers is the conjunction that produces NiranMonadic the room emptiesAbsence, the way a locked door is absence. People feel excluded and never rejected: the soul pushes nobody away. It simply does not include themNames of closure. The Seal · The Closed Book · The Vault · The Ledger-Keeper · The Silence. Cozbi’s title is Monadic in origin: the name of a soul that counts everything and shares the tally with no one

Why the Accord fears the Monadic. A sealed system produces no readable output. A system the instruments cannot assess is a system the Accord cannot price, and a system the Accord cannot price is a hole in the ledger.
Sancta Lux considers it a doctrinal problem, because the Scale cannot weigh what will not present itself to the measurement.
Common people do not call Monadic practitioners anything, because Monadic practitioners do not give them the chance.

Where the Weather Comes From
The Third Name has a mechanism, and it is the cheapest thing in the Crystal.
Stage, Level, Wellspring and Form have no hand in the Archetype, which is why identical instrument profiles produce opposite rooms. It is produced by Passive Traits.
A Passive Reflection is a law stabilized by long habit and continuous exposure, always running, costing almost nothing to hold and impossible to switch off. It shows in posture, in gait, in thermoregulation, in scent, and in the ambient behavior of a room somebody has been sitting in for an hour. The trained sense a soul’s power and argue over it openly enough. The Third Name is read off something else: a soul’s standing habit, at the only amplitude that never stops broadcasting.
This is why the Third Name is stickier than the other two and why it cannot be renounced. A title can be surrendered and an instrument profile changes at every Threshold (the melting and rebuilding that lifts a soul to its next Stage, whether by crisis or out of a bottle). A Passive Trait is the shape of a life already lived, and it goes on expressing at the same amplitude whether the bearer is fighting, sleeping, or sitting quietly in a room full of people who have not been told who he is.

The crowns’ spy-clerks worked this out two centuries before the Archives did. Every agent’s file records Passive Traits first and stat profile second, because the profile is what an enemy can only learn by fighting him and the Passive is what a stranger learns by sharing a bench.
Which means the unawakened have Third Names and nothing else.
Passive Traits sit in the soul’s own material and require no Crystal to run. An unwoken midwife who settles a room settles it for the same reason a Constant Grandmaster does, at a fraction of the amplitude, with no coil in her history and no token in her belt. The village named her forty years ago and the Accord has never heard of her.
Every quarter is full of these names. The Still Woman at the ford. The one they send for when a child will not stop screaming. The man nobody sits beside on the wagon and nobody can say why. The folk naming tradition is reading the only layer that was ever readable from outside, which makes it, on this one axis, more accurate than the Accord’s entire apparatus.
The Archives has recorded the observation three times. It has never been actioned, because a system built to price output has no use for a name attached to a person who produces none.

How Titles Are Made

A title accretes, and nobody confers it. The world watches long enough to identify the pattern, the pattern produces a name, and the name sticks because names that accurately describe a lived experience are the stickiest things in any language.

I · The Reputation. It begins as gossip. The tender at Greyshaft Twelve tells the next shift that the new practitioner settled the array by walking past it, and within a month the syntax has compressed to a name, and nobody remembers who said it first because nobody did. It arrived the way weather arrives: from a direction you can point at and from a source you cannot name. Heralds cry it next and minstrels rhyme it, usually wrongly, and by then the bookies have it chalked beside the odds. Rival names fight it out for a season or two, and the most famous wins.
II · The Confirmation. The title survives its first test in circumstances that differ from the ones that produced it. It has crossed from description to prediction, and a title that predicts is a title that means something, and a title that means something is a title people start using in the practitioner’s hearing.
III · The Claim. Acceptance ratifies the name. Rejection demonstrates that the name has enough weight to require rejection, which is itself a form of ratification. The only response that kills a title is indifference, and indifference is difficult to sustain toward a name that accurately describes something your soul is doing whether you choose it or not.
IV · The Record. It enters the Accord’s filing, the guild’s archive, or the crown’s peerage register and becomes a legal fact.

A Third Name that has survived all four stages is, for every practical purpose, the practitioner’s real name, and the name their parents gave them is the alias.

Where Your Name Places You
Constant titles place their bearers at the center of institutions. The Accord’s entire architecture is designed by and for Constant practitioners, which is why the Accord works, and why it is so profoundly unsettling to everyone who does not fit inside it.
Aberrant titles place their bearers at the edge. Field assets, frontier specialists, the kind of problem-solver you send to a situation that has already destroyed the standard response. They are valued and they are unwelcome, and the distance between the two is the Aberrant practitioner’s entire social experience.
Elegiac titles place their bearers apart. Sacerdotal: the spaces reserved for grief, memory, and the cultural work of holding the dead in the minds of the living.
Bound titles place their bearers below and above simultaneously. Subordinate to what holds them and superior to anyone without an equivalent endorsement: the class confusion that surrounds every temple-warrior, oath-knight and consecrated servant in the four quarters.
Ascendant titles place their bearers above. Full stop. Aristocratic in the original sense: the thing that claimed them does not claim the second-best, and the room reorganizes around that fact whether the practitioner asked it to or not.
Catalytic titles place their bearers in motion. Institutions that employ them discover the practitioner has changed the institution more than the institution has changed the practitioner.

Monadic titles place their bearers nowhere. A Monadic title sounds like a door closing, reads like a refusal, and functions as a reminder that classification requires the classified to participate.
They cannot be placed because they have not provided the information placement requires, and the world’s response to a person who cannot be placed is the world’s most honest confession of what placement was for in the first place, which was control.

What the Archives Has Not Filed
The titles the dead keep are the one gap the Division treats as urgent, and the reason is the cutting (inscribing a working into stone or metal). A name cut into stone by an Engraver three centuries dead is still legible, still doing work, and still attached to a Third Name nobody alive can verify. The wall says who he was. There is no living instrument that can check.

The Kharven death-houses carry the hardest version. The inscriptions name their Engravers. Several of the names belong to no lineage the seat can trace, and the Accord’s position is that the records were lost. The Kharven position is that the records were taken.

Stripped-title ceremonies exist, are rare, and fail to do what the ceremony implies. A guild can revoke a title and strike a profile from its register. It cannot stop a room from settling when a Constant walks into it, and every stripped practitioner discovers within a season that the only name that survived the ceremony was the one nobody had the authority to grant.

Still unfiled: per-kingdom title conventions, historical title lineages, inheritance and succession, and the civilian conventions by which a village names a practitioner it has decided to keep.

the-magic-system/practice-and-institutio.title: Training and Sects
the-magic-system/practice-and-institutio.content:
How a woken practitioner grows, who teaches them, what a sect has that money cannot buy, how they are ranked, and what fame and contest do to them. For the whole system in brief, see How Magic Works.
The Copper Kites and the Iron Aunts of Hollin Ford have hated each other for fourteen generations, and on ranking day the whole town shuts to watch. In the year everyone still talks about, the Kites sent out an inner disciple named Perrin Dace, nineteen, in the school’s burnt orange, against the Aunts’ core disciple Sunniva Holm, who outweighed him by two sacks of flour and had never lost on that ground. For a quarter of the water clock she walked him down, Aunts’ song going up from the east bank, and his left collarbone was already broken when he stepped inside her swing on a strange slanting half-pace, planted, and put his palm through her guard into her breastbone, and Sunniva Holm sat down in the river. The Kites went mad. And in the Aunts’ box the school’s grandmother, who was ninety and had not spoken in public for a decade, stood up on two sticks and asked in a voice that carried over the whole ford who had taught that boy their third step. By nightfall it was out: one winter, a kitchen boy, four silver, a copy of the Aunts’ inner manual. The Kites’ elders struck his name to save their own necks. The Aunts’ bounty went up on every door along the river before morning. The song says twelve hunters came after him; the Aunts’ accounts pay two, and record a right hand, taken at a ferry. Children on both banks still play at that half-pace in the street, and the Aunts still beat them for it.
Note what that boy paid four silver for. A Stage can be had for coin, by anyone with enough of it, and nobody on the river would have stolen a manual for something a wool merchant could buy his son. He stole a step. Training is where all of it is decided: what you can do, who owns it, and who comes for you if you carry it off. What follows is how the thing runs.
What it is
A practitioner (a person whose Soul Crystal, which is the soul itself, is awake) grows by cultivation: breath and pulling, hard fighting, tempering, and seclusion before each Threshold (the melting down and rebuilding of the Crystal one Stage, one step of sixteen, higher). Practitioners are common, and their ranks are common knowledge. Schools, houses and sects teach them, rank them, guard their secrets and hunt their deserters, while the guilds sneer at fighters and the world cheers the great ones.
Money buys the climb, and sects sell the rest. Drafts and blessings can supply a Threshold’s Catalyst (the particular experience a Stage demands), so a Stage can simply be bought. Everything a fighter does with it comes from somewhere else, and for most of them that is here.
How it looks
Cultivation, five ways.



































PracticeWhat it doesWhereBreath and pullingLong, slow breathing that pulls Aether (the world’s medium of power) from the ground and air around the practitioner into the Crystal and refines it to Essence (the practitioner’s own power). Trains the pull, the measuring-out and the speed of recoveryAt a Wellspring site (a place where one of the sixty kinds of Aether pools, a Core in common speech, most of them inside a dungeon somebody cleared), or anywhere the Aether is dense: a guild yard on rich ground, a shrine, a mountain spring. Rich ground fills you faster and thin ground starves you, and schools fight over the differenceSparringDrills, forms and practice bouts. Builds technique, timing and the read. Skills rise with use and show as Grades on the sheet; techniques are named things done with themThe school’s yard, every dayReal fightsHunts, duels, wars, dungeons. Barring a blessing, the only thing that raises Level (the count of how often the Crystal has densified), because only real consequence does. Level moves by danger overcome, so one kill of something stronger moves it more than a hundred weak ones, and crews argue over who got the killWherever the danger isTemperingMelting the Crystal down and rebuilding it layer by layer, which refines Essence and makes it stronger, while the body gains Traits. Essence Drafts, rendered by alchemists from monster cores, feed it, and Traits level with itA guarded room, and a billSeclusionMonths alone before a Threshold, working the self toward the Catalyst, under guard. A Draft or a blessing can stand in for the Catalyst, and those who can afford one spend the same months waiting on the meltA sealed room, a cave, a cell under a school
A seclusion is guarded because a practitioner deep in one is helpless, and because a Crystal near its melt is a prize to an enemy. It ends in a breakthrough, the full transformation the hall can see, the soul passing the Great Work in its own Path’s terms (nigredo, albedo, citrinitas, rubedo: broken down, purified, woken, fixed), or in slag (a remaking that set wrong and cost the soul ground), or it does not end at all.
Each school its own basics. There is no common curriculum. The Accord’s Apprentice’s Primer teaches the glyph grammar to the registered, but how to breathe, stand, pull, reinforce and strike is each school’s own, and a fighter’s first form tells a trained eye who taught them. A school’s methods and forms are secrets worth stealing and worth killing over.
Each school its road, mostly. A soul has one life’s time to spend and a school can only fill so many years of it, so most of them teach down one Path. The Body yards drill hands, footing and what a thing will do under load. The Spirit halls drill reading, projecting and the written line. Each will tell you over dinner that the other is not really an art, and each has buried students who found out otherwise. Any good school lets a student study the other roads for knowledge and small uses, which opens no gates. A school that promises you two is selling about two and a half times the years and a rough seat, and some of them are honest about it. Fate is the odd one out. A yard can teach reach, weight in a room and the keeping of a word, and there it stops, because a real pull cannot be drilled in or reasoned out. The Moto teach more, to their own blood, and any sect advertising otherwise is after your silver.
What a sect has that money cannot buy. A bought Stage arrives with no Release, and a sect teaches what comes after: Releases, Domains, techniques, skills, and the rites for their Wellspring (the governing idea that transforms how a soul uses Aether; a person may get one at a Core in a dungeon, from a school, from a Draft or blessing, or by birth, and the school’s rites are how it stops being a small thing and starts, after years of mastery, to reach double its effect on its home Path, or half again at most away from it). A Release must be found and mastered by fighting, and a sect is where someone knows what you are looking for. Anyone at Stage VIII can have a Domain, their own concept made real, and the same elders know how it is coaxed out and how it kills you. None of this is on any market. It is paid for in years, duty and an oath, and the sect decides whether to take you, so every great school has a story about the rich heir who turned up at Stage VII with forty servants and was handed a broom. The cleverest houses buy the Stage and then send the child to sweep.
Schools are clubs. A school has colors, songs, grudges, a style you can spot at fifty paces and a following that has never thrown a punch and will fight you about it anyway. Tavern walls are chalked with who beat whom. A boy will tell you his family has been Kite since his grandmother’s day, and a Kite marrying an Aunt is a matter for both priests and both elders.
The three shared arts. Aura coat, Pressure and sensing are taught in every yard and belong to nobody, and each culture has its own name for each and its own argument about them. In a bout-ring of the western quarters the coat is the shine, Pressure is the weight and sensing is the nose, and a fighter is priced by all three. A Moto house says matoi, the wearing, and considers it coarse to show color at table; it says atsu for Pressure and kehai, the sign of someone there, for sensing, and holds that a person who must look has already lost. The lineage halls say hùtǐ, wēiyā and shénshí, and have spent four centuries of commentary on which must be learned first. On a Guild roll they are reinforcement, Pressure and Gnosis Perception, and the Measurewrights who write those words will gladly explain why every other school has the order wrong.
The ranks.

























WhoRanks, low to highSchools, houses and sectsOuter disciple, inner disciple, core disciple, elder. A sect’s grandmaster over allGuild hallsThe nine titles, Initiate to Paragon, grading trust in that trade; among the makers Apprentice still comes by the seven-year term and Master by the masterpieceAcademiesScholar, Licentiate, Master, Doctor, ChairFighting guildsThe same nine titles, read off the Stage table, because a fighter’s trade is the fight
Disciples rise by ranking contests, set bouts held on a school’s calendar, and by the elders’ word, which can lift a disciple who lost or hold back one who won. A rank opens secrets (the next forms, the inner manuals), resources (Drafts, the bottled workings that feed growth; hours at the school’s Wellspring site; a better room) and standing. It also demands duty: missions, teaching the ranks below, fighting when the school is challenged, marrying where the house says. A defector is hunted for what they carry out in their head and their hands.
Guilds sneer, the world cheers. To a guild examiner a fighter who works by voice and body is a mouth, someone who could not afford to learn to cut. That is a feud, and everyone outside the halls disagrees. Crowds pack the bout-rings, armies follow named fighters, sects court them, and children play at their techniques in the street.
Renown, by audience. A name is known differently to the street, the guild halls, the schools and sects, the crowns and the Accord, and the underworld, and each keeps its own account. Heralds cry the results, minstrels spread songs that get the details wrong, and bookies keep the only figures anyone trusts. Renown opens doors and draws challengers in equal measure: every young fighter with a point to prove wants to beat the person everyone has heard of. Epithets are mostly given by others, some of them wrong and some unkind, and they travel ahead of a fighter down the road. A fighter who names himself is laughed at until it works, and then the name is his.
Warrants and bounties. The guild halls post warrants: lawful, public, payable for an unlicensed high worker or a corrupted practitioner, brought in alive where the warrant says so. Sects, houses, guilds and lords post bounties: private, for what someone stole, knew or did, with terms nobody writes down. A monster that gets famous earns a name, an epithet and a bounty like anyone else, and its core is the part of the bounty worth the most.
Tournaments. Contests are fought in brackets by Stage, and a fighter may enter above their own Stage but never below. A fighter may yield at any time, by word or a hand flat on the ground. Killing is forbidden, and the killer forfeits and owes blood-price; it still happens, most often in the high brackets, where a full blow cannot be pulled in time. A fighter’s own power is allowed: Traits (the soul’s standing laws), techniques, releases (a Trait let loose in a learned form), vows (conditions sworn for power) and a bonded weapon. Bought power is banned: fight Drafts, purchased tags (prepared runed strips), hired arrays (standing runed workings). A bought Stage cannot be banned, since it is the fighter’s Stage for good and the coil reads it the same however it was crossed (it reads the seat differently, and no bracket reads the seat), and the crowd handles that part itself, at volume, with fruit. Prizes are resources (Drafts, a season at a Wellspring site, rights to pull at a Core, a worked Wellspring site), places (an inner-disciple seat, an academy letter, a house commission) and fame.
What it costs

Seclusion: months out of the world, a guard who must be trusted and paid, and the risk of slag.
Entry: fees, a seven-year indenture, or an oath to a house or crown sworn before the first lesson.
What the sect teaches: years you could have spent buying, and an oath. A rich heir pays this like everyone else, usually with worse grace.
Rank: duty, and secrets that bind. The higher a disciple climbs, the more they know, and the harder they are hunted if they leave.
Fame: a stream of challengers, a price on the head in some ledgers, and an epithet that may not be kind.
Bouts: wounds, the Drafts drunk to recover from them, and the occasional death the rules forbid.

How it is beaten

Study the school. A taught form is a documented form. A fighter who learned a rival school’s basics can read its disciples before they finish their first step.
Find the secluded. A practitioner in seclusion cannot fight. Get past the guard, or bribe him.
Steal the manual. A school’s power is its secrets; take them and the school is ordinary. Ask Perrin Dace, if you can find him, and shake his left hand.
Find the bought ones. A fighter who bought their Stage carries the ceiling, the door and the color, thin underneath, and has not done the fighting. Make them improvise, and see whether there is a Release under it.
Make them choose. A disciple bound by duty can be pressed through it: challenge the school in public and someone must answer.
Use the yield. In a bout, a fighter losing badly may live to fight the next season. In a feud there is no yield, and a disciple raised on bouts sometimes forgets that.

Example
Wil Ashdown wakes at nine and is taken as an outer disciple of a mountain school whose basics start with breath at a cold spring before dawn. For six years he sweeps, carries water and drills the school’s first forms until the elders can read his stance from the gate. At sixteen he wins two ranking bouts and loses the third, and the elders lift him to inner disciple anyway: he lost to a core disciple, and he lost well.
Inner rank opens the school’s second manual and its Wellspring hours, and sends him with three others to guard a salt convoy. A real fight on that road gives him more Level than a year of sparring, and the first night’s kill sets him and the other three shouting at one another about whose bolt it was. His window keeps its own count, in the hill speech he grew up with:
[Level: 61 to 63]
[Skill: Measure, Initiate to Apprentice]
[Reserve: 22% ▓▓░░░░░░░░]

A night holding a pass beside one of the others leaves a bond between them that carries weight: a Spirit Axis (the bond with another soul that Stage IV demands). He goes into seclusion for four months under a core disciple’s guard and comes out Flourishing, the hall watching his color settle.
The next spring he enters the Stage IV bracket at the river games and draws Rafe Tressilian in the final, a wool factor’s son who drank his way to Flourishing at fifteen, on two Drafts that cost more than Wil’s village, with the ceiling, the color and a very good coat, and a Level of about twenty under them. Neither has a Release yet. Wil has been hit before, and he has the deeper reserve by three times over. He wins a season’s Drafts and a nickname he hates, and he finds a challenger waiting at the school gate the morning after, and a letter from Tressilian’s father asking what the school would want for a place.
Read next: Blessings and Curses, for the road that needs no school.
