the-magic-system/practice-and-institutio.title: Vows and Oaths
the-magic-system/practice-and-institutio.content:
How a soul binds its own odds, what the window shows, what lands when you break one, what your own denial does after that, and what you are risking when a court hands you the book

IT COUNTED.
Chalked on the river stair at Cask Row in Waxgate, on the last day of every February that has one, by persons unknown

Maud Ferrier kept a cooperage on Cask Row in Waxgate, and on the twenty-ninth of February in the year 684, the nameless day when the law sleeps, a Sable Lancer named Ser Aymer Roake rode her brother down in the street for a joke, knowing that no court in the Concord could hear of it. She went down to the river stair that night with nobody there, no priest and no friend, a cooper’s hammer in her right hand and her whole aura going up smoky red over the black water, and she bawled it at the far bank.
"Not One More Word Out of Me Till Aymer Roake is Down! And This Hand's the Price!"
Her throat shut like a bung going home. Her eyes went to the middle distance, and she read it there, where nobody else ever would:
[Vow: "Not one more word out of me till Aymer Roake is down."]
[Bargain: Ardency one step up · Voice gone until then]
[Breach: right hand dead, and the step with it]

Maud Mum, the river called her, and in eleven years she became one of the great sights of the Concord. She came up through the brackets from Stage V to Stage VII, an Expert the whole way, in a leather apron without a battle cry, a taunt or a single call of a technique, in a sport that runs on all three, and crowds came in their thousands to hear her not say anything. She married a chandler by nodding. She had a son, and taught him his letters on a slate. Every kept morning went into her Crystal like a hoop onto a cask, and she never bought a Draft in her life.
In the summer of 695 she got Roake in the ring at the Sealhall bone arena, with forty thousand people on their feet. He had a Stage on her, and she walked him down it with the hammer, one rib at a time, until he was on one knee with his mouth full of blood and she had the swing already coming. His second knew the terms, because by then everyone did. A rail gave way in the third tier, as it had been paid to, and a boy of nine came off it above the stone.
"TAM!"
It landed at once, before the boy did. The red went out of her like a blown lamp, her right hand opened by itself, and the arm hung off her dead to the shoulder for the rest of her life. Roake got up. A pie seller caught the boy, and is still drinking on it. Maud Ferrier lost the bout, her jaw and nine teeth, and she would have told you, if you had asked her that night, that she would do it again.
The bill for that was fair and it was finished. The trouble came from the wording-men. Her husband’s advocate pointed out that a vow sworn on Munahi, on a day no instrument binds, had surely never been a vow at all, and the Waxgate assize, asked politely, agreed that it would not enforce one. Her window said otherwise, in plain words, every morning. She took the advocate’s side. For nine years she told every room in the Concord that it had not counted, that she had never meant it, that eleven years of her life had been a misunderstanding about a calendar, and that her brother had been a fool who rode too near the horses. Then the law her soul had been running since that night on the stair turned round on her. She had held her tongue for eleven years and now she could not hold it at all. She talked through meals and through her sleep, hoarse and then bleeding, for the last two years of her life, and she died in a room over the chandler’s in the winter of 706, in the middle of a sentence, explaining.
Every clause of the subject is in that story, and this page takes them in order.
At a Glance
What it is. A vow is small Fate: a person binding their own probability, spoken aloud, with a price on it. It is the shallow end of the Fate Path, and it is anyone’s to make, because every soul has the layer it is made on. Fate at large is a good deal more than this, and people fight and wage wars with it; a vow is the smallest thing done on that plane and the only easy one. An oath is the same small Fate attached to a promise before someone with the standing to hold you to it.
How it looks. A line on the window with the bargain and its terms, and a price that shows on the body at once.
What it costs. Whatever you said. Narrower terms and a heavier forfeit buy more.
How it is beaten. Learn the terms and arrange the morning on which keeping them costs more than the fighter can pay.
Example. Hob Garrow, a Stage VI caravan guard on a pass road, swears aloud that he will not take a step back. His technique climbs to the top of its step on the Measurewrights’ scale, his stack line counts it toward the cap, and the raider across from him now knows exactly what to try.
What a Vow Is
A person says aloud what they will do or will not do, and what it costs them if they fail. Fate attaches. The Essence Core takes the restriction up as a standing law, and from then on the odds around that person lean, by a small and exact amount, toward its being kept. A vow is the only part of the Plane of Fate that needs no bloodline, no Stage and no permission. Real Fate Arts are rare and mostly run in the blood. Everybody has a mouth.
It is made on the Attraction Layer. That is the part of the Soul Crystal that holds a soul’s own share of fate, its bonds, oaths, claims and odds, and every soul has one whatever Path it walks, the unwoken included. A hitter who swears is working the same plane as a nun who swears, with less practice. The Fate Path is what you call it when a soul has learned to lean on that layer: there the binding bites harder and a kept vow pays more, and everybody else makes do with what a mouth and a price can buy. The Path goes far past promises, into the odds of a blow and the hour an army arrives, at a price no vow has ever charged, and The Three Paths has that side of it.
It needs no witness. The stair at Cask Row was empty. The Continuum (the whole lawful order of reality) is the audience, and it does not need to be told twice. A witness is for the person who wants to be held to it, or wants the crowd to know, and the priest Sigrun Ox-Hand swore in front of at Cullen Fair was there to make it a better show.
It must be spoken. A thing resolved in the privacy of your heart is an intention, and intentions have never moved anything on a window. The words go out and the line arrives.
It is anyone’s. The unwoken make them too, and a baker who swears on her mother’s grave never to serve stale bread gets a line on her little sheet and a small and real lean in the way her mornings go. Most of what any of them buy is measured in luck and loaves. A practitioner’s buys more, because a practitioner has more for the odds to act on.
The bargain. The law is the old one, and it is short: the narrower the condition and the heavier the forfeit, the greater the return. “Against those who deserve it” buys nothing. “Only against the Sable Lancers, and if I break it this hand is gone” is a vow.





















What you stakeWhat it buysA condition, sworn aloudUp to the top of the working’s step on the scaleA great vow, staking life, a limb or Crystal massOne full stepYour secret: the working’s true mechanism, stated aloud in the target’s hearing before you use itEvery advantage of surprise goes, and the output rises to match. It is the one sound reason for a villain’s monologue
Each vow counts on the stack. Vows are self-boosts, so every one counts against the cap of two steps on the hidden scale, read from the sustainable figure on the card. See Stacking and Spending. They do one thing nothing else in a fighter’s own hands does: a vow, or a breakthrough, is the only way across a gap of two Stages, and it still shows in the room first.
A kept vow pays twice. Tempering Coherence is the match between a person’s stated law and how they live, and it is the Crystal’s honest scale at every Threshold. A vow kept buys that with conduct and not with money, so it is the cheapest advancement in the world, priced in the rest of your life. It clusters where Drafts do not reach: soldiers, hedge-workers, the orders and the poor. It is also the most reliable way ever found to grow a Fate Path, since Hyeon Do-sun sitting at the fourth gate at Kell Harbor was a vow being kept, daily, for seven years, in front of a Crystal that was counting.
Enough of them is a Path. The Crystal goes by what a life has been spent on, and it does not ask what you thought you were doing. A hitter with three great vows and twenty years on them may read as having Walked the Fate Path on an honest assay, three parts in ten of her practice gone down that road, and she gets the force bonus and the rough seat that go with two roads, having never once intended either. Plenty of old soldiers discover this at a Threshold.
The filing clerks keep two old drawers for all this, and both now sit under the one Form, Bind. A vow’s working is Votia, a working whose currency is a declared price, and the seal it sets on the soul is Claustra, the only seal whose anchor is the bearer’s own behavior. See Forms.
The Window
A vow shows its terms, in full, in your own tongue, because you wrote them.
[Vow: "This hand stays down until he is dead."]
[Bargain: Ardency one step up · Left hand dead until then]
[Breach: lands at once]

That is the difference between a vow and a blessing, and it is the whole of the difference in what the wording-men charge. A blessing’s line was written by somebody else and may lie. A vow’s line is the one honest contract you will ever sign, and if it turns out badly, the author is available for comment. It stays until it is kept:
[Vow: kept. Bargain ended.]

The Breach and the Break
The old books run these together, and a good many people have died of the confusion.
A breach lands at once, by its own terms. It takes no witness, no court, no enemy and no ill will. The moment the terms are broken the forfeit arrives, in the same beat, and the bargain ends with it. The window reports it after the blow:
[Vow: broken]
[Right hand: dead. Will not answer.]
[Ardency: down a step]

Being forced does not help, and neither does a good reason. Maud Ferrier shouted for a falling child and it took the arm all the same. A breach is a debt paid. A great many people have paid one, lived on for decades with a dead hand, and owed the universe nothing more.
A Shear Break comes after, and only from denial. The Core has been running a law, and the law was built out of something true. A Shear Break is what happens when the bearer repeatedly denies the truth behind it: says it did not count, says it was never meant, lives as though the thing the vow was made from had never been so. The Trait grown out of that truth collapses, inverts or turns on the person carrying it. See The Trait System. It is the commonest death for someone who has changed their mind about who they are and not told their soul.
So the orders do not treat a lapsed vow as a disciplinary matter, or not at first. They put the person in a quiet room with somebody who knew them before, get them to say out loud that they broke it and why, and only then ask who is to be punished. It is regarded as an emergency, and the good infirmarians will leave a supper to go and do it.
What a vow can stand. The Resilience Sub-Stat called Oath measures how well an active vow or contract holds against someone trying to sever, invert or weaponize it. Almost nobody places points there before the first time it happens.
Oaths and the Book
An oath is a vow with an audience that can bill you. A proper court, a sect, a crown or a hold makes you swear before it, and two things then bind you: the law, which has its own penalties, and small Fate, which attaches to the words whether or not anyone is watching. A soul that swears falsely under a proper oath pays on its own window.
Fate can be set on an oath by someone who knows how. A Fate Path master can attach terms to one so that it holds with nobody present to enforce it, and the old Moto and Kharven bindings that made a clan’s word structural were works of that kind, some of them lost. Most oaths are plainer. A Marrowkin Cask-Oath runs “while the brew lives”, sung over the barrel, and a Marrowkin who cannot say that word over a thing has not promised it. A Kharven swears by the hand that cut it, a moment before something gets thrown.
The sworn sheet
Nobody can see your window, so hiring takes proof and a court takes your word, on oath. A proper court makes you swear to what your sheet shows. If you lie, the cost lands where only you can read it:
[Oath: "Level 140, as my sheet shows." Sworn false.]
[Terms: every chance goes against you until it is unsaid.]

Only an assay can check what you said, and it reads numbers and says nothing of your intentions. So the lawyers eat well.

The wording governs. As my sheet shows and as I am are different oaths, and half the advocates on Wording Row have a favorite.
A lying line protects you. A person who swears honestly to a blessing that lies, or to a window a mind-worker has tampered with, has told the truth as far as they knew it. The current reading at Waxgate is that you are bound to your own understanding of the words, which is why a wording-man will tell you never to read your line too closely before a hearing.
Unsaying it works. The terms run until the lie is taken back, in front of the same bench. This is rare, and the fines are heavy, and there are people who have paid them with tears of relief.

The Paper, the Book and the Word
Three things get called a promise, and they fail differently.





























Who holds youBreaking itOn the nameless dayAn instrument (a contract, a charter, a bond, a seal)The lawFines, forfeits, the bailiff, and a judgmentVoid. The chancery has no date-form for it, and this has been tested twiceAn oath before a court or a houseThe law and small FateBothNo court will hear it. Fate was not asked to take the day offA vowNobody but the soulLands at once, by its own termsHolds
Munahi is the day the law sleeps and Fate does not. On February 29, every fourth year, no instrument binds, no debt falls due, and nobody can be summoned or sealed. See The Sky, the Hour and the Year. Every quarter has its customs for that day and few of them are pious. A vow spoken on it holds exactly as it would on any other morning, and each leap year some young fool stands up in a tavern, swears something ruinous on the grounds that it does not count, and reads his window.
How It Is Beaten
Every vow can be answered, and the price of knowing one is usually a round of drinks.

Learn the terms. Fighters bluff about their vows and lie about them. A vow that is a matter of public record is a loaded weapon pointed at its owner.
Make them choose. Maneuvering a sworn fighter into breaking their own word is legal everywhere, universally despised, and has ended more careers than any duel. Ser Aymer Roake died rich, and nobody ever ate with him again.
Fight what it left out. A vow binds exactly what it says. No step back says nothing about the step sideways, or the step you were knocked.
Wait. Some vows have a clock, a sunset, a season, and the price arrives when it runs.
Press the denial. If a fighter has broken one and will not say so, you need not lay a hand on them. Mention it, in company, every chance you get. It is the cruelest thing on this page.

Famous Vows
Told in taverns, and told wrong. I have checked what can be checked.
The Ox at Cullen Fair. Sigrun Ox-Hand swore she would not set the ox down till the sun went behind the church, having looked at the sun first. It took four minutes and nearly killed her, and the priest has told it at every wedding since. See Stacking and Spending.
The Fourth Gate. Hyeon Do-sun swore at nineteen that he would walk through Kell Harbor’s gate on the day his brother’s ship came home. He let his mother die to keep it, One-Ear Pask refused to pay on it, and the Crystal entered it as Fate. See The Three Paths.
Old Gammer Pell. At the sack of Ostley a very small woman told a Free Company captain she would not die in that house. He set fire to it, with some ceremony. She was found the next morning in the road outside, burned to the waist, having crawled two hundred yards to be right, and she lived another eleven days to enjoy it.
What They Call It













































WhoThe wordThe argumentA Guild roll, a MeasurewrightA vow, a binding, VotiaIt is a price stated in advance, and the books can carry itNorthern commons, crewsSwearing it, being swornDid he say it out loud? Then he meant it. Stay out of his wayMotoSeiyaku (誓約), the sworn pledgeSworn onto the ground, and the ground takes it. A person’s word is entered, and the register has no eraserMarrowkinKurme, the swearing itselfThere is no lighter word. A Marrowkin who says it has already done the thing, in the only grammar that countsKharvenGiving your word before witnessesA word is the one thing a poor man can hold against a rich one, and everybody knows what it is worth by the winterThe lineage hallsShìyuē (誓約), the oath-bondIt binds the line as well as the mouth, and your grandchildren can be suedThe faithsA vow, a sacrament, a penanceEach has its own answer to who was listening. Sancta Lux claims jurisdiction over every oath sworn inside its reach, and it keeps very good files
Read next: Blessings and Curses, for the line somebody else wrote, and Who Pays for the Lamp, for what the rest of the world does all day.

the-magic-system/practice-and-institutio.title: Who Pays for the Lamp: The Living Crafts
the-magic-system/practice-and-institutio.content:
A working is a thing a person does, and a person wants paying, and may on any given morning decline. Everything else in this chapter is detail.
Note on the flyleaf of the Southbank rolls, in an archivist’s hand

On the eve of the Midsummer Fair the lamp-wardens of Southbank walked off their rounds over a single copper. The company had taken one more copper in the silver out of the round-fee, and Nan Tallowgate, who had kept Kettle Bridge alight for twenty-six years and whose aura had settled to the deep yellow of a good egg yolk, climbed onto the bridge rail at dusk with three hundred wardens behind her in their soot-blue hoods, sang the first line of the Wardens’ Round very badly, and closed her fist. The lamp over her head went out. Then the next one did, and the next, down both banks of the river, the amber and rose and kingfisher green of eleven hundred lamps folding back into the hands that kept them, street after street, a darkness running away from the bridge faster than a horse, and the whole fairground, mouths full, cheered it as though it had been laid on for them.
The Provost had an answer ready, and his answer was Magister Lucan Hale, a man of Master standing whose coat you could read a letter by at forty paces. Hale walked out onto Kettle Bridge in violet silk, raised both arms, and lit all eleven hundred at a stroke.
Southbank went the color of a cathedral window. Nan Tallowgate sat down on the rail, took out a heel of bread and an onion, and waited, because she knew what he had never had to learn. Lighting a lamp is nothing. Keeping one till dawn is the trade. A warden feeds each flame a filament no thicker than a hair, out of ground she has walked since she was twelve, and she knows which lamps on Cooper’s Row burn greedy in the wet. Hale was holding eleven hundred filaments out of a single reserve, on thin river ground that could not fill him as fast as he spent. By the second bell of the night his hands shook and the violet had paled to lilac. By the third there was blood down the silk. A little after midnight he went over on his face on Kettle Bridge, and every lamp in the quarter went out together, and in that dark a cart went off Tanner’s Stair into the river and a dropped tallow dip took the ropewalk. Nine people were dead by morning, and both sides have been blaming the other for them ever since. The company gave back the copper and added another. The minstrels put the wardens at three thousand and give Nan Tallowgate a sword. Hale’s heirs still pay double on that side of the river, and they have stopped asking why.
Hold on to that night, because the whole of this chapter is in it. Magic in a city or a village is done by living hands. Every lamp, every ward and every warm stone has a price, a keeper, an argument, and a person you can hate, and any one of those people may refuse you.
I. The Trades
Aether was always in the ground and the air, thick in some places and thin in others. The Long Reckoning discovered nothing here and priced everything. The cities were worked first and most thoroughly, and their lights, their heat, their clean water and their warded doors are kept by hired people on regular rounds; past the last warden’s round the trades thin out, the towns and the wilds still burn oil, and when something goes wrong somebody sends a boy for the hedge-worker.
Ground is graded by the density it carries (Aetheric Density, in the scholar’s term), because a warden on rich ground fills fast and works cheap while a warden on thin ground starves and charges for it. The grade is stamped at intervals on the corner-stones in Accord Chancery Hand, so that any searcher in any kingdom reads the same mark, and a map of a city’s rents is very nearly a map of its ground.



























































TradeWhat they doHow they are paidHow they refuseLamp-wardensKeep street and door lamps, by the round, dusk to dawnRound-fee from a company or parish; a household by the monthWalk off the round, or simply pass your doorWard-cuttersCut and re-cut wards into lintels, thresholds and strongroomsBy the job, and by the glyphLeave the last stroke uncut until the balance is settledHedge-workersEverything in the country: frost off the orchard, a charm on the well, a fever talked downIn kind, usuallyIt is a long walk to the next oneCore keepersHold a worked Core, which is a dungeon somebody cleared, and sell hours at itBy the hour, the season, or an old obligationClose it, or stop bleeding the poolGuild craftsmenSmiths, dyers, renderers and engineers of contraptions, under guild mark, up to what their title lets them makeBy the pieceDecline the commission, loudly, in front of your rivalsPetty folk artsOne small power and one small livingA copper here and thereShut the stallSoul-mendersClose what a Spirit strike or a haunted place leaves in a soul: read it, set it true, hold it while it knitsBy the sitting, quoted before the first and paid before the second; a house by retainerSend you home at the reading, or will not sit a patient who is still fightingCordwrightsMake knot-cutters, the worn pieces that take one knot’s debt off a Fate fighter and break doing itBy private treaty, by the pieceAre in bed for weeks after the last one, and say so
Lamp-wardens. A street lamp is a glass and a glyph-cut stem, and without a warden it is an ornament. An Essence lantern costs three to eight silver, and the inscription fee on top is the expensive part. Wardens walk at dusk with a boy and a pole, and each lamp burns the color of whoever keeps it, because what it burns is a hair’s worth of that person’s own Essence, so that an old resident can tell you whose round she is on with her eyes half shut.
Ward-cutters. Chisel, chalk and a good eye. A ward is a working inscribed in material, it wears like any other cut, and the tap of a cutter’s chisel on a lintel is the most reassuring sound in a poor street and the most alarming one in a rich street, where it means somebody has been robbed. The cutter’s mark goes under the ward, and every trace examiner can read it.
Hedge-workers. They work by voice and hand in the country beyond any company’s bounds, one for every few villages, and most of them have never seen a primer. The schedules forbid taking pay for a working without a license. They have never defined an egg.
Core keepers. A Wellspring is a governing idea, an alchemical and spiritual transformation that changes how a soul uses Aether, and in the scholars’ account it is one of sixty types of Aether that affect the Soul Crystal differently. A place where one of them pools is a Core in common speech, and left to itself it does not stay a place. Most Cores lie in dungeons, which grow down in floors around the Core with something guarding the heart, and the rest are said to lie out in vast territories nobody has finished walking. A worked Core is a dungeon somebody cleared and now holds. Under every respectable pool in the city is a stair, a seat of old stone, and somebody’s great-grandmother’s account of what it cost. A worked Core recharges by the season if it is not bled, and it has keepers, who may be an order, a sect, a temple or one stubborn family, and they sell hours at the pool, to anyone who can pay to pull there or to take a Wellspring from it. Half the wardens in a city top up at a Core they do not own. The keeper can close it, and when one does, every working in the district that depends on those hours goes thin within the week. A keeper can also simply stop bleeding it, and the place remembers what it was, as the Ferrants of Hollowhay learned at a wedding. The old soldier’s version of the same thought: to beat a Core-fed enemy, take the fight off rich ground and onto salted, bled or thin ground, and let him find out what he had been standing on.
Parish stones rise at street level: iron-bound, waist-high, warm, and unlovely. A cutter sets one and a warden keeps it charged, and it is the public working point of the street, where you bring a pot to boil and a child to thaw. In a good district it stands in a railed enclosure and is opened by a company man. In a bad one it stands in the road and has been opened by everybody.
Assay posts stand wherever one fee-band meets another, each holding a brass fork in a glass case, the fork ringing truer as the ground thickens and the reading going down in a book. A post is brass, slate-backed, locked, and searched quarterly, because a street’s fee hangs on its grade. The lock is the point. The fork is honest, and the case is where the argument about what it said takes place.
Guild craftsmen shout the names of their works and brag about their marks in the street, and their contraptions misfire in funny and terrible ways. Master Hobb’s Self-Turning Spit, Perpetual In All Weathers, has twice roasted a cat and once a bailiff, and there is a waiting list.
Petty folk arts are everywhere, because about one person in ten wakes a Crystal and very few of those ever climb far. The noodle seller’s knife that has never dulled, the laundress who dries a sheet between her palms, the rat-charmer of Pudding Lane who is at war with the rat-charmer of Pudding Lane’s other end. Each one costs money, each one has a bad day, and each one can tell you to come back tomorrow.
Soul-menders. A lamp over a door, usually near the physician’s and never on good terms with him. A mender is a Spirit Path practitioner who closes the wounds no surgeon can find: the soul knocked out of true, the dread that will not lift, the cut that took a color or a brother’s name. A reading is 1 to 2 silver and a shallow sitting 2 to 6, or a few copper and a prayer at a temple door; a course for a deep wound is 10 to 60 gold the season, which is a laborer’s year at the bottom. A deep wound left past a season sets for life, so most of what a village calls a changed man is a set wound nobody had the silver to read. Soul Wounds and the Menders has the bench’s whole price list.
Cordwrights. The rarest door on this page, and it has no sign. A Fate fighter who pulls a thread owes the world a knot afterward, and a cordwright makes the one thing that will carry such a debt: a knot-cutter, a ring of twisted iron or a cord with a lead seal, which takes one knot onto itself and breaks. Every cordwright reads at least Fate IV, the rung the folk call Knotwright, which nobody reaches without a grip, a bloodline’s Work or a blessing, and the trade took another name on purpose, after a century of clients who thought the rung and the craft were the same purchase. The price is a good warhorse for a small one and a small estate for a large, by private treaty, and the maker is in bed for weeks after. Half the cutters on any market are fakes. The Tell and the Knot has the law of it.
Pourers and chanters, for the record, belong on the ordinary side of this page. A Drafter is a guild craftsman paid by the bottle and a chanter is paid by the hour sung, and neither is doing anything stranger than the warden on his round.
II. The Hum
A kept street is audible. The sound is faint and hardly sound at all, but every ward and lamp carries the note of its own Wellspring, and a district thick with them has a floor under it that everybody in it stops hearing by the second week and hears immediately when it stops.
The hum is the single most reliable orientation instrument a city person has. They navigate by it without knowing. They sleep in it. Children raised on a kept street find quiet countryside physically difficult and are widely reported to be poor sleepers away from home, which the companies cite as evidence of nothing and the physicians cite as evidence of something.

When the wardens walk, the silence arrives before the dark does. People come to doorways. The companies have known for eighty years that a stoppage produces crowds within four minutes and schedule their own repairs accordingly, which is to say between three and five in the morning. The wardens have known it for eighty years too, and they walk at dusk.

III. The Fee and the Seal
Every lawful working for hire carries a seal, and the seal is the whole of the trade in one object.
It is a lump of stamped lead on the lamp stem or a mark pressed into the lintel’s wax. It says who did the work, what was paid and until when, and it is the property of the company rather than of the householder. Breaking a seal is a specific offense with its own fine, prosecuted more reliably than assault, because the seal is the instrument by which the company exists.
Grades of work:

Sealed household. Heat, light, warded doorframes, a working stove. Paid by the month, capped, cheap, and adulterated in the sense that the work delivered is below what the fee implies and everyone knows it. Three to five silver a month for one room; eight to twelve for a clerk’s house with every doorframe done. It is the largest line in a poor household after rent, and it comes due whether the family has coin that month or not.
Trade work. Stronger, dearer, and searched twice a year: two to five gold a month. Any workshop that cuts, pours or renders hires this.
Bonded work. Uncapped, individually warranted, and issued against a name. Practitioners of standing, Accord premises, and three of the great houses. A bonded contract is a legal fact about a person before it is a service.
Unsealed. Illegal, universal, and effected with a stolen glyph and a nerve. The companies call it foreign work. Everyone else calls it a botch.


A botch stands well clear of Mechanica (forbidden working that takes power without lawful consent). What it robs is a lawful company of its fee, which makes it a magistrate’s business. The distinction matters enormously in law and not at all to the man freezing in the room upstairs.

IV. The Companies
The Accord, a coalition of guilds across many nations, runs none of this directly. The trades are run by chartered companies, one to a trade in each city or quarter, signed on with the Accord for shared rank, enforceable contracts and passage, licensed under its seal, and owned by whoever bought the charter.
They are monopolies. They set fees, they hold the Core rights, they employ the searchers, and they answer to a licensing body that depends on their fees. The Accord regulates the companies and is funded by them, and this has been raised in council eleven times.
The searcher is the characteristic figure of the whole arrangement: a man with a seal press, an assay fork, a book, and the authority to strike a household from the round, on ten to eighteen gold a month and the gifts nobody records. He is seldom much of a practitioner. He is frequently not liked. He is the only representative of the entire magical apparatus to whom most people will ever have to answer.
V. Who Can Refuse
Everything on this page is done by hands, so all of it can stop, and everybody in a city lives with that fact the way a sailor lives with weather.
The stoppage. Illegal under most charters and common under all of them. Wardens walk a street at a time or a quarter at a time, ward-cutters down chisels with half a gate cut, and a keeper’s whole family sits on the steps of the pool eating lunch. Bills go up on doors overnight, hand-copied in bad letters, and criers sell the news of it by the corner. Bookies take odds on how long the company lasts.
The passed door. Quieter and meaner. A warden who has been cheated, insulted or merely bored by a house walks past it, and no law requires otherwise until the searcher has been fetched, and the searcher drinks with the wardens. A street can go a year with one dark door and everybody on it knowing why.
The overcharge. In a hard winter a warm stone costs what its keeper says it costs. Ask anyone who has paid it.
The fee strike. The refusal runs the other way as well. A whole street stops paying, the company sends the snuffers, and the street stands in the road with its sleeves rolled. The great fee strikes have been won by the street exactly as often as the company has been willing to lose its snuffers.
The answer. A company on the wrong end of a stoppage has three replies: bring in strangers from another town, who do not know the lamps; pay; or hire somebody grand. The Southbank rolls record what the third one costs, and yet some provost tries it every decade, because the grand somebody always swears he can hold it.
VI. Bad Work
Work delivered below the fee is the ordinary condition of poor districts, and it has consequences that are physiological rather than merely commercial.
Residue accumulates where the work is cheap and the ground is thin. Every working leaves Aetheric Residue (the trace left in a place by what was done there), and residue thins on a schedule set by local density, so thin ground clears slowest of all. A crowded quarter relit every night by the cheapest hands available, at poor yield (η, the share of an expenditure that arrives as effect) and with the lost share going off hot into the walls, never finishes clearing one night’s leavings before the next night’s arrive. Residue is a persistent alteration to the field of the place it sits in. The affected streets read wrong on any instrument and read wrong to the people living in them, who describe it as a heaviness and are told it is damp.
Over a generation it goes like this. For ten years, nothing anyone would swear to. Then an apprentice’s ward cut over an old ward cut over an older one starts failing in two years instead of ten, so it is cut again, cheaper, on top. The lamps on the stair burn a shade off their keeper’s color. Milk turns early, dogs will not settle, and the street’s old people start saying the street has gone heavy. Thirty years on the grandchildren are waking at the wrong ages or not at all, one family on one staircase has something strange it passes down, and rent has fallen far enough that only the poorest come, who can only afford the cheapest work.
The documented effects are unspectacular and cumulative: poor sleep, low-grade Gnosis (perception) noise in anyone sensitive, Crystal awakening (the soul itself opening) at abnormal ages in children, and a Trait (a standing law carried in the soul) incidence in long-settled families that the companies have never commissioned a study of. The Physicians’ College has requested one four times.

The Southbank finding, and what happened to it. A company surveyor established in a single quarter that residue concentration tracked tenement density and inversely tracked fee band, and submitted it.
The report was accepted, the surveyor was promoted, and the recommendation was referred to a committee that has met twice. Nobody suppressed the finding. It is available. It has simply never been the business of anybody with the authority to act on it.

Two Measurewrights of my acquaintance dispute whether the heaviness comes from the residue at all or from a lifetime of being told it is damp. They have been disputing it for nineteen years, in the same tavern, on a thin-ground street, and neither sleeps well.
VII. Bolt and Proof
The crossbow is ordinary and old, and it is the reason nobody sensible has ever stopped wearing armor.
A bolt is cheap. A working is not. A bolt costs three coppers at the fletcher’s and a practitioner’s expenditure is pulled against a reserve that took years to build, so the economics of an engagement between the two never favored the practitioner and still do not. Every missile carries a threat Grade fixed by its kind, from the sling stone and the hunting arrow through the war-bow shaft and the crossbow bolt to the ballista bolt, a worked one taking its maker’s Grade, and a dodge or a catch is the defender’s speed, read on the same scale though no person wears the letter, against it. A fighter whose speed stands in the bolt’s own step “can read a crossbow bolt loosed across a room and slip it, if they see the loose”, and that last clause has buried more proud people than any Domain.
Proofed harness is armor tested by loosing at it and marked with the result. The proof-mark is the whole trade: a stamp naming the house, the bow tested, and the range. Harness proofed against a hand-spanned bow at twenty paces carries a different mark from harness proofed against a windlass arbalest at fifty, and the marks are forged constantly.

A proof-mark is a promise about a specific bow at a specific range, made by a workshop that may no longer exist, on a piece of steel that has since been repaired twice. Every soldier who has bought his own harness knows this and buys anyway, because the alternative is buying nothing.

VIII. Road, Beacon and the Rest
The kept road is a street that does not stop. Ward-cutters do its bridges, road-wardens its waystones, and a waystation’s stones are cut in tuned pairs: the warden fills one in the station, and its twin under a carrier’s cart-bed takes the heat across a hand’s breadth of air by Transference (a Wellspring of Fate, the living exchange, whose law binds two tuned things so that what one holds the other can use, with nothing carried between them) and burns nothing. The road is the reason the companies matter beyond their own walls: every town it reaches is a town on somebody’s fee, and a company with a road through its country negotiates with every waystation on it.
The beacon line. Hilltop fire-towers in sight of one another, lit by wardens in shuttered colors, Judicium’s arc-blue against Pyreveil’s ember-orange, and read by clerks whose Crystals have never woken. The beacon line is the first apparatus in the world’s history that lets an ordinary person send something faster than a horse, and its cultural effect substantially exceeds its technical one. It is a Guild line at a Guild price, a silver for twenty words with the addresses counted, carrying information as a licensed commodity, and the Accord guards it in the tone of an institution that knows exactly what it would lose. Everybody else has relay riders, ships, heralds, minstrels who get the details wrong, and hand-copied bills posted on doors.
Workshops run on trade work, raise no chimney, and employ a great many people who have never woken to operate processes that are magic from end to end. A dye works uses Ignivale at workshop scale by having thirty men each perform one licensed step badly.
IX. The People Who Tend It
Core-tenders work the lip of a site, in pairs, with an assay fork and a lamp, clearing and bleeding the pool, in what used to be a dungeon and would like to be one again. The work is wet, cramped, and pays badly, and the residue exposure is continuous and undocumented. The ones who live longest learn to mention to someone when a gallery they know has moved.
Seal-clerks press and record. Fee-walkers walk. Snuffers attend when a household stops paying, strip its lamps and scratch through its wards, and are the most despised trade in any city and the best paid of the four.

None of these people are screened. Core-tenders spend careers at the edge of a worked pool, at densities that would be recorded as an Active Concentration (a density that alters bodies over time) if a surveyor found the same reading in open country, and no baseline is taken because no baseline exists for the unawakened.
The trade knows what it does to a man over twenty years. It has a word for the late stage, the word is in no company document, and a physician who has never worked a pool will diagnose it as something else with perfect confidence.

Read next: On Walking Into the Current, for what the same current does to someone with no warden’s fee to protect them.

the-magic-system/reference-and-craft/for.title: Forms
the-magic-system/reference-and-craft/for.content:
Big Maud Skerritt sold herring on the Skerry quay, and she threw them, flat and hard, at sixty paces, at customers who were slow with the coin. A herring from Maud would crack a tankard in a man’s hand and leave a silver bruise that smelled for a week. When a Guild assessor came to ask which hall’s token she carried, she knocked his hat into the harbor, and the Accord convened a public hearing to establish what, in law, she was doing. Eight Measurewrights (the Guild’s sworn measurers) sat on it. The bookies of Skerry opened the book before the benches were full: Vectra at two to one, Arts at three, Manifestus at twelve for the romantics, and forty to one on Mechanica, the forbidden one, which the fish-merchants’ guild was paying somebody to argue for. Four days, three fistfights among the bench, one Measurewright in tears, and a demonstration that took the presiding examiner’s coif off on the fifth herring.
They entered her under Arts, with a dissent. Vectra’s backers rioted in a small way. Maud paid forty silver in fees, in herring, and raised her prices.
I have told that story to every apprentice I have ever had, because a table of this kind looks like a law of nature and it was written by people like those eight. The register they were fighting over had twenty-six headings. The trade has since folded them into the twelve below, and under these Maud is a Strike, with a dissent for Shape, and the bookies would still open. Most of what the old headings said was sound, so it has been kept here under the Form it belongs to, and the old names go on being used wherever they earn their keep. All of it has been fought over by someone with money riding on the answer.
Forms sort workings, the things a person does with power. They do not sort people or their trades. A chant, a rune, a tag and a Draft are all done by whoever has leveled the skill, under whatever guild will have them.
The Five Lines
Every art answers five questions, and nothing else classifies it.



































LineThe questionWhere it is writtenPathWhich layer of the Crystal does it lean on? One [[The Magic System/The Soul and the Climb/The Three Paths Routing, Recognition and the GatePath]], or a named pair. This picks the [[The Magic System/The Soul and the Climb/Classes and the Three LaddersLensWhich [[The Magic System/The Foundations/The Sixty Wellsprings/The Sixty WellspringsWellspring]] (the governing idea it runs on), and of what kindFormWhat are the hands doing? One of the twelve belowThe artGatesWhich Sub-Stats and Stages does it need open?The artSourceHow did this person come by it: Lived, Taught, Inherited, Bought or Blessed?The person’s card, since the same art can be all five in one family
Three of them, laid side by side:

































ArtPathLensFormGatesRusashinBodyCoagulatio (Wild)ShapeGnosis Analysis past 100A cut ward on a doorSpiritFixatio (Medium)WriteA woken Crystal, and real harmonization with what is cutA Work of Hataraki taking holdFateNone needed, since a grip does not depend on a lensPullThe Work’s own grip, and Dominion Fate against the target’s Persistence and Continuity
The Twelve



















































































FormHomeWhat the hands doThe clerks’ old wordsStrikeBodyPut power into a blow, a block or a body in motionArts, CorporisShapeBodyTell matter, force or heat what to do, by hand or at reachKinesia, VectraReadSpiritFind out what is there, what it was and where it leansManteia, Mnemata, Auguria, AethericaWriteSpiritSet a sentence of law into something that outlasts the sayingGlyphica, ScriptiaRiteSpiritDo it slowly and in order, with others and with an offeringRitus, Turgia, TransitusMakeSpiritBuild a thing that acts apart from the makerAnimatria, Crystalia, the Spirit ForgeSingSpirit and FateCarry it in tone, from one soul across to anotherHarmonia, Synergia, ConcordiaBrewBody and SpiritStabilize a working into a substanceDrafts, Alchemia, ConjunctionCallFateAsk something that already exists to comeVocatiaBindFateHold a thing against its own nature, or hold yourselfClaustra, VotiaClaimFateSay that this ground, or this absence, is yoursDomain Weaving, SilentiaPullFateTake hold of a thread and move what a result depends onThe Fate Arts
A home is a qualifier and never a lock. It works the way a Wellspring’s kind does. Any Path can take up any Form, and each will do it in its own layer’s terms: a Body cutter’s ward stops the bottle, a Spirit cutter’s is taken for a wall, and a Fate cutter’s sets a term on her own share of the odds. A Form is cheapest at home. Away from home the work is clumsier and dearer than it looks in the manual: yield (η, the share of the spend that arrives, as a distillation has its yield) falls, and the lost share is paid in the worker’s own coin, heat for a Body hand, hollowing for a Spirit one, a heavier knot for a Fate one. The rung it reads is still whichever one the art’s Path line picked. The same fighter routinely has two techniques under two Forms, and a bookie will quote you both.
Each Form below keeps what the old register knew about it.
Strike
Structured, discipline-based styles blending movement, form, and the flow of power: controlled Flux (the flow of what a soul holds through the body, which is the Charge, raw Aether packed in the Shell, for a Body fighter, and Essence for anyone else), martial shaping, embodied Aether expression. Strike is often a practitioner’s first structured magic regardless of eventual Path, since the truth held in the Essence Core (the Crystal’s inner layer) and the expression of the Aether Shell (its outer layer, which turns power into force) already speak the same language here. A clerk who says Corporis means the case where the body is the conduit and cannot be separated from the technique.
You have seen it as: Resonant Forms · the Iron Bison · Nadi · a herring at sixty paces.
Shape
Direct control of a working in real time, the technique being the act. The old heading Vectra covered motion, direction, velocity and spatial gravitation, and it is still what trained mouths call anything that is fundamentally about where force goes. Shape climbs Body Mastery rung by rung: matter as an object, through contact, by recognition, by law, as a whole system. What it spends on the Body Path is raw Aether (mana), drawn in, packed in the Shell and driven out through it, and the lost share burns in the Shell’s furnace and comes off as heat.
A trade feeds the climb. On a material that a Body fighter’s trade skill knows at Journeyman or better, they work one rung up the Material Force: contact reaches recognition, and so on up. A smith reads steel deeper than she reads anything else, a mason stone, a butcher the joints of whatever is in front of him. The lift applies to that material and no other, and it never carries anyone past the Body Mastery ceiling of their Stage. Marta Kell, on the Skills page, is the case the examiners quote.
You have seen it as: Gravity Folding · Aetherstep · Spatial Collapse · the Material Force.
Read
Reading and sensing through a lens. Mnemata reads backward: memorycraft and echo work, dream records, ancestral fields, temporal imprints and historical echo-law, the practiced discipline behind Lattice Memory and Crystalline Memory, extended outward to other souls’ records. The Wellsprings of remembrance and depth (Anamnesis, Phreatis, Somnalis) are its most natural partners.
Auguria reads sideways, and it is the reading of outcome weight, causal load, and probability distribution: what is leaning, with what will happen left to happen. Mnemata reads backward into what a thing was; Auguria reads sideways into what a thing is being pulled toward. The answer must be received by a Core capable of holding it without resolving it into narrative, which is the failure mode: an Auguria reading that arrives already interpreted has been interpreted by the reader.
Auguria is the licit, open end of the Plane of Fate, because it only looks. Moving the weights it reads is a Pull, and it is another matter.
Aetherica is the old name for the measuring trade, the Measurewrights’ own: Flux, Aether Units, Yield (Efficiency in the older rolls), Density, Coherence. Its readings are often right about how much and never about why. A practitioner of it might never cast in their life, instead ensuring everyone else’s workings are measured against the same scale. It is also the shelf that keeps the window, the soul reporting its numbers to its owner, unseen by anyone else: the window gives its bearer numbers, ranks, percentages, bars and Level, Aetherica holds the EU, AU/s and yield behind them, and its scholars argue about who built the thing.
You have seen it as: Outcome Reading · Tide-Sense · the crow’s sight (Yukari) · water-scrying practices with no register entry · Dreamfolding · Echo Archives · Solution.
Write
Glyphica is the Parun-based language of law, the syntax by which the Continuum (the whole lawful order of reality) recognizes and authorizes transformation, explicit in sigils and scripts or implicit in internalized chains. It governs the Four Glyph Roles: Authorization, Boundary, Direction, Sealing. It is the Essence Core’s intention made legible. A practitioner with sloppy internalized chains still casts, and what comes out is slightly different from what was intended: a quiet, accumulating error.
Scriptia is the clerk’s word for cutting it into something. Every cut or prepared sentence files here. A rune goes on working in its material after the cutter has gone home, and a tag is prepared ahead, fueled per tag and fired only by a practitioner; both are skills anyone with a woken Crystal can level. The home is Spirit, and it is Fate only for writing on Fate itself, as a written blessing does. What a glyph is and what a fault in one does are on the Master Glyph Index.
You have seen it as: Wordform Chains · runes and cut wards · tags · Parunic Script Weaving · the Spirit Rune Arts.
Rite
Formal rituals built on Wellspring harmonics, Realm laws, and Parunic syntax. A typical sequence: Intention → Space → Circle → Offering → Invocation → Catalyst → Seal. Ritus anchors are temporary and ceremonial. A rite is performed, not built, and the Essence Core’s posture during the rite matters more than any glyph’s placement. It is also the ancestor of every field-capable discipline that later internalized what the circle used to externalize. Turgia is the clerk’s word for the kind that leaves a lasting change behind it.
Transitus is the old name for the crossing of a body, soul, or object between planes, and for the making and holding of the apertures through which crossing occurs. Shape moves a thing to somewhere else in the world. Transitus moves it out of the world it was in, across the Veil’s inner fold. A crossing requires three things at once and fails if any is missing: a body that survives arrival, a Core that stays coherent through the transition, and a claim on the far side that has agreed to receive it. Uninvited crossings resolve as the receiving plane sees fit.
You have seen it as: Rite of Hollow Union · Pale Root Binding · Choir of Severance · Transference Crossing · Gate-Work · Veil-Thinning.
Make
Animatria is the shaping and projection of consciousness into constructs, fields, or avatars. An Animatria construct is a small detached fragment of the caster’s Essence Core given temporary independent operation, closer to a deliberately-shaped Essence Shard than a Domain. This is why Animatria fails completely in Silence Realms (regions where no lawful working can be authorized): the construct’s continuity depends on a connection back to its source, which Harmonic Silence severs. The Spirit Forge does the same job in ore, bone or glyph-cut stone.
Crystalia is the engineering, forging, and refinement of Soul Crystals and related lattices, the practiced discipline behind the Crystalia Constraint: harmonization with three relevant Wellsprings, certified understanding of the subject’s Path and Wellsprings, sufficient Temperance to survive exposure to another soul’s Essence Core. Its object is the Core, and its method is physical: forging and tempering done with hands and instruments on a lattice that happens to also be a soul.
The discipline’s hard limit is that nucleation cannot be manufactured at the bench. A Crystalia practitioner can widen conductivity, repair a fracture, and prepare a lattice to receive a melt cleanly. With hands and instruments they cannot supply a seed, because a true seed is a law the subject survived into existence and no instrument makes one. Everything the trade sells past that point is a Draft under another name, a seed out of a bottle, and the Accord’s halls distinguish the two on paper and nowhere else.
A Master Work is the far end of Make: a piece that does what its Grade and material should not be able to, made once at the end of a lifetime, always Unique or Mythic, and named.
You have seen it as: Eidolon Crafting · Spiritchain · Fractal Alignment · Core Rebinding · Tempered Latticework.
Sing
Magic of tone, vibration, and resonance. Harmonia sits on two Paths because tone originates in the Essence Core, what the soul means, but only becomes Harmonia once it travels outward to affect other Crystals, by way of the Attraction Layer, what the soul reaches. Mismatched Resonant Tone produces Echo Fracture (the failure state of tone-work). A chant files here, or under Write when the sentence matters more than the note, and a chant stops when the speaker does.
Synergia is emergent resonance from multiple souls, Wellsprings, or Domains interacting, birthing shared Temperance fields and collective intent. A Synergia field is several Soul Crystals briefly sharing one Essence Core, Shell, and Layer, which is why souls harmonized to the water Wellsprings anchor these fields most easily.
Concordia is the apex: aligning multiple Aether bodies, Wellsprings, and Domains into a single coherent field, Synergia and Harmonia scaled up and made durable rather than momentary. It requires both homes: Spirit-side precision to align many Essence Cores without flattening any, and Fate-side reach to hold that alignment as a lasting Domain rather than a passing chord. A successful Concordia working is functionally a Major Shared Realm (a Domain that has outlived its founders and become a place)‘s founding moment, performed deliberately, and it is what people reach for to heal a damaged Wellspring vein or begin closing a Hollowing (a region’s slow loss of the capacity for lawful working).
You have seen it as: Veilsong · Lunar Chorus · Frequency Collapse · Affinity Fields · Severance Choirs · Guild Choirs · Concord Domains · Nexus Formation · the Harmonic Arts.
Brew
Alchemical procedures channeling a Wellspring’s process through Parun glyphs (signs in the root script of law). Drafts are formulaic: Aether + Essence + Vessel + Glyphica = Reaction. Though Drafts touch all three Soul Crystal layers, the decisive variable is how cleanly the Essence Core’s intention survives the journey into the crucible, and hands alone can pour one, so a Crystal that never woke can level the skill. Conjunction is the bench operation that weds prepared laws, Essences or Traits in a vessel, and it requires strict compatibility: opposed laws need mediation glyphs, and failing that the Rupture Event follows. A clerk’s Conjunctia means one practitioner’s working on two lenses at once, which needs no heading of its own.
Brew is also where the money lives. A Draft or a blessing can supply a Catalyst, the change a Crystal needs before it passes a Threshold, so Stages can simply be bought; the great houses hoard the top Drafts for that reason. A monster’s core renders into Essence Drafts used for tempering, with Creature-Sourced potency and the risk of Identity Contamination, and a Crystal cut from a dead practitioner makes the strongest Draft of all and the worst crime in every realm. A breakthrough Draft follows the Path of the soul it is brewed for: Salt-based for a Body-led soul, Core stock for a Spirit-led one, and for a Fate-led one the Layer reagent, the dearest of the three and the most criminal. A Fate Essence Draft made on that reagent is a Master Work, a piece no ordinary bench can make: extremely hard, and very coveted. There is no fight Draft for Fate at all, since a Fate fighter’s reserve is Essence and Core stock refills it.
You have seen it as: Coagulation · Distillation · Sublimation · monster-core tempering Drafts · Apotheosis Fusions · Absolution Weaves.
Call
Invocation by recognition and correspondence: Titans, Archons (the fourteen great powers that embody cosmic law), World Spirits, lesser entities, Realms. Vocatia never dominates. It negotiates shared resonance, the practice-form of Invocation and Consent. A Vocatia working addressed to an unwilling higher being is, at the level the Continuum reads intention, an attempted Usurpation, regardless of correct surface syntax. Successful Vocatia is always an act of the Current of Recognition, never Refusal. Nothing is pulled down, which is why it can be learned in a yard at all.
You have seen it as: Titan Echo · Archon Descent · Concord Summons · the Spirit Summoning Arts.
Bind
Claustra is the binding, sealing, and lawful imprisonment of a thing against its own nature: souls, entities, Wellspring processes, Phenomena mid-event, and other practitioners’ workings. Where Write supplies the Sealing role as one of four, Claustra is the discipline of making that role carry the whole weight of a working indefinitely. The seal’s syntax is Soul Plane precision while its duration is a Fate-side claim that must be renewed by something. A Claustra working that loses its anchor opens, all of it, at once. It is the home of the Vow Clause: a vow is a seal a practitioner sets on themselves, and it is the only Claustra working whose anchor is the bearer’s own continued behavior.
Votia is the old name for workings whose operative currency is a declared and irrevocable price: an offering made before the effect, a restriction accepted permanently, a thing given up so that a law will answer more readily than the practitioner’s Temperance should permit. What is being altered is the Essence Core’s posture rather than its output. A Votia working makes a practitioner stronger by making them narrower, and the Continuum answers narrowness with power.
The sacrifice arts are Votia at its far end, where the thing given up cannot be given twice: an eye, a hand, a year of life, a name. They stand outside the ordinary accounts the way a blessing does. A sacrifice opens what the practitioner’s gates have not opened, and what it lends is not counted on the cap of two steps over the sustainable figure, because the soul is not lifting itself: it has paid something else to do the lifting. That is the whole of the good news. It works once, for the one working it was offered for. The price is ruinous, taken from the body on the spot and written on the Ledger besides, where it goes on being collected after the wound has closed, and no hall I know of will teach one to a student it expects to see again.
The Vow Clause, stated mechanically. A vow declares a permanent restriction and the Core adopts it as a standing law. Tempering Coherence measures the alignment between a practitioner’s stated law and their lived behavior, and it is the structural prerequisite for Threshold eligibility. A vow kept is therefore a direct purchase of Coherence by conduct rather than by expenditure, which is why vows are common in every hall and camp, and commonest in the populations that cannot buy Drafts: soldiers, hedge-workers, the orders, the poor.

It is the cheapest advancement mechanism in the world and it is priced in the rest of your life.

A broken vow lands at once by its own terms, and repeated denial of the truth behind it makes a Shear Break. The Core has been running a law the bearer has now denied, and the law does not negotiate its own withdrawal. This is why the orders treat a lapsed vow as a medical emergency rather than a disciplinary one, and why the disciplinary response follows only if the practitioner survives.
A vow is small Fate, a person binding their own probability, and anyone can make one. It spends the soul’s own share and pulls nothing down, so a vow kept leaves no knot. Spoken, it shows in the bearer’s window with the bargain and its terms, and what it buys counts toward the two-step cap like any other boost of one’s own. See Vows and Oaths.
You have seen it as: Dragon Binding · Null-Anchors · The Veil’s standing closures · Oath-Seals · Gisei · Sacrament and Oblation · Disclosure practices.
Claim
Domain Weaving is the deliberate reshaping of local Continuum behavior so that a chosen law becomes easier to sustain within a defined space. The practitioner does not enforce the law directly; they alter what the region is willing to do cheaply. A Domain is a standing negotiation with the Plane of Fate rather than an application of force. It persists exactly as long as the Attraction Layer keeps recognizing the claim, which is why a Domain fails all at once rather than fraying. Every Domain is a claim by the Layer, on every Path, and it needs no Fate Mastery and pulls no thread. Anyone at Stage VIII can have one, held by a Second Release or, on Fate, by the One, their own concept made real, and money cannot buy it: a sect teaches it, or the fighter finds it. Concordia aligns many existing fields into one; Domain Weaving builds a single field from a single soul’s claim.
Silentia is the removal of magical possibility from a region, a body, or a working. Counterspelling and shielding are other trades. This is the deliberate production of an absence in which lawful transformation cannot be authorized at all. Mechanica removes recognition and substitutes extraction. Silentia removes recognition and substitutes nothing, which is why Silence Realms sever Animatria constructs from their source and why a soul held inside one reports the sensation as loneliness rather than weakness. It is the counterplay Form: every other entry here describes something being done, and Silentia describes the conditions under which none of them work.
You have seen it as: Aspect Sovereignty · Standing Claim · Law-Bias Fields · Harmonic Silence · Null Zones · Aether Suppression · the Hollow’s quieter effects · Talos.
Pull
A pull moves the weights Auguria reads, to work outside what reality already knows and to control the fate of a thing. At one end it is a Fate Path fighter’s single lean on the odds, rare, ruinous and often a failure. At the far end it is a Fate Art, and that is rare, mostly by bloodline and considered incredibly overpowered. A pull comes down from above through the Veil’s outer face, and it always reads Fate Mastery on top of whatever else is being paid. What it spends is Thread, which is never held: it is pulled for the one working and paid for out of the soul’s own share of fate, and every pull leaves a knot that the world collects later, sized to how far the pull stood from likely. It moves only what already has a way of happening. The Works of Hataraki are inherited grips on it, and a grip lifts Fate Mastery past the second rung, where every soul without one stops, and lowers the chance of failure, and never the price or the knot; the edit types of the Ketsumyōgan are others, and a personal grip can be won, once, though only a Work or a blessing lifts the rung.
You have seen it as: the rotten pile at Akagawa · Danshi’s cut · an involuntary Fate-pull that took somebody somewhere they did not ask to go.
Seam Arts

A ward is a wall, and a wall stands on one side of something. Ask the cutter which side, before you pay.
Proverb of the Ward-Cutters’ Company, Sallow Quay

Two of the twelve Forms have two homes. Brew sits on the Body and the Spirit, and Sing on the Spirit and Fate. For nearly everyone who practices them that is a filing matter: a Draft is poured at a bench, a chant is sung in a choir stall, and both are trades and skills that anyone may level, under whatever guild will have them. Nothing in this section is about those people.
A Seam Art is a combat art whose Form crosses two Paths and is worked where the planes themselves join. The Veil has two such places. Its inner fold runs between the Physical World and the Soul Plane, and a Brew worked there is one working that is matter and meaning together. Its outer face is where the lower realities meet Fate, and a Sing worked there carries a tone out of the Core and along the bonds a soul holds on its Layer. Where the fold and the face come together, the trade says seam, and the name has stuck to the arts.


























SeamFormPathsWhat the working isWhat it spendsThe inner foldBrewBody and SpiritA working stabilized into a substance in the middle of a fight, in a wound, a breath or the fighter’s own blood, so that it acts on the flesh and on the soul wearing it in the same strokeCharge through the Shell for the matter and Essence through the Core for the meaning, both at once, on a card that carries the splitThe outer faceSingSpirit and FateA tone carried from one soul across to others along what binds them: an oath, a debt, a love, a name held in commonEssence through the Core for the note, and the singer’s own share of fate for the carrying. Where the song pulls a thread it reads Fate Mastery on top and leaves a knot like any pull
Why they are feared. Every counter in the manuals stands on one plane. Plate, Durability and a Body ward stop what arrives as matter. A soul-ward stops what arrives as meaning. Soundness, a kept oath and reaching the puller answer Fate. A Seam Art arrives as two of these at once and belongs wholly to neither, so the defense that stops one half lets the other through, and a fighter who has only ever drilled against one road finds that the drill has nothing to say. A Measurewright asked to grade one will ask which road’s Mastery to read it on, and the honest answer is both, each half on its own.
Why they are rare. They are unstable, and the instability is in the seam and no fault of the practitioner. A working held across two planes has to stay true on both, and the Veil is thick in one street and thin in the next. On thick ground the halves come apart and the art does half its work at full price. On thin ground it does more than was asked. It demands two Paths walked in earnest, with all that costs in years, and its failures are its own: a Brew at the fold that curdles does so in the brewer’s body and Core together, and a Sing at the face that slips its key rings back along the singer’s own bonds first, since those are the nearest. Most who attempt one are dead or ruined before the art has a name, and the halls do not teach them. They are found, or inherited, or taken off the dead.
Two that are still spoken of. Neither has been assayed by anyone who came back to file the paper, so what follows is casework and report.
The Red Vintage. Odo Sacheverell kept a wine shop in Harrowmouth and killed eleven sworn duelists across nine years, every one of them better than he was on any measure the Accord keeps. He brewed in the wound. Each cut he made he fixed as a substance in the opponent’s own blood, a ferment that was part poison and part grief, so that the body sickened and the soul soured together, and a man warded against venom died of despair with his veins clean while a man warded in the soul died of the venom. The surgeons who opened his victims found the blood gone thick and dark as lees. He was taken in the end by a fishwife’s son with a boathook who gave him no time to cut, which is the counter the casebook recommends, and by then a third of his own blood had turned, by the examiners’ estimate, from the brews that had curdled in him over the years.
The Kin-Knell. A sung art out of the hill chantries, credited to a cantor the registers call only the Widower of Low Tessaly. He sang one sustained tone at one person, and it did nothing to them that anyone could see. It went out along what bound them. A captain’s sworn company dropped their shields forty paces behind him. A mother three valleys off sat down in her kitchen and did not get up that day. The Concord’s casework holds that the tone was an ordinary soul-strike, which a soul-ward on the target stops perfectly well, and that this is of no use at all, because the target was never where it landed. Its known answers are to have no bonds, which is the answer of a certain kind of villain, or to kill the singer in the first breath. The Widower’s own name is said to sit wrong in the mouths of those who knew him, and nobody now alive will say for certain what it was.
Villains favor these arts for the plain reason that they punish the prepared, and a hall that learns one is at large in its district generally posts the bounty before it posts the warning.
Mechanica, the Crime
Mechanica is no Form, because it is any of them done as theft. It covers forbidden constructs bypassing Soul Crystals, Wellsprings, or Glyphic Syntax. Mechanica coerces transformation without lawful Wellspring participation, consuming the resonance around it and damaging the Continuum. Every Form involves recognition: of Wellsprings, Domains, other souls. Mechanica is what remains when recognition is removed and replaced with extraction: Conjunction’s compatibility deleted, Glyphica’s authorization skipped, Drafts performed without consent. Statute XXVI, Mechanica Irreversibility, exists because this is the one practice that leaves scars the Continuum doesn’t forget. The long account is Mechanica: Extraction Without Recognition.
You have seen it as: Soul Splicing · Aether Inversion · Trait Collapse Engines, and a very great many bad nights in the cellars of very respectable houses.
What No Form Covers
Forms sort what somebody does. These are done by nobody in particular, or they are what the doing is done with.
Phenomena are large-scale anomalies where Aether law bends under overload: semi-autonomous, self-sustaining events marking major law stress, the Singularity of Statute XIV. Once triggered, Phenomena are no longer cast. They have outrun any Attraction Layer, which is why Counter-Phenomena are so dangerous: the trigger has an author, but the Phenomenon itself does not. Echo Collapse, Worldbirth, Aetherquake and Memory Storms are the ones that get into songs.
Manifestus is the old word for short-lived Wellspring emissions and flares triggered by high emotional density or sudden pressure, reflecting current Temperance and Essence posture. An involuntary Trait preview: Overtone Bloom given external form. The trigger is always a spike in the Core and the expression is a flare that briefly exists physically. Early-Temperance souls experience this far more, and it is what Trait Awakening looks like from outside. Maud’s backers at twelve to one were arguing she could not help it.
Traits are standing laws carried in the soul’s own material and expressed through the Crystal once there is a Crystal to express them: Primary, Secondary, Inherited, Passive and Compound Reflections.
Traits are not encoded by Temperance. Primary and Inherited Traits are woven into a soul’s original Essence, the rest are forged by what the soul lives through, they run in the unwoken whose Crystal will never open, and awakening arms what was already there rather than granting anything new. What Temperance does is the reverse of encoding. At a Threshold the Crystal melts, and Traits are the only structures that survive the heat, because a law the Continuum has accepted as reliable does not stop being reliable at temperature. The new lattice cools around them. This is why Traits govern advancement rather than merely decorating it.
A Trait is held in the Core, and its most legible expression is almost always physical, and the expression is literal rather than figurative. A Trait biases the Aether Shell’s conductivity permanently, and because the Shell is the Material-Plane layer the bias is laid down in tissue: mineral into bone, altered myelination, rebuilt vasculature, a resting core temperature off the population mean. A body is a Trait record and a corpse is a better one. So the Tempering that melts the Soul Crystal down and rebuilds each layer also leaves the body with its Traits written into it. A Trait can be leveled and refined like a skill. Its level rises with use, grows with overall Level and skill, and shows on its bearer’s sheet; the law itself stays the law it was.
The Wellsprings are the Lens line and nobody’s Form. The Sixty are the nouns; everything else is a way of using them as verbs. Temperance governs how much of each process a soul can bear, and a Wellspring defines what law and emotional grammar are available.
The Guild’s Naming Table
A clerk’s form has a box for this, and the clerk needs one word. The root is the Affinity (the face of a lens’s idea a person works: fire, not Pyreveil, gives Pyromancy its root). The suffix says what the worker is doing with it, and it places them before they have finished introducing themselves. Nothing here is a law of the world, and three separate halls have tried to make it one.

Nobody has ever coined a suffix for Call, Bind, Claim or Pull that stuck. Those trades have other names, mostly unfriendly ones, and the people who do them have rarely filled in the form.
Where the Old Headings Went
For anyone reading an older book, an older register or a technique entry that still carries its tag. The tag tells you the Form, and it tells you nothing about the Path, which the old alignment tags never did reliably.

the-magic-system/reference-and-craft/ind.content:
There is a dent in the oak table of the Guild’s reading room at Altherion, left by two Measurewrights (the Guild’s sworn measurers) and one lectern in the Duel of the Two Ruptures, and these are the pages they were fighting over. Consulted rather than read. The Field Manual is the compilers’ own: how a working gets written down, with what magic is left to the rest of the shelf.


Forms The five lines every art states, the twelve Forms with their home Paths, Big Maud, the Guild’s naming table and where the old headings went. Consulted, not read.
The Lexicon of Magic — Master Terminology Every term, defined, windows, classes, monster cores, titles and blessings included. Consulted, not read.
The Working Vocabulary — Trade Jargon and Its Metaphysical Extensions The trade words of lamp-wardens, assayers and glasshouses, carried over into the metaphysical case.
The Practitioner’s Field Manual — The Forge The compilers’ own. How a working gets written down rather than what it is, with the sheet, the class and the climb, and the design notes behind the working trades.


Next: the workbook, Fracture of Worlds — The Living System. Back to The Magic System.
