Mechanism · The same object described in two frames, they say, yields two entirely different sets of numbers and one unchanged object, since nothing is created or lost in a transformation and the quantities are merely re-expressed. By their reckoning Transmutatio applies this to failed workings, which are spent substance in an inconvenient basis with none of it destroyed, and the Wellspring supplies the transformation that makes them usable again. It is the one account in the guild’s books that the benches would sign, if it said who does the saying.
Vantabriel · The Wellspring of Night

Folk name the Night (what carters, soldiers and the commons call it; each culture may add its own beside it).
The idea The night that keeps. Enduring by carrying everything that was lost, with none of it put down.
Kind Wild
Titan Chronaeus: accumulated consequence, with nothing ever put down.
Operation Conjunction: everything lost is joined to the one who carries it, and none of it is ever let go.
Hue Near-black with a retained faint glow, because it keeps everything it has taken and gives none of it back, save the warmth of all it carries, which cannot help showing.
Ground Favors darkness, silence, Aether-thin ground and ruins, places that have long kept everything that was lost in them; hates Aether-rich ground, crowds and active Domains, where nothing is let stay lost.
Contrary Pyreveil (burning it down against keeping all of it); Catharsis (setting it all down against carrying it all); Aurevane (emission against absorption).
On the Body What strikes the practitioner stays in them: the blow goes into muscle and bone and nothing comes back out, no recoil and no spray of force, only a slow heat from inside. Every fight they have survived is still in the flesh, which is how someone who moves like an old man comes to stand under a maul.
On the Spirit Thrown from the Core, a working on this lens reflects nothing and reports nothing. Whatever it takes joins the pile, and a ward it swallows becomes one more thing the caster must carry for life.
On Fate The lost stay bound to them, every dead friend, broken oath and failed cause keeping its pull on the Attraction Layer, so such a person trails a slow heavy pull that the sensitive feel as an empty chair, and survivors of ruined companies find their way to that door. Calling the whole weight down at once, so that a general who has beaten them five times looks up on the sixth field and finds all five defeats drawn up against him under one banner, is done once if at all, and the holder has to carry everything it brings, the knot with the rest.
Spirit Temperance through absence. The confessors’ reading: carrying what was lost.
Alchemy The black that keeps: char that holds everything it has ever taken. (the trade’s reading)
Stat Effect Strengthens Resilience Continuity, Harmonics Attunement, Tempering Longevity. The character endures by carrying the memory of what was lost rather than replacing it.
Glyph [DmN] Dominion; attested on one more.
Failure The night keeps everything and puts none of it down, and everything kept has to be carried by someone. Past what the soul can carry, the kept load has nowhere to go but into the body and soul holding it. The Measurewrights call it thermal saturation.

The Measurewrights’ account. This is the guild’s theory, often right about how much and never about why.
Analogue · Near-total absorption and hysteresis. Retained state dependent on history.
Mechanism · An ultra-absorptive surface, they say, returns almost nothing and converts what it receives into internal heat, and a hysteretic material’s present state depends not on current conditions but on the path it took to arrive. By their reckoning Vantabriel combines them: what strikes the practitioner is kept rather than reflected, and the Crystal’s condition is a function of everything it has ever absorbed. Endurance here is loss carried, with none of it replaced.
Verdantia · The Green Pulse

Folk name the Green (what carters, soldiers and the commons call it; each culture may add its own beside it).
The idea Growth without end. A self with no final size, which feeds on simply being out in the world. It comes through accumulation rather than rupture, one good day on top of another.
Kind Wild
Titan Florwyn: growth itself, her breath in every green thing.
Operation Fermentation: the soul is fed a little at a time from the world it stands in, and grows on that feeding without end.
Hue Chlorophyll green, because it is the color of everything that grows and has not yet stopped.
Ground Favors thick living growth, mild weather and ground close to blood, places where life has long gone on adding to itself; hates barren ground, bitter cold and Aether-thin soil, where nothing grows.
Contrary Monolithion (the finished monument against the self with no final size); Mortalis (more life against the boundary of life).
On the Body The body never settles on a final size and recovers simply by being outdoors, so a long fight on open ground tends to leave the Verdantia fighter bigger at the end than at the start. Keep them in a cellar and they grow long, pale and useless.
On the Spirit An inscription keeps growing after its author has walked away, and a line written on a wall in spring has put out new clauses by autumn. Nobody has found a way to make it grow in the direction they wrote.
On Fate A name spreads the way a root system does, quietly and in every direction, until the holder has cousins and tenants in towns they never visited, and after decades an invading army may find itself buying its bread and hiring its guides from all of them. A Domain (a region where the world runs on a practitioner’s terms) raised on this lens keeps creeping outward for as long as it is held, at a growing cost that neighbors resent and the holder, thinning out at the center, eventually cannot feed. A pull along those roots leaves a knot that goes on growing until the world collects it.
Spirit Temperance through growth.
Alchemy The Feeding: growth given a little at a time and never all at once. (the trade’s reading)
Stat Effect Strengthens Vitality Regeneration, Tempering Yield, Harmonics Synergy. Passive Essence recovery accelerates. The character heals by growing rather than repairing.
Glyph [El] Life, [Eld] Elderwood, [WL] Wildlaw, [Blm] Bloom, [Flo] Bloom-Root; attested on seventeen more.
Failure A self with no final size cannot stop growing, even when the world has stopped feeding it. Shut away from the open air it grows on anyway, all length and no substance, until it cannot hold itself up. The Measurewrights call it etiolation.

The Measurewrights’ account. This is the guild’s theory, often right about how much and never about why.
Analogue · Carbon fixation and indeterminate meristematic growth.
Mechanism · A plant, they say, does not have a final size: meristem tissue remains embryonic for the organism’s whole life, and photosynthesis converts ambient energy into structure continuously rather than in bouts. By their reckoning Verdantia gives the Crystal indeterminate growth and continuous ambient conversion, which is why its practitioners recover while doing nothing and why they are difficult to exhaust in a long engagement. Every gardener in the realm could have told them, and did, for a fee.
Outside the Sixty · Vohrin · The Stillwater Core

This entry is the register’s one exception, and it is marked as one. The Sixty are fixed, and Vohrin is not among them. It is the power of a Titan, the Prime Cryotheic of Niflheim, worked directly at Wellspring level, where the other thirteen Titans reach a soul by way of the Sixty. The note sits on this page because a cold that stills is still a thing you can point at in the physical world, and because fighters keep writing Vohrin into their entries as one of the sixty, and somebody has to tell them what they have written.


Folk name the Still Cold (what carters, soldiers and the commons call it; each culture may add its own beside it).
The idea The cold that stills. Prometheus burns what is false, Zar’thuun unmakes what is excess, and Vohrin stills what is left so it can be built upon. Cold here is no fire of its own. It is a deficit, heat let go of and held as a discipline.
Kind Wild
Titan Vohrin itself: stillness after the end, the settling of motion and thought once everything else is done, which the Measurewrights call entropy’s peace. No Wellspring stands between this power and its Titan.
Operation Coagulation, in the old bench’s sense of congelation: what still moves is stilled and set where it stands, so that it can be built upon.
Hue Ember-orange banked down nearly to brown, under a skin of rime, because the fire is never put out, only banked and held; the cold that shows is what it has let go of. The blue belongs to the ice.
Ground Favors cold air, deep ice and the long northern winters, places where everything has long since settled and gone still; hates warm air, where a stilling costs many times as much, and ground already at rest, where there is nothing left to still.
Contrary Heat or motion forced back in faster than it can be stilled, which is why Pyreveil and its like are the standard answer. It stands outside the Sixty, so its contrary is read from its idea and no entry names it back.
On the Body The blow carries stillness into the wound, heat let go of rather than thrown, and the holder’s own blood runs slow and steady under it.
On the Spirit Projected from the Core, the cold stills what it reaches and holds a thing at what it already is, and a hurrying thought or a half-finished working simply stops where it stood.
On Fate What is held stays held: a bond stops moving in either direction, and with the whole of a life’s discipline a charge can lose its reasons halfway across the field, or a war about to happen can sit in camp through the last of the good weather. The result has only been put off, the knot waits with it and thaws on the same day, and whoever is holding it off grows steadily colder in the fingers and then in the purpose.
Two levels One power, worked two ways. The frost arts of the hunters and the northern schools work it at Wellspring level or as a Titan-derived current, each at the Stage floor its own entry states. The Titan-Keyed Stillwater Rite works it at the Titan’s level and is gated at Revelation.
Where it pools A cold site is a Titan-touched site. Surveyors and renderers read a Vohrin gallery the way they read a Core, with the same care and the same rope, and it does not go on any list of the Sixty’s sites.
Stat Effect None of record, since it has no row in Part Thirteen. In use, Vitality Tolerance answers for the cold.
Glyph No primary of its own that the register accepts. Its arts write in common forms such as [Vor] Return and [Cro] Cycle, and the Codex’s frost rows, [FrTh] FrostThrone and [ObsG] Obsidian-Glacier, still stand under Cymorath’s name (see the Cymorath entry).
Failure A stilling has no end of its own. Whatever is held still has to go on being held, and past what the holder can carry the stillness settles in them instead: the fingers, the lungs, then the mind, with purpose going before pain. A stillness that is only held is also broken by heat or motion forced back in faster than it can be stilled, which is how flame ends the Stillwater Rite. The Measurewrights call it cold soak.
Signature The aura is ember-orange banked down nearly to brown under a skin of rime. The blue that people remember is the ice, and the aura is not blue. Sound is a long creak of settling ice and then the sound of the room falling away; the air smells scrubbed and then of nothing; heat leaves the skin toward the working. The practitioner’s lungs ache and small purposes slip. The tell is frost running out from the feet, with the breath stopping in the air before it has gone anywhere.

The Measurewrights’ account. This is the guild’s theory, often right about how much and never about why.
Analogue · Heat extraction. Conduction down a held gradient and the minimum work of a heat pump, which climbs steeply as the cold end falls; at the Titan’s level, the zero-flux condition of a body that neither emits nor absorbs.
Mechanism · Cold is never emitted, they say. A region goes cold only when energy leaves it, so by their reckoning the Shell takes heat out along a gradient that already exists and has to put it somewhere: the lungs, the air behind the practitioner, the bank of a field. In cold air the heat is cheap to move and in warm air it costs many times as much, and in thermal equilibrium there is nothing to pump at all; at contact the ordered cold crystallizes the working’s path through a wound. Their figures for the warm-air price are good. They have never said where the heat goes at the Titan’s level, where nothing leaves at all.

Read next: the hub, for the kinds, the lens, the Titans and the Paths; and the other three kinds: Spirit, Fate, Medium.

the-magic-system/index.title: The Magic System
the-magic-system/index.content:
At the midsummer fair of Hallingsgate, in front of four thousand people and the entire fish guild, Gudrun Halfdane stepped into the Accord’s brass coil to prove what the minstrels had been singing about her for three years. They called her Gudrun Infinite. She stood six and a half feet in a coat of red and gold, she had a move called INFINITE FIST and a purse with every coin she owned on it riding at the bookies’ tables, and she had told the whole of the Fishgate that the coil would read her a Master. The clerk, a small man with a clear voice, read out Stage III, a Journeyman, and a Flux of eighty-one.
The fair howled, the fish guild loudest of all. Bookies ran for the boats. Gudrun looked at the coil for a while, and said something the clerk declined to enter, and hit it.
It rang for two days. Dogs left town. Her hand broke in three places, and the clerk, when he had climbed out from under his table, read her again, because procedure requires it, and the reading was the same.
She went north to the wars. Eleven years later she came back with one arm and no red coat, stood in the same coil at the same fair in front of a crowd who had come specifically to laugh, and it read Stage VII. She said nothing to anyone. She walked out along the Hallingsgate breakwater, set her feet, turned her one fist on the gray-green sea and called the name, the same stupid name, in a voice you could have stood a spoon in. There is a gap in the breakwater sixty feet wide. The harbor still charges her heirs for it, and no child in Hallingsgate has ever laughed at the word Infinite, though they have all tried it on each other.
Everything in this section is in that story. She could not argue with the number, and it went up when she had survived something, and it cost her an arm. The Measurewrights will tell you it was the Stage that made the name true. Her family says the name came first, and I have stopped having this conversation at weddings. The heir of the fish guild, who laughed loudest that first midsummer, read Stage VII himself by the age of thirty, at the cost of most of his father’s fleet in Drafts, and has never put a hole in anything. The harbor does not charge him. He comes to the fair each year and stands a long while looking at that gap.

The Continuum grants no power. It measures a soul, reports what the measurement found to the soul’s owner, and permits exactly as much as the architecture will bear. Everything in this section is an account of that measurement: what it reads, what it refuses to read, and what it costs to move the reading.
“You call Temperance a buff. It is a confession of how much you have survived.”
Where the numbers live. Everything on this page is the account. The arithmetic underneath it is Fracture of Worlds — The Living System, filed at the foot of this section in twenty-four Parts across ten pages. Levels and the Stages they hold, the scale of thresholds under every number, the Sub-Stat ceiling per Stage, all sixty-four Path gates, Threshold Catalysts, Resonant Pairs, Strike Force and Durability benchmarks, the yield (η) by Mastery, the yield table, Domain costs. Some of its Parts still carry the older reckoning (Bands, Tiers of Standing, three class ladders), and How Power Grows reads them in the present terms.
Read it when a value is in question, not before. This page tells you what the system is. Fracture of Worlds tells you what the number has to be.

The Six Things That Carry the System
Everything after these is detail.

































NumberThe ruleOneReality is spoken of as three planes. Matter, soul, and fate: matter and soul are the two lower realities, and fate, a plane by courtesy, stands above them and is everything that can happen in them. Every act of magic crosses all three at once. Remove one and the working fails, without exception and without appeal.TwoAether is the ocean. Essence is your water. Foreigners say mana and spiritual energy, and they mean the same two things. Aether is infinite and belongs to no one. You pull it from the world around you, and nobody has ever worked a drop of it they did not first pull inside. What you do with it then is your road, and the three roads spend three different things. On the Body Path you pack it raw into your Shell as the Charge, shape it there and drive it out unrefined, and what you lose burns in the Shell’s furnace and comes off you as heat. On the Spirit Path you refine it in your Crystal into Essence, stamp it with your identity and spend it through your Core, and what you lose is paid as a hollowing there. On the Fate Path you hold nothing: you pull Thread down for the one working, and what you lose stays behind as a knot the world collects later. There is only ever as much as you have earned or paid for. Essence is your soul’s own substance, so spending it is spending yourself. Charge is the world’s, so spending it is spending the world, and your body pays for the handling. Rich ground fills you faster; thin ground starves you. A Wellspring represents an alchemical and a spiritual transformation and concept. You can see it as a source of power to pull from, and it is more the governing idea that transforms how your soul uses Aether: a lens on magic already potent, which shapes whatever your Path works (raw Aether in the Shell, Essence in the Core, the claim on the Layer) and in time can double its effect on its home Path, half again at most away from it. There are sixty, and the scholars explain them as sixty types of Aether with one law of physics apiece.ThreeYou cast through a Soul Crystal, and the Soul Crystal is your soul, literally. A wand, a word and a will are decoration. The Crystal has three layers, one per plane, and its architecture decides what you are capable of long before your ambition gets a vote.FourPower is refined. Nothing accumulates, because Temperance is subtraction. Sixteen Stages, each one a structural reorganization of the Crystal: Tempering melts it down and rebuilds each layer, refines your Essence and makes it stronger, and the body gains Traits. Your soul climbs Stages, and each asks one thing of you, its Catalyst; your life climbs Level, by everything hard and real you have done; your hands climb skills, by use. A Stage opens when its Catalyst is met and Level can hold it. A crisis, a seclusion or a tribulation can supply the Catalyst, and so can a Draft or a blessing, so Stages can simply be bought and the wealthy are stronger because they are wealthy. A bought Stage opens the door and no more: the soul stands Overgrown until its Level catches up, and a Release must still be found and mastered by living its own Catalyst.FiveEverything costs. Power is spent, and nobody has ever summoned any. Charge bills the body, Essence bills the self, and a pulled thread leaves a knot. Domains bleed. Traits fatigue. Overchannel scars. Drafts cost money, and the best of them cost someone else’s life. A practitioner who tells you a technique is free is either lying or has not yet paid the invoice.SixThe system does not lie and it does not forgive. Your numbers are the Continuum’s honest assessment of the soul carrying them, and your soul reports them to you in windows that no one else can see. They can be improved. They cannot be argued with. The one line on the sheet that can lie is a blessing’s, because the giver wrote it.
The Four Axes
One number has never described a practitioner. Four independent measurements run alongside each other, and the gaps between them are as diagnostic as the values themselves.
THE FOUR AXESFour independent measurements of one soul; the gaps between them are the diagnosisTHE SOUL CRYSTALCoreShellAttractionSTAGEsixteen Stages, said as rankhow far the Crystal is remadePATH & MASTERYthree Paths, a rung on eachthe road, and how much arrivesTHE NUMBERSsixty-four Sub-Statsread on the hidden scaleWELLSPRING LENSsixty Wellsprings, by kindwhat the numbers meanBody: the Shell  ·  Spirit: the Core  ·  Fate: the Attraction Layer  ·  each with its own MasteryStage, said as rank, sets the ceiling, and Level places Mastery under it. The numbers report the magnitude.The Mastery of the Path in use decides how much arrives. The lens decides what it means.






























AxisWhat it tells youWhere it is readStageThe ceiling. How far the Crystal has been remade, said as a rank (Initiate, Apprentice, Journeyman, Adept, Expert, Master, Grandmaster, Archmaster, Paragon): every stat’s cap, what can open, and how high Mastery may go. It can be boughtThe Sixteen StagesLevelThe life. Everything hard and real the soul has come through. It holds a Stage open, sets the reserve and the stat points, and places Mastery under the Stage’s ceiling. The numbers it buys decide a contest, a full step ahead on the Measurewrights’ scale winning outright; no person ever wears the scale’s letterHow Power GrowsPath, with its MasteryThe road. Which layer of the Crystal the soul leans on, what that opens and shuts, and how much of the magnitude arrives: the Mastery of the road in use, Body, Spirit or Fate, sets the share. It cannot be boughtThe Three Paths, Classes and MasteryThe lensThe meaning. The Wellspring a soul has tempered on, and it changes what the magnitude does without changing the number by a single point: over years of mastery on its home Path it can double the effect, half again at most away from it, while the reading stands where it wasThe Sixty Wellsprings

The four do not move together, and that is the whole of the diagnosis. Stage opens Mastery’s ceiling and Level places the rung under it, so a rich heir can stand under a very high roof on a very low rung, Overgrown and spilling. Path and lens both apply after the numbers are read, so neither has ever moved a number. A Class, the name a soul offers from Glory on, sits beside all four and says what it has made of your life.
Two practitioners at identical stat values and identical Stage can produce wildly different results if one is Body III, Resonant as the smiths say, and the other Body I, Muridic. The stats are the same. The delivery is not.

The Grammar of a Working
Newcomers ask how to learn a spell. The question is malformed. Workings are built, and the building starts with a person: what they refuse, what they survived, and the one wild concept they can explain in a breath, soup or debt or doors. The lens comes after that, the idea’s operation, its price and its flaw, and the Codex (the Accord’s master register of laws) is only asked at the end what to file it under. Once it is filed, every named art in the Continuum answers the same four lines, and its owner’s card answers a fifth.





























LineWhat it saysPathThe layer the art leans on, one or a named pair, and so the Mastery that reads it: matter reads Body, a soul or a meaning reads Spirit, a condition reads Fate. A true pull reads Fate Mastery on top of whatever else is being paid.LensThe Wellspring it is worked through, and that Wellspring’s kind, which names a home and locks nobody out.FormWhat the hands do. Strike and Shape are at home on the Body; Read, Write, Rite and Make on the Spirit; Sing on Spirit and Fate; Brew on Body and Spirit; Call, Bind, Claim and Pull on Fate. A home here is a qualifier too.GatesThe Sub-Stats it needs opened, each with its Path and Stage.SourceOn the card and not the art: Lived, Taught, Inherited, Bought or Blessed. The same art can be any of the five in different hands.
Under those lines sit three old words the trade still uses every day. The Affinity is the particular face of a Wellspring’s idea a person works, fire within Pyreveil or weight within Petralon. The Ability is the internalized governing system a Crystal has developed for it, Pyrokinesis for instance, which does nothing visible on its own: it is the platform. A Technique is a specific, repeatable application on that platform, with defined inputs, outputs and limitations, and it is what you actually do.
And every working, whatever its Form, is at bottom one sentence of Parun, the language of law, with four roles: Authorization says by what right a limit is set, Boundary sets it, Direction says which way the law runs across it, and Sealing ends it. The Wellspring supplies the law and the glyph tells it where to stop, and the stopping lands on the layer the working leaves through: a physical limit on the Shell, what a thing is taken to be on the Core, a term or a prerequisite on the Attraction Layer. So the same Exuroth in the same hand, with the same boundary, cracks a stone on the Body and proves a liar on the Spirit.
The Scholars’ Nine Methods
Older books sort every working by a Method, encoded in the suffix of its name, and the Guild’s clerks still name disciplines that way. A Method is no tier of the grammar above. It is a scholar’s name for a road and a trade taken together: Corporis is the Body speaking, Scriptia is cutting, Alchemia is pouring. The name itself is built on the Affinity: fire, not Pyreveil, gives Pyromancy its root.

Physical manipulation in real time.ShapeTurgia-turgyRitual and creation. Forging lasting change.Rite, MakeCorporis-kinesis (body)Martial integration. The body itself is the conduit.StrikeScriptia-graphyInscription. Magic carved permanently into materials. It is Spirit’s work, and it touches Fate only when the writing is on Fate itself.WriteAlchemia-genesis / -synthesisAlchemy. The Eight Primaries
Eight Primary Stats, eight Sub-Stats beneath each, sixty-four values in total. A Primary is the combined total of its eight Sub-Stats, with one exception: Dominion’s Throne sits outside the total, so Dominion is read over seven. Points are spent on the grain, most of them by the life a person leads and a few placed by choice at each Stage; the category is the arithmetic afterward. The Temperance ceiling and the Path gates bind the Sub-Stat, and the register prints a Primary’s mean beside its total. Two characters at identical Primary totals can be radically different practitioners because their distributions tell different stories, and a specialist can read modest on an assessor’s ledger while three Sub-Stats at the ceiling do the actual work.


















































PrimaryWhat it measuresPlaneVitalityThe body’s capacity to carry power without breaking. Fortitude, constitution, tolerance, regeneration.MaterialArdencyRaw output through the layer in use: raw Aether for Body, Essence for Spirit, Thread for Fate. Flux, compression, penetration, overchannel. How hard the working hits and how fast it leaves you.MaterialGnosisPerception and comprehension. Analysis, forecast, retention, cognition. The stat that reads the room before the room moves.SoulDexterityPrecision and control of the body in motion. Celerity, reflex, economy, evasion, feint.MaterialHarmonicsResonance and bond. Attunement, empathy, breadth, synergy, axis. How honestly output reflects the inner state.FateResilienceStructural persistence under assault. Integrity, ward, anchoring, persistence, hardening.SoulTemperingRefinement itself. Coherence, maturity, ceiling, capacity, longevity. The stat that governs how a remaking takes.SoulDominionCommand over local metaphysical law. Radius, sovereignty, gravity, pressure, throne. The stat of sovereignty.Fate

Two Sub-Stats gate everything else. Tempering Coherence is the structural prerequisite for Threshold eligibility, the Crystal’s internal plumb line. Tempering Maturity is the Sub-Stat the Crystal consults first when evaluating whether you are ready.
A practitioner obsessed with Ardency and negligent of Tempering mounts a very impressive trebuchet on a hay cart, and the first shot settles which of them was the better idea.

The Paths
Sub-Stats are gated behind Path commitment. Every soul has all three layers of the Crystal, and a Path is the one it has learned to lean on: the direction advancement actually took, assessed retroactively and recorded whether the practitioner agrees or not. Nobody picks one at registration.
Body Path · the Aether Shell, in the Physical World, and the literal understanding and manipulation of physical reality. It works raw Aether: drawn in, packed unrefined in the Shell as the Charge, shaped there by the lens and driven out through the Shell, with the lost share burned in the Shell’s furnace and shed as heat, and the body paying for the handling. The shortest road and the most reliable. Direct multiplicative bonus to Strike Force, Durability, and Lifting Strength, from roughly five percent early to twenty percent at Stage XII and above. The trade is reduced Range and Aura Pressure, so low down a Body Path practitioner must close distance to spend their advantage. The road climbs by Mastery, whose best-known teaching is Matla: matter commanded as an object, then through contact, through recognition, through law, and at last as a complete system. High up a Body fighter’s reach runs as far as there is matter to read, still needing existing substance and paying in recoil through body and Crystal.
Spirit Path · the Essence Core, on the Soul Plane, and everything to do with spiritual reality: souls, spirits, the dead, and what a thing means. It spends Essence, refined and stamped, through the Core, and its loss is a hollowing in the Core and never heat. Perception, inscription, clarity, processing, and force at range, which is force on souls: a soul knocked out of true, dread laid on a mind, a Core wounded (see Soul Wounds and the Menders). The Shell is the only door into matter, so a Spirit practitioner who wants a stone moved moves it through their own Shell, at their own Body Mastery, or leaves it where it is. Gates most of Gnosis and much of Tempering’s refinement architecture.
Fate Path · the Attraction Layer, on the Plane of Fate, and the hardest road there is. Fate sits above the two lower realities and is what has to be so before anything can happen, the law and construction of the world itself, and “plane” is a courtesy. A Fate fighter’s everyday weapons are Range, Aura Pressure, presence and bonds. On the rare day they can pull a thread of Fate down, they move what a blow, a wall or a march depends on, and the result arrives without having been forced, at a ruinous price and often not at all. What they pull is Thread, which is never held: it comes down through the Attraction Layer for the one working, is paid for from the soul’s own share, and leaves a knot the world collects later. The Path’s shallow water is bond, recognition, reach, command: it gates nearly all of Harmonics and the majority of Dominion. Its far end holds the high gates: Persistence, Continuity, Ceiling, Sovereignty, Fate, Throne. Almost nothing at the far end unlocks below Stage V, and its terminal Sub-Stats do not open below Stage XIII.
No road is better. Body needs existing substance, must close until very high, pays in recoil and has no purchase on a soul. Spirit needs a soul or a meaning to work on, has a fragile body and dies out of position. Fate is ruinously hard, slow to set, moves only what already has a way of happening and loses a straight exchange, and being above the lower realities makes it harder and never better. So Body beats Spirit by getting there, and Spirit beats Body by going past the Shell. Body beats Fate with force and soundness, and Fate beats Body through what closing depends on. Spirit beats Fate by reaching the hand on the thread, and Fate beats Spirit because one wrong read is enough. Stage, ground and preparation decide which of these holds on the day, and this is why some people combine Paths.
Mastered, Walked, Studied. A Path stands on a sheet in one of three ways. Mastered means its gates are no obstacle at the person’s Stage. Walked means three parts in ten of their practice or more have gone down it. Studied is knowledge and small uses, open to anyone, and it opens no gates. A card carries each road’s Path Stage, the highest Stage whose gates it has opened, so that Mastered means the Path Stage equals the soul’s, and the clerk writes Body VII Mastered · Fate VI Walked 35%. One Path masters fastest, at the full force bonus and on a clean seat. Two take about two and a half times as long, at three-quarters of the bonus on each for life, on a rough seat. Three take about six times as long, past a mortal span, at half the bonus, with the highest steps of the scale shut, and the world looks down on anyone trying.

The three-and-four question, settled. Older registers and gate tables name a fourth Path, Attraction. They were looking at the shallow end of Fate and calling it a road of its own, and an Attraction gate in an old table is a Fate gate at the same Stage. Fate takes the smallest line in a table of force modifiers because a real pull goes around force: the cut that lands is an ordinary cut, and what moved was everything it depended on. Its small line there is a fact about force rather than a fact about Paths.
The deeper difference is how commitment is recognized. Body and Spirit are demonstrated by what a soul routes, Charge through the Shell or Essence through the Core, and the shallow water of Fate by results that keep going your way past what luck allows, by the sworn company that keeps its word and the room that turns. The far end gates Persistence, Continuity, Ceiling, Sovereignty past 400, Stability on Wellspring-absent ground, Fate and Throne, none of which concern output at all, so deep Fate commitment is recognized by what a soul refuses to let end. No drill produces it and no instructor assigns it.
Which is why the Measurewrights read the far end as a late-tier extension. It arrives on time, and it stays invisible until somebody has held something long enough for the holding to count. Full treatment in The Three Paths.

The Wellsprings on the Paths. A Wellspring’s kind names its home plane and locks nobody out. Thirty-three are Wild, transformations of matter, things you can point at, which a soul shapes what it spends around: raw Charge on the Body road, Essence on the Spirit. Fifteen are Spirit, purely spiritual, and they usually do little or nothing to the physical world and give a fighter no fire on any Path, showing instead in what the person can bear, know, keep or let go. Six are Wellsprings of Fate, working on bonds, debts, names and odds. Six are Medium, at home on all three. Any Path can use any Wellspring: at home it can reach double with years of mastery, and away from home it runs at poorer resonance and higher cost, and half again is the most anyone has got out of it. Off its home plane a Wellspring changes target and never idea: on the Body it acts on matter, on the Spirit on what a thing means and holds, on Fate on what a thing could have been.
How each road tires. The shared tells stand for everyone, at half, a quarter and a tenth of the reserve, and each Path adds its own on top. The Body runs hot and cracks: heat-haze on the skin, then steam and cramps, then a Shell drawing on the flesh. The Spirit runs hollow: flat colors, a cold and a slipped word, then names and memories. Fate runs unlucky: small luck curdling, things going wrong nearby, a name that sits wrong in other mouths. You can read a Path by watching its walker flag.
What Your Soul Shows You
A window is the soul reporting its numbers to its owner, in the owner’s own tongue, and no one else can see it. Scholars argue about who built it. It comes in short blocks, fights included, for damage, skill gains and reserve, and it shows numbers, ranks, percentages, bars and Level, while EU, AU/s and yield stay with the instruments and the notes. A normal look gives the sheet:
[Corra Vell · Human · Level 196 · Stage VII, Refraction · Path: Body]
[Class: Yard Breaker]
[Mastery: Body II]
[Vitality 1,720 · Ardency 1,840 · Gnosis 560 · Dexterity 1,100]
[Harmonics 290 · Resilience 520 · Tempering 600 · Dominion 250]
[Reserve: 100% ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓]
[Trait: Bank the Fire]
[Skills: Hammerwork, Expert · Tracking, Journeyman · Bargaining, Apprentice]
[Blessing: none]

The sheet. Race and lineage show on it and shape base stats and what comes easily. The Eight Primaries show as totals of their Sub-Stats, with no letter, since letters are for things, and the register prints the mean beside them, so a working fighter’s sheet reads lower than her fists: Corra’s Flux and Fortitude stand well above her Ardency’s mean. A Sub-Stat appears when it is used or when it moves; the full set remains to study.
Skills rise with use and show on the nine ranks, the same words as a Stage’s rank: Initiate, Apprentice, Journeyman, Adept, Expert, Master, Grandmaster, Archmaster, Paragon. A trade has no cap and can reach Paragon with no Stage behind it; a fighting skill never ranks above its owner’s own Stage rank. Drafts, runes, tags and chants are skills and trades like any other. Traits stay as filed in their Four Reflections and their laws, and carry no level of their own: a Trait works at its owner’s Mastery of the lead road, and at its base below Glory. Techniques are named things done with a skill. They show no level; one jumps when its skill gains a rank and a fight pushes it past its old limit, and takes a bigger name.
Class. A name, never a number, that the soul offers for how the person has lived, first at Glory with Mastery I. It evolves each time the lead Mastery rises, each evolution bringing one move that fits it and a lean on where life spends the stat points. The one wild concept stays the person’s own.
Mastery, one rung for each road, read from Glory: how well a soul works its own road’s substance, I to V and Ω at the top, written Body III · Spirit I. It sets the yield for workings through its own layer, on one table for all three roads. The Stage sets the ceiling and Level places the soul under it (I at Glory, II at Refraction, III at Transcendence and Invocation, IV at Realization and Dissonance, V from Emanation to Zenith, Ω for the Paragons; rung I from Level 115, II from 150, III from 215, IV from 260, V from 340), so a bought Stage raises the ceiling and not the rung. A Walked second road reads a rung behind until mastered, and a Studied one two behind, stopping at II. Fate climbs with Level like the others, but without a grip, which is a bloodline’s Work or a blessing, it stops at II, and its price is the knot. Each road keeps its own folk names for the rungs: on the Body Muridic, Harmonic, Resonant, Luminous, Radiant; on the Spirit Listener, Answerer, Confessor, Shepherd, Ferryman; on Fate Touched, Drawn, Spinner, Knotwright, Weaver. The older books kept them as three separate ladders, the Aether, Essence and Thread Classes, each with a lateral sixth rung (Voidic, Sin-Eater, Severer) that is now the Inverted mark, a feared and wrong way of holding any rung. Classes and Mastery has the one table.
Level is the life, and it moves by anything hard and real: danger overcome above all, so killing something stronger moves it more than a hundred weak kills and crews argue over who got the kill, but a flood night held or fifty years at a trade move it too. It holds a Stage open (Stage II at Level 5, III at 15, IV at 30, V at 101, VIII at 201, XV at 500), and it runs on whether or not the next Catalyst comes; only past the top of a rank group with no Catalyst met does the pressure build as Residual Strain. How Power Grows walks the climb end to end.
Reading someone else. A stronger Gnosis Perception reads a weaker Resilience Ward, and everything else is an estimate said aloud, which people can hide or fake.
What Money Buys
The Catalyst was for a long time the Accord’s favorite argument that the climb was fair. Drafts and blessings can supply one, and everybody with a vault has always known it. Stages can be bought, the great houses hoard the top Drafts, and a coil at a noble’s wedding reads like a ledger of the family’s holdings. The poor rise by dungeon luck, guild patronage and blessings, and the great houses lose more sleep over one commoner with a monster core than over any rival.
Money stops at the door it opens. A purse can buy the Catalyst for any Stage, and at Zenith a Hollow Throne must still recognize the buyer, so there money buys the attempt and not the seat. Sects teach what it cannot buy: Releases, Domains, techniques, skills and the rites for their Wellspring. A rich Stage IX may have no Release at all while a poor Body fighter at the same Stage has all three, since the lead Path sets the count: three on the Body, two on the Spirit, one on Fate, the One, at Refraction. Anyone at Stage VIII can have a Domain, their own concept made real, once the Second Release that opens it, or on Fate the One, has been found. The boost cap of two steps on the hidden scale stays, and only outside help goes past it.
A monster’s core is in a way its Soul Crystal, worth more the stronger the monster, and an alchemist renders it into the Essence Drafts used for tempering. The core’s road decides the Draft: Body cores render to Salts, Spirit cores to Core stock, and the rare Fate core to a reagent for the Layer that only the black market sells. Swallowed raw it gives everything at once, and most who try die or come out wrong. A Crystal cut from a dead practitioner makes the strongest Draft of all, the worst crime in every realm and the most profitable. Monsters themselves level by killing, evolve, share the Stage and Level scale and are known and bountied by Grade, and dungeons grow down in floors around a Core, alive and learning, with something guarding the heart. The Bestiary has the rest.
Fate and Blessings
The Plane of Fate is the control of Attraction Force and Obsession Force and the workings of reality itself: manipulating probabilities to work outside what reality already knows, to control the fate or predestiny of something. All spirits and all physical things have fates. It can attach to oaths, where it is small and anyone’s to use (see Vows and Oaths), and it is more tied to blessings. Fate Arts are rare, mostly by bloodline, reached late by some high-Stage masters along the Fate Path, and considered incredibly overpowered. Hataraki can take back or remove a blessing, which is a good part of why that bloodline is feared, though it takes two Works or two Moto, because each Work is an inherited grip on one function, which lowers the chance of failure and never the price.
Vows and blessings are its small uses. People also fight and wage wars with Fate, and the Moto are the model of how deadly a lineage with it is, though it is the hardest thing in the system. Fate is the law and construction of the world itself, most if not all of the Archons and the great principles they embody are Sovereign across all three planes, this one included, and understanding gets no purchase on it, because understanding is made of the thing it would be used against. Some Archons are deemed greater than others, and Uurgath and Urion are unparalleled in Fate, because what they are cannot be conceived. An ordinary Fate Path fighter mostly fights with Range, Aura Pressure, presence and bonds. A real pull moves what a blow depends on, so a guard slips and an ordinary cut is already there, and it is rare, ruinously expensive and often fails, and landed or failed it leaves a knot, a debt the world collects from the puller later. Moving a whole field is a life’s masterwork at high Stage or a bloodline’s art. It moves only what already has a way of happening, it has a charge and a tell, and it is contested: Dominion’s Fate Sub-Stat against the target’s Resilience Persistence and Continuity. See The Three Paths, The Tell and the Knot for how a pull is seen coming and what it leaves owing, and Counterplay for how such a fighter is beaten.
A blessing grants a power out of a person’s natural reach, even in Level. It need not go through Fate, but most do. Higher spirits, Archons, Epochs and people of higher Temperance give them, because they are spiritually stronger, and a great giver spends almost nothing. Epochs and Archons act rarely, and it shakes the world. A blessing is listed on the sheet as its own line and can lie, because the giver wrote the line. A curse is often a blessing with terms you did not read. See Blessings and Curses.
What Corruption Looks Like, By Law
Every Wellspring has a terminal failure state, and its entry in the Sixty names its own, read from the flaw in its idea. Physicians see them in a few shapes, by what the law was doing to the person who could not put it down. The early symptoms are indistinguishable from enthusiasm.

Entries
The section is filed in six shelves and a workbook. Each shelf has its own page, and each shelf ends by pointing at the next. This list is the reading order, the one that visits everything. Start Here and First Steps offer short routes through it for readers in a hurry.
I · First Steps
The newcomer’s road. Read these four first and everything after them will make sense.


How Magic Works The whole system in brief, for a newcomer: the soul and its windows, Wellsprings as lenses, Traits and skills with their levels, classes, Stages for sale, monster cores and dungeons, guild titles, gear, Fate and blessings.
The Measures at a Glance Every number a practitioner, a monster or a piece of gear is read by, what it decides, and one fighter read on all of them, window included.
One Exchange, Annotated A single exchange between two fighters, with every rule that decided it marked and each fighter’s windows shown as a worked example.
The Core Vocabulary The words. The first three pages explain each one as it comes; this is where they are kept, and it stays open beside everything after.


II · The Foundations
What a working is, the laws it conditions, and the boundaries every working is written in.


The Physical Account: Two Sets of Books The Measurewrights’ own book. Their account of a working in natural philosophy, set beside the canon reading by the lens, and where the power actually comes from. Often right about how much, never about why.
The Sixty Wellsprings The laws being conditioned. Read the hub, then whichever kind you need: Wild, Spirit, Fate or Medium.
The Master Glyph Index — 136 Attested Forms The boundaries imposed on those laws.
The Spell Index Every attested working, written in those boundaries.
The Master Codex The canon workbook, and where each of its sheets lives here.
The Descent of Parun — The Fourteen Hands The fourteen ways of writing a boundary down, and what each one changes. Its child, The Counted Speech, is why almost nobody says it aloud.


III · The Soul and the Climb
What a soul carries, what advancement does to it, and how it reads from outside.


The Trait System: Law, Function and the Forge What a soul carries before any of the above touches it.
The Three Paths: Routing, Recognition and the Gate The route a working takes out of a soul, what each road spends and what it costs, how the Crystal recognizes it, and what it gates.
The Sixteen Stages What advancement does to a person, told four ways per Stage.
The Ladder and the Draft — Temperance, Advancement and Essence Drafts How the climb joins the rest of the system, what Drafts and monster cores buy, and what money cannot.
How Power Grows The climb in one reading: Stage as rank, Catalyst and Level, Mastery, skill ranks, Releases by Path.
Tier Grade, Bands & the Aether Shell The numbers, and who wins.
Windows and the Sheet The soul’s private report, and everyone lying about it.
Classes and Mastery What your soul thinks you are, what it hands you for it, and the Mastery that says how far your reach runs on each road.
Skills and Their Ranks What rises by doing it, the nine ranks it is read in, and the few points that are yours to place.
Release Forms The soul’s law let off its limit in a learned shape, three on the Body, two on the Spirit and the One on Fate.
Releases and Domains by Path What a Release and a Domain do on each road: the flesh and the field for Body, the line and meaning for Spirit, the claim and conditions for Fate.
Domains The seed, the true Domain and the Realm: a space where one soul’s law outranks the world’s, how it is called, and how fields clash.
Soul Wounds and the Menders What a Spirit strike does past the Shell, how the hurt shows and how long it stays, who closes it and for how much.
The Tell and the Knot: Pulling a Thread How to see a pull coming, how long you have, and what the world takes back afterward.
The Color of Essence What all of the above looks like from outside.



The Concordant Crystal: One frame shared by several souls, and what fuses and what does not.

IV · Power in Use
How power is put into the body, stacked, spent, carried in tags and beaten.


Reinforcement The coat of one’s own aura over the body’s base, what it costs, and when it fails.
Stacking and Spending How boosts stack to the cap, how the reserve runs down, and how the body tells on it.
Runes and Tags Workings cut into objects ahead of time: who fuels them, who fires them, who cuts them.
The Working Trades The ways a working can be set down, the skills and trades behind them, and the old guild feuds that follow.
Counterplay: What Beats a Practitioner What beats a practitioner, and in what order the decision is made.


V · Practice and Institution
Who may practice, what they are called, how they are trained, and what the practice is set against.


The Gate: Who May Learn Magic Why nearly everyone carries a Crystal, why about one in ten is taught to wake it, and who holds the door on the rest of the lesson.
The Standing and the Title: Guild Titles as Trust The nine titles every guild shares, what each one lets a stranger hand you, and the two other names you carry.
Training and Sects Schools, disciple ranks, seclusion and the tournament ladder.
Blessings and Curses What a thumb grants, how the line on your window lies, and who can take it off again.
Vows and Oaths Small Fate, anyone’s to make: what a vow buys, what breaking one does, and the one day the law sleeps.
Who Pays for the Lamp: The Living Crafts How a city’s magic really gets done: lamp-wardens, ward-cutters, hedge-workers and Guild craftsmen, paid by the job, who can strike, overcharge or refuse.
On Walking Into the Current — Wellspring Encounter and Recovery What happens to a body that meets a Wellspring without meaning to.
Mechanica: Extraction Without Recognition The practice everything above defines itself against.


VI · Reference and Craft
Consulted rather than read. The Field Manual is for whoever has to write a working down: how magic is recorded, not what magic is.


Forms The twelve things hands do, each with its home Path, and what every art must state. Reference. Consulted rather than read.
The Lexicon of Magic — Master Terminology Every term, defined. Consulted rather than read.
The Working Vocabulary — Trade Jargon and Its Metaphysical Extensions The trade words of lamp-wardens, assayers and glasshouses, carried over into the metaphysical case.
The Practitioner’s Field Manual — The Forge How a working is written down rather than what it is.


The Workbook · Fracture of Worlds — The Living System
The stat framework itself: a reference you open with a specific question already in hand.

How to use it. Statting a character: open I for the point economy, then II for the ceiling their Stage permits and the Path gates on their Sub-Stats. Writing a fight: II for the gap in numbers on the Measurewrights’ scale, III, Force of Hand, for what the strike actually does to masonry and bone. Writing a working: V for the Wellspring’s stat effect, VII for how much of it survives the Shell. Writing advancement: VI for the Catalyst the Crystal is waiting on. Writing a Domain: VIII. Pricing a working (in EU, or in joules by the Measurewrights’ conversion): IX. Reading gear, a beast or a Commission on its ladder: X. The Sub-Stats themselves are IV.


Elsewhere in the wiki. The named arts live under The Disciplines. The material register lives under Materials, Alchemy & Trade. Monsters and their cores are under The Bestiary, with Dungeons beside them. Item Grade, Rarity and Master Works are in Grade and Rarity. The Apprentice’s Primer, the in-world first reader that condenses this entire section for a newly registered practitioner, sits under In-World Documents.

the-magic-system/the-soul-and-the-climb/.content:
New to the climb? Begin with How Power Grows: the soul climbs Stages, the life climbs Level, the hands climb skills. This page is the two things read off them that people talk about most, the Class the soul offers and the Mastery that says how far a soul’s reach runs on each road. The older registers filed it as Classes and the Three Ladders.


“Your soul has been watching you for years, and at Stage VI it tells you what it thinks. Bring a drink.”
Advice to new Experts, chalked on the wall of the assay house at Waxgate, and renewed by somebody every time the wall is painted.

Every army in the Hundred Crowns has marched through the Painted Rivers at least twice, and every one of them has used the ford at Threeways, because it runs knee-deep on a good day between banks thick with yellow flag, and because there is a perfectly good ferry beside it that nobody wearing a crown has ever paid for. Bess Tolliver grew up on that ferry. At Glory, Stage VI, her window (the soul’s private report of its own numbers) offered her Pole-Hand, as it has offered every ferry child who lived that long. A rung of Mastery later it offered her Riverblade, which is what any ferry town produces when you hit people with a long wet pole for ten years and then someone gives you an edge. She was one of a few thousand. A rung after that she came out a Floodbreaker, one of a few hundred, and the quartermasters of the Midmarch had started putting her name in their letters.
On the morning the levies of Pennycrown came down to Threeways, eleven hundred spears in yellow and blue, four carts of baggage and a king who owed her father nineteen crossings, she walked out to the middle of the ford with her skirts tied up, stood knee-deep in bright green water, laid a blade flat across the current, and let the whole valley have it.
"Nothing crosses."
The first rank came on at the march and walked in. Water presses on whatever is under it according to how much of it is piled above, density times gravity times depth, which is why divers go home with their ears bleeding. Bess had Abython, the Abyssal Pulse, for a lens, which teaches a soul to match the pressure of the deep by teaching it exactly what that pressure is, and her years on the Body Path had taught her that a thing you can read in matter you can also tell to matter. She told that one stretch of river how deep it was. It looked exactly as it had. It was still knee-deep to the eye, and it bore down on those men’s shins with the weight of the sea at its deepest sounding. A body can stand a great deal of weight pressed evenly all over it, which is how the deep fish live, and it cannot stand that weight from the knee down with nothing above to push back. Their greaves folded like wet pasteboard, the blood and the soft meat went up inside their legs, the knees burst, and the front rank knelt in a foot and a half of sunny water and could not be pulled out by their friends, who stepped in to try. The king of Pennycrown sent the nineteen crossings that afternoon, in coin, by a herald under a white branch, and took his host home by the long road with the front rank carried on hurdles.
Her window arrived that night:
[Threshold reached: Body IV, Luminous]
[Your life has earned:]
  The Unforded
[Choose.]

There was one name on it, and it told her to choose anyway. No one else in the Archives has ever held that class. The art charges in its own coin, as the big ones do: nothing crosses, and the river has never made an exception for the woman who said so. She has not set foot over running water since, her mother lives on the east bank, and for nineteen years the two of them have spoken across two hundred yards of green river or not at all. Tavern rankings put the Unforded among the most frightening classes in the North. Her mother is old now, and all of Threeways knows that when she is buried Bess will stand on the west bank for it.
Three things happened to Bess Tolliver at those thresholds, and they are most of the subject of this page. Her soul named her. The name changed as she lived. And the idea she carried from the first day to the last, that nothing gets across, stayed hers alone. The rest of the page is the Mastery her Level was reading off while it happened, and the same rungs on the two roads she never set foot on.
What a Class Is
Taverns run two things together that the assayers keep apart: the Class, and Mastery.
A Class is what the soul makes of a life. It is a name, never a number, offered at thresholds, fitted to how the person has lived, and it arrives on the window in the owner’s own tongue. It is first offered at Glory, with Mastery I, and it evolves when the lead Mastery rises. Each evolution brings one move that fits the new name and a lean on where life spends the person’s stat points. It has no rung of its own. No coil has ever read one. A class name is known to its owner, to anyone with Gnosis Perception (the stat of sensing what a soul is) strong enough to read it off them, and to everyone else exactly as far as the owner cares to tell it, which is why half the Wallbreakers in the Midmarch are something else.
Mastery is what the instruments read. It is one rung for each Path a soul walks, and it measures how strong a person’s reach is through that Path’s layer. Body Mastery is the Aether Shell (the Crystal’s outer layer, which turns inner power into outward force) and their influence on the physical world. Spirit Mastery is the Essence Core and their influence on spiritual reality. Fate Mastery is the Attraction Layer and how much of Fate they can pull down and hold. From Glory each sets the yield (η: the share of each spend that arrives as intended effect, as a distillation has its yield) for workings through its own layer. A practitioner stands in the coil, the brass assay instrument, and the clerk writes Body III on the slip, and the old clerks add Resonant out of habit, and for a second fee will read the roads the soul has only walked or studied, which on most slips is a waste of a second fee.
The Archives file the full law of the Shell under Grades, Ranks and the Aether Shell, with its anomalies, and in Fracture of Worlds, Part Seventeen. Every soul has all three layers, whichever Path it leans on, and Mastery is read on every road the soul walks, Mastered, Walked or Studied: the Body rung of a Fate Path auditor who studied the Shell, the Spirit rung of a Body Path brawler who walks the Core besides. A road a soul has never set foot on reads nothing. What follows is first about the name and what people do once they have one, and then about Mastery.
The Offer
When. The first offer comes at Glory, Stage VI, with the first rung of Mastery, where the coil first reads one. Stages I through V are unclassed, and the unwoken have no class at all: a baker’s window shows her Level, her trade skills and her health, and waking opens the rest of it without yet naming her. After Glory, the offer comes again each time the lead road’s Mastery climbs a rung. A Fate-led soul with no grip on the thread stops at the second rung, and its class stops with it, which is how a Fate Path fighter with no grip on anything comes to carry the same name for forty years and complain about it the whole time.
What arrives. A short block, in the owner’s tongue, with one name or several:
[Threshold reached: Body II, Harmonic]
[Your life has earned:]
  Riverblade
  Toll-Breaker
  Oath-Hand
[Choose.]

That one belonged to a ferryman’s son at Chainbridge who chose wrong, and knew it about a year later. The three names were all true of him. He had fought for the river, he had cheated the chain, and he had sworn to a lord’s steward, and his soul laid out the three roads his life could honestly be said to have taken. Most people get two or three. A soul that has only ever done one thing gets one thing, and a soul with a false account of itself finds the window declining to share that account, which has embarrassed a number of paladins.
Which way it leans. The offer comes through the layer the soul leans on, and it has that layer’s accent. A Body soul hears mostly names of work, weight and matter: Pole-Hand, Wallbreaker, Winter Porter. A Spirit soul hears names of souls, meanings and things kept: Auditor, Bone-Reader, Calls Them In. A Fate soul hears names of bonds, debts and odds: Oath-Hand, Contract Hand, Turncoat. It is a lean, and the soul allows itself surprises. Body-led ferrymen have been offered Oath-Hand, the Archives hold a Spirit Path abbess whose window said Wallbreaker and would not be argued with, and the surprise is usually the truest name on the list.
What it cannot be. A class is never picked off a list of what you would like. A duke’s son who dreams of being a Stormblade and has spent his life at his father’s elbow will be offered a name for the life he has had, and it will not be Stormblade. An offer left unanswered keeps the old name at the new rung and goes on waiting, and a few stubborn people have carried a first-rung name up three rungs out of spite, giving up the moves the soul had for them. Once taken, the name stays until the next rung. Nobody has ever handed one back, sold one or had one cut out, though the fair-stall trade in promises to do so is brisk.
The bought Stage. A Stage can be bought, as The Ladder and the Draft explains at length, and Mastery cannot. It is read from Level under the Stage’s ceiling, a bought Stage opens the ceiling and leaves the Level where it was (the table is under Mastery, below), and a Stage held above its Level runs Overgrown, its Mastery reading low or not at all. The offer cannot be bought either, because the offer reads the life. House heirs who take Glory in a quiet room with a physician standing by have opened their windows to Well-Attended, Second Son and Kept Indoors. Great families pay good silver to keep those names quiet. Commoners with Gnosis to spare pay good silver to find them out.
What a Class Gives
The name carries real goods. In rough order of how often they turn up:

One move. Each offer brings one move that fits the name, a small lawful trick listed on the window when gained, the kind of thing a person might have spent years failing to learn. It runs on the owner’s reserve at the owner’s yield and costs what it costs, and it often arrives with the skill it runs on already started: a Riverblade wakes up with Wet Footing and Long Measure on the window and a sure foot on planks. See Skills and Traits.
An easier road. Certain kinds of move come quicker, and the teachers notice. A Wallbreaker’s elbows learn in a month what a Bookkeeper’s elbows will never learn.
A lean in growth. Life spends most of a person’s stat points by what their lead layer does, and a class leans on that: what the name is about grows a little faster, and what it ignores a little slower. Every Wallbreaker in the four quarters has roughly the same shoulders.
A shape in the aura. The Wellspring a person has tempered on longest sets their base color, any others add texture and sound, and a class or a big Trait adds a shape, which a good eye can spot at fifty paces. People read strangers off it in every market on the continent, or think they can:


Cherry-red, temper-blue at the edges, smelling of quench oil: an Exuroth lens. A Riverblade’s shape, running in a flowing band around the shoulders.
“Fire school, river town, and he’s hiding a limp.”

The gain shows when it lands:
[Class: Wick-Trimmer]
[Body III]
[Gained: Clean Thread. A flame held to a bootlace's width keeps all its heat.]

What a class never gives is power out of nothing. It adds no step on the scale, it does not lift the two-step cap on boosts, it opens no Release and it builds no Domain. Those are the person’s to find. The yield comes from Mastery, by the clarity of each layer, and the name merely sits beside it.
How It Evolves
A class grows at each rung of the lead road’s Mastery into a form chosen from what you have actually done. When that rung climbs, the old name is offered back changed, or offered back in pieces, according to how it was lived. Two Auditors going up from the second rung can come out as a Reckoner and a Debt Collector, and they will not be speaking by then. Bess Tolliver’s record is the one every guild hall tells:

Her kit is still one idea: nothing crosses.
There is no tree. Every few years somebody at a fair sells a beautifully inked chart of what a Wallbreaker becomes, with arrows, and guild halls have been known to hang them. The charts describe what happened to the last few people and predict nothing. The Archives hold eleven Wallbreakers who became Siegebreakers and one who became Gentle Hands, after a very bad year, at a rung and a yield that the eleven would have killed for. Parents plan around the charts regardless, and it costs them.
You cannot drill for one. Sects have tried, for centuries, because a known class is an easy thing to put on a recruiting bill. What a sect can do is give its students the same life, the same drills, the same enemies and the same bad food, and the classes do cluster: a school’s colors and a school’s class names come to march together, and a style you can spot at fifty paces gets a name you can guess. The one who goes over the wall to see her dying father comes out of the next threshold with something else, and that one is usually the student the elders start watching.
Conquest has never chosen a name. A good day’s killing is Level like any hard thing, and Level moves the rung, so a famous fight reaches the class in the end, by the long way round, as the Shell’s page sets out. What the new name is, the soul decides from the whole life. Conquest has moved a great many names, and named none of them.
Common Classes and Classes of One
Common classes are famous. A class shared by thousands has songs, slang, a reputation in the bookies’ mouths and a joke the other classes tell about it. Crews advertise for them: wanted, one Wallbreaker, one Ferryman, share of the core. Taverns rank them, the rankings disagree, and fights over the rankings have closed more taverns than fire. A commoner who comes out a Riverblade has a trade anywhere there is water.
Rare classes are a calling card. A few hundred Floodbreakers means that every one of them has heard of the others. Lords hire them by the name. Rivals look for them on purpose.
Classes of one are feared. Some names have been held by exactly one person in the history of the Archives, and those people tend to be the ones the heralds cry and the bounty boards carry. The name is the first thing anyone wants to know about them, and the last thing they can check. Children know the great ones the way they know the names of monsters, and a false claim to one is a good way to be challenged by someone who knows the real holder.
There is one complication the Measurewrights enjoy. A one-person class is one person’s life, so no teacher can prepare you for it, no chart lists what it gives, and no one can warn you what it costs. The Unforded found out about the river by trying to go home.
By People and Region
Peoples tend toward classes and Traits of their own, because a class fits how a life is lived and a place decides a great deal of that. These are tendencies and never locks. There is a Marrowkin Riverblade working the barges below Chainbridge, and he is sick of hearing about it. The names below are gathered from assay-house gossip, sect rolls and three lawsuits, and each arrives on the window in its owner’s own language, so the Common forms are what foreigners call them.

Moves, and the One Concept That Stays Yours
A kit has one wild concept, the thing you can explain in a breath. The concept is the person’s own, and no class has ever supplied one. A class is what the soul says about a life. A concept is what the person decided to do about it. The class gets no vote: a Stage VII Auditor may well fight with soup.
What the class does is shape the moves, the way a trade shapes a hand. Take two Riverblades out of the same ferry town, with the same footing and the same long measure on the sheet, the same way of keeping the blade low and letting the wet plank do half the work.

Bess Tolliver’s idea is that nothing crosses. Her Riverblade moves are all cuts laid across a line: Wake Cut, a flat stroke that leaves a seam of pressure standing in the air behind it, and whoever walks through it finds out.
Old Latch of Chainbridge’s idea is doors. His Riverblade moves are all cuts that open something: Latch-Lift goes in low at the same angle Bess uses and leaves a neat hinged flap in a man’s mail, his ribs, or on one celebrated evening his brother-in-law’s strongroom.

Same class, same stance, same aura-shape, and a bookie who has seen both will quote you different odds. The class is why they look alike. The concept is why they fight nothing alike.
As the class evolves the moves get new bones, and the name of a move gets bigger at each jump, with the old name staying in use. Techniques themselves show no level on any window.

Read down the right-hand column and it is one idea getting louder. Read the two middle columns and you see what the soul kept handing her to do it with.
Trait, Release and Domain are that same concept escalating: the idea, the transformed body, and the world obeying it. A class stays in its own lane through all of that. It shows in how the body carries the Release and in the shape around the aura, and the song writers, who cannot tell any of this apart, will credit the class regardless.
Mastery
Every name above sits beside a rung, and the rung is what decides how much of a practitioner’s power gets out of them. Mastery is how well a soul works its road’s own substance: one rung for each Path a person walks, numbered I to V, with Ω above them for the very few. The slip prints it in one line:
[Body IV · Spirit II]

That line belongs to a hitter with a very clean Shell and some schooling in souls, and like nearly everyone alive she has never walked the Fate road at all, so the slip says nothing of it.
Each road’s rung sets the yield for workings through its own layer, and each layer works a different thing. The Core authors everything, and the layer it lands through sets the rung. A blow by hand, or a burn that lives in the tissue, is raw Aether (mana, in plain words): drawn in, packed unrefined in the Shell as the Charge, shaped there by the Wellspring’s lens and driven out through the Shell. None of it is ever refined into Essence, and it reads Body Mastery. A working authored in the Core is paid in Essence (spiritual energy: Aether refined in the Crystal and stamped with its owner), spent through the Core, and reads Spirit Mastery. A pull takes hold of Thread, drawn down through the Attraction Layer and paid for out of the puller’s Essence, and reads Fate Mastery.
Fighters name the three styles for what they spend: Aether Manipulation, Essence Manipulation and Thread Manipulation. The halls used to wince at the first of those, and it is now the literal truth, since a Body fighter is handling the world’s own Aether with her Shell and nothing else. Measurewright Odo Farrant of the Waxgate assay house, who has grumbled about bracket slang for forty years, has merely changed grumbles. His present one concerns the young hitters who hear “Aether Manipulation” and conclude that power which is not theirs must be free. It is not theirs and it is not free. Spending Essence is spending yourself, and spending Charge is spending the world, and the body pays for the handling in heat, torn fiber and recoil, to the last copper. Farrant keeps a jar of teeth on his desk from people who thought they could skip the body’s bill. The Three Paths has the whole list of which layer reads what, trade by trade. One person can be clean in one layer and roaring in another, so a yield on a slip is only ever a yield for something. The name changes; the share that arrives follows the layer. A Riverblade at Body II leaks what a Bookkeeper at Body II leaks, whatever the songs say.
The one table: Stage against rung
Mastery is never tracked. The Stage sets the ceiling, and the Level places the soul under it. A Stage says how high a road may go. It has never carried anyone there, and neither has practice on its own: the rung follows Level, and Level follows everything hard and real a soul has done. A bought Stage opens the ceiling and leaves the Level where it was, which is how a rich Stage XII can stand under a roof marked Radiant, Overgrown, and read three rungs short of it, or nothing at all. This is the one table on the subject, and every other page in these Archives points here.

The roof rises a rung at a time up the whole climb, so the numeral means something at every height, and a soul fresh across a Stage reads a rung under its new roof until its Level grows into the Stage. A new Refraction soul at 130 reads I and reaches II at 150; a new Transcendent at 201 reads II and reaches III at 215; a new Realization soul at 230 reads III and reaches IV at 260; a new Emanation soul at 320 reads IV and reaches V at 340.
The early grip. One exception breaks the silence below Glory. A soul born to one of the Epochs’ lines and holding that line’s instrument, a Moto with a Work of Hataraki, a Zettari with Matla, a Yukari with Null-Light, reads rung I on that instrument’s road from Ascension, the third Stage, and only rung I until Glory. The blood opens one ladder early, and the assay houses keep a separate book for those children.
Inverted. Any rung can be held Inverted, a feared and wrong way of working it, in which the soul takes where it ought to give and empties where it ought to fill. It is a mark beside the rung and never a rung of its own: Spirit IV Inverted. Most souls never see it.
Which rung you stand on follows your road.

The Mastery of your leading Path reads from your Level, up to the Stage’s ceiling, and your Class evolves when it rises.
A Walked second Path, thirty parts in a hundred of the practice or more, reads a rung behind until that Path is mastered.
A Studied Path reads two rungs behind the lead and stops at II.
A road you have never walked or studied reads nothing.
Fate reads like the others, with one hard limit, set out under Fate Mastery below.

The Stages in the table are a ceiling and the Level places a soul under it, so a Stage XI who reads Body II on a road she only studied is common, and nobody thinks less of her until she leaks on them. Mastery is read from Level for everyone, and the Archives keep no list of people who stand above it. Where an old record shows someone working past the rung their Level gives, that was an overreach: done once, in that moment, at a price, and the record stands as the night they reached past themselves, never as a rung they hold. The Measurewrights still charge extra to write it up. The Crystal’s look is a separate reading again: how the whole stone looks, following the Stage, as the Shell’s page sets out.
Body Mastery: the Shell
How strong your influence on the physical world is. Its mechanism is clarity: how cleanly the Shell works raw Aether, the Charge packed in it, into matter, force and heat. Bess Tolliver climbed this one. It is the rung the old registers mean when they say “Class” with a numeral and nothing else, since for a long while it was the only one anybody paid to have read.
