The right-hand column is a habit, and the Archives have stopped calling it a rule. Plenty of Radiant souls carry names a fishwife would blush at, and a Muridic class can be as famous as any.

Spirit Mastery: the Core
How strong your influence on spiritual reality is: souls, spirits, the dead, what a thing means. A wall will tell you nothing about Spirit Mastery, and its great holders have often been people you could knock down with a loaf.
For eleven years the Pennycrown Yellows drilled in the Bellmarsh. They had died there to a man in a single afternoon, four hundred spears in yellow and blue, and nobody had told them. Reed-cutters heard the sergeant’s count at dawn, the fen villages sickened with a homesickness that had no home in it, and two bishops and a Sancta Lux exorcist in scarlet went out in turn with bell and banner to order the dead to lie down, and came back hoarse. Then the villages took up a collection and sent for Dorrit Quill, a wide, cheerful laundress from Tallow Row in a mustard-yellow apron, on the Spirit Path these thirty years, whose slip read Spirit III, and who by her own account could not crack a walnut at the first try. She walked out into the marsh with a basket of new bread and stood at the end of their line. She commanded nobody. She called the company roll, in the voice of a woman calling children in to supper, all four hundred names, which had taken her a year to collect out of the parish books, and four hundred voices no living ear could quite hear answered here. Then she turned round and walked home, and they fell in behind her. It took nineteen days. Every market on the road went quiet as she came through with the dogs lying flat and a cold wind at her back, though not a reed bent and not a cup spilled from one end of that road to the other. At each village a few of the Yellows fell out of the file and went in at their own doors, and that night someone in that house slept. Her window arrived on the sixth day, somewhere south of Tollgarth:
[Threshold reached: Spirit IV, Shepherd]
[Your life has earned:]
  Calls Them In
[Choose.]










































RungWhat it can doUnreadThe Core holds identity, memory and Traits, as every Core does, and reaches nobody else’s on purpose. An unread soul in a haunted house gets a cold neck and a bad night. Most hitters never read on this road at all and are no worse for itI · ListenerThe Core starts to hear. The dead in a room, the grief soaked into a coat, the lie going sour in a man’s voice all reach them, and none of it can be answered. Most Listeners think at first that they are going mad, and a few areII · AnswererThe Core can reply and be understood. A shade or a bound spirit will talk to them, and a thrown working holds together across a yard of air, because it now means something when it arrivesIII · ConfessorReaches into a soul and finds what is lodged there. A willing soul can be relieved of a poison, an unwilling one can be told what it has been hiding from itself, and a line written on a thing carries their say on what the thing is. Output arrives at near-full fidelity for the first timeIV · ShepherdHolds many souls at once. A frightened company steadies around them, a dying man’s soul stays where it is put until morning, and the lost will follow them homeV · FerrymanCarries souls across. The Veil (the threshold between the planes) opens to them, the dead know them by name, and a soul can be walked from one side and set down on the other. Output begins exceeding what the raw numbers suggest. A Ferryman guides, questions, lays to rest, carries a message and binds a lingering dead, and never returns a life. Nobody has ever rowed one back, though a great many have paid to see it triedInvertedThe Core takes in where it ought to speak. Spirits vanish into them, a read finds nobody home, and names and griefs go in and do not come out. A soul an Inverted Core has worked on is short of something and cannot say what. A mark on any rung; the old books called it Sin-Eater, or HollowΩ · AbsoluteThe Core dissolves as a boundary, and there stops being a clear answer to whose grief this is. Nobody who holds it has filed it
What a Ferryman does, and the one thing she does not. The rung has five works, and the temples list them in this order. She guides: a soul that has lost the road is walked to it and across. She questions: the dead will answer her, truthfully as far as they know, for as long as she can hold the crossing open. She lays to rest: what lingers is set down on the far side and stays there. She carries a message, one way or the other, word for word, and is paid well by widows and badly by heirs. And she binds a lingering dead: a shade that will not go and cannot be let loose is tied to a place, a thing or a term, until someone can do better by it. Every one of those moves a soul or a word across the Veil. None of them moves a life back. The dead stay dead, and a Ferryman who is asked will say so before she names her fee, which is how you tell her from the other kind. Anything closer to a return than a message is no Ferryman’s work at all: it is a blessing of the sort that shakes the world, from a giver who can afford it, and by every account on file it comes back as a curse. Soul hurts short of death are another trade’s business, set out in Soul Wounds and the Menders.
A Spirit Ferryman has nothing to do with the Ferryman on a crew’s bill, who is a class and works a boat. Everyone concerned has complained.
Fate Mastery: the Layer
How much of Fate you can pull down and hold. This is the hard one. A Fate Path fighter’s everyday weapons, Range, Aura Pressure, presence and bonds, work at any rung, and anyone can keep a vow, because a vow binds a person to themselves and pulls nothing down: a vow spends the soul’s own share, and a pull reaches above it. The share is part of the reserve, so a vow drains it like any working, spent through the Layer, and it refills the same way. The rung measures one thing only, which is what happens when you reach up.
What a Fate soul holds is Essence. It refines Aether in the Crystal as a Spirit soul does, and it pays its pulls from that. Thread is never stored. It is pulled down for one working and is gone when the working is, which is why no window has a Thread bar, why Core stock refills a Fate worker as it does a Spirit one, and why a Fate fighter who has run herself dry is hollow and cold as well as unlucky.
Fate climbs with Level like the other two roads, and its grip sets the ceiling. Without a grip on the thread a Fate soul stops at II, however long it lives and however many vows it keeps. A grip is a Work or a blessing. A Work of Hataraki is an inherited grip on one function, which lowers the chance of failure and has never lowered the price; a blessing that grants a grip lifts the ceiling the same way. Either lifts it to the Stage’s own and never past it. Blood alone is not a grip, and the cadet lines of the great Fate houses, who have the blood and were never given a Work, stop at II like anyone else and are bitter about it in every generation. A holder of an Epoch’s Work reads Fate I from Ascension, the early grip, which is why a Moto child can read the first rung at an age when other children are reading their sums, and why the rest of the world dislikes hearing about it. Fate’s yield reads from the same table as everyone else’s, and no drill helps the reading: everything you understand is made of the thing you are trying to move, as The Three Paths explains at more length than anyone enjoys. Fate’s price is not the yield. It is the share a pull costs, below, and the knot after it.
Pell Oakshot, called the Long Odds, gave twenty-three years to the Fate Path and was known from Sealhall to the Wend as the dullest duelist on the circuit, a thin woman in a plum-colored coat who stood still, talked too much and lost on points. In the final at the Saltgate Cod Fair she drew Anders Holm, a Stage above her and a head taller, in a gilt harness his cousin had mended cheap, and for four exchanges he broke things on her while the crowd bayed for the finish. Then she went still in a different way. Her breath held on a count that was not the count of the exchange, and the ring went slightly too tidy, and people along the rope stopped chewing without knowing why. Holm’s left greave strap, which had been going for a month, let go as his weight came onto it, his foot slid a hand’s width on the wet boards, and her cut, an ordinary cut, was already there, and it went in under his arm. She fell over a moment after he did. This is what she was reading, face down:
[Pull: landed · Fate II, Drawn]
[Essence: 6% ▓░░░░░░░░░]
[Hit: both eyes bleeding. Sight dimmed by half.]
[Knot: one, small. Owed within days.]

The bookies paid at forty to one and watched her for a repeat for the rest of her career, which ran eleven more years. It never came. She had no grip, and a lean that size from a soul without one is a thing that lands once, if ever. Asked at the Fair how she had done it, she said that if she knew, it would not have worked.









































RungWhat it can doUnreadHas a fate, an Attraction Layer and a perfectly good ability to keep a promise, and holds no thread of anything. Nearly everyone aliveI · TouchedHas felt one. They know the strap is about to go and the bridge is a bad idea, and on a rare day they can lean on that for most of a reserve and a nosebleed, and it often fails anywayII · DrawnCan bring one thread down on purpose and hold it, for one thing that was already on its way to happening. One lean on the odds in a fight, if the fight lasts long enough to set it. As far as anyone without a grip has ever goneIII · SpinnerCan hold a thread long enough to twist it: one prerequisite of one blow taken away or handed to somebody else, at a ruinous priceIV · KnotwrightCan tie threads to one another and set them beforehand, so that one thing’s happening hangs on another’s: the wall stands until the bell, the company breaks when the flag does. A few at once, and the holder is then in bed for a weekV · WeaverCan move a whole field: weather, supply, panic, the hour a column arrives. The old woman under the plain banner at Akagawa did this, once, with eleven years behind it, and four of her people carried her home. Each side’s first job in a war is to find these peopleInvertedCuts where the others pull. A bond, a debt, an inheritance, what ties a blow to its landing: parted, and nothing in the world is quick to tie it again. Taking a blessing back, which Hataraki can do with two Works or two Moto, looks very like it from outside. A mark on any rung; the old books called it SevererΩ · AbsoluteThe Layer dissolves as a boundary, and the holder is part of what is being pulled on. The Archons, Sovereign across all three planes, stand here, and Uurgath and Urion stand somewhere the table cannot describe
The yield, one table
The three roads side by side, with what is lost on the way at each rung. All three share their figures, and the folk names are each road’s own word for the rung.





























































RungBody (the Shell, raw Aether into matter)Spirit (the Core, Essence onto souls)Fate (the Layer, a pull)Yield (η)UnreadBlows and the coatSmall stamped work, and a line on a soulRange, Pressure and bonds, and no pullthe Stage’s own figure: about 0.30 at Murmuring, 0.35 at Welling, 0.40 at Ascension, 0.45 at Flourishing, 0.60 to 0.70 at SplinteringIMuridicListenerTouched0.60 to 0.70: roughly 30 to 40% lostIIHarmonicAnswererDrawn0.75 to 0.85: roughly 15 to 25% lostIIIResonantConfessorSpinner0.90 to 0.95: roughly 5 to 10% lostIVLuminousShepherdKnotwrightabout 0.97: almost nothing lostVRadiantFerrymanWeaver1.00 and above: more arrives than the numbers promise, and about 1.2 on the practitioner’s own ground at ArchmasterΩAbsoluteAbsoluteAbsoluteno longer a measurement
An Inverted rung carries no figure of its own and reads the yield of its numeral.
Where the lost share goes depends on the layer, and the three are not alike. What the Shell loses burns in its own furnace, and shows as heat on the skin and in the air: the Shell is the athanor, the furnace that never goes cold, and that heat is the furnace burning, never power thrown away. What the Core loses is paid in the Core as a hollowing, a cold and a flattening of color, and never as heat. What a pull loses stays on the Layer as a debt, the knot, which the world collects later.
The jump from II to III is the largest single gain in fidelity on any road, which is why a Spirit III Auditor walked the Barn to death around the Harl Cross market. The full account of that night is on the Shell’s page, where the field average by rank also lives, with the rule for which to read: a read rung overrides the rank’s figure. And a good figure on the Fate column buys clean delivery and never an easy pull. A Fate V Weaver still pays in years, in blood and sometimes in everything, because what she is spending against is the distance of the result from likely, and no rung has ever shortened that.
What a pull costs
A pull is priced by Fate Mastery against distance from likely, as a share of the reserve, which for a Fate worker is Essence. The Measurewrights keep this table in pencil, and the people on it do not fill out forms. Read it for one result in one fight. A whole field is a great many of these, set beforehand, and it is paid for in years on top.





















































Fate MasteryAlready on its way (the strap is going)Could go either wayAgainst the oddsLong oddsNext to impossibleI · TouchedMost of the reserve, and it often failsAll of it, and it usually failsOut of reachOut of reachOut of reachII · DrawnAbout halfMost of itAll of it, and it often failsOut of reachOut of reachIII · SpinnerAbout a thirdAbout halfMost of itAll of it, and it often failsOut of reachIV · KnotwrightAbout a fifthAbout a thirdAbout halfMost of itAll of it, and it usually failsV · WeaverAbout a tenthAbout a fifthAbout a thirdAbout halfAll of it, and it may still fail
A registered card’s own price for its own pulls governs its holder, as a card’s own yield does. A Work moves the failure on that table and leaves the share alone. A vow appears nowhere on it, because a vow spends the soul’s own share and reaches for nothing above it. The table is also only the first of two bills. Every pull on it, landed or failed, leaves a knot that the world collects afterward, sized by the same distance from likely, and no Work has ever shrunk one. How to see a pull coming, how long the warning runs and what the knot does are set out in The Tell and the Knot. And what lies past the right-hand column is the Stage XII soul emptied to the floor with nothing to show for it, which the Archives hold on file several times over.
The older registers kept these rungs as three ladders, Aether Class, Essence Class and Thread Class, Ø to Ω, each with a sixth lateral rung; an old slip’s Aether III is Body III now, and its sixth rungs, Voidic, Sin-Eater and Severer, are the Inverted mark.
What People Do About It
They brag. The class is the first thing on a fighter’s lips and the first thing on a slate, chalked beside Stage and Path and color. It costs nothing to claim, and the coil cannot contradict it.
They lie. Only a stronger Gnosis Perception against a weaker Resilience Ward can read the name, and everything else is an estimate said aloud. Every crew has met a Stormblade whose aura had a suspiciously ferry-shaped band about it. A sworn statement of your class before a proper court is another matter, because an oath is small Fate, and Windows and the Sheet sets out what it costs.
They hire by it. A class on a commission bill is shorthand for what a person will be good at on the worst day of the job. Merchants pay more for an honest Contract Hand than for a Stage over her.
They get embarrassed by it. The name arrives on the window at the moment of greatest pride, and it is usually a remark about the owner’s character. Coward’s Patience has held the Cutwall stair for twenty-six years and answers to it.
They argue about what it proves. Measurewrights will tell you for free that the offer proves the Continuum (the whole lawful order of reality) reads biography, and for a fee that it proves no such thing. The priests of half a dozen faiths claim the name as a calling and the other half as an accusation. The Measurewrights’ hall has produced four monographs on whether a class names a person’s life or nudges it, and the only settled finding is that Wallbreakers have stopped reading them.
Read next: Windows and the Sheet, for where the name and the rungs show up; Skills and Traits, for what it hands you; The Trait System, Release Forms and Domains, for the one concept getting louder; Soul Wounds and the Menders and The Tell and the Knot, for what the Spirit and Fate roads leave behind; and The Sixty Wellsprings, for the lens it all comes through.

the-magic-system/the-soul-and-the-climb/.content:
The place where a soul’s own law outranks the world’s: how it first flickers, who can call one, how long it holds, what happens when two meet, how it grows at last into a Realm, and what it does to the person holding it when it goes out

“When belief holds, the world begins to answer.”
Guild proverb, carved over the door of the assay house at Sealhall, and scratched out and recarved by somebody with a grudge at least twice a decade

Justiciar Ambrose Tick, Stage VIII, heard land cases at Hawes Bridge on the Kessen for thirty-eight years, a long thin man in a plum gown with a permanent cold in his head, and the song calls him the most tedious person who ever drew breath, which he would have taken as a professional compliment. In the autumn of 662 two armies of the Hundred Crowns came down both banks to settle a boundary he had already ruled on, four thousand men in yellow and green with their trumpets going and the bookies riding behind them on mules. He walked out to the middle of the bridge with his clerk and a folding stool. He sat down, blew his nose, and said what he had said at the opening of every sitting of his working life, not very loudly.
"ORDER."
His aura came up the dull gold of old sealing wax and it did not stop at his skin. It ran out along the planks and down over both banks, until three hundred yards of the Kessen valley had gone the color of a lamp in a records room. A lancer of the Greens at full gallop came to a walk and looked down at his horse in astonishment. Every sword inside that light slowed as it rose and stopped a finger’s width from whatever it had been meant for, and it stayed there, humming, because nobody in the field could now do anything to anybody until their case was called. The clerk opened the book. That was the Long Sitting, and for the eight hundred men inside it the law of swords had been adjourned. The other three thousand stood outside the edge with their mouths open, and then, this being the Midmarch, sat down and started a book of their own.
He called them in order, and each man stated his grievance. A surprising number found they did not have one, sheathed, and went home. At the hour of lamps Dame Hild Aske, Marshal of the Yellows, Stage VIII and in no mood, rode to the edge and bawled her own art across the river, and a wall of furnace red rolled over the meadow and met the gold in a seam you could have walked along. For a quarter of an hour the two of them fought for that ground on nothing but the weight of their souls, while eight hundred men with their swords in the air watched the light change on one another’s faces. Her Dominion was the better, and the seam came on toward the bridge. Then the clerk, who had done this to better advocates, stood up and read her case out of order: her name, her father’s name, and the toll he had owed on that bridge since before she was born. She turned her head to answer. The gold went back over her like a tide over a sandcastle, and he found against her, with costs.
He held it for nine hours, and then his reserve fell to a tenth and it went out. A Domain pays when it ends. The collapse came off the bridge in one ring of struck air that took out the middle span and put the Justiciar, the stool and the clerk into the Kessen, and every blow still hanging over a case he had not reached fell at once, about four hundred of them. Then came the bill in the coin of the idea, as it does with the big ones. A court that sits must hear its list. Ambrose Tick lived another twenty-six years, and for all of them he could not walk past an argument. He stopped, unfolded the stool and heard it out, both sides, in the rain, on a bridge, in a burning house. His family wrote to him. The bridge at Hawes is a very bad place to start a fight to this day.
A child can say the whole of it: inside his yard, you wait your turn. What follows is how the Measurewrights say it, with the reasons.
At a Glance
What it is. A Domain is a space where a practitioner’s inner law becomes local law: a soul whose doctrine the ground takes as its own. It is the third size of one idea: the Trait is the idea, the Release is the idea worn on a transformed body, and the Domain is the world obeying it.
How it looks. That depends on the road. On the Body road the owner’s aura leaves the skin and fills the ground, the light, air and temperature change to suit, and everyone inside feels it as a pressure behind the eyes. A Spirit Domain leaves the room looking exactly as it did, and a thing in it has stopped being what it was. A Fate Domain is dust lying still and flames standing straight, and a thing that cannot happen until something else has. All three are called aloud and form as they are named. See On Each Road, below.
What it costs. Reserve for every second it stands, more for a larger or shakier field, and far more inside someone else’s. When it goes out, a shockwave that spares nobody, its owner included.
How it is beaten. Step out of it, outlast it, break the holder’s attention, read what it rests on, or arrive two Stages up.
Example. Corra Vell, Stage VII, says “Smelter’s Yard” and a courtyard goes forge-hot and orange. That is a seed. It holds about three minutes from a full reserve and it dies if somebody shouts the right name. See Release Forms.
What It Is
A soul has three layers, and the Attraction Layer is the one that holds bonds, vows and claims. A Domain begins when that layer claims territory on the Plane of Fate (the plane of Attraction Force and Obsession Force, where what is possible can be moved) and the claim reflects downward into physical and spiritual law. Inside the line, the owner’s doctrine outranks the world’s settled habits for as long as it is held, and the ground gives way exactly as far as the owner’s soul has truly become that doctrine. A soul has grown heavy enough to dent reality, and reality has stopped resisting the dent.
Domains are grown, and then they are called. No technique stands in for one and no manual contains one. The soul comes to it by living, and what nobody has ever done is call a Domain the soul has not grown. Once it is there, the owner opens it on purpose, by name, as deliberately as throwing a punch and a good deal more expensively.
The Stage grants a Domain, and a Grade never does. A ten-year veteran with a magnificent Dominion at Stage VI has a very heavy presence and no Domain. A Stage VIII with a modest one can have a small, bad, real Domain. Dominion and the lead road’s Mastery decide how wide it runs and how steady it stands. The Stage decides whether it can stand at all, and anyone at Stage VIII can have one, their own concept made real, with the fame, the rivals and the bounties that follow it around.
A Domain is Fate’s business, whoever holds it. The claim is made by the Attraction Layer, a soul’s own share of fate, so every Domain stands under the authority of the Plane of Fate, whichever Path its owner came up by. A hitter at Stage VIII can have one as surely as anyone. What the Fate Path buys is more say inside it, and that is the whole of its advantage here.
Every Domain needs no Fate Mastery and pulls no thread. The claim comes out of the soul’s own share, which every soul has, so a hitter who has never felt a thread can stake one. Holding it is another matter, and the upkeep reads the Mastery of the holder’s lead road. On the Body and Spirit roads it is the Second Release that calls and holds one; on Fate, the One.
On Each Road
The claim is the same everywhere, and what the field rules follows the road.





















































BodySpiritFateThe field rulesMatter. Weight, heat, the state of stone. Everyone can see it: the air goes forge-hot and the light turns orangeMeanings. What a thing is taken to be. The room looks unchanged, nobody’s hair moves, and the blade in your hand has stopped being a bladeConditions. What has to be so before anything can happen. The Long Sitting is one: no blow lands until its case is calledWhat calls and holds itThe Second ReleaseThe Second ReleaseThe OneThe upkeep readsBody MasterySpirit MasteryFate MasteryWhat holds it smallThe Fate gates. Radius, Sovereignty and Gravity stop at 400 without the Fate Path (its Path Stages V and VI open them), so a Body holder’s Domain is real, tight and easily out-heldThe same gates, and a body that dies out of position while it holdsReserve, since the gates stand open, and the ground: rich Aetheric ground crowds the radius, and heavy Thread Weight extends itWhat pays the upkeepCharge, and it throws heatEssence, and it hollowsEssence, spent through the Layer as the soul’s own share. No Thread is pulledWhat it adds to forceThe Body bonus as usual, and no moreThe Spirit bonus at range, on souls, and no more. It moves no matter[[The Magic System/Fracture of Worlds — The Living System/III. Physical Force (Part Eleven)A fighter on two roadsField on the lead road, gates of the road behind a Stage late, all bonuses at three-quartersThe sameThe same
No Domain on any road pulls a thread, so none leaves a knot for the world to collect later. Releases and Domains by Path sets the three beside each other, with what each spends on upkeep and how each holder flags.
So a hitter’s Domain is a small hard yard, a line-writer’s is a room where the words have changed, and a Fate holder’s is a very large place where the conditions are somebody else’s, and the last of those is the one the bookies refuse to price.
Any concept will serve. The Archives hold a Domain of the way out, one of a toll bridge, one of a shut door, one in which the bell decides who may rest, and one that has never been described by anybody who agreed to go back.
The Road, Stage by Stage
The road has two kinds of step that are easy to run together, and the old literature did. One is the flicker, which happens to a person once, at a Threshold (the crossing from one Stage to the next). The other is the calling, which a person learns.



























































StageWhat happensHow longWhat it needsThe Threshold into VIIThe flicker. A one-time burst of the person’s own Trait, the first fragile territory, which is the lived Catalyst for Refraction. It follows the road: a Body flicker rules matter (the pints fell upward), a Spirit one meanings, a Fate one conditionsSeconds, as a rule. Gaffer Tom Underhay’s ran four, and every pint in the taproom fell upward. Penny Thyra’s ran four minutes on the Ottermouth bridge, and the Guild is still cross about itNo Release. It cannot be repeated by wanting toVII · RefractionThe seed. With a Second Release, or on the Fate road the One, the flicker can be called back and held, as a fragile field the size of the room or yard it stands inMinutes. Set on the card as time from a full reserveThe Second Release or the One, found and mastered by fighting. Far fewer people have one than have reached this StageVIII · TranscendenceThe true Domain. A piece of the soul’s lattice accepts the signature for good. It is grown by living and called aloudHours. It survives small disruption, and it takes real force to shake itThe Stage, the Second Release or the One, and the livingThe Threshold into IXThe first flicker of a Realm, on the same terms: once, unbidden, the Catalyst and no more, and on the same road as the Domain under itA momentNo ReleaseX · Realization, and aboveThe Realm. A Domain grown into a field that can hold other fields inside it, with the Wellspring’s second color at its edge. Pacts, artifacts and law begin to set into the terrain, and the Continuum (the whole lawful order of reality) has to make room. It opens by each road’s own door, and most who hold one get there at Dissonance or EmanationAll day, if the reserve allowsThe road’s own door (The Realm, below): the Third Release on the Body road, the Second grown whole on the Spirit road, the One on Fate, and the door’s own Catalyst on topXI to XII · Dissonance, EmanationThe leak. Effects run without active holding, and a mood becomes weatherAlwaysHaving lived through the middle of the ladderXIII · PrincipalityThe registered law. The Continuum enters a law the person embodies, and the land carries itLonger than they willXIV · ZenithNo seam. Domain and person cannot be told apart
The Catalyst at each of those Thresholds is the one demand met in the lead layer’s terms, as The Sixteen Stages sets out floor by floor: the seed comes out of a body pressed past holding, a truth faced aloud, or a vow held where it should break. A soul that goes into seclusion for it does so on its own road’s ground, Aetheric Density for the Body, Echo Depth for the Spirit and Thread Weight for Fate.
So a person reaches Stage VII on one involuntary flash and may then spend twenty years unable to do it again. That is the commonest shape of a career at Refraction, and every veteran corps has someone who will tell you about the night the beer turned green.
The bought road. A Draft called the Domain Seed Vitrifier sells the flicker, and a blessing can too. It is poured by road, like every breakthrough Draft: on a Salt base for a Body soul, on Core stock for a Spirit one, and on the Layer reagent for a Fate one, which is the dearest of the three and a crime to hold in every realm. Neither sells what comes after it. A bought Stage VIII has the right to a Domain and nothing to open, because the Second Release, or the One, must be found and mastered by fighting, and no purse has ever opened one. Sects teach the road, and that is a large part of what they are for. See The Ladder and the Draft.
Calling One
The name goes first. A true Domain forms as it is named. The volume belongs to the person: a showman bawls it across a valley, and Asahina Shigeko said Kaerazu no Mon almost too low to hear. A Second Release on its own may go out silent, weak and without its first rise, as its page sets out, and it will hold a field that way. Nobody has ever opened a true Domain without saying what it is, and the beat that costs has killed people.
The window fills. The holder’s own window shows the name, what changed and a bar draining, whatever the room is doing, and it is for the holder alone:
[DOMAIN: THE LONG SITTING]
[Changed: within the field no blow lands until its case is called]
[Workings: one Grade up · cap counted]
[Held: ████████░░]
[Reserve: 71%]

It counts on the stack. Inside a field the Second Release or the One lifts the owner’s workings one Grade, and a Third lifts its one stated effect by two. All of that counts toward the cap on self-boosts, two steps on the hidden scale over the sustainable figure on the card, and only outside help goes past it. See Stacking and Spending.
What the old headings are. The Guild files what a Domain does under behaviors, and every working fighter ignores the filing until it matters, since each one leans on a different stat. There were six for a very long time, and all six describe a field that rules matter, because the clerks who drew up the list could see those. The Bench has since marked each with its road and added the two it had been misfiling.



























































The headingThe roadWhat it does inside the lineWhat governs itLow-G, High-GBodyWeight changesDominion SovereigntyHushBody, for sound and force. Spirit, where what will not carry is a thrown lineSound, force or a working will not carryDominion Pressure, Harmonics SuppressionHeat-Invert, Phase-StabilizeBodyA set temperature or a set state of matterThe WellspringVectoringBodyBolts curve, distances lie, approaches slide offDominion Sovereignty, Dexterity FinesseConstruct SustainBody, for made matter. Spirit, for a spirit called and keptWhat was summoned stays without attentionDominion Gravity, Ardency DensityInertial DominionBodyMoving things stop, turn or leap at the holder’s wordDominion Sovereignty, Vitality AbsorptionGlossSpiritA thing is taken to be something else. Nothing in the room moves, and a blade is not a blade, or a man’s saber is not hisDominion Sovereignty and Gnosis Analysis, against the Integrity and Anchoring of whoever is insidePreconditionFateA thing cannot happen until something else has. Nothing is stopped by forceDominion Sovereignty and Dominion’s Fate Sub-Stat, against Persistence and Continuity
For a generation the Long Sitting was filed under Inertial Dominion, since every sword in it stopped. It is a Precondition with a docket: not one of those blades was held by force, and each simply lacked leave to land. A Fate Path holder gains the most from any of the eight: inside a formed Domain, that Path’s amplification can pass a Body Path fighter’s raw advantage outright.
When Two Meet
A field meeting a field is the great spectator sport of the upper ladder. The border shows as light changing color across the ground, bystanders feel both, and the odds-men move fast. The Continuum settles it in order.

Stage first. A field two or more Stages above the other simply overwrites it. Nobody fights for that ground, and the lower field goes out with its owner standing in it.
Otherwise Dominion holds the ground. Between fields closer than that, the owner with the higher Sovereignty and Gravity holds the territory, and the weaker field erodes from its edge, costing its owner more with every yard.
A read can flip it. Find what the field rests on, the owner’s focus, its edge, or the thing they are guarding, press there, and the border moves back. Dame Hild Aske had the better Dominion. She also had a father.
The Wellsprings have a say. Fields built from contrary Wellsprings, which each entry in the Sixty names, grind each other down, and neighbors may lie easy together. The ideas decide who holds; whatever is left over at the border behaves as the world always has, so heat against frost still leaves the seam steaming.
At dead level, the truer one. A Domain built from an honestly lived truth is denser than one built from adopted belief. Tempering Coherence and Maturity are the tiebreak, and this is the part that makes rich people angry.

A Realm can do what no Domain can: go round another field and close, and hold it inside, still running, with its owner in it. Ask anyone from Dornhold, which burned for nineteen years afterward.
The Realm
What closed round the marshal’s field at Dornhold was a flicker, the one a soul is given at the crossing into Invocation, once, with no release behind it. The Realm proper is the far end of the climb. It opens no earlier than Realization, the tenth Stage, on any road, and only through that road’s own door, with a Catalyst of its own done under contest and never bought. A bought Stage X has no door.

































RoadWhat it needs firstThe door’s CatalystWhat the Realm rulesWhere it breaksBodyThe Third Release, heldAnother’s world carried, and not let fallThe ground other fields stand onIt cannot grip: whatever lifts or pulls away parts itSpiritThe Second, held as a true Domain for yearsAnother’s whole meaning held inside your own, and both left trueThe sense in which other fields are readWhat means nothing, or will not be read, gives it nothing to holdFateThe OneA claim others stand on, kept for themThe leave under which other fields may standIt falls the moment its holder breaks a word of their own
Each takes its price in its own idea: the Body holder grows heavier by every world they bore, the Spirit holder comes out of every holding a little persuaded by the person they fought, and the Fate holder’s standing pays for every claim it warranted that was later broken. A Realm still yields to a field two Stages up. Releases and Domains by Path gives the three doors in full.
What It Costs

Reserve, continuously. A Domain drains by its width (Dominion Radius), by how shaky it is (Dominion Gravity), and by how hostile the ground is. Holding one inside someone else’s costs a great deal more. The drain is written on the card as time from a full reserve, and it is paid in what the holder holds: Charge for a Body holder, Essence for a Spirit or a Fate one.
The ground. Each road’s field is cheaper on its own ground, Aetheric Density for a field of matter, Echo Depth for one of meanings, Thread Weight for one of conditions. Rich Aetheric ground also crowds a Domain’s radius, and a Fate holder’s Range with it, while heavy Thread Weight extends them, which is why the Long Sitting ran three hundred yards on a bridge where thirty-eight years of boundaries had been decided, and would have run a good deal less in a mine.
The limit. It ends on its own when the reserve falls to a tenth. Below that lies Starvation, which takes a Body holder in the flesh and a Spirit holder in the memory. A Fate holder’s reserve is Essence, so it takes her in the memory too, with her luck curdling on top.
Afterward. The Second Release or the One leaves the Crystal Overgrown (swollen and spilling) until a full night’s sleep, and the Third or a Realm for a day and a night. Held past the limit, a Second or the One means a Crystal Fracture Event, and a Third or a Realm may cost the Trait.
Collapse. A field that fails produces a Resonance Shockwave, sized to its width and density. It strikes everything in the former territory, and that includes the owner. A seed’s is a slap of hot wind and flying cobbles, and it will put a fighter on his back. A true Domain’s takes bridges with it.
Its own price. A big art charges in the coin of its own idea, on top of everything above, and the card says how. The toll-keeper must pay the toll, the landlady is the last one out, and the Justiciar hears the list.

How It Is Beaten
Most Domains can be answered by someone at their own Stage, and none is owed such an answer: a field keeps the flaw its idea gives it, and some have no answer short of somebody two Stages up. Under every way on this list lie the four answers the benches teach: the contrary idea, a soul further refined in the holder’s own idea, ground that already holds another idea (deep Echo, heavy Thread Weight, another Domain), and a flat refusal of the claim.

Before. The name costs a beat and the aura leaves the skin first. Strike into the beat, or be somewhere else.
Walk out. Every field has an edge, which is the most useful fact on this page. Three thousand men at Hawes Bridge sat that afternoon out.
Outlast it. The clock is the counter, on a bar only the owner can see. Make them hold it, keep your distance, and take the fight onto salted, bled or thin ground, where the reserve cannot refill.
Break the attention. A seed collapses when attention breaks: a wound, a shout, a name that matters. A true Domain shrugs off the small ones and takes real force.
Read it. Every law has a thing it rests on and a thing it left out. A docket can be read out of order, from either side.
Bring someone two Stages up. It is expensive, and it never fails.
Stand clear of the end. If the owner is going to lose it, be outside the line when they do, and make sure they are inside.

What They Call It













































WhoThe wordThe argumentA Guild roll, a MeasurewrightDomain, seed, RealmIt is an Attraction Layer claim, and the rest is decorationBracket crowds, in CommonGoing loud; his yard, her yardIs it a yard or is it a seed? The Climb as the Archives Now Reckon It: Stage, Level and the Hands

“The soul climbs, the life piles up, the hands learn. Everything else is somebody reading one of the three.”
Chalked over the door of the assay house at Waxgate, where the old wall of figures used to be. The clerks painted the figures out themselves and say they sleep better.

In the autumn lists at Harl Cross, in the year the Wendle locks were rebuilt, the house of Stanmere sent its youngest son to the sand in a coat of blued plate with gilt at every rivet and a long sword the Appraisers’ stall had priced aloud that morning as Grade A and Very Rare. Leofric Stanmere was nineteen. He had been bought to Glory, the sixth Stage, by four breakthrough Drafts in four quiet rooms, and he was an Expert by rank on every slate in the Cross. When he walked out, the lamp flames along the rail leaned toward him like grass in a wind, and the unwoken in the cheap stands bent at the knee without meaning to, which is what an Expert does to people who have never woken. The bookies made him one to nine.
His opponent was Elswyth Ashby, the lock-keeper at Wendle, an Adept, Stage IV, in a leather jerkin her mother had worn and a quarterstaff with an iron shoe. She had held the Wendle gates through three flood nights while the river tried to take the town, and she had pulled eleven people out of the race with a boathook on the worst of them. Everyone who drank in the Cross knew two things about her. The water in the lock would not lie flat when she stood near it, and had not for a year. And she had never once been offered a Stage, by a Draft or a sect or anybody else.
Stanmere’s first blow put her through the barrier and into the stands. The second she took across the staff and the forearms, and the staff held, and the forearms did not, and she did not fall. Witnesses on the east side swear the sand under her went dark and wet, as if the river had come up through it, and that the heat came off her in a wave they felt on their faces. Then she stood up straight out of the wreck of the rail, and she was Splintering, the fifth Stage, and an Expert like him, and he had never in his life been hit by anyone who meant it.
She broke his sword hand at the wrist on the next exchange and his collarbone on the one after. He had the weight of a Glory soul behind every swing, and his blows were very heavy, and they went where a boy who had trained for three years in a walled garden sent them. His Crystal spilled power into the air every time he moved and none of it would gather into anything he could use. Hers had been ready for a year and had only been waiting for a reason.
The Archives keep the slate from that day under glass. Three marks are chalked beside each name: the Stage, the Level and the staff or the sword. The bookies at Harl Cross had read the first one. This page is about the other two, and about why the first one is still the one everybody says.
The One Sentence
The soul climbs Stages, and each Stage asks one thing of it. The life climbs Level, by everything hard and real a person has done. The hands climb skills, by use. Everything else is read from those three.
That is the whole of the reckoning, and the Archives would like it chalked over every hall door in the four quarters, as the assay house at Waxgate has done. Older books carried a dozen more measurements than this, each with its own ladder and its own clerk, and the halls spent a generation discovering that every one of them was a way of reading one of these three badly.

Stage is the soul. It is what the Crystal has become, crossing by crossing, and it is the thing that matters and the thing people say.
Level is the life. It is the count of what a person has lived through and done, and it is what lets a Stage hold.
Skills are the hands. They rise by doing, and they are what a fight is actually made of.

Leofric Stanmere had a great deal of the first and very little of the other two. Elswyth Ashby had the other two in full and was owed the first.
Stage, Said as Rank
There are sixteen Stages, and nobody outside a hall says their names in ordinary talk. What people say is the rank, one of nine words that every child in the four quarters knows, and the Stage name is the precise term for when precision is wanted: “a Journeyman, Ascension, and close to Flourishing.”




























































































































StageNameRankThe Crystal looksLenses 
The Crystal’s look is how the stone looks to anyone who can see a soul, in the jewelers’ words: Clouded through the four lowest Stages, Faceted through the Expert years, then Fire, Flawless, Starred and Absolute. It follows the Stage. It is a description, and nobody climbs it.
Lenses. A soul holds one home lens, its first Wellspring, through the Adept years. From Expert it can safely harmonize one more at each rank, so a Master holds three and a Paragon six. A Clouded soul may try for a second lens early, and some do, and the menders see the tears. The base hue a person’s aura shows is the lens they have tempered on longest.
The same words serve two worlds. A fighter’s rank is their Stage. A tradesman’s rank is the Accord title for their trade, earned by the work, as The Tiered Path sets out. So a Master smith may be an Apprentice by Stage, and Master Venn at the Waxgate forge, who makes swords for Grandmasters, is an Apprentice the moment he steps onto the road. People mix the two up constantly, and a fair share of the Accord’s lawsuits begin with a merchant who thought he was hiring one kind of Master and got the other.
The Sixteen Stages gives every Stage in full: its story, what it is from inside, what it looks like and what the folk call it.
What Opens a Stage
A Stage opens when two things are true at once. Its Catalyst has been met, and the soul’s Level can hold it.
The Catalyst is one deed to each Stage, and the Crystal asks it in the terms of the Path the soul leans on: in the flesh and in matter for a Body soul, in a soul or a meaning for a Spirit one, in a bond, an oath or the odds for a Fate one. It comes by crisis, by a long guarded seclusion, by tribulation, or it is handed over in a breakthrough Draft or a blessing. Stage II’s Catalyst is the first lens itself: a Wellspring’s raw Aether, touched under pressure, which is how most people learn which Wellspring they belong to. The Sixteen Stages carries all three forms of every Catalyst, floor by floor.
A Stage is rare, and it is paid for. The Level climbs all year, and the hands get better every week a person works them; that is the climb anyone can watch. A Stage is another thing. Most fighters cross only a handful in a lifetime, and the great ones cross perhaps one in a hard year, sometimes none in five. Every road to it costs blood. A crisis leaves its wound, a seclusion is months of something going wrong in a locked room, and a tribulation takes somebody standing too near. Ask anyone who has crossed what it cost them, and they will tell you, or they will change the subject, and both are answers.
The hold. Each Stage is held from a Level, and below that Level the Crystal has opened a door it cannot yet fill. The Stages of one rank hold close to its floor, so a soul that has crossed into a new rank soon has the Level for the next Stage or two of it.



























































StageHolds from LevelStageHolds from LevelI · Murmuring1IX · Invocation215II · Welling5X · Realization230III · Ascension15XI · Dissonance301IV · Flourishing30XII · Emanation320V · Splintering101XIII · Principality401VI · Glory115XIV · Zenith420VII · Refraction130XV · Revelation500, and Level runs on past it, unnumberedVIII · Transcendence201XVI · ApexThe last approach, which the Codex declines to number
Buying is the door and nothing more. A breakthrough Draft or a blessing will supply any Catalyst on the ladder, and the Crystal goes to the melt and comes out a Stage higher, in a quiet room, with nobody for miles the wiser. The Level is still owed. So is the Mastery, and so is every Release. A purse can open the door. Whatever comes after it has to be lived.
Overgrown. A Stage held under its Level leaves the Crystal Overgrown. Power spills out of it with nowhere to go: lamps lean toward the person, tempers stain the air around them, their Mastery reads low or not at all, and no Release will come, whatever they do, until Level catches up. It makes no difference whether the Stage was bought by a great house or met early by a prodigy who walked into the right disaster at fourteen. The heir and the prodigy are the same case, and the halls can spot either one from across a yard. Leofric Stanmere was Overgrown, and every lamp at Harl Cross said so before he drew.
Residual Strain. The opposite case is worse to stand beside. A soul may climb a long way in Level inside its rank, and that is ordinary: most fighters grind up toward the top of their group for years, and nobody thinks the worse of them. The trouble begins at the old gates. When Level passes the top of the soul’s group with no Catalyst to the next Stage, the pressure builds in the Crystal with nowhere to go:





























The soul stands atStrain begins past LevelStages I to IV, Initiate to Adept100Stages V to VII, the Expert years200Stages VIII to X, Master300Stages XI and XII, Grandmaster400Stages XIII and XIV, Archmaster500
The veteran stuck at the gate is the strange one, and the dangerous one. The Strain shows in the room: water that will not lie flat, dogs that will not settle, a cold or a heat the season does not explain. Held long enough, it can fracture the Crystal. It can also break a seal that was never broken, and this is the most important thing the Archives have learned about it: Strain can wake the unwoken. A commoner who has lived hard enough for long enough builds pressure in a sealed soul until something cracks it open, and late wakings, in a widow of fifty or a drover of sixty, are a known thing in every quarter, and are not always a happy one.
Any real work moves Level. Danger overcome moves it most, and beating something stronger than you most of all, which is why crews still argue over who landed the last blow. But a flood night held moves it, and a plague nursed through, and fifty years at a trade. A baker can stand at Level 140 and never have been in danger in her life. There is one Level, and a lifetime’s work counts toward everything Level is read for once the soul wakes. Elswyth Ashby’s Level was flood nights and boathooks, and the Crystal did not care that none of it had been done with a sword.
Mastery: How Far the Reach Runs
Every soul works its Path’s own substance, and Mastery is how well it does. There is one rung for each Path a person walks, numbered I to V, with Ω above them for the very few. Nobody tracks it. The Stage sets how high it may go, and the Level says where under that ceiling the soul stands.
The ceilings. Below Glory, Mastery is not read at all, and the soul works its road by blows, the coat and the Stage’s own figure. The roof then rises a rung at a time up the whole climb, so that the numeral means something at every height: at Glory the ceiling is I; at Refraction, II; at Transcendence and Invocation, III; at Realization and Dissonance, IV; from Emanation through Zenith, V; and Ω only at Revelation and Apex.
The early grip. There is one exception to the silence below Glory. A soul born to one of the Epochs’ lines and holding that line’s instrument (a Moto with a Work of Hataraki, a Zettari with Matla, a Yukari with Null-Light) reads rung I on that instrument’s road from Ascension, the third Stage. The blood opens one ladder early, and the assay houses keep a separate book for those children.
The rungs by Level. A soul reads I from Glory’s hold at Level 115, II from 150, III from 215, IV from 260 and V from 340, each no higher than its Stage’s ceiling allows. A soul fresh across a Stage therefore reads a rung under its new roof until its Level grows into the Stage: a new Refraction soul at 130 reads I and reaches II at 150, a new Transcendent at 201 reads II and reaches III at 215, a new Realization soul at 230 reads III and reaches IV at 260, and a new Emanation soul at 320 reads IV and reaches V at 340.
Shown above the rung. Mastery is read from Level for everyone, and the Archives keep no list of people who stand above it. When a soul is seen working past the rung its Level gives, that was an overreach: done once, in that moment, at a price, and the record stands as the night they reached past themselves, never as a rung they hold.






















































RungBody reads matterSpirit reads souls and meaningsFate reads odds and conditionsShare lost on the way outIas the object in handit hearsa leanroughly 30 to 40 parts in a hundredIIby contactit is answereda lean, heldroughly 15 to 25IIIby recognitionit reads a soul whollya prerequisiteroughly 5 to 10IVby lawit holdsa prerequisite, surealmost noneVby law, and wideit holds manya fieldless than none: more arrives than the numbers promiseΩas a whole systemall of itall of itthe question stops meaning anything
The last column is the yield, the share of what a soul puts into a working that reaches the world, as a distillation has its yield. It reads from the Mastery of the Path a working lands through, on this one table for all three roads.
The folk names. The card says Body IV, and so does the assay slip. The people of each road keep their own word for the rung, from the ladders the halls used to chalk:









































RungOn the Body roadOn the Spirit roadOn the Fate roadIMuridicListenerTouchedIIHarmonicAnswererDrawnIIIResonantConfessorSpinnerIVLuminousShepherdKnotwrightVRadiantFerrymanWeaver
A hitter in a Hallenfeld tavern will tell you she is Luminous, and a mender in a Sum-gol temple will tell you the old woman upstairs is a Shepherd, and both mean the fourth rung.
Inverted. Any rung can be held Inverted, a feared and wrong way of working it, in which the soul takes where it ought to give and empties where it ought to fill. It is a mark beside the rung, never a rung of its own: Spirit IV Inverted. The halls do not teach it. Some people arrive at it anyway, and the ones who do are written about.
Fate’s grip. Fate climbs with Level like the other two roads, with one hard limit: without a grip on the thread, a Fate soul stops at II, however long it lives. A grip is a Work or a blessing. Blood alone is not one, and the cadet lines of the great Fate houses, who have the blood and were never given a Work, stop at II like anyone else and are bitter about it in every generation. A grip lifts the ceiling to the Stage’s own, and a blessing that grants one lifts it that far and no further. Fate’s yield reads from the same table as everyone else’s. Its price is the knot, which the world collects later, as The Tell and the Knot explains.
Two Paths. A Path on the card is Mastered, Walked or Studied. A Walked Path, thirty parts in a hundred of the practice or more, opens its gates a Stage late and reads a rung behind the lead until it is mastered. A Studied Path reads two rungs behind and stops at II. All of it reads from Level like the rest, and The Three Paths gives the gates.
No Letter on a Person
The halls used to give people letters. They have stopped, and the Archives were glad to see it go.
Grades are for things. A sword has a Grade and a Rarity, and an Appraiser will tell you both for a fee. So does a crossbow bolt, a ballista shaft, a beast and a bounty. A person has none, aloud or anywhere else. Stanmere’s sword was Grade A. Stanmere was an Expert who had bought his way there, and that is all anyone at the Cross now says of him.
The card keeps the numbers. Every one of a person’s sixty-four Sub-Stats is still on the card, with the points spent on them, and each of the eight Primaries is their total. When two people contest a thing, the numbers are compared under the Stage-gap rules, and the assayers keep the old scale underneath for their arithmetic: a stat a full step ahead on it wins its exchange outright, and a self-boost, whatever its source, stacks no more than two steps over what the card can sustain. Only outside help goes past that. Nobody says the scale aloud of a person, and a clerk who forgets is not thanked for it.
Gear multiplies a whole Primary, all eight of its Sub-Stats together, and all the gear a person wears together lifts any one Primary by half again at the most. A piece above its wearer’s Stage works at half, or fights them. The piece itself still fights at its own Grade and Rarity.
Beasts keep a Stage, a Level and a lean toward one Path underneath, the same as anyone, and are known and bountied by Grade. The Accord says which title may take which Grade of bounty, and every board from the coast to the passes posts the Grade beside the price. The beasts themselves are in The Bestiary.
Pressure on the unwoken reads by the fighter’s rank. An Initiate or an Apprentice brings dread into a room. A Journeyman brings weight, so that people feel it in their shoulders. An Expert bends their knees, as the cheap stands at Harl Cross found out.
The Hands
Skills read as the nine ranks: Initiate, Apprentice, Journeyman, Adept, Expert, Master, Grandmaster, Archmaster, Paragon, the same words as a Stage’s rank and an Accord title. “A Journeyman by Stage and a Master at the anvil” means exactly what it says, and a good deal of the world’s trouble comes from people who only heard the first half.
Trades go anywhere. A trade skill can reach Paragon with no Stage behind it at all. There is a bread-oven in Stannvaard that has been a pilgrimage for forty years, kept by a woman who never woke, and her Baking reads Paragon.
Combat is capped by Stage. A fighting skill cannot rank above its owner’s own Stage rank: a Master’s sword stops at Master, and an Expert’s at Expert.
A trade skill still feeds the Body road. At Journeyman or better with a material, a Body fighter works one rung further into that material than their Mastery would otherwise reach, and never past their ceiling. The mason who fights is a different animal from the soldier who does.
Techniques jump when two things happen together: their skill gains a rank, and a fight pushes them past their old limit. A jump gives one of four things, power, reach, speed or a lower cost, and a bigger name, and the old name stays in use.
Traits have no levels. A Trait reads at the lead Path’s Mastery, and its Release and Domain are the same idea escalating. Below Glory, where Mastery is not read, a Trait works at its base. Skills and Trait Levels holds the older account.
Class: The Name the Soul Offers
A Class is a name, never a number, that the soul offers for how the person has lived. It is first offered at Glory, with Mastery I, and it evolves when the lead Mastery rises. Each evolution brings one move that fits the new name and a lean on where life will spend the person’s stat points from then on. The one wild idea at the heart of a person’s power, their Trait, stays their own through all of it. Bess Tolliver of Threeways, who was Pole-Hand and Riverblade and Floodbreaker before she was anything worse, is the story everyone tells, and Classes and the Three Ladders tells it.
Leofric Stanmere, at Level 74 and Glory, had been offered nothing. His Mastery did not read. The soul offers a name for a life, and he had not had one yet.
Releases, by Path
A Release is the soul’s own law let off its limit in a shape found and mastered by fighting, and the Path decides how many a soul can have. Each one is deeper than the last, and each has its own Catalyst.

































Stage IVStage VIIStage VIIIStage IXBodyFirst ReleaseSecond ReleaseDomainThird ReleaseSpiritFirst ReleaseSecond ReleaseDomainFateThe OneDomain

The Body has three. The First comes of the body broken, refusing to fall: beaten past what it can take, by something that means it, and still standing. The Second comes of a material known so well it obeys at range: one stone or steel or water read to the grain until it answers across a yard of air. The Third comes of the body remade around a wound: a new wound, taken in the fight that asks for it, with the Wellspring helping to build the body again around the break.
The Spirit has two. The First comes of the self said aloud, and true, declared to the face of someone who denies it. The Second comes of a meaning borne for someone else, the sin-eater’s office: a grief or a guilt that another has set down, carried whole.
Fate has one, the One, at Refraction, and it comes of a claim staked on the soul’s own life, and kept: a claim over something outside the self, the claimant’s life forfeit if it fails, held through a whole contest. A claim kept by pulling a thread does not count, because a pull is not a claim. The One is deeper than any First and counts as a Second: it opens the Domain and powers it.

Every Release Catalyst counts only from the Release’s own Stage, must be met against something that means it, and cannot be bought. If a deed would answer both a Release and the next Stage, the Stage takes it. One met while the Crystal is Overgrown prints on the stone and stays locked until Level holds.
Two roads, one count. A soul walking two Paths has the Releases of its lead Path, and no more. The Walked road colors them, so that a Body soul who walks the Spirit road throws a First Release with meaning in it, and it brings none of its own.
Domains stand as they always have. A seed may flicker once at Refraction as the Catalyst that carries a soul into that Stage. Anyone at Transcendence may have a Domain. Only a Second Release, or Fate’s One, can call one up and hold it. Domains has the whole of it.
The Realm is the far end of the climb, and every road reaches it late, by its own door. The crossing into Invocation still carries a first flicker of one, once, on every road. The door itself opens no earlier than Realization, and never for a bought Stage:

































RoadWhat it needs firstThe door’s CatalystWhat the Realm isIts priceBodythe Third Releaseanother’s world carried, and not let fallthe ground other fields stand onthe holder grows heavier by every world they boreSpiritthe Second, held as a true Domain for yearsanother’s whole meaning held inside your own, and both left truethe sense in which other fields are readthe holder comes out a little persuaded by everyone they foughtFatethe Onea claim others stand on, kept for themthe leave under which other fields may standevery broken claim it warranted is billed to the holder’s standing
A Body Realm cannot grip, so whatever lifts or pulls away parts it. A Spirit Realm gives nothing to hold to what means nothing. A Fate Realm falls the moment its holder breaks a word of their own. Release Forms and Releases and Domains by Path give the forms in full.
Drafts, Blessings, Sects and the Accord
Drafts. A tempering Draft gives Level, at the risk of Identity Contamination, which is what happens when a dead monster’s core goes into a living soul and some of the monster comes with it. A breakthrough Draft gives a Catalyst. A fight Draft refills the reserve and leaves a crash that pays for it. All of them are priced about threefold a Stage, and counterfeits are common. The Ladder and the Draft has the trade.
Blessings. A blessing can grant Level, a Catalyst, or both. A Stage blessed in above its Level runs Overgrown like any other.
Sects teach the road to the Catalysts. They put their students into the danger and the truths that meet the Stage and Release Catalysts, teach their techniques and their style, and keep the lore of which lens and which Path suit whom. It is the one thing in the climb a purse cannot buy outright, and the sects know precisely what they are selling when a duke’s daughter turns up at the gate at Glory asking to be hit.
The Accord. Accord titles are earned by commissions. A fighting guild also asks the title’s own rank in Stage, so a Journeyman’s title needs Stage III behind it. A trade guild asks none.
How a Card Reads Now
An assay slip, or a card in the Archives, carries the reckoning in two lines and a third for the roads:

Stage VIII Transcendence · Master (Fire)
Level 238 · Refined · Floodbreaker
Body VIII Mastered, III · Spirit VII Walked 35%, II · Lenses: home + 2

The first line is the Stage, its rank and the Crystal’s look. The second is the Level, the Crystal’s state (Refined when it is sound, Overgrown when it spills, Fractured when it has broken) and the Class. The third is each Path the soul walks, with how far that Path has opened, how it is held and its Mastery, and last the lenses it carries.
Old Words
Old books and old people use a good many words the reckoning above has set aside. They are worth knowing, because most of the world still says them. Where an old card in the Archives reads otherwise than this page, the reckoning wins. Whatever its holder was seen to do still happened, and where it ran past the rung their Level gives, the Archives file it as an overreach on the night it was done.

Tier of Standing. The older registers numbered the nine ranks as Tiers, so that a Master was a “Tier Six” on a hall token. The number is gone and the word is kept.
The Bands. Mortal Foundation, Awakened, Sovereign, Mythic and Absolute were five blocks of a hundred Levels, each with a gate. People still call a Master-rank fighter “a Sovereign” in the North. The edges of the old Bands survive as the hold Levels of Splintering, Transcendence, Dissonance and Principality, 101, 201, 301 and 401, and the old gates are where Residual Strain begins.
The class ladders. Aether Class, Essence Class and Thread Class were three ladders, one to each layer of the Crystal, that the coils used to read. They are Mastery now, and their rung names are the folk names in the table above. Their sixth rungs, Voidic, Hollow and Severer, were the old way of saying Inverted.
The Clear Crystal. The jewelers once had a Clear look between Faceted and Fire. A Refraction soul reads Faceted now, and an old slip that says Clear means the same.
Trait levels. A Trait used to carry a level of its own. Now it reads at the lead Path’s Mastery, and an old card’s Trait level is a guess at the same thing.
The T-tiers. Beasts were once graded T1 to T9. The bounty boards dropped the tiers and post the Grade, and old hunters still say “a T5” of anything that killed someone they knew.
The craft ranks. Skills were once read on six craft ranks of their own, Novice, Apprentice, Journeyman, Master, Grandmaster and Legend, and before that in the fighters’ letters. They read on the nine ranks now, and an old letter crosses plainly: Hollow, F and E are Initiate, D Apprentice, C Journeyman, B Adept, A Expert, S and SS Master, SSS Grandmaster, X and EX Archmaster, and EX+ Paragon. Old masters still call a lifetime’s craft “a Legend’s hand”.
A person’s Grade. “An A-Grade fighter” was ordinary talk a generation ago and is still heard in the dockside rings. The letter belongs to the sword now. The scale under it is still there, in the assayers’ arithmetic, where nobody has to hear it.

Back to The Soul and the Climb.
