the-magic-system/the-soul-and-the-climb/.title: Release Forms
the-magic-system/the-soul-and-the-climb/.content:
How a practitioner turns their own Trait loose, in a form the whole room can see. For the whole system in brief, see How Magic Works.
The Widow Ansa Brack kept the Three Keys at Sallow Ferry for thirty-one years, and the song says she never once raised her voice before the night the Tollgate Free Company came in without paying. The song is wrong, as songs usually are, because the whole town knew that voice. A hundred and forty men in red-and-yellow quarters filled her yard with their horses and their opinions, Harry Stott leaned on her doorpost and told her what he thought the ale was worth, and she came out onto the step with a slop pail and said what she had said at closing every night of her married life.
"EVERYBODY OUT."
Her hands went first, black as old door iron to the wrist. The ring of keys at her belt rose and stood straight out on the air, jangling, and her aura slammed to its full color, a silver shot through with deep violet that lit every face in the yard from underneath. The crowd has always called that one Door-Iron. Then one of the keys turned, by itself, in nothing.
The light went violet from wall to wall, and every man in that yard felt the ground decide he had no business standing on it. They left. They left through the gate, through the hedge and through the side of the stable, in one long bright spill of armor and horses that came down across the river meadow and broke four dozen collarbones. Harry Stott, who had a good grip, went with the rest and left his hand on the doorpost, where it stayed, and it hung over the bar for the next sixty years. That was the Second, the Outgang, a field that ruled the ground of her yard and the weight of everything standing on it.
The bill came with the law, as the big ones do. A landlady is the last one out of a house she closes, and Ansa Brack closed that one with herself on the step. She never set foot inside the Three Keys again. She stood on that step for nineteen years and served through the window. She walked the Body road, which can hold three releases, and the minstrels gave her the Third she never had, an error that has cost several people money.
A child can say the whole of it: she tells you to leave, and you leave. What follows is how a Guild Measurewright says it, at somewhat greater length.
What it is
A release is a practitioner’s Primary Trait (the deepest standing law in their soul) let off the safety limit of the Soul Crystal (the soul itself, in its working form) on purpose, in a shape the Crystal has learned to hold: the same force as an overchannel (forcing the Crystal past its safe ceiling), rehearsed until it keeps a form, a price and a name. A technique is something the practitioner makes with the Trait; a release changes the practitioner, and every technique fired inside it runs through the released Trait.
One idea, three sizes. Trait, Release and Domain are a single concept escalating. The Trait is the idea, the Release is the idea worn on a transformed body, and the Domain is the world obeying it. A kit that reads as three unrelated powers has been filed wrong, and any Measurewright will tell you so for free. See The Trait System for where the idea comes from.
How it looks
RELEASES BY PATHThe lead Path sets how many, each deeper than the last; a Walked Path colors them and brings noneTHE BODYthree ReleasesFirst ReleaseStage IV · Flourishingthe body broken,refusing to fallSecond ReleaseStage VII · Refractiona material known so wellit obeys at rangeThird ReleaseStage IX · Invocationthe body remadearound a woundTHE SPIRITtwo ReleasesFirst ReleaseStage IV · Flourishingthe self said aloud,and trueSecond ReleaseStage VII · Refractiona meaning bornefor someone elseFATEone ReleaseThe OneStage VII · Refractiona claim staked on your life,and keptDeeper than any First, itcounts as the Second: it opensthe Domain and powers it.Domainfrom Stage VIII · TranscendenceA seed may flicker once at Refraction. Only aSecond Release, or the One, calls a Domainup and holds it.The Realmfrom Stage X · RealizationEvery road reaches it late, by its own door:Body through the Third, Spirit through theSecond grown whole, Fate through the One.
The releases. Every release follows one pattern: the body changes, the aura flares, the sound comes, and the Trait’s power rises.









































First ReleaseSecond ReleaseThird ReleaseWhich roads, and from which Stage (step on the soul’s sixteen-step ladder)Body and Spirit, from IV, FlourishingBody and Spirit, from VII, Refraction. Fate’s One opens here too and stands in its placeThe Body alone, from IX, InvocationThe lookOne signature change to the body or the weapon, in any shape the soul takes: skin, eyes, hair, wings, armor, a weapon’s new formThe change spreads into the ground around them as a field. On the Body road it is one where light, air and heat obey the Trait, and everyone inside feels the color shift. A Spirit field leaves the room looking as it did, and a Fate field shows as dust lying still (the table below)The field takes a second color at its edges, the Wellspring’s own (the type of Aether their Crystal is tuned to, the governing idea that changes how their soul uses its power, with its own alchemical character and its own law), and the Wellspring’s voice joins the soundThe powerThe Trait’s workings strike at the top of their Grade (the letter band their force reads in, as a blade’s or a bolt’s does)Inside the field, one full Grade higherInside the field, the Trait’s stated effect becomes local law, two Grades over its base, for that effect aloneThe reachThe body and what it touchesA field the size of the room or yard it stands inThe Second’s field, rimmed in the Wellspring’s color and carried by a body the Wellspring helped rebuildThe soundIts own, called once: a bellows drawn hard, a struck bell, a crack of iceThe sound held as a standing noteThe Wellspring’s note beneath the owner’s
The road sets the count. The Path a soul leads on decides how many releases it can ever have, and each is deeper than the one before. The Body has three, at IV, VII and IX. The Spirit has two, at IV and VII. Fate has one, the One, at Refraction, deeper than any First, and it counts as a Second: it enlarges the claim and the Pressure as a First would, and it lays the field that opens and powers the Domain, as a Second does. Below Refraction a Fate fighter has no release at all, and fights with Range, Aura Pressure, presence, bonds and vows, which grow with the Stage and are quite enough to be going on with. A soul on two roads has its lead road’s count and no more. The road behind colors those releases and brings none of its own.
What it does on each road. The pattern above holds for everybody, and what the release acts on follows the road. A first release transforms whatever the lead layer does, and the field rules what that layer rules.









































BodySpiritFateReleasesThree: First at IV, Second at VII, Third at IXTwo: First at IV, Second at VIIOne, the One, at VIIThe first transformsThe flesh and the blow: what the body is made of and what a hit does. Raw Aether floods the Shell, and the body runs hotter and heavierThe line and its reach, on souls: what a thrown working can carry to a soul and how far it holds. It moves no matterThe One transforms the claim and the Pressure: how much of the room already answers to themThe field rules (the Second’s, or the One’s)Matter: weight, heat, the state of stone. Everyone can see itMeanings: what a thing is taken to be. The room looks exactly as it did, and the door has stopped being a doorConditions: what has to be so before anything can happen in hereThe clock readsBody MasterySpirit MasteryFate MasteryA two-Path fighterReleases on the lead road, with the lead road’s count. The road behind shows in the texture and takes no field and no release of its ownThe sameThe same
Each road also spends its own thing and tires in its own way, and Releases and Domains by Path lays the three side by side with a famous case of each.
A bloodline art does not change the road. A Moto’s release follows the layer that Moto leans on, and a Work used inside it is still a pull, paying a pull’s price and leaving a pull’s knot on top of the release’s clock. Neither the release nor the field ever pulls a thread.
The form is free. A release takes whatever shape the person’s soul would take: wings, plate, a changed blade, a beast’s outline, a crown of something that should not burn. A practitioner tempered on Ascensio (the Ladder of Ascent, a Wild Wellspring of rising) may release as a white crane. What the form does still comes from the Trait and its Wellspring (the lens it works through), so the crane’s wings strike as weight and muscle strike, by the world’s old habits, and the rising is the lens’s own business.
The aura. A release drives the aura to the practitioner’s full color at once: the hue of the Wellspring they have tempered on longest, at their Stage’s clarity. At Stage IV that is a smoky flare, charcoal with the hue clouded through it; at Stage VIII it is clear enough to throw light. Where that light falls is the road’s affair. A Body fighter’s flare sits on the skin and lights the room in its own color. A Spirit fighter’s stands a half-step off the body, lights the holder and the struck, and bends the shadows more than it brightens the walls. A Fate fighter’s is a thread of hue at the edge of the eye, and what the room gets is stillness: straight flames and settled dust.
The Domain. The Second Release opens and powers the Domain (a space where the practitioner’s inner law outranks the world’s), and on the Fate road the One does. The flicker of a seed that carries a soul into Stage VII is a one-time burst of the Trait and needs no Release, and it follows the road as the field later will: a Body flicker rules matter, a Spirit one meanings, a Fate one conditions. The Second, or the One, is what lets a seed be called and held. At Stage VII the field is a seed: it lasts minutes and collapses if attention breaks. From Stage VIII it is a true Domain, grown by living and called aloud, held for hours and steady under small disruptions, and anyone at Stage VIII can have one, their own concept made real, with the fame, rivalries and bounties that follow. The Stage grants it, and a Grade never does. The crossing into Stage IX carries a first flicker of a Realm on the same terms, once, on every road, with no release behind it. The Realm itself, a field that can hold other Domains inside it, is the far end of the climb and opens no earlier than Stage X, by each road’s own door (The Realm, below). From Stage XI the first of a soul’s releases no longer needs calling: it is simply how they are.
When fields meet. Stage comes first: a field two Stages up simply overwrites the lower one. Otherwise two release fields, or a field and another’s Pressure (the weight a strong soul puts on a room), contest the ground by Dominion (the stat of authority over ground and presence) before a blow lands. The border shows in the room as light changing color across the floor, bystanders feel both, and the weaker side starts the fight already paying. A read can flip it: find what the field rests on, the owner’s focus, its edge, or the thing they are guarding, press there, and the border moves back.
The window. The Crystal is the soul, and it reports to its owner. When a release fires, the owner’s window (the soul’s report of its own numbers, seen by nobody else) fills with the release’s name and what changed, and a timer bar starts to drain. Percentages, bars and the Grade of what the Trait throws, and never a letter on the owner: the exact figures stay with the assayers.
[FIRST RELEASE: KILN SKIN]
[Heat workings: top of Grade]
[Forge heat on every blow landed · bonded hammer carries its share]
[Time: ██████████ full]
[Reserve: 96%]

Nobody else sees it, so the man across from you is left to read the skin, the shimmer and the breath, and he has been known to read them wrong.
The bonded weapon. A weapon its owner has carried for years can carry part of the release: the blade burns with the owner’s heat, the staff holds the edge of the field. Its part is written on the owner’s card, and is lost with the weapon.
Called or silent. The owner chooses. Called, the release’s name goes out as it fires, in its owner’s own tongue, with the meaning landing in the same beat through a witness or a knowing second. A showman bawls it in capitals and a cold killer may barely breathe it, and either way the call costs a beat, buys the full rise, and is a tell everyone within earshot can use. Silent, it costs no beat and gives no spoken tell, but it still flares and still sounds, and it comes in weaker: the form without the call’s rise. The card says exactly what silence costs each release.
Who carries them. Any practitioner with a woken Crystal and an armed Primary Trait; an unwoken soul (the sealed Shell) carries Traits but cannot release them. How many a person can have is the road’s, three on the Body, two on the Spirit and one on Fate, and having the right to one is a long way from having it. Most who fight their way to Stage IV on the Body or the Spirit road earn a First in time. Far fewer earn a Second, or the One. A Third is the mark of a Body fighter the ballads already know. A Stage bought in a Draft or granted in a blessing opens the door and nothing past it, so a rich Stage IX may have no release at all while a poor Body fighter at the same Stage has all three, and there is steady money for bookies in knowing which is which.
What they are called. The Archives say First, Second and Third Release, and on the Fate road the One. Every people has its own street words for the three, as it does for the Stages: bracket crowds in the Common tongue call them going big, going loud and going home, the last because a certain number do not. A person’s own art may count its tiers in its own word, Acts, Verses, Knots, Entries, so that the count itself becomes a threat, and there is no more unpleasant sentence in a duel than “that was the First Knot.” Bloodline faculties release too, by the bloodline’s own law and stages, kept as a family secret and written on the bloodline’s page.
How one is learned. A release must be found and mastered by fighting, and no sum of money has ever changed that. A bought Stage comes without one and no purse opens one. A sect can teach the road to it, and that is much of what a sect is for: the drills, the rites for its Wellspring, the sparring ladder, and elders who will hurt you in the right places. Like the Trait, the shape itself is survived into being, and the shape that comes is the fighter’s own. Each release has its own Catalyst (What Opens Each One, below), and it is reached by one of three roads. Crisis is the commonest road to a First Release: the Trait breaks its limit in a fight the practitioner should have lost, and the Crystal keeps the shape. Seclusion is the commonest road to a Second and to the One: months working the Trait alone on what the last fights showed, until it claims the ground around them, and then back out to prove it against someone who means it, because a field that has never been contested will not hold. The ground is chosen by road. A Body fighter secludes on Aetheric Density, a mine head or a wild valley, where the Shell can be packed and emptied all day. A Spirit fighter goes into Echo Depth, a charnel house, an old temple or the home she grew up in. A Fate fighter sits under Thread Weight, on a battlefield or at a crossroads, and the sects that own such ground charge for the bench. Tribulation is how every Third arrives: the Wellspring’s own Aether comes down on the flesh of a Body fighter and tests the claim before it agrees to share the law, and not everyone survives the test. The first time a release holds, it prints on the Crystal, and the transformation is the kind people remember seeing. Command of it comes after that, in bout after bout, as the time on the bar lengthens and the price shrinks toward what the card says.
It deepens with the person. A release keeps its core for life but grows new aspects as its owner advances, survives and changes, and a great turn in a life can reshape it. Each new aspect is added to the card when it first shows.
What Opens Each One
A Stage has its Catalyst, and so does every release, and the benches spend a good deal of breath keeping the two apart. Five things hold for all of them.

The release’s own Stage first. A release Catalyst counts only once the soul stands on the release’s Stage: IV for a First, VII for a Second and for the One, IX for a Third. The same deed done a year earlier is a story and opens nothing.
One deed, one door. A deed meets one Catalyst and no more. Where it would answer both a release and the next Stage’s crossing, the crossing takes it, because the crossing is the louder demand, and the release waits for another day. Every Expert who hopes to buy two doors with one bad night is told this, and most of them try anyway.
Met under contest. Every release Catalyst is met against something that means it: a fighter, a beast, a flood, a court, another field. The deed is the trial, and the shape that prints is the fighter’s own.
Never bought. No Draft and no blessing has ever supplied a release Catalyst. A purse buys a Stage’s door and nothing past it.
Overgrown waits. A release Catalyst met while the Crystal is Overgrown prints on the stone and will not let the release out until Level reaches the Stage’s hold. The fighter knows it is there and cannot reach it, which is its own kind of education.

The Body’s First: the body broken, refusing to fall
The body breaks in a fight, truly breaks, bone or joint or the Shell itself, and the fighter stays on their feet and goes on acting with what is broken, by their own will and nobody else’s, until the fight ends one way or the other.
A quarry foreman at Adept takes a mace across the forearm, hears the bone go, and keeps the gate with the other hand and the broken one tucked against his ribs until the raiders give it up. That meets it. A caravan guard has her knee smashed by a drake’s tail, fights the rest of the bout on one leg and a spear butt, and loses, and that meets it too, because winning was never asked. A duelist with a cracked collarbone who is held up by his second while he finishes the bout fails: somebody else refused for him. So does the fighter whom a vow holds on his feet, since the Crystal reads the vow and not the body.
The room sees the break, a limb wrong or a rib line gone, and a fighter who does not sit. The Charge comes up through the break as a smoky flare of the base hue packed tight against the skin, the heat over the broken place plain to see, and the people watching go quiet, because they have all seen a broken man fall and this one is not doing it. Ever after, the First very often comes up first in the limb that broke.
The Body’s Second: a material known so well it obeys at range
One material the fighter knows to the grain, stone or iron, timber, bone, river water or the salt in blood, obeys them across open ground with no hand or weapon on it, in a contested fight, at their word and on purpose.
A smith of thirty years, a Journeyman with the sword and a Master at the anvil, makes an opponent’s mail go heavy and tight across the yard and fights him inside it. A mason at Refraction, in a siege breach, tells the fallen stones of the wall twenty paces off to stand, and they stand while the storming party is still coming over them. Both meet it. The tavern fighter whose pints fell upward for four seconds when he was pressed past holding does not: that was the seed that carried him into Refraction, unaimed and unwanted, and it opens nothing else. Nor does the smith who moves the mail with her hand on it, or through her hammer’s contact, which is an older rung and asks nothing new. A trade at Journeyman or better on the material makes the deed easier and is never required.
The material moves first, before the field: the stone stands, the mail cinches, the water in the ditch goes still and hard. Then the Charge leaves the skin and runs out along the ground in the fighter’s hue, and the Measurewrights in the stands start writing, because the line it draws is where the Domain will one day stand.
The Body’s Third: the body remade around a wound
In the tribulation, when the Wellspring’s own Aether comes down on the flesh to test the claim, the fighter takes a new wound from it and does not heal back to the body they had. The body is remade with the wound as part of its plan, the Wellspring sharing the work, and the fighter fights in that body before the day is out.
A Fractura fighter’s tribulation opens a seam of light down his sword arm that never closes; the arm is rebuilt along it, and his Third comes up through that seam every time. A Pyraeon hunter’s burns her hands to the bone. She lets no physician touch them, and when the burning stops her hands are forge-colored and hold heat as a crucible does, and she takes a contract the next morning with them. Both meet it. The Master whose tribulation wound a priced mender closed clean, the body left as it was, survived the test and kept nothing of it, and the Crystal has nothing to build a Third around. The fighter who offers up an old wound to be remade has mistaken the floor: an old wound made to bear weight is Transcendence’s work, done already or still owed, and the Third asks a new one, and asks to share it with the Wellspring.
The room sees weather that has found its target, the ground around one body taking the lens’s look, and then a body that should have been destroyed standing up changed, the wound lit at its edges in the Wellspring’s second color, the color that will rim the Third’s field from then on.
The Spirit’s First: the self said aloud, and true
The soul says what it is, aloud, in its own words, to someone or something that denies it and has the power to make the saying false, and in the same contest it proves the saying true by what it does.
A temple scribe at Adept, told by a Shepherd of the dead that she is a thief of other people’s grief, answers that she is a keeper of it, and then keeps a dead child’s mother from the thing that came for her. A sellsword called a coward for nine years tells the man who said so that he is a man who runs to save his own and will not run today, and does not. Both meet it. The young thrower who declares herself the finest in the province before a bout and is beaten by an honest Journeyman fails, because the saying was a boast and the fight proved it untrue. So does a true saying with nobody in the room able to deny it: a self said to friends has met no contest.
The benches keep it apart from two neighbors. Flourishing’s own Catalyst for a Spirit soul is being known, another soul seeing this one whole, shame and all, and not putting it down, and that is received; the First is given, declared outward at risk. Refraction’s seed comes when a soul faces aloud a truth about itself it did not want to know, which is a confession of what it found, where the First is a declaration of what it is. One deed meets one of them, never two.
Very little shows in the room and a great deal in the people. The aura rises a half-step off the body in its full hue, the one who denied finds the words have gone into him past any armor he wore, and bystanders remember the sentence for years and quote it slightly wrong.
The Spirit’s Second: a meaning borne for someone else
The soul takes up a meaning that belongs to someone else, a grief, a name, a last word, a guilt, the sense of an oath, which that person cannot carry, and carries it whole in their name, in its true sense and not its own, while something contests it: a power that wants the meaning broken, changed, buried or taken.
A sin-eater’s daughter at Refraction eats the bread over a murdered magistrate and takes his last ruling into her Core, and when his killers come to the burial to have it unsaid, she says it, his words and not hers, and it stands. A soldier carries the meaning of his dead captain’s surrender, given to save the company, through a court that wants it called treason, and holds it as mercy, which is what it was. Both meet it. A widow who carries her own husband’s death as her own grief and makes it bear weight has done Transcendence’s work, because the meaning was hers. The bearer who carries another’s meaning and tells it as she would have liked it to be fails too: the Crystal reads the bending and counts nothing.
This is the deed that opens the Domain on the Spirit road, and the benches say why: a field of meanings is a soul holding what things mean for everyone who stands in it. Nothing moves when it is met. The bearer’s aura takes something of the other person’s coloring at its edge, people who knew the one whose meaning is carried feel for a moment that they are in a room with them, and then the line of the field runs out along the floor, and inside it the meaning is simply so.
Fate’s One: a claim staked on your life, and kept
The soul names aloud a claim over something outside itself, a ground, a gate, a people’s standing, what may happen in a place, with its own life as the forfeit, against a contestant who has the power to take the claim and the life together, and keeps the claim, unyielded, until the contest ends.
A toll-reeve at Refraction stands at the middle of her bridge and says that nothing crosses it armed while she lives, to a company that can kill her, and holds it through the night. She meets it whether they turn back or she is carried off the bridge alive at dawn with the claim still standing. A bonded guardian claims a child’s right to her mother’s seat before a house that wants the child dead, stakes his life on it in their own hall, and keeps it through the season they spend trying to break it. A Fate fighter who holds the same bridge by pulling a thread, so that the company’s horses go lame on the approach, has made a pull and not a claim: it leaves a knot and counts for nothing. So does the claim staked and then yielded at the last hour to save the claimant’s life, however wise that was.
A vow is a word about one’s own act, and Refraction’s own Fate seed is a vow held for a few seconds at the moment it ought to break. The One is a claim over something outside the self, held for the whole of a contest, and it has exactly the shape of a Domain, which is why it opens and powers one. When it is met the dust lies flat from the claimant’s feet to the edge of what was claimed, flames stand straight, and the people inside it find they have stepped back to give it room before anyone told them to. When the contest ends with the claim still standing, the stillness stays on that ground for a day, and animals will not cross it.
The Realm
The crossing into Invocation carries a first flicker of a Realm, once, needing no release, on every road. The Realm itself is the far end of the climb: a field that can hold other fields inside it, still running, with their owners in them. No release makes one. Every road reaches it late, by its own door, from Realization at the earliest: the Body through the Third, the Spirit through its Second grown whole, held as a true Domain for years, and Fate through the One. Each door has its own Catalyst, met under contest and never bought, and a bought Stage X has no door at all. Releases and Domains by Path gives the three in full, with what each Realm is, where it breaks and what it costs.
What it costs
The shape spreads the strain. Because the release is a learned shape, the Crystal carries it without structural damage, provided it is held inside its limit. Past the limit it is a raw overchannel again.



































First ReleaseSecond Release, or the OneThird ReleaseDrainSet on each card and written as time from full: how long it holds if started on a full reserve (the store of power they carry, held mostly as Charge in the Shell by a Body fighter and as Essence in the Core by a Spirit or a Fate one). One person’s First Release may sip; another’s may burn like a ThirdSet on the cardSet on the cardThe limitEnds on its own when the reserve falls to a tenth. Below that is Starvation: sagging stats and flickering Traits, and then the road’s own form of it. In Charge Starvation a Body fighter’s Shell (the Crystal’s outer layer) draws on the flesh itself. In Essence Starvation a Spirit fighter’s Core frays, names first, and so does a Fate fighter’s, since her reserve is Essence too, with her luck curdling on topThe sameThe sameAfterwardsSpent and shaking; the pain the fight was shrugging off arrivesThe Crystal runs Overgrown (swollen and spilling) until a full night’s sleep: power spills, and the owner’s moods stain the air around them. No lasting harmOvergrown for a day and a night, and an ache through the body like the end of a fever. No lasting harmHeld past the limitA plain overchannel, with its fracture riskA Crystal Fracture Event (a crack in the Crystal)The Trait itself may fail, in a way the card names

The call costs a beat every time.
Its own price. A big release also charges in the coin of its own idea, on top of reserve and body tells, and the card says how. A landlady ends up on the step. A heat release blisters the hands that carry it.
Outside a fight a release may be held at the same cost: a First Release worn through a court audience to make a point, a Second spread over a winter camp to keep the snow off. The clock runs the same.
On the stack a release counts toward the cap of two steps on the hidden scale over the sustainable figure on the card, which is read with the gear off, and a Third already stands at it for its one effect, so nothing more stacks there. Only outside help goes past the cap, and a blessing counts as outside help, a point Measurewrights have settled several times.

How it is beaten
Most releases can be answered by someone at their own Stage, before, during and after, though none is owed such an answer: a release keeps the flaw its idea gives it. Under each way below lie the four answers the benches teach: the contrary idea, a soul further refined in the same idea, ground that holds another idea, and a refusal of the claim.

Before. A called release costs a beat, and the aura flares and the sound comes before the power rises. A fighter who reads the tell can strike into that beat, or get out of reach. A silent release skips the beat but still flares, still sounds, and comes in weaker.
During. The clock is the counter, and it runs on a bar only the owner can see. A release spends reserve fast and ends at a tenth, so outlasting it is a real plan: keep distance, make them chase, and fight on ground that raises their cost: cold and wet against heat, shallow ground with no memory in it against a Spirit release, light ground where nothing was ever decided against a Fate one, and salted, bled or thin ground (ground with little Aether to pull) against anyone, since a reserve refills only from what the ground can give. Rich ground cuts one way that surprises people: it fills a Fate fighter as it fills anyone, and it crowds her Range and the reach of her field while it does. A Second Release or the One at Stage VII collapses when attention breaks: a wound, a shout, a name that matters to them. Every field has an edge; step out of it. Contest the ground with a stronger Dominion, or read what holds it up. Take the bonded weapon and its part of the release goes with it.
After. The aftermath is a window. A First Release leaves them spent; a Second, the One and a Third leave the Crystal spilling and easy to read.

This is how a lower-Stage fighter beats a higher one across one Stage: survive the release, read it, and strike in the aftermath.
Example
Corra Vell is a Stage VII hired hunter on the Body Path, harmonized to Pyraeon (the Ember Crown, a Wild Wellspring and so at home on her road), with a heat Primary Trait. Her color is Pyraeon’s banked ember-orange at Refraction’s clarity: gray and orange sharing one field without mixing. She has fought eleven years with the same forge hammer, and it is bonded. She found Kiln Skin in a bad fight in a culvert in her fifth year, and Smelter’s Yard over one winter of hard contracts and a hard teacher. Her card carries two releases:

KILN SKIN (First Release). She says “Kiln Skin” and her skin goes the dull cherry-orange of iron at forging heat, from the hands up over the forearms to the collarbones, and the air around her shimmers like the air over a forge bed. There is a sound like a bellows drawn once, hard. Every blow she lands carries forge heat into the wound, and her heat workings strike at the top of their Grade. Her bonded hammer takes the heat with her: its head glows the same cherry-orange and keeps it, and the forge heat in her hammer blows is the hammer’s share, lost if the hammer is. From a full reserve it holds about six minutes, and it ends on its own when her reserve falls to a tenth; afterwards her palms are blistered and she cannot pull heat for an hour. Released silently, it takes the color and the shimmer but not the call’s rise, and her heat workings strike at the middle of their Grade, not the top. The counter is in the beat of the call, which can be struck into, in cold and wet ground, which makes every second cost more, and in the blistered hands afterwards, which cannot hold a weapon properly.


SMELTER’S YARD (Second Release). She says “Smelter’s Yard” and the heat leaves her skin and fills the ground around her, about the size of a courtyard: the air goes forge-hot and dry, the light turns orange, and everyone inside feels the color change as a pressure behind the eyes. The bellows sound becomes a low, steady roar for as long as it holds. This is her Domain seed, and inside it her heat workings strike one full Grade higher. From a full reserve it holds about three minutes, and it collapses at once if her attention breaks; afterwards her Crystal runs Overgrown until she sleeps, and heat leaks off her with her temper. Released silently, the yard forms without its first roar and her workings strike at the top of their own Grade inside it, not one higher. The counter is to break her focus with a wound, a shout or a name that matters, to step out past the edge of the yard, to contest its ground with a stronger Dominion, and to strike while her spilling Crystal is easy to read.

On a dockside job Corra meets a Stage VII duelist tempered on Judicium (the Wellspring of Truth, which runs arc-blue) who opens his own field, a ring of arc-blue that makes every hair in the yard stand up. She answers with Smelter’s Yard, and the two fields meet in a seam across the cobbles where orange light and blue light grind against each other. His Dominion is higher, and the seam starts walking toward her. Then she reads him: his field is centered on his left hand, which never moves from his belt. She throws the hammer at it. He flinches to guard the hand, his attention breaks, and his field goes out like a doused lamp, with the slap of hot air and flying cobbles that every collapse pays, a Resonance Shockwave of the small kind, which puts him on his back. The orange floods the yard to the water’s edge. Only she can see the rest of it:
[SECOND RELEASE: SMELTER'S YARD]
[Heat workings: one Grade up]
[Field: holding · his has collapsed]
[Time: ████░░░░░░ about a minute left]
[Reserve: 47%]

She is going to need her hammer back.
Read next: How Power Grows, for where the releases sit in the climb; Domains, for what the Second Release and the One open; Releases and Domains by Path, for what each road spends and how each one flags; Stacking and Spending, for what it adds to everything else; The Three Paths, for which road the release is on; and The Sixteen Stages, for where on the ladder each one opens.

the-magic-system/the-soul-and-the-climb/.title: Releases and Domains by Path
the-magic-system/the-soul-and-the-climb/.content:
How many releases each of the three roads holds, what a Release, a Domain and a Realm do on each, what each one spends, and how to tell which you are standing in before it is too late to matter

“The first one cooked the ring. The second one I never saw at all, and I was looking straight at her. The third one I only noticed when I found I had already bet on him.”
A turnstile-keeper at the Sealhall brackets, on the afternoon of the Three Roads

The Sealhall autumn brackets of 688 are remembered for one afternoon on which three fighters called a release inside the same hour, one from each road, two Firsts and then the One, and eleven thousand people in guild colors got the plainest lesson in the Paths the Midmarch has ever been given for the price of a seat.
Bram Oxley, the Dray, went first. He was a carter’s son from Garrow Lock with a neck like a mooring post, and he bawled “FULL LOAD” loud enough to lift pigeons off the far stand. His skin went the dull red of a brick kiln from the scalp down, the sand under his boots sagged into two bowls, and the front rows put their hands up against the heat coming off him. His opponent hit him with a quarterstaff and the staff caught fire.
Mother Edda Quill went second, and half the stands thought she had declined to. She said “Plain Speaking” in the voice of a woman asking for the salt. Nothing in the ring changed. No sand stirred, no banner moved, and her pewter-gray aura hung where it had been, a half step off her body. Then she said one further sentence to the swordsman in front of her, at the same volume, and every person in the top tier heard it as if she were sitting beside them. The swordsman sat down on the sand and wept, with his blade still in his hand, and could not afterward say what he had been fighting about.
Tobias Marl went third. He walked the Fate road, which has nothing to release until the seventh Stage, and he had spent eleven years at the Sealhall rope on presence and Range alone before he stood at Refraction and had something to call. The argument over whether he said anything at all lasted years. The account the Guild accepts is that he said “The House” while adjusting his cuff. The dust in the ring lay down flat. A coin a boy had dropped under the stands landed on its edge and stayed there. The marshal found he had already stepped back to give the man room, the crowd found it had already gone quiet, and his opponent, a perfectly sound Stage V spearman, discovered that everybody in the building including himself had been treating the bout as settled for some time.
A child can say the whole of it: the first one changes his body, the second one changes what reaches you, and the third one changes whose room it is. What follows is how a Measurewright says it.
At a Glance







































































BodySpiritFateThe layer in useAether ShellEssence CoreAttraction LayerWhat the Release spendsRaw Aether (mana), held unrefined in the Shell as the ChargeEssence (spiritual energy), refined and stamped in the CrystalEssence as well, spent through the Layer as the soul’s own share of fate. It pulls no threadTopped up withA SaltCore stockCore stock. There is no Draft for FateReleasesThree: First at IV, Second at VII, Third at IXTwo: First at IV, Second at VIIOne, the One, at VII, counting as a SecondThe first release transformsThe flesh and the blowThe line and its reach, on soulsThe claim and the PressureThe field (the Second’s, or the One’s) rulesMatterMeanings. The room looks unchangedConditionsThe ThirdThe body remade around a woundNoneNoneThe clock and the upkeep readBody MasterySpirit MasteryFate MasteryThe door to a Realm, from Stage XThrough the ThirdThrough the Second, grown wholeThrough the OneRun long, itRuns hot and cracksRuns hollowRuns unlucky
The pattern every release follows, the Stages, the calling and the learning are set out in Release Forms, and the claim itself in Domains. This page is the three roads laid side by side.
What Holds for Everybody

The road sets the count. The lead Path decides how many releases a soul can ever have: three on the Body road, at IV, VII and IX; two on the Spirit road, at IV and VII; and one on Fate, the One, at VII. Each is deeper than the last, and each has its own Catalyst, set out in Release Forms.
Called or silent. Called aloud, a release takes its full rise and costs a beat. Silent, it costs no beat and comes in weaker. The owner chooses each time.
The Second, or the One, opens and powers the Domain. At Stage VII it holds a seed for minutes. Anyone at Stage VIII can have a true Domain, their own concept made real. A seed can also flicker once, unbidden, as the Catalyst that carries a soul into Stage VII, with no Release behind it, and it cannot be done again by wanting to. The flicker follows the road as the field will: a Body flicker rules matter, a Spirit one meanings, a Fate one conditions.
Found on the road’s own ground. A release is found and mastered by fighting, and the seclusion that so often comes before a Second or the One is kept where the lead layer feeds: on Aetheric Density for the Body, in Echo Depth for the Spirit, under Thread Weight for Fate. A Stage’s bought Catalyst is poured by road too, on a Salt base, on Core stock, or on the Layer reagent, the last being the dearest and the most criminal. No bench has ever poured a release.
The cap. Self-boosts stack to two steps on the hidden scale over the sustainable figure on the card and no further. A Third Release fills that cap alone. Only outside help goes past it. See Stacking and Spending.
One idea. Trait, Release and Domain are a single concept growing, whichever road carries it.
A fighter on two roads releases on the lead road, with the lead road’s count. The road behind colors those releases, shows in their texture, and brings no release and no field of its own.

The Body Road
The First Release is a flood. A Body fighter works raw Aether, drawn in and packed in the Shell unrefined, and that packed store is the Charge. Called, the First Release opens the Shell to all of it at once, shaped on the spot by the Wellspring’s lens. The flesh changes and the blow changes with it: the body runs hotter and heavier, the skin takes the release’s look, and every hit carries the Charge into what it lands on. The lost share burns in the Shell, which is the furnace that never goes cold, and comes off him as heat, which is why the front row at Sealhall shielded their faces. None of it is Essence. It is the world’s own power worn like a second hide, and the body pays the bill for carrying it.
[FIRST RELEASE: FULL LOAD]
[Strike Force: top of Grade · weight on every blow]
[Shell: flooded · running hot]
[Time: ███████░░░ ]
[Reserve: 68%]

The Second Release rules matter. The Charge leaves the skin and fills the ground, and inside the line weight, heat and the state of stone obey the holder. Everyone can see a Body field. The air shimmers, the light changes color and the cobbles do something cobbles should not.
The famous one. Big Annet Rudge of the Hask Moor threshers held the smallest true Domain on the Guild rolls, THE THRESHING FLOOR, eleven paces across and not a hand more. Inside it everything weighed three times what it should, and Annet did not. Men laughed at the size of it for twenty years, generally from twelve paces off. A Stage VIII knight of the Hundred Crowns rode into it at a canter in 671, and what the horse did to itself coming down on its own forelegs is the reason the Moor holds no jousts. He was cut out of his breastplate with shears. The edge of the Floor is marked in whitewash to this day, and the drovers repaint it.
The Third Release is the body remade. Only the Body road has one. It comes out of the tribulation at Invocation, a new wound the Wellspring gives and helps rebuild the body around, and from then on the Third comes up through that wound and the field takes the Wellspring’s second color at its rim. Inside it the Trait’s stated effect becomes local law, for that effect alone, and stands at the cap by itself. The songs call it a Realm. It is the Body road’s door to one, which is a different thing, and the door is a long way further on.
What holds it small. Radius, Sovereignty and Gravity are Fate gates, and without the Fate Path they stop at 400. A Body Domain is therefore real, tight and hard, and a holder with the gates open will out-hold it yard for yard. Annet’s answer was that eleven paces is a long way when you are inside them.
Run long. At half the heat-haze thickens on the skin. At a quarter steam comes off the shoulders, the big muscles cramp and fibers tear. At a tenth the release ends on its own, and a fighter who forces it past that finds the Shell drawing its Charge out of the flesh: the skin splits in fine bright lines like glaze on an overfired pot. Past that lies heat stroke, burst vessels and a Shell that may not close. Bram Oxley held Full Load nine breaths too long in the final and spent the winter wrapped in wet sheets.
The Spirit Road
The First Release lengthens the line. A Spirit fighter spends Essence, refined in the Crystal, stamped with identity and sent out through the Core. The First Release transforms the line that Essence travels and how far it holds: what a thrown working can carry, and to how many souls at once. Its force is force on souls. It knocks a soul out of true, lays dread on a mind, wounds a Core, and it goes past plate and hide as if they were not there, since armor does not cover what it strikes. It moves no stone. The Shell is the only door into matter, and a Spirit fighter who wants the stone moved does it through their own Shell, at their Body Mastery, like anybody else.
So a Spirit release shows on the holder and on the struck, and hardly at all on the room. The aura flares to full color and the sound comes, as with every release. The sand stays where it is.
The Second Release rules meanings. The field governs what a thing is taken to be. The room looks exactly as it did, nobody’s hair moves, and something in it has stopped being what it was. There is no Third on this road. The Second is the deepest a Spirit soul releases, and its door to a Realm is that same Second, held long enough to grow whole.
The famous one. Jessamy Crake kept a pawnshop on Tally Row in Waxgate and reached Stage VIII behind its counter. Her Domain was called UNREDEEMED, and inside it nothing was yours until she said it was paid for. A duelist’s bonded saber, carried nineteen years, lay in his hand like a stranger’s property: the steel was the same steel, and his soul no longer knew it, so the share of his release it carried was simply not there. Men forgot which of their own arts belonged to them. Three collectors from a Kharven house walked in to settle her account in 659, and they walked out again unhurt, and it was a week before any of them could be persuaded that their own boots were theirs to put on. Nothing on her shelves had moved an inch.
What holds it small. The same Fate gates as the Body road, and a body that is no stronger for any of this. A Spirit holder dies out of position while the field stands, to a spear that does not care what it means.
Run long. The lost share is paid in the Core, never as heat, so a flagging Spirit fighter does not sweat. At half the colors near them go flat. At a quarter comes a hollow cold and a slipped word. At a tenth the release ends, and held past it names and memories start to slip. Maxed, a memory goes for good and the holder faints. Mother Quill, in her last season, finished a bout and asked the marshal quite politely which city this was.
The Fate Road
Nothing to release until Refraction. From Adept through the Expert years a Fate fighter fights with Range, Aura Pressure, presence, bonds and vows, and all of those grow with the Stage. There is no First on this road and no Third. What comes at Refraction is one release, the One, deeper than any First and counted as a Second, because it does both jobs the other roads split in two.
The One enlarges the claim. It transforms the claim and the Pressure: how much of the room already answers to the holder before anything has been done in it. It is paid from the soul’s own share of fate, the same purse a vow is paid from, and that purse is the reserve: a Fate soul refines its Aether into Essence as a Spirit soul does, holds it in the Core, and spends it out through the Layer. Tobias Marl kept a flask of Core stock in his coat like any thrower. The release pulls no thread, so the release itself leaves no knot behind. What shows is very little on the body and a good deal around it. Dust lies still, flames stand straight, coins land face up, and people give ground they did not decide to give. A vow spoken inside it sits heavier, and so does the holder’s name.
A true pull made from inside a Fate release is another matter. It is still a pull, it pays a pull’s price on top of the release’s clock, and it leaves its knot like any other.
The One also lays the field, and the field rules conditions. It governs what has to be so before anything can happen in it, and it opens and powers the Domain as a Second does on the other roads. Nothing is prevented by force. The thing simply lacks leave to occur.
The famous one is the Long Sitting of Justiciar Ambrose Tick at Hawes Bridge, told in full on the Domains page: three hundred yards of river valley in which no blow could land until its case was called. It is the model of a Fate field, wide, quiet and held for nine hours, and it shows the other half of the road as well, because the bridge went into the Kessen when it ended.
What holds it. The gates stand open on this road, so reserve is the leash, and the ground is the other. Rich Aetheric ground fills a Fate holder as it fills anyone and crowds the radius of the field and the holder’s Range while it does. Heavy Thread Weight, a battlefield, a court, a crossroads, extends both, and a Fate holder chooses where to stand accordingly. Inside a formed Domain the Fate amplification can pass a Body fighter’s bonus outright, which is the whole of what the road buys here, and it is a great deal.
Run long. At half small luck curdles nearby: a cup slips, a buckle gives, a friend’s dice go cold. At a quarter things go wrong around the holder in earnest and at once. At a tenth the release ends, and forced past it the holder’s own name begins to sit wrong in other mouths. Maxed, every knot the holder has ever left outstanding comes due together. Under all of it runs the Spirit road’s bill, because the reserve being emptied is Essence: a Fate holder below a tenth is losing names as well as luck. Marl overheld the House exactly once, in a card room in Verath, and the roof came in on that table and no other.
Every Domain Is a Layer Claim
Whatever the field rules, the claim that stakes it is made by the Attraction Layer, which every soul has.

It needs no Fate Mastery. The claim spends the soul’s own share and reaches for nothing above it, so a hitter who has never felt a thread can stake a Domain as surely as a Moto can.
It pulls no thread and leaves no knot. Holding a Domain, of any kind, for any length of time, adds nothing to what the world will collect from the holder later. The Domain’s bill is the reserve, the collapse, and the price in the coin of its own idea.
Upkeep reads the lead road’s Mastery. A Body holder’s field is kept at their Body Mastery and paid in Charge, and it throws heat. A Spirit holder’s is kept at their Spirit Mastery and paid in Essence, and it hollows. A Fate holder’s is kept at their Fate Mastery and paid in Essence through the Layer, with nothing to see but the luck going off. See How Power Grows.
The Fate gates measure it. Radius, Sovereignty and Gravity decide how wide a field runs, how well it holds contested ground and how steady it stands, and they stop at 400 for anyone who has not walked the Fate Path. That one fact is why Body Domains are yards, Spirit Domains are rooms and Fate Domains are valleys. The gates open by the Fate Path’s own Stage, which climbs with the soul like any road’s, so a Fate holder needs no high rung of Mastery to hold a valley.
The ground has a say. Each field is cheaper on its own road’s ground, and rich Aetheric ground crowds any Domain’s radius while heavy Thread Weight extends it.

The Realm, by Road
A Realm is a Domain grown into a field that can hold other fields inside it, still running, with their owners in them. Its edge takes the Wellspring’s second color, pacts, artifacts and law begin to set into the terrain, and the Continuum has to make room. It is a claim, owes no knot and can be held all day. The Archives read it by the road beneath it: a Body Realm rules the matter another Domain stands on, a Spirit Realm what the fields inside it are taken to mean, and a Fate Realm whether a field inside it has leave to stand at all.
The flicker comes first, and early. The crossing into Invocation carries a first flicker of a Realm, once, needing no release, on every road and in that road’s terms. The Ember Deacon’s field closing round the marshal’s at Dornhold was such a flicker, and it was enough to burn a town for nineteen years.
The door opens at Realization, on every road, and never before. Realization’s own Catalyst is the Domain made a thing the Continuum must make room for, and no door can open before the Continuum has been made to do it. So a Realm is a Stage X thing at the earliest, and most who ever hold one get there at Dissonance or Emanation. That is late enough to be rare and early enough that a Stage X Master with a Realm is a soul the Concord’s Strategic Division keeps a file on.
Each road needs what came before. The Body’s door needs the Third Release held. The Spirit’s needs the Second held as a true Domain for years, grown whole. Fate’s needs the One. Without them there is no door to open. Each door has its own Catalyst on top, a single deed done at Stage X or above with another soul’s field in the holder’s hands, met under contest, one deed for one door, and never bought. A bought Stage X has no Realm and no door, and nothing sells one.
The holder’s own idea rides on top. A Realm is the same concept as the Trait, the Release and the Domain, at its last size. What follows is how each road holds other fields, and the holder’s own concept brings its own flaw and its own price on top of these.
The Body: through the Third
The door’s Catalyst: another’s world carried, and not let fall. With the Third released, the holder lets another soul’s true Domain stand on their own ground and bears its whole weight in the remade body for its full span, an enemy’s at full strength or an ally’s in collapse, without breaking it and without letting it fall on what stands beneath. A Body Master who catches a dying ally’s Domain as its owner’s reserve fails, and carries it in her own body until it spends itself so that the collapse never reaches the town beneath, meets it. So does the Master who stands under an enemy’s field for the whole of its hour, every weight it lays on the ground taken into his frame, so that the people sheltering behind him are never inside its law. A Master two Stages up who simply overwrites the enemy’s field from above has carried nothing, since any field two Stages up does that. The holder who carries it until the body gives, and lets it come down on the street, has failed the one thing asked: the deed is the not letting fall.
What the Realm is. Matter as foundation. The holder’s field becomes the ground other fields stand on, so a Domain inside a Body Realm keeps running and keeps its own law, and every grain of matter it rests on belongs to the holder.
Its idea is the foundation that bears worlds: to be what other law stands on. The masons’ benches call it Petralon’s idea at the size of a soul, and the operation is coagulation, the holder fixed as the ground and set to bear.
Its flaw. A foundation bears whatever presses down on it, and nothing ever asked it to hold on. A Body Realm cannot grip. Whatever lifts away, uproots or draws out from it parts it, and a field inside that chooses to rise rather than press goes out through the top.
Its contrary is the pull and the rising: a Fate pull on what the ground is there for, a field built on ascent or on slipping the load (Ascensio and Cymorath stand against it among the Sixty), and ground already holding another idea.
Its price. What is ground is walked on, and what bears a world keeps some of it. Each holding leaves the weight of the fields carried settled in the holder’s body for good. They grow heavier by the size of what they bore, floors give under them, horses will not carry them, and in the end they cannot be lifted, carried off a field wounded or pulled out of the water. The Measurewrights call it settling.
The Spirit: through its Second, grown whole
The door’s Catalyst: another’s whole meaning held inside your own, and both left true. Inside their own Domain, the holder takes in a rival’s true Domain and understands its law so wholly that it runs inside their field meaning exactly what its owner means by it, while the holder’s own meaning stands around it unchanged, for the whole of the contest. A court mancer who holds a heretic’s Domain inside her own for the length of his trial, so that the bench hears what his law truly is and judges that, meets it, and she may judge against him anyway. A Spirit Master facing a rival’s field of grief who takes it in whole, every mourning in it meant as its owner means it, and goes on fighting from inside her own, meets it too. The Master who holds the rival’s field by taking it to be something else, a madness, a lie, a trick, has laid her own reading over another’s law, and the Crystal counts nothing. So does the holder whose own meaning yields to what she took in. She held one meaning, and the door asks two.
What the Realm is. Meaning as the reading of readings. The holder’s field becomes the sense in which other fields are read, so a Domain inside a Spirit Realm keeps its law and has that law taken in the holder’s understanding.
Its idea is the interpreter’s house, every meaning inside it held whole and given its true reading: the sin-eater’s office grown into a law, or the interpreter between two courts whom both trust because she lies to neither. The operation is conjunction, two meanings joined in one vessel and each kept.
Its flaw. A reading needs something to read. What means nothing, and what refuses to be read, silence, the unrecorded, a thing with no name to read it by, gives it nothing to hold and passes through. And whatever part of a field the holder has not truly understood is not held at all.
Its contrary is unknowing: a working that withdraws recognition (Null-Light’s Mugan is its direct contrary), forgetting on purpose, the hollow law, and the refusal of a soul that will not be read.
Its price. What is wholly understood is half believed. Each holding leaves the held field’s doctrine in the holder’s Core as a second voice that argues, and the holder comes out of every Realm a little persuaded by the person they fought. The old ones carry a crowd of enemies inside them and agree with most of them about something.
Fate: through the One
The door’s Catalyst: a claim others stand on, kept for them. The holder grants standing to another’s claim, a rival holder’s Domain, a truce between two holders, a city’s charter, by putting their own One beneath it as surety, life and standing pledged; and when the other claim is broken or attacked, the holder keeps it for them at their own cost, against whoever breaks it, kin and allies included. A Fate Master who stands surety on his One for a truce between two Domain holders, and enforces it against the elder of them when she breaks it, though she is his grandmother, meets it. So does the Master who pledges her One beneath a free town’s charter when a duke comes to revoke it, and holds it against the town’s own council when they try to sell it. The surety who keeps the truce by pulling threads, so that each side’s attack never quite happens, has made pulls and not a claim, and opened nothing. The surety who stands by while the claim breaks has failed, however good the reason.
What the Realm is. Condition as warrant. The holder’s field becomes the leave under which any field inside it may stand at all, so a Domain inside a Fate Realm runs only on the holder’s leave, and the leave can be given or withdrawn.
Its idea is the warrant and the surety: to be the condition under which other claims stand, as the surety answers for another’s default and the tithing answers for each of its own. The operation is sublimation, the holder’s claim raised above the others into the vessel their leave comes down from.
Its flaw. A warrant is only as good as the one who warrants. The Realm stands on the holder’s own standing, so if the holder breaks a word of their own while it stands, inside it or outside, every field in it loses leave at once, theirs first. And it governs only what needs leave: a thing that is simply so, a sound body with no strap to give or an avalanche with nothing to exploit, passes through it untouched.
Its contrary is necessity and soundness, whatever needs no leave; the refusal of a soul that does not recognize the holder’s standing; and ground that already holds another idea.
Its price. The surety answers for the default. Every claim given leave inside the Realm that is later broken, whenever and by whomever, is billed to the holder’s standing, and never as a knot: their word weighs less in every mouth for a season, and a holder who has warranted too many faithless claims comes at last to a day when their own vow will not take.
All three

On the stack a Realm counts as the field beneath it does, toward the two-step cap over the sustainable figure, and only outside help goes past it.
Cost and collapse. Reserve for its span, written on the card as time from full, and Overgrown for a day and a night afterward. Held past its limit, the Trait may fail as the card names. A collapse is a Resonance Shockwave sized to everything inside it, the held fields included, and at Dornhold that was a great deal.
Against Stage. A Realm still yields to a field two Stages up. Holding another field is not out-ranking it.

Reading the Road Across a Ring








































You seeIt isWhat to do about itHeat on your face, footprints sinking, the light gone the color of the auraA Body releaseKeep away from the hands. Make it run: cold, wet and distance all raise the cost, and the body pays itNothing at all in the room, and a fighter who has stopped looking at your guardA Spirit releaseWard the Core, close the distance and hit the body, which is no tougher than it wasStill dust, straight flames, and the feeling that you have already lostA Fate releaseBe sound: check the straps, keep your footing, and get to the holder before the room finishes agreeingA fighter sweating steam and splitting at the knucklesA Body release run longWaitA fighter gone pale and vague who has just called you by the wrong nameA Spirit release run longWaitA fighter whose bootlace has just snappedA Fate release run longWait, from further away
