the-magic-system/the-soul-and-the-climb/.title: Skills and Traits
the-magic-system/the-soul-and-the-climb/.content:
“Fifty years at one thing will make anyone frightening. It will not, as a rule, make them alive afterward.”
Guild surgeon’s note, Tollgarth, in the margin of an invoice

Marta Kell had kept the block on Tollgarth’s Tripe Row for fifty-one years, under a striped red awning, with sausages in ropes overhead and a yellow cat on the scale. She was a wide old woman in a wet apron who had never woken a Crystal in her life. Her window held a Level you could count on your fingers and one line that made Measurewrights take their hats off. When Captain Gorr Ashtooth of the Iron Mandate came down the Row collecting for his company, a Stage V hobgoblin in a black coat and a scale shirt, carrying a mace the size of a churn, he told her the levy had doubled. He leaned across her block to take a ham by way of first installment, and he did not bother to run his aura down that arm, since she was a fat old butcher and he had done this on four hundred streets.
"Hold still, love."
She had a boning knife with a blade worn thin as a willow leaf and the arm of a woman of seventy, and she brought nothing to that moment you could put on a force table. Her Ardency read nothing worth writing down. She had also taken apart something over two hundred thousand animals, and her hand knew where a shoulder comes undone the way your tongue knows your teeth. The knife went in through the gap at the armhole of the scale shirt, along the top of the arm bone, and round the ball of the joint, where the capsule (the sleeve of gristle that holds a joint together) can be opened by anyone who knows its seam with no more force than it takes to joint a chicken. It took her about as long as it took him to look surprised. Then the arm slid off onto her block, ham and all, with the mace still in its fist, and the blood came out of him in a hot red rope that went clear across the Row and wet the sausages.
He hit her with the other hand. It went through the awning post, the back wall and the wall of the tannery behind that, with her in front of it.
She lost. She lost the fight, the shop, four teeth and the use of a hip. Captain Ashtooth, coat flaring to the socket and white as lard, walked to the end of the Row on his own feet and has been Ashtooth Red-Sleeve in every song from there to Undaar-Gorr. And her window, when she could read it, in a bed at the guild surgeon’s, went like this:
[Hit: left hip broken. Four teeth gone. Ribs uncounted. Health 31%]
[Level: 9 to 23]
[Skill: Butchery, Paragon, 97%]

She keeps a new stall now on the same Row. The Iron Mandate’s collectors no longer walk it.
Everything about that afternoon sits on this page. A trade skill can go as high as the ranks go with no Stage under it, and it can do things force cannot. It still leaves you standing in front of a Stage V with a boning knife, and the rank decides how well you do what you do, while the stats decide what happens next. How the whole climb fits together, Stage, Level and the hands, is set out in How Power Grows.
The Things That Rise
Five things are counted over a life. Four of them rise by roads of their own, the fifth rides on another, and the window reports each differently.









































What risesBy whatShown asHas a ceilingLevelAny real work, danger overcome most of allA number, 1 to 500 and past it at Paragon500 below Stage XV; Residual Strain past the old gates without a CatalystStatsMostly what your life spends, by what your lead layer does, a few placed by you at each StageNumbers, never a letter; a Sub-Stat when used or when it movesThe Stage’s ceilingSkillDoing itOne of the nine ranks, with a percentage rising to the nextNone for a trade; a fighting skill ranks no higher than its owner’s Stage rankTraitNothing of its own: it reads at the lead Path’s MasteryNo number at allThe Mastery ceiling of the StageTechniqueIts skill gaining a rank, and a fight or a scene that pushes it past its old limitNo level at all; a bigger name when it jumpsNone
The class has its own page, and it hands you skills and shapes moves on top of all this.
Skills
A skill is one thing a person does and has got better at by doing it. Swordwork, haggling, tracking, brewing Drafts, cutting runes, folding tags, chanting, laying out the dead, lambing. Every practitioner has them, and so does everybody else, since a baker has a Baking skill and a little sheet. Anyone can level most of them, and everyone can pour or bake; cutting a rune, folding a tag and chanting want a woken Crystal. There is no gate of birth or Stage on picking up a skill beyond that, which has made a great many teachers unhappy.
A skill rises with use and shows on the sheet on the nine ranks: Initiate, Apprentice, Journeyman, Adept, Expert, Master, Grandmaster, Archmaster, Paragon, the same words a Stage’s rank and an Accord title use. Between ranks the window gives a percentage when something moves it. Work done under real weight counts for more than work done idly, the way danger moves Level: a hundred sparring cuts shift a Swordwork line a little, and one cut that decides whether you see supper shifts it a good deal more, which is why sect elders put their students in real danger and call it teaching.
[Skill rising: Footwork, Journeyman, 91%]

[Skill: Measure, Initiate to Apprentice]

The names are the soul’s and not yours. Your window files what you actually do, in your own tongue, and it does not flatter. A shepherd is told he has Lambing, Shearing and Laying-Out, the washing and dressing of the dead, because he buried his own in a hard winter. A veteran finds Bearing Blows on the sheet above his Swordwork, and a duke’s son finds Obedience, and is surprised how high it has climbed.
What a sheet of them looks like
A normal look gives you the skills in play. A long look gives you all of them, and most people’s are longer than they would have guessed.
An adventurer on an Accord commission, thirty-one and doing well:
[Skills]
[Hammerwork Expert · Wet Footing Journeyman · Tracking Journeyman]
[Bearing Blows Journeyman · Bargaining Apprentice · Knots Apprentice]
[Riding Journeyman · Field Dressing Apprentice · Reading a Bill Journeyman]

A Draft-pourer in a sect’s hall, who has fought twice in her life, and badly:
[Skills]
[Pouring Master · Rendering Journeyman · Herb-Lore Journeyman · Ledger Journeyman]
[Bottle-Cutting Apprentice · Sums Journeyman · Deference Journeyman]
[Knife Initiate]

A second son of a great house, Stage VIII by his family’s purse:
[Skills]
[Riding Journeyman · Courtly Address Journeyman · Dancing Journeyman · Fencing, Salon Apprentice]
[Obedience Journeyman · Dice Master]

Marta Kell’s, before Tripe Row got interesting:
[Level 9 · Health: sound]
[Skills: Butchery Paragon · Sums Apprentice · Curing Master · Haggling Journeyman]

What a skill does and does not do
A skill’s rank says how well the thing gets done. It puts no force behind it. The stat in use decides a contest, by its numbers, and the force tables on Grades, Ranks and the Aether Shell read stats. Brawling at Journeyman behind an arm with nothing in it is a beautifully placed punch from someone who cannot hurt you. Hammerwork at Apprentice behind an Ardency the assayers whistle at is a barn door falling on the wrong house.
Where skill earns its keep is everywhere the stats tie and everywhere they are not asked. Where two fighters’ numbers sit within a step of each other, exchanges are settled by technique quality, tactics and position, and a Master by Stage who is a Master with the sword makes a Master who never drilled look like a child. It also decides what can be built: techniques are named things done with skills, so an art built on a skill you do not have is a shout and a surgeon’s bill.
Fifty years at one thing can make a Paragon of a trade with no Stage to speak of. The Stage’s ceiling binds Sub-Stats and caps the fighting skills, and it has never bound a trade. These mundane masters are real, they are rare, and they are frightening: a mason who can tell by leaning on it which stone in a keep comes out first, or a barber who has shaved a duke every morning for forty years and has never once been searched. They usually still lose a fight. Sensible lords keep them fed and on the right side of the wall.
The ranks, read by ear. Nothing on file fixes how long a rank takes, and a person with a good teacher and a bad year goes faster. A rough guide, as the guild halls talk about it:













































RankReads asInitiateYou have started and someone has noticedApprenticeUseful at home, and then someone would pay you for itJourneymanA living, in a town with some competitionAdeptThe name people give when asked who does this round hereExpertKnown across a province, and you have opinions about the othersMasterStudents travel to youGrandmasterRivals write lettersArchmasterYour work is argued over in halls you have never visitedParagonA lifetime with nothing else in it; fifty years will do it. The Archives list three claims to something past it, and the three claimants disagree
The older sheets gave skills the fighters’ letters, and a later generation read them on six craft ranks of their own, Novice, Apprentice, Journeyman, Master, Grandmaster and Legend, now retired. An old letter reads across plainly: Hollow, F and E are an Initiate, D an Apprentice, C a Journeyman, B an Adept, A an Expert, S and SS a Master, SSS a Grandmaster, X and EX an Archmaster, and EX+ a Paragon.
The cap on fighting skills. A trade is free to climb as high as a life will take it, to Paragon with no Stage behind it. A fighting skill is not: the hands cannot learn to fight past what the soul behind them can carry, so a combat skill never ranks above its owner’s own Stage rank. A Master’s sword stops at Master, and an Expert’s at Expert.
Skills and trades
Drafts, runes, tags and chants are skills and trades like any other, open to anyone who will put in the years, though all but the pouring want a woken Crystal. Any soldier may learn to pour. Any woken pourer may learn to cut a seal. A trade is what happens when someone does a skill well enough for money, and a guild is what happens when enough of them would like to keep the money. The old quarrels between the pourers’ halls and the cutters’ halls are guild feuds now, and they are carried on with the same vigor as ever.
A skill is what you can do, and a title is what you are trusted to do. The nine guild titles, Initiate through Paragon, grade trust in a trade. A smith’s title caps the Grade of work she may lawfully make, and a merchant’s caps the Rarity he may sell. The two drift apart all the time, and the gap is the business of half the market. A Paragon of the anvil with a Journeyman’s token sells under the counter. A Grandmaster’s son who is a Journeyman at Smithing has apprentices who hide their work from him. See The Standing and the Title.
Trade skills on the Body Path
A trade skill is knowledge of a material, and the Body Path is the working of materials, so the one feeds the other. The schools teach the Body road as the Material Force, a ladder of five rungs: matter commanded as an object, then through contact, then through recognition, then through law, and at the far end as a whole system. A soul’s Body Mastery says which rung a fighter stands on. On a material that a Body fighter’s trade skill knows at Journeyman or better, they work one rung up, so that contact reaches recognition on that material and no other. A smith reads steel deeper than her Shell has any right to, a mason reads stone, and a butcher reads joints. It never carries anyone past the ceiling their Stage sets for Mastery, so a fighter already at the ceiling gets nothing from it but a neater cut.
Marta Kell is the case, and she shows which half of it needs no Crystal. Her Shell was sealed and held no Charge, so she worked no Aether on Tripe Row and had no rung to stand on. What she had was the knowing, at Paragon, and a hand that recognized a shoulder so completely that a thin knife and an old woman’s arm were enough to open it. Her sister’s grandson, Pell Kell, did eleven years at her block before a company took him, and his window reads Butchery at Journeyman. He is a Stage VII on the Body Path whose Shell reads Body II, a rung short of what his Stage allows until his Level reaches 185, so against a wall or a breastplate he must lay a hand on a thing to command it, like anyone on the second rung. On meat and joint he works at recognition. He does not need to find the seam of a shoulder, because he knows it across a yard the way his great-aunt knew it under her thumb, and the men who have sparred with him say it is like fighting someone who has already read the bill of fare. The Iron Mandate now asks recruits what their fathers did for a living, and writes the answer down.
When a technique jumps
Techniques show no level. A technique is a named thing done with a skill, and its strength is that skill’s rank, shaped by the Trait under it: the Trait sets what the technique can do, and the skill sets how well it is done. A fire-law under Swordwork at Journeyman is a competent burning cut. The same law under Swordwork at Master is the same cut, placed where nothing can be done about it.
A technique jumps when two things have both happened. The skill it runs on gains a rank, and a fight or a scene pushes the technique past its old limit. Neither is enough alone. A rank gained in the practice yard leaves every name on the sheet where it was, and a desperate night with no new rank under it is only a desperate night. Sect elders know this, which is the other reason they put students in danger.
A jump gives exactly one of four things: power, reach, speed or a lower cost. It may also add a condition, and the larger jumps usually do. The technique takes a bigger name, and the old name stays in use for the smaller version, which is why a veteran’s sheet reads like a family tree. Dob Harrow, a ferry-guard on the Ward river, threw Short Right Hand for nine years. His Brawling went from Apprentice to Journeyman in the spring, and that summer a river pirate stood a full stride outside his arm with a boathook. The window notes it and moves on:
[Skill: Brawling, Apprentice to Journeyman]
[Short Right Hand is now THE RIGHT HAND OF THE RIVER WARD]
[Gained: reach · Condition: both feet planted]
[Short Right Hand: kept]

Traits
A Trait is a standing law a soul carries, formed by what it survived, and The Trait System gives the whole of its law: the Four Reflections, the four offices and the ways it goes wrong. All of that stands. What this section adds is how loud it runs, and the answer is that a Trait has no number of its own. It reads at the Mastery of its bearer’s lead Path, so it grows as that Mastery grows, and its Release and Domain are the same law escalating. Ibbet Lowe’s Trait kept a street’s linen clean for forty-one years, and on one afternoon it took all the blood out of a knight in a white surcoat, and those were the same law at two amplitudes.
[Trait: It Comes Up White]
[Reads at: its base]

How it grows. Below Glory, where Mastery is not read, a Trait works at its base, and its base can be a frightening thing in a soul that has lived hard. From Glory it reads at the lead road’s rung, and it climbs when that rung does. Four things feed the climb, all of them by way of Level and the hands:

Use. Lean on the law and the life piles up, and the life is what Level counts. A Body fighter’s Trait is driven out through the Shell, a Spirit worker’s worked through the Core on souls and meanings, a Fate worker’s on bonds, oaths and odds, and all of it is real work.
The rest of the climb. A fighter who has spent thirty years leaning on one law carries it far higher than a prodigy who has merely had it longer, because thirty years of leaning is a great deal of Level, and the skill the law runs through has had thirty years to rank.
Refinement. A tempering course feeds Level, Salts for a law that runs through the Shell and Core stock for one that runs through the Core, and a teacher can show a practitioner where the law has more room than they have been giving it.
A Threshold. Tempering melts the Crystal down and rebuilds each layer, the lead layer first, and a Stage that lifts the Mastery ceiling lifts the Trait’s with it.

The mark a growing Trait leaves on the body follows the Path as well, dense and warm on the Body road, light and still on the Spirit, and next to nothing on Fate, where it shows in the street around the bearer. The Trait System has it under What a Trait Does to the Body.
[Level: 214 to 215]
[Spirit: III]
[Trait: Look Twice, now read at III]

[STAGE VII: REFRACTION]
[Bank the Fire: ceiling lifts to II]

What a rung buys. Each rung presses harder on the Trait’s four offices: a steeper Bias on the stats it touches, more that it Permits, a stronger seed in the melt and a higher Ceiling. It also buys a heavier Rigidity Effect, since the more absolute a law becomes, the less room its bearer has to contradict it. A Trait read at the fifth rung is a magnificent thing to have and an awful thing to disagree with.
How the Bias shows on the sheet. It depends on whether the law is always running. An always-on Trait shifts the stat itself, and the window simply shows the shifted figure, with no mark on it to say where the number came from. A porter whose Trait is Carries What Is Given reads Fortitude 210 every hour of his life, and only an assay with the Trait damped would show the 160 underneath. A situational Trait shows conditionally, with the plain figure first and the lifted one after it, and the condition named. Ibbet Lowe’s law runs only while there is something to be washed out:
[Absorption 140 · 190 while It Comes Up White holds]

The line changes the moment the condition does, and a fighter who has been leaning on the second figure learns a good deal from watching it go back to the first. Both kinds count on the two-step cap on boosts, so a soul whose Trait already lifts a stat a full step on the assayers’ scale has one step of room left there for a vow, a Release or a Draft.
Before waking. The great majority of the world’s Traits sit in bodies that will never be screened, refining by the Weathering, the slow hardening along the way a soul is used. A commoner’s window shows only Level, trade skills and health, so the law sits unlisted and goes on working. Ibbet Lowe’s window read Washing and nothing else for forty-one years. Waking opens the rest, and a Trait turns up already worn deep into the soul, sometimes far deeper than anyone in the room expected, to the alarm of everyone in it.
Monsters have them too. A Moor Tyrant’s Pack Hunter reads at the beast’s own Mastery like anybody else’s, and it is usually higher than you would like. See The Bestiary.
The older sheets gave every Trait a level of its own, a number that rose with use, and an old card’s Trait level is a guess at the same thing the lead road’s Mastery now says plainly.
Stat Points, and Placing Them at a Stage
Life spends most of your stat points. A few are yours. Every Level brings an allotment, and every Stage’s Threshold (the crisis that refines a soul to its next rung) brings a larger one. Most of it lands where the pressure went, by what you actually do, which for a practitioner means by what the lead layer does, and a farrier’s points do not wander into Feint because he would have liked them to. That is why a cobbler’s son and a duke’s son at the same Level read so differently, and why a sheet read properly is a biography.
The law, unchanged from Fracture of Worlds, Part Three. Points go on Sub-Stats only. A Primary is the total of its eight Sub-Stats, and the assayers read its mean (Dominion’s over seven, since Throne stands outside its total).



































LevelsPoints per LevelConcentration cap per Sub-Stat, per level-up1 to 100125101 to 200155201 to 300188301 to 4002110401 to 5002412
A Threshold grants the Stage number multiplied by 100 in points, so Stage VI awards 600 and Stage XIII awards 1,300, landing on the same terms. No Sub-Stat may pass the ceiling of the current Stage. Points refused by a ceiling are not lost: they sit as pressure until a Threshold enlarges the vessel.
The road leans the grant. A soul’s Path is the layer it leans on, the lead layer does most of the work in a life, and so it does most of the spending. Level by Level the points follow what that layer was doing. At a Threshold the lean is plainer still, because the melt rebuilds the lead layer first and the large grant lands while it is hottest.

























Lead PathThe Threshold grant leans towardBecauseBodyArdency, Vitality, Dexterity and TemperingThe Shell hits, bears, moves and holds its ChargeSpiritGnosis and HarmonicsThe Core reads, and tunes itself to what it worksFateDominion and ResilienceThe Layer claims, and keeps its own
It is a lean and no more. The points still go on Sub-Stats, the caps and ceilings stand, and a life lived against its road will drag the grant after it: a Spirit worker who has spent a Stage being hit comes out of the melt with more Vitality than her tutors ordered. A soul on two Paths takes the lean of its lead Path, and the second road gets what its share of the practice has earned.
A farrier’s Level. Odd Brannick shoes carthorses at Ostler’s Cross, and the week a gray mare put him through the side of his own forge he went from Level 14 to Level 15. That is under Level 100, so twelve points, and his life spent all twelve without asking him. Five went on Fortitude, which is the most one Sub-Stat can take from a single Level that low, because he had just been kicked through a wall. Four went on Grapple, for nineteen years of holding up the hind leg of something that did not want it held. Three went on Threshold, for the kick. Nothing went to Feint, or to anything else he might have chosen, and he will not be asked for an opinion until a Stage gives him a bar to place.
What the owner sees. None of that arithmetic appears on a window. Your soul tells you which Sub-Stats moved, and it gives you what is left to place as a bar:
[Threshold passed: Stage VI, Glory]
[Your life has spent it: Fortitude, Threshold, Flux]
[Points to place: ▓▓░░░░░░░░]
[Place where?]

You place by thinking it. The window answers with whichever Sub-Stat moved:
[Reflex: rising]
[Points to place: ▓░░░░░░░░░]

[Ward: at ceiling. Refused. Held as pressure.]

Between Stages it has nothing to say on the subject. Jory the gaff-man’s window said it flatly the morning after his first real fight: Points to place: none until your next Stage.
The placing is the whole of the owner’s say, so people argue about it for years. The handful you steer is small beside what your life has spent, and it is the only part you get to aim. The main schools of thought, shouted in any sect refectory:

Feed the peak. Put it where you already fight. A contested exchange is decided by the Sub-Stat in use, and a full step ahead on the assayers’ scale wins it outright, so the next step on your best Sub-Stat wins fights. This is what most fighters do and what most crews want them to do.
Patch the hole. Your life will never spend on what it never does, so the placed points are your one way to fix what it left out. A brawler with a Ward the assayers would not bother writing down dies the first time he meets a mind-worker. Old teachers who have buried students say this one.
Pay the register. Institutions measure the mean and fights are decided by the peak, so a point in a neglected Sub-Stat lifts the Primary an assessor prints. A house with a marriage to arrange or a title to secure will instruct its heirs accordingly, and the heir will look magnificent on paper until he meets someone who has read that paper.
Save the gate. The Path gates and the Resonant Pairs ask for a figure on particular Sub-Stats. Someone who knows where they mean to go can place toward a door years ahead. Most people who think they know this are wrong.

A bought Stage pays out too, and the Threshold points land on the same terms, most of them where the life has been spending itself, leaning toward the lead Path’s Primaries like any other grant. A second son who takes Transcendence in a quiet room receives a very fine helping of Finesse, Economy and whatever his years of obedience have trained, with his bar to place on top of it. This is what the family’s tutors are for, and why the great houses employ men whose entire job is to stand behind an heir at the moment of a Draft and tell him where to put it.
Race and lineage set where you start and what comes easily: they show on the sheet and shape base stats, so the same placed point lands on a different number for a Marrowkin and a Serpentkin. They are tendencies you can argue with, at some length, for a lifetime.
Read next: Windows and the Sheet, and The Ladder and the Draft.

the-magic-system/the-soul-and-the-climb/.title: Soul Wounds and the Menders
the-magic-system/the-soul-and-the-climb/.content:
What a Spirit strike does once it is past the Shell, how the hurt shows, how long it stays, who closes it and for how much, and what the Spirit road does to its own walkers when they overspend

“He had not a mark on him. That was how we knew it was bad.”
A ringside surgeon at the Sealhall Lantern Brackets, giving evidence in the matter of the purse.

Gorm Hadrick, called the Anvil, went into the third round of the Lantern Brackets at Sealhall in a harness of blued Marrowhold plate with brass rivets the size of thumbnails, behind a Durability the slates had chalked at three hundred and forty, and he had not been put down in six years. Across forty paces of raked sand stood Sister Odalys Wren of the Quiet Bell, a thin Confessor in a saffron habit with ink on her cuffs, whom he outweighed by a second person. The crowd had come to see how long she could run.
She did not run. She raised two fingers, said one word in the temple tongue, and something the color of old honey crossed the sand between them faster than the eye liked. It touched nothing. The plate did not ring, the rivets did not start, the sand under his boots lay as it was raked. Gorm Hadrick took one more step, stopped, and sat down in the ring like a man who has remembered he left a pot on the fire. He was not bleeding. His aura, which had been a good loud forge orange, had gone the color of weak tea, and when his second ran out and asked him what day it was he gave the right answer and then could not say what his second’s name was, which was Tobb, and Tobb was his brother.
His window had it before the surgeons did:
[Hit: Core struck out of true. Soul wound, deep.]
[Lost: the color orange. Taste dulled. Tobb, gone thin.]
[Stays until mended.]

The plate was sold that winter to pay the mender. It had never been touched, and it fetched full price.
That is a soul wound, and it is the reason every hitter in the four quarters who has fought a thrower once keeps a charm on a cord and a mender’s name in his purse. The rest of this page is the law of it.
I. The Door Past the Shell
Armor answers a blow. Durability answers a blow. Both belong to the Aether Shell, the soul’s outer layer, the one that meets the Physical World, and a strike from the Spirit Path is not going to the Physical World at all.
A Spirit fighter spends Essence (spiritual energy: Aether refined in the Crystal and stamped with the person who refined it), authored in the Essence Core and sent out through the Core. What leaves her is a say about a soul, carried on her own substance, and it lands on the layer it was made in: the other person’s Core. Spirit force is force on souls. It does not dent bronze, lift a stone or scorch a coat, and a Spirit fighter who wants a wall moved has to move it through her own Shell like anyone else, at whatever her Body Mastery will bear. The Shell is the only door into matter. The Core is the door into people, and a breastplate does not cover it.
What stands in the way is the target’s own soul. Integrity is how hard the Core is to cut, Anchoring is how firmly it sits in true, and Ward answers a read rather than a blow. A hitter with Durability in the three hundreds and Integrity under a hundred is a castle with the gate open, and throwers can tell at a glance, which is most of why they look so calm.
A Spirit strike does one of three things, and the surgeons have learned to ask which.

























The strikeWhat it doesHow it reads on the dayKnocked out of trueThe soul is shoved off its seat in the body, the way a blow shifts a rider in the saddle. Nothing is cut. Will and limb stop agreeing for a moment, and a working half-made comes apart in the handA stagger with no blow behind it, a lag between meaning to move and moving, a dropped guard. Usually shallowDread laid on a mindA feeling is set in the Core with the striker’s stamp on it, and the mind takes it for its own. Dread is the common one, because it is the cheapest to author, and grief, shame and homesickness have all been thrown in angerThe knees go before the reason does. The victim can tell you there is nothing to fear and cannot make his legs agree. Shallow if it lifts with the fight, deep if it does notA Core woundThe Core itself is cut: identity, memory or a Trait’s seat opened, and something leaks or is lostColor goes out of the aura and out of the world, a sense dulls, a memory thins. Deep by nature
Anything that works on souls can give one. A Spirit Path fighter is the usual source, and a spirit, a lingering dead thing or a beast of the Soul Plane will do it just as well and with less ceremony. A Body Path fighter cannot, however hard she hits, because matter has no purchase on a soul, and the hitters who claim otherwise are describing a concussion.
II. How It Shows
A soul wound is a status line, like any wound, and it stays until someone treats it. It sits on the window beside the broken collarbone and the missing ear, in the owner’s own tongue, and it says what has been lost.
[Hit: dread laid, shallow. Knees unsteady while it holds.]

[Hit: Core cut, deep.]
[Lost: green, the smell of rain. Your mother's voice, gone thin.]
[Stays until mended.]

From outside there is no blood and no bruise, and the tells are quieter than a body’s. There are three, and a good second knows them all.

Lost color. The victim’s aura fades toward gray at the place it was struck, and the world fades for the victim to match. It is rarely all color. It is one, or a family of them: Gorm Hadrick lost orange, which was his own hue, and for a season his forge fire looked to him like dishwater. People notice it first in their food.
A dulled sense. Taste, smell, the feel of cloth under the fingers, the pitch of a known voice. The organ is whole. A physician will test the ear and find it sound, and the patient will tell you music has gone flat.
A memory gone thin. The memory is still there, and that is the cruelty of it. The victim knows he has a brother, and knows the name if told it, and it will not stay. A thin memory has no weight: it does not come when called, it carries no feeling, and it reads to its owner like something he was told about a stranger.

The body follows on. A soul out of true makes a clumsy hand, a deep wound makes a poor sleeper, and a fighter carrying one works at a loss: a working authored in a cut Core arrives ragged, and Traits seated near the wound stutter. None of this is heat, and none of it is fever. A surgeon who bleeds a soul-struck man is treating the wrong layer and should be stopped.
The pale place. Anyone with Gnosis Analysis worth the name can read a soul wound directly, as a tear or a dislocation in the Core, and can say how deep. A healed one still reads. It leaves a pale place, a patch of Core with the color washed out of it, and it stays for life the way a scar stays. Assayers note it on a slip without being asked. Opponents with the stat to see it note it too, for their own reasons, as section III explains.
III. How Long It Lasts

























DepthLeft aloneMendedShallow (knocked out of true, a dread that lifts, a nick)Closes by itself in days, a week or two at the outside, with rest and no spendingA sitting or two, and the fighter is back in the yardDeep (a cut Core, a dread that has set, a loss on the window)Does not close. It spreads slowly, and the thin memory gets thinnerSeasons. A course of sittings through one season at the least, often twoSetFor lifeFor life. A mender can make it bearable and cannot make it go
Two things set a wound, and both are common.
Left past a season. A deep wound untreated for a full season sets where it lies. The Core closes around the loss the way bone knits around a break nobody splinted, and what was thin is then gone: the color, the sense or the memory is no longer missing, because there is no longer a place for it. Most set wounds in the four quarters belong to people who could not pay in the first month and had the money by the fourth.
Struck twice in the same place. A second wound on an open one, or on the pale place a healed one left, sets at once, on the day, and no mender alive has undone it. This is why a pale place is worth knowing about, and why a certain kind of thrower pays an assayer for the reading on an opponent before a bout. The halls call that scouting. The menders have another word for it.
Tam Corrow of the Hallenfeld barges took a Core wound from a drowned thing under Chainbridge at nineteen, lost the pitch of voices, paid a mender through one hard summer and had it back, with a pale place left of center to remember it by. Eleven years later a rival who had bought his slip put a second stroke on the same spot in a tavern yard. Corrow is a Stage VII Riverblade with a good name on the water, and he has not heard a tune since. He can tell you a fiddle is playing. He says it sounds like someone describing one.
Mending draws on the patient. A soul wound closes with the patient’s own Essence, re-stamped across the gap, since nobody else’s will take. So a fighter under a mender’s care is a fighter spending reserve on being whole, and one who goes back into the ring half-closed is spending from a purse with a hole in it. Menders refuse to sit a patient who is still flagging, and the good ones refuse a patient who fights between sittings.
IV. The Menders
Soul-mending is a trade, with a bench, a fee and a reputation to lose, and it has nothing to do with the miracle sellers at the fair. A mender is a Spirit Path practitioner, at Spirit II at the least for shallow work, an Answerer as the road says it, and at Spirit III, a Confessor, or better for anything deep, since the work is reaching into a willing soul and finding what is lodged or torn there. Temples keep them, the great houses retain them, the fighting halls have one on a stipend and complain about the stipend, and a working town of any size has a mender’s door with a lamp over it, usually near the physician’s and never on good terms with him.
What a sitting is. The patient sits. The mender reads the wound, sets the soul back in true if it has been shifted, and then has the patient do the long part, which is to tell the thin thing over: the brother’s name and the brother’s face and the day they stole the pears, again and again, while the mender holds the edges of the cut together so that what the patient says has somewhere to stay. It is slow, it is dull, and it leaves both of them gray and cold. A mender cannot put back what is gone. She can close a wound around what is left, stop it spreading, and keep a deep one from setting.
What it costs. The prices below are the Guild-city rate, set against a physician’s visit at 1 to 3 silver and a surgeon’s operation at 5 to 40 gold on What Things Cost. The fee is quoted before the first sitting and paid before the second.








































ItemPriceNoteA reading1 to 2 silverThe mender looks, says how deep, and says whether it is hers to treat. Honest ones send set wounds home at this priceA sitting, shallow2 to 6 silver; a few copper and a prayer at a temple doorOne or two close most shallow wounds. A hall fighter’s stipend usually covers itA course for a deep wound10 to 60 gold the seasonTwo or three sittings a week through a season, by a Confessor. A laborer’s year at the bottom and a clerk’s several at the top. Houses pay it without blinkingA course by a Shepherd100 gold and up, by private treatyFor wounds near a Trait’s seat, or on someone whose name is worth it. She can hold the soul still while she works, which halves the timeKeeping a set wound1 to 3 silver the monthNo cure. A sitting now and then so the edges stay quietA soul-ward5 silver for a temple charm; 2 to 30 gold for worked piecesA charm, a reliquary or a warded band, worn. Worked ones lift Ward and Harmonics by a real margin and draw a little on the wearer to stay lit. The fair-stall kind lifts nothing
Who goes without. The arithmetic is the same as for a broken leg. A rich fighter takes a deep wound on a Tuesday and is under a Confessor’s hands by Wednesday, and by harvest has a pale place and a story. A poor one waits to see whether it will close by itself, and a deep wound never does, and the season runs out. The unwoken take soul wounds too, from haunted ground and from fights they were standing too near, and most of what a village calls a changed man, a woman who came back from the fen wrong or a child who stopped laughing is a set wound nobody had the silver to read.

A warning from the bench. There is a brisk trade in “restoring” a set wound, sold to the families of the well-off. What is sold is a second stamp laid over the place by someone else’s hand. It takes, for a while, and the patient is delighted, and what he has got back is somebody else’s memory of pears. The Guild fines for it. The temples have a harsher word.

V. The Second Case
Lady Maren Aldous of the Banner Houses took a laid dread at the Assize of Greywater, from a rival’s hired Answerer in the gallery, in the middle of her own testimony. It was meant to be shallow, a moment’s disgrace in front of the bench. It did not lift. Her window read dread laid, deep, the color blue went out of her banners as far as she could see them, and for nine weeks she could not climb a stair without her hands shaking, and knew perfectly well there was nothing on the stair.
Her house had a Shepherd under retainer. He sat her four times a week through the autumn, at a fee the house has never disclosed, and by first frost she was back before the same bench, where she won. The pale place is still there, low on the Core, and her enemies have paid to know exactly where. She has worn a reliquary of worked silver over it ever since, changes menders every year so that no one of them knows the whole of her, and is said to be the only woman in the Midmarch who fences with her back to the gallery wall.
The rival’s Answerer was fined eight gold for a working thrown in a court. The Lady considered this the most insulting part.
VI. Flagging on the Spirit Road
The wounds above are done to a soul by somebody else. The Spirit Path also does a quieter version to its own walkers, every time they overspend, and a watcher who knows the signs can tell a Spirit fighter from across a yard by how she tires.
Every practitioner shows the shared tells as the reserve falls: at half the breath shortens and the aura dims, at a quarter comes tremor and a thinning color, at a tenth the aura flickers and the Trait stutters. On top of those, each road flags in its own way, because each spends a different thing. A Body fighter is working raw Aether through the flesh, and what she loses comes off as heat. A Spirit fighter is spending Essence, which is to say herself, and what she loses is paid in the Core as a hollowing. It is never heat. She does not sweat and she does not steam. She goes cold.

























ReserveWhat a Spirit fighter shows, on top of the shared tellsHalfThe colors near her go flat. Cloth, banners and painted shields within a few paces look washed, and she sees it worse than anyoneA quarterA hollow cold comes off her, with no frost in it, and she slips a word: the wrong name for a thing, a sentence that ends somewhere elseA tenthNames and memories slip. She knows the face in front of her and cannot find what to call it, and the working she is holding starts to forget what it was forMaxedA memory gone for good, and a faint. She wakes not knowing what she has lost, which is the nature of the loss, and someone who loves her has to tell her
The last row is a soul wound in everything but the name, self-dealt, and it sets on the day because there is nothing left to mend it with. Old Spirit masters keep a book in their own hand for this reason, and reading it back is said to be the worst hour of the year.
For comparison, and so that the other roads are not mistaken for it: a flagging Body fighter runs hot, with heat-haze thickening on the skin, then steam off the shoulders and cramps, then the skin splitting in fine lines as the Shell cracks, and at the end heat stroke and burst vessels. A flagging Fate fighter looks well, and the trouble is around her: small luck curdles nearby, things begin going wrong within reach, her own name sits wrong in other mouths, and at the end every knot she owes comes due at once. The Three Paths sets the three side by side.

Cost. A shallow wound costs days and a few silver. A deep one costs a season, a year’s wages or a house’s indifference, and a pale place for life. A set one costs whatever it took, for good.
Counter. Integrity and Anchoring, raised honestly, and Ward against the read that finds the weak place. A worked soul-ward. Distance closed before the working is authored, since a Spirit fighter caught out of position has an ordinary body. And a mender’s name, known before the bout and paid before the season is out.
Read next: The Three Paths, for the road that deals these; How Power Grows, for the Spirit Mastery a mender climbs; Windows and the Sheet, for how a wound sits on the line; and The Tell and the Knot, for what the third road owes.

the-magic-system/the-soul-and-the-climb/.content:
A Visual Taxonomy of Essence Hue, Temperance Clarity, and Wellspring Color Across the Continuum. Compiled for the Archives. Companion to The Sixty Wellsprings, The Sixteen Stages, the Provenance Doctrine of The Bench of Attribution, and The Standing Index.

On the last night of the Boat Fair at Tarn Quay, the lamps along Fishmonger’s Row went ochre one after another from the harbor end, a full ten minutes before there was anybody to see. The paper lanterns went first, then the oil in the glass, then the pale evening over the net lofts, and a fine dust of harbor silt began to settle on the eels. Nobody on that quay had ever read a line of the Refinement Spectrum, and every one of them knew exactly what it meant. The Red Crane school and the Tanners’ Boys, who had been brawling up and down the Row all week in scarlet and blue, stopped in mid-punch and straightened each other’s collars. Every stall on the quay began taking in its awning. Then Grandmother Seok Bo-ok came up the Row in wooden clogs, Stage XII, Basilithe to the bone, carrying the color of a quarry at sunset on everything she passed, and it was already bleaching toward white at its edges. She had come for a pair of boots a tanner had owed her since they were both twelve. He paid, in both hands, in front of everybody, and handed over his front teeth along with them without being asked. It cost the Row three weeks of sweeping, and he told the story for the rest of his life.
Ochre for the Wellspring, the white edge for the Stage, and nobody on the quay needed the Archives for either. The Archives, however, has opinions.
Preface

On the question of whether Essence (spiritual energy, the soul’s own stuff of power) has color, the Archives’ position has always been that it does, that the color is not decorative, and that anyone who dismisses it as merely aesthetic has never been in a room with a Zenith practitioner.

Essence color is determined by two independent variables. The Wellspring (one of the Sixty, the governing idea that changes how a soul uses its power) a soul has tempered on longest assigns the hue. The Temperance Stage (how far the soul has climbed) of the Soul Crystal (the soul itself, in its working form) assigns the clarity. Hue without clarity is noise. Clarity without hue is an empty vessel. Together they produce the practitioner’s Essence Color: the visible expression of who they are and what they have survived.
The hue comes from the Wellspring a soul has tempered on, and from the person before that. A soul that has yet to temper on any Wellspring shows a color of its own, which belongs to no lens and answers to nothing but the person wearing it. Once it has tempered on one, that Wellspring sets the hue, and a soul with several takes its hue from the lens it has tempered on longest. Either way the hue is there from the first Stage, clouded low down. Older books have the color coming from an inborn bias of the soul, and the trade has given that up: a soul’s color changes when what it has tempered on changes, and an inborn bias would have no business doing that.
An aura is built in three coats, and a good eye reads all of them. The Wellspring a soul has tempered on longest sets the base color. Every lens adds texture and sound, the grain and the voice of the thing: a tint laid over the base, the way it moves, the note it holds. A class or a big Trait adds a shape, a set of antlers in the glare, a door-frame standing around a landlady, a coil of smoke that will not leave a man’s left shoulder. Three people on one Wellspring in one Stage will never be mistaken for one another, and no two people have ever agreed on who looked best.
Hue follows the idea. Every hue is what its idea looks like held up to the light, the Wild ones as surely as the rest. A Pyreveil practitioner reads ember-orange because fire that renews stays in the soul where it was lit and never flares off into smoke, so what shows is the steady orange of iron holding its heat. A Judicium practitioner reads arc-blue with colored fringes because a thing truly told apart shows its parts at the edge, each in its own color. Penance is dull iron, darkening, because the soul is hardest where it has gone back most, and Benediction warm red-gold because a bond freely given is warm in the hand and weighed like gold. The Measurewrights will tell you, with a chart, that Pyreveil is orange because that is the color heat takes in iron and Judicium blue because that is the color current makes in air, and the chart has the shade exactly right and the reason backward. The Wellsprings did not choose their colors. The colors chose the Wellsprings, because a color is what a law looks like from outside.
Clarity follows refinement. Every woken aura shows its own hue from the first Stage, clouded and smoky low down and clearing as the Stage rises. A Murmuring Crystal reads nearly black because it is full of noise, contradiction and unresolved identity, and its color comes through that like a coal through ash. A Zenith Crystal passes light like spring water because almost everything that was not essential has been burned away, and the eye looking through it reports mostly brightness. Temperance is subtraction, and the Refinement Spectrum is what subtraction looks like from outside. There is one color in a soul, the lens’s, and the Spectrum says only how much cloud still stands between it and the eye. Color says what. Clarity says how high.
Part One · The Refinement Spectrum
Temperance clarity across the Sixteen Stages. The hue is present in every row, smothered at the bottom and clearing as you read down. Nothing in this table is a color of its own: the black at the head of it is cloud, and the white at the foot of it is daylight coming through.
The metaphor is smelting. Raw ore is dark, dense, full of impurity. Heat and pressure drive the impurities out, and what remains brightens with each pass of the forge. The Soul Crystal is the ore. Temperance is the forge. The Refinement Spectrum is the color of what comes out.
The assay houses prefer a jeweler’s bench to a smelter’s floor, and they grade a soul the way they would grade a stone: by its color for kind, and by its clarity and depth for worth. Clarity is how little stands in the light’s way. Depth is how far into the color the eye can go before it stops. A Spectrum reading is those two things and nothing else, and a clerk who writes “gray” on a slip for a Glory fighter has described the cloud and forgotten the man. The Rank column gives what people call a soul at each Stage, and the Crystal column the look the stone takes there (Part Three).











































































































StageRankCrystalClarity and characterI · MurmuringInitiateCloudedClouded nearly to black, with the hue already in it. Coal dust on a smith’s palm before the bellows touch it, and the one live coal somewhere underneath. Opaque and turbid. No coherence: noise rendered visible, a dark smear with a stain of its own color, gone before it travels a handspan. Others with sufficient Gnosis (the stat of perception and understanding) perceive it only as a quality of wrongness in the ambient light, the way a room feels heavier when someone in it is afraidII · WellingApprenticeCloudedDark char with the hue stirring beneath, like a dye in dirty water. First detectability outside the body: a thin aura clinging to the hands during sustained working. Mancers (practitioners who read and sense through magic) describe reading Stage II as trying to read a book by holding it against a dark wall in a dim roomIII · AscensionJourneymanCloudedSmoke, tinted plainly with the lens’s color: a brown smoke over a fire school, a blue one over a storm hall. The first genuine clearing. What the soul works now shows as its own, holding a consistent tint rather than cycling through murky interference: on a Spirit or a Fate soul that is the identity stamped on its Essence at refining, and on a Body soul, whose Charge carries no stamp, it is raw Aether settling into the lens’s shape. Often the first time a practitioner sees their own output and recognizes it as theirsIV · FlourishingAdeptCloudedWarm charcoal with a rumor of the hue in it, the color of good charcoal when the ember bed has been worked to consistency. Identity has settled; the Signature (the resonance pattern unique to one practitioner) is readable at distance by any competent Mancer. At this Stage the color is a suggestion, not a declarationV · SplinteringExpertFacetedFracture-streaked. The crisis Stage, and the color shows it. Hairline veins of the lens’s clear color run through the smoky field, appearing and vanishing with emotional spikes. A Splintering practitioner’s Essence flickers. Gnosis-grade observation shows a field at war with itself, the old architecture refusing to make room for the new. Those veins are the first faces the stone takesVI · GloryExpertFacetedA thin haze with the color standing in it, and the first Stage where genuine luminance enters. The color no longer has to fight its way through, and the aura begins to keep an outline. This is the Stage where civilians begin to see practitioners as visually markedVII · RefractionExpertFacetedClear, with the last of the cloud lying in it like breath on a pane. Haze and color occupy the same field without mixing. Prismatic: the Essence shifts hue depending on angle of observation, as a clean stone does when it is turned in the fingers. A Refraction Domain (a region where the world runs on the practitioner’s terms) held on the Body road manifests as an environmental color-temperature shift perceptible to anyone standing inside it. A Spirit seed changes no light at all, and a Fate seed shows as dust lying stillVIII · TranscendenceMasterFireClear enough to throw light, and the light it throws is the lens’s color. The first Domain threshold. Dark with light in it has become light with the memory of darkness in it. Bright enough to illuminate in low light. A Body aura casts the hue onto nearby surfaces, a Spirit aura lights its owner and bends the shadows, and a Fate aura is as bright as either to a reader and lights nothing (Part Three)IX · InvocationMasterFireBright, and no longer uniformly the practitioner’s own. A second hue enters at the edges of the field, the Wellspring’s rather than the soul’s, surfacing during invocation and receding after. The first Stage at which a Mancer reads two authors in one Essence and the reason experienced readers ask who else is in there before they ask anything elseX · RealizationMasterFireClean through. The cloud has receded to a whisper and the color dominates without competition, deep enough that the eye goes into it and does not find the back. Aetheric Residue (the trace a working leaves in the surrounding Aether) now holds the hue for hours and sometimes days, staining the Continuum (the lawful fabric of reality) the way dye stains cloth. Ground a Stage X practitioner worked on keeps their color long enough that a Mancer arriving a week later can still say who was hereXI · DissonanceGrandmasterFlawlessBrilliant, with visible interference grain. The second crisis Stage. Textures like the standing ripples in a struck basin fluctuate with the Crystal’s internal pressure, objectively brighter than Realization and reading as unstable: the brightness of pitch flaring on a torch, where a steady lamp would hold. Mancers describe the passage out of Dissonance as the moment the soul stops arguing and starts speaking, and it is the most dramatic single-Stage change in the spectrumXII · EmanationGrandmasterFlawlessThe color begins to bleach toward white at its edges, where the field has grown clear enough to bend the daylight around it. The passive aura projects far enough that the color change in a room’s ambient light announces them before they arrive. The bleaching is the first visible sign that identity and Continuum-law are beginning to mergeXIII · PrincipalityArchmasterStarredWashed in light, near-white to the eye, the way tinted glass looks held against the sun rather than against shadow. The color has gone nowhere. There is simply nothing left in the stone to stop the light. Difficult to look at directly, whatever its brightness, because the eye processes its saturation as pressure. Reads as a statement rather than a phenomenonXIV · ZenithArchmasterStarredNear-white with the faintest ghost of the lens’s color. The sun seen through colored glass. The canonical ceiling of mortal progression. The ghost of hue is all that distinguishes one Zenith Crystal from anotherXV · RevelationParagonAbsolutePressurized white: every color held in compression, the way white light contains the full spectrum. Witnesses perceive it as containing all color simultaneously, and none of them has called it colorless. Two recorded practitioners; neither produced effects describable in color terms. The descriptions default to temperature, pressure, and the specific quality of fear that accompanies encountering something the Continuum treats as a peerXVI · ApexParagonAbsoluteAbsolute white. The distinction between soul and Continuum dissolves, and the color distinction dissolves with it. What observers report has stopped being a visual phenomenon: they report the experience of standing inside a law rather than looking at one. No practitioner has reached Apex within the documented age
The dark lenses prove the rule. Tenebra, Nihiloth and Abython have no brightness to gain, and they climb the Spectrum like everyone else. A Murmuring Tenebra is a dirty dusk, brown at the edges and leaking. A Principality Tenebra is a dark with an edge you could cut bread on, perfectly clean, and the lamps beside it look tired. A student who was taught that the high Stages go white was taught by someone who has only met the bright lenses, and the white in the rows above is what a clear stone does with daylight when its own color has light in it.
The aura, Stage by Stage
The aura a person wears is the same reading at arm’s length, and it changes its manners as it clears.
Low down it is smoke. From Murmuring to Flourishing an aura has no edge. It shows only during a working, clings to the hands, drifts off the shoulders in tatters like breath on a cold morning, and loses itself within a handspan at first and an arm’s length by the end. It stains what it touches and lights nothing.
In the middle Stages it clears and takes a shape. Splintering runs clear veins through the smoke, and from Glory the aura keeps an outline when its owner stands still, which is why Glory is where a civilian first sees one. Glory is also where the soul first offers a class, and the third coat, the antlers or the door-frame or the coil of smoke at the left shoulder, arrives with it. By Refraction the shape holds at rest and in a wind, and from Transcendence it is clear enough to throw light. On a Body fighter, whose aura is Charge showing through the Shell, that light lands on the wall behind. On a Spirit fighter it stays with the figure a half-step off the body, and what the wall gets is a shadow leaning the wrong way. On a Fate walker there is no light for anyone but a reader, and the wall is merely free of dust.
At the top it bends light. From Emanation the edges bleach, and from Principality the aura does to light what a full glass does to a spoon. A doorpost seen past the shoulder stands a finger off where it is, a lamp flame beyond them leans without a draft, and their shadow carries a bright rim. Nobody needs a Mancer to read that, and nobody who has seen it once mistakes anything else for it.
The unwoken show nothing. A sealed Crystal puts out no color at all, and a reader with the Gnosis for it finds only the dark stone of Part Three.
Part Two · The Sixty by Hue
Essence hue by Wellspring, each one its own, with the short form on that Wellspring’s entry in the register. The assignment is causal, and anyone who calls it symbolic should be kept away from Mancers: each hue is what its idea looks like held up to the light, and the line after the color says why. A kind of neighborhood shows, since fire tends to orange, stone to ochre and water to teal, but the hue belongs to the Wellspring and nothing above it.
Wild, at home in the Physical World













































































































































WellspringHue and characterAbythonNear-black. A density in the air more than a color, like looking through glass that is not quite clean, and the darkest of the grays, because the soul has made its peace with the deep by matching itself to the dark there, and keeps no light of its own to set against itAnima SpirareBright arterial red. Oxygenated blood, copper patina, the wet red inside an open wound, because a body that remembers being whole sends all its blood running to the smallest hurt. The most viscerally uncomfortable color on the list to observe: the hue triggers the mammalian recognition-response to blood. The observer’s pulse accelerates, attention sharpens, and there is a faint nausea that has nothing to do with the magic and everything to do with a body that has evolved to treat red coming from inside another body as a signal to actAscensioSteel gray with pulley-lines. The lines are the load being taken up, each one a step that will bear it, and the gray is the color of a height climbed by rope and tackle, a step at a time and never by one heaveBasilitheOchre-gold with quartz-clear lines. Clay, wet stone, mineral veins in quarry rock, because the soul has become a standard: the gold is what every weight is read against, and the clear line is the one note in it that nobody can retune. Reads as heavy, with a visual density few other hues have, and it may be the most immediately identifiable color in the spectrum. Like the other stone lenses it routinely leaves physical residue: a fine dust of the local substrate settling on surfaces where the practitioner has been workingCataclysmWhite-orange flash with a pale ring. Part Three · The Crystal, the Aura and the Body
The Crystal is the soul itself, as literal as a liver, standing where the Material, Soul and Fate planes overlap, and it has observable physical properties. One of those is color.
The Crystal’s color tracks the Refinement Spectrum but is not identical to the Essence’s color. Essence is what the Crystal produces. The Crystal is what produces it, and the distinction matters at the extremes.
The Crystal’s look
The Crystal passes through seven named looks, one for the sealed stone and six for the woken one, each how the whole stone looks at its Stage, all three layers together. They follow the Stage and nobody climbs them. The names are a jeweler’s, and each one describes what a reader with the Gnosis for it actually sees in the chest.

Seed (the unwoken) · The grower’s word for the small first crystal a stone is raised from. No Essence output, but the Crystal exists and can be perceived: dark, inert, dimensionally flat. A black stone in the chest with no luminance and no depth
Clouded (Stages I–IV) · Cloud is the bench word for the milk inside an unworked stone. The Crystal has opened and is circulating, the color is in it, and the eye cannot get past the surface. The aura over it is smoke for the same reason
Faceted (Stages V–VII) · The stone has taken faces. Splintering cuts them, and each one returns the light the same way twice, which is the recurring rhythm the Continuum can at last read consistently. Turned in a reader’s sight it flashes and goes dark and flashes again, and by Refraction a reader sees into it and through it, with the last cloud lying in the heart of the stone like breath on a pane
Fire (Stages VIII–X) · The jeweler’s word for light split into color and thrown back out. The Crystal stops only passing light and begins to give it, in the lens’s hue, and the first true Domain stands on that
Flawless (Stages XI–XII) · Nothing in it under any glass: no cloud, no feather, no seam between what the person is and what the person’s law does. The color runs so deep that a reader looking in reports no back to it
Starred (Stages XIII–XIV) · A star caught inside the stone, with its rays running out to the faces. A reader sees the person in it, whole and exact, and has usually looked away by then
Absolute (Stages XV–XVI) · Output virtually indistinguishable from Continuum-law. The Crystal reads as a source of light that does not behave the way light should, because what shines there is identity, rendering itself visible by sheer force of coherence

The progression is not uniform:

Seed to Clouded is the smallest color change and the largest qualitative change: dead stone to a bellows breathing on its own, and the visual difference is barely perceptible.
Faceted to Fire is the first moment the Crystal produces enough light to be seen without mantic assistance.
Flawless to Starred is where the Crystal stops reading as an object inside a person and shows what it has been all along: the person. The color is the soul, expressed.

The old names. Old books, the north-road songs and any assay slip written before the renaming call them Dormant, Awakened, Harmonic, Resonant, Radiant, Sovereign, the Crystallized Soul and Absolute, in that order, eight names for what were then eight looks, the jewelers keeping one called Clear between Faceted and Fire. The Measurewrights retired the old names because three of them are also folk names for rungs of Body Mastery and two were the names of old Bands, and a clerk who writes Resonant on a slip ought to mean one thing by it. They retired Clear because it was only the last of Faceted, and an old slip that says Clear means a Refraction stone.
A look follows the Stage, and a Stage can be bought. A bought Stage gets the look of its Stage on schedule, because the look follows the Stage. What it does not get is the Level to hold it, and a soul held above its Level is Overgrown, which shows in the reading as a color that is clear and shallow, bright at the surface with cloud still standing a little way in. Depth is the part of the reading that money has never moved, and it is why the coil is asked for depth as well as a Stage. Tier Grade, Bands and the Aether Shell has what each tier can structurally do.

The three at the Gull. Tarn Quay still talks about the evening three Masters, all at Transcendence and none acquainted, took the one free table at the Gull and Anchor. Brannoch Vey, a Pyreveil shipwright off the slips, wore his ember-orange close as a shirt, and when he set his mug down the handle glowed the color of his hand for a moment after. What the climb does to the body
The same three roads show in the flesh, slowly, and a Stage or two behind the aura.
The Body Path grows dense. The Shell is the layer that lives in matter, and a soul that leans on it lays the leaning down in bone and fiber. A Body fighter is heavier than they look from the first Stages, heavier than they have any right to be by Glory, and warm to the touch in any weather, a hand like a loaf just out of the oven. Ferrymen charge them double and are right to. High up, from Invocation, the eyes catch light like a cat’s, a flat coin of the lens’s color in a dark doorway, and snow does not lie long where they have been sitting.
The Spirit Path grows light. A soul that leans on the Core wears its flesh more loosely. The tread goes quiet, the weight goes off the stair, and in strong light, from about the same Stage, there is a faint translucence at the edges of them: the rim of an ear, the web of a hand held up against noon. What every animal notices long before that is the stillness. Horses stop fidgeting, a hall full of dogs goes quiet, and birds do not get up when they walk through.
The Fate Path shows almost nothing. A Fate walker at Emanation can look like a clerk on half pay. What changes is the world around them: the weather they walk under, which is theirs more often than chance allows, fair or foul by the person; the crowd that parts without knowing it has; the queue that happens to be short. The body keeps no record at all, and that is why the careful reader watches the street and not the man.
How each road looks when it tires is a different picture, heat and split skin for the Body, flat color and slipped names for the Spirit, curdled luck for Fate, and it is set out with the three roads.
Part Four · The Essence Matrix
The full Essence Color of any practitioner is the intersection of hue and Temperance clarity: sixty Wellsprings across sixteen Stages. Left edge of each row: the color at its most clouded and least refined. Right edge: clearest, deepest and most refined, with daylight coming through it. Every practitioner in the Continuum sits somewhere on this grid, and their position can be estimated by anyone who looks and read outright by anyone whose Gnosis Perception outranks their Resilience Ward.

The applications are diagnostic. A field Mancer assessing an unknown practitioner reads two things at once: the hue tells them what the practitioner works, the clarity tells them how long they have been working it.
A bright saturated Pyreveil reading is a high-Stage fire practitioner, and a bright rose-gold looks nearly as warm and is one of the Spirit kind (Part Five). A dark murky Anima Spirare or Mortalis reading is an early-Stage healer or necromancer who has not refined past the noise. Taken together, the single most reliable field-assessment tool available to a Mancer who does not have time for a full Gnosis workup and needs to know, in the next three seconds, whether the person in front of them is dangerous.
The answer, for the record, is nearly always yes.

Schools know all this and dress to it. A Pyreveil sect’s scarves are ember-orange and its members will fight you over the shade, a Thaloré hall sings about teal, and half the brawls at any Stage bracket start with somebody’s cousin wearing the wrong color in the wrong stand.
Part Five · How Each Wellspring Reads in the Room
What a soul works does what its Wellspring’s law would do if that law were visible, and when a practitioner pushes it, it shows. The table gives each Wellspring as it reads on its home road, and the room’s report follows the road in use: worked through the Shell a lens does these things to the air and the furniture, worked through the Core it does them to the people in the room and leaves the furniture alone, and worked through the Layer it does them to what happens next. The aura flares in their own color, the lens’s hue at their Stage’s clarity, sitting where their Path puts it (Part Three): a smoky smear of it on the hands at Welling, a flare a civilian can see from Glory, a light that colors the walls from Transcendence. The harder they push, the brighter it burns, and a release drives it to its full color at once. A good eye reads the physics first and the color with it.

The road in use decides, and the kind only says where a lens is at home. A Wild lens on a Spirit worker reports like a Spirit lens. Sister Maud of the Ash Door threw Pyreveil through the Core for thirty years and never warmed a griddle: the people in the room felt a grudge they had carried since childhood go to cinders, and the candles burned on as they were. The other way about holds too. A Spirit lens on a hitter still gives no fire to throw, and it reports through the flesh, in what that body can bear and let go, at the poorer resonance any lens has away from home. A Mancer who reads the hue and then assumes the manners has made the commonest mistake in the trade.

Three arts so famous that no two peoples agree what to call them and no two taverns agree how they work.
The color a practitioner wears is also the first art anyone learns to use on purpose, and two more go everywhere with it. A Guild roll says reinforcement for the aura coat (the constant visible coat of a practitioner’s own aura, bought with reserve), Pressure for the weight a strong soul lays on a room, and sensing for the trained read of another person’s power. Hardly anybody else on the continent says any of that, and the words they do say carry their arguments with them.





















































Who says itThe coatThe weightThe noseA Guild roll, a MeasurewrightReinforcementPressureSensingBracket crowds, in CommonThe shine (“he’s lost his shine” means he is nearly out of reserve)The weight (“she leaned on the room”)The noseKharvenThe hideThe low skySmelling a man’s stackMotoMatoi, the wearingAtsu, the pressKehai, the sign of someone thereMarrowkinOn shiftThe loadSounding you, as a rock face is sounded for a bad seamThe MahuoGabot, armorNureum, the pressing-downNunchi, reading the roomThe lineage hallsHùtǐ, guarding the bodyWēiyā, majesty that pressesShénshí, the spirit-sense
The Moto hold that a coat anyone can see is badly worn and that showing color at table insults the household. The Kharven hold that a man who hides his hide is lying about his price. The Marrowkin enter the whole affair in the Tally, a shift worked and a load carried, and argue about who pays, and they will read a Moto lord’s quiet matoi off his color like the heat of a pour and tell him to his face that it runs cold. The lineage halls teach that a junior lowers the eyes before wēiyā, and a fair number of the feuds between the halls and everyone else began with somebody who did not. Every grandmother among the Mahuo teaches nunchi before letters, on the sound reasoning that a child without it gets hit. Measurewrights maintain that all of this describes one phenomenon, and have been wrong about the details in every generation so far.
How the coat works. Stats sit in the body as a passive base, and the coat is the active layer over it, surging at the point of contact and glowing brighter as its owner pushes. It can be focused to one place at the cost of a thin rest and extended into held gear, and it is lost asleep, drugged or surprised, which is why so many famous people have died at dinner. What the coat covers follows the road. A Shell coat, worn at the wearer’s Body Mastery, is the only one that hardens a body. A Spirit fighter’s coat is Essence and wards the soul, so a thrower who wants her ribs kept as well wears both and pays for both. A Fate fighter’s coat is the claim worn as presence: Pressure, and the room settling around the wearer, and nothing a blade would notice.
How the weight shows. It shows in the room first, in smoke, frost, lamp flames and animals, and then in bodies. One Stage up bends attention. Two brings sweat and nausea. Three or more drops people where they stand, and a gap of a whole Crystal look changes the weather. The unwoken take it by the fighter’s rank: dread from an Initiate or an Apprentice, a weight in the room from a Journeyman, knees bending from an Expert. Only after all that does the window (the soul’s report of its own numbers to its owner, seen by nobody else) catch up and report it as a line, by which time the knees have usually formed their own opinion:
[Pressure: far above you · Focus down a step]

A title lends no weight. A Grandmaster merchant with no fighting Stage has no Pressure at all, whatever his manners suggest, and many a fighter has been embarrassed in a counting house by assuming otherwise.
How the nose reads. A stronger Gnosis Perception reads a weaker Resilience Ward: Level, Stage and rank, Mastery and the numbers, on the reader’s own window, as plain as a price, and never a letter, since a person carries none. A stronger Ward leaves the reader with question marks. Everything else in the trade is an estimate said aloud, and that is why fighters talk about each other so much and so loudly. People can hide it or fake it. A Moto lord banks his coat down until a Stage XI looks like a tired Stage VI, and a Free Company sergeant with a bad hand and a loud mouth will run his aura hot enough to pass for two Stages over what he is. Trained noses know both tricks, and both tricks still work on someone.
How the spending shows. The color tells on its owner at fixed marks, whatever the words used for them. At half the reserve the breath shortens and the aura dims. At a quarter come a tremor and a thinning of the color. At a tenth the aura flickers and the Trait stutters, which the Guild calls Starvation, Charge Starvation on a Body fighter and Essence Starvation on a Spirit or a Fate one, whose reserve is Essence. Past that lie heat, blood and a cracking aura. Each road adds its own tells on top of those (Part Three): the Body runs hot, the Spirit runs hollow and Fate runs unlucky. Waste is loud and hot, mastery is quiet, and a good nose reads all of it from across a market. The owner has the same news sooner and more exactly, as [Reserve: 41%] on a window nobody else can see, which is the whole reason a practiced fighter can fake a tremor at half.
Read next: The Sixty Wellsprings, for every Wellspring’s entry and its Titan; Release Forms, for the color at full burn, and Reinforcement, for the coat in use.
