the-war-cycle/the-army/the-order-of-batt.title: The Order of Battle
the-war-cycle/the-army/the-order-of-batt.content:
The costliest lawsuit in the history of the contract companies was Mother Gorse’s Own against the Yellow Jacks, and it began with a parade. On muster day at Ansley Bridge, with the whole town on the walls and the Jacks’ fifes going, Captain Lorimer Dogwood marched past the Accord’s commissioner at the head of six hundred men in wasp-striped hose. Forty of them he had hired for the morning from Mother Gorse, whose company wore green, and their stripes were still wet. The commissioner paid on six hundred. Nine weeks later at Sedge Ford those same forty, back in green and on the other side, loosed their crossbows into the Jacks’ flank, and a three-copper bolt went through Dogwood’s visor while he was still shouting at them by name. His widow sued for the muster money. Mother Gorse countersued for forty men’s back pay, on the reasoning that the roll still listed them as Yellow Jacks and nobody had settled up. The arbiters found for Mother Gorse. Both companies still sing the affair to one tune with the names swapped, and when they meet at an inn the landlord carries the good benches upstairs.
Everything in that quarrel is in this document: the muster and the fraud, the captain paid by the head, the crossbow, the commission that binds on paper and the men who go wherever the money goes. The Strategic Division tells it with the fifes taken out. Read it with them still playing, because the men on these rolls had favorite songs and owed money at the sutler’s, and every number below had a nickname.
What an Army Is Made Of, and Who Owns It

Issued by the Strategic Division. Distributed to Crown staffs under the reciprocity provisions of Article IV, with the establishment tables for the Vanguard Orders and the Black Concord omitted from all external copies.
Second of the War Cycle.

What Marches

A Legion of twelve thousand moves roughly thirty thousand people.
Officers who have not seen it assume the difference is exaggeration. Officers who have seen it assume the figure is low.

An army is a town that walks. The fighting establishment is the smallest part of it, and every commander who has planned a campaign on the fighting establishment alone has run out of food on the eleventh day.
For every hundred men on the muster there are between one and two hundred others: servants, carters, drovers, smiths, harness-menders, cooks, sutlers selling what the commissary does not issue, surgeons and their assistants, laundresses, wives, children born on the march, clerks, Scribes discharging the Law of Witness (every battle must be recorded by a Concord Scribe or Seer, and an unrecorded war is an illegal one), and the priests and keepers who bury what the day produces.
The Accord’s establishment tables acknowledge a ratio of one to one and a half. Field returns from contested campaigns routinely show one to two.
Baggage runs at roughly one wagon per ten combatants, rising to one per six where tentage and the equipment of Sealwrights (the Accord’s binding and containment specialists) are carried, and the wagon train is the reason armies move at the pace of oxen rather than the pace of men.
The three tails





















TailWhat it isThe necessary tailCarters, smiths, surgeons, cooks. Cannot be reduced without reducing the army. The Division has attempted it four times and abandoned it four timesThe tolerated tailSutlers, hawkers, licensed followers. Feed and clothe the army at no cost to the treasury, and are the reason troops do not desert to find these things elsewhere. Every commander despises them and every commander licenses themThe unacknowledged tailWives without contract, children, camp women, the destitute who attach to an army because an army eats. Regulated on paper, present in fact, and the first to be abandoned when the column is pressed
What the fighting part carries
The spear is the line: cheap ash, a long iron point, a man who has been shouted at until he stands still. The crossbow is the reason nobody sensible goes without armor at any Stage. A bolt costs about three coppers at the fletcher’s, an ordinary one carries about 100 J and a heavy steel-bowed arbalest about 440 J, and it carries the crossbow bolt’s threat Grade, met by the target’s Speed like any missile’s, so a fighter quick enough for a D-Grade shaft “can read a crossbow bolt loosed across a room and slip it, if they see the loose”. A volley does not wait to be seen. Harness is what the man who can afford it wears: mail, brigandine and such plates as a smith can fit, carrying a proof-mark that promises resistance to a named bow at a stated range. The engines (trebuchets, mangonels, rams) come with their own guild masters, who paint them, name them and shout about them. Relay riders and the beacon line carry the orders, when somebody has remembered to pay them.
How Troops Are Raised
Five systems operate across the four quarters, frequently within the same army, and the friction between them is the principal cause of operational failure in the record.
The Concord Call
Under Article IV, every signatory contributes combatants, specialists or logistical assets in proportion to Wellspring capacity, population and strategic reach. The proportion is calculated by Logistics and Supply and disputed by everybody.
A Call produces a coalition rather than an army. Contingents arrive under their own officers, with their own drill, their own field words, their own dietary and burial requirements, and their own understanding of who they are actually obliged to obey. The Division’s field manuals devote more pages to reconciling contingents than to fighting.

Wellspring capacity as the basis of assessment produces the political grievance that underwrites half the Accord’s internal politics.
A realm rich in veins pays in practitioners. A realm poor in veins pays in bodies. Both are described in the assessment as contributing proportionally, and the eastern quarter has filed the objection eleven times.

The other four






























SystemWhat it isIts characteristic failureCrown levyService owed for land. Cheap, slow, seasonal, and legally limited in durationA levy that reaches its term walks home and is within its rights, which is why levy campaigns end abruptly and often at the worst moment. Cannot hold a line contested by a Domain (ground made to obey its maker’s law), cannot be marched far from their own districts without dissolutionIndentureA captain contracts to deliver a stated number of men of stated quality for a stated term at a stated rate. The dominant system in the Old World and the most flexibleThe muster. A captain paid per head has an interest in heads, and borrowing men from a neighboring company on inspection day is old enough to have its own vocabulary in three languages. Commissioners now count by Lattice signature (each sworn man’s mark on the Accord’s web of oaths), which has reduced the fraud and raised its priceGuild companyChartered houses fielding their own formations under Accord commission. Well-equipped, well-paid, technically excellentContractually specific. A guild company that has completed the object of its commission stops, and no appeal to the situation on the ground will move it, because the Lattice recorded the object at signature and will record the deviationContract companiesFree companies hired by the season. The Accord’s public position is that they are a regrettable necessity. Its actual practice is that a third of any large Concord force is contracted, because contracted men can be sent where the Law of Reversal makes it awkward to send Legion troopsUnpaid contract companies mutiny, and a mutinied company skips the road home and takes the nearest town in lieu of wages
Colors, songs and bounties. A company is also a club. It has a color you can spot at a quarter mile, a song with rude verses about its neighbors, an epithet for its captain, some of them unflattering, and a grudge handed down from dead men. Heralds cry its victories, minstrels get them wrong, lords post bounties on its captains and bookies quote its chances. All of this moves the price. A famous company signs for more, deserts less and draws recruits who have never met it, and a famous captain discovers that the name arrives at every town ahead of him and sometimes gets there with a crossbow. The Division’s tables have no column for any of this and every commissioner knows the going rate by heart.
The Legion
The Strategic Division’s own establishment. Smaller than every Crown believes and more specialized than any of them can match.
Aether Knights · The striking arm. Fielded in numbers the Division does not publish. Committed late, protected obsessively, and reviewed after every engagement in which one is lost.
Domain Engineers · Construct battlefield Domains. Doctrine now directs them to seat toward their own formations rather than toward the enemy, on the finding that a patch of ground where the sound is right is worth more than a patch where the enemy’s is wrong.
War-Priests of Urion · Read the Lattice hum for enemy movement and remaining capacity. A staff function rather than a combat one, and the Division’s principal instrument for the costing-out doctrine (make a practitioner spend their reserve on things that do not matter, then hand them to the infantry). They also keep the running log of small things going wrong, which is how an enemy’s Fate user is found, and those are pinned first, ahead of even the champions.
Fate Officers · The ordinary sort is a practitioner on the Fate Path with long Range, heavy Aura Pressure and a sworn company that fights better for having him: read him as a captain whose regiment fights a step better than its muster, and cost him out like anyone. The rare sort is the Fate commander, a life’s masterwork at high Stage or a bloodline’s art, who spends on what the field depends on: weather, supply, panic, the hour a column arrives, the company that breaks first. The establishment table carries no such line, and The Practitioner Problem says why. See The Three Paths for why nobody does this casually.
Thread-hunters · A light-horse troop and two clerks attached to the War-Priests’ log, whose whole work is to read that log for a run of bad luck that luck would not produce, find the old woman under the plain banner, and reach her before the result arrives. Each side’s Fate users are pinned first, ahead of even the champions, and these are the people who do the pinning. A troop that spends six days failing has still made her spend six days hiding, and that is entered as a success.
Inspectors of the Line · The Division’s inspection regime, carried on the establishment as quartermaster’s staff: every bridge walked, every horse shod on schedule, pay on the day, and two roads to every ford. A Fate hand moves only what already has a way of happening, and these people go round closing the ways. The cheapest metaphysical defense in the arsenal is a man with a list, and the Crown auditors who keep cutting him do not know what they are paying for.
Lattice Pilots · Guide Concord fleets and Gate crossings through dimensional instability. The Legion’s strategic mobility rests entirely on perhaps two hundred people across four quarters and the Division is aware of the exposure.
Couriers · Relay riders, beacon clerks and boys on fast ponies. Not a separate order and always listed last. The Legion’s greatest advantage and its softest target.
Enforcement, attached

Enforcement Division formations are not Legion troops and do not answer to the High Marshal, a distinction that has cost engagements.
Vanguard Orders · Elite strike teams bearing the Sealwright Mark, able to fight on metaphysical planes. Attached to a Legion by Concord Writ and withdrawn without consultation.
Sealwright Teams · Containment circles, barrier fields, dimensional anchors. Slow, fragile, decisive, and credited for nothing.
Null Wardens · Silent, throats sealed by vow, sensing corruption through harmonic dissonance. Universally disliked by the troops they protect.
Tribunal Marshals · Senior executioners of the Codex. Their presence in a column means somebody in it is already condemned and has not been told.

Command, and Who Actually Holds It

The High Marshal commands the Legion. The Crown commands the ground. Neither commands the other and both are told they do.

A Concord force operating in a Crown’s realm sits inside an unresolved authority. The Crown holds sovereignty, the ground, the law, the levy and the supply. The Legion holds the practitioners, the arrays, the Writs and the credit. Neither can conduct the campaign alone and neither will subordinate.
The formal resolution is the Concord Writ. The practical resolution is that the High Marshal’s staff writes the plan, the Crown’s marshal signs it, and both record their reservations for the Arbitration review that follows every engagement.

Where the two conflict in the field, law gives way to possession: the deciding factor is who is holding the Wellspring site the campaign depends on, and the answer has been the Citadel and its Divisions since Year Zero.

Officer ratios
Legion · Roughly one officer to twenty, plus a staff establishment that Crown officers consider grotesque. The staff exists because the costing-out doctrine is arithmetic and arithmetic requires clerks.
Crown levy · One to forty or worse, with officers appointed by tenure rather than competence, and a command chain that breaks the moment the named lord is unhorsed.
Contract company · One to ten. The best ratio in the four quarters, because a captain paid by result invests in the men who deliver it.
What proportion ever fights
In a formed line, the front two ranks. Everything behind is pressure, replacement, and the moral architecture that keeps the front two ranks in place.
Across a campaign the figure is different and worse. Of a Legion that marches out, roughly one man in six will stand in a line at any point in the season. The remainder garrison, escort, forage, dig, carry, guard, or lie sick.

The sick are the largest category by a considerable margin.
The Division’s own returns for a hard campaign show more men lost to camp disease than to every enemy in the field, and this has been true of every army in the record.

Unresolved Entries

Wellspring-based assessment Objected to eleven times by the eastern quarter and revised none. The objection is that realms poor in veins pay in bodies. The Division’s reply is that the assessment measures capacity, which is true and answers nothing.
Contract companies and the Law of Reversal Whether contracted troops acting on Accord commission bind the Accord for purposes of the Law is unsettled, has never been tested, and is the largest unexamined risk in Accord military practice.
Lattice Pilot establishment Two hundred people, four quarters, no reserve, no school capable of replacing losses at campaign rate. Raised in four consecutive assessments. Funded in none.
Vanguard withdrawal Enforcement may withdraw attached Orders without consulting the Legion commander they were attached to. Three engagements in the last century turned on this. No revision has been proposed by either Division.


Read next: The Practitioner Problem, for what a practitioner does to all of this; The Three Paths, for the Fate user every side pins first.

the-war-cycle/the-fighting/sack-and-cont.filePath: The War Cycle/The Fighting/Sack and Contribution.md
the-war-cycle/the-fighting/sack-and-cont.title: Sack and Contribution
the-war-cycle/the-fighting/sack-and-cont.content:
The town of Little Perrot keeps a receipt in its church, in a gilt frame, under a lamp, and every harvest they take it down and dance. Dickon Brazier rode up the valley road with three hundred horse in orange sashes, a drummer and a clerk on a mule, in the year the western wars reached the perry country, and he sent the clerk ahead with the sum already written. Alys Fenn, who brewed the town’s perry and had buried two husbands and frightened both of them first, met him at the bridge with a table and two cups. They were at it until dark. She beat him down by a third and a tun of the good stuff, the clerk wrote it out and sealed it, and Brazier danced with her in the square with his spurs on while his men paid for their drinks. Across the ridge, Over Perrot had sent back the clerk with his ears boxed. The smoke of it stood up for four days, straight as a column in the still weather, and you could see it from the dance floor, and everyone at the dance could see it. Over Perrot is the second row of the table at the bottom of this page. Eight years later another captain came up the road, with a different clerk, and he was very polite about the receipt.
The Arbitration Division prepared the following, and the Strategic Division was invited to comment and declined. It is the one document in this cycle I would ask you to read sober.
What War Does to People Who Are Not In It

Prepared by the Arbitration Division. The Strategic Division was invited to comment and declined.
Sixth of the War Cycle.

The Object of War Is Usually a Countryside

You do not have to beat a Crown. You have to make its country stop producing revenue, and that is a task for cavalry and fire.

The pitched battle is a gamble. The siege is expensive. The reliable instrument for breaking an enemy is to ride through his country and burn the means by which he pays for an army.
A raiding column moves fast, avoids fortified places, times itself to the harvest, and destroys mills, barns, stores, seed grain and standing crops across the widest front it can manage. It does not seek battle and will refuse one. Its object is the tax base.

Its secondary object is political and is the sharper of the two. A Crown that cannot protect its people has demonstrated that it is not a Crown, and the demonstration is made to the people rather than to the Crown.

Contribution
The refinement, and the instrument that funds most campaigns in the four quarters.
A district pays to not be burned. The sum is assessed, demanded in writing, and collected under threat, and the threat is credible because the alternative has been demonstrated in the next valley.
Contribution is more profitable than plunder, less destructive, and repeatable, which is why competent commanders prefer it and why it has become the ordinary means by which an army in the field pays itself.

A campaign conducted entirely on contribution can be self-financing and occasionally profitable. The Logistics Division’s own accounts record two seasons in which the Legion’s field expenditure was met from contribution and the surplus returned to the Citadel.
The distinction between contribution and extortion is that contribution is assessed, receipted, and taken by an army with a legal position.
The distinction is invisible to the district paying it.

Quarter, Ransom, and Who Is Worth Keeping
Quarter · Given to those worth taking and refused to those who are not. This is not stated in any code and is observed in every army. A knight, an officer, a practitioner or anyone whose family can pay is captured. Common soldiers in a broken line are killed, because a prisoner has to be fed.
Ransom · The economy underneath the convention. A great capture can fund a campaign, and a truly great one can beggar a kingdom for a generation. This is why the wealthy survive battles at rates the poor do not, and why the mercy extended to a lord is indistinguishable in practice from a commercial transaction, because that is what it is.
Practitioners · A costed-out practitioner (one whose reserve has been spent to nothing) taken alive is worth more than the engagement, which is why the doctrine says capture and why the men who reach one rarely comply.

The convention’s honest description is that it protects those who can pay and licenses the killing of those who cannot.
And that it is called chivalry by the people it protects.

The Storm
The position
Concord Writ does not recognize forfeiture of protection. The inhabitants of a stormed place retain their status. The Codex Protocols bind the storming force in full. The Law of Witness (every battle must be recorded by a Concord Scribe or Seer) applies throughout and the Scribe’s record is admissible.
The Division has issued this position without variation for four centuries.
What happens
Three days is the customary figure, and the customary figure is observed in the sense that it eventually ends.
What occurs in a stormed town is documented in the Scribes’ records and in the returns of the surviving population, and the two do not agree.

The pattern of disagreement is consistent. The Scribes record the first hours accurately and the later hours thinly, which is a function of where a Scribe can safely stand rather than of any intent.
And is why the Division’s own evidentiary standard is weakest exactly where the conduct is worst.

The men who do it are the men who did not do it the week before, at the end of a siege, having watched their friends die of the flux in a ditch for four months on account of a decision made by the garrison commander they are now looking at.

The Division offers this as no justification, and offers it anyway, because a doctrine that does not account for it produces regulations that fail.

Why the Accord’s record is what it is
Nine reviews. No prosecutions. The Division’s explanation is evidentiary and is technically correct.

The Guild of Measurewrights, who have no standing in the matter, filed a note observing that a legal standard which cannot reach the conduct it exists to govern describes where the record stops, and does nothing else.
The note was entered. It has not been answered.

Afterward
A district that has been raided does not recover in the season. It recovers in the generation, or it does not.

























IntervalWhat happensThe first yearThe stored grain is gone, the seed grain is gone, and the draft animals are gone. There is no planting. What the raid did not take, the following winter doesThe second yearNothing has been sown, so nothing is reaped. The population that survived the first year leaves, and the ones who leave are the young and the able, which is the population that would have rebuiltThe generationFields go to scrub. The mill is not rebuilt because there is nobody to grind for. The district’s assessment falls permanently. Half the depopulated country in the western quarter was depopulated in a single season two hundred years ago and has never been resettledThe deadBuried improperly, at scale, by people with neither the time nor the rites. And the districts concerned will tell you about what followed at length, and will not be believed
Unresolved Entries

The evidentiary gap · The Scribes’ records thin exactly where conduct worsens. Four proposals to require Scribes to remain present through the third day have been drafted. None has been adopted, and the drafting officers’ own notes record why.
Which is that it would kill the Scribes.

Contribution and the Law of Reversal · Whether systematic contribution constitutes aggression for purposes of the Law has not been tested. The Strategic Division’s declining to comment on this document is not unconnected.
Quarter as a property qualification · Raised by the Arbitration Division itself in a session whose minutes were sealed. The seal is the only public evidence that the question was asked.
Reparation · No mechanism exists. Contribution is receipted and never returned. Sacked towns have petitioned the Division on ninety-one occasions in four centuries. The Division’s response in every instance has been to acknowledge receipt.

Read next: What Things Cost, for what is taken; The Crossing, for what is left behind.

the-war-cycle/the-fighting/index.content:
Trumpets, painted engines and a Master’s violet stroke across the sky are what people pay the minstrel to hear about. The wars themselves were settled by a ditch and a receipt.
Investment, reduction, the breach, and what war does to the people who are not in it.


Walls and What Beats Them Investment, reduction, the breach
Sack and Contribution What war does to people who are not in it

the-war-cycle/the-fighting/walls-and-wha.title: Walls and What Beats Them
the-war-cycle/the-fighting/walls-and-wha.content:
The siege of Carrick Ness took fourteen months, and the only part anyone sings is the trebuchet. Mistress Wenna Holt of the Engineers’ Guild built it on the beach in full sight of the garrison, painted it blue with gold teeth, named it the Bishop’s Apology, and stood on its frame bawling her guild mark at the walls while forty apprentices hauled down the beam. The first stone went backward through the besiegers’ brewhouse. The fourth took the top off a tower. The garrison’s answer was its master mason, old Fergus Ruck, who had been feuding with Holt’s guild for thirty years over a bridge contract, and who rebuilt by night whatever she knocked down by day and carved a new rude face into every repair. In the sixth month the besiegers hired a Master at a ruinous price, and he unmade the outer face at noon with one violet stroke the fishing boats saw from six miles out, and found behind it a ditch, a second face, and a great many crossbows. What took Carrick Ness in the end was a team of Sealwrights nobody noticed, three quiet weeks of striking entries off the walls’ old workings, and the flux, which had by then killed more of the besiegers than Holt, Ruck and the Master combined. Holt’s guild still claims the victory. Ruck’s descendants still have the faces.
Keep the Bishop’s Apology in mind while you read, because she is the part of the siege that gets painted, and the Strategic Division’s document below is about the rest.
Investment, Reduction, and the Convention of the Breach

Issued by the Strategic Division, with the reduction schedules for Accord-held fortifications omitted from all copies issued outside the Citadel.
Fourth of the War Cycle.

Why the War Is About Places

Battles are the exception. A campaign is a list of places, and most of them have walls.

A fortress cannot be walked past. It sits on the road, the river, the bridge or the vein, and a force that leaves it behind has left an enemy on its own supply line with cavalry and time.
So armies besiege. Most of the days of most campaigns are spent sitting outside somewhere, digging, waiting, dying of camp fever, and negotiating. The pitched battle that the histories record is what happens when a relief force arrives and both commanders decide simultaneously that the risk is acceptable, which is rare, and which is why the histories have so few of them and so many sieges.
The Lines
A besieging force digs twice. Inward against the garrison, outward against relief.
The inner line · Faces the walls. Pens the garrison, blocks sorties, and provides the platforms from which the reduction proceeds. Begun out of bowshot and dug forward in covered trenches, each one nearer the wall than the last.
The outer line · Faces away. Protects the besieger’s back from the field army that is always coming. An army that has invested a place without an outer line has put itself in the position it intended to put the garrison in, and the record contains several examples of exactly that outcome.

Both lines must be held continuously by ordinary soldiers, in weather, for months, the clearest illustration in warfare of the currency distinction.
No practitioner has ever invested a fortress. Investment is time converted into ground and there is no other instrument for it.

What Walls Are Built Against Now
Fortification design has passed through three answers to three different threats, and every standing wall is a fossil of the threat it was built against.

























FormBuilt againstWhat happenedThe high wallEscalade and starvationTall, relatively thin, designed so nobody can climb it. Effective for centuries and obsolete the moment a besieger could bring a practitioner capable of unmaking masonry at range, which made every tall wall in the world a target rather than a defenseThe low workPractitionersThick, low, earth-backed, angled so every face is covered by crossbows and workings from another face. A practitioner can unmake a section and finds behind it a ditch, a second face, and enfilade (loosing down the length of a line instead of across it). The reduction now costs Essence per section rather than Essence per wall, and the arithmetic of the costing-out doctrine turns against the attackerAnchored workEverythingPrincipality Mortar (the mortar that seats a Domain, ground made to obey its maker’s law, into a foundation), and the eleven structures raised on it. A Domain anchored at Realm scale registers in the Continuum as terrain rather than as building. It is not reduced. It is not mined. It cannot be removed by its own builders, and four of the eleven now stand in places nobody governs

Why nobody builds anchored work. Cost, the Bench’s reservation, and the fact that a fortification which cannot be removed is a fortification your grandchildren will have to garrison whether or not the border still runs there.
The Division’s own assessment is that anchored work is a strategic liability disguised as an asset, that the eleven were built by regimes which did not expect to end, and that all eleven regimes ended.

Reduction
Engines
Trebuchets, mangonels, rams, belfries and bores. Each is a guild master’s own work, built on the spot from the nearest good timber, named, painted, and shouted about, and each carries the guild mark somewhere the enemy can read it. They throw stone, fire pots, dead horses and on one recorded occasion a bishop’s letter. They misfire in ways their makers describe as rare, and an engine crew is paid by the piece and can walk off a siege as readily as any other trade. Against bare masonry they are slow and sure. Against a wall with its inscription intact they are mostly slow.
The Sealwright approach
A Sealwright team (the Accord's binding and containment specialists) leaves the walls standing and unmakes what is in them.
Every fortification above the crudest carries inscription: ward-plate, seated chains, anchored foundations, the accumulated metaphysical work of however many generations have held the place. Sealwright work strips that, chain by chain, from outside, slowly, in a process that resembles nothing so much as a clerk going through a ledger and striking entries.

Stripped, the place is masonry. Masonry falls to ordinary engines, ordinary mining, and ordinary time.
The Sealwright team’s contribution is invisible from the walls and decisive, and garrisons that have watched a siege proceed with no apparent progress for three weeks have surrendered on the fourth without understanding what changed.

Mining
Old and unchanged. Dig under, prop with timber, burn the props, drop the wall. Counter-mining is the defender digging to intercept, and the fighting that happens underground is the worst fighting in warfare and the least described.
Against Domain-anchored foundations mining does not work, because the foundation is registered as terrain and terrain does not care that the earth under it has been removed. Sappers have reported galleries in which the ceiling simply continued to be there.

Three attempts against anchored work are recorded, all abandoned, and one of the three abandoned the sappers.

Starvation
The oldest instrument and still the most successful. A well-provisioned town holds a year and a poorly provisioned one holds a season, and the arithmetic that matters is the population’s, far more than the garrison’s, since a town holds many more mouths than soldiers and the soldiers eat first.
The sequence is documented and identical everywhere. Horses first, then the animals kept for other purposes, then what was stored for planting, then what is not food.

Disease arrives before starvation completes and does most of the work.
The besieging camp gets the same disease at approximately the same time and frequently loses more men to it than the garrison loses to everything, which is the central absurdity of siege warfare and the reason competent commanders want terms.

Terms, and the Breach
Everything a garrison does after the breach is practicable is judged against a convention nobody signed and everybody enforces.
A garrison may surrender on terms while resistance remains meaningful, and will ordinarily be allowed to march out with its arms, its colors and its honor. Mercy has nothing to do with it: the besieger is buying the place cheaply rather than buying it with a storm.

Once a practicable breach exists and the garrison refuses terms and forces a storm, the convention holds that the garrison and the town have forfeited protection. Quarter may be refused. The place may be sacked.
Every commander in the four quarters knows this and every garrison commander weighs it, and the weighing is the most consequential decision anyone makes in a siege, because it is made on behalf of a population that does not get a vote.

The Accord’s position
Concord Writ (the Accord’s warrant for war) does not recognize the convention. Arbitration’s stated position is that a stormed town’s inhabitants retain full protection, that the storming force remains bound by the Codex Protocols, and that the Law of Witness applies throughout.
The Division’s own after-action record for stormed places contains a consistent discrepancy between the Scribe’s account and the returns of the populations concerned.

The discrepancy has been noted in review on nine occasions. No prosecution has followed any of them.

Unresolved Entries

Anchored work Eleven structures, four in ungoverned territory, none removable. No policy exists for what happens when an anchored fortification stands in a place the Accord no longer wishes to hold.
The third mining attempt Abandoned. The sappers were not recovered. The gallery was sealed by Enforcement and the sealing is maintained annually at Division expense.
Sealwright stripping and the ownership of inscription Whether stripping a fortification’s accumulated inscription constitutes destruction of property has been argued twice and settled neither time. The stakes are large: several of the places in question hold inscription older than the Accord.
The storm discrepancy Nine reviews, no prosecutions. Entered at the insistence of the Guild of Measurewrights, who have no standing in the matter and filed anyway.


Read next: The Working Trades, for the wards cut into the stone; Domains, for what a high Stage does to a wall; The Order of Battle, for who goes up the ladder.

the-war-cycle/index.title: The War Cycle
the-war-cycle/index.content:
Every child in the Arrow valleys can sing you Ser Aldric and the Cart. In the fourth summer of the Marrowmere war Ser Aldric Noon walked out onto Harrow Field at sunrise in a coat of aura the orange of a kiln mouth, a Master on a lord’s retainer with a herald running ahead of him to cry his name, and before the porridge was ready he had unmade twelve hundred of the Lady of Sallowby’s spearmen, with their banners, their drums and a fair part of the hill. Camp followers on both sides climbed onto the wagons to watch. A bookie in the Sallowby baggage paid out at nine to one with tears running into his beard. The Lady’s quartermaster, a one-eyed carter’s widow named Bet Oxley, did not look up from her tally. She sent four hundred men and sixty wagons around the far side of the hill to the mills at Cobb’s Reach, where they sat down and started digging. Ser Aldric could not be in two valleys. By harvest his side had eaten its horses, by the first frost it had walked home, and in the song he is still standing on Harrow Field, unbeaten, shining like a forge, asking where everybody went.
The eleven documents in this cycle are the explanation of that song. The Divisions of the Guild Accord wrote them in the voice of people who have counted the wagons, and I, who keep these shelves, have left that voice alone and added windows only where a reader would otherwise suffocate. War is bodies, money and names. The minstrels look after the names.

A practitioner converts Essence into effect. An army converts time into ground.
Every document in this cycle is an elaboration of that distinction, and every failure in the record is a commander who did not believe it.

The Cycle
Eleven documents issued across four Divisions of the Guild Accord, each answering a question the one before it opened. The first six are about the army. The last five are about the body.
ITHE PRACTITIONER PROBLEMwhy four thousand men are there at allIITHE ORDER OF BATTLEwhat an army is made of, and who owns itIIITHE LONG MARCHbread moves. Essence does notIVWALLS AND WHAT BEATS THEMinvestment, reduction, the breachVTHE CAMPnot held in this archiveVISACK AND CONTRIBUTIONwhat war does to people who are not in itVIITHE CROSSINGwhat happens to a Soul Crystalwhen the body stopsVIIITHE RITESburial, exclusion, and the consent of the deadIXTHE PHYSICIAN'S EYEreading a body, and what will not closeXTHE LONG ILLNESSdisease, trade sickness, and timeXITHE RUNNERShow a kill becomes a reagent

































































DocumentIssuing DivisionThe finding it rests onI · The Practitioner ProblemStrategicGround is held by bodies. It has never been held by anything elseII · The Order of BattleStrategic, distributed to Crown staffsAn army is a town that walks, and the fighting establishment is the smallest part of itIII · The Long MarchLogistics and Supply, jointly with StrategicA practitioner is refilled by the ground they stand on, or not at all, so the vein map (the chart of where rich ground lies) is the road mapIV · Walls and What Beats ThemStrategicNo practitioner has ever invested a fortress. Investment is time converted into ground and there is no other instrument for itV · The Camp—Cited by every other volume. Not held hereVI · Sack and ContributionArbitration. Strategic was invited to comment and declinedA legal standard which cannot reach the conduct it exists to govern describes where the record stops, and does nothing elseVII · The CrossingResearch and ArchivesGrade IV (Crystal Draw, the stock rendered from what carried a Soul Crystal) is intercepted from the Wellspring, in transit, before arrival, and the dead lose nothing by itVIII · The RitesResearch and Archives, over the objection of the BenchSeven traditions, one problem. The body has nine days of work to do and somebody has to see it is left alone to do itIX · The Physician’s EyeLegion surgeons and Anima Harmonic assessorsThe wound is an instruction, partially executed, still executingX · The Long IllnessResearch and ArchivesEvery occupational mechanism has been understood for a century and no polity operates a schemeXI · The RunnersCompiled for the Guild of Measurewrights. No runners’ guild was consulted because none existsThe factor sets the grade and the runner has no instrument
What the Cycle Argues
Read in order, the eleven documents make one case and it is not a flattering one.
An army cannot be beaten by a practitioner and a practitioner cannot be beaten by an army, so wars are fought over ground, and ground is held by ordinary men in numbers. Those men are chained to fodder arithmetic, and the practitioners among them are chained to geology, which means campaign routes run vein to vein and half the sieges in the record are of places nobody valued.
Most of a campaign is therefore spent sitting outside somewhere, digging, waiting, and dying of camp fever. And the reliable instrument for actually breaking an enemy is neither the battle nor the siege. It is riding through his country and burning the means by which he pays for an army.

Which puts the Accord in a specific position. It is incapable by its own founding oaths of a war of conquest: the Law of Reversal sees to that (if the Concord turns aggressor, the Lattice, the web of sworn resonance that binds the Accord, strips its whole army of power). It is also the institution whose own after-action record for stormed towns contains a consistent discrepancy between the Scribe’s account (every battle must by law be recorded by a Concord Scribe or Seer) and the returns of the surviving population.
Nine reviews. No prosecutions. The explanation is evidentiary and is technically correct.

The Missing Fifth
Sack and Contribution is the sixth of the cycle. The Practitioner Problem is the first, the Order of Battle the second, the Long March the third, and Walls the fourth.
The fifth is The Camp, cited by name in the Long March as the document describing what happens to an army’s water and to the men who drink it. It is not held in this archive.
Its absence is load-bearing. Every document in the cycle points at camp disease as the largest killer in warfare, the Order of Battle records more Legion men lost to it than to every enemy in the field, and Walls records besieging camps losing more to it than the garrison loses to everything.

The cycle’s largest cause of death is the one volume nobody has.

Entries
The Practitioner Problem sits with the Guild Accord, under the Strategic Division that issued it. The Camp is not held in this archive. The remaining nine are here.


The Order of Battle
The Long March
Walls and What Beats Them
Sack and Contribution
The Crossing
The Rites
The Physician’s Eye
The Long Illness
The Runners
The Fisc — Paying for a Siege

the-war-cycle/the-wounded-and-the-dead/t.title: The Crossing
the-war-cycle/the-wounded-and-the-dead/t.content:
For eleven years the best seed loaf in Tarrowby was baked by a dead woman. When Annot Kettlewell died of a spring fever her husband Perkin paid a hedge-necromancer with her mother’s gold earrings, and on the tenth morning she was back at the trough in her blue apron, kneading, with flour to the elbows and her head tilted the way she had always tilted it. She took the ribbon at the Harvest Fair three years running. She remembered who liked the heel. People came from two towns off for those loaves, and they went home crying over them without knowing why, and then the butcher at the corner began reciting her wedding vows in his sleep, the girl who swept the shop could suddenly name every one of Annot’s dead sisters, and every dog on the row sat down facing the bakery door. Null Wardens (the Accord’s silent corruption-hunters, throats sealed by vow) came in the twelfth year, in their gray, with half the street standing across the road to stop them and Perkin Kettlewell at the front of it with a peel. They broke what was at the trough in the time it takes to say so. The corner of that shop still reads wrong to any instrument you care to bring, the dogs still will not settle on the row, and I am told the bread there now is merely good.
The Research and Archives Division explains below what was standing at that trough, what a corpse is holding, and who is owed it. This is the most important document in the cycle and it was written by people who would rather not have known.
What Happens to a Soul Crystal When the Body Stops

Issued by the Research and Archives Division. Section VI was prepared at the request of the Arbitration Division and the Bench of Attribution jointly, and neither has acknowledged it.
Seventh of the War Cycle. Companion to The Rites.

Three Things Leave

The Crystal comes apart, into three products with three destinations and three separate laws.
Everything difficult about death in the four quarters follows from the fact that they do not leave together.

A soul has three layers because three hands made it, and each of the three goes back its own way. The Essence Core becomes the Echo. The Aether Shell becomes the Temperance residue, which leaves through the body. The Attraction Layer becomes the Name-record.

      
      
      
      
      within hoursnine days, by diffusion through the bodyfiled permanentlyDEATHthe lattice disassemblesTHE ECHO, from theCorememory, habit, voiceprint,the texture of how aperson movedTHE TEMPERANCERESIDUE, from theShellevery Threshold crossed,every stage climbed,every seated carry andharmonizationTHE NAME-RECORD,from the Layerthe bare fact of theperson:that they existed, whatthey were calledTHE SOUL PLANEspirit lawTHE WELLSPRINGthe Wellspring's own lawTHE ARCHIVE OF NAMESOrder
These three were one lattice for the whole of a life. Death separates jurisdiction, and the separation is the actual event.

When people say a person has died they mean that the three products have parted and are now the property of three different laws. The heart stopping is a physical fact of no metaphysical consequence.

The Sequence, and the Windows
The Echo goes first
Within hours, and the departure is perceptible to anyone with even passive sensitivity to the Veil (its inner fold is the membrane between the living world and the Soul Plane), which is most people at a deathbed even if they have no vocabulary for it. An Echo leaving is the ordinary course of a death. It is the Echo that cannot leave, or will not settle once it has, that gets anyone called out at night.
This is how death is actually determined in the four quarters. A body whose Echo has departed is dead in the sense the law means. A body whose Echo has not is not, whatever the breath and the pulse are doing, and the practice of sitting with the dying until the room changes is universal, ancient, and correct.

It is also why the fear that troubles other traditions runs the opposite direction here.
Nobody in the four quarters fears being buried alive. They fear being buried too late, because the second window is closing while the family argues.

The Temperance residue takes nine days
The residue diffuses, slowly, back into the Wellspring, and it diffuses through the body, which remains its medium until the process completes.
Nine days is the figure. It varies with Stage, with the Wellspring concerned, with saturation at the site, and with what the body is doing, but nine is the number the practice is built on and the number the law uses.

On the ninth day the residue is gone, the Wellspring has received what it was owed, and what remains is meat.

Meat is a body with no Temperance left in it. The Trait tissue stays. A Trait is laid down in the body itself, mineral into bone, and it does not diffuse with the residue, so the remains of anyone who bore a Crystal go on holding their Traits after the ninth day, as passive carry with nothing active in it. The rendering houses race the nine days for the Temperance. The Trait tissue waits, which is why a Crystal-bearer’s grave-dirt and bone-ash still read Grade IV.
Everything difficult in this document occurs inside those nine days.
The Name-record files last and does not close
The Archive receives the Name-record and the Archive does not release it. A name entered is entered permanently, which is why the Law of Silence forbids naming captured Outer Realm entities, and why the destruction of a Name is a category of violence distinct from killing and considerably worse.
What the Road Changes
Every soul leaves all three. Which one is heaviest depends on what the soul spent its life leaning on.
A Path is the layer a Crystal learned to lean on, and a layer leaned on for fifty years is a heavy thing to set down. The Path sets the heaviest product.

























The dead ofHeaviest productWhat it means in practiceThe Body PathThe residueThese are the dead the renderers race for. A Body master’s corpse is the richest stock in the trade, the family counts days, and the guards at the wake are armed for a reasonThe Spirit PathThe EchoThey haunt. The Echo goes on time and goes heavy and clear, and it does not settle quickly. Nobody buys a Spirit master’s house for a generation, and the Melancholic Erosion described below comes on early and comes on hardThe Fate PathThe Name-recordThey leave vows still binding. The name is filed and whatever was tied to it stays tied, with no one left to release it. A dead Moto swore a bridge on the Tobi would never carry a Shirogane, and the Shirogane still go round
Who is repaid
The residue goes to the lens the soul tempered on longest, whatever else it took up on the way, and it is that Wellspring which is repaid. A soul with five lenses pays one creditor. The unlensed, who are most of the world, feed the ground they lie in, and every parish knows without being told why a good graveyard grows good beans.
Cutting the Crystal
The lattice takes those nine days to finish coming apart, and for that long it can still be found in the body, which is why a Crystal can be cut from a corpse inside the window and never after it. What the cutter takes is the lattice with the residue still in it. The ninth day leaves nothing to cut. Monster Cores gives the trade’s side of this, and the law’s side is the worst crime in every realm.
Rebirth
Rebirth moves pattern and never a person. Bloodlines repeat, Traits resurface three generations on, and an Echo set into a successor gives the successor a dead woman’s reflexes and her grief. All the faiths have fine words for this, and the Division has no quarrel with the words. The woman is still dead. Every death in the Division’s returns is permanent, and the roads that claim otherwise are entered under fraud or under the section below.
What a Corpse Is Holding

Prepared at the request of the Arbitration Division and the Bench of Attribution. Neither has acknowledged receipt and both hold copies.

A body inside the nine days is a medium through which a Wellspring is being repaid.

Grade IV rendering, correctly described, is the interception of that repayment.
The Crystal Draw (Grade IV stock, rendered from something that carried a Soul Crystal) taken from a corpse leaves untouched the person, who has already gone, and the family, who never owned it.
It is taken from the Wellspring, in transit, before arrival.

Grade IV material is stolen from the world rather than from the dead. This is the correct account and it is not the comforting one. The dead are not harmed. The Wellspring is short. Every unit of Grade IV in circulation represents Temperance a Wellspring did not receive, and the arithmetic of that shortfall across four centuries has never been performed, because performing it would require knowing the volume of the trade, which is the figure the Bench has declined to establish.
The nine-day window explains the entire trade’s structure. Why Grade IV must be rendered fast. Why the rendering houses sit near the assizes and the battlefields and the almshouses. Why a body that has been argued over is a body worth nothing. And why Gravemark Ink specifies grinding within nine days of the donation, and every alchemist knows the figure without knowing why it is nine.

The Law of Return is an anti-rendering provision and has never been read as one.
The Codex Protocol states that any Accord soldier who dies defending a Wellspring becomes part of its flow and that their Essence cannot be reclaimed. This is presented as an honor.
Structurally it is a prohibition on Grade IV rendering of Accord war dead, drafted before the trade existed, in language that does not mention the trade. Whether it was foresight or accident is not recorded.
It has held for four centuries and it protects only the soldiers who died at a Wellspring.

Necromancy
The prohibition is structural, and its distance from morals is the whole of the law.
Raising the dead cannot be done, and summoning them is a different discipline governed elsewhere.

Necromancy holds the three products together after they should have parted.

What that produces
A construct that is not a person and is not a corpse. The Echo is present and cannot reach the Soul Plane. The Temperance residue is present and is not diffusing, so the Wellspring is not repaid and will not be. The Name-record is filed and is therefore in the Archive as a completed entry attached to something that has not completed.
The construct behaves. It moves, it may speak, it may retain skill and preference and something an observer would call recognition. Families have kept them. This is the reason the prohibition requires enforcement rather than merely announcement.
Why it is prohibited
The debt does not clear · A Wellspring owed Temperance that is not returning does not merely go unpaid. The shortfall persists as a standing deficiency at the vein, and the deficiency is cumulative across every construct maintained anywhere that pulls on it.
The Archive holds a false entry · A completed Name attached to an incomplete thing is a corruption of the Archive itself, and the Archive is what every oath, every Lattice binding and every Trial of Resonance is measured against.

The Echo does not survive it. An Echo held out of the Soul Plane degrades. What is left after a year is the residue of the person’s memory being prevented.
Proximity produces the documented Melancholic Erosion: uncontrollable weeping and the taking-on of memories that are not yours.
The families who keep constructs are the first casualties of keeping them, and they are always the last to be persuaded of it.

So the prohibition has nothing to do with respect. A necromantic construct is a hole in three separate systems, maintained deliberately, and the hole does not close when the construct is destroyed. It closes when the residue finally diffuses, which for a construct maintained past its nine days can take decades, and for some has not yet.
Drift, Echoes, and the Hollow

























FormWhat it isLawful Echo Class IIDesaturated, gray, tied to an anchor. Not dangerous in itself and hazardous by proximity, sustained exposure produces Melancholic Erosion. The remedy is removal from the site, and the folk remedy is grounding tea, which does nothing and helpsSoul DriftInvoluntary partial crossing by a living person. Commonest in thin-Veil zones and in the recently bereaved, whose Attraction Layer is reaching for an anchor that has moved. Treated as a medical emergency requiring re-anchoring. Grief is the commonest cause of Veil injury in the four quarters and is not classified as a cause of anything in the Accord’s own returnsEcho BeastsCorrupted soul-forms condensed from unresolved Soul Plane content pouring through a rupture. Produced in volume by battlefieldsThe Hollow Class VStatic, purple silence. What is left where the Crossing was prevented at scale and long enough. Contact produces Dissonance: cracks in the Crystal, misfiring, apathy. The field guides advise fire or flight and the field guides are not being dramatic
Battlefields

The Division was asked to explain why old battlefields are what they are. This is the explanation and it has not been circulated.

An engagement produces several thousand bodies in one place inside one hour, each entering the nine-day window simultaneously, at a site whose ambient saturation has just been violently disturbed by whatever was done there.
Nothing in any funerary tradition in the four quarters is built for that. Rites assume a household, a body, a parish, and nine days of attention. A battlefield supplies none of those and supplies four thousand of them at once.

The Echoes go together · Thousands departing across a few hours through a membrane already strained. This is the rupture, and the dying cause it, afterward, in the quiet, when the fighting has already gone home.
The residue does not diffuse cleanly · Thousands of simultaneous returns into one saturation basin. The Wellspring cannot take it at that rate. What does not diffuse pools, and pooled residue at a disturbed site is the precondition for the Echo Beast and the Hollow.
The bodies are not buried in nine days · They are stripped in one, left for two or three, and pitted by conscripted locals on the fifth or the eighth or the twelfth. Every day past the ninth is a body that has completed its diffusion in the open at a site that cannot absorb it.
The rendering houses arrive · Inside the window, lawfully or otherwise, for the flesh, the bone and the residue still diffusing through them. The license reaches the body and stops at the Crystal: cutting the lattice out of a corpse is a different act and the worst crime in every realm, which is why the night-cutters work the same fields after dark, behind the licensed carts. This is the largest single source of Grade IV material in the four quarters and it is legal, and the legality is the reason Enforcement releases fields on a schedule that the rendering houses know in advance.
The result is that a battlefield is a metaphysical wound with a known etiology, a known progression, and no treatment, and that the districts which hold old fields have been telling the Accord about it for four hundred years and have been recorded as superstitious in the Division’s own summaries of their complaints.

Unresolved Entries
The nine days · Varies by Stage, Wellspring and site, and the variance has never been characterized. The law uses nine because the practice uses nine and the practice uses nine because it always has.
Cumulative Wellspring shortfall · Four centuries of Grade IV rendering represents Temperance that was not returned. No estimate exists. Producing one requires the volume of the trade, which the Bench has declined four times to establish. One Guild auditor has set the question beside the Withering and observed that the two columns look alike. The Division has noted the observation and holds no position.
Constructs whose residue has not completed · At least three are known to the Enforcement Division. The oldest is not dated in the public record. The entry states that the matter is monitored.
Whether the Law of Return was drafted as a rendering prohibition · No record survives of the drafting. The Division’s position is that the question is unanswerable and that the provision should not be amended in either direction until it is.
Old fields · Nine districts have petitioned. All nine petitions are held. The Division’s standing summary describes the complaints as consistent with local tradition, which is true and is not a finding.

Read next: From Omnara to a Blow, for where the three layers came from; The Three Paths, for what each road leaves heaviest.

the-war-cycle/the-wounded-and-the-dead/t.title: The Long Illness
the-war-cycle/the-wounded-and-the-dead/t.content:
Cressing was the richest cloth town in the west the summer the barge Fair Constance came up the river with southern silk and a sick bargeman. Every street of Cressing dyed its own color, and the Cress ran madder on Mondays and indigo by Thursday, with red-armed women on the tenter frames shouting across the water and the weavers’ guilds fighting pitched battles over who walked first at the fair. The spotted death came ashore with the silk. The rich left in the first week, in painted litters, by the road that was closed behind them in the second. The dyers would not stop, because a vat left standing is a year’s wages lost, so through that whole summer the river went on running gold and blue past shut houses with the well locked in among the sick. In the sixth week the council found the cause in the washerwomen of Tenter Row, who were disliked, and it burned their row with some of them in it. In the tenth week the sickness left, when the trade had stopped, and the guilds resumed their quarrel over a much shorter procession.
The Research and Archives Division consolidated what follows from four registers nobody had ever read side by side. It is about what bodies do over time, and it is also about who keeps the count. You will find the sword hardly appears in it, and that the dead are many more.
Disease, Trade Sickness, and What a Body Does Over Time

Compiled by the Research and Archives Division. The occupational tables consolidate the hazard registers previously held separately by the Guild of Measurewrights, the alchemical trades and the Logistics and Supply Division.
Tenth of the War Cycle.

Epidemic

An army is a disease delivery system that also fights.


The flux Fouled water and worse latrines. Arrives within days of any body of people standing still and does not leave. The commonest cause of death in warfare, in cities, and in sieges, and the least written about in every quarter.
Camp fever Carried in the seams of clothing nobody has changed in six weeks. Kills besieger and besieged at the same rate in the same week.
The spotted death Plague. Arrives with trade, moves with trade, and stops when trade stops, which every quarter has worked out and none can afford to act on. The response is the same everywhere: shut the roads, shut the houses, and let whoever is inside a shut house take their chances.
The wasting cough Chronic, slow, and the disease of anybody who breathes anything for a living. Miners, grinders, calciners, and the poor of any city with workshops in it.


The social response is identical in all four quarters regardless of what the local doctrine says: the wealthy leave, the roads close, somebody is blamed, and the blame lands on whoever the district already disliked.
Quarantine. Isolation works and is enforced unevenly, and corruption has little to do with the unevenness. A shut house contains the well alongside the sick, and everybody knows it, and the officers doing the shutting have families in the district.
The Accord’s position is that quarantine is a Logistics matter rather than an Enforcement one, which sounds like an administrative detail and means that nobody with the authority to compel is required to attend.

The Trades
Consolidated from four registers previously held separately. Every entry has an onset figure, a progression, and no compensation scheme in any quarter.


















































ConditionTrade and onsetCourseTender’s shakeArray service (tending standing runed workings) · ~8 yearsTremor, permanent, progressive. The largest single occupational cohort in the four quarters and the one with the strongest documentation and no schemeCrucible palsyAlchemical bench · ~9 yearsTremor beginning in the writing hand, progressing to head and jaw, accompanied by a withdrawal of manner that families notice before physicians do. The reason a master’s later formulas are dictatedVein coughCalcination, sulfide roast · 20 yearsChronic. The commonest cause of retirement in the alchemical tradesGrinder’s rotStone dust · early onset, fast progressionThe figure that matters is expectancy: a boy set to dry-grinding at ten does not commonly reach thirty. Known for a century. Wet grinding halves it. Wet grinding is slowerThe renderer’s markGrade III handlingDiscoloration in the sclera and under the nailbeds, keyed to what has been handled most. Cosmetic, diagnostic, and socially ruinousThe appetiteGrade III carry off predator stock, seated in a person who works with it dailyNot a disease, and recorded here because nothing else records itThe quietLong-service DistillationA flattening of affect beginning as professional detachment and continuing past it. Classified as an occupational condition. No treatment proposedLaw-fragment burnContact with corrupted product · acuteThe injury continues after contact ends because the fragment does not know it has left the vessel

The pattern. Every entry above has three features in common.
The onset is long enough that the worker has no other trade by the time it appears. The mechanism has been understood for at least a century. And no polity in the four quarters operates a compensation scheme of any kind.
The Accord’s position is that occupational injury is a matter for the employing house. The employing houses’ position is that it is a matter for the guild. The Arbitration Division has never been asked to rule, because ruling requires a petitioner and the petitioners cannot hold a pen.

Childbirth
The most dangerous thing most people in the four quarters will ever do, undertaken repeatedly, attended almost entirely by women, and absent from every military and guild register in the Accord.
The per-birth danger is real and moderate. The cumulative danger across a life of births is what actually kills, and it is why the figure quoted by physicians and the figure understood by women are so different, and why the women’s figure is the correct one.
Who attends · The midwife, licensed by the parish where she is licensed at all, trained by apprenticeship, and the most experienced practical clinician most people will ever be touched by.
What goes wrong · Obstruction, malpresentation, hemorrhage, and the fever afterward, which is the one that takes the woman who survived the birth.
The Wellspring dimension · A birth is the formation of a Crystal, and thin-Veil districts record what the Accord’s literature describes as an elevated incidence of complication and what the districts describe considerably more precisely. Nobody has studied it. The proposal has been made three times by midwives and has never been made by a physician.

What the Accord counts · Nothing.
Maternal death does not appear in any Accord register because no Division holds the file.

Hunger, and Age
Famine
Progresses in stages anyone who has seen it can name: hunger, wasting, the swelling that families mistake for recovery, then the apathy, then whatever ordinary illness is passing through.

Famine kills less often by starvation than by removing the body’s ability to survive the flux, and the flux is always available.
The metaphysical dimension is documented and unstudied: a district in genuine hunger produces measurably fewer Welling-stage children in the following decade, and the Measurewrights hold the series and have no explanation for it.

Age
Life expectancy at birth is low and misleading. What kills the figure is the children. Anyone who reaches twenty can reasonably expect their fifties, and Tempered practitioners considerably longer, which is one of the more resented facts of the age.
What the old suffer · The stone, the cataract, the joints, the cough, and the loss of teeth, which is not fatal and is what actually ends a person’s independence.
What the old Tempered suffer · Everything above, later, plus the specific deterioration of whatever they spent their life doing. A practitioner’s body records their Path more legibly than their face records their years.
Who keeps them · Family, then the parish, then nobody. Guild pensions exist for certified practitioners and are the single most valuable thing certification confers, which is why people pursue certification long past the point where the rank is any use to them.
The Fracture Log, from the Other Side

The character sheet records a Fracture Log as a list of what a soul has survived. A physician’s casebook records the same events as a list of what a body has been asked to absorb.
The two documents almost never agree.

The Log records the event. The casebook records the accommodation. A Splintering appears in one as a fracture and in the other as nine months of altered sleep, appetite loss, a change in gait that never came back, and a marriage that did not survive the year.
The Log is proud of things the casebook is worried about. Every entry in a Fracture Log is an achievement in the sense that the practitioner is still here. The casebook has no such register and records the same entry as damage that has been compensated for rather than repaired.
The casebook sees the pattern first. A practitioner’s third fracture presents like their first two, and the assessor who has the earlier notes can predict the accommodation before the practitioner has noticed they are making it. Assessors are consequently disliked.

The practical instruction for any physician handed a Tempered patient is to ask for the Log and to read it as a record of injury regardless of how it is written, because the patient will not describe it that way and will be irritated at the suggestion.

Unresolved Entries

Compensation No scheme exists anywhere in the four quarters for any occupational condition. The obstacle is procedural: Arbitration requires a petitioner and the affected cannot petition.
Thin-Veil birth complication Proposed three times by midwives. Never proposed by a physician. Never studied.
Maternal mortality Held by no Division. Not counted. Consequently not addressed.
Post-famine Welling cohorts The Measurewrights hold the series and offer no explanation. The series is now four generations long.
The quiet, again Two askings, no answer.


Read next: On Walking Into the Current, for Wellspring exposure; The Crossing, for where the long illness ends.

the-war-cycle/the-wounded-and-the-dead/t.title: The Physician's Eye
the-war-cycle/the-wounded-and-the-dead/t.content:
Ragna Steen, surgeon to the Legion at Ostermere, once ruined a duke’s dinner from a tent door. His son had taken a thrust through the forearm from a Wellspring-charged blade, and the boy lay on cloth of gold with three physicians in scarlet around him, all agreed that they had never seen so clean a wound, nine days old, not a trace of pus, pink at the margin, a credit to everyone. Steen had been passing with a sausage. She stopped in the doorway, sniffed, walked in chewing, put her ear down next to the wound with the whole scarlet college staring, and listened for a while to nothing, and it was a very particular nothing, because the talk in that tent had thinned around the spot the way sound thins in deep snow. She said to take the arm off above the elbow by supper. The duke laughed, and when he was finished laughing he had her put out of the tent. They cut the wound back clean on the eleventh day and again on the fourteenth, and on the fifteenth the margin had moved. She took it off on the seventeenth at the shoulder, with the boy cursing her in three languages and the duke holding the lamp. By then her own hands had begun to go the way surgeons’ hands go, and she had to tie the last vessel with her teeth.
Her casebooks are in this compilation with those of many others. I have read them all. They are the only documents in this archive that made me look up from the page and check who was in the room.
Reading a Body, and What Will Not Close

Compiled from the casebooks of Legion surgeons and the Anima Harmonic assessors. Supersedes the fragment circulated as the Alchemist’s Eye, which was a diagnostic aid for chemists and was never intended for use on the wounded.
Ninth of the War Cycle. Companion to The Long Illness.

What a Surgeon Can Actually Read

There is no instrument. There is a hand, an eye, a nose, and thirty years, and the thirty years are the instrument.


Color Pallor and the specific gray of serious blood loss. The dusky purple-black of tissue that has stopped receiving. The advancing red of spreading infection, which is read by marking its edge with a fingernail and looking again in an hour. Yellow in the sclera.
Smell The most underrated instrument in surgery and the one that carries furthest. Sweetish rot means gas in the tissue and means the limb. The flat foul stench of hospital rot. Voided bowel means the abdomen is open whether or not you can see where. Experienced surgeons diagnose from the tent doorway and are right.
Heat, by hand Local heat is inflammation. General heat is fever. Cold and clammy is the body giving up its extremities to keep its center, and it is the worst sign available to a hand.
Texture Crepitus under the fingers, which is gas and is a death sentence. Boggy edema. The hardness of a mass. The give of an abscess.
Sound The wet suck of an open chest. The rattle. And the absence of sound where sound is expected, which is the surgeon’s tell for a Wellspring wound.
The pulse Fast and thin is the body running out. The single most useful number available without instruments, and every competent practitioner takes it before they take anything else.


What cannot be read. Internal bleeding until it is too late. The depth of an infection. Organ damage that has not reached the surface. Whether a man will survive an amputation, which is unknowable and is guessed at daily. And whether a wound is carrying a fragment.

Why Some Wounds Will Not Close

A blade wound is an injury. A Wellspring wound is an injury and an unfinished sentence, and the body cannot heal around a process that is still running.
This is the central distinction of the discipline and the one that separates a field surgeon from a butcher with a saw.

A blade opens tissue and stops. The damage is total at the instant of contact and everything afterward is the body’s own work.
A wound inflicted by a Wellspring process does not stop. A portion of the process was invoked into the body and was interrupted by the body, and what remains is a fragment attempting to complete itself in the tissue it landed in.

Read the wound as an instruction, partially executed, still executing. A surgeon who reads it as a hole will lose the patient.

How a surgeon recognizes one

























TellWhat it looks likeIt does not granulateOrdinary tissue reaches for ordinary tissue. A fragment-carrying wound stays open at the margin, clean, and wrong, and the wrongness is that it looks better than it should for longer than it shouldThe margin behavesAdvances, retreats, or holds against pressure. Surgeons describe fragment wounds as attentive and are not being fancifulThe silenceSound behaves oddly at close range, and this is the tell most surgeons use and none can explain. Old practitioners put their ear near the wound. The gesture looks superstitious and is diagnosticIt does the same thing to the next tissueA fragment moves. Debridement removes tissue and does not remove the instruction, and the surgeon who cuts back to clean margin three times and finds it there again on the fourth has understood something about the injury that no amount of cutting will change
What can be done

Sealwright referral The only genuine treatment. A fragment is a Parunic problem (a matter of Parun, the glyph tongue in which a working’s boundaries are written) and requires a Parunic answer, closure of the unfinished sentence rather than removal of the tissue.
Amputation proximal to the fragment Works, if the fragment has not traveled, and the surgeon cannot know whether it has. The commonest treatment in the field, and a bet made with somebody else’s limb.
Containment Sealed dressing, isolation, and a rule that nobody touches the dressings without the Sealwright’s own materials. Fragments transfer, which is why a surgeon working fragment wounds has a shorter career than one who does not.
Nothing The commonest, because Sealwright teams are attached to sieges rather than to infirmaries, and a Legion in the field carries perhaps two for four thousand men.

The Three-Layer Model, Read Backward
The combat literature describes a strike in three layers. A surgeon meets the same three in reverse order and cannot always tell which they are looking at.
The Physical layer · What the surgeon can see. Torn tissue, broken bone, opened vessel. Treated conventionally and successfully, and this is the majority of the work.
The Essence layer · What the surgeon infers. Conduction channels cut, resonance nodes disrupted, the patient reporting that a technique they have used for twenty years does not answer. Not visible, not treatable by the knife, and frequently the injury the patient actually cares about.

A practitioner who has lost a hand and lost a harmonization will grieve the harmonization.

The Hermetic layer · The fragment. The layer that will kill a patient the surgeon has otherwise saved.
The diagnostic difficulty is that all three present at the same site and the surgeon has hours rather than days. The standing instruction is to treat the Physical, note the Essence for the Anima Harmonic assessors, and refer anything that will not granulate.
Triage
Somebody has to decide. Everything else in this document is technique and this is the job.
The sorting is by salvageability rather than by severity, and it produces four groups in every army in every quarter.

























GroupWhat is doneWill live untreatedWalking wounded. Dressed, sent back, and resented by everyone for the noise they make about itWill live if treated nowThe whole purpose of the surgeon’s day. Everything the establishment exists for is spent on this groupWill die whatever is doneAbdominal wounds, open chest, massive hemorrhage, the fragment cases that arrived too late. Given what is available for pain and left. The Legion’s instruction is that somebody stays with them and the instruction is met about half the timeWill die slowly whatever is doneThe worst category and the one no manual names. Days, sometimes, and lucid for most of it, and the surgeon has to keep walking past
The Legion sorts without regard to rank and states this proudly. Crown forces sort by rank and state nothing. Both are lying slightly: the Legion’s sorters know who the Aether Knights are and no instruction is required to make that matter.
What the Surgeon Costs Themselves
The hands · Fragment transfer, chronic. A career working Wellspring wounds ends in a specific documented deterioration of the hands that the Anima Harmonic assessors can recognize across a room.
The fever · Surgeons take what the camp has and take it earlier, from working among it. Camp fever kills surgeons at a rate higher than any other specialization in a Legion establishment including the line.

The sorting · No physical mechanism and the most reliably reported injury in the entire literature.
Surgeons who have sorted for a decade describe a flattening that they can name and cannot arrest, and the description is close enough to the alchemical condition documented as the quiet that the Archives have been asked twice whether they are the same thing and have not answered.

Unresolved Entries

Fragment travel Whether and how fast a fragment migrates is not established. Every field practice around amputation depends on the answer and there is no answer.
Sealwright establishment in infirmaries Two per four thousand. Requested at four per thousand in nine consecutive returns. Not funded, on the stated ground that Sealwright teams are an Enforcement asset and infirmaries are a Logistics responsibility.
The quiet Whether the surgeon’s flattening and the Distillation specialist’s flattening are one condition. Asked twice. Not answered.
The fourth category No manual names it. Four surgeons have proposed naming it. The Division’s position is that naming it would not change what is done about it, which is correct.


Read next: The Physical Account, for why the blood is only the report; Stacking and Spending, for reserve tells.
